## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III**

A chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices; corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating their subject matter; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes:

The first is an index of subjects, by consulting which one can see at a glance whatever each Father has written on any given topic. The second is an index of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader can readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture and in which places of their works they did so.

This is the most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the modesty of its price. Above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but brought together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# Exegetical Works of the Venerable Bede, Anglo-Saxon Priest, or Part II of All His Works

## Section One — Genuine Works

[Col. 0009]

### Note

Among ecclesiastical writers, the Venerable Bede, priest and Benedictine monk, holds no inferior position; among the English he easily claims the first place. For if one considers the solidity and uniformity of the doctrine he transmits, who ever wrote more holily or more truthfully? If one considers the multitude of his books, who wrote more abundantly? If one considers the variety of his many treatises, who ever attained so successfully to so many kinds of disciplines and sciences? Thus, in this one man, it is possible to admire an excellent grammarian, no less skilled in Greek than in Latin; a poet, not insignificant for his age; an orator; an astronomer; an arithmetician; a chronographer; a cosmographer; a historian; a philosopher; a theologian; and, above all, an outstanding interpreter of Sacred Scripture.

With good reason, therefore, William of Malmesbury says of him in his *Book of the Deeds of the Kings of the English*: “A man whom one can more easily admire than praise worthily, who, born in the farthest corner of the world, struck all lands with the flash of his learning.” He seems to have borrowed these words from the writer of Bede’s own life.

Although he was exceptionally well versed in all the liberal arts and in both divine and human sciences, and although, as Pithaeus writes, he learned them accurately, knew them solidly, retained them firmly, and taught them clearly, so that in his age he had scarcely any equal and certainly no superior, his principal and almost sole study was devoted to meditating on the Sacred Scriptures. He directed the whole course of his labors, his vigils, and his nocturnal studies toward their perfect understanding.

Bede himself testifies to this in his *Epitome*, where he says:

> From that time on, spending the whole course of my life in the habitation of that same monastery, I devoted all my effort to meditating on the Scriptures. In the midst of the observances of the rule and the daily duty of singing in the church, I always found it pleasant either to learn, to teach, or to write.

For this reason he is rightly praised by Acca, bishop of Hexham, in the letter usually placed before Bede’s *Commentaries on the Gospel of Luke*, as one who spent days and nights in vigilant meditation on the law of the Lord. Boniface, bishop of Mainz and apostle of the Germans, calls him “the most discerning investigator of the Scriptures.”

Writing to Cuthbert, or Ubert, the abbot, Boniface says:

> Meanwhile, we ask that you kindly send us some written extracts from the little works of Bede the monk, that most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, whom we have recently heard shone among you in the house of God, like a lamp of the Church, through his knowledge of the Scriptures.

And in his letter to Archbishop Egbert:

> Now, eagerly desiring this, we earnestly beg you, for our joy and remembering us, to take care—as you have done with me before—to send us some portion or spark from the lamp of the Church which the Holy Spirit has caused to shine in the regions of your province; that is, send us whatever portion you may graciously provide from the treatises which Bede, the spiritual priest and investigator of the Holy Scriptures, composed by opening them up.

[Col. 0011C]

Since Bede spent his entire life meditating upon and expounding the Scriptures, it is truly astonishing that the first of all the works which he himself listed in his catalogue has been absent from every edition until now and has not seen the light of publication in our time: namely, four books on the beginning of Genesis, extending to the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Ishmael.

Thus it should be read “four books,” not “three books,” as it is commonly printed. This is confirmed by three ancient manuscripts of Bede: one, extremely famous, written six hundred years ago for the monastery of Saint Ouen at Rouen; another of approximately the same age from the monastery of Saint Martin at Séez; and a third from Vendôme. They are supported by the edition and by the ancient Saxon version, or paraphrase, of Chifflet, corrected and prepared against other manuscript codices. Sigebert likewise supports this reading: in chapter 68 of his *Book on Illustrious Men*, he reports Bede’s catalogue of his works in Bede’s own words.

Add to these Honorius of Autun, a priest, who writes of our Bede in his *Book on the Lamps of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Bede, a monk and priest of the English province, wrote innumerable works, among which are these: four books on Genesis.

Trithemius says the same in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Bede, monk and priest of the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, which is in England, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man most devoted to and highly learned in the divine Scriptures … composed the following works: four books on Genesis, extending to Isaac.

The most ancient six codices support this reading. In them this work of Bede is divided into four books: one, elegantly written about nine hundred years ago in the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury; two others from Corbie; a fourth from Dijon, Saint-Bénigne, whose script indicates an age of more than eight hundred years; a fifth from Clairvaux, approximately six hundred years old; and a sixth from Saint Vincent at Metz, of approximately the same age. These codices almost all deserve greater confidence because they approach Bede’s own age more closely.

Bede did not, however, compose these four books in one continuous effort. He first undertook to expound only the first three chapters of Genesis, up to Adam’s expulsion from paradise, intending to devote himself to what followed after completing his exposition of Ezra, which he was then planning. This he did by adding three books in which he commented on the events extending from Adam’s expulsion from paradise to the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Ishmael.

He divided the earlier work, undertaken at the urging of Acca, bishop of Hexham, who took great pleasure in Bede’s companionship, into two books, as is clear from the dedicatory letter to Acca. These two books later became one when he completed the work, as may be gathered from an ancient Corbie codex. In that manuscript the earlier division appears in such a way that, after the exposition of the *Hexaemeron*, one reads, “Here ends the first book”; then, after the expulsion of Adam from paradise, one again reads, “Here ends the first book.” This is because, after the three later books were added, those first two were combined into a single first book.

We had prepared these books for publication many years ago, but only recently learned that they had already been published in England. For some time we therefore hesitated over whether to print them again. But since that edition has scarcely crossed the sea and is found in only the rarest libraries, and since we have been unable to obtain it despite our efforts, our friends persuaded us—though we hesitated and almost resisted—to commit these excellent books to the press, since they would benefit not only the English but also the French and other nations.

This seemed especially appropriate because we present them after collating several manuscript codices with the greatest diligence and labor, adding variant readings in the lower margin and some notes, and because we have purged the earlier part of the first book—the only part previously published—of almost innumerable errors. Finally, since these books everywhere breathe Bede’s spirit and his reverence for the holy Fathers, and since they repeatedly quote their words, usually without naming them, we have undertaken, insofar as possible, to record the citations of the Fathers and the books from which they were taken.

# The Hexaemeron, or Four Books on the Beginning of Genesis, Extending to the Birth of Isaac and the Election of Ishmael

## Preface to Acca, Bishop of Hexham

[Col. 0009A]

To the most beloved and most reverend bishop Acca, Bede, the humblest servant of Christ’s servants, sends greetings.

Many have said many things about the beginning of the Book of Genesis, in which the creation of this world is described, and many have left to posterity monuments of their talent. But, as far as our small capacity has been able to learn, the principal writers are Basil of Caesarea, whom Eustathius the interpreter translated from Greek into Latin; Ambrose of Milan; and Augustine, bishop of Hippo.

The first, in nine books; the second, following in his footsteps, in six; and the third, in twelve books and again in two others written specifically against the Manichaeans, poured forth for readers abundant streams of salutary teaching. In these works they fulfilled the promise of Truth:

> Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.  
> (John 7:38)

Augustine also treated this primordial creation in some measure in his *Confessions*, in the books he composed with exceptional skill against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets, and in various other short works scattered throughout his writings, always with an appropriate exposition.

### Note

Among others, Rhodon, an Asian by birth who was instructed in the Scriptures at Rome by Tatian, composed elegant treatises on the *Hexaemeron*, as Jerome testifies in chapter 37 of his *Book on Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*. Jerome says the same about Candidus in chapter 48, about Appion in chapter 49, and about Hippolytus in chapter 61.

Yet these works are so extensive and so profound that scarcely anyone except the wealthy can acquire so many volumes, and scarcely anyone except the learned can penetrate their depths. It has therefore pleased your holiness to assign me the duty of gathering from all these works, as from the delightful fields of a widely flowering paradise, whatever might appear sufficient for the needs of the weak.

Nor was I sluggish in carrying out what you graciously commanded. Rather, as soon as I had examined the volumes of the Fathers, I collected from them and arranged in two little books what could instruct the still inexperienced reader, so that the educated reader might learn from them to ascend to a higher and more difficult reading of the works of the great Fathers.

In this work I tried to set forth throughout the thought of the Fathers mentioned above and of other equally Catholic Fathers—sometimes in their own words, sometimes, for the sake of brevity, in my own; sometimes without naming them, and sometimes naming them, according as the circumstances of the passage required.

I carried the work as far as the point at which Adam, expelled from the paradise of pleasure, entered the exile of temporal life. I also intend, if God wills and your intercession accompanies me with its help, to write something about what follows in the sacred history. First, however, I planned to examine briefly the Book of the holy prophet and priest Ezra. In it, under the figure of the ending of a long captivity, the restoration of the temple, the rebuilding of the holy city, the return to Jerusalem of the vessels that had been carried away, the rewriting of God’s law that had been burned, the correction of the people concerning foreign wives, and their conversion with one heart and soul to the service of God, the mysteries of Christ and the Church are represented. Ezra composed these events both as prophet and historian.

### Note

The printed editions, together with one Corbie manuscript, read “foreign.”

Once I have briefly examined this book and, with God’s favor, made some of the mysteries mentioned above clearer to diligent students, I shall do so.

Farewell always, most loving bishop, remembering us in the Lord.

# Here Begins Book One

[Col. 0013]

## “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

In indicating the creation of the world, divine Scripture fittingly reveals at once, in its very first word, both the eternity and the omnipotence of God the Creator. For when it declares that he created the world at the beginning of time, it plainly indicates that he himself existed eternally before time. And when it says that he created heaven and earth at the very beginning of creation, it declares, by such speed of action, that he is omnipotent, for whom to will is to accomplish.

### Note

Another reading: “whose.”

To complete his work, God’s omnipotent hand had no need of delay, because it is written:

> He has done whatever he willed.  
> (Psalm 113:3)

Human weakness, when it undertakes something—for example, when we build a house—first prepares the material at the beginning of the work. After that beginning, we dig down into the earth; then we place stones in the foundation; then, as the rows of stones increase, we add the walls. Thus, advancing gradually toward the completion of the work we have undertaken, we finally arrive at its perfection.

It was therefore fittingly said that “in the beginning God created heaven and earth,” so that it might be clearly understood that both were made by God simultaneously.

### Note

The printed editions read “by him.”

Although human beings cannot say that the two were made simultaneously, the prophet says:

> At the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord.  
> (Psalm 101:26)

Here the Lord is said to have created heaven and earth in the beginning. It follows plainly that the making of both elements was completed at the same time, and with such speed through the power of God that not even the first moment of the world’s birth had yet passed.

It may also reasonably be understood that God made heaven and earth “in the beginning,” that is, in his only-begotten Son. When the Jews asked him what they ought to believe concerning him, he replied:

> The Beginning, which I also speak to you.  
> (John 8:25)

### Note

Thus read by two older manuscript codices, one from Fleury and one from Corbie. The holy Fathers Ambrose also read it so: *Hexaemeron*, book 1, chapters 2 and 4; *On the Faith to Gratian*, book 3, chapter 4; and book 5, chapter 4. Augustine likewise read it so in his unfinished *Commentary on Genesis Literally*. An ancient manuscript codex of the Gospels from the greater monastery, written eight hundred years ago, reads the same. The printed editions, together with the smaller Corbie manuscript, read “and I speak.”

For in him, as the Apostle says, all things were created in heaven and on earth.

> (Colossians 1:16)

But one must pay close attention, so that each person may devote himself to allegorical meanings in such a way that, by allegorizing, he does not abandon the plain truth of the historical account.

What and what kind of heaven was made in the beginning together with the earth is suggested by the words that follow:

## “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss.”

Why does Scripture introduce these words about the earth while passing over heaven, unless it wished us to understand that nothing of this kind applied to heaven? For the heaven in question is the higher heaven, which remains forever at rest, separated from every revolving condition of this world and from all its movement, in the foreknowledge of the divine glory.

As for our heaven, in which the lights necessary for this age have been placed, Scripture explains later both how and when it was made.

The higher heaven, therefore, which is inaccessible to the sight of all mortals, was not created empty and void like the earth, which in its first creation produced no green shoots or living animals. It was immediately filled with its inhabitants when it was created—that is, with the most blessed hosts of angels.

That they were created in the beginning together with heaven and earth, and that immediately afterward they praised the Creator for their own creation and for the beginning of all creation, is testified by the Creator himself. Speaking to his holy servant Job, he says:

> Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?  
> (Job 38:4)

And shortly afterward:

> When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy.  
> (Ibid., 38:7)

By “morning stars” he clearly means the same angels whom he calls “sons of God,” distinguishing them from holy human beings, who were to be created later and who, like evening stars, would set through the death of the flesh after confessing and praising God.

One of these morning stars, because of his contempt for the praise offered by his companions to God, deserved to hear:

> How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning! You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations, who said in your heart: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne.”  
> (Isaiah 14:12)

In explaining this passage, Saint Jerome also speaks of the higher heaven. He writes:

> “Either he was saying these things before he fell from heaven, or after he had fallen from heaven. But if he was still placed in heaven, how does he say, ‘I will ascend into heaven’? Yet since we read, ‘The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord,’ while he was in heaven—that is, in the firmament—he desired to ascend into the heaven where the Lord’s throne is, not through humility but through pride. But if he speaks these words after he had fallen from heaven, we should understand them as words of arrogance: even though he has been hurled down, he does not rest but still promises himself great things—not that he will be among the stars, but above the stars of God.”  
> (*Commentary on Isaiah*, book 6)

Thus it is rightly said that the heaven of heavens was not made empty or void. Nor is it said that darkness or an abyss has any place there, for the Lord God illuminates it, and the Lamb is its lamp.

The earth, however, was rightly empty and void, since it was still covered entirely by the abyss—that is, by an immense depth of waters.

Darkness was rightly over the face of the abyss, since the light that would drive it away had not yet been created.

We must not listen to those who criticize God and say that he created darkness before the light. God did not create any darkness in the water or the air. Rather, in the distinct order of his providence, he first created the waters together with heaven and earth, and afterward, when he willed, adorned them with the grace of light. We see him doing this even now, both in water itself and in the air, through the daily rising and setting of the sun.

It is not lawful to believe that the waters were not made by God. Although Scripture does not say this openly here, it plainly signifies it when it indicates that they were illuminated by God and ordered at his command. The psalm also clearly says:

> And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord, because he spoke, and they were made.  
> (Psalm 148:4)

Here one should observe that, together with heaven, two elements of this world are expressly said to have been made in the beginning: water and earth. Yet it is clear that the other two were already contained in them—fire in iron and stones, which were then hidden throughout the earth’s interior, and air in the earth itself.

We know that air is mixed with the earth because, when the earth has been moistened and has received the sun’s warmth, it immediately exhales abundant vapors.

Fire, too, implanted in the inner parts of the earth, is revealed by hot springs.

### Note

The printed editions read “come forth,” which is less suitable.

When these waters flow over certain metals deep below, they emerge upon the surface of the earth not merely warm but even boiling.

These elements were not, as some argue, mixed together shapelessly. Rather, the earth, bounded on every side within the same limits as now, was then wholly such as still remains in part beneath the deepest depths of the sea.

The waters covered its entire surface to such a height that they reached those places where, even now, some waters remain above the firmament of heaven and do not cease to praise the name of God the Creator together with the heavens of heavens.

### Note

Fleury reads: “beneath the earth, in the depth of the sea.”

### Note

Another reading: “as far as those places.”

Moreover, that material from which Scripture testifies that the world was made is formless. In praising God, Scripture says:

> You who made the world from formless matter.

Everything that we see in the world together with the waters and the earth either took the beginning of its nature from them or was made from nothing. The earth itself and the waters themselves were called “formless matter” because, before they came into the light, they had no source from which they might possess beauty or form.

What is improper about the world’s material having dark beginnings, so that, when light came upon it, what had been made might be rendered more beautiful, and so that the condition of the human being who would later progress might be signified in this way? The Apostle explains this when he says:

> For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts.  
> (2 Corinthians 4:6)

And elsewhere he says:

> You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.  
> (Ephesians 5:8)

That is, in him who, when darkness was over the face of the abyss, said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

## “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

We must not childishly imagine that the Creator Spirit—of whom it is written, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7)—was borne over the things that were to be created merely by occupying a particular place.

Rather, we should understand that he surpassed the creatures by divine power, possessing in his own authority the time when he would illuminate the abyss of the waters, the time when he would gather them into one place so that dry land might appear, and the time and manner in which he would arrange the remaining creatures according to his will.

He was like a craftsman whose will is accustomed to be applied to the materials from which something is to be made.

This also concerns the distinction of the higher heaven, in which, once everything had been perfectly arranged, the presence of the Holy Spirit immediately shed light upon all things.

But here below—that is, among the creatures of this world—he intended to bring the beginnings of creation gradually from their temporal origin to perfection.

Moses mentioned the higher world so briefly because he had undertaken to speak about this world, in which the human being was made, for the instruction of the human race. He thought it sufficient to include the whole state and adornment of spiritual and invisible creation under the single name of “heaven,” which he said was made in the beginning. By contrast, he described bodily, visible, and corruptible creation more fully and in order.

That is, he set before human beings those things that God had commanded or promised to them, leaving unspoken matters too lofty for human inquiry and too difficult for them to investigate.

For this reason he also entirely passed over the fall of the transgressing angel and his companions, since that belonged to the state of that invisible and spiritual creation.

Saint Basil speaks of this higher and invisible creation in the second book of his *Hexaemeron* as follows:

> “For we believe that if anything existed before the establishment of this perceptible and corruptible world, it was certainly in the light. Neither the dignity of the angels, nor the entire heavenly host, nor whatever else may exist—whether something named or capable of being addressed, some rational power, or a ministering spirit—could dwell in darkness. Rather, it possessed in light and joy the condition appropriate to it.”

When he had declared at the beginning that God—that is, the Father in the Son—made heaven and earth, Bede fittingly added a mention of the Holy Spirit:

> And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

Thus he indicated that the power of the whole Trinity cooperated in the creation of the world.

## “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.”

It is fitting for God’s works that the adornment of the world should begin with light. God himself is the true light and dwells in inaccessible light. The angels created in the heavens of heavens had already begun to enjoy the blessedness of beholding him. It was therefore appropriate that, in adorning this age as well, he first grant the grace of material light, so that there might be a means by which the other things he would create could be seen.

When God is said to have spoken, whether that light should come to be or anything else, this should not be understood in our manner, as though he spoke through the bodily sound of a voice.

### Note

The printed editions add “made,” but this is absent from the manuscripts and is unnecessary.

Rather, God’s “speaking” should be understood in a higher sense: he said that the creature should come to be because he made all things through his Word—that is, through his only-begotten Son.

The evangelist John states this more clearly:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him.  
> (John 1:1–3)

What John says—that all things were made through the Word of God—is what Moses says when he writes that God said, “Let there be light”; “Let there be a firmament”; “Let the rest of creation also come to be.”

This is what the psalm says when it adds the person of the Holy Spirit:

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.  
> (Psalm 32:6)

If it is asked in what places light was made at God’s command, since the abyss still covered the whole expanse of the earth, the answer is clear: that original light shone forth in the upper parts of the earth, which the daylight of the sun still customarily illuminates.

Nor should we be surprised that, through divine action, light could shine in the waters. Human activity also frequently makes them luminous. Sailors, when submerged in the depths of the sea, pour oil from their mouths and thereby make the water around them clear and bright.

### Note

This is taken from Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book 1, chapter 9.

If a human being can accomplish such a thing through the oil of his mouth, how much more should we believe that God can create through the breath of his mouth, especially since the waters should be believed to have been much more rarefied at the beginning than we now see them on earth, before they were gathered into one place so that dry land might appear.

### Note

The manuscripts omit “for if.”

### Note

The printed editions read “so that they might appear gathered,” which is entirely wrong.

## “And God saw that the light was good.”

God did not suddenly see the light as something previously unknown and then praise it by saying that it was good. Rather, he knew that he would make it worthy of praise, and, once it had been made, he declared it worthy of praise and admiration among human beings.

But because the infusion of light did not drive away all the darkness of the world—for it belongs to the age above to enjoy fixed and perpetual light—God illuminated one part of the world and left another part dark. Therefore Scripture rightly adds:

## “And he divided the light from the darkness.”

He divided them not only by their qualities but also by their locations: he spread the light through the upper part of the world, where human habitation was to be, while allowing its lower regions to remain in their ancient darkness.

## “And he called the light Day and the darkness Night.”

This is said for the sake of our understanding. For in what language did God call the light “day” and the darkness “night”—Hebrew, Greek, or some other language? The same question can be asked about everything else that he named: in what language did he name it?

But in God there is pure understanding, without the noise and diversity of languages.

“And he called” means “he caused it to be called,” because he distinguished and ordered everything in such a way that days could be perceived and receive names.

We speak in the same way when we say, “That head of the household built this house,” meaning that he caused it to be built. Many similar expressions are found throughout the books of divine Scripture.

## “And evening came and morning came, one day.”

### Note

Another reading: “And evening came, as the light gradually disappeared.”

Evening came when the light gradually set after the completion of the period of daylight and passed beneath the lower parts of the world, just as now happens at night through the customary circuit of the sun. Morning came when the same light gradually returned over the lands and began another day.

Thus one day was completed—namely, twenty-four hours. By commending this expression, Scripture carefully admonishes us to understand that the light which was made traversed the lower regions of the world in its setting.

For if it had not done this, but had instead gradually disappeared altogether when evening came and then gradually risen again at dawn, it would not have called one day complete at the morning of the following day. It would rather have called it complete in the evening of the first day.

For this reason Scripture preferred to speak of evening and morning rather than of night and day. It wished to indicate that the movement of the original light operated in a circuit, just as the circuit of the sun now produces day and night.

### Note

Another reading: “unless on account of.”

The sole difference is that, after the stars were created, night also became filled with its own light, although lesser than the light of day.

During those first three days, however, it remained completely dark and obscure. For it was altogether fitting that the day beginning with light should be extended into the morning of the following day, so that it might be signified that the work of him who is the true light, and in whom there is no darkness at all, begins from light and is brought entirely to completion in light.

God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters”; and God made the firmament and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament. And it was so. God called the firmament Heaven, and evening came and morning followed: the second day.

Here the creation of our heaven, in which the fixed stars are set, is described; it is established as having been made firm in the midst of the waters. For we see that waters are placed beneath it in the air itself and in the lands; and that waters are placed above it, we learn not only from the authority of this Scripture [Col. 0018C], but also from the words of the prophet, who says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, you cover its upper parts with waters” (Psalm 103:2).

Thus it is established that the starry heaven was made firm in the midst of the waters, and nothing prevents us from believing that it was even made from waters. For we know how great is the firmness, and how great the transparency and purity, of crystal stone, which is certainly produced from the congealing of waters. What, then, prevents us from believing that the same arranger of natures solidified the substance of the waters into the firmament of heaven?

If, however, anyone is troubled about how waters, whose nature is always to flow and to descend to lower places, can stand above heaven, whose shape appears to be round, let him remember the Scripture that says of God: “He binds up the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth together downward” (Job 26:8). Let him understand that the one who binds up waters beneath heaven for a time, whenever he wills, so that they do not all fall together—not supported by any ledge of firmer substance, but held only by the vapors of clouds—could also suspend waters above the round sphere of heaven so that they would never descend, not by vaporous tenuity but by the icy solidity of their suspension.

But even if he wished to establish liquid waters there, is this a greater miracle than that he hung the mass of the earth, as Scripture says, upon nothing? For when the waves of the Red Sea or of the river Jordan are raised high and fixed like walls for the passage of the Israelite people, do they not plainly indicate that waters can also remain fixed in their station above the revolving roundness of heaven [Col. 0019A]?

Certainly, what sort of waters they are there, and for what purposes they have been reserved, the Creator himself knows. But that they are there, because holy Scripture has said so, he has left no one any room for doubt.

What it means to say that God said, “Let this or that creature come into being,” has already been explained above. He “said” that it should come into being when, in his co-eternal Word—namely, his only-begotten Son—he arranged all things in creating them. When, therefore, we hear, “God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters,” we should understand that, in the Word of God, there existed the decree that it should come into being; in that Word he foresaw, before all time, whatever God later brought forth externally in time.

But when we hear, “And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament, and it was so,” we should understand that the creation and arrangement of heaven and the waters did not exceed the boundaries prescribed for them in the Word of God, in accordance with the Psalmist’s statement: “He established a decree, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148:6). The same should be understood of the creatures reported as having been made during the following four days.

When we hear added, “And God saw that it was good,” we should understand that, in the goodness of his Spirit, the thing pleased him—not as though it became pleasing after he had learned that it had been made, but rather that it pleased him to remain in that goodness in which it had pleased him to come into being.

It should be noted that the addition of this phrase is not found here in the Hebrew text. It is remarkable that, among all the things that God is said to have created, this testification of divine vision is omitted only here—that is, in the works of the second day. Yet these works are shown, together with the others that he made, to have appeared good to God when it is said later: “And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good.”

Unless perhaps, as some of the Fathers explain, Scripture wished us to understand by this that the number two is not good, because it divides from unity and prefigures the bonds of marriage. Hence, in Noah’s ark, all the animals that entered two by two are unclean, and an odd number is shown to be clean.

Concerning what has so far been expounded—that is, concerning the creation of the first and second days—it is reported in the history of Saint Clement that the apostle Peter said [Col. 0019D]:

> “In the beginning, when God had made heaven and earth as one house, the earth itself, having become a shadow from the bodies of the world, gave forth from itself darkness to the things enclosed within. But when the will of God introduced light, that darkness which had been made from the shadow of the bodies was immediately swallowed up. Then light was assigned to the day, and darkness to the night. Now the water that was within the world, in the midst of the space between that first heaven and the earth, as though congealed like ice and solidified into crystal, was spread out; and by this kind of firmament the spaces between heaven and earth were enclosed as if in the middle. The Creator called that firmament heaven, naming it by the name of the earlier heaven, and thus, when the whole structure of the world was one house, he divided it into two regions. The reason for this division was that the upper region might provide a dwelling for angels, while the lower one might provide one for human beings” (*Recognitions of Saint Clement*, book 1, chapter 27).

I have wished to insert these few words into our work so that the reader may recognize how far they agree with the understanding of the Fathers.

God then said: “Let the waters that are beneath heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear”; and it was so. The waters that had filled all the space between heaven and earth were withdrawn and gathered into one place, so that the light that during the preceding two days had shone brightly through the waters might shine more brightly in the pure air; and so that the earth, which had been hidden and had remained muddy [Col. 0020B] and weak beneath the waters, might, when they withdrew, become dry and suitable for receiving seeds.

If anyone asks where the waters were gathered that had covered every part of the earth up to heaven, let him know that it could have happened that the earth itself, sinking far and wide at the Creator’s command, provided other parts as hollow basins into which the waters flowing together could be received. Thus the dry land appeared in those parts from which the moisture had withdrawn [Note: [Col. 0019D] Printed editions: “had departed.”]

It can also reasonably be believed—as we mentioned above—that the primordial waters were more rarefied, covering the lands like a mist [Note: [Col. 0019D] Another reading: “clouds”]. Through their gathering they became denser, so that they could be contained in the places assigned to them, while the dry land appeared elsewhere.

Although there are many seas, he rightly says that the waters were gathered into one place, because all these waters are joined by an unbroken and continuous flow to the Ocean and to the great sea. Even lakes that appear to be enclosed within themselves are said to be pierced by hidden channels and caverns, through which they send their passages into the sea [Note: [Col. 0019D] Another copy adds: “through hidden channels.”] The diggers of wells also prove this, since the whole earth is filled with waters flowing through invisible veins, and these waters derive their origin from the sea.

And God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of waters he called Seas. Earlier, for the distinction of the waters, he had called the entire more solid part of the world “earth,” when he said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; and: “The earth was formless and empty.” But now, after the world has begun to take shape, and after the face of the earth appeared as the waters withdrew to their appointed place, the remaining portion—which was able to be dry—received the name “earth,” in distinction from that part of it which was still pressed down by the waters [Note: [Col. 0020D] Another reading: “was called.”] It is so called in Latin because it is worn down by the feet of living creatures.

The gatherings of waters are called “seas,” evidently because of their greatest part [Note: [Col. 0020D] Printed editions: “the nearest.”] For among the Hebrews, they say that all gatherings of waters—whether salty or fresh—are called seas. Appropriately, then, he who earlier said that, because of the continuity of all the waters upon the earth, they had been gathered into one place now names their gatherings in the plural, and says that they are called “seas” in the plural, because of their many-branched inlets, which themselves receive different names according to the names of the regions [Col. 0021A].

And God saw that it was good. The earth had not yet produced vegetation, nor had either the earth itself or the waters produced living creatures; yet God is said to have seen that it was good when, as the waters withdrew, the dry land appeared. For the Creator and evaluator of the universe, foreseeing what was to come, praises as already completed things that are still only at the beginning of their first work. This is not surprising in one for whom the perfection of things lies not in the completion of the work but in the predestination of his will [Note: [Col. 0021D] Another copy omits “the Creator and evaluator.”]

And he said: “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation producing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth” [Col. 0021B]. And it was so. And the earth brought forth green vegetation, bearing seed according to its kind, and trees making fruit, each having seed according to its own kind [Note: [Col. 0021D] Another reading: “according to its species.”] And God saw that it was good, and evening came and morning followed: the third day.

It is clear from these words of God that the world’s adornment was perfected in the springtime. For it is then that green plants usually appear upon the earth and trees become laden with fruit. At the same time, it should be noted that the first shoots of the herbs and trees did not come from seed but came forth from the earth. At the one command of the Creator, the earth, which had appeared dry, was suddenly adorned with herbs and clothed with flowering groves; and these immediately produced from themselves the fruits and seeds proper to each kind [Note: [Col. 0021D] Another reading: “brought forth.”]

For it was necessary that every form of created thing should first come forth perfect at the Lord’s command. In the same way, human beings themselves, for whose sake all things were made on earth, must be believed to have been formed perfect—that is, at the age of youth.

But God said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven.” In a suitably ordered sequence, the world proceeds from unformed matter to an appropriate form. After God had created heaven, earth, and water before any day of this age—that is, the higher and spiritual world with its inhabitants, and the unformed matter of this entire world—in accordance with what is written, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sirach 18:1), he made light on the first day of this age [Note: [Col. 0022D] Another reading: “so that he might make the other creatures.”], so that he might make the other creatures capable of possessing form.

On the second day he solidified the firmament of heaven—namely, the higher part of this world—in the midst of the waters. On the third day, in the lower regions, he separated the sea and the lands within their own boundaries and, as the water withdrew, spread out the air in its appointed places. It was therefore fitting that the elements should receive the progress of a greater adornment in the same order in which they had been created: on the fourth day, heaven should be distinguished by lights; on the fifth, air and sea should be filled with their creatures; and on the sixth, earth should be filled with its living beings. The fact that on the third day the earth was clothed with herbs and trees belongs not to its adornment but, so to speak, to the surface of its own form [Col. 0021D].

[Col. 0022A] God therefore said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day from the night.” This is the division that is explained more clearly in what follows: the sun should illuminate the day, while the moon and stars should illuminate the night. For after the heavenly bodies had been made, this was added to the increase of the primordial light, so that the night too might become luminous, illuminated either by the splendor of the moon, or of the stars, or of both—whereas until then it had known nothing except its ancient darkness.

Although night often appears dark and blind to us, because the air nearest the earth is obscured by cloudy whirlwinds, those higher regions that are designated by the name “ether,” extending from this turbulent air up to the starry heaven, are nevertheless always made bright by the radiance of the heavenly bodies as they revolve.

The heavenly bodies that arose also offered this gift of divine generosity to the world, together with an increase of light, so that through them the distinctions of passing times might also be recognized. Hence it follows:

“And let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years.” Before the heavenly bodies were made, there was nothing by which the order of times could be marked by signs. There was no means of recognizing the midday hour before the fiery sun climbed to the middle of heaven; nor was there any means by which the other hours of day and night could be marked, until the stars divided the pole equally among themselves between day and night.

Thus the lights are for signs, seasons, days, and years—not because seasons began from their creation, since it is clear that they began at the beginning, when God made heaven and earth; nor because days and years began only when God said, “Let there be light,” and light came into being. Rather, it is because by their risings and settings the order of seasons, days, and years is marked.

For that entire preceding period of three days had passed in the undifferentiated course of its progress, without any precise measurement of hours. The primordial light still filled all things generally and had no fixed head or source such as it now receives from the sun. Nowhere had more intense rays shone, nor had any more remote shade grown cool beneath a rock or tree.

Apart from the marking of times, the lights are also signs necessary for the uses of this life. Sailors observe them for navigation, as do travelers in the sandy deserts of Ethiopia, where, at the slightest impulse of wind, every track of travelers that may be found there is immediately smoothed over [Col. 0022D]. Therefore those traveling in those regions need the signs of the heavenly bodies by night and day no less than those who sail upon the sea.

There are also signs by which we sometimes foresee, through their observation, what the condition of the air will be [Note: [Col. 0022D] Another reading: “because”; another: “which.”]

“So that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth”; and it was so. As we have said, the lights always shine in the firmament of heaven and bathe the regions nearest to it in bright radiance, but at appropriate times they illuminate the earth.

Sometimes a cloudy air obstructs the light, so that neither the moon, when it is small, nor the light of the stars appears upon the earth. The rising sun also prevents the moon and stars from illuminating the earth with its greater light. Hence the sun received its Latin name, because alone, when it has obscured the stars together with the moon, it shines upon the earth by day.

God also made two great lights. We may understand “great lights” not so much by comparison with other things as by their function, just as we speak of the great heaven and the great sea. The sun is indeed great, filling the circle of the earth with its heat; and the moon, by its light, illuminates everything on earth wherever they are in the heaven, and both are equally seen by everyone.

The evident proof of their greatness is that their disk appears the same to all human beings throughout the world. If it appeared smaller to those farther away and shone larger to those nearer, that would reveal their smallness [Col. 0023B].

“The greater light, to rule the day, and the lesser light, to rule the night, and the stars”; and he placed them in the firmament of heaven.

The greater light is the sun, not only because of whatever form its body possesses, but also because of the magnitude of its light, by which it is believed to illuminate both the lesser light and the stars. It is also greater in the power of its heat, by which, when it rose, it warmed the world, although during the preceding days before its creation the world had possessed no heat at all.

They say that the moon is seen to be of equal size with the sun because the sun travels much farther from the earth and at a greater height than the moon; therefore its true magnitude cannot at all be discerned by us, who live on earth. Everything placed farther away ordinarily appears smaller [Col. 0023C].

“And the lesser light,” he says, “to rule the night, and the stars; and he placed them in the firmament of heaven.” For although the moon is sometimes seen by day in every month, and larger stars may also occasionally be seen, it is nevertheless certain that they bring some consolation of light not to the day but only to the night.

“To shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness.” These words can be understood both of the great lights and of the stars, with this distinction: the phrase “to rule the day” applies specifically to the sun; the phrase added, “and the night,” applies to the moon and stars; while the final phrase, “and to divide the light from the darkness,” applies equally to all the heavenly bodies. Wherever they travel, they carry light with them; wherever they are absent, they leave everything dark [Col. 0023D].

If, however, someone asks what the daylight could have been like before the creation of the heavenly bodies, it is not unreasonable to believe that it was like what we see each day at dawn: as the sun’s rising approaches but is not yet visible upon the earth, the day is indeed illuminated by the muted rays of the stars, but it does not yet shine brightly [Note: [Col. 0023D] The printed editions add “it is right to believe”; these words are absent from the manuscripts but appear to be understood.] until the sun rises [Note: [Col. 0023D] Another reading: “until the sun’s rising shines forth.”]

Thus at that time there could have been no distinction of times except between day and night. Accordingly, after the heavenly bodies had been made, it was rightly said: “And let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years” [Col. 0024A].

For the alternation of times began to be distinguished from the moment when, on the fourth day of the world’s birth, the sun, proceeding from the middle of the eastern sky, consecrated the spring equinox by its rising. Then, advancing each day by climbing to the heights of heaven and afterward gradually descending from the summer solstice to the lowest points, it completed the span of the year in four clearly distinguished seasons and in fixed days, repeatedly returning from the lowest and wintry regions to the equinoctial circles without delay.

The full moon, appearing in the evening, also fixed by its first rising the times that were to be observed for the celebration of Passover. For this is the hour at which not only that ancient people of God but also we today observe the beginning of the celebration of Passover: after the day of the equinox has passed, the full moon appears in the evening—that is, on the fourteenth day [Col. 0024B].

For immediately afterward, when the Lord’s Day has arrived, the appropriate time for celebrating the Lord’s resurrection is at hand, and the prophet’s word is fulfilled literally: “He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting” (Psalm 103:19) [Note: [Col. 0024D] Another reading: “for appointed times.”]

The stars also are for signs and seasons, apart from what we mentioned above: by their appearance they show what kind of weather is to come, and by their course they indicate which watch of the night it is [Note: [Col. 0024D] Another reading: “apart from the fact that.”] They are for signs and seasons because, as they come into the sky, some mark the summer season and others the winter.

They are also for days, because some accompany the sun in the spring days and others in the autumn. They are for years, because those that now rise in the morning at the spring equinox come into the face of heaven at that same equinox every year; and those that now rise in the evening or morning at the solstice always rise at those same hours during the solstice [Col. 0024C].

There are also certain stars that astrologers call planets—that is, “wanderers”—which complete longer years through their circuit, returning to the same place in the sky. The star called Saturn is said to return to the same regions of the heavens in thirty years; Jupiter’s in twelve years; and Mars’s in two solar years, after completing their circuit of the sky.

The moon, too, makes a common year when it has completed twelve periods of its course—that is, 354 days. In order that its circuit might correspond with the solar year, every second or third year it adds a thirteenth month, which those who calculate the calendar call an embolismic year; this produces a year of 384 days.

[Col. 0024D] And God saw that it was good. Holy Scripture necessarily repeats many times that God saw the things he had made to be good, so that the piety of the faithful might be formed by this. Yet this does not mean that human beings, who often take offense even at good things whose causes and order they do not know, should judge visible and invisible creation according to human understanding. Rather, they should believe and submit to God, who praises it.

For each person comes to know something more easily by making progress in understanding to the extent that he has first believed God more reverently, before understanding it [Note: [Col. 0024D] Another reading: “before recognizing it.”]

God therefore saw that the things he had made were good, because the things that had pleased him as things to be made pleased him as things that had been made and were to remain, according to the measure of existence or permanence that so great a maker had appointed for each thing [Col. 0025A].

And evening came and morning followed: the fourth day. This is that memorable evening on which the people of God in Egypt offered the lamb in celebration of Passover; and this is the morning that it saw first after throwing off the yoke of long slavery and beginning its journey of freedom.

It is written, as the Lord said to Moses: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. On the tenth day of this month each person shall take a lamb for his families and houses, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the entire assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening” (Exodus 12:2), and so forth [Col. 0025B].

On that same evening, in order to complete the sacramental observances of the legal Passover, our Lord, after eating the lamb, symbolically inaugurated for us the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated. When morning dawned, like an unblemished lamb, he redeemed us by his blood and freed us from slavery under demonic domination.

This day of the fullest moon occurred in the creation of the world on the fourth day. But at the time of the Lord’s Passion, by the grace of a higher sacrament, it fell on the fifth day of the week, so that the Lord, crucified on the sixth day, might rest in the tomb on the Sabbath itself, consecrate the first day of the week by his resurrection, and grant us faith and hope that on that day on which light was made we too might rise from the dead and enter everlasting light [Col. 0025C].

God also said: “Let the waters bring forth the moving creature having a living soul, and let birds fly above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” After the face of heaven had been adorned with lights on the fourth day, the lower parts of the world—the waters and the air—were next adorned on the fifth with those things that move by the breath of life. These elements are joined both to one another and to heaven by a kind of kinship.

They are joined to one another because the nature of water is close to the quality of air. Thus the air is shown to be enriched by their exhalations, so that it gathers clouds and can support the flight of birds, as Scripture testifies: “Suddenly the air is condensed into clouds, and a passing wind drives them away” (Job 37:21).

Indeed, even on clear nights the air produces dew, whose drops are found in the morning upon the grasses [Col. 0025D]. It is joined to heaven in this way because this air is so near to it that it sometimes receives the same name, as Scripture calls the birds “of heaven,” although it is clear that they fly in the air.

The Lord himself speaks to the crowds, who had not recognized the time of his coming from the signs of the elements, saying: “When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, ‘A rainstorm is coming,’ and so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be heat,’ and it happens. Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of the earth and the sky, but how do you not interpret this time?” (Luke 12:54).

Here it is clear that by “the face of heaven” he means no other thing than the changing state of this air.

[Col. 0026A] God therefore said: “Let the waters bring forth the moving creature having a living soul, and let birds fly above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0025D] The manuscripts omit “the moving creature.”] And lest anyone perhaps suppose that, because there are aquatic creatures that move not by crawling but by swimming or walking on feet, and among birds there are some that have wings but are entirely incapable of flying, some kind of flying or aquatic creature had been omitted from the Lord’s word, Scripture carefully adds:

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Florence manuscript: “God created.”]

“And God created the great sea creatures and every living and moving creature that the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind.”

No kind, therefore, was excluded. Together with the great sea creatures, every living creature that the waters had brought forth in their various kinds was created [Note: [Col. 0026D] The Florence manuscript omits “of them.”]—that is, creatures that crawl, creatures that swim, and flying creatures, as well as those that are not suited to any kind of movement but remain fixed, attached to rocks, such as the many kinds of shellfish [Col. 0026B].

The statement “and let birds fly above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven” presents no obstacle to reason or truth. For although an immense intervening space lies between them, birds nevertheless fly beneath the starry heaven when they fly above the earth. In the same way, we human beings, placed upon the earth, are truly and correctly said to be beneath heaven and the sun, as Scripture testifies: “There were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5); and: “What more does a human being have from all his labor by which he labors beneath the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1:3).

According to another translation, some are troubled by the statement: “And birds fly alongside the firmament of heaven” [Col. 0026C]—that is, “near the firmament of heaven.” But it should be understood that birds are said to fly beneath the firmament of heaven because this name also indicates the ether: that upper region of the air extending from this turbulent and dark place in which birds fly [Note: [Col. 0026D] Another reading: “move about.”] all the way to the stars, and which is rightly believed to be entirely calm and full of light.

Indeed, Scripture said that the seven wandering heavenly bodies, which are said to be carried along in their wandering course through this region of the ether, were placed in the firmament of heaven. Therefore birds are rightly said to fly near the firmament of heaven, because these turbulent regions of the air, which support the flight of birds, are—as we have said—near the ether.

Nor is it surprising that the ether is called the firmament of heaven, since the air is called heaven, as we have explained above [Col. 0026D].

It should not be passed over that, when God was said to have created every living creature, “mortal” was added, evidently to distinguish it from the human being whom he was about to make in his own image and likeness. If human beings kept his commandments, they would live forever in blessed unchangeability. The other animals, however, were made from the beginning in such a way that either some would become food for others or, growing weak through old age, would themselves perish.

And God saw that it was good, and he blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.” And evening came and morning followed: the fifth day.

The words “increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea” apply to both kinds of living creatures made from the waters—that is, to fish and birds. For just as fish cannot live anywhere except in water, so there are many birds that, although they sometimes rest upon the land and propagate their offspring there, feed not so much from the land as from the sea, and prefer marine habitats to terrestrial ones [Note: [Col. 0027D] All manuscripts omit “fish.”] [Note: [Col. 0027D] Thus all manuscripts; the printed editions read “nevertheless.”]

The following words, “and let the birds multiply upon the earth,” refer to both kinds of birds: those that feed from the waters and those that feed from the land. Even those birds that cannot live without water—so that they often lie beneath deep waters for much of the year like fish—nevertheless sometimes come out onto the land, especially when they are laying eggs and feeding their young [Col. 0027B].

God also said: “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: cattle, creeping things, and beasts according to their species.” And it was so.

After heaven had been illumined by the stars, after the air had been filled with birds—air which, because of its proximity to heaven, as we have said, deserved the name “heaven”—and after the waters had been enriched with their living creatures, waters that are themselves joined to the air by a great natural kinship—for from them the air derives living creatures, and from them it also derives rain, snow, hail, and other things of this kind—it followed that the earth too should be filled with its living creatures, that is, with creatures generated from itself.

The earth itself also has a special kinship with the waters, since without their moisture and irrigation it could not merely fail to bear fruit but could not even continue to exist. Peter testifies to this when he says: “For the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water, by the word of God” (2 Peter 3:5) [Col. 0027C].

God therefore commands the earth to bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth. Since the term “beasts” is understood to include everything that rages with its mouth or claws, except snakes; since the term “creeping things of the earth” also includes snakes; and since the term “cattle” designates animals used by human beings, where is the category of the other four-footed animals described—deer, does, buffalo, goats [Note: [Col. 0027D] Another reading: “young goats”], and other creatures of this kind? Perhaps we might say that these too, because of the ferocity of their untamed disposition, have been counted among the beasts.

According to the ancient translation, however, in which it is written, “Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to its kind: four-footed animals, creeping things, and beasts of the earth” [Col. 0027D], there is no question at all. For under the name “four-footed animals” everything is included that the earth produced apart from beasts and creeping things, whether animals under human care or those that are wild and untamed.

And God made the beasts of the earth according to their species, and cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth according to its kind. The alteration of the wording should be noted. Above, it was said that God commanded the earth to bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth. Now, with the order changed, God is said to have made the beasts of the earth, cattle, and every creeping thing of the earth.

This should be understood to mean that everything he willed came into being more quickly than the word could be spoken, and that it makes no difference that human speech names first, in the order of creatures, those things that divine power created all at once [Col. 0028A].

When the text continues, “And God saw that it was good,” it is reasonably asked why there is not added here what was said concerning the living creatures that the waters had brought forth: “And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the earth.”

Or perhaps, because God commended the first creation of living creatures with these words, he left it for us to understand the same words concerning the second creation—especially since he was about to add many other things in the works of this day. Concerning the human being, however, he took care to repeat them, saying: “And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” lest anyone should think that sin was present in honorable marriage and that the marriage bed should be compared with the disgrace of fornication.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] Such was the error of the Encratites, concerning whom Saint Augustine writes in *On Heresies*, chapter 25: “They condemn marriages and make them altogether equal to fornications and other corruptions; nor do they admit into their number anyone who uses marriage, whether male or female.” Before them, Saturninus declared that taking wives and begetting children came from Satan, as Epiphanius testifies in *Heresy* 23; Epiphanius attributes similar views to the apostolic heretics in book 2, *Heresy* 61.]

Now that the dwelling of the world had been made and adorned, it remained for the human being himself—on whose account all things were being prepared—to be created as its inhabitant and lord. The text continues:

And he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Now it becomes clearer why it was said of the herbs and trees that had been created, of the fish and birds, and also of the terrestrial animals, that each had been made according to its own kind and species. For the future creation of one was foreseen who would correspond not only in likeness and species to his own kind, [Col. 0028C] but would also be made according to the image and likeness of his Creator. The nobility of this creation is also attested by the fact that, unlike the other creatures, God did not say, “Let man be made,” and man was made; or, “Let the earth produce man,” and the earth produced man. Rather, before he was made, the words “Let us make man” are spoken, so that, since a rational creature was being fashioned, he might appear to have been made, as it were, with deliberation. He is formed from the earth, as though through a carefully conceived work, and raised up by the Creator’s inspiration through the power of the life-giving spirit, so that he might exist not through the command of a spoken word, but through the dignity of an act of workmanship, because he was made in the image of the Creator.

[Note: The printed editions and one manuscript read *jussionis vocem* (“the command of a voice”).]

When it is said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” the unity of the holy Trinity is openly proclaimed. Indeed, that same undivided Trinity had already been mystically suggested in the preceding formation of things, when it was said: “And God said, ‘Let it be,’” and “God made,” and “God saw that it was good.” But now this same mystery is indicated more plainly, when it is said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And rightly so, because, until there was one to be instructed, the preaching of the Godhead lay hidden in the depths; but when the creation of man began to be anticipated, faith was revealed and the doctrine of truth shone forth clearly.

In the word “Let us make,” the operation of the three persons is shown to be one; in what follows, “in our image and likeness,” the one and equal substance of that same holy Trinity is indicated. For how could there be one image and likeness if the Son were less than the Father, if the Holy Spirit were less than the Son, or if the glory of the whole Trinity were not consubstantial and of one power? Or how could the words “Let us make” be spoken if there were not a cooperating power belonging to the three persons in the one Godhead? God could not have said to the angels, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” because no reason at all permits us to believe that the image or likeness of God and the angels is one and the same.

But in what respect man was made in the image and likeness of God, the Apostle testifies when he carefully exhorts us to recover within ourselves, through the grace of that same Creator, what we lost in our first parent. “Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God, in righteousness, holiness, and truth” (Ephesians 4:23). Adam, therefore, was created from the earth as a new man according to God, so that he might be righteous, holy, and true, subject and humbly attached to the grace of his Creator, who exists eternally and perfectly righteous, holy, and true.

But because Adam corrupted this most beautiful newness of the divine image in himself through sin, and begot from himself a corrupted lineage of the human race, from it came the second Adam, namely, the Lord himself and our Creator, born from a Virgin, created incorruptibly and unchangeably according to the image of God, free from every sin and full of all grace and truth, so that he might restore his image and likeness in us through his examples and gifts. He is truly the new man created according to God, because he took from Adam the true substance of flesh in such a way that he drew from him none of the stain of vice.

To follow his example according to our capacity, to cling to his gifts, and to obey his commands is to recover in the new man the image of God that we lost in the old man. Man, therefore, was created in the image of God not according to the body, but according to the understanding of the mind.

Nevertheless, the body itself also possesses a certain feature that indicates this: it was made upright in stature, so that by this very fact man might be admonished not to pursue earthly things, like cattle, whose entire pleasure is from the earth. Hence [Note: Read “toward the earth.”] all other creatures are bent and prostrate, whereas, as one of the poets most beautifully and truly said:

> While the other animals gaze downward upon the earth,  
> He gave man a face held high, and commanded him  
> To look upon heaven and raise his countenance  
> Upright toward the stars. (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 1)

His body, therefore, corresponds to his rational soul—not according to the outlines and shapes of his limbs, but rather according to the fact that it is raised toward heaven, [Col. 0030A] to contemplate the things that are above in the bodily structure of the world, just as the rational soul ought to be raised toward those things that excel most in spiritual nature, so that it may set its mind on things above, not on things upon the earth.

The text rightly adds:

> “And let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heavens, and the beasts, and the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.”

For man was made especially in the image of God in this respect: that he surpasses irrational creatures. He was created capable of reason, through which he could rightly govern all that had been created in the world and enjoy recognition of the one who created everything. [Note: Another reading, *possit*: “may be able.”] If, placed in this position of honor, he does not understand how to act well, he will be compared with those same senseless animals over which he was set, as the Psalmist testifies (Psalm 48:13). [Note: The Florence manuscript reads *sensatis* (“sensible animals”) for *insensatis* (“senseless animals”).]

“And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him.” What he had said earlier—“in his own image”—he repeated for the sake of confirmation by adding, “in the image of God he created him,” so that he might impress more carefully upon us what sort of beings we were made by God, and fix more firmly in our minds the hope of receiving the image of God again. Thus, though we walk in the image of God, we should not be troubled in vain, storing up treasures in the uncertainty of riches; rather, we should thirst for the Lord, awaiting the time when we shall come and appear before his face, confident that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

What is now said—“in the image of God he created him”—although above it was said, “Let us make him in our image,” signifies that the plurality of persons does not mean that we are to believe in several gods. Rather, because of the Trinity it was said, “in our image”; and because of this, “in the image of God,” we are to understand one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“Male and female he created them.” More fully, in what follows, the place and manner in which God made the first-formed pair are explained. But for the sake of brevity they are now merely reported as created, [Note: The printed editions read *tunc* (“then”).] so that the work of the sixth day and the consecration of the seventh may be explained along with the rest, and so that at the proper time this and other matters worthy of mention that had been passed over may be discussed more freely.

God first created one male and one female—not like the other animals, of which he created not one individual in each kind but several—in order by this means to bind the human race together in a closer bond of love, since it would remember that the whole of it had arisen from one parent. For this reason, when sacred Scripture said, “And God created man; in the image of God he created him,” and immediately added, “Male and female he created them,” it did not wish to add, “in the image of God he created them.” For the woman was created in the image of God insofar as she too possessed a rational mind. But Scripture did not think it necessary to add this about her, because, on account of the unity of their union, it left it to be understood also of her; indeed, it indicated that everything said about them was to be understood of the whole human race that arose from them.

Every human being, even now, insofar as he uses reason, bears within himself the image of God. Hence John says: “He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world” (John 1:9). This is the light of which the Psalmist glories in the Lord, saying: “The light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7).

It is fitting, indeed, that in this passage male and female are mentioned as having been created, even though the manner of that creation has not yet been reported, so that the account of the divine blessing might have its appropriate place. It follows:

“And he blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it.’” This increase of human beings and filling of the earth could be accomplished only through the union of male and female. But if the human race grows and multiplies by God’s blessing, how worthy of condemnation are those who forbid marriage and condemn the arrangement of the heavenly decree as though it had been devised by the devil?

Marriage, therefore, must not be condemned. It was instituted by the grace of heaven’s blessing for the propagation of the human race and the filling of the earth. Rather, virginity is to be honored and is worthy of a greater blessing: after the earth has been filled with human beings, it desires, with a chaste mind and body alike, to follow the Lamb wherever he goes—that is, the Lord Jesus—in the heavenly places, and to sing the new song that no one else can sing to him.

For our God and Lord, who at the beginning of the world being born fashioned woman from the man’s side, to teach that the earth was to be filled through their mutual union, [Col. 0031C] himself, at the end of the age, took a man from the flesh of a Virgin, free from every defilement and perfect in the entire fullness of divinity, to show that he loved the glory of virginity more than marriage.

“And rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the heavens, and all the living creatures that move upon the earth.” It is reasonably asked for what benefit man received dominion over the fish, birds, and all the animals of the earth, and for what uses or consolations these were created for man, if he had never sinned.
