[Note: So all manuscripts; the printed editions read *creati hominis* (“of created man”).] For, as the following words of this Scripture make clear, in the first creation he was granted not these creatures as food [Note: Tertullian (*On Fasting*, chapter 4), Origen (*Homily 1 on Genesis*), Basil (*Oration 1 on Fasting*), Chrysostom (*Homily 27 on Genesis*), and Jerome (*Against Jovinianus*, chapter 10) teach that before the Flood permission to eat flesh had not been given.] but only the fruits of herbs and trees.

Unless, perhaps, it must be said that God foreknew that man would sin, and that the one whom he had created immortal would become mortal through sin; and for that reason he instituted for him from the beginning those consolations by which a mortal could protect his weakness—namely, nourishment from these creatures, clothing, and assistance for labor or travel.

Nor is it worth asking why man does not even now rule over all living creatures. After he himself refused to be subject to his Creator, he lost dominion over those creatures that his Creator had subjected to his authority. Indeed, we read testimonies of the first creation: birds rendered service to holy men who served God humbly; the jaws of beasts yielded; and the poison of serpents could not harm them.

“And God said: ‘Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and every tree that has within itself the seed of its kind, to be food for you, and for all the animals of the earth, and every bird, and everything that moves upon the earth and in which there is a living soul, so that you may have them for food.’” [Note: Edition and Corbie manuscript: “so that they may have.” The printed editions add *sint* (“may be”).]

Here it is clear that before man’s guilt the earth produced nothing harmful: no poisonous herb, no barren tree. For it is plainly said that every herb and every tree was given as food to human beings, birds, and all the animals of the earth. It is clear, therefore, that the birds themselves did not live by snatching weaker creatures, nor did the wolf lie in wait around the sheepfolds, nor was dust the serpent’s bread; rather, all creatures fed together in harmony on green herbs and the fruits of trees.

Yet amid these matters a question must not be omitted: how was man made immortal above the other animals, while nevertheless receiving the same earthly nourishment as they? We must observe here that there is one immortality of the flesh, which we received in Adam at the first creation, and another which we hope to receive through Christ in the resurrection.

Adam was made immortal in such a way that he could avoid dying if he did not sin, but if he sinned he would die. The children of the resurrection, however, will be immortal when they are equal to the angels of God, so that they can neither die nor sin any longer. Therefore, after the resurrection our flesh will require no nourishment from food, because it will suffer no decline from hunger, weariness, or any other weakness. [Note: Another reading, *egebit*: “will need.”]

Adam’s flesh before sin was created immortal in such a way that, aided by the support of temporal nourishment, it would remain free from death and pain until, through bodily growth, he reached the age that pleased the Creator. Then, after many descendants had been created, by the Creator’s command he would also partake of the tree of life. Having thereby become perfectly immortal, he would no longer require the supports of bodily food.

Thus the flesh of the first human beings was created immortal and incorruptible so that they might preserve that immortality and incorruption by observing God’s commands. Among those commands was this: they were to eat from the trees of paradise that had been permitted, but abstain from eating the forbidden one. Through the former food they would preserve the gifts of immortality implanted in them; by touching the latter they would encounter the ruin of death.

Our flesh will be incorruptible and immortal at the end in such a way that, after the likeness of angelic exaltation, it will remain forever in the same condition and, since there will be no bodily foods in the spiritual life, will be unable to experience any need of them. For when angels are read to have eaten with the patriarchs, they did so not from necessity but from kindness, so that by acting in this way they might conform more graciously to the human beings to whom they appeared. [Note: Two manuscripts read *congruerent* (“might be fitting”).] The Lord also ate with his disciples after the resurrection, not because he needed nourishment, but to show that after death he had truly recovered flesh.

“And it was so”—that is, so that man might rule over all things created on earth or in the waters, and might receive the ability and authority to eat the fruits of the earth, together with the birds of heaven and the animals of the earth.

“And God saw all that he had made, and it was very good.” Since it had been said individually of each of God’s works that he saw that they were good, it was rightly stated in conclusion, when everything had been completed, with the addition that he saw all that he had made and that it was very good.

But it is reasonably asked why, concerning man after he had been made, the separate statement “And God saw that it was good” was not added, but his creation was reserved for universal praise among the other things. Was it because God foreknew that man would sin and would not remain in the perfection of his image, and therefore wished to call him good not individually but together with the rest, as though intimating what was going to happen? [Note: Another reading, *facturum*, is “what he was going to do”; the Florence manuscript has *venturum*, “what was going to come.”]

Before sin, then, man was good in his own kind; but Scripture omitted saying this so that it might instead say something that foretold what was to come. For God is the best creator of natures but the most just arranger of sinners, so that even if individual things become deformed through wrongdoing, the universe as a whole nevertheless remains beautiful with them.

“And evening came and morning came, the sixth day. Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment.” The number six is evidently perfect, because it is filled by its own parts: the sixth, namely one; the third, namely two; and the half, namely three. One, two, and three make six. Such a number is found nowhere among the units except here, nor among the tens except in the number twenty-eight.

God therefore completed all the adornment of heaven and earth in six days, so that he who established all things in measure, number, and weight might also teach, by the number in which he worked, that his works were perfect.

“And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made.” In another translation it says that God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made. This presents no difficulty at all, since the clear account indicates what was done in it. But it is reasonably asked how our edition, which descends from the source of the Hebrew truth, can say that God completed his work on the seventh day, when no new creation is recorded on that day.

Perhaps we may say that he made the seventh day itself at that time and completed his work in making it, because by doing so he completed the measure and number of the days, whose cycle would thereafter carry all the ages forward to the end. For in the cycle of times the eighth day is counted as the same day as the first.

[Col. 0034A] “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made.” He brought to an end on it the total number of the days he had made, adding that seventh day, [Note: Another reading: “among them.”] which he wished to be called and to be the Sabbath, because he endowed it above the others with a mystical blessing and sanctification, as what follows teaches.

Hence the day of judgment and the consummation of the age, because it will come after the seventh, the Sabbath, is called the eighth in Scripture, evidently because only seven days precede it. For in the title of the Psalms it is said: “For the end; with hymns, a psalm of David for the eighth.” That this was written concerning the day of judgment is shown by the entire text of the following psalm, in which the prophet, fearing the anger of the coming Judge, cries out: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Psalm 6:1), and so forth.

The day of the Lord’s Resurrection is likewise called the eighth in the title of another psalm, although it was to come after so many thousands of days, because it followed the seventh and was to be the first day of the following week—that is, the very day on which in the beginning God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made. The psalm itself proves that it was written concerning the Lord’s Resurrection, for the one who speaks in it says: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Psalm 11:6).

It may also rightly be understood that God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made in that he blessed and sanctified the day itself. For neither blessing nor sanctification is no work at all. Nor should Solomon be said to have done no work when he dedicated the temple he had made; indeed, it is an outstanding work of God when he has glorified eternally by blessing and sanctification the things he has made. [Note: The printed editions read *glorificat* (“glorifies”).]

Finally, concerning this work that he performs on the eternal Sabbath-day, he himself says in the parable of the faithful servants: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, and make them recline, and passing by will minister to them” (Luke 12:37). He who girds himself, prepares a place at table, passes by, and ministers is certainly working. Yet by all these words nothing else is indicated than that the Lord blesses and sanctifies his saints forever—that is, after the good works he has graciously produced in them, he rewards them with the vision of his glory.

“And he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.” God did not rest, like human weakness, as though tired from excessive labor after the world’s structure had been completed. Rather, he is said to have rested from all his work because he ceased to establish any new creation.

Scripture often uses the name “rest” to indicate the cessation of a work or speech, as in the Apocalypse concerning the living creatures: “And they had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty” (Revelation 4:8). This means that they did not cease continually to sing these words. For the greatest and only rest of the saints in heaven is to proclaim with unwearied voice the praise of the supreme Trinity, which is God.

The Lord’s resting from all his works may also be understood in a deeper sense: not that he needed those works in which he might rest, since his rest in himself, without beginning or end, is always true, but that he made works solely because of his goodness, works that might rest in him. [Note: Another reading omits *scilicet* (“namely”); another reads *ullis* (“any”) for *illis* (“those”).] This is more readily understood by remembering that human need labors daily above all so that it may find rest in its works, as the Lord says to man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 3:19).

But God, who before the creation of the world eternally possessed perfect rest in himself, after creating the world also rested—not in the works he had made, but from all the works he had made. He had no necessity within himself that required him to rest in creatures; rather, he himself grants rest to rational creatures, while he always rests perfectly in himself and is blessed by that good which he himself is to himself. [Note: Another reading: *perfecto* (“perfect”).]

“And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” This was the blessing and sanctification that he later made known more fully to his people in the law, saying: “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work” (Exodus 20:8). And shortly afterward: “For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11).

For this reason the Lord blessed the seventh day and sanctified it. This blessing and sanctification of the seventh day was made as a type of a greater blessing and sanctification. Just as, through the frequent—indeed daily—sacrifices of the law, the blood of the Lord’s Passion, which was to be shed once for the salvation of the world, was signified, so too through the rest of the seventh day, which was always accustomed to be celebrated after the works of the six days, that great Sabbath-day was prefigured on which the Lord was once to rest in the tomb.

He would rest there after all his works had been completed and perfected on the sixth day—those works by which he restored the world, which he had perfected on the sixth day but which had already been lost. On that day, as though recalling the ancient work, he declared openly that he had now completed the salvation of the world. For when he had received vinegar, he said: “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30).

This sanctification and blessing of the seventh day, and God’s rest on it after his very good works, also signified that each of us, after the good works that he himself works in us both to will and to accomplish, moves toward the rest of heavenly life, in which we may enjoy his eternal sanctification and blessing. Hence it is rightly not written that the seventh day had an evening, because it signifies our perpetual rest in that day.

“And he blessed,” it says, “the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.” That is, once the adornment of the world had been completed, he ceased to establish new kinds of things.

This should not be considered contrary to what he says in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). He was answering those who complained that, on the authority of this Scripture’s ancient commendation of God’s rest, the Sabbath was not observed by him.

He had ceased on the seventh day from creating kinds of creatures, because thereafter he created no new kinds. But from then until now he has continued to administer those same kinds that were instituted—not as though, even on the seventh day, his power ceased to govern heaven and earth and all the things he had made; otherwise they would immediately fall apart. [Note: The Florence manuscript reads *ut ipso*; one Corbie manuscript, *ita ut ipso*.]

Thus far, it is enough to have discussed the beginnings of the nascent world according to the literal sense. But it is pleasing briefly to indicate how the sequence of those six—or seven—days in which it was made [Note: Another reading adds “the world.”] corresponds to the same number of ages.

The first day, on which God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, corresponds to the first age. At its beginning the world itself was made, and man was placed amid the delights of the paradise of pleasure, where, in the presence of the grace of his Creator, he enjoyed freedom from and ignorance of every evil.

But this day had already begun to decline toward evening when the first-formed pair, by sinning, lost the happiness of their heavenly homeland and were cast into this valley of tears. This was also signified by the time when, after his transgression, Adam heard the Lord walking in paradise at an hour after midday. The Lord walked in order to signify that he had withdrawn from the human being in whose heart he had formerly remained at rest; and he did so at an hour after midday so that man might recognize that the light of divine knowledge and the fervor of divine love had been diminished in him.

The full evening of this day arrived when, as the vices of the human race increased, all the earth was corrupted before God and filled with iniquity, so that all flesh deserved to be destroyed by the Flood except those whom the ark had enclosed.

On the second day the firmament was made in the midst of the waters. In the second age of the world, the ark in which the remnant of the human race—and, so to speak, the seed of the following ages—was preserved was placed in the midst of the waters, which were poured out in rivalry from one side by all the fountains of the abyss bursting forth and from the other by the floodgates of heaven opened above.

But this day too inclined toward evening when the nations, having forgotten the recent anger or mercy of God, turned to build a tower of pride. It received its full evening when the society of the human race was broken apart through the confusion of languages.

On the third day, when the waters flowed together into their places, dry land appeared, and soon it was clothed with green herbs and leafy groves. At the beginning of the third age, the idolatrous nations were separated into their places. Their error was unstable and moved by every wind, like the teachings of empty images; thus they were aptly signified by the name “sea.”

The seed of the patriarchs was separated from their society and made fruitful by spiritual produce, when the Lord said to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house into the land that I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you” (Genesis 12:1), and so forth, until he says: “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

Within this nation, the distinct orders of the faithful, like green herbs and fruit-bearing trees, emerged from one and the same earth, [Note: Another reading: *prodebant*, “produced.”] receiving the heavenly rain of the divine words. [Note: Two manuscripts read *suscipiente* (“receiving”).]

But here too the day began to incline toward evening when that same Israelite people, abandoning both the faith of the patriarchs and the ceremonies of the law given to it, became polluted with the crimes of foreign nations and was oppressed by servitude. Evening came when that nation itself, together with the king whom it had chosen for itself while neglecting God, was for the most part destroyed by the sword of foreigners.

On the fourth day the heavens received their luminaries. In the fourth age, the aforementioned people of God became conspicuous with a new brightness through the rule of David, Solomon, and the other kings who reigned with God as their author; through that most noble temple that Solomon built for God; through the signs of the prophets, which did not cease to flourish throughout the times of those kings [Note: The manuscripts do not contain “of those same kings.”]; and especially through the fact that the Lord swore to the first and most eminent of the kings who pleased him: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon my throne” (Psalm 131:11). [Note: So the manuscripts; the printed editions read *tuam* (“your [throne]”).]

Yet here too the day began to decline toward evening when, later, those kings and the people themselves, scorning the temple and the laws of God, were devastated and torn apart by their enemies. A very grievous evening, and not merely evening but night, followed when that entire kingdom was overthrown, the temple burned, and the whole people led captive into Babylon.

On the fifth day the waters brought forth creeping things possessing living souls, and flying birds over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven. In the fifth age the children of the captivity increased and multiplied in Babylon, which is often represented by the name “waters.” Many of them remained there like fish in the waters. Yet among them were some who, like great sea creatures, preferred to rule over the great waves of the world rather than serve them, because they could not be perverted into idolatry by any terror.

Others, when the captivity was released, returned to the land of Israel as though they had received wings of freedom, and like flying creatures sought heavenly things with their whole purpose. Thus they strove to rebuild the temple and city of God and to restore his law with the greatest zeal.

But evening was approaching when, amid other darknesses of crime, they later began to quarrel among themselves in domestic conflicts and became traitors to their own country on behalf of the Romans. That evening also arrived when it befell them not only to become tributaries but also to be subjected to the rule of a foreign king.

On the sixth day the earth brought forth cattle, beasts, and creeping things. On that same day God created the first man, Adam, in his own image, and from his side, while he slept, he created the woman Eve.

In the sixth age of the world, amid the many reprobates who could rightly be compared with serpents and beasts, because of their savagery and because they were born to cling with their whole spirit to earthly cares or pleasures, there are also many saints among the people of God. Like clean animals, they know how to ruminate on the word of God, keep the divided hoof of discernment on the road, carry the yoke of divine law in good works, and warm their work with wool. The Gospel appropriately mentions both kinds.

Among them appeared the second Adam, namely the mediator between God and human beings, in whom the entire fullness of the image of God was present. From his side, as he slept on the cross, flowed blood and water; from these sacraments the Church is born and nourished. She is the mother of all who truly live throughout the world, as the name Eve signifies.

Therefore the Lord himself says concerning these same sacraments: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55).

We now see the evening of this day drawing near, when, as iniquity abounds everywhere, the love of many grows cold. A far darker evening will come when the man of sin, the son of iniquity, appears—he who is exalted and lifted up above everything that is called God or worshiped—and such tribulation occurs that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error.

Immediately afterward comes the hour of universal judgment, concerning which it is written: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

[Col. 0038C] On the seventh day God rested from all his works, sanctified it, and blessed it. The seventh age is the perpetual age of rest in the other life, in which God rests with his saints forever after the good works that he works in them throughout the six ages of this world.

This age of supreme peace and rest is and will be eternal in God. But for human beings it began when the first martyr Abel entered bodily into the dwelling of the tomb and, in soul, into the joy of eternal life. There the rich man, while he himself was tormented in the underworld, saw the poor man at rest.

This Sabbath-rest of holy souls will continue until the end of the world. When the final age of the world, after its evening of which we have spoken, reaches its end, with Antichrist slain by the Lord Jesus, [Note: Another reading, *perfecerit*: “will have completed.”] then this Sabbath-rest too will be bestowed upon bodies through the greater blessing and sanctification of resurrection unto perpetual life.

Therefore it is rightly not said that evening followed the seventh day, because this seventh age will have no sadness to bring it to an end. Rather, as we have said, it is completed in the greater joy of the eighth age—that is, the age which will then begin through the glory of the resurrection, when this whole life has passed away, and which will never be changed from the contemplation of God’s face by any end or alteration of things.

[Note: Here the printed editions end. At this point the first book of the two books that Bede dedicated to Acca the bishop before writing on Ezra also ended, as is established by the smaller Corbie manuscript, which reads here: “The first book ends.” What follows up to the second book constituted the other book dedicated to Bishop Acca. Later, however, these two books were joined into one, namely when he added the following three books. Hence the aforementioned Corbie manuscript, after the second of those books, again has: “The first book ends.”]

[Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039D] Alternatively: “these are.”] These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created. [Note: [Col. 0039D] Thus all manuscripts; in the Vulgate it reads, “were created.”] By this conclusion Scripture addresses those who assert that the world has always existed without a beginning, or who indeed think that it was made by God, but from matter which God did not make, and which, coeternal with him, existed without beginning alongside the Creator. [Note: [Col. 0039D] Such were Aristotle with his followers and Plato. Of the former, Saint Ambrose says in Book I of *The Hexaemeron*, chapter 1: “Aristotle takes it upon himself to say that the world has always existed and will always exist”; of the latter he says: “Men have adopted such a great opinion that some of them established three principles of all things: God, the exemplar, and matter, as did Plato and his disciples; and they asserted that these were incorruptible, uncreated, and without beginning, and that God made the world not as the creator of matter, but as a craftsman directing his attention toward the exemplar—that is, the idea—and making the world from matter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “governings” (*gubernationes*).]

For he calls “the generations of heaven and earth” the very order of the divine creation, by which their adornment, through the works of the six days, reached that perfection described above, in accordance with what the Creator himself said in the Decalogue of his law: “For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Exod. 20:11). But what follows—“On the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose on the earth, and every plant of the land before it germinated”—should by no means appear contrary to the statement of God just mentioned. It must plainly be understood that here Scripture uses “day” for the whole period during which the primordial creation was formed.

For heaven was not made, or illuminated by the stars, on any one of the six days; nor was the earth separated from the waters and planted with trees and grasses on one particular day. Rather, following its customary manner, Scripture uses “day” for “a period of time,” just as the Apostle, when he says, “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2), means not one particular day but the whole period during which, in the present life, we labor for eternal salvation. Likewise the prophet speaks not of one particular day but of an extended time of divine grace when he says: “On that day the deaf shall hear the words of this book” (Isa. 29:18).

[Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “on this day”; alternatively: “on one day.”]

Otherwise, it is difficult to understand how on this day God made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every plant of the land, unless perhaps we say that all creation was made together in unformed matter, in accordance with what is written: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). Yet he certainly did this before every day of this age, when in the beginning he created heaven and earth. Although the earth was then “formless and empty,” and darkness was over the abyss, nevertheless within the nature of the earth itself and of the abyss—that is, of the waters—there lay hidden, as it were through a seminal substance, those things which, though created together in the substance of the earth and abyss, were afterward not to be brought forth from them all at once through the Creator’s work. [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “work” (*opera*).] Therefore, if we say this, the question mentioned returns to the same conclusion: we must understand the designation “day” as used to signify the period during which God created all these things together in the beginning. “On the day,” he says, “when the Lord God created earth and heaven and every shrub of the field before it arose on the earth, and every plant of the land before it germinated.”

If, then, by the “day” he mentions we understand the designated period when all things were made together before any day of this age, the meaning is readily apparent: every plant and every tree was made causally within the substance of the earth itself before they visibly arose or germinated from the earth. [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively, omitting *ipsius*: “within the substance of the earth.”] But if—as we more reasonably judge—we take the designation “day” as referring to the period during which this world was made and adorned over six days, we can understand that Scripture now wished to explain more clearly how it had earlier said that “the earth brought forth green vegetation bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit.”

For the earth did not produce these things at the beginning of creation in the manner in which it now does, when, after receiving an irrigation of waters by God’s ordering, the earth spontaneously bears fruit. [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “had produced.”] Rather, by a wholly more marvelous work of the Creator, before any fruits had arisen or germinated from the earth through growth, the plains, mountains, and hills were suddenly covered with grasses and trees [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “all the plains and hills were suddenly covered.”] possessing their appropriate height and stature, spreading branches, leafy shade, and an abundance of fruits. They did not receive these things gradually by rising or germinating from the earth and advancing through successive growth, but acquired them suddenly by coming forth from it.

The words that follow also seem to support this interpretation, for it is said:

> “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the ground, but a fountain was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

Who does not see that these words could not have been spoken of the first creation of the earth, when it was still formless and empty and darkness was over the face of the abyss? Surely there was no need at that time to say that rain had not descended upon the earth, when the earth itself could not yet receive rain, nor the air release it, because the waters still filled all the regions belonging to each of them. [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “filled.”] Nor could a fountain rise from the earth to irrigate it while the whole earth was covered by the abyss. Hence, unless I am mistaken, it remains to be understood that when it is said above, “On the day when the Lord God created earth and heaven,” and so forth, the period of those first six days is indicated, during which the whole creation of the world was formed. [Note: [Col. 0040D] Alternatively: “is mentioned.”]

In this context it rightly recalls that God had not rained upon the earth and that there was no man to work the ground, so that we may understand how far the first germination of the earth differed from that of the present time. Now the earth spontaneously germinates through the irrigation of rains, and through human industry and cultivation much is produced in gardens, fields, and groves. But the first creation of grasses and trees was completed in a very different manner. By a new command of the supreme Craftsman, the dry earth, without rain and without human labor, was suddenly and far and wide filled with many kinds of fruit. “But a fountain,” he says, “was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

Before discussing this fountain and its rising upon the earth, let us first observe that the earth’s first germination, which the preceding statement mentions, took place without any irrigation of waters, at God’s command. The irrigation of this fountain, whatever it was, came afterward, once the earth had been clothed with grasses and trees. This is also proved by the very wording of Scripture. After saying in the past tense that “the Lord God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field, and every plant of the land,” it immediately added, in the pluperfect tense: “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work the ground.” This shows that before the creation of the shrubs and plants God had not sent rain.

What happened afterward it immediately appended in the imperfect tense, saying: “For a fountain was rising from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” By the form of the verb it indicates that this did not happen only once but repeatedly: it does not say “it rose” but “it was rising.” Since the fountain is said to have risen from the earth and watered its entire surface, it is reasonably asked in what manner it rose. There is no obstacle to believing that it rose and returned in alternating cycles to irrigate the earth, just as to this day the Nile annually rises to irrigate the plains of Egypt; or as the Jordan once irrigated the land of the Pentapolis, of which Scripture says: “For the whole region was watered like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt” (Gen. 13:10); before God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.

As Saint Augustine testifies:

> “It is reported of certain springs that, at a fixed interval of years, they undergo a marvelous alternation, flooding in such a way that they irrigate the entire region which at another time they supply with sufficient water for drinking from deep wells. Why, then, is it incredible,” he says, “if from one source of the abyss, flowing and ebbing in alternating change, the whole earth was then watered? And if,” he says, “excluding that part of the abyss which is called the sea, we understand its immense extent as surrounding the lands with evident depth and bitter waves, while in that part alone where the earth contains it within hidden recesses all the springs and waters distribute themselves through different regions and channels and burst forth in their respective places; [Note: [Col. 0041D] The manuscripts lack “waters,” but it occurs in the text of Saint Augustine cited here.] if Scripture wished to call this a fountain rather than fountains because of the unity of its nature, and if it rose from the earth through innumerable ways of caverns and fissures, watering everywhere the whole face of the earth as though with scattered strands of hair—not in one continuous expanse like the sea or a pond, but as we see waters travel through the channels of rivers and the winding courses of streams and, overflowing them, soak the neighboring areas—who would not accept this, except one who is troubled by a contentious spirit? The whole face of the earth can indeed be understood to have been watered in the same way that an entire garment is said to be colored, even if this occurs not continuously but in spots; especially since, in the earth’s early condition, it is believable that although not all regions, at least many of the plains were then open, allowing the streams bursting forth more widely to spread and extend themselves. Therefore, concerning the size or multiplicity of this fountain—which either had a single outlet somewhere, or was called the one fountain of all great and small springs because of some unity among themselves in the earth’s hidden recesses, from which all waters gush over the earth, rising from the earth through all its dispersions and watering its whole face; or, more plausibly, because Scripture does not say, ‘one fountain was rising from the earth,’ but ‘a fountain was rising from the earth,’ and uses the singular for the plural, so that we understand many fountains throughout the whole earth watering their respective places or regions, just as ‘soldier’ may be said while many are meant, and as locust and frog were spoken of in the plagues by which the Egyptians were struck although the locusts and frogs were innumerable—let us no longer labor over the matter.” [Note: [Col. 0041D] Alternatively: “among themselves.”]

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Saint Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book V, chapter 10.]

Accordingly, when it had been said that God created the grasses and shrubs, with no rain yet descending and no man existing to work the earth, the creation of man is next introduced, and it is said:

> “Then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.”

Here the making of man is described at greater length. He was indeed made on the sixth day, but his creation was mentioned there only briefly and is explained more fully here: namely, that he was made with respect to the substance of body and soul. [Note: [Col. 0042D] Alternatively: “substance.”] His body was formed from the dust of the earth, while his soul was created from nothing through God’s breathing; and the woman likewise was formed from his side while he slept.

In this statement we must avoid the poverty of a carnal understanding, lest we imagine that God formed the human body from clay with bodily hands, or breathed into the face of the formed man with throat and lips so that he could live and possess the breath of life. When the Prophet says, “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. 119:73), he speaks more in a figurative than in a literal manner—that is, according to the customary way in which human beings work. [Note: [Col. 0042D] Alternatively: “proper.”]

For God is spirit, and only the unlearned believe that his simple substance is composed according to the outlines of bodily limbs. God formed man from clay: by his word he commanded that man be made from clay. He breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul: that is, he created for him the substance of soul and spirit in which he would live. For this is rightly understood as God’s breathing into the face of man and creating the breath by which he would live, just as it was understood above that “God called the light day” means that he caused it to be called by human beings.

God is rightly said to have breathed into man’s face so that he might become a living soul, [Note: [Col. 0043D] Alternatively: “God.”] because the spirit implanted in him contemplates the things outside him, since the anterior part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is situated toward the forehead. The sense of touch, too, which is spread throughout the whole body, is shown to have its passage from this same anterior part of the brain, proceeding backward through the crown and neck to the spinal cord. The statement made above concerning man agrees with this:

> “He created him in the image of God. Male and female he created them.”

What is said concerning the image of God is rightly understood to refer only to the soul; what is added concerning male and female refers only to the body.

Therefore those who think that the soul is a part of God must not be heeded, as though the human soul were a part of God and thus could neither be seized by itself nor by anyone else, nor be compelled by any necessity to do or suffer anything evil, nor be changed at all for better or worse. That breath of God by which he animated man was made by him, not from him. The breath of a human being is neither a part of another human being, nor does a person make it from himself; rather, it is drawn from the air and expelled.

God, however, was able to create from nothing a living and rational being—something man cannot do. Nevertheless, some think that the first man was not then animated when God breathed into his face and he became a living soul, but that he then received the Holy Spirit. However either of these may be shown to be more credible, we must not doubt that the soul is not a part of God, nor a nature created or brought forth from his substance, but was made from nothing.

Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed. We must believe that God planted the paradise from that beginning when he commanded the whole earth, after the waters covering it had been removed, to produce grasses and fruit-bearing trees. In it, however, he placed man on the sixth day, on which he had also formed him. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Alternatively: “whom.”]

There is no reason at all to doubt that the paradise in which the first man was placed [Note: [Col. 0043D] Alternatively: “first.”]—although it represents either the present Church or the homeland of the future—must nevertheless be understood according to the literal meaning as a place: an exceedingly pleasant region shaded by fruitful groves, and both extensive and richly watered by a great fountain. Instead of “from the beginning,” our edition, which was translated from the Hebrew truth, has in the ancient translation “toward the East.” Hence some wish the location of paradise to have been in the eastern part of the world, although it was separated from all the regions now inhabited by the human race by an immense intervening distance of either ocean or land. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Alternatively: “a very great distance.”] Therefore even the waters of the Flood, which covered the entire surface of our world to a great depth, could not have reached it. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Alternatively: “could have reached it.”]

But whether it was there or elsewhere, God knows; we may not doubt that this place was and is earthly. Finally, in the words that follow, Scripture explains more fully how God planted it, saying:

> “And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and pleasing for food, and also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

This is understood to have happened on the day when the earth, at God’s command, produced the other fruit-bearing trees as well. But it is necessarily repeated here so that we might know what kind of place paradise was, [Note: [Col. 0044D] Alternatively: “might be able.”] especially since particular mention had to be made of the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In the one there was a sign of the obedience owed by man; in the other, the sacrament of eternal life, which he would merit through that obedience.

The tree of life was called by that name because, as we have said, it received from God the power by which whoever ate from it would have his body strengthened with lasting health, would never be changed for the worse by sickness or age, and would not even decline into death. Yet this occurred bodily in such a way that it was also a figure of a spiritual sacrament: namely, of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is said in praise of wisdom: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her” (Prov. 3:18). And in the Apocalypse of Saint John: “To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will grant to eat from the tree which is in the paradise of my God” (Apoc. II, 18).

This plainly means: “To the one who conquers the temptation of the ancient serpent, by which Adam was conquered, I will grant what I would have granted to Adam if he had conquered, so that he may be refreshed forever by the present vision of the glory of Christ.” Therefore no assault of death can touch him, because the Lord Christ—the power and wisdom of God the Father—is in the paradise of the heavenly kingdom, which he also deigned to promise, together with the other saints, to the thief who confessed him on the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0044D] Thus the manuscripts. Earlier they read “the tree of knowledge,” as in the Vulgate.]

> “And the tree of the wisdom of good and evil.”

Concerning this tree Saint Augustine says:

> “As I consider the matter again and again, I cannot say how greatly I am pleased by the view that that tree was not harmful as food. For he who had made all things very good would not have established anything evil in paradise; rather, the evil was the transgression of the command. It was necessary, however, that man, placed under the Lord God, should be prohibited from something else, so that the very obedience by which he sought to please his Lord would be his virtue. I can say with complete truth that this alone is the virtue of every rational creature acting under God’s authority; and that the first and greatest vice is the swelling of pride leading to ruin, the desire to use one’s own power, whose supreme name is disobedience. There was therefore no way for man to conceive and recognize that he had a Lord unless something were commanded him. That tree, then, was not evil, but was called the tree of the knowledge and discernment of good and evil, [Note: [Col. 0045D] Alternatively: “of knowledge and of discerning.”] because, if after the prohibition man ate from it, through the transgression of the command that would follow he would learn by experience the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Accordingly, this must be understood not figuratively but as a real tree, whose name was imposed not from the fruit or apple that grew upon it, but from what was to follow when it was touched contrary to the prohibition.”

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Saint Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book VIII, chapter 6.]

And a river went out from the place of delight to water paradise—that is, those beautiful and fruitful trees that shaded the whole region. We must believe that this occurred in the same way that the Nile irrigates the plains of Egypt in the land we inhabit. Hence, as we also stated above, it was said of the land of Sodom: “The whole region was watered like the garden of the Lord and like Egypt” (Gen. 13:10).

In his provident ordering, the Lord and Creator of all things wished our world to contain some likeness of that homeland for which we were created in our first parent, so that he might admonish us by a nearby example to seek its return and merit its possession—especially through that river which is known to flow from paradise. For the Nile, which irrigates Egypt, is the Gihon, which is later said to proceed from paradise. Likewise, by overthrowing the cities of Sodom, which once were watered like the garden of the Lord, he established an example for those who would act impiously, so that by seeing in the world the sure traces of the destruction of the wicked, we might flee their eternal punishments with vigilant care.

> “From there it divides into four heads. The name of one is Pishon.”

It is established by the most reliable authorities that the sources of all these rivers, which are said to go out from paradise, are known in our world. The source of the Pishon, which is now called the Ganges, is in the regions of the Caucasus Mountains; the source of the Nile, which Scripture, as we have said, calls the Gihon, is now far from Mount Atlas, which is the westernmost limit of Africa. The Tigris and Euphrates, moreover, arise from Armenia. From this it must be believed that the location of paradise itself is exceedingly remote from human knowledge and that the four divisions of the waters proceed from there. The rivers whose sources are said to be known must at some point run beneath the earth and, after passing through lengthy stretches of other regions, emerge where they are said to be known as though at their own sources. For who does not know that some waters commonly do this? It is known there because they do not run beneath the earth for long.

Indeed, historians report that those same rivers—the Tigris, Euphrates, and Nile—disappear into the earth at many places and, emerging again after a considerable intervening distance, resume their customary course. This too must be believed to have been arranged by the Lord as an indication of that course by which the rivers flow to us from paradise through the earth’s more hidden recesses and longer channels.

“Pishon” is interpreted as “change of mouth,” and rightly so, because it displays to us, for our benefit, another face of its own—that is, a much lower one than it has in paradise.

> “It is the one that circles the whole land of Havilah.”

This is the region of India, bearing its name because after the Flood it was possessed by Havilah, son of Joktan, who was the son of Heber, the patriarch of the Hebrews. Josephus also reports that Havilah, together with his brothers, possessed the region from the river Cophene and the land of India as far as the place called Hiera.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] *Jewish Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 20.]

> “There gold is born, and the gold of that land is excellent.”

Pliny the Elder says that the regions of India abound in gold veins more than other lands. Hence their islands received the names Chryse and Argyre from the abundance of gold and silver.

> “And there bdellium and the onyx stone are found.”

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Alternatively: “bdellium.”]

Bdellium, as the same Pliny writes, is an aromatic tree, black in color, the size of an olive tree, with leaves like those of the oak and fruit like the wild fig; its nature is that of gums. Its tear—or resin—is clear, somewhat whitish, smooth, fatty, evenly wax-like, and easily softened; it is bitter in taste and has a pleasant odor, though it becomes more fragrant when mixed with wine. The Book of Numbers also mentions it: “The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like that of bdellium” (Num. 11:7), that is, clear and somewhat whitish.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] *Natural History*, Book XII, chapter 9.]

Onyx is a precious stone, so called because it contains a whiteness mixed into it resembling a human fingernail. For the Greeks call a fingernail *onyx*. Arabia also produces it, but the Indian variety has fiery gleams surrounded by white bands, whereas the Arabian is black with shining bands.

The ancient translation has “carbuncle” and “prasinus stone” in place of these. [Note: [Col. 0046D] Alternatively: “prasinum.”] A carbuncle is, as its name also shows, a stone of fiery color, which is said to illuminate even the darkness of night. A prasinus is a stone of green appearance; hence it received its Greek name from the leek, which they call *prason*.

> “And the name of the second river is Gihon. It is the one that circles the whole land of Ethiopia. The name of the third river is Tigris. It flows toward the Assyrians. The fourth river is the Euphrates.”

For this reason Scripture does not say where the Euphrates flows or what lands it circles, because, flowing nearby through the land of promise, it could easily be known by the people of Israel who were situated there and would read these words.

Since through the waters of regeneration our return to heavenly things is opened to us, it is entirely fitting to the dispensation of divine mercy that the very element by which we are led back to our heavenly homeland should be shared with paradise, where the first man was placed. Just as grace, invisibly restoring us, prepares us for entrance into the heavenly kingdom, so also, invisibly, the same water by which he restores us should spring forth from paradise through the veins of the earth into the world of the Lord.

Therefore, just as “the Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice but do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8), [Note: [Col. 0046D] Alternatively: “do not know.”] so it was fitting that the water by which the Spirit sanctifies those whom he wills should come to us from paradise by unknown paths and return to places unknown to us, since it is established only that it has its origin in the paradise of delight.

Then the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise of delight, to cultivate and guard it.

What he says—“to cultivate and guard it”—seems to refer back to the place where it was said, “And there was no man to work the ground.” But let us also set down, in explaining this word, the words of the holy Father Augustine:

[Note: [Col. 0047D] *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book VIII, chapter 8.]

> “What was he to cultivate or guard? Did the Lord perhaps intend the first man to practice agriculture? Or is it not believable that before sin he had condemned him to labor? We would indeed think so, unless we saw some people cultivate the land with such delight of spirit that it is a great punishment for them to be called away from it to something else. Whatever delight agriculture possesses, it was certainly much greater then, when nothing adverse occurred either to the earth or to the sky. For it was not an affliction of labor but an exhilaration of the will, when the things God had created came forth more joyfully and abundantly with the assistance of human work. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Alternatively: “had created.”] Thus the Creator himself would be praised more fully, since he had given the rational soul, placed within an animal body, both the reason to work and the ability to do so—to the extent sufficient for a willing soul, not to the extent to which bodily need would compel an unwilling one.”

“To cultivate it,” he says, “and to guard it”—that is, to guard that same paradise for himself, lest he commit anything by which he might deserve to be expelled from it. Finally, he also receives a command, so that he may have something to guard in paradise: namely, that by preserving it he might not be cast out. For someone is rightly said not to have guarded his property if he acted in such a way as to lose it, even if it remains safe for another who either found it or deserved to receive it.

There is another meaning in these words, which I think should not undeservedly be preferred: namely, that God himself was to cultivate and guard the man. For just as a human being cultivates the earth not in order to make it earth, but to make it cultivated and fruitful, so God, all the more, cultivates the man whom he himself created so that he might be a man, in order that he might be righteous—if the man does not withdraw from him through pride.

Thus God placed man in the paradise of delight to cultivate and guard it: to cultivate it, that he might be good and blessed; to guard it, that he might remain whole, humbly submitting himself to God’s dominion and protection. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Alternatively: “safe.”]

And he commanded him, saying:

> “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

It must not be believed that anything evil naturally existed in that tree, as we have also taught above. Rather, man was prohibited from a tree that was not evil, so that the preservation of the command itself would be good for him and its transgression evil.

In the end, the sinner desired nothing else except not to be under God’s dominion, when he committed the very act in which, to prevent its commission, he ought to have considered only the command of the one who ruled. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Alternatively: “dominion.”] If that command alone had been heeded, what else would have been loved except God’s will? What else would have been preferred to the human will except God’s will?

Nor can it happen that the self-will of a person does not fall upon him with the heavy weight of a great ruin if, by exalting it, he places it above the will of one superior. Man experienced this when he despised God’s command; and by this experience he learned the difference between good and evil: the good of obedience, but the evil of disobedience—that is, of pride, defiance, perverse imitation of God, and harmful freedom. This object received its name from what could happen through the object itself, as was said above.

> “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.”

He does not say, “If you eat, you will be mortal,” but: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” For man died in soul when he sinned, because God, who is the soul’s life, withdrew from him. As a consequence of this, bodily death followed when the soul, which is the body’s life, departed from him. [Note: [Col. 0048D] Alternatively: “the dead.”] This death came upon the first man when he reached the end of the present life, not long after he had eaten what was forbidden.

It may also be understood that the death in question was brought about in them by that day on which they sinned. [Note: [Col. 0048D] Alternatively: “and thus.”] The Apostle laments it when he says:

> “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:22–24).

It would not have been enough for him to say, “Who will free me from this mortal body?” [Note: [Col. 0048D] Alternatively: “would suffice.”] Rather, he says, “from this body of death.” Likewise: “The body,” he says, “is dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10). There too he does not say “mortal,” but “dead.” Although it was certainly mortal because it was going to die, we must not therefore think that those bodies were such from the beginning. They were indeed animal bodies, not yet spiritual, but they were not dead—that is, they were not bodies that necessarily had to die. This occurred on the day when they touched the tree contrary to the prohibition.

And the Lord God said:

> “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself.”

This speech of God must be believed to have been made not through a bodily voice emitted outwardly into the air, but inwardly through the divine reason of his will, by which all things were created, in accordance with what we taught above concerning the words: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

If someone asks for what purpose this helper ought to have been made, let him hear the answer of Saint Augustine, whose words above we have often set down without mentioning his name:

> “Nothing else plausibly occurs to me except that it was for the procreation of children, just as the seed is helped by the earth so that a plant may arise from both. [Note: [Col. 0048D] Alternatively: “earth.”] For this too had been said at the first creation of things: [Note: [Col. 0049D] Alternatively: “creation.”] ‘Male and female he made them,’ and he blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule over it.’” [Note: [Col. 0049D] Alternatively: “rule over them.”]

This purpose of the creation and union of male and female, together with the blessing, did not cease even after the sin and punishment of man. For it is according to this purpose that the earth is now filled with human beings who rule over it. [Note: [Col. 0049D] Alternatively: “rule over them.”]

Although it is recorded that, after they had been sent out from paradise, they came together and begot children, I do not see what could have prevented them from having honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage-bed even in paradise, if God had granted this to them while they lived faithfully and justly and served him obediently and diligently. Thus offspring could have been generated from their seed without any restless burning of lust and without any labor or pain of childbirth—not so that children would succeed parents who were dying, but so that, while those who had begotten them remained in some fixed condition of bodily form, and drew bodily vigor from the tree of life planted there, those whom they begot might also be brought to the same condition.

Then, when the appointed number had been completed, if all lived justly and obediently, that transformation would occur in which, without any death, their animal bodies would be changed into another quality. Since they would serve the spirit governing them at every command and would live solely through the spirit that gave them life, without any support from bodily nourishment, they would be called spiritual bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The following material does not follow the preceding passage in Augustine, but comes from chapter 6 of the same book.]

For if Enoch and Elijah, who did not die in Adam and who carry in the flesh the succession of death—which they are believed to return to this life in order to discharge and, after so long a delay, undergo—now exist in another life where, before the resurrection of the flesh and before the animal body is changed into a spiritual one, they do not waste away through sickness or old age, how much more justly and plausibly would that have been granted to the first human beings, who lived without any sin of their own or of their parents, so that after children had been born they might pass into some better condition? From there, when the age of the world had ended, they and all the posterity of the saints would be changed into an angelic form—not through the death of the flesh but through the power of God, and with far greater blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book IX, chapter 3.]

Therefore, after the Lord God had formed from the soil all the animals of the earth and all the birds of the sky, he brought them to Adam. If anyone is troubled that he did not say, “having formed from the soil all the animals of the earth and from the waters all the birds of the sky,” but seems to have formed both kinds from the earth, let him understand the words “Therefore the Lord God, having formed from the soil all the animals of the earth and all the birds of the sky” in two ways: either that he has here omitted the material from which he formed the birds of the sky, since it could be inferred from the omission that the Lord did not form both from the earth; but that we should understand, even though Scripture is silent, from what he formed the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky; or that “earth” is being used universally together with the waters, just as it is used in that psalm where, after the praises of the heavenly beings have been concluded, the discourse turns to the earth and says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons, and all abysses” (Ps. 148:7), and so forth. Nor is it subsequently said, “Praise the Lord from the waters.” For wherever all the abysses are that praise the Lord from the earth, there also are the creeping things and winged birds that likewise praise God from the earth [Note: [Col. 0050D] Alternatively, “also from the earth”; alternatively, “the Lord.”], according to this universal designation of “earth.” In this same sense it is also said of the whole world: “God who made heaven and earth”; whether from dry land or from the waters, whatever was created is rightly understood to have been created from the earth.

[Col. 0050B] And he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them. We must not think in a bodily way that God brought the animals of the earth or the birds to Adam as a shepherd usually drives his flock from one place to another. Rather, we should understand that, just as by divine power he created these creatures from the waters when he wished, so also, by the hidden motion of his power, when he wished he brought the same creatures before the man to be seen. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Alternatively, *eadem* (“the same”) is omitted.] In the same way, all the birds and four-footed animals of their kinds are read to have come to Noah’s ark and entered it—not gathered by human hand, but moved by God—though they themselves did not know why they were coming, while the man knew, and received them as they came into the ark, God bringing and commanding them.

[Col. 0050C] For every living creature that Adam called by name, that was its name; and Adam gave their proper names to all the animals of the earth, all the birds of the sky, and all the beasts of the earth. It is established that Adam gave names to the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky in the language spoken by the whole human race up to the building of the tower, when languages were divided. But when, at the overthrow of the tower, God granted each people its own distinct language, then we must believe that he also distinguished for them the names of animals, as well as those of other things, according to each people’s manner of speech. Yet it is also clear that afterward people in many nations gave animals names according to their own preference for many things that perhaps appeared as new to them, and that they still customarily do so today. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Alternatively, *sibi nova* (“new to themselves”).] Finally, Scripture says nothing about fish being brought to Adam so that he might give them names. Nevertheless, it is credible that, as the fish gradually became known, people gave them different names according to the diversity of nations. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Alternatively, “the first language was Hebrew.”]

The first language of the human race, however, seems to have been Hebrew, since all the names that we read in Genesis up to the division of languages are evidently in that language. The reason why all the animals of the earth and the birds of the sky were brought to Adam, so that he might see what he would call them and give them names, is this: God thereby demonstrated to the man how much better he was than all irrational animals. For it is evident from this that man is better than cattle by reason itself, since only reason, which is superior, can distinguish them and discern them by name.

But no helper corresponding to Adam was found for him. Therefore the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh, and the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman. The fact that the woman was made from the man’s side must be believed to have occurred in order to commend the power of that union. But what was done to him while he slept—that a bone was taken away and flesh supplied in its place—was done on account of a deeper mystery. For it signified that from the side of Christ, who was put to sleep in death upon the cross, the sacraments of salvation would come forth, namely blood and water, from which the Church, his bride, would be formed. For if so great a sacrament [Note: [Col. 0051D] Alternatively, *tanta* (“so great,” feminine)] were not to be foreshadowed in the creation of woman, why was it necessary for Adam to sleep so that God might take from him a rib from which to make the woman, when he could have done the same while Adam was awake and without pain? Why was it necessary that, when the bone taken from the man’s side—out of which the woman was formed [Note: [Col. 0051D] Alternatively, *in feminam* (“into a woman”)]—was removed, flesh rather than another bone should be supplied in the bone’s place, unless it was because it was being signified that Christ would be weak for the sake of the Church, while the Church would become strong through him? For this reason, also for the sake of the same mystery, Scripture used a typological word and did not say, “the Lord God made,” or “formed,” or “created,” as in all the works mentioned above, but said, “the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman”—not as though it were a human body, but as though it were a house. And we are that house if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope. For it was fitting that the origin of the human race should proceed through God’s work in such a way that, through harmonious figures, it might bear witness to the redemption that, at the end of the age, was to come through the same Creator.

And he brought her to Adam. And Adam said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” Since Adam, when all the animals of the earth and the birds had been brought to him, had found none among them like himself [Note: [Col. 0051D] Alternatively, *similem* (“similar”)], he rightly recognized now, when he saw the helper corresponding to him made and brought to him, and exclaimed: “This now is bone from my bones.” “Now,” that is, because earlier, after seeing the other animals, he had not seen among them one like himself. But “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” was said because he knew that the other creatures he had seen, which possessed bone and flesh and which he had distinguished by name, had been made not from his substance but from the earth or the waters. And just as he had given names to those creatures when they were brought to him, so it remained for him to give a name to the one whom he recognized as like himself and created from his own body.

“This one,” he said, “shall be called woman [virago], because she was taken from man [viro].” Just as the Latin etymology corresponds in these names—since she is called *virago* from *vir*—so too does the Hebrew etymology correspond. In that language, as may be observed, a man is called *’îš* (*his*), and a woman derived from this name is called *’iššâ* (*hissa*). Finally, that *his* is the Hebrew word for man is also attested by the name Israel, which is interpreted as “a man seeing the Lord.”

It also fits most appropriately with the mysteries of Christ and the Church that Adam wished the woman created from his flesh to share in his name, because our Lord Jesus Christ likewise gave to the Church—whom he redeemed by the price of his body and blood and adopted as his bride—a share in his name, so that she might be called Christian from Christ and, from Jesus, that is, from the Savior, seek eternal salvation. [Note: [Col. 0052D] *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book IX, chapter 19.]

Nor must it be passed over that the sleep, or *ecstasy*, that is, an excess of mind, which the ancient Translation has, “the trance that God cast upon Adam,” is rightly understood, as Saint Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0052D] Alternatively, *ipsius* (“of it/him”)], to have been “sent for this purpose: that first, through ecstasy, the mind might become a participant, as it were, in the angelic court, and, entering into the sanctuary of God, might understand the final things. Finally, when he awoke [Note: [Col. 0052D] Alternatively, *vigilans* (“while awake”)], as though filled with prophecy, and saw the woman who had been brought to him as his own, he immediately poured forth what the Apostle commended as a great mystery: ‘This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man’; and what follows.”

Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Although Scripture itself attests that these words were first spoken by the man, the Lord nevertheless made clear in the Gospel that God had said them. For he says: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’?” (Matt. 19:4). From this we understand that, because of the ecstasy that had preceded in Adam, he was able to say this divinely, as a prophet.

If therefore Christ clung to the Church so that the two might be one flesh, how did he leave the Father, and how did he leave the mother? He left the Father because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6). This is what it means that he left the Father: not that he abandoned or departed from the Father, but that he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father. In the same way, he left his mother by leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and clinging to the Church, which he gathered from all nations, so that, in the peace of the New Testament, the two might be one flesh. For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh our participant, so that we might be the body of that head.

Now both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed. “And rightly so: for what was there to cause shame when they had perceived no law in their members resisting the law of their mind—the punishment for sin that followed them after the transgression had been committed, when disobedience seized what had been forbidden and justice punished the deed? Before this occurred, they were naked, as it is said, and were not ashamed. There was no movement in the body to which shame was owed; they thought nothing needed to be covered because they had perceived nothing that needed to be restrained.” [Note: [Col. 0053D] Augustine, *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 4.]

But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made. This serpent can be called more cunning than all the animals not by its own irrational soul, but through another spirit already present in it, that is, a diabolical spirit. For however much the transgressing angels may have been cast down from their heavenly seats on account of their perversity and pride, they are nevertheless by nature superior to all the animals of the earth because of the excellence of reason. What wonder, then, if the devil, already filling the serpent by his impulse and mingling his own spirit with it, had made it the most cunning of all the animals of the earth, in the manner in which seers are accustomed to be filled by demons? Or, as another edition has it, he made it “the wisest of the beasts,” according to the irrational living soul by which living creatures live?

“If therefore it is asked why God permitted the man to be tempted, when he knew beforehand that he would consent to the tempter, the true answer is that it would not have been a matter of great praise for the man if he could live rightly for the reason that no one persuaded him to live wrongly, since by nature he was able and by his own power willing not to consent to the persuader, though assisted by him who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Nor should it be thought that this tempter would have cast the man down if there had not first arisen in the man’s soul some pride [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, *quaedam* (“some”) is omitted] that needed to be restrained, so that through the humiliation of sin, which he had falsely presumed upon himself [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, *praesumpserit*], he might learn the truth—for it is said: ‘Before ruin the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled’ (Prov. 16:18).

“Some people [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, *si autem* (“but if”)] are disturbed by the fact that God permitted the first man to be tempted, as though they do not now see the entire human race continually harassed by the devil’s snares [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, “pressed hard”; alternatively, “to contend”]. Why, then, did God permit this also? Is it because virtue is tested and exercised, and it is a more glorious crown not to consent when tempted than not to be able to be tempted? But if it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, “to be tempted”] especially through the serpent, this was done for the sake of signification—not because [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, “what”] the devil wished to signify anything for our instruction, but because he could not approach in order to tempt unless permitted, nor could he approach through anything other than what he was permitted to use. Whatever, then, that serpent signified must be attributed to that providence under which the devil himself has a desire to harm, but no power except what is granted either for overthrowing and destroying the vessels of wrath, or for humbling, or testing, the vessels of mercy. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Alternatively, “or testing” is omitted.]

“Therefore the serpent did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman. For its soul must not be thought to have been changed into a rational nature, since even human beings, whose nature is rational, do not know what they are saying when a demon speaks through them in that condition for which the exorcist seeks a remedy. How much less would the serpent understand the sounds of words that the devil produced through it and from it in that manner—sounds that a human being speaking would not understand if he heard him while free from diabolical affliction?” [Note: [Col. 0054D] Augustine, same work, chapters 4, 5, 6, 12, and 28.]

Therefore he said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of the garden?” The woman answered him [Note: [Col. 0054D] Alternatively, “answering”]: “We may eat from the fruit of the trees that are in the garden; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the garden, God commanded us not to eat from it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.” “The serpent first asked and the woman answered this so that the transgression might be inexcusable and it could in no way be said that the woman had forgotten what God had commanded.” [Note: [Col. 0054D] Augustine, same work, chapter 30.]

But the serpent said to the woman: “You shall certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” What else is understood here than that she was persuaded [Note: [Col. 0054D] Alternatively, “them”] not to wish to be under God, but rather to be in her own power without God, so that they would not observe his law, as though he begrudged them the ability to rule themselves? They would not need his eternal light, but would live by their own providence, as though by their own eyes, to distinguish good and evil, which he had forbidden.

In these words we should note with what great skill of wickedness the devil tempted the human being from the beginning. [Note: [Col. 0054D] Alternatively, “had tempted.”] He not only taught him disobedience and contempt for his Creator, as though the Creator begrudged him something, but also proposed that he believe in a plurality of gods, saying, “You will be like gods.” Thus, even if he could not perhaps draw him into disobedience, he would corrupt the chastity of the faith by which they worshiped one God; but if he did draw him into disobedience, he would emerge victorious in both respects. [Note: [Col. 0054D] Alternatively, “who”; alternatively, “because.”]

“When, however, would the woman have believed by these words that she had been divinely forbidden something good and useful, unless there had already been present in her mind that love of self-rule and a certain proud presumption about herself which was to be exposed and humbled through that temptation? Finally, not content with the serpent’s words, she considered the tree, and saw, as Scripture says, that it was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold. Not believing that she could die from it, I think she supposed that God had said, ‘If you eat, you will die,’ for some symbolic reason; and therefore ‘she took from its fruit and ate, and gave it also to her husband,’ perhaps even with a persuasive word, which Scripture leaves unstated but invites us to understand. Or perhaps there was no need for the man to be persuaded [lacuna] when he saw that she had eaten that food and had not died.” [Note: [Col. 0054D] Alternatively, *suadere* (“to persuade”).] [Note: [Col. 0055D] Augustine, same work, chapter 30.]
