**And he ate. And the eyes of both were opened.** “Opened to what, except to desiring one another, to the death of the flesh conceived as the punishment of sin? The body was no longer merely an animal body, which, if they had preserved obedience, could have been changed without death into a better and spiritual state, but had become the body of death, in which the law in the members resisted the law of the mind.” [Note: [Col. 0055D] Augustine, same work, chapter 31.]

For they had not been made with closed eyes, nor had they wandered about blind and groping in the paradise of delights. The same is meant in the Gospel when it says of the two disciples, one of whom was Cleopas, that when the Lord had broken bread for them, their eyes were opened and they recognized him whom they had not recognized on the way—not that they had been walking with closed eyes, but that they had been unable to recognize him. Thus the eyes of the first human beings were opened to what they had not previously been open to, although they had been open to other things.

When they realized that they were naked, they sewed together fig leaves and made themselves loincloths. “The rational soul was ashamed of the beastlike movement in the members of its flesh and cast shame upon it, not only because it perceived there what it had never before perceived, but also because that shameful movement arose from the transgression of the commandment. For there it perceived the grace with which it had previously been clothed, when in its nakedness it suffered nothing indecent. Finally, in their confusion they rushed to fig leaves, which they perhaps found first in their distress, and sewed loincloths, that is, coverings for the waist; and because they had abandoned what was glorious, they covered what was shameful. Nor do I think that they considered that something in those leaves was suitable for covering the members that now tingled with such a movement. Rather, by a hidden impulse they were driven to this in their confusion, so that, even without knowing it, the sign of such punishment would convict the sinner and teach the reader who encounters it in writing.” [Note: [Col. 0055D] Augustine, same work, chapter 32.]

Saint Ambrose briefly but clearly explained the mystery of this tree, under which the Lord also saw Nathanael still situated, saying: “Blessed are those who bind their horses under the vine and the olive, consecrating the course of their labors to joy. But the fig tree, that is, the seductive itch of worldly pleasures, still overshadows me—lowly in its height, fragile for labor, soft for use, barren for fruit.”

And in another passage: “What is more serious, he says, is that Adam girded himself at this place according to this interpretation [Note: [Col. 0055D] Alternatively, “at that place”], at the place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For in the loins with which we gird ourselves, certain seeds of generation are said to be found. Therefore Adam was wrongly girded there with useless leaves, where he signified not the future fruit of generation but certain future sins.” [Note: [Col. 0056D] Ambrose, *On Paradise*, chapter 13.]

And when he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden at the afternoon breeze, Adam hid himself, and his wife with him. After the afternoon, those who had fallen away from the light of truth had now become fit to be visited. Thus appropriately the Lord ascended the cross at midday and, after promising the robber a dwelling in paradise, gave up his spirit in the afternoon, that is, at the ninth hour. In this way, at the same hour in which the first man had touched the tree of transgression, the second man ascended the tree of redemption; and at the hour of the day when he had driven the transgressors from paradise, he brought the confessing robber into paradise.

“Adam hid himself,” it says, “and his wife from the face of the Lord God among the trees of the garden.” “When God turns his face away inwardly, we should not be surprised that things occur which resemble madness, through excessive shame and fear, while that hidden impulse also continues, so that they unknowingly do things that signify something, which their descendants, for whose sake these things were written, would one day understand. For [Note: [Col. 0056D] Alternatively, *namque* (“for”) is omitted.] those who sin hide from the face of God because they render themselves unworthy of the sight of divine mercy. They hide from the face of God not so that the inner judge may fail to see their conscience, but so that they themselves may never behold the glory of his face except by repentance.” [Note: [Col. 0056D] Augustine, same work, chapter 33.]

And the Lord God called Adam and said to him: “Where are you?” He did not ask because he was ignorant, but reproved him and admonished him to consider where he was—in the state in which God was not. For, since he had eaten from the forbidden tree, he had already died the death of the soul, when it is said that life had departed from it.

“And this too certainly pertains to a particular signification: just as the commandment was given to the man, through whom it would reach the woman, so the man is questioned first. For the commandment came from the Lord through the man to the woman; but sin came from the devil through the woman to the man. These things are full of mystical meanings—not because those involved in them were consciously doing this, but because the most powerful wisdom of God was acting through these events. We are not now recounting what was signified, but defending what was done.” [Note: [Col. 0056D] Augustine, same work, chapter 34.]

He said: “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” It is sufficiently probable that God was accustomed to appear to those first human beings in human form, through a creature appropriate to such an action. Yet he never allowed them to notice their nakedness, raising their attention toward heavenly things, until after the sin they had perceived the shameful movement in their members and the punitive law of their members. Thus they were affected as human beings are accustomed to be affected in the sight of other human beings; and such an affection was part of the punishment of sin: they wished to hide from one whom nothing can escape. For what they were now ashamed of in relation to each other—and for which they had made themselves loincloths [Note: [Col. 0056D] Alternatively, “their loincloths”]—they were much more intensely afraid to be seen in that state by the one who, as though in a familiar manner, brought visible human eyes through a visible creature in order to see them.

“Therefore the Lord, wishing now to punish the sinners by the manner of justice with a punishment greater than that shame which they were already forced to feel, said: ‘Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?’ For death, conceived because of God’s sentence, by which he had threatened them in this way, caused the members to become aware of desire. This is where it is said that their eyes were opened, and what caused shame followed.” [Note: [Col. 0057D] Augustine, same work, chapter 35.]

And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” “Did pride say, ‘I have sinned’? It possesses the deformity of shame, but not the humility of confession. These things were written for this reason, and the questions themselves were evidently posed so that they might be usefully recorded, in order that we might observe how people today labor under pride [Note: [Col. 0057D] Alternatively, “through pride”], trying to attribute to the Creator whatever evil they have done, while wishing whatever good they have done to be attributed to themselves. ‘The woman whom you gave me as a companion,’ he says, ‘gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate,’ as though she had been given for this purpose rather than to obey the man herself, and for both of them to obey God.”

“And the Lord God said to the woman: ‘Why have you done this?’ She answered: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate.’ She too does not confess her sin, but transfers it to another. Though the sexes are unequal, their arrogance is equal: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate,’ as though anyone’s persuasion ought to have been preferred to God’s command.” [Note: [Col. 0057D] Augustine, same work, chapter 35.] She too refers the cause of her fault to the Creator, who created the serpent in the garden as the instrument through which she would be deceived.

And the Lord God said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all the animals and beasts of the earth.” “Since the serpent was not asked why it had done this, it may be understood that it had not done it by its own nature and will, but that the devil had acted through and by means of it; the devil had already been destined for fire because of the sin of his ungodliness and pride. Therefore what is said to the serpent [Note: [Col. 0057D] Alternatively, “concerning the serpent”], and is certainly also referred to the one who acted through the serpent, was unquestionably figurative. For in these words that tempter is described as he would be toward the human race.” [Note: [Col. 0058D] Augustine, same work, chapter 36.]

“Upon your breast you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life.” The serpent walks upon its breast because all the devil’s steps are wickedness and deceit. For by “breast” he indicates the cunning and trickery of the devil’s thoughts, by which he creeps toward those whom he wishes to deceive. For this reason the ancient Translation has: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly.” He crawls upon his breast when he suggests earthly thoughts to human beings whom he desires to make his members. He crawls upon his belly when, after overcoming them through gluttony, he stirs them up into the heat of lust. For everything that crawls drags its body along the earth. The devil’s body consists of all the reprobate. He crawls upon his breast and belly when he presses them down to the lowest things through wicked thoughts or the enticements of feasting and luxury.

He devours the earth when he feeds upon and delights in the error of sinners, and, leading them astray, drags them to destruction. For just as the saints are often designated by the name of heaven, so those who set their minds on earthly things are designated by the name of earth. Thus, later, it is said to Adam: “You are earth, and you shall go into earth,” which our Translation has as: “You are dust, and you shall return to dust.” As a sign of this spiritual devouring, the irrational serpent itself—an instrument that the devil used to deceive the man—is now commanded to eat material earth, although previously, together with the other animals of the earth, it had been permitted to eat the herbs and fruit of the trees. [Note: [Col. 0058D] Alternatively, “of the grasses.”] [Note: [Col. 0058D] Alternatively, “fruit.”]

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The woman’s seed is the entire human race; the devil’s seed are the transgressing angels, who were corrupted by the example of his pride and rebellion. His seed is the perverse suggestion; the woman’s seed is the fruit of a good work, by which the perverse suggestion is resisted. How much the human race suffers from the enmity of this serpent and its seed, and how greatly all the elect exercise enmity against it by living rightly, is clear to all the faithful, clearer than the sun. A sign of this enmity also appears in the nature of the irrational serpent, which, because of the plague of poison implanted in it, is always hostile to all the animals and beasts of the earth. This is to be believed to have been implanted in it from the time of this curse, and not before.

“She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.” The woman crushes the serpent’s head when the holy Church, having detected the devil’s snares and poisonous suggestions at their very beginning, drives them away and, as though trampling them down, reduces them to nothing. She crushes the serpent’s head when, by humbling herself beneath the powerful hand of God, she often resists the pride by which Eve was deceived; for pride is the beginning of every sin.

The serpent lies in wait for the woman’s heel because, as the devil circles around the Church like a roaring lion, he seeks someone to devour and strives to overturn the steps of our good action. He lies in wait for the heel when he attempts to snatch us away at the end of the present life. Since the heel is the end of the body, it not improperly signifies the end of our life. Both meanings are also figuratively proclaimed by the condition of the serpent itself: all who can do so are accustomed to crush it, while it never ceases to lie in wait to strike human footsteps.

[Col. 0058D] And to the woman he said: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you shall bear children.” “These words of God to the woman are also more suitably understood figuratively and prophetically. Nevertheless, since the woman had not yet given birth, and since the pain and groaning of childbirth arise only from the body of death that was conceived through the transgression of the commandment, this punishment also refers to the literal sense. For in what follows—‘You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you’—although it is not fitting to believe that the woman was made [Note: [Col. 0058D] Alternatively, “made”] otherwise even before sin than so that the man should rule over her and she should live under his authority, it can rightly be understood that a servitude was signified which is a matter of condition rather than love. Thus even the kind of servitude by which human beings afterward began to be servants of other human beings is found to have arisen from the punishment of sin.

“The Apostle did say: ‘Through love serve one another’ (Gal. 5:13), but he would never say: ‘Rule over one another.’ Therefore spouses can serve one another through love, but the Apostle does not permit a woman to rule over a man. This sentence assigned authority rather to the man, and the husband earned dominion over the woman not by nature but by fault. Yet unless this is maintained, the fault will be further corrupted and increased.” [Note: [Col. 0059D] Augustine, same work, chapter 37.]

Figuratively, however, these words aptly apply to the Church, the spouse of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0059D] Alternatively, “come.”] Her hardships are multiplied in this life after the guilt of the first transgression, so that she may reach eternal life after being chastened. Her conceptions are also multiplied when she strives to beget spiritual offspring for God by preaching and living rightly. Thus the outstanding preacher says to that offspring: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). She bears children in pain when, in anxiety, she fears that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so their minds may be corrupted and they may fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ.

She acts under the authority of her husband because she serves the Lord in fear and rejoices in him not in security but with trembling. If she had never sinned, she would be joined to him only in the embrace of secure love. And he will rule over her, restraining her carnal impulses and continually advancing her toward the perception of heavenly life through the discipline of instruction from above. [Note: [Col. 0059D] Alternatively, *receptionem* (“reception”).] If she had never departed from that life, she would always reign with him in shared freedom.

And to Adam he said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat, the earth is cursed in your work. In toil you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth,” and so forth.

“Who does not know that these are the labors of the human race upon the earth, and that they would not exist if the happiness that had been in paradise had been preserved?” [Note: [Col. 0060D] Augustine, same work, chapter 38.] Because of the man’s sin, the earth was cursed so that it would produce thorns—not that it should itself feel punishments, since it is without sensation, but so that it would continually place the crime of human sin before human eyes, by which they might at some time be admonished to turn away from sins and turn toward God’s commandments. Poisonous plants, too, were created either as punishment or for the exercise of mortals.

This should also be noted in relation to sin: after sin we became mortal. Through unfruitful trees, too, human beings are reproached, so that they may understand how shameful it is to be without the fruit of good works in God’s field, that is, in the Church, and may fear that God will abandon them, since they themselves also abandon unfruitful trees in their own fields and apply no cultivation to them. Before the man’s sin, therefore, it is not written that the earth produced anything except grass for fodder and fruitful trees. After sin, however, we see many dreadful and unfruitful things growing, for the reason we have mentioned.

Mystically, however, the earth that is said to have been cursed in the work of Adam’s transgression is best understood as the flesh. For it now produces thorns and thistles for us, because, propagated through the desire of the flesh, we suffer from the flesh itself the prickings and incentives of vices.

“In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are dust and you shall return to dust.” Here understand the bread of which he says: “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven” (John 4:51). We eat this bread in the sweat of our faces because we ascend to the sight of divine majesty only through the labor of necessary affliction.

[Col. 0060B] And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. It is established that Adam gave this name to his wife by divine inspiration, and it most appropriately corresponds to the holy Church, in whose unity alone—the unity called catholic—the door of life lies open to all.

And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them. This was done for the sake of signification, yet it was nevertheless done. For by such clothing the Lord indicates that they had already become mortal; skins, after all, which are taken only from dead animals, contain the figure of death. Thus [Note: [Col. 0060D] Another reading: “those who oppose.”], when man, contrary to the commandment—not through lawful imitation but through unlawful pride—desired to be God, he was cast down to the mortality of beasts. Indeed, they themselves had made loincloths from fig leaves to cover their shame; but God made tunics of skins for them, with which to clothe their whole bodies. For they, having lost through transgression the glory of innocence, set before themselves a veil of excuse by which they might transfer their guilt to the Creator; while the Creator himself, by the sentence of a just judgment, [Note: [Col. 0060D] Another reading: “having offered.”] took away their state of unchangeable life and punished both soul and flesh with the penalty of mortality.

The Gospel parable relates that the compassionate father, when his prodigal son returned to him through repentance, among other gifts also ordered the first robe to be brought forth and the son to be clothed in it. Mystically, this indicates that the elect will receive again in Christ, at the end of the age—and indeed with a more abundant grace—the garment of immortality that they lost in Adam at the beginning of the world. For Adam was made immortal in such a way that he could have remained without dying, had he kept the commandment; but the children of the resurrection will be immortal in such a way that they can neither ever die nor be affected by fear of death. Concerning the receiving of this robe the Apostle says: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53). Here “put on” signifies that the nakedness which Adam and Eve recognized in themselves after the sin and were ashamed of has certainly been taken away.

And he said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” Concerning this Saint Augustine says:

“However and in whatever manner it may have been spoken, since God nevertheless said it, what he says—‘like one of us’—must be understood in no other way than that the plural number is used on account of the Trinity, just as it had been said, ‘Let us make man,’ and also as the Lord says of himself and the Father: ‘We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him’ (John XIV). Thus the outcome desired by the proud one, who coveted what the serpent had suggested—‘You shall be like gods’—was repeated to his face. ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘Adam has become like one of us.’ These are the words of God, not so much insulting him as warning the others not to become proud on whose account these things were written: ‘He has become,’ he says, ‘like one of us, knowing good and evil.’ What else should be understood except that an example intended to inspire fear has been set forth? For he not only did not become what he had wished to become, but did not even preserve what he had become. Concerning this, elsewhere: ‘They are not,’ he says, ‘the words of God confessing, but rather reproaching’ [Note: [Col. 0061D] Augustine, same work, chapter 39].”

“Behold, Adam has become like one of us,” just as the Apostle, when he says, “Do me this wrong” (II Cor. XII, 13), clearly wishes the words to be understood in the opposite sense.

“Now, therefore, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life, eat, and live forever, the Lord sent him forth from the paradise of delight, to work the ground from which he had been taken. The preceding words are God’s; this action, however, followed because of those words. For, alienated not only from the life which he would have received with the angels had he kept the commandment, but also from that which he enjoyed in paradise through a certain blessed condition of the body, he necessarily had to be separated from the tree of life—whether that happy condition of the body was sustained by that tree through an invisible power proceeding from a visible thing, or whether the tree contained also a visible sacrament of invisible wisdom. He had to be removed from it, either because he was already about to die or because he was like one excommunicated, just as in this paradise—that is, in the Church—ecclesiastical discipline ordinarily removes people from the visible sacraments of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0061D] Augustine, same work, chapter 40].

And he cast out Adam, and placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life. The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “And he cast out Adam, and placed him opposite the paradise of delight, and appointed the cherubim and the flaming sword,” and so forth.

“If we follow this,” Augustine says, “we must believe that this too was done for the sake of signification, yet that it was nevertheless done: the sinner was to dwell opposite the paradise in which blessed life was also spiritually signified, and therefore in misery. But since God is said to have placed before the paradise of delight the cherubim and the flaming sword, this must certainly be believed to have been done through heavenly powers in the visible paradise, so that by angelic ministry there might be a certain fiery guard. Nor should it be doubted that this was not done in vain, since it also signifies something concerning the spiritual paradise” [Note: [Col. 0062D] Augustine, same work].

This guard is rightly asserted to be turning, because the time would eventually come when it could also be removed. It was removed for Enoch, when he was transferred away from sinners; it was removed for Elijah, when he was carried away in a fiery chariot; it was removed for all the elect when, after the Lord was baptized, the heavens were opened to him; it is likewise removed for each of the elect when they are washed in the baptismal font; and it is removed from them more perfectly when, released from their bonds, each in his own time ascends to the glory of the heavenly paradise.

Furthermore, because *cherubim* is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge,” or “knowledge multiplied,” it is rightly said that the cherubim and the flaming sword were placed to guard the way to the tree of life. For through the discipline of heavenly knowledge and through the labor of temporal afflictions, the way of return to our heavenly homeland is opened to us, from which we departed through the folly of transgression and through the desire for carnal pleasures.

And it is rightly said not simply that a flame, but that a flaming sword, was placed before paradise, so that it might indicate that the enticements of temporal desire are to be struck down in us by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, if we desire to penetrate to the tree of life, which is Christ the Lord.

And it is rightly reported that the same sword was turning, to indicate mystically that this sword is not always necessary for us, but, as it is written, “there is a time for war and a time for peace”: war, namely, when in the contest of this life we fight against the powers of the air or even against the vices of our mind and body; peace, however, when we are crowned with complete victory and are perpetually satisfied without weariness by the fruit of the tree of life.

But the adversary of the Law and the Prophets asks: “If this tree that bore the fruits of life in paradise existed, for whose benefit was it?” Saint Augustine answers him:

“For whom, unless for those first human beings who had been placed in paradise? Then, after they had been expelled from paradise on account of their deserts, it remained as a memorial signifying the spiritual tree of life, which is the wisdom of the blessed, the immortal food of souls. Whether anyone now feeds upon that food—unless perhaps Enoch and Elijah—I do not think should be rashly affirmed. Yet unless the souls of the blessed were nourished by that tree of life which is in the spiritual paradise, we would not read that paradise was granted on that very day to the soul of the thief who believed in Christ, as a reward for his piety and most faithful confession: ‘Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise’ (Luke XXIII, 43). To be there with Christ, however, is to be with the tree of life; for he himself is Wisdom, concerning which it is written: ‘She is a tree of life to all who embrace her’ (Prov. III, 18). Amen.”

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0063]

Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore [Note: [Col. 0063D] Another reading: “a son, Cain.”] Cain, saying: “I have acquired a man through [Note: [Col. 0063D] Another reading: “the Lord.”] God.” From this point, after the delights of paradise and the guilt of the first transgression, the events of this age and mortal life are related: the first parents, who had been created immortal, after receiving the condition of death, began to beget from themselves mortal offspring, all conceived in iniquity and coming forth from the maternal womb in sins.

Cain is interpreted as “possession”; his mother herself explained the reason for the name when she said: “I have acquired a man through God.” By this statement our mother, already with catholic discernment, teaches us that she bore a son subject to the sin of her transgression, yet that he possessed, as a gift of divine creation and the first blessing, the fact that he was born a human being—that is, a being consisting of [Note: [Col. 0063D] Another reading: “from the soul.”] soul and body, [Note: [Col. 0064D] Another reading: “from disposition.”] through the effect of divine creation [Col. 0063B].

And again she bore his brother Abel. Abel is interpreted as “mourning” or “miserable,” a name by which the condition of his premature death was foreshadowed from his earliest age. For although the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, once they have tasted the cup of saving passion, nevertheless, as far as human perception is concerned, it is exceedingly mournful that we have departed so far from the innocence of our original condition that even those who were the first brothers born on earth could not maintain peace and harmony between themselves, but one killed the other out of envy, while they alone, still with their parents, possessed the whole world. Already then they plainly foreshadowed that the saints in this life would suffer oppression and death at the hands of the reprobate. Here we should also note that Cain was born first in this life, but Abel was taken from this life first, because this life properly belongs to the wicked, from which they are precipitated into eternal death; whereas the life of the elect properly belongs to the future, and in order that they may reach it more happily, they are put to death daily in this life and are regarded as sheep destined for slaughter.

After many days, Cain brought an offering to the Lord from the fruits of the earth; Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. It is plainly shown that both brothers had faith in God, and that both, either naturally admonished or taught by their parents, knew that gifts were to be offered to God and that the guilt of their father’s [Note: [Col. 0064D] Another reading: “transgression.”] transgression was to be washed away by sacrifices offered to him [Note: [Col. 0064D] Another reading: “gifts.”]. But because they offered with unequal dispositions, the vows of the two were not equally accepted.

I do not think Cain sinned in either practicing agriculture or offering God gifts from the fruits of the earth, but because he labored in the care of the flesh with less perfect piety and approached the offering of gifts to God with less perfect devotion. After all, Noah too was a farmer: he worked the ground and planted a vineyard; and Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, offered bread and wine from the fruits of the earth. Cain, therefore, was not rejected because the kind of his offering was contemptible. He offered God what he himself was accustomed to live upon; but because of the impious mind of the one offering, he himself, together with his gifts, was rejected by him who examines hearts, as the following words make clear:

And the Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but he did not look upon Cain and his offerings. For it does not say, “The Lord looked upon Abel’s offerings and upon Abel himself; but upon Cain’s offerings and upon Cain himself he did not look.” Rather, it first testifies that the person of the one offering was acceptable or unacceptable to God, and then that the gifts were regarded or not regarded. Human beings are often reconciled by the gifts of those by whom they have been offended; but God, who discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart, is appeased by no gift more than by the pious devotion of the one offering. When he has approved the purity of our mind, he will consequently also receive the vows of our prayers and works.

And Cain was exceedingly angry, and his face fell. How did Cain know that the Lord had looked upon Abel and his offerings, but had turned his face away from him and his offerings, unless it was because, as some have interpreted it, the Lord kindled a fire over Abel and his sacrifice, but did not kindle one over Cain and his sacrifice—that is, he received Abel’s offering by sending fire from heaven, something we very often read of having happened when holy men offered sacrifices? Cain himself, however, ought to have consumed his sacrifice with fire. The Apostle also seems to signify this when he says: “By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts” (Hebr. XI, 4). God therefore bore witness to Abel’s gifts through fire, receiving them from heaven; and by the Apostle’s testimony we are taught that Abel’s offering was made acceptable to God through the devotion of his faith. Conversely, we should understand that Cain was rejected because he did not serve his Creator with undivided faith.

And the Lord said to him: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, will not your sin immediately be at the door?” Why, he says, are you angry, tormented by the envious bitterness of jealousy toward your brother, and lowering your face toward the ground? If you do well—if you offer sacrifice with a pure mind—you will receive, since the Lord will look upon you and your sacrifice. But if you do evil, your sin will immediately be at the door, and with such a gatekeeper you will always be accompanied as you enter and leave, instead of the Lord guarding your entrance and your exit. As it is said of Wisdom: “Whoever keeps watch for her from the light will not labor. He will find her sitting at his doors” (Wis. VI, 15). And again: “For she herself goes about seeking those worthy of her, and on the paths she shows herself to them, and in every providence she meets them” (ibid., 17).

But under you shall be its desire, and you shall rule over it. According to the idiom of the Hebrew language, he used the indicative mood in place of the imperative, as in numerous examples: “You shall love the Lord your God; you shall love your neighbor; you shall not commit fornication; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Deut. VI, 5), instead of saying: “Love, and do not kill; do not commit fornication; do not steal; do not bear false witness.”

“Under you,” he says, “shall be its desire, and you shall rule over it.” Because you possess free will, I warn you to oppose and restrain the desire for sin, so that it may no longer rule over you as it grows, but that you, by living more correctly, may rule over it.

The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still, for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.” An offering is made rightly to God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered. But it is not divided rightly when the places or times of offering are not properly distinguished, nor the things offered themselves, nor the one who offers, nor those to whom what has been offered is distributed for eating; so that by “division” we may understand discernment.

In which of these matters Cain displeased the Lord cannot easily be determined. But because the Apostle John, when speaking of these brothers, says, “Not like Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother. And for what reason did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s righteous” (I John III, 13), it may be understood that God did not regard his offering because Cain himself divided it wrongly, giving God something of his possessions but himself to himself. This is what all do who follow not God’s will but their own: that is, who live not with a right but with a perverse heart. Yet they offer God a gift by which they think he can be bought off, so that he may not help heal their depraved desires but assist in fulfilling them.

“Be still,” he says, “for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.” Cease wasting away through the sin of envy against your brother, because the turning of that same sin will be toward you, your iniquity will recoil [Note: [Col. 0065D] Another reading: “will recline.”] upon your own head, and you shall rule over it, having the power, through the grace of divine assistance, to drive away from your heart the wickedness conceived there [Col. 0065D].

God spoke these words to Cain in the manner in which he had spoken with the first human beings through a subordinate creature, as though their companion, in an appropriate form. But because Cain was admonished not inwardly but outwardly, he nevertheless carried out the crime he had resolved upon—the killing of his brother—even after the word of divine admonition and correction. The text continues:

And Cain said to Abel his brother: “Let us go out into the field.” And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. Here too Cain’s treachery and Abel’s innocence are shown together. Abel’s innocence is shown in that, although his elder brother was inflamed with hostile hatred toward him, he simply followed his brother as he was ordered. Cain’s treachery is shown in that, intending to kill his brother, he led him outside, as though in a more secluded place he could evade the divine presence. He did not consider or understand that he who knew and reproved [Note: [Col. 0065D] Another reading: “knows.”] the hidden things of his heart could also see where he withdrew and what he did in secret.

And the Lord said to Cain: “Where is Abel your brother?” He did not ask as one ignorant, seeking information from him, but as a judge questioning the guilty person whom he would punish.

He replied: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” A response at once foolish and proud: foolish, because he thought he could deceive the one who, as the knower of hidden things, had exposed the sinner’s conscience even before the crime of fratricide was committed; proud, because, like a stubborn servant, he denied that he was his brother’s keeper, although, if any danger threatened, he ought, as the elder brother, to have cared for and protected his younger brother from approaching harm.

And he said to him: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground.” Blood has a great voice—not only Abel’s blood, but also that of all who have been killed for the Lord. Their blood is the voice of their steadfast faith and the fervor of their charity, through which they were worthy to suffer for the Lord.

It cries out to the Lord from the ground. For even if, like Abel, they were killed by the impious in the hidden recesses of the earth, the very cause of their death nevertheless stands precious and clear before the judgment of the inner [Note: [Col. 0066D] Another reading: “Judge.”] Judge, rightly demanding that those who were unjustly slain in their simplicity be crowned, and that those who unjustly persecuted and slaughtered them be condemned.

The blood of the slain therefore cries out to the Lord—those whose life before death is also shown to have cried out to him, who are accustomed to say: “I have cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I will seek your justifications” (Ps. CXVIII, 145). For the one who cries out to the Lord with his heart is the one who asks for great things, prays for heavenly things, hopes for eternal things, and seeks from him not the glory of this age but the keeping of his justifications.

The Apostle teaches from where this cry arises in the hearts of the righteous, saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6). He says that the Spirit cries to the Father in our hearts because, when he fills them, he himself kindles these things in us so that we may cry out.

John shows that the souls of the martyrs also possess this cry of devout faith after death, when he says: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” (Apoc. VI, 9).

These souls of the saints cry out not from hatred of their enemies but from love of justice, which they have learned always to hunger and thirst for, and also from the desire to receive again their bodies, which they had given over to death for the Lord, so that [Note: [Col. 0066D] Another reading: “in this.”] in these immortal and incorruptible bodies they might be worthy to stand before the Lord. Great is the voice of their cry, and great is their desire for justice.

When the blood of the saints cries out to the Lord—that is, when it seeks just vengeance for its unjust death—the fate of their persecutors is subsequently revealed, when the Lord says to Cain:

“Now, therefore, you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work it, it shall not give you its fruits; you shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.”

The just Judge also appoints the measure of vengeance according to the measure of the sinners’ wrongdoing. When Adam ate what was forbidden, he himself was not cursed; rather, the earth was subjected to a curse in his work—not so completely that it denied fruit to the one who worked it, but so that, for the laborer who toiled and sweated, it brought forth its fruits to its cultivator, and so that the labor might at some time end and eternal rest begin.

He was also condemned to the death of the flesh. This was done as a benefit, so that he might not labor and suffer forever; only those who do not understand how miserable is the life of the present age doubt this.

Cain, however, knowing the transgression and condemnation of his parents, added to the same guilt of transgression which he had inherited from his lineage [Note: [Col. 0067D] Another reading: “root.”] a more serious guilt of treachery, envy, murder, and falsehood. Hence he is deservedly punished with a harsher penalty: first, so that he himself should be cursed upon the earth which, hitherto unstained by his brother’s blood, he had polluted with it; second, so that he should labor uselessly in cultivating the earth, with no abundance of crops answering his efforts; third, so that upon that same earth he should always be a wanderer and fugitive, not daring to have a settled dwelling anywhere—or, as another translation has it, that he should live upon the earth trembling and groaning.

But [Note: [Col. 0067D] Another reading: “that.”] when he heard the penalty of so great a curse, he did not wish to beg for pardon. Instead, multiplying sins upon sins, he considered the crime so great that God could not forgive him. Finally, he answered the Lord:

“Greater is my iniquity than that I should deserve pardon. Behold, today you cast me away from your face, and I shall be hidden from your face and from the earth, and I shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.”

“I am cast away,” he says, “from your sight, and, unable to bear the light itself because of the consciousness of my crime, I shall hide [Note: [Col. 0067D] Another reading: “and conceal myself.”] and remain concealed.”

Or certainly: “You cast me away from the face of the earth,” so that I may not be permitted to remain safe and free in any region of the earth or among any of its inhabitants; “and I shall be hidden from your face,” so that I may no longer be worthy to see it, since until today I lived more happily by looking upon it so often and hearing your voice.

“Everyone, therefore, who finds me will kill me.” This means that, whether from the trembling of his body and the frenzy of one who trembles, or from the instability of a wanderer and fugitive, he understands himself to be one deserving to be killed [Note: [Col. 0068D] Another reading: “will understand.”].

But God, unwilling to end his torments by a shortcut through death and unwilling to hand him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, said:

“By no means shall this be so; but whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

You will not die as you suppose, nor receive death as a remedy; rather, you will live for a very long time as an example to the rest, so that they may not dare to sin in this way. And I am so far from wishing you to be killed by anyone [Note: [Col. 0068D] Another reading: “by anyone whatsoever.”] that, if someone kills you, he will be punished sevenfold—that is, with the heaviest vengeance—because, even warned by the severity of your condemnation, he was unwilling to restrain his hands from shedding blood.

A human being ought not to kill a human being to whom God had granted life despite his sin, whether to increase the punishment of Cain himself or to provide an example of caution and correction to others.

Scripture often uses the number seven to signify the fullness of the matter of which it speaks. Thus in Leviticus: “If you walk contrary to me and are unwilling to hear me, I will add to your plagues sevenfold” (Lev. XXVI, 21). And shortly afterward: “I will strike you seven times for your sins” (ibid., 24), meaning “many times.” The Psalmist uses the number in a good sense: “Seven times a day I have given praise to you” (Ps. CXVIII, 164), which is another way of saying: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII, 2).

But when the ancient interpreters said, “Everyone who kills Cain shall pay seven avenges” [Note: [Col. 0068D] Another reading: “shall discharge seven punishments.”], the meaning is this: You will live until the seventh generation, and you will be tormented by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you, according to the twofold interpretation, will either do so in the seventh generation or free you from great suffering. It does not mean that the one who kills Cain will be subjected to seven punishments, but that he will discharge upon the slain the seven acts of vengeance that ran their course through Cain, killing the one who had been left alive for punishment.

For Lamech was the seventh from Adam, and Cain is said to have been killed by him. By his death, Lamech released this same Cain from the seven acts of vengeance which, by sinning sevenfold, he had deserved.

His first sin was that, when offering to God, he did not divide rightly; the second, that he envied his brother; the third, that he acted deceitfully when he said, “Let us go out into the field”; the fourth, that he killed him; the fifth, that he denied it insolently: “I do not know”; the sixth, that he condemned himself: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon”; the seventh, that even after being condemned he did not repent.

And God placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. This sign was evidently that he would always live trembling, groaning, wandering, and fleeing: continually reminded by his own misery that he could not be killed indiscriminately by anyone; but whoever killed him would either free Cain from great miseries or, by doing so, subject himself to sevenfold vengeance.

And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord—that is, from the inner rooms of the dwelling in which, until then, he had lived with his parents and had often been accustomed to see the Lord in angelic form.

He dwelt as a fugitive in the land east of Eden. Eden is interpreted as “pleasure” or “delights,” a name by which paradise is designated, concerning which it was said above: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight at the beginning.” The ancient interpreters translated this as: “And the Lord God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east.” From this it is understood that paradise was established in the eastern region of the world.

Cain therefore dwelt not east of paradise—for otherwise he would have dwelt beyond this world—but in the eastern regions of the world, which are near paradise, although paradise is inaccessible and unknown to mortals.

All that is said literally concerning Abel’s righteousness or [Note: [Col. 0069D] In former times, especially around Bede’s period, the title “martyr” was given not only to those who were killed out of hatred for Christ on account of their faith, but also to all who were unjustly killed for any reason—for example, out of envy. Thus Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, is called a martyr, although Ebroin killed him solely out of envy. Likewise Lambert, bishop of Utrecht, who died in a similar circumstance. Hence below Abel is called the first martyr.] martyrdom, and concerning Cain’s wickedness and condemnation, bears witness mystically to the Lord’s passion or his life in the flesh, and to the persecution and destruction of the Jews.

For the Lord himself does not say to those same Jews without reason: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V, 46) [Note: [Col. 0069D] Another reading: “for it was about me.”].

Cain, therefore, was the firstborn, and Abel the second. The earlier people, the Jews, were God’s possession, just as he himself said to Moses: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV, 22) [Note: [Col. 0069D] Another reading: “the second people followed.”]. The second is the people of the Gentiles, for whose life above all the Son of God deigned both to be born in the flesh and to die [Note: [Col. 0070D] Another reading: “having become incarnate.”].

Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and the Lord says: “I am the good shepherd” (John XI, 14). Cain, however, was a farmer, because the Jewish people devoted themselves to earthly and temporal affairs, either seeking only these things or serving the Lord with regard to them, since they understood carnally the things which the prophets spoke to them mystically concerning the heavenly promise: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. [Col. 0069C] II, 19).

For Cain offered the Lord gifts from the fruits of the earth, because that people thought they pleased the Lord through good works pursued for the sake of an earthly reward.

Or certainly he offered gifts from the fruits of the earth when that people, believing that it was justified through an earthly circumcision, an earthly Sabbath, earthly unleavened bread, and an earthly Passover, disdained to receive the righteousness of faith which is in Christ.

Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. For the Lord, interceding with the Father for the saints, offers him, according to the form of the humanity he assumed, their vows—namely, their good works and the richness of inward love. These are the firstborn of his flock and their fat.

The Lord looks upon Abel, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII, 5). He also looks upon his offerings, because God the Father graciously accepts the life of the elect which he offers to him and, as though by fire from heaven, kindles his offering. For those who have taken care to mortify themselves for the Lord, he inflames with the power of his Spirit, so that they may burn more intensely in heavenly things—or rather, may become wholly heavenly.

But he does not look upon Cain and his offerings, because, reproving the carnal works of the Jews, he says through the prophet: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full; I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of bulls, goats, and calves” (Isa. I, 11). And shortly afterward: “For your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves; be clean”—that is, through faith in the grace of Christ.

Cain becomes angry against his brother’s piety, and, though reproved by the Lord, does not recover from the fury conceived through envy. How violently the Jews raged against the Lord and his grace because of their resentment toward the New Testament, and how often, although rebuked or admonished by him, they nevertheless persisted in their evil undertakings, the Gospel history sufficiently reveals.

They are aptly compared with Cain, of whom it is said that his face fell. For they could not contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. They had lost that joy of divine grace concerning which the righteous, exulting, say: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. IV, 7).

Cain led his brother outside and killed him in the field. The Jewish people led the Lord outside their city, Jerusalem, and crucified him at the place of Calvary. Through the location of each passion we are typologically admonished to go out to the Lord outside the camp, bearing his reproach—that is, having abandoned the fellowship and society of the world and the wicked, to endure willingly whatever the world casts away, for love of our heavenly homeland.

When the Lord asked Cain where his brother Abel was, Cain replied that he did not know and that he was not his keeper. To this day the Jews say to the faithful who question them—namely, to the members of Christ—concerning Christ, that they do not know him. Yet they would in some way be Christ’s keepers if they had wished to receive and preserve the Christian faith. For one who keeps Christ in his heart does not say, like Cain, that he does not know his brother or that he is not his keeper.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Another reading: “The Lord says”; another: “And God said.”] God said to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.” Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the Holy Scriptures.

The blood of Christ has a great voice upon the earth, when, after it has been received by all the nations, they answer: “Amen.” [Note: [Col. 0070D] Here he alludes to the ancient custom of the Church by which the faithful, upon receiving the Eucharist in communion, said “Amen.” See, if desired, what we have said in Book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 4, article 10.] This is the clear voice [Note: [Col. 0070D] Another reading omits “of the blood.”] which the blood itself expresses from the mouths of the faithful redeemed by that same blood. Concerning this the Apostle rightly says to the faithful: “You have approached Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks more eloquently than Abel’s” (Heb. XII, 24).

For the blood of Christ speaks more eloquently than Abel’s, because Abel’s cried out to the Lord for the condemnation of a fratricide, whereas Christ’s raises its voice to heaven for the salvation of Christ’s faithful brothers.

“Now, therefore, you shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.” By “earth” he means the Church. For it is she, and no other, who opens her mouth to taste mystically the blood of Christ, which was poured out by the hands of the Jewish people.

Upon this earth that people is cursed, because the more closely it clings to the love of its Creator, the more gravely it understands that the people hostile to him is accursed, although, still proud, it boasts that it alone is specially blessed.

When you work it, it will not yield its fruits to you. [Col. 0071B] That people worked upon the same earth which Christ, the head of the Church, carried—that is, upon his flesh—for our salvation, crucifying him who died for our sins; yet that earth did not give them its fruits, because they were not justified by faith in his resurrection, who rose for our justification. Therefore, when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, just as the earth did not show Cain, who worked it, the fruit of its strength, so that that seed might be sown. But the Jews worked the earth that is the Church, through their persecutions causing it to advance further in God; often also raging against many even to the point of death, but they were not worthy to see the fruit of the faith and precious death of those whom they killed.

As for Cain’s reply to the Lord, “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon,” [Col. 0071C] “Behold, you drive me out today from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden, and I shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth”—this is manifestly and unmistakably about the Jewish people. Its iniquity is greater than can deserve pardon, because it killed the Son of God; and therefore those from among it who receive pardon through repentance are certainly saved beyond what their merit deserves, by the grace of divine mercy. It is clear that it was driven from the face of the earth—that is, from the portion of the holy Church—and hidden from the face of divine contemplation. It foreshadowed this for itself when it veiled Christ’s face during his Passion; and heavenly signs also foreshadowed it for that people when, after he had been crucified, the sun concealed the radiance of its light. Having lost its kingdom, it became a fugitive and wanderer, scattered throughout the world wherever it was dispersed, fearing that even its temporal life might be taken away. It therefore says, as Cain does: [Note: [Col. 0071D] Another copy has, “For everyone.”] “Everyone who finds me will kill me.”

But what did God answer it? “By no means shall this happen; rather, whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance”—that is, the carnal Jewish people, the wicked race, shall not perish by bodily death. For whoever destroys them in this way shall pay sevenfold vengeance: that is, he shall remove from them the sevenfold vengeance with which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s death. Thus, throughout this whole period, which unfolds according to the sevenfold number of days, the fact that the Jewish nation has not perished makes it sufficiently evident to faithful Christians what sort of subjection those deserved who killed the Lord in their proud kingdom.

We have placed this exposition of the passage [Col. 0072A] according to the ancient translation because we took it from the writings of Saint Augustine, who followed that translation, as we have also extracted many other things from him.

And God placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him. The Jewish nation, whether under pagan rulers or under Christian ones, bears the sign of its law, by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples. Every emperor or king who finds them in his kingdom finds them with that sign and does not kill them—that is, he does not cause them to cease being Jews, distinguished from the fellowship of the other nations by a certain distinctive sign of their observance—except for those among them who have passed over to Christ.

And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and dwelt in the land as a fugitive, toward the eastern region of Eden. “In the presence of the Lord” [Col. 0072B] is ordinarily understood as his recognition, by which he manifests himself and is recognized. Rightly, therefore, the people that withdrew from the grace of divine knowledge is said to dwell in the earth. For it cannot say with the elect: “But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ” (Phil. 3:20).

The Seventy Translators rendered this passage as follows: “And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord God and dwelt in the land of Naid, opposite Eden.” *Naid* is translated as “fugitive”; or, as we find in the Book of Hebrew Names, “unstable movement and fluctuation.” Some, including Josephus, agree that this was the name of the place where Cain dwelt. [Note: [Col. 0071D] *Jewish Antiquities*, book I, chapter 3.] Our translator, however, understood this not as the name of a place but as signifying the condition itself [Col. 0072C], because Cain was destined always to be unstable, wavering, and without a fixed dwelling. How [Note: [Col. 0072D] Another copy has, “only.”] well this corresponds to the present condition of the Jews, the whole world bears witness.

He is also rightly said to dwell opposite Eden. [Note: [Col. 0072D] Another copy has, “to have dwelt.”] For Eden signifies “pleasure” or “delights.” That faithless people, the more it turns away from knowledge of the truth and entangles itself in earthly affairs, lives a life increasingly opposed to heavenly delights; and because it thirsts only for temporal joys, it stands with the dry throat of its heart opposed to the torrent of divine pleasure from which the righteous drink.

Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he built a city and called its name after his son Enoch. Just as, from the beginning of the world, the sufferings of the saints were indicated in Abel’s death, while the faithlessness of the wicked was signified in Cain’s envy and persecution—both of which would remain in the world until the end of the age—so also, in the city Cain built, it was typologically signified that the whole hope of the wicked would be fixed upon the kingdom and happiness of this age, since they had neither faith in nor desire for future blessings.

Of this city the Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea: “I am God, and not man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 2:9). Neither Abel nor Seth, who was born in his place, is read to have built a city [Col. 0073A] or [Note: [Col. 0073D] Another copy has, “houses.”] houses. [Note: [Col. 0073D] Another copy has, “to have built.”] They represented—or rather, they were the first fruits of—those who rejoice to say to their Creator: “For I am a sojourner with you, a stranger like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13).

This promise of the Lord, which we mentioned above, aptly suits them: “I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst.” For the more they make themselves strangers to the fellowship of the worldly city, the more worthy they become of the indwelling of their Creator.

Appropriately, Cain called the city’s name after his son Enoch, thereby indicating that he would have successors like himself, who, excluded from the heavenly homeland, would root their hearts in the pleasures of this life. Enoch is rightly interpreted as “Dedication,” because the wicked, while wishing to rejoice in what they do in the present, dedicate, as it were, the city they build for themselves in the first generation. By contrast, in that lineage of the human race which descends through Seth to Noah, Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is born; he is said to have walked before God and not to have appeared, because God took him away. For the rest and joy and hope of all the elect are found only in the future Sabbath. After they walk with the Lord in this life, humbly following his commandments, they are taken by him into the life of perpetual rest and no longer appear among mortals, because they live immortally with him.

They themselves are his city and temple: now they strive toward perfection through daily progress in good works; then, their labors ended, they reign with him. In their own dedication—which will continually be celebrated through the presence of the Holy Spirit—each of them rejoices, as it were, in the name Enoch. [Col. 0073C]

Moreover, Enoch begot Iram, [Note: [Col. 0073D] Another copy has “Iran, and Iran”; another, “Irad, and Irad.”] and Iram begot Maviahel, and Maviahel begot Matusahel, and Matusahel begot Lamech, who took two wives: the name of one was Ada, and the name of the other [Note: [Col. 0073D] Another copy has “Sella.”] Sella; and Ada bore Jabel. [Note: [Col. 0074D] Another copy has, “Cain was the firstborn.”]

Cain’s descendants are counted through the seventh generation, and in that generation Cain himself was killed by Lamech and released from the sevenfold vengeance which he had miserably borne for so long. In that entire offspring which had sprung from him, after it had been further polluted by Lamech’s adultery, adding to the curse, it perished when the flood came upon it. In the sixth generation it was defiled by adultery; in the seventh it was destroyed by the flood. Spiritually this signifies that the city of the wicked—that is, the entire society of the reprobate—will corrupt itself through crimes during the six ages of this world, but in the seventh, which is future, will perish forever.

For just as Enoch, the seventh from Adam, was taken up into paradise and no human being saw him, because he lives in peace with God, so Jabel, the seventh from Cain, whose name is interpreted “Changed,” was destroyed with his brothers and the whole of his offspring in the flood, and no human being saw him, because, punished with eternal death and removed from the worldly glory he had loved, he was changed into the punishment he had not foreseen. In these things, as we have said, it is clearly signified that after the six ages of this world the saints proceed to rest in another life, while the reprobate proceed to punishment, as the Lord’s account of the poor Lazarus and the proud rich man also clearly demonstrates.

“Adah,” he says, “bore Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and of shepherds; and the name of his brother was Jubal. He was the father of those who play the lyre and the organ. Sella also bore Tubal-cain, who was a forger of every work in bronze and iron.”

All these things which Lamech’s sons are reported to have invented or practiced pertain to the cultivation, adornment, or enticements of this life. Abel is not read to have done anything of this kind, nor [Note: [Col. 0074D] Another copy omits “anything of this kind.”] is Seth, who was born in his place, nor their descendants; rather, they are shown to have led a simple life as strangers on the earth.

Although Abel was a shepherd of sheep, he did not wish to devote himself so completely to this occupation that he would weave tents in which he could practice it more conveniently. As for the lyre and pipe, far be it from so great a man to devote any time to them. Anyone who carefully considers all the works made of bronze and iron clearly understands that, if the human race had rightly observed the natural law, even though expelled from the joys of paradise through the guilt of transgression, it would have had no need of all these things. Thus it is clear that all these inventions originated with the sons of the curse, although later, as the human race degenerated from the purity of its first way of life, even good servants of God sometimes occupied themselves with such things for the sake of social life.

There is, however, a great difference. The reprobate took pleasure in such things as though they were their highest good, [Note: [Col. 0074D] Another copy has, “delighted in them.”] whereas the elect either renounce them entirely or use them for some benefit of this life, until they reach eternal life, as a traveler uses an inn or provisions while passing through.

The patriarchs, for example, dwelt in tents, but as strangers in the world, in contrast to those who habitually lived in cities and houses as citizens of the earth. The psalmists used the lyre and pipe, but to praise the Lord with them. Conversely, the prophet reproves those who made music on the lyre, tambourine, and lyre at their banquets. There were learned men among the people of God skilled in every work of bronze and iron, as well as of silver and gold; but the Lord himself commanded these men to apply this craft to the adornment of his tabernacle.

The prophet, too, proclaiming the joys of the Lord’s Incarnation, foretold that harmful works of iron would be removed and transformed for the better: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war anymore” (Isa. 2:4).

Nor should we carelessly overlook the fact that when human beings began to defile themselves with adultery, to devote themselves excessively to pasturing cattle, to dissolve themselves in musical modes, and to apply themselves to smithing arts, they were then destroyed when the flood came upon them.

We must therefore be especially careful lest the last day find us entangled beyond measure in such things. The Lord, speaking of the day of judgment and recalling this period, urges us to vigilance, saying: “For just as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and [Note: [Col. 0075D] So in the manuscripts; copies corrected by another hand read *nuptui* (‘for marriage’). I find *nuptum* (‘marriage’) in the very ancient manuscript of the church of Tours, written more than eleven hundred years ago, and in two other manuscripts of the church of Saint Martin, one written a thousand years ago in gold letters and the other about nine hundred years ago. Two other, somewhat less ancient, manuscripts from Marmoutier also agree with them.] giving themselves in marriage until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away; so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24:38).

The sister of Tubal-cain was Noema. [Note: [Col. 0075D] Another copy has “Noemma.”] Noema is interpreted as “Pleasure.” It is fitting that Cain’s lineage ends with the birth of a woman, and that this woman is called Pleasure, because the whole intention of the wicked serves the enticements of the world and desires to end life in the fulfillment of carnal pleasures.

After this woman was born, however, the whole cursed offspring was soon afterward brought to an end by the flood. For when they bow the neck of the mind to the pleasures of the world and say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them. [Col. 0075B]

It should be noted that enjoyment or pleasure is commonly understood in two ways: in good and in evil. It is understood in the good sense when it is said: “But the meek shall possess the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. 36:12). And again: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure” (Ps. 35:9).

Paradise is also named from this pleasure, because humanity was placed there so that, in the presence of its Creator, it might enjoy forever the most blessed and holy delights of flesh and soul. In the evil sense pleasure is understood when the Apostle identifies certain people as lovers of pleasure rather than of God. The name Noema is appropriately applied to them, [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy has *Noemmae*, and this name is consistently written with a double *m*.] since in her generation the first age of the world was destroyed, with few exceptions.

The human race had therefore departed from Eden—that is, from the delights of inward goods—and, abandoning heavenly things, was occupied with the earth. It reached the birth of the woman called Noema, that is, Pleasure; [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy has, “reached.”] and not long afterward the whole race perished in the cataclysm. Thus the birth of such offspring and the disaster that followed signified that all who neglect spiritual things and subject themselves to the pleasures of the flesh rightly hasten toward ruin.

Noema was born in the seventh generation from Cain. If, however, you wish to count Cain’s generations from Adam himself and include all of Lamech’s sons, you will find Naamah in the eleventh place. Lamech is the seventh from Adam; when his four children are added, the eleventh number is completed.

The number eleven, which exceeds ten, commonly signifies sin, since sin is committed through transgressing the Ten Commandments of the Law. Therefore the wicked lineage rightly ends and perishes at the number eleven, and does so in a woman, because, while despising the precepts of the divine law, it strives to be satisfied with its own wicked pleasures and builds sudden destruction for itself.

And Lamech said to his wives, Adah and Zillah: “Hear my voice, wives of Lamech; listen to my speech, for I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise.” The man or young man whom he mentions signifies Cain. Lamech killed him, but not intentionally, as Jerome testifies is written in a certain Hebrew volume. He killed him “for his wound” and “for his bruise,” because by this act [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy omits “in this.”] he also brought death and condemnation upon himself: he killed the one whom God had granted life.

“Vengeance shall be taken sevenfold on Cain, but on Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” Vengeance was taken sevenfold on Cain because, until the seventh generation, he paid the penalties of his fratricide and envy as a wandering fugitive. On Lamech it was seventy-sevenfold because, as Jerome testifies that he had learned from the Hebrews, and as Josephus likewise affirms, [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy has, “revealed.”] [Note: [Col. 0076D] *Jewish Antiquities*, book I, chapter 3.] seventy-seven persons were born from Cain’s stock and perished in the flood. [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy has, “revealed.”] They say that in this number vengeance was exacted from Lamech, because his race endured until the flood.

Lamech is interpreted as “Striking” or “Struck”; both interpretations suit the same man, who struck Cain and, because of that very act of parricide, was himself struck by divine vengeance.

Mystically, Lamech signifies the human race: struck by the deception of the ancient enemy in its first parent, and striking itself through the daily increase of its sins. Vengeance was taken upon it seventy-sevenfold because, until the coming of Christ—who appeared in the world in the seventy-seventh generation—the guilt of the first transgression oppressed the human race. Then he came and [Note: [Col. 0076D] In one manuscript, written by a second hand: “who would take away.”] took away the sins of the world and brought us into the eternal life which we had lost in Adam, opening the gate of the heavenly kingdom through his baptism or Passion.

At that point vengeance on Lamech ceased, because, through the Lord’s Passion and resurrection, the sting of death and sin was broken, and the human race returned to the heavenly kingdom.

Adam again knew his wife, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, saying: “God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel.” After recounting the death of Cain the fratricide and repeating how his offspring was again cursed in the seventh generation, he returns to explain the restoration of the holy seed [Col. 0076D], and relates how this seed would remain perpetually while the wicked perished. [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy has, “and that this”; another, “and what.”] [Note: [Col. 0076D] Another copy, written by a second hand, has “remaining.”]

Seth is interpreted as “Appointment” or “Resurrection.” The reason for the name is explained by the parent’s words:

“God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” He was appointed in Abel’s place not only in the order of birth but also in the merit of virtue, filling his brother’s place. His devotion of mind is shown to have passed even to his offspring, when it is added:

“But to Seth also a son was born, whom he called Enosh. He began to invoke the name of the Lord.” Enosh is interpreted as “Man” or “Human Being.” Therefore it is rightly said that the one who bears this name begins to invoke the Lord’s name, imploring the help of his Creator in daily prayers with all the greater urgency because he remembers that he was made of fragile nature.

Mystically, just as Abel, killed by Cain, signifies the Lord suffering, so Seth, born in his place, signifies him raised from the dead. Accordingly, among the Septuagint Translators, his father or mother is fittingly said to have declared at his birth: “For God has raised up another seed for me in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.” He is rightly called “another seed” according to the mystical sense, although the same Lord who was killed rose again, because he was killed as mortal and rose immortal. He died so that we would not fear death; he rose so that he might give us hope and faith of rising from death.

The Apostle clearly distinguished these two kinds of seed when speaking of our resurrection: “It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it shall rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it shall rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15:42–44). And of the Lord himself he says: “Although he died through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

Enosh, the son of Seth, figuratively expresses the Christian people, [Note: [Col. 0077D] Another copy has “of Christians.”] which is born daily throughout the whole world from water and the Holy Spirit through faith in and the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection. Preferring the grace of its regeneration to its first birth, it has become accustomed in all that [Note: [Col. 0077D] Another copy has, “says.”] it does to invoke the help of the Lord’s name, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9), and so forth, in that same prayer of the Lord, or in the other prayers by which we beseech his grace, without which we can do nothing.

Thus we are also rightly called Enosh, that is, “Human Beings,” because of our awareness of our frailty; but because of our hope of future immortality, we are sons of Seth, that is, of “Resurrection.”

This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created humanity, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them, and he blessed them. This is the book of humanity’s first creation: God made it in his likeness so that, through participation in his goodness, it might remain forever good, immortal, and blessed. He made them male and female and illumined them, once made, with the grace of his blessing.

Such was Adam’s generation with his wife on the day when he was created. But alas, what grief! [Note: [Col. 0077D] Another copy has, “was profaning.”] He profaned the likeness of God by believing the enemy rather than the Creator. His firstborn contracted a heavier punishment of the curse by envying and killing his brother. Lamech, the seventh from Adam, corrupted the law established for male and female, of which it had been said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), by taking two wives and joining three persons in one flesh. As evils multiplied everywhere, the human race withdrew so far from the likeness of its Creator and from the original blessing that, in the tenth generation, it deserved to be entirely destroyed, except for the few whom the ark contained.

Nevertheless, the Creator himself granted us a return to that likeness and blessing by deigning to be born in the likeness of our nature, to be cursed, and to die, so that, redeemed through him, we might deserve to say of him: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), and to hear from him: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you” [Note: [Col. 0078D] Another copy has, “which has been prepared for you.”] “from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

And he called their names Adam on the day when they were created. Adam, like Enosh, is interpreted as “Human Being,” but Enosh is said to sound like “a man” in such a way that it applies only to males; Adam, however, is so formed that it can be applied to either sex. Thus it is rightly said that he called their names Adam, that is, “Human Being.”

Just as the Latin word *homo* derives its etymology from *humus*, “earth,” because the origin of flesh is drawn from the earth, so among the Hebrews Adam is named from the earth, because humanity was formed from the clay of the earth. Adam may therefore also be interpreted as “Earthly” or “Red Earth.”
