Among the Greeks, however, “human being” has another etymology. It is called *antropos*, from the fact that a person ought to contemplate what is above and raise the eyes of the mind to behold heavenly things.

In the name Adam, apart from the interpretation by which it signifies “human being,” there is another mystery that should not be passed over in silence. It has four letters—A, D, A, and M—and from these letters the four regions of the world, when named in Greek, take their beginnings. They are called *anatole*, “east”; *dysis*, “west”; *arctos*, “north”; and *mesembria*, “south.” It was therefore most fitting that the name of the first-formed human being should mystically contain all the regions of the world, since through his offspring the whole world was to be filled.

When it says, “And he called their names Adam,” [Note: [Col. 0078D] Another copy reads “saying.”] and adds, “On the day when they were created,” [Note: [Col. 0078D] Another copy omits “and.”] it plainly indicates that Adam and his wife were made on one and the same day—that is, on the sixth day of the newly created world—and that the wife was not created separately from his side after the sixth or seventh day.

[Col. 0078D] Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and begot a son in his likeness and image, and called his name Seth. Adam was created in the image and likeness of God because he was created immortal in soul and body. But after he corrupted the image and likeness of God in himself through sin, he begot a son in his own likeness and image—that is, mortal, corruptible, capable of reason, bound by the guilt of his transgression, and able to be released only by the grace of that same Creator.

It should be noted that where our manuscripts, transmitted from the Hebrew source, have that Adam lived [Col. 0079A] one hundred and thirty years and begot Seth, the ancient translation has two hundred and thirty instead of one hundred and thirty. Where our manuscripts continue, “And the days of Adam after he begot Seth were eight hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters,” that translation has seven hundred instead of eight hundred.

Where, in conclusion, it adds, “And all the time that Adam lived was nine hundred and thirty years, and he died,” both translations give the same total. The same distinction of numbers is maintained in all the generations down to the flood: according to the Septuagint Translators, each person is read to have lived one hundred years more before the birth of a son, and one hundred years fewer after the birth of a son, than in the Hebrew text. At the conclusion, however, both translations give an equal total—except in the sixth generation, where both manuscripts state that Jared, at the age of one hundred and sixty-two, begot Enoch and lived eight hundred years after his birth; and in the ninth, where a new kind of difference occurs.

According to the Hebrew text, Lamech begot Noah when he was one hundred and eighty years old and lived five hundred and ninety-five years after Noah’s birth. In the Septuagint Translators’ manuscripts, Lamech is found to have lived one hundred and eighty-eight years before Noah’s birth and five hundred and sixty-five afterward. Thus [Note: [Col. 0079D] Another copy has, “thirty-four.”] Lamech is found to have lived twenty-four years longer in the Hebrew manuscripts than in those of the Septuagint Translators.

Through this difference among the translators, Methuselah’s lifetime appears to extend fourteen years beyond the flood. The years before the flood therefore amount, according to the Hebrews, to one thousand five hundred and fifty-six; according to the Septuagint Translators, whom the chronographers follow, to two thousand two hundred and forty-two.

The most learned Augustine, however, states that even in the Septuagint translation, in fewer but more reliable manuscripts, Methuselah is found to have died six [Note: [Col. 0079D] Another copy has “years.”] years before the flood. When he investigated most diligently the cause of the discrepancy between the translations, he did not wish to detract from the reliability of the Septuagint Translators, whom the apostles and evangelists are shown to have followed in many passages; and he himself believed that, in translating the Scriptures, they had relied more on a prophetic gift than on the professional duty of interpretation. He therefore concluded as follows:

“More plausibly, then, someone might say that when these books first began to be copied from the library of Ptolemy, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Another copy has “of Ptolemy.”] something of this sort could have happened in one manuscript, but in the manuscript first copied from that source, from which the reading then spread more widely; and [Note: [Col. 0079D] Another copy has, “something.”] there could indeed have been a scribal error. But in that question concerning Methuselah’s life, it is not absurd to suspect this.”

And after a little further on:

“I would in no way hesitate to affirm that it was rightly done that, whenever something different is found in both manuscripts—since both cannot be true with respect to the historical facts—the language from which the translation into the other language was made through interpreters should rather be trusted.” [Note: [Col. 0079D] *The City of God*, book XV, chapter 13.]

According to the Hebrew text, therefore, Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot Seth. Seth lived one hundred and five [Note: [Col. 0079D] Another copy has “years.”] years and begot Enosh. Enosh lived ninety years and begot Cainan. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has “Caian.”] Cainan lived eighty years and begot Malalehel. Malalehel lived sixty-five years and begot Jaret. Jaret lived one hundred and sixty-two years and begot Enoch. Enoch lived sixty-five [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has “sixty-six.”] years and begot Mathusalam. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has “Mathusalem.”] He [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy adds, “Enoch.”] walked with God.

After he begot Methuselah, he lived three hundred years and begot sons and daughters. “He walked with God” means that he followed God’s will and commandments in all things. With God dwelling in him, possessing and ruling his heart, he practiced good works outwardly, according to the prophet’s saying: “I will show you, O human being, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: certainly, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God” (Mic. 6:8). And as Zechariah says: “I will strengthen them in the Lord, and they shall walk in his name, says the Lord” (Zech. 10:12).

This does not mean that Enoch walked with God for three hundred years only after Methuselah was born, as though he had not obeyed divine commands before his birth. Rather, the sentence simply indicates that after Methuselah’s birth he served God in this life through good works for no more than three hundred years. When these were completed, he followed his guidance into the joys of the further life. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has, “is.”] The text continues:

“And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years; and he walked with God, and he did not appear, because God took him.” It is beautifully said that the one who first walked with God in this life by obeying his commandments afterward walked with him by passing from this life into another, where he would live in the greatest peace and happiness of flesh and spirit. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has, “whom then.”]

The universal faith of the Church nevertheless holds that before the day of judgment—that is, when the coming of Antichrist is imminent—he will return with Elijah for the conversion of this age, so that by the authority and teaching of such great men human hearts may be instructed and strengthened to endure and overcome the persecution of that son of perdition. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has “the persecution.”] After completing their martyrdom, they will then be admitted to the joys of immortal life, according to what [Note: [Col. 0080D] Another copy has, “in the Apocalypse.”] the Lord says to John in the Apocalypse: “And I will give to my two martyrs,” that is, witnesses, “and they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth” (Rev. 11:3)—that is, living in great self-restraint and anguish for three and a half years.

A little later he says: “And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, and will conquer them and kill them” (ibid., 7).

We anticipated above that just as Lamech, cursed in the seventh generation from Adam, signifies the destruction of the reprobate, which they find in the future age where they ought to have hoped for rest, so Enoch, translated from the world in the seventh generation, demonstrates the true rest of the elect, which they receive without end after the labors of this life, which pass through six ages.

Accordingly, Lamech is rightly read to have taken two wives, contrary to the decree of the one who said, “The two shall be one flesh,” and to have begotten children devoted to the works and enticements of the world; and thus, after committing murder, to have been cursed by the sentence of his own mouth.

Enoch, on the other hand, is said to have walked with God. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Another copy has “because.”] What greater praise could there be for a human being? None, [Note: [Col. 0081D] Another copy has, “as.”] since he is God’s inseparable companion and follows the traces of the divine command in all his actions. Had Adam [Note: [Col. 0081D] Another copy has, “when he had done this.”] done this, he would never have turned his steps away from the companionship of the Creator to listen to the serpent’s conversation; he would have remained in paradise with his entire race to this day.

The statement that all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years—the number of days [Note: [Col. 0081D] Another copy has, “is introduced.”] contained in the solar year—mystically signifies that throughout the whole period of this age those who faithfully serve the Lord and strive toward eternal rest will never cease. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Another copy has “will never fail.”]

Nor is it without reason that the three hundred years during which Enoch is especially said to have walked with God are mentioned separately. Among the Greeks this number is customarily represented by the letter T. The letter T has the shape of a cross; and if it had received the single stroke missing in the middle, it would no longer merely have the figure of a cross but would visibly display the very sign of the cross.

Thus Enoch, whose name means “Dedication,” walked with God for three hundred years, because he embodied—or rather, himself lived—the life and conduct of those who, in faith in the Lord’s Passion, await the joy of eternal salvation, denying themselves, taking up their cross daily, and following the Lord. In other words, they walk with God and strive toward entry into paradise.

It should be noted that although Scripture carefully traces the offspring of Seth down to Noah and then to Abraham, it describes Cain’s lineage down to Lamech and his children without mentioning any ages, as though silently impressing upon us the Psalmist’s words: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish” (Ps. 1:6).

Methuselah lived 187 years and fathered Lamech. Lamech lived 182 years and fathered Noah, saying: “This one will console us from our works and the labors of our hands on the land which the Lord has cursed.” By prophetic spirit Lamech foresaw what kind of man his son would be and how great his virtue would become: that in his days the nation of the wicked would be exterminated, and that through him, after the Flood had passed, the generation of the faithful would be restored. By “works and labors of our hands,” I believe he meant no others, nor greater ones, than those by which the offspring of the elect at that time was oppressed by the wickedness of evil men. He called this “his own and his people’s consolation” because, when the world that then existed had been destroyed by the Flood, and all the things and inhabitants of the world had been removed, they foresaw that a new race of the righteous would arise, with the face of the age renewed. [Note: In another copy, *nos* (“us”) is absent.]

Even now, the consolation of the good is that, when they see the day of judgment drawing near amid the increasing ruins of the world, they know that on that day, after the whole company of the wicked has been consumed, they themselves will possess with the Lord the kingdoms of the age to come.

For what our edition has, “he will console,” the ancient interpreters said: “This one will make us rest from our works” [Note: Another copy reads, “they would declare beforehand”; another, “they would learn beforehand.”]—which seems more appropriate to the name Noah. For Noah is interpreted as “Rest.” In the literal sense, this can be understood to mean that in his time all the former works of human beings came to rest through the Flood. In the spiritual sense, the rest is the same as the consolation of the saints: namely, to behold, as the end of the world approaches, both the destruction of the wicked and the arrival of the time of rewards for the faithful.

Well, then, Noah—through whose merits devoted to the Lord rest and consolation were to be given to the age—is born in the tenth generation from Adam, because eternal rest and life are granted to us through the fulfillment of the Decalogue of the Law. Again, when Scripture said that he had fathered sons, it did not wish to name only one of them, lest in a perfect man the number eleven should seem to have some place as a transgression of the number ten. Rather, speaking mystically of a man of virtue, it reports that three sons were born to him at once.

“Noah,” it says, “when he was five hundred years old, fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” [Note: Another copy reads, “and Ham.”]

Noah was therefore born in the tenth generation because he both represented and enacted the life of those who are perfected in the observance of the Decalogue. [Note: Another copy reads *et figuram tenet et egit* (“and represents and enacted the figure”).] He fathered three sons so that he might signify, even through the fruit of his physical offspring, that he had served the Lord in faith in the Holy Trinity and had produced the fruit of spiritual virtues. Nevertheless, even according to the historical sense, it was fitting that the man in whom the seed of the world that was perishing was to be left for the world that would be born again should have three sons, so that through the descendants of his three sons the three corresponding regions of the world might be filled. For the sons of Shem chiefly possessed Asia, the descendants of Ham Africa, and the offspring of Japheth Europe.

When human beings began to multiply upon the earth and fathered daughters, the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. By “men” he means the offspring of Cain, who had turned away from contemplating the divine will and subjected their minds solely to human affairs. By “the sons of God,” however, he means those who were born from the lineage of Seth and who, following the example of their father’s devotion, preserved with unshaken minds the service they owed to God.

By this distinction [Note: Another copy reads, “which [serves] for distinction.”] the Lord also distinguished his disciples in the Gospel from the rest, saying: “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16:13). After receiving their answer, he said: “But you—who do you say that I am?” He wished them to be understood as superior to men and to be counted among those of whom he himself says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6).

Some manuscripts have “the angels of God” instead of “the sons of God,” which is certainly understood in the same sense. For the righteous are rightly called angels of God when, according to the measure of their capacity, they strive to live an angelic life on earth. To such people the Apostle says: “But you, brothers, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9). And again: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

It therefore appears that, as long as the generation of Seth was not mingled with the offspring of Cain, it preserved the unblemished standard of its chastity. But after it fell into lust and joined itself to the accursed offspring through desire for wicked women, then it too, having marred the beauty of a sober mind, began to become a sharer in that curse. Hence, in the Law, the children of Israel are carefully and repeatedly commanded not to enter into marriages with foreigners, lest, he says, “her daughter seduce your son, and they follow their gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4).

And God said: “My Spirit will not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be 120 years.” Explaining these verses, Saint Jerome says [Note: *Questions on Genesis*]:

“In Hebrew it is written: ‘My Spirit will not judge these men forever, because they are flesh’; that is, because the condition of the human being is fragile, I will not preserve them for eternal punishments, but here I will repay them what they deserve.” [Note: Another copy reads, “because it is a condition of frailty.”]

Thus the Hebrew does not convey God’s severity, as it is read in our manuscripts, but his clemency, since the sinner is punished here for his crime. Hence an angry God also says to certain people: “I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication, nor their brides when they have committed adultery” (Hosea 4). And elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; nevertheless, I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88).

Moreover, lest he seem cruel because he had not granted sinners a place for repentance, he added: “And his days shall be 120 years” (Genesis 6:3)—that is, they would have 120 years in which to practice repentance. But because they scorned repentance, God did not wish to wait for the appointed time. Instead, cutting short the period by twenty years, he brought on the Flood in the hundredth year, which had been appointed for the practice of repentance.

Now giants were upon the earth in those days. By “giants” he means people born with enormous bodies and endowed with excessive power. We read that many such men also existed after the Flood, that is, in the times of Moses or David. In Greek they are called *gigantes* because, according to the fables of the poets, the earth gave birth to them.

They appear to have been begotten at the time when the descendants of Seth chose wives from the lineage of Cain on account of their beauty, contrary to the law of their own dignity. For the text continues:

“For after the sons of God had gone in to the daughters of men, and they had borne children, these were the mighty men from of old, men of renown.”

It should be noted that here, instead of “giants,” the Hebrew reads “the fallen,” that is, *annasilim*. The meaning is straightforward and complete: in those days there were men who had fallen to the earth, that is, who clung to earthly desires after losing the state of rectitude devoted to God. Giants, however, are properly called *Rafaim* in their language.

The term “giant” is sometimes also used in a good sense [Note: Another copy reads, “that passage concerning the Lord”], as in this passage concerning the Lord: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:6). Here it refers to the singular power by which he justly transcended the rest of the human race and accomplished the mystery of the Incarnation with wondrous power. In the same way, a lion sometimes signifies the Lord and sometimes the devil: the devil on account of his pride and ferocity, and the Lord on account of his power. [Note: Another copy reads, “signifies.”] Yet in the Hebrew text the verse of the aforementioned psalm is written: “He rejoiced like a mighty man to run his course.”

When God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great on the earth, and that every inclination of their heart was directed toward evil, he regretted that he had made man on the earth. Scripture says that God regretted this—not because God truly regrets any of his deeds as a human being does, since his judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain—but because Scripture uses such expressions to make itself, in a way, more familiar to us. We ourselves normally begin to change something and transfer it into another state only through regret.

Although divine providence appears, to those who contemplate it with a calm heart, to govern all things according to an entirely certain order, Scripture nevertheless accommodates and adapts itself to the humble understanding of the slower-witted, who are by far the greater number. Thus it speaks as though, through God’s regret, those things are removed which begin to exist but do not persist as long as they were expected to persist. Something similar is found in what follows: [Note: Another copy reads, “and that too.”]

“And being touched inwardly with grief of heart, he said: I will destroy from the face of the earth the man whom I created, from man to animals, from creeping creature to birds of the air; for I regret that I made them.”

God is said to grieve in human fashion when he sees that the people whom he himself created cling to the hostile power of evil by sinning rather than to him by living piously, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “A foolish son is the grief of his father” (Proverbs 19:13). And again: “A foolish son is the anger of his father and the grief of his mother who bore him” (Proverbs 17:25).

But by also announcing the destruction of all earthly and flying creatures, he declares the magnitude of the coming disaster. For he threatens destruction to irrational animals, as though they too had sinned.

“These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generations; he walked with God.”

Noah is praised with the same commendation as Enoch: namely, that he followed the traces of the divine command with the straight steps of good works. Therefore, when the world was about to perish, Enoch was transferred to paradise, while Noah was saved in the ark as the world perished.

Noah was righteous and perfect [Note: Another copy adds *est* (“is”)]—not as the saints will be perfected in that immortality in which they will be made equal to the angels of God, but as people can be perfect in this pilgrimage. For this reason the text adds, “in his generations,” signifying that he was righteous not according to consummate righteousness but according to the righteousness of his generations—namely, those generations in which Seth, Enos, Enoch, and the other holy and perfect men of that time lived. The subsequent text of Holy Scripture indicates that his sons Shem and Japheth also belonged to these generations.

When God saw that the earth was corrupt—for all flesh had corrupted its way—“all flesh” means every human being, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). Birds and quadrupeds had not corrupted their way by sinning, just as they would not see the Salvation of our God, that is, Christ; rather, every human being would see him.

And he said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them [Note: Another copy omits *a facie* (“from the face/presence”)], and I will destroy them together with the earth. Make yourself an ark of planed wood,” and so forth.

A many-sided mystery is contained in the construction of the ark and in the coming of the Flood. First, as the Lord himself shows through the sudden inundation of the Flood, the unforeseen hour of the final judgment is signified: “And as it was,” he says, “in the days of Noah, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking, marrying wives and giving them in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark. And the Flood came and destroyed them all” (Matthew 24:38–39).

The construction of the ark, which took place over 100 years, signifies the entire period of this age, during which the holy Church is built and brought to its perfect completion. There is no doubt [Note: Another copy adds, “that”] that the number 100 signifies perfection [Note: Another copy reads, “represents”]—either because it is completed by ten decades, or because it passes from the left hand to the right, expressing the activity which in this life is exercised, as it were, on the left, but in the future life is brought to completion, as it were, on the right.

When the ark had been made and all that was to be saved had been brought into it, the Flood came and carried away everything that was outside it. So, when all who have been predestined to eternal life have entered the Church, the end of the world will come, and all who are found outside the Church will perish.

According to this interpretation, the ark plainly signifies the Church; Noah, the Lord who builds the Church in his saints [Note: Another copy reads, “who built it”]; and the Flood, the end of the age or the final judgment. [Note: Another copy reads, “signifies.”]

Yet, apart from the construction of the ark, Noah—because his name is interpreted as “rest,” and because it was foretold that he would cause human beings to rest from the works and labors of their hands in the land which the Lord cursed [Note: Another copy omits “and labors”]—also represents the image of the Lord and Savior. For he consoles us [Note: Another copy reads, “he will console”] through the illumination of his Spirit, who is therefore called the Paraclete, that is, the Consoler. He rescued us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us. He calls those who labor to rest: “Come to me,” he says, “all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29). [Note: Another copy omits “from me.”]

In truth, among his generations—that is, in the entire congregation of the saints—he alone was righteous and perfect in all things, since he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

According to another interpretation, equally pious and catholic, the ark signifies the Church, and the Flood the water of baptism, by which the Church itself is washed and sanctified in all its members. In this sense the Apostle Peter explains:

“When the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water. In the same way baptism now saves you by a corresponding figure—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:20–21). [Note: Another copy reads, “toward God.”]

When he says that we have been saved in baptism through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, he briefly explains what the number of the eight souls who were saved through water mystically signifies. [Note: Another copy reads, “what . . . signifies.”] For the day of the Lord’s resurrection is the third day from the day of his Passion, but from the day of the first creation it is the eighth day.

Some of the Fathers also frequently interpret the waves of the Flood as the temptations of this age, by which the holy Church is assaulted every day but not overcome. Indeed, through being exercised by temptations [Note: Another copy reads, “having been exercised”], she is lifted up from earthly desires toward the things that must be sought in heaven.

Whatever is outside the ark is drowned by these same temptations of the world, just as it is said that the waters, multiplying and overflowing with great force upon the surface of the earth, lifted the ark high above the earth, but destroyed whatever was outside the ark. This interpretation corresponds to the Lord’s parable of the two houses, one built upon rock and the other upon sand. When both were struck equally by rain, winds, and rivers, the one founded upon the rock of faith was tested by temptations, whereas the one that had placed its hope in the fleeting pleasures of this life, as though upon sand, was shaken and collapsed.

What Noah, the builder of the ark, is there [Note: Another copy reads, “the builder and ruler Noah”], the foundation-rock is in the house of faith; and what the corrupt and earthward-inclined mind of the giants is outside the ark, the piled-up sand expresses in the house of unbelief.

Thus let the ark signify the Church; let the Flood signify the baptismal font by which she is washed; let the waves signify the temptations of the world by which she is tested; and let it signify the end in which she is crowned. Moreover, Noah, the builder of the ark, typologically announces either the Lord and our Savior himself or any devoted ruler of that same holy Church.

“Make yourself,” he says, “an ark of planed wood.”

Not only the human beings who were saved in the ark, but also the animals that entered it with them, and even the wood from which it was made, mystically signify the faithful of the holy Church. The wood from which it was made is therefore commanded to be planed, because whoever is placed in the structure of the Church [Note: Another copy reads, “in the construction”] by coming to the faith must first be cut away from the root of his former way of life through the instruction or correction of those who preceded him in Christ. He must remove whatever he discovers in himself that is harmful, crooked, or deformed [Note: Another copy reads, “harmful,”], and must conform himself entirely in mind and action to the rule of catholic faith and truth, so that, in the order of the heavenly building, the new man may be suitably placed in his own position at the proper time.

For “planed wood,” an ancient translation has “squared wood,” which likewise refers to the perfection of the elect. However one turns a square, it will stand and cannot be vulnerable to any fall. So, too, the mind of the elect remembers to preserve the unshaken state of its devout purpose, whatever temptations may confront it.

“You shall make compartments in the ark.”

All the dwellings in the ark were arranged as receptacles for the various animals that were to enter it. Likewise, in the Church there are many orders of discipline according to the diversity of those who come to the faith. The life or conduct of married people and of the continent, of sinners and of rulers, should not be one and the same.

To one person it is said: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: you shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness” (Matthew 19:17), and the rest of this kind. To another it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor” (ibid., 21).

Therefore, concerning the reward of eternal recompense, the Lord also says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). There are thus compartments in the ark because not everyone in the Church has the same merit, nor is everyone at the same stage of progress in the faith, although all are contained within one faith and are washed in the same baptism.

“And you shall coat it with pitch inside and outside, and thus you shall make it.”

Pitch is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive. Its property is that wood smeared with it [Note: Another copy reads, “coated with it”] can neither be eaten away by worms nor dissolved by the heat of the sun, the blasts of the winds, or the inundation of waters. What else, then, can pitch mystically signify but the steadfastness of faith?

The ark is pitched inside and outside and is thus perfected in its entirety, when both the thoughts and the works of the elect are fortified in every respect by the power of faith, so that they may neither be overcome nor deceived by any assaults of vices.

“The length of the ark shall be 300 cubits, its width 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits.”

The length of the ark signifies the long-suffering of patience, by which adversities are bravely endured; its width, the breadth of charity, by which even those who inflict adversities are embraced; and its height, the loftiness of hope, through which eternal recompense is granted in heaven.

The length of the ark is rightly commanded to be 300 cubits, a number which, as we have indicated above, is represented in Greek by the letter Τ (*tau*). This letter is written in the form of a cross, because the holy Church, while enduring adversity undefeated and steadfast, follows the traces of the Lord’s Passion, mindful of his saying: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:38).

Its width extends to 50 cubits. In this number the Holy Spirit is sent, and in the Law universal rest and remission are granted to the people of God, because the love of God is poured into our hearts not through the merit of our action but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

This is our rest and the remission of our debts [Note: Another copy reads, “of our sins”]: when we love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength; our neighbor in God as ourselves; and our adversary for God’s sake.

Its height is 30 cubits, because this is the one and only hope of the elect: that through observance of the Decalogue of the Law, which is fulfilled in love of God and neighbor, they may ascend to contemplation of the Holy Trinity. Three times ten makes thirty.

There is another noteworthy mystery in the form of the ark: it is shown to have been shaped according to the measure of the human body. The length of the human body, from the crown of the head to the feet, is six times its breadth, which extends from one side to the other, and ten times its height, measured from the back to the belly, as when one measures a person lying on his back or face down. From the head to the feet, the body is six times longer than the breadth from right to left or left to right, and ten times longer than its height from the ground.

Thus the ark was made 300 cubits in length, 50 in width, and 30 in height. Since the Apostle says that the Church is one body and one spirit in Christ, it was fitting that the ark, which bore this figure, should be formed in the likeness of a human body. For Christ himself, our God and Lord, also willed to become incarnate for us and, through the sacraments of his humanity, to wash and consecrate us from sins.

It was therefore fitting that he should command the ark, in which he had decreed to save the remnants of the human race while the wicked perished, to be made in the form of a human body. Likewise, the temple that Solomon made for the Lord prefigured not only his Church but also his very flesh, which he took from the Virgin. He testified to this himself when he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The evangelist adds: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21).

So, too, the ark that Noah made in the figure of the human body bore the type of us, of whom the Apostle said: “Until we all attain to a perfect man” (Ephesians 4:13). It also bore the type of the Lord himself, who, through the mystery of his Incarnation, deigned to gather us into the unity of faith, cleanse us from sins by the grace of the Holy Spirit—which the dove, bringing the *oliva* (olive [branch]) to the ark, signified—illuminate us, and save us from the destruction of the perishing world.

“You shall make a window in the ark, and you shall complete its summit with a cubit.” [Note: Another copy reads, “in cubits.”]

The window is commanded to be made in the ark so that, after the rains had ceased and the ark had come to rest, Noah could send out a bird through it to determine whether the waters had already ceased, whether the earth had dried out, or whether it had begun to produce vegetation. Through the opened window he could also see the light of heaven.

Hence, in Hebrew, the term for window is said to mean “midday,” because windows are ordinarily illuminated most brightly by the midday sun. This also agrees most suitably with spiritual mysteries. For the window that illuminated the inhabitants of the ark with the splendor of the midday sun only after the Flood had passed signifies the knowledge of heavenly mysteries, which is more fully revealed to baptized believers.

The statement that the summit of the ark was completed with one cubit [Note: Another copy reads, “in cubits”] appears to mean that at the bottom it had 300 cubits of length and 50 cubits of width. As the corners were gradually drawn inward, however, it was gathered at the top into a space of one cubit, becoming proportionately shorter and narrower as it became higher.

As far as the practical demands of rain and Flood are concerned, no other form of ark could have been more suitable than one from whose narrow roof peak the torrents of rain could run off while the floodgates of heaven were opened and rain fell for so long a time. But this form of the ark also mystically suits the condition of the holy Church.

Just as the ark was broader below, where it is believed to have held the beasts, and narrower above, where it contained human beings and birds, until it reached the measure of one cubit at the summit, so the Church contains more carnal people than spiritual ones. It has more people who, like quadrupeds, are inclined toward the desire for earthly things with the whole gaze of their minds than those who, on the wings of the virtues, seek heavenly things. And the holier people are within it, the fewer they are found to be, until one arrives at the Mediator between God and human beings, who appeared among human beings as a human being, yet is God blessed above all forever.

“You shall place the door of the ark in its side, below.”

This door, through which the human beings and all the animals that were to be saved in the ark entered [Note: Another copy omits “both human beings and all”], signifies the unity of faith, without which no one can enter the Church: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. It is appropriately commanded to be placed in the side of the ark because it signifies the door that was opened in the side of the Lord and Savior, who had been placed upon the cross, by the soldier’s spear. Immediately blood and water came forth from it. Through these sacraments each of the faithful is received into the fellowship of the holy Church, as into the interior of the ark.

The door of the ark is commanded to be made not only in the side but also below, so that the humility either of the Lord himself, through which he died for us, or of ourselves, without which we cannot be saved, may be signified.

The door of the ark was also made below and near the ground so that the human beings or animals that were to be saved could enter through it and, once inside, immediately ascend to their respective places above. Thus the Lord, appearing in the depths of this mortality, was wounded for our iniquities, so that, redeemed through the sacraments of his wounds, he might lead us by an invisible ascent to the heavenly dwelling places of the virtues and, in the present life, to the rewards above in heaven.

This is also aptly signified in Solomon’s temple by the door through which one ascended to the upper rooms. [Note: Another copy reads *quod* (“which/that”) for *quo* (“through which”).] Of it, it is written: “The door of the middle side was on the right side of the house.” Some understand this statement as though it meant that the temple had an entrance on its southern side, but that was far from the case. If this were what Scripture intended, it could simply have said: “It had a door toward the south,” or “toward the south wind.”

Instead, the temple itself had its entrance toward the rising of the sun. When it says, “The door of the middle side was on the right side of the house,” the right side of the house is called the southern part of the house. In the middle of that side was the door through which one ascended to the upper rooms. The entrance began on the eastern part of that same side, namely, at the very corner, and proceeded gradually upward through the interior of the middle wall to the upper chambers. [Note: Another copy reads *protendente* (“stretching onward”).] Hence what follows is added: “They ascended by a spiral stairway to the middle chamber, and from the middle chamber to the third.”

Since the Lord, when he said to the Jews, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), was speaking about the temple of his body, is it not plainly evident that the door on the right side of this temple is the very door that was opened in his right side after his Passion, as we said above? Through its opening we pass from the present life of the holy Church to the eternal rest of souls in the future life, following the example of those who entered through the right side of the temple and ascended by a spiral staircase to the middle chamber.

After the blessed rest of souls, we will also reach the reception of spiritual bodies, ascending as though from the middle chamber to the third. From there we shall rejoice with God in the perpetual immortality of both together—that is, of soul and body. [Note: Another copy reads, “with the Lord.”]

“You shall make chambers and three stories in it.”

“Three stories” signifies a threefold roof. For *stegē* in Greek means “roof”; hence the ancient interpreters rendered this word by “having two chambers” and “having three chambers.” Indeed, in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Apostle Paul raised from the dead [Note: Another copy reads *suscitavit* (“raised”)] the young man who had fallen, he is said to have fallen from the third roof or chamber. In Greek it is written that he fell from the *tristegon*.

The chambers and the three stories, as the ancient translators said—being two-chambered and three-chambered—were made in the ark so that animals of different kinds might remain in seats divided in various ways. [Note: Another copy reads, “in many ways.”] The beasts were presumably below, the clean animals above them, and human beings and birds in the highest places.

For it is clear that where the human being sat, there too were the raven and the dove, and consequently the other birds as well, in the vicinity of the window, which must be believed to have been made in the highest parts of the ark. Through it Noah sent out the birds mentioned above to see what the surface of the earth was like.

Various compartments were also made in these stories, as was said above, to separate the same animals and birds, lest some harm others—lest the fiercer harm the gentler.

It was not without reason that Scripture said that chambers and three stories were made in the ark, or that it was made two-chambered and three-chambered, when it could have said in one word that it was arranged with five chambers or roofs. It called it two-chambered to signify that circumcision and uncircumcision, Jews and Greeks, would be saved in the Church.

It called it three-chambered on account of the threefold fruit of the Gospel seed: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. Thus in the lowest chamber marital chastity dwells, above it widowhood, and above that virginity.

Origen says that the lower part of the ark was made two-chambered so that the lowest region might receive refuse and the second be assigned to the preservation of food. In the upper part it was three-chambered, so that in the first section the beasts might have their lairs, in the second the gentler animals their stalls, and in the highest human beings their dwelling.

“Behold, I will bring the waters of the Flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall be consumed. And I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark—you and your sons,” and so forth.

The waters of the Flood brought upon the earth killed all flesh that was found outside the ark, but Noah and all that were in the ark were saved. The water of baptism, washing the world, saves all whom it finds faithfully remaining in the unity of the holy Church. Those who receive baptism outside the Church from heretics or schismatics perish unless they recover by returning to catholic unity.

Likewise, when the moment of the final judgment arrives, all who are found persevering in faith and action within the holy Church will be saved forever. Those who are separated from the Church either in faith, or in works, or in both, will perish.

Take with you, therefore, from all the foods that can be eaten, and store them with you; and they shall be food both for you and for them. [Col. 0092A] And the Lord filled his Church in many ways with the nourishment of spiritual life: [Note: [Col. 0091D] Al.: “in diverse ways” (*multifarie*).] he invited the multitudes of the faithful to receive heavenly rewards through the general ordinances of his commandments, and called all who were more perfect, through the disciplines of stricter observance, to the higher gifts of that same everlasting kingdom.

But it is commonly asked whether the ark, with the capacity attributed to it, could have carried all the animals said to have entered it, together with their food. Origen attempts to resolve this question by the geometric cubit, asserting that Scripture did not say without reason that Moses had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who loved geometry. He says that a geometric cubit was worth as much as six of our cubits. If, therefore, we understand such large cubits, [Col. 0092B] there is no question that the ark had sufficient capacity to contain all those things. [Note: [Col. 0091D] St. Augustine, Book I, Questions on Genesis, question 4.]

It should be noted, however, that if Moses had learned geometric cubits, he nevertheless knew that the people for whom he was writing the book were unacquainted with these arts; nor did he wish to deceive them by writing what that people could not truly understand, but only he himself together with the most learned Egyptians could understand. We must also observe that Moses, when writing about the construction of the tabernacle, recorded cubits not of another kind but of the same kind that he had used for the ark. [Note: [Col. 0091D] Al.: “marked” (*notabat*).] For, writing in the same work and for the same readers or hearers, he could not have introduced something different. [Note: [Col. 0092D] Al.: “contrary” (*adversum*).] If, then, he also used geometric cubits there, the tabernacle itself was not, as we read, thirty cubits long and ten cubits high and wide, but, with this number multiplied sixfold, [Col. 0092C] it had [Note: [Col. 0092D] Al.: “multiplied sixfold” (*sexcuplato*).] a length of one hundred eighty cubits and a height and width of sixty cubits. Thus it was much longer and wider than Solomon’s temple, which had only forty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width. [Note: [Col. 0092D] Al.: sixty.]

The boards of the tabernacle itself, which are said to have been ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide, would have been sixty cubits long and nine cubits wide; [Note: [Col. 0092D] Al. reads “ninety cubits” (*nonagenos*) for “nine” (*novenos*).] and they would have been larger than either ordinary forests generally produce, or such a building requires, or human hands could easily carry. The coverings, too, with which it was covered, each said to have been thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, would have been one hundred eighty cubits long and twenty-four wide. But Josephus also prevents us from understanding these measurements in this way. [Note: [Col. 0092D] Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book III, chapter 6.] Writing about the construction of the tabernacle, he says:

> “The ark, then, was made five palms long and three palms wide. For this reason Moses wrote in Exodus that the ark was two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide; and, according to Josephus’s testimony, these are to be understood as ordinary, not geometric, cubits.”

Concerning Noah’s ark, therefore, we must take a deeper view: everything that happened in it or in relation to it was filled with miracles of divine power. [Col. 0093A] For if matters had proceeded according to ordinary human custom, how could eight people have sufficed to provide daily food and drink for so great a multitude of birds, cattle, beasts, and reptiles, and to perform all the other services that necessity demanded? [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al.: “to bring” (*afferre*).] [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al.: “requires” (*poscit*) for “demands” (*deposcit*).] Especially since Scripture reports no command from God concerning water to be brought into the ark. How could the dung and urine of so many animals fail either to make the place intolerably foul for the animals themselves or to damage the bottom of the ark, however well it had been coated with pitch? [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al. omits *non*: “would damage.”] How could birds that remained in one place for an entire year without flying, and quadrupeds without walking, fail to lose the use of flight or movement?

The Lord himself, therefore, who preserved the ark and all that it carried unharmed, and who guided it so that it would not drift into the sea but settled it in such a place among the mountains [Col. 0093B] that all the animals contained in it could easily and readily leave by the door it possessed, also provided for them how they might feed in the ark and remain safe. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al.: “foresaw” (*praevidit*) for “provided” (*providit*).] It is not unreasonable to believe, as some maintain, that Noah prepared for each animal entering the ark food sufficient for one day’s use, and that, after each had been refreshed, they thereafter remained quiet—or even fell asleep—by divine direction until the day of their departure. This signified the mystery that in the Church all of us are refreshed according to the measure of our individual capacity by the food of life.

Thus Noah did everything that God had commanded him. And the Lord said to him: “Enter, you and your whole household, into the ark,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al. reads: “Enter into the ark, you and all your household.”] He did everything that God had commanded: that is, he built the ark and, after arranging the compartments, stored food in it for all the animals. [Col. 0093C]

“Of all the clean animals, take seven and seven, male and female; but of the unclean animals, two and two, male and female. And likewise of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, so that their seed may be preserved upon the face of the whole earth.” [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al. omits “of the sky.”] [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al. omits “whole.”] When he says “seven and seven,” he does not wish seven pairs to be taken from each species, but only seven, one of which, left over from the pairs, could be offered to God after the flood. He says “seven and seven” because of the many species of animals that had to be included in this number.

Similarly, when he says “two and two,” he does not designate two pairs in each species of unclean animal, but only two, a male and a female. [Note: [Col. 0093D] Al.: “two pairs.”] He says “two and two” because the same pairs had to be taken from many species of animals. Here it is readily evident to anyone that, if the matter had been undertaken only for the preservation of the species and not for the sake of a higher mystery, a smaller number of animals would have sufficed for preserving the restoration of their offspring. [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al.: “for restoring.”]

But since not all who undergo the washing of baptism in the Church also preserve the purity of good works, unclean animals enter the ark together with the clean. And appropriately the clean are contained under the number seven, because the grace of the Spirit is sevenfold, by which the hearts of the faithful are cleansed and sanctified. The unclean are included under the number two, because false Catholics receive the sacraments of faith with a divided heart: in this life wishing to rejoice with the world, and in the future to reign with Christ. Of such people James says: “Let that man not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord, being a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:7). [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al. omits “is.”]

Thus Noah did everything that the Lord had commanded him. He was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood inundated the earth. [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al. omits “upon the earth.”] And Noah entered, with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, with him into the ark, and so forth. [Col. 0094B]

Noah’s age signifies the great perfection of those who enter the Church and attain eternal joys through faith and action worthy of faith. Six times one hundred makes six hundred; and the number six, in which the world was made or formed, appropriately signifies the perfection of good action. [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al.: “signifies the actions of good perfection.”] The number one hundred, which, as we recalled above, is transferred in digital reckoning from the left hand to the right, especially suits those who at the final judgment will stand at the Judge’s right hand and hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34). Therefore the number one hundred, multiplied by six, signifies that perfection of spiritual virtues which is not displayed outwardly for human approval, but is accomplished for the glory of the Creator in hope of heavenly reward. And rightly the master of the ark, in which the state of the Church is represented, also signifies, in the time of his life, the devotion of those who enter it in such a way that they may deserve to pass into eternal salvation through the merits of good action. [Col. 0094C] [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al.: “to have passed.”]

This may also rightly be understood in the following way: when the waters of the flood signify the wave of baptism, Noah’s age indicates the perfection toward which those who are baptized ought to strive. But when the time of the final judgment is prefigured, that same number of his years figuratively declares what sort of people will enter with the Lord into everlasting rest—for “Noah” means “rest”—namely, those worthy of entrance into heaven through the accomplishment of good works and the intention of a pure heart.

“And when seven days had passed, the waters of the flood inundated the earth.” The seventh day, the Sabbath, indicates the rest of the life to come. When, therefore, the flood signifies the water of baptism, it appropriately comes after seven days from the completion of the ark, because we are baptized in hope of everlasting rest. [Note: [Col. 0094D] Al.: “in hope.”] But when the waves of temptations are represented by the waters of the flood, they likewise rightly come after seven days, because on account of their faith the righteous suffer persecution in hope of future blessings from those wretched people who prefer earthly goods to heavenly ones and temporal things to what endures. When, however, the flood is compared with the arrival of the final judgment, it likewise fittingly inundates the earth after seven days, because then all the elect who have borne Christ’s gentle yoke and light burden find rest for their souls.

“In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, all the fountains of the great abyss were burst open, and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.”

Among the Hebrews, months are counted only according to the course of the moon, from one new moon to the next. Their first month, in which it was commanded that the Passover be celebrated and in which the world was made, is called Nisan, which we call April. The second is Jair, which we call May. On its seventeenth day—that is, when the moon of that month was seventeen days old—the flood came, when on that very day Noah had entered the ark with all the people, animals, and birds that were to be saved through it. This is what follows:

“On that day Noah entered the ark, together with Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his sons, his wife, and the three wives of his sons. They and every animal according to its kind,” and so forth, until it says: “and all the birds entered in to Noah into the ark.”

All the animals, therefore, entered the ark on one and the same day. Noah did not labor with great effort and over a long period to gather them and bring or drive them into the ark; rather, compelled by divine direction, they all came of their own accord, each according to its number. Noah himself went first with his children and wives; the animals followed in order, and, with the Lord directing them, each entered its own compartment as though by its own will. This is the force of what is said about the birds: “They entered in to Noah into the ark,” and earlier, in general terms: “Of everything that moves upon the earth, two and two entered in to Noah into the ark.”

On that same day, that is, on the seventeenth day of the second month, the following also took place:

“And the Lord shut him in from outside, and the flood was upon the earth for forty days.”

This was the eighth day from the time the entire structure of the ark had been completed. [Note: [Col. 0095D] Al.: “the building of the ark was completed.”] From this it is evident that the ark was made on the tenth day of that same second month, in a great mystery. [Col. 0095D]

The first month can suitably be understood as that ancient people gathered from the Hebrews by God. The second month, however, signifies the people of the New Testament. For this reason the Law commands that anyone who was unclean because of a dead body, or was far away on a journey, [Note: [Col. 0095D] Al.: “on a journey.”] or was prevented by any other necessity from celebrating the Passover in the first month, should celebrate it in this second month with the blood of the lamb and unleavened bread, on the fourteenth day at evening.

We are signified by the addition of this month: we could not celebrate the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion with the former people of God, since we were still far away from the fellowship of the saints, unclean, indeed dead in sins. But after those sacraments of the Lord’s Incarnation had been accomplished, we came to faith and, as it were, in the light of the second month celebrate the Lord’s Passover. On the tenth day of that month the ark was completed, because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, promised us the denarius of the heavenly kingdom and granted us, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, the ability to fulfill the Decalogue of the Law.

That grace may also be represented by the number seven of the days during which, after the ark had been completed, its entry and the arrival of the flood were awaited. [Note: [Col. 0095D] Al.: “which” (*qui*).] For once the promise of the kingdom, expressed by the denarius, has been received, the grace of the Spirit is given to the faithful, through which they may be joined to the members of the holy Church.

We may also rightly understand why the ark was drenched by the flood on the seventeenth day of the month and not earlier: each of the faithful must first be catechized in faith for receiving true rest and the heavenly denarius—that is, the image of the eternal King—and only then be admitted into the fellowship of the Church through the washing of regeneration.

But because the fountains of the great abyss were burst open on account of the flood, and the floodgates—that is, the windows of heaven—were opened, Scripture’s name “the great abyss” signifies the Old Testament. [Note: [Col. 0096D] Al. omits “of heaven.”] For a long time it had been closed by the veil of the letter and could not open the veins of spiritual understanding to the world; but, revealed through the Lord, it now also supplies the Church with very abundant fountains of saving knowledge. The opened floodgates of heaven signify the outpouring of evangelical and apostolic preaching, which visibly irrigates earthly hearts from above. Since, therefore, we are confirmed in the faith of regeneration both by the revealed words of prophecy and by the heralds of the New Testament preaching openly, it is rightly said that, to bring about the flood, all the fountains of the great abyss were burst open and the floodgates of heaven opened.

The Lord shut the ark from outside because he always protects his Church, rejoicing in the cleansing of holy baptism, with heavenly protection, so that none of those whom he has predestined for life may perish by any means. He also guards the Church, laboring amid the waves of the world, on every side, so that it cannot be crushed or submerged by the pressures or pleasures of the age. “The Lord sends his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.” [Note: [Col. 0096D] Al.: “will send” (*immittet*).]

On the day of judgment, too, the Lord shuts Noah and the inhabitants of the ark in from outside, [Note: [Col. 0096D] Al.: “will shut in” (*includet*).] when, having placed his elect with him in his Father’s house, he permanently bars the door of the kingdom against the lost—even those who repent too late—according to the Gospel parable of the ten virgins, where it is said that those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, “and the door was shut,” and so forth.

It is rightly said that it rained upon the earth for forty days and forty nights. [Note: [Col. 0096D] Al.: “it should rain” (*plueret*).] Ten multiplied four times makes forty, because every guilt of sin committed against the ten commandments of the Law, throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts, is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism—whether that guilt was contracted during the “days,” through prosperity in worldly affairs, or during the “nights,” through adversity in worldly affairs.

“And the waters increased and lifted the ark high above the earth; the waters inundated the earth exceedingly, and everything was filled upon the surface of the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0097D] Al. omits “the waters.”] The waters of baptism and of faith, multiplied throughout the whole world, raise the Church from desire for earthly things toward the hope and longing for heavenly life. The tribulations that frequently assail the Church also raise it: the more violently they filled everything, the more forcefully they drove it to seek the joys of the life to come. [Note: [Col. 0097D] Al.: “to acquire” (*ad acquirenda*) for “to seek” (*ad quaerenda*).] This is well represented in sacred history when it says that the Amorite oppressed the sons of Dan in the mountain and did not give them room to descend to the lower ground.

“Amorite” means *bitter*; “Dan” means “judging” or “judgment.” And whom else do the sons of Dan signify but those who carefully examine everything they do, to determine whether it is right, on the scale of truth; who, walking by the light of God’s word, swear and resolve to keep his judgments of righteousness? And whom do those represented by the Amorite signify but those who attempt to disturb or even overturn the sweetness of the saints’ life through the bitterness of tribulations?

The Amorite oppresses the sons of Dan in the mountain and does not allow them to descend to lower ground when so great a storm of persecutions generally afflicts the elect that they are in no way permitted to indulge in weak thoughts for any length of time. Rather, living in complete restraint, they must continually devote themselves to prayers, fasts, and meditation on the divine Scriptures, so that through greater exercise of the virtues they may overcome the greater struggles of temptations.

Moreover, the ark was carried upon the waters, and the waters prevailed exceedingly, and all the lofty mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The mountains signify all the proud who exalt themselves in the glory of this age. The waters cover these mountains, but the ark is carried above the waters themselves, because the flood of temptations crushes and submerges the proud and ungodly, while it is overcome by the righteous, who do not cease, with a free course of good works and an eager mind, to make for the harbor of eternal salvation.

This was well prefigured when Peter crossed the sea toward the Lord, because the Church, treading underfoot the waves of the world, was destined to reach the tranquility of heavenly life. Likewise, the waters of the flood raise the ark on high, cover and conceal the mountains, because the sacrament of baptism, by which the Church is exalted, despises the proud height of the world and shows it to be worthless. And because we are baptized in hope of the future rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies to eternal life, which carnal wisdom does not know, it is rightly added:

“The water was fifteen cubits higher than the mountains that it had covered.” [Note: [Col. 0097D] Al.: “cubits.”]

Seven and eight make fifteen. Seven pertains to the rest of souls that will follow death, since the Lord rested in the tomb on the seventh day, the Sabbath. But because after the Sabbath, that is, on the eighth day, he rose from the dead, eight most appropriately indicates the time of our resurrection. Thus the water rises fifteen cubits—that is, seven and eight—above the lofty mountains, because the faith of the Church, sanctified in the fountain of saving baptism, surpasses in hope of future rest and immortality every arrogance of carnal philosophy. That philosophy knows how to argue subtly about the creation of the world, but knows nothing to say about the Creator of the world or about the life of the saints that exists above the world.

“And the waters prevailed over the earth for one hundred fifty days.” This number also pertains to the same mystery as the number fifteen. Since seventy is named from seven and eighty from eight, the two numbers joined together make one hundred fifty. For one hundred fifty days the waters prevailed over the earth, commending and confirming, as I have said, the same action of baptism in consecrating the new man to hold fast to faith in rest and resurrection.

“And God remembered Noah, and all the animals and all the cattle that were with him in the ark, and he brought a spirit over the earth, and the waters abated.”

The Spirit himself, the life-giving Spirit of God, may be understood by the name “Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 0098D] Al. omits “of God.”] Of him it was said at the beginning: “And the Spirit of God was moving over the waters” (Genesis 1:3). There is no doubt that, just as then, by gathering the waters together, he dried the earth in one place, so now, by removing the waters of the flood, he again revealed the face of the earth.

This airy wind may also be called “Spirit,” according to the Psalmist’s words: “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still” (Psalm 106:25). Through its frequent blasts, waters are often diminished or moved from their place. Thus it is said in Exodus: “And when Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord took it away, blowing with a strong wind throughout the whole night, and turned it into dry land; and the water was divided” (Exodus 14:27). [Note: [Col. 0098D] Al.: “and the water was divided.”]

“And the fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven were closed, and the rains from heaven were stopped; and the waters returned from the earth, going and returning, and began to diminish after one hundred fifty days.”

In saying that the waters returned from the earth, going and returning, the text plainly indicates, in its literal sense, that all the courses of rivers and streams return through the hidden veins of the earth to the primal abyss, according to Solomon’s words: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, there they return, so that they may flow again” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

Mystically, however, after one hundred fifty days the fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven are closed, the rains cease, and the waters return because, after the words of the sacred oracle have instructed us in faith and hope of perpetual rest and immortality, they will no longer teach us. They will have nothing greater to promise after they have brought us, perfected in the immortal glory of flesh and spirit, to the blessed vision of our Creator. [Col. 0099A] [Note: [Col. 0099D] Al. reads “might have brought [us]” (*pervenerent*) for “have brought [us]” (*adduxerint*).]

Hence the Book of Psalms, which is contained in the number one hundred fifty, is fittingly completed in divine praise. It begins with blessedness arising from self-restraint and meditation on the divine Law, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Psalm 1:1), and so forth. Near its end it commends the new joys of the future age, saying—and at the very end completes everything in the praise of God—“Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the saints” (Psalm 149:1), [Note: [Col. 0099D] Al.: “praise” (*laudatio*) for “his praise” (*laus eius*).] concluding in this way: [Note: [Col. 0099D] Al.: “concluded” (*conclusit*).] “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Psalm 150:6). The one hundred fiftieth psalm is rightly sung and fulfilled entirely in the praise of God, because the sum of all our blessedness is that, dwelling in his house, we may praise him without end.

“And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Armenia.”

That the ark rested in the seventh month refers back to the seventh rest of which we have spoken so often, because all who are perfect, and who, through the steadfastness of a thought fixed upon God, are as though square and firm, tend toward rest. Fittingly the ark reached rest on the twenty-seventh day of that month, since according to arithmetic this number is the solid square of three.

The number three corresponds to the devotion of our mind: through memory we recall God, through understanding we know him, and through the will we love him. But for this trinity to proceed from a simple and straight line to a square, multiply three by three, and the result is nine. For the same square to acquire height and become solid, multiply nine by three; the result is twenty-seven. Thus you complete the solid square of the number three, in which the ark rested, because the Church, as though squared by the stability of its mind and action, both awaits rest in this life and receives it eternally in the life to come.

It rested upon the mountains of Armenia because, having trampled underfoot the summit of worldly pomp, the Church, even while living this pilgrim life, draws near in spirit to heavenly joys.

“But the waters continued and receded until the tenth month.” The tenth month may signify the time when the saints enter with the Lord into the joys of eternal light. In the Gospel, too, under the name of the denarius given to the workers in the vineyard, he signifies the reception of that same heavenly kingdom. A denarius contains ten obols.

The waters, therefore, which had washed over the ark proceed and recede until the tenth month, because the washing of baptism, once it has fulfilled its office in each of the faithful, ceases. For no one, if he sins, can be cleansed again in the same fountain of holy baptism. Rather, baptism sends those already washed and sanctified once to the hope of heavenly life, namely, to the time when they will come and appear before the face of God. [Col. 0100A]

“In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared.”

The first day of the tenth month may be understood as the beginning of that perpetual life in which, even while placed in this life, the saints taste and see that the Lord is good. On that day the tops of the mountains appear, because the more perfectly this takes place in their pure hearts, the more clearly the worldly height that vainly inflates itself is exposed.

“And when forty days had passed, Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent out the raven,” and so forth.

We said above concerning the window of the ark, which is opened after the flood has passed, that it represents the mysteries of heavenly things by which the baptized are specially initiated. But some use these same mysteries for the allurements of the age, while others use them for works of piety. The former are represented by the raven, the latter by the dove.

The fact that forty is completed by ten multiplied four times may appropriately signify, in the number of forty days, the fulfillment of the divine Law, which is perfected through the grace of the Gospel. The Law is contained in ten commandments; the teaching of the Gospel is set forth in four books. Fittingly, after the beginning of the tenth month, after the tops of the mountains have appeared, forty days pass, and then Noah, opening his window, makes an entrance for the new light into the ark.

For Christ reveals to his faithful the future life that they will receive, and, by revealing the pride of those who stand outside the Church and boast of worldly glory, he also shows his faithful that the commandments of the Law must be fulfilled not by the powers of human freedom but through evangelical grace, by his gift. Once they have received both this faith and the humility of asking for divine assistance in all things, they then deserve to know the higher gifts of the heavenly homeland, as though the window in the ark had newly been opened.

But, as we have said, some use this same knowledge of heavenly gifts to their own destruction, while others use it for salvation. [Note: [Col. 0099D] On *eadem … cognitione*: the verb *utor* is not rarely construed with the accusative, as in Cicero, *Academica*: “and they used what they had received from their predecessors”; and in Varro: “let us use what is useful rather than abuse what is useless.”] Hence what follows concerning the raven sent out from the ark is appropriate.

“Which went out and returned until the waters were dried from the earth.” He does not say, “It went out and returned into the ark,” but says, “It went out and returned until the waters were dried from the earth.” [Note: [Col. 0100D] Al. omits “from the earth.”] It flew uncertainly back and forth, sometimes beginning to depart, sometimes returning to the ark as though it were about to enter, [Note: [Col. 0100D] Al.: “then” (*tunc*).] yet not returning to the window from which it had gone out. Rather, it wandered outside until, when the waters had receded, it found rest and a dwelling for itself outside the ark.

Those who have indeed been instructed and imbued with heavenly sacraments but do not put off the blackness of earthly pleasure, preferring the broad paths of the world to the confines of ecclesiastical life, are rightly compared with its departure and wandering. [Note: [Col. 0100D] Al.: “then.”]

“And he also sent out the dove after it, to see whether the waters had now ceased from the face of the earth. But when it found no place where the sole of its foot could rest, it returned to him into the ark. For the waters were upon the whole earth. And he stretched out his hand, took it, and brought it into the ark.”

As we have said, the dove represents the spiritual and simple mind of the elect. Once the window of heavenly contemplation has been opened to them, the more cautiously they despise everything that rolls about below, the more deeply they behold the joys that endure forever. Like this dove, such people look down upon all the pleasures of the age as though flying higher, so that they do not wish to touch them even with the lowest traces of their minds. For they can find no true rest for themselves in this world, whose adversities and prosperities alike are carried along, wandering and uncertain, like waters.

They strive not only to remain within the enclosures of the Church themselves, but also, as far as they can, to bring others into it by their example or exhortation. Hence it is rightly added:

“And after waiting seven more days, he again sent the dove out of the ark. And it came to him toward evening, carrying in its beak a fresh olive branch with green leaves.”

The olive branch found outside and brought into the ark in the dove’s beak represents [Note: [Col. 0101D] Al.: “brought inside from the dove’s beak.”] those who indeed receive baptism outside the Church, but, fruitful through the richness of charity and whole in pious intention, are green like leaves. Many of them, at a later time, as though toward evening, are recalled to the Church through the reconciliation of spiritual men, as though by the mouth of the dove. This rightly happened after seven days from the time the dove itself had found no rest outside.

The number seven of the days is mystically suited to the light of spiritual grace, because spiritual men, after withdrawing their minds from carnal desires, attempt, prompted by that same spirit of grace, to withdraw others from them as well. [Note: [Col. 0101D] Al.: “and the dove may be able to signify.”]

The dove, which, after the flood, brought an olive branch into the ark through the opened window, may also be understood to prefigure what happened when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan: the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. When the individual sons of the Church receive baptism, the bishop lays his hand upon them through the anointing of the most holy chrism, so that they may receive the Holy Spirit and the door of the heavenly kingdom may be opened to them.

This figure is appropriately matched by the fact that the raven had gone out before the olive was brought in through the dove, [Note: [Col. 0101D] Al.: “after” (*post*) for “before” (*ante*).] and did not return to the ark. Thus the prophecy did not pass over in silence the faithlessness of Simon. He was baptized in the Church, but, before he received the grace of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, he was expelled from the Church, because, being full of the gall of bitterness, he bore in his heart not the innocence of dove-like simplicity but rather the blackness of the raven, in a heart not pious but malicious.

Noah understood, therefore, that the waters had ceased from the earth. Nevertheless, he waited another seven days and sent out the dove, which did not return to him again. [Col. 0102A]

The dove that, when the waters had ceased, went out from the ark upon the earth and did not return signifies the souls of the saints leaving this life for the free light of the heavenly homeland and no longer returning to earthly existence. In that homeland, just as prophecy will be abolished, knowledge will pass away, and tongues will cease, so also the water of baptism will dry up. But charity will never fall, through which the unchangeable truth and life will forever be seen and praised as ever present. [Note: [Col. 0102D] Al.: “the water of baptism.”] [Note: [Col. 0102D] Al.: “will not fall.”] [Note: [Col. 0102D] Al.: “the unchangeable way and truth.”]
