And because it is not only a heavenly gift that we may do good, but also that after good works we may attain eternal life, the dove rightly went out not only after seven days to bring an olive shoot into the ark, but, after bringing the olive, went out again after another seven days, so that it might enjoy the open sight of the sun and, as it were, of a new world.

“For the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus,” and “from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace”—namely, the grace of reward in return for the grace of good action.

Therefore, in the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters [Note: [Col. 0102D] Another reading: “were diminished.”] had changed upon the earth. Noah opened the covering of the ark and looked out; and he saw that the surface of the earth had dried.

By “the covering of the ark” he means its uppermost board, concerning which it had previously been said: “And you shall finish it to a cubit at the top.” In this covering, one cubit long and wide, we said that the Mediator between God and humanity is signified: he wished to be joined humanly to the members of his Church, yet by the dignity of his power he uniquely transcended her and protected her entirely from above.

Noah opened this covering when the flood had withdrawn, because, once the sacrament of baptism has been celebrated, it is necessary that the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation be disclosed more diligently, in due course, by the mouths of teachers, so that, having learned what he did and taught in the flesh, the faithful may follow his footsteps by imitating him according to their ability.

And very appropriately this is said to have happened first after six hundred years, in the first month, on the first day of the month, so that the beginning of the year, month, and day might also indicate the new beginning of spiritual life that was to be undertaken by the faithful. Indeed, the same month in which the Passover was commanded to be celebrated is called the month of new things, surely on account of the great mystery of the renewal of our former life through Christ’s Passion.

In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was completely dry. It was said above that at the beginning of the first month the surface of the earth had dried; and now, when the second month was nearly complete, the earth is described as having become dry throughout, because then the soil was dried on the surface, where green grasses were growing, so that it could become green again and produce anew the grasses that the water had consumed. Now, however, it had also dried so thoroughly within that it could support the footsteps of those walking upon it, and it was so clothed with flowering grasses that it was also suitable for feeding sheep and cattle.

God spoke to Noah, saying:

“Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives with you. Bring out with you every living creature that is with you, of every kind of flesh, both birds and beasts and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth. Bring them out with you, and enter upon the earth. Increase and [Note: [Col. 0103D] Another reading: “multiply upon it.”] multiply, and fill it.”

So Noah went out, and his sons, and all the rest.

The same mysteries of Christ’s Church are often repeated in many forms and through many kinds of figurative representation. Accordingly, Noah’s departure from the ark onto land cleansed by the flood, together with the human beings and animals whom he had brought in with him, corresponds figuratively to that time when each of the faithful, washed in the fountain of baptism, proceeds with Christ as his guide—that is, with the spiritual Noah—to perform good works even publicly, and grows and multiplies through the continual increase of spiritual virtues.

“Go,” he says, “into all the world and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Figuratively speaking, this means: bring every kind of living creature into the ark to be cleansed by the waters. He immediately adds: “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid., 20), as though he were saying typologically: After the flood, let the animals go out from the ark and enter upon the new face of the earth, verdant with fresh flowers, [Note: [Col. 0103D] Another reading: “where.”] and there let them multiply and grow.

The fact that they leave the ark on the twenty-seventh day of the month—which, as we stated above, is a solid number, the square of three—signifies the perfection of faith that is consecrated in baptism. It cannot waver in any respect, but must always remain unconquered and steadfast against all the snares of the devil.

It should be noted, in a manner consistent with the literal sense, that those who entered the ark on the seventeenth day of the second month remained in it for a complete solar year, since they came out after a year, on the twenty-seventh day of that same month. For if, for example, on the present day, at the Kalends of April, the moon were seventeen days old, then in the following year, on the day before those same Kalends, it would be twenty-seven days old, after three hundred and sixty-five days had passed in sequence—the number by which the solar year is completed. [Note: [Col. 0103D] Another reading: “the whole year.”]

Thus they were in the ark for an entire year: that is, until the sun, having traversed the zodiacal circle through its twelve months, illuminated all the regions of the world, so that, just as the water covered and washed the whole earth, so the sun, as though cooperating with it, traversed the whole earth during the same period of time and irradiated it with the light of its splendor.

The Lord is figuratively called both the Fountain of Life and the Sun of Justice. [Note: [Col. 0103D] Another reading: “the Fountain who regenerates, the Sun who illuminates us.”] He is the Fountain because he regenerates; the Sun because he illuminates us, according to the Psalmist’s words: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

And during a complete solar year Noah, together with the animals and human beings that were to be saved from the flood, was in the ark, because throughout the entire time of this age and through all the regions of the world the Lord both washes his Church with the water of the saving bath and illuminates her with the grace of his Spirit.

Noah built an altar to the Lord. Taking from all the clean cattle and clean birds, he offered burnt offerings upon the altar.

As a righteous and truly perfect man, after surviving so great a disaster, he immediately gives thanks to the Creator once the altar has been built, while also imploring him not to allow the world to deserve to be struck by such a blow again. And because he makes his petition devoutly and piously, he quickly becomes worthy of being heard. For the text continues:

“The Lord smelled the odor of sweetness, and said to him: I will no more curse the earth because of human beings.”

It was fitting that, as Abel had consecrated the beginning of the first age of the world through sacrifices offered to God, so this holy man, mindful of the future, should consecrate the beginning of the second age after offering sacrifices to God. Abraham and Melchizedek are likewise remembered as having done this at the beginning of the third age. David, king and patriarch of the fourth age, did the same thing on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. Jesus the great priest, and Zerubbabel at the beginning of the fifth age, after restoring the altar destroyed by the Chaldeans, are also reported to have done so in the same place.

All these events prefigured our supreme King and true High Priest, who consecrated the beginning of the sixth age—or rather, the entire sixth age—through the offering of his body and blood to God upon the altar of the holy cross. [Note: [Col. 0103D] Another reading: “would dedicate.”] As for the statement that, when Noah offered his sacrifice, the Lord smelled the odor of sweetness, this does not signify that odor of sweetness which, rising from burning sacrifices, could delight human nostrils; [Note: [Col. 0104D] Another reading omits “of sweetness.”] rather, it signifies the odor of virtues which, proceeding from the most pure heart of the one making the offering, rose into the presence of the divine Majesty.

It was this odor that the patriarch Isaac perceived in his son Jacob when he said: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). [Note: [Col. 0104D] Another reading omits “plentiful.”] It is also the odor of which the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

According to the mystical meanings, Noah very appropriately offers sacrifice after the flood, because this too is the order of our consecration in Christ: first we are washed in the fountain of life, and afterward we are refreshed at the sacred altar by the offering of the Lord. Hence the Apostle says: “But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified” (1 Corinthians 6:11)—washed, namely, in baptism; sanctified by the saving sacrifice; justified by good works. [Note: [Col. 0104D] This indicates the ancient rite of the Church, by which the baptized, raised from the sacred font, immediately became participants in the sacrament of the Eucharist, as we have shown in Book I, On Ancient Church Rites.]

The burnt offerings that were offered to the Lord after the flood from clean animals can also most appropriately signify the holy martyrs. After the washing of baptism, they not only preserved purity of life but also poured out their blood for the Lord.

A holocaust is so called because it is wholly burned; that was the name given to those sacrifices which were entirely consumed by the sacred fire, and from which nothing passed into the use of the offerers. Accordingly, such sacrifices aptly and figuratively correspond to the holy martyrs, who deserved to glorify God not only in their lives but also in their deaths.

The altar upon which these burnt offerings are offered is the heart of the elect, built by our Noah, Christ, and imbued from heaven with the fire of his Spirit, which he sent upon the earth and desired to be kindled intensely.

There are many burnt offerings, but one altar, because the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one, and there was no division among them. The Apostle says: “Be careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:13).

Burnt offerings are offered from all the clean cattle and birds because, from every nation, every kind of human being, and every age, the faithful have attained the palm of martyrdom.

If it is right to believe that there is a distinction between the clean cattle and the clean birds, then the cattle offered as burnt offerings designate those who became martyrs from the common life of God’s people; the birds, however, designate those who, accustomed to seek heavenly things through the frequent flight of contemplation, were also crowned with a precious death.

Thus both clean and unclean animals, whether winged or not, leave the ark washed by the flood, but sacrifice is offered to the Lord only from the clean ones. The faithful rise from the bath of baptism having received forgiveness of sins, yet many of them return after baptism to the filth of sin. Others persevere firmly to the end in the purity of life they have received. Some take such care to preserve the purity once received that they even lay down their lives to guard it.

Since the clean animals and birds had entered the ark seven by seven, it is clear that the burnt offerings offered to the Lord were taken from those that had survived in pairs. And appropriately the birds or cattle numbered seven are appointed for the Lord’s sacrifice, on account of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, whose gift enables the faithful not only to believe in the Lord but also to suffer for him.

The glory of virgins may also most fittingly be signified by the cattle and birds found in the number seven and made into the Lord’s burnt offering. It is contained in an unequal number because, free from the bond of marriage, it chose to lead a celibate life; and it is offered as a burnt offering to the Lord when, neglecting carnal concerns and actions, it consecrates itself entirely to the Creator through the fire of supreme love.

Concerning these John says in the Apocalypse:

“These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were purchased from among humanity as first fruits for God and for the Lamb.” [Note: [Col. 0105D] Another reading: “and they follow.”]

When Noah offered the burnt offerings, the Lord smelled the odor of sweetness, because God the Father graciously accepts, through the grace of Christ, either the passion of the blessed martyrs or the virginal life of the faithful, consecrated and offered to him.

And he said to him:

“I will no more curse the earth because of human beings, for the sense and [Note: [Col. 0105D] Another reading: “knowledge.”] thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from youth. I will not, therefore, strike every living creature again as I have done.”

The Lord promises that he will no longer curse the earth or strike every living creature, because human beings are so prone to sin that even if they were punished again by a flood, nevertheless, once it had passed, they would again entangle themselves in vices and crimes.

Here we must observe [Note: [Col. 0105D] Another reading: “who.”] that, although the sense of the human heart is said to be inclined toward evil from youth—an age from which the incentives of carnal desires ordinarily begin to arise within us—it does not follow that we first become subject to sins from the time of puberty, although from that point a wanton age urges us to commit greater offenses.

There is also that divine sentence [Note: [Col. 0105D] Another reading: “which is said.”] which says: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they go forth from their mother’s womb” (Ecclesiasticus 40:1)—namely, the yoke of the first transgression, on account of which we were all conceived in iniquities and born in sins. From the beginning of youth, however, we willingly add many sins to those burdens under which we came into this world not by our own will but because of the guilt inherited from our father. From all these things we are liberated only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ.

“I will not, therefore,” he says, “strike every living creature again as I have done.” But he makes clear how far this promise of mercy extends by adding [Note: [Col. 0106D] Another reading: “it is said.”]:

“All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease.”

When he had said “all the days,” he immediately added “of the earth,” so that you might understand that during all the days in which the earth will retain its present condition, human beings are to be secure from the assault of a universal flood. Yet there will not fail to come a time [Note: [Col. 0106D] Another reading: “concerning the future time when.”] when, with this yearly succession of passing things having ceased, the entire world together with its living creatures will perish by fire, as Peter testifies:

“The heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and through the water by the word [Note: [Col. 0106D] Another reading: “Word.”] of God; by these the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But the heavens and the earth that now are, by the same word are kept in store, reserved for fire against the day of judgment” (2 Peter 3:5).

Here we must note that the heavens which he says were destroyed by water or will perish by fire should be understood as nothing other than this turbulent air, which is close to the earth and from which the birds are called “birds of heaven” because they fly in it. The ethereal or sidereal heavens will not be consumed by fire, just as they were not consumed by water.

God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them:

“Increase and multiply, and fill the earth. Let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth [Note: [Col. 0106D] Another reading: “living creatures.”] and upon all the birds of heaven, together with everything that moves upon the earth. All the fish of the sea are delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. Just as I gave you the green plants, I have given you everything.”

The literal sense is clear: the second age of the world, like the first and the other ages, is blessed by the Lord at its beginning. Noah is blessed together with his sons—that is, with all those who, born from him in the flesh and endowed with faith and obedience, truly show themselves to be his sons. His offspring are commanded to fill the earth, as is known to have happened. Human beings are declared destined to be a terror to all the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, and these, together with the fish, are granted to them for food, just as they had received the green plants for food [Note: [Col. 0107D] Another reading: “until.”] up to the time of the flood.

Here we must note that, when he commands their terror and dread to be upon the animals, he certainly forbids it to be upon human beings. It is contrary to nature to desire to be feared by one’s equal through pride. Yet it is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects when they discover that those subjects scarcely fear God at all. In demanding fear from those who live perversely, rulers exercise dominion, as it were, not over human beings but over animals, because in whatever respect their subjects are beastlike, in that same respect they ought also to lie subject to fear.

According to the spiritual understanding, Noah is blessed together with his sons—that is, our Lord and Savior with the apostles, whom he also deigned to call sons [Note: [Col. 0107D] Another reading: “to call them sons.”], saying: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew 9:15).

God the Father commanded these men to increase and multiply throughout the whole world when the Lord said to his disciples: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:14)—that is, to all nations.

All the commands of the Lord and Savior are, of course, the commands of the Father. For he himself said: “The things therefore that I speak, even as the Father said to me, so I speak” (John 12:50).

The Father subjected all the animals that move upon the earth, all the birds of heaven, and all the fish of the sea to their authority [Note: [Col. 0107D] Another reading: “lordship.”] when he said: “Whatever you bind [Note: [Col. 0107D] Another reading: “shall bind.”] upon earth shall be bound also in heaven [Note: [Col. 0107D] Another reading: “in the heavens.”]; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

The animals [Note: [Col. 0108D] Another reading: “also.”], birds, and fish signify persons of various dispositions and ways of life. All these are given as food to the sons of Noah after the flood, because, after the Lord had brought the gift of the saving bath to the world, he also wished it to be administered to all nations, saying to the apostles: “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

These creatures are given as food to the sons of Noah in accordance with what was said to Peter when all the four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth were shown to him on a mystical sheet: “Arise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). That is: destroy the Gentiles from the condition in which they had lived wickedly by preaching the truth, and bring them into the members of the Church by initiating them into the sacred mysteries. Hence it is rightly added here:

“Except that you shall not eat flesh with blood.”

Blood appropriately signifies carnal desires and the carnal sense. Blood is poured out when people renounce the carnal allurements and thoughts in which they had lived wickedly, so that they may say with the Apostle: “I live, now not I; but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:29). And again: “Immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood” (Galatians 1:16).

Otherwise, when baptism begins to incorporate into the unity of the holy Church those who continue in their former crimes, it is as though they were eating the animals given [Note: [Col. 0108D] Another reading: “given.”] to them by the Lord together with their blood, because it receives into fellowship people whose former way of life is still held, as though suffocated, within their conscience. It is reported that this was the greatest transgression of the giants: they ate flesh with blood. Therefore, after the Lord had destroyed them by the flood, he permitted human beings to eat flesh [Note: [Col. 0108D] Another reading: “flesh.”] but forbade them to do so with blood.

“For I will require your blood, the blood of your lives, at the hand of every beast, and at the hand of humanity; at the hand of every man and of his brother I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.” [Note: [Col. 0108D] Another reading: “his blood.”]

By “the blood of your lives,” it is figuratively said [Note: [Col. 0108D] Another reading: “it is said.”] that he means the very life by which human beings are sustained, nourished, and live in the flesh through the soul. Likewise, by “the hand of beasts” he figuratively means the act of devouring by which they kill a human being. For who, being in sound mind, would truly believe that human blood belongs to the substance of the soul? Yet the same lawgiver elsewhere appears to speak more explicitly: “For the life of all flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:14).

This was said in the same manner as: “The rock was Christ”—not because it literally was Christ, but because Christ was signified by it. The Law would not have wished to signify the soul through blood—an invisible reality through a visible one—unless blood, diffused through all the veins from the heart itself, held greater dominion in our body than the other fluids, so that wherever a wound has been inflicted, it is blood itself, not another fluid, that emerges.

Thus the soul, which invisibly prevails over all the elements of which we consist, is better signified by that which visibly prevails over all the elements of which we consist.

It is readily understood how God requires the life of a human being from the hand of another human being, seeking vengeance from the one who sinned. But it can rightly be asked how he also requires it from beasts, which lack reason, unless we can understand that the mystery of the future resurrection is indicated here: at that time all the bodies of the human race that were devoured by wild animals, consumed in any other way, or corrupted will be restored incorruptible, and the souls of all human beings, separated from their bodies by whatever kind of death, will each be returned to their own bodies, so that in judgment they may receive eternal life for good merits or eternal death for evil merits together with those same bodies.

Appropriately it is then added:

“Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.”

How many have shed human blood, yet their blood has not been shed? Others have killed a human being by poison or hanging, and yet, although the person has died, no blood has been shed. How, then, will the Lord shed their blood in such a person, when the killer did not shed blood? It is because, as we have said, the blood of a human being must be understood as the very life by which he exists. Whoever sheds it—that is, whoever kills a human being by any kind of death—will have his own blood shed, because through sinning he loses eternal life.

“For the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20). The same meaning is found in what is said to Peter: “For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword.” It is as though he were saying plainly: All who unjustly kill a human being perish in their own soul through that killing.

Appropriately it is then added:

“For humanity was made in the image of God.”

For this reason it is a greater crime to kill an innocent human being: whoever does so not only destroys the work that God made but also corrupts his image.

For this reason God requires human lives from beasts or from human beings by whom they had been driven from the body, because he made humanity in his own image, inasmuch as he willed it to remain for eternity and not to perish [Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “to have perished.”] with the death of the body like the animals. It is also because of this mystery that flesh may not be eaten with blood, so that we may continually be reminded by this command that we were created according to the substance of the soul in the image of our Creator and that we must fear corrupting that same image within us through sin.

God also said this to Noah and to his sons with him:

“Behold, I will establish my covenant with you and with your offspring after you,” and so forth, up to the statement: “Never again shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of the flood, neither shall there be a flood thereafter to destroy the earth.”

The literal sense is clear: the world need no longer fear judgment by water, but judgment by fire. Through frequent repetition the heresy of Origen is refuted and condemned—Origen dared to assert as a dogma that the cycles of infinitely many ages, always running in the same order, would recur.

Mystically, however, the fact that the water of the flood does not return upon the earth signifies that the water of baptism, once received, cannot be repeated. Whoever has been washed does not need to wash again, as the Lord himself testifies (John 13:10). Those who have once been washed by the waters of tribulation and have attained perpetual salvation are not to be immersed [Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “be plunged.”] again in the same waters for purification, but joyfully will sing to their Redeemer forever: “We went through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (Psalm 65:12).

Nor should it seem contrary to the meaning of the saving bath that the waters of the flood are described above with the words: “I will no more curse the earth because of human beings,” or that it is said here: “There shall not be a flood thereafter to destroy the earth,” since the water of baptism ordinarily brings not a curse or destruction upon our mind or flesh but rather blessing and salvation.

We should understand instead that in baptism the Lord in a certain way curses our former way of life and destroys it [Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “these things.”], when he commands us to renounce the devil, all his works, and [Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “his pomp.”] all his pomps. Thus, cleansed at last by a new confession, we may deserve to attain the grace of eternal blessing. [Note: [Col. 0109D] Another reading: “by the confession of a new life.”]

“I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. And when I cover [Note: [Col. 0110D] Another reading: “when I shall have covered.”] the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant with you and with every living soul which gives life to flesh (carne), [Note: [Col. 0110D] Another reading: carnem, “flesh” in the accusative, rather than carne, “by flesh.”] and never again shall the waters of the flood be for destroying all flesh.”

To this day, whenever the bow in the sky is seen, it recalls to our memory the sign of the divine covenant: the earth will not again be destroyed by a flood. But, if it is carefully considered, it also sets before our eyes a sign of the future judgment that will come upon the world through fire.

For it does not shine with a blue and reddish color together without reason. The blue color bears witness to the waters that have passed, while the reddish color bears witness to the flames that [Note: [Col. 0110D] Another reading: “are to come.”] will come.

Appropriately the celestial bow, which they call the Iris, is set as a sign of divine favor. For that bow commonly shines in the clouds and responds, as it were, with a pleasing confession to the rays of the sun by which the dewy darkness is illuminated.

Christ is therefore the Sun of Justice; the clouds illuminated by him are the saints, whose names are written in heaven. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 35:6).

When the bow appears in the clouds, the Lord remembers his promise not to destroy the earth by a flood, because, through the intercessions of the saints—who know how to shine not from themselves but from him—he will show favor to the faithful when they raise the eyes of their minds toward heavenly desires and recognize his glory in the deeds, sayings, and even [Note: [Col. 0110D] Another reading: “lest they themselves.”] their silences, as it were, of the righteous who preceded them, as though in his own clouds.

“And there shall be a bow in the clouds, and I will see it, and I will remember the everlasting covenant that was made between God and every living soul of all flesh that is upon the earth.”

God is said, in human fashion, to remember his covenant when he sees the bow in the clouds. On account of the merits of the saints, who are glorious and heavenly because he himself illuminates them, he spares and has mercy upon our weakness. But he does not himself newly remember anything, since he can never forget anything.

“For he remembered his covenant forever” (Psalm 110:5). Yet he seems then to remember the covenant he made with us when, as we lie in tribulation, he extends the aid of his protection. Hence, appropriately, in the psalm, in the voice of certain afflicted people to whom the help of divine [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading: “power.”] mercy seemed delayed, it is said: “Why do you turn your face away? Do you forget our poverty and our tribulation?” (Psalm 43:24).

“Noah, a husbandman, began to cultivate the earth and planted a vineyard,” and so forth.

It is pleasing often to repeat the Lord’s saying to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote of me” (John 10:46).

For in this reading as well, while Moses constructs the history of Noah and his sons, he figuratively announces the Lord’s Passion, the devotion of the peoples who believe in him, and also the unbelief of those who contradict the faith.

Noah cultivated the earth and planted a vineyard because the Lord, caring for the human race, established the Synagogue among the Jewish people. The Psalmist also mentions this vineyard when he says: “You brought a vineyard [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading: “from Egypt.”] out of Egypt” (Psalm 79:9). And in the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: “A man planted a vineyard, and set a hedge around it” (Luke 20:9), and so forth to the end of the parable, where he says: “What therefore will the lord of the vineyard do to those husbandmen?” They say: “He will destroy those wicked men miserably, and will let out the vineyard to other husbandmen.”

“Drinking wine, he became drunk, and he was uncovered in his tent.”

The Lord drank wine when he accepted the cup of his Passion. He became drunk through drinking when, suffering for us, he reached the extremity of death. He was uncovered in his tent when, among the Jewish people whom he had made his own and among whom he had long been accustomed to dwell as in his own tent, he endured insults and mockery and finally underwent the punishment of the cross, revealing most clearly to all the truth of the mortal substance that he had deigned to assume.

When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw that his father’s nakedness had been exposed, he told his two brothers outside. But Shem and Japheth took a cloak and laid it upon their shoulders; walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away, and they did not see their father’s nakedness.

Ham, who saw his father’s exposed nakedness [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading omits “exposed.”] and mocked him, signifies the Jewish people, who contradicted the faith and did not believe. Facing destruction rather than salvation through it, they took greater pleasure in treating the Passion of our Lord and Savior with contempt than in honoring him. Ham also told his brothers outside what had happened to his father, because through him the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, which had been hidden in prophecy, was disclosed and in a certain way made public.

until we come to the gift of the second generation; hence the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

The two sons—the eldest and the youngest—represent those to whom he subsequently refers, saying: “But to those who are called, Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God; for what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading omits “and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.”] and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.”

Together they carry upon their backs, as one cloak, the one and same mystery of the Lord’s Passion, already past and completed. They do not look upon their father’s nakedness, because they do not consent to Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading: “in Christ’s death.”]; yet they honor it with a covering, as though knowing from where they were born, so that they might be sons of mercy, though in their first birth they had been sons of wrath.

The middle son—that is, the Jewish people—is in the middle because it neither held the primacy of the apostles nor was the last among the Gentiles to believe. He saw his father’s nakedness because he consented to Christ’s death [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading: “in Christ’s death.”].

It is rightly said of the other two that, with their faces turned away, they covered their father’s shame, like those to whom the deed of that wicked vineyard was displeasing. [Note: [Col. 0111D] Another reading omits “namely.”] This vineyard—that is, the Jewish people—figuratively revealed, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, how far it had degenerated [Note: [Col. 0112D] Another reading: “degenerates.”] from the nobility of its father: when the Lord was thirsty on the cross, it offered him vinegar instead of wine. For he thirsted for the faith and love of that people, but instead of the sweetness of faith and the warmth of love, it gave him to drink the bitterness of hatred and unbelief.

Noah awoke from his wine, and, when he learned what his younger son had done to him, he said:

“Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers.”

Awaking from his wine, Noah curses the offspring of the one who mocked him; but those who honored him as a father he rewards with the blessing that was their due. In accordance with the voice of the psalm (Psalm 3:6), the Lord, when he had slept in death and rose immortal, struck all those who opposed him without cause and crushed the teeth of sinners. Upon his own people, however, he poured out the blessing of perpetual salvation.

Canaan is subjected not only to the curse but also to the service of his brothers. For what else is that people today except a kind of archive of the Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s claim, so that we may honor, through the mystery, what it announces [Note: [Col. 0112D] Another reading omits “announces.”] in the letter? [Note: [Col. 0112D] Bede took these words from Saint Augustine, Book XII Against Faustus, chapter 23. Similar statements occur in Psalm 40, no. 14; Psalm 56, no. 9; and frequently elsewhere.]

And he said:

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant.”

We said that in Shem, Noah’s firstborn [Note: [Col. 0112D] Another reading omits “son.”] son, the primitive Church gathered from the Israelite people is signified, while in Japheth, the younger son, the election of the Gentiles who followed is represented. Hence it is rightly said:

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem.”

Although he is the God of all nations, in a certain sense he is also called, by a proper name, the God of Israel, even among those nations [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading: “among those very nations.”]. And how did this come about, except through the blessing of Japheth? For in the people of the Gentiles the Church has occupied the whole world.

This is precisely what is foretold [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading: “was foretold when it was said.”] when the following words are spoken.

God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading: “let him dwell.”]. For Japheth dwells in the tents of Shem because the Church, on earth as a pilgrim, dwells in the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, in the prophetic Scriptures, and in the spiritually understood sacraments of the Law. We customarily use tents in war or on a journey; and we, who have come from the nations to Christ, dwell in the tents of the Israelite people, since, so long as we are placed on the road of this life and yearn for our heavenly homeland, and so long as, with Christ as leader and helper, we struggle against the snares of the ancient enemy, we must always retain the words, deeds, and works of our ancient fathers as an example of life and profession. Thus, protected by their authority, we may press forward with greater certainty and security, through a perfect contest, toward the palm of reward.

The name Japheth, which means “expanse,” also aptly corresponds to the growth of the holy Church, by which it has filled the whole world. Therefore, alluding to the name itself, Noah says: “May God enlarge Japheth,” that is, grant him “expanse” [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading: “in expanse.”]. It is fitting, moreover [Note: [Col. 0113D] Another reading omits “moreover.”], that what had been said of Shem is repeated concerning Japheth as well: “And let Canaan be his servant,” because the faithless Jews, though with an impious mind, render the service of salvation to both peoples of believers—not only insofar as they assist them by the authority of the sacred books [Note: [Col. 0114D] Another reading: “in place of authority.”] and strengthen them in the faith, but also insofar as they persecute them to the extent of their power. For by persecuting them on account of righteousness, they make them more deeply participants in eternal blessedness; and, through their offense and the hardness of their blindness, they also urge them to give greater thanks to their Redeemer and Enlightener.

The name Canaan, which is interpreted as “Commotion,” most aptly suits this people. For it cannot say, “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm 39:3); rather, uncertain and wavering, it is always in motion.

It should also be noted, according to the literal sense, that when Ham sinned, it was not Ham himself but his son Canaan who was cursed—especially since Canaan was not Ham’s firstborn but his last son. For it is written: “The sons of Ham were Cush, Saba, Mesraim, Phut, and Canaan.” He foresaw in the Spirit that the descendants of Canaan would sin far more than the other branches of Ham’s sons, and therefore would become worthy either to perish by a curse or to groan under subjection to slavery. This was demonstrated especially by the Sodomites, who sprang from the race of Canaan, both through their unspeakable crime and through the dreadful vengeance inflicted upon them; and it was also demonstrated by the extermination or enslavement suffered by the Canaanites after the Israelite people, descended from the stock of Shem, came out of Egypt.

The Ethiopians arose from Cush, the Egyptians from Mesraim, and the Libyans from Phut, as the names by which these same peoples are still known among the Hebrews testify. Scripture records nothing of the other peoples concerning such a crime or punishment as it relates concerning the Sodomites and Canaanites.

God also enlarged Japheth, so that he dwelt in the tents of Shem and Canaan became his servant, when the Greeks or Romans—who certainly arose from the race of Japheth—possessed the kingdoms of Asia, where the descendants of Shem lived, and among others made the Canaanites tributary to themselves.

[Col. 0114B] Noah lived for three hundred and fifty years after the Flood. All the days of his life were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died. Just as Noah’s six hundred years of life, completed before he entered the ark, signify the perfection of the faith and profession of those who enter into the Church’s sacraments of heavenly grace and everlasting reward, as we have explained above, so also the three hundred and fifty years during which he lived after the Flood represent the great perfection of those who, having received the sacraments of life, faithfully serve the Lord until death.

We have said that the number three hundred, because it is represented in Greek by the letter tau (and tau is written in the form [Note: [Col. 0114D] Another reading: “figure.”] of a cross), most aptly signifies those who glory in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus Gideon, at the Lord’s command and with his help, overcame the innumerable army of the Midianites with three hundred men, teaching figuratively that by faith in the Lord’s cross we would conquer the battles waged against us by both this world and our vices.

Scripture teaches that the number fifty signifies, in figure [Note: [Col. 0114D] Another reading: “because it signifies a figure.”], the rest promised by the Law: every fiftieth year it ordained that the whole people of God should receive the greatest remission of all labors and freedom from servitude. For this reason, through a certain mystery, Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the Flood, to indicate that, having received the washing of baptism, we ought to endure labors for the Lord in hope of heavenly rest and blessedness. He lived three hundred years so that we might be patient in tribulation; he lived fifty also so that we might rejoice in hope.

But since seven times fifty make three hundred and fifty, the number seven signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, while fifty signifies the true rest bestowed through that same Spirit upon the elect; thus the numbers correspond figuratively.

We may also interpret the mystery of this number in the following way: the one who lives three hundred and fifty years after the Flood is the person who, throughout the whole period following the reception of baptism, aided by the gift of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0114D] Another reading: “by the gift of spiritual oil”; this reading may not be wrong.], does not cease to labor for eternal rest in heaven [Note: [Col. 0115A] Another reading: “in the churches”]. Such a person will see the happy death of the flesh—or rather, will pass from death to life, which alone ought to be called true life—if he completes the course of the present life with such a fullness of perfection. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0115A] Another reading: “The second book ends. The third book of Bede the priest’s Hexameron begins” [Col. 0116A]. In another copy there is no title.]

The second book on Genesis by Bede the priest ends.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115A] These are the generations of the sons [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading omits “sons.”] of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and sons were born to them after the Flood. The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: “Chiras.”].

The account of Noah’s line begins with his youngest son and ends with the eldest; this is customary language in the sacred Scriptures. Mystically, it signifies that the lesser people of the nations would be preferred in the greater faith to the greater people of the Jews, when Christ came in the flesh.

The sons of Noah who are mentioned are each believed to have been the progenitor of a particular nation. They divided the world among themselves in such a way that Shem, the firstborn, obtained Asia; Ham, the second, Africa; and Japheth, the last, Europe. This is to be understood with the qualification that, since Asia is much larger in extent than either Europe or Libya, the descendants of Ham and Japheth also held some portion of Asia.

“Seven sons were born from Japheth, who possessed the land in Asia from Mount Amanus and the Taurus, the mountains of Coele-Syria and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: “Phanaum”; another: “Tanais.”]. In Europe they extended as far as Gades, leaving their names to places and peoples. Later many of these names were changed, while others remain as they were. Gomer means the Galatians; Magog, the Scythians; Madai, the Medes; Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks—hence the Ionian Sea; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also called Spaniards, taking this name from the river Iberus, and from them come the Celtiberians, although some suppose them to be Italians; Meshech, the Cappadocians, among whom a city is still called Mazaca, also named Caesarea after Augustus Caesar. The Seventy Interpreters, moreover, consider the Captorim to be Cappadocians; Tiras means the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered.”

The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: “Niphath.”], and Togarma. Ashkenaz means the Sarmatians, whom the Greeks call R[h]iginians; Riphath, the Paphlagonians; Togarma, the Phrygians.

“The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: “Donanim.”]. From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, arose the Elishah people, who are called the Eleans; hence the fifth language of Greece is called Aeolic, which they call the *pente dialecton*, ‘fifth dialect.’ Josephus considers Tarshish to mean the Cilicians, saying that the aspirated letter in *Thar* was corruptly changed by later generations into *Tar*; hence their metropolitan city is called Tarsus, celebrated for the apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0115D] Another reading: “Tarsus.”]. [Note: [Col. 0115D] The parenthetical sentence is absent from Saint Jerome.] Some think that Tarshish, from which gold was brought to Solomon, is a region of India. Kittim means the Kitians, from whom the city now called Cyptotium takes its name [Note: [Col. 0116D] Another reading: “Cyprocitium”; another: “and Ipso-citium.”]. Dodanim means the Rhodians; for it is better read as Rodanim or Rodim, as the Seventy Interpreters translated it [Note: [Col. 0116D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*], and as our own translator also rendered it in the Book of Hebrew Names. For the similarity of the letters daleth and resh often causes this error among the Hebrews, so that one is read in place of the other. Rhodes is the largest of the Cyclades and was once a very powerful city in the Ionian Sea, renowned for naval warfare and, because of its exceptionally safe harbor, a refuge for all merchants.”

From these the islands of the nations were divided into their regions, each according to its language [Note: [Col. 0116D] Another copy omits “its.”] and family, in their nations.

“Let us read the histories of the ancients [Note: [Col. 0116D] Namely, the books of Varro on antiquities, those of Sinnius Capito, the Greek Phlegon, and other learned men, as Jerome says.], and we shall see that almost all the islands, the shores of the entire world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers [Note: [Col. 0116D] Another reading: “by Greeks.”]. As we said above, they possessed all the maritime regions from the mountains of Amanus and Taurus as far as the Britannic Ocean [Note: [Col. 0116D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

When it says that each was according to his language and family in his nations, it clearly shows that, according to the common opinion, each of the sons of Noah mentioned here—or the grandsons of Noah’s sons—established a separate nation or kinship with a different language. For, after the descendants of Ham and Shem have also been listed, the same point concerning the variety of generations and languages is added.

The sons of Ham were Cush, Mesraim, Phut, and Canaan.

[Col. 0116D]

“Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mesraim, Egypt; Phut, Libya, from which the river of Mauretania is still called Phut, as is the entire surrounding region, the land of Phut. Canaan, moreover, obtained the land that the Jews later possessed after expelling the Canaanites.

“The sons of Cush were Saba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah [Note: [Col. 0116D] Another reading: “Recina.”], and Sabtahca. Saba gave his name to the Sabaeans. Virgil says: ‘The Sabaeans alone possess a branch of fragrant incense,’ and elsewhere: ‘A hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense’ [Note: [Col. 0116D] Add the other occurrence, as in Jerome.]. Havilah gave his name to the Getulians, who dwell alongside the desert in a more remote part of Africa. Sabtah gave his name to the Sabatheni, who are now called Astabari. Raamah and Sabtahca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what names they now bear in place of the old ones [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “it is unknown.”; Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

Nevertheless, because Ezekiel says in his vision of Tyre that the merchants of Sheba and Raamah—or, as the Seventy Interpreters said, Regma—were Tyre’s merchants, it appears that Raamah also formed its own people, and, since it is joined with Sheba, that its region was near that province.

The sons of Sheba were Raamah and Dedan [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “Dadanus”; another: “Dodanim.”].

“This Sheba is written with the letter shin, whereas the Sheba mentioned above is written with samekh; from the latter, as we said, the Sabaeans received their name. The present Sheba therefore means Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we read, ‘The kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall offer gifts’ (Psalm 71:10), the Hebrew has ‘the kings of Sheba and Sheba’: the first name is written with shin, the second with samekh [Col. 0117B] [Note: [Col. 0117D] The parenthetical sentence is absent from Jerome.] (which resembles our letter). Dedan is a people of Ethiopia in the western region [Note: [Col. 0117D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be powerful on the earth, and he was a mighty hunter before the Lord.

While the descendants of Shem and Japheth remained in the innocence of a simple way of life [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “remaining”], a cursed man was born from the stock of Ham [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “the accursed man”], one who would pervert the condition of human society through a new manner of living. Exalted by singular power, he first lived by hunting; then, having gathered an army, he sought to exercise an unprecedented tyranny over peoples; finally, he is said later to have possessed a kingdom and built very great cities. Scripture testifies that he was the first to do this when it says: “He began to be powerful.” He began, because he was the first to do it.

He was powerful on earth because, neglecting heavenly things—in which the righteous are powerful—he learned to seek what is lowly and to place his hope in it.

From him the proverb arose: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” It became a proverb because his deeds were unprecedented in those ages. The addition “before the Lord” intensifies the enormity of the crime, since it was exceedingly rash and arrogant for a man on earth to presume to live in such a way before the Lord, who looks down from heaven upon the sons of men. This proverb makes clear that many at that time avoided doing such things out of fear of the heavenly gaze, although another edition reads that “Nimrod was a giant hunter against the Lord.”

Because of the ambiguity of the Greek word *enantion*, both interpretations are possible. Thus, in the Psalm where we sing, “Let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 104:6), the word is *enantion Kyriō*—“before the Lord.” The same word occurs in the Book of Job, where it is written: “You have broken out in fury against the Lord.”

The meaning concerning the giant is therefore readily apparent: he was a powerful hunter of wild animals, like a mighty man; but he was also an impious man who led an arrogant life against the will of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “like a man.”].

His kingdom began with Babylon, Arach, Archad [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “Achad.”], and Calneh in the land of Shinar.

How Babylon came to be is explained more fully below. Here, however, what is passed over there is mentioned in advance: Nimrod was the founder of that city and of its exceedingly proud tower.

His kingdom began with Babylon because it was either the first of his cities to be founded or, on account of its size and beauty, was regarded as the capital of his kingdom.

“Arach is the city now called Edessa [Note: [Col. 0117D] Another reading: “Arcah.”]; Archad is now Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia [Note: [Col. 0118D] Another reading: “Nisibi”; another: “Nisibius.”]; Calneh is now Seleucia, named after King Seleucus, or perhaps the city now called Ctesiphon [Note: [Col. 0118D] Another reading: “and Esiphon”; another: “Ephison.” Read, as in Jerome, the Greek form *Ctesiphon*] [Note: [Col. 0118D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

The phrase “in the land of Shinar” appears to apply to all four cities. Shinar is said to be a plain of such great extent that it could easily contain Babylon itself and many other cities.

Because Babylon, together with the cities of which it is the head, signifies the proud glory of this world, which is subject to confusion—for Babel means “confusion”—its founder aptly and figuratively announces the devil, the head of all evils.

The name Nimrod, which signifies “tyrant,” “fugitive,” or “transgressor,” also suits him well. He is a tyrant because, rebelling against the Creator, he strives to seize the citadel of divinity and the kingdom of the world. He is a fugitive because, having fallen from heaven and been cast out from the fellowship of the angels who remained steadfast in their state, he exults in his misery. He is a transgressor because he scorned to obey the will of his Maker.

The role of hunter is also not unfittingly assigned to him. In the forest of this world he lays the snares of his ambushes and, deceiving human beings who are pure by nature and disposition [Note: [Col. 0118D] Another reading: “whom”], hunts them to death like stags and does. He is the opposite of those hunters who seek to capture human souls by their teaching for the very purpose of drawing them to eternal life. To them the Lord says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:39). Their homeland was therefore called Bethsaida, that is, “House of Hunters,” because they were hunting human beings for life.

Nimrod is the son of Cush, which is interpreted as “Ethiopian” [Note: [Col. 0118D] Another reading: “Aethiops”], because the ancient enemy is always born anew, as it were, from the obscure people of the faithless through the execution of wicked teaching or action.

From him the proverb still remains to this day, so that it is said: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” It may most truly be said of those who imitate the devil and belong to his party that, when they hunt human souls to destruction by word or example, they follow the deeds of the ancient transgressor and deceiver.

From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh and the squares of the city.

By “that land” he means the land of Shinar, from which the empire of the Assyrians sprang. They founded the great city that the Hebrews call Nineveh, naming it after Ninus, son of Bel.

Since Scripture appears to say nothing about the origin of Asshur, from whom the Assyrian people arose, but only states from what land he went out to build Nineveh and the other cities it mentions, some of the Fathers understood this Asshur to be the son of Shem, who is mentioned below.

But whether he was the same Asshur or another, it is certain that the first kingdom, that of the Babylonians, and the second, that of the Assyrians—whose capital was Nineveh—arose from the same land.

Mesraim fathered Ludim, Anamim, Laabim [Note: [Col. 0119D] Another reading: “Nephtum.”], Nepthuhim, Phethusim, and Chesluim, from whom the Philistines and the Capturim came forth.

These appear to be names of peoples rather than individual men, since it is expressly said that the Philistines came forth from the Casluhim. They all end in *-im*, which among the Hebrews is characteristic of the masculine plural; and their interpretations likewise indicate a plural rather than a singular number.

The Lehabim are the Libyans, the Philistines the Palestinians, and the Caphtorim the Cappadocians, as we find stated in the Book of Hebrew Names according to the opinion of the Seventy Interpreters. The names of the other peoples are unknown to us [Col. 0119C]. They possessed the land from Gaza to the borders and frontiers of Egypt.

Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites.

“From Sidon, the firstborn of Canaan, the famous Phoenician city of Sidon is named; formerly it was the northern boundary of the Canaanites. The Arkite founded Arcas, a town situated opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it was another city called Sim [Note: [Col. 0119D] Another reading: “Sini.”], which, later destroyed by the varying fortunes of war, preserved only the ancient name of the place. The Arvadites are those who possessed the island of Aradus, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait [Note: [Col. 0119D] Another reading: “channel.”]. This island, situated near Tyre, is still seen to be a fortified city and to have the town of Antaradus lying opposite it [Note: [Col. 0119D] Another reading: “Amaradus.”]. The Samarites are Emesa, a distinguished city of Syria [Note: [Col. 0119D] In Saint Jerome: “Edessa.”]. Hamath is still called by both the Assyrians and the Hebrews, even in our own time, by the name it bore among the ancients. The Macedonians who ruled in the East after Alexander called it Epiphaneia. Some think that Antioch was so named [Note: [Col. 0119D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

In fact, there were two cities called Hamath: one was Great Hamath, now called Antioch, “great” serving to distinguish it from the lesser Hamath, which is called Epiphaneia. It was in the latter that Nebuchadnezzar blinded Zedekiah’s eyes.

The boundaries of Canaan were established for those coming from Sidon: Gerar as far as Gaza, until one enters Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lesha [Note: [Col. 0119D] Another reading: “Sela,” in place of Lesha.].

For Lesha the ancient translation has Laisa. It is the place now called Callirrhoe, where hot springs burst forth and flow into the Dead Sea [Note: [Col. 0120D] Saint Jerome reads it thus; our manuscripts pronounce the name variously: “Callir-Noe,” “Caltur-Noe,” or “Calliso hoe.”]. Sidon, therefore, was the northern boundary of the Canaanites, Gerar the southern boundary, and Gaza lay near Egypt.

[Col. 0120B] From Shem also were born the fathers [Note: [Col. 0120D] Another reading: “from the father.”] of all the sons of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth.

He calls Eber the brother of Japheth, but leaves unmentioned the fact that he was also the brother of Ham, because he understands that those whom he knows to be united in the faith of piety should rightly be called brothers [Note: [Col. 0120D] Another reading: “true brothers.”]. He shows that the faithless man, although born of the same parents, is alien from the fraternal fellowship of the righteous.

This sentence appears to signify that, although many sons born from Shem fathered many peoples, the particular descendants who followed his faith and piety were those who descended through Eber to Abraham and the Hebrew people. Hence Shem is specifically called the father of them—that is, of all the sons of Eber.

Finally, only in the house of Eber, who lived in that age, as is related below, did the original speech of the human race remain when the tower was being built, as Scripture says, “the language of the whole earth.” The Hebrew names of people in the succeeding age clearly prove this. It is to be believed that Eber deserved this because, following the faith of his forefather Shem with his household, he kept himself free from the conspiracy of that proud undertaking.

Nor was it without reason that Abraham chose to be called a Hebrew. He knew how to imitate the life of this Seth [the text reads *Seth*, evidently for Shem], and therefore wished to bear the name as his own surname and to leave it to his descendants thereafter.

The sons of Shem were Elam, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram.

“These occupied the part of Asia [Note: [Col. 0120D] Another reading: “of Syria.”] from the Euphrates River as far as the Indian Ocean. Elam gave his name to the Elamites, the princes of Persia. It has already been said concerning Asshur that he founded the city of Nineveh. Arphaxad gave his name to the Chaldeans; Lud, to Lydia; Aram, to the Syrians, whose capital is Damascus. In the Hebrew language Syria is called Aram.”

The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Uz held the principality of Trachonitis and Damascus, between Palestine and Coele-Syria [Note: [Col. 0120D] Another reading: “Coeles”; another: “Coele.”]. Hul gave his name to the Armenians. Gether gave his name to the Arcanians or Carians [Note: [Col. 0120D] Another reading: “Arnanians”; another: “Acarcanians.”]. Mash, for whom the Seventy Interpreters read Mosoch, gave his name to those called Maeonians [Note: [Col. 0121D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

Arphaxad fathered Shelah [Note: [Col. 0121D] Another reading: “Saleh”], from whom Eber arose. From this Eber, Abraham and the people descended from him, as we have said above, are surnamed Hebrews.

Two sons were born to Eber. The name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; the name of his brother was Joktan.

He calls the division of the earth the division that took place in the confusion of languages. He named his son Peleg, that is, “Division,” so that he might leave a perpetual memorial of his devotion to his descendants, since, when the languages of the faithless were divided on account of their pride, he himself, by the merit of his faith, preserved the original speech of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] One Corbie manuscript reads: “Sceleps, who fathered Joktan.”] Joktan fathered Helmodad, Saleph, Asarmoth, Jare, Adura, Uzal, Decha, Ebal, Abimael, Saba, Ophir, Evila, and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan.

Jerome testifies that he was unable to discover the later names of these peoples. “But to the present day,” he says, “because they are far from us, either they are called by their original names, or the names that have been changed are unknown [Note: [Col. 0121D] Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*].”

We read above that Pishon, one of the four rivers of Paradise, which our people call the Ganges and which is undoubtedly in India, flows around the entire land of Havilah. This land appears to have received its name from this Havilah.

Josephus relates that Havilah, together with his brothers, possessed the whole region of India called Hieira, from the river Coephere [Note: [Col. 0121D] Another reading: “Cophere.”]. The Books of Chronicles also relate that Solomon’s servants went by way of the Red Sea to Ophir and brought back from there gold, thyine wood, and very precious gems [Note: [Col. 0121D] Another reading: “they went … and brought back.”]. It is credible that Ophir was a region of India and that it received its name from Ophir, the son of Joktan.

All these were sons of Joktan. Their dwelling extended from Mesha, for those journeying, as far as Sephar, the eastern mountain [Note: [Col. 0121D] Another reading: “of those journeying.”].

We said above that Shem, Noah’s firstborn, signifies believers from the ancient people of God; Japheth signifies believers from the nations; while Ham, laughing at his father’s shame and therefore cursed, signifies that part of the same people which, remaining as it were in the middle, was unwilling either to belong first to its own kinsmen or later to share the faith of the nations.

The places of their habitations therefore correspond most aptly to these figures. The sons of Eber, who is shown to be the most prominent of Shem’s descendants, are said to have extended their dwelling from Mesha to the eastern mountain called Sephar.

Mesha is a region of India whose interpretation is said to be “Elevation.” It signifies not a blameworthy and proud arrogance, but rather that elevation of mind [Note: [Col. 0122D] Another reading: “exaltation.”] to which the Apostle exhorts us when he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1).

But what is the eastern mountain except the one of which Isaiah says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob” (Isaiah 2:3)? It is rightly called a mountain because it lifts all who ascend to it from the desire for lowly things to the desire for heavenly things [Note: [Col. 0122D] Another reading: “longings.”]. It is rightly an eastern mountain because it reveals the rising of the true light to all who gather to it. It is also rightly called Sephar, that is, “Book.” For it is the book of life, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden and in which the names of all the elect are written.

The dwelling of the sons of Joktan—Joktan being interpreted as “Little One”—therefore extended from Mesha, that is, “Elevation,” for those journeying, as far as the eastern mountain called the Book. The holy people, following the humility of the earlier righteous, of whom it is said, “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Psalm 114:6), raise their minds above earthly contamination at the beginning of their religious life, so that they may deserve to ascend to behold the brightness of the eternal Sun and to be instructed from the book of life, which is the Lord Christ, when the pages of eternal wisdom have been opened.

Likewise, when it is said concerning the sons of Japheth, “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their regions,” does this not most clearly indicate, even by the name “nations,” the churches throughout the world? Like islands amid the waves of the sea, they are continually battered by the swollen and bitter storms of the age, yet they are not overcome. At one time the world flatters them, and they glide as though touched by gentle waves [Note: [Col. 0122D] Another reading: “are brushed.”]; at another, when it rages, they are struck as though by waves raised high into the deep adversities. Nevertheless, they remain unconquerable in the stability of their faith.

By contrast, the sons of Ham have the beginning of their kingdom in Babylon, that is, “Confusion,” which is in the land of Shinar, that is, “their stench.” This kingdom is in a plain because the reprobate do not climb the mountain of contemplation, by which they might seek heavenly things, nor do they approach the tranquility of the islands of understanding, by which they might transcend the cares of the passing age with a loftier freedom of spirit. Instead, they rejoice in being carried about in the unrestrained wantonness of their earthly desires [Note: [Col. 0122D] Another reading: “unbridled”; another: “to run wild.”].

A fitting end follows such a beginning, when it is said that the boundaries of Canaan extended for those coming from Sidon through Gerar as far as Gaza, until one enters Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah [Note: [Col. 0122D] Another reading: “Admah.”], and Zeboiim, as far as Lesha.

Sidon is interpreted as “Hunt of Sorrow,” because here nothing else should be understood than the hunt by which the ancient enemy hunts souls to destruction. It is rightly called “Hunt of Sorrow,” because all whom he captures he subjects to eternal pains. Nimrod, that giant who is called “the mighty hunter against the Lord,” signifies such a hunter [Note: [Col. 0123D] Another reading: “Nimrod.”].

There is no doubt that Sodom, Gomorrah, and the neighboring cities signify the eternal torments of the impious.

These are the families of Noah according to their peoples and nations. From these the nations were divided on the earth after the Flood.

Let the diligent reader list in order the names of the men or peoples who are said to have been born from the three sons, and they will be found to number seventy-one: thirteen from Japheth, thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-six from Shem. From these, it is believed, an equal number of languages and nations filled the world—or rather seventy-two, as the more widespread tradition has it [Note: [Col. 0123D] Another reading: “and they will be found”; another: “they will be found.”], if one of them was the ancestor from whom two nations and peoples later arose.

Unless perhaps we should understand there to have been two men named Asshur, who created two peoples: one who went out from the land of Shinar and built Nineveh, and another who was the son of Shem. In this way the number of seventy-two nations would be completed.

It does not seem unreasonable that the Lord sent seventy-two disciples to preach because there were that many nations and languages to which the word of preaching was to be entrusted. Just as he first chose twelve apostles because there were twelve tribes of Israel to be called to the faith, so afterward he appointed seventy-two teachers to signify the salvation of all the nations, which were comprehended in that same number.

The earth was of one language and of the same words. Since he had previously said that the sons of Noah divided the earth among the nations according to their kinships, languages, and regions, he now returns to show how human beings were separated from one another.

Here it is made entirely clear that, so long as the human race served its Creator with due humility, it was also united in peaceful love among its own members. But when it raised its proud neck against its Author, it was immediately and justly punished, and could no longer maintain peace even with itself [Note: [Col. 0124D] Another reading: “with itself.”].

The grace of that same Lord, our Creator and Redeemer, testifies how great the happiness of human beings could have been even after their expulsion from Paradise, if they had then been willing humbly to serve their Creator. By sending the Spirit from above to the disciples who faithfully adhered to him, he granted them knowledge of all languages.

Thus, through a wondrous transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, just as here the nations were scattered throughout the whole world because of the division of languages brought about by pride, so there, on account of the merit of humility, a diversity of languages was united. People gathered from every nation under heaven resounded with praise and proclaimed God’s mighty works in one confession and one undivided faith.

With good reason, therefore, this city, in which languages were divided and nations scattered, is called Babylon, that is, “Confusion”; while the other is called Jerusalem, that is, “Vision of Peace,” because in it, with the speech of all nations united in praise of God, harmony has been established.

But we shall discuss this more fully later. For now, let us examine the literal text.

As they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. These words show that the first human beings also occupied the eastern region. It should therefore be regarded as the head of the world, not only because the light of the stars rises from there, but also because the human race first inhabited it.

And the one said to his neighbor: “Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire.” And they had bricks instead of stones, and bitumen instead of mortar. Perhaps they used bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar because in those regions there was not enough stone to complete so great a work; or because they knew that a brick wall would resist the danger of fire more strongly. Bitumen is made from trees, and also from earth or water; hence it is written below concerning the land of Sodom: “The wooded valley had many wells of bitumen.” And the Dead Sea is called in Greek the Lake of Asphaltos [Note: [Col. 0124D] Alternatively, “asphalt”], that is, of bitumen, because bitumen floating on its surface is customarily gathered there. This makes it seem all the more likely that the walls of Babylon were constructed with it.

And they said: “Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven, and let us make our name renowned before we are dispersed throughout all the lands.” The phrase “whose summit” signifies not the summit of the city but of the tower—that is, of the citadel—which they intended to make higher than the other walls, on a more elevated site. It is certainly astonishing with what intention they planned both to raise the summit of their tower all the way to heaven and nevertheless to declare that they would be dispersed throughout all the lands—unless perhaps, with utterly vain and proud minds, they were planning to divide themselves throughout the world so that, if they should eventually become weary of earthly habitation, or if the waters of the flood should once again rush upon the earth, they might by means of it seek the upper regions of the air or of heaven.

But the Lord descended to see the city and the tower that the sons of Adam were building. Instead of “sons of Adam,” the Old Translation has “sons of men”—that is, not sons of God, but those who, living according to man, would deserve to hear from the Lord: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like men” (Psalm 81:6). God is not moved from place to place, since he is always wholly present everywhere; but he is said to descend when he does something on earth that, being performed miraculously beyond the ordinary course of nature, in a certain way manifests his presence. Nor does he learn by seeing for a time, since he can never be ignorant of anything; rather, he is said for a time to see and know what he causes to be seen and known. That city, therefore, was not seen in the manner in which God caused it to be seen when he revealed how displeasing it was to him. Yet it may be understood that God descended to that city because his angels, in whom he dwells, had descended, so that the statement which follows—“And he said: ‘Behold, they are one people and all have one language,’” and then the addition, “Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language”—may be a recapitulation demonstrating how what had been said, “The Lord descended,” came to pass. For if he had already descended, what does “Come, let us descend” mean, which is understood to have been spoken to the angels, unless he had descended through the angels, who was present in the descending angels?

“Behold,” he says, “they are one people and all have one language; and they have begun to do this, nor will they desist from their plans until they complete them in action.” There is a great difference in the gravity of sin between those who despise God’s commandments so completely that they have among themselves some righteous imitators and worshipers [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, *justos* (“righteous persons”)], and those who with unanimous agreement all contradict the heavenly commandments. There is likewise a great difference between those who sin, for example, during the time of youth but later, when old age follows, intend to repent of their offenses, and those who in the evils they commit harbor no intention of correction. Thus, to demonstrate here the unanimity of sinners, the invisible Judge says: “Behold, they are one people and all have one language.” [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively: “in order to add the intention not to repent.”] And he adds the intention not to repent: “They have begun to do this, nor will they desist from their plans until they complete them in action.” To them aptly corresponds the beginning of the Thirteenth Psalm, where it is said: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1)—that is, Nimrod [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, *Nembrot*], the craftsman of the wicked enterprise—and afterward, concerning the craftsmen of the ruined city: “They are corrupt; they have become abominable” (ibid.). The inner Judge speaks these words, of which we are speaking, to the ministers of his powers in a manner incomprehensible to us [Note: [Col. 0125D] The alternative reading omits “to us”]. His speaking to them is the display to their hearts of his hidden and invisible judgments, so that whatever they ought to do, they read in the very contemplation of truth. It is as though what is inspired in those who see is said to those who hear. Thus, when God poured into their hearts the punishment of vengeance against human pride, he said:

“Come, let us descend and confuse their language there.” “Come” is said to those who were present because never to diminish from divine contemplation, but always to increase in divine contemplation, is to come continually; and never to withdraw in heart is, as it were, by a stable movement always to come. To them he also says: “Let us descend and confuse their language there.” The angels ascend insofar as they behold the Creator; the angels descend insofar as they repress by the judgment of strictness [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, “of distinction” (*distinctionis*)] the creature raising itself unlawfully. To say, therefore, “Let us descend and confuse their languages” is to display to them within themselves what may rightly be understood, and through the force of inward vision to inspire judgments in their minds by hidden movements. And he rightly does not say, “Come, and, after descending, confuse them,” but “Let us confuse their language there,” showing that he works through his ministers in such a way that they themselves are also God’s fellow workers, as the Apostle says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, “co-workers”].

“Let us confuse,” he says, “their language there, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor.” The evil inclination is justly punished even when the deed does not succeed; and since the authority of one who commands resides in the tongue, pride was condemned there, so that the one who had refused to understand in order to obey God’s command might not understand the one commanding him.

And so the Lord dispersed them from that place throughout all the lands, and they ceased building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused.
