The language was rightly confused for the sake of dispersion [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, “in dispersion”], because they had wickedly conspired together for an impious speech. The power of speech was taken away from the proud rulers, lest, in contempt of God, they should be able to teach their subjects the evils they had begun [Note: [Col. 0125D] Alternatively, “had wickedly begun” (*male*)]; and thus the judgment of divine severity was turned into an aid to human usefulness, so that by falling silent they would cease from the work to which they had perversely gathered themselves through their speech. Thus, when the Lord descended and saw the city of arrogance, it came about that it was called Babylon, that is, Confusion. The city of truth, however, is sufficiently contrary to it both in name and in condition: it is called Jerusalem, that is, Vision of Peace. There, when the Lord saw the gathering of the faithful and humble in spirit, he sent the grace of the Holy Spirit, who granted them knowledge of all languages. Instructed by these languages, they summoned all the peoples who were present in diverse tongues into unanimous assembly for the construction of that same holy city, namely, the Church of Christ; and those who had humbly applied their ears to the truth opened their mouths sublimely to proclaim the knowledge of truth throughout the whole world.

It should also be noted that Scripture indeed says that, after the builders had been dispersed throughout the world, the building of the city ceased; but it does not say that inhabiting it ceased. Hence it seems that, while others descended from there and ceased from the building, Nimrod, the author of the work, remained there with his household and family until, after offspring had been produced from his lineage, he could rule there more powerfully and add other cities to his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0126D] Alternatively: “and add other kingdoms to his kingdom”]. For, unless I am mistaken, the statement made above about him cannot otherwise be understood: “The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, and Arach, and Achad [Note: [Col. 0126D] Alternatively, “Acadh”], and Chalanne in the land of Sennaar.” Yet it is reported that Ninus, or his wife Semiramis, later made that same city of Babylon larger and more magnificent in the course of time. Hence comes the poet’s statement [Note: [Col. 0126D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book IV; alternatively, *quam* rather than *quod*], which is said to have been:

> Semiramis once enclosed the city with baked-brick walls.

And especially Nebuchadnezzar, accumulating its ornaments from the spoils of Jerusalem, said in his pride: “Is this not great Babylon, which I have built as a royal residence, by the might of my strength and for the glory of my magnificence?” Concerning its size and splendor Jerome relates the following [Note: [Col. 0126D] On Isaiah, chapter 14]:

> “Babylon was most powerful and situated on a plain in the form of a square; from corner to corner its wall extended sixteen thousand paces”—that is, all around its circuit [Note: [Col. 0127D] Another edition of Jerome has: “that is, altogether around its circuit, forty-eight stadia.” But in a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Marmoutier, written eight hundred years ago, it reads: “that is, altogether around its circuit, sixty-four”]. Herodotus (Book I), and many others who wrote Greek histories, report [Note: [Col. 0127D] Alternatively, “fifty-three, but read sixty-four”]. The citadel—that is, its Capitol—was the tower which was built after the flood and is said to have extended four thousand paces.”

Orosius mentions it in this way in his histories (Book I, chapter 6):

> “This city, visible from every side across the level plain, in a location most pleasant by nature, was laid out as a camp in the form of a square, with equal walls. The strength and size of its walls, scarcely credible to report, were fifty cubits in width and four times that in height. Its circuit, moreover, enclosed four hundred and eighty stadia [Note: [Col. 0127D] Alternatively, “surrounded”]. A wall of baked brick, joined with bitumen poured between it, enclosed it, while a broad ditch outside, flowing around it like a river, surrounded it. On the front of the walls were a hundred bronze gates. The width itself, at the completion of the battlements [Note: [Col. 0127D] Alternatively, “on both sides”], contained dwellings for the defenders, and, with an interval arranged between them, held four-horse chariots [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively: “situated chariots”; another reading, “its own chariots”]. The houses within, rising with threatening height to four times the usual size of dwellings, were marvelous [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively, “astonishing.”]”

Since, according to the spiritual meaning, Babylon is the city of the devil—that is, the entire reprobate multitude of humanity—who are the builders of Babylon except the teachers of error, who either introduce a worship of divinity contrary to the truth or attack the acknowledged faith of the truth through evil deeds or words?

The whole earth had one language and the same words as long as people remained in the East. But when they moved their feet away from the East, they were immediately separated from one another because of words or works of pride, and were driven farther from their Creator. The region of the East, from which the world customarily receives the light of the stars at their rising, rightly signifies him who said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). As long as people remain in him, they have one language and one voice, because there is one confession of faith, the same purity of conduct, and a common charity and hope of eternal things; for all who persevere in Christ are illumined. But those who withdraw from contemplation of the true light can have neither peace with the Lord nor peace with one another, because there is not, just as there is one standard of faith, one and the same standard of unbelief. Rather, there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God, in whom is the salvation of the elect. But the reprobate have many lords, diverse winding paths of faithlessness, diverse mire-pools of pollution [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively, “of defilements”], and diverse gods of the nations, by whom all the wretched are dragged toward one common destruction. This was well signified [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively, *significat* (“signifies”) or *signavit* (“signified”)] by the figure of those two cities when, after the languages had been divided in Babylon, no one could recognize the voice of his neighbor. In Jerusalem, on the other hand, when the languages of all were joined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the faithful understood the voices of all the foreigners who had arrived, and together, joined in one bond of charity and faith, praised the same God and Lord.

They departed from the East and found a plain in which to dwell, because the reprobate, withdrawing from the light of righteousness, found for themselves the broad ways of the world in which, with unstable minds, they might remain; and this amid the stench of carnal vices. For, as we have said, Sennaar is interpreted as “their stench.” And what is expressed by the land of Sennaar except the putrid torpor of carnal desire [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively, “the beginnings of carnal desire”], in which all who do not avoid dwelling—that is, remaining with secure and fixed attention—soon, as wickedness increases, provoke even their neighbors to injury against the Creator and to wicked deeds?

For it follows that one said to his neighbor: “Come, let us make bricks for ourselves and bake them with fire.” Thus they kindle one another to make bricks with which they may establish Nimrod’s [Note: [Col. 0128D] Alternatively, *Nembrod*] city in the plain of Sennaar. For the whole multitude of the impious serves the devil through muddy, filthy, earthly works, and by living wickedly builds for him no other city than themselves. By contrast, the city of Jerusalem, in which David and Solomon—namely, the Strong of Hand and the Peaceful—reign, is built not of brick but of stone, and not in a plain but on a mountain, as its king says to it: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order, and I will found you on sapphires” (Isaiah 54:11). And concerning it the Prophet says: “Mount Zion, the sides of the North, the city of the great King” (Psalm 47:3). For the city of the devil—whose name Nimrod signifies “fugitives,” namely, transgressors and tyrants—that is, the entire multitude of the reprobate, wanders about as a vagrant through the fleeting corruption of the present life. But the Church, the city of Christ, is built from living stones, that is, from souls made strong by faith and action. Speaking of its king, its wise architect said: “Coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen and honored by God, you also, as living stones, are built up” (1 Peter 2:4). Nor is this done in the plain of Sennaar, but on the holy mountain of the Lord, because the elect do not seek to relax themselves in the weak pleasures of carnal things, but strive rather to constrain and raise themselves toward heavenly desires. Hence they say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

The fact that they mold mud into bricks, which are customarily made with equal sides in a square and from which they also receive their name, demonstrates the composition and ornament of secular eloquence. Through this, the proud city of the devil—whether in deceptive philosophy or in heretical cunning—appears for a long time to rise greatly, but at the judgment of the strict Judge it will be revealed how deserving it is of condemnation and confusion.

They baked the bricks they had made with fire—clearly with that fire of which it is said: “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hosea 7:4), and of which Isaiah says: “Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11). This fire is the love of vices and the desire for human approval. With this fire, foolish teachers of the deceived labor to confirm and harden doctrines of falsehood once discovered, so that they cannot be overcome by any contest with truth or heavenly teaching. Nevertheless, when the army of truth prevails, as Scripture says, “Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen” (Revelation 18:2), by a twofold fall [Note: [Col. 0129D] Alternatively, “of the twofold”]: in the present, cast down through the manifestation of truth; and in the future, condemned by the sentence of final severity.

In former times the Israelite people made such cities in Egypt from mud and brick, because they too, not yet instructed by hearing the Law, served vices and errors and expressed their figure in their works. They also prefigured those who, still held in the obscurity of unclean spirits and still enslaved by the harsh commands of the Egyptians, had learned to possess no faith or hope of acquiring their heavenly homeland; therefore they knew only how to cling to and be subjected to the allurements of this world.

The bitumen that the builders of Babylon used instead of mortar, drawn from the earth or from wells, clearly represents the purpose of earthly and base pleasure, by which the people of this age strengthen all their works [Note: [Col. 0129D] Alternatively, “will strengthen”], since they do not, through any hope or knowledge of heavenly goods, lift themselves toward seeking the joys that are in heaven. Therefore everything they do is done for the sake of temporal pleasure or human approval. In contrast, we read that the builders made the Lord’s temple with mortar. Mortar is made from stones that have been burned and reduced to ash. Through fire, those who had previously been individually firm and strong [Note: [Col. 0129D] Alternatively, *viri tam firmi* (“men so firm”)] are softened by the addition of whiteness; joined to one another by water poured among them, they are connected more securely and can themselves connect other stones placed in the wall. Not long afterward they recover a stronger firmness than they seemed for a short time to have lost.

Who, then, ought to be understood as being in the mortar except those who, repeatedly baked in the furnace of temporal tribulations, first changed within themselves all the darkness of vices into the whiteness of virtues, saying to their Creator: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:9); and then strive also, through their exhortations or examples, to whiten their neighbors [Note: [Col. 0129D] Alternatively, “their own”] and bind them to one another with the bond of love [Note: [Col. 0129D] Alternatively, “in the bond”]? Of them it is rightly said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). The more they are humbled and softened by the flame of tribulations, the stronger they become for strengthening and sustaining the hearts of their neighbors amid tribulations.

The temple is also built of white stone, as David said to Solomon when he gave him the resources and showed him the measurements for constructing the temple: “And he prepared an abundance of Parian marble” (1 Chronicles 29:2). For the Church of Christ is gathered from the souls of the elect, made radiant by strength in faith and action. The marble of the island of Paros [Note: [Col. 0130D] Alternatively, “Parian”] is known to be of strong quality and white color. But the builders of Babylon, lacking either an abundance of this material or concern for it, cement their bricks with the bitumen of wells, because they attempt to fortify the whiteness of innocence, the strength of faith, and the harmony of brotherhood with the arguments of their disputations.

“Come,” he says, “let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose summit may reach to heaven.” Evil teachers make a city for themselves when, abandoning the heavenly city whose architect and builder is God—that is, the holy Church—they gather their own assemblies. All the reprobate make a city for themselves when, neglecting the protection of God’s commandments, they follow the thoughts and desires of their own hearts in what they do or say [Note: [Col. 0130D] Alternatively, “which they themselves desire”]. They build the Babylonian city when they perform works deserving of confusion. They also make a tower whose summit reaches to heaven when they raise impious tongues even against the injury of their Creator; when, in the words of the Psalmist, they speak iniquity against the Most High [Note: [Col. 0130D] Alternatively, “in the highest place”]; when they set their mouth against heaven. The Gentiles do this by worshiping many gods, heretics by polluting faith in the one God with errors, Jews by denying Christ the Son of God, and false Catholics by profaning the right faith through evil works or schisms. To all of them the Psalmist’s statement to the Lord applies: “The pride of those who hate you continually rises” (Psalm 74:23)—rises toward you, that is, into the memory of your just judgment.

When the pride of the wicked rises toward heaven like the summit of an impious tower, it is right that the Creator of heaven, descending, should destroy the united undertakings of the wicked; and that he should first grant them this benefit: that, since they are unable to complete what their hands have begun, they may not be condemned more severely forever. Then, by dividing them among themselves through a harmful conspiracy split apart, he also ensures that they do less harm to the good.

The Lord did this once for himself by descending from heaven; he does it daily in the Church through his preachers. For he confuses the tongues of the proud Jews, who, against the grace of the Gospel that he preached, all rebel with unanimous agreement and, as it were, with one tongue; and by restraining them from their impious efforts, he scattered them throughout the whole world. He also brings down and divides, through Catholic teachers, the tongues of heretics, and by separating them from one another prevents them from raising the gates of hell against his Church. There is no heresy that is not attacked by other heretics; no sect of secular philosophy that is not exposed as falsehood by other equally foolish philosophical sects. Thus it happens that, while the reprobate have confused tongues among themselves, so that no one recognizes the voice of his neighbor as one who shares the same understanding, they demonstrate that the name Babylon—that is, Confusion—suits them, and they do less harm to the Vision of Peace in which the Church rejoices. For it is evident that the more wicked teachers or evil workers are separated from one another by a divided disposition, the more time they grant for the Church to be gathered.

These are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the flood. Once the structure of Babylon has been destroyed, Scripture hastens, by enumerating the generations of the second age of the world—the first having run from the beginning to Noah and the flood—to reach Abraham the patriarch of the third age, indeed of all the nations. Through his faith and obedience, the foundations of the holy city would again be laid, and in his offspring the dispersion of the nations would return to one confession and faith in the worship of God.

The number one hundred, which is transferred from the left hand to the right, commonly signifies great perfection, whether of good action, hope, or heavenly life. Accordingly, Shem, the son of blessing, fathered a son in the hundredth year of his life, whose lineage would extend through Eber to Abraham. Abraham himself, by the grace of the same mystery, fathered Isaac, the son of promise, in the hundredth year of his age. Following his example, we, made sons of promise and placed meanwhile by hope, as it were, at the right hand of our Judge, await the blessing of heavenly life through good works.

For the two sons whom Shem fathered before his hundredth year, Elam and Asshur, as was read above, were placed outside the holy seed and, as though still being held in the left hand, produced from themselves citizens of the earthly city, that is, of this world. One became the ancestor of the Elamites, that is, the Persians; the other became the ancestor of the Assyrians.

But according to the literal sense a major question arises: how can Shem be said to have been one hundred years old two years after the flood, when above he is said to have been born in Noah’s five-hundredth year, and the flood is recorded as having come in Noah’s six-hundredth year? If he was born in the five-hundredth year of his father’s life, then, when Noah was six hundred years old and the flood came, Shem was one hundred years old; therefore, two years after the flood, he was one hundred and two years old. Thus, so that the number of years may not contradict itself, it must be understood either that Noah was more than five hundred years old by two years when Shem was born, or that he was less than six hundred by two years when the flood came, or that Shem was one hundred and two years old when he fathered Arphaxad. Scripture sometimes speaks in this manner, so that even if a little remains over or is lacking, it nevertheless gives the sound of a full and complete number in its reckoning.

It seems most likely, in my judgment, that Noah was two years beyond five hundred when Shem was born. For Scripture did not speak falsely when it said that he was five hundred years old, even if he was five hundred and two, since the smaller number is contained within the larger. Scripture itself indicated how freely it spoke at that point when it said that Noah, being five hundred years old, fathered three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. No one doubts that one man could not father three sons by one wife in one and the same year. Perhaps for this reason the sacred historian took care to explain the matter more carefully here by saying that Shem was one hundred years old two years after the flood, because he remembered that he had noted the year of his birth somewhat carelessly.

And Shem lived five hundred years after he fathered Arphaxad, and he fathered sons and daughters. Nowhere throughout this entire sequence of generations is there added, as in the age preceding the flood, the statement “and he died,” because among all this group of those being born there was no one concerning whom it could be said, in contrast with the others, as it was said there of Enoch: “He walked with God, and he was not seen, because God took him” (Genesis 5:24).

Arphaxad lived thirty-five years and fathered Shelah. In this place the Seventy Translators placed one additional generation beyond the Hebrew truth, saying that Arphaxad, when he was one hundred thirty-five years old, fathered Cainan, and that Cainan, when he was one hundred thirty years old, fathered Shelah. The evangelist Luke appears to have followed their translation at this point. But when the Greek chroniclers discovered this discrepancy, they corrected the sequence of generations in accordance with the Hebrew authority by removing Cainan. Nevertheless, they did not take care to correct, according to that authority, the number of years in the generations that they shared with the Hebrew books. Rather, following their own authority, they assigned to the age extending from the flood to Abraham a total number of years that was one hundred thirty years less than the edition of the Seventy Translators, but six hundred fifty years greater than the Hebrew truth.

Shelah likewise lived thirty years and fathered Eber. The Seventy Translators have one hundred thirty.

Eber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg. The Seventy Translators have one hundred thirty-four.

Peleg lived thirty years and fathered Reu. The Seventy Translators have one hundred thirty.

Reu lived thirty-two years and fathered Serug. The Seventy Translators have one hundred thirty-two.

Serug lived thirty years and fathered Nahor. The Seventy Translators have one hundred thirty.

Nahor lived twenty-nine years and fathered Terah. The Seventy Translators have seventy-nine.

Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. In this one generation the Seventy Translators differ in nothing from the Hebrew truth. Up to this point the second age of the world extends, comprising, according to the Hebrew truth, 192 years; according to the Seventy Translators, 1,072 years; and according to the reckonings established by the chroniclers, 942 years.

When it is said that Terah, having lived seventy years, fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran, the meaning is the same as when Noah, before the flood, is said to have fathered three sons when he was five hundred years old, even though one man could not father three sons by one wife in a single year [Note: [Col. 0133D] Alternatively, “beget”]. It is understood that, when he was seventy years old, he fathered Abram, who is now called Abraham, and afterward his brothers at a later time. Scripture took less care to express the time of their births because the single notation of the time when Abraham was born was enough and sufficient to indicate the significance of that age [Note: [Col. 0133D] Alternatively, “was expressed for the significance”; alternatively, “was expressed and could suffice”].

These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Terah’s was the one household from which Abraham was born, in which the worship of the one true God existed and, as is credible, in which alone the Hebrew language had by then also remained. Yet he too, just as the people of God later became more manifest in Egypt, is reported by Joshua as having served foreign gods in Mesopotamia. The others descended from his ancestor Eber gradually flowed into other languages and other nations. Therefore, just as in the flood of waters Noah’s one household remained for the restoration of the human race, so amid the flood of many superstitions throughout the world Terah’s one household remained, in which the planting of the city of God was preserved.

Finally, just as there, after the generations up to Noah had been enumerated together with the number of years and the cause of the flood had been explained, before God began to speak to Noah about building the ark, it is said: “These are the generations of Noah,” so here too, after the generations from Shem, the son of Noah, to Abraham have been enumerated, a similarly significant transition is placed, so that it is said: “These are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.” There, the second age of the world was being recounted; here, a patriarch of the third age was being born.

Haran fathered Lot, and Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. The phrase “before Terah” can designate both presence and time: time, because he died before his father; presence, because he departed this life before him—that is, while he was present. Indeed, some manuscripts read: “He died before the sight of Terah his father.” But the phrase “in Ur of the Chaldeans” appears to be the name of the place in which he was buried; its mound is still shown today, as Josephus reports [Note: [Col. 0133D] Jerome regards this account as a fable in his *Questions on Genesis*]. From this it seems that Haran had possessed some great excellence or dignity.

Since among the Hebrews *Ur* means “fire,” they relate that he was consumed by the fire of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 0134D] *Jewish Antiquities*, Book I, chapter 7]. For, recognizing the true God together with his elder brother Abraham, he refused to worship the fire that they worshiped. Therefore, when both were cast into the fire by the Chaldeans, Haran was consumed by the flames, while Abraham, by the merit of his more exalted faith, was delivered by the Lord. Hence later the Lord says to him: “I am the Lord, who brought you out of the fire of the Chaldeans.” Because of this dispute, although Abraham escaped the fire, he could not remain among the Chaldeans; rather, together with his kindred, he was transferred by his father to another land.

The words of Achior, leader of all the Moabites and Ammonites, agree with this. As a renowned man, he could not have been ignorant of what had happened among a neighboring people related to him—indeed, a people from whom he himself had sprung. Speaking of the people of Israel to Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, he says: “This people is descended from the Chaldeans. It first dwelt in Mesopotamia, because they would not follow the gods of their fathers, which were in the land of the Chaldeans. Thus, abandoning the rites of their fathers, which consisted in the worship of many gods, they worshiped the one God of heaven, who also commanded them to depart from there and dwell in Haran” (Judith 5:6) [Note: [Col. 0134D] “It is therefore” is absent in the alternative reading].

Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. Our elders say that Iscah was this same Sarah, Abraham’s wife [Note: [Col. 0134D] Alternatively, “Sarai”], since the full brothers Abraham and Nahor had as wives the two sisters, daughters of Haran. If this is so, the Haran who was their father cannot be understood to be the same person who was the younger brother of Abraham and Nahor, but another man of the same name [Note: [Col. 0134D] Alternatively, “the man is absent”]. For it is established that Abraham was only ten years older than his wife Sarah, since he himself says before the Lord: “Do you think that a son will be born to one who is a hundred years old, and that Sarah, who is ninety, will bear a son?” (Genesis 17:17). How, then, could his younger brother have had a daughter who was ten years younger than he, while she was herself only seven or at most eight years younger than Abraham?

Sarai was barren and had no children. This happened by the design of divine providence: she was barren in her youth so that, giving birth to the son of promise in old age, she might foreshadow the holy Church, to which it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear” (Galatians 4:27), and so forth. For it was fitting that she who, as a figure of our one faith and hope, was to bear one son by promise should give birth to him not in Chaldea, not in Mesopotamia, but in the land of promise.

So Thare took his son Abram, and Lot, the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans [Col. 0134D], to go into the land of Canaan. The Old Translation has “he led them out of the region of the Chaldeans,” which presents no difficulty at all. But what is said according to the Hebrew truth, that he led them out of Ur—that is, from the fire or conflagration of the Chaldeans—can rightly be understood in this way: he led them out of that region where fire was worshiped, so that the meaning is, “he led them out of the idolatry of the Chaldeans.” But when it is said that they were to go into the land of Canaan, and it is immediately added, “they came as far as [Col. 0135A] Haran and dwelt there,” and “the days of Thare were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran,” this reveals Thare’s intention. For when he fled from the Chaldeans, he was indeed thinking of going into the land of Canaan; but when he reached Haran and found there a suitable and secure dwelling for himself and his people, safe from the pursuit of the Chaldeans, he postponed visiting the land of Canaan as a place of exile any farther, and remained in the city to which he had come until his death [Note: [Col. 0135D] Alternatively, “passed over.”], so that he did not even take the trouble to move his foot from it when his son Abraham and his grandson Lot left it at the Lord’s command. For the statement that he died there when he had lived two hundred and five years is plainly understood to have occurred long after their departure. Indeed, Abraham, who was born when his father was seventy [Col. 0135B] years old, was seventy-five years old when he left Haran, which makes one hundred and forty-five years [Note: [Col. 0135D] Alternatively, seventy-five.]. He therefore left Haran when his father was that age, namely, sixty years before his father’s death. But Scripture, anticipating the death of Thare before Abraham’s departure, joined it to Abraham’s arrival and dwelling in Haran, so that thereafter it would have free scope for narrating the story of Abraham and Lot.

Haran, moreover, is a city of Mesopotamia beyond Edessa, which is called Charra to this day [Note: [Col. 0135D] Alternatively, Carran.]. Among the Romans it is famous for the death of the consul Crassus, and among us for the dwelling of the patriarchs. It is also reported to have been ennobled in the book of the holy father Tobit by the hospitality shown to the archangel Raphael.

But the Lord said to Abram: “Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house into [Col. 0135C] the land that I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed.” Since the Lord speaks distinctly of land, kindred, and father’s house, Abraham’s land is to be understood as the region of the Chaldeans, from which he had already departed; his kindred, his brother Nachor with his family, whom he had already left; and his father’s house, in which he was then living at Haran. How, then, is he now commanded to go forth with his father’s house also from the land and kindred from which he appeared already to have departed? Unless perhaps it is to be understood that, with the intention we have already described above, he had left his land and kindred together with his parent so that, once the Chaldeans had been reconciled, he might return there in a later age. But now the Lord commands him to turn his mind away from returning to Chaldea, and likewise to withdraw both mind and body from dwelling in Mesopotamia; leaving the land in which a city of pride had been built and, by the Lord’s judgment, confounded, he was to come into the land in which he would receive the grace of heavenly blessing and, by the merit of his faith and obedience, produce from himself a new and better offspring.

For what he says, “I will make you into a great nation,” properly concerns the people of Israel. Of the other peoples who likewise were to arise from him—namely, the Ishmaelites, the Idumeans, and the peoples who were to be born from Chettura, his second wife after Sarai [Note: [Col. 0135D] Alternatively, “spouse.”]—he says to him later: “I will make you grow exceedingly, and I will place you among nations, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” This is a greater and far more excellent promise of blessing than the former. The former is earthly, this one heavenly; for the former signifies the propagation of carnal Israel, while this signifies spiritual Israel. The former concerns his people, born from him according to the flesh; this concerns the people saved in Christ from all the families of the earth, among whom are also those who, although born from him according to the flesh, wished to imitate the piety of his faith. To all of these the apostle Paul says: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring” [Col. 0136B] (Gal. 3:19).

Therefore, what he says, “and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed,” is as though he said, “and in your offspring the families of the earth shall be blessed.” To speak in the words of the Apostle, Mary was already then in Abraham’s loins, from whom Christ was to be born, when these things were said to him.

And wondrous is the fitting dispensation of heavenly severity and mercy [Note: [Col. 0135D] Alternatively, “of severity and mercy, fittingly.”]. Because men had joined together for a proud undertaking, they deserved to be divided from one another among different languages and kindreds. But when one man left that province and voluntarily became an exile at the Lord’s command, he heard that all the nations—divided among various provinces and languages—were to be gathered together in him through a common blessing.

It should also be noted that, although the third age of the world is commonly reckoned from Abraham’s birth, nevertheless, by this oracle of the Lord to Abraham, the beginnings of the third age were specially consecrated according to the full unfolding of events [Note: [Col. 0136D] Alternatively, “established.”]. For at that time the holy seed was set apart from the nations, and the Savior who was to be born from it was foretold as the Savior of all nations. Until that time, all the faithful and righteous had used that moral knowledge of life [Note: [Col. 0136D] Alternatively, “mortal.”] which they had learned either under the guidance of nature or had originally received from the teaching of their parents [Note: [Col. 0136D] Alternatively, “because.”]. But now they received knowledge also through the coming work of the Savior who was to appear in the flesh, in whom blessing and salvation were to come to all the holy ones—both to those who would precede his incarnation by being born earlier [Note: [Col. 0136D] Alternatively, “preceded it.”], and to us, who were born later and, through the name of that same Lord Jesus, believe that we are saved, as Peter says, just as they were.

[Col. 0136D] So Abram departed as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. From this number of Abraham’s years it is clear that, as explained above, he left Haran while his father was still alive. There can be no doubt that the number seventy-five is mystical, since in that year he himself received the promise of divine blessing and, when he died, left Isaac his son as heir of the same blessing. To speak briefly about it: seventy, being seven times ten [Col. 0137A], signifies the perfection of good action, when by the grace of the Holy Spirit—which the prophet describes as sevenfold—we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue. Five is added to these so that, with the help of the Spirit’s grace, we may carry out the same divine commands through all the senses of our body.

Abram was seventy-five years old when, departing from Haran at the Lord’s command—or in response to his promises—he entered the promised land. This showed that he too, by the help of the Spirit, after renouncing the errors of Babylonian conduct, would keep God’s commands; and that in everything he did by living, hearing, tasting, or touching, there would be nothing at all in his body that he did not offer in obedience to the heavenly commands, enlightened and assisted by the gift of that Spirit [Col. 0137B]. It also signified that all the other heirs of the same promise were to lead their lives in a similar order.

For the fact that he was commanded to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s house is plainly something to be imitated by all the children of his promise, among whom we also belong. We leave our land when we renounce the pleasures of the flesh; our kindred when, insofar as is possible for human beings, we strive to strip ourselves of all the vices with which we were born; and our father’s house when, for love of the heavenly life, we strive to leave this world together with its prince, the devil. For because of the guilt of the first transgression, we are all born in this world as children of the devil [Note: [Col. 0137D] Alternatively, “are born into the world.”]. But through the grace of regeneration, all who belong to the seed of Abraham [Col. 0137C] become children of God. Our Father who is in heaven says to us—that is, to his Church: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11). Accordingly, Haran, from which Abraham departed, is aptly interpreted as “Wrath.” Canaan, toward whose land he is invited, is called “Changed” or “Merchant.”

Therefore Abraham did not depart alone with his brother Lot to come into the land of Canaan. Rather, all the elect who have been born through the bath of regeneration also certainly depart from Haran and come into the land of Canaan. All the elect, when they reject the anger of their first guilt from the pattern of their lives and, abandoning the habit of vices, devote themselves to virtues, apply themselves in a most blessed exchange to temporal labors so that they may obtain eternal rewards. They scorn earthly riches so that they may receive heavenly ones; they despise the joys of human kingship so that they may deserve to have a share in the kingdom of God.

For this is the land that the Lord promised to show his followers: it cannot be discovered by human ingenuity or wisdom as the path of good actions on which one should walk; rather, in all things the guidance of him is to be sought to whom the Psalmist says: “You have held my right hand [Note: [Col. 0137D] Alternatively, “the hand of my right hand.”], and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 2:24).

So Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot the son of his brother, and all the property they had acquired, and [Col. 0138A] the persons whom they had made in Haran; and they departed to go into the land of Canaan. The phrase “the persons whom they had made” is used instead of “the sons whom they had begotten.” For in Scripture a human being is sometimes indicated by the name of the soul alone, and sometimes by the name of the flesh alone. By “soul,” as it is said: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20); by “flesh,” as in the Psalm: “All flesh shall come to you” (Ps. 64:3). Yet neither flesh without soul can come to God, nor can soul sin without flesh; rather, the whole person is signified by one part.

Nor do those who think that, just as flesh is begotten from flesh, so soul is begotten from soul, derive any support from this statement. For, as we said, the whole person is designated by the word “soul.” It is not Abraham and Lot who are to be understood as having made, that is, begotten, persons in Haran [Col. 0138B], but their households and servants; for the subsequent course of sacred history testifies that the patriarchs themselves were still without children.

And when they had come into it [Note: [Col. 0138D] Alternatively, “when he had come.”], Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the illustrious valley. At that time the Canaanite was in the land. And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him: “To your seed I will give this land.” And he built there an altar to the Lord.

It is read above that, while Abram was still dwelling in Haran, the Lord addressed him and, after promising him manifold blessings, commanded him to depart from there and come into the land that he would show him. When Abram had done this and willingly obeyed the divine commands, he immediately became worthy of a greater grace from God [Col. 0138C], so that he deserved to enjoy not merely his address, as before, but also his vision.

When, through that same divine vision and address, he learned that this was the land which God had promised to give him for his possession, he immediately, like a man devoted to God, took care to dedicate it to him by setting up an altar and consecrating it for offering sacrifices to him.

But because sacred history is full of typological mysteries, it should be noted that this appearance of the Lord and the erection of the altar are said to have occurred at Shechem and in an illustrious valley. What else can the illustrious valley figuratively be understood to signify except humility? This is the first virtue that we, called by the Lord away from the labors and burdens of this world, ought to possess, as he himself says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29).

The place of Shechem mystically corresponds to the bearing of this burden [Note: [Col. 0138D] Alternatively, “to a portion of this burden.”], because it is mentioned together with the illustrious valley. For Shechem is rendered in Latin as “shoulders,” since with humility of mind we ought to undertake the burdens of good works that must be carried. When we diligently strive to do this, we shall soon deserve to receive the grace of the Lord’s visitation and consolation, so that little by little we may be able to ascend to higher stages of virtue. Hence, appropriately, concerning the stages of Abraham’s journey, which signify progress in good works, it is added:

And from there, crossing over to the mountain that was opposite Bethel on the east, he pitched his tent there, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. He also built an altar there to the Lord and invoked his name.

After the valley he climbed into the mountains, because through humility in despising ourselves we ought to ascend to the sublimity of action devoted to God. There also, just as in the valley, he built an altar to the Lord and invoked his name, because both our humbling ourselves in the Lord’s presence and our performing lofty works of virtue are gifts of divine favor. For both we ought to offer him praises of thanksgiving.

And because there ought always to be progress toward higher things in the practice of virtue, it is suitably added:

Abram continued on his way, going farther and farther toward the south. The southern region, from which the hotter sun customarily illumines the world [Col. 0139B], mystically displays the fervor of love [Note: [Col. 0139D] Alternatively, “because.”]. By this fervor the hearts of the elect, lest they grow sluggish in the desire and pursuit of lowly things, are always kindled from above by the Sun of righteousness, namely Christ, shining upon them [Note: [Col. 0139D] Alternatively, “when he shines upon them.”].

Thus Abraham, desiring to see and know the land that he was to receive as a possession, proceeded in a human sense out of curiosity, “going farther and farther toward the south.” But in its mystical significance he taught that he, ascending from virtue to virtue, continually advanced in divine love, as do all the elect, until they are granted to see the God of gods in Zion.

Now a famine occurred in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there. After receiving the promises of blessing, after entering the promised land, after building an altar to the Lord there, and after invoking his name, Abraham was tested by famine—and by such a famine that, as soon as he had seen and entered the land he had received in the promise, he left it because of the famine’s severity.

Isaac too, and Jacob and his sons, were similarly compelled by necessity to leave that promised land. As the Psalmist sings, “They passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people” (Ps. 10:13). This should be believed to have happened not by chance but certainly by heavenly providence [Note: [Col. 0139D] Alternatively, “divine providence.”], so that they themselves, and all the heirs of the same promise, might understand that they had received the gifts of divine blessing in such a way that nevertheless in this life they must endure temporal labor and affliction, while in the future they should await everlasting rest and blessedness [Col. 0139D].

It was also made clear that the land of Canaan was promised to Abraham and his seed as a possession in such a way that it signifies rather the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, of which it is written: “But the righteous shall possess the land as an inheritance, and they shall dwell upon it forever and ever” (Ps. 36:29). It is clear that this was not spoken of the land of this age, which is common to the just and unjust, since it is said that the righteous alone will possess it forever and ever [Note: [Col. 0140D] Alternatively, “by the righteous alone.”].

The land of Canaan is therefore promised to Abraham and his seed, and after the long labor of Egyptian servitude it is restored under the leadership of Jesus [Col. 0140A], to signify mystically that the heavenly homeland once promised to us will be restored through Jesus Christ our Lord after the affliction of our present exile.

But even in that same land of Canaan the children of the promise never ceased either laboring or fighting against enemies, so that they might understand, as we said above, that after this life they must seek another homeland, in which they will truly enjoy heavenly blessing and eternal rest.

To this dispensation of divine providence also aptly belongs the fact that, while Abraham was sojourning in Egypt, he was endangered because of his wife, but when endangered he was aided by divine protection so that she would not be harmed. Thus it might be made clear that in this life the righteous must endure with the reprobate not only the general evils of the world—such as famine, disease, and captivity—but also suffer particular tribulations from the reprobate themselves, and that for all these things they will receive in the future those rewards which the reprobate do not know. It follows.

And when he was near entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: “I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife,’ and they will kill me, but they will preserve you. Say, therefore, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you,” and so forth, up to the point where it is said: “But the Lord struck Pharaoh and his house with very great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife” [Note: [Col. 0140D] Alternatively, “Abraham’s wife.”]. And Pharaoh summoned Abram and said to him: “What is this that you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? For what reason did you say that she was your sister, so that I might take her as my wife?”

Abraham told no lie when he called his wife his sister. She was indeed also this, because she was related by blood, just as Lot, although he was the son of his brother, was also called his brother by that same relationship. Thus he concealed that she was his wife but did not deny that she was his sister, entrusting the protection of marital chastity to God while avoiding human danger as a man. For if he did not avoid danger insofar as it could be avoided, he would be tempting God rather than trusting in him.

In the end, what Abraham had expected from the Lord came to pass. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who had taken her as his wife, was severely afflicted and restored her to her husband. Far be it from us to believe that she was polluted by another’s intercourse, since it is much more credible that Pharaoh was not permitted to do this because of the great afflictions.

It may also be said that, according to the book of Esther [Col. 0140D], any woman who pleased the king was anointed for six months with myrrh oil and for another six months used various perfumes and spices, and only then entered the king’s presence. It could have happened that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entrance to him was being prepared over the course of a year, and while Pharaoh had given many gifts to Abram, Pharaoh was subsequently struck by the Lord, while she still remained untouched by intercourse with him [Note: [Col. 0140D] Alternatively, “it might be possible.”].

So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything that he had, and Lot with him, toward the southern region. He does not mean the southern region of Egypt, but [Col. 0141A] that of the promised land. For he did not travel southward from Egypt, since anyone who did so would move farther away from the promised land; rather, leaving Egypt altogether, after visiting the part of it that he had entered, he first ascended into the southern region of the promised land, which was nearest [Note: [Col. 0141D] Alternatively, “which was the greater part.”].

It should also be noted in the literal sense that Abraham is said both above to have gone down into Egypt and now to have gone up from Egypt, because the land of Egypt is said to lie lower not only than the land of Canaan but also than the other regions of the world. Conversely, the region of the Scythians is said to rise higher than the other parts of the earth. This can easily be inferred from the courses of the rivers, which flow into Egypt from elsewhere and flow out from it.

It is most fitting to the typological meaning that the land of Canaan should be higher than Egypt, since the former signifies the promise of the heavenly homeland, while the latter signifies the pressures and labors of the present life. The Lord both promised the former and gave it as an inheritance to his people Israel. In Egypt, Abraham was endangered, although the Lord very quickly protected him; his descendants were oppressed there for a much longer time by the gravest servitude, although they too were finally wondrously redeemed and led out.

The promised land is therefore higher than the boundaries of Egypt, although it lies nearby, because, even if the righteous and the reprobate seem to live outwardly the same common life in this world [Note: [Col. 0141D] Alternatively, “with the reprobate.”], citizens of heaven by the great sublimity of their devoted minds surpass all lovers of this world.

Thus the statement that Abraham went up from Egypt and came with all his people [Col. 0141C] to the southern region signifies typologically that both he, while living in the flesh, and all the elect—the children of the same promise—turn their thoughts for a time toward lowly things to care for the body’s necessities, but as soon as that care has been completed, recall the whole attention of their minds to contemplate the things above and seek renewal through the fervor of love and the light of heavenly grace from the Sun of righteousness.

Mystically, then, to go up from Egypt and come to the southern region means to seek from the Lord, with diligent attention, progress in heavenly light and love after the necessities of the flesh have been fulfilled. It is beyond doubt that by such a desire and intention of mind we make our way toward the heavenly homeland. Hence it is aptly added:

He returned by the way by which he had come, from the south to Bethel [Col. 0141D]. For us, to proceed through the south toward Bethel means to hasten, through the light of heavenly knowledge and the inspiration of inward love, toward entry into the house of God—which is what Bethel signifies—by repeated steps of good works. This is the house which, as the Apostle says, is “not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1). The Prophet desired to see it when he said: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the tabernacle of your glory” (Ps. 25:8) [Note: [Col. 0141D] Alternatively, “the place of your dwelling.”].

As far as the place where he had first pitched his tent, between Bethel and Ai, at the place of the altar that he had previously made; and he invoked the name of the Lord. It should be noted that blessed Abraham, representing the journey of the elect through his own journey, is said to have returned from the south, or through the south, to Bethel, but it is not added that he entered that city. Rather, he is said to have reached the place between it and Ai, and there to have invoked the Lord [Note: [Col. 0142D] Alternatively, “to invoke the Lord.”].

It is mentioned above that this place of prayer was situated on a mountain. For the elect, still held by the bond of the flesh and engaged in progress through the virtues, strive with the whole intention of their minds to reach the house of the heavenly dwelling; they hasten toward it by continuous steps of good works. But they cannot yet enter it, nor yet behold its citizens and King in his beauty [Note: [Col. 0142D] Alternatively, “in their heart.”]. Between the reception of faith, by which they have been consecrated to the Lord, and entry into the kingdom in which they desire to see him, they climb the height of good action as though to the summit of a lofty mountain standing between them.

Ai, or Aggai, as the ancient translators rendered the name of that city, is interpreted as “Question” or “Festivity.” This name most aptly corresponds to the time when each of the faithful is consecrated to the Lord through the sacraments of salvation. Concerning this the Apostle admonishes: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30). For what great festivity of mind it is to be redeemed from the power of darkness and, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, to become the seal of the true King!

This city of unconquerable faith can also rightly be called “Question.” For through it either the elect have learned to seek the Lord, from whom they had wandered farther away [Note: [Col. 0142D] Alternatively, “from whom they had strayed.”], or the Lord himself, like a good shepherd, has made known that he sought them as his sheep, according to what he says: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

The saints build on the aforesaid mountain of good conduct an altar to the Lord—nothing other, of course, than their own body and soul—and on it they invoke his name, knowing that without the help of his name they can neither begin the way of righteousness nor bring the course of their good purpose to completion.

We have taken care to explain this matter of Abraham’s altar more fully, lest anyone think that blessed Moses wished to describe so carefully, for the sake of history, and not rather with a view to spiritual understanding, the place of his tent, altar, and prayer by repeating the narrative.

Here too it should be noted that Abraham is described as making an altar or invoking the Lord not in Egypt, nor in Chaldea, nor in Haran, but only in the land of Canaan, which he received in the promise. For we are able to perform perfect works and offer vows worthy of God only within the unity of the catholic faith and only in hope of the heavenly promise.

Bethel itself is the place formerly called Luz. Jacob gave it the name Bethel after, while sleeping there, he had seen heavenly miracles and hosts. Like Ai, it is a city situated approximately twelve miles from Jerusalem on the road to Neapolis.

[Col. 0143A] Lot, who was with Abram, also had flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and tents [Note: [Col. 0143D] Alternatively, “tents, herds, and sheep.”]. The land could not contain them so that they might dwell together, for their possessions were many and they were unable to live together. Hence strife arose between the herdsmen of Abram’s flocks and those of Lot, followed by the rest of the account, which relates in order how Lot departed from Abraham without any breach of charity. Abraham preferred to separate his dearest and most holy brother from himself bodily rather than keep him with him amid the scandal and quarrels of the weak [Note: [Col. 0143D] Alternatively, “of the infirm.”].

Yet although separated from him in body, he did not separate him from the inward love of his mind, as the following events of sacred history most clearly prove. When Lot was captured by enemies, Abraham vigorously rescued him and all his people; and rightly so, because Lot himself, even while living apart, did not in any respect alter the work of virtue and faith that he had been accustomed to practice with his elder brother [Col. 0143B].

So Lot lifted up his eyes and saw all the region around the Jordan, which was everywhere watered before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah [Note: [Col. 0143D] Alternatively, Gomorrha], like the paradise of the Lord and like Egypt as one approaches Segor. Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan and departed from the east; and so forth, up to the point where it says: “But the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord.”

The text praises the fertility of the land while at the same time noting the wickedness of its inhabitants, so that they may be understood to deserve a greater condemnation because they turned God’s greatest gifts not toward the fruit of piety but toward the increase of luxury. At the same time, blessed Lot is implicitly praised, because while dwelling in that land among its native inhabitants, he could not be corrupted in the least either by the richness of the soil or by the example of those living with him, but preserved the integrity of his purity [Col. 0143C].

The sins to which the Sodomites were enslaved—apart from that unspeakable one which Scripture records later—the prophet Ezekiel sufficiently explains when he speaks to Jerusalem: “Behold, this was the iniquity of Sodom your sister: pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and leisure for her and her daughters; and they did not extend a hand to the needy and poor. They were lifted up and committed abominations before me” (Ezek. 16:49).

That blessed Lot was free from all these things is testified by the text of sacred history, which declares that he received angels as guests and was rescued through them from the impious who were perishing. It is also proved by the statement of blessed Peter the Apostle, which says: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the outrage and conduct of the ungodly” [Col. 0143D] (2 Pet. 2:7). He was righteous in sight and hearing, dwelling among those who day after day tortured his righteous soul by their wicked deeds.

What good merit could he have lacked, when the apostolic voice asserts that he was righteous? Those present could hear from him nothing but the reputation of righteousness; and the crimes of his neighbors, heard and seen by his pure eyes and ears, were nothing to him but torment and affliction.

But when it is said that he departed from the east toward Haran, this signifies [Note: [Col. 0144D] “and Mesopotamia”; alternatively, “and from Mesopotamia.”] Mesopotamia also, from which he had long before departed bodily under Abraham’s leadership [Col. 0144A]. But because the reader might doubt his intention—whether he was still held by love of his kindred and homeland, or whether he too had perfectly departed from his land, kindred, and father’s house as Abraham had—the text took care to make clear specifically concerning him that he had withdrawn from those places and inhabitants not only bodily but also mentally, and that for the sake of faith and hope in divine blessing he consented to remain wherever it pleased Abraham, as a perpetual guest and exile.

That Haran is a city situated to the east of the promised land is attested by Scripture, which later says: “So Jacob set out and came to the land of the east” [Note: [Col. 0144D] Alternatively, “the eastern region.”], since he had in fact traveled from Bethel to Haran.

[Col. 0144B] And the Lord said to Abram after Lot had separated from him: “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, the east and the west. All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed forever.”

Some manuscripts have “for an age,” both expressions being translated from the one Greek word *aionion*, αἰὼν [Note: [Col. 0144D] Some manuscripts omit *aionion*]. If it is read “forever,” it reasonably raises the question how Abraham’s seed can possess that land forever, since human life in this world cannot be everlasting. But if it is read “for an age,” and understood as we faithfully hold it—namely, that the beginning of the future age proceeds from the end of the present one—there will be no question. For although the Israelites have been expelled from Jerusalem, they nevertheless remain in other cities of the land of Canaan and will remain there until the end; moreover, the whole of that land is inhabited by Christians, and they themselves are Abraham’s seed [Col. 0144C].

The statement may also be understood mystically as spoken to blessed Abraham: “All the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed forever.” The region of the heavenly homeland, which that promised land prefigured, is received by all the elect—the seed, namely, of Abraham—in such a way that they remain in it without end, in accordance with what is said of the fire of the burnt offering in [Note: [Col. 0144D] More properly, in Leviticus 6:13]: “This is the perpetual fire, which shall never go out from the altar.”

For that material fire by which sacrifices were burned in the tabernacle could not be perpetual, since the tabernacle itself, the altar itself, and the priesthood itself have long since been taken away. But the fire of love, by which the elect are kindled to offer God the sacrifices of prayers and good actions, never goes out from the altar—that is, from their hearts, which were represented by that Mosaic altar. For in this life they burn with divine love, and in the future, seeing God, they will love him more perfectly with their whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength [Note: [Col. 0144D] Alternatively, “mind.”]. You will find many such things in the ceremonies of the law which, although they are said to be performed or to remain under perpetual obligation, are nevertheless shown not to have been perpetual except when understood spiritually.

Moving his tent, therefore, Abram came and dwelt beside the valley of Mambre, which is in Hebron. Hebron is a city approximately twenty-two miles south of Jerusalem. In the time of Moses it was called Arbe, or Chariatharbe—that is, “City of Four”—because Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam the first-formed were buried there, as it is written in the book of Jesus. Later it received the name Hebron from one of the sons of Caleb, as the Books of Chronicles relate.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that it is now called by this name, even before the time of the sons, let him understand that the name Ebron could have been added here by Ezra the priest when he renewed the sacred Scripture that had been burned by the Chaldeans. Those learned in the sacred letters find many such additions made by him in the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0145D] Alternatively, “the unlearned.”].

[Col. 0145B] And he built an altar to the Lord. This is the third altar that Abraham built: for he had built the first near the place of Shechem, and the second between Bethel and Ai. In all these instances it should be noted that Scripture nowhere records that he offered a sacrifice, but only that he invoked the name of the Lord; nor is he found in the passages that follow to have offered any victim or sacrifice to God, except for the one ram which he offered as a burnt offering to the Lord in place of his son, in which the passion of the Mediator between God and human beings was most clearly prefigured. Nor is his son Isaac read to have offered any victim to God, but only to have built an altar to the Lord. Likewise, although Jacob built an altar at the Lord’s command, he too is not found to have slaughtered any victims, except when, having left the promised land, he was about to enter Egypt on account of Joseph. For then, when he arrived at Beersheba, he is said to have received a divine oracle, after slaughtering victims there; yet neither their kind nor their number is mentioned. Nor is any victim found to have been offered to God by the fathers from that time onward through all those years, until the time of Passover, when the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt.

What, then, does it mean that from the time when the promise was made to Abraham until the time when the law was given, no victims were offered except the one alone which the father sacrificed for his son as a figure of God the Father, who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, while afterward such an abundance of victims was continually offered each day under the law? It means that it was plainly foreshadowed [Col. 0145D] that the grace and truth promised to Abraham and his seed would be bestowed upon the world not through the offerings [Note: [Col. 0145D] Alternatively, “of the victims.”] of sacrifices, but through Christ’s passion. Through faith in him and the sacraments of his passion, not only we but also the righteous who preceded the time of that passion were saved.

The same figure is supported by the fact that Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, who lived in the time of the patriarchs, is read to have offered the Lord not the blood of victims but bread and wine, and to have presented the form not of the legal priesthood but of the evangelical priesthood. He also blessed Abraham himself, to whom the blessing had been promised and in whom the blessing of all nations was promised, so that it might be evident in every respect that the promise given to the fathers was to be fulfilled not through the ceremonies of the Mosaic law but through the grace of the Lord’s passion.

It happened at that time that Amraphel, king of Shinar, Arioch, king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, and Thadat, king of the nations, entered into war against Basra, king of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0145D] Alternatively, “Bara.”] and against Bersa, king of Gomorrah [Note: [Col. 0145D] Alternatively, “Gomurra.”], and the others. The account relates how Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites—that is, of the Persians—waged war against the Pentapolis with the kings allied to him and conquered, and what peoples they killed when, hastening toward this battle, they encountered them along the way.

We must not suppose that the author of sacred Scripture committed these things to memory merely from a historian’s interest [Note: [Col. 0146D] Alternatively, “recorded them”], and not rather with a view to commending heavenly grace to us. Through Abraham’s victory, by which he overcame so many kings with a few men, Scripture teaches us what is the power of the faith with which he was fortified, and how great is the grace of divine blessing with which he was endowed: for by that same faith the saints who were afterward to be born would conquer kingdoms, perform justice, and obtain the promises.

There is also another very important reason, which must by no means be passed over, why the battle of the kings, the initial flight of the Sodomites, and their subsequent rescue were recorded—those same people are plainly shown in what follows to have been utterly overthrown by heavenly wrath. For God, seeing their crimes, first chastised them through this slaughter and captivity at the hands of their enemies. But soon, through his faithful servant [Note: [Col. 0146D] The word “servant” is absent in the alternative text.], he rescued them from that captivity together with everything that had been captured, for the sake of blessed Lot, who faithfully served God among them. Thus, aided by and delivered from evils through such a gift of divine protection, they might learn to serve God themselves after abandoning their errors, and might follow the example in good works of the one through whose merit and by whose agency they had been saved by God’s grace.

But since neither divine chastisements nor gifts caused them to be corrected from their iniquity—indeed, they continually piled fresh crimes upon the ancient offenses of their depravity—it remained that they should be condemned forever by heavenly wrath. The course of this chastisement and punishment continues to be carried out in the same way against the impious and sinners even to this day, indeed until the end of the age: those who do not care to be corrected either by benefits or by heavenly scourges are afterward punished by heavenly vengeance [Note: [Col. 0146D] Alternatively, “are punished with condemnation.”].

[Col. 0146D] In the same way, the world itself will consume its course without end, when human beings throughout the whole world, persisting both in ingratitude toward heavenly gifts and in insensibility toward scourges, will suddenly be swept into eternal destruction by the storm of the final judgment [Note: [Col. 0146D] Alternatively: “Thus … will consume its own state at the end.”].

But when it is said, “All these came together in the Valley of the Woods, which is now the Salt Sea,” the place where the battle was fought is briefly indicated in advance. For what follows explains the cause of the conflict and by what route the hostile army arrived there after carrying out such slaughter, so that the greater the strength of the adversaries is shown to have been, the stronger Abraham’s faith appears, through which he very easily shattered all their power.

The Valley of the Woods is the region in which the Pentapolis—that is, the territory of Sodom and the neighboring cities—then lay. Now, after the conflagration, the waters poured over it from the Jordan, and it is called in sacred Scripture the Salt Sea, or the Dead Sea, while by Greek historians it is called Lake Asphalt, that is, “of bitumen” [Note: [Col. 0147D] Alternatively, “of pitch.”]. It lies between Jericho and Segor.

“And they struck the Rephaim in Astarothcarnaim, and the Zuzim with them, and the Emim in Save, Kiriathaim.” *Raphaim* is the Hebrew name; in Greek they are called *Giants* [Note: [Col. 0147D] “Are called” is supplied in the alternative text.]; in the singular, a Repha is called a giant. Their land, called Astarothcarnaim, lay on the heights above Sodom. Indeed, even to this day a village called Carnea is shown beyond the crossings of the Jordan.

Astarothcarnaim is interpreted as “sheepfold of horns,” since it was clearly the dwelling place of mighty men. Save was a city of the Emim, situated above the region of Sodom, and it is still called by that name. What is added, “Kiriathaim,” is interpreted as “their city.” The sense is therefore: “They also struck the Emim in Save, their city,” just as the Septuagint translators rendered it. That the Emim, like the Zuzim, were a very powerful people is also proved by the meaning of their names: for Zuzim means “Terrible,” while Emim means “Horrible.”

“And the Horites in the mountains of Seir.” At a later time, the sons of Esau—who was also called Seir because he was hairy—drove out the Horites and possessed these mountains together with the neighboring regions. Yet it seems likely that this was not that same Seir, but another Seir, from whom the mountains received the name Seir: namely, the patriarch of the Horites, from whose stock Esau took a wife. Scripture says later:

“Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon the Hivite” (Genesis 36:2).

A little later, after Esau’s lineage has been enumerated, the text explains who this offspring was and from where it came, concluding as follows:

“These are the chiefs of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, wife of Esau. These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs [Note: [Col. 0147D] Alternatively, “Oholibamah.”]—he is Edom” [Note: [Col. 0147D] The words “he is” are absent in the alternative text.].

Immediately a new heading follows:

“These are the sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, and Zibeon.”

And shortly afterward:

“These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys [Note: [Col. 0147D] Alternatively, “she-asses.”] of Zibeon his father. He had a son, Dishan, and a daughter, Oholibamah [Note: [Col. 0148D] Alternatively, “Oholibama.”].”

Since, therefore, Esau had a wife from the race of the Horites—Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon, son of Seir—it is certainly established that the mountains of Seir, in which the Horites were struck [Note: [Col. 0148D] Alternatively, “they struck.”], received their name not from Esau, who was born much later and began to possess those places, but from Seir, the patriarch of those same Horites [Note: [Col. 0148D] *Chorreorum* in the Corbie manuscript; that manuscript nevertheless reads *Horreos* above.].

“And they turned back and came to the spring of Mishpat. This is Kadesh.” Mishpat is interpreted as “Judgment.” Hence the older translation states the matter more explicitly: “They came to the spring of judgment.” This too is spoken by anticipation, since the place received that name much later, because there the Lord judged the people who had come out of Egypt [Col. 0148A].

“And they struck the whole region of the Amalekites.” This must be joined to the preceding verse, so that it is understood that the people of Amalek were struck near Kadesh-barnea, where Miriam encamped and Moses, after striking the rock, brought water from the stone for the thirsty people.

But what follows—“and the Amorite who dwelt in Hazazon-tamar”—belongs to another place, namely the town now called Engaddi, fertile in balsam and palms. Hence Hazazon-tamar is interpreted as “city of palms,” for *tamar* means “palm.”

“And they drew up their battle line against them in the Valley of the Woods.” In place of “Valley of the Woods,” the Hebrew has “in the Valley of Siddim,” which signifies pleasant and wooded places. Such was the Pentapolis, which, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, deserved not only to be consumed by fires but also to be hidden forever from the sight of all living beings beneath the abyss of waters.

“And behold, one who had escaped came and reported to Abram the Hebrew.” From this passage it is clear that those who suppose the Hebrew people were surnamed *Ebrei* from Abraham’s name are greatly mistaken, since Abraham himself is also called a Hebrew—namely, from Heber, son of Joktan, in whose days the division of languages took place.

*Hebrew* is interpreted as “one who crosses over,” a meaning that plainly corresponds to Abraham’s faith and merits. For he transcended temporal desires and hastened to pass from the present age into future joys. [Note: [Col. 0148D] Alternatively, “spirit.”] The saint is not an inhabitant of the earth but a traveler and a stranger, saying to his Creator: “For I am a sojourner with you on the earth, and a pilgrim, like all my fathers.”

It was not without reason that, although both brothers—Abraham, that is, and Lot—descended from the stock of Heber, they were not both called Hebrews, but Abraham alone was so called. He also left this name to the people of God born from him. But because he himself crossed beyond the world more perfectly and transmitted his own passage to his descendants as though it were an inherited right, the additional gift he had received beyond his brother is indicated by the name.

Appropriately, Abraham is first called a Hebrew, that is, “one who crosses over,” at this point, when he was about to rescue his brother from his enemies. Scripture silently intimated that it properly belongs to those who save others from the dangers of temptation through their teaching or intercession that they themselves do not weakly succumb to the trials of vices, but know how to cross beyond them with a vigorous spirit.

Abraham rescued his brother Lot, a man devoted to God, from his enemies; he also rescued the Sodomites, men greatly hated by God. This mystically prefigured that through his merits and intercessions both the elect among the people of Israel and the reprobate would often be instructed through temporal evils, although only the elect can be saved from eternal destruction.

It should also be noted that, while the province of Sodom still remained and had not yet been punished, the righteous Lot was afflicted with temporal losses because of the reprobate, while, because of righteous Lot, the reprobate were mercifully withdrawn from temporal afflictions. But when the judgment of the final severity fell upon the reprobate citizens, then neither could the righteous in any way be touched by the punishments of the wicked, nor could any of the wicked share in his wondrous salvation. Only the good were then saved; only the wicked were destroyed.

In this the state and end of the whole world are clearly expressed, since in this life the good are sometimes afflicted temporally because of the proximity of the wicked, and the wicked are temporarily rescued from adversities because of the proximity of the good. But at the moment of the final judgment, only the wicked will be lost eternally, and only the righteous will be delivered without end.

“When Abram heard that his brother Lot had been captured” [Note: [Col. 0149D] “Had been” is added in the alternative text.], “he counted his trained servants, three hundred and eighteen, and the rest.” It is indeed a great miracle of divine power that Abraham, with so small a cohort, inflicted such slaughter upon so many enemies. But that number of soldiers with whom he conquered contains a deeper mystery of the faith in which our spiritual battle must be overcome.

There were three hundred and eighteen. In that number the sign of the most victorious cross and the name of our Savior Jesus Christ are indicated, through whom this sign has been consecrated as a defense of our salvation. Among the Greeks, three hundred is represented by the letter Τ, which is shaped like a cross. For if it had received a crossbar in the middle, not merely the figure of a cross but the actual sign of the cross would plainly have been represented.

Eighteen, among them, is represented by Ι and Η, which are the first letters of the name Jesus. Therefore, when three hundred and eighteen is written in Greek letters, it is not far from being read as “the cross of Jesus.”
