Abraham therefore rightly conquered the enemies and rescued his brother through three hundred and eighteen companions, so that he might mystically prefigure the one who would be born from his seed and who, through the passion of the cross, would recall the world from death. He too would stand forth exalted and worthy of worship throughout the whole world by the name of Savior, that is, Jesus. Moreover, all who belong to salvation would attain salvation only through this venerable sign and through his fearful name [Note: [Col. 0150D] Alternatively, “through which.”].

“And he pursued them as far as Dan. Dividing his forces, he fell upon them by night, struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is to the left of Damascus.”

The whole sequence of sacred discourse is filled with mystical figures. Not only its words and deeds but also the places and times in which these events occur correspond to the apostolic statement: “All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our sake” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Dan is interpreted as “Judgment,” Hobah as “Condemnation,” and Damascus as “Cup of blood.” Thus, while pursuing the enemies, Abraham found them at Dan and struck them unawares and secure by night. They had boasted of their savagery up to that point and rejoiced as though they had captured their prey. In the same way, sinners who exalt themselves in the riches of this life and in the oppression of the innocent are permitted to glory in their deeds until the crisis of divine judgment.

But when, blinded by heedlessness and placed as though in the middle of night, they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them. Hence it is rightly said that he struck them and pursued them as far as Hobah, that is, “Condemnation,” which must be understood as nothing other than sudden and eternal destruction.

“This,” it says, “is to the left of Damascus.” Damascus, as we have said, is interpreted as “Cup of blood,” by which name the pleasure of vices is rightly signified. For what is the pleasure of sin except a cup of blood, when someone strives without any hesitation to fulfill the things that belong to flesh and blood?

Hobah, where Abraham struck his adversaries, is to the left of Damascus, because the condemnation that will punish the impious will thrust them into everlasting punishment with the devil and his angels, which is customarily signified by the left.

Damascus is a famous city of Phoenicia and was once the metropolis of all Syria. Dan too was a town of Phoenicia and marked the boundary of the province of Judea toward the north, where Paneas is today, once called Caesarea Philippi. Hence the Jordan also received its name, since it flows from Lebanon. Dan is one of its sources; the other is called Jor, which is interpreted as “stream.” When these two sources, which are not far from one another, join into a single stream, it is thereafter called the Jordan.

“But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing out bread and wine—for he was priest of God Most High—blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands.’ And he gave him tithes of everything.”

First, it should be noted in this reading that the patriarchs had foreshadowed what the apostles preach: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:25).

When Lot was suffering adversity, Abraham suffered with him. When they rejoiced in their rescue and victory, Melchizedek rejoiced with them, and he poured heavenly blessing upon the victor who had exposed himself to danger for the sake of his brother’s distress. He magnifies not only the human victor but also the Lord, the giver of the victory, with worthy praise, in accordance with the evangelical saying: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Next, it should be considered that Abraham is blessed after the struggle and victory, and this by the king and priest of God Most High. For all of us who belong to the promise of our heavenly homeland await, after the labors of good works, the blessing of the everlasting kingdom prepared for us from the foundation of the world by the great King and Priest, namely Jesus Christ, Mediator between God and human beings.

Concerning his kingdom, which he possesses equally and eternally with the Father, the Psalm says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’” (Psalm 109:1), and so forth. Concerning his priesthood, in which he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father for us, the same Psalm adds: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (ibid., 4).

Since the Apostle has completed the greater part of his Epistle to the Hebrews by discussing and explaining most sublimely the exposition of these verses and the priesthood and kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ, which were prefigured in Melchizedek, it is appropriate for our small work to speak and treat of them here only very briefly, following his footsteps and inserting here a few of the many things that he set forth.

Thus Melchizedek signifies the Lord Savior: first, as the Apostle says, “he is interpreted as king of righteousness,” and then “king of Salem,” which means “king of peace” (Hebrews 7:2). In these words the blessed Apostle demonstrates how the figure of Melchizedek is to be understood, and teaches us most clearly to seek in the writings of the Old Testament the meanings not only of things but also of names.

Just as Melchizedek, through his name and person, figuratively proclaims Christ as King of righteousness, so also, through the name of his city, he announces the Church of the saints, the city of the great King. Of it it is written: “And his place was made in Salem, that is, in peace” (Psalm 75:3).

Salem is the city later called Jerusalem by King David, and it became the metropolis of the entire province of Judea because he purchased the site of the temple there [Note: [Col. 0151D] Alternatively, “chose it”; another alternative, “bought it.”] and left the expenses of its construction to his son Solomon [Col. 0151C]. All this and countless other things that are read to have been done or said concerning that city are plainly understood by all readers to pertain to the Church.

By the very kind of his sacrifice, of which he also made Abraham a participant when he blessed him, Melchizedek prefigured the offering of the New Testament. Our Lord himself first offered it as the sacrament of his body and blood, and left it to the Church to be offered continually for the remission of sins. He taught that all the children of the promise were to be blessed through participation in it alone, so completely that no one can be a participant in everlasting life without sharing in it:

“Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54).

Thus, in the significance of a great mystery, the priest Melchizedek blessed Abraham by bringing him a portion of the sacrifice which he had offered to the Lord in bread and wine. He clearly intimated in a typological way that not only we, who came after the Lord’s passion in the flesh, but Abraham himself, who had received the promises, and all his elect seed were to be endowed with eternal blessing through the offering of the Lord’s passion.

Abraham had indeed heard from the Lord: “I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed.” He had heard: “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” But before any son was born to him who would be a coheir of that same blessing, and before he offered any sacrifice to God in thanksgiving for the blessing bestowed, Melchizedek, king of Salem, appeared, bringing out the bread and wine that he had offered to God, and blessed him. Thus Abraham might plainly understand that he would receive the blessing promised to him, together with all his seed, through the King of righteousness and author of supreme peace, through the outstanding high priest, and through the mystical sacrifice of bread and wine.

Therefore, let the Jews not boast of the Levitical priesthood against Christians, since they offer victims of flesh to the Lord, while we offer bread and wine. For our sacrifice surpasses theirs both in time and in dignity. In time, because Melchizedek offered this before Abraham, or the priests who later descended from him through the tribe of Levi, offered that. In dignity, because it was concerning this sacrifice, not theirs, that the Father said to the Lord Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

Only a fool and an impious person denies that this has been fulfilled in the work itself and is now manifest throughout the whole world. It is therefore established that Melchizedek was a greater priest than the patriarch Abraham. For, as the Apostle says, without any contradiction, “the lesser is blessed by the greater” (Hebrews 7:7).

The sacrifice of Melchizedek was greater than the victims that Abraham is read to have offered later, because the former was to be offered by Christ the Lord, while the latter was to be offered by Aaron; the former by the priests of the New Testament, the latter by those of the Old.

Hence it is rightly added: “And he gave him tithes of everything.” The Apostle understood and explained this with great sublimity: Abraham gave him tithes not only on his own behalf but also on behalf of all those who were to be born from him, among whom were the very priests who would receive tithes from the people.

“For through Abraham,” he says, “even Levi, who received tithes, was tithed; for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him” (ibid., 9).

Therefore, just as the Levitical tribe—that is, the priestly people—from whom he received tithes was superior to the people, so Melchizedek was superior even to those priests and Levites when he received tithes from them in their father Abraham [Note: [Col. 0152D] Alternatively, “received them.”], for they were still in his loins.

Here Abraham signifies the people of Israel together with its priesthood; Melchizedek, on the other hand, singularly expresses the Mediator between God and human beings, together with the priesthood that he also left to the heirs of the New Testament.

Abraham is blessed and tithed by Melchizedek because even those who were distinguished within the law and the Levitical priesthood could be saved only by being blessed by the Lord Jesus Christ, by referring all the virtues they might possess to him, and by confessing that they were his grace.

Hence Peter, when the grace of the Gospel had already begun to shine, speaking as though of the priesthood that was promised to come according to the order of Melchizedek, said to those zealous for observance of the law [Note: [Col. 0152D] Alternatively, “legal observance”]:

“Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke of servitude which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they also were” (Acts 15:10).

Abraham therefore gave tithes of everything to Melchizedek the priest, from whom he had received a blessing, because Abraham thereby understood the type and image of a better priesthood than the one he himself represented. Abraham represented the legal priesthood; Melchizedek bore the figure of the evangelical priesthood [Note: [Col. 0153B] Alternatively, “of the Gospel.”].

Abraham was to bring forth from himself a temporal priesthood maintained through successive high priests. Melchizedek, however, is read to have had neither a beginning nor an end of priesthood, neither a predecessor nor a successor. Hence he fittingly presents the image of the one to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Let this suffice for what has been said briefly about Melchizedek, insofar as it seemed sufficient for our work. But whoever desires to know fully about him and about the mysteries that he prefigured should diligently read the entire Epistle to the Hebrews.

Then the king of Sodom said to Abram: “Give me the persons, and take the rest for yourself.” He replied to him: “I raise my hand to the Lord God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the warp to a sandal strap I will take nothing of all that is yours,” and so forth.

It should be carefully noted and drawn upon as an example for moral living that Abraham, truly compassionate toward the needs of his neighbors [Note: [Col. 0153B] The word “truly” is absent in the alternative text.], had exposed himself to danger for the liberation of Lot; as one devoted to God, he had given tithes to the priest who blessed him; and, as one who despised money, he refused to accept anything from the spoil he had recovered, even when he offered it to him as the king whom he had defeated. As a lover of justice, he did not neglect to distribute among the soldiers who had fought with him their proper shares.

Such a conscience deservedly rises ever higher through new benefits of heavenly grace, so that it may more swiftly reach the citadel of the virtues. Hence, when these matters had been completed [Note: [Col. 0154B] “Immediately” is absent in the alternative text.], he is rightly made at once a participant in the gift of a heavenly oracle and divine blessing. We shall reserve these matters for better consideration and treatment in the reading of the following book.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0153]

[Col. 0153C] After these things had taken place, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: “Do not fear, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward is exceedingly great.”

The Lord himself confirms the blessing that Abraham had received from the priest Melchizedek. The priest had said: “And blessed be God Most High, by whose protection your enemies are in your hands” (Genesis 14:20). The Lord says: “I am your protector.” The priest had said: “Blessed be God Most High” [Note: [Col. 0153D] Alternatively, “Blessed be Abram by God Most High.”]. God himself says: “And your reward is exceedingly great.”

He speaks of a reward not only for the love he had shown toward his brother when he was in distress, but also for the whole love [Note: [Col. 0153D] Alternatively, “for the devotion, because he himself.”] with which, from the time he had left his homeland and parents, he had served the Lord himself with an undivided heart.

And Abram said: “Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go away without children, and the son of the steward of my house is this Damascus Eliezer.” Abram added: “But you have not given me offspring; and behold, my servant [Note: [Col. 0153D] Alternatively, “one of my household servants.”] will be my heir.”

He does not waver as one doubtful of God’s promises, but simply asks what reward he is to receive from the Lord. Since he has no son in whom he might rejoice as the heir and participant in the divine promise, he will instead have his servant as heir.

That servant was called by two names, namely Damascus and Eliezer. From him, they say, the city of Damascus both received its foundation and its name.

The Lord, favoring Abraham’s desires, promised him the reward he was seeking, when he immediately added:

“This man shall not be your heir, but one who will come forth from your womb will be your heir.”

Reason proves that this was said of Isaac and his seed; concerning him Abraham later heard: “In Isaac your seed shall be called.” For although the sons of the concubines were Abraham’s seed, they could not be participants in his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0154D] Alternatively, “and of the inheritance.”]. And since only heavenly souls belong to this inheritance beloved by God, in which divine protection and a great reward were to be found, the text appropriately continues:

“And he led him outside and said to him: ‘Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can.’ And he said to him: ‘So shall your seed be.’”

The righteous and elect are rightly compared with stars, not only because, like the stars, they cannot be counted by human beings, but also because they are exalted by heavenly blessedness, since they transcend the low and base desires of this life with great elevation of mind; because they shine among the reprobate like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life.

Of such people it can rightly be said at the end: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

When he says, “So shall your seed be,” he speaks not only of those elect who were to be born bodily from his stock, but also of us, concerning whom the Apostle says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3:29).

Hence, when he was still inside, he rightly heard: “But one who will come forth from your womb will be your heir,” on account of those who, coming forth from his seed, were also to become coheirs of the promised blessing and inheritance.

Later, however, bringing him outside, he commands him to count the stars, if he can: “So shall your seed be,” he says [Col. 0155A], on account of those who were not to be begotten from his womb but were nevertheless to be gathered from the whole world into his seed.

Accordingly, to the believing centurion, who belonged to Abraham’s seed not bodily but spiritually, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I tell you that many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11).

He therefore led him outside so that he might learn that he would receive the seed of blessing throughout the breadth of the whole world. He commands him to look up at the sky and count the stars so that he might understand that, in the heavenly homeland, he would be enriched by this inheritance.

“He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

The Apostle recalls this statement (Romans 4:3) in order to commend the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0155D] Alternatively, “to entrust it”], lest circumcision boast and refuse to admit uncircumcised nations to faith in Christ. For when this happened—when faith was credited as righteousness to Abraham who believed—he had not yet been circumcised.

Faith is therefore credited as righteousness, not an idle and naked faith, but one that works through love. The faith of one who, although he does not yet have the opportunity to act, nevertheless possesses a perfect will to act, is also credited.

The faith of the thief was credited as righteousness. Although, when the moment of death was imminent, he could have no opportunity to act, it was nevertheless judged so perfect by the examiner of the heart that on that very day it was rewarded with him in the dwelling of paradise.

The faith of Cornelius and his household was credited as righteousness, so that even before the washing of regeneration they received the gift of the Holy Spirit, because, once conceived in the heart, it was immediately prepared to work through love.

So too Abraham’s faith proved how far it was sufficient to be credited as righteousness [Note: [Col. 0155D] “To be credited” is absent in the alternative text], since it was prepared, at the Lord’s command, to offer even his only son as a burnt offering.

“The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17)—by that faith, namely, which is prepared to work through love and, when it has the opportunity, does work.

And he said to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land and that you might possess it.”

Some think that Ur is the name of a place. But since *Ur* is interpreted as “fire,” it is better understood, in accordance with the tradition of the Hebrews, as we also said above, that he was rescued from the fire of the Chaldeans. When he refused to worship and adore the fire which they themselves worshiped as a god, they wanted to consume him in the flames [Note: [Col. 0155D] Alternatively, “they wished to do so.”], but because God protected him, they were unable to accomplish this [Note: [Col. 0155D] Alternatively, “could not.”].

But he said: “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?”

We must not think that, after Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, he failed in faith by saying, “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?” For he does not seek a sign, as though he still lacked faith, to which he might then give credence. Rather, he begs that some likeness of the matter he had believed might be presented to him, by which its manner might be understood.

Hence the older translation has the more significant wording: “Lord Ruler, according to what shall I know that I shall be its heir?” [Note: [Col. 0155D] Alternatively, “how shall I do it?”]. This is like the case of the Virgin Mary, who was not expressing doubt when she said, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34). She was certain that what was to happen would happen; she was asking how it would happen.

And when he had asked this, he received an answer. Here too, finally, a likeness was given through animals—a heifer, a goat, a ram, and two birds, a turtledove and a dove—so that by these signs he might know what was to happen, although he did not doubt that it would happen.

The text continues:

The Lord answered: “Take for me,” he said, “a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, as well as a turtledove and a pigeon.” [Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading omits “for me.”] Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and placed the two parts opposite one another, but he did not divide the birds. For, whether the heifer signified the people placed under the yoke of the Law, the she-goat that same people destined to become sinful, and the ram [Col. 0156B] that same people also destined to reign, these animals are called three-year-old because that people grew to maturity in the third age of the world and entered the promised land [Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading has *ingressus est* (“entered”) for *intravit* (“entered”).] The first age extended from Adam to Noah, the second from Noah to Abraham himself, and the third from Abraham to David; in that age the people were saved from Egyptian slavery [Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading has *salvatus est* (“was saved”) for *salvatus* (“saved”).] and transferred into the promised land [Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading has *salvatus* (“saved”) for *translatus* (“transferred”).] Or, if these things signify something else more suitably, I nevertheless would in no way doubt that spiritual people were prefigured [Col. 0156C] in the addition of the turtledove and the pigeon. Therefore it was said: “But he did not divide the birds.” For carnal people are divided among themselves, whereas spiritual people are divided in no way—whether they withdraw from the busy dealings of human beings like the turtledove, or dwell among them like the pigeon. Yet both birds are simple and harmless, signifying that even within the Israelite people, to whom that land was to be given, there would be undivided peoples of the promise and heirs who would remain in the happiness of the eternal kingdom.

Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. These divided birds, which descended upon the carcasses, signify not something good, but certain spirits of this air, seeking their own sustenance from the division of carnal people; or certainly the carnal adversaries of that same people, who, following the counsel of Balaam the diviner, sought to snatch an opportunity for victory from their crimes. Of them the prophet says: “Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of the sky” (Lamentations 4:19).

Abram drove them away because Israel was often delivered through his merits both from the distress of temporal evils and from the snares of evil spirits.

What follows—“As the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark terror seized him”—signifies the great disturbance and tribulation that will come upon the faithful near the end of this age. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matthew 24:21).

And it was said to him: “Know beforehand that your offspring will be strangers in a land that is not theirs; they will subject them to slavery, and they will afflict them for four hundred years,” and so forth. This is most clearly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who were destined to serve in Egypt. It does not mean that this people would spend four hundred years in that slavery under their Egyptian oppressors; rather, within those four hundred years this future event was foretold.

The four hundred years are mentioned on account of the completeness of the number, although the actual period is somewhat longer—whether one begins the calculation from the time when these promises were made to Abraham, or from the birth of Isaac, on account of the offspring of Abraham concerning whom these things are proclaimed. From Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the first promise was made to him, to Israel’s departure from Egypt, there are four hundred and thirty years. The Apostle refers to them in this way: “This is what I mean: the Law, which [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading: “which.”] came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to abolish the promise” (Galatians 3:17).

Thus these four hundred and thirty years could be called four hundred, since they are not much more; how much more so when several of that number had already elapsed at the time when those things were shown and spoken to Abraham in the vision, or when Isaac was born to his father at the age of one hundred, twenty-five years after the first promise. At that point, of the four hundred and thirty years, four hundred and five remained, yet the Lord wished to call them four hundred.

“In the fourth generation they will return here” [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading: “they will return.”] Caath entered Egypt with his father Levi; Caath’s son was Amram, Amram’s son was Aaron, and Aaron’s son was Eleazar. Eleazar, being the fourth from Caath, departed with his father Aaron from Egypt [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading omits “from Egypt.”] and, after Aaron had died in the wilderness, he himself entered the promised land [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading: “that land.”]

When the sun had set, a dark gloom came to be, and a smoking furnace and a fiery lamp appeared, passing between those divided pieces. This gloom and fiery furnace, which came after the setting of the sun, signifies that at the end of the age the carnal will be judged by fire. Just as the affliction of the City of God—such as is expected to occur under Antichrist and such as has never previously been—was signified by Abraham’s dark fear around sunset, that is, when the end of the age was already approaching, so at sunset, that is, at the very end, this fire signifies the day of judgment, separating through fire the carnal who are to be saved in fire from those who are to be condemned in fire.

On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: “To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.” By “the river of Egypt” he means the Nile, which he does not call great but small; it forms the boundary between Egypt and Palestine, where the city of Rhinocorura is located [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading: “Rinocorura.” The name of this city is found in various forms among authors: Rinocolura, Rhinocurara; but Ptolemy and Josephus read Rhinocorura.]

The Lord therefore made a covenant with Abram on the day when he had offered animals and birds as sacrifices to him. The covenant was that he himself and his offspring should always offer to the Lord, with faithful hearts, the vows of their prayers and sacrifices, while the Lord would give to him and to his offspring the land of Canaan to possess forever.

[Col. 0158B] Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had not borne children. But she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, and she said to her husband: “Behold, the Lord has closed me off from bearing children. Go in to my maidservant, so that perhaps I may receive children from her.” When he consented to her request, Hagar the Egyptian, his maidservant, was taken ten years later, after he had begun to dwell in the land of Canaan, and given to her husband as a wife; he went in to her, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress, and so forth.

The Apostle fully explains in his Epistle to the Galatians how Hagar and Ishmael designate [Note: [Col. 0157D] Another reading: “signify.”] the Synagogue and the Old Testament, just as Sarah and her son Isaac signify the Church and the New Testament. As for the historical matter itself, however, Abraham must in no way be accused or branded with a crime on account of this concubine [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: “The accusation against Abraham began with this concubine.”] He used her to beget offspring, not to satisfy lust; nor did he act insultingly, but rather obeyed his wife, who believed that her sterility would find consolation if, by her will, she made the fertile womb of her maidservant [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: *fecundae* (“of the fertile woman”).]—something nature could not provide—her own [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another readings: *quo* (“by which”) and *quoniam* (“because”).]. In accordance with the right expressed by the Apostle: “Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Corinthians 7:4), the woman made use of another woman for bearing a child whom she could not bear herself.

Finally, when the pregnant maidservant became proud toward her barren mistress, and Sarah, with the suspicion natural to a woman, had blamed her husband for this [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: “Sarai.”] [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: “had charged him with it.”], Abram [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: “showed.”] showed even then that he was not a lover but a free father, and that he had preserved chastity toward his wife Sarah through Hagar [Note: [Col. 0158D] Another reading: “toward his wife Sarai.”]; he had fulfilled not his own will but hers. For he said: “Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; use her as you please.”

When the angel found her sitting beside a spring of water in the wilderness that lies on the road to Shur, he said to her: “Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?” The Egyptian woman was evidently hurrying along the road to Shur, which leads through the wilderness toward Egypt. The wilderness of Shur extends as far as the Red Sea, which reaches the borders of Egypt.

“Behold,” he said, “you have conceived and will bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael.” Ishmael is interpreted as “Hearing of God,” and the reason for the name is explained immediately afterward: “because the Lord has heard your affliction.”

It should be noted that Ishmael was the first, and Isaac the second, to receive a name from the Lord before being born, certainly by the grace of a particular mystery: namely, that the heirs both of the Old Testament, signified in Ishmael, and of the New, signified in Isaac, were foreknown in the divine election before the ages.

“He will be a wild man; his hand will be against everyone, and everyone’s hand will be against him, and he will pitch his tents opposite all his brothers.” This signifies that his offspring would dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, with uncertain dwelling places, who attack all the nations bordering the wilderness on its side, and are attacked by everyone. But that was in ancient times. Now, however, his hand is so against everyone and everyone’s hands are against him that they oppress all Africa throughout its length under their rule, and also hold the greater part of Asia [Note: [Col. 0159D] Another reading: “of Assyria.”] and some part of Europe, hated and opposed by all.

When he says, “He will pitch his tents,” he shows the ancient custom of the people, who were accustomed always to dwell in tents rather than in houses.

She called [Note: [Col. 0159D] Another reading: “his name.”] the name of the Lord who was speaking to her: “You are the God who saw me.” For she said: “Surely here I have seen the back of him who sees me.” Therefore she called that well “the Well of the Living One who sees me.”

These words make it clear that Hagar was able to see not the face of the angel speaking with her, but only the back of him as he departed from her. Yet she recognized that he had looked upon her in mercy and that he was the Living One—that is, the true God—or that he had come to her in the person of the Living God.

The woman’s wisdom was remarkable—or rather, not remarkable, since she belonged to Abraham’s household—in that she wished the well beside which she had been strengthened by the divine oracle to bear a name derived from that same God. She seems to have understood openly that the well signified the deep mysteries of the divine purpose [Note: [Col. 0159D] Another reading omits “divine”; perhaps one should read “of the divine purpose.”], by which he would have mercy on her affliction, command her to return to her mistress, and foretell that her offspring would become great.

And just as in that well or spring, as it was named above, she saw living and perennial water, so she understood the depth of the divine substance as ever-living and enduring without end or beginning, and believed that the well was rightly named after it.

Corresponding aptly to this figure, when the Psalmist had said: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41:2), he immediately added: “My soul thirsted for the living God” [Note: [Col. 0160D] Another reading: “for you, the living God.”]—so that we might understand that, just as springs possess living and unfailing waters, so God possesses life abiding in himself.

It should also be noted that Hagar’s well is still shown today between the wilderness of Kadesh and Barad, and rightly so, as a testimony to her faith and confession.

After he had begun to be ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said: “I am God Almighty. Walk before me and be perfect. I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.”

Thus, when Abraham was one hundred years old, his name was enlarged, the covenant of circumcision was given, and the birth of Isaac was promised, so that in a great mystery the one-hundred-year-old, already circumcised, might receive the son of promise.

He walks before the Lord so that he may be perfect: whoever remembers at every moment that he stands in the sight of the Divinity and has been placed, as it were, in its service. Thus Elijah, who says, “The Lord lives, before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17:1), indicated that he always kept ready service to God and the presence of his Creator in his mind. And because humility is the first step toward perfection, it is rightly added:

“Abram fell forward upon his face.” In the earlier passages of sacred history we read that holy men invoked the Lord, offered him sacrifices of praise, and lived innocently in his sight; but no one before Abram had fallen forward upon his face before the Lord.

Yet the higher the gifts he received beyond those granted to earlier men, the greater were the thanks he rendered to the giver of gifts by humbling himself. And because, by falling to the ground, he humbly remembered his own frailty, he immediately deserved to recognize sublimely the eminence of divine power. For it follows:

“And God said to him: I am, and my covenant is with you.” What does it mean for the Lord to say, “I am,” except that he openly declares the state of his eternity, in which he is always the same? Concerning this the Psalm also says: “But you are the same” (Psalm 101:28).

The Gospel agrees with this passage where the Lord said to the Jews: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58). Appearing in the flesh, he taught that he himself was the one who had once appeared to Abraham in spirit. He repeated to the Jews the same testimony to his existence that he had given to Abraham. But the Jews, because they had heard, “Before Abraham came to be, I am,” were troubled; Abraham, because he heard, “I am,” rejoiced and did not doubt that God existed before he himself came to be.

Therefore, because he faithfully heard the word of divine eternity, he received as an increase of his reward that he should both be called and become the father of many nations. The Jews, however, because they could not grasp the hidden mysteries of divinity once they had heard them, were cast out from Abraham’s stock and counted among the offspring of vipers.

Finally, they took up stones to throw at him; but he hid himself from them and went out of the temple (John 8:59), so that, hidden from their stony hearts and going out, he might come to reveal to the nations the knowledge of his majesty. At that time also, after going out from the temple, he gave sight to the man born blind, as a figure of the grace by which he was to enlighten the hearts of the Gentiles. It follows:

“You will be the father of many nations, and your name will no longer be called Abram, but you will be called Abraham, because I have appointed you the father of many nations.”

Because blessed Abraham abandoned his kindred and his father’s household at the command of the Lord, he rightly received this also as a gift of recompense: that he should become the father of many nations. Indeed, of so many that they would include not only those who were descended from his seed according to the flesh, but also those who, deriving their bodily origin elsewhere, would follow the footsteps of his faith and obedience, as the Apostle fully explains in his Letter to the Romans.

It should be known that Abram means “Exalted Father,” whereas Abraham means “Father of Many,” with “nations” understood.

“And I will establish my covenant between me and you and between your offspring after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.” The Old Translation reads: “And I will establish my testament.”

It should be noted that wherever in Greek we read “testament,” the Hebrew has “covenant” or “pact,” that is, *berith*. It is not surprising that God’s testament or covenant with Abraham and his offspring is an everlasting covenant, so that he may be their God. This covenant will be preserved without interruption throughout the whole time of this life, in the successive generations of the elect following one another in due order, and it will be celebrated without end in the age to come.

What follows—“I will give to you and to your offspring the land of your sojourn, the whole land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession” [Note: [Col. 0161D] Another reading: “as an eternal possession.”]—requires a more elaborate explanation of how it is to be understood as fulfilled, or still awaited for fulfillment, since no earthly possession can be eternal for any nation.

It should be known, however, that our interpreters translate as “eternal” what the Greeks call *aionion*, a word derived from *aion*. In Greek, *aion* means “age.” But the Latins did not dare to translate this as *saeculare*, lest they convey a very different sense. For many things are called *saecularia* when they are carried out in this age even though they pass away after a short time. But what is called *aionion* either has no end or extends to the end of this age.

Therefore, as we said above, the land of Canaan is given to Abraham’s offspring as an everlasting possession because Christians—whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles, that is, the offspring of Abraham—are believed never to be lacking in it until the end of this present age.

Again God said to Abraham: “And you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall observe between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.”

In gracious providence the Lord first established the covenant of his grace with blessed Abraham and his offspring; then he required from them a covenant of obedience, so that the labor of the struggle might frighten them less after they had first heard of the reward of everlasting recompense.

The flesh of the foreskin was therefore commanded to be circumcised as a sign of the covenant between God and human beings, so that by this sign the faithful of that time might be reminded that they must be cleansed from every pollution of flesh and spirit and bring sanctification to completion in the fear of God.

But in a deeper mystery that physical circumcision was performed as a sign of the covenant between God and Abraham’s offspring, because it was given as the sign of the covenant of which it had earlier been said to Abraham: “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” No believer doubts that this pertains to the grace of the New Testament.

Therefore no believer doubts that circumcision was given as the sign of this covenant, and that Abraham and his offspring were circumcised in the flesh of their foreskin, so that the one who was to be born from that offspring might be typologically prefigured—the one who would cleanse his elect from every stain of sin [Col. 0162B] and grant them everlasting blessing. To the sacrament of this cleansing the following statement aptly corresponds:

“An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you.” For on the eighth day the Lord, that is, after the Sabbath, rose from the dead. In imitation of his passion and resurrection we are baptized, released from the oldness of our vices and renewed as though by spiritual circumcision. The Apostle explains this, saying: “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3).

This number can also most suitably correspond to the time of our resurrection, when we shall universally be clothed with the immortality of the flesh that we laid aside through death, and shall suffer neither sin nor corruption any longer in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0161D] Another reading omits “anything.”].

Our resurrection too is not inappropriately represented by the number of the eighth day: after the six ages of this world and the seventh Sabbath, that is, the rest of souls now celebrated in the other life, it will come. Thus infants were commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day as a sign of the divine covenant, so that it might mystically be indicated that all the elect, by God’s grace, would in this number be released from every iniquity, cleansed from all corruption of the flesh, and freed even from the death that they incurred through the guilt of the first transgression [Note: [Col. 0162D] Another reading: “from eternal death.”].

“Every male throughout your generations, whether born in the household or purchased, shall be circumcised, as well as anyone who is not descended from your stock.” This signifies that the grace of regeneration and immortality pertains to all the faithful, whether they derive their bodily origin from Abraham’s stock or from elsewhere.

“My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.” By this covenant it is signified that he will clothe your flesh and soul together with perpetual renewal and immortality.

“Any male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.” By this sentence the greater mystery of the same circumcision is disclosed. It is not only a sign of the future renewal in Christ, but also of the abolition of the transgression committed in Adam. What baptism now accomplishes in the faith of Christ, circumcision accomplished from that time onward on the eighth day, by which Christ’s resurrection was signified.

The difference was that, before the Lord rose from the dead and opened the gate of that kingdom to all his elect by ascending into heaven, entry into the heavenly kingdom was not yet open to those who were circumcised. This is why they were especially circumcised on the eighth day: to signify that they could truly be cleansed from every stain of vice only through the effect of the Lord’s resurrection.

One may ask how it can be said, “That soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” [Note: [Col. 0163D] Another reading: “shall perish”], when the child bears no guilt, although the text says that his soul will perish, and he himself has not broken God’s covenant; rather, the elders failed to take care that he should be circumcised.

The answer is that even infants, not according to the particular character of their own life but according to the common origin of the human race, all broke God’s covenant in that one person in whom all sinned. Since circumcision was the sign of regeneration, and since generation rightly destroys the infant through original sin—the sin by which God’s covenant was first broken—unless deliverance sets him free, these divine words must be understood as though they said: “Whoever has not been regenerated shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken God’s covenant,” since, in Adam, he too sinned along with all the others.

And the Lord said to Abraham: “You shall not call your wife Sarai by the name Sarai, but you shall call her Sarah. I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son. I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from him.”

Here the promises concerning the calling of the Gentiles in Isaac, the son of promise, are clearer. This signifies grace rather than nature, because a son is promised from an old man and a barren old woman. Although God also brings about the natural course of procreation, wherever the work of God is evident—where nature is impaired and has ceased—there grace is understood more clearly.

And because this was to happen not through generation but through regeneration, circumcision is now commanded. When a son is promised from Sarah, the names of the parents are changed; everything resounds with newness, and the New Testament is shadowed forth in the Old.

Sarai is interpreted as “My Princess,” whereas Sarah means “Princess.” The reason for the change of name is that previously she was called “My Princess,” that is, the mistress of one household only; afterward she is called simply “Princess.” For it follows:

“From her I will give you a son, whom I will bless; he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from him” [Note: [Col. 0164D] Another reading adds “of peoples.”]

Significantly, the Hebrew does not read as we find it in Greek: “God said to Abraham, ‘Your wife Sarai shall not be called Sarai.’” Rather, it has: “You shall not call her name Sarai,” that is, “You shall not say to her, ‘You are My Princess.’” For she was destined already to be the princess of all nations. Hence the Apostle Peter, instructing women in their way of life, says: “Thus formerly the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You are her daughters when you do what is good and do not fear any disturbance” (1 Peter 3:5).

Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: “Can a son be born to a man who is one hundred years old? And can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear?”

Abraham’s laughter was the exultation of one rejoicing, not the mockery of one who doubted. Nor were the words he spoke in his heart words of doubt, but of amazement. The Apostle also bears witness to this when he says of him: “He did not waver through unbelief concerning the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:20).

And the Lord said to Abraham: “Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac.” Isaac is interpreted as “Laughter,” and there is no doubt that he was given this name because, when he heard of his birth, Abraham laughed in his heart.

That laughter aptly signifies the joy of the New Testament, in which the children of promise, with the Lord dwelling in them, will rejoice forever.

As for what follows—“I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him,” and so forth—the phrase “his offspring” refers to those who, by imitating Abraham’s faith, deserve to hear from the Lord: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). The Apostle joins himself to such people when he says: “We, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac” (Galatians 4:28).

More particularly, the name Isaac, that is, “Laughter,” which is born from the promise, aptly applies to the Mediator between God and human beings. Concerning his birth the angel said to the shepherds: “Do not fear; for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10).

He was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and Ishmael his son had completed thirteen years at the time of his circumcision. Thus Abraham was one hundred years old and Ishmael thirteen when they were circumcised. Was this so that, after Isaac was born a year later, Abraham, at the age of one hundred, and Ishmael, at fourteen—that is, twice seven—might have completed their years perfectly? Certainly this occurred in a great mystery, because Isaac held the figure of the New Testament and Ishmael that of the Old.

When Isaac was born, his father was one hundred years old, to indicate that the grace of the New Testament brings the children of its promise to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. As has often been said, the number one hundred in the reckoning of the digits passes from the left hand to the right, and the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, is rightly signified by the right hand. Those who are permitted to enter it will also stand at the Judge’s right hand at the final judgment.

At Isaac’s birth Ishmael had completed two weeks of years, on account of the mystery of the Sabbath, which was observed in the Old Testament. Thus, when the fifteenth year was beginning, Isaac was born as though as a sign of the resurrection, that is, of true circumcision. Here it was typologically made clear that, when the observance of the Law given through Moses passed away, the grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ would succeed it.

When Isaac was born, prefiguring the grace of the New Testament, his older brother Ishmael, who represented the Old Testament, had completed the number seven in his years. For it was fitting that observance of the Law—within which the Sabbath held the chief place—should extend to the time of grace.

The fact that this same number seven was doubled pertains to the perfection of that mystery. The Law desires us to be at rest from servile things—that is, from evil works in the body and harmful thoughts in the mind. The number seven is doubled because the Law commands its followers to have rest for their bodies in this life and promises rest for their souls in the life to come.

When Isaac was born and was beginning the first year of his life, Ishmael was beginning his fifteenth year. This means that when the grace of the Gospel appeared, the Law itself, understood spiritually, was discovered to be full of heavenly mysteries and to proclaim the glory of the resurrection.

But when Isaac had grown, Ishmael was cast out with his mother at Sarah’s command. This must by no means be understood as meaning that the Old Testament should be abolished through the succession of the New Testament. Rather, it signifies that the carnal observance of the Law, together with those who insist that it must still be observed carnally even while the grace of the Gospel shines forth, must be expelled from the boundaries of the Church. The Law itself, understood in a spiritual sense, will not lose even one iota or one letter-stroke until all things have come to pass.

The Lord appeared to him as he sat in the valley of Mamre at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and so forth. This appearance of the Lord is plainly more sacred than all the earlier appearances in which he had so often been seen by blessed Abraham.

And rightly, after receiving the sacrament of circumcision and after his name had been enlarged to signify that he would be the future father of all nations, he came to know the more hidden mysteries of God. Since not only circumcision but also the foreskin was to share in those mysteries, it is rightly recorded that the appearance took place in the valley of Mamre.

For Mamre, as we read above, was an Amorite by birth, but he had entered into a covenant with Abraham together with his brothers. Accordingly, the valley of Mamre aptly signifies our humility. We who have our bodily origin among the Gentiles have Abraham as our father in spirit and faith. To us the Apostle speaks, drawing from Abraham the origin both of flesh and of virtue: “We announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us. What we have seen and heard we announce to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us” (1 John 1:2).

Indeed, apart from its spiritual meaning, this reading greatly edifies those who read it: Abraham saw unknown men and immediately ran to meet them, as though he were about to offer the grace of hospitality to strangers; approaching them, he humbly worshiped upon the ground; he asked them to await and accept his service; and, when they agreed, he hastened to provide it. Nor did he accomplish this through servants and maidservants, but through himself and Sarah.

For if, when he first saw them, he did not believe that they were human beings, it would be remarkable why he wished to bring them water for washing their feet; why he asked them to rest beneath a tree as though they were tired from walking; and why he urged them to refresh and strengthen [Note: [Col. 0165D] Another reading: “by refreshing.”] their bodies as though they were worn out by fasting.

But whoever seeks to examine this reading more deeply will find it everywhere fragrant with spiritual meanings. The Lord’s appearing to Abraham as he sat at the door of his tent aptly corresponds both to Abraham’s devotion and to that of all the heirs of the same promise, who testify that they are strangers and inhabitants of this world but citizens of another life, that is, of the heavenly homeland.

We usually use tents on a journey or in war, but a house in our homeland. In this mystery Isaac and Jacob too are read to have dwelt in tents.

Anyone remains in the middle of his tent who knows that he is a stranger and will not live forever in this age, yet is not ashamed to entangle himself, insofar as he can, in the affairs and enticements of the world. But Abraham and his followers, who engage in worldly things only from necessity and not for pleasure, sit at the door of their tent [Note: [Col. 0166D] Another reading adds: “so that already.”], because they are already prepared to depart from the world and await the entrance into the life to come with a joyful heart ever extended toward future rewards.

It is rightly added: “in the heat of the day.” The heat of the day in which Abraham sat at the door of his tent signifies the power of love with which his mind burned in contemplation of the Sun of righteousness. Such a time and place were fitting for one who was about to see the Lord and enjoy conversation with him: one who was represented as a stranger in this world, irradiated by the light of true heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 0166D] Another reading adds: “that is.”], and ardently inflamed with love for divine contemplation.

[Col. 0166C] And when he had lifted up his eyes, three men appeared to him standing near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of the tent, bowed down to the ground, and said: “Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant,” and so forth.

The fact that three men appeared to him is a mystery of the Holy Trinity. Indeed, when he saw three, he worshiped one and prayed to the Lord, because although there is a Trinity in persons, there is nevertheless one equality of the ruling Godhead, one to be worshiped together. So also in Isaiah, when the angelic powers were singing the glory of the Holy Trinity, saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” they immediately add the unity of dominion and divinity: “The Lord God Almighty; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

And it is rightly said that Abraham lifted up his eyes in order to see the angels, [Col. 0166D] because surely whoever desires to see the citizens of heaven, and to know the glory and mysteries of the divine Majesty, must raise the whole gaze of his mind away from lowly desires and open it with diligent attention toward the light of the true Sun.

It is rightly added that, when he had seen the angels, he ran to meet them, worshiping them and asking them not to pass him by, because whenever we conceive in our spirit some taste of inward sweetness, we must immediately strive with every desire and with ready steps of good works lest that same sweetness quickly leave us. Rather, what has been tasted for a time should, through the memory of heavenly sweetness, refresh our minds for somewhat longer, and, drawing them away from the pleasures and cares of this world, suspend them in contemplation of eternal things.

Perhaps some are troubled by the question of how, both in this passage Abraham and in the following one Lot, seeing angels, received them as guests as though they were human beings and refreshed them with human food as though they were mortal, while nevertheless they spoke with them as with God and received their words no differently from heavenly oracles.

“But it is believable,” as Saint Augustine says, “that Abraham recognized the Lord in the three men, and Lot in the two; and they spoke to him in the singular number, even when they thought them to be human beings. For they did not receive them in this manner for any other reason—so as to minister to them as though they were mortals and in need of human refreshment—but there was certainly something in which they excelled, although they were regarded as human beings, so that those who offered them hospitality could not doubt that the Lord was in them, as he is accustomed to be in prophets. Therefore they sometimes addressed the men in the plural and sometimes the Lord in them in the singular.” Scripture testifies that they were angels, not only in this book of Genesis, where these events are narrated, but also in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where hospitality is praised: “Through it,” he says, “some, without knowing it, received angels as guests” (Heb. XIII, 2). [Note: S. Aug., book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 29.]

Yet in this reception another interpretation may suitably be understood: it was divinely arranged that the patriarchs, seeing angels, should indeed receive them as human beings but venerate them as God, so that by this distinction [Note: Another reading omits “such.”] of service and devotion there might be prefigured what was one day to occur: that the Lord himself, appearing in the flesh, would be nourished with bodily food [Note: Another reading: “would be sustained.”] and received into human hospitality. In that hospitality, however, he would devote himself more to proclaiming the Gospel and healing the weak than to eating and drinking, as the Gospel history very often testifies.

Finally, the interpreters of the sacred Scriptures understood as fulfilled here what the Lord said to the Jews: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII, 56). He saw the Lord’s day when, seeing three angels, he worshiped one and addressed the Lord, because in the distinction of the three persons he recognized the essence of one Majesty.

[Col. 0167D] He refreshed them with food set before them, because he understood that one would be born from his seed who, although God before the ages and consubstantial with the Father, would appear as a true human being at the end of the ages and truly dwell among human beings. The foods with which he refreshed them are themselves full of spiritual [Note: Another reading: “mysteries.”] sacraments, as is recorded:

[Note: Another reading adds “however.”] “Abraham hastened into the tent to Sarah and said to her: ‘Hurry; mix three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.’ He himself ran to the herd, took from it a tender and excellent calf, and gave it to the servant, who hastened and cooked it.”

Here one must first observe that everything is done quickly, as is fitting for the service of receiving God: Abraham hastens, he orders Sarah to hurry, and the servant promptly completes the task assigned to him. Thus it is clearly shown that blessed Abraham truly, in accordance with the Lord’s word, “rejoiced that he might see his day; and he saw it and was glad” (John VIII, 56). Likewise, all who are touched in spirit by consideration of divine grace immediately leap forth into the service of the heavenly will with joyful steps of good works and thoughts, and by diligent exhortation urge themselves and their hearers to hasten in observing the heavenly commandments.

The fine flour that Sarah mixed in order to refresh the angels is the inward sweetness of God’s word, which the prophet promises to heavenly Jerusalem, that is, to the Holy Church, saying of the Lord: “He has made your borders peaceful, and he satisfies you with the richness of wheat” (Ps. CXLVII, 14). Immediately, explaining more clearly what the richness of wheat is, he adds: “He sends forth his word to the earth.”

There are three measures of that same fine flour because in Holy Scripture there is a threefold sense of understanding: the historical, the allegorical, and the anagogical. For example: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. XXV, 8). According to the historical sense, he desired that the beauty of the house which Solomon built for the Lord should remain inviolate, with the Lord’s people praising him there. According to the allegorical sense, he desired the beauty of the Holy Church to shine throughout the whole world; to it the Apostle says: “For you are the temple of God” (II Cor. VI, 16). According to the anagogical sense—that is, the sense that leads upward—he desired to see the beauty of the heavenly homeland, namely, the house not made with hands but eternal in the heavens. The Lord also mentions this threefold measure in the Gospel parable: “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

The woman hides the Gospel leaven in three measures of flour so that the whole may be leavened when the Holy Church, represented here by Sarah, whether it proclaims the historical sense in Scripture, reveals the allegory, or lifts the eye of its interpretation toward the contemplation of heavenly things, always establishes in its words the power either of love of the Lord or of love of one’s neighbor. Let no one think that he has correctly understood Scripture if he has not been able to find in it the establishment of charity.

A *satum* is a unit of measure among the Palestinians, holding one and a half *modii*.

As for Sarah’s making cakes baked under the ashes, this is highly relevant. While cakes baked under the ashes are cooking, they themselves are hidden together with the fire by which they are cooked [Note: Another reading: “with the fire by which they are cooked”]; only the ash piled above them is visible to the eyes of those watching. But when they have been cooked, the ash is removed and the clean loaves are brought before the mouths of those eating. For truly, “the words of the Lord have been tested by fire” (Ps. XVII, 31), namely by the Holy Spirit, through whom Scripture itself was composed. Yet at times, because of the poverty and simplicity of its style, the Spirit may possess such profound knowledge within it [Note: Another reading: “possesses”] that what warmth of spiritual fervor and what measure of heavenly nourishment it contains is not [Note: Another reading omits “easily.”] [Col. 0169A] easily apparent. But when, through the ministry of the preacher, the veil of the letter is removed and the sweetness of the spiritual meaning is disclosed to the hearts of the hearers, then, as though the ash had been shaken off, the sweetest loaves are offered to refresh the faithful. [Note: Another reading: “the sweetness of the spiritual sense is restored to their hearts.”]

The tender and excellent calf that Abraham took from the herd signifies the Mediator between God and human beings, whom the most merciful Father, according to the Gospel parable, slaughtered for the younger son returning to him—that is, for the people of the Gentiles. He is the tender and excellent calf taken from the herd for slaughter and cooking, uniquely for the citizens of heaven, because from the whole human race he alone was specially chosen, by whose blood the world would be redeemed, and through whom not only the things on earth but also those in heaven would be restored in him, as the Apostle says.

This calf is rightly called tender and excellent. For what is as tender and as excellent as he who humbled himself to raise us up: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Ps. II, 8)?

He also took butter and milk, and the calf that he had cooked, and set them before them. By milk he expressed the beginnings and, as it were, the elements of the Mosaic Law; by butter, the perfection of evangelical teaching. By milk, the simplicity of the letter in Scripture; by butter, the power of the mystical sense that is usually generated from the letter. Or certainly, milk signifies the beginning of faith, while butter indicates the perfection of works produced from faith.

Abraham set all these things before the men whom he had received so as to signify that the children of promise would always offer spiritual banquets to the Lord: namely, the loaves of holy readings, the calf of the Lord’s Incarnation, milk as faith or historical perfection, and butter as spiritual meanings or good works. Accordingly, it is well added:

“But he himself stood near them beneath the tree,” because we must feed the Lord—or rather delight him—with the banquets of faith and virtues by living well in such a way that we always remember to stand in his sight, in accordance with blessed Elijah’s saying: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (III Kings XVII, 1). And as the Psalmist says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you” (Ps. CXXXVII, 1). And we must do this beneath the tree of the Lord’s Passion, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI, 14).

When they had eaten, they said to him: “Where is Sarah, your wife?” He replied: “Behold, she is in the tent.” He said to him: “I will return to you at this time, with life accompanying me, and Sarah your wife shall have a son.” [Note: Another reading: “I will return to you, coming back.”]

Both masters of the household, Abraham and Sarah, prepare the refreshment with the greatest haste. But, as in a well-ordered house, Abraham, with the prepared food, approaches the Lord more boldly; Sarah, with womanly fear and modesty, confines herself in the tent—indeed, behind the entrance of the tent—and no longer dares to approach, but listens from hiding to what her husband is saying with the Lord.

Therefore, because she was both devoted to God and properly subject to her husband, she heard the joy of the birth that she greatly desired; and not merely of any birth, but of that birth through which she herself in the future, and all nations, would receive blessing. It is fitting that after the angels had eaten they promise that a son would be born to their host, because when the Lord has received the banquets of our good works and faith, he rewards us with the grace of his blessing.

The angels ate—or rather, appeared to eat—as Saint Raphael explained to Tobias, in order to represent the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, in which the Angel of the great counsel would eat as a human being: not merely by appearing visibly, but also by sitting at a human table and eating. Yet, as that same Raphael says, they used invisible food—that is, food which cannot be seen by human beings dwelling in the flesh—namely, the joy of contemplation. Concerning this the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). They always see him—that is, even when they come outwardly to minister something to us.

It is believable, however, that the food they ate, as soon as it touched [Note: Another reading: “came into contact with.”] their spiritual or [Note: Another reading: “aerial.”] ethereal body, was consumed like water poured upon a blazing flame, and did not nourish their body for refreshment as water poured upon parched earth usually does in us when we eat.

[Note: Another reading omits “now.”] Now both were old and advanced in age, and Sarah’s periods had ceased. To magnify the power of heaven, he says that both were old; and, in addition, that Sarah, although she had been barren, was now also deprived of menstrual blood, so that she could no longer give birth even if she had not been barren.

Moreover, if a woman is so advanced in age that her customary female flow still occurs, she can bear a child by a young man but not by an older one—although that older man may still be able to beget a child by a young woman, as Abraham was able to do with Keturah after Sarah’s death, because he found that she was still vigorous in age.

This, then, is what the Apostle commends when he says: “He believed in hope against hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been said to him: ‘So shall your offspring be’; and, not weakened in faith, he did not consider his own body already dead, since he was nearly a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah; and he did not hesitate at the promise of God” (Rom. IV, 18).

For this reason he says that Abraham’s body was already dead: at that age he could no longer beget a child from every woman who still had some final period of fertility [Note: Another reading: “she herself.”]. We must understand the body to have been dead in some respect, not in every respect; for if in every respect, then old age would no longer be the age of a living man but the corpse of a dead one.

She laughed inwardly, saying: “After I have grown old and my lord is an old man, shall I give myself to pleasure?” The Apostle Peter recalls this statement when, exhorting women to obey their husbands, he adds: “As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.” [Note: Another reading: “So also Sarah.”]

A passage similar to this one appears to be read above concerning Abraham, where, upon hearing that Sarah would bear a child, he fell on his face and laughed in his heart, saying: “Shall a son be born to one who is a hundred years old, and shall Sarah, who is ninety, give birth?” He added, saying to God: “Would that Ishmael might live in your sight!”

But because the Apostle says that Abraham did not hesitate through unbelief, while the following speech of the Lord makes clear that Sarah did hesitate, the Lord says to Abraham:

[Col. 0171B] “Why did Sarah laugh, saying: ‘Shall I truly, an old woman, give birth?’”

It remains to understand that, when Sarah heard that she would bear a son, Abraham had first laughed in wonder and joy, while Sarah herself afterward doubted in joy. Yet her doubt was immediately removed when the reason for divine power was given, as the angel said to him:

“Is anything difficult for God? At the appointed time I will return to you”—that is, at the same time, with life accompanying me—[Note: Another reading omits “and.”] “and Sarah shall have a son.”

When she heard this statement, all doubt was so entirely removed and she was so firmly established in faith that the Apostle rightly says of her: “By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive offspring.”

When he says, “I will return to you,” and adds “with life accompanying me,” he speaks in human fashion, as though he were saying, “if life accompanies me.” But it must be understood more deeply: the angels always dwell with life, whether they remain in heaven or descend to earth—that life of which it is said: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.” Through the vision and illumination of this life, angels and holy human beings become perpetually blessed.

This passage should rightly be compared by contrast with the actions of the first human being. After the guilt of transgression, he is said not to have seen the Lord God but to have heard the sound of him walking in the garden. Abraham, here, kindled by faith, hope, and love of the future blessing, saw the Lord standing, because while this remained with him, contemplation of the divine glory had not departed from him.

The first man, hearing the voice of the Lord God, hid himself trembling, because he was ashamed that he had sinned. Abraham, seeing the Lord, immediately ran to him joyfully, believing that through his obedience he had pleased him. The first man was visited by the breeze after midday; Abraham was visited in the very heat of the day. The latter burned with the fire of divine love; the former, by sinning, had driven away from himself the light of divine protection and love.

Abraham receives the Lord as a guest and refreshes him, so that by the bodily food set before him he might signify that he refreshed him in his heart by living piously on spiritual food, in accordance with the Lord’s own promise to his lovers: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20). [Note: Another reading: “I will go in.”]

The first man, that is, the progenitor, who ate what had been forbidden and lost the perpetual delights which he could have possessed in the presence of the Lord and his angels, was also visibly excluded outside from the tree of life, so that it might clearly be shown that he had lost the incorruptible fruit of wisdom, of which he used to enjoy invisibly.

And because blessed Abraham, by the merit of his pious devotion, had already tasted for a while the fruit of wisdom and life, which is Christ, he is rightly said to have seen and received the Lord while standing beneath the tree.

There Eve, abandoning divine fear and disregarding her husband’s counsel, rashly approached the serpent in whom the devil was speaking. Deceived by him into eating what was forbidden, she also made her husband an accomplice in her transgression. Therefore, after receiving the sentence of just condemnation with her husband, she heard among other things: “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16); and she first bore Cain, a son of the curse and a fratricide.

Here Sarah, subject to divine fear [Note: Another reading: “submissive”], and at the same time following her husband’s religious faith and conduct, waited at home when the Lord appeared, until her husband went to meet him and learned what had to be done. Although food had been prepared for the Lord’s reception, she nevertheless modestly kept herself at home and rejoiced that her husband should go before the Lord with them and offer to him both his own gifts of devotion and hers.

Therefore both received the reward of their good deed in the promised offspring—not just any offspring, but that one through whom all nations would be blessed. And rightly so: there the guilt of transgression in the first Adam was punished by due vengeance; here the time of redemption through the second Adam was both foretold as future and prepared.

It follows:

[Note: Another reading: “And when.”] Therefore, when the men had risen from there, they directed their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham walked with them, escorting them.

When the men are said to have risen from there, it is shown that Abraham, while they were seated [Note: Another reading: “as they returned”], stood beside them and ministered to them, although he had first seen them standing. They directed their eyes toward Sodom so that, just as they rewarded the faith of blessed Abraham with joyful promises, they might destroy the unbelief of the impious city with avenging flames.

This accords with the Psalmist, who, after first declaring the Lord’s kindness toward the holy when he said, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII, 16), immediately adds his severity in avenging the wicked: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (ibid., 17). [Note: Another reading: “promised.”]

As for Abraham’s walking with the angels and escorting them, one should believe that he did this out of the customary devotion of hospitality. Yet blessed were those steps by which a human being was worthy to walk with angels on earth [Note: Another reading: “in the land”] and, when they had come to visit him, escort them [Note: Another reading: “those who had come with him”] as they returned to heaven. Blessed now also is the life of those who follow an angelic manner of life on earth: living soberly, justly, piously, and chastely, and always devoting themselves, as far as is possible for a mortal, to divine praises.

But blessed Abraham, because he received the Lord’s coming with such joy [Note: Another reading: “joyfully”] that he even took care to escort him as he departed, as though he were a member of his household [Note: Another reading: “as a domestic”], deserved to learn the higher mysteries of divine works. Understanding that the severity of heavenly judgment was coming upon the world, he showed himself previously devoted to God in receiving guests and afterward showed himself solicitous for his neighbors by interceding for them.

The Lord therefore said: “The cry of Sodom and [Note: Another reading: “of the Gomorrhites.”] Gomorrah has been multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave.”

By the cry of Sodom he means the report—or rather the infamy—of its crimes. The Apostle prohibits this from us when he says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, and shouting, and blasphemy, be taken away from you, together with all malice” (Eph. IV, 31). This cry is opposed by the cry of the elect, concerning which they confidently beseech their Creator, each saying: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Ps. CI, 2).
