Their great cry is their sublime merit and the intention of faith that seeks heaven alone, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Because they desire neither earthly wealth, nor empty and fleeting glory, nor the dying pleasures of the flesh, but only the goods above, everything they do is lofty and resounds, as it were, like a cry.

But since the cry of sinners, that is, their monstrous crime, has been multiplied, let us see what follows.

“I will descend,” he says, “and see whether they have completed in action the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

When the Lord therefore said that he would descend to see whether that cry was true, he did not display ignorance of his own, for he possesses knowledge of all things; rather, he instructs our rashness, so that before we have learned matters fully we may not presume to condemn the actions of our neighbors.

He teaches us the same thing in the building of the tower, where it is written that the Lord descended to see the city and the tower that the sons of Adam were building. What could he fail to see from heaven on earth [Note: Another reading: “would see”], of whom it is written that hell is naked before him and no covering exists for destruction?

They turned away from there and went to Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the Lord. Drawing near, he said: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? If there are fifty righteous in the city, will they perish together?” and so forth, until he said: “But if ten are found there?” And the Lord said: “I will not destroy it for the sake of the ten.”

It is read below that two angels came to Sodom and were received by Lot. It therefore seems likely that here the two angels departed from Abraham, and that he spoke with the one who remained with him [Note: Another reading: “with him”] and interceded for the doomed city.

In this intercession, above all, the humility of blessed Abraham must be weighed. Although he had such standing with God that he received him in hospitality as one of his household and interceded with him for others as with an intimate friend, he nevertheless remained lowly and despised in his own estimation. Thus, in his second prayer, he says to him:

“Since I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes.”

By this statement he plainly rebukes our pride. Although we are far from the height of his merits and, because of our sluggishness and inertia, far removed from divine conversation, we are nevertheless puffed up by the image of arrogance and scarcely remember that we shall become ashes and dust.

Blessed Abraham, the nearer he drew to the purity of the divine vision, the more clearly he dispersed and cast away the weakness and lowliness of his own frailty. But we [Note: Another reading adds “because”], who are excluded from the sight of inward brightness by the cloud of our perversity, lament the darkness of the misery implanted in us all the less because we are accustomed to see nothing beyond it.

Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the city gate. It is not without reason that the angels who had come to Abraham at midday are said to have come to Sodom in the evening. They came to announce prosperity and joy to Abraham, but to bring adversity upon Sodom. He was burning toward heavenly things through the fruit of light; Sodom, besieged by the darkness of vices, was drawing near to eternal destruction.

When Lot saw them, he rose and went to meet them. He bowed face-down to the ground and said: “I beg you, my lords, turn aside into the house of your servant, remain there,” and so forth.

A great and perfect example of hospitality devoted to God is displayed in blessed Lot. When guests entered the city, he was not only ready to meet and receive them, but also earnestly begged them to turn aside to him and rest with him.

At first they refused to enter his house, but afterward, when he urged them, they consented, so that in this way they might test his diligence in hospitality more carefully and reward it more worthily by rescuing him and his household from the destruction of the sinners.

But before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from the boy to the old man—all the people together. They called Lot and said to him: “Where are the men who came in to you at night? Bring them out to us, so that we may know them,” and so forth.

This is what the prophet Isaiah says concerning the people of Israel who sinned beyond measure: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not hide it” (Isa. III, 9). They proclaimed their sin like the Sodomites and did not hide it when, without regard for any sense of shame, all the males, from childhood to extreme old age, regularly practiced obscenity with males, to such an extent that they did not even conceal their crimes from guests and strangers, but tried, by inflicting violence upon them, to make them like themselves in crime and involve them in their offenses.

When they were raging to commit such an outrage, Lot said among other things: “I have two daughters who have not yet known a man. I will bring them out to you, and you may abuse them as you please, provided that you do nothing harmful to these men.”

Since he wished to prostitute his daughters as compensation, so that his guest-men might suffer nothing of this kind from the Sodomites, it is rightly asked whether compensation for crimes or for any sins ought to be admitted—whether we should do something evil so that another may not do something worse—or whether this statement should rather be attributed to Lot’s bewilderment and not to deliberate counsel. Such compensation is certainly admitted only with the greatest danger. If it is attributed to human confusion and to a mind disturbed by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated.

And behold, the men reached out their hands, drew Lot inside to them, and shut the door. They struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door, and so forth, up to the point where Lot said to his sons-in-law: “Rise, leave this place, for the Lord will destroy this city,” and he seemed to them to be speaking in jest.

The fact that the angels shut the door behind Lot, lest the Sodomites be able to drag either him or anyone from his household outside to destroy them, clearly signifies that the wickedness and persecution of the reprobate will not destroy any of God’s elect [Note: Another reading adds “is.”]. The Lord says of his sheep: “I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John X, 28).

The fact that Lot, although the angels gave him the opportunity and he tried very hard, could not bring any of the faithless citizens—even his own relatives or friends—to salvation signifies that no human labor can add even one soul to the number of the predestined, who were chosen by the Lord before the foundation of the world: “The Lord knows those who are his.”

Yet although our frailty hides from us who belong to the lot of the elect, we must not therefore cease caring for our salvation, nor restrain our tongue from instructing our neighbors. Like blessed Lot, we must live chastely and devote the service of piety to correcting those who err. For although we may be unable to save those predestined to destruction, we do not lose the reward of the kindness we extend toward their salvation.

They led him out and placed him outside the city. There he said to him: “Save your life; do not look back, and do not stand anywhere in the surrounding region. Rather, save yourself on the mountain, lest you perish together with them.”

In general, the burning and destruction of Sodom, from which Lot was rescued, signifies the punishment of the final judgment. When, at the end of the age, the full number of the elect has been completed, all the impious will be swept into eternal fire. The Lord explains this when he says: “Just as it happened in the days of Lot: they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building; but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all. So shall it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed” (Luke XVII, 28).

The Apostle Jude also bears witness to this: “Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, which in the same way committed fornication and went after other flesh, have been made an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire” (Jude VII).

The same Sodomite fire may also appropriately signify the flames of vices by which the reprobate are burned in this life and prepared for everlasting fire. Since they do not cease now to burn with earthly desires and the allurements of the flesh, then they will never cease to burn in the fire of punishment. [Note: Another reading: “they do not cease”; another: “they assist.”]

The Lord affirms—and indeed teaches—this meaning when he says: “In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his belongings in the house, must not go down to take them; and whoever is in the field must likewise not return backward. Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 31).

For we are taught not to abandon the summit of upright conduct and turn our minds downward toward worldly desire when the final moment of judgment is at hand; nor, having left behind the plow of spiritual cultivation, should we look back, when no further correction of our works remains for us but the accounting for what we have done is imminent.

Rather, as judgment approaches, this exhortation [Note: Another reading: “reason”] is given to the faithful: let them persist in the good and salutary things they have begun, lest, returning carelessly to the contagion of the vices they left behind, they imitate Lot’s wife, who, when she heedlessly looked back at Sodom burning with sulfur, was turned into a pillar of salt. [Note: Another reading omits “was turned into a pillar of salt.”]

Therefore, when the Lord forbids us to imitate Lot’s wife, he clearly shows that the burning of the city toward which she had turned her eyes expresses the flames of vices, which we both can and must avoid.

Hence the angels’ exhortation, by which they warned Lot, once led out of Sodom, not to look back or remain anywhere in the surrounding region, but to seek the mountain where he would be saved, must be understood spiritually and followed with the greatest possible attention. We must not carelessly [Note: Another reading: “carelessly”] return to the heat and incitements of vices from which we seem for a short time to have escaped; nor should we consent, as far as possible, to remain in the neighborhood of sinners, lest by their example we stray from the path of our uprightness, in accordance with the Psalmist’s description of the blessed man: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. I, 1). Rather, we should hasten to climb to the summit of a demanding way of life.

Lot said to them: “I beg you, my lord, since your servant has found favor before you, and you have magnified the mercy that you have shown me in saving my life, I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me. Behold, there is a small city nearby to which I can flee, and I shall be saved in it.”

Blessed Lot did not seek the protection of the neighboring city as though he feared that some punishment or disaster would come upon him if he could reach the mountain. Rather, he wished to turn aside to the nearby city so that, while he sought the mountain—which was farther away—the flame threatening the impious nearby might not consume him on the journey itself. [Note: Another reading: “he sought.”]

He said to him: “Behold, I have also granted you this request, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken,” and so forth.

O what depths of divine compassion! God not only frees the righteous from the destruction of sinners, but on account of that same righteous person grants many of them the life they did not deserve, so that in those who perish he might show what impiety deserves, and in those who remain indicate how powerful the intercession of the devout is with God.

Therefore the name of that city was called Segor. Segor is interpreted as “Little,” and it was so called because Lot had said, “Is it not a small one?” Previously, however, it was called Bale, as is read above: “And against the king of Bale, which is Segor itself.” Bale is interpreted as “devouring”; the Hebrews say that it was so called because it was swallowed up by an earthquake on the third occasion.

Just as burning Sodom signifies the flames of vices, and the mountain to which Lot is ordered to ascend suggests the summit of virtues, so Segor [Col. 0177B] designates a certain less-perfect degree of good conduct. Although it is still far removed from the height of the perfect, it has nevertheless already been set apart from the contagion [Note: [Col. 0177D] Alternatively, “contagions.”] of the wicked. For example, one who rightly preserves married life has indeed escaped the sulfurous flame of fornication, but has not yet climbed the mountain of continence [Note: [Col. 0177D] Alternatively, “immediately climbed it”]. One who turns hand and mind away from robbery and greed, and is accustomed to give to the poor from the possessions he has, has not yet been able to abandon everything. He has escaped the conflagration of the Sodomites and entered the walls of the little city in which he could avoid the danger of destruction, but he has not yet ascended the fortress of virtue in which he might already stand forth as perfect—and so forth in similar cases.

“The sun had risen over the earth, and Lot had entered Segor; then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah [Col. 0177C] sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven; and he overthrew those cities and the whole surrounding region.” The rising of the sun over the earth, together with which Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown [Note: [Col. 0177D] Alternatively, “Sodom was overthrown,” with “and Gomorrah” omitted.], signifies the manifestation of the final judgment, when, after all the righteous have been rescued, sudden destruction will overwhelm the wicked.

And it was rightly done by God’s judgment that those who had tried to ensnare blessed Lot, while he greatly labored and resisted, in their crimes, should, when sudden day arrived and they saw him rescued, themselves utterly perish; and that those who had burned in the darkness with the foul pleasures of the flesh should, when morning suddenly appeared, be consumed by sulfur and fire. For all who secretly serve vices in the blindness of their minds are openly struck by the strict Judge when the knowledge of their crime is revealed.

It should also be noted that on one and the same night Lot rejoiced in the Lord as his guest and was defended from his enemies, while the Sodomites labored to heap up their crimes, even by defiling Lot together with his guests. When the sun had risen, Lot was delivered on account of his righteousness, while they were condemned for their wickedness. For in the night of this world the saints rejoice to receive in the chambers of their hearts the One who said, “Behold, I shall come and dwell in your midst” (Zech. X, 11), and in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door for me, [Col. 0178A] I shall enter in to him, and I shall dine with him, and he with me” (Apoc. III, 20). The wicked, however, seek through their temptations either to corrupt the works of the faithful or to corrupt the faith itself. But when the morning of the coming age appears, the former receive the crown of life, while the latter incur the punishment of everlasting death.

The Sodomites perish by a punishment worthy of their crimes. Because they led their wicked lives in the rottenness of lust and the heat of desire, they are rightly punished not only with the flames of fire but also with the stench of sulfur. Nor should we doubt that by such a punishment they have been condemned not only for the present but also for eternity, since the apostle John says: “But for the timid, the unbelieving, the accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the pool burning with fire and sulfur” (Apoc. XXI, 2). [Col. 0178B]

The punishment and vengeance are therefore proportioned to the kinds of sins, in accordance with what the wise man, interpreting the plagues of the Egyptians, says: “So that they might know that by the things through which one sins, by those same things one is also tormented” (Wis. XI, 17). Conversely, blessed Lot deserved to be delivered according to the manner of life he had led. Because he had been hospitable, he happened to be saved from destruction after receiving good guests.

Nor should we doubt that after death he was received by those same guests into the eternal dwellings, so that he who had brought citizens of heaven into his hospitality and refreshed them with his feasts might himself be led by them into heavenly habitations [Note: [Col. 0177D] Alternatively, “tabernacles.”], where he would be refreshed forever with the bread of angels—that is, with the glory of the vision of divine brightness.

[Col. 0178C] As for the statement that “the Lord rained sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven,” the persons of the Father and the Son are plainly distinguished, and the heresy of Sabellius is rejected, for Sabellius says that the Father himself is the one who is the Son. “The Lord rained from the Lord”: the Son from the Father. Hence elsewhere it is said to the Father, “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24), that is, in the Son. Similar is the Psalmist’s statement, where he describes the persons of the Father and the Son as two, while nevertheless indicating one divinity in two persons: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. XLIV, 7). “Your throne, O God,” is said to God the Son; “God, your God, has anointed you” then refers to God the Father.

[Col. 0178D] “His wife looked back, and she was turned into a pillar of salt.” This should truly be believed to have happened literally. Indeed, Josephus reports that even in his own time the same pillar of salt remained at the gates of that city. [Note: [Col. 0178D] Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book I, chapter 22.]

The woman, overcome by fear born of feminine weakness, looked back at the sudden cry of those who were perishing and at the crashing of the flames falling from heaven. Nevertheless, she represents in this weakness those who, having once renounced the world and begun the arduous path of virtues, suddenly return with an unstable and, as it were, womanly heart to the desires of the world that they had abandoned. Concerning them the apostle Peter says: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered [Col. 0179A] to them” (II Pet. II, 20). [Note: [Col. 0178D] Alternatively, “It would have been better.”] [Note: [Col. 0178D] Alternatively, “after recognizing.”]

By contrast, Lot, who left behind everything he possessed, destined to perish with the sinners, signifies those who truly renounce the world and do not regret having renounced it. Blessed Noah also clearly represents them: he too left behind all his possessions, which were to be consumed with the reprobate—by fire in Lot’s case, by the waters in Noah’s.

But the fact that Lot’s wife, when she turned away from the road that the Lord was showing, perished and was changed into a pillar of salt aptly indicates that those who turn aside from the way of truth by returning to vices themselves perish in their depravity, but by the example of their destruction leave others something like a seasoning of wisdom. Thus, remembering their ruin, others may guard themselves more cautiously and circumspectly in the purpose of righteousness they have undertaken. [Col. 0179B]

Finally, the Lord, warning the faithful not to abandon the path of faith they have begun, as though offering them a rock of salt so that they may taste his words more sweetly, says among other things: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke XVII, 32). Whoever therefore desires to escape the fire of vices and the final judgment must, forgetting what lies behind, continually direct his attention toward the joys of the divine promise that lie ahead.

“Lot went up from Segor, and he remained on the mountain, and his two daughters with him.” For he had been afraid to remain in Segor. He hastened to ascend from Segor to the mountain because he understood that this was more pleasing to the angels through whom he had been rescued. He feared that the city which, at that critical moment, had escaped the danger of death through his intercession might afterward, because of the crimes of its citizens, be consumed in destruction like the neighboring cities. [Note: [Col. 0179D] Alternatively, the phrase “the same” is absent.] [Col. 0179C] He was especially afraid because he knew that it had previously been destroyed by frequent earthquakes [Note: [Col. 0179D] Alternatively, “he greatly feared,” with the intervening phrase absent.]. Hence it was also called Bale, that is, “falling headlong” or “devouring.”

According to the spiritual interpretation as well, since Sodom signifies the flames of vices, Segor the still modest beginning of good works, and the mountain the height of virtues, it is necessary that when someone has approached the beginning of virtue after escaping the fire of vices, he should not remain sluggish at that beginning. Rather, he must always strive to advance and hasten with an eager step toward the higher progress of good action.

“The elder daughter said to the younger: ‘Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth. Come, let us make our father drunk with wine, and let us sleep with him, so that we may preserve offspring for ourselves from our father,’” and so forth. This passage relates how Lot’s daughters made him drunk with wine, slept with him, conceived, and bore Moab and Ammon, the patriarchs of the Moabites and Ammonites.

This story indeed appears to have occurred contrary to the natural custom of human conception, but the event cannot be doubted, since such great authority reports that it happened. Lot may seem excusable because he endured such an incestuous crime unknowingly rather than committing it himself. Yet he is not excused in that, having so recently forgotten the [Col. 0180A] destruction of the wicked, he indulged in wine to such an extent that he could not discover what was being done to him.

The daughters too appear excusable, since they did not commit incest with their father out of lust, but because they believed that no men remained on earth and that all the others had been consumed by the same punishment of flames. They suspected that, just as after the Flood the human race had been restored through Noah’s three sons and their three wives, so now it would have to be renewed through themselves and their father, who alone had survived the fires. They therefore judged that the act should be carried out during sleep, lest their father, knowing of such a union, reject and disdain it. [Note: [Col. 0179D] Alternatively, “lest he disdain to look upon it.”]

They may therefore seem excusable because they believed that by such an act they were rendering service to the divine dispensation. But they are not excused in failing either to seek the will or counsel of their father in such a matter or to await a delay of time until they might learn more certainly what had happened to the human race throughout the world. [Col. 0180B]

In the moral sense, however, we can understand from this event that no condition of earthly habitation, however exalted it may seem, can be free from the contagion of tempting guilt. For behold, blessed Lot escaped the foul flames of the Sodomites, avoided the ruin of Segor, an equally sinful city, and climbed to the summit of the mountain. Yet where you might have supposed him placed in the lofty fortress of virtues, there you see him at night made drunk and suddenly defiled by his daughters. This happens because those who, through the illumination of heavenly grace, had overcome other temptations of vice often afterward, through the inertia of their own weakness, succumb feebly to others. [Col. 0180C]

The angelic guidance signifies the heavenly assistance by which we are delivered from the dangers of sins [Note: [Col. 0179D] A variant reads, “by which we are freed from sin.”]. The daughters of blessed Lot express even the carnal thoughts of exalted men [Note: [Col. 0180D] Alternatively, “carnal thoughts of vices.”], through whose negligence such thoughts sometimes arise in them, so that even from a devout heart a less-worthy word or deed may be conceived, as though it were a wicked child.

For we should not doubt that the sons of Lot born from his daughters, who produced gentile peoples alien to their father’s faith, signify those works of holy men that belong not to the rule of holiness but rather to the depravity of evil. Such were David’s adultery, King Hezekiah’s pride, and King Josiah’s rash advance into the battle in which he was killed and thereafter exposed the [Col. 0180D] Davidic kingdom to its enemies; and likewise, finally, the denial of the most blessed prince of the apostles.

Moreover, as often happens, times correspond to events [Note: [Col. 0180D] Alternatively, “events and times.”] For Lot, who had been rescued from Sodom at the dawning of morning [Note: [Col. 0180D] Alternatively, “blessed Lot”], was at nightfall made drunk and deceived. For the fact that we are saved from dangers belongs to the grace of God, who gives light; the fact that we relapse into vices belongs to our blindness and weakness.

Moab and Ammon are generated from Lot’s daughters. That they signify sins is also attested by the commandment of the law, which says: “The Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord until [Col. 0181A] the third and fourth generation, and forever” (cf. Deut. XXIII, 3). For errors and vices, as we have said, are in no way counted among the number of the virtues by which the Church is perfected and adorned; rather, they are covered over by the accumulation of good works, so that they may not appear.

The names of Lot’s sons also fit the habit of vices appropriately. The first is interpreted from the father, and the second as “My people.” [Note: [Col. 0181D] Alternatively, “because of.”] These names signify that vices are not implanted in us by God the Creator, but arise from the origin of our first condition. I call Ammon “my people,” that is, “my people,” because I recognize that this too must be applied to me and not attributed to the Creator of natures.

It should carefully be noted that the name of the people is properly interpreted as *merosus* [the reading is uncertain]. “My people” is called Ammon [Note: [Col. 0181D] Alternatively, “Ammi.”], and this too does not differ from the signification of sins [Col. 0181B]. For just as we ought to rejoice in the growth of virtues that are bestowed on us by the Lord, so it is necessary that we be pierced with salutary sorrow over the rise of vices, which plainly proceed from the corruption of our nature.

These, then, are the sons of Lot conceived through incest. Isaac, on the other hand, who was born from the promise and whose name is interpreted as “Joy,” signifies the grace of virtues.

“Abraham departed from there into the southern land, dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar.” Abraham’s coming into the southern land signifies through his earthly journey the heavenly progress of the mind, by which he, like the other saints, was accustomed always to ascend toward more perfect works of virtue.

[Col. 0181C] The southern land, being nearer to the light and heat of the sun, often indicates, in the moral sense, that life of the faithful which, after dispelling the torpor of worldly desire, is accustomed to be renewed more and more each day by the inward light of heavenly love. Abraham seeks the southern land after Sodom has been destroyed, when each of the elect, seeing the destruction of the wicked, girds himself more devotedly for the service of his Creator, so that he to whom it has been inwardly granted to survive the destruction of the evil may deserve to share eternally in the joys of the good. “When the pestilent is scourged, the simple becomes wiser.”

The words that follow also aptly correspond to the spiritual progress of the elect: Abraham dwelt between Kadesh and Shur and sojourned in Gerar. Kadesh is interpreted as “Holy” or “Changed,” Shur as “Strong,” [Col. 0181D] and Gerar as “Sojourning.”

Abraham therefore went into the southern land and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur because all the elect, when they are inwardly illumined by the recognition of truth and burn with love for the vision of God, also strive to practice works of holiness. They take care to lead among human beings a changed life—that is, a heavenly life instead of an earthly one, an angelic life instead of a human one—and they do not cease to cling through the strength of unconquered faith to the One who is uniquely strong, each saying, “For me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28). [Note: [Col. 0182D] The words “all saying” are absent in another witness.]

It should be noted that among the Hebrews Shur is one of the ten names of God, by which his omnipotent power is customarily signified [Col. 0182A] [Note: [Col. 0182D] Alternatively, “by which his omnipotent power is usually signified.”]. He therefore dwells between Kadesh and Shur who, through works of virtue, daily longs for the vision of his Creator. Since this vision is ordinarily reserved for the future, while in the present age those who have learned to hope for an eternal homeland in heaven confess themselves to be sojourners, the text rightly continues:

“And he sojourned in Gerar.” Both the verb “to sojourn” and the name Gerar, that is, “sojourning,” fittingly portray the life of the saints, which, insofar as it is devoted to divine commands, is alienated from temporal joys. Hence the Apostle, glorifying the life of these same patriarchs, said: “By faith Abraham sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise; for he awaited the city having foundations, whose architect and founder is God” (Heb. XI, 9). And shortly afterward: “In faith all these died, not having received the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (ibid., 13).

Those who say these things signify that they are seeking a homeland. Gerar was formerly the southern boundary of the Canaanites and a metropolitan city of Palestine, situated between Kadesh and Shur—that is, between two deserts. One of these is joined to Egypt, toward which the people arrived after crossing the Red Sea; the other extends from Kadesh to the wilderness of the Saracens [Note: [Col. 0182D] Alternatively, “stretches.”].

The text continues:

[Col. 0182C] “And he said concerning Sarah his wife, ‘She is my sister.’ Therefore Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her.” Why Abraham said this about Sarah, and why we should believe that, although she was taken into the king’s house, she was nevertheless not touched by the king’s intercourse, has already been explained above, where she was similarly taken by Pharaoh but, at the Lord’s command, restored to her husband.

When the text continues:

“God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: ‘Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband’; but Abimelech had not touched her and said: ‘Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation?’”—and the rest of this passage—

Abimelech appears both to have known the worship of the true religion and to have diligently practiced it with all his people. For how could a man alien to the knowledge and fear of God deserve to be rebuked by God when he had sinned, or receive with such humility the words of God rebuking him? He demonstrated the innocence of his nation when he said, “Will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation?” He likewise showed the purity of his heart and conduct when he added, “In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this.”

Therefore, because he answered the Lord prudently and humbly, he immediately deserved to be praised and consoled by the Lord’s second word:

“And I know that you acted with a simple heart; therefore I guarded you, lest you sin against me.”

The fact that he immediately rose during the night, summoned all his servants, and [Col. 0183A] told them what had happened to him, and that they, having heard of the danger of guilt into which the king had fallen, were all greatly afraid, teaches how devoted to righteousness were the minds of both—the king himself and his servants. For when the king said to Abraham, “What have you done to us? What have we sinned against you, that you have brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin?” he plainly indicated that he did not regard the sin of ignorance as trivial, since he confessed that it was harmful not only to himself but also to his kingdom.

He therefore did not believe that it was enough for him to have deserved forgiveness for his offense from God—or rather, to have deserved, through God’s favor, to be guarded from sinning—unless, after returning Abraham’s wife, he also gave the man against whom he had unknowingly sinned a large amount of money, so that he might be reconciled to him, as is read in what follows. [Col. 0183B]

It should not, however, be surprising that uncircumcised men could at that time be worshipers of the truth, since blessed Job and his friendly kings too are believed to have served the Lord faithfully with all their people, after the institution of circumcision, without the sacrament of circumcision. Moreover, it is established that the patriarch Shem, together with Arphaxad, Shelah, and Eber, his sons or grandsons, was still living in the flesh at that time and led a life pleasing to God without the law of circumcision.

It therefore seems probable that the sign of circumcision was given only to Abraham, his descendants, and his household, while among the other nations there could still have been some who served God devotedly through a natural knowledge of the law [Note: [Col. 0183D] Alternatively, “through knowledge of the law by nature.”]—either by the offering of sacrifices or certainly by the [Col. 0183C] profession of true faith, having been cleansed from the stain of the first transgression. This was especially possible while those who still remembered either the destruction of the human race in the Flood, the building of the tower and the division of languages, or the destruction of Sodom were still alive.

The historical account of Genesis, consulted on this matter, testifies that Shem himself lived in the body until the fiftieth year of Jacob’s birth. Blessed Pope Gregory agrees with this judgment when he says that we should in no way believe that so small a number of men in those times attained everlasting life, since the lawgiver Moses appears to have included them in the very brief record of his writings.

When Abraham satisfied the king, who earnestly pressed him and persistently asked why he had called his wife his sister, he said, among other things: “But indeed she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father and not the daughter of my mother.” The old translation puts it more appropriately: “Indeed, she is truly my sister by my father, but not by my mother”—that is, she was the daughter of his brother, not of his sister.

In Scripture, brothers and sisters are sometimes called relatives when they belong to one family—that is, one paternal line—which the Latins interpret as *paternitates*, “paternal relationships,” when a multitude of descendants spreads from one root. Otherwise, how could it be that Abraham, a righteous man, took his father’s daughter as his wife, when Scripture does not even name this practice among the first human beings for the sake of the health of their ears, preferring that it be understood rather than spoken?

When the king said to Sarah:

“Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother; this shall be for you as a covering of the eyes [Note: [Col. 0183D] Alternatively, “as a veil.”] among all who are with you, wherever you may go; and remember that you were exposed” [Col. 0184A],

he spoke in jest because she had said that Abraham was her brother. He says that she had been exposed because, by disguising the truth and calling the man who was her husband her brother, she had concealed it. He urges her to remember this in the future, lest, exposed through a similar pretense, she should again incur the same disgrace.

If one takes pleasure in perceiving an allegorical meaning in this passage, in which Sarah, with Abraham’s permission, is loved and carried off by kings but, through the Lord’s providence, is restored undefiled to her husband, it signifies [Note: [Col. 0184D] Alternatively, “that the Church . . . is to be assailed.”] that the Church is often assailed by the temptations of worldly powers. This occurs by the permission of the Lord, who has deigned to be called her husband because of the gift of heavenly protection [Col. 0184B] and grace, so that, tested by adversity, it may become clear how firm her faith is, with what purity she is devoted to God, and how greatly her Creator’s protection must always guard her from all the plots of her enemies; nor is she ever to be corrupted from the simplicity of her faith.

When, on returning Sarah to Abraham, the king also gave him sheep and oxen, male and female servants, and a very large amount of money, this signifies the time when the kingdom of this world was to submit its neck to the Christian faith and to hold in veneration the religion that it had once striven to destroy.

The fact that Sarah was twice desired and carried off by kings, yet was not polluted—once as a young woman by Pharaoh, and now, more advanced in age, by Abimelech—signified that although the Church would always be exercised by hardships in this life, it would nevertheless undergo [Col. 0184C] two persecutions greater than the rest: one from the Roman Empire, which, as though in her youth, she endured and, with the Lord’s strongest and most glorious assistance, overcame; the other from Antichrist, which, as though in her old age—that is, as the end of her temporal life approaches—she will suffer and, through the mercy of that same Lord, conquer.

Sarah’s great beauty, by which she could be loved even in advanced age because of the grace of her appearance, signifies that the Church will at that final time be adorned with such glory of virtues that the fierce enemy and his minions will greatly envy her. Therefore he will strive to conquer her by every artifice of his plots and powers, fulfilling the prophecy spoken concerning her children: “They will still multiply in fruitful old age, and they will endure well, so that they may proclaim” [Col. 0184D] (Ps. XV, 19)—that is, so that they may steadfastly preach the faith in which they glory amid the evils they suffer.

The fact that both kings were preserved, through God’s providence, from violating Sarah signifies that, through the Lord’s mercy, the fury of persecutors will be restrained in such a way that none of those who truly belong to the Church can be seduced from the purity of faith and charity that is in Christ.

The fact that each king was compelled by plagues to restore Sarah to her husband, and that he corrected his rash abduction by giving money as well, signified that persecutors would often be restrained from injuring the faithful by adversity and the loss of temporal [Col. 0185A] possessions. It also signified that they would be changed into reverence for, or fellowship with, those same faithful—a change that we know has occurred several times during persecutions and believe will occur in the final persecution, which will be greater than the others. This will happen through the prayers of spiritual bishops and through the indulgence and mercy of the Lord and Savior, who has deigned to unite the holy Church to himself by the covenant of marriage.

Blessed Abraham, praying for Abimelech, appropriately signifies both the Lord and Savior himself, who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us, and the pastors and rulers of that same Church. Because they care for her chastity, they do not neglect to beseech the Lord on behalf of her adversaries, so that they may be unable to defile her and may quickly desist from the harmful undertakings they have begun.

[Col. 0185B] Nor should it seem inappropriate that Abimelech, a good man who feared God, can represent the persecutors of the good. In Scripture it is customary for good things to be signified through evil persons and, at times, evil things through good persons. Thus blessed Pope Gregory did not hesitate to place the most wicked kings Saul and Jeconiah in the role of the Lord and Savior; conversely, he says that the perfidy of the Jews was signified by the deed of the most faithful Uriah. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 4.]

“The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised her, and he fulfilled what he had spoken to her. She conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold to her.”

God is said to have “visited” Sarah as though she were sick and had already despaired of all fruitfulness in offspring, so that what nature appeared to deny might be bestowed by the presence of divine grace. This word aptly corresponds to all the children of the promise, who are saved not through the decision of their own free will but through the election of grace, not through the effort of their own labor but when the Lord visits their hearts and fulfills the gift of grace that he promised. [Col. 0185C]

“Abraham called the name of his son whom Sarah bore to him Isaac.” Isaac is interpreted as “Laughter” or “Joy,” and this name itself suits all the faithful, to whom, among the other goods of the heavenly inheritance, their Redeemer promises: “But I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John XVI, 1).

“And he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was one hundred years old.”

Just as Isaac was born in the time of the Old Testament but, by his very birth, signifies the heirs of the New Testament, so the circumcision by which he was consecrated is indeed a sacrament of the Old Testament, but was given beforehand as a figure of the grace of the New Testament, by which the world was to be cleansed in Christ from every stain of sin [Note: [Col. 0185D] Alternatively, “from sin”], death, and mortality.

At that time circumcision released the faithful from the bond of original guilt; nevertheless, it was given as a type of the higher grace by which the whole reign of sin and death was to be destroyed through the Lord’s passion and resurrection. In accordance with this figure, we are absolved from all sins in baptism, and on the last day, renewed from every corruption and mortality of body and soul, we shall attain eternal life. There, as the Lord says, the children of the resurrection “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven; for they can no longer die” (Mark XII, 25). [Col. 0186A]

And because the Lord rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the Sabbath—and because we too hope to rise in the eighth age, circumcision was rightly commanded to take place on the eighth day. There are six ages of this world; the seventh is the Sabbath-rest of souls in the other life; the eighth is our resurrection itself and the universal judgment [Note: [Col. 0186D] Alternatively, “of this age.”].

The fact that Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born and the son of the promise was circumcised corresponds most appropriately to the perfection of that same promise. Since one hundred is a perfect number—and this is especially demonstrated by the fact that it is transferred from the left hand to the right—[Col. 0186B] it mystically belongs to heavenly and everlasting goods. Isaac is therefore rightly born at that age, since by his birth, wonderfully granted to aged parents [Note: [Col. 0186D] Alternatively, “given to his parents”], he signifies heirs not of a temporal and lowly kingdom but of the eternal kingdom in heaven.

In the same sacramental meaning, Noah’s ark was built over one hundred years, Abraham dwelt one hundred years in the land of promise, and Isaac, sowing in Gerar, received a hundredfold in that very year. The court of the tabernacle was one hundred cubits long; in the parable of the Gospel seed, the good soil produced a hundredfold; and the Lord promises those who leave their possessions a hundredfold in this time and, in addition, eternal life. In all these instances, the number one hundred signifies either the joys of everlasting life or the good works by which one reaches them.

[Col. 0186C] “The child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.”

Isaac is nourished with milk when each of the elect—the child of the promise, newly begotten in Christ—receives the first rudiments of faith. Although he is not yet capable of investigating the highest mysteries of divinity, he is nevertheless delighted by the sweetness of heavenly rewards and strives to persist in good works, through which, with God’s help and generosity, he may deserve to receive greater things, in accordance with the words of the apostle Peter: “Therefore, putting away all malice, and all deceit, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet.”

But Isaac is weaned and reaches the nourishment of bread when the elect, progressing through the growth of faith, learn not only to confess Jesus Christ, and him crucified, but also to add that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Abraham made a great feast on the day of Isaac’s weaning because a great solemnity indeed comes to the minds of the foremost teachers when they see those whom they have educated ascending to the citadel of wisdom and virtue.

When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing, she said to Abraham: “Cast out this slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” [Col. 0187A]. Some manuscripts read: “the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with Isaac his son,” which is not found in the Hebrew. But whether he played with Isaac or played in Isaac’s presence, Sarah did not want the slave woman’s son to become a teacher of play for her son [Note: Another reading: “for”]; she did not want the one whom the aged woman had received in the promise to be made unworthy of the promises and heavenly blessing through the ignoble examples or companionship of a bastard. Hence the Apostle did not hesitate to call this play “persecution.” For he persecutes his brother not only one who pursues him with swords, hatred, or insults, but also one who seeks, by playful or foolish conversation, to turn him away from the uprightness of his purity through flattery. Thus also the Psalmist says: “The wicked have told me tales, but not as your law, O Lord; all your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me; help me” (Psalm 118:85) [Col. 0187B]. For he too, because he loved the law of the Lord and the commandments of truth, endured tellers of tales as persecutors; and therefore he implored divine aid to overcome them.

The Apostle, however, clearly showed what each of Abraham’s two sons signifies typologically when he wrote to the Galatians: “It is written [Note: Another reading: “because”] that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; but the one who was born of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one who was born of the free woman was born through the promise—things which are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, producing slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, corresponding to the present Jerusalem, and it is in slavery with its children; but the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4:22) [Col. 0187C].

When he says that the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but the son of the free woman through the promise, he plainly indicates that custom gave birth to the one, demonstrating nature, whereas promise gave the other, signifying grace. Ishmael was born as human beings are born, through the customary law of nature, by the union of the two sexes; hence it is said, “according to the flesh.” This is not because these benefits are not God’s gifts, but because, where God’s gift was to be signified—as God’s grace bestows on human beings what they have not earned—it was fitting that the son should be given in a way not owed by the processes of nature.

Isaac, therefore, was not born to Abraham according to the flesh, but from the promise—not because he had not been brought about through the flesh [Col. 0187D] [Note: Another reading omits “brought about”], but because Abraham had received him from the depths of utter hopelessness. Unless God, who made the promise, had been present, the old man would no longer have dared to hope for descendants from the womb of his aged wife.

Explaining the law, the Apostle adds: “But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. But just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the spirit, so also now” (Gal. 4:28). He does not condemn the Old Testament as though it were opposed to the New, lest he confirm by his authority the insane doctrine of Manichaeus—God forbid! Nor would he in any way place the apostles and evangelists above Moses and the prophets who composed the Old Testament. Of their common grace he says elsewhere: “But having the same Spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13) [Col. 0188A].

Rather, he censures and judges worthy of expulsion from the houses [Note: F.: “house”] of the kingdom those who understand the law, which is spiritual, in a carnal manner; those who, from observance of the law, seek from the Lord temporal benefits and a temporal kingdom, rather than eternal goods in heaven. He reproves those who trust that the letter of the law is sufficient for their salvation without assisting grace—an attitude characteristic of the Jews, of whom he likewise says: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:13). He rejects them and declares them persecutors of the faithful: when the Gospel was shining forth, and the grace of the New Testament was already illuminating the whole world through the Lord’s Incarnation, they nevertheless insisted that circumcision, sacrifices, and legal ceremonies were necessary for those baptized in Christ. It was chiefly against these people that his intention was directed when he wrote this, as a careful consideration of the whole text of this Epistle plainly teaches. Finally, he immediately attaches to the words we have quoted the following:

“But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.’ Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ freed us. Stand firm, and do not again submit to the yoke of slavery. Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. 4:30) [Col. 0188C].

By these words he plainly shows that he does not teach that the Scriptures or the writers of the Old Testament are to be expelled from the boundaries of the Church like the slave woman and her son. Rather, he says that the carnal observance of that same Testament, after the grace and freedom of the Gospel had shone forth through Christ, was to cease and, transformed into a spiritual meaning, was faithfully to be fulfilled by the heirs of the New Testament.

For this is how we must understand what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things have taken place” (Matt. 5:18). Whatever the law and the prophets plainly speak concerning faith in the truth, righteousness of works, or purification of the heart for seeing God [Note: Another reading: “speaks”] must always be received according to the letter [Col. 0188D]. But whatever was commanded to the still-carnal people for carnal observance—such as circumcision itself, the offering of sacrifices, and the daily careful cleansing of leprosy, not only of persons but also of houses and garments, together with innumerable things of this kind—these had to be observed according to the letter until the time of the Lord’s Incarnation.

But after the Lord, rising from the dead, opened the disciples’ minds so that they might understand the Scriptures and recognize the riddles of prophecy in manifest light, it was proper that these things should indeed be read in the Church because of the authority of prophecy; but, because of the illumination of grace, they were to be observed spiritually and not carnally [Col. 0189A]. The primitive Church in Jerusalem nevertheless observed many legal ceremonies even according to the letter, while those who had been called from the nations to the faith also practiced Judaizing, until the Church, spread far and wide throughout the world, began to have priests and teachers from the nations—men who had no concern for Jewish observance, but rejoiced simply as Christians to listen to the apostolic and evangelical decrees.

The figure of Abraham’s sons corresponds most beautifully to this ecclesiastical arrangement. Before Isaac was born, Abraham and Sarah rejoiced over Ishmael as though he were their only son, since he had not yet displayed any pride or frivolity in mind or conduct. In the same way, before the Lord’s Incarnation and the revelation of grace, all who were spiritual under the law rejoiced that the people themselves guarded the law according to the letter with sincere devotion of heart [Col. 0189B]. And rightly so: that people was not resisting grace or preferring the law to the Gospel; rather, with faithful minds it followed the commandments of righteousness that alone had been given to it.

But after Isaac was born and was not yet weaned, Ishmael’s affection began to grow contemptible [Note: Another reading: “the lover”], since the parents rejoiced at Isaac’s birth as though he were the proper son of them both. Yet they were not then considering the expulsion of Ishmael or his mother. For when the grace of the Gospel had been revealed, and the apostles were preaching Christ, the Church of believers rejoiced, and its teachers rejoiced over the promise of the kingdom of God bestowed upon them; nevertheless, they did not immediately strive to reject circumcision and the sacrifices and festivals of the law as superfluous.

For they could not suddenly repel as harmful those things which they knew had been established by God, especially since, amid such observances, the tender and still almost nursing infancy of the holy Church was being nourished.

But when Isaac had been weaned, Sarah saw the slave woman’s son playing and decreed that he should be expelled with his mother. For after the Church from the nations had grown strong in faith in Christ, certain people came from Judea, carnal in understanding, truly sons of the slave woman, not yet made free in the spirit of grace for Christ. They taught the brothers and said: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1). This was more a matter of play [Col. 0190A] and vanity than of evangelical truth. Indeed, it was no small persecution to wish to lead back into the shadows of figures those who were already enjoying the gift of the manifest light. Therefore, through the council of the apostles, the mother Grace soon decreed that this doctrine, together with its authors, was to be cast out.

“For the son of the slave woman,” she says, “shall not be heir with my son Isaac” [Note: Another reading omits “my”] [Col. 0190C]. The Apostle wrote “with the son of the free woman,” because false teachers are in no way to be received alongside the heralds of truth, who preach that we must be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus—false teachers who assert that this grace benefits us only if we are also consecrated by circumcision according to the rite of the law.

Rather, those who deny the power of that grace, which is in Christ, or exalt themselves through works without grace, will remain eternally excluded from the inheritance of grace [Col. 0190B].

Even today there are some in the Church who have been imbued with the sacraments of the New Testament but, because of the carnal intention of their minds, belong to the Old Testament and to the figure of Hagar and Ishmael. This is not because they truly follow the commandments of the Old Testament—for the Lord says of them, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17)—but because, neglecting eternal benefits, they seek temporal benefits from the Lord. They embrace more readily what the old Scripture, understood according to the letter, sometimes seems to proclaim through the prophet: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. 1:19), than what he says through himself: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Matt. 5:3).

Of such people the Apostle says: “For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21) [Note: Another reading omits “are”] [Col. 0190C]. Whether they persist until death in wicked conduct among good Catholics, or whether because of heresies and open schisms they are expelled from the Church by priestly judgment like the sons of the slave woman by Sarah the free woman, nonetheless all who have not corrected themselves beforehand will be made strangers and exiles from the inheritance of blessing at the future judgment:

“For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin; but the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. Therefore, if the Son makes you free,” he says, “you will truly be free” (John 8:34).

[Col. 0189]

# COMMENTARIES ON THE PENTATEUCH. (G,S)*

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST BOOK OF MOSES, CALLED IN HEBREW *BERESITH* AND IN GREEK *GENESIS*

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0189D]

## In the beginning God created heaven and earth.

Certainly, not at the beginning of time, for God made time. Therefore, before God made time, there was no time. We cannot therefore say how God acted before he had made anything. The Beginning, then, is Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you.” For this reason the Son is not mentioned here in the same way because he is the Word, but only because he is the Beginning. The beginning of a still-imperfect creation is being indicated. The Son is mentioned because he is the Word in what is written: “God said, ‘Let it be made.’” For the perfection of creation is indicated there.

What is therefore said—“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—reveals the matter of the whole creation, rational and corporeal, that is, of the angels and of this world. God therefore made both matter and form, just as voice and word come into being together, although voice is prior in origin. Finally, Scripture says: “You who made the world from formless matter.” Matter, however, was made from nothing, while the appearance of the world was made from formless matter.

Accordingly, before every day and before all time God created two things: the angelic creature [Col. 0191B] and formless matter. For although all things were made together—for Solomon says, “He who lives forever created all things together”—still, as we have said, the origin of matter was formed into appearance, just as voice precedes the word.

Thus God did not make everything from nothing, but created some things from nothing and some things from something. From nothing he made the world, the angels, and the soul; from something he made human beings, cattle, and the remaining creatures. This is according to the historical sense.

Spiritually, however, in this Beginning, Christ, God made heaven and earth—that is, spiritual people who contemplate heavenly things, and carnal people who savor earthly things.

It should be known that among the Hebrews this book is called *Beresith*, just as volumes receive their names from their beginnings.

Let us return briefly to the beginning. Some inquire into the person, place, and time of this statement, and say that the Spirit first spoke it through Moses. There are three kinds of prophecy: prophecy about the past, as in “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and what follows; about the present, as in “Christ seated at the right hand of God the Father”; and about the future, as in “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead,” and what follows.

“In the beginning he created.” Some refer this Beginning to the beginning of the creation of all things, since nothing was created before these two; or to the beginning of time, since time was not reckoned until heaven and earth had been made; or to the beginning of dominion, since heaven and earth hold dominion over all things. But, as we said above, this is more properly to be understood of the Son, as many testimonies confirm. Among them is this one, according to the Apostle: “For from him and through him and in him are all things.” The Prophet also says: “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands.”

John likewise speaks in the person of Christ: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” and: “In the beginning was the Word.” Many other testimonies concerning this expression—“In the beginning,” and what follows—are found in Scripture. Among them is the passage in the prophet: “I will crush his head in the sea, from the first to the second” [wording uncertain]. Another prophet says concerning this: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.” Elsewhere: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me.”

Solomon also spoke of this: “All the torrents go into the sea, from them onward” [wording uncertain]. Here too it should be recalled that it is said: “I am the First and the Last.” Both expressions are contained in the Law and in the Apocalypse, where it is said: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God also gave him.”

“He created”—as though he were saying, “he constructed.” Strictly speaking, “to create” is used of making without matter, while “to make” is used of making from matter. Here Moses first speaks of God by this title, although the serpent had spoken of him earlier, saying: “For God knows,” and what follows.

“Heaven” is so called either because it conceals mysteries, or from its height, or from its ornamentation. “Earth” is so called because it is trodden.

How he created heaven and earth, another passage shows when it says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” as though they were a double house with the firmament set between them. Elsewhere: “Stretching out heaven like a skin,” and: “Stretching out heaven like a garment,” as though it were a chamber.

Of the earth it is said that it was founded: “You founded the earth.” In this heaven and earth differ: one is stretched out, while the other is founded. Elsewhere we find these words written in a different order: “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” From this it is understood that they were made together.

Although heaven is here spoken of in the singular, in many places of Scripture heavens are found in the plural, as in: “The heavens declare the glory of God”; “He who made the heavens with understanding”; “Bless God, Lord of the heavens”; and “Praise him, heavens of heavens.”

Here “heaven” is spoken synecdochically, that is, the part for the whole. “Heavens” is used properly here because there are many, as in:

> The golden-hued ether of the sevenfold heaven is split apart;

their names are air, ether, Olympus, the fiery expanse, the firmament, the heaven of angels, and the heaven of the Trinity.

Jerome, however, lists the heaven of the Trinity first, the heaven of angels second, and the firmament third [Col. 0192C].

This statement—“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—may seem contrary to the saying: “When I made heaven and earth, the angels praised me.” Yet there is no contradiction, because all things were made together.

Heaven and earth have a beginning and an end for us; with God they are regarded as without beginning, that is, in his presence, like a man making a chest.

Many heresies are forestalled in this statement. Some said that heaven and earth had existed without a beginning, and not God; that other gods had made them, and that God had not existed beforehand. These heresies are refuted in this verse.

Jerome, however, reveals what this volume concerns when he says: “Genesis is evidently most clear, for in it are written the creation of the world, the beginning of the human race, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the people of the Hebrews as far as Egypt” [Col. 0192D].

Others say that, in the phrase “heaven and earth,” the soul and body, or spiritually the New and Old Testaments, may be understood.

## Now the earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the abyss.

These words seem to signify the formlessness of corporeal matter. Earth and water are more tractable than the other elements when worked upon. That abyss is surely the one in which the devil and his angels are designated in the Gospel, where it says: “The demons begged him not to command them to go into the abyss.”

The earth was empty when there was no one to inhabit it, and [Col. 0193A] unformed, since it had not yet been distinguished from the sea.

Spiritually, our earth—that is, our flesh—was empty and void before it received the form of teaching. “And darkness was over the abyss,” because our flesh was covered by the deep darkness of ignorance.

## And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

The Spirit of God was borne over them not in bodily places but in the excellence of power, because whatever he had begun to form and complete lay subject to the Creator’s will.

Here the Trinity is mentioned, when Scripture says: “In the beginning”—that is, in the Son—“God made,” that is, God the Father. The reason the Holy Spirit is not placed immediately after the mention of the Father and the Son, but earth, darkness, the abyss, and water are inserted, is that the Spirit of God—meaning the will of God—had to rule in such a way that there would be things over which it could be borne, not spatially but in power, and which would lie subject to the Creator’s will.

“Water” is not named here in such a way that we should understand the water we see and touch. Nor is “earth” the sort of earth that can now be seen and handled. Rather, by the names of heaven and earth the whole creation is signified, which God made and brought into being.

These things are called by the names of visible objects because of the weakness of little ones, who cannot comprehend invisible realities.

It is not unreasonable that this formless matter over which the Spirit of God was borne should be called water, because everything that is born on earth—whether animals, trees, or plants—begins to be formed and nourished from moisture.

“The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” [Col. 0193C]—that is, the Spirit of God was borne over our fluid and dark heart. By his breath we are all brought to life, and in him we subsist and find rest.

The statement that the Spirit of God “was borne over” the waters, rather than “entered” or “supported” them, forestalls the heresy that God might not be said to be greater than all creatures.

Spiritually, earth may be understood as the Church, which was empty—that is, without good works—and void—that is, without rewards. “Darkness” signifies the darkness of ignorance and sin. “The face of the abyss” signifies the multitude of human beings. “The Spirit of God” signifies the spirit of prophecy, which was borne over the waters—that is, over the prophets.

The statement that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters also prefigures the Holy Spirit’s descent upon Christ from the water of baptism in the form of a dove [Col. 0193D].

This statement, from “In the beginning” through “over the waters,” signifies three laws: the law of nature, the law of the letter, and the law of the New Testament.

## And God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light.

How did God speak? By what voice, and to whom did he speak before all time? He spoke to the Word, coeternal and unchangeable with himself—not by the bodily sound of a voice, but by inward and eternal reasons.

Spiritual light was made when he said, “Let there be light”—that is, the angels and heavenly powers, of whom it is said: “Wisdom was created before all things.” This same spiritual creation was called heaven when it was said: “In the beginning the Lord created heaven and earth.”

Thus, when God said, “Let there be light, and there was light,” the creation is understood to have been converted and illuminated by being recalled to him [Col. 0194A].

“Let there be light” means: let the illumination of faith appear in us.

Others say that the statement “Let there be light” refers to pale light, that “he said” refers to the Son, and “let there be” to the Father.

In another interpretation, light signifies the New Testament or the spiritual understanding, which is divided from darkness—that is, from the Old Testament or the letter.

In yet another, light signifies the soul, which is superior to the flesh. Darkness signifies the flesh with its vices, as the Apostle says: “I know that nothing good dwells in my flesh.”

## And God saw that the light was good.

That is, it pleased him well.

## And God divided the light from the darkness, and what follows.

The division of light from darkness signifies the distinction of the formed thing from the formless. The naming of day and night indicates this distinction.

It does not say, “He made darkness,” because darkness is not a creature; rather, darkness is the name given to the absence of light.

When it says, “He called the light day, and the darkness he called night,” by what language did he call them? “He called” means that he caused them to be called, since he distinguished all things so that they could be discerned and receive names.

“Evening” throughout those three days, before the luminaries existed, may quite reasonably be understood as the end of completed work. “Morning” signifies the operation that was to follow.

## One day.

Perhaps “day” here is the name of the whole of time, and by this term all the ages of the world are included. For this reason it does not say “the first day,” but “one day.”

Allegorically, “God divided the light from the darkness” means that he divided sinners who depart from the truth from the righteous who remain in that same light.

The fact that it does not say that he made the darkness shows that he is not the maker of evils but the arranger of merits. “Evening” signifies the sin of rational creation; “morning” signifies its renewal.

## And God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters.”

It may rightly be asked whether the heaven now came into being that surpasses all the regions of the air and in which the luminaries were established on the fourth day, or whether the air itself is called the firmament.

Many assert that there cannot be water above the starry heaven, because the weight of water has been so ordered that it either floats upon the earth or is carried vaporously through the air near the earth.

One who agrees with them demonstrates that this air is called heaven, just as in ordinary speech we say “clear heaven” and “cloudy heaven.” Scripture also calls birds “birds of heaven,” although it is clear that birds fly in the air.

It is called the firmament because its interval divides certain water vapors from those visible waters that float upon the earth.

We, however, should not doubt in the least that these waters are above the highest heaven, whatever they may be and however they exist there. The authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human intellect.

We know that the Lord did not say “Let this or that creature be made” as many times as the words “God said, ‘Let it be made’” are found in this book. For he generated one Word, in which he spoke all things before they existed.

But Scripture speaks as to little ones when it indicates that the eternal reason of each kind was created by God’s word.

When we hear “God said, ‘Let it be made,’” we understand that it was in the Word that the thing should be made. When we hear “and so it was made,” we understand that the creature was made and did not exceed the limits prescribed in God’s Word.

When we hear “And God saw that it was good,” we understand that, in the goodness of the Spirit, it pleased him that what had pleased him to be made should remain made.

But when it adds, “And God made,” why is “And God made” not said in the creation of light? Because on the first day, when light was made, the condition of spiritual creation is disclosed. In that nature the holy angels and powers are understood.

Therefore it is not repeated, because the spiritual creation recognized its conformation—that is, it was formed by the illumination of truth, toward which it was converted [Col. 0195B].

Other things are created in such a way that they first come into being in the knowledge of rational creation and afterward in their own kind. Therefore it says, “It was made so,” that is, in the knowledge of spiritual creation; and afterward it repeats, “And God made,” that is, in its own kind.

To discuss the shape of heaven—whether it covers the earth from above or surrounds it on every side like a sphere—does not belong to this work.

Allegorically, “God made the firmament in the midst of the waters and divided water from water” means the solidity of the holy Scriptures.

He distinguished above this firmament the waters, the heavenly powers, of which it is said: “The waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,” because Scripture is not always needed by those who see God.

He placed this firmament over the lower peoples who possess understanding of Scripture [Col. 0195C].

It is also not inappropriate to call our inner person heaven, as in the Gospel: “Let your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” The firmament is so called because of its eternity, and because it must distinguish between spiritual and carnal things, as between water and water.

Others say that “firmament” is used for all the heavens.

“In the midst of the waters”: the waters above the firmament are there so that they may temper the angels in their divinity, so that the angels might endure the face of God, as Origen says.

In another interpretation, the firmament signifies the Church in the midst of the waters—that is, between the two laws; or between holy teaching and heresy, which divides water from water, that is, the New Testament from the Old, or holy doctrine from heresy [Col. 0195D].

“He divided”—through the words “under the firmament”—means that the Old Testament and heresies are under the Church. The New Testament and holy doctrine are above the Church.

“He called the firmament heaven” means that the Church is called heaven because of its height.

The firmament also signifies perfected understanding, which itself is called heaven because of its height. “To divide water from water” means to distinguish practical from theoretical understanding: practical understanding beneath itself, and theoretical understanding above itself.

## And it was made, and evening came, and morning came: the second day.

These repetitions are to be understood as above.

## Then God said, “Let the waters under heaven be gathered together,” and what follows.

Some say: If everything was full of water, how could the waters be gathered into one place? [Col. 0196A]

But it has already been stated that “waters” is the name given to the matter from which God was going to form all things. The gathering of the waters into one is itself their confirmation in the form that we see.

“Let the dry land appear,” so that this matter might receive the visible form that the earth we now see possesses.

Allegorically, he gathered the lower waters into one—that is, unbelieving human beings, who are shaken by the storm of carnal thoughts. From them he separated the dry land, namely, the people thirsting for the fountain of life.

We may also understand these waters as sins that are under heaven—that is, subject to our reason. If they are separated, then our dry land will no longer be dry but fruitful.

The gathering of the waters is called “seas,” either because of its greatness—for the sea is understood as something great—or because “sea” is derived from bitterness.

For this reason the gathering of the waters is called “seas,” because among the Hebrews every great body of water is called a sea.

“Let the waters be gathered into their place” means: let sinners and heretics be gathered into hell, because the seas are so called on account of the bitterness of sins.

“And let the dry land appear” means: let the Church appear.

## And God said, “Let the earth bring forth the herb of pasture,” and what follows through “the third day.”

The creation of herbs and trees is distinct from the form of the earth and water, since they are said to emerge from the earth separately allotted and made solid.

“And so it was made. And God saw that they were good.” Yet, because they are fixed to the earth and connected to it by their roots, he wished them to belong to the same day.

At this point heretics customarily say: If God commanded herbs and trees to grow, who commanded thorny or fruitless trees? Certainly, before the human sin, it is not written that the earth produced poisonous or fruitless things.

Therefore, after human sin, the earth was cursed and produces thorns and thistles. This was not so that the earth itself would feel punishment while bringing forth growth because of human crime, but so that human beings might always have punishment in this. Poisonous herbs were created either as punishment or for the testing of mortals.

Spiritually, after God restrains the proud within their proper limits, the faithful people produce various fruits of good works according to their kinds.
