Loving the neighbor through bodily assistance, and possessing within himself seed according to his likeness, he should, out of his own weakness, have compassion on the weak, producing a strong tree, sturdy in strength, fruitful and beneficial [Col. 0196D].

Each person can also cause useful herbs and fruitful trees to germinate within himself when he possesses various virtues.

And God said: “Let there be two luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth,” and so forth, up to “the fourth day.” What does it mean that the earth germinated before the luminaries came to be in heaven? It was said above that by the name “light” the spiritual [Col. 0197A] creature is understood to have been formed on the first day. On the second day the higher part of this world, namely heaven, was formed. On the third day came the earth with its herbs and trees, because although trees and herbs move through growth, they are nevertheless fixed in the earth by their roots. Thus it was not the earth that first received its ornament, but heaven. The first day is assigned to the spiritual creature; the second and third to this visible world, on account of its two greatest elements, heaven and earth; on the fourth day the luminaries were placed in heaven, and just as heaven was made first, so it was adorned first.

But what does it mean that they were appointed “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years,” when this seems obscurely to imply that time began on the fourth day—as though the preceding three days could have passed without time? Or as though time could have existed before the stars, when days, hours, years, and months are distinguished by the stars? Yet we said above that He calls it “night” because a work has been completed, and “day” because another work is about to begin. It is uncertain whether the statement “Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years” applies to all the stars, or whether “signs” and “seasons” apply to the others, while “days” and [Col. 0197B] “years” apply only to the sun.

Many people inquire at length what sort of moon was made—whether it was created full or as a new moon—but that question does not belong to this little work.

Spiritually, the luminaries are made in the firmament: namely, holy teachers who advance in Scripture and display the light of knowledge to those below. The diversity of the stars is the diversity of graces. We can also understand luminaries as existing within ourselves. Let us strive to become heaven; then we shall have within us luminaries—Christ and His Church. For He is the light of the world, and He illuminates the Church, just as the moon is said to receive light from the sun so that it may itself be illuminated. In the same way, the Church, having received the light of Christ, illuminates those blinded by the darkness of ignorance.

These stars divide day and night; [Col. 0197C] that is, teachers divide between the light of the perfected and the darkness of the wicked. They are “for signs,” namely, of virtues; they are also “for seasons and for years.” They live within their own appointed times and pass away, but “the word of the Lord remains forever.” Each one of us, through the illumination of Christ and His Church and through the various graces that are like stars, divides between vices and virtues.

“The greater luminary,” and so forth, is “for the beginning of God.” For if we begin to advance through the illumination of the Church—which nourishes the little ones and, like the moon, moderates the night—and if we are found worthy to be called children of God, then we shall indeed be illuminated by Christ. He illuminates the perfected.

Some say that the sun receives its name from the fact that it alone shines during the day, or from the solemnity of light; [Col. 0197D] the moon, from shining—*luna* from *lucendo*—or as though it were “born light.” The sun is said to have been made from the nature of the angels, while the moon is made from pale light, and so is the star. The function of the stars is to shine, and from them the souls of animals are created. Human souls, however, are somehow brought forth from divinity. Hence it is said of them: “Do not the souls of human beings ascend into heaven?” But of the others it is said: “Do not the souls of beasts descend below?”

The luminaries were placed in the firmament of heaven because the other heavens could not support them. They are “for signs,” that is, for navigation, for punishment, or because they signify certain things that have been spoken. They are “for seasons,” that is, for circles or clocks. They are “for days,” that is, to show the length or shortness of the day. They are “for years,” as when one speaks of a solar or lunar year.

[Col. 0198A] “The greater luminary,” and so forth. This luminary is said to be greater than the moon in four respects: in size, in its greater length or distance, in brightness, and in duration.

The stars are said to be carried by angels, whose ministry is to carry the stars, as another writer has discussed on the basis of the Apostle’s testimony, where it is said: “Are they not ministering angels?”

It is said that the stars themselves are not seen by us, but their radiance; and the position of the sun is said to be in the form of a tablet. The moon does not increase or diminish, but turns like a half-white sphere, as we said above: kindled by the sun, then waning until it is kindled again.

“And let them divide day and night”: that is, let holy teachers divide all those things which, as we said above, are signified by day and night.

And God said: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls, [Col. 0198B] and birds beneath the firmament of heaven,” and so forth, up to “the fifth day.” Now, in the lower part of the world, those creatures that are moved by the breath of life are made. The nearest element produces the nearest creatures from the waters, because air is the element next to water in quality. This air is so close to that heaven in which the luminaries are placed that it too has received the name “heaven.”

This air is called not only “heaven” but also “heavens,” just as one also speaks of “earths”; and nothing other than that which is singularly called “earth” is signified. For we say “the globe of the lands” and “the globe of the earth.” When “heavens of heavens” are mentioned, the starry heavens are understood as being above these aerial heavens, like higher heavens over lower ones.

We read in a certain letter said to be Peter’s that these aerial heavens perished in the flood. I do not know how this can be understood except as meaning that the nature of the waters [Col. 0198C] was changed into a denser form of this air. Otherwise they did not perish but were raised higher, when the waters occupied their place. Yet we more readily believe, on the authority of the Letter, that they perished.

It is asked why birds, which fly through the air, are produced by the waters. It must be understood that the air is misty and humid and is reckoned with the waters. It condenses and becomes thick through the exhalations of the sea and the earth; it becomes somewhat heavy, so that it can support the flight of birds. Therefore it also forms dew during clear nights, whose drops are found in the morning on the herbs.

One must not suppose that the air has been omitted from this Scripture, since the world consists of four elements: heaven, air, water, and [Col. 0198D] earth. The uppermost part of the air, which does not receive moist exhalations, is assigned to heaven. The lowest part of the air, in which winds and rains occur, is assigned to the earth; and this part receives living creatures only from the waters.

Therefore it is written: “Let the waters bring forth reptiles and birds,” not in the firmament of heaven, like the luminaries, but beneath the firmament—that is, in the air—so that creatures extended vaporously for birds and flowing creatures may be assigned to it. “Reptiles with living souls” means, as it were, “with living souls.”

Dragons are also said to be without feet, to rest in caves, and to be lifted into the air. The air extends from the boundary of the luminous heaven down to the flowing waters and to the earth. Stirred by winds and violently agitated, it draws in fires and thunder, gathers clouds, [Col. 0199A] and produces rain; when the clouds freeze, it produces snow; when denser clouds freeze in greater turbulence, it produces hail. When stretched out and clear, it makes fair weather, all by hidden commands and the work of God.

Allegorically, “the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls” means human beings renewed to life through the sacrament of baptism. Birds are also made: holy souls flying toward heavenly things.

We may understand this passage in another way, if our mind has been illuminated by our sun, Christ. It is then commanded to bring forth from the waters within it reptiles and birds—that is, to bring good or evil thoughts into the open, so that a distinction may be made between good and evil. Both kinds proceed from the heart, as from waters. Thus we should separate from ourselves the thoughts that crawl upon the earth, while allowing the higher thoughts, like birds, to fly toward [Col. 0199B] exalted things.

“Let the reptiles multiply in the waters,” that is, in worldly things; and “let the birds multiply upon the earth,” having earthly things beneath them. Let the waters bring forth reptiles. Everything that crawls upon its belly, or whose feet are short, is a reptile. Everything that flies is called a flying creature, except the body of the devil, which was made not by necessity but as a wound of sin.

“Grow,” through the pouring out of seed, “and multiply,” through giving birth, “and fill the waters of the sea,” by living in them.

By the waters, teachers may be understood, for they bring forth reptiles and birds—that is, sinners and saints. By the great sea creatures may be understood great sins, which God is said to create, though this means by permitting them and not desiring them.

But if sinners are understood by reptiles, how do they appear good to the Lord? [Col. 0199C] Certainly because the saints are tested through them.

“And He blessed them”: that is, the holy teachers, who are commanded to grow in the law of nature and to multiply in the law of the letter. To fill the waters means to fill the law of the New Testament. To multiply the birds means to multiply the saints in good works or rewards, upon the earth—that is, the Church, or the land of the living. God blesses them and commands them to grow in hope and to multiply in faith. To fill the waters of the sea means to fill souls with love.

And God said: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind,” and so forth, up to “they are good.”

Animals were created in three ways: some are useful to us, some harmful, and some superfluous. Through harmful creatures we are either punished, disciplined, or frightened. Through superfluous creatures we are neither harmed nor helped; through useful creatures we are helped. [Col. 0199D]

Therefore, make use of what is useful, beware of what is harmful, and leave aside what is superfluous. In all things, however, observe measure, number, and order, and seek the craftsman.

It is fitting, then, that the other part—properly called earth—should be adorned with animals, whether beasts of burden such as horses, oxen, sheep, and the rest; reptiles such as snakes and whatever other creatures there are; or wild beasts such as lions, bears, and the rest. Whatever creature created with hooves is savage may appropriately be called a beast.

It is asked why only the animals of the waters were deemed worthy of blessing, like human beings. Perhaps it should have been said of one kind of creature so that it could be understood consequently of the others, which grow through generations. But it was necessary to repeat this concerning humanity, lest anyone [Col. 0200A] say that human beings are sinful in the act of generation, as they are in lust or fornication.

The generation of harmful animals is also commonly questioned: were they created after the sin of the first human being as a punishment, or rather, having already been created harmless, could they—or did they—begin to harm sinners only afterward? Nor is this surprising, since in the times of this laborious life no one is so righteous that he dares call himself perfect.

They were therefore created to punish us, or to discipline and test us. These creatures could thus have been created without harming anyone if there had been no cause for punishing or testing human beings. But if someone asks, “Why do they harm one another?” we reply that perhaps some were given to others so that the latter might feed upon them. [Col. 0200B]

According to mystical interpretations, the earth brings forth a living soul because holy Church, abstaining from dead works, gives birth to living shoots of virtues according to their kind—that is, by imitating the life of the saints.

It also brings forth beasts: human beings powerful in worldly affairs, or fierce through the arrogance of pride. It brings forth cattle: the faithful who live simply. It also brings forth harmless serpents, namely holy men who, through the vitality of their shrewdness, distinguish good from evil. For He says: “Be wise as serpents.”

Nor is it surprising that the Church—that is, the earth—is said to bring forth a living soul, as well as beasts, cattle, and serpents, since according to the Gospel it gathers fish of every kind.

As we said above, birds and animals produced from the waters may be understood as all the movements of our soul, [Col. 0200C] which are brought forth from the depth of the heart, as from waters. In the same way, by animals produced from the earth we can understand the movements of our outward person, in which nothing winged is indicated.

“For I know that good does not dwell in me,” that is, in my flesh. Now let us consider what follows.

And God said: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness,” and so forth, up to “the sixth day.”

Whereas in the other works God says, “Let there be,” here He says, “Let us make the human being,” indicating a plurality of persons, on account of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0200D] Yet He immediately teaches that the unity of the divinity must be understood, saying, “And God made the human being.”

When it is said, “In the image of God,” this does not mean that the Father made the human being in the image of the Son, or the Son in the image of the Father. Otherwise it would not truly have been said, “in our image.” Rather, “in the image of God” is said as though one were saying, “God made the human being in His own image.”

The human being is said to have been made in the image of God according to the inner person, where reason and understanding are found—not on account of the body, but on account of that power of God by which the human being rules over all living creatures.

It is not said here, “And it was so,” but only, “And God made the human being,” because this creature too is intellectual, like the light that was made first. In irrational creatures, the phrase “and it was so” signifies that the knowledge of the creature came about through the word of God; then “and God made” demonstrates that the kind of irrational creature itself came into being.

Some have supposed that the inner person [Col. 0201A] was made at this point, while later, when it says, “And God formed the human being from the clay of the earth,” the body was formed. They did not notice that male and female could come to be only through the body.

How the human being could have received, together with the other living creatures, every tree and fruit of trees as food, while before sin he was immortal, is difficult to say. For although “Grow and multiply” seems impossible apart from the intercourse of male and female, it can nevertheless be said that another mode may have been possible for immortal bodies: children could have been born through the sole affection of holy love, neither destined to succeed deceased parents nor themselves destined to die, until the whole earth was filled with immortal human beings.

No one, however, will dare say that the need for food could exist except in mortal [Col. 0201B] bodies.

When it says, “And so it was done,” and introduces the giving of herbs as food to human beings and animals, this derives from the passage where He says, “Behold, I have given you,” and so forth.

He does not say separately of the human being, “And God saw that it was good.” Rather, after the human being had been made and had been given authority to rule, He included everything by saying, “And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good.”

It is rightly asked whether, because God foresaw that the human being would sin, He wanted to call him good not separately but together with the others, as though indicating what he would become.

Individual things are called good, but all things together are called very good, because the body and its members are beautiful even individually; yet they are much more beautiful in the structure of the whole body.

Others inquire in what respect the inner person [Col. 0201C] possesses the image and likeness of God—that is, in eternity and in character, according to Origen.

According to Faustinus, however, our inner person was made in the likeness of God in six ways: immovable, swift, invisible, incorporeal, subtle, and eternal.

“God created the human being,” and so forth, up to that point. Here it is shown that the souls of man and woman were created; and here heretics are guarded against, since they do not think so.

Adam was not formed until the sixth day because, until everything had been created, it was fitting that he not be formed—as though his house had first to be prepared for him.

Spiritually, as was said above, the earth is said to signify the Church. The beasts of burden signify the Jewish people, and the reptiles the Gentile peoples. [Col. 0201D] Fish signify heretics and worldly philosophers, over whom the human being—that is, Christ—presides.

Alternatively, if understood in a good sense, fish signify good teachers; birds signify saints, over whom the human being, Christ and the Church, rules, as in the words, “Have dominion,” and so forth.

When it says “every herb,” it signifies that the Jewish people are to be entrusted to the apostles, and by the trees are signified the Gentiles.

Spiritually, God made the human being in His own image: namely, the perfect human being, who does not imitate just any saint but imitates the Truth itself and practices righteousness. For Christ suffered for us and left us an example, so that we might follow in His footsteps.

He also received authority over fish and birds and all beasts of burden, because the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one.

[Col. 0202A] What follows, “Male and female God made them,” shows spiritually in the Church the obedient as well. What follows, “Grow and multiply,” means either through languages or through the spiritual degrees of understanding, so that by the understanding of reason they may rule over all carnal disturbances.

Every herb and every tree given as food to human beings signifies the faithful, who share from their offerings. Hence the Apostle also says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you”; and these are fruitful trees.

God said, “Let us make the human being,” and so forth. Consequently, according to what we explained above, He wishes such a human being as we have described to exercise dominion over the aforementioned beasts, birds, and other creatures. We explained allegorically how they should be understood when we said that the water is commanded—[Col. 0202B] that is, the mind of the human being is commanded—to bring them forth, so that he may rule over them and they may not rule over him.

“Male and female He made them.” The inner person consists of spirit and soul. The spirit is called male; the soul may be called female. If these are in harmony with one another, they can generate children—good and useful thoughts—through which they may fill the earth, that is, the flesh.

What follows, “Behold, I have given you every grass,” can be understood of carnal affections. For example, if we use anger for correction—which is something we share with the other animals—we feed usefully on the fruits of the earth. The same may be understood of desire and the other movements.

## CHAPTER II

Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and so forth, up to [Col. 0202C] the statement, “God created in order to make.”

The number six is perfect because it is completed by its parts. One is its sixth part, two its third, and three its half; if you add one, two, and three, the total is six. For this reason it is called perfect. The same is not found in the other numbers.

Therefore God completed His works in this number. No one is so foolish as to dare say that God could not have made everything in one day, if He had wished.

When it says, “God rested on the seventh day from all His works,” what else does this signify except the holy rest that He will give us from our works, if we have done good?

According to this figure of speech the Apostle says: “The Spirit Himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings.” [Col. 0202D] The Holy Spirit does not groan, but He causes us to groan.

God proclaimed, while resting from all His works on the seventh day, that day on which Christ was to rest in the tomb. For He rested in the tomb on the Sabbath day, after completing His works on the sixth day.

What is said in the Gospel—“My Father is working until now, and I am working”—is not contrary to this passage, in which God is said to have rested from all His works. God rested from creating the kinds of creatures, because thereafter He did not create any new kinds. From then until the end, however, He continues to work in administering those same kinds that were instituted at that time.

Evening is the end of the preceding day; morning is the beginning of the following day. Thus night belongs not to the following day but to the preceding one. Therefore, when the sixth day had been completed, [Col. 0203A] after its evening came morning—not signifying the beginning of the creation of another creature, but signifying the beginning of the continuing and resting of everything that was spoken of in the rest of the One who created it.

Therefore the seventh day began from morning and ends in no evening.

It is not unreasonable to understand evening and morning as the knowledge of the creature in itself—the knowledge possessed by the spiritual creature—and as praise of the Creator on account of the creature that had been made.

He blessed the seventh day, that day certainly which has no evening.

Spiritually, after the works of these six days, human beings hope for profound rest of mind when established in the spiritual paradise, which signifies the blessed life.

Thus far the works of the six days have been explained according to the historical account: how they were narrated [Col. 0203B] and how they are understood in the Church. Next it must be set forth what they signify as an image of the ages of the world.

God completed all His works in six days and rested on the seventh. The six ages of the human race in this world, through the succession of times, signify the works of God. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth thereafter until the coming of the Lord; the sixth, which is now taking place, until the world comes to an end. The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints, which has no evening because no limit closes it.

Let us therefore proceed through these ages of the world and distinguish their differences.

[Col. 0203C] In the first age, human beings were made like light in paradise. In that age God divided the children of God, under the name of light, from the children of human beings, as from darkness. The evening of this day was the Flood.

In the second age there was made, as it were, a firmament between water and water: namely, the ark that floated amid rain and seas. The evening of this age was the confusion of languages.

The third age came when God separated His people from the nations through Abraham, distinguishing them like dry land from the waters. It brought forth the shoot of herbs and signs—that is, the saints—and the fruit of the holy Scriptures. Its evening was the sin committed in the wickedness of the evil king Saul.

The fourth age began with David. In it God established luminaries in the firmament of heaven: the splendor [Col. 0203D] of the kingdom like the excellence of the sun, and the Synagogue obedient like the appearance of the moon, together with its rulers as stars. The evening of this age was found in the sins of the kings, through which that people deserved to be taken captive to Babylon.

In the fifth age, that is, in the Babylonian captivity, there came to be, as it were, animals in the waters and birds of heaven. For then the Jews began to live among the nations as in the sea, and had no stable place, like birds in flight. The evening of this day was the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, who were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus.

The sixth age was the age of Christ’s coming. For just as on that sixth day the first human being, Adam, was formed from the clay of the earth in the likeness of God, so in this sixth age of the world the second [Col. 0204A] Adam, that is, Christ, was born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary.

And just as on that day the earth produced the kinds of serpents and wild beasts, so in this age of the world the Law gave birth to nations seeking eternal life. The vessel shown to Peter makes this meaning clear.

And just as on that day male and female were created, so in this age of the world Christ and the Church are revealed.

Of the evening of this day it is said: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes He will find faith upon the earth?” After this evening comes morning, when the Lord Himself will come in glory. Then the saints will rest with Christ from all their works.

After works that are very good, we must hope for rest on the seventh day, which has no evening.

What follows is a recapitulation of the created order.

“These are the generations of heaven and earth,” and so forth, up to [Col. 0204B] “upon the face of the earth.”

Here he says that heaven and earth were made in one day, although above he does not recall that they were made in one day, but recalls that one day was made by God—that is, the spiritual creature, as we said, was made in knowledge, while the rest were made within it.

God’s creatures are known to the angels in one way and to us in another. To the angels they are known primordially, just as they were first created. To us they are known according to the administration of all things through divisions of time, by which God continues to work until now. It is also well understood that this one day signifies all time.

For God made all time together with all temporal creatures.

When, after naming heaven and earth, He created the shrub of the field and was silent about the other things that are in heaven and [Col. 0204C] on earth, He included in “the shrub of the field” the things that spring forth from the earth. Before they arose, they were created causally upon the earth, when God created everything together.

What follows—“For the Lord God had not yet caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no human being to till the earth”—is as though it said that God did not make those things in the same way as He now makes others, when He sends rain.

Other things are mentioned as having been made without rain and without human labor. Now they are said to have been made so that the power of His word might be understood: God made all things together.

What does it signify mystically that, after naming heaven and earth, He added “the shrub and the herb of the region” and was silent about the earth, unless by “the shrub of the field” He understands the invisible creature, such as the soul?

It is called “the shrub of the field” because of the vigor of life; “the herb,” because of that same [Col. 0204D] life as it withers.

Then, when He adds, “Before it arose upon the earth,” the soul is understood before it sinned. Once soiled by earthly desires, it is rightly said to have arisen or been born upon the earth.

Hence He added: “For the Lord had not yet caused it to rain upon the earth,” as though He openly said: Before the soul sinned, God had not yet granted through the clouds of Scripture the rain of teaching to water the soul.

What He then added—“And there was no human being to till the earth”—means that no human being worked in the virgin from whom Christ was born. For He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands.

“But a spring went up,” and so forth. Here, as far as I think, the things that occur through intervals of time are indicated—things deriving from that first creation in which all things were made together. The account rightly begins with the element [Col. 0205A] from which all kinds of animals, herbs, and trees arise.

What this spring is may rightly be asked. If it watered every plain, how is it said to have watered the whole surface of the earth? But if it watered the whole earth, there would have been a flood, and the earth would not yet have been separated from the water.

It is credible that he did not say “one spring,” but used the singular “the spring” for a plural number, so that I may understand springs throughout the whole earth, watering their own places—just as “the frog” and “the locust” are mentioned among the ten plagues of Egypt, although their number was incalculable.

The principles of all creatures exist in one way—unchangeable in the word of God; His works, in another way—those from which He rested on the seventh day; and these present works, in yet another way—those which He continues to perform until now.

[Col. 0205B] Of these three, the last is to some extent known to us; the first two are remote from our senses. Therefore all those things existed from the beginning, not through bodily mass or magnitude, but through the force of causal power.

What the shrub of the field signifies spiritually was explained above, when the earth brought forth the herb of pasture.

The spring is wisdom, which waters the whole Church.

Alternatively, the virgin earth is Mary, of whom it is written: “Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior.” The Holy Spirit watered her, and in the Gospel the Holy Spirit is signified by the name of spring and water.

Then God formed the human being from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.

Even in the body itself the human being possesses a particular characteristic: an upright [Col. 0205C] posture. This was intended to admonish him not to pursue earthly things, like cattle.

But how did He make him? Was it suddenly, at a perfected age—that is, at manhood—or as He continues to form human beings in the wombs of mothers?

If the causes of all future things are now implanted, how did God create all things together? Adam was made in no other way when he was formed from the clay of the earth—as is now credible—than at a perfected age and manhood, which existed in those causes in which God made the human being through the works of the six days.

It is therefore commonly asked whether the animal body was first formed for the human being from the clay of the earth—the kind of body we now possess—or whether it was a spiritual body, such as we shall have when we rise.

The Apostle’s judgment on this matter is not obscure. He says: [Col. 0205D] “The spiritual was not first, but the animal; afterward the spiritual.”

A question arises here: How are we renewed if we are not renewed in Christ to what we first were in Adam? From where, then, is the first robe brought forth for the returning son, if he does not receive the immortality that he lost in Adam?

If Adam had not sinned, he would not have died bodily. How, then, could he not have been immortal, if the animal body is renewed from the oldness of sin?

He will not be renewed into the former animal body in which Adam existed, but into a spiritual body, when we shall be equal to the angels.

We are renewed in the spirit of our mind according to the image of the One who created us, which Adam lost through sin. We shall also be renewed in the flesh, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, so that it may be a spiritual body.

We have not yet been changed into that body, but Adam would have been changed if, by sinning, he had not deserved bodily death.

For before sin, by one consideration that body could be called mortal, because it could die; and by another immortal, because it could avoid dying. [Col. 0206A] For it is one thing to be unable to die and another to be able not to die.

In this latter sense the first human being was created immortal: this was bestowed upon him through the tree of life. After he sinned, he was separated from it so that he could die; if he had not sinned, he could have refrained from dying.

He was therefore mortal by the condition of his animal body, but immortal through the benefit of the Creator.

Concerning the soul that the Lord made by breathing into him, I affirm nothing except that it is from God: it is not the substance of God; it is incorporeal, not a body but a spirit; it was not begotten from the substance of God, nor does it proceed from Him, but was made by God.

It was made in such a way that its nature is not another creature into which it could be converted. Thus it was made from nothing, and it is immortal according to a certain mode of life that it cannot lose.

[Col. 0206B] According to another kind of mutability, by which it can become either worse or lower, it is not without reason called mortal, since true immortality belongs only to Him of whom it is said: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.”

Mystically, God formed the human being from the clay of the earth: Christ was formed from the seed of David according to the flesh, as from the clay of the earth.

“And He breathed into his face the breath of life”: namely, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, who wrought the human being Christ.

“And the human being became a living soul”: so that He who was perfect God might also be believed to be perfect human being.

Others inquire from what earth Adam was formed, if paradise was a distinct place. It was certainly [Col. 0206C] from the common earth, as is shown where it says: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

They say that the Lord breathed into his face for this reason: the spiritual part of the body is the head, which is the first part to develop in human beings and contains the principal senses, distributed through the brain. The first part contains sight, hearing, taste, and smell; the second understanding; and the third touch, which is spread throughout the whole body.

These writers also say that the words “Let us make” through “our” pertain to the formation of Adam’s soul, while the formation of the bodies is signified by the statement, “Male and female He made them.”

The word “formed” here pertains to the formation of the limbs themselves; “breathed,” unquestionably, pertains to the soul.

The body of a son derives from the body of his father its corporeal substance and a hidden power—that is, [Col. 0206D] sin; from the soul it derives immortality and prudence.

Now the Lord God had planted the paradise of delight, as at the beginning, and so on, up to the place where he says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die.” I am not unaware that many have said many things about paradise. For some understand paradise only corporeally, others spiritually, and still others in both ways. It follows that the human being should be understood as having been placed in a corporeal paradise, and that paradise should be understood as a certain place—namely, the earth where the human being would dwell—a most lovely earthly place, covered with fruitful groves, large as well, and made fertile by a great spring.

The Lord therefore planted paradise in delights, that is, in Eden. As for what follows, “He brought forth from the earth every tree,” and so on, it should be understood that the trees established in paradise were of the same kinds as those which the earth had already brought forth causally on the third day, so that even now the earth produces such things through temporal processes. The words of God on the sixth day, when he said these things, were not uttered in an audible voice, but as the creative power in his Word. Yet when it is said that God spoke to human beings without temporal sounds, this could only have been expressed through temporal sounds. For it was destined that the human being should use these things as food.

What follows—“also the tree of life in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—must be considered more carefully. Perhaps it compels us to turn to allegory, so that these were not trees but signified something else under the name of “tree.” But just as there is an eternal Jerusalem in heaven and another Jerusalem on earth, so too there is the tree of life, in which there was a sacrament, while the other trees provided nourishment. What else is the sacrament than wisdom? Concerning it, it is said: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her.”

There is no doubt that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a visible tree. I certainly do not suppose that anything harmful was in it, since God made all things very good; rather, evil lies in the human being’s transgression of the commandment. It was necessary, however, that the human being, placed under God, should be forbidden something, so that the virtue by which he might win the favor of his Lord would consist precisely in obedience.

As for the four rivers of paradise proceeding from one spring, from this we infer that they were well known and widely reported among nearly all peoples. [The text is uncertain here.] It must be believed that these four rivers emerged from that part of paradise most remote from human knowledge, just as the most trustworthy Scripture testifies; and that they flowed for a considerable distance and, after traversing neighboring regions, emerged in other places where they are said to be known as though at their own sources.

These four rivers signify the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Prudence itself is contemplation of the truth, alien to every human mouth: thus Phison is interpreted as “change of mouth,” which, when speaking, gives birth to rather than brings forth what it conceives; this is signified by Evilath, which is interpreted as “she who gives birth.” It possesses gold, the discipline of living, which is free from every stain like pure gold; carbuncle, the truth which no falsehood conquers, just as the carbuncle’s radiance is not overcome by night; and prassinum, eternal life, signified by the stone’s greenness because of the vigor of life.

The river that circles the whole land of the Ethiopians, hot and burning, signifies fortitude, lively and tireless in the heat of action. The third, the Tigris, runs against the Assyrians and signifies temperance, which resists lust. Hence the Assyrians are often placed in Scripture in the role of adversaries. The fourth is not said to where it goes or what land it circles. For justice pertains to all the parts of the soul.

Phison is said to be the Ganges, and Gyon the Nile. The Tigris and Euphrates still retain these same names. The Euphrates, moreover, is a river of Mesopotamia. The Tigris is called by this name because of its speed, running with excessive swiftness like a beast.

Regarding the statement, “God had planted the paradise of delight at the beginning,” some say it can be understood to mean that, before he made heaven and earth, he planted the paradise of delight, in which the will of God was present. What he says about its being “beautiful to look at” pertains to the soul; to the body it pertains that it was pleasant to eat.

By the river, they say, a migration from paradise is signified, because Adam migrated to the common earth. By the river, the unity of the Godhead; by the four heads, the four Gospels, in which the Euphrates is narrated historically. It is not assigned specially to any particular region because it is near the Hebrews; through it the Gospel of John is signified, and it pertains to contemplation, to which the Church is near. The other Gospels have their own properties.

By the tree of life, spiritual teaching may be understood; by paradise, that is, the Church; by the river, baptism; and by the four heads, the four virtues, as we have said above. Alternatively, paradise signifies the body; the tree of life, the sense of prudence; and the river, the teaching that is said to exist in a human being composed of four elements, as though four heads—that is, cold and hot, moist and dry.

As for the statement, “to work the earth and keep it,” this does not mean servile labor but an honorable disposition of the soul. We may understand “to work the earth” as meaning to work paradise and to keep oneself. He was not to be kept from wicked human beings, since there were none, but perhaps from beasts. Yet how could this be? Were beasts then raging against human beings, something that would not have happened except through sin?

There is another meaning in these words: God himself worked and kept the human being. For just as a human being works the earth not in order to make it earth, but to make it cultivated and fruitful, so God works the human being whom he created so that he might be human, in order that he might be just.

Allegorically, however, “the Lord God had planted paradise” means the Church, as it is said of her: “A garden enclosed is my sister.” “At the beginning,” because the Church was founded by Christ. The river flowing from paradise is Christ, who irrigates it; concerning him it is said: “The Lord our God, a glorious river, leaping forth upon thirsty land.” The four rivers of paradise are the four evangelists. The fruitful trees are all the saints. The tree of life is Christ; if anyone stretches out his hand to it, he lives forever.

Phison is interpreted as “mouth of the people,” or “change of mouth.” Ethiopia signifies darkness or gloom. Evilath means “grieving” or “giving birth.” Geon means “breast” or “foreskin.” We can say that the Assyrians are those who direct. Tigris means “swiftness.” Euphrates is interpreted as “fruitful.”

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is free choice itself, placed in the midst of us for discerning good or evil. If anyone, having abandoned God’s grace, tastes from it, he will die.

“God took the human being and placed him in paradise.” God assumed flesh and became the head of the Church, in order to work and keep her—that is, according to the Father’s will, so that he might fill the Church from all the nations—in accordance with the saying: “Those whom you gave me, I have kept.”

God also said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone,” and so on, up to: “And the two shall be one flesh.” In this recapitulation, when God is said to have made all the beasts of the earth and all the birds of heaven from the earth, he calls the earth universally together with the waters.

As for the statement, “It is not good for the human being to be alone,” it is difficult to investigate how God said this: whether temporally, with words and syllables uttered; or whether the rational principle recalled here was itself principally present in the Word of God; or perhaps whether it was in the mind of the human being himself, as in the Psalm: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me”; or whether some revelation concerning this matter was made to the human being, concerning the human being, through an angel; or whether the voice itself resounded through a corporeal creature.

If it is asked for what purpose this helper ought to be made, nothing else seems probable except the procreation of children. For this had been said at the first creation: “He made them male and female, and blessed them, saying, ‘Increase,’” and so on.

Now it must be considered why all the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven were brought to Adam so that he might give them names, and necessity might thus appear to bring about the creation of the female from his side, since no similar helper had been found among those animals. It seems to me that this was done for some prophetic signification. Why, then, are the fish also mentioned in this connection? It must be believed that names were gradually assigned as the kinds of fish became known.

That the woman was made from the man’s side perhaps commends the power of that very union. But why from a sleeping man? Why was bone, rather than flesh, taken? Why a rib? Why was its place filled with flesh, and not another rib? Why did he not make her, but build her? There is no doubt that these things were indeed done in this way; nevertheless, they were done to signify something—namely, Christ and the Church.

How the animals were brought to Adam is a matter of inquiry. God’s command came not only to human beings, nor only to birds and cattle, through angelic ministry, but also to the creatures in the waters, as to the whale that swallowed Jonah. If God granted a human being the ability even to tame wild animals, how much more can angels do what I have described. Angels, however, cannot in any way establish or create a nature. God alone is the Creator—that is, the Trinity itself.

As for how Adam was put into a deep sleep, and how his rib was removed from the structure of his body without any sensation of pain, these things perhaps could have been done through angels. But no one could form or build the rib into a woman except God, by whom all nature subsists.

What follows—“Bone of my bones,” and so on—consists of the words of the first human being; nevertheless, the Lord declares in the Gospel that the Lord spoke them. For he says: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife’?” Thus we are to understand that, because of the ecstasy which had preceded in Adam, he was able by divine inspiration to prophesy this.

Certainly, the question debated concerning the soul of the woman—whether she received a soul from Adam’s soul, just as she received a body from elsewhere, like Adam himself; or whether souls are born from souls, as bodies from bodies; or whether they are sent by God in some other way—is not relevant to the work at hand.

When he said, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die,” it is as though he had said: “You will be assigned to death.” This does not mean that he died on that same day, but that he became mortal, because he was expelled from paradise; or that he died on the very day on which he sinned, although nine hundred and thirty years intervened.

Adam was formed, it is handed down, on the sixth day—the day on which he sinned and died. Christ, however, was born on the sixth day; he made wine from water and suffered.

The Lord God also said, “It is not good for the human being to be alone.” Heretics are refuted by this—those who think that Christ was merely human and not also God. “Let us make a helper like him,” because in the human being he assumed, the Church was joined to God.

Adam gave their proper names to all the animals, birds, and beasts, signifying that they would be saved in the Church and would receive through Christ a name which they had not previously possessed, as in the saying: “I will call my servants by another name.”

But no helper like Adam was found for him, because, although someone may be good, he cannot equal Christ. For it says: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.” No one could free the human race from death except Christ.

God cast Adam into a deep sleep. Christ slept on the cross; his side was pierced by a lance, so that the Church might be formed from the sacraments flowing from it. Concerning this sleep it is said: “I slept, and began to sleep, and arose.”

“And he put flesh in its place.” He put his flesh in place of the Church.

“Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” Whether spiritual and strong or less perfect, they are one body of Christ.

“This one shall be called woman,” just as Christians receive their name from Christ.

Therefore, “a man shall leave father and mother,” and so on. Christ left the Father when he said: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world.” He also left his mother, the Synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament and which was his mother according to the seed of David; and he clung to the Church in the peace of the New Testament, so that the two might be one flesh. For although he is God, he became our participant, so that we might be able to be the body of that head.

After this she will be called Eve, meaning “life” or “calamity”: a meaning fitting for us, since here we have calamity and in the future life.

Some say that the statement, “And he filled flesh in its place,” pertains to God’s mercy, in place of the power of divinity.

The rib was built into a woman, concerning whom it is said: “Who will find a strong woman?”

They also say that the rib together with flesh signifies the soul together with flesh. The woman is said to have received from the man corporeality, hidden power, immortality, and prudence.

The first prophecy in this world is said to be contained in this sentence: “Therefore he shall leave,” and so on, up to “one flesh.”

## CHAPTER III

Now both were naked—Adam, that is, and his wife—and they were not ashamed, and so on, up to the place where he says: “To guard the way of the tree of life.”

Truly, the bodies of the two human beings in paradise were entirely naked, and they were not ashamed. For what would have made them ashamed, when they perceived no law in their members opposing the law of their mind?

This serpent is said to have been more cunning than all the beasts, not by means of its irrational soul but through another spirit—that is, a diabolical spirit. For what is surprising if the devil, filling the serpent by his own impulse in the manner in which seers are accustomed to be filled by demons, made it the wisest of all the beasts?

Nor should we suppose that the devil chose for himself the serpent through which he would attempt to persuade the woman. Rather, since the desire to deceive was in him, he was able to act through the animal through which he had been permitted to act.

It is asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted when he foreknew that the human being would yield to the tempter. We should not suppose that this devil would have been permitted to tempt in order to overthrow the human being unless a certain pride requiring restraint had first arisen in his soul. For it does not seem to me that the human being would have deserved great praise if he could live well only because no one persuaded him to live badly. He had both the nature and the power, if he wished, not to consent.

If someone is troubled by this temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, let him consider that the entire human race is ceaselessly tempted by the devil’s snares. Why, then, does God permit this also? Is it because virtue is tested?

If, therefore, the serpent spoke to the human being, why did the she-ass on which Balaam was sitting speak to a human being, unless the former was the devil’s work while the latter was angelic?

The serpent asks, “Why did the Lord command you?” and so on. The woman replies, and so on, so that the transgression might be inexcusable. For the transgression is more evident when the commandments are retained in memory.

“You shall be like gods,” and so on. We see that sin was persuaded by these words through pride. For this is the force of what was said: “You shall be like gods.”

As for the statement, “You shall certainly not die,” it pertains to what was said: “Because he is a liar, and the father of it.”

She gave it to her husband, for whom persuasion was unnecessary, since he saw that she had not died from eating that food.

“And the eyes of both were opened,” because, as a punishment for sin, they had become objects of mutual desire and had received the death of the flesh.

They sewed fig leaves together. Those who had abandoned what could be gloried in covered what was shameful.

“In the evening,” and so on. Because they had fallen away from the light of truth, they hid themselves, and so on.

Let us not be surprised that these things occurred, since they resemble the madness produced by excessive shame and fear.

“Where are you?” This is the voice of one reproving, not of one ignorant. From God, through the man, sin reached the woman; through the woman, from the devil, it reached the man. And just as the man has primacy, so he is questioned first.

“The woman whom you gave me,” and so on. Pride never said, “I have sinned.”

Finally, the woman did not say, “She deceived me” [Note: Perhaps one should read: “Finally, he did not say, ‘The woman deceived me.’” Ed.]; rather, she said, “The woman whom you gave me,” and so on.

When questioned, the woman said: “The serpent deceived me.” For this reason the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived.”

Was the woman deceived because she had limited understanding, and for this reason the Apostle does not attribute the image of God to her? For he says: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. But the woman is the glory of the man.” This does not mean that the woman’s mind cannot receive that same image, but perhaps that she had not yet perceived what she would gradually receive from the image of God and from the man who ruled and administered.

“The serpent deceived me.” It is as though someone’s persuasion ought to have been preferred to God’s commandment.

And the Lord God said to the serpent, and so on, until he said: “And you shall lie in wait for his heel.”

This entire sentence is figurative, and the faithfulness of the writer and the truth of the narrative owe it nothing except that we should not doubt that it was given. The serpent was not questioned because it was not itself, in its own nature, the agent; rather, the devil worked through it, by means of it, and in it. Therefore, what is now said to the one who spoke in the serpent is figurative.

“Because you listened to the voice of your wife, cursed is the earth in your works.” Who does not know that human labors exist in the earth because of this? And since there would have been no labors in the earth if the happiness that existed in paradise had been preserved, this too must not be doubted.

The “works” here are not, as many think, the cultivation of the land, but sins.

“Tunics of skins.” This too was done for the sake of signification, but it was nevertheless truly done.

“Behold, Adam has become like one of us.” These are God’s words—not so much mocking them as warning the others not to become proud in the same way. He had not only become what he wished to become, but had not even preserved what he had become.

“And he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword.” This must certainly be believed to have been done through the heavenly powers, even in visible paradise.

When he says, “Lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and also take from the tree of life,” he shows that Adam had to be separated from the tree of life because he had been estranged from life. He was estranged from it because he was destined to die, or even as one excommunicated. Alternatively, since the expression is ambiguous, it may be understood in this way: “And he sent him into this misery, lest perhaps, after his labors, he might again eat from the tree of life and live forever.”

“Now both were naked,” and so on. It should be understood that, if they had been clothed, it could certainly be said that they were clothed—but with innocence.

The serpent is so called from crawling. The devil speaks to the woman because he saw that he could deceive the woman and not the man, or because he thought that only the man had been formed in the likeness of God, and not the female.

“Why did the Lord command you?” and so on. This is said to have been the first question in the world.

When he says, “You shall certainly not die,” this is likewise the first lie.

The devil is said to have persuaded them concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because the Lord had forbidden it. For the devil always persuades against Christ’s commandments; hence he is also called Satan, “the adversary.”

“And you shall be like gods.” Here unity is first divided, and here idolatry also first arose.

Although the woman was deceived and not Adam, both nevertheless experienced the punishment. This is like someone being deceived at a gathering while another remained at home, yet both suffered the loss, although the deception was reckoned to the one.

Eve sinned in five ways: in persuasion, delight, consent, exaltation—that is, in knowledge, as in the words, “knowing good and evil”—and in pride, as in the words, “You shall be like gods.”

“The eyes were opened,” that is, by guilt. For guilt opened the eyes which innocence had closed. They were opened, that is, so that they might see evil. At first they had seen only good.

That they sewed fig leaves signifies that, abandoning immortality, they took on a laborious life, as in “In the sweat” and so forth.

That it is said of both, “They sewed,” signifies their cooperation in the transgression of idols; alternatively, the bitter fig leaves signify the bitterness of punishment.

When he says “fig leaves,” he indicates that there were many trees in paradise.

When he speaks of the Lord walking about, as though he were unstable, he signifies their expulsion from paradise and that God’s assistance had been taken away from them.

“Toward the breeze,” or “toward evening,” shows that God comes in the manner in which he finds each person.

“After midday,” that is, after they had despised immortality.

When he says, “In the midst of the tree of paradise,” it is shown that even now it lies within his own will whether he chooses life or death.

“And the Lord called Adam, and called him, and did not expel him.” Thus, too, teachers ought to act according to the Lord’s rule.

It is rightly said, “Where are you?” while he was hiding.

“Where are you, Adam?” Perhaps he called them both by the one name, Adam, because one sin had joined them together.

“Where are you, Adam?” These three parts signify that he sinned under the three laws. The present tense, moreover, signifies perseverance in punishment.

Just as death entered the world through the man, the woman, the serpent, and the tree, so through the man, the woman, the serpent, and the tree of the cross, the lost life is restored in heaven.

The first rebuke is in the words: “Where are you, Adam?” The second: “Who told you?” The third, when he says to the woman: “Why did you do this?” According to this rule, teachers ought to rebuke three times. And if a person does not repent even after this, he is expelled from the Church, just as Adam was expelled from paradise.

“Because you have done this, you are cursed,” and so on. The corporeal serpent is now said to have received venom, although it did not previously possess it, and for this reason it is said to be cursed. Or, if the statement pertains to the devil, he is called cursed because he cannot repent.

“Among all living creatures,” that is, because they preserved their nature.

“And among the beasts of the earth,” that is, human beings.

“Upon your breast you shall walk.” For the serpent is said to have walked on feet before this, though I would not dare to affirm it.

“And you shall eat earth,” that is, historically, dust for the serpent.

“Until you return to the earth,” that is, to paradise, to the common earth.

“For you are dust,” and so on. This shows that it was the gate of life.

He does not rebuke and curse in the same order. He rebukes the man first and then the woman. But this is determined by the difference in guilt and by the cause of their advancement. He curses the serpent first, then the woman, and finally the man, according to the order of guilt and delight.

Adam is expelled from paradise so that he would not eat from the tree of life and be mortal—because we have been healed through death—or as though he had not known Eve in paradise.

Another person says of paradise: Paradise is a place of the earth not separated by any intervening sea; but divine wisdom separates us from it.

The fire of the cherubim is also called corporeal by some, since it drove out corporeal beings so that they could not return to paradise; I do not, however, strongly affirm this.

Spiritually, Christ receives this commandment, and we have received it in him, because every Christian may appropriately bear the person of Christ, who says: “As long as you did it for one of these least of mine, you did it for me.”

It is therefore said to him—that is, to us: “You shall eat from every tree of paradise.” This signifies spiritual delights: the fruit of the Spirit, love, peace, and so on.

Let us not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the midst of paradise—that is, let us not wish to become proud of the nature of our free choice, which is placed in the middle, so that, deceived, we may experience both present good and evil.

That serpent indicates the devil, who is called a serpent because he moves about with winding cunning. He deceived through the woman, and not through the man, because our reason cannot be deceived unless bodily delight has preceded it.

Sin is committed in three ways: through delight, suggestion, and consent. Through the serpent we understand suggestion; through the woman, the animal sense of the body; through the man, reason. The serpent suggests, delight obeys, and reason consents.

Morally, this serpent signifies the hidden cunning of heretics, who seek out new things. Through Solomon, speaking in the person of the heretics, it is said: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is pleasant.”

“You shall be like gods.” Thus all heretics in general profess the worth of divinity, promising the opening of the corporeal eyes so that the inner eye may be darkened.

The woman took fruit from the tree and ate. For carnal people more easily persuade others to sin than spiritual people do.

She gave it to her husband, who ate. For after the delight of carnal desire, reason too is subjected to sin.

They sewed fig leaves together. Thus those who embrace the bitter world cover themselves, since they will be patched together on account of the origin of carnal pleasure. Those deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace gather coverings of lies like fig leaves for themselves, making girdles of perversity when they speak imperfectly about the Church or about Christ.

When they had heard the voice of the Lord walking about in paradise, toward the breeze after midday, God walks about in them—he does not stand—because they did not stand in his commandment. And appropriately it says “toward the breeze after midday,” because that more fervent light of truth was being taken away from them as the darkness of error approached.

“They hid themselves,” and so on. For the one who has turned away from God hides himself in the midst of the tree, living according to the desires of his error and his free choice.

God called Adam and said, “Where are you?” Therefore no sinners whatsoever should despair, since even the ungodly are summoned to the hope of forgiveness.

After this it is said to the serpent: “You are cursed among all the living creatures of the earth; upon your breast and belly you shall crawl.”

By the name “breast,” pride of mind is signified; by the name “belly,” the desires of the flesh.

“Or else you will deceive through earthly desire all the days of your life,” that is, for the entire time during which you exercise this power.

“I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The seed of the devil is perverse suggestion. The seed of the woman—that is, of the mind—is the fruit of a good work, which resists perverse suggestion.

“She shall crush your head,” if the mind excludes it at the beginning of the evil suggestion.

“He lies in wait for her heel,” because he who does not deceive them by his first suggestion attempts to deceive them at the end.

Some understand the statement, “I will place enmity between you and the woman,” as referring to the virgin in whom God was born. The seed of the virgin Mary is Christ; the seed of the devil is perverse human beings. “You shall strike him down so that he may die; he, having conquered you, shall rise again.” “She shall crush your head,” which is death.

“In pain you shall give birth to your children.” For when carnal will wishes to overcome some evil habit, it suffers pains at the beginning and gives birth to a good work, as to children, upon a better habit.

“Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” This signifies that carnal will, which gives birth to children through pain, must obey reason, as a husband who rules, lest it fall.

Thereafter she is called the mother of all the living—that is, of those who act rightly—whose opposites are sins, signified by the name “dead.”

By the sentence pronounced against the man, our reason is accused. If it has been removed from the blessedness of paradise, it bears the curses of earthly activity and the pains of temporal cares, like thorns and thistles.

He is therefore dismissed from the paradise of blessedness so that he might work the earth—that is, labor in this body—and establish for himself the merit of returning to the life signified by the name paradise, so that he may be able to stretch out his hand to the tree of life and live forever.

The stretching out of the hands signifies the cross, or the torment of repentance, through which life is recovered.

He received a tunic of skin; by this name the mortality of the body is signified.

Cherubim is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The revolving sword, placed to guard the way of the tree of life, signifies bodily punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of troubles and fullness of knowledge—that is, through love of God and neighbor. For the fullness of the law is love.

## CHAPTER IV
Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, and again bore Abel. Cain is interpreted as “acquisition” or “possession,” because Eve said, “I have acquired a man through the Lord.” The birth of Adam’s two sons bears the likeness of two peoples. Just as Cain’s sacrifice from the fruits of the earth [Col. 0215D] is rejected, whereas Abel’s sacrifice from the sheep and their fat is accepted, so the faith of the New Testament, praising the Lord through the grace of innocence, is preferred to the earthly riches of the Old Testament.

But how did Cain know that God would look upon Abel’s gifts and not look upon his own? It can only be because Theodotion’s interpretation is true, in which he says, “God was inflamed toward Abel and his sacrifice; but toward Cain he was not inflamed”—that is, by fire. We read that fire customarily came from heaven to consume sacrifices, as at the dedication of the temple under Solomon and on Mount Carmel under Elijah.

Let us return briefly to the beginning and inquire how the name Adam is pronounced in three languages. In Hebrew it is called *Adam*, in Greek *anthropos*, and in Latin [Col. 0216A] *homo* (“man”). Since we are discussing the name, its significance in the three languages mentioned above must be understood.

Among the Hebrews, the dignity of a name is expressed through a multitude of interpretations, as *Adam* is interpreted in many ways. For *Adam* means “man,” “ground,” “earth-born,” “red and bloody earth,” and “begetter”; and these interpretations retain their significance in ground, blood, earth, and creation.

Among the Greeks, the significance lies in many combinations, as is seen in their treatment of Sarah, where they added another rho. Among the Latins, the dignity of a name lies in its multiplicity, as in Publius Cornelius and Scipio Africanus.

The name *Adam* appropriately consists of four letters because he was composed of four substances—moist and dry, hot and cold; because he was destined to rule over the four regions of the world; and because the second Adam, that is, Christ, is signified, who is proclaimed in the four Gospels and through the four laws. One of these letters, doubled, signifies Adam’s change from paradise to common earth and from common earth to paradise.

The first and the new Adam correspond in the four letters and in the four laws; they differ, however, in what the Apostle says: “The first Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a living spirit.” The letters of the first are changed, but those of the second are not changed. This signifies the changeability of the first and the immutability of the second, as with the *Tetragrammaton*, that is, the Lord’s name written in four Hebrew letters: iota, vau, he, and heth.

We cannot say what name was written with these four letters on the golden plate [Col. 0216C] until the day of judgment. These four letters of the name *Adam* have proper names in the names of the regions: *anatole*, *disis*, *arctus*, and *mesimbria*—that is, east, west, north, and south. This property signifies that Adam would rule in the four regions of the world mentioned above.

The fact that this name begins with A signifies that he holds primacy among the angels. That second Adam too—who, according to the Apostle, is Christ—is placed first in honor and also in the order of the letters.

Here others also ask who first gave Adam his name, along with the remaining questions. We give only their answers, saying that God first named Adam when he said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Adam, however, named all living creatures, as the Spirit says through Moses: “And he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them.” In these statements, the Lord’s dominion over Adam and Adam’s dominion over all living creatures are signified.

Adam is properly named by the Lord, who says, “Let us make man”; or, as others hold, he is named appellatively. Yet it is easier to understand the name as proper when Adam is compared with the animals.

These letters are called as follows in the three languages: aleph, alpha, *a*; daleth, delta, *d*; mem, *mi*, *m*. Among the Hebrews, *mem* changes the form of the letter when it occurs at the beginning and end of a word.

“She conceived in the womb and bore,” that is, brought forth. Some compare conception—if Adam had not sinned—to the cooperation of one man’s hands, without any pleasure. Others say that a spiritual meaning is intended in the statement, “He knew his wife”: namely, Christ and the Synagogue of the Jews, which conceived under the law of nature and bore under the law of the letter; or conceived under the law of the letter and bore under the New Testament.

It is not inappropriate for the Jewish people to be signified by Cain, on whose behalf the Synagogue gives thanks, just as Eve did for him, and who served the Lord with the good things of the earth, as in the words, “You shall eat the good things of the earth,” since Cain is written here as having been a farmer.

In the moral sense, Adam signifies the perfected understanding and Eve the flesh. Cain signifies the evil understanding, and Abel the good understanding, which guard the other senses, just as Abel was a shepherd of sheep.

“After many days” means “until he had something that he could offer.” This shows that God does not demand from a person what he does not possess.

Then God said to Cain: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For although the Jews did many things rightly, they are nevertheless guilty of unbelief because, when Christ came, they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old.

If Cain had obeyed God, aided by an understanding of grace, he would have ruled over his sin and would not have killed his innocent brother. Likewise, the Jews—whose figure was represented in these events—would have ceased from their agitation if they had recognized the time of salvation and the remission of sins. They would have heard Christ saying that he had not come to call the righteous but sinners, so that they might turn from their sin and be saved through confession.

But now, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness. They burned with anger against Christ, and, seeing that his works were acceptable to God, they grieved.

Abel, the younger, is killed by his elder brother; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people.

“Will you not, if you do well, receive”—that is, abundance or fire? “But if you do evil, your sin clings at the door”: this is understood as a sign of falsehood. In the statement, “But it will be under you,” he assigns repentance: “its desire,” that is, the desire of sin. “And you will rule over it,” as though he were saying openly: “It is under your power, depending on whether you act well or badly.”

When Cain says, “Let us go out,” he speaks deceitfully. When the Spirit says of him, “When Cain rose up,” this signifies “when he rose up with hatred or at the devil’s prompting.”

“Where is Abel your brother?” He does not ask as one ignorant, needing to learn from God, but as a judge questioning a guilty person whom he intends to punish. Even now, when we ask the Jews about Christ, they answer that they do not know Christ. They would in some sense be guardians of Christ if they guarded the Christian faith.

God says to Cain, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth.” Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in Scripture. The blood of Christ has a great voice in the earth, when, having received it from all nations, the response is “Amen.” This is the clear voice that the blood itself expresses from the mouths of the faithful.

In saying “your brother,” he recalls their thought so that they might be pierced with repentance.

“You shall be cursed upon the earth”—that earth which God gave to Abraham’s seed, in which they shed Christ’s blood. Or else, “from the earth,” that is, from the Church, which opened its mouth in confession of sins to receive the blood of Christ, poured out for the remission of all sins, from the hand of the persecutor who refused to be under grace but chose to be under the curse. For all who are of the works of the law are under the curse.

“When you work, it shall not give you its fruit.” For in the earth which Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, but their own destruction. Therefore, when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified.

In the historical sense, however, Cain was cursed with poverty. In the statement, “Cursed is the earth,” and what follows, up to “from your hand,” it may be understood that the blood of the righteous diminishes the fruit of the earth, but not the blood of vengeance according to the law.

“A wanderer and fugitive,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “groaning and trembling.” Who, then, does not see how the people of Israel are wanderers and fugitives among the nations, groaning after the loss of their kingdom and trembling with fear under innumerable Christians?

Therefore Cain answered, saying: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness,” and what follows. Truly Judas, a wanderer and fugitive, groans and trembles lest, having also lost his earthly kingdom, he be killed by this visible death. He declares this to be a greater cause than the fact that our land does not give the Jews its fruit, and, hidden from the face of God, he has God angry with him.

Cain is charged with seven sins. First, he divided wrongly, as in: “But toward Cain and his gifts he did not look.” Second, he was envious, as in: “And Cain was angry.” Third, he was sorrowful, as in: “His face fell.” Fourth, murder, as in: “He killed him.” Fifth, lying, as in: “He answered, ‘I do not know.’” Sixth, he did not repent, as in: “What have you done?” up to “to me.” Seventh, he despaired of himself, as in: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness.”

The statement, “It shall certainly not be so,” is to be understood as though he had said: “Not as you say, that everyone will kill you, but one person will.” And what follows, “God placed a sign,” is to be understood in light of what is said, “It shall certainly not be so.”

The events that took place between Abel and Cain can also be referred morally to the good and evil understanding: through the shedding of Abel’s blood, the good understanding turned away by the evil may be signified. As was said above, they may also refer to Christ and the Jewish people, since both are sons of the Synagogue. The latter also led Christ outside—that is, outside the city of Jerusalem—to be crucified, and rose up with the devil or with hatred of Christ to carry out this deed.

“Am I my brother’s keeper?”—“Am I a rabbi?” This is thought to be the meaning.

“Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Or, as the Septuagint translated it, “shall pay seven acts of vengeance.”

Let us first discuss according to the historical sense what is signified by “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Certainly God did not wish to bring his torment to an end by the convenience of death. Cain seems to have desired this when he said, “Everyone who finds me will kill me.” God speaks to him, as it were, in this way: “You will not die as you think, nor will you receive death as a remedy. You will live until the seventh generation and be tormented by the fire of your conscience. Or whoever kills you—whether in the seventh generation or with great torment—will free you.”

It does not mean that the one who killed Cain would himself be subjected to seven punishments, but that he who killed Cain released him from the seven torments that had continued together in Cain for so long, or that Cain was to be killed in the seventh generation.

Adam begot Cain; Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Gaidad; Gaidad begot Malaleel; Malaleel begot Mathusalem; Mathusalem begot Lamech, who was seventh from Adam and unwillingly killed Cain. He says that he killed a young man, not because Cain was young, but because he was wandering and unstable.

Spiritually, who does not see that whoever has destroyed the impious race of the carnal Jews “pays seven acts of vengeance”—that is, removes from them the seven acts of vengeance to which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s murder, in this age that revolves according to the number seven days?
