God placed Cain as a sign, so that everyone who found him would not kill him. The Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or Christians, did not lose the sign of the Law and circumcision; and whoever found them with that sign did not kill them.

So Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Naid. In Hebrew, Naid is called Nod, which is interpreted as “commotion” or “unstable.” It signifies not so much the name of a place as Cain’s—or the Jews’—instability. As fugitives, they dwell in carnal agitation and disturbance against the joy of God, that is, against Eden.

Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch, and he built a city. At the very beginning of the world, the offspring of the impious built a city, because all the impious are founded in this life, where they have their treasures; but the holy are guests and pilgrims.

Hence Abel, like the pilgrim Christian people, did not establish a city on earth, for the city of the righteous is above. Enoch is interpreted as “possession” or “dedication”; in his name the city was founded, that is, earthly Jerusalem, where nothing beyond what is seen is hoped for.

It should be noted that no female offspring is mentioned in the progeny of Seth, but one is mentioned in the progeny of Cain. Carnal people arise from the union of husbands and wives.

Others say that the statement “Cain knew his wife” signifies that vengeance would cease if Cain had not taken a wife.

“And he called his name”—up to “Enoch.” This is the first city in Scripture to be called by the name of a man; through this, idolatry can also be signified.

Morally, Cain signifies the evil understanding, or each sinner. He knows his wife—that is, the flesh subjected to sins—which conceives in thought and gives birth to sin in evil action. What follows, “he built,” signifies that the evil understanding or sinner does not immediately abandon sin, but increases it.

His genealogy is recalled so that the truth concerning the generations of Cain and Lamech might be announced. Cain prefigures the people of heretics, generating other heretics. Lamech was the first to take two wives, as though he were saying, “He was the first to commit adultery.”

Jubal was the first to build houses, according to some; according to others, he was the first among those who kept livestock. Jubal was the first harpist. Through Lamech, the people of heretics are signified with the two churches of heresy; or, in a good sense, Christ is signified with his two churches.

Through Jubal, the Jewish people dwelling in tents are signified—that is, dwelling in the things of this age. Through Jubal, the Christian people among the nations are signified, singing with the harp—that is, through history—and with the organ—that is, through understanding.

Tubal-cain was the first worker in iron and bronze. He signifies each holy person as guardian of his own body and soul.

“And Lamech said to his wives,” and what follows, up to “of Lamech, seventy-sevenfold.” According to the historical sense, it is said that from Adam to Christ there are seventy-seven generations, through which the sin of Lamech—that is, of the whole world—was dissolved by the shedding of Christ’s blood.

Some say that seventy souls from the family of Lamech were received in the Flood, and that vengeance was exacted from Lamech in this number. Indeed, among the Jewish people also, seventy acts of vengeance were established on account of the murder of Christ, according to the saying that one must forgive a brother not merely seven times but seventy-seven times, if he repents, for Christ’s forgiveness.

Others say that Cain sinned sevenfold, and therefore was to be punished sevenfold for the sins we enumerated earlier.

The acts of vengeance inflicted upon Adam, Cain, and Lamech are not alike because those who sinned later had greater knowledge of God, including through the preceding acts of vengeance, which they knew had occurred earlier. Thus vengeance is now observed under the three laws.

It is also said that vengeance was added in Lamech’s case because of adultery.

When Lamech signifies Christ, the killing of Cain demonstrates the killing of the devil. This is announced by Christ to his wives [Col. 0220C]—that is, to the churches—which he commands to listen to his word.

The statement “in my wound” signifies that the devil was killed because of lust in the death of Christ. “And a young man”—that is, the devil—because of lust and eternity. “In my bruise,” that is, not without pain.

Alternatively, the killing of Cain demonstrates the killing of the good understanding, or of the Christian people, when a heretic is represented by Lamech.

Adam again knew his wife, and she bore a son and called his name Seth. From Seth a son was born, whom he called Enos. Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” which is Christ. Enos is interpreted as “man,” and he began to invoke the name of the Lord.

What does this mean except that every human being who is a child of resurrection lives through confession while he journeys on earth? Or, as the Hebrews think, Enos began to invoke the name of the Lord because it was then that an idol was first fashioned in the likeness of the Lord’s name.

Enoch, seventh from Adam, was translated and pleased God. He signifies the seventh rest, to which every human being is transferred who is formed on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age of the world—through the coming of Christ.

The fact that through Seth the number ten is indicated from Adam to Noah signifies the fulfillment of the commandments represented in the works of the Church. But the fact that the progeny from Adam through Cain ends with the number eleven signifies the transgression of the commandments, or sin. For if Lamech, who is seventh from Adam, is added, together with three sons and one daughter, the number eleven is completed.

Hence Lamech’s daughter herself, Noema, is interpreted as “will.”

“This one began to invoke the name of the Lord.” Others say that this should be understood to mean that Enos first discovered another name among the twelve names of the Lord by which he is called among the Hebrews, namely *Het*.

Spiritually, Adam and his wife signify Christ and the Synagogue. From them was born a son—that is, the people of the nations brought to faith—who is rightly called Seth, meaning “placed in truth.”

The statement “another seed in place of Abel” signifies the good people of the New Testament in place of the patriarchs, prophets, and martyrs who were killed by the evil part of the Jewish people. Enos signifies the successors of the Christian people, who invoke the name of the Lord.

Morally, Adam and his wife signify each holy person and the flesh. Through the son, the perfected understanding is signified. Through “another seed in place of Abel,” good understandings are signified in place of the good.

## CHAPTERS V–VIII

“This is the book”—up to “Adam.” This signifies the evangelist’s wording when he says, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ appeared,” and so forth. This expression is properly said of God and of an angel or devil: “and he begot”—up to “his own,” that is, because Adam was made in the image and likeness of God, whereas human beings were made in the likeness of Adam.

“And he called his name Seth.” This shows that Adam did not lose the spirit of knowledge and prophecy in the naming of his sons.

Adam’s 939 years signify virtues and the three laws, or hope, faith, and charity, or the age of Christ.

Through this genealogy, one who generates holy teachers is signified, and these in turn generate others. The fact that the years of Adam’s sons decrease signifies that the years of the succeeding generations would diminish.

“And Enoch walked with the Lord”—that is, in his manner of life; “and he walked with the Lord”—that is, in his ascension, bearing the figure of Christ.

And he called his name Noah. In this naming Lamech’s foreknowledge is present, when he says: “This one will console us,” up to “the works of our hands.” Noah is interpreted as “consolation” or “comforter,” because people were consoled in Noah’s days when they were extinguished from sin in the Flood. Another interpretation of Noah is “rest,” because he provided rest in the ark for all living creatures. Noah is interpreted as “rest,” because in his time all provisions came to rest through the Flood, and therefore he is called “rest.” [Col. 0221D]

When it says, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years,” this means that they would have one hundred and twenty years in which to do penance, not that the span of human life had been fixed at that length.

As far as can be inferred from the measurements given, the ark had four corners, rising from a single base; these were gradually drawn inward toward the top until the structure was reduced to a space of one cubit. For it is reported that its foundations were three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high, but that it narrowed toward the summit, so that its width and length at the top were one cubit. The compartments in it appear to have been made so that the various kinds of animals and beasts could more easily be separated into individual chambers. [Col. 0222A] The Hebrews, however, relate that Moses—who, as Scripture says of him, was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians—set down the number of cubits in this passage according to geometry, which the Egyptians especially cultivated. Among geometers, according to that calculation which they call *virtus*, one unit is reckoned from a solid and a square, or one unit for every six cubits.

In every respect Noah signifies Christ. Noah is interpreted as “rest,” and the Lord says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Noah alone was righteous; Christ alone is without sin. To him seven human souls are given, that is, perfect human beings, through the sevenfold grace.

Noah saves his own through water and wood; [Col. 0222B] Christ saves Christians through the cross and baptism. The ark is constructed from undecaying wood; the Church is built from human beings who will live forever. For this ark signifies the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. Its being said to be made of squared timber signifies the stability of the life of the righteous. “Inside and outside”—that is, whether by those who are inside or by those who are outside—they are never to be dissolved.

This people, which is saved in the Church, is rightly compared with those human beings and animals that were saved in the ark. Since their merits are not all the same, they do not all have the same dwelling-place in the ark. Although all are held within one faith in the Church and cleansed by one baptism, their progress is not the same. [Col. 0222C] Of them it is said: “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord.” The multitude of irrational cattle, and even of beasts, is kept in the lower places. Those who live by rational knowledge are very few. For “many are called, but few are chosen.”

The words of Lamech, Noah’s father, do not apply to Noah when he says: “This one will console us from the works and labors of our hands on the earth which the Lord cursed”; rather, these words apply to Christ. [Col. 0222A]

The ark’s length of three hundred cubits signifies that the number one hundred is perfect and complete. Thus we read in the Gospel that someone who has one hundred sheep, when one of them has gone astray, leaves the ninety-nine on the mountains and goes down to seek the one that was lost. [Col. 0222D] Here the number one hundred signifies the number of the whole rational creation. Since it does not subsist from itself but from the Trinity, it descended and received from the Father, through the Son and the Holy Spirit, the length of life—that is, the grace of immortality. It is therefore tripled, so that we who have fallen through ignorance from the number one hundred may be restored through recognition of the Trinity to three hundred.

The width contains the number fifty, a number consecrated to remission and indulgence. According to the Law, remission took place in the fiftieth year. Spiritually, therefore, Noah—that is, Christ in his flesh, namely in his Church—placed this number fifty in the Church. For unless he had granted believers the remission of sins, the breadth of the Church would not have been spread throughout the world.

The number thirty, representing the height, [Col. 0223A] contains a sacrament similar to that of the three hundred. What is represented there by three hundreds is represented here by three tens. The total is called the sum of the entire construction because there is one God the Father, from whom all things come; one Lord; one faith of the Church; and one baptism. You will find much about these matters in Scripture when you have leisure.

Joseph is brought out of prison at the age of thirty. Jesus is reported to have been thirty years old when he came to baptism. We find the fiftieth day and feast consecrated to the offering of new crops, and the fiftieth part of the spoils of the Midianites was owed to the Lord. Abraham defeated the Sodomites with three hundred men, and Gideon overcame them with three hundred men who lapped water with their tongues.

The addition, “It was at the side,” is a sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from Christ’s side. According to the Septuagint, the interior of the ark is divided into two or three chambers: into two because the Church gathers a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision; or into three because of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the whole world.

The fact that seven clean animals and two unclean animals are found does not mean that there are fewer wicked than good people, but that the good preserve the unity of the sevenfold Spirit, whereas the wicked, represented by the number two, are readily divided into schisms.

Noah himself is the eighth, because in Christ the hope of our resurrection appeared: he rose on the eighth day, after the Sabbath. [Col. 0223B] Outside the ark no flesh is saved, because outside the unity of the Church the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only has no efficacy but is even harmful. [Col. 0223C]

The forty days and forty nights during which the Flood rained signify the Ten Commandments joined to the evangelical number. The fact that the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains signifies, through the sacrament of rest and resurrection, that the Church transcends the height of the mountains. In each of the numbers set down here, anyone may discern a sacrament.

As for the raven, which is said not to have returned to Noah, it either perished in the waters or settled upon the floating corpse of some dead creature. It signifies people rendered most foul by the uncleanness of desire, intent upon the things outside, in this world. The dove that was sent out and returned because it found no place of rest shows that, through the New Testament, rest has not been promised to the saints in this world.

The fact that it brought back a fruitful olive branch [Col. 0223D] signifies that some who have been baptized even outside the Church can, if they have not lacked the richness of charity, at a later time be led into unity in the dove’s mouth, as though by a kiss of peace. But when it was sent out after another seven days and did not return, this signifies the end of the age, when there will be rest—not still in the sacrament of hope by which they are joined together in the present time, as long as what flowed from Christ’s side is seen—but already in the perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, and when, in that clear contemplation of unchanging truth, we will need no bodily ministers.

Why is the roof of the ark opened in the six-hundred-and-first year of Noah’s life—that is, after six hundred years had been completed? When the sixth age of the world has ended, the hidden sacrament and promise will be revealed. [Col. 0224A] Why is the earth said to have dried on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, as though the necessity of baptism had already ended, in the number fifty-seven? It is indeed the twenty-seventh day of the second month; this number, arising from the joining of spirit and body, contains seven times eight, with one added because of the bond of the Trinity.

Noah and his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives enter the ark separately, but they leave the ark joined together. Noah and his wife, his sons, and his sons’ wives are thus mentioned because continence is necessary in the ark, as in the Church; and because of the procreation of children outside the ark. For when we, saved through the spiritual ark, have risen, the flesh will cleave to the spirit in perfect peace. For now, meanwhile, they oppose one another. [Col. 0224B]

What does it signify that Noah and his wife were separated, and that his sons were separated from their wives, during the time of the Flood? That all the animals are given to them for food, just as Peter is told, “Kill and eat”; and that they are commanded to eat the flesh after its blood has been removed, so that the former life may not remain in the conscience as though suffocated, but may have something like an outpouring through confession.

God established a covenant between himself and human beings—the bow in the clouds—so that the Flood would not destroy them. Those do not perish in the Flood who recognize Christ in the prophets and divine Scriptures, as though in the clouds of God.

Let us briefly touch, at the beginning of this reading, on what has been passed over in this exposition. [Col. 0224C] Shem, Ham, and Japheth are Hebrew names; their interpretations are rendered in Latin as “placement,” “cunning,” and “breadth,” on account of the knowledge by which they were so called. These three, together with Noah in the ark, also signify three peoples with Christ in the Church: the peoples of the Law, of nature, and of the letter—which is also said to signify the Gospel.

In the statement that the sons of God saw them, the seed of Seth is signified. Seth may appropriately be called the Son of God, because he was born in place of Abel, whose offerings the Lord regarded. By the daughters of human beings are understood the daughters of Cain’s seed. Their union with Seth’s seed caused the Flood to come upon the earth, something that also frequently happened to the Jews.

The punishment on account of foreign wives is signified in the Church, in which even now the sons of God—that is, good thoughts—would receive evil thoughts, which are shown by the daughters of human beings. [Col. 0224D] They are called beautiful, that is, pleasurable.

God said, “My spirit will not remain in human beings,” meaning the spirit of vivification, because they are flesh—as though he were saying, “because they are fragile and easily inclined to sin.” Alternatively, by “spirit” in this passage the spirit of anger is understood, as though he had said: “Because human beings have fragile material, I will not be angry with them forever,” as it is said elsewhere concerning this: “I will not reserve them for eternal torments, but here I will restore to them what they deserve.”

The giants mentioned here indicate great sins, for they were born from the greatness of sin. When it says, “men of renown,” it should be understood as though it said, “the proud” or “the strong.”

The Lord is said here to repent, but in the manner of human beings. [Col. 0225A] This is the first repentance of the Lord found in Scripture concerning the creation of humanity: that he had made human beings on the earth. Historically, this refers to the fact that he had made them with free choice, while they made no progress but sinned more and more. It may also refer to his taking precautions for the future—that is, lest they add further sins. Or it may refer to the fact that human beings cannot live with giants. From human beings to cattle, he left nothing halfway; through these things the vices of soul and body may be understood.

Noah is said to have found grace before the Lord, not because Noah’s goodness preceded the Lord, but because he was righteous in comparison with the others. No one is naturally good except God alone. Noah was not, however, righteous and perfect—that is, in word and deed—as is sung of the Lord: [Col. 0225B] “The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works.”

“The earth was corrupt,” that is, its fruit was corrupted by iniquity. “Every one,” up to “his own way,” means “his own nature.” Bitumen and pitch are said to be the same. Bitumen is mud. A cubit is said to contain six palms, from the thumb to the end of the finger; yet it was stated above that Moses measured the ark according to Egyptian cubits, one of which equals six Roman cubits.

“A window,” that is, as is thought, an oblique opening, so that it would not allow rain and wind to enter, while light could nevertheless enter through it. “Upper rooms,” “third stories,” and “small chambers” mean the same thing.

“I will establish my covenant with you,” that is, “I will be your co-worker.” Two unclean animals are introduced into the ark solely for the sake of reproduction. Seven of the clean animals are introduced for the sake of offering them after the Flood. [Col. 0225C]

Spiritually, when it says, “Make an ark there,” the counsel of the Father to the Son concerning the assumption of flesh may be understood. “From smoothed timber,” that is, from Jews fashioned by the Law. Noah with his sons in the highest place signifies Christ with his apostles; the birds in the second place signify the saints; the livestock in the third signify the innocent; the beasts in the fourth signify worldly people. Through the fifth place, together with the dung, hell is signified.

Alternatively, these five levels show the ascents of the Church: catechumens, baptized persons, married people, penitents, and saints. By the bitumen, patience and bodily and spiritual continence are signified. Enough has been said about the ark’s measurements.

The fact that the number of clean animals is greater than that of the unclean [Col. 0225D] signifies that more will be with Christ in the Church, and in the future, than will be unclean. The rain after seven days may be understood as the voluntary rain after the Old Law, concerning which it is said: “You will give voluntary rain, O God, to your inheritance.”

“Upon the earth,” that is, Noah did everything. This is a figure of Christ obeying the Father unto death, and of every saint. The phrase “because of the waters of the Flood” shows that one enters the Church through baptism or because of persecution. The phrase “for seven days” shows baptism after the Old Testament, or judgment after the present age.

“All the fountains of the great deep were broken open,” that is, the testimonies of the Old Testament were turned toward a spiritual meaning. When it says, “The Lord shut him in,” it shows that Christ [Col. 0226A] guards his Church from persecutors.

“All the mountains were covered beneath the whole heaven,” that is, including Paradise while he is on earth, or excluding Paradise while it was being guarded by the Cherubim. When it says, “All flesh was destroyed,” it warns against heretics who suppose that others escaped the Flood, as was said concerning Methuselah.

“He sent forth the spirit,” that is, the wind; “and the waters diminished,” that is, heresies and persecutions diminished. Through the cataracts of heaven, the proud are shown. When it says, “going and returning,” it signifies punishments directed against persecutors and heresies, returning upon the heretics.

The raven sent out and not returning represents the sinner or the devil, who does not return to the kingdom of God. The dove signifies Adam returning to Paradise through Christ, or [Col. 0226B] each righteous person returning to the Church; its foot—that is, its understanding—does not find rest in this world. “He brought it into the ark,” that is, Christ, by his assistance, brings those who come to the Church inside.

The olive branch in the dove’s mouth signifies the confession of the Trinity in the mouth of each saint, “with green leaves,” that is, with perfect works. Alternatively, the Holy Spirit is signified by the dove, bringing peace through spiritual teaching when heresies and persecutions over the earth—that is, over the Church—have ceased.

The other seven days signify the New Testament after the Old. Noah leaving the ark with his wife signifies Christ leading his Church to heaven after the persecutions. The altar built by Noah signifies the Church of the New Testament, in which holocausts are offered [Col. 0226C] from both the Gentiles and the Jews—that is, bodies and souls—as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord.

“I will not curse the earth,” historically means “in punishment”; alternatively, it refers to the Church in the New Testament, on account of sinners. “Sowing and harvest” signify doctrine and Scripture. “Cold and summer” signify chastity and faith; winter also signifies chastity. “Night and day” signify the Old and New Testaments.

Alternatively, if “sowing and harvest” are taken in a negative sense, they signify the teachers and Scriptures of heresy. “Cold and summer” signify unbelief and will; “night and day” signify heresies in both Testaments.

## CHAPTER IX

“God blessed Noah,” up to “I have given everything to you.” This means the Father [blessing] Christ with his apostles. [Col. 0226D] “Your terror and dread shall be upon them”: this is said with reference to the offering, or as though this consolation were given after punishment.

“All the fish of the sea have been delivered into your hands,” that is, to be eaten under fear; and “everything that moves,” up to “as food.” Here flesh is first commanded to be eaten. “You shall not eat flesh with its blood,” that is, although it is distinguished from the body, this does not teach anything concerning the soul.

“Whoever sheds human blood,” up to “his blood.” Here the first commandment after the Flood is enforced by punishment, and this is the first prohibition.

“My bow in the clouds, and I will see it.” Here the bow is given to Noah and his sons as a sign that the Flood would not come again. It also signifies that God had perceived fear of the Flood in their hearts. For this reason it is placed not on earth but in heaven, so that it may be seen by everyone.

The bow has two colors, namely those of water and fire, which are signified by it. The bow did not exist before the Flood, but after the Flood it was given by the Lord to Noah and his sons as a sign of security from the Flood. Thus baptism is a sign of the security of Christ’s Church from punishment. For human beings are saved in baptism through water and the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Alternatively, the bow is said to have three colors: hyacinth-colored, *onidis*, and *pubinum*—that is, the stumbling-block of repentance, active life, and spiritual ardor in the meaning of baptism. Alternatively, the bow signifies spiritual teaching. The color of water signifies the Old Testament; the color of fire, the New Testament and its spiritual meaning.

Morally, [Col. 0227B] if someone can turn away from the flowing and transitory things of the world when evils are flooding in, and can hear the word of God and the heavenly commandments, that person builds within the heart an ark of salvation and establishes within himself a library of the divine word. In it he places length, breadth, and height—that is, faith, charity, and hope. Faith shows the Trinity and the length of life and immortality; breadth establishes the disposition of charity, mercy, and kindness; height raises the hope toward heavenly things.

He refers the total sum of his arches to the one. For he knows that although all run, only one receives the prize—namely, the person who is not divided by a multiplicity of thoughts. Yet he constructs this library not from rough and unpolished timbers but from squared wood, that is, not from the volumes of secular authors but from prophetic and apostolic books. These alone, with all vices cut away and removed, [Col. 0227C] contain a squared life, balanced on every side. The authors of secular volumes may indeed be called lofty timbers, but they cannot be called squared, because in them it is not life but speech that is balanced.

“Make upper rooms and third stories in it”: these are historical narratives. Learn, therefore, the great mystery fulfilled in Christ and in the Church. Learn also to correct your conduct and cut away your vices, placing nests of various virtues within it.

You shall coat it with bitumen inside and outside: carrying faith in the heart and displaying confession with the mouth, possessing knowledge within and works outside, in the ark. Therefore, in the books of God—or, alternatively, in the faithful soul—you ought to introduce clean and unclean animals.

It is easy to say what the clean animals signify: memory, learning, [Col. 0227D] understanding, examination, and judgment concerning what we read, together with other things of the same kind. It is more difficult to pronounce upon the unclean animals. Nevertheless, I think that desire and anger, when they are present, are necessary for all these things in the soul. Accordingly, since neither the succession of offspring nor desire is restored without them, and since no correction is possible without anger and no discipline can endure without it, they should necessarily be preserved.

“And Noah began to be a man,” and the rest. This means that Christ began to exercise the Church through the teaching of the New Testament, and that he also planted a vineyard. He drank wine, that is, he fulfilled in action what he had taught, as it is said: “What Jesus began to do and teach.”

Shem and Japheth signify the sun and the moon, placing a covering upon their shoulders—that is, their splendor beside the cross. Their faces are turned away, that is, through their turning away they are directed toward darkness. Noah’s awakening signifies Christ rising from his Passion. [Col. 0228A]

“When he learned that his younger son…” The younger son signifies the Jewish people. “Cursed be Ham”: this appears to prefigure punishment upon the Jews. Ham is said to have been the servant of Shem and Japheth; by this it is understood that the evil part of the Jews must be bent beneath the good part of the Jews and the Gentile people. For Ham represents the Jewish people, Shem the good part of the Jewish people, and Japheth the Gentile people.

“May God enlarge Japheth,” up to “Shem.” Historically, Japheth inhabited Europe and occupied the western region of Asia.

Now, however, [Col. 0228B] who could fail to see that what is said after the Flood—that Noah became drunk from the vineyard he had planted and was exposed naked in his house—concerns Christ? He was stripped when he suffered, stripped when he was crucified in his own house, that is, among his own people. Then the mortality of his flesh was exposed. Seeing this nakedness—that is, the Passion—Ham mocked it, that is, the Jews.

But Shem and Japheth, like two peoples from circumcision and uncircumcision, placed a garment upon their backs and entered backward, covering the nakedness of their father. In a certain way we cover the Passion—that is, we honor it through the sacrament—and, explaining the meaning of that mystery, we cover the Jews’ disparagement.

Their backs signify the memory of past events, because the Church celebrates Christ’s completed Passion and does not look ahead to a future one. Ham, that is, the Jews, is in the middle. [Col. 0228C] He is in the middle because he neither held the primacy of the apostles nor believed among the last peoples, the Gentiles. He announced outside to his brothers what had been secret in prophecy.

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; let Ham be his servant.” For what else is the Jewish people than a kind of servant of the Christian people, carrying the Law and the Prophets, so that we may honor through the sacrament what they announce through the letter?

Shem was the elder, and his name is interpreted as “he himself”; he is the one from whom the prophets and apostles were generated. Japheth, that is, “breadth,” is the father of the Gentiles. In accordance with Noah’s prophecy, we see Japheth dwelling in Shem’s tabernacle—that is, the Church building itself rather in the house of the Law and the Prophets.

Ham is interpreted as “hot.” [Col. 0228D] He signifies not only the Jews but also heretics. They announce Christ’s Passion, which was signified by that man’s nakedness, correctly in their prophetic utterance, but dishonor it by their evil conduct. When Ham sins, his descendants are condemned, because the reprobate sin in the present but receive condemnation in the future. The Jews, too, transmitted condemnation to their descendants when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

## CHAPTER X

From Japheth fifteen sons were born, from Ham thirty, and from Shem twenty-seven: seventy-two in all. From them arose seventy-two nations, among whom the Lord sent seventy-two disciples.

From Japheth: Gomer, that is, the Galatians; Magog, that is, the Scythians; Matham, the Medes; Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, and from whom come the Celtiberians; Mosoch, the Cappadocians. [Col. 0229A] Hence among them there is the city Mazech Tyrastrates, whose name has not been sufficiently altered.

From Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is the land now called Ethiopia by the Hebrews. Mizraim is Egypt. Put is Libya; from it the river of Mauretania is also called Put, and the whole region around it is called Phutensis. Canaan, moreover, occupied the land that the Jews later possessed.

Ashur went out from that land and built Nineveh and the streets of the city. From this land the empire of the Assyrians sprang forth, because they founded, from the name of Ninus son of Bel, the great city which the Hebrews call Nineveh.

From Shem: Ham, Ashur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. These peoples hold the part of Asia from the Euphrates River as far as the Indian Ocean. [Col. 0229B] Hela—perhaps Elam—is the ancestor of the Elamites and prince of Persia. It was said of Ashur that he founded the city of Nineveh. Arphaxad was the ancestor of the Chaldeans. Lud was the ancestor of Lydia. Aram was the ancestor of the Syrians, whose metropolis is Damascus. Heber was the ancestor of the Hebrews.

He prophetically gave his son the name Peleg, which is interpreted as “division,” because in his days the languages were divided. After the Flood, Nimrod was the first to seize tyranny and became the instigator of building the tower. Since he attempted to penetrate the heights of heaven beyond his nature, he is appropriately compared with the devil, concerning whom it is said: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.” When he is called “a hunter of earthly souls,” this means a deceiver who captures the human race for death.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0229C]

The tower signifies the pride of this world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they had been moved from the east—that is, had departed from the true light—they came to the land of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking off the teeth,” or “their stench.” Immediately, in opposition to God, the pride of the perverse built the tower. They were separated among themselves by differing errors, as though by the discord of language; the Trinity condemns them, since they offend against it when it says: “Come, and let us confuse their languages.”

Only in the house of Heber did the language that had existed before remain. Now also, only in the Church is there unity of confession. Babel, which is also Babylon, is interpreted as “confusion,” because there the languages were confused. It was the city of Nimrod’s kingdom, whom Josephus affirms to have been the leader in building the tower. The Hebrews call Babel “confusion.”

Aram [probably Haran] died before his father Terah, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. [Col. 0229D] The Hebrews relate that Aram was thrown into a fire because he refused to worship the fire that the Chaldeans revered; by God’s help he was delivered and fled from the fire of idolatry. This, they say, is what is now meant by the statement that he died before the sight of Terah his father in Ur of the Chaldeans—that is, in the fire of the Chaldeans. For *Ur* is interpreted as “fire.” Thus, because he refused to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire.

The statement, “Ashur went out from that land,” prefigures Christ going out from the world. He is strong and conquering, as it is said: “No one can enter the house of the strong man unless he first binds the strong man.” When it says, “He built Nineveh,” it signifies the Church built by the Lord, [Col. 0230A] concerning which it is said: “The Lord builds Jerusalem.”

Resen, which is said to lie between Nineveh and Calah, signifies the two Laws. They were divided from one another until after the Flood—that is, by Christ and his Church after baptism. When it says, “The earth had one language,” it signifies unity among the Gentiles: “up to Noah and his sons,” that is, up to Christ with the three Laws, or with faith in the Trinity.

They are therefore said to build the tower because they feared the Flood, as some say; or so that they might preserve a memorial before they were divided among the lands, which Scripture confirms.

The Lord descended to see the city and the tower. The Lord is said to descend both for punishment and for assistance, [Col. 0230B] as when he takes care of the human race. By the city and tower he designates the Church of the heretics. In saying “the sons of Adam,” he recalled Adam’s sin. And thus he divided them, because they did not do what they were doing [the wording is uncertain], yet he nevertheless did not wish to destroy them.

## CHAPTER XII

God speaks to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house.” Christ, having left his land, his kindred, and his father’s house—that is, the Jewish people—is enriched among foreigners and prevails among the Gentile people.

Following his example, we too must go out from our land, that is, from the possessions of this world; from our kindred, that is, from our former conduct and habits and from the vices joined to us from birth as though by blood relationship; and from our father’s house, that is, from every memory of this world as though from a Gentile condition. Thus, renouncing these things, we may be enlarged into the people of God and, when the time comes, brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

Two promises are given to Abraham: one concerning the land of promise, namely that his seed would possess it; and another: “All nations shall be blessed.” When it says, “I will make you into a great nation,” it shows virtues, as it is said: “A great nation is a multitude of virtues.”

The statement, “Go out from your land,” is said to be intelligible as referring to the Law of nature. “From your kindred” refers to the Law of the letter. “From your father’s house” refers to the Law of the New Testament. [Col. 0230D] “Into the land” means “into heaven.”

Abraham’s wandering signifies and expresses the wandering or instability of his people. Abraham’s people became greater through its instability than when it dwelt in its own land. Thus the Church, journeying away from carnal habitation and toward resurrection, will receive greater rewards.

Abraham, the head of faith, is a figure of Christ or Peter; the testimony mentioned above is a figure in the books of Solomon. At the beginning there is the teaching of the child, in the second place the teaching of the man, and in the third the teaching of the soldier. The teaching of the child is to go out from paganism; the teaching of the man is to go out from one’s sins; the teaching of the soldier is to go out from the memory of this world.

Abram was first called by this name, meaning “exalted.” Then he was called Abraham, meaning “exalted father.” Abraham means “father of many,” that is, of nations: first, when he had no son; second, when he had a son; third, when he had Isaac. [Col. 0231A] When names are changed, works also are changed. Abraham was therefore called by these three names because he embodied the three forms of teaching mentioned above.

“Blessed,” that is, abundance: Israel historically, but the Church through the virtues of heaven. “And I will bless you” means abundance for those who bless you, as happened in the case of Joseph and Pharaoh in Egypt.

When it says, “I will curse those who curse you,” followed by “all the tribes of the earth,” [Col. 0231B] it means that what everyone would have wished to become, like the people of Abraham, was fulfilled especially in Christ, who is blessed in virtues. Those who bless him will themselves be blessed, namely angels or faithful people who bless the saints in holiness. Those who curse him will be cursed, as Christ and Sathiel cursed those who opposed the saints, whether in ways, vices, or heretics.

When it is later said to Sarah, “In you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed,” this signifies that they are blessed through many examples of the righteous.

“Abraham went out,” that is, as a figure of Christ obedient to the Father unto death, or of every saint. The statement, “Abraham passed through to the place of Shechem,” reveals Christ through the patriarchs and prophets, directed toward the Church, or toward every righteous person.

“To the bright valley” means the Church situated in humility, which is illustrious, as it is said elsewhere: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” By the Canaanite, worldly and Gentile people are then signified.

The Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him: “To your offspring I will give this land.” This expression is not often used except of three persons: God, an angel, or the devil. What it says, “The Lord appeared to Abraham,” signifies God the Father appearing to Christ, or to each righteous person in the Church. What it says, “To your offspring,” spiritually signifies Christ as the offspring. “This land” means either the present land or the kingdom given to all the saints. Abraham, building an altar, builds the Church of God the Father in humility. In all these matters, however, Abraham represents Christ or any one of the saints.

His tent between two cities signifies the Church between two laws; and his second altar signifies the new Church. Egypt signifies the world, into which Christ descended. Sarai, however, represents the soul of a saint or the wisdom of a teacher. The Egyptians signify heretics, who judge the teacher’s wisdom wrongly. Abraham and Sarai’s plan signifies that each saint invokes his soul, or that a teacher invokes wisdom, on account of which he is healed. Thus it is said here: “That it may be well with me because of you.”

The princes who reported to Pharaoh signify demons or heretics, wishing to separate wisdom from the teacher, the holy soul, or the Church from Christ, and unite it with Sathiel. The same things are shown in the offering of the woman in Pharaoh’s house. The meaning of the sheep, cattle, and the other things mentioned here is clear. The Lord struck Pharaoh with illness, or with the barrenness of his wife. This signifies that Christ scourges heretics who retain the soul, wisdom, or the Church; and, once scourged, they are dismissed, as it says here: “Behold, your wife; take her.”

Pharaoh understood—that is, either naturally or through a vision. Abraham and his wife signify Christ and the Church, and Lot signifies the holy people. They went up from Egypt—that is, from the world. The meaning of what follows is clear.

Abraham was seventy-five years old when he departed from Carrhae. From this an insoluble question arises. For if Terah, Abraham’s father, begot Abraham when he was seventy years old, while he was still in the land of the Chaldaeans, and afterward died in the land—that is, in Carrhae—in the two hundred and fifth year of his life, how is Abraham now said to have departed from Carrhae after Terah’s death at the age of seventy-five, when it is shown that from Abraham’s birth to his father’s death there were one hundred and thirty-five years?

The tradition of the Hebrews that we mentioned above is therefore true: Terah departed with his sons from Ur of the Chaldaeans, and Abraham, surrounded by the Babylonian fire because he refused to worship idols, was rescued by God’s aid. They therefore say that his days and the period of his life are reckoned from the time when he confessed the Lord, scorning the idols of the Chaldaeans. It may also be that, since Scripture has left the matter uncertain, Terah departed from Chaldaea a few years earlier and came to Carrhae, where he died; or certainly that he came to Carrhae after the persecution and remained there for a longer time.

## CHAPTER XIII

When Abraham had returned from Egypt, from which he had come, his brother Lot departed peacefully into the land of Sodom, preserving their mutual affection and avoiding discord, because they had become exceedingly wealthy and their shepherds were quarrelling.

The statement, “And they brought her into Pharaoh’s house,” can be excused in the case of Sarah. For, according to the Book of Esther, any woman who had pleased the king among the ancients was anointed for six months with myrrh-scented myrtle oil and adorned for six months with various perfumes; only then did she enter the king’s presence. It may therefore be that, while her entrance to the king was being prepared throughout that year, Pharaoh was struck by the Lord and she remained untouched.

Others say that Lot’s flocks signify the various virtues of the holy people. When it says, “The land could not contain them,” Lot appears to represent the person and people of the heretics, whom the Church, together with the Christian people, cannot contain. The Canaanites and Perizzites signify demons, sins, or vices—in that land, among that people of heretics.

From the perspective of the saints it is said, “Depart from me, I beg you,” while the teachers of the two peoples quarrel among themselves. This signifies what is said to sinners: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire.” What it says, “If you go to the left,” signifies unbelief or hell; “to the right,” worldly prosperity. When Abraham chose these two alternatives, the right hand signified faith or the kingdom of the saints, while the left signified the breaking of the will.

In this passage Jordan displays the teaching of the heretics, because the whole land was watered—that is, by rivers and springs—like the paradise of the Lord, since that is how their Church appears to heretics. “Coming” means “boundaries.” The meaning of what follows is clear.

The people of the heretics dwell in Sodom—that is, in sins. To Christ with the Church it is said: “Lift up your eyes to heaven,” that is, away from the world: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens.” The four directions signify the four Gospels. The whole earth is given to him, as elsewhere: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth, forever”—that is, for the length of the ages. What follows here applies spiritually to Christ with his Church.

## CHAPTER XIV

“And they struck Ephraim in Astaroth-Carnaim, and the Susim with them.” Susim is interpreted as “terrible” and “horrible.” The Rephaim—that is, giants—were struck in their city, which is still called by that name today. This signifies that the four kings who came from Babylonia killed the giants and also the strong men of Arabia: Astaroth-Carnaim, a certain land of giants on the heights above Sodom.

“And they struck the whole region of the Amalekites, and the Amorite dwelling in Asalonthamar.” This is the town now called Engedi, fertile in balsam and palms. Asalonthamar is interpreted as “city of palms”; for *Thamar* means “palm.”

The four kings who overcame the five may signify opposing powers—heresy, paganism, hypocrisy, and avarice, which is the worship of idols. They are called kings because they exercise the power of a kingdom on a large scale. The five kings overcome by them may be understood as the five bodily senses, since they too are kings, because through them our outward human nature is governed.

“They turned their backs.” Until Abraham, the exalted father, after defeating the four kings mentioned above, recovers the spoils and rescues Lot, his kinsman who had turned aside, from their power—that is, from evil. The statement that the five kings withdrew from the four signifies that the opposing power chiefly persecutes those whom it had previously held in slavery.

The fact that the exalted father is said to have had three hundred and eighteen servants signifies that, through the elect who are established amid the persecution of the virtues, grounded in faith in the Trinity and possessing the fullness of the Decalogue, they rise with Christ on the eighth day, the day following the Sabbath.

As Abraham was returning, Melchizedek met him, bringing bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High and blessed Abraham. Paul, speaking of this Melchizedek as “without father, without mother,” refers him figuratively to Christ, who was without a father on earth and without a mother in heaven, and who is priest forever. Melchizedek means “righteous king,” as in the passage: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways.”

This is a mystery, so that we may offer in sacrifice not the victims of animals but an offering of bread and wine—that is, of the body and blood.

After the blessing, Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth. Spiritually, he knew that a priesthood among the people of the nations would be better than the Levitical priesthood, which was to arise from him in Israel.

The name Melchizedek is interpreted as “king of peace” or “king of righteousness,” and is rightly applied to Christ. For it says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace.” The Hebrews think that this Melchizedek was Shem, the son of Noah; by calculating his years, they show that he lived as far as the time of Isaac. Every firstborn son, until he exercised the priesthood of Aaron, was a high priest.

Salem is Jerusalem, which was formerly called Salem. Salem signifies the Church, whose king is Christ, bringing forth his body and blood, the priest of God the Father Almighty. From this priest Abraham was blessed—that is, the Christian people.

What it says, “His enemies are in his hands,” displays demons and heretics under the power of the Christian. The tithes Abraham gives signify the good works that the people mentioned above offer to Christ through the ten senses and the ten words of the Law.

The king of Sodom signifies the devil, envious of Christ because of the many souls.

What it says, “I lift up my hands,” is a form of oath-taking. What follows, “From a thread beneath the coverings as far as the things that are yours” [Latin reading uncertain], indicates that Christ accepts nothing from the devil into his Church.

“What the young men have eaten” means the apostles, teachers, and their successors. “And the portions of the men, as far as Mamre”: in this expression the three peoples, the laws, or all who believe in the Trinity are displayed.

## CHAPTER XV

“Do not be afraid, Abraham.” This is said to a teacher, a righteous man, and a ruler. When he says, “What will the law of Moses give me?” he shows that it belonged only to the good things of the earth. The request for a son is expressed where he says: “I am going away childless.” After this there was a twofold figure of the promised offspring, while he was concerned about his household.

God showed him the stars of heaven, saying: “So shall your offspring be.” That is, the Christian nation, whose father he is through faith and which shines with the light of the resurrection.

He also showed him the sand, saying: “So shall your offspring be in multitude.” This means that the nation of the Jews will indeed be numerous, but barren and unfruitful like sand.

He asked for a sign, not as one doubting whether it would happen, but seeking to know how it would happen. The fact that Abraham inquires not about his own time but about his household after him displays Christ’s concern for his apostles. In the same way Moses was concerned for his people, and good rulers anticipate the needs of their churches.

The statement, “Immediately the word of the Lord came to him,” displays a form of mercy. The Lord said to him: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a pigeon,” and so forth.

The three-year-old heifer signifies the people placed under the yoke of the Law. The three-year-old she-goat signifies the same people as sinners. The three-year-old ram signifies the same people as destined to reign. These animals are called three-year-old because of the successive periods extending to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to David. That people grew to maturity as though passing through a third age.

The turtledove and the pigeon signify the spiritual people within that nation. Their temporal age is not stated because, meditating on eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires.

But what does it mean that the three animals are divided and set in opposite parts, except that the carnal are divided among themselves both in the ancient people and now? The birds, however, are not divided among themselves because spiritual people are indivisible and do not contemplate schism. Whether they withdraw from the crowds or live among them, they act like the pigeon; both birds are simple and innocent.

The birds descending upon the divided carcasses are unclean spirits, seeking some kind of food from the division of the carnal. Abraham drove them away. This signifies that Israel will be liberated in hope because of the merits of the righteous.

Around sunset terror fell upon Abraham. This signifies the great disturbance that will come upon the saints through the Antichrist near the end of the world. When the sun had set, darkness came, and a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between the divided pieces. After the end of the world, God’s judgment will separate the rejected from the elect.

“They will afflict them for four hundred years”—not because they served the Egyptians for four hundred years, but because this number was completed from the time when these promises were made to Abraham.

We may also understand the three-year-old heifer, ram, she-goat, turtledove, and pigeon as signifying all the souls that will come to faith. They are said to be three years old because they will believe in the mystery of the Trinity. Since the holy Church contains not only carnal but also spiritual people, the Church is signified by the animals and the birds. The rest, to the end of the parable, agrees with the meaning stated above.

In a moral sense, we have proposed understanding the heifer as virtue, the she-goat as bodily substance, and the sheep as a spiritual gift, together with the turtledove and pigeon—that is, chastity and innocence. All are called threefold, as though fortified by a triple confession, because he divides the animals into two parts. Let us also observe what those in authority and those subject to them ought to do, so that everything of ours may be carried out in due order.

He does not divide the birds. We must not divide ourselves in such a way that one thing is done publicly and another before God; by the same reasoning and innocence, we must remain undivided.

The birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. He calls the birds “refugees,” because they always wish to defile the sacrifices offered by you to the Trinity; but, because of the principal senses, he does not permit such a division to be confused.

When the sun had set, darkness came. When the mind’s reason lies prostrate, our entire breast is occupied by darkness, so that we do not see what we lack.

“A smoking furnace and a flaming torch passing between those divisions.” When a sinful person realizes that he is enveloped in the darkness of sins, his breast, like a furnace burning hot, exhales the smoke of ignorance; afterward he is deemed worthy to possess the lamp of divine light.

The Lord made a covenant with Abraham. This is said to signify the law of circumcision. The statement “from the river of Egypt to the great river” is understood spiritually as extending from the law of the Old Testament to the New. The Canaanites and Jebusites signify vices.

## CHAPTER XVI

Sarai, Abraham’s wife, signifies the Church of the synagogue. At that time Abraham—that is, Christ—did not beget children, because there were then few believers. The Egyptian maidservant represents the worldly Church from the nations.

“Go in to my maidservant; perhaps I may receive children from her.” This is said by the Father to Christ the Son, who also wished Christ to receive children from the nations. When he consented to her request, and so forth, the interpretation of the name Sarah is especially fulfilled: “my princess.”

After ten years—that is, after the words of the Law—the maidservant, having conceived, despised her mistress. This signifies the synagogue being despised by the Church of the nations after the latter had come to faith. For the establishment of the synagogue of the Jews and the Church of the nations did not occur until the maidservant had given birth—that is, until the Church of the nations had faith.

What it says, “Your maidservant is in your hand,” assigns the Church of the nations to the authority of the faithful Jews—that is, the apostles. What it says, “Use her as you please,” prefigures the statement: “When the fullness of the nations has come, then all Israel will be saved.”

When Hagar fled, the primitive Church is understood as afflicted by the synagogue with God’s consent. The angel, finding her beside the spring—Christ found her beside baptism—in the wilderness, that is, in the world, said: “Return to your mistress.” We understand this as Christ’s commendation of peace: “He who makes both one.” And “humble yourself under her hands”: thus Christ teaches humility to the Church of the nations, before the primitive Church because of its multitude—that is, of believers.

“Behold, you have conceived and shall give birth”: the Church conceived in baptism and gave birth in faith and works.

Ishmael means “hearing of God.” He signifies the people of believers, who are called a wild man—that is, opposed to demons and heretics. “He shall pitch his tents opposite all his brothers,” that is, the Church beside the worldly peoples.

He called his name, in worship, “You are God who saw me”—that is, in persecution. By saying that he saw the back of the one who saw him, he shows that here the Church sees through a mirror.

“The well of the one who sees” means the people of the nations; “the one who sees” means God or the angel. Between Kadesh and Barad—that is, between the two laws—there is baptism.

## CHAPTER XVII

“My covenant between me and you” displays the Law between Christ and the Church. It is multiplied through the multitude of the faithful people; through the covenant of circumcision, it signifies the carnal people.

“Kings shall come forth from you”—that is, the apostles from Christ. What it says, “an everlasting covenant,” is fulfilled in the New Covenant or in the future. “For an everlasting possession” means in heaven.

“This is the covenant that you shall keep”: the law of circumcision for the carnal people and the spiritual people—that is, the New Testament for the spiritual people. After this he received the sign of circumcision.

“Every male among you shall be circumcised; an infant eight days old shall be circumcised,” and so forth. What does circumcision signify except renewed nature through baptism, after the stripping away of the old man? And what is the eighth day except the New Testament, in which we are renewed through the Savior’s resurrection on the eighth day, after the Sabbath, and, once circumcised from every vice, become new people? Christ rose after the completion of the week, after the Sabbath.

The fact that he commanded not only sons but also servants and purchased slaves to be circumcised testifies that it pertains to the whole grace of redemption. There the names of the parents are changed, so that everything may resound with newness.

For Abram is interpreted as “exalted father”; Abraham as “father of many,” that is, of nations. By this name it was announced that many nations would follow the traces of his faith. What follows—“of nations”—is not contained in the name but is understood.

Nor is it surprising that among the Greeks and among us a letter appears to have been added, while we have said that the letter *e* was added in Hebrew. It is the idiom of that language to write *e* but read *a*; conversely, they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*. Those are mistaken who think that Sarai was first written with one *r* and that another *r* was later added to it.

She was therefore first called Sarri. When *e*, which is read as *a*, was added, she was called Sarra. Sarai is interpreted as “my household’s princess”; Sarra, “princess.”

Circumcision was commended to Abraham so that he might be under the Law, just as Adam was under the command not to eat from the tree, so that it might be tested whether he would fulfill it. They are circumcised on the eighth day because infancy could not endure it earlier. The circumcision of the eighth day signifies the circumcision of eight vices in the new tenderness.

This member is circumcised on account of chastity, or because pleasure is located in it, so that it too may be circumcised in us. Circumcision is given in one part of the body because it signifies the body and hell, in which filth and refuse are produced; it is not given in the upper part, which signifies heaven and the soul, in which there is no evil but every good.

This law would not have been given to Abraham if Adam had kept the law given to him. Three differences are said to exist between the Jews and the nations: the Law, offerings, and clothing.

Isaac, born through Abraham at the age of one hundred and through Sarah at the age of ninety, signifies Christ, who was to be born amid the perfection of the hundred and the nine orders of angels. And just as Isaac was born through prophecy, so Christ was foretold through the patriarchs and prophets.

What it says, “He will beget twelve leaders,” can be understood both historically and spiritually: the twelve apostles in that period, that is, under the law of the letter; and in the other year—that is, in the New Covenant.

## CHAPTER XVIII

“After these things, three men appeared to Abraham,” and so forth. It should be noted that Abraham has a threefold representation: first, of the Savior, when he departed from his land; second, of the Father, when he sacrificed his son; and third, in this passage, of the saints who received the Lord’s coming with joy.

Abraham’s tent is Jerusalem itself, where the apostles were for a time and where the Lord was first received by believers. In the three men who came, his coming is announced. Two angels accompanied him, whom many think to be Moses and Elijah: one proclaiming the Lord’s coming through the Law, the other the one who would come at the end of the world before Christ comes. Indeed, they were also seen with him on the mountain.

When he saw the three men, he worshiped one. This signifies the Lord and Savior, whose coming he had awaited. Hence the Lord says: “Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.” He then beheld the future mystery. He also washed their feet, to show that they would be washed in purification at the end of time. The feet signify the last things.

He prepared for the feast a fattened calf. This fattened calf is the body of the Lord Jesus. The calf is slaughtered for the returning son. The richest butter is the teaching of the Gospels. Milk, according to the Apostle, represents the ancient Law. Abraham set the calf before them to eat with milk and butter, because the Lord’s body cannot exist without the milk of the Law or the butter of the Gospel.

The three measures of flour signify the three sons of Noah. From them the human race arose; believing in the divine Trinity, they were to be kneaded from the water of baptism through the Church, whose image Sarah was, and reduced into one bread, the body of the Lord. The cakes baked under the ashes signify that, cooked by the heat of the Holy Spirit through repentance for past sins, they may become food pleasing to God.

He says that they sat beneath the tree. This was a sign of the Lord’s passion, whose heralds they are. It may also be understood that Abraham signifies the rational sense in a human being, while Sarah signifies the flesh. When both received God, they carried different pastures of virtues.

Mamre is Hebron. Mamre was also the name of one of Abraham’s friends. Some say that this valley signifies humility. Through humility the Lord comes to each person. The door signifies faith, and the heat of the day the warmth of faith. The three men signify the three laws, although in one of them above all the Christian people worship the Lord.

Historically, it displays Abraham’s perfection that three men came to him in the heat of the day. The Lord came to him especially because at that time there was no one better than he, so that the judgment against the cities and the fact that Sarah would have a son might be announced to him.

Lot, however, is seen as less perfect because two men came to him, and they came in the evening.

The three measures signify hope, faith, and charity; or thought, word, and deed, which are joined together in faith. The cake baked under the ashes signifies humility.

Through the boy whose son is given, the Jewish people are signified. “And he cooked him” means Christ in his passion. “He also took”—that is, the perfected people.

But it must be asked how they are said to have eaten. Some understand it as meaning that they ate historically when they assumed bodies; alternatively, that food was offered to the poor by divine power.

“Around this time I will return”: this does not refer to times but to the correspondence of his coming, when the faithful people was to be born through the promised Son. This is Sarah, the barren woman, to whom it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth.”

Sarah’s laughter is not doubt but prophecy: either because there would be laughter for unbelievers at Christ, or because he would laugh at all his enemies in the judgment. Hence Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.”

What it says, “I cannot hide,” should be understood as though he had said, “I do not wish to hide.” What it says, “with life accompanying,” speaks in the manner of a human being.

And God said: “The outcry of Sodom”—that is, because of their wickedness, or because it had been heard by human beings and angels. “I will go down” means “for vengeance”; “I will see” means “in mercy.”

After this promise, Sodom and Gomorrah are turned to ashes. But what does it signify that the Lord says the city would be saved if up to ten righteous people were found in Sodom?

He chose the number fifty because of repentance, in case they might turn and be saved. The fiftieth Psalm is the Psalm of repentance. He says that the city would not perish down to ten, as though in each of the Ten Commandments the name of Christ’s protection were found; whoever possessed it would not perish. The number ten also displays the cross of Christ.

The fact that five cities were burned signifies that all who have indulged the five bodily senses lustfully will be burned in the judgment.

## CHAPTER XIX

Lot himself, who deserved to escape from that conflagration, signifies the saints who groan among the wicked and ungodly, do not consent to their deeds, and will be delivered from them at the end of the world.

Lot’s wife represents the class of those who, called by God’s grace, look back. The fact that she was turned into salt offers an example for seasoning the faithful, from which others may be salted. Hence the Lord says: “Remember Lot’s wife as she fled from burning Sodom.”

Lot came to Zoar and did not ascend to the mountains. This signifies those who avoid unlawful desires of the flesh but nevertheless cannot attain the summit of contemplation. That is, Lot went out from Sodom but did not reach the mountains, because a condemnable way of life is abandoned, but the height of contemplation is not carefully maintained.

What follows, “Is it not a little place, and my soul shall live?” signifies a life that is neither entirely separated from the cares of the world nor alienated from the joy of eternal salvation.

Lot signifies one thing here and another when his daughters were with him. At that time he signifies the Law, which some, misunderstanding it, intoxicate themselves with; by using it unlawfully, they produce works of unbelief. “The Law is good,” the Apostle says, “if one uses it lawfully.”

His two daughters may signify the scribes and Pharisees, who wrongly beget carnal children from the Law.

In another sense, Lot signifies the Law. Nor is it inappropriate that among us *lex*—“law”—is declined as feminine, while in Greek it retains the masculine gender.

His wife signifies that people who, having been freed from Egypt and from Pharaoh’s persecution as from the fires of Sodom, again desired the carnal pots of Egypt, looked back, and fell in the wilderness. There the Law left and lost the first people, as though they were looking back, in the form of the wife.

From there he came and dwelt in Zoar, of which he says: “It is small, and I shall hide in it.”

Lot is said to have refused to ascend the mountain for three reasons: historically, because of fear of wild beasts and serpents; because of the plague that occurred; or because he wished to save the city.

A city is so called from the gathering of many, because it gathers the lives of many and holds them together as one. Those who live according to the Law have a small way of life as long as they understand the Law according to the letter. There is nothing great in observing Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision of the flesh, and the rest in a carnal manner. But if one begins to understand them spiritually, those observances that were small when practiced carnally will become great.

After this he went up to the mountain and lived there in a cave, he and his two daughters. The Law too should be understood as having ascended, because there it approached ornament through the temple constructed by Solomon. When the house of prayer was made, evil people turned it into a den of thieves.

Lot therefore lived in the cave, and his two daughters, whom he describes by saying that they were two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah. Some identify Oholah with Samaria and Oholibah with Judah. Thus the people, divided into two parts, made two daughters of the Law.

These desire to propagate a carnal offspring and strengthen the power of an earthly kingdom with numerous descendants, putting their father to sleep and inducing sleep in him—that is, covering and observing his spiritual meaning, they derive from it only an understanding of the flesh. From this they begot such sons that their father cannot even acknowledge them.

Zoar is interpreted as “small,” from what Lot said: “Is it not small, and shall I be saved in it?”

Some ask why vengeance is given from heaven. Because their wickedness was great, vengeance is given; it was given outside the ordinary course because they sinned outside the ordinary course.

The sulfurous fire came upon them because there is no other fire in which corruption exists. Sulfur is indeed the fire of a certain wood, whose nature burns in part; because of this resemblance, the fire is also called sulfurous.

Two fires are signified here because they committed both natural and unnatural sin. The two angels who inflict punishment hold the type of the two Laws, which punish those who do not fulfill them.

Lot is said to be excusable in the sin he committed because he was unaware. He is also excusable because he had drunk wine to such an extent. His daughters likewise are excusable because they acted for the sake of creating offspring. Yet they are inexcusable because they saw Zoar safe and the world not destroyed, and still acted for the sake of the two cities alone.

In a moral sense, Lot signifies the rational sense and the manly spirit. His wife, who looks back, signifies one devoted to carnal desires.

Take care lest, when you have escaped the flame of the world and evaded the fires of the flesh, and have surpassed even little Zoar—which is a certain moderate and civic progress—and ascended to the height of knowledge as to a mountain, your two daughters, who follow you, lie in wait for you.

When he ascends the mountain—that is, pride—the elder sister, vainglory, lies in wait. They are called daughters because they arise not from outside but from within us. In the cave of the breast they lie in wait, so that from us, while we sleep and are unaware, they may beget children—reprehensible thoughts and actions.

Lot went up from Zoar and sat on the mountain, for he was afraid to remain in Zoar. The question is asked: Since at first he preferred Zoar to fleeing to the mountain, why does he now move from Zoar to the mountain? The Hebrews relate that Zoar was frequently shaken by earthquakes. It had first been called Bela and then Salisa. Lot was afraid and said: “If, while the cities stood upon the earth, it was often overturned, how much less will it be able to escape now in the universal destruction?”

He called its name Moab—that is, “from the father.” The younger daughter gave birth to Ammon—that is, “son of my people.”

## CHAPTER XX

Abraham said that Sarah was his sister, confident in God that he would not allow her to be violated, just as previously by Pharaoh.

Sarah, however, signifies the Church, which during this pilgrimage and among foreign peoples is not permitted to be polluted, so that she may be without stain or wrinkle for her husband. The Church rightly lives in the glory of Christ, so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, just as Abraham was honored because of Sarah. Kings offer her gifts, as Abimelech offered them.

It is remarkable that she could be loved but could not be violated. For the Church is the Lord Jesus’ wife in secret; in spiritual concealment, the human soul or the Church clings to the Word of God, so that the two may be one flesh.

What was then prefigured first and afterward in Abimelech was fulfilled in the earthly kingdom, of which Abimelech bears the type, through the earlier and later kings. At first they persecuted the Church and wished to violate her, but could not; afterward they honored her.

The Church is Christ’s sister, not from his mother. For she is commended to Christ not according to earthly generation but according to heavenly generation, according to which we are spiritual. We received this generation not from the synagogue, Christ’s mother according to the flesh, but from God the Father.

Whose wife she is is concealed; whose sister she is is not concealed. For it is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined to the Word of God. But the fact that the saints are Christ’s brothers through a hidden kinship is made abundantly clear from Christ’s words in the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXI
The very great banquet that Abraham made on the day Isaac was weaned signifies the banquet of Christ on the new day of the perfection of the Christian people. Their children were weaned in the fifth year, or, according to others, in the second year. When Sarah saw Isaac playing with Ishmael, she said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” It must be asked why Sarah earlier wished her husband to receive a son from the slave woman, but now orders the slave woman and her son expelled from the house. She did this not inflamed by jealousy, but compelled by a mystery. Hagar—that is, the Synagogue—bore the former people into slavery; Sarah—that is, the Church—bore the Christian people into freedom. The loaves indicated this: the ancient priesthood carried the loaves of the Presence with it. But the waterskin failed; the purification of judgment is signified. Their carnal doctrine was destined to fail in a dead skin, that is, in the flesh of the old man. That Hagar was in the wilderness with her son signifies the Synagogue, expelled with its people from its own land without priesthood, and the priesthood wandering and ignorant of the way that is Christ.

[Col. 0242B] That the boy perished from thirst signifies that the people had no spiritual purification. That she cast her son beneath a tree and, when the angel showed it, saw a spring signifies that some from that people would seek refuge beneath the shadow of the wood of the cross and, with their eyes opened, see the spring of living water—that is, Christ. This angel is a likeness of Elijah, through whom this one will come to faith. When it is said, “I will make him into a great nation,” this means either that the Jewish people would rule as a numerous people in the world, or that those among them who believed would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom. As for the fact that he first speaks of an angel and afterward calls him Lord, we must believe that this was the Son, who always spoke through the Law and the Prophets and who is also the Angel of Great Counsel.

Beersheba is interpreted as “the seventh well,” or “the well of the oath”: either because Abimelech received seven ewe-lambs from Abraham, or because they swore the covenant there. For *Sabee* means either “oath” or “seven” in Hebrew. It should be noted that Isaac was born not at the oak of Mamre but in Gerar, where the town of Beersheba still exists today. Scripture bears witness to this when it says: “Abraham dwelt in the land of the Philistines.”

Others say that Christ’s figure is preserved where it says: “I shall not see the boy dying.” This signifies that the Jews handed Christ over to the Gentiles for crucifixion, and that they themselves did not crucify him. When it says, “What are you doing, Hagar?” they understand it as though he were saying: “What are you doing in the Law of the letter?” In all these matters Hagar displays the portion of the Jewish faithful, to whom it is said:

[Col. 0242D] “Rise”—that is, in faith; “and take”—that is, the work of faith. The statement that she held his hand signifies the Church’s cooperation. “He opened her eyes”—that is, her understanding in faith. The waterskin, once filled, signifies the old Law fulfilled in spiritual understanding, which is given to the Christian people to drink. That Ishmael is called an archer appropriately suits the Jewish people, namely, in slaughtering the sacrifices of the Law.

Of the banquet Abraham made it is said elsewhere. A banquet is made when Isaac is weaned, and there is great joy for the exalted father. But the supreme teacher makes a banquet for those who no longer need milk but strong food, who, according to their capacity to receive it, have their faculties trained and possess discernment of good and evil.
