But there can be no banquet for those of whom the Apostle says: “I gave you milk as food.”

That Sarah became angry when she saw Ishmael playing with Isaac signifies that the flesh, whose person Ishmael represents, was flattering the spirit, who is Isaac. Although such play of the flesh with the spirit may be permitted in pleasures, it nevertheless greatly offends Sarah, who is virtue.

Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman; yet both were Abraham’s sons, although not both were free. Therefore the one born of the slave woman does not become heir with the son of the free woman to receive the promise. Spiritually, then, all who come through faith to the knowledge of God may be called sons of Abraham. But among these there are some who come because of love and others because of fear of the coming judgment. It is said: “The one who fears is not perfect in love”; but “perfect love casts out fear.”

[Col. 0243B] We may also understand morally the matter concerning Abimelech, king of the Philistines: that he wished to take Sarah as his wife, that Abraham called her his sister, and that God restrained Abimelech on her account. I therefore think that Sarah, whose name is interpreted as “princess,” signifies the virtue of the soul. This virtue, then, is joined to the wise man as his wife. Finally, the Lord says: “Whatever she tells you, listen to her voice in everything in which she gives her counsel.” Abraham therefore does not wish virtue to be called his wife. For as long as virtue cannot share itself with others, it cannot be called a wife. But when we have come to perfection and become capable of teaching others, then we should no longer confine virtue as a wife within our bosom; rather, we should join it as a sister to others who desire it. Hence it is written: “Say that Wisdom is your sister.”

Accordingly, Abraham called Sarah his sister. Pharaoh too once wished to possess Sarah, but not with a pure heart; and virtue can agree only with purity of heart. This Abimelech, however, is far different from Pharaoh. It seems to me, therefore, that this Abimelech represents the diligent and learned men of the world who devote themselves to philosophy but do not understand the rule of piety sufficiently to attain it. Nevertheless, they perceived God and the King of all. Thus, as far as moral philosophy is concerned, they are shown to have pursued it even with a purified heart, but God did not permit them to attain this grace.

[Col. 0243D] For this grace was being prepared to be handed on to the Gentiles not through Abraham but through Christ. God heals Abimelech, his wife, and his slave women—whom we take to signify natural philosophy and the diverse and varied inventions of the schools. Meanwhile Abraham desires to share the gift of divine virtue with the Gentiles, but the time has not yet come for the grace of God to pass from the former people to the Gentiles.

According to this allegorical meaning, Pharaoh, whose name is interpreted as “destroyer,” could not take Sarah, that is, virtue. Virtue therefore remains with Abraham and remains in circumcision until the time comes when, in Christ Jesus, perfect virtue passes to the Church of the Gentiles. Then Abimelech’s household and his slave women give birth to sons for the Church. For this is the time when the barren woman gives birth—and this occurs through Abraham’s prayer, that is, through the people prophesying by means of the patriarchs and prophets. Hence it is also said there: “Return the wife to her husband, because he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you shall live.” Later he adds: “When Abraham had prayed, God healed Abimelech,” and the rest.

## CHAPTER XXII

“God tested Abraham.” Here God mentions his beloved son in order to increase the weight of the test, and he tells him to go to the land of the vision, so that, while walking and making the journey, he might be torn apart by his thoughts. He reached the place on the third day, so that throughout this very long interval he might gaze upon his son. The father ate with him, and the boy ate in his father’s lap, so that the test might be increased in every respect.

But what follows—“After we have worshiped, we shall return to you”—what do you say, Abraham? Are you speaking truthfully to the servants, saying that you will worship and return with the child, or are you deceiving them? If you are speaking truthfully, then you will not make him a burnt offering; but if you are deceiving them, it is not fitting for such a patriarch to deceive. What, then, does this statement express in your mind?

“I am speaking the truth,” he says, “and I am offering the boy as a burnt offering. For this reason I am also carrying the wood with me, and with the boy himself I shall return to you. For I truly believe—and this is my faith—that it is possible for almighty God to raise him from the dead.”

Finally, what did the Lord say to Moses when he came to the place God had shown him? “Remove the sandals from your feet, because the place on which you stand is holy.” Nothing of this kind was said to Abraham, nor even to his son Isaac. Perhaps Moses, although a great light of the Church, coming from Egypt, had certain bonds of mortality fastened to his feet. Abraham and Isaac, however, had none of these.

Abraham loved his son Isaac, but he placed love of God before love of the flesh. We have spoken of these matters historically; otherwise, they have been explained above according to their meaning.

Abraham is blessed a second time, signifying that just as he is the father of circumcision, so also he is the father of those from the Gentiles who believe. This may also be understood morally, because God renews his promises in order to show you that you too must be renewed. The first man was earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. He does not remain in the old things, lest you too remain an old man. He speaks of heaven so that you may also receive the image of the heavenly one. What benefit is it to you if he speaks these things from heaven while you hear them as coming from the earth?

[Col. 0244D] “Offer him upon one of the mountains.” The Hebrews say that this is the mountain on which the Temple was afterward founded, namely Mount Moriah, where there is the golden vessel of the Jebusite. “And he went to the place on the third day.” It should be noted that the journey from Gerar to Mount Moriah takes three days, and consequently the text says that he arrived there on the third day.

When Abraham sacrificed his son, he represented God the Father. The fact that Abraham fathered him in old age signifies that Christ would be born near the end of the world. God does not grow old, but his mystery was pointing far ahead. Sarah’s old age signifies that, at the end of time, Christ would be born from the people of holy souls. Her fertility indicates that the Church was barren for many ages but now, under grace, has many children of life.

Alternatively, Sarah’s barrenness signifies that we came late into this world and were all born in Christ, as in Isaac. At the end of time, the Church, by God’s wondrous grace rather than by natural fertility, bore these children to the Father.

Just as Abraham offered his one son, and just as Isaac himself carried the wood for himself, so Christ carried the wood of the cross upon his shoulders. The two servants who were not brought to the place of sacrifice signify the Jews divided into two peoples because of Solomon’s sin; serving the Law carnally, they did not understand Christ’s passion. The donkey is the senseless folly of the Jews: it carried the mysteries but did not understand what it was carrying.

What follows—“Wait here with the donkey,” and the rest—means: “After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” “After we have worshiped,” he says, as though he had said: “After we have caused them to worship, we shall return to Israel.”

The three-day period in which they reached the place of sacrifice signifies the three ages of the world: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In this third age the mystery of the cross was fulfilled.

Isaac, bound, is placed upon the pile of wood; Christ, crucified, is hung upon the wood of the cross. The ram sacrificed in Isaac’s place signifies that, while his divinity remained unharmed, he was crucified according to the flesh; or it signifies that the same Christ was born as a son. The sacrificed ram was caught by its horns. The cross indeed has horns, as it is written: “Horns are in his hands.” The ram caught by its horns signifies the crucified Lord.

[Col. 0245C] The evening signifies human sins. “With the thorns of sins,” he says, “this people has surrounded me.” Others have understood this ram bound by its horns to signify the same Christ, before he was sacrificed, crowned with thorns by the Jews.

When the sacrifice had been completed, God said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed.” This is written in the Psalm: “Let all the ends of the earth turn to the Lord.”

He called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” because the Lord caused himself to be seen, namely through the Incarnation. Others say that the fire signifies the Passion and the sword the hatred of the Jews. In the fact that Isaac said, “My father,” they say that Christ was prefigured, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

Morally, however, Abraham signifies every righteous person. Rising at night signifies rising from unbelief. Saddling the donkey signifies subjecting his body to the Law. The two young men signify the two Laws. Isaac the son signifies perfect understanding. The wood that is cut signifies perfected works, and the place signifies the Church. When he says, “Wait here with the donkey,” it should be understood as though he were saying: “Restrain the flesh; I and the boy”—that is, his understanding—will go on.

Isaac said to his father: “Where is the victim, father?” This signifies understanding fearful of sufferings and torments. The fact that he says “Abraham, Abraham” twice is the voice of one reproving. When he says, “I will bless you and multiply your seed,” this signifies the hundredfold reward of the saints in the present and the multiplication of rewards in the future.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0246A]

“And they departed from Beersheba”—that is, toward baptism—“and he dwelt there”—that is, in the Church. Then Sarah dies in the one hundred and twentieth year of her life. But what does it mean that she is buried in a double tomb, unless it is that the soul which dies to the world in order to live for God is received into a twofold rest, namely in the practice of good works and in contemplation of the Divinity?

She was buried in the city of Arbea, that is, “four,” because Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam himself were buried there. Sarah may also signify the virtue of the soul, which is joined to the wise man like a wife. Sarah’s sleep, however, is the completion and perfection of virtue. Whoever possesses perfected virtue must always be engaged in some form of instruction. Therefore, while Sarah slept, Abraham took another wife.

Cethura is interpreted as “offering incense.” Through the exercises of the virtues, one becomes the good odor of Christ. According to this interpretation, you may appear to have taken as many wives as the virtues in which you are strong.

The cave is called double—that is, two tombs—so that, by another interpretation, the double cave signifies the two Laws through the intervention of the letter. The field signifies the breadth of Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXIV

What is meant by Abraham’s requesting an oath-bound pledge from his servant—“Place your hand beneath my thigh, and I adjure you by the God of heaven”? What does the God of heaven have to do with Abraham’s thigh, unless it is so that the mystery may be recognized? For by the thigh a lineage is understood. This, then, was the oath by which it was signified that Christ would come from his lineage in the flesh.

This senior servant bears the image of the Law, through which the Church was betrothed as a bride to Christ; he is called senior because of its antiquity. He therefore went to Mesopotamia and stood beside the spring, seeking a bride for his master’s son. So too the Law, which came after faith to the spring of baptism and prayed there, encountered the virgin Rebekah—that is, the Church.

He saw the boy—that is, the prophetic word. She bowed down—that is, she received faith. The ornaments, earrings, and bracelets signify understanding and action. Thus she followed the boy and came to Isaac: the Church, following the prophetic word, came to Christ. She is led on a camel because she is found among the Gentiles in crooked and vicious ways of life.

When Rebekah saw Isaac, she dismounted, because, having come to know the Lord, she abandoned the vices of the Gentiles. Remembering, she covered herself with a cloak, because our flesh is put to shame by the error of our former life.

As the day declined, Isaac entered the field, because, coming at the final period of this world, Christ went out into the field, as it were, into the open. Although invisible, he presented himself visibly to the Church. The Church found him at the Well of Vision—that is, in contemplation of truth—or beside the water-bath where she might be purified. From there she was joined to her bridegroom, clinging to him in glory, eternity, and kingship.

The Hebrews say that Abraham swore at his sanctification, that is, at his circumcision; but we say that he swore by the seed of Abraham, that is, by Christ. Others say that Rebecca’s nurse signifies the discipline of the Holy Spirit; her son who was with her signifies the Synagogue of the Jews; the drink signifies doctrine; and the camels signify penitents who use the ten words of the Law.

The vessel fell upon her arm, that is, while she remained in humility, and it displayed the two Laws. The bracelets weighed ten shekels, that is, the ten words of the Law.

The house of Sarah into which Isaac entered after her death is the house of the Synagogue, to which the Church of the Gentiles came to believe after the Synagogue. Isaac led Rebekah into the tent, that is, Christ led the Church of the New Testament into the Church of the apostles.

The straw signifies the many forms of the Holy Spirit’s teaching that are given to penitents. Rebekah’s mother signifies the Gentiles; her father, Bethuel, signifies the devil.

## CHAPTER XXV

It should not be supposed that Abraham took Cethura because of incontinence, especially since he was very old, or for the sake of producing children, since a seed like the stars of heaven had been promised to him through Isaac. But just as Hagar and Ishmael signify the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Cethura and her sons signify heretics who think that they belong to the New Testament.

Yet both women are called concubines. For it is said: “He gave gifts to the sons of the concubines.” Sarah alone is always called his wife. “My dove is one,” he says.

Cethura is interpreted as “joined” or “conquered.” For this reason the Hebrews suspect that she was the same as Hagar, who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine to being a wife. They thereby seem to excuse Abraham’s now-declining age, so that an old man might not be accused of indulging in new marriages after the death of his aged wife. Leaving aside what is uncertain, we shall say this: Abraham’s sons were born from Cethura.

Abraham therefore gave everything he possessed to his son Isaac, but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts and separated them from his son Isaac. We must note what this signifies: certain gifts are given to heretics—that is, to the carnal—but they do not reach the promised kingdom. Neither heretics nor Jews receive it. For apart from Isaac there is no heir, because it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are counted as the seed.

When it is said to Rebekah, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples are divided in your belly,” this was figuratively fulfilled, and even unbelieving Jews know how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and how the Jewish people, greater in time, served the lesser Christian people.

In us too there are two nations and two peoples: virtues and vices. The former is lesser, the latter greater. For vices are always more numerous than virtues. Yet in us also, by the grace of God, the greater people has served the lesser. The flesh serves the spirit, and vices serve virtues. If we are like Rebekah and deserve to conceive from Isaac—that is, from the word of God—then vices will yield to virtues.

Esau came forth first, red and entirely like a hairy skin. Then his brother Jacob came out, and his hand was entwined around Esau’s heel. But why was he entirely red and hairy? Truly, because the former people, stained by the blood of the prophets and of Christ, remained polluted by sin and surrounded by the filth of wickedness. The younger one held his heel because, mystically, the lesser people overcame the greater.

For the fact that Esau himself sold his birthright to his brother for food and afterward was deprived of the promised first blessing signifies that same people, which was called God’s firstborn, lost not only the honor of its primacy for the sake of the profits of the present world but also failed to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. Hence it is said to them: “The kingdom of the world will be transferred from you.”

The birthright itself was a priestly garment, in which the firstborn, clothed with their father’s blessing, offered sacrifices like high priests. Through their desire for earthly love, the Jews lost this gift together with the glory of the future kingdom.

The fact that Esau is called a man skilled in hunting and a man of the field signifies the Jewish people: he is called a hunter because of the hunt, and a farmer because, for the sake of the goods of the earth, he served God alone.

Jacob, however, is simple—that is, the people of the Gentiles, for whom the cross of Christ is not regarded as being in the tents, that is, in the Church. When it is said that Isaac loved Esau because he ate from his hunts, this signifies the Jewish people, loved by God the Father when it was good in the Law and in sacrifices.

Jacob, selling the stew, signifies the Christian people, selling unbelief and vanity for the sake of the heavenly kingdom. He eats a hundredfold in the present—that is, with the body; he drinks—that is, with the soul; and he departs—that is, from the face of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Afterward, when a famine arose over the land, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar. There, out of fear, he pretended that Rebekah was his sister. The foreign king learned that she was Isaac’s wife when he saw him playing with her.

What could it mean, in the mystery of Christ and the Church, that such a great patriarch played with his wife? Once that marriage had been recognized, everyone surely saw that he must not, by erring, sin otherwise in the Church, but must carefully contemplate the secret of that husband in the Holy Scriptures. And he found that the one who is equal to the Father in the form of God had briefly concealed himself in the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be capable of him; in this way he adapted an appropriate manner of proceeding to his wife.

For what is absurd—or rather, what is not suitably adapted to the pronouncement of future things? If God’s prophet played in some way, it is carnal for his wife’s affection to take hold of him, since the very Word of God became flesh in order to dwell among us.

After this Isaac undertook the work and began to dig the wells that his father Abraham’s servants had dug. But the Philistines, envying him, stopped them up by filling them with earth. Who is this one if not our Savior? When he descended into this torrent of Gerar, he first began to dig the wells that his servants had dug—Moses, David, Solomon, and the prophets—which earthly and dirty understanding had nevertheless filled. When Isaac wished to cleanse their mouth, he showed that whatever the Law and the Prophets said, they said about him.

The Philistines quarreled with him—that is, the Jews, strangers to the kingdom of God. Isaac therefore dug, or rather Isaac’s servants dug, a new well. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark,

[Col. 0249A] Luke, John, and the other apostles. They all dug the well of the New Testament and found a spring of water leaping up into eternal life. Yet those who look to earthly things still quarrel over these matters. To them it is said: “Since you judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, we shall go to the Gentiles.”

After this Isaac dug a third well and called it “Broadness,” saying: “Now the Lord has given us room.” Isaac was truly enlarged and filled the whole earth with knowledge of the Trinity, establishing the Church’s breadth throughout the world.

But why did he call Abraham’s wells, which Isaac reopened, by the same names as his father had, unless it is because among us Moses is called Moses, and each prophet is called by his own name?

These things are mystical. “I am the God of your father Abraham,” as though he were saying: “Since I am your father’s God, I shall be merciful to you.”

He extended his tent—that is, the Church—and commanded his servants, that is, the apostles, to dig a well, that is, the apostles’ teaching in their own writings.

It should be understood that Abimelech, whom we have said signifies philosophers and learned men, does not always have peace with Isaac: sometimes he disagrees, sometimes he seeks peace. Philosophers neither always agree with the word of God nor are they always opposed to the one God. Many philosophers write that there is a God who created all things. Some have even added that God made or created all things through his word, and that the word of God is what directs and governs everything. In this they agree with the Law and the Gospel.

They disagree with us when they say that matter is coeternal with God; when they deny that God cares for mortal things, restricting his providence to the region above the lunar sphere; when they say that human beings depend upon the courses of the stars at their birth; and when they say that this world is eternal and will be closed by no end. There are many other matters on which they disagree and agree.

“Let an oath be made between us and you.” For whoever wishes to approach the Law of God necessarily says: “I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness.” In the words that follow, they seem to ask forgiveness of sins in return for their satisfaction.

Then follows: “And he made them a banquet.” For whoever ministers the word is indebted to the wise and to the foolish.

When Abimelech, Ochozath, and Phicol had come from Gerar, Isaac spoke with them. Abimelech is interpreted as “my king.” Ochozath is interpreted as “holding.” Phicol means “the mouth of all.” These three, as I think, represent the whole of philosophy, because among them philosophy is divided into three parts: logic, physics, and ethics—that is, rational, natural, and moral philosophy.

The rational part is that which confesses God the Father of all, as represented by Abimelech. The natural part is that which is fixed and holds all things together, relying, as it were, upon the powers of nature itself; it is represented by Ochozath, whose name means “holding.” The moral part is that which is in everyone’s mouth and concerns everyone, through the banquet-like likeness of its precepts; it is represented by Phicol, whose name means “the mouth of all.”

All of them therefore come to Isaac—that is, to the Law of God. After the banquet they swear to one another. When they have been refreshed by spiritual mysteries and received the gift of baptism, God promises to forgive them all their debts if they forgive everything.

These three may also signify the three Magi who came to Jesus from the eastern regions, instructed by the teaching of their ancestors.

Isaac dismissed them peacefully to their own place. According to others, this signifies what is said elsewhere: “Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called.”

He called it “Abundance,” that is, the four rivers of the apostles.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0250B]

Esau, being forty years old, took two wives. This signifies the people of heretics, who think that by means of four they can lead two churches—the churches of heretics—which both offend the soul of Isaac and Rebekah, that is, Christ and his Church.

When it says that Isaac’s eyes grew dim, this signifies that divine inspections do not see the faults of sins. Morally, however, Isaac is described as digging wells among a foreign people, teaching us by this example that, placed in the misery of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts. Until the waters of true forgiveness answer us, the hands of our inquiry must not grow slack in drawing out the earth of the heart.

Yet the Allophyles, lying in wait, filled those wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us digging diligently, direct toward us degrading thoughts of temptation.

The blessing of Jacob itself follows, as Hippolytus the martyr repeated it. “Isaac,” he says, “bears the image of God the Father; Rebekah, the image of the Holy Spirit; Esau, the image of the former people and of the devil; Jacob, the image of the Church and of the saint.”

The fact that Isaac grew old signifies the completion of the world. The fact that Isaac’s eyes grew dim signifies that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been cast aside.

That the elder son is named signifies the reception of the Law by the Jews. The fact that the father loved his food and his catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts through teaching.

The word concerning the promise is the blessing and hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ. Rebekah bears the figure of the Holy Spirit, who knew beforehand what would take place in Christ. In Jacob, however, she deliberates.

She speaks to her younger son: “Go to the flock and bring me two young goats.” This prefigures the Savior’s coming in the flesh, by which he would especially free those who were held liable for sins. For throughout the Scriptures young goats are understood as sinners.

Why does she order two to be brought? Because the taking up of two peoples is signified: she shows them to be tender and good, teachable and innocent souls.

Esau’s robe signifies the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, with which the people of the Gentiles were afterward clothed. The skins wrapped around his arms signify the sins of both peoples, which Christ fastened with himself to the cross in the extension of his hands.

Isaac’s asking Jacob why he had come so quickly marvels at the swift faith of believers entering the Church. The delightful foods that are offered signify a sacrifice pleasing to God, the salvation of sinners. The blessing that follows, and his enjoyment of its fragrance, openly proclaim the power of the resurrection and the kingdoms that have been opened.

He is blessed in this manner:

“Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.”

The fragrances of Christ’s name fill the world like a field. His blessing comes from the dew of heaven, from the rain of divine words, and from the richness of the earth—that is, from the gathering of peoples and the abundance of grain.

This multitude, because it gathers from the mystery of his body and blood, serves him, having turned to him from the Gentiles. The tribes—the peoples believing from the circumcision—worship him in faith. He is the Lord of his brothers because he rules over the Jewish people. The sons of his mother will worship him because he was born from her according to the flesh.

Whoever curses him is accursed, and whoever blesses him will be filled with blessings. Who does not know that the Jews, cursing Christ, are accursed, while the Christian people, blessing Christ, are blessed?

Isaac blessed one in place of another, then trembled and recognized what had happened. Yet he was not angered when the mystery was reported to him; rather, he confirmed it, saying: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.” This is the blessing given to the lesser Christian people.

But we must not think that the elder son was despised, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved. The prophecy of this blessing is: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be”—in the richness and fertility of the earth, that is, of material things, and in the power of the kingdom, which belonged to that people; and in the dew of heaven, that is, in the divine utterances, since the utterances of God were entrusted to them.

“You shall live by the sword.” Because that people was devoted to bloodshed at the beginning, it exercised these things against Christ or against the prophets.

“You shall serve your brother,” and the rest. This signifies that the Idumeans will serve the Jews, and that a time will come when they will cast the yoke of servitude from their neck.

Spiritually, however, “You shall serve your younger brother” means the Christian people. A time will come when you will shake off his yoke, and the rest: when, through acknowledgment of his faith, you have turned to the grace of Christ and are about to lay down the burden of the Law; then you will no longer be called the servant of the lesser people but, through faith, its brother.

After his father’s blessing, Esau, stirred by the goads of envy, devised his plot deceitfully. The Jewish people also premeditated this against Christ: it not only handed the Lord over to the cross but also persecuted those who believed in him to the shedding of blood.

Others say that “Behold, the fragrance of my son” should be joined to the place where it says: “He perceived the fragrance of his garments,” and the rest. This statement applies so specifically to Christ that it also applies to the Christian people.

The fragrance of Christ is the teaching of the Holy Spirit through the Gospel, or in the apostles, so that “we are the good fragrance of God,” and it applies to each teacher in his teaching and example.

All that follows applies historically both to Jacob and to the Christian people; when spoken from the person of Christ, it applies to the Christian people.

“From the richness of the earth”—that is, the people of Christ. But when Christ says to a saint, “from the richness of the earth,” he signifies the richness of heavenly rewards reserved for the future, as it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

The abundance of grain, wine, and oil historically refers to the three places in which the children of Israel dwelt: the abundance of grain in the land of Canaan, where Jacob received Isaac’s blessing; of wine in Egypt; and of oil in the Promised Land.

Alternatively, these three are spoken of as the abundance of the Promised Land. In another interpretation, the abundance of grain signifies Joseph’s abundance of grain in Egypt; the abundance of wine, the abundance of manna in the wilderness; and the abundance of oil, the abundance of the Promised Land.

Through the abundance of grain, wine, and oil, it is desired that the Church offer Christ an abundance of perfected works, together with hard and easy commandments, when Christ abundantly desires these things for every saint.

Grain, wine, and oil signify thought, word, and deed. Grain grows; oil, when it produces its liquid, does not grow. So thought grows into word, and word grows into deed, while deed stands firm.

Thus everything that follows applies historically to Jacob, to Christ from God the Father, to the Christian people from Christ, and to each saint, as was explained above.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Jacob, fleeing his brother’s plots and leaving his ancestral home, goes to a distant region to take a wife for himself. Christ likewise went among the Gentiles, away from the people and from his ancestral home—that is, Jerusalem—and took the Church for himself from there, as it is written: “I called my people, not my people.”

As Jacob proceeded to Mesopotamia, he found a place called Bethel and placed a large stone beneath his head. While sleeping, he saw a ladder set up with its support resting against heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending. Bethel is interpreted as “house of God,” which is the Church, where Jacob slept—that is, where Christ’s Passion is proclaimed. Jacob’s sleep is therefore Christ’s Passion. The stone beneath his head likewise signifies Christ: the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. And since he was anointed, who does not know that Christ is named from anointing (*unctio*)? To him it is said: “Your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” Through the ladder likewise Christ is understood, [Col. 0252D] who says: “I am the way, and no one can come to the Father except through me.” The raising upright of the stone signifies Christ’s resurrection.

According to the allegorical interpretation, it is not inappropriate that Jacob, the stone, and the ladder should all be understood as Christ for different reasons, as we find in many passages. The ascending and descending angels are the holy preachers. They ascend when, in order to understand his most exalted divinity, they rise beyond the whole of creation so as to find him in the words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” They descend when they find him in the words: “Made from a woman, made under the law.”

That ladder from earth to heaven—that is, from the flesh to Christ—[Col. 0253A] signifies that carnal people advance through it and become spiritual as they ascend; and spiritual people descend to nourish them with milk, when they cannot speak with them as with spiritual people but only as with carnal people. He himself is above in his head, and he himself is below in his body, which is the Church. We therefore understand him as the ladder, because through him one ascends in order to understand lofty things; and to him one descends, so that the little one may be nourished among his members. Through him alone people raise themselves up, so that they may await him on high; and through him they also humble themselves, lest they proclaim him in a lowly and merely temporal manner.

That Jacob did not see this spiritual vision in the land of Canaan signifies that no one sees spiritual visions unless he abandons sins and vices; and after he has abandoned them, he will undoubtedly see. [Col. 0253B] The fact that Jacob saw this vision after sunset signifies that each holy person sees spiritual things in the Church after the setting of worldly goodness.

Jacob, who carried the stone, signifies the Christian people. The stones from which the stone—that is, Christ—was carried signify the Jews, who are called stony because of the hardness of their hearts. Christ is called a stone because of his firmness and stability, since he assumed flesh from the Jews. He is also placed beneath the head, that is, beneath the leadership of the Christian people. Jacob’s sleeping signifies the mortification of that same people for Christ, with respect to vices and sufferings. The fact that Jacob did not sleep until he came to the stone signifies that the Christian people do not possess the aforesaid mortification until the coming of [Col. 0253C] Christ. Because of his coming and the mortification of vices, each holy person sees spiritual things, just as Jacob saw the vision after his sleep.

According to others, the ladder Jacob saw is said to signify the two laws. The pieces of wood, that is, the steps of the ladder, signify the order of the commandments. These steps are also said to number fifteen, corresponding to the fifteen psalms inscribed “A Song of Ascents.” The ascending and descending angels are the angels who minister to human beings—that is, the merciful and the unmerciful.

Alternatively, those who begin repentance but do not complete it are signified by the ascending angels. In another interpretation, this ladder shows the life of each believer, and its two pieces of wood signify body and soul. The statement that they were ascending and descending signifies that the spirit of each person rises and falls between the active and contemplative life.

Alternatively, “ascending and descending” means that those ascending from the earth are understood as Elijah and Enoch, while those descending from heaven are demons, who are also called angels, though not angels of God. For the Apostle calls them angels when he says: “An angel of Satan was given to me to buffet me.”

Or one may understand the ascent and descent as Christ’s descent, when, having left the right hand of the almighty Father, he came into the world, assuming flesh, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber; and his ascent as occurring when, after breaking the powers of death, he was gloriously victorious and, leading captivity captive, was lifted up into heaven before the eyes of his disciples.

Historically, [Col. 0254A] this signifies with respect to Jacob that he would eventually ascend again to his own land, although he was then descending to Mesopotamia while fleeing Esau’s anger over the blessing deceitfully obtained through his mother. Jacob descended to Mesopotamia because, by the situation of the place, it is lower than the land of promise. The fact that God spoke about the ladder signifies God’s speaking to human beings about his commandments:

> “The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed.”

Historically this is fulfilled; spiritually, the land of the Church was given to Christ and to his seed, that is, to the Christian people. In this passage, the west signifies the setting of worldly goodness; the east, future goodness; the north, the breaking of the will; and the south, the warmth of faith.

What are the gates of heaven except the commandments, or the apostles, [Col. 0254B] who are called gates because through their teaching one enters into belief in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? The oil poured upon the stone signifies the proclamation either of his incarnation, his divinity, or his mercy.

## CHAPTER XXIX

After this vision, as Jacob journeyed from that place, he saw sheep, shepherds, a well of water, and a large stone placed over it. Figuratively, the sheep are the peoples of the righteous; the shepherds are the prophets, who, cleansed by the Holy Spirit until Christ’s coming, governed the people of Israel. The stone placed over the well prefigured the Lord; the well was the Holy Spirit, which remained covered because Christ, the Word of God made man, had not yet come.

Alternatively, the well signifies baptism and the field [Col. 0254C] this world. The fact that they are called flocks signifies faith in the Trinity, or the three laws reclining with the aforesaid people—that is, in humility. The animals watered from it signify the simple who find the grace of baptism. The stone by which the mouth of the well was closed signifies the hardness of unbelief; once this is cast away, people can receive baptism. In this passage the shepherds are the apostles, and Christ removed the stone from the well—that is, unbelief from baptism.

Alternatively, the well is the Old Testament. The three flocks are those practicing physics, ethics, and logic; the animals are the people of the old law, hoping for the goods of the earth. The stone, however, is the letter of the law, which concealed its spiritual meaning and which Christ, on coming, removed.

[Col. 0254D] Accordingly, as Jacob proceeded to Mesopotamia, he took two wives, daughters of Laban, Rebecca’s brother: first Leah, then Rachel; and Leah’s maidservant, named Zilpah, and Rachel’s maidservant, named Bilhah. From these four women he fathered twelve sons.

Jacob’s two free wives can represent the two lives proclaimed to us in Christ’s body. One is temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we contemplate God’s delight. Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” and Rachel as “beginning of sight.” The activity of this life, through which we live by faith, is laborious and uncertain in its works, since it is uncertain whether, at the end, it will benefit those whom we wish to assist. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife; consequently she is described as having weak eyes. “The thoughts of mortals are fearful,” whereas the hope of the contemplation of God, possessing knowledge, is Rachel. [Col. 0255A] Hence she is said to be beautiful in appearance. Every lover devoted to beauty loves her, and for her serves the grace of God.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Through that grace sins, which are like scarlet, are whitened like snow. Thus one serves Rachel, not Leah. For who would desire the active life for its own sake? Yet, when night has been imposed, he experiences its fruitfulness. The active life, through examples and teaching, generates many children. When anyone, under the grace of whitening, has been established by the seven commandments of the law—love of neighbor and endurance of labor among them—and has cleaved to it amid various temptations, then, as if at night, the unexpected Leah is joined to him. He endures her in order to reach Rachel, receiving another [Col. 0255B] seven commandments, as though serving another seven years: to be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and a peacemaker.

A person would wish, if it were possible, to reach the delights of beautiful contemplation immediately, without any endurance of labor. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying. Hence it is said: “It is not customary in this place for the younger to be given before the elder.” She is not absurdly called “elder,” because she is earlier in time. The labor of good works comes first in a person’s education, before the repose of contemplation.

It must also be understood that after Jacob had been deceived by Leah and received her as his wife instead of Rachel, his father-in-law Laban told him to complete seven days after the wedding of the first sister and then to take Rachel, for whom he would serve another seven [Col. 0255C] years. Therefore, contrary to what some wrongly believe, he did not take Rachel as his wife after another seven years, but after seven days of the first wedding. For the text continues: “And he went in to Rachel, and he loved her more than Leah, and he served him another seven years.”

Thus both of Jacob’s wives were free women; both were daughters of the remission of sins, that is, of Laban’s whitening. One is loved, the other endured. For the sake of fruitfulness, the labor of the righteous has the greatest fruit in those whom they generate for the kingdom of God amid many tribulations.

Rachel, bright in appearance, approaches God in mind and sees, in the beginning, the Word of God with God. She wishes to give birth but cannot, for “who will recount his generation?” She is therefore barren because she does not come to the aid of those in their various afflictions. [Col. 0255D] At times she herself burns with the desire to give birth; for she wishes to teach what she knows, and she grieves that people hasten instead to that virtue which attends to their needs rather than to her.

## CHAPTER XXX

Rachel envied her sister. Since what is spiritually produced from the pure substance cannot be expressed in carnal words, Rachel chose, through every kind of bodily likeness, to receive children from her husband through her maidservant rather than remain without children.

Bilhah is interpreted as “grown old.” From the old life, devoted to carnal senses, we conceive images whenever something is heard concerning the unchangeable substance of truth. She receives sons through Leah and her own maidservant, out of love for a more numerous offspring.

We find that Zilpah is interpreted as “gaping mouth.” [Col. 0256A] She signifies those whose mouth was present through preaching, but whose heart was absent. Christ says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” Yet offspring is also received from Zilpah; or, as the Apostle says, “whether Christ is proclaimed through pretense or in truth, in this I rejoice.”

There are also certain affections in men, though produced by Rachel’s benefit, when, after receiving the mandrakes from Leah’s son, she allows her husband—who was to lie with her on the appointed night—to sleep with her sister. We know that the mandrake is beautiful and sweet-smelling, but weak in taste; here it signifies good worldly reputation. Hence the Apostle says: “The Church must have a good testimony from those who are outside.” Such people often provide the brilliance of praise and the fragrance of a good reputation to those through whom their interests are cared for.

[Col. 0256B] Those who are engaged in the dangers and labor of active deeds reach this glory first. Therefore Leah’s son finds the mandrakes when he goes out into the field—that is, when he walks honorably before those who are outside. But higher teaching, fixed in contemplation, does not attain this popular glory unless it has a testimony from those who labor amid the popular crowds. Thus, in a certain way, the mandrake fruits come through Leah to Rachel, while Leah herself receives them through her firstborn son—that is, through the honor of her fruitfulness.

Many people gifted with good intelligence, although they could have been capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid this and are carried into the leisure of teaching as into Rachel’s beautiful embraces. [Col. 0256C] Since it is good that this life too, becoming somewhat more widely known, should earn popular glory, it is unjust for it to obtain that glory if leisure suitable for administering ecclesiastical responsibilities holds back its lover and he does not provide governance for the common good.

Therefore Leah says to her sister: “Is it too little for you that you have taken my husband, and that you also seek popular glory?” Accordingly, in order that he may be shared justly, Rachel gives her husband to her sister: so that, if they love to devote themselves to knowledge, those who are capable may nevertheless undertake governance for this reason; but they are not compelled to undertake it.

This is signified by the statement: “When Jacob came in from the field, Leah went out to meet him and, detaining him, said: ‘You will come in to me, because I have hired you for the mandrakes of my son.’” It is as though she were saying: “Do you wish to confer a good reputation? Do not flee from the labor of leisure.” Anyone who notices these things being enacted in the Church perceives them. [Col. 0256D]

Leah can also signify the Church. Leah, the synagogue of God, gave birth to the people. She is read as being pregnant in her eyes because she could not see the spiritual meaning in the letter. Rachel, the younger—that is, the Church later in time—is beautiful in appearance and holy in body and spirit. She remained barren until the synagogue had given birth to the spirit.

Why did Jacob serve for Rachel, while Leah was placed before him? Because the Lord, in order to take up the Church, first joined the synagogue to himself. Jacob served for the two wives for seven years; this signifies the time of the present life, since time unfolds through seven days. During this time the Lord took the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death. He served for the sheep.

[Col. 0257A] And the Lord says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.” He fed the sheep and said: “I am the good shepherd.” Through the profit of his wages he acquired for himself a varied flock; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations. He placed three rods, cut by hand, in the watering troughs so that, by looking at them, the sheep might multiply; and our Lord, in the water of baptism, set before the faithful people the new reality of the three Persons, so that whoever looks upon it with a full heart may become a sheep of God.

For this reason some say that the first month was spent without payment, because he was then a guest. Laban also said to Jacob regarding chastity: “What wages will you accept,” or “in return for your love of her?”

[Col. 0257B] The fact that Leah is joined to Jacob at night signifies the synagogue joined to God in the darkness of the letter. Leah’s company of friends signifies the multitude of patriarchs and prophets. Rachel, however, is joined in the daytime—that is, the Church of the Gentiles in the day of the New Testament. The crowds of her friends signify the apostles, who are friends of God and of the Church of the Gentiles.

“And he called his name Reuben,” which signifies the perfect teacher in the Church: “seeing sons,” that is, seeing them in the Church; or seeing the sons of heretics and not permitting them to dwell in the Church.

Simeon signifies the Christian people, who hear the law in the time of the New Testament. Leah’s two sons together signify the Church’s two peoples: Reuben, the Jewish people, who live by the law; Simeon, the Gentile people, who hear the law from the apostles and teachers. As it is said elsewhere: “The eye that sees bore witness to me, and the ear that hears blessed me.”

“And he called his name Levi,” which is interpreted as “union” [Col. 0257C]: he signifies the Christian people, who through their teaching join all the saints to Christ.

Judah held the figure of Christ, saying: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth.” Or he signifies the Christian people, who confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When Rachel joined Bilhah to Jacob, she signifies the synagogue of the Jews, but, through the apostles, the part joining the Church to Christ.

Reuben went out and found mandrakes. Some say that this kind of tree resembles a human being in its hands and feet, or in its fingers and head; yet it has no head—that is, it lacks Christ, who is the head of the Church.

[Col. 0257D] Laban signifies the ignorant people who teach souls to be white through heresy and black through sin, when the appointed time arrives—that is, the time for shearing the sheep or for division. Laban, whose figure he bears here, was discussed shortly before.

Jacob undoubtedly signifies Christ. The three rods signify the three laws; the carnal elements signify the examples of the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles; and the water placed in the channels signifies baptism through the examples of those mentioned above. The varied sheep signify the souls of the saints, diverse in their virtues; the rams signify the apostles, of whom it is said: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God, even the rams.”

Just as all the sheep of diverse colors are assigned to Jacob, so the souls of the saints, diverse and distinguished by various virtues, are assigned to Christ.

Alternatively, the three rods signify Christ, the Holy Spirit, and Mary; Jacob signifies God the Father; [Col. 0258A] the water, the teaching of the Gospel; the sheep, as above; the carnal elements, the bodies of the saints; and the rams, the holy teachers.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“You have changed my wages ten times.” This is said either because of the magnitude of the matter, or according to the customary manner of human speech, or with reference to the five years during which Jacob served Laban. In those five years he had ten changes, because the sheep of Mesopotamia are understood to become pregnant twice a year.

Jacob entered Laban’s presence alone; so Christ entered the world singly against the devil. And just as Jacob became rich from Laban’s substance, so Christ was enriched from the devil’s substance.

What does this signify: after a long servitude, Jacob fled with his wives without Laban’s knowledge; Laban pursued him, caught him on the mountain, [Col. 0258B] and searched for the idols Rachel had stolen, but did not find them?

Laban signifies the devil, although earlier he signified something else. Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Although the devil is dark, he transforms himself, by merit of his disguise, into an angel of light. Jacob served him—that is, in part the reprobate Jewish people served him, from whose flesh the Lord came incarnate.

Laban can also represent the world, which in its fury pursues Jacob’s chosen ones, who are the members of our Redeemer, and attempts to crush them. Jacob took away Laban’s daughters—that is, the daughters of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined to himself the Church from both Gentility and circumcision, drawing her out of her father’s house, as it is said: “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

What is signified by the idols except greed? [Col. 0258C] Hence the Apostle says: “Greed, which is the service of idols.”

Laban came to Jacob but did not find them, because, after displaying the world’s treasures, the devil found no traces of earthly desire in our Redeemer. But Rachel covered by sitting what she did not possess in her actions. Through Rachel, who is called the sheep of God, the Church is signified. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance.

Rachel therefore covered them by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Of this covering of sins it is said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,” and so forth.

Rachel signifies us: by sitting we suppress idols, and by repenting we condemn the guilt of greed. [Col. 0258D] This impurity of greed occurs not to those who run manfully, but especially to those who, walking with an effeminate step, are dissolved through the flatteries of this world. Hence Rachel’s words there are, according to the custom of women: “It is happening to me now.”

After Laban had pursued Jacob, Laban and Jacob made a covenant. Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar, which Laban called “Heap of Witness,” while Jacob called it “Heap of Testimony.” The heap is among the faithful, and the prominent stone—that is, Christ—is a witness both to Jews and to Gentiles; the heap of stones is the multitude of saints.

All Jacob’s substance that he carried signifies the Christian people. The servants signify those who fear Christ. [Col. 0259A] The camels on which the substance is placed signify the strong in faith or the crooked; the asses, however, signify the simple.

Just as Jacob carried his entire household along the banks of the Euphrates to the land of promise, so Christ carried the Christian people along the banks of baptism to the New Testament or to the kingdom of heaven.

Jacob’s journey to Isaac signifies Christ’s journey to the Father in heaven. The statement that Jacob did not wish to confess to his father-in-law signifies Christ’s concealment from the devil, so that he might complete that for which he had come. The following statement—“Beware lest you speak anything harshly against Jacob”—signifies God the Father’s refusal to permit the devil to harm Christ or the Christian people.

“And you will drive away my daughters”: these are the words of the devil’s person, if he had been able to speak to Christ.

The fact that Laban and Jacob both came across the Euphrates signifies two peoples coming through baptism. [Col. 0259B] Laban’s return, together with all who were with him, signifies those who do not fulfill the dignity of baptism and return to the letter.

The mountain signifies the Church of the New Testament; the banquet, the flesh and blood of Christ.

Jacob said to his brothers: “Let us gather stones.” After gathering the stones, they made a heap. Laban called it “Heap of Witness,” and Jacob called it “Heap of Testimony.”

In the Hebrew language, a heap is called *adnerotes*. Again, in Syriac, a heap is called *Gar*, while “testimony” is called *utha*. Jacob called it *Galaat*, Laban *Gat*, and in the language of his people he called it *Seduth*.

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter”; Israel as “prince with God”—and this because he prevailed with God.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0259C] “With my staff I crossed the Jordan.” It is as though he had said: “I was in the midst of love, when I had nothing except a staff.”

The staff signifies weapons held in both hands. If this statement is referred to Christ, Christ’s staff is the Father’s help in the Passion and in the resurrection. Christ now goes forth with two companies—that is, with two peoples—through baptism. A company (*turma*) is said to be smaller than a crowd (*turba*).

If the statement “Deliver me from the hand of Esau” can be referred to Christ, it must be understood with respect to the flesh. Alternatively, Jacob’s prayer in this passage displays Christ’s prayer for his people.

The gifts Jacob sent to Esau signify those whom Christ handed over to the devil’s power.

[Col. 0259D] After these events, Jacob sent messengers to his brother Esau and sent gifts. After leading everyone across the torrent, he himself remained alone. A man wrestled with him alone, and Jacob prevailed; he did not release him until he had wrested a blessing from him and received a sacred name.

The man signifies Christ. Jacob prevailed over him because the people of Israel, whose figure Jacob then bears in the Passion—that is, in the torrent—prevailed over the Lord and wrestled, as it were, with Christ in his weakness according to the flesh. Nevertheless, Jacob obtained a blessing from the angel whom he overcame; the bestowal of his name was indeed a blessing.

Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” or “a prince with God.” This will be the reward of all the righteous at the end.

The Angel touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame; thus Jacob [Col. 0260A] was blessed and lame: blessed in those from that people who believed in Christ; lame in the unbelievers. For “thigh” signifies the breadth of a race or multitude. Many from that people, straying away, limped into the errors of their own seed. “They have limped,” he says, “from their paths.” That people not only limps but can no longer generate sons.

Finally, Jacob’s statement that he had seen God face to face, although earlier he had narrated that a man wrestled with him, signifies that the same God was to become human, the one who wrestled with the people of Jacob.

Historically, the man who wrestled with Jacob signifies God’s favor, so that Jacob might know that God would not grant him that. Jacob himself greatly feared his brother; he could not have overcome him—that is, he would have wished to overcome him.

[Col. 0260B] He answers: “Why do you ask my name?”—and it is impossible for Jacob to express it, because, as Jerome says, we use the customary name until the day of judgment. Phanuel, however, is interpreted as “face of God.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

The first, second, and last groups in Jacob’s multitude signify the peoples of the Church. The servants and maidservants sent first signify married people. Leah and her sons, in the second place, signify penitents or the continent. Rachel and Joseph, in the last place, signify the saints who are close to Christ.

The fact that he sent gifts to his brother signifies those whom Christ, through freedom of choice, handed over to the devil, as we said above.

The statement that Jacob bowed seven times signifies Christ’s body serving the persecuting people amid persecutions, [Col. 0260C] through the seven [periods] of this world. He therefore sent gifts first in order to appease him before seeing him, and for that reason bowed his head to him, because Esau was the firstborn, or because of fear of him. Alternatively, this was so that the prophecy of his father might be fulfilled, in which he said: “The time will come when you will shake his yoke from your neck,” and so forth.

Those who go before are close to Esau, that is, to the devil.

Others say that Jacob saw the vision at night because he could not have seen the one whom he saw at night during the day; or that this signified that Jacob was unlike Moses, who saw a vision by day. This signifies the law of the New Testament. Jacob saw by night, signifying the old law.

[Col. 0260D] Just as Jacob was able to see the likeness of the appearance he saw, and yet it did not bring death to him, so it is shown that he was able to see Esau’s appearance and bring death to him.

Jacob’s encounter signifies the Christian people, who were opposed to Christ before baptism. The striking of the sinew with a sword signifies the striking of sinful desire with the sword of God’s word. The lameness of one foot shows that we use one spiritual foot after casting away the vice of the flesh.

Jacob, in this passage, with his twelve sons signifies Christ with the twelve apostles; and his one daughter signifies the one holy Church.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

After this, Shechem, the son of Hamor, violated Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. She had gone out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, the son of Hamor [Col. 0261A] the Hivite, ruler of that land, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and slept with her, forcibly overpowering the virgin. His soul became attached to her, and he soothed her grief with flattering words.

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region when each negligent mind, abandoning its own studies and attending to the affairs of others, wanders outside its proper habit and order. Shechem, the ruler of the land, overpowers her: that is, when the devil finds the mind occupied with external concerns, he corrupts it. Her soul became attached to him because he regards her, once united to him, as belonging to him through wickedness; and, after recognizing her guilt, she recovers her senses and attempts to weep.

The corrupter places empty hopes and assurances before her eyes so as to remove the usefulness of grief. [Col. 0261B] Appropriately the text adds: “He soothed her grief with flattering words.” Sometimes he speaks of the more serious deeds of others; sometimes that what has been done is nothing; sometimes of God’s mercy; sometimes he promises repentance. He prolongs the time that follows, so that while the deceived mind is led along by this means, it may be suspended from its intention of repentance. Thus it receives no good things, just as no evils then distress it; and afterward it is more fully overwhelmed by punishments, while now it rejoices in pleasures.

According to the preceding explanation, however, Dinah signifies the Church joined to the devil through Gentility before baptism, or after baptism through crimes. Her father and brothers—that is, Christ and the apostles—avenge her, avenging the Church, who is the apostles’ sister. Dinah is avenged through deceit; so the Church is avenged by Christ against the devil through deceit.

[Col. 0261C] Two acts of vengeance are inflicted upon Shechem, namely circumcision and slaughter. Thus the devil received a double vengeance, in the present and in the future; and so did sinners. The fact that vengeance was taken on Shechem on the third day signifies vengeance against the devil and sinners through the third law.

Alternatively, Dinah signifies the soul of each sinner, or a person entering into marriage with a heretic, whom Christ and the teachers avenge.

Others say that the vengeance carried out by Simeon and Levi did not displease the Lord. This is shown by the fact that they were delivered from the hand of their enemies, or because they avenged God’s law and circumcision, since the circumcised man had used force against one who came from circumcision.

Alternatively, this did displease the Lord, since Shechem and his father received circumcision from Jacob; nevertheless Simeon and Levi were healed according to the merit of their father.

## CHAPTERS XXXV–XXXVI

[Col. 0261D] The idols that Jacob buried beneath the tree signify vices and sins hidden beneath the wood of the cross. The earrings signify disobedience. The changing of the men’s clothing because of the vengeance at Shechem signifies that evil works must be changed into better ones, as it is said elsewhere: “Strip off the old man with his deeds.”

Then God speaks to Jacob so that he might dwell at Bethel. While giving birth there, Rachel bore Benjamin and died. But what does it mean that Rachel gave birth to this same Benjamin and called his name “My sorrows,” except that she prophetically foretold that Paul would arise from that tribe, one who would afflict [Col. 0262A] the Church during the time of persecution?

Alternatively, Benjamin represents earthly Jerusalem, which was in the tribe of Benjamin. Its people inflicted great sorrow upon their mother by shedding the blood of all the prophets and, moreover, by crying out impiously at Christ’s death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Others say that Jacob’s journey to Bethel signifies Christ’s journey to the Church of the New Testament, since he did not offer sacrifice until he came to Bethlehem.

The statement that the flocks passed by is thought to be spoken by anticipation, because Jacob’s flock dwelt there, or because it signifies the flock of angels who ministered at the Lord’s birth.

[Col. 0262B] “And he came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, in the land of Canaan.” How is Salem now called a city of Shechem, when Jerusalem, where Melchizedek reigned, has already been called Salem? Either, then, the same name belonged to a city and a place in different tribes; or we should say that this Salem, which is now called Shechem, is here interpreted as “consummated” and “perfect,” while the other, which is elsewhere called Jerusalem, means “peaceful,” which is how we translate it in our language. For with a slight alteration of accent this word has both sounds.

The Hebrews report that Jacob’s lame thigh was restored and healed there, and that for this reason the same city received the name “healed” and “perfected.”

And God said to him: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name”; and he called his name Israel. Previously no name had actually been imposed on him; rather, what was to be imposed was foretold. What is therefore promised as future there [Col. 0262C] is taught here by example.

“And Jacob, son of Zore”—instead of “of Bosra.” Some suspect that this Jacob was added at the end of the volume; the Hebrews, however, assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor.

Meanwhile, Reuben violated his father’s concubine. Through Reuben the firstborn people of Israel from circumcision are signified: he polluted his father’s concubine, that is, he repeatedly stained the law of God in the Old Testament by transgression.

Paul teaches why the old law is called a concubine, saying: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman; these are the two Testaments.”

Reuben is interpreted as “son of vision,” or “seeing son,” or “seeing in the midst.” For his mother said: “God has seen my humiliation.”

Simeon means “hearing,” since his mother said: “The Lord has heard me.”

[Col. 0262D] Levi means “attachment” or “joining”: “For,” she says, “my husband will be joined to me,” or “he will be mine”; or, better, “my husband will follow me.”

Judah is interpreted as “confession,” since his mother said: “Now I will confess to the Lord.”

Dan means “judgment,” since his mother Rachel said: “God has judged me.”

Naphtali means “those who converse,” or “he has enlarged me,” or “certainly he has entangled me,” for his mother said: “God has compared me with my sister.”

Gad is interpreted as “temptation,” or “little bandit,” or “fortune,” since his mother said: “In fortune I am embittered,” declaring: “I am life.”

Issachar means “reward.” This is because Reuben had lawfully purchased for himself, with his mandrakes, the entrance that was owed to Rachel; or because she said: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband.”

Zebulun means “dwelling,” for she said: “My husband has dwelt with me.”

[Col. 0263A] Dinah is interpreted as “case,” since she became the cause of the quarrel at Shechem.

Joseph means “increase,” from his mother’s desire that another be added to her.

Benjamin means “son of the right hand,” the father having changed the name that his mother had given as Benoni—that is, “son of sorrow”—because of the difficulty of the birth.

## CHAPTERS XXXVII–XXXVIII
Joseph, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, whom his father loved more than the other sons, signifies Christ the Lord, whom the Father preferred, according to the flesh, to the other brothers descended from Abraham’s seed. Hence it is also said there: “For Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age.” As the world was growing old, the Son of God came.

The many-colored tunic which his father made for him signifies the diversity of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ. [Col. 0263B] That dream, moreover, by which his brothers’ sheaves bowed down before his sheaf, is what is fulfilled in Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him.” He is the one whom the sun, the moon, and the stars adore. For the excellence of the saints adores him under the name of the sun, the splendor of the Church under the image of the moon, and the multitude of all peoples in the figure of the stars.

Therefore his father rebuked him, saying: “Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed bow down before you?” This rebuke by his father signifies the hardness of the people of Israel, who, because they know that he was born from them, disdain to adore him.

Jacob sent his son Joseph to inquire after his brothers. God the Father likewise sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. “For God,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” to see whether all was well with his brothers and the sheep. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothaim. Dothaim is interpreted as “failure” or “decline.” Truly they were in decline, since they had conceived the murder of their brother. When they saw him from a distance, they planned to kill him. The Jews, seeing the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus, likewise formed a plan to kill him, saying: “Crucify him.”

A most evil beast devoured him—that is, the Jewish beast killed him. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am sending you out among wolves.”

Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his many-colored and long tunic. The Jews, through the death of the cross, stripped Christ of his bodily tunic. The many-colored tunic means one adorned with the diversity of all virtues.

They sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a kid, because, accusing him by false testimonies, they declared him guilty of death through envy, although he was granting forgiveness for all sins.

Others, however, ask what is meant by the phrase “the most evil crime.” “He accused his brothers of a most evil crime.” They therefore think that this was said either of the worship of idols or of the crime of the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans.

Others also say concerning Joseph’s tunic that it may signify Christ’s immortality. When the sun and the moon concealed their light beside Christ’s cross, turning themselves into darkness, they adored him.

How these things were fulfilled historically is clear; [Col. 0264A] but some of them may be applied only incompletely to the correspondence between Christ and Joseph.

Joseph’s father adored him, but not his mother; Christ, however, was adored by his mother, but not by his heavenly Father. The man who found Joseph wandering in the field signifies the prophetic word, which found Christ as though he were wandering. For the one who seeks the wandering is called “wandering.” That man—that is, the prophetic word—served Christ’s passion.

What he says, “They have departed from their place,” signifies that the Jews had departed from their place, from the labors of the Law, by worshiping idols.

Reuben, who attempted to rescue the boy from his brothers’ hands, signifies those who did not wish for Christ’s cross. He is spoken of as a figure of Pilate, because they cooperated in the matter of Christ’s cross.

Pilate, who is in solitude—that is, in good works—for it is said, “There is none who does good, not even one.” And what is said, “Keep your hands also innocent,” signifies that it was not the Jews but the nations who kept their hands undefiled.

Then he is cast into a cistern, that is, a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell. From the cistern he is raised and sold to the Ishmaelites, that is, to the Gentiles. Christ, after he emerges from hell, is purchased by all the Gentiles through the commerce of faith.

Joseph is sold for thirty pieces by Judah’s counsel; Christ is sold for thirty silver pieces through the counsel of Judas Iscariot.

Finally, Jacob, mourning the loss of his posterity because the father was grieving for his lost son, wept as a prophet over the destruction of the Jews. At last he tore his garment, which we read was done by the high priest in the Lord’s Passion. The veil of the Temple was also torn, so that prophecy might show both that his people had been laid bare and that his kingdom had been divided.

Thus Joseph descended into Egypt, and Christ into this world. A eunuch purchased him, namely, a people chaste through the disciplines of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“He was beautiful in face.” He was “fair in form beyond the sons of men.” And the woman cast her eyes upon him in order to commit adultery. This woman was a figure of the synagogue, which, as it is written, often “committed adultery after foreign gods.”

In the same way she wished to retain Christ in the crime of her adultery, so that he would deny that he was God and observe the teachings of the Pharisees and the doctrines of the scribes rather than the commandments of the Law, which was like her husband.

Christ, however, refusing the unlawful adulterous teaching of the synagogue, was seized by the adulteress by the garment of his body; he stripped himself of the flesh and, death having been destroyed, departed to heaven.

The harlot therefore slandered him when she could not hold him. In the end, neither did prison hold Joseph, nor did hell hold the Lord Jesus. Although he had descended there as though he were to be punished, he departed from it after freeing others.

Finally, he found two eunuchs from the king’s household. They signify the figure of two peoples, namely, believers and unbelievers, who were confined under sin and held liable through Adam’s transgression. They are called eunuchs because they received a chaste rule of discipline. On the third day, therefore, when the Lord rose from hell and the obscurity of the Law was dispelled, as Joseph revealed the dreams, the people of believers were released from sins and, freed from the prison of hell, restored to the service of divine Law.

But the unbelieving people of the Jews, because they did not believe in the wood of confession, is hung upon the wood of transgression.

## CHAPTER XL

Moreover, Pharaoh recounts a dream, and Joseph interprets it. But what do the seven years signify, which were shown in seven full ears of grain or in seven fat cows, except the gifts of the seven spiritual charisms, through which the abundance of faith overflows with generous piety? [Col. 0265B] Conversely, the seven barren and thin ones showed the famine of the word of God in the last times.

Joseph gathered an abundance of all crops during seven years—that is, he stored the grain of faith in the storehouses of the saints. This was through those seven charisms, as though through seven years, so that when the seven years should begin—that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital crimes should arise under Antichrist—when there should be a famine of faith and salvation, then the just and faithful alike would possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, so that their faith would not fail, weakened by scarcity.

Others say that the spices carried on camels signify two laws: the resin signifies the law of the books of the Law, and the stacte signifies the law of the prophets.

The fact that Joseph was not freed through Judah’s counsel signifies [Col. 0265C] that Christ was not freed, in the flesh, through the late repentance of Judas Iscariot.

Elsewhere it is said: “They sold him to the Ishmaelites for thirty silver pieces.” When the thirty silver pieces are mentioned in writing, others say that they signify faith in the Trinity, because Christ is purchased by the Church of the Gentiles.

The fact that Reuben came to the cistern and did not find the boy signifies what is written in the Gospel: “He is not here, but he has risen.”

What is said about Jacob’s unwillingness to accept consolation signifies the Christian people suffering with Christ, refusing consolation in the present but accepting it in the future.

What he says, “I shall go down to my son, mourning, into hell,” historically signifies the grave, or that by his prophecy he foresaw that the souls of human beings would go down into hell before the Lord’s coming.

The Midianites, then, as far as Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch. Some inquire here how this eunuch was one. For eunuchs are called eunuchs in three ways: those who have been made eunuchs by human beings; those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of Christ God; and those who were made eunuchs from their mother’s womb.

Potiphar, however, was made a eunuch in none of these three ways. Rather, according to the opinion of scribes and teachers, Potiphar was a priest of the idols of Heliopolis, a handsome man, and beautiful in face. Then, as it is said, “the love of him” [the reading is uncertain] seized Pharaoh’s sense, so that they became like Sodomites with one another. Pharaoh then took him away from his idol and made him the eunuch of his wife, after his loins had been dried up for many years, when Pharaoh had entrusted his wife to him because of passionate desire. Thus he is said to have become a eunuch for this reason.

## CHAPTERS XXXVIII–XL

Judah said to his son Onan: “Go in to your brother’s wife.” In this statement the Law is found by the son—that is, by the shepherd.

Odollam was a city. Thamnas, however, is a terrestrial region, that is, a garment [the Latin is uncertain: “palium”].

“She sits at the crossroads,” either so that she might be thought to be a prostitute or so that Judah would not pass her by.

Judah recognized her and said: “Thamar is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” In Hebrew it is thus: “Thamar is more justified than I”—not that she was righteous, but that, by comparison with her, they did less evil; they did not commit outright shamefulness, but sought more freely.

Phares is interpreted as “division,” because he divided the limbs in the womb. [Col. 0266B] Zara, second in order, is interpreted as “rising” or “east,” either because he appeared first or because many righteous people were born from him.
