In the book of Chronicles it is written: “In Thamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law.” The Jewish people are understood here, to whom kings from the tribe of Judah were owed as husbands. And fittingly her name is interpreted as “bitterness,” for she gave the cup of gall.

There were two kinds of people among the populace who did not act rightly: one kind harmed others, while the other did no good. They are signified by Judah’s two sons. One was wicked; the other spilled his seed on the ground so that he would not give seed for the conception of Thamar’s offspring.

Nor are there more than two kinds of people useless to the human race: those who do harm and those who refuse to be useful. And because the one who harms is worse than the one who does no good, the wicked one is therefore called the greater.

Her is interpreted as “leathery,” referring to the tunics with which the first human beings were clothed, they having been condemned as a punishment.

Onan is interpreted as “their sorrow,” referring to those who do no good even though they have the means by which they could do good.

The greater evil is the taking away of life, signified by wars, rather than the failure to give life, signified by “their sorrow.” Nevertheless, God is said to have killed both, where it is figured that he removed the kingdom from people of such a kind.

The third son of Judah, who was not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings from the tribe of Judah began no longer to arise for the Jewish people. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Thamar, who was herself of that same tribe of Judah, did not receive him; yet no one from it reigned. Hence Shelah is interpreted as “his division.” Holy men who knowingly rendered service by prophesying do not properly belong to this interpretation.

Judah signifies Christ coming to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel. He came with his shepherd, an Odollamite named Hyras, to shear his sheep at Thamna.

Thamna is interpreted as “failing,” for the ruler had already failed from Judah, as had all anointing.

He came with the shepherd Hyras. Odollamite is interpreted as “testimony in the waters.” The Lord came with precisely this testimony, possessing testimony greater than John’s.

Hyras is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” John truly saw his brother; he saw his brother according to the seed of Abraham. Therefore “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.”

He saw him when he said: “Behold, the Lamb of God.” He saw what many wished to see and did not see. Therefore, as a true Odollamite, he bore witness in the water.

The Lord came to shear his sheep—that is, to unload the burdens of all sins.

Then Thamar changes her clothing and her name. For her name may also be interpreted as “changing,” and thus she signifies the transition from synagogue to Church. Yet in that synagogue they had served the Lord gall in the bitterness of water, whereas she signifies the one in whom Peter wept bitterly.

The clothing of a prostitute is a confession of sins. Thamar bears the type of the Church. Sitting in her clothing at the crossroads, she advances in love of neighbor and, as though walking forward, strives toward perfection. Hence David says: “Make your ways known to me, O Lord.”

And she secretly received a ring and a bracelet, as it is found in the Septuagint. The necklace and the staff signify calling; she is adorned by justification and exalted by glorification: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.” But these things were done secretly, where the conception of holy fruitfulness might take place.

A kid is sent to her as to a prostitute. The kid is the reproach of sin, sent through the same Odollamite, as though he were rebuking her and saying: “Brood of vipers,” and the rest. But the reproach of sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had changed her.

By the public signs of the ring and bracelet—or, as in the Septuagint, the necklace and staff—she may also be understood to have overcome the Jews who judged rashly; Judah himself at that time also represented their persons. They say that this people does not belong to Christ, but when the surest proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forward, they blush and confess that we are more truly justified.

The Church is accused by the Jews as an adulteress against the Law, but she displays the staff, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the legitimacy of the Law; and the bracelet, the pledge of immortality.

When Thamar was giving birth and had twins in her womb, the first, called Zara, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it. But when he withdrew his hand inward, the other, who was called Phares, came forth in birth. Figuratively this corresponds to the fact that Israel extended its hand toward the works of the Law but drew it back stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. Afterwards the people of the Gentiles burst forth, so that “the first shall be last, and the last first.”

Concerning Jacob it is said that he came to his father Isaac at Mambre, the city of Arbae, which is also Hebron. It should be known that Mambre is the same city, named so in antiquity after Abraham’s friend.

And Esau fathered Eliphaz. This is the Eliphaz whom both Scripture and the book of Job mention.

Esau, Edom, and Seir are the names of one man. In Hebrew, Esau is interpreted as “red,” from the color of his body. But he was entirely hairy, hairy like a skin. Edom means “red” or “reddish-brown,” from the red or tawny stew which he received in exchange for his birthright.

When it says, “The Horites, inhabitants of the land,” the repeated account of Esau’s sons explains who had earlier been prince in Edom before Esau: he was of the race of the Horites, who in our language are interpreted as “free.”

The book of Deuteronomy plainly records how the sons of Esau killed the Horites and possessed their land. There were the sons of Jonath the Horite; there were also Onies, Lodan’s sister, and Tenna. The latter was the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn.

The Horites are therefore recalled because Esau’s firstborn took a concubine from among their daughters.

Others, however, say that the shepherd and the aforementioned Edom signify every teacher who announces the Incarnation of the Lord coming to the Church; and that the three months during which the Church was not found in the good portion signify the three Laws [the wording is uncertain].

By these interpreters the midwife is said to signify the teaching or discipline of the Holy Spirit, which tied the scarlet thread—that is, spiritual grace—to the people of the Gentiles. This people was shown first through the good of nature, but how this was previously explained.

“We suppose [the reading is uncertain] the wind” means “the substance of my womb”—that is, the assumption of the Law by the people of the Gentiles.

“And the Lord was with him”—that is, God the Father was with Christ as his helper.

The fact that Joseph is said to dwell in the house of his lord signifies Christ dwelling in the synagogue of God the Father and ministering his teaching to the Jewish people. Through him the Father blessed the Church throughout the world and multiplied it both in kids and in lambs—that is, in souls and bodies.

“He knew nothing except bread.” In this is prefigured what is said concerning Christ: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

She seized the edge—that is, the hem—of his garment. The cloak is said to signify the letter of the Law, which was left to the synagogue, the wife of the devil, abandoned by God.

Alternatively, through this woman’s husbands the Jewish people is signified.

Those who saw the dream did so not because of their own merits, but so that Joseph might be magnified.

[Col. 0268C] “I was taken from the land of the Hebrews.” These words are spoken by anticipation.

And here the innocent one is in the pit—that is, Christ is in hell for Adam’s sin, although he himself committed no sin.

“Three branches,” that is, three boughs; “buds,” that is, clusters [the reading is uncertain: “bolca”].

Pharaoh and Herod are especially recorded as having adorned the day of their birth, because they thought that at the hour of their birth their succession to the kingdom had been arranged. They performed a similar act of adoration, as it is said: “Their impiety was equal, and their solemnity one.” Hence Joseph, who bore the type of Christ, deserved the chariot.

## CHAPTER XLI

A herald went before him, proclaiming before him, and he appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. [Col. 0268D] So also our Lord, betrayed by Judah as Joseph was by his brothers, rose from the prison of hell, mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is said: “The chariot of God is multiplied by tens of thousands.” He received power from the Father to preach and to judge.

The Apostle says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name.”

He also received a ring, namely, the priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation, and on our foreheads and hearts the figure of the eternal King is impressed in the form of the cross.

He was clothed in a linen robe—that is, holy flesh, the appearance of splendor, and the robe of immortality.

He also received a golden chain, that is, good understanding.

A herald goes before him—that is, John the Baptist, who precedes his way and proclaims: “Prepare [Col. 0269A] the way of the Lord.”

He has another herald: the voice of the archangel with the trumpet of God.

Joseph is called in the Egyptian language “savior of the world.” This is clearly about Christ, when, under the figure of Joseph, the Savior is shown to be not merely the savior of the land of Egypt but of the whole world.

Joseph was thirty years old when he stood in the presence of King Pharaoh. Christ is likewise read to have been thirty years old when, in the presence of this world under the type of Pharaoh, he disclosed what had been revealed.

He therefore received a wife from the Gentiles, that is, the Church. From her he fathered two sons, that is, two peoples gathered from Jews and Gentiles.

After the years of abundance, famine prevailed throughout the whole world, rightly, because there was no one who did good.

After this Joseph saved Egypt from the scarcity of grain, and Christ freed the world from the famine of the word of God. [Col. 0269B] He opened his storehouses: Christ, throughout the whole world, subjected everything by the distribution of his grain.

For unless Joseph’s brothers had sold him, Egypt would have perished; unless the Jews had crucified Christ, the whole world would have perished.

Joseph is interpreted as “increase” or “enlargement,” but that Joseph enlarged only Egypt. In our Joseph, however, the whole world deserved to have increase.

He distributed wheat; our Joseph distributes the word of God. “For their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

## CHAPTER XLII

Jacob said to his sons: “There is grain in Egypt.” God the Father also says: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Ten more perfect men therefore went down—that is, from the catalogue of the Law, established in the number. [Col. 0269C] Although he himself recognized them, he was not recognized by them. Christ also recognizes the Hebrews, but they do not recognize him.

They gave him money; but Joseph—that is, Christ—gave them grain and returned their silver, because Christ is not purchased with money but with grace.

Joseph saw Benjamin, his little brother. Mystically, too, the Lord saw Paul when light shone around that little one.

It is asked when this happened. When he guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen, he was not yet perfect.

Joseph wept; and Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping.

Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus came to be seen by many.

Then the silver cup was placed in the sack of the youngest alone, and it was found in Benjamin’s sack.

Joseph’s cup, in Paul’s body, shone forth as the eloquence of heavenly teaching while he was learned in the Law, because he was not yet subject to it. The cup was inside the sack: teaching was inside the Law; the lamp was inside the measure, having been sent.

Then Ananias laid on his hand and opened the purse. When the purse was opened, the silver shone forth. When the scales fell away, as though the sack had been loosened from certain bonds—that is, when the veil of the Law had been removed—he obtained the grace of freedom, and with unveiled face he preached the word of the Gospel.

Thirty silver pieces were given to him, together with five excellent garments. Whoever preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ receives thirty silver pieces from Christ. Therefore Paul says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

He received five garments of the wise: the manifold disciplines of all five senses. Paul therefore excels. His portion of merits overflows, yet the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace.

The two garments signify confessing that Christ is God and human. Accordingly, it is read in Proverbs: “All her household are clothed in double garments,” that is, with mystical or moral understanding.

Gifts are also sent to the father. The son honors the father. Christ invites his people to promised gifts.

Donkeys carry these gifts: the Gentiles, useless and laboring. Now, having become useful, they carry gifts as a type of Christ; they carry them in the Gospel of the giver of gifts.

Let us now briefly take up what has been omitted.

When Joseph says, “You have come to inspect the fortified places of this land,” he wishes to terrify his brothers in revenge for his sale, and he does this as a figure of Christ.

For just as Joseph took revenge and did not take revenge, so Christ took revenge by not taking revenge. “We rightly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother.” This may be understood as spoken in the person of the Jews, as though they were saying: “We rightly suffer these wounds as vengeance for the cross.”

It may also be understood in the person of the perfect, in that same vengeance, according to what Reuben said: “Did I not tell you: Do not sin against the boy?”

## CHAPTERS XLIII–XLIV

Judah said to his father: “Send the boy with us.” Historically, this signifies that he would later receive the principate from him.

The gifts sent by Jacob to Joseph signify gifts of hope, faith, and charity, or of thought, word, and deed. [Col. 0270C]

The grain signifies eternal rewards.

The money has a twofold history and meaning, or signifies body and soul.

“Put the loaves,” and the rest. These three possessions, which are described as existing here, show the difference of merits in the future, as it is said: “God will repay each according to his work.”

Benjamin, as explained above, signifies Paul. Others, however, inquire where Paul’s greater love for Christ, compared with that of the other apostles, is shown. They answer it in this way: Paul was caught up to the third heaven; he heard words that cannot be uttered; and after the resurrection he deserved to be taught by God things that the others did not deserve.

In the other matters that follow, the meaning is clear. In the statement, “They drank and became drunk,” the drunkenness of the Church is understood as the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

The filling of the sacks with grain signifies the filling of the bodies of the saints with eternal rewards in the future.

## CHAPTER XLV

“He made me like a father to Pharaoh.” Pharaoh is said in this passage to hold the figure of the Christian people, whose father is Joseph, that is, Christ.

What he says, “Do not leave anything of your possessions,” signifies that we ought not to abandon the good that we have begun when we come to Christ.

Joseph dismissed his brothers, who announced to their father, saying: “Joseph your son is alive, and he is lord over all Egypt.”

Jacob was terrified. The unbelieving people, however, after learning of Christ’s deeds, revives in spirit; and the one who seemed dead is called back to life through faith in Christ’s resurrection. [Col. 0271A] He is therefore vivified by his sons, that is, by Peter, Paul, and John.

The Jewish people is invited to grace. Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession,” meets it, because confession now goes before those whom unbelief previously possessed.

The statement made to Jacob, “Joseph will place his hand over your eyes,” may signify that Jeroboam was from the tribe of Joseph. He made two golden calves in order to lead the people back to worship them, and by this, as though placing his hands over them, he blinded and closed Israel’s eyes so that they would not see their own impiety—or perhaps under the appearance of piety.

These things were said by the Lord under the appearance of what was to come.

We may also say that, just as our Lord, in the manner of Joseph, placed his bodily hand over the eyes of a blind man and restored his sight, so he placed his spiritual hand over the eyes of the Law, which had been blinded by the understanding of the scribes and Pharisees, and restored its sight, so that, for those whose spiritual senses he opened, sight and understanding might appear in the Law.

## CHAPTER XLVI

Israel therefore departed and came to the well, and saw in a vision by night, and the rest.

Others understand this in the following way: no one saw God unless he reached baptism and perfect works, just as Jacob reached the water of the oath and, after the slaughter of the sacrifices, heard God through a vision.

## CHAPTER XLVII

Pharaoh invited Israel and his sons. This signifies the stronger portion of the Christian people inviting the weak to spiritual teaching in the Church.

Afterward Joseph came to meet him. He had already received the seed in old age, in the last times, signifying the Jewish people, not according to the election of his grace.

He placed his hand over his eyes and removed his blindness. He delayed removing his blindness so that, at the end, those who had previously thought that belief was impossible might believe.

Hence the Apostle says: “For a blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.”

After this Joseph gave his parents and brothers the rich land of Goshen, providing them with food because famine had seized the land.

So also the Lord chose the best land for his parents—that is, for the patriarchs and prophets from whom Christ was born according to the flesh—or for all the saints, concerning whom he says in the Gospel: “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father.”

To these, therefore, he gives the land of promise, the kingdom of God. Concerning it the Prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

Others say that the land of Goshen, which is interpreted as “nearness,” signifies the Church, which is near the kingdom of heaven or near the world.

The fact that the sons of Israel carried Jacob signifies that the Christian people carries him with itself to faith, or carries the weak to the stronger part of the Church, as we said above concerning Pharaoh.

The little ones and the women signify the difference of persons in faith, or the inexperienced perceptions of the soul.

The wagons signify examples of the righteous or the commandments of Scripture, by which the successors of the people are carried toward the unity of the Church, so that one people may be formed.

Finally, in the Septuagint translation it is written: “And the famine overcame them.” The Egyptians were oppressed by famine, but famine did not hold Jacob and his sons. Although it is written that famine prevailed, it is not written that it prevailed over the sons of Israel.

Earlier, after all, it is written: “Abraham went down into Egypt,” because famine had prevailed in the land of Judaea.

How carefully this is written concerning the saints: it is reported that famine prevailed in the land, whereas concerning the impious it says that they were overcome by famine. Famine held neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor their sons.

What is therefore an exercise of virtue for the righteous is a punishment for sin among the unrighteous. Those who think according to the earth suffer a famine of the word of God, because famine prevails in the land. But the righteous, as it is written, “shall be satisfied in the days of famine.”

You will find that those who are born from the seed of Abraham went down into Egypt; and again, that the sons of Israel went up from Egypt.

Finally, it is also said concerning Abraham himself: “Abraham went up from Egypt, he and his wife and everything that belonged to him.”

And it is said to Isaac: “Do not go down into Egypt.”

The Ishmaelites also, who carried incense, resin, and stacte, and who likewise came from Abraham’s seed, are said to have gone down into Egypt.

And shortly afterward: “The brothers went down,” he says, “into Egypt.”

And shortly afterward: “They went up from Egypt and came to their father in the land of Canaan, and they said: Joseph your son is alive, and he is lord in all the land of Egypt.”

These matters concerning ascent and descent may at present provide an occasion for reflection to diligent students.

What is said, “Joseph your son is alive,” and the rest, was not said without purpose. For if he could have been overcome by lust, this would perhaps not have been announced to his father. If he had certainly done this, he would not have been alive. “The soul that sins shall itself die.”

What is said, “He himself is lord in all the land of Egypt,” is truly a great thing for him: he brought Egypt under his power.

To trample upon lust, flee luxury, and restrain and curb all the pleasures of the flesh—this is to exercise dominion over the whole of Egypt.

But if there is someone who subdues certain vices of the flesh while yielding to others, it cannot properly be said of him that he exercises dominion over the whole land of Egypt; he will appear to exercise dominion over perhaps one, two, or three cities.

The fact that the father and brothers were not in Joseph’s presence signifies that in the present we see Christ “through a mirror and in an enigma.”

What he says, “The days are evil and few,” should be understood as though he were saying: “Would that my days in the present had been long!”

Alternatively, it signifies the judgment of the Christian people after its dwelling in this world. The days appear few in comparison with the rewards that will be received in the future, and evil in comparison with the days to come.

After this it is said that Joseph subjected the whole land of Egypt to Pharaoh, as each person sold his possessions. No one was free in Egypt. Pharaoh subjected them all to himself.

Perhaps for this reason it is said: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery.”

It is said concerning the Hebrews that they were violently reduced to slavery. But Pharaoh easily reduced the Egyptian people to slavery.

Through Joseph the whole land of Egypt is handed over to Pharaoh. Joseph is easily excused in this matter, for the Egyptians had sold themselves.

Paul did this when he handed over to Satan the man who was unworthy of the fellowship of the saints. Let no one therefore say that Paul acted harshly when he expelled the man from the Church, so that, after being expelled, he might learn not to blaspheme.

The Egyptians sold their land to Pharaoh. Spiritually, this signifies that Christ purchased the whole world with his teaching and his body.

What he says, “Sow the fields,” signifies bodies; the crops signify the thoughts and perceptions daily rendered to Christ; and the portions left over signify the active life, which Christ leaves to us if we use the five senses rightly.

What is said, “Our salvation is in your hand,” signifies that our salvation has been placed in Christ’s power.

The land of the priests, which was free, signifies that the Church is free from the tribute of the world.

The priesthood of certain people signifies a twofold honor: a hundredfold reward here and rewards in the future.

“Under the thigh.” Jacob is said to have asked an oath under the thigh for three reasons: so that, if Joseph violated the oath under the thigh—that is, under the organ of generation—his seed would not continue; or so that he might swear under the member by which the Lord gave the sign, namely, the sign of circumcision; or so that he might swear under the member from which, as we explained elsewhere, Christ’s generation would come.

Then there is the command that his sons and grandsons should fulfill after him the oath of their father.

“And show me mercy,” that is, do not bury me in Egypt.

“And truth,” that is, the fulfillment of the oath.

“Turning toward the head of the bed”: this signifies that he was secure concerning his request.

## CHAPTERS XLVIII–L
Then Joseph, hastening to receive his father’s blessing, presented his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and so forth. Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” signifies the Jews who forgot their Lord. Of them it is said: “They forgot God, who saved them.” Ephraim, however, the younger, whose name means “fruitfulness,” signifies the Christian people, who overflow with the abundance of grace.

When Jacob wished to bless them, Joseph placed Ephraim on his left and Manasseh [Col. 0273D] on his right. But Jacob, crossing his hands and prefiguring the mystery of the cross, transferred his right hand to the younger and placed his left over the elder. Thus the likeness of the cross over their heads prefigured scandal for the Jews and future glory for the Christian peoples: through the mystery of the cross, the elder was made left from right, and the younger right from left. For when the Jews fell into our desolation, we attained their glory; and by such a sacrament the younger people of the nations was set above the greater people of the Jews. Hence the Patriarch said to them: “This one shall indeed become a people, but this one shall be exalted above all.”

The souls who entered Egypt with Jacob were seventy-six; [Col. 0274A] sixty-six souls came forth from Jacob’s loins and entered Egypt, and nine souls. We should know that in the Hebrew text, instead of “nine,” there are two. For Ephraim and Manasseh were born of Asenath, daughter of Potiphar, in Egypt, before Jacob entered Egypt and before the time of famine came upon them.

There is also what we read above: “The sons of Manasseh were those whom his concubine bore: Machir; and Machir begot Gilead. The sons of Esrom, the brother of Manasseh, were Sudalam and Tahan; the sons of Sudala were Medem.” It has been added because what we read later is described as having occurred by anticipation. For it is not recorded that, at the time when Jacob entered Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim were of such an age that they could beget sons. From this [Col. 0274B] it is clear that all the souls who entered Egypt, descended from Jacob’s loins, numbered seventy-six. After they had entered, three souls were found in Egypt—Joseph, namely, together with his two sons. Jacob himself was the seventieth.

The Seventy, however, said in Deuteronomy that Jacob descended into Egypt with seventy souls. Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, gave seventy souls, lest he should appear to contradict the Seventy, who at this time are not regarded as possessing great authority.

“And I have given you one portion above your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow.” He gives him Shechem, which is Sichem. They say that “bow” and “sword” signify the justice by which they were freed after Sichem and Hamor had been killed. Others say that by the bow justice is signified, and by the sword labor. [Col. 0274C]

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow; foremost in gifts, greater in authority, poured out like water, you shall not increase, because you went up onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

The sense is this: “You are my firstborn, greater among my sons, and you sat according to the order of your birth, by which the firstborn were truly entitled to receive the priestly kingdom.” Here he demonstrates honor-bearing and great strength. But because you sinned and, like water that cannot be held in a vessel, were poured out in the impulse of your will, I therefore command you not to sin any longer. Thus, lamenting the penalty of sin in the least of your brothers, you mourn what you lost—the rank of the firstborn.

“The beginning [Col. 0274D] of sorrow” is every firstborn, because for him the parents’ innermost feelings are first stirred.

“Simeon and Levi are brothers; instruments of iniquity are their weapons. Let my soul not enter their counsel, and let my glory not be joined to their assembly; for in their anger they killed a man, and in their will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their anger, because it was obstinate, and their indignation, because it was harsh; I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

This signifies that it was not by his counsel that they killed the men allied with Sichem and Hamor; instead, during a time of peace, they shed the blood of the innocent under the guise of friendship and, seized by a kind of furious cruelty, destroyed the city walls. Hence he says: “Cursed be their anger,” because Simeon did not receive a separate inheritance but, among all the tribes, possessed only a few cities for dwelling. Concerning Simeon it is written in the book of Joshua that he did not receive a territory by lot, but received some from the tribe of Judah. [Col. 0275A]

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness—who will rouse him?”

Because Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written of Judah: “Your brothers shall confess to you,” or “shall praise you.” Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, according to the literal sense it signifies that kings would be generated from David’s stock and that all the tribes would worship him. For he does not say, “The sons of your mother,” but “the sons of your father.” What follows—“You have gone up to the prey, my son”—shows that he would bring back a captive people; and, according to the more sacred understanding, that he ascended on high and led captivity captive. Or, as I think better, captivity signifies the Passion, and ascent signifies the resurrection. [Col. 0275B]

“Tying his colt to the vine, and his she-ass to his vine.”

This evidently means that he joined the colt of the she-ass on which Jesus sat—that is, the people of the nations—to the vineyard of the apostles, who are from the Jews; and that he tied the she-ass on which he sat to the vine—or, as the Hebrew has it, to Soreth, that is, “the chosen vine”—namely, the Church gathered from the nations.

When he says, “My son,” he makes an apostrophe—that is, a sudden turn toward Judah—showing that Christ would accomplish all these things here.

When it is said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations,” this signifies that rulers did not fail to arise from Judah until the time when Christ was born, he who was sent by the Father and is the expectation of the nations. [Col. 0275C]

“Issachar: astute and strong, lying between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; he placed his shoulder beneath the burden and became a servant subject to tribute.”

Because he had previously said concerning Zebulun that it would possess the shores of the great sea and reach Sidon, Phoenicia, and the remaining cities, he now returns to the inland province. Issachar, who was to possess the most beautiful region of Galilee beside Naphtali, is made by his blessing an inhabitant [Col. 0275D] of it. He calls him a strong she-ass, and speaks of his shoulder for bearing burdens, because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea what was born within his borders, also carrying tribute to the kings.

The Hebrews, however, say that by metaphor—that is, transformation—it signifies that, meditating on the sacred Scriptures day and night, he devoted his zeal to labor; and for that reason all serve him, as though carrying gifts to a teacher.

“Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe in Israel. Dan is a serpent on the road, a cerastes on the path, biting the horse’s hooves so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.”

Samson, the judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. He therefore says this, seeing in the spirit that Samson would grow his hair and, as a Nazirite, triumph over the other enemies: that, like a serpent or a basilisk lying in wait on the roads, he would permit no one to pass through the land of Israel. But if some reckless man, trusting in his own strength as though in the speed of a horse, wished to escape him in the manner of a plunderer, he would be unable to do so.

He speaks of the whole matter metaphorically, in terms of a serpent and a horseman. For when I saw that the Nazirite was so strong, that he died because of a prostitute, and that, while dying, he killed our enemies, I thought, O God, that he himself was Christ, your true Son, so strong because he died and rose again and was once more led away captive. For another Savior of my race is still to be awaited. Let him come, to whom all things have been reserved; he is the expectation of the nations. [Col. 0276A]

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded afterward.”

This signifies that, when he returned after fourteen years to the sons whom he had left beyond the Jordan as their possession, before Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he found a great battle awaiting him against the neighboring nations and, after defeating the enemies, fought bravely. Read the book of Joshua son of Nun and Chronicles. [Col. 0276B]

“Naphtali is a released hind, giving words of beauty”; or, “Naphtali is a watered field.” For the Hebrew word *anioala* [reading uncertain] signifies both—a forest.

This signifies either that warm waters arise in that tribe, or that the Lake of Gennesaret was watered by the streams of the Jordan. The Hebrews, however, understand “watered field” because of Tiberias, which appeared to possess knowledge of the Law, and interpret it as prophesying words of beauty. “A released hind,” on the other hand, indicates seasonal crops and the swiftness of a more fertile land. [Col. 0276C] But it is better if we refer everything to teaching, since the Savior taught there above all, as it is also written in the Gospel:

“Joseph is a son increasing, Joseph is a son increasing and beautiful in appearance; daughters ran along the wall, and they embittered him, quarreled with him, and envied him, carrying arrows. He sat in the strength of his bow, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob; from there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel.”

“O son of Joseph, who are so beautiful that the whole crowd of the girls of Egypt gazes at you from the walls, towers, and windows: they envied you and provoked you to anger, your brothers, carrying arrows of envy and wounded by darts of jealousy. But you placed your bow and weapons of warfare in God, who is a strong defender; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosed and broken by him. From your seed the tribe of Ephraim is born, strong and steadfast, set upon a harder stone, and also ruling the ten tribes of Israel.” [Col. 0276D]

Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils. That this is a most explicit prophecy concerning Paul is clear to everyone: in his youth he persecuted the Church, and in old age he became a preacher of the Gospel.

The Hebrews, however, explain it as follows: the altar on which the sacrifices were offered, and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured out, was located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. They say, therefore, that this signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning and in the evening divide what has been collected for them by the people. They apply the interpretation of the bloody, ravenous wolf to the altar, and the division of the spoils to the priests who served the altar and live from the altar.

Thus much concerns the historical sense. Spiritually, however, Reuben appears to have represented the person of the firstborn people, to whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn son.” For, in accordance with what belonged to the firstborn, it was his to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. It is added: “You are my strength,” certainly because from that people came the foundation of faith, and from that people came the power of God, who is Christ.

But how is he himself “the beginning of sorrows”? Truly, because he was always inflicting sorrow upon his father, turning his back toward him and not his face. He was first in gifts, because to them were first entrusted the divine utterances, the giving of the Law, and the covenant—or promise. He was greater in authority, certainly because of the magnitude of his strength, since that same people ruled more extensively than the others in this world.

But “poured out like water”: by sinning against Christ, he was poured out in an impulse of will, like something that cannot be held by a vessel. Therefore he adds: “You shall no longer increase,” because, after that people had been dispersed throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished.

But why did it deserve such things? He adds this explanation: “Because you went up upon your father’s bed.” The Jews refer this to the sexual violation committed by Reuben with his father’s concubine Bilhah. Yet this more properly pertains to prophecy, because he is speaking of future events; for he says: “That I may announce to you what will happen in the last times.”

He proclaims the audacity of the firstborn people, which went up upon its father’s bed and defiled his couch when it seized the Lord’s body—in which the fullness of divinity rested—hung it upon the cross, and stained it with iron. Alternatively, he polluted the bed of the concubine upon which he climbed—that is, the Law of the Old Testament, which he often defiled by transgressing it.

That the old Law is represented in the person of the concubine, Paul taught when he said: “Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. These are the two covenants.”

Morally also, through Reuben—whose name may be interpreted as “son of vision,” or “see the carnal son”—he signifies the visible human being. For although our outward man is corrupted, the inward man is renewed. At first, every person in this world lives according to the flesh and is moved according to the flesh; and the first carnal movement is in the desire of lust. When this besieges the time of early youth, it makes a person harsh and reckless, as well as wanton—one who climbs upon his father’s bed and pollutes his father’s couch; that is, even the commandments and defenses of the natural law that is within us, which our Father now says we transgress.

“Simeon and Levi, brothers, are weapons of iniquity for warfare.”

By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes and Pharisees and the priests of the Jewish people. The scribes among the Jews were associated with Simeon; from the tribe of Levi came the high priest. They formed the plan to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him, concerning which plan it is said: “May my soul not enter their council.”

He shuddered at all the crimes that the Jews were going to commit in the last times, because in their fury they would kill the man—that is, Christ—of whom it is said: “Behold, a man; Dawn is his name.” And elsewhere: “A woman shall surround a man.”

They pierced the wall—that is, the most solid spiritual wall that guards Israel. They pierced him with a lance. “Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn”: when, inflamed with fury and anger, they handed Christ over to Pontius Pilate, saying: “Crucify, crucify!”

“And their indignation, because it was harsh”: when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the Prince of life be crucified.

“I shall divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel,” because some of them believed, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separated from them and came to the faith are said to have been divided; those whose homeland and Temple were overthrown, and whose unbelieving race was scattered throughout the world, are said to have been dispersed.

Perhaps these three sons of Jacob signify the three movements of the human soul: the appetitive, the irascible, and the rational. Reuben held the form of appetite, since he slept with his father’s concubine. Simeon held the second form, anger, which is shown by the reproach of his fury. Levi held the third form, reason, to whom the keeping of the Church’s law was entrusted.

These three forms, therefore—that is, every soul in its proper condition, when it comes into this world—first act culpably, until, weighed down by the burden of evils, it can reach the place of repentance.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you.”

Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is represented, who was born according to the flesh from his tribe. His brothers will praise him—namely, the apostles and all his coheirs, who through adoption have been made sons of God the Father and have become Christ’s brothers by grace, although he himself is their Lord by nature.

“Your hands shall be upon the necks of your enemies.” By those same hands and through the same trophy of the cross he both sheltered his own and healed his enemies and opposing powers. In accordance with this, the Father also promised, saying: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.”

“Your father’s sons shall adore you,” when many of Jacob’s sons adore him, having been saved through the election of grace.

“Judah is a lion’s cub”: when, by being born, he became small, as it is written: “A little one has been made for us.”

“You have gone down to the prey, my son”—that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples; and those whom that opposing lion had attacked, you rescued by dying. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive; resting, you lay down like a lion.

Most manifestly Christ lay down in his passion, when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit, or when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a kind of sleep of the body.

But why “like a lion,” or “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion because he fulfilled this not by necessity but by power, as he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down myself.” And he was also like a lion’s cub, because he died from where he was born.

Natural philosophers, moreover, write concerning a lion’s cub that, when it has been born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then, at the father’s growl or roar—when the place of the den is said to have been shaken—the sleeping cub is awakened.

This is very suitably applied to Christ’s death in the passion: lying for three days and three nights in the chamber of the tomb, he completed the sleep of death. Therefore Christ rested like a lion, who not only did not fear the bitterness of death, but even in death itself conquered death’s dominion.

But when it is said, “Who will awaken him?” the meaning is that no one will do so except himself, in accordance with what he himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it.”

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah and Israel.”

This most clearly refers to Judah. For succession to the kingdom remained undefiled among the Jews from his seed until Christ was born; and we have spoken of this above.

“Binding his colt to the vine.” His colt is the people from the Gentiles, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been placed. He joined this colt to the vine of the apostles, who are from the Jews; for the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.

“And his she-ass to the vine.” For he himself says: “I am the true vine.” To this vine, therefore, he binds his she-ass, upon which the Church gathered from the nations sits. He bound her to the vine of his body by the bond of love and by the discipline of the Gospel, so that, living in imitation of him, she might become God’s heir.

Others interpret this she-ass as the Synagogue, slow-footed and weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law.

“He washed his robe in wine”—or his flesh in the blood of the passion—or that Church in the wine that “will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

“And his cloak in the blood of the grape.” The nations are the cloak, which he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as a garment.”

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” Christ’s eyes are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the Church with the light of knowledge. Their commandments surpass the austerity of wine—that is, of the ancient Law—because they are more enduring.

“And his teeth are whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy teachers, who cut people away from errors, and those who, in eating, transmit the body of Christ. They have become whiter than the milk of the old Law: they chew and distribute the solid food of the word, and they are rightly called whiter. For all who supply the Church with the nourishment of Scripture ought to be pure and unstained.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the landing-place of ships.”

Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of beauty” and signifies the Church. She dwells on the shore of the sea and at the landing-place of ships, so that she may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

Against all the storms of this world—that is, against its upheavals—she stands with solid firmness and awaits the shipwreck and tempests of Jews and heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Although she is beaten by the waves, she is not broken.

She extends as far as Sidon—that is, as far as the Gentiles. It is also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from there, and that the Lord often taught in those regions, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the people sitting in darkness, saw a great light.”

Sidon is interpreted as “hunter” or “huntress.” Who are the hunters except the apostles? As we said above, they were taken from those regions, concerning which it is said: “I will send my hunters, and they will hunt you on every mountain.”

Morally also, Zebulun—which can be interpreted as “nocturnal flow”—signifies that, after Judah, that is, the soul, has been turned toward repentance through confession, all the things it did in the night of ignorance are removed from it and cease. It extends itself even to the hunters, so that it may learn to hunt.

Whenever wild beasts or deceitful foxes—that is, demons or exceedingly wicked thoughts—break into its heart and wish to destroy the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, let it seize them and become a praiseworthy hunter of evil thoughts.

“Issachar is a strong ass.”

Issachar is interpreted as “reward.” They refer this to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his own people. This Issachar is written to be a strong ass because formerly the Gentile people were like a tributary and wanton animal, existing without any rational order; but now it is strong, offering its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer and bearing the yoke of evangelical discipline.

“Lying down between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent.”

To lie between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of this world, seeking nothing of the things that now exist in between, but desiring the final things. The strong ass saw the good rest and the excellent land when the simple Gentile people raised themselves to the strength of good works for this reason: because they were striving toward the eternal homeland of life.

Therefore he also places his shoulder beneath the burden, because, while desiring to reach the promised rest, he bears all the commandments honorably. Hence he became one who serves tribute: that is, offering to the King and to Christ the good works of faith and the gifts of good works.

Morally, we have shown the person who, having wandered through the threefold movement of the soul—in fact, through the sickness of the whole soul—erred through desire. We distinguished that Reuben, Simeon, and Levi can signify prudence that is not rightly directed. But here we have shown the penitent already turned away from the error of envy, and in Zebulun turned in large and substantial part toward repentance.

In Issachar, whose name is interpreted everywhere as “reward,” we see one awaiting the reward of good work, because he has not only cast away every evil but also continually desires and seeks every good. He dwells or rests midway between the boundaries, inclining neither to the right nor to the left.

“He saw that rest was good and the land excellent.” After he had driven away and expelled the struggle of flesh and spirit, his spirit rested in God. Then he saw that the land was good, when he was conquering his flesh by vices and desires; and when he produced the fruit of righteousness in good works, he placed his shoulder beneath the burden. He became one serving tribute when he carried that evangelical burden—very light indeed—upon the shoulders of his soul and rendered it to God.

“Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe in Israel. Let Dan become a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path,” and so forth.

Some say that these words prophesy that the Antichrist will arise from this tribe. Others pronounce these words concerning Judas, by whom the Lord was betrayed, and wish the rider and the horse to designate the Lord together with the flesh he assumed. They understand “fall backward, upon the earth from which he was taken.” But because he rose on the third day, he said: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord”; for he says: “You will not leave my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.”

Others, as we said above, transfer this prophecy to the Antichrist, because in this passage Dan is asserted to be a serpent, and one that bites. The fact that Dan was the first among the tribes of Israel to camp toward the north signifies the one who says that he will sit at the sides of the north. Concerning him the prophet says figuratively: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard.” He is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent.

For in Greek, *cerasta* means “horns.” That serpent is said to be horned, through which the Antichrist is suitably represented: he will be armed against the life of the faithful not only with the bite of poisonous preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? “Let him become a serpent on the road,” because in the breadth of the present life he urges those to walk whom he seems, as though sparing them, to encourage—not by flattering them, but by biting them. He consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty.

Again, “let him become a horned serpent on the path,” because when he finds those who are faithful and sees them constraining themselves within the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks them not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also destroys them through the terror of power. In the anguish of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

The horse signifies this world, which through its pride foams along in the course of passing times. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the final times of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves.

To bite the hoof is to touch the extremities of this world by striking them.

“So that its rider may fall backward.” Whoever is exalted in the dignities of this world is the rider of its horse. He is said to fall backward, not forward, as Paul is remembered to have fallen.

To fall forward is for each person in this life to recognize his own sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward, where one does not see the fall, is suddenly to depart from this life and not know that one is being led to punishments.

And because the Jews, caught in the snares of their error, await the Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob rightly says in the same passage, suddenly converted into the number of the elect: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord.” That is: like the faithful, I shall faithfully believe not in the Antichrist but in the true Christ, who is to come for our redemption.

Morally also, this may be understood of the one who, having long ago been said to have advanced through Issachar—[the text reads “Misachar” here]—and to rest in the commandments, and having become the cultivator of his soul, now advances to the point of having acquired the understanding necessary to distinguish and judge his people—that is, the thoughts of his heart—as one of the tribes of Israel; that is, to bring everything back into unity and harmony, so that there may be no disagreement among his thoughts.

Thus he becomes a serpent, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Be wise as serpents.” We ought to act wisely in the life of this world, inclining neither to the right nor to the left. Let us not walk along the broad road that leads to death, but along the narrow one that leads to life.

For this reason the horned serpent is also added to the path: the path is narrower than the road.

“Let him bite the horse’s heel,” doing what the Apostle says: “I discipline my body,” and so forth. He does this so that the rider may fall backward. Such a person always fears pride and exaltation, and prefers that his soul fall from an evil height into good humility, so that he may learn from Christ, who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.”

If, therefore, he recalls his soul backward from its height and returns after Christ’s humility, he awaits salvation from the Lord.

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him.”

This girded Gad expresses the person of the Lord, who at his first coming, by fighting, confronted the coming of the Antichrist, girded with the sword of God’s word, concerning which it is said: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one.” With it he divided enemies—that is, son from father, daughter from mother, and so forth. “I have not come,” he says, “to bring peace, but a sword.”

But when he says, “And he himself shall be girded afterward,” the love of the Lord is shown at the second coming. When the Antichrist comes, Christ will again follow in his footsteps and confront him with a swift coming, so that he may kill him with the breath of his mouth. Hence Gad can also be interpreted as “a bandit,” and “afterward”—that is, late—as a form of a bandit leaping out in an unexpected arrival. “For just as a thief in the night,” he says, “so is Christ.”

Thus before Antichrist he comes against him in humility; after him, in majesty. Morally also, our human being, whom we have described above as having advanced somewhat in the ways already mentioned, must come to the point of being tested by the enemy, so that the constancy of his purpose may be proved, because an untested man is not approved.

Let us gird ourselves before and afterward, so that we may carefully attend to the things that have happened and those that are to come.

“Asher has rich bread, and he gives delicacies to kings.”

Asher, whose name signifies “riches,” is therefore Christ, because the height of his riches in wisdom and knowledge is beyond counting. He became poor for us so that we might become rich. His bread became rich—namely, his flesh; whoever eats it will not die forever.

He also supplies the delights of wisdom to kings: to those, namely, who rule their own senses well and bring their bodies into servitude.

Some refer this passage about Asher to Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, who, prophesying about Christ with Simeon, supplied many delights to kings—that is, to the apostles and the other saints.

Morally also, Asher, which is interpreted as “blessed,” is perhaps the one whom we led back from error to repentance and gradually brought through each stage to an increase of blessedness. After his conversion, after spiritual understanding, after temptation and victory, his bread is rich.

He eats that bread which descended from heaven and gives life to this world. And this one, whose bread is now rich, will also give delicacies to kings—not to the poor or foolish, but to kings. For “we speak wisdom among the perfect.”

“Naphtali,” which is interpreted as “expansion,” signifies the apostles and holy preachers. Their teaching has been spread throughout this world, and many of the apostles were from this tribe.

He is called “a released stag,” because the apostles and preachers, springing forth with a swift leap like stags, transcend entanglements and, contemplating lofty and exalted things, give forth beautiful speech, proclaiming the Savior’s teaching to all nations.

Morally also, our inward man, who shortly before was feeding on rich bread—bread that strengthens the human heart—is not inappropriately called “a released stag,” because, despising all earthly things, he feeds in high places like the stags. He places his entire treasure in heaven, where, according to the Gospel, rust and moth do not destroy it. Then he brings forth beautiful words—that is, proofs of heavenly contemplation.

“Joseph is a growing son,” certainly among the Gentiles. When he had left the synagogue because of its unbelief, he gathered for himself an innumerable people from the Gentiles. Concerning him David says: “All the ends of the earth shall be converted to the Lord.”

It follows: “Beautiful in appearance.” For his beauty surpasses everyone’s, concerning whom it is said: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.”

“Daughters ran along the wall”—that is, the generation or the churches that believed in Christ. Upon the solidity of faith, as though upon a wall, they run upward through love of Christ’s beauty, in order to behold the true bridegroom through contemplation and join themselves to him with the kiss of love.

“But they provoked him,” when, slandering him with false testimonies, the people of the synagogue plotted to oppress the Lord’s holy one.

“They envied him, and they also had arrows.” For no one actually shot arrows or any weapon of injury at Joseph. But this happened particularly to Christ. Yet “his bow was strong.”

Christ placed his bow and weapons of warfare in God, by whose power all the wickedness of the faithless is shattered. And the bonds of his arms were dissolved—the bonds with which his brothers led him bound to Pilate, or with which they crucified him, hanging him upon the wood.

For they were cut apart by the hand of mighty Jacob—that is, by the God of Jacob, from whose seed the Lord himself, the good shepherd, came forth: the stone and firmness of believers in Israel.

“The God of your father will be your helper.”

Who helped the Son except God the Father, who are one in unity? Yet this is said in reference to the person of the body, because he needed divine assistance, just as it is said in the Gospel: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.”

“By blessings from heaven above, by blessings from the abyss lying below.” For he subjected all things to him: heavenly things through the blessing of heaven, and earthly things through the blessing of the abyss, so that he might rule over angels and human beings.

“By blessings of the breasts,” or of the two Testaments, one of which proclaimed him and the other displayed him; or by the blessings of Mary’s breasts. Hence that woman in the Gospel says: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you suckled.”

“By blessings of the breasts and of the womb.” Here his mother’s womb is blessed, which, being virginal, brought forth the Lord for us.

“The blessings of your father have prevailed over the blessings of the fathers of your servants.” For, beyond every merit of the holy patriarchs and prophets, the Father’s blessing prevailed in the Son, so that none of the righteous could be compared with him, until the desire of the eternal hills should come.

The eternal hills became those who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Concerning them the Lord says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see.”

They are therefore called hills because of the excellence of their holiness; they are also called eternal because they obtain eternal life.

“Let them be upon the head of the Nazirite,” concerning whom it is written: “He shall be called a Nazirite.” The same is Joseph, according to the language of the Egyptians, “savior of the world,” among his brothers—that is, among the saints whom he himself calls brothers.

Morally also, the one who has grown so far through progress in faith and through the stages mentioned above that he provokes his adversaries even to envy is rightly called “growing.” He is said to grow not once but twice.

Every perfect person grows in faith and in work, and is called beautiful because the beauty in which he was naturally made is renewed in him. Because of this beauty, the daughters saw him from the wall and desired him. Holy souls, founded upon the wall of faith, desire to see and imitate his perfection.

But demons provoked such a holy person, possessing fiery arrows of wickedness. For they prepare their arrows to shoot at those who are upright in heart.

“His bow was strong”: the bow of his virtue is set in his advances in divine things, from which he now sends forth the arrows of his prayers to pursue his enemies. And the bonds by which the enemies wished to bind him were dissolved through the power of the God of Jacob.

Then he begins to be a shepherd of souls, and, like a very hard stone, he is not overcome.

For the God of his father—that is, of the righteous who preceded him, who are spiritually our fathers—is the helper of every saint. To each such person this is promised: “And the Almighty makes him abound in strength through blessings from heaven above and blessings from the abyss lying below.”

For he is filled by contemplation of heavenly things and by understanding the Scriptures, which he rightly calls “the abyss” because of the obscurity of their mysteries. And just as eternal rewards are promised to the saints through the blessing of heaven, so through the blessing of the abyss certain consolations in the present age are proclaimed to them.

“By blessings of the breasts and of the womb.” It is clear that there are apostolic breasts, from which those still new in the faith, like little children, receive nourishment so that they may reach the more perfect food of preaching.

Hence the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food,” possessing, that is, the words of the two Testaments, or the love of God and neighbor.

This Church has a spiritual womb, which not only gives birth to children but, if they should perhaps turn away from the way of truth, gives birth to them again.

“The blessings of your father have prevailed over the blessings of your fathers.” Our Father is the one to whom we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” who, raising his hands in Bethany, blessed us through the blessing of the apostles.

The fathers are Christ’s patriarchs, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is descended according to the flesh”; each person in the Church makes use of their prophecies and blessings.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” Then the desire of the saints will come, when, according to the Apostle, they go to meet Christ; and thus they will always be with the Lord.

“Let them be upon the head of Joseph the Nazirite,” as we said above: let the blessings mentioned above remain upon the head—that is, the mind—of each person.

For, as the Apostle says: “Our outward man is corrupted, but the inward man is renewed day by day.”

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.”

As we said above, this prophesies concerning the apostle Paul. Some, however, refer it to the city of Jerusalem, which is situated in the territory of the same Benjamin. For just as Benjamin receives the final blessing, so the people of Jerusalem are the last to be saved. “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

He is called a ravenous wolf because that people shed the blood of the prophets.

“In the morning he eats prey.” That morning signifies the time when he received the Law; for then the first illumination of knowledge was given to the world. He eats in the morning because he still consumes and meditates upon the Law he received—namely, following the law of righteousness, which, seizing it before all others and devouring it as prey, he does not reach the law of faith.

“But in the evening he divides the spoils.” The evening is the final time, when they will be converted. Then he sees, and then he understands that the letter must be divided from the spirit; then he recognizes that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” And then he will begin to do what, although meditating on it all day, he did not do before.

Morally also, nothing else presents itself except that perfect person whom we mentioned above seizes the kingdom of heaven in Benjamin as a ravenous wolf. “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” He attacks, as though hungry and ravenous, the things he had read in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel.

And when, in this time—as in the morning—he has seized this prey, at the evening of death he will begin to divide the spoils. That is: through different labors he will begin to possess different rewards, which, after he has overthrown his enemies, he will deserve to hold as one who is now victorious.

But why did Jacob honor all those whom he fathered by free women and slave women equally, unless to show that the Lord Jesus Christ grants the kingdoms of heaven equally to all nations? For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, slave or free, because Christ is in all.

## EXPLANATION OF THE SECOND BOOK OF MOSES, WHICH IN HEBREW IS CALLED *VELLESEMOTH* AND IN GREEK *EXODUS*

[Col. 0285]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0285B]

These are the names of the sons of Israel. Some say that this sentence of the prophet Ezra extends as far as “the Seventy,” and constitutes the beginning of the book: “Now Joseph was,” and what follows. The title of this book is *Joseph*, which says: “From Egypt, golden vessels,” up to “Moses fasted forty days and forty nights.” This title may be called the root of the word. The word itself is the book, extending to the end. It is the custom of divine Scripture to plant the root of a word before it discloses its mysteries.

Jacob is also called the root of his sons and the son of the people. Thus Christ is the root of the apostles, and the apostles are the root of all believers. This sentence signifies the evangelical statement in which it is said: “These are the names of the twelve apostles.” Yet this is the present, recapitulated statement: the names mentioned in Genesis are now mentioned here. The ordering in Genesis and here in Exodus signifies the twelve prophets in the Old Testament and the twelve apostles in the New Testament.

The sons of Israel are mentioned here before their father because the people will be closer to them than to Israel. This book may also be called the book of life, by which the entire canon is likewise designated, since the names of these people are said to have been written in the book of life—of the patriarchs in the Pentateuch and of the apostles in the Gospel.

“Israel” means “strong man.” In those matters to which this designation is said to apply—namely, birth, the firstborn, and blessings—it signifies Christ: strong in the resurrection, in conquering the devil through the three temptations, and in the release of the underworld.

Joseph’s going down into Egypt with Jacob and his sons signifies Christ’s apostles preceding him into this world. From Reuben to Asher, the order of narration is understood. The patriarchs are numbered according to four orders. First, the order of birth, as in Genesis, where their births are narrated. Second, the order of blessing. Third, the order of freedom, as in their service concerning the tabernacle. Fourth, the order of narration, as here in Exodus, which does not preserve the three orders mentioned above.

These orders also apply to the apostles. First is the order of birth, that is, calling by Christ, as with Peter and Andrew. Second is the order of freedom, as is said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Third is the order of blessing, as with John in the rewards. Fourth is the order of narration, that is, the way in which they are numbered in various combinations.

What is said—“each with his household”—is to be understood as referring to living beings, whether men and women; mystically, the Apostle is said to signify each person together with his churches. And what is said—“they entered into distress”—according to some refers to the passage: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

After all, the seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob, and the seventy disciples were sent to preach the word of God throughout the whole world. They are said to have descended as “souls,” since it is customary to call human beings souls. These are the souls who came forth from Jacob’s loins. I do not think that just anyone can beget a human soul, unless perhaps he is like the one who says: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel.” Such are those who beget souls, as he says elsewhere: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

Others either do not wish or are unable to undertake this kind of begetting. Accordingly, Adam says: “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and not “soul of my soul.” By this he seems to confess that the things which are from the earth are his, but he does not dare to say that those things which he knows are not from the earth are his. Laban likewise says to the devil: “For he is my bone and my flesh”; he added nothing more, except what earthly kinship acknowledges.

There is another begetting of souls, which is associated either with Jacob as he descends into Egypt or is attributed to the other saints in the mystical enumeration of their descendants.

“After Joseph had died, the sons of Israel increased and grew exceedingly strong.” After the true Joseph had tasted death for all, the people of the faithful multiplied. For if the grain of wheat had not fallen and died, the Church would certainly not have produced abundant fruit.

Morally, the same applies to you: if Joseph dies in you, if you receive the mortification of Christ in your body and put your member to death with respect to sin, then the sons of Israel—that is, good and spiritual understandings—multiply in you. For each day, as vices die in you, the number of virtues increases. And you multiply in the land—in your flesh, that is—through which the virtues are administered.

It follows: “Another king arose.” First, we must see who this king is who knew Joseph, and who the one who did not know him is. As long, therefore, as our king—that is, the spirit of our mind—retains the memory of Joseph, that is, of Christ—for this king in Egypt remembers him, namely, our spirit in our flesh, which is not improperly called Egypt—the sons of Israel, that is, rational understandings or virtues, are not afflicted, nor are they consumed by clay and bricks, that is, by earthly concerns; nor are the males killed, that is, works already perfected.

But if our understandings do not know Christ, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its own people—namely, bodily pleasures—and, having summoned the leaders of the vices, takes counsel against Israel concerning how he may be oppressed by the evils already mentioned.

Therefore, you who hear these things: if, after the gift of baptism, you perform the works of this world, know that another king has arisen in you, one who does not know Joseph.

The king of Egypt who does not know Joseph may also be the devil, who said in his heart: “There is no God.” He speaks, as it were, to his own people, that is, to the apostate angels: “Behold, the Israelite men have increased and grown stronger than we”—namely, those who are able to see the Lord with the mind.

The devil then perceived that the people of Israel were strong, for Israel often went forth and was often overcome. But what he fears is that war might one day arise among them, that they might join their adversaries, and that, after defeating them, they might descend from their land.

He showed that he had perceived what the patriarchs and prophets had foretold concerning the coming of Christ, and from this he knew that war threatened him. He perceived that Christ was coming, and that with confidence he would triumph over him. He teaches Israel to build cities—Pithom, which is interpreted as “failing mouth” or “mouth of the abyss”; and Rameses, which is interpreted as “the moth’s agitation”; and Heliopolis, that is, “city of the sun.”

See what kinds of cities Pharaoh ordered to be built for him: “failing mouth.” The mouth indeed fails when it speaks a lie, when it falls short of truth or proofs; or it is “the mouth of the abyss,” because the abyss is the place of perdition.

Another city is “the moth’s agitation.” Those who follow that path gather their treasures there “where moth destroys and thieves break in.”

Even if we give thanks with a completely clear conscience, he also says concerning us: “The sons of Israel have grown exceedingly strong against us.” What he says—“lest they perhaps join our adversaries”—signifies that, if we join the preachers of truth, we will prevail over him and become strangers in his land: putting off the old man with his deeds, or abandoning the image of this earthly man and putting on the image of the heavenly one.

Others say that by the adversaries to whom Pharaoh feared Israel might join, the commandments pertaining to Christ are understood. “And they will go out from the land”: that is, they will be without Egyptian servitude. This too the devil fears in the present age: that they may go out from the land of their body if they do not serve sins and vices.

By the taskmasters whom Pharaoh placed over the sons of Israel, the heretics appointed by the devil according to his own judgment are signified, so that they might afflict the saints with the burdens of sins. Or, morally, as we briefly explained above, they signify evil understandings seeking to corrupt good ones.

What is said—“The more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied”—signifies that, the more the saints suffer temptations from the devil, the more abundantly they receive rewards from Christ. When “they multiplied” refers to the saints, it pertains to faith; when “they grew” refers to the work of clay and bricks, it pertains to the vices of body and soul.

“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives,” and what follows. According to the historical narrative, this seems impossible. It is said that “the midwives did not do what Pharaoh commanded.” Yet they are not found to have failed to preserve alive the females whom Pharaoh commanded to be kept alive. And if they did not do this, they ought, according to the command, either to have preserved the males alive, contrary to the king’s command, or to have killed the females.

This is said for those who are friends of the letter and do not think that the Law is spiritual. Spiritually, however, according to the meaning accessible to one who can understand God and seek the things above, Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, hates the male and desires to destroy him. Whatever belongs to the flesh he wishes not only to preserve alive but to increase, so that all who are upon the earth may think according to the flesh and no one may raise his eyes toward the heavenly homeland.

This Pharaoh attempts to corrupt the midwives. One of them was called Sephora, which is interpreted as “sparrow”; the other was called Phua, which among us may be rendered “reddish” or “blushing.” Through them he wishes to kill the males and preserve only the females.

Some have said that these midwives represent the form of rational instruction. Midwives occupy an intermediate position and attend both males and females. Such rational instruction reaches almost everyone, enters into every understanding, and nurtures all. If someone has a manly spirit within it and wishes to seek heavenly things, through this instruction he will come more readily to the understanding of divine matters. One midwife is like a sparrow, teaching higher things; the other, whose name means “reddish” or “modest,” is moral instruction, which orders conduct and teaches modesty.

But since Scripture says, “The midwives feared God and did not carry out the king’s command,” these two midwives may more appropriately signify the two Testaments. Sephora, whose name means “sparrow,” signifies the spiritual Law. Phua, who is called “reddish” or “modest,” signifies the Gospel, which shines red with the blood of Christ and the radiance of his passion.

The souls born in the Church are therefore, as it were, treated by these midwives, because through the reading of the Scriptures every form of instruction is supplied in that medicine. Nevertheless, afterward Pharaoh attempts to kill the males of the Church, when he suggests heretical interpretations of the divine Scriptures to earnest students. But the foundation of God stands immovable.

For “the midwives feared God”: that is, they taught the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom.

It follows: “The people increased”—the people of the Church, certainly, because the midwives feared God—“and he built houses for them.” Those who teach the fear of the Lord from Scripture build houses for the Church. According to the letter, this sentence does not seem to fit: that houses were built because God was feared. Perhaps we should understand, “He built houses for them” to mean, “He built for them a household and a lineage.”

Because these women acted well toward the people of God, God multiplied their offspring. These midwives did not preserve alive the females whom Pharaoh desired to preserve: they neither teach vices in the churches nor nourish sins.

Morally, you too, if you fear God, will not carry out the command of the king of Egypt. You will not live in luxury; you will not desire present things. If you fear God, offer service to your soul.
