Preserve alive the male—your inner man—which is in you. Then God will build a house for you, that is, an abundance of virtues.

But when Pharaoh saw that through the midwives he could not kill the males of Israel, he commanded all the people, saying: “Cast every male into the river; preserve every female alive.”

See what the ruler of this world commands through his decrees, so that they may seize our infants and cast them into the river. See at once what threatens you as soon as you have been born—or rather, reborn. This is what you read in the Gospel: when Jesus had come up from baptism, he was led by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil.

This, therefore, is what Pharaoh commanded his people: to drown the infants of the Hebrews in the waters. Of these waters the prophet says: “The waters have entered even to my soul.” And now the Egyptians lie in wait, in case a male should be born among the Hebrews, so that he may immediately be killed and no one may observe and conceal every male offspring.

## Chapter II

But a man of the tribe of Levi fathered a male child. When he saw that the infant was beautiful, he hid him for three months.

Therefore, if I give alms, because it is the work of God, I beget a male child. But I must do it in such a way that it becomes known to human beings: my almsgiving has been snatched away by the Egyptians.

It follows: “A man went out from the house of Levi and took a wife from his own lineage. She conceived and bore a son. Seeing that he was beautiful, she hid him for three months,” and what follows, up to the words: “She called his name Moses, saying, ‘Because I drew him from the water.’”

The daughter of Pharaoh is the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Although she has an impious father, nevertheless it is said to her: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear.” She went out from her father’s house and came to the waters to be washed from the sins that she had contracted in her father’s house.

This Church therefore found Moses abandoned in the marsh and gave him to be nourished by her own people. He is nourished among his own and spends his infancy there. But when he had grown stronger, Pharaoh’s daughter took him and adopted him as a son.

Moses signifies the Law. When the Church came to the waters of baptism, she also received the Law. Yet the Law was inside a little basket of reeds, woven from many shoots—or made from papyrus—and sealed with pitch; the infant lay within it.

The Law therefore lay hidden within such coverings, smeared with pitch and bitumen. That is, enclosed by cheap and earthly things, it was soiled by the traditions of the Jews. The Church took him from the marshes so that he might stand within the halls of wisdom and royal roofs.

He spent his infancy among his own. Among those who do not know how to understand it spiritually, the Law is small and has the food of infants. But when it came to the Church, it became stronger.

What, however, does it mean that the woman who had nursed the Law—namely, the one among whom the Law was born and raised—received a reward for its nourishment from Pharaoh’s daughter? The synagogue received this reward from the Church: that it should no longer worship an idol. When the synagogue sees those who are from the Gentiles converted to the Lord in such a way that they no longer worship idols, it is itself ashamed to worship idols. Thus the synagogue received this benefit from the Church: it appeared to have nourished the Law when it was still small among the Jews.

Moses may also signify Christ, whom Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, the Church—found at the river, the river of the washing. The infant wept because he was wounded for our sins, or because he is said to have wept, as when he raised Lazarus, in order to raise those who are dead in sin.

The Church therefore gathers Christ from the synagogue, his carnal mother, as from one who had cast him away like an infant, when he appeared small because he was seen in human form. She found Moses enclosed in a little vessel made from many shoots. The Church finds Christ hidden in the hearts of the saints, who, joined by the glue of unity, have become one body.

Some say that the man who went out from the house of Levi signifies the Law, because the Law was given to the Levites, that is, to Moses and Aaron. The three months during which the synagogue concealed Christ signify three laws: the law of the letter, the law of nature, and the law of prophecy. At the end of these, Christ is revealed by the synagogue in the assumption of flesh. This is signified appropriately by the little basket smeared with pitch and bitumen—that is, by the evil suspicion held by the synagogue concerning Christ’s body and divinity.

What is said—“and he placed him in the reeds”—signifies that the synagogue placed faith in Christ among the Jews. As the reeds enclosed him there, so the Jews surrounded Christ bodily, harboring envy against him. Through his sister, therefore, the Jews are signified: they do not nourish him but guard him.

One of the maidservants who was sent signifies the prophecy of the prophets, who prophesied that Christ would descend for the assumption of flesh, disclosing the obscurity of the mysteries. “She saw,” that is, she believed.

Alternatively, the man from the house of Levi signifies Christ going forth from the Law; and his wife signifies the Church giving birth to a son, that is, the Christian people. She hid him for three months, that is, in the inner man, in faith in the Trinity.

What is said—“She took a little basket from the reeds”—signifies belief in the flesh expressed through good works. The river’s current signifies the teaching of the Holy Spirit. The sister standing at a distance signifies either the second synagogue or the Church of the apostles, which is called the second Church of the synagogue, while its mother is the primitive Church.

Pharaoh’s daughter descended in humility. The boy’s sister said to her: “Shall I go and call,” and what follows. This signifies the Church of the Jews in relation to the Church of the Gentiles. What is said—“He adopted him as a son”—makes it clearly understood that it is not the Church of the Gentiles but the synagogue that gives birth to Christ.

Moses is interpreted as “taken,” “taking,” or “water-born.” These interpretations apply to the Church of the Gentiles, which receives from Christ. She is “water-born” in baptism; she is snatched away in faith; she takes Christ’s cruelty upon herself and offers sacrifice in the sanctification of Christ’s divinity and incarnation.

Morally, we too had Pharaoh as a father, if the king of Egypt begot us through evil works. When we come to the washing, let us take up Moses—that is, the Law of God—and place him within the royal chambers of our heart. Let us abandon what is crooked and make Moses strong and great. For everything that is spiritual is great.

Meanwhile Moses freed a foreign brother from an Egyptian and did not allow the deed to go unavenged: he killed the Egyptian. The devil is exceedingly injurious to us in this pilgrimage; he was killed by Christ for our sake.

What Moses seized, slain, in the sand signifies that the devil has been bound in the hearts of the reprobate, who possess no stable foundation but build their house upon sand.

When Moses could not reconcile the two Hebrews who were quarreling, he departed for the land of Midian. Since the Law of God could not unite the quarreling scribes and Pharisees with the rest of the people, it remained among the Gentiles.

Midian is interpreted as “contradiction.” Through this, the Law is signified: the divine Law first encountered contradiction among the Gentiles. The same Law defended the seven daughters of the priest of Midian—that is, it defended them against the philosophers and wise men of this world. The Church of the Gentiles, although born from a Gentile father, was born through the Law of God.

Accordingly, he took one of the seven. For although the Church is sevenfold, she was born through unity. “One is my dove,” he says.

After the Gentiles had been joined to the Law, it is said that the king of Egypt died.

Others say that in this matter Moses bears the figure of Christ; the two who were quarreling signify the two peoples; and the one perpetrating the wrong signifies the Jewish people, to whom it is said: “Why do you strike your neighbor?”—that is, the Gentile people. “Who appointed you ruler or judge?” This prefigures the fact that in the Gospel the Jews denied that Christ was the king of the Jews. “Do you intend to kill me?” This too, they affirm, can be said by the Jewish people to Christ.

In what follows, it is not difficult to refer the passage to Christ: through Moses’ fear, the fear of Christ according to the flesh is proclaimed, as in the words: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Through this flight, Christ’s flight through Mary and Joseph into Egypt from Herod’s power is signified. As Moses fled from Pharaoh, so the following events also refer to Christ.

But they wish the seven daughters to signify the seven churches of Asia, and the sheep the peoples under the yoke of the churches; these churches Christ defends. The daughters’ return, however, signifies the portion of unbelievers returning to the devil. The devil is amazed when they come with a compunction of heart, as it is said here: “Why have you come so quickly?” What is said—“An Egyptian man”—applies to Christ according to the flesh.

“Why did you dismiss the man?” and what follows, up to “bread.” This applies to the devil, who wishes through his own invitations to entice Christ’s body—that is, his saints—to his will. For thirst occurs both before and after bread, and so do desires.

These three things, morally understood, apply to every good teacher who sits beside spiritual instruction. In this sense, Midian signifies Christ, and his daughters signify souls instructed through the sevenfold Spirit, drawing up the waters of repentance.

Therefore it is said: “They sought what they could scarcely obtain.” This signifies carnal bodies on account of the power of the body; the flocks signify perfected understandings; the shepherds, evil men who drive away the girls—that is, souls.

Moses signifies the teacher; the sheep, thoughts; and the return to Jethro, the return of souls to Christ when they are tempted. Christ says to them: “Why have you come?”—that is, “Why are you inexperienced?”

The teacher is called an Egyptian because he teaches worldly things; or the Law is so called because of marriage.

Moses therefore swore an oath. In this too he signifies Christ: “swearing,” that is, prophesying immutably, the assumption of flesh. “That he might dwell with him”—that is, with the devil—in this world, overcoming him upon the cross.

The daughter who was joined to Moses has been discussed above. The son whom she bore to him, namely Gershom, whose name is interpreted as “stranger,” signifies the people of the Gentiles, who were strangers to the Law.

The death of the king of Egypt has also been discussed above: his power was broken in the world through Christ’s passion.

The sons of Israel groaned—that is, because of the greatness of their servitude. Likewise, the saints groan because of the temptations of demons, evil people, and vices, on account of the works—that is, the sins—of evil teachers.

Their cry ascended to the Lord, in the sense that he heard it. Through this cry, the prayer of the saints is signified as ascending to the Lord.

What is said about the people of Egypt after the death of their king signifies that vices or sins come into the world after the devil. He heard their groaning—that is, the groaning of the people or of the saints in their labors.

Alternatively, as was said above, the king of Egypt signifies imperfect understandings. When he dies, the sons of Israel—that is, the perfect—groan while subject to vices in their bodies.

“And he remembered the covenant” made with Jacob, and what follows.

Some customarily ask why the Lord is not here said to have remembered the covenant of Adam and his son Abel; and why not that of Enoch, who first consecrated the clouds in his ascent; or of Noah, through whom the world was rebuilt after the Flood.

But the covenant is recalled through Abraham: that is, the law of circumcision that was given to him. He did not transgress it but fulfilled it; therefore the covenant is recalled through him.

Adam transgressed the commandment that he had received from God. Enoch’s sin likewise hindered him. Abraham was the first to fulfill the Law that he had received.

Alternatively, the law is not considered to have been given specifically to Enoch and Noah; rather, the covenant is recalled only through Abraham, to whom the second law was given, and who did not transgress it after receiving it. Therefore the covenant is recalled through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for the people of Israel—either because after the Flood there were no better men, or because they are the foundation of the Church, or because in both works and figures they are worthy in some way to bear their respective types: Abraham, the type of the Father; Isaac, of Christ; and Jacob, of the Christian people. They were also the first to receive the fullness of knowledge, which was called Midian.

After Adam, Abraham was the first to possess physics, by which nature led him to worship God and through creatures he came to know him. Isaac possessed ethics, because he did not take a wife while his mother was alive, lest love of a wife surpass love of his mother. Nor did he take a wife until his father commanded him.

Jacob possessed logic, which is understood in the choosing of blessings and in the choosing of foods.

## Chapter III

“Moses, a young man, was tending sheep”: Christ feeds the saints daily through the examples of the Gospels.

Jethro, the priest of Midian, signifies the devil. Others say that Midian was an idol and Jethro its priest.

The flock that Moses led signifies the saints; the inner regions of the desert, the mysteries; and the mountain of God, Horeb, the holy Church.

Then the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush. There was a flame in the bush, and the bush was not consumed: the Law of God was among the Jews, yet the sins of the Jews were not consumed. The flame is the Law of God; the bush is the sins of the Jews, which the Law could not burn up. For the Apostle says: “The Law brought nothing to perfection.”

Others wish to understand in the burning yet unconsumed bush the Church, set ablaze by persecutions and yet not destroyed, because the Lord speaks within her. Others wish the holy Mary to be signified by the bush, in whom divinity burned without suffering any harm.

That the Lord is read as having appeared to Moses in that same bush signifies that he appeared to believers nowhere other than in the Church.

Moses’ removal of his sandals signified that no one can worthily see God unless he lays aside all earthly things and mortal vices. Yet there is another figure in Moses’ being commanded to remove his sandals: he was not to approach the Church, which was represented by the bush, as a bridegroom; this was reserved for Christ.

The Hebrews say that the Lord appeared to Moses in a bush and not in another kind of wood so that the Jews might not perhaps carve an idol from that same wood. God always removed from them the occasion for idolatry.

Others say historically that the Lord appeared through fire to show that illumination had been granted to the Lord’s people. The vengeance upon Egypt, which is also displayed from the middle of the bush, showed that he would pass through the mind of servitude just as the flame passed through the narrow spaces of the bush.

The burning bush that was not consumed signifies that the labor of servitude in Egypt would not consume the sons of Israel. What is said—“Why is the bush not burned?”—shows the ignorance of human beings regarding spiritual meanings.

The Lord is then said to call Moses when he went to see. From this we understand that the Lord gives us help to see what we had not previously seen when we come out from the freedom of our will, so that we may no longer do what is carnal according to our desires.

“Remove your sandals from your feet,” and what follows. It is as if he were saying: “There are no serpents in this place.”

Alternatively, the sandals signify unbelief, which constricts your understandings, or Pharaoh’s fear arising from your understandings.

“The place on which you stand is holy ground.” This seems contrary to what was said: “Cursed is the earth,” and what follows. Unless the place was sanctified by God’s presence.

And he said: “I am the God of your father,” and what follows. This statement shows that God held on to the father’s love because of his son’s love.

Moses hid his face, demonstrating his weakness. Just as Moses could not endure the sight of God’s face, so Pharaoh could not endure the face of Moses.

What is said—that the Lord saw the affliction, and what follows—strengthens Moses so that he would not fear Pharaoh when liberating his people.

“Descend,” that is, for Pharaoh’s punishment.

“To a good land,” and what follows. The Lord mentions that it is a land because he knew that the impulse of desire existed in Moses.

All the things we have mentioned also apply to Christ, who appears in the midst of the Church in a flame of fire—that is, with the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

Moses signifies the Christian people, whom the Lord calls. Whenever something earthly is attributed to this Moses, it can be referred to the tenderness of the Christian people, and likewise to his obedience and the people’s obedience to God.

The Lord’s descent, of which he says, “I have descended,” may be referred to the descent by which he came down for the redemption of this world through the assumption of flesh and through his passion.

The cry that he heard may appropriately be understood as that of the patriarchs and prophets, inviting the Lord to assume flesh and redeem the human race.

To them a good land—that is, the Church—is promised, with hundredfold and beautiful rewards; or good and beautiful in the faith of divinity and incarnation; or in rewards for bodies and souls. Alternatively, the good land signifies the kingdom of heaven.

“Milk and honey” signify the Old and New Testaments in the Church. Alternatively, milk and honey signify nourishment for bodies and souls.

Egypt, together with its people by whom the sons of Israel were oppressed, signifies the Gentile world together with demons, evil people, and vices, from which we are liberated through the Lord.

“Remove your sandal,” which is a testimony, signifies the evangelical statement in which the apostles, sent to preach the word, are told to cast off human fear and fear God.

The bush likewise signifies the body of each individual saint together with the fire of compunction, or the letter understood spiritually.

That the Lord sent Moses to Pharaoh to punish him and finally to bring about his death signifies that the Lord would send the Law for the mortification of the devil’s strength and the liberation of the human race. And just as it was not Moses but the Lord who liberated the people from Egyptian servitude, so it was not the Law but Christ, through his passion and resurrection, who liberated the world.

“Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?”—that is, as though he had said: “I can do nothing without God’s help.”

“And I will be with you”—that is, in the assumption of flesh.

“And you will have a sign,” and what follows. This signifies that we have God’s help together with the Law, and that the Church has been liberated from sins and vices. Just as Moses went to the sons of Israel, so the Law goes to human beings.

“The God of our fathers”: this makes it understood that God the Father sent the Law to human beings.

“If they say to me, ‘What is his name?’” This also shows that the Lord disclosed the name that is “the Lord.”

The Lord said to Moses: “I am,” that is, “the one who was with your fathers”; “who am,” that is, “with you”; or, “I am who I am,” that is, “without past or future.”

Alternatively, “I am” means “the Son”; “who am” means “the Holy Spirit”; and “who is” means “the Father.” The person of the Son is mentioned first here because afterward the salvation of the world is administered through the person of the Son.

Alternatively, “I am who I am,” as it is said to him, is spoken from the perspective of the faithful. Alternatively, “I am” refers to the Old Testament; “who am” refers to the New; and “who is” sent me, that is, into this world.

“Go and gather the elders,” and what follows. The gathering of the elders signifies that like things must be gathered with like things. An elder ought to announce the word to elders.

Spiritually, the Law is also said by the Lord to gather the saints into the unity of peace.

Dominion is signified through “Lord,” and freedom through “God.”

“He will surely visit us.” This indicates the weakness of the people. Alternatively, “visiting” is fulfilled in the Old Testament, while “he has visited” is fulfilled in the New. Or, “visiting” refers to the ten plagues, and “I will visit” to the Red Sea. Or, “visiting” refers to the present Church, and “he will visit” to the day of judgment or vengeance. Or certainly, “visiting” refers to the hundredfold increase, and “he visited” to the rewards.

“They will hear your voice,” and what follows. The Lord is understood to speak this to the Law: the men of Israel—that is, the righteous—hear the words of the Law.

“You will enter,” and what follows, up to “Egypt.” This signifies the Law entering with the righteous to overthrow the devil, who was king of the world before Christ’s coming.

Alternatively, through Moses the principal understandings are signified, and through the elders the good virtues, going to the king of Egypt—that is, against the devil.

“But I know that he will not let you go.” Through this prophecy the Lord took precautions, lest they should incur envy if he had not foretold what would later occur.

## Chapter IV
After this, when Moses asks for a sign, he is told: “Throw down the staff that you carry in your hand.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent, and he fled in fear. Then he grasped its tail, and it became a staff again.

The serpent signifies death. For through the serpent death was brought upon humanity. The staff, however, is Christ. The staff changed into a serpent: [Col. 0296A] Christ changed into death. But Moses’ flight signifies what is read in the Gospel: that the apostles, abandoning Christ, fled, and withdrew from the hope in which they had previously stood. The tail, once grasped, became a staff, because after he had been killed—having completed everything for which he had been sent—he was changed back through his resurrection into what he had been.

Historically, the staff that had been in Moses’ hand and was changed into a snake signifies that Moses should trust in God’s power, and that the people should trust Moses, and that Moses should not fear Pharaoh. Alternatively, the staff changed into a snake signifies the plague sent by God that would harm the Egyptians but not harm Israel; Moses’ flight likewise signifies the people’s flight from Pharaoh’s presence, or Moses’ unbelief; and the snake’s transformation back into a staff signifies the people’s release from Egyptian servitude.

[Col. 0296B] Another sign is then given to Moses. He put his hand into his bosom, and it was found to be white—that is, unclean. Whiteness on the skin is leprosy, not brightness. For God’s inheritance—that is, his people—was sent out from him and became unclean. But what follows, “He brought it back, and it returned to its former color,” signifies that the Jewish people, now alienated from God’s bosom, will return at the end of the world to its former color when it recognizes the Savior, when the last will be like the patriarchs.

These two signs are set forth in different ways: the first on the ground, the second in the bosom. This signifies the plague upon the perceptible and imperceptible in Egypt. Leprosy, moreover, is said to signify the Jews’ unbelief in the Son, which was not present toward the Father. [Col. 0296C] Yet only the hand is said to be white, while—in their assessment of what is good, as they seek a cause—it is then like the rest of the flesh: how will they believe both? The healthy hand, before it was put into the bosom, signifies belief in the Father. The bosom signifies the obscurity of faith. The three signs together—that is, the two on the mountain and the third directed toward Egypt—signify the three laws.

Next, when Moses pours the water onto the ground and it is changed into blood, the people are changed into faith in the blood of Christ. Or they pour out their blood through martyrdom and are changed by Moses, because through the fullness of the Law they find faith in Christ. As for those who are the waters of the people, the Apocalypse bears witness: “The waters are the peoples.” [Col. 0296C]

## CHAPTER V

After this Moses and Aaron entered before Pharaoh. “A journey of three days.” The way is Christ, who says: “I am the way.” This way must be traveled over three days. For whoever confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead on the third day will be saved. This is the journey of three days by which one comes to the place where the sacrifice of praise is to be offered and rendered to the Lord. [Col. 0296D]

In a moral sense also, we depart from Egypt on a three-day journey if we preserve ourselves from every defilement of flesh, soul, and spirit. And, according to the Apostle, may spirit, soul, and body be kept whole for the day of the Lord. We depart from Egypt on a three-day journey if, removing natural reason and moral wisdom from worldly matters, we turn them toward divine ordinances. We depart from Egypt on a three-day journey if, purifying within ourselves what has been said, done, or thought—for through these things people ordinarily sin—we become pure in heart.

But the king of the Egyptians wishes to let God’s people depart on a three-day journey; for he wishes to signify sinning in deed or word, and, if not in word, then failing in thought. Moses, however—that is, the Law—wishes to lead you out of Egypt and away from the work of straw, provided that you listen to him and wish to go into the desert, that is, to a place empty of the disturbances of this world. When you have come to this place of rest, there you will be able to sacrifice to the Lord. [Col. 0297A]

Alternatively, by the way of three days the faith of the Trinity is shown. By the desert we understand freedom from sins and vices, and by the mountain the holy Church of God.

When Moses says that he is not eloquent, and that from yesterday and the day before—since the Lord spoke to him—he has been slow and impeded in speech, this signifies that all human beings, in comparison with the divine Word, must be considered not only ineloquent but mute. For until Moses went into Egypt, he did not acknowledge himself to be slow of tongue. Egypt possessed a resonant voice and incomparable eloquence; when he began to hear the voice of God, he then perceived that he was slow of tongue. But because he was thereby perfected so as to recognize himself, he rightly heard from the Lord: “I will be in your mouth.” [Col. 0297B]

Moses’ mouth is not opened alone, but Aaron’s also. For it is said: “I will be in your mouth and in his mouth.” Aaron meets Moses in the desert. You too meet the Law of God, and when you have entered into its meaning in a desert place—that is, when you have withdrawn from varied occupations—your mouth will be opened.

As for Moses’ statement that he was not eloquent “from yesterday and the day before,” some think that he said this out of humility; or, according to the truth, that he was not eloquent in the Hebrew language. They understand “from yesterday and the day before” as though he had said, “From my youth,” referring to the past period in which he began to speak with the Lord.

“He who made the mouth of man,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “No one other than I.” And just as I made the mouth of man, so I can also make him eloquent.

Spiritually, the mouth of man signifies the Law of the people. “Who made the mute and the deaf?” Spiritually, the mute signifies the people of the Gentiles, and the deaf the Jewish people, who, though they possessed the Law, did not listen. The one who hears and sees signifies the Christian people. The blind signifies the unbeliever, because he did not see the way of truth. [Col. 0297C]

“And I will be in your mouth.” By this the Lord is signified as dwelling in the Law. This testimony also prefigured what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not consider what you are to say,” and so forth.

Moses and Aaron together signify the Law and the priesthood. The mouth of Moses and Aaron is mentioned; thus the priesthood was the mouth of the Law. Moses, interceding between God and Aaron, signifies the Law interceding between God and the priesthood; the priesthood, in turn, between God and the people.

“And take the staff,” that is, after he had seen the Lord at Horeb. Jethro said to him: “Go in peace.” In this passage Jethro signifies God the Father, commanding Christ to go to assume flesh. [Col. 0297D]

Then the Lord said to Moses—that is, in another vision or in the same one. Moses’ wife, whom he brought from Egypt, signifies the Church, which the Lord brought out of the Egypt of this world. His two sons likewise signify the two peoples. The donkey upon which he placed [them] signifies the apostolic people. His return to Egypt signifies the return of the Law or of Christ into this world. The staff that he carries signifies the teaching of the Holy Spirit or the cross of Christ; and what he says before Pharaoh indicates what pertains to him. [Col. 0298A]

“And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” that is, through the exercise of his own free choice—or this is said as punishment, as though [an OCR reading here is uncertain: “not finding the head beforehand”] he did not prophesy to him. It is as though the Lord were saying: “Nevertheless, I know that Pharaoh will not let you go.”

Alternatively, the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart through the deserved judgment arising from Adam’s sin; or, when the punishment of sins is imposed, the heart is hardened.

“My firstborn son is Israel,” that is, in the Law’s designation, the people Israel; or he said in the New Testament: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” [Col. 0298B]

Immediately Zipporah took a very sharp stone, that is, the Church of the Gentiles took the teaching of the Holy Spirit or of Christ. And she circumcised the foreskin of her son, that is, of the Gentile people; and the blood touched his feet. These things signify the circumcision of the person within and without.

But when the prince of Egypt says, “I do not know God,” and so forth—“I will not let them go”—see in the Gospels how those who have been tormented utter this cry. For the demons cried out, it says, and said to the Lord: “Why have you come to torment us before the time? We know that you are the Son of God.” When they felt the torments, they recognized the Lord. Before the scourges he says, “I do not know God.” Pharaoh likewise does not know the Lord before the blows. After the blows he asks that supplication be made on his behalf. [Col. 0298C]

It follows: “Why do Moses and Aaron trouble the people? Go to your works.” As long as the people are with him, he does not consider them perverse. But if he says, “I wish to go on a three-day journey,” he says that the people have been perverted.

Even today Moses and Aaron—that is, prophetic and priestly speech—trouble the soul toward the service of God. Then the ruler of this world compels it still more strongly toward its former works.

Pharaoh then said, “Many are the people.” This signifies the devil’s counsel against his own satellites: the devil’s desires and works. The devil envied the multitude of the Christian people.

The people scattered over the whole land of Egypt signify the scattering of the human race into slavery under the devil’s power, to gather straw—that is, vices. They were scourged—that is, by the devil. [Col. 0298D]

“By a strong hand,” and so forth: “I will show my power through the signs that I shall perform.”

## CHAPTER VI

“I am the Lord who appeared,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: “Just as your fathers came to know my power when I took vengeance on their enemies, so you too will know it in the vengeance taken on your enemies.”

“And I did not make my name Adonai known to them,” which is interpreted as “Almighty” or “Lord of hosts.” This is to be understood as though he had said: “I did not make it known”—indeed, I did make it known to them, and so I shall make it known to you. Or, when they pleased me, I nevertheless did not make this name known to them as I shall make it known to you.

Alternatively, this may be understood mystically as though he had said: “In the Old Testament I did not make it known as in the New,” or “In the New I did not make it known as on the day of judgment.” [Col. 0299A]

“And I remembered my covenant”: this is understood to mean that the Lord remembered, against the devil, the oppression of the saints. And he remembered Israel because of the promise that he had made, namely: “And I will give you this land,” and so forth.

The Egyptian prison signifies the temptations of this world; its slavery signifies the slavery of demons. From these the saints are delivered by an exalted arm—that is, by God’s power, or in the Son—and by great judgments, that is, historically through the plagues of the Egyptians, or spiritually through the plagues of demons on the day of judgment. What follows here applies to the Church delivered from the devil’s power.

“Over which I raised my hand,” that is, in the customary manner of swearing. “I am the Lord,” that is, the one who can do what I say.

“Because of the anguish of spirit,” that is, because he confined faith through envy; “and the harshest labor,” that is, temptation, follows. [Col. 0299B]

“We sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord.” For the Egyptians disdain eating sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate, we offer. The simplicity of conscience, which the wise men of this world consider folly, the righteous sacrifice to the Lord as an offering.

From the time Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the Lord’s people are afflicted more severely. For once the word of God has entered the human mind, the crafty enemy rises up more fiercely.

Some, enclosed under many blows, confess that they are Pharaoh’s people, saying: “Why do you afflict your people?” Overcome by blows, some indeed fall away from the faith and say to Moses and Aaron: “Ever since you entered before Pharaoh, you have made our odor detestable in his presence.” For prophetic speech is a sweet odor to believers, but to the doubtful and unbelieving it becomes a detestable odor. [Col. 0299C]

“Behold, the children of Israel do not listen to me,” and so forth. Just as Moses here objects that Pharaoh would not listen to him because the children of Israel had not listened, so the Law objects that the devil will not listen to it if the saints do not listen to the command addressed to the children of Israel—that is, to the example of all the plagues.

The years of Levi’s life were 138. Levi’s years are specifically enumerated here so that the truth of Moses’ and Aaron’s birth and generation may be understood. Reuben and Simeon are placed before Levi because of the order of birth, but the tribe of Levi is nevertheless mystical.

The number of Levi’s years signifies a mystery. The people rise from great to small, descending into humility. One hundred specifically signifies perfection; thirty, faith in the Trinity; eight, the New Testament. [Col. 0299D]

And just as the greatest leaders are mentioned in this genealogy, so in the Church those who hold the greatest authority are mentioned, and those second to them, as in the case of Moses and Aaron.

The years of Gath are enumerated. His years and Levi’s have the same meaning, through the last three who are signified in the Law. Reuben and Simeon, whose years are not enumerated, represent the figure of penitents. Levi and his sons, whose years are enumerated, represent the figure of the perfect. Amram and Jochebed represent Christ and the Church, from whom the Law and the priesthood are born. Their years likewise have the same meaning.

For this reason Levi’s genealogy also mentions Esau—that is, on account of Korah, or on account of the evils that arise for them afterward. So also in the Church the good and the wicked are mentioned as an example. [Col. 0300A]

Aaron took a wife. This is mentioned on account of Phinehas. These events also apply figuratively to teachers, who give birth to teachers, just as saints give birth to saints. The birth of Korah, however, represents heretics giving birth to others.

“This is Aaron and Moses.” Some say that this sentence belongs to the prophet Ezra, or to the Holy Spirit speaking through Moses, or to the translator; or that someone was speaking from Moses’ perspective. “He said it.”

Aaron is mentioned first here because he is the older. This also fits the figure: Christ, whom Aaron represents here, is older than the Law.

“To whom the Lord God commanded,” and so forth. Some investigate in what ways this is said. There are three: truly, falsely, and by designation. Truly, as “God Almighty”; falsely, as “the gods who did not make heaven and earth”; by designation, as “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh.” This testimony figures the evangelical saying: “Whatever you loose on earth,” and so forth. [Col. 0300B]

Whenever the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt through Moses is mentioned in this book, it signifies the exodus of human beings from the world to the kingdom of heaven through the Law and the priesthood.

Where Moses is mentioned before Aaron, it signifies that the Law displayed its own form before the priesthood. Moses is said to be uncircumcised in lips; this signifies that the Law did not speak salvation from itself, but from Christ.

## CHAPTER VII

“Behold, I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh,” and so forth. By this the power of the Law is demonstrated. “Aaron, your prophet,” that is, your preacher.

“And I will multiply signs and wonders.” By “signs” the plagues are understood; by “wonders,” what he did in the sea. “My hand over Egypt,” that is, it signifies power over this world. “I will bring out my people and my army,” that is, the saints and the Christian people. [Col. 0300C]

There is also a mystical meaning in the years of Moses and Aaron: fifty signifies men of repentance; thirty-three, what we explained above concerning the ages.

Moses’ staff devoured the staffs of the Egyptians. This signifies that the Word made flesh emptied the dreadful poisons of the ancient serpents through the remission of sins.

The staff is the Word made straight, bearing royal power and the distinguished insignia of rule. The staff became a serpent: he who was the Son of God became the son of man through the incarnation. Like that serpent suspended in the desert, he poured the medicine of wounds into humanity. [Col. 0300D]

Moses’ staff, changed into a dragon, swallowed the magicians’ staffs. And Christ, after the dignity of his glory, becoming obedient unto death, through that very death destroyed the sting of death.

“The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” because these things harden the devil on account of sin, so that he is never softened by the compunction of repentance. As it is written concerning him in Job: “His heart will be hardened like a stone.”

When the plagues are mentioned, the question is asked how many kinds of plague there are. There are four: the first is an incurable plague, by which the enemy is struck without reversal; the second occurs in the manifestation of powers, as with the blind man in the Gospel; the third is on account of a future sin, as when Paul received a thorn so that exaltation might not come to him; the fourth is on account of a past sin, as with David concerning the numbering of the people. [Col. 0301A]

The kind of incurable plague is said to have happened to the Egyptians. But according to some, four kinds of plagues are also found here: the kind of incurable plague in the Red Sea, and [the others] on account of the ascent of virtues.

“I have appointed you so that I may show my power in you.” This concerns a future sin: Israel would not have been abandoned because of its pride if it had not received a plague. It concerns a past sin because they retained what had been given to illuminate them in former times.

The ten plagues in Egypt are spiritually fulfilled in the world, of which Egypt is a figure.

It must be understood that one passage says, “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” while another says, “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.” Yet it is not said that it was hardened by the Lord, but as though of its own accord. The Apostle indicates this when he says: “But according to the hardness of your heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath.” By this he condemns the one who hardens himself voluntarily. [Col. 0301B]

Elsewhere it is said: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.” But this must be observed: among the ten plagues, some blows were inflicted by Aaron, some by Moses, and some by the Lord himself. This signifies that in some matters we are cleansed through sacrifice and the observance of the priesthood, which Aaron signifies; in some we are purified through knowledge of the Law, which Moses’ office signifies; and in others, which are more difficult, we need the power of the Lord himself.

Moses, coming to Egypt and carrying the staff, chastising Egypt, signifies the Law, which rebukes the world through the ten plagues of the commandments. [Col. 0301C]

The staff by which Egypt is chastised and Pharaoh overcome is the cross of Christ, through which the world is conquered and the ruler of this world is triumphed over.

The fact that the staff thrown down became a serpent signifies wisdom. For it says: “Wise as serpents.”

The fact that it devoured the magicians’ serpents signifies the cross of Christ, whose preaching, though it appeared folly, surpassed all the wisdom of the world. That it contains the mystery of the cross the Lord declares when he says: “For he wrote about me.”

When the staff was thrown onto the ground, it was then changed into a serpent. For when the cross came to human belief, through the mystery of the cross it made the wisdom of this world foolish. [Col. 0301D]

But the fact that the waters of the river were changed into blood is suitably explained: the river to which they had handed the Hebrews over for cruel death gave the authors of the crime a cup of blood in return.

Allegorically, the rivers of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers. When they have deceived the immature in sense and understanding, and the cross of Christ has poured the light of truth into this world, the penalty of their death and the liability of their blood are exacted.

## CHAPTER VIII

The second plague, in which frogs are produced, signifies, as I think, the poets’ songs. Through a certain empty and inflated modulation, like frogs with their sounds and songs, they have introduced into this world tales of deception. For this animal is useful for nothing else except that it produces the sound of its harsh voice through untimely cries. [Col. 0302A]

After this the gnat is produced. This creature is suspended on wings, flying through the air, but it is so delicate and minute that it escapes the eye’s sight unless one observes sharply. Yet when it falls upon the body, it pierces it with an exceedingly bitter sting, so that one who cannot see what is doing the stinging nevertheless feels it.

I therefore think that this kind of creature is most appropriately compared with the art of dialectic, which penetrates souls with the minute and subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such cunning that the deceived person neither sees nor understands from where the deception comes.

At the third sign the magicians ascended, saying: “This is the finger of God.” Those magicians possessed the type—or the hostility—of heretics. The Apostle makes this clear: “Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses.” Through this very correction they were most restless in mind; at the third sign they failed, confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them. For the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is placed third. Hence, failing at the third sign, they say: “This is the finger of God.” [Col. 0302B]

Just as the Holy Spirit, reconciled and planted within us, grants rest to those who are gentle and humble in heart, so, when opposed to the rich and proud, he stirs up an agitation that torments them. This agitation was signified by those very small flies, under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.”

In the fourth place Egypt is struck by flies. The fly is an insolent and restless creature. What else, then, is signified by it except the insolent anxieties of carnal desires? Egypt is struck by flies because the hearts of those who love this world are driven about by the restlessness of their desires.

Moreover, the Seventy Translators rendered *cinomia*—that is, “dog-fly”—by which the behavior of dogs is signified. Thus, when the world has been deceived in each of these ways, the Law of God arrives and chastises it in such ways that, from the character of the punishments, it may recognize the character of its former errors. [Col. 0302C]

## CHAPTER IX

The fact that Egypt is struck in the fifth place by the death of animals or cattle rebukes the stupidity or folly of mortal human beings, who, like irrational cattle, bestowed the worship and name of God upon images impressed on wood and stone—not only images of human beings, but also of cattle: worshipping Ammon-Jupiter in a ram, Anubis in a dog, and also venerating Apis in a bull. Therefore the monsters which Egypt admires, and in which it believed divine worship resided, are seen to become pitiable punishments.

After this, ulcers and inflamed blisters are produced in the sixth blow. It seems to me that the ulcers rebuke solitary and deceitful malice; the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; and the inflammations, the madness of fury and anger. Thus far punishments are tempered for this world through figures of its errors. Afterwards, however, there come from above the thunderings of a voice—namely hail and fire running about. Observe the moderation of divine mercy. It does not strike in silence, but gives a voice and sends teaching from heaven, by which the chastened person may recognize his fault. It also gives hail, by which the still tender, newly sprouting vices are ravaged. It gives fire as well, knowing that there are thorns and briars which the fire ought to consume. Then the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth”; for by this the incitements of pleasure and lust are consumed. [Col. 0303A]

## CHAPTER X

The fact that locusts are mentioned here is thought by some to refute, through this kind of plague, the inconsistency and discord of the human race, which disagrees with itself. For although the locust has no king, it leads its army in a single battle line; human beings, although made rational by the Lord, have not been able to govern themselves in an orderly fashion. In another sense they are to be understood as representing the mobility of frivolity, like wandering and leaping souls flying about in this world.

The ninth plague is darkness, whether to show that their minds are accused of blindness, or so that they may understand that the nations are most obscure to divine providence. For God made darkness his hiding place; and those who boldly and rashly desire to investigate it, asserting one thing after another, have fallen into the thick and tangible darkness of errors. [Col. 0303B]

## CHAPTERS XI–XII

Finally, destruction is inflicted upon the firstborn. Egypt’s firstborn are destroyed, that is, its principalities and powers; or the rulers of this world, or the authors and inventors of the false religions that existed in this world, whom Christ’s truth extinguished and destroyed together with their authors. This is the mystical sense.

Morally, too, while each soul lives in errors in this world, it is placed in Egypt, that is, in this world. If the Law of God begins to draw near, it changes the waters into blood: that is, it changes the fluid and slippery life of youth into the blood of the New or Old [Testament]. Then it draws from it empty talk and a fabric of words like frogs, directed against God’s providence. [Col. 0303C]

For it purifies the soul’s evil thoughts, and with the biting of gnats drives away the stings of lust. Through the bites of flies it destroys the folly and beastlike understanding by which the person has been compared to foolish animals. The ulcers rebuke the swelling of sins and arrogance, and extinguish the heat of fury. From these and after these come the voices of the sons of thunder, that is, evangelical teachings.

And it removes the chastisement of hail, so as to restrain luxuries and pleasures. At the same time it applies the fire of repentance represented by the locusts, and withdraws the soul from their example, so that all its restless and turbulent movements may be bitten and consumed, and everything may be done in proper order. [Col. 0303D]

But when it begins to confess what the finger of God is, and receives a small measure of recognition, then it sees the darkness of its deeds. Once it has seen this, it will deserve that the firstborn of Egypt within it be extinguished—those firstborn being the sins of youth and ignorance.

At first the movement rushes into sin; but if it refuses to join the Israelite people, it will not be able to escape from the depths.

We may understand the same thing in another sense. Just as there were ten acts of opposition by the Egyptians against the people of Israel, so there were ten acts of vengeance by the Romans against Christ and against the Christian people.

There the first plague was the changing of water into blood. Here the first plague, under Nero, required that the blood of those dying should be there, whether through the corruption of morals in the city or through wars throughout the world, like blood. There it occurred both in the wells and in the rivers. [Col. 0304A]

There the following plague consisted of frogs making a clamorous and wanton din in the inner rooms, almost causing hunger for the inhabitants and for those among them. Here the following plague, under Domitian, similarly drove the attendants of that ruler—who carried out the commands of the bloodiest prince through their wicked and unrestrained raids—to poverty among all the faithful Romans and citizens, who were driven into exile and scattered.

There the third affliction consisted of gnats, namely the most depraved and savage flies, which, gathered densely together, ordinarily settle upon the hair of human beings or animals. Here the same plague, under Trajan, was the third plague that stirred up the Jews. Although they had been scattered everywhere, they suddenly raged against him.

There the fourth plague consisted of dog-flies, or flies from the light, which are the rottenness of worms. Here the fourth plague, under Marcus Antoninus, was a pestilence announced or inflicted upon many provinces. It also gave the Italian army of the Romans, scattered along distant frontiers, over to both rottenness and worms. [Col. 0304B]

There the fifth chastisement was completed by the sudden death of cattle and beasts of burden. Here likewise, in the fifth vengeance under the emperor Severus, who was near to the most famous civil wars, the vital organs and beasts of burden of the state and of the provincial populace, as well as the soldiers’ regions, were crushed.

There the sixth affliction included feverish boils and flowing ulcers. Here the puncture of [an uncertain OCR reading: “equisex”], which occurred after the persecution of Maximian, ordered that bishops and clerics in particular, leaving aside the common crowd, be slaughtered. Inflamed repeatedly by anger and envy, it brought about not the slaughter of the common people but the deaths of rulers through wounds. [Col. 0304C]

There the seventh vengeance is counted: the air, compressed by hail, was drenched with it, and this brought sufficient destruction upon human beings and animals. Here the seventh, under Gallus and Volusianus, which followed after the persecutor Decius had been killed, was a plague poured through the air. It spread throughout the whole extent of the Roman realm, from East to West, and brought nearly the entire human race to death.

There the eighth devastation of Egypt was brought about by locusts raised everywhere, terrifying all things. Here the eighth was brought by peoples raised everywhere like horses for the overthrow of the world; through slaughter and fires they destroyed all the provinces.

There the ninth disturbance consisted of prolonged darkness, threatening altogether more danger than it inflicted. Here likewise the ninth chastisement occurred when Aurelian stirred up persecution. A terrible and mournful lightning bolt fell with dreadful disturbances at his feet, showing what such a powerful avenger could accomplish when vengeance demanded it, unless he were merciful and patient. Nevertheless, within six months three emperors who followed him in succession—Aurelian, Tacitus, and Florianus—died for different reasons. [Col. 0304D]

There the tenth plague was the killing of the sons whom they had begotten as their firstborn. Here likewise the tenth, that is, the final punishment, was the destruction of all the images that they had first loved and made.

At the beginning, there the king felt, tested, and feared God’s repentance [i.e., relenting]; and for this reason he permitted God’s people to depart free.

“This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year.” What wonder if this month had been first, in which heaven and earth were created, in which the Flood both occurred and ended, in which the people of Israel were liberated, in which the Law is said to have been given to the others, and in which Christ’s preaching and his passion took place? [Col. 0305A]

Nor is it surprising that the month in which all these things occurred should have been suitable for this purpose, since among the Hebrews it is called Nisan and among the Latins it is called March.

This month is designated as the beginning of the months of the year because the Hebrews had not previously observed the order of the months properly, but according to the custom of the Gentiles, among whom they had earlier lived.

Some think that *mensis* (“month”) is derived from *metiri* (“to measure”), because weeks, days, hours, and moments are measured together within it.

The first month signifies the natural law; the month of the year signifies the Law of Moses and the prophets; the year signifies the whole world.

Meanwhile Passover takes place. Christ is killed at the killing of the year, of whom it is said: “Behold, the Lamb of God.” [Col. 0305B]

The fact that the lamb is taken on the tenth day of the month but is not sacrificed until the fourteenth signifies that Christ’s passion was indeed prefigured through the Law. Yet the course of the Gospel also suffered beforehand [the printed reading is uncertain]. The number ten belongs to the Law because of the ten words of the Law; the number four belongs to the New Testament because of the four Gospels.

What follows—“If the smaller number is not sufficient to eat the lamb, he shall take his neighbor,” and so forth—signifies that one who is unable by himself to fulfill or understand the mystery of faith ought to inquire of someone wiser, cling to him, and trust him, since he knows what that person ought to do in order to eat the lamb’s flesh.

[Col. 0305C] The lamb shall be without blemish. This applies to Christ, of whom it is said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” A year-old lamb is sacrificed, and Christ suffered at a mature age.

It follows: “According to this rite you shall also take a kid.” This kid, too, appropriately signifies Christ himself, since he is the sacrifice for sin. For, as he says, “He who knew no sin was made sin for us.” The lamb is sacrificed in the evening, because Christ suffered in the evening of the world. The lamb’s blood is placed on both doorposts. We too are marked in heart and body with the sign of Christ’s cross, and we say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.”

Others say that the Passover celebrated in Egypt signifies the Passover of the Old Testament, from which there has not yet been a passage away from the willful desires; after the crossing of the Red Sea, it signifies the figure of the Passover of the New Testament in the Church, which after baptism has been deserted by the desires of men. Yet after the Passover in the desert, the Passover of the promised land remains; so also, after the Passover of the New Testament, the Passover of judgment remains for the saints—that is, the kingdom of heaven.

It is said to be the tenth day of the month, not the tenth night, either so that it might be distinguished by the notable part, or because the day was created and not the night. Thus, “each one” means each ruler.

Morally, however, the tenth day on which the lamb is sacrificed signifies that Christ is introduced to us for belief through the ten senses, and that he is sacrificed through innocence. The families and households signify the senses of soul and body.

Here there seems to be a difficulty, because according to the historical account he did not give a definite number; nevertheless, the interpretation explains the meaning. The number suited to eating the lamb appears to signify those who see well through the six days during which the world was unfolded; or seven men, that is, those living according to the sevenfold teaching; or twelve, that is, those fulfilling the teaching of the apostles. For these numbers daily receive Christ in the Church—that is, those who were found worthy.

The lamb is also said to have been sacrificed on behalf of Joshua and Caleb, signifying those kids who fell in the wilderness. In another sense, the lamb and the kid now suggest to us belief in the divinity and incarnation of Christ.

“And you shall keep watch over it,” and the rest: Christ was watched over through the Law, as we have said; morally, we ought to watch over him in our hearts until the fourteenth day—that is, until he comes through the work of the Decalogue. “Of this month,” that is, of the Gospel—historically, because Christ suffered in it, as we have said.

“The whole congregation,” that is, the multitude of Jews crucifying Christ; or, in the mystical sense, the multitude of believers; or, morally, the multitude of perfected senses.

“In the evening,” that is, at the completion of the Old Testament; or, morally, evening signifies the completion of the prosperity of this age.

“And they shall eat the meat on that night,” that is, in the obscurity of the mysteries; or, morally, in the ignorance of sin.

“Roasted with fire,” that is, with the fire of the Passion. The houses in which the meat is eaten signify either the soul or the body.

The command to eat unleavened bread with wild lettuce signifies that, while leading a life restored from every leaven of malice, we must always possess the bitterness of compunction of heart, which the lettuce signifies. When eaten, lettuce is so salty and bitter that it brings tears to the eater’s eyes. Thus, when receiving the heavenly bread, we too ought to water our faces with tears.

The lamb’s meat is not cooked in water, but only by fire, because Christ’s Passion is not understood through the wisdom of this world but through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“You shall devour the head with the feet and the entrails.” In the head is the sign of divinity; in the feet, of humanity. The entrails signify the more secret and hidden mysteries, all of which we ought to devour—that is, believe.

And what is said, “Nothing of it shall remain until morning,” signifies that before the dawn of the time of future judgment, we must believe and fulfill everything that has been written. [Col. 0306D] If anything is exceedingly obscure and too profound for us, it must be reserved for the Holy Spirit, who is a consuming fire. When he comes in this way, he will recall to us everything that has been said. This is signified by the statement: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.”

What is said, “You shall not eat any of it raw,” is understood by some as meaning that those eat it raw who understand Christ only in a carnal way. “The head with the feet,” that is, Christ together with the two Laws or with the apostles. “You shall burn it with fire”: morally, this can be understood to mean that with the fire of compunction we ought to burn whatever we have failed to retain of good works.

“You shall gird your loins.” This signifies the correction of human concupiscence. Concupiscence occurs in the loins of men, but in the navel of women. We too are told: “Gird the loins of your mind,” that is, gird your minds. Or, as is said, the part is understood for the whole.

“You shall have sandals on your feet,” that is, let us have the twofold charity in our senses, or, following the example of the prophets and apostles, in body and soul.

“Holding staffs,” that is, weapons held in both hands. Our weapons, by which we defend ourselves and with which we fight, are the two Testaments; or, morally, the aid of both substances. “In your hands,” that is, in your works. “In haste,” that is, spiritually.

We ought to believe in Christ in haste, before the day of judgment; or, morally, in haste the Church proceeds from earthly things before the day of death.

Passover is interpreted as “passing over,” that is, the Lord’s passing over to vengeance. Then it is said to Israel: [Col. 0307B] “Eat in haste,” before vengeance.

The interpretation given above is appropriate in many ways: first, through the Lord’s passing over to vengeance, as it is said: “I will pass through the land of Egypt.” Or it may mean that vengeance passed through the people of God, or a passage in the cloud.

Spiritually, the passage is understood as the passage through the vengeance of judgment, or as the passage from the world, together with all the saints, to the kingdoms of heaven. The Lord’s passing over in the cloud signifies his aid together with the saints.

The people of Israel went out from Egypt at midnight, and the firstborn were killed. Likewise, judgment is thought to come at that hour, and the saints of Israel go out from the world after eating the lamb—that is, Christ. Then all the strength of worldly men is shattered.

At midnight the people of hell were released, while the devil and his attendants were bound. Here, too, Peter’s release at midnight is appropriate.

Historically it is said to Israel: “Let each one take,” and the rest—that is, to determine whether it is good.

As we explained above, the lamb represents those who escaped to the land, that is, of promise; the kid represents those who perished in the wilderness. The firstborn of Egypt were killed in place of the firstborn of Israel. The firstborn signify sinners, because they sacrificed them to idols. For those who are full of malice deserved full vengeance.

Regarding the statement, “He executed judgment among their gods,” the Hebrews maintain that on that night when the people of Israel went out, all the temples of the Egyptians were destroyed, without an earthquake. Spiritually, this signifies that when we go out from the errors of the world, the idols collapse and are shaken.

After the leaven has been removed, they set out in this way. We too, as we leave the Egypt of this world, must not walk in the leaven of malice.

They ate unleavened bread for seven days. We too must eat purely and simply throughout the seven days by which this world is completed; the lamb must be sacrificed for us daily, and daily we must celebrate Passover.

The destruction of these temples of idols also signifies Christ’s coming into Egypt, by which the images of Egypt were destroyed. The killing of rational and irrational creatures signifies the killing of human beings and animals in the Red Sea, or of bodies and souls, or the punishment of sins in the present and in the future. The firstborn of the Egyptians were killed so that this might deter the Egyptians from persecuting Israel.

[Col. 0308A] “The soul shall perish from Israel,” that is, whoever among us sins shall perish from among the holy.

“From the first day until the seventh,” that is, from the beginning of the New Testament to its end; or from the beginning of the work to its end; or from the persecution of souls to the persecution of bodies.

“The first day shall be holy,” that is, free from labor. Thus the day of the New Testament is solemn, abounding in spiritual goods and free from the labors of sins. In both substances, except for those things that pertain to the active life, these matters likewise apply.

“On that same day and forever,” that is, on account of the benefit the Lord granted them on the day of Passover; this also applies to the righteous in the New Testament, whom Christ redeemed.

The fourteenth day demonstrates faith in Christ: through the ten commandments and the four Gospels; or in relation to receiving Christ’s flesh, through the ten senses and the four elements of which a human being consists.

The sacrifice of the lamb on the fourteenth day is appropriate, because Mesraim, on the fourteenth day from Adam the first, sacrificed blood to idols, up to the twenty-first day—that is, in figures of the two Laws and of their unity. “Of the same month,” that is, of the New Testament.

“Of the resident aliens,” and the rest. The resident aliens signify the Gentiles; the natives, the Jews; the land, the Church.

Hyssop is a lowly herb; because it cleanses the breast, it bears the figure of Christ, lowly in the assumption of flesh. A bundle of hyssop—that is, belief in the incarnation and divinity of Christ—must be present in bodies.

Therefore the people took the kneaded dough, that is, the letter of the Law together with carnal good works. The Christian people, binding the Law dispersed through understanding onto stakes—that is, to the yoke of life—hear: “If anyone wishes to come after me,” and the rest. For life is the fulfillment of the commandments.

Then God commanded them to ask the Egyptians for what they had lent them. Thus, as the people departed, they stripped the Egyptians of gold and silver at God’s command, who commands nothing unjustly.

The gold, silver, and clothing of the Egyptians signify certain teachings learned through a useful diligence from the customs of the Gentiles. In another sense, the gold and silver of the Egyptians are souls, together with their bodies; the clothing signifies those who join themselves to the people of God.

What Rameses and the other stopping places signify, we shall explain when we begin to discuss the stopping places.

“No foreigner shall eat of it.” No unbeliever feeds on the flesh of Christ.

“Every purchased slave shall be circumcised, and then he shall eat.” Everyone whom Christ purchased with his blood must be a servant of Christ, be circumcised of vices, and then eat Christ’s body.

“The resident alien and the hired servant shall not eat of it.” The resident alien is one who has recently come to the faith, such as the newly baptized. The hired servant is one who labors only for earthly profit and seeks no future reward. Such people are certainly not worthy to receive Christ’s body.

“It shall be eaten in one house,” that is, in the Church. For, he says, “My dove is one”; it must not be carried outside, beyond the Church, into the congregation of heretics.

We are forbidden to break the bones of the lamb in the Passover rites. The Lord’s bones were not broken on the cross. Or, in the words, “You shall not break his bones,” he forbade us to divide Christ’s divinity by unbelief.

“Every male of it,” that is, everything masculine belonging to it, in sin.

“The children of Israel did,” up to Aaron. Moses and Aaron very frequently signify the Law and the priesthood; the children of Israel signify believers.

“In one,” meaning every firstborn. This first sacrifice is required, as though the Lord were saying: “Sacrifice your firstborn, since the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed on your account.”

We too must offer our works to God spiritually, as is said elsewhere. We are also commanded always to celebrate Passover—that is, our passage from worse things to better—and to consecrate the firstborn of our works to God, who killed the demons on our behalf.

## CHAPTER XIII

That which opens the womb is sacrificed to God as a figure of Christ opening the womb of the virgin Mary.

“From the house of slavery,” that is, from Egypt, which is called the house of slavery because Israel served there. Or because they served the idols of the Egyptians; or because a fifth part was given to the kings.

“In the month of new things,” that is, in the new [month], as it is said: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

“Seven days,” and the rest. Elsewhere it is said concerning this: “Every solemnity among the Hebrews must end on the seventh day.”

“You shall kill the firstborn of the donkey.” This means that a good virtue should be changed in place of a vice. If someone does not possess a good virtue instead of a vice, nevertheless let him kill his vice.

“Moses took the bones of Joseph.” Here it is shown that children ought to fulfill the oaths of their fathers after their death.

“God went before them,” and the rest. This light is said to go before the children of Israel, as it is said: “God went before them and, in some manner, came after them,” when he stood between the people of Israel and the Egyptians who perished.

The material of the columns is indicated as follows: just as the column of cloud remained from night into day, so the column of fire became present from day into night. These columns were in the air, between heaven and earth.

The cloud by day signifies the old Law together with the obscurity of the letter. The column of fire signifies the Law of the New Testament, as in: “The words of God are fiery,” and: “A fiery law was in his right hand,” that is, Christ is at the right hand of God the Father.

In another sense, the day in which the cloud was present signifies the prosperity of this world together with the Old Law: “The good things of the earth,” and the rest. The column of fire at night signifies the New Testament in the obscurity of its mysteries, or in comparison with the life to come. For just as the New Testament is preferred to the Old, so the day of judgment surpasses it.

“They walk by night and by day,” as a figure of those who walk in sins and in righteousness, from among their descendants. In another sense, such a walking in darkness and in light signifies that some of them would be in the letter, concerning which it is said: “The letter kills”; others would be in the meaning, concerning which it is said: “The Spirit gives life.” Thus the honor of God would be alike in day and night.

“And he went before them,” that is, God the Father. Christ went before us in the New Testament, showing the way of truth, as it is said: “What Jesus began to do and teach”; or in his resurrection, ascension, and sitting at the right hand of God the Father.

“By day and night,” that is, through the active and contemplative life, or through the two Laws.

The column of cloud and fire signifies the teaching of the Holy Spirit, differing according to letter and meaning. In another sense, just as the work was unbound, so too were the columns unbound. The two columns also figure the two Churches, that is, of the Old and New Testaments, in which he speaks.

In another sense, the column of fire at night signifies divinity in the flesh of the virgin Mary, as it is said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.”

“At both times,” that is, both here and in the future. “The column was never absent,” and the rest. This signifies what is said elsewhere: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

## CHAPTER XIV

Pharaoh therefore harnessed his chariot, that is, the devil’s four-horse chariot. The devil’s chariot is each sinner together with gluttony, fornication, anger, and pride.

Moses struck the waters with his staff, and the children of Israel crossed. The Red Sea signifies baptism, consecrated by Christ’s blood. The staff with which the sea is touched, as was said above, is Christ’s cross, which we receive through baptism. For we were buried with him through baptism.

The enemies pursuing with their king, who die behind them, are past sins, which will be washed away; and the devil is drowned in the spiritual washing, that is, in baptism.

The Egyptians press hard; sins persist. But as far as the water was concerned, the people’s right side was against the Egyptians, while the left side was against the sea—that is, the Christian people in the Church, which lies between the world and the kingdom of heaven; or between the two deaths, of body and soul.

He desired to enter Egypt, that is, the desires of this world. Three worked together for Israel’s salvation: God, Moses, and the staff. Thus we too are delivered through three laws, through faith in the Trinity, and through thought, word, and deed.

Between two walls, one of which was in the east and the other in the west. Likewise, this signifies between the two Laws, among which there is one that does not exact vengeance upon the righteous. Or, between two walls, it signifies the path between body and soul, as it is said: “Neither to the right nor to the left.”

The bitterness through which they went out signifies the bitterness of fulfilling the word of God.

Why did they go out with weapons, flocks, and clothing? In the same way, through baptism, we go out with hope and good works. The weapons, and the rest. The vessels signify the various virtues in the Church.

The waters through which the children of Israel went out signify three kinds of weeping: the weeping of repentance through the Red Sea, as it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn now,” and the rest; through the Arnon, the weeping of compassion, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0310D] “Bear one another’s burdens,” and the rest; through the Jordan, weeping directed toward the kingdom of heaven, as in: “I desire to depart,” and the rest. We ought to bring forth these tears through thought, word, and deed.

The burning wind from the south—that is, the Holy Spirit from Christ—drives the temptations of this world away from the saints.

The three sons delivered from the furnace, the children of Israel from the sea, and Noah in the flood correspond to Christ together with the saints.

“In the fourth watch,” that is, after the four Gospels have been fulfilled, the saints will be delivered from the world.

“Behold, the Lord looked,” and the rest. The Lord looks from the column of cloud and fire toward vengeance, when demons and the impious are killed through the three Laws and the wheels of the devil are overturned.

“Into everlasting time,” that is, until the release of the men of hell, or without end.

There are two fathers: the father of darkness and the Father of lights.

## CHAPTER XV

After the crossing of the Red Sea, with the Egyptians and Pharaoh submerged, the people sing a song to God. Now, in another sense, the faithful, after they rise from the washing, send forth a hymn of praise when their sins have been destroyed.

Although there are many songs in the divine books, this song is nevertheless the first of them all. You will speak these words better and more worthily if you have a tambourine in your hand—that is, if you have crucified your flesh together with its vices.

Let us see what it says: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored.” As though “He has been glorified” were not enough, it adds, “He has been gloriously honored.” To glorify and to honor gloriously are different things.

Christ was glorified when he came to his Passion, when, as he says of himself: “Father, glorify your Son.” Yet that glory was not glorious but humble. For, he says, “He humbled himself unto death.” But when he comes in his majesty, and kills the true Pharaoh—that is, the devil—with the breath of his mouth, then he will be gloriously glorified.

“He cast horse and rider into the sea.” There are horses whom the Lord rides, concerning which it is said: “Your riding is salvation.” And there are horses that have the devil and his angels as riders. Therefore all who persecute the saints are horses and have demons as riders. Such horses and riders are plunged into the sea of this world, driven back from us with the Lord’s help.

“This is my God, and I will exalt him.” Christ is our Father, who begot us and made us. Therefore God the Father is our God, and the God of our father Christ, who says: “I ascend to my God and your God.” We glorify him if we recognize that God the Father is our Father. We exalt God with a higher understanding when we comprehend how Christ called him his God, whom by nature he calls Father.

“God who crushes wars,” and the rest. He overthrows not only the wars of visible things but also invisible horses, and likewise the chariots—that is, those united in wickedness.

They are called *ternistatores* [three-man charioteers], because there is a threefold way of sinning: by word, deed, or thought. These *ternistatores* are wicked angels from Pharaoh’s army.

“The sea covered them,” because on the day of judgment they will be handed over to waves of fire and, like extremely heavy stones, will be submerged, since they will not be living stones.

“And by the spirit of anger,” that is, of the Lord’s correction, the water is divided. This means that through the desires and pleasures of this world the people escape, while unbelievers are drowned in them. Or certainly God saves the righteous through the water of baptism. In the water he kills vices, as though in anger.

“There is none like the Lord among the gods of the nations.” There is none even among the saints, who in many places are called gods, although the Apostle John says: “We shall be like him”—not by nature but by grace.

“The earth devoured them with its vegetation.” For the earth has always devoured those who set their minds on earthly things, who occupy themselves with earthly matters and do not seek things above. But the Lord will govern his people, whom he has freed through the holy washing, in righteousness and lead them into refreshment.

“Pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia.” As far as the historical account is concerned, it is clear that the Philistines, Moabites, Edomites, and Canaanites were not present at the signs that occurred. How, then, are they said to tremble, hurry, or be angry?

Spiritually, however, the Philistines—whose name means “those falling by the cup”—and Edom, which is interpreted as “earthly,” trembled.
