The rulers of these people, that is, the demons, hurriedly fear, bound by pains, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, penetrated by the one who descended into the lower regions of the earth to rescue those possessed by death.

“Fear seized them,” those who perceived the greatness of his arm. Hence all the inhabitants of Canaan departed; Canaan is interpreted as “changeable.” They saw their kingdoms shaken, the strong man bound, and his vessels plundered.

“Fear falls upon them” when they see the sign of the cross in us.

“Let them become like a stone,” not because human beings are changed into stones, but because they become immovable like stones, unable either to persecute or to flee.

Spiritually, this signifies that the Jewish people would be like a stone, remaining in hardness, until the people of the Gentiles became Christian; and then all Israel will be saved.

“Bringing them in and planting them.” God does not wish to plant us in Egypt but on the mountain of his inheritance, that is, in the Church.

“In the dwelling place you have prepared.” For others labored, and you entered into their labor.

“Your sanctuary, O Lord,” and the rest. We are God’s sanctuary, that is, his holy building; we were not made by human hands but are God’s cultivation.

“Lord, you reign forever and unto ages of ages.” This too signifies a kingdom without end.

“For the horsemen entered.” We have spoken of this above.

But we, who are the children of Israel, should walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea, in the midst of a crooked nation, holding fast the word of life. It is enough to have said these things briefly, lest the reader be wearied.

Mary, the sister of Aaron, holding a tambourine, signifies the sister of the true priest, that is, the Church, which is Christ’s sister. All the women signify the Churches with choirs and tambourines, that is, with the Old and New Testaments.

After crossing the sea, the people are led into the desert: namely, all who have been baptized are led through the desert of this world, and Christ does not abandon them there. The column does not depart, nor do they return in their hearts to Egypt.

After this the people murmur, unable to drink the bitter waters; hence the place is named from its bitterness. Moses casts wood into the waters, and they become sweet.

Understand the bitter waters as having the figure of the killing letter and of the Law. If wood is cast into them—that is, the sacrament of the wood of the cross—then the water becomes exceedingly sweet, and the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness of the understanding of the spiritual meaning.

So that you might be able to drink the bitter water, God shows you what is cast into it, so that whoever drinks may not die. Solomon says concerning wisdom: “She is a tree of life to all who grasp her.”

This wood, then—that is, the wisdom of Christ’s cross—was cast into the water of the Old Law and provided a most health-giving drink for the faithful people, who previously could not drink from it.

For what is more bitter than, on the eighth day, to receive the wound of circumcision and to serve at various sacrifices?

In another sense, the bitter waters made sweet by receiving the wood indicate that the bitterness of the nations will one day be changed into the service of sweetness through the wood of the cross.

From this bitterness of the letter the people came to springs. One passes from the Old Testament to the New, to the twelve springs of the apostles. There they find seventy palm trees; likewise, seventy others were sent to preach the word of God.

## CHAPTER XVI

After this the people murmur on the fifteenth day of the second month, after they had gone out from the land of Egypt. Recall what was said in the laws concerning Passover: there you will find that this is the provision establishing a second Passover for those who were unclean in soul or engaged on distant journeys.

At this time the manna descended; it did not descend on the day when the first Passover was celebrated. The first Passover belongs to the first people; the second Passover belongs to us.

We were unclean in soul, because we worshiped idols, and, occupied with worldly affairs, we were living far away in a foreign land. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Guests of the covenants.”

Nevertheless, manna is given from heaven not at the first Passover but at the second. For the bread that descended from heaven did not come to those who celebrated the first Passover, but to us.

“Behold, I will rain bread from heaven,” and the rest. The statement, “On the sixth day they gathered twice as much,” shows that manna was first given from heaven on the Lord’s day. For from the Lord’s day, the day of preparation for the Sabbath, the sixth day is counted.

From this the Jews understand that already then our Lord’s day was preferred to the Jewish Sabbath, since no grace descended to them on their Sabbath. On our Lord’s day, however, God always rains manna from heaven. Throughout the whole period of the New Testament, the divine words are ministered to us.

Manna is said to be fine and minute. For what is as subtle and minute as the spiritual meaning? It is white because it is darkened by no ignorance.

“Manna” is interpreted as “What is this?” When we hear the Law of God being recited, we say to our teachers: “What is it?” For it is exceedingly subtle, like coriander seed. It has something of a vegetable in it, by which it can nourish the weak. “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables.”

It has something cold in it, and therefore it is like hoarfrost.

What does it mean that twice as much is gathered on the feast day? The sixth day is the present life, in which we are commanded to gather twice as much. For in six days God made this world. On this day, therefore, we should store up as much as will suffice for the future day. For if you acquire any good work here, it will be your food in the age to come. “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.” Therefore let us not sow what perishes, but what will endure until tomorrow.

When the unbelievers kept some of the manna, worms boiled out of it, and it rotted. What was stored up for the sake of the Sabbath did not decay; but if you hoard only for the sake of the present life, worms immediately boil out—worms, that is, which do not die.

These are the worms produced by greed and by nothing else. In us, worms arise from the manna, that is, from the word. For he said: “If he had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin;” but after receiving the word of God, if anyone sins, the word itself becomes a worm for him, gnawing at his conscience.

The bread given to the Israelite people is said by some properly to be counted as the bread of angels, as in: “The bread of angels.” But it was said of Christ: “Whom angels desire to look upon.” Every saint eats him.

“I will rain bread,” and “a voluntary rain,” and the rest. These two expressions are said to have the same meaning; both designate divine wisdom.

It follows: “In the evening you shall know that I am the Lord; but in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord.”

In the Gospel they find these things written: “When the evening of the Sabbath came, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb, and a great earthquake occurred. For an angel descended from heaven, and the guards became like dead men.”

Through these events he was recognized by the Church in the evening; he was recognized through the power of the resurrection, while in the morning his glory was seen. When the other women came very early on the first day of the week, they found angels in great brightness saying: “Tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead.”

The glory of the Lord’s majesty was therefore seen in the morning, when it was announced through the angels.

It follows: “In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.” In the evening of this world the Word became flesh, and by that flesh which he assumed from the Virgin we recognize the Lord.

No one ate this flesh of the Word of God in the morning or at midday. Christ came in the evening of this world. But he says: “In the morning you shall be filled with bread.” The bread for us is the word of God; for he is the living bread that descended from heaven, and the rest.

But since it is said that this bread was given in the morning, although we have said that his coming in the flesh occurred in the evening for this world, I think it should be understood as follows: the Lord indeed came in the evening of this world, but by his coming—because he himself is righteousness—he restored a new day for believers at evening, since he displayed a new light of knowledge.

Like the sun of righteousness, he produced his own morning, whose ray he has now brought forth for us; and in this morning those who receive the commandments are filled with bread.

Do not be surprised that the Word of God is called both flesh and bread, since milk and vegetables are also named according to the measure of those who partake.

This too can be understood: after his resurrection, which we have shown to have occurred in the morning, he filled believers with bread because he gave us the previously unknown books of the Law and the Prophets. Thus he himself is the bread in the Gospel, while the other books—many books of the Law and the Prophets—are called loaves, from which the righteous are filled.

We can also understand his meaning as applying to each of us: morning is the time when we are enlightened and ascend to the light of faith. In that morning we cannot eat the flesh of the Word of God—that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine—but only after long exercises.

When we are already near evening and the very end of our imperfection, only then do we become capable of more substantial food.

This manna, according to each person’s disposition, produces a flavor suited to that person. If you are troubled, this manna—that is, the word—consoles you, saying: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.”

If you are angry, it calms you, saying: “Cease from anger and forsake wrath.”

If you lack sight, the Lord illuminates the blind.

It is also possible to understand the food of birds as signifying the words of the Old Law, which, through words sent by God, lifts up the carnal people as carnal people. They are given through flying creatures in the evening because everything given in a carnal manner has an end.

From the manifest light of faith, manna is given to the people of God—that is, Christ, who is the living bread.

Among the Hebrews this kind of bird is called *coturnix* (“quail”); among the Greeks, *ortigometra*; in Latin, a sea bird.

Others say that the quails can be understood as Christ’s humanity, and the manna as his divinity. The quail is struck in the evening, signifying the killing of Christ’s flesh. In the morning, the manna marks the superiority of divinity over the body, and for us it marks the mystery of wisdom and of Christ’s body, until we have gone out from the world through baptism; just as manna was not given to the people as long as they were in Egypt.

Manna pounded with a pestle signifies Christ’s body on the cross. “In the day,” that is, in the new [day], as it is said: “You are sons of light,” and the rest, up to “night.”

Manna is given to the righteous and the unrighteous; so the word of God is given to everyone.

The flesh given in the evening signifies the statement: “I know that nothing good dwells in my flesh.”

The bread in the morning displays the enlightened soul, like honey—that is, the letter together with its meaning.

They ate manna between the Red Sea and the land of Egypt, the Arnon and the Jordan, and the land of Canaan—that is, between the world and baptism, repentance, the fire of judgment, and the heavenly kingdom.

The sixth day, on which they were commanded to gather twice as much, can also signify the sixth age of this world, in which we now live. For during the five days—that is, the past periods of this world—people served worldly advantages so that they might eat earthly goods: from Adam to the Flood; from the Flood to Abraham; from Abraham to Moses; from Moses to David; and from David to Christ.

But we, to whom not worldly rewards but the kingdom of heaven is promised, gather twice as much on this sixth day—that is, from Christ to the end of this world—because we prepare for ourselves not only the present rest but also the rest of the future.

The *gomor* that was stored up so that it might remain there before the Lord [perhaps: “for perpetuity”] signifies, assuredly, Christ’s body, which, joined to God, cannot fail to know itself. 

## CHAPTER XVII
Then the rock was struck and poured forth water, signifying Christ: for Christ, struck upon the cross, poured out the laver of grace for those who thirst. “The rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ.” But the people, thirsting, murmured against Moses, and he showed them the rock from which they were to drink. This signifies that if anyone murmurs against Moses—that is, against the law which is displeasing according to the letter—the same law shows him the rock, that is, Christ, so that he may drink from him. The place where the rock was struck is called “Temptation”; and at the place of the Passion a great temptation arose, when all his disciples abandoned him and fled.

After this Moses went up the mountain, while Jesus fought against Amalek. What is signified by this except that Moses—that is, the law—could not defeat the adversaries obstructing our journey? For the law brought nothing to perfection; but Jesus fought and conquered, he who is our Savior. Moses stood at the summit of the hill: that is, the law rises into spiritual understanding. And he sat upon a stone: that is, he rests in the Church.

What follows, “Moses’ hands were heavy,” signifies that he did not bring forth sinners with mercy, but struck them with strict severity. Aaron and Hur, however, supported his hands. Aaron is interpreted as “mountain of strength”; Hur, “fire.” This mountain, therefore, which signifies strength, is Christ: for he is the mountain, the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain. Fire signifies the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said, “I have come to cast fire.”

Aaron and Hur support Moses’ hands because the mediator between God and human beings, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, makes the heavy commands of the law—which could not be borne in a carnal manner—more tolerable for us by means of spiritual understanding. Moses, moreover, was full of God and spoke with God face to face—a matter of great wonder.

## CHAPTER XVIII

He received counsel from Jethro, that is, from a gentile, and did everything he said. But he gives the rulers an example of humility and indicates an image of the sacrament that was to come. For it was destined that, at some time, those things lacking in the law would be completed through the people gathered from the gentiles, and that the law’s deficiency would be fulfilled at the prompting of the Gospel.

Jethro’s bringing Zipporah and both sons to Moses signifies that the holy preachers of the Church would then bring forth to the divine law both sons from both peoples; through their counsel and interpretation the same law would be confirmed. The tribunes signify those who fulfill the three laws, or those who believe in the Trinity. The centurions signify the perfect; the fifty-men and the tens, those who fulfill the Decalogue.

## CHAPTER XIX

“When I carried you upon eagles’ wings.” The wings are Moses and Aaron; in the spiritual sense, however, the two wings are the two laws, while the eagle is Christ.

“Beware lest you go up onto the mountain”—that is, into the assembly, into the Church—“or touch its boundary,” that is, the three multitudes. “He shall surely die”: that is, in repentance. “The hand shall not touch him”: that is, human action. “But he shall be overwhelmed with stones”: that is, with testimonies. Whether it be an animal—that is, a gentile or a foolish person—or a human being—that is, a Jew or a wise person—the trumpet signifies the word of God.

Then he went up onto the mountain. This shows that God invites the multitudes into the Church. “He sanctified it”: that is, by sacrifices or by circumcision. Circumcision sanctified, the law purified, and grace justified. And Moses descended—that is, Christ descended from heaven—so that the law might come down from the Church to distinguish marriage.

Clothing signifies works. “On the third day”: that is, in the law of the New Testament; or in action after thought and word; or in faith in the Trinity. What he says, “Do not approach your wives,” signifies that the Church has cast out marriage. Alternatively, wives signify every softness of pleasures.

When Moses descended from the mountain, this signifies the descending law; or Christ descending from heaven; or the holy person descending from the summit of perfected works to active life. Moses, in the historical sense, calls the people; the law and the Lord Christ call the whole world; holy people call others to their own example; likewise, good understanding calls others into itself.

“Morning”: that is, of the New Testament, of repentance, of death, and of the day of judgment. The law being given on the third day signifies that the third law would come to them again; they too ought to await the law in patience, while the law preached repentance.

It had also been arranged that the law should be given on the mountain, since the law was lofty and was given with darkness as well. For the old law was given with the darkness of the letter that kills, but the new with splendor, because the Spirit gives life. On one mountain there were signs only of the living, while on the other there were signs of both the living and the dead. The first law was given only to the living—that is, to those who served the goods of the earth. The second profits both in life and after death.

There the one Lord addressed them, because that law profited not many. Here, however, five address Christ, because the new law summoned more people to Christ than the old did. Darkness and everything that was obscure signify the letter; the mountain and everything that was bright demonstrate spiritual understanding. Everything gentle and luminous belongs to the faithful, while all terror and darkness belong to unbelievers.

The law is therefore given throughout with severity so that the people might fear and honor the law and Moses. The three who went up the mountain with Christ signify the nearness of the saints to Christ. This was not so in the giving of the old law, because the people of the New Testament are nearer than those of the Old.

There are three groups: the first is the people of the law of nature; the second, the people of the law of the letter, who were nearer to God; the third, the people of the new law, who have been united to God in the Church. This mountain is the first Church, and this group signifies married people; the second signifies the people of repentance; the third, the saints with Christ. In these three multitudes, thought, word, and deed are signified.

Nor should this be passed over: “Moses went up onto the mountain, and the Lord descended.” The mountain is the height of contemplation, onto which we climb so that we may be lifted to behold those things that lie beyond. But the Lord descends into it because, when the righteous are making great progress, he discloses to their understanding that only a little is lacking for them.

On the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated, the law was given to Moses. Likewise, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion, the Holy Spirit was given to one hundred and twenty people, constituted according to the number of the Mosaic age.

In the voices and thunderclaps, the cry of preaching is understood; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the sound of the trumpet, the forceful preaching of the saints. All these things were fulfilled at Christ’s coming.

The Lord’s descending in fire and smoke signifies that at his coming the Lord illumines the faithful with his splendor and darkens unbelievers through the smoke of errors. That the Lord was in darkness signifies that he gave the law to the Jews, as though through the darkness of the letter, so that “seeing they may not see.”

Others say that the following sentence is signified by the thunder: “Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire”; and by the lightning, “The righteous shall shine like the sun.” By the trumpet are signified command and prohibition; by the horn, the word of God. “Greater,” that is, as the law grows; and “longer,” that is, as it teaches through stages of increase.

They stood, both the steadfast and the unsteady, as a figure of the two laws. “A terrifying mountain”: that is, the Church to the impious; or each holy person is terrifying to vices. “Boundary”: that is, faith toward the Church, since no one enters the Church except through faith.

## CHAPTER XX

Finally, the Lord established the law in ten words. No number increases further except up to ten: if you count twenty, you have two tens; if thirty, you have three tens. Thus, however far you progress, you will find the number ten. By this means he established the fullness of the commandments in the fullness of the number. Some distinguish these commandments in such a way that three pertain to love of the Trinity, while seven pertain to brotherly love, through which human society is not harmed.

The first commandment pertains to God the Father, when he says: “I am the Lord your God. You shall have no other gods. You shall not make for yourself a graven image,” and so forth. This is so that, hearing these things, you may not offend by your fornication against many gods.

The second pertains to the Son, where he says: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”—that is, you must not think that the Son of God is a creature, since every visible creature is subject to vanity.

The third commandment, concerning the Sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit, whose gift promises us eternal rest. By the gift of the Spirit we are sanctified; hence it is also said here: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” Thus, in the six ages of this world we labor, as in six days; on the seventh day—that is, at the end of this world—eternal rest will be granted to us.

After the three commandments comes the number seven, pertaining to love of one’s neighbor. It begins with love of parents, from whom we receive our beginning in this life. This commandment is fourth in order, yet the first of the six among the seven. Hence, according to the Gospel, it is called the first, since it is first on the other tablet.

Perhaps the reason they are called not one tablet but two is that these ten commandments pertain to love of God and of one’s neighbor. The fifth is, “You shall not commit adultery”; the sixth, “You shall not kill”; the seventh, “You shall not steal”; the eighth, “You shall not bear false witness”; the ninth, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; the tenth, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.”

Or certainly the commandments should be distinguished in this way: the first is, “You shall have no other gods”; the second, “You shall not make for yourself a graven image”; the third, “You shall not take”—and so in order, until the statement is joined in which he says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife.”

When he says, “You shall have no other gods,” he did not deny that such beings exist, but prohibited the person to whom these things are commanded from having them as gods. This accords with the Apostle, who says: “For although there are those who are called many gods and many lords, yet for us there is one God.” Many gentiles call demons gods, or indeed angels, to whom he entrusted the nations to be governed; it is agreed that they are called gods as though given by God, and lords as though they had received authority. For he says: “He established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.”

“You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness.” To make a graven image is one thing, and to make a likeness another. He makes a graven image who fabricates something that does not exist at all, merely according to the invention of his heart. He makes a likeness who makes the likeness of something—for example, of a quadruped, serpent, or bird.

“You shall not adore, nor worship.” Some adore unwillingly, or under compulsion of fear, or seduced through greed. Those worship who venerate with their whole affection. Delayed by extremely obscure questions, we have exceeded the limits of the brevity we desired.

“You shall not adore other gods”: that is, you shall not adore vice or gluttony, as those are read of “whose god is their belly,” nor avarice, nor fornication, nor the many other things that are the service of idols, as the Apostle confirms. Because of this the wrath of God comes. Adam first sinned through gluttony; Judas, Gehazi, Ananias, and Sapphira fell through avarice; and such was the case with Sodom and Gomorrah through fornication.

“You shall not make for yourself a graven image” is spoken of evil thoughts. For just as an iron tool cuts a piece from wood, so an evil thought does the same, as in the Gospel: “Evil thoughts defile human beings.”

“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain,” as in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all.”

“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” is spoken of the New Testament, and so forth. For just as he sanctified the Sabbath day and rested on it, so through the New Testament he sanctified us and made us rest from sins.

“Honor your father and your mother.” The Father is the Lord, and the mother is the Church: that is, “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” The Church is the house of God, the father and mother of all the righteous in baptism, confession, and repentance.

“You shall not kill”: that is, you shall not hate your brother. For he says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; and again: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.”

“You shall not commit adultery”: that is, you must cleave to God alone and not hand over to the devil what belongs to God, but render to God what is God’s—in works, words, and thoughts. Finally, the Prophet also says: “Indeed, it is good to cleave to God.”

“You shall not steal”: that is, what a person can do but does not do, as in the psalm: “But God said to the sinner, as far as the words ‘backward’” [the surviving citation is incomplete].

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” his house and everything belonging to him. By “neighbor” we understand the world, as in the saying: “Do not love the world,” and “Do not store up treasures on earth.” For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

I do not affirm that the author of this little explanation begins at the passage “You shall not adore other gods”—that is, “You shall not adore vices”—since I do not know the author. It is for the elders to establish this.

It follows: “Visiting the iniquity upon the third and fourth generation.” On the basis of this testimony heretics say that it is incompatible with the good God to condemn one person for another’s sin. For the sins of the fathers are visited upon the sons, upon the third and fourth generation, but they are not visited upon the fathers themselves, since he said nothing about the fathers.

The devil is the father of all sins. For the Lord says: “You are of your father the devil.” As long as the world stands, the devil does not receive back his sins; they will all be reserved for him in the future. Yet they are visited upon the sons whom he has begotten. For, through sin, people placed in the flesh are punished by the Lord, who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live.

We seek out sinners as ministers and accomplices of sin; the devil has them as a third or fourth generation. God scourges them when they sin in the present, so that they may endure more lightly in the future.

Finally, the devil begot Judas through sin. Satan entered into him, and Judas went away to the chief priests; for he could not accomplish the crime of the cross by himself. Then the chief priests stirred up and persuaded the people; thus a fourth generation arose from Judas.

“But he shows mercy to thousands of those who love him.” Those who love correction have no need of this, but to them he grants mercy alone. For “blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy.”

The law was written on two tablets because of the two Testaments, or because of love of God and neighbor. The stone tablets signify the hardness of the Jews’ hearts.

It is added: “You shall not make for yourselves gods of gold or silver,” so that we may not accept any superfluous meaning, however radiant it may seem, or empty eloquence.

“You shall make an altar of earth for me.” To make an altar of earth is to hope in Christ’s humanity. And we offer a gift of offerings on an altar of earth if we establish our actions firmly in faith in the Lord’s Incarnation.

It follows: “But if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones.” The hewn stones are those who divide unity. Christ does not receive such people into his body, whose figure that altar foreshadows.

Of unhewn stones it is said: “As living stones, be built up.” No iron has been applied to these, because they have not received the darts of the evil one.

It follows: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar.” That is, you shall not reach me by gradually preferring one person to another. This is what the Arians do, dividing the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The statement “You shall make an altar of earth,” which we discussed above, is taught by others to be the third distinction between gentiles and Jews. They differed in their bodies, in their clothing, and in the altar of earth. This altar of earth is also said to signify that the Jews had a heart of flesh; the stone altar, that the gentiles built with a heart of stone.

These altars also prefigure two Churches: by the altar of earth, the Church of the Old Testament; by the stone altar, the New.

## CHAPTERS XXI–XXII–XXIII–XXIV

[Col. 0321A]

Many commandments of the law are then given, which we shall pass over briefly. Since we do not find them explained and understood simply by our predecessors, they edify the hearers.

After this it is commanded: “If a Hebrew boy should happen to come into slavery, let him serve for seven years, and in the seventh year let him be released from slavery. But if he does not wish to leave slavery, his ear shall be pierced, and he shall be a slave forever.”

We too, serving throughout the six ages of this world, are freed in the seventh year—that is, in the eternal Sabbath—provided that we wish to be free and are Hebrews, that is, people passing through this world. While we are in this world, we serve worldly desires. If we wish to be freed from them, the ear shall be pierced in testimony of disobedience; and when we have been freed with our wife and children whom we have produced—that is, with the flesh and works of sin—we shall be slaves forever.

This Hebrew slave can also be understood as signifying the whole human race, which was freed in the seventh year—that is, in the rest of the New Testament.

“With whatever garment he entered, with such let him go out”: that is, let him come from the law of nature into the new law with faith, which was also a garment. His master is over all.

The good teacher gave him a wife: that is, he joined his soul to him. The sons and daughters signify good understandings and thoughts according to this interpretation.

He himself will go out with his clothing—that is, with the law of nature or faith—and will be brought to the door—that is, to the rulers. The doorposts are the second law. He will pierce his ear with an awl—that is, he will preach him through preaching—and he will be a slave, that is, of Christ or of the teacher.

The two men who quarrel are two disputants arguing about certain questions of Scripture. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing; the servant of the Lord must not quarrel.”

The pregnant woman is the soul that has recently conceived the word of God. She is called a woman because of her weakness. Struck by the quarreling men, she casts away the word of the Lord, which she had conceived only slightly.

The one who struck her shall be subject to a penalty in whatever amount the woman’s husband demands. He will be afflicted through repentance because he afflicted a weak person. The penalty is for the whole teaching that pleased Christ, because the faithful soul already has a proper husband. Or, certainly, it is whatever the teacher demands, since he stands on behalf of Christ’s Church.

It may be that he instructs and restores the one whom he injured. But if death follows, “he shall give life for life.” This is to be understood at the judgment before the Judge, who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.

Or it may be that one who is conscious of such a great scandal—of having spiritually killed a human soul—should also give his own soul for the soul of the one whom he scandalized, and, if necessary, work for God even unto death, so that the other may return and be restored to the faith.

If he injured an eye—that is, disturbed the soul’s understanding—the turbulent understanding with which he injured his brother shall be taken away.

But if he injured his brother’s tooth—that is, the understanding by which he was chewing Scripture in order to reach its inner meaning—his tooth shall be removed, since he did not properly chew the foods of Scripture.

His hand is the soul’s power, by which it can seek and grasp something; alternatively, it signifies his action. So too his foot is that with which he walks toward good and evil.

Therefore, if the soul suffers scandal not only in faith but also in actions, the things signified by the hands shall be cast out; the feet shall be removed because they provided a stumbling block; and the hands by which he does not work well, together with the feet by which he does not walk well, shall be removed. He receives the punishment of the burned because he burned the soul.

Through each of these details it is shown that this striker, with all his members mutilated, is to be cut off from the body of the Church, so that the others may be afraid.

After this the Israelite people are commanded to offer God tithes and firstfruits of everything. The firstfruits indicate the beginnings of good works, or the good will itself, which precedes the work—something the Pelagians claim for themselves by attributing it to their own power. When God commands that these be offered to him by us, he shows that they belong to his grace.

Every number grows up to ten, and therefore we take the tenth, the beginning of the completion of works, as the inclination toward consummation.

What is said, “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep,” signifies that the donkey is impurity, while the sheep is innocence. To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to turn the beginnings of an impure life toward the simplicity of innocence, so that, after an unjust person has practiced impure things—which the Lord rejects—he may bring forth for practice those things that are clean and suitable to place upon God’s altar.

It follows: “You shall not redeem it; it shall be killed,” because an impure mind, if it is not changed for the better, will be killed by eternal death.

## CHAPTER XXV

In the Ark of the Covenant the tablets had been stored, signifying the observance of the old and new law in the Church.

The Ark is made of incorruptible wood. The Church is built from saints in mind and body. It ought to radiate like gold, both inwardly through the splendor of life and outwardly through the brightness of doctrine.

The golden crown around it is the unity of the Church. The four rings are the four Gospels, preached in the unity of the Church, by which she is girded and stretched out through the four regions of the world.

They also make poles of setim wood, which are inserted into those same rings. These signify strong and persevering teachers, who are to be sought as incorruptible, always clinging to the holy Church through instruction in the sacred volumes, constantly proclaiming unity, and, as though inserted into the rings, carrying the Ark. They are also commanded to cover them with gold, so that when they have instructed others by their speech, they too may shine with the splendor of life.

This Ark contains two tablets; the Church contains the two Testaments. It also contains a golden urn, which we understand as Christ’s flesh, and within it has the manna of perpetual divinity, pure and stored away.

Aaron’s rod is the scepter of the true high priest, Jesus, which he entrusted to the holy Church.

The mercy seat above the Ark indicates Christ himself, who, standing between God and human beings, intervenes as mediator and propitiator. The mercy seat is placed upon the Ark; thus Christ is the head of the Church. At his right and left stand two cherubim, signifying the fullness of knowledge, that is, love of God and neighbor.

Others understand the two cherubim as the two Testaments, which overshadow Christ’s sacred humanity. They look toward the mercy seat with faces turned toward it, when the Testaments are turned in spiritual understanding; then they agree with each other for the better.

That altar signifies Christ’s body, or all the saints, in whom the divine fire always burns and in whom the flesh is consumed.

The table is the faith of the Church, or Scripture, on which one is nourished with various foods.

The lampstand bore the image of the Holy Spirit, who illumines the Church with a sevenfold grace. That lampstand is also said to be that of “the four Romans” (quatuor Romanorum; sense uncertain). Others understand the lampstand as Christ, bearing the seven Churches in which the sevenfold splendor of the Holy Spirit flashes forth.

This lampstand had tongs, which can signify the two Testaments, by which vices are cleansed. Outside, the true lampstand burns, because the grace of the Holy Spirit shines forth without the veil of the ancient law.

The oil taken from olive trees signifies that same grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the light of truth is hidden in our hearts.

## CHAPTER XXVI

The tabernacle allegorically signifies the Church, established in the wilderness of this world and constructed in various forms. The tabernacle is made partly of less valuable and partly of beautiful materials, demonstrating that some are righteous and others impious, though all the faithful are constituted within the Church.

The columns are the holy apostles, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Those who were regarded as pillars.” They are silver-plated when they proclaim the divine utterance.

The bases are rightly the prophets and apostles. For holy teachers place the Church upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles.

The golden capital of the columns is the one of whom it is said: “The head of the man is Christ.”

The gilded boards are teachers expanded in preaching.

What else are the rams’ skins than the leaders and superiors who signify the Church? Since they are compelled to devote themselves to temporal concerns, they must endure the winds and rains of temptations arising from the adversities of this world, so that those within the Church who are spiritual, shining like linen, purple, and hyacinth, may meanwhile be radiant while their rulers labor outside against the storms of this world.

The veil in the middle of the tabernacle signifies that the people of the Church are not permitted to see the things that are near until they arrive. For now we see through a mirror; we have not yet reached the Holy of Holies.

Those things in the present may be called “holy,” but the Holy of Holies is the kingdom of heaven, into which one enters once for all, where there is a multitude of knowledge, that is, the cherubim.

Meanwhile, in the present Church we possess the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, shining as in a purest lampstand.

This veil can also signify the period that existed under the law, because what the law and the prophets foretold remained hidden. But through Christ’s Passion this veil was torn, and what had been obscured from the Jews was revealed to Christians.

That the bases are silver and the boards gilded shows that the commandments of the apostles are clearer than those of the prophets.

## CHAPTER XXVII

The tents sewn with loops, suspended from rings, and attached by ropes signify the remaining multitude of the believing people, which hangs upon the ropes of faith.

Twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth, it signifies the law and the Gospel. The fact that it was seven and twenty and eight, while there were ten curtains, signifies the Decalogue. These curtains are joined to one another by fifty rings, because all the righteous are united by the gift of the Holy Spirit through the bond of charity.

For on the fiftieth day after the Passover the Holy Spirit came upon the eleven disciples, in a number exceeding ten. Sinners are signified because the number exceeds ten, yet they become part of the Church, and the goats’-hair covering itself is joined by fifty loops because of the image of the remission of sins; hence the fiftieth signifies remission.

The figure of the former tabernacle is a type of the Church, and the various gifts signify the gifts of merits by which the Churches are adorned.

Wisdom is compared with gold; the speech of preaching, with silver. The fact that men offered gifts together with women signifies that both stronger deeds and the deeds of the weak contribute to the adornment of the Church. This offering is not forced but voluntary, because faith is voluntary.

The bracelets that bind the arms demonstrate the works of superiors laboring greatly; the earrings, the obedience of those subject to them; the rings, the seal of hidden things; the armlets, good works; the golden vessel, understanding of the Divinity; the hyacinth, hope of heavenly things; the purple, understanding of the Passion; the twice-dyed scarlet, charity, which adorns love of God and neighbor; and the linen, the most splendid whiteness of holiness, for linen is exceedingly white.

The goat hair, from which the roughness of sackcloth is woven, signifies the harsh affliction of repentance. Through the extended diversity of works, one tabernacle is made.

The setim wood, which is incorruptible, signifies the minds of the saints, since in the flesh they are incorruptible. Precious stones are the apostles, confessors, and all the saints. The ointment is the chrism with which all the righteous are anointed.

Morally, each one of us can also construct a tabernacle within himself. He ought to have shining silver columns of virtues and spread out courts when he has enlarged his heart, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Be enlarged, you also.”

He can also strengthen it with poles when he binds it together in unity, and have two bases. When it is placed upon the foundation of the words of the apostles and prophets and has gilded capitals on its columns, Christ is the righteous head of all the living.

He ought to have an altar fixed within himself: namely, a clean heart. With the knife of continence he should sacrifice; he should slaughter pride like bulls, anger like rams, and lust and every desire like a goat. Yet he should know how to separate from these sacrifices the right arm, the whole breast—which is described as correptum (“taken” or “corrected”; uncertain)—and the jaw, for speaking the word of God.

He should know that the lampstand is to be placed among the holy things, so that they may be lamps always burning. For “the lamp of your body is your eye.” Let him place this lampstand in the south so that it looks toward the north.

When the light has been kindled—that is, with a vigilant heart—he must always look toward the north and watch him who comes from the north; that is, he must observe the devil’s cunning, from which the enemy may snatch him away.

The table of the Presence, bearing twelve loaves, should also be placed on the northern side, looking toward the south, so that it may possess knowledge of the New Testament, by which we are all nourished, and the apostolic word both in power and in number. Let it look toward the south, from which the Lord came.

Within the innermost chambers of his heart he has an altar of incense, so that he may say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ.”

He also has the Ark of the Covenant, in which are the tablets of the law, so that he may meditate on his law day and night and so that his memory may become an Ark of the books of God.

Within him there is also an urn containing manna—that is, a stored understanding of the word of God—which should be subtle and sweet—and Aaron’s rod, priestly teaching and the flowering severity of discipline.

The incense made from four most fragrant spices, ground to great fineness—namely, stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense—signifies the prayers of the righteous, as the Apocalypse shows, although in its form it indicates four kinds of elements.

These four are arranged so that frankincense, which is soothing, may be compared with air; stacte with water; galbanum and onycha with earth and fire. Thus, through this, everything that is in heaven, and below and within, and below, and in the waters, may be pleasing to God. Incense is the praise of every creature.

The blood with which Moses sprinkled the people and everything else signifies Christ’s blood, by which Christ’s people—the faithful people—are sprinkled. The faith of the Church is signified by the fat, whose breast is wrapped and whose lobe of the liver is offered upon the altar.

The breast itself and the right arm are given to Aaron and his sons. The fat with which the breast is wrapped signifies the thoughts with which the heart is enclosed, according to the saying: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?”

Desire is in the liver. But after the fire of the Spirit has burned the fat of the breast—that is, all the thoughts with which the breast is enclosed—together with the lobe of the liver, that is, the desire for lust breaking forth through the eyes, then the reward of the mind is the breast and the arm: in the breast, pure thoughts; in the heart, knowledge of the law and of doctrines; in the arm, good works and battle against the devil.

Thus, what they have conceived, they present by example. They are commanded to have these things on the left side: these offerings concerning vices and the things offered to the priests are given to the Lord.

The jaw signifies one who speaks and is learned, so that what we have conceived in the breast we may bring forth with the mouth.

By the belly he shows that, for minds consecrated to God, whatever we eat is cast into the privy. Hence it is said: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods.”

## CHAPTERS XXVIII–XXXI
The common garments of the priests are linen breeches, which reach to the knees and the hamstrings. They conceal the private parts, and their upper portion is tightly fastened below the navel, so that, whenever they slaughter victims unencumbered, carry burdens, or should they fall, no indecency may be exposed. This type of garment is called in Hebrew *maraste*, and by our people *femoralia*, “breeches,” reaching to the knees. Josephus, however, says that they are made not of twisted byssus [Col. 0326A] but of linen. The tunic *poderis*, that is, a full-length tunic, is made of double linen; Josephus calls it *byssina*, “of byssus,” and it is called *catonath*, which in the Hebrew language is rendered *linea*, “linen.” It clings to the body and is so tightly drawn by its close-fitting sleeves that there is no wrinkle at all in the garment, and it descends to the legs. The priests use this tunic so that, while wearing the beauty of the garments, they may move swiftly without being naked.

The third kind of garment is what they call *Bonet*, which we may call a belt, girdle, or sash. It has the appearance of a serpent, because it was woven round in such a way that, having been extended, you might think it a longer purse; or it was made beneath a covering of scarlet, purple, and hyacinth, with a linen warp, for beauty and strength. It was so ornamented by the *polymita* technique that it displayed various flowers and gems, not woven by the artisan’s hand but rendered as though they had been made according to his design. [Col. 0326B]

They fasten the linen tunic mentioned above between the navel and the breast with this belt. The belt is four fingers wide and hangs down for the most part toward the legs; when the priest needs to perform the sacrifices with greater freedom of movement, it is thrown back over his left shoulder.

The fourth kind of garment is a round cap, such as we see painted on *mulixi* [reading uncertain], as though its rough middle were divided and one part placed upon the head. The Greeks call it *Enarradarum* [reading uncertain], while some call it a *galerus*. It has no peak at the top and does not cover the whole head as far as the hair; rather, it leaves a third of the forehead uncovered and is fastened at the back of the head like a fillet. It is thin and not easily lifted from the head. It is made of byssus [Col. 0326C] and so skillfully covered with linen that no trace of the needle appears on the outside.

The four garments are therefore: the breeches; the linen tunic; the girdle, which is covered with purple, scarlet, linen, and hyacinth; and the cloak of which we have just spoken. Both priests and Levites use these. The remaining garments belong specifically to the high priests. The first of these is the *millioli*, that is, a full-length hyacinth-colored tunic with sleeves sewn to its sides from the same material. At the upper part, where it is put on around the neck, it is open—what ordinary people call the neck-opening—and this is adorned with very strong, self-woven work so that it will not easily tear. At the lower edge, that is, at the hem, there are seventy golden bells and as many pomegranates, woven in the same colors as those mentioned above for the girdle. Between two bells there is one pomegranate, and between two pomegranates one bell, so that when the high priest enters the sanctuary he may proceed entirely vocal. If he does not do this, he dies immediately. [Col. 0326D]

The sixth garment is the shoulder-piece, called by the Hebrews *Ephoth*. This type of garment belongs only to the high priests; nevertheless, those who are Levites are also said to have worn an *Ephoth*. For there is another kind, woven in four colors—hyacinth, linen, scarlet, and purple—and also in gold, as though it were plain: strips of linen and gold leaf, that is, sheets of gold, are wonderfully stretched at the edges, from which cut threads are twisted. Together with a covering of three colors—hyacinth, scarlet, and purple—and with a linen warp, and vermilion thread, it forms a little cloak of extraordinary beauty. It dazzles the eyes like a *caracalla*, but without its hood. [Col. 0327A]

Nothing is woven across the breast, since a place is left for the future breastpiece. Between the two shoulders are two enclosed and distinct stones, one on each side, which Josephus calls sardonyxes, agreeing with the Hebrew text and with Aquila; they were intended to indicate either the stones’ color or their origin. On each stone are written six names of the patriarchs. On the right shoulder are the elder sons of Jacob, and on the left the younger, so that when the high priest enters the holy place he may carry upon his shoulders the names of the people for whom he is about to entreat the Lord.

The seventh is the garment called in Hebrew *Ossen* and in Greek *Logion*; we may call it the *rationale*, or breastpiece. It is a short square cloth, worked with gold and with the same four colors as the shoulder-piece. It is a span in size, square, and doubled so that it will not easily tear. Set into it are twelve stones of extraordinary beauty, arranged in four rows, with three stones in each row:

- in the first row, sardius, topaz, and emerald;
- in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper;
- in the third, ligure, agate, and amethyst;
- in the fourth, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx.

On each stone, according to the order of the tribes, the names of the twelve tribes are written. Four rings belonging to the four parts of the breastpiece, made of gold, are placed opposite the shoulder-piece. Another set of four rings is placed opposite them, and the two sets are joined to one another by hyacinth-colored ribbons. Moreover, lest the size and weight of the stones tear the woven threads, they are bound above and enclosed in gold. But since this would not be sufficient to remedy their weakness, chains of gold were made and covered, for beauty’s sake, with golden clasps. The breastpiece would have its upper two larger rings, which were fastened to the neighboring golden rings of the shoulder-piece, and two others below. Behind, on the shoulder-piece opposite the breast and stomach, there were golden rings on either side, which were joined and connected by chains to the lower rings of the breastpiece. Thus the breastpiece and shoulder-piece were joined together, or fitted together, so that, when connected, they appeared to those looking at them to be one woven fabric. [Col. 0327C]

The eighth is a golden plate on which the name of the Lord is written or engraved in Hebrew, namely, in the four Hebrew letters *loth*, *He*, and *Vau* [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. This is placed upon the linen cap, and it is common to all priests. In the case of the high priest something more is added: a hyacinth-colored fillet on the forehead, together with the whole splendor of the high priest.

The Hebrews say that the four colors signify the four elements, from which the universe is composed. Linen is assigned to earth, because it grows from the earth; purple to the sea, because the *cocculus* is dyed from it; hyacinth entirely to the air, because of the similarity of its color; scarlet to fire and air. In place of scarlet, according to Latin usage, the Hebrews write *thothati*, that is, vermilion. They also recall that it was fitting for the high priest to pray to the Creator of all things not only for Israel but for the whole world. For this world and its elements consist of earth, water, air, and fire.

The first garment, the linen one, signifies earth; the second, the hyacinth-colored one, signifies air [Col. 0328A] because of its resemblance in color. The hyacinth-colored garment itself, extending from the head to the ankles, indicates that the air reaches downward as far as the earth. The pomegranates and bells placed below signify lightning and thunder, or earth and water, and the harmony of all the elements. The fact that the colors mentioned above are woven into the purest gold signifies that the divine meaning penetrates everything through providence.

The shoulder-piece and the two stones signify the hemispheres, one of which is above the earth and the other beneath the earth; or the sun, which shines above, and thunder, which resounds. The breast of the priest is enclosed by these. They interpret the linen tunic, by which the earth is girded, as the Ocean, placed around the earth in the middle; and they say that the earth, although it contains all things like a point, is surrounded by the elements. The twelve stones on the breastpiece are interpreted either as the circle of the zodiac or as the twelve months. The changing conditions of the earth, of time, of heat, and of cold descend from the course and order of heaven. Hence the breastpiece is also fastened more tightly to the *Ephod*. [Col. 0328B]

What is said to be revealed in the breastpiece—“manifestation and truth”—means that the truth of God is not falsehood, but is manifested to human beings through many arguments. Above all, the *cidaris* and the hyacinth-colored fillet signify heaven; the golden plate on the forehead of the high priest, with the name of the Lord written upon it, signifies that everything beneath the earth is governed by God’s judgment. It was therefore right that the high priest, bearing in his garments the food of all created things, should indicate that all things need the Lord’s mercy. [Col. 0328C]

Concerning the linen breeches they usually say this: the principle of seeds and generation belongs to the flesh and is assigned to the earth. For, he says, “You are earth, and to earth you will go.” The cause of this matter—how from the smallest seeds and the most repulsive beginnings the whole multitude of human beings and the beauty of all things arise—is hidden and does not lie open to human eyes.

Wrapped in the excessive obscurity of spiritual mysteries, we have exceeded the limits of brevity. But Aaron, the great priest, gives life to the one to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever.” The priestly garment is the Church. The breeches, by which the private parts are concealed, can signify that the Church of Christ must possess chastity and integrity. Priests do not receive the garments unless they first wash their ways. For new wine must be put into new wineskins, because we must be cleansed by the precepts of the Law. And when we have removed our tunics, then, purified by baptism, we put on the garments of Christ.

The linen tunic *poderis*, that is, the full-length tunic, signifies Christ’s humanity, which is from the earth. Linen arises from the earth; alternatively, the linen tunic signifies the body made white through baptism. The belts by which the priestly breast is girded signify the choir of the saints, who embrace Christ in the unity of faith.

The *cidaris*, that is, the *thara*, signifies the splendor of divinity. Thus the one and the same person appears adorned according to his human nature by the weight of the garment and according to the *cidaris* by its ornament. We too can say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord.” The hyacinth-colored fillet signifies understanding of heavenly things. [Col. 0329A] Hyacinth shines with the color of air, so that the holy Church may think upon the things above, if its manner of life is in heaven.

The pomegranates signify the unity of the Church. For just as many seeds are protected within a single outer rind in a pomegranate, so the unity of the holy Church gathers countless peoples, whom an inner diversity of works holds together. The bells among the pomegranates signify the prophets and holy teachers placed in the midst of the Church. These bells are situated at the lower part of the garment, and therefore they continually discuss the end of this world and the future.

The shoulder-piece signifies the Savior’s power and kingdom, “whose government is upon his shoulder.” The shoulder-piece and breastpiece may also be understood as our works and our reason. The two stones on the right [Col. 0329B] signify the Church, or the two peoples: the Gentile people on the right and the Jewish people on the left; or Christ and the Church; or spirit and letter.

The breastpiece placed upon the breast, distinguished by its fourfold arrangement of stones, figures the evangelical message, because it sets forth the teaching of truth in a fourfold order. The twelve names inscribed upon it signify the examples of the patriarchs, placed before the holy apostles for imitation. The breastpiece’s being doubled signifies that evangelical doctrine is both covered and hidden, and both simple and mystical. The golden plate shines on the forehead: learning in all things is of no benefit unless we are crowned with the knowledge of God.

Morally, too, gold shines in the high priest’s vestment when understanding gleams forth; joined to it is hyacinth, so that through everything he handles there may arise a love of heavenly things. [Col. 0329C] Royal purple is mixed with it, so that, as though by royal authority, he may suppress the suggestions of vices. Scarlet, twice dyed, is also joined to it, so that before the eyes of the inward Judge the good works of all virtues may be adorned with charity. Charity depends upon love of God and neighbor and shines, as it were, in a twofold dye; to this twice-dyed scarlet the twisted linen is joined.

Linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance and is therefore white; by it bodily chastity is signified. This, twisted together, is fastened to the beauty of the shoulder-piece, because chastity is then led to the perfect whiteness of purity when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence. It is also girded with the belt, by which the incitements of lust and sexual desire are restrained.

When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is surrounded by the bells on the tunic [Col. 0329D], so that he may possess the voice of preaching and not, by silence, offend the judgment of the heavenly Judge. The pomegranate is also joined to the bells, so that through them the unity of the doctrine of faith may be signified.

The fact that the high priest entered the first part of the tabernacle daily to offer sacrifices prescribes for us continual daily diligence, so that every day we may offer a spiritual sacrifice of confession and praise—that is, humility in the chastity of our souls. “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.”

The fact that he entered once a year, leaving the people, into the Holy of Holies signifies our high priest Jesus Christ, who was placed in the flesh and remained with the people throughout the whole year. Of him it is written: “To call the accepted Lamb to the Lord” [wording uncertain]. He therefore enters the Holy of Holies once in that year, on the day of the Presentation; that is, having completed the appointed dispensation, he penetrated the heavens and entered to the Father, so that he might make him favorable toward the human race. For we have him as an advocate with the Father. [Col. 0330A]

When Moses clothed Aaron in these garments, nothing is added concerning the breeches. I think the reason is that the Law does not put its hand upon our genitals; rather, we ourselves ought to cover and veil what is more secret. For other virtues—for example, wisdom, courage, and justice—may also be judged by others. Only the conscience knows chastity, and human eyes certainly cannot be its judges, except for those who, like brute animals, have given themselves indiscriminately over to lust. The Apostle says concerning virgins [Col. 0330B]: “I have no command of the Lord”—as though Moses too were saying: “I do not clothe anyone in breeches, nor impose an obligation on anyone; whoever wishes may clothe himself.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

Then Moses descends from the mountain and breaks the tablets, indicating that a people consecrated to deceit is unworthy to receive the Law. He burns the calf that the Israelites had made, crushes it into fragments, scatters it in water, and gives the people the powder [the transmitted *polum* is uncertain] to drink.

Through this calf, that is, through the body of the devil, evil people are signified—human beings of whom the devil himself is the author. The gold appears to signify the rites of idolatry, whether instituted by the wise or fashioned by them. Moses, that is, the divine Law, therefore burns this calf, meaning the whole fellowship of the nations, with that fire of which it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” When the nations believe in him, the Savior crushes the devilish [Col. 0330C] form within them completely by the fire of his power; that is, he humbles and breaks apart that evil unity. He casts it into water, so that this calf—that is, the people who worship the idol—may be transferred by the Israelites, that is, by holy preachers, into their members, namely, into the Lord’s body, through baptism.

It should be understood that, according to the historical account, Moses transferred this calf to the people as a drink, as though he had thrown it upon the earth, or into water and fire. The point was plainly that the people devoted to idolatry might pass the whole thing through their bowels, so that they would be ashamed to worship their own excrement.

Moses’ command that many of those who had fashioned the idol be killed signifies the death of the vices into which they had fallen through that same idolatry. For the Apostle commands us to rage against such vices: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication and impurity.” [Col. 0330D] “You went from gate to gate”—from vice to vice—so that death might advance against the mind with the sword of rebuke.

But the number itself, three thousand slain, indicates the threefold form of the unlearned. For every sin is committed either by deed, by word, or by thought.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Moses therefore ascends the mountain again and receives the Law a second time. The first tablets, which were broken, signify the former Law, which ceased immediately because of the people’s sin. The others, however, are not broken, because the words of the New Testament will endure. Thus [Col. 0331A] the second reception also signifies the new.

Two writings are attributed to the Lord: the first on stone, the second on earth. This signifies that those to whom the Law was given on stones were harder, while those for whom it was written on earth were more pliable. The first writing was on bodies, and the second on souls. In both cases the writing was written by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

The ten commandments correspond especially well, since they are written upon the ten senses of body and soul. These ten commandments together with the two tablets make the number twelve. This is fitting because Christ gives admonition through the twelve apostles. And just as the two tablets preserve the ten commandments, so too did our sense once possess a dual form.

The fact that the tablets were restored after the worship of idols [Col. 0331B] signifies the renewal of the Law with Christ, following the worship of idols in the Old Testament. The fact that the same words were written the first and the second time signifies that the Law which is broken and the Law which is restored are the same.

Moses’ search for the material of the tablets demonstrates that we possess free choice and that the material of the Law lies before our reason. It belongs to God to inspire and inscribe upon the tablets. These tablets are broken until the day of judgment and are renewed. The tablets are broken, but the words are not broken, as it is said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

The ten words, multiplied through the five books of the Law, are multiplied into the five volumes of the Law. So too new inscriptions [Col. 0331C] are multiplied through the four Gospels.

Moses fasted for forty days. Elijah fasted for the same number, and the Lord himself also fasted. Through this we are instructed by the Law and the Prophets, and by the Lord himself in the Gospel, to restrain our appetite from all the enticements of this world by the fast of temperance, until the perfection of the Law’s Decalogue is completed through the four parts of this same world—that is, through preachers throughout the whole earth—so that ten multiplied by four may signify the number forty.

Joshua, going up to the mountain with Moses as his minister, signifies Christ, who was the minister of the Law and went with the Law.

These same days in Moses, Elijah, and the Lord alike signify the New Testament. The forty days of the Flood’s bodily punishment and of bodily healing in the Old Testament figure the Law. [Col. 0332A] In forty days there are six weeks. For the Law ought to be given through the number six, since the Law taught servitude for six days.

The fact that the days and nights are not counted separately by the Lord signifies that anger and understanding are together in the Law. Alternatively, it indicates the two peoples who would later profit from the Law: they are called the sons of light and the sons of night.

Then, because Moses feared to see the brightness of God, he received the answer that he could not see the one whom no human being could see and live. This signifies that, although human nature may progress after the resurrection as far as angelic brightness, it still cannot fully see his essence; even angelic perfection, whatever it may be, does not attain to knowing it completely. The Trinity alone knows itself perfectly, together with the humanity assumed, which is the third person in the Trinity. [Col. 0332B]

It follows: “There is a place with me, firm upon the rock, and you shall see my back.” We stand upon the rock so that we may see the back of God. We stand within the Church, and through the Gospels we see the back of God—that is, the humanity of the mediator between God and human beings. We cannot see his face and live, because, while we remain in the flesh, we do not yet rise fully into contemplation of his divinity.

Or certainly, what is said to Moses—“You shall see my back”—signifies that the Jewish people, whose person Moses now represents, would believe at the end of time when they stood upon the rock, that is, in the solidity of faith, at the time when he would show his hand, that is, his power, to the Jewish people. Some say that this was fulfilled because, according to the Gospel, Moses saw the back of God—that is, when, at a later time, he spoke with him on the mountain. [Col. 0332C]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

When Moses descends from the mountain, his face appears glorified, but it is nevertheless covered with a veil. This signifies that the Law is covered and concealed among the faithful by a mystical veil. The language of the Law possesses the glory of knowledge, but it does not disclose the secret; and it has the horns of the two Testaments, with which it advances armed against false doctrines.

Whenever Moses placed the veils of the Law, Scripture says that the veil was placed over the heart of the Jews; thus it speaks of those who cannot sustain the glory of the Law. But if they turn to the Lord, the veil of the killing letter will be removed, so that the spiritual meaning may be revealed.

# EXPLANATION OF THE THIRD BOOK OF MOSES,

which in Hebrew is called *VAICRA*, and in Greek and Latin *LEVITICUS*.

[Col. 0331]

## CHAPTERS I–III

[Col. 0331D]

The Lord called Moses and spoke to him, and so forth. Some customarily ask whether there is an order corresponding to the order of these books of the Law. The answer is as follows: Genesis signifies the statement, “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls”; Exodus, “giving wisdom to the simple”; Leviticus, “showing forth the commandment of the Lord and enlightening”; Numbers, “the judgments of God, truly justified.” These four books, by their number, prefigure the four Gospels. Deuteronomy, however, signifies the whole Gospel, since *Deuteronomy* is interpreted as “the renewed law.”

But we must explain how the order just mentioned corresponds to the order of the books. The first statement is suitably assigned to Genesis because Genesis declares that all things were created by the word of God—and for that reason it is called “law.” It also contains the conversion of souls: from life to death, as in Adam, and from death to life, as in Noah. Exodus, “giving wisdom to the simple,” is fulfilled in what God promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob concerning the land of promise. For all are simple in their cooperation with God. Leviticus, “the enlightening commandment that gives light,” distinguishes between clean animals. Numbers contains the true judgments of God, especially in the prophecy of Balaam, in the blessings and the curses.

There is one calling found before this one, namely, in the knowledge of God under the law of nature: “And God made man,” and so forth. There are many callings after this, because we are called from the law of nature to the law of the letter—not by abandoning the former, but by advancing through the laws—and from the letter to the New Testament: “Come to me, all you,” and so forth.

“And Moses called,” and so forth: this signifies the whole world, which is called by God through faith from paganism to baptism, and to repentance, or to faith in the Trinity, or from the body to the future life; or it may refer to the judgment, as in: “Come, you blessed,” and so forth. In the wording, the dignity of the person is displayed, since the Lord called not someone else but Moses; at the same time, his lowliness is shown in comparison with the one who rules.

It may also be understood in the statement “The Lord called him from the tabernacle” that God the Father calls Christ from heaven to the Incarnation. God the Father commands him to speak to the children of Israel—that is, to all believers. “And the Lord called him,” and so forth, signifies Christ calling the apostolic people from the law of the letter, to whom it is said, “Preach the Gospel to every creature”: that is, among the second people, as in Peter’s preaching to the three thousand. Or the primitive people call the second people from the tabernacle—that is, from the Church. Alternatively, each teacher calls Moses, that is, every believer. By “the children of Israel,” moreover, the understanding of the perfect may be indicated.

A *hostia* is properly so called because it is killed before the entrance of the tabernacle—or from the notion of “display.” An *oblation* is when a victim from the flocks is offered, which is then killed. A *holocaust* means “wholly burned,” that is, something brought to completion. A *sacrifice* is made from bread; a *libation*, from liquid. Alternatively, *oblation* derives from what is signified to the priests by the people, and *victim* from nourishment offered in sacrifice.

In all these oblations in Leviticus, a spiritual meaning must be sought. As it is said elsewhere: Just as the word of God, proceeding into this world, was covered by the appearance of flesh, so that one thing was seen in him and another understood—the appearance of flesh being open to all, but recognition of his divinity available to very few—in the same way the word of God is proclaimed through the Lawgiver and the prophecies, while the veil of the letter covers it. The spiritual meaning is hidden within and was altogether apparent to only a few.

At the beginning of Leviticus, the kinds of the principal offerings that are commanded to be offered to the Lord are described: first, a calf; second, a lamb; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, fine flour mixed with oil. The remaining sacrifices were offered according to the nature of the circumstances.

It is not without significance that it says, “If anyone from among you offers a gift,” as though a person could offer something other than a human being, even though “If anyone from among you offers a gift” would have sufficed. Elsewhere it says, “If a soul offers a gift.” Thus one passage says that a man offers, another that a soul offers, another that a high priest offers, another that a synagogue offers, another that a ruler offers, another that a single-minded person offers, and another that the people of the land offer.

Christ was sacrificed in the calf on account of the power of the cross; he himself was the lamb on account of innocence; he himself was the ram on account of sovereignty; he himself was the goat on account of the likeness of sinful flesh. In the turtledove and the dove, on account of God and man; in the fine flour, on account of the Church, which is his body, gathered from many members as from many grains, ground by the mill of the Law and the Gospel, mixed with the water of baptism, anointed with the oil of chrism, and made firm by the Holy Spirit.

Morally, we too offer a calf to God when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational impulses; a young goat when we conquer wantonness; a dove when we preserve simplicity of mind; and a turtledove when we maintain chastity. This species of bird is said to preserve a single and chaste marriage. We offer unleavened bread when we walk not in the leaven of malice but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

But when it is said, “Let him place his hand upon the head of the victim,” this may be understood historically as though it said, “Let the one who brings the sacrifice to the priests hold it.” It must also be understood spiritually: the work must be placed upon the cruelty [or: severity] of Christ’s divinity, since the divinity of Christ is indicated by the head of the victim.

That man who first placed everything before the Lord as a gift for sacrifice not inappropriately signifies the human race. Of him the Gospel says, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” He offers the calf—the fattened calf that the father slaughtered when his son had advanced and been restored to him. This man, therefore, because he possessed nothing of his own substance, found this calf sent from heaven, yet coming through the succession of the patriarchs and generations.

For this reason it does not simply say “a calf,” but “a calf from the cattle.” It is male or female. Truly male is the one who knows nothing of sin, which belongs to feminine weakness, and who had no stain of sin. He offers it not in the tabernacle but at the entrance of the tabernacle: for Christ suffered outside the gate, or because he came to his own and his own did not receive him.

The blood is offered by the sons of Aaron. This may be understood of Annas and Caiaphas and the others who took counsel to seize and kill Jesus by deceit, pronounced him guilty of death, and shed righteous blood with impious voices. The blood is poured out beside the base of the altar, because a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem.

He places his hand upon the head of the calf—that is, the sins of the human race. For he is the head of his Church, the one who bears the sin of the world.

It follows: “After removing the victim’s skin, they shall cut its limbs into pieces,” and so forth. He removes the calf’s skin who takes away the veil of the letter from the word of God and divides its inner spiritual mysteries. He places these limbs not upon the ground but upon the altar, because he does not disclose divine mysteries to unworthy people, but to those who are God’s altar, in whom the divine fire always burns and in whom the flesh is continually consumed.

To divide the limbs means to distinguish appropriately the stages of spiritual progress: whether one has touched Christ’s fringe, washed his feet with tears, anointed his head, or reclined upon his breast. Whoever knows how to express these matters according to the progress of each person can be that priest who removes the skin and divides the limbs.

Then, after wood has been brought, fire is kindled upon the altar, signifying the divinity of Christ. For divinity is from above, whither this fire hastens. The fire burns upon the altar when a teacher discusses not only something concerning Christ’s Incarnation but also something concerning his divinity.
