The wood signifies the works performed in the Savior, in which his burning divinity was displayed. Or certainly the wood may signify the Passion: Christ’s Passion continued up to the wood. But when he was suspended upon the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was completed. This holocaust of his flesh, sacrificed through the wood of the cross, joined human things to divine things.

Meanwhile, he commands the inner parts and the feet to be washed with water: this signifies that the inner parts—that is, the conscience—and the feet—that is, the senses—are cleansed.

Morally, as we said above, we too possess a calf, and indeed a proud one, which we should offer: namely, our flesh. If we wish to offer it as a gift to God, let us bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle, so that it may be able to receive the divine hearing. Let it be male and know nothing of the female; let it seek nothing dissolute or soft.

What does “Place your hand upon the victim” mean? It means: place upon it the bridle of self-restraint, and do not remove from it the hand of discipline, as did the one who says, “I discipline my body,” and “Sacrifice it to the Lord”—that is, “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.”

The sons of Aaron offer the blood. They are called the priest or his sons, for they alone understand the Lord. Through them you must offer the blood, so that you may chastise carnal desires rationally. There are indeed people who offer, but not through the priest, because they do not understand and do not act according to the Law.

The second victim is the lamb, which, as we said above, signifies Christ on account of his innocence: the very lamb who takes away the sins of the world. He is also the young goat, because through his death the devil, the author of sin, is recognized and slaughtered.

The lamb is sacrificed at the side of the altar that faces north. Christ suffered for this purpose: to overthrow the prince of the north. For, “plundering the vessels of the strong man, he first bound the strong man,” and so forth. What follows concerning the lamb is explained in the same way as what concerns the calf.

The third sacrifice is the turtledove or the dove. The turtledove may signify Christ’s humanity, as Solomon says: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove.” The dove signifies the Holy Spirit: “When you see the Spirit descending,” he says, “as a dove.”

Accordingly, a man offers Christ’s humanity joined to the Holy Spirit—that is, either the human race, as we said above, which Scripture often recalls under the name “man”; or every person living rationally; or certainly Jesus Christ, who offered himself. The man mentioned above offers sacrifices in these ways.

Fourth is the soul. This may be the Church, which offers fine flour mixed with oil—that is, a life adorned with charity—or the soul, namely, the animal man, who according to the Apostle does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. His gifts are far inferior to those of man, that is, of the perfect person. He has neither a calf, nor a lamb, nor a young goat, nor a dove to offer; he offers only fine flour, that is, this ordinary life, for example, a life devoted to agriculture or navigation. Nevertheless, he offers a gift to God, fine flour anointed with oil. For every soul needs the oil of divine mercy.

Frankincense is also offered with this sacrifice, because whatever weakness we perceive in our actions must be entreated by persistent prayer, so that with the prophet we may say: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

By the oven, the weight of temptations is suitably signified; by the frying pan, steadfastness of soul and strength of mind; by the griddle, manifold assault.

In the various offerings, apart from the sacrifice for sin, after certain portions have been sacrificed upon the altar, the remainder is assigned to the use of the priests. These portions either fulfill what properly belongs to the Lord, such as fasting and self-restraint, or accomplish what must be done for our neighbors, such as giving alms, reconciling those who are at odds, and so forth.

The fact that honey was not offered in God’s sacrifice signifies that nothing pleasurable or sweet belonging to this world should please us; rather, it should possess something of the biting quality of truth. Hence the Passover too is eaten with bitterness.

Salt is commanded to be mixed into every sacrifice, so that in everything we offer in honor of Christ we may possess the discernment of rational salt.

We offer only the firstfruits of leavened bread and honey; we do not place them upon the altar, because at the beginnings of faith we possess imperfect works, according to the Apostle: “We receive milk as drink, not solid food.” When the time comes for us to place perfect gifts—that is, good works—upon the altar of the heart, we abandon all that is imperfect.

For this reason the command concerning firstfruits follows. It signifies that we must consecrate to God the beginning of our works, enlightened by the fire of divine love, and that we must perform acts of discernment between good and evil when, stripping off the old man, we put on the new.

The remaining matters concerning the qualities of the offerings can be understood from what has already been said. But we must know that in offerings of well-being not only males but also females are selected. When peace exists in a person who is engaged in battles against vices, not only stronger works but also weaker works are of great value.

The stronger works are chastity, contempt for all possessions, love of enemies, and so forth. The lesser works are restraint within marriage, giving alms from one’s possessions, doing good to enemies, and so forth.

## CHAPTER IV

The command concerning the soul that sins through ignorance follows. How beautifully it calls it “soul,” not “spirit,” since Scripture does not say that the spirit sins. For “the fruit of the Spirit is love and joy.” Nor does it call it “man,” in whom the image of God is corrupted by the coming of sin and is renewed through baptism in knowledge.

It follows: “If the priest who has been anointed sins.” In this third case mercy is shown as well: the one who is a priest, even though anointed, is not free from fault; nevertheless, he is commanded to offer a sacrifice for his sin, by which he demonstrates God’s clemency toward him.

The calf is sacrificed in two ways: once as a gift and once for sin. The text then appears to repeat corruptly: “but the one offered as a gift, once for sin.” But the one offered as a gift is consumed upon the altar of the holocaust; the one offered for sin is commanded to be burned outside the camp, together with its hide, in the place of refuse and dung, while only its fat is offered upon the altar.

See the mighty Jesus, who through his blood reconciles, according to the Apostle, “the things on earth and the things in heaven.” He is the calf who was offered in heaven, not for sin but as a gift. On earth, however, where death reigned from Adam to Moses, he was offered for sin—that is, he suffered outside the camp of the angels. Of these Jacob says: “This is the camp of God.”

Outside that camp, therefore, is every earthly place in which we dwell and in which Christ suffered in the flesh. The statement that it is burned “with the dung and in the place of refuse” signifies that, in comparison with heavenly bodies, this human body is figuratively called dung. For what else does that dung signify except the martyrdom of the humanity he assumed?

Although these matters have been discussed boldly, the hearing of the righteous can nevertheless be nourished by them. The same things are to be understood concerning that calf by the whole congregation.

When the priest’s sin is mentioned, the text does not say that he sins unknowingly, because that priest signifies Christ, in whom no ignorance can be found. Although he committed no sin, he was made sin for us; and for that sin which he received and bore from us he offered the calf—that is, an undefiled flesh—and thus he himself is both priest and victim.

What follows, “causing the people to sin,” is understood of Christ in this way: just as he brings life to believers, so he brings death to unbelievers. For he has been set, it says, “for the fall and resurrection of many.” He caused the unbelieving people to sin because he could be killed in the flesh. If he had not come in the flesh, his blood would not have come. For he says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.”

Morally, this priest signifies the sense of piety and religion within us, which functions as a kind of priesthood through the prayers we pour out before God. If this sense commits some offense, it causes the entire people of good works within us to sin. For if the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness?

The whole congregation may be understood as the people of virtues mentioned above. The ruler signifies the power of reason within us, as though reason itself were to sin and we were to do something foolish.

We must fear what is said: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has become foolish, it is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside,” and so forth.

This person therefore has his own victim. It follows: “If one soul from the people of the land sins.” Why does it add “from the people of the land,” unless because the soul that sins does not belong to that people? Of them it is said: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

You too, if you come to the grace of baptism, have offered a calf. Since you are baptized into Christ’s death, you have offered a goat for martyrdom, because you have slaughtered the devil, the author of sin. When you give alms and pour out the affection of mercy toward the needy, you have honored the sacred altar with well-fed young goats. If you forgive your brother’s sin from the heart, lay aside the swelling of anger, and gather a gentle spirit within yourself, you have sacrificed yourself as a ram or lamb of faith.

Moreover, if you are instructed in the divine readings by meditation, and become a turtledove in the law of the Lord, whose murmur sounds more like a groan than a song; if you turn a sinner away from error and restore him to the simplicity of the dove; and if, by clinging to the saints, you make him imitate the fellowship of the turtledove, then you have offered a turtledove or dove to God.

If charity abounds in your heart, so that you love your neighbor as yourself, you have offered breads together with them, kneaded in the oil of charity and without any leaven of malice. If you have disciplined your flesh and made it dry through fasts and much self-restraint, you have offered a sacrifice from the frying pan and the griddle.

## CHAPTER V

It follows: “If a soul sins and hears the voice of one who swears,” and so forth. Historically, it is clear that we must not pollute our consciences with another person’s sin—not only by acting together with it, but also by failing to disclose what has been done unlawfully.

Spiritually, however, that soul of which it is written, “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” hears the voice of the one who swears, as the scribes and Pharisees do. They are always meditating upon these things, yet they do not wish to announce them to the people while remaining silent, nor do they confess the coming of Christ.

It follows: “The soul that touches anything unclean,” and so forth. See how unsuitable is the Jewish interpretation that observes these things according to the letter. What uncleanness does a person contract by touching a dead animal or the body of a dead person? What if it were the body of a prophet or of a patriarch? What if a dead body were raised by Elisha’s body?

The Apostle says: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” This act is unclean. For if anyone looks at a woman in order to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart. The vice of desire has therefore touched his heart, and his soul is unclean.

Whoever touches anything through desire for a woman or through greed for money must understand how to offer a sacrifice and how he may be made clean, according to what we have discussed.

The dead body of a person is touched by one who follows or imitates someone dead in his sins. Those who add the simpler people to their own simplicity touch the filth of sins by that touch by which, we say, they touch a dead animal. Of such animals it is said: “You will save human beings, O Lord.”

Whoever utters an oath, whether to do something good or something evil, “shall offer a lamb to God,” and so forth. To utter an oath means to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service. When we promise good works, we pledge ourselves to do good—for example, when we give food or drink to the needy, or rescue someone from unjust oppression.

When, however, we recognize that through abstinence and the mortification of our flesh we do ourselves harm, we make a present pledge to do evil to ourselves. Or, since flesh and spirit oppose one another, we do good to the spirit through the same works by which we see that we do harm to the flesh. “Power is made perfect in weakness.” For he says: “I kill and I give life”: he kills the flesh in order to give life to the spirit.

Although anyone may be perfect, no one is so free from sin that he does not sin even within his very vows.

A female lamb from the flocks, or a she-goat, is commanded to be offered: that is, we offer to God either an active and simple life, or a contemplative life through the she-goat, which often seeks pasture in the heights. The lamb is rightly commanded to be offered from the flocks, because the active life belongs to many, whereas the contemplative life belongs to few.

But when our virtue is sometimes insufficient to be offered, we must offer two young doves or a pair of turtledoves, because they possess the sound of a groan rather than a song. Through them a double groaning of repentance is signified: for what we have failed to do rightly and for what we have done wrongly. Thus we offer one turtledove for sin, because we give a groan for guilt, and from the other we make a holocaust.

We call a holocaust something wholly burned. For the good we have neglected to do, we hand ourselves over to the fire and burn in the fire of grief.

The varieties of victims and the rites of sacrifices are beyond our powers, since much has been omitted by earlier authorities. We are not able to explain every detail, because they remain concealed, except for a few chapters that have readily presented themselves to us.

Nearly every victim has something that signifies Christ, for every victim is summed up in him. When he was offered, all those victims ceased.

The calf, therefore, as we said above, may signify Christ either as a gift or for sin. The fat covering the inner parts may signify his holy soul, which covers his inner parts—that is, the hidden things of his divinity—or his humanity, adhering to him from his parents, as though a middle gate between the flesh and the divine fires, to be illumined and preserved for heaven.

The small branches [*ramunculi*] handed over to the fires signify that there are no movements of Gentile parts in Christ. In the sevenfold application of the blood, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is signified. The four horns of the altar indicate the four Gospels, which refer to Christ’s Passion.

In the liver, anger is slaughtered. In the liver’s *piscina* [“basin”], the stirring of fury is displayed. The remaining blood at the base of the altar signifies that grace by which all Israel will be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered: it is placed at the base of the altar, or, at the final calling, the Church will receive the Passion of Christ.

Whoever sins through error in things that have been sanctified shall offer a ram. He sins in sanctified things who transgresses God’s commandments and abandons the words of Scripture.

Whoever offers a ram as a holocaust, purchased for two shekels, seeks Christ through faith and works; for Christ suffered for each soul.

What follows, “He shall add a fifth part,” some understand simply to mean that, when restoring the loss, one must add a fifth of the damage inflicted: if someone took five coins, he should return six. Yet this should not be understood of thefts, but of those who take something for their own use from things that have been sanctified.

Others, examining the matter more cautiously according to the Greek wording, understand it as follows: if someone takes ten silver coins, he must return those ten and restore another ten, adding the fifth part—that is, adding two silver coins.

The ram must be purchased according to the sanctuary’s weight; that is, Christ must be sought according to the meaning of Scripture.

If someone has harmed himself by transgressing God’s commandments, he must restore what he neglected, and must not merely benefit himself but also benefit others. He must labor further, adding the fifth part and fitting the fullness of the bodily senses to spiritual things.

For the number five often pertains to the five senses. Or the fifth part means that he should join knowledge of the divine Law to good works; the number five signifies that Law on account of the Pentateuch of Moses.

## CHAPTER VI

The command concerning the soul that denies having received a deposit from its neighbor follows, and so forth. Remember, too, that the term used is “soul,” not “human being.”

In these chapters, those who are incapable of the mystery are instructed according to the letter. Spiritually, however, we have received from God a deposit belonging to our neighbor, namely, the soul in which he impressed his image.

If you are merciful, just as your heavenly Father is perfect, you have preserved your neighbor’s deposit as you received it. If you imitate, according to your capacity, those qualities that he possesses by nature, the image of God is safe in you. But if, instead of being merciful, you are cruel, and instead of pious, impious, you have denied the good deposit to the Lord.

We have also received the Holy Spirit as a good deposit. As long as he remains in us, we do not sin. But if we live [the text is materially corrupt here: *rebus habitamus*], that is, whether by reason or by other gifts in the things that the Lord wills, this is to deny the deposit.

When it says, “If he has brought a false accusation, or has found something lost,” it shows that we accuse God when, because of our evil deeds, his name is blasphemed among the Gentiles. We find something lost when we hear testimonies corrupted by heretics; these we must restore to the Catholic faith and join to the perfect meaning.

Above we explained what it means to offer a ram. Here, however, a price is mentioned, and the shekel is not named. There is a difference between sinning in sacred things and sinning outside sacred things, as it is said in the Books of Kings: “If someone sins against a human being, the priest will pray for him; but if someone sins against God, who will pray for him?”

The command concerning the Law follows. The holocaust must now be burned, the priest must be clothed, and the fire must always burn.

If you wish to be God’s priest—for you exercise a royal priesthood—do not let the fire leave your altar, which God desires to burn. Let the fire of faith be nourished upon the altar of the heart. Let the priest put on a tunic: stripped of his former garments, let him assume the wedding garment. Let him be clothed in tunics and wear undergarments, so that he may restrain lust. Enough has already been said concerning the undergarments.

We must know that the priest is clothed in one set of garments when he is engaged in the ministry of sacrifices and in another when he goes out to the people. Paul, the wise priest, did this among the assembly of the perfect. As though placed within the holy ones, he put on the robe of the highest teaching, saying: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, though not the wisdom of this world,” and so forth.

When he goes to those who are incapable of understanding, he changes his robe and teaches lower things, saying: “I gave you milk to drink, not food.” Christ too spoke to the crowds in parables, but to the apostles, as to those who were more perfect, he set forth deeper matters.

It has already been sufficiently stated that what is not leavened signifies that God’s sacrifice must not contain the leaven of malice.

But how is it that only males eat, while females do not? No one doubts that the holy flesh must be eaten by the one who has become a man according to the Apostle and has put away the things of childhood. Such a man should eat the holy flesh not in any place but in a holy place.

In the Church the holy flesh—that is, the flesh of Christ, which all those sacrifices signified—must be received. Let the heretics hear this, those who presume to receive Christ’s flesh outside the Church.

When it is said, “Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified,” this does not accord, according to the letter, with the sacrifices of the Jews. If an unholy person or a parricide had touched the sacrificial flesh, he could not thereby have been called sanctified. But whoever touched Christ, like the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, was immediately sanctified. For we have seen all the Gentiles, receiving Christ’s body in baptism, become sanctified.

“In the court of the tabernacle.” Here they are commanded to eat, because the present Church is the court of the future one.

He rightly says “fine flour mixed with oil,” because whoever has shown mercy to the poor has poured Christ’s sacrifice into God. The ministry that he carries to the saints displays the sweetness of the turtledove.

Aaron and his sons eat the remaining portion of the fine flour. Whatever remains from the spiritual matters of martyrdom, reserve for the priest, its author, your understanding. Let him eat it himself; let him examine it himself.

The command concerning the offerings of Aaron and his sons follows, and so forth. In the other sacrifices the priest performs a service for the people; in this command he attends to what is proper to himself.

He is commanded, from the day on which he is anointed, always and forever to offer fine flour. Perhaps this priest’s sacrifice is the Law itself, given through Moses. He commands that this Law be divided into two parts, namely, letter and spirit, and orders the middle portion—that is, the portion of the letter—to be offered.

“Morning” means the first period of the Law, when it was given to them in its various forms according to the letter. The New Law brought forth a new day. He commanded half of it to be offered in the evening.

For in the evening—that is, in the later times—the spiritual meaning of the Law is offered to us, with Christ’s coming. “From the frying pan” means that he wishes the priest to be broken and parched. The Law is called eternal according to that part of it which is spiritual.

The command concerning the law of the victim for sin follows, and so forth. It must be understood that some commands are given to the children of Israel, others to the sons of Aaron, others to Moses and Aaron, and others to Moses alone, so that even Aaron does not share in a certain command, as in the statement, “As the Lord commanded Moses.” To examine all these matters belongs neither to our small capacity nor to this brief exposition.

It must nevertheless be understood that each person receives in proportion to his progress. Do not look among mute animals for what you ought to offer; seek it within yourself. The herds of oxen and the flocks of sheep and goats, in which the patriarchs were blessed and multiplied, are eternal birds within you. Nor should you be surprised that, in a certain sense, you also possess the sun and the moon.

These chapters have been well explained earlier. We must nevertheless know that God’s great kindness is commended when the holocaust is offered, so that the one who has sinned may understand that, if he repents and slaughters a sacrifice of a contrite spirit, he can stand in the holy place and be joined to those who belong to the Lord.

When it adds, “It shall be most holy,” it signifies that the one offered for sins—the only-begotten Son of God—is the Holy of Holies.

When it says, “The priest who offers it shall eat it,” it shows what the Apostle says concerning Christ: since he offered himself, he himself is both priest and victim; he himself ate and consumed our sins, for he is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

It follows that the priests of the Church, ministers of the true priest, should also eat the sins of the people. Receiving the sins of the people, they should grant them remission of sins in the holy place, in the Church, in which sins are forgiven.

Of the things offered, some are granted to the priests for eating, while others are given to God as fuel for the fire. We are permitted to grasp certain things from Holy Scripture; certain things must be reserved for the Lord. The same applies to the offering for sin and to the offering for guilt.

In Scripture, “sin” is frequently used for “guilt,” and “guilt” for “sin.” Here, however, he did not wish to show any difference in the matters in which he divided the sacrifices. Some think that guilt is a lighter offense than sin, since Scripture speaks of “sin unto death” but does not say this concerning guilt.

Or guilt occurs when we fail to do what we ought to do, whereas sin occurs when we commit what we ought not to commit. The same reasoning must be applied to the sacrifice for sin.

If the fat that covers the inner parts is offered, together with everything fatty from the kidneys, then every fault of lust is cleansed, and you have offered a sacrifice as a pleasing fragrance.

The skin is this outward and mortal life; when it is not offered, it encloses the inner parts. Earthly matters, without which a human being—because God has commanded it—cannot be holy at all, belong to the service of God.

The oven may be understood as the human heart, according to the saying: “Their hearts burned like an oven.” If the devil has not inflamed our hearts with the fire of vices, but Christ has inflamed them with the fire of the Holy Spirit, then the loaves of the divine Scriptures are baked for sacrifice in the oven.

He says that there are three forms of sacrifice: from the oven, from the frying pan, and from the griddle. The oven, according to its form, can signify the deeper and more ineffable matters in Scripture; the frying pan, those matters that can be explained if they are turned over repeatedly; the griddle, those things that are open and without any covering.

There are therefore three kinds of understanding of the divine Scriptures: historical, mystical, and moral.

## CHAPTER VII
The commandment concerning peace offerings made to the Lord follows. He divided the peace offering into two parts: one he assigns to thanksgiving, the other for a vow; yet both are offerings of peace. But the leavened loaves, which he altogether rejected in the sacrifice, are now commanded to be added. It must be understood, however, that here they are not set against the sacrifice itself but against the mystery of the sacrifice. [Col. 0343B]

Thus it is said: “Leavened loaves also with the sacrifice of thanksgiving”; he does not say that the loaves themselves are the sacrifice, but that they are offered with the sacrifice. One of them is offered to the Lord not for the sacrifice but for the firstfruits.

Leaven signifies teaching, according to the saying, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.” Human teaching, whether grammar, rhetoric, or dialectic, is not to be accepted in those matters that must be believed concerning God. Yet clear and more eloquent speech, and rhetorical brilliance, may appropriately be admitted for the service of the word of God. Paul takes this leaven into the service of the word of God when he says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.” He also appropriated testimonies from the philosophers.

Who, then, can offer so great and worthy a peace offering, whether as thanksgiving or voluntarily and by vow, except one who by all his actions causes God to be praised—[Col. 0343C] whose works people see and glorify the Father who is in heaven?

Concerning the sacrifice of well-being it is said, “It shall not remain until morning,” just as it was said concerning the Paschal sacrifice: “Remember.” But concerning the sacrifice made by vow or voluntarily, delay is permitted: “Until the next day.” If anything remains until the third day, it must be given over to the fire. We shall understand this distinction as follows: one day is either a period of time or the present, in which the whole mystery of Christ’s passion must be received by us and must not be reserved for the future. Or certainly “one day” is understood generally as Holy Scripture; the two days are the Old and New Testaments, in which the holy flesh must be sacrificed—that is, the mystery of Christ’s cross must be sought out and [Col. 0343D] distinguished. We must accept no other authority except divine Scripture. But whatever the two Testaments do not distinguish must be reserved for the fire of the Holy Spirit.

He sets forth a threefold uncleanness. The first is that the holy flesh must not be touched by any uncleanness; the second, that the one who eats must be clean; the third, that the one who eats, though clean, must not touch any uncleanness. Uncleanness touches the holy flesh—that is, the divine words—when evil heresies are mixed with sound doctrine.

The one who eats must be clean. For the praise of God is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. Once he has become clean, it remains for him not to touch uncleanness, lest he be defiled by the sins of others.

Next he forbids the things sacrificed to the Lord—that is, the fat of cattle, sheep, and goats—to be eaten, and [Col. 0344A] so forth. In the passage mentioned above, when we were discussing the calf, we said that the fat signifies the soul of Christ. In the present passage, however, the fat not incongruously signifies that soul for which Christ gave his own soul, namely, the Church, which is truly his soul. The one who eats the fat scandalizes one of the little ones who believe in Christ.

Blood is forbidden to be drunk. According to the preceding interpretation, the Israelite people may be understood here. They descend not from faith or from the spirit of Abraham, but only from his blood. The Apostle does not wish this people to be offended when he says: “You will say then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in,’” and the rest.

But he permits the fat of an animal that has died of itself or has been partly eaten by a wild beast to be used for various purposes, and so forth. [Col. 0344B] For there are many testimonies which, having been found among the nations, are spiritually dead. Yet we appropriately receive those whom the evil beast has killed, if not for authority, then for usefulness. They may indeed be called “fat,” because they have formed opinions in their own way.

When he says, “He shall hold in his hand some part of the sacrifice,” he signifies that it is works which commend our sacrifice to God. The rest has been explained above.

When he says, “This is the anointing of Aaron and of his sons,” he does not add what the anointing was, since he does this in what follows. It may, however, be understood of the breast of elevation and the arm of separation, especially since these have been inserted under the sacrament of spiritual anointing.

Finally: “This is the law of the burnt offering, and of the sacrifice,” and so forth. This is a repetition of the preceding chapters.

## Chapters VIII–IX

[Col. 0344C] When he says, “Take Aaron,” and the rest, what follows has for the most part been explained above, when the discussion concerned Aaron’s garments. It must nevertheless be observed that Moses first washes him and afterward clothes him. “Let Moses wash you”—that is, the Law. “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” Then you put on Jesus Christ, and you will have the wedding garment.

All who offer sacred gifts are priests, and to them it is said: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.”

Moses gathered the people. For the presence of the people is required when a priest is ordained, so that the ruler may be chosen on the testimony of many.

In Exodus eight kinds of garments are designated; here only seven are counted. [Col. 0344D] The undergarments are omitted. We have said that these signify chastity, because they restrain the sexual organs. Perhaps they are omitted for this reason: Scripture does not always say that these parts were restrained in those priests. They are not to be granted indulgence in the power of generation and the succession of offspring.

The priests of the Church, too, must sometimes pour in the seed of the divine word, so that they may instruct the minds of their hearers; at other times they must remain silent, lest they cast pearls before swine. They must have a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent.

## Chapter X

The sons of Aaron, who placed alien fire upon the altar, were consumed by divine fire. They signify those who, having despised divine teaching, pursue perverse doctrines. To them it is said: “You have rejected the commandment of God in order to [Col. 0345A] establish your tradition.”

In another sense, someone kindles alien fire when he lights within the sanctuary of his heart the fire of some desire and dares to approach God’s altar, which receives only that fire of which it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.”

They were cast outside the camp. Such people are not counted among the saints who excel in merit. What is said next—“Do not uncover your heads,” and the rest—must be discussed below.

He commands the priests not to drink wine or strong drink, especially when they approach the ministry of wine. This is appropriate even according to the historical sense, since the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.” Spiritually, it means that your hearts must not perhaps be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this world.

The remaining matters concerning the breast, [Col. 0345B] the arm, the sacrifice for sin, and the command that the priests eat this in a holy place have been explained in scattered passages.

## Chapter XI

Now we must consider the fact that the Law did not permit certain animals to be eaten as unclean, while it permitted others. God is not concerned with animals as such. Through them, therefore, human conduct is portrayed, and the ways in which human beings themselves are clean or unclean.

Thus those who chew the cud are clean: they always carry food in their mouths, namely, the divine commandments. Those who divide the hoof possess the two Testaments and divide the letter from the spirit.

The Jews indeed chew the words of the Law, but do not divide the hoof: they do not believe in the two Testaments, nor in the Father [Col. 0345C] or the Son, and therefore they are unclean. Heretics divide the hoof and accept the two Testaments; but because they do not profess the doctrine of truth with their mouths, they are unclean.

Since this must be understood of human beings rather than cattle, we must see how we eat clean people and reject the unclean. Every person gives his neighbors a taste either by answering or by speaking. If the one from whom we receive the taste is good, we take clean food. But if he is unclean and perverse in mind, we take unclean food. Thus one’s neighbor becomes clean or unclean to each of us.

Among the creatures born in the waters, those with fins and scales are eaten. These fish, having fins and scales, rise toward the upper [Col. 0345D] waters. They signify those who seek the freedom of the spirit. Although they are surrounded and weighed down by the waves of this world, they strive to rise toward heavenly things.

The scales signify the gravity of conduct and the firmness of one’s way of life. The fin signifies the understanding of those who think about heavenly things. Those who lack these are people of frivolous and effeminate conduct who do not think about heavenly things.

When he forbids the camel, he condemns a shapeless life. When he forbids the pig, he reproves a filthy and muddy life. When he accuses the hare, he condemns men deformed into women. Through the lizard he denotes the uncertain variety of life. Through the weasel he condemns theft. Through the gecko he execrates the stains of minds. Through the hawk, kite, and eagle he hates plunderers. Through the vulture he condemns rapacity. Through the [Col. 0346A] raven he condemns dark pleasures. Through sparrows he condemns intemperance. Through the swan he condemns the lofty necks of pride. Through the owl he condemns variations that flee the light. Through the other similar creatures he censures various vices.

## Chapter XII

The commandment concerning the uncleanness of childbirth follows. It is not said without purpose that a woman who gives birth to a male after conceiving seed is called unclean, since this distinguishes her from the woman who conceived the Son, Jesus Christ, without seed. The burdens of the Law do not weigh upon her. Thus it is not superfluous but mystical that he says, “Having conceived seed.”

When it says that, if she has borne a male, she will be unclean for seven days and purified on the seventh day, this signifies that, as long as we remain in the present age—which revolves through seven days—we cannot be completely [Col. 0346B] pure until the eighth day has come. The eighth day is the time of the age to come, in which the male is commanded to be circumcised.

Then, as we have said, we shall be thoroughly cleansed from all superfluous actions, words, and thoughts, when God is all in all. Then the mother who has borne the male also becomes clean. Once cleansed within, the one who has acted in a masculine and manly way, possessing nothing feminine or soft within himself, will receive flesh and resurrection. For, he says, the effeminate will not enter the kingdom of God.

But the one who remains lax and effeminate in his actions will be cleansed neither in the present week nor in the future one. His sins are not remitted from uncleanness, either in this age or in the age to come.

What follows is:

[Col. 0346C]

> “For thirty-three days she shall remain in the blood of her purification.”

This period may signify the time during which in this world we strive to fulfill and possess the commandments of the Law and the sacrament of faith. Thirty-three consists of three units and three tens; this pertains to faith in the Trinity and to the Law.

We remain in purification for that length of time so that we may be found pure. We labor as long as we remain in this life. Through this labor we shall be found purified in faith and works in the present life and in the life to come, when death has been conquered and God is all in all.

Then we shall touch holy things and enter the sanctuary, when that which is perfect has come. We shall contemplate heavenly things not through a mirror but face to face.

Concerning the woman [Col. 0346D] who bears a female, it was stated above how we shall be purified in the present time and not in the future.

## Chapter XIII

The discourse concerning the plague of leprosy follows. There are six kinds: the first is on the skin and living flesh; the second extends over all the living flesh, from head to foot; the third is in the place of a healed ulcer; the fourth is in the place of a burn; the fifth is on the head or beard; the sixth is on baldness or complete baldness.

Leprosy is false doctrine. Hence lepers are rightly understood as heretics, because they stain the purity of the Church with various errors.

Those bear leprosy on the skin who try to commend external and carnal things, such as the Cerinthians, who suppose that the future resurrection consists in the desires of the flesh, and the Luciferians, who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh.

The one devoted to various heretical doctrines bears leprosy over his entire [Col. 0347A] body and stains his whole life.

Someone has leprosy in the place of a healed ulcer when, after acknowledging his error and receiving medicine, he seeks some trace of his former error, like a dog returning to its vomit.

The Manichaeans bear the leprosy of fire in the place of a burn. Through the torture of an empty abstinence they exhaust their bodies and, through unbelief, produce not uncleanness but leprosy. Of such people the Apostle says: “Forbidding to marry and commanding abstinence from foods that God created to be received.”

He carries leprosy on his head who blasphemes the Divinity or sins against Christ, who is the head of the Church—such as the Arians, the Manichaeans, or indeed the Jews.

Those who think perversely about the apostles and holy preachers, and pretend that they [Col. 0347B] preached anything false, display leprosy in their beard. For just as the beard is an ornament to a man, so the apostles and teachers are an ornament to the body of Christ.

Those who, after casting away superfluous and dead desires, become entangled again in greater sins and are corrupted by perverse doctrine show leprosy on baldness or complete baldness.

When he adds the colors of the leprosies, he shows the various forms of heresies. Heresy is pale through false brothers; red through martyrdom, which they undergo although it is fruitless; white through the color of false righteousness; livid through certain useless fasts; black through perverse doctrine; and dark through the mysteries of error.

There is also a leprosy that is cleansed through the rite of sacrifice—that is, through a contrite and humbled heart. For he says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” [Col. 0347C] This is done at the command of the priest—that is, through the teaching of some Catholic man—by a purification lasting seven days, namely, through acknowledgment of the sevenfold Spirit, outside the fellowship of the Holy of Holies, so that the person, once cleansed, may afterward be received within the holy Church.

There is another kind that water cleanses through baptism. But the kind of leprosy that cannot be cleansed belongs altogether to those who say that penitents cannot obtain forgiveness, or who refuse to turn back from error.

When it is said that lepers leaving the camp must sit outside until their leprosy is cleansed, this signifies that heretics must be cast out of the Church until, having driven away their own error, they return to the Lord.

“With torn garments”—that is, with all his secrets made manifest. “With uncovered head,” so that the exposure of his mind may be seen by everyone. “With his mouth covered,” lest he [Col. 0347D] teach impiety any further.

When leprosy is said to be lower than the rest of the flesh, who does not see that perverse doctrine is humbled and despised? Let the leper pronounce himself unclean, so that through confession he may receive healing.

These things written concerning leprosy are brief; in other respects they bear an image of the truth.

Leprosy on a linen garment signifies perverse conduct—people who are very harsh and, through a certain color of righteousness, are more severe toward sinners than is proper, provoking them to despair rather than to healing and, contrary to the Apostle, not bearing one another’s burdens.

Leprosy on a woolen garment signifies those who, out of flattery, do not wish to correct wrongdoers but consent to those who do evil; or certainly those who live softly [Col. 0348A] and do not strive to act manfully.

Leprosy in the warp may signify the vices of the soul, through which the body is made to stand and flourish. Leprosy in the woof signifies sins committed through the body. For the soul subsists in the body as the warp does in the woof.

The skin is the external life and carnal conduct of human beings. Hence Adam and his wife are said to have been given tunics of skin because of their sin.

Leprosy on the skin is a bad example in the conduct of this life, through which the uneducated are led into error.

Leprosy on the walls of a house signifies perverse doctrine in the thoughts of heretics. Concerning this the prophet says: “[Text uncertain: the supplied reading is *O divi Ecclesiam malignantium*].”

All the kinds are separated for seven days, because no one is cleansed except through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

The priest enters [Col. 0348B] to examine the leprosy outside the camp, because the leper does not enter the camp. A worthy teacher is near to all in compassion, as was the one who said: “I have become all things to all people.”

## Chapter XIV

The discourse concerning the sacrifice of the leper who is cleansed follows. He is commanded to offer two sparrows. Each sparrow signifies a person turning away from sins, to whom it is said: “Cross over to the mountain like a sparrow.”

Since the two sparrows signify the substance of flesh and soul, it is lawful to feed upon them, just as it is said to Peter: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” He in some manner feeds the holy teachers and the angels with the one who turns away from sins. One sparrow is sacrificed over living waters; the other, sprinkled with the blood of the first, is released [Col. 0348C] into the field. The latter must be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.

For this reason the flesh in some sense dies, so that the living soul may fly more strongly into the field of evangelical discipline and may bear fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or, if it progresses in this way, a hundredfold.

Such a victim is sacrificed over living waters so that, turning neither to the right nor to the left, it may observe the disciplines of the Gospel, which are called water. Whoever drinks this water becomes in himself a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

The earthen vessel signifies human conduct, in which we labor while we remain.

Cedar wood is also added. For it is impossible for the leprosy of sin to be removed without the wood of the cross.

Scarlet signifies the blood of Christ, which flowed from his side.

[Col. 0348D] Doctors report that hyssop cleanses harmful humors from human chests; so through confession the sins of penitents are cleansed. These things are necessarily received as an aid to our salvation.

When he has washed his garment and shaved all the hair of his body, then, once cleansed, he enters the camp. When through the bath we have laid aside our former sins, which are the garments of the old person, and have cast away every hair—that is, whatever superfluity arises within us—then we enter the camp of God.

Indeed, the holy person who possesses no work of death must preserve every hair. As long as he is not defiled by superfluous words, deeds, or thoughts, iron does not come upon his head. Of him it is said: “His leaf shall not fall, and [Col. 0349A] all that he does shall prosper.”

What it means for a person to be sprinkled seven times has often been stated.

Certainly it is not idle or without mystery that it is said: “He shall remain outside his tent for seven days.” He must shave every hair of his head, as well as of his beard and eyebrows. It is as though he wished to say that even what he had previously stated—“Let him shave all the hair of his body”—would not yet be sufficient.

When someone is joined to the camp, that is, to the Church, he does not immediately enter his own house, that is, the house of the virtues, concerning which it is said: “Take up your bed and go to your house.” You have been healed; see that you do not again bring guilt upon your head.

The sin of the head is to think something contrary to the true faith. In the beard, let mature manhood lay aside its guilt; in the eyebrows, [Col. 0349B] lay aside arrogance.

They are also commanded to cleanse their garments and body again, although the body had previously been washed; but these things are to be done within the camp. Whatever arises in us after baptism and pure faith must be cut away through repentance and devotion to a perfect life, but not outside the Church. Thus all these things are to be done within the camp.

After all this it is said: “Let the one who is cleansed offer for himself two unblemished lambs, one year-old ewe, and the rest.”

The first lamb, which is offered for transgression, may signify the virtue assumed by the one who had been in sins, a virtue by which he was able to repel the affection for sin from himself.

The second lamb signifies the recovered virtue through which, after casting away all vices, he offered himself whole.

The ewe taken after the lamb [Col. 0349C] signifies the fruitfulness of the one who, after turning away from sin, offered himself entirely to God and makes use of the fruits of good works.

Since there are three victims—the first by which sins are forgiven, the second by which the soul turns to the Lord, and the third by which the convert displays fruitfulness—he therefore adds three measures of fine flour, so that we may understand that purification cannot take place without the mystery of the Trinity.

He has fine flour from which to make clean bread, and this is mixed with oil. He divides the oil of the one who is to be purified for two purposes, so that the person’s bread may become rich and so that, on account of mercy and knowledge, he may place light upon his head through the hands of the priest.

It belongs to the priest to establish him, so that he may be steadfast and not be moved by every wind of doctrine.

Blood and oil are poured on [Col. 0349D] the ear so that his hearing may be pure; on the hand so that his work may be clean; and on the feet so that they may be directed only toward good work. All these things are done on the right, since he is not permitted to have anything left-handed in himself.

The priest sprinkles the oil seven times before the Lord, so that he may invoke the sevenfold Spirit upon the one who is cleansed, pouring out prayers to the Lord and saying: “Strengthen me, Lord, with your principal Spirit.”

Or certainly the shaking of the finger seven times signifies the expulsion of demons, which God plainly declares in the Gospel to be driven out of a person.

The Lord—or rather, the Spirit of the Lord—is designated through the image of the oil, so that the one who is cleansed may not only obtain remission of all sins but also deserve to be filled with the Holy Spirit.

What the lamb signifies that the poor man offers, or the two turtledoves or young pigeons, has often been stated.

## Chapter XV

[Col. 0350A] After this it is said: “The man who suffers from a discharge of blood is unclean.” He signifies one who does not know how to impose restraint upon his words and cannot escape sin through excessive speaking.

Good seed is the word of evangelical teaching, which grows in the hearts of hearers as in good soil. Conversely, bad seed is perverse doctrine, which the enemy sows over it.

A man who suffers from a discharge of blood is unclean because he considers neither persons nor times, does not remember that there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent, does not remember that what is holy must not be given to dogs, and does not distinguish good from evil. He is therefore unclean.

Hence the Apostle [Col. 0350B] says: “Do not be led astray by various and foreign doctrines.”

His conduct, in which he lies inert as though on a bed, is also unclean. Whoever has been touched by his teaching needs to be washed with the water of life, that is, with instruction.

He remains so until evening—that is, until the end of the empty doctrine or perverse will that he has commended.

“The man from whom the seed proceeds shall not be received,” and the rest: this refers to one who, joining with carnal desire as with a woman, labors to teach in a way that provokes people more to laughter than to mourning, although it is written: “Woe to you who laugh.” And again: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you.”

He shall be unclean until evening. Evening is the end of the day and the beginning of night; so repentance is the end of empty joy and the beginning of saving sorrow.

“Blessed are those who read now, for they shall be comforted.”

“The woman who, when it returns,” and the rest. Through women is signified anyone effeminate who possesses nothing manly within himself. When the time of desire returns, he pours out blood—that is, if he possessed any natural goodness, he loses it through negligence. He is separated for seven days so that he may recognize that he is subject to seven demons.

The woman who pours out blood not at the time of menstruation but continually signifies one who in no way resists inwardly and lies empty of every good; and, if the blood has stopped after seven days have been counted, he may be found cleansed and healed on the eighth day, having received the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

## Chapters XVI–XX

[Col. 0350D] After this it is commanded that Aaron not enter the sanctuary—which is within the veil—at every hour, and so forth. Through this we are instructed daily, so that we may know in what garments and at what time we should approach God’s altar.

The spiritual Aaron, the ancient priest Christ, does not enter at every hour but once in the year of his life, concerning which it is said: “Call the acceptable day of the Lord.”

How he himself is the priest, and how he is signified in the calf and in the ram, is not difficult to understand.

The linen tunic signifies his flesh, which is called holy because his holy flesh was conceived not from the seed of a man but from the Holy Spirit.

The undergarments signify the chastity of his flesh, through which his flesh was open neither to lust nor to the begetting of children.

The linen sash signifies the same chastity, since there was no lust in his [Col. 0351A] loins.

The turban is an adornment of the head; therefore it signifies the glory of the resurrection, through which God gave him the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father, and the rest.

How these things apply morally to priests was stated above.

How he who was washed receives these things is not doubtful, since Christ, though he had no stain, did not refuse washing. He prayed for himself and for his household when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit,” or when he prayed once and again a third time.

He prayed for his household when he said: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me.”

Now we must consider the two [Col. 0351B] goats over which lots are cast, one for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat.

If all the people of God were holy, there would not be two lots over the goats, but one lot and one victim. But since many are called and few are chosen, the portion of the victim that is offered by the people is sacrificed to the Lord, while the other portion is cast away. Yet the lot falls upon both, so that each may be received or rejected according to his merit.

The goat is both the one that is sent away and the one that is received. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.

The one who falls to God’s lot is killed, because for his sake we are put to death every day: “We have died, and our life is hidden.”

But prayers are poured over the one who is sent into the wilderness, so that he may carry the people’s sins into solitude, because all righteous blood comes upon sinners, and the rest.

[Col. 0351C] The wicked always practice iniquity. Likewise, those who possess righteousness have further increase added to them in perfection. For, he says, “To the one who has, more will be given.” In the same way, the one who has sins will have the sins of his ancestors repaid to him unto the third and fourth generation, by the most just judgment of God, who judges all things most justly.

He is sent into solitude because the wicked are those alone who have been abandoned by God and abandoned by every good thing. Perhaps this solitude is what the Gospel calls the outer darkness or the eternal fire.

Concerning the ram that is taken with the goats, what was said above concerning the ram may be understood. Or these things may be said concerning Jesus and Barabbas: one, coming by the lot of Jesus the Lord, was killed; the other, accursed, was sent into the wilderness of the Jews, carrying the people’s [Col. 0351D] sins while they cried, “Crucify him!”

The man who led the goat may be Pilate, by whose sentence the one who is said to have been washed was released. Having taken water, he washed his hands before all the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.”

Finally, Jesus may be called the goat, both because God made him sin and because he is the victim for sin; and Barabbas is the goat who must be placed on the left.

The prepared man who leads the goat into the wilderness signifies Christ, to whom all judgment has been given, so that he may place the sheep on the right and the goats on the left. His garments are filthy, concerning whom it is said: “And I saw Jesus the high priest clothed in filthy garments.” He washed the robe of the world in the wine of his blood and made it clean.

In another sense, the two goats signify the two peoples, bearing a symbolic form.

But what does it mean for the goat to fall to the lot of the Lord except that the people of believers are [Col. 0352A] fellow heirs and co-partners of Christ? His blood is mixed with the blood of the calf, so that, having become partners in Christ’s passion, we may become participants in his glory.

But the Jewish people, who refuse to believe in Christ, accumulating sins upon sins, withdrew into a place deserted by God.

The fact that he sprinkles toward the east signifies that propitiation comes from the east. For from there is the man whose name is “Rising.”

When it is said, “Let no one be in the tabernacle when the high priest enters,” it means that whoever is able to follow Christ and ascend with him to the heights of heaven will no longer be human. “They will be,” he says, “like angels in heaven.” Or, while placed in the flesh, he will no longer be human, because his conduct is in heaven.

“I have said,” he says, “you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”

Concerning the censer and the [Col. 0352B] other matters narrated here, discussion has been offered elsewhere.

But whoever kills a sheep or an ox and does not offer it at the door of the tabernacle must be charged with bloodguilt. For every victim of our works, if it is not brought under the authority and power of the Church, is empty; and it not only does not help but greatly harms.

We omit the remaining matters, because some of them have been discussed above, while others are not very obscure. Some, however, must for now be reserved according to the literal sense.

## Chapter XXI

If the daughter of a priest is caught in adultery, she shall be burned with fire.

Every Christian is a priest. If the thought that he himself has [Col. 0352C] generated within himself is found to be alienated from God, it ought to be consumed by the fire of compunction, so that it may cease to be adulterous.

We are commanded that, when we have planted fruit-bearing trees, we should remove their firstfruits. We remove the firstfruits of the trees when we do not approve the beginnings of our works that have arisen from the very stain of weakness. Even when the beginnings of good works are still being praised, it is unworthy that they should continue to feed the worker’s mind in this way.

In the fourth year all their fruit shall be sanctified. Our works are then sanctified through the Incarnation, when we perfectly believe in the humanity of the Mediator, which is announced through the four Gospels.

In the fifth year we eat the fruit, when, observing the Law spiritually, we add the perfect work of faith.

[Col. 0352D] The commandment concerning the great priest among his brothers follows, upon whose head the oil was poured, and the rest.

The great priest among his brothers is Christ, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever.” Rising again, he says: “Go to my brothers.”

Oil of anointing was poured upon his head, concerning which it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you.”

“He shall not uncover his head.” The head of Christ is God. No one has ever seen God except his only-begotten Son. Therefore do not seek on earth what is poured over the head of the priest, whose hands have been consecrated, since he displayed them in his passion for the expiation of the whole world.

Or Christ has consecrated hands because he committed no sin—something that does not apply to any human being, however holy he may be.

He does not tear his garments, because he does not permit his [Col. 0353A] Church to be divided by heresy or schisms. The Church clings to him as a garment; its figure was that seamless tunic of Jesus which was not torn during the passion.

“He shall not return to any dead person,” that is, to one who is dead in sins. For when the soul sins, it dies. “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul.”

“He shall not be defiled by father or mother.” Every human being who enters this world is defiled by father and mother, from whom he derives original sin. For, he says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sin.”

Christ alone was not defiled when he was born of a virgin, because he was conceived not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit. Nor was he defiled in his mother, because he was born from a virgin womb not through the pleasure of the flesh.

Finally, he himself said through Solomon: “When I was more good, I came into a defiled body.” The body was not defiled by his mother. Therefore he was not contaminated in his mother.

In another sense, we are defiled in our father when through sin or unbelief we offend God, while in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Our Father who are,” and the rest.

We are defiled in our mother when, believing in God, we injure the Church, which is the mother of us all, to whom [Col. 0353B] we are born in place of fathers. Or we offend our mother when we stain the freedom of our heavenly mother with the unworthy slavery of sin; the Apostle calls her the mother of us all.

Christ was defiled neither in mother nor in father. He committed no sin, and deceit was not found on his tongue.

“He shall not go out from the holy places.” The one who slips after receiving help from the [Col. 0353C] virtues goes out from the holy places; Christ never did this. For he alone was without sin. Or, by assuming flesh, he descended into this world in such a way that he never abandoned heaven, because he is wholly present everywhere.

A widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute he shall not take as wife. The widow, the divorced woman, and the prostitute signify the synagogue of the Jews, when Jeremiah says in his lamentations: “How the city sits solitary; she has become a widow, the mistress of the nations.” Of her it is said: “What is the bill of divorce of your mother, with which I dismissed her?” To her it is said: “You will prostitute yourself under every leafy tree.” For the virgin is the Church, to whom the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one man, as a chaste virgin.”

Alternatively, the widow is the soul which, departing from the yoke of the law, does not keep the evangelical commandment; the divorced woman is she who, by sinning, is separated from the body of Christ; and the prostitute is she who has admitted loves—that is, things opposed to virtue—which desire her beauty in order to deceive her. Such women do not belong with Christ.

“Let him take a wife from his own kind”: namely, the Church, which was born not from the will of the flesh but from God. And therefore she is of his kind, whence he himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my mother, brother, and sister”; or, “let him take a wife from his own kind,” that is, the soul which is joined to the faithful.

It can also be understood in this way: when he says “from his own kind,” we should know that Christ’s soul is from the kind and substance of all human souls. “He did not defile his seed”—that is, the word of God—when he said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” and: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” Therefore the Apostle says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to those who are outside everything is in parables.”

Morally, these things also apply to every priest and to the other members of Christ. He says: “He shall not uncover his head”—that is, the mysteries of Christ, because honor concerning the mysteries is his covering. “And they shall not tear their garments,” lest he pass over into heresy or schisms, tearing apart Christ’s commandments, which are his garments.

“He shall not enter upon any dead person.” He does not approach any sin that leads to death; or certainly, he will in no way consent to one who is dead in sins.

“He shall not defile himself on account of father or mother”: he must not indulge his affection for the death of his parents so far that he offends his God. For whoever loves father and mother more than God is not worthy of him.

“He shall not go out from the holy things,” so that he may always be mindful in holy deed and thought. For whoever speaks, does, or thinks anything blameworthy goes out from the holy things.

“A widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute he shall not take as wife”: he must not embrace anything from the former life, which is a widow, a divorced woman, and a prostitute; rather, he should possess a virgin—that is, a life flourishing in complete purity—from his own kind, that is, he should imitate the life of the saints, to whom he is close through faith.

After this it is commanded that whoever has a blemish must not offer the breads to the Lord: if he is blind, if lame, and so forth. Everything is referred to a defect of the soul. For it is conduct in a person, not nature, that is condemned.

The blind priest is one who does not understand the meaning of the Scriptures and, through ignorance, does not know where to direct the step of his teaching or conduct. Of such people it is written: “All his watchmen are blind.”

The lame man is one who indeed understands what he ought to teach, but does not fulfill the commandments that he teaches.

He has a small nose who is not capable of maintaining the measure of discernment. He has a large and crooked nose who is furious and threatening, with arrogant pride or immoderate discernment.

He has a broken foot or hand who does not strive to follow the way of God that he teaches.

The hunchback is one whom the weight of earthly desire depresses and who is slow to direct his attention to heavenly things.

The bleary-eyed man is one whose intellect flashes toward knowledge of the truth, but who obscures it by living carnally.

He has a white spot in his eye who is blinded by the arrogance of wisdom or righteousness.

He has a continual scab who is incessantly dominated by the wantonness of the flesh.

He has an eruption on his body who is ravaged in mind by avarice. If he is not restrained in the smallest matter, it surely expands without measure.

The heavy man is one who does not practice shameful conduct in deed, but is burdened in mind by continuous activity without moderation.

If such men enter the holy places, they cannot possess the title of bishop.

A certain likeness is also presented through the sons of Aaron the priest, who are commanded not to defile themselves by the deaths of their fellow citizens, except only by those of blood relatives and close kin, and so forth. This applies to certain teachers who, although wise and faithful, nevertheless involve themselves in worldly affairs as far as they can.

They permit lighter matters to those weighed down by sins, in order to release them from heavier matters, because those who are burdened by many vices cannot avoid heavy and light faults at the same time. Through this they are allowed, in a certain manner, to be defiled by the death of relatives, just as they are allowed to be defiled by the death of fellow citizens.

Fellow citizens are all the faithful whom the wall of faith encloses, even though they may be sinners. Relatives are those who, although they are weighed down inwardly, nevertheless strive to attain one rule of conversion.

Your father is he who taught you. Your mother is she who, when you were a little child, nourished you with the milk of her teaching. Your brother or sister is a virgin if he or she shares with you one pursuit or one discipline under the same teacher. And if you have become stronger, show consideration for these relatives, as we said above.

But nothing of this is granted to the high priest, because the supreme teacher or ruler of the Church, who is separated from worldly affairs, ought to offer no base example, nor any feeble or contemptible teaching.

Whoever touches anything unclean shall be unclean; his unclean touch shall last until evening. For then we are cleansed from all uncleanliness and defilement, when, at the evening of this world, Christ the Sun of righteousness set through his Passion, and we were released by the washing of baptism.

## CHAPTER XXII

It follows: “A man who offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the Lord, whether fulfilling vows or offering voluntarily, shall offer an unblemished lamb,” and so forth.

First, a blemished animal is rejected from the sacrifice—that is, those in whom there is a diversity of sins and who are moved by various crimes. He also rejects the blind, that is, one who neither sees the Lord nor cares for him.

The broken animal is likewise rejected, that is, one tormented and crushed by carnal vices.

An animal with a scar is also rejected, because it does not lament the wounds of its sins with worthy satisfaction, but still bears inwardly the mark of its former illness.

The animal with a pustule is rejected, signifying one who burns with the itching of lust and the heat of desires. Likewise the scabby animal signifies one who completes the sin of the flesh through the contagion of deed.

An animal with an eruption signifies the assembly of heretics, which frequently inserts itself into the body of the Church; and an eruption causes distress.

Those whose ears have been cut off signify people who do not attend to the word and do not fulfill what has been commanded. He has a cut-off ear who does not steadfastly preserve the good that he begins.

A defect or a crushed testicle indicates those who, although they are male in body, become effeminate again and are therefore rejected from God’s sacrifice.

Nor is the bread of a foreigner offered to God—that is, the teaching of heretics, or the empty pursuits of secular literature, which are foreign to the Church. Such offerings are rejected by the Lord.

An animal whose ear or tail has been cut off is accepted for a freewill sacrifice, but a vow is not fulfilled with it. This signifies that those who possess the innermost and highest vows of religion, or elevated ranks, must live irreproachably, according to the standard by which the Apostle designates what a bishop or deacon ought to be.

For one who is of lower rank, or without rank, his vows and whatever good he voluntarily performs are acceptable.

Regarding the ox, sheep, and goat, he says that they are to be nourished for six days at their mother’s breast, and then may be offered to the Lord. This signifies that all whom Mother Church gives birth to must first be nourished with the milk of teaching, and then, perfected by the sevenfold grace of Christ, become the Lord’s offering.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When he commands that we bring sheaves of the first fruits to the priest, who will elevate and sanctify them on the day after the Sabbath, this signifies that then the true priest, Christ, to whom we ought to offer the first and chief of our works, elevated and sanctified our works after the Jewish Sabbath had passed.

The second day—that is, the day of the New Testament—and the time of grace arrived; and thus our works were accepted.

By commanding that, when reaping the grain, we not gather the ears that remain but leave them for the poor and for foreigners, he shows that, when from the labor of our earth—that is, of the flesh—we prepare eternal fruits for our needs, we ought to come to the aid of our neighbors and of those who are still weak. Thus, relaxing something of our severity, we may bend down to raise those who lie fallen, and may benefit them by example, exhortation, or prayers. For “the prayer of a righteous person has great power.”

The poor person is one in whom desire is present but works are lacking. The foreigner is the novice who has abandoned his former error and recently entered within the boundaries of the Church.

## CHAPTER XXIV

When he commands oil to be prepared for arranging the lamps, it is joined outside the veil in the tabernacle, on the most pure lampstand, as in the case of the most holy teacher.

But within the Holy of Holies—that is, in the heavenly places—we do not need the light of the Scriptures, since the Lord himself is the everlasting light there.

The son of an Israelite woman, whom she had borne to an Egyptian man, who quarreled in the camp and blasphemed the Lord, signifies the heretics. They are begotten from the devil as father and expelled from the womb of Mother Church like abortions; through false teaching they blaspheme the Lord.

These are the people of whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” Of them the Gospel says that “an enemy sowed weeds over the wheat.” By the Lord’s command, they are to be buried beneath the stones of testimony outside the camp of the Church by the entire holy people.

## CHAPTER XXV

When he says, “For six years sow your field,” and so forth, but in the seventh year “there shall be a sabbath of rest for the land of the Lord,” he intimates to us that the person who has diligently labored in perfect charity through the four virtues by which human life is ordered—fortitude, prudence, justice, and temperance, joined with faith and hope—for these virtues make progress when they are adorned with certain faith and hope in future goods, will rest without labor and without fear.

“For perfect love,” he says, “casts out fear.”

Then our land also keeps sabbath, that is, our flesh, resting in charity when the labors of vices have ceased, spontaneously produces spiritual fruits. These fruits are for not only us but also for servants and maidservants, or hired workers and resident foreigners—that is, for every kind of person whom the evangelical net draws to the shore.

The examples of the saints are nourishment for the faithful.

Servants are those who have not yet come to the adoption of sons. Hence the Lord says to the apostles: “I will no longer call you servants, but sons.”

Maidservants are those who live softly and remain under ecclesiastical discipline, compelled more by some necessity than inflamed by desire.

Hired workers are those who labor in the Church for present profits.

Resident foreigners are newly arriving novices, who, however they may be, are nevertheless in the Church and, as we have said, assume a certain covenant through the examples of the perfect.

Concerning the Jubilee, that is, the year of remission, we can say that after seven weeks of years—forty-nine years—the fiftieth year teaches a certain rest: the flesh has been subdued and resists lust more gently, when childbirth also ceases for women. Then each person will return to his own possession.

At that time, who will be able to possess the household of the perfect and of the virtues, which the law could possess before it sinned, or certainly through baptism?

# EXPLANATION OF THE FOURTH BOOK OF MOSES, CALLED IN HEBREW VAIEDABBER AND IN LATIN NUMERI

[Col. 0357]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0357B]

At the beginning of Numbers, the Lord speaks to Moses in the second month and in the second year after their departure from Egypt. This shows that the time of the law, which was earlier and belonged to the past, is passing away with the coming of the time of the New Testament, which is later, in which the Lord spoke in the flesh. For he says: “The old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new.”

In this statement, in which he spoke, four things are shown. First, the dignity of the person, since he speaks to Moses and not to another. Second, mercy, since a human being did not deserve to have the Lord speak to him unless the Lord’s mercy provided it. Third, human manner of expression, because it is said of the Lord, “The Lord speaks,” as though it were said of a human being. Fourth, the Lord’s speech itself is understood.

Through this, mystically, the inspiration of God concerning the law is signified.

“The Lord spoke to Moses in the desert.” By the desert, this present world is signified according to its prosperity.

Historically, however, Moses said, “He spoke through the Spirit to Moses,” so that Moses’ person might be honored by his people, since he spoke not to another man but to him.

The Lord’s two utterances—one in the bush and the other in the tabernacle—signify two laws.

By the first day, the entire span of the present age is shown; by the second month, the future life, or baptism and repentance.

At the beginning of this book, the branch of arithmetic is understood, which may be interpreted as numerical reckoning. The sons of Israel are counted in three ways: by clans, households, and names. This shows that the saints are to be counted by three things: hope, faith, and charity; or by knowledge, word, and deed; or through faith in the Trinity.

Historically, what is said “by clans” is to be understood in this way: “Who are the sons of Jacob and the sons of Levi?” That is, it indicates the name by which each one of them was called.

For this reason, the people were now counted, so that they might carry the tabernacle. There is a great difference in the counting of the people between Moses and David. The census made by Moses and Aaron was commanded by the Lord, and they conducted it not for self-exaltation but in obedience, so that the sons of Israel might carry the tabernacle in due order.

David’s census, however, was made for self-exaltation and was not commanded by the Lord; therefore it deserved punishment.

By this testimony also—“Take the sum of the sons of Israel,” and so forth—it can be signified that “many are called, but few are chosen.”

“From the age of twenty years”: that is, in history and in meaning. The fact that this number does not end signifies that the number of the Church is not to be ended until the end of the world.

The fact that they are counted individually signifies that all the names of the saints are counted in heaven, since their names are written in heaven.

The names of sinners are recalled for two reasons: first, so that they may not be imitated in their conduct; second, so that punishments may be added to them.

Those who are passed over are those who did not deserve remembrance in divine Scripture.
