A saint who is not mentioned is one who, although he has healed his understanding by his work, has nevertheless left no one an example.

Everything that is said is presented in four ways: good well, as here, where the Lord spoke to Moses; evil badly, as when someone speaks a word against God; good badly, as when you are that person’s disciple; evil well, as when “males passed through males,” and so forth.

The twelve princes chosen by Moses and Aaron signify the twelve prophets and the twelve apostles, chosen by the law and the priesthood to govern the Church of God the Father.

Four persons cooperate in the adornment of the tabernacle: God, Moses, Aaron, and the people. In the same way, the Church is adorned by these four persons: God, the law, the priesthood, and the people—and by the four Gospels.

Every saint is also adorned with four virtues, as we have said in certain passages; or with the four elements of which a human being consists: moist and dry, hot and cold.

The fact that women and children are not counted signifies that the soft and effeminate, and those who are children in faith, have not yet attained unity in perfection. They are not counted in the camps of the saints because we cannot stand in the battle that we must wage daily.

All these matters must be joined to the place where it is said: “You shall count them by companies,” and so forth.

“Of Reuben: Elisur son of Sedeur.” Here the order of narrating or counting is shown.

The father’s name is mentioned with the son’s because the father was more distinguished than his son—or because it was said earlier: “Take the sum of the sons of Israel by their clans, their households, and their names.”

When this census is referred to the Church, it is shown that all the saints are counted through many virtues; and by “heads,” that is, principalities; by forty, the four Gospels; by six, the age of the world; by five hundred, the five books of Moses’ law; by fifty, penitents; and by three hundred, faith in the Trinity.

All the numbers that have been counted up to this point bear another figure of the world.

The Levites, however, were not counted with them because they were dedicated to the Lord.

“But you shall appoint them over the tabernacle.” This signifies the saints whom the Lord appointed over the Church, to carry it from the world to heaven; or it signifies each saint who, with perfected senses, is carried toward the kingdoms of heaven, as it is said: “All these things happened to them as a figure for us.” Or, as the Apostle says: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called.”

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0359B]

“Let Judah pitch his tents toward the east.” Here the first arrangement of the tribe of Judah is shown, because it was before the tabernacle.

The tribe of Judah is placed before Issachar because Judah was a warrior, as it is said: “Judah is a lion’s cub,” and so forth; or because Christ would take flesh from him; or so that they would not later envy him when he assumed the kingdom, since God’s judgment had appointed him beforehand; or because the sons of freedom and servitude had been joined together, so that they might have peace with one another; or so that it might be shown to the people that they had pitched their tents as equals before God.

Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun pitched their tents east of the tabernacle; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad to the south; Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh to the west; Dan, Asher, and Naphtali to the north.

Dan is not unfittingly placed last, because Samson was from Dan, and he bore a figure of Christ. Thus the Church begins with confession and ends with judgment.

The sons of Israel are placed in three ranks around the tabernacle, so that none of them might be in excess or lacking.

It is asked: when they pitched the tabernacle in this manner, so that they could see it, was this done for the sake of reverencing God’s tabernacle? And the Levites, guarding it and carrying the ark, are appropriately arrayed against all its assaults.

These four ranks correspond to the chariot in Ezekiel: the human being, the lion, the calf, and the eagle.

The lion belongs to Judah, since it is said of him: “Judah is a lion’s cub.” The calf belongs to Levi, since it was the custom of the Levites to sacrifice calves for the people. The eagle belongs to Benjamin. The human being corresponds to human beings.

What else does the tabernacle signify in this place except the Church of the Old Testament?

The twelve princes around the tabernacle signify the twelve prophets around the synagogue, or the twelve apostles around the Church, together with those who believed with them.

Alternatively, Judah before the tabernacle bears the figure of Peter, who before all the others believed in the divinity present in the man, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Luke before the tabernacle signifies Peter before the Church. Just as the guarding of the tabernacle begins with Judah and ends with Dan, so the Church begins with confession, as we said above, and ends with judgment.

Eight ranks are shown here; so also the Church is surrounded by the eighth rank of the New Testament.

There were eight ranks in the middle, which encircle it, and four outer ranks, which defend the tabernacle and bear the figure of worldly believers.

The four former ranks that we mentioned appear to be our acts of reverence and the service of the Church of God. The four ranks in whose midst the ark stands signify the ranks of the saints who defend the Church from heretics and sinners.

Each person preserves his own order, as it is said: “Let everything be done in due order.”

These ranks are established by God’s command. Likewise, two orders are established in the Church by God’s command: the order of marriage and the order of virginity.

There were four ranks outside and four inside. So also in the Church there are four ranks, namely the four Gospels.

Three tabernacles were placed toward the east. They signify faith in the Trinity, or the Church, to which it was said: “For those who fear the name of the Lord, the Sun of righteousness will rise.”

The three toward the south signify faith in the Trinity, or the Church, to which at the end of life it is said: “Come, blessed ones,” and so forth.

## CHAPTERS III–IV

The three before Aaron toward the east, the three second behind Aaron on his right, and the three west of Aaron signify those to whom it is said: “If anyone wishes to come,” and so forth.

The three toward the north signify those to whom it is said: “Depart, you accursed,” and so forth.

All were gathered around the tabernacle and separated by signs. So also all the saints are gathered in faith in the Trinity and separated by their works.

Of worldly people it is said: “You will know them by their fruits.”

The raising and lowering of the tabernacle signifies the Church, which is raised daily among believers and lowered among those who deny.

When the tabernacle is lowered, certain things in it are not rolled up, while certain others are covered by a double veil. This is because Holy Scripture, which can signify the tabernacle, is sometimes manifest and sometimes veiled. For they are covered by a twofold or threefold hope; the allegory has indeed been set free.

Now it is wrapped in a hyacinth-colored veil, now in a purple one, because Holy Scripture often discusses Christ’s incarnation or his Passion, and often the figure of martyrdom, and often heavenly mysteries.

To the extent that the sons of Levi are worthy, they will approach the holy things; and to the extent that Christians are worthy, they will approach the divine secrets.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0360D]

“Let lepers, those who suffer a discharge, and those defiled by a corpse be cast out of the camps.”

Lepers are heretics. Those who suffer a discharge are those who are polluted in thought or excessively wordy. Those defiled by a corpse are unclean in deed.

Such people are separated from the camps of the Church, lest through the contagion of their conduct they pollute the life of the innocent.

The tabernacle of each saint can also be signified together with four ranks, that is, the four Gospels, or the four substances of which a human being consists.

Within, every saint possesses the four principal virtues. It begins with Ruth—that is, confession—and ends with Dan—that is, judgment—having within it Aaron, that is, perfected understanding.

Its eastern rank signifies the saints of preaching, because “the righteous will shine like the sun.”

The right-hand rank signifies the warmth of faith; the western rank, the setting of the prosperity of this world; the northern rank, opposition from the devil.

“They kindled strange fire.” It is called strange fire because these men were not appointed by the Lord, or because the fire was not sent from heaven, or because the deed was performed out of pride.

The death of these priests likewise signifies the teaching of heretics and the death of heresy: of those who offer in vengeance, or of those who kindle the fire of lust in vengeance.

The sons of Israel were not placed in the same order because they were separated in all their ministrations.

After this the Lord warns: “When a man’s wife has gone astray and despised her husband, and has slept with another man, and her husband has been unable to discover it,” and so forth, he is to bring her to the priest, and so forth.

This man whose wife she was is the shepherd of the Church; his wife is each of his subjects. The priest to whom they come is Christ; the water is Scripture.

When a leader cannot detect the crime of a subject but nevertheless suspects that she has committed adultery through some vice, he should, through zeal for justice, bring her to the priest—that is, reserve the matter for God’s judgment, lest he judge before the proper time.

The priest himself, the Lord Christ, despises hypocrisy through the bitter waters—that is, through the discipline of divine Scripture—and reveals sin, either here or certainly in the future. For, as it says, “Nothing is hidden that will not be known.”

Christ says in the Gospel: “The word that I have spoken to you will judge you on the last day.”

Thus the bitter water is called divine Scripture because it does not spare sinners; but to the righteous it is sweet, since it promises eternal rewards. Thus for some the water is blessed, and for others accursed.

The Apostle also says something similar: “To some we are the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life.”

Others say that the offering made for the woman signifies the blood of Christ, which was poured out for the soul of every human being.

The offering is placed upon the altar—that is, the body of Christ in the Church.

The handful signifies faith in the Trinity. The tenth part signifies the Decalogue. The measure of barley flour demonstrates the power of the flesh.

“He shall not pour oil over it, nor place frankincense upon it”: that is, mercy and prayer.

When he says, “He shall put some of the dust from the floor of the tabernacle into it,” he signifies that a commemoration is to be placed in it through the teaching of the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints.

When he says, “He shall uncover her head,” he signifies the disclosure of sin from the principal understanding of the soul.

Through the writing and the water he demonstrates the teaching of Christ and the shedding of blood.

## CHAPTER VI

The Nazirite is commanded not to drink wine, anything that can intoxicate, or anything made from grapes; nor to drink vinegar or eat anything made from dried grapes.

What does the name “Nazirite” signify except abstinence of life?

Luxury is forbidden to these people in wine; different desires are signified by different drinks.

Those who do not drink wine but drink other beverages are people who, in order to deceive others, pretend to possess certain shadows and images of virtues.

Those who eat dried grapes are people who, for the sake of human approval, stain themselves with the pallor of abstinence in order to win glory from human beings.

Those who drink vinegar are people who fall from the holiness of life into the oldness of former vices and take pleasure in the corruption of their former wickedness.

Therefore God commands those who assume the title of holiness to abstain from all these vices and to retain no memory of them.

It is then commanded that the Levites be sprinkled with water of purification and shave the hair of their flesh, because those who are taken up into divine service ought to be cleansed by the health-giving water of teaching and appear before God’s eyes free from superfluous conduct or thoughts, lest they deform the beautiful appearance of the soul as though with fruitful hairs.

In the phrase “He shall restore him,” some say that repentance for sin is signified.

In the further mention of a week, they understand confession through the sevenfold teaching of the Holy Spirit.

The eighth day demonstrates the New Testament.

The sacrifices that follow have been discussed sufficiently above.

## CHAPTER VII

The six wagons can signify the six days, and the twelve princes the twelve prophets; similarly, the twelve oxen signify the twelve apostles.

Alternatively, the wagons signify [uncertain]; the covered ones, however, signify the contemplative life.

The bowl and its foliage signify body and soul, both filled with fine flour.

The young goats signify perfected works.

The ten-shekel mortars signify the body with its ten senses, filled with incense—that is, prayer—through the fire of compunction.

The ox signifies a teacher, but the two oxen show the senses of body and soul.

The five goats likewise signify the five senses.

One goat signifies either Christ’s flesh or the people of any one group of heretics.

All the ornamentation, gold and silver, signifies history and meaning, by which the Church is adorned.

Alternatively, an ox from the herd prefigured the spirit from the Jews.

The twelve days bear the figure of those living according to the teachings of the apostles.

The water of purification signifies the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or tears in repentance.

## CHAPTER VIII

The law commanded the Levites to serve in the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year until their fiftieth year, and after their fiftieth year to cease serving; they were then to be guardians of the vessels and ministers of their brothers.

What else is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which youth arises in us, except the battles against each vice? And what else is signified by the number fifty, in which those of the Jubilee rest forever, except the outward rest expressed after the battle of the mind has been subdued?

What else are the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful?

The Levites serve the tabernacle from the twenty-fifth year and become guardians of the vessels at fifty, so that those who still endure the struggles of attacking vices through the consent of pleasure do not presume to take responsibility for others.

When they have subdued the battles of temptations and are secure in themselves concerning eternal tranquility, they are entrusted with the guardianship of souls.

But who can completely subdue these battles, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind,” and so forth? Yet it is one thing to endure battles bravely, and another to be enfeebled and conquered by battles.

## CHAPTER IX

Afterward it is commanded that those who were unable to take part in the Passover in the first month should assemble in the second month.

They were commanded to do this in the second month, which is clearly understood as a type of the people of the Gentiles. They had seemed, envious in soul, to have committed fornication with all the demons; but, cleansed by a saving confession, they are commanded to pass over to a second birth, as though to the second month.

## CHAPTER X

Two silver trumpets are also commanded to be made, by which the multitude can be summoned.

The army is summoned by two trumpets because through the two Testaments, or through the two commandments of charity, the people are called to the battle line of faith.

They are silver so that the words of preachers may shine with the brilliance of eloquence and not confuse the minds of their hearers with any obscurity.

They are hammered because those who preach the life to come must grow through the cuttings of present tribulations.

It is rightly said: “When the sound is interrupted, the camps will move,” because when a subtler or more minute word of preaching is handled, the minds of the hearers are stirred more ardently against their battles.

From the place in Exodus where it is said that the sons of Israel came from Rephidim into the desert of Sinai, where Moses ascended Mount Sinai, everything that is read up to the end of Exodus, the whole of Leviticus, and what the book of Numbers contains up to the present place were written at this encampment, that is, at Mount Sinai.

After this, coming from the Lord’s mountain, they arrived in the wilderness of Paran. This encampment is called “the Grave of Lust” because of what happened there.

## CHAPTER XI

This people, disdaining the heavenly bread, desired Egyptian meat; therefore a fire devoured them.

From this we learn that those who have abandoned the conduct of this world and rejected the Egyptian pots—that is, the desires of carnal longings—ought not to murmur against the heavenly bread or desire the drunkenness of the Egyptians, but should seek the simple food of manna, that is, the life of heavenly things.

Otherwise, if after a perfected life we wish to desire our former inclinations, we will swallow nausea and will immediately be tormented by the Lord’s fire.

Our desire will be turned into a tomb, so that we may become whitewashed tombs.

Historically, however, it must be understood why the sons of Israel desired meat while possessing manna. The answer is that manna had the likeness of every food except meat.

So also Holy Scripture contains every kind of nourishment that benefits, except the sinful will.

The Lord also gave meat so that he would not be thought to possess only limited power. Nevertheless, because they asked improperly, he punished them.

Thus the will is granted through Scripture—not in one day, that is, not in the unity of faith; nor in two laws; nor in five volumes. The Decalogue is signified; the twenty-two laws are signified. “By one Moses,” that is, by the present time. “Through your nostrils.” Just as they did not ask according to custom, so they are punished.

Joshua sacrifices through Moses, signifying Christ sacrificing through the law.

At this encampment, the Spirit descended upon the seventy men. The Lord descended in a cloud, withdrew the spirit that was in Moses, and placed it upon the seventy men.

In his descent, the grace of the Holy Spirit was spread throughout all the flesh of Christ through faith, over the chosen peoples and the seventy languages of the nations.

All that gift of power which had once been in Moses and the prophets came upon them.

## CHAPTER XII

After this Aaron, entering upon the occasion of offense with his sister Miriam, reproached his brother because he had taken a wife from a foreign people.

Immediately Miriam broke out with the contagion of leprosy.

This signifies that that priestly people of the Fathers would disparage Christ the Savior because of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, and would not return to God’s tabernacle until the time of the fullness of the Gentiles had been completed.

Then that same people will be able to recover its former health, when the knowledge of the sevenfold Spirit of grace has interceded for them unto pardon.

## CHAPTER XIII
After these events, twelve scouts are sent to inspect the land. The scouts sent to inspect the fertile land, who terrified the people, signify the scribes and Pharisees. For just as those men were sent by Moses [Col. 0364C] to examine the land’s fertility with careful attention, so these were sent through the Law and the Prophets to investigate the fertility of Scripture and discern the Lord’s coming: he who arose from the holy land—that is, from the body of the virgin Mary, in whom the grace of the Spirit abounded. Or, certainly, they were to consider the land of Christ’s flesh, through which they might attain the kingdom of God as the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life.

But just as those scouts terrified the people so that they would not believe God’s promises, so these men persuaded the Jewish people not to believe Christ, who promised forgiveness of all sins and the kingdom of heaven. They desired to return to Egypt, that is, to this world; while receiving the manna of faith, they sought the black pots of sins, the rotten onions of blasphemies, and the decaying melons of vices and lusts.

That cluster hanging from the wood is Christ hanging from the wood of the cross, from the land of the virgin mother Mary according to the flesh, poured forth from the womb of the stock of the earth. The two bearers are the two peoples. The first, the Jewish people, gave Christ their back and not their face; they did not see him whom they bore in the Law. Of them it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see,” and so forth. The second is the people of the nations, who, believing in Christ and always bearing him, see him and, like a servant, follow his lord.

This is the cluster that poured out the wine of his blood, shed for our salvation, through its crushing. The Church, sharing the burden, followed him with pomegranates. For just as pomegranates contain many seeds within a single outer rind, so the Church, fortified by the unity of faith, contains many peoples, or all the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the bond of charity. The fig that they carried with the cluster presented an image of the Law, as we are taught in the Gospel examples. For neither can the Law exist without Christ, nor Christ without the Law.

Others also say that these twelve men, carrying a branch with grapes, signify the twelve apostles. They likewise believe that the branch with grapes signifies Christ’s body together with his divinity, carried from the north toward the right—that is, from the letter of the Law toward the warmth of faith.

## CHAPTER XIV

Caleb prefigures good teachers; the others who terrified the peoples signify evil teachers. That the rebellious man, without God’s command, went up the mountain’s summit, his head darkened, and was overcome by the Amalekites and Canaanites signifies that anyone who trusts in his own virtues, darkened by ignorance and climbing the summit of pride, and who wishes to resist opposing powers, will immediately be led away without God.

## CHAPTER XV

Next comes the account of the man who dared to violate the Sabbath day, for which reason he was removed from the people. He represents the figure of the one who is signified today in Christ. He is found performing a carnal work, namely, gathering wood, hay, and straw suitable for the food of eternal fire. While he gathers these things, he is killed, caught by the people; when he is judged by spiritual persons, he is spiritually killed, overwhelmed by the stones of the testimonies of divine Scripture [Col. 0365C].

The command that they make tassels at the corners of their garments, placing violet-blue cords in them, signifies that commandments which seem excessive, if they are kept for the sake of heavenly life—signified by the violet-blue color—and for the sake of the aerial warmth, are greatly beneficial. For whoever despises small things gradually falls away, so that, whether we eat or drink, we may do everything for the glory of God.

Historically, the tassels are commanded so that there may already be, in the people’s garments, a distinction between the children of Israel and the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XVI

Korah, Dathan, and Abiron, who resisted Moses and Aaron the priest through perverse efforts, signify heretics, who attempt to create heresy and schisms and deceive many by drawing them along with themselves. Contradicting Christ’s priests and profaning the truth of the Lord’s sacrifice through false sacrifices, they are plunged into the cleft of the earth—that is, swallowed up by earthly teachings together with those who adhere to them, and made food for the eternal fire.

Korah is interpreted as “baldness”; Dathan as “their gift”; and Abiron as “my exalted father.” Through these names all heretics are signified: adorned with every appearance of the beauty of virtues, they nonetheless bear baldness. For, as it is written, “baldness upon every head,” they seem to possess their gift, and not God’s, and they arrogate to themselves exalted predecessors.

“And alive they descend into hell”—because they err not through ignorance but through contempt, with a perverse mind. The sons of Eliab are the sons of the devil, or those whose name is interpreted as “unrighteous.” Fire fell upon Dathan because the one who offered strange fire had to be consumed by fire. The earth also swallowed them because they contended to hold dominion on earth, since the material of greed was in them. It swallowed their livestock together with all their property. For just as livestock and other possessions are guarded for God’s sacrifices, so livestock from which no sacrifice is offered to God are destroyed.

They suffered this unusual death because they had performed an unusual work for the Lord. This happened by day, not by night, so that it might be seen by everyone; sacrifice was not customarily performed at night. It happened before the whole multitude so that all the others might fear.

Historically, they all descend into hell [Col. 0366B]. For just as men are raised into heaven, so these men descended into hell. This agrees with the saying: “Let them go down alive into hell, for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst,” as Moses says: “But I cried out to the Lord, and the Lord will save me.”

Some also say that they had laid down judgment, because they did not heed the Lord through Moses and Aaron, the ten plagues, and the preaching in hell, as it is said: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven,” and so forth. Alternatively, those who did not add sin to Adam’s sin were freed by Christ; conversely, those who added sin were not freed.

The statement, “Let them descend alive into hell,” indicates that hell is beneath the earth. Alternatively, “hell” is understood as the grave. Through fire and earth, the letter and the meaning are also said to be understood mystically. For earth appropriately designates the letter, because it proclaims the good things of earth; and therefore the meaning is designated by fire, because the divine words are fiery: “A fiery law is in his right hand.” Through all the property and tents, sins and bodies are designated.

Afterward Aaron took a censer and confronted the destruction. Standing between the living and the dead, he halted the plague. This priest is Christ; this is the one who came from heaven and halted our plague; this is the one who was born or died between the living and the dead. Or certainly, as it is written of him: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.”

And so, taking the censer of his passion, he suspended the destruction of eternal fire and endured hostile death [Col. 0366D]. The fact that Moses and Aaron judged the people can also be understood in this sense: the saints will judge sinners on the day of judgment. “You will sit and judge,” and so forth.

After the new Law—that is, after the people’s placement in relation to the tabernacle—these men transgressed. Therefore they received this punishment as a figure of Ananias and Sapphira, who were the first to sin under the New Covenant.

Eleazar signifies every good teacher. He takes up the censers, that is, sinners lying in the fire of desire, and applies them to the altar of the Church, so that incense—that is, prayer—may be made from them.

## CHAPTER XVII

Aaron’s rod, which blossomed because of its dryness [Col. 0367A], signifies Christ’s flesh, which, having been put to death, came back to life. Thus the rod becoming green after its dryness is Christ rising after death. We understand both the flower itself and the rod itself: in the rod, the power of the ruler is shown; in the flower, his beauty. Hence it is said elsewhere: “I am the flower of the field.”

Others think that this rod, which produced a flower without a grove, represents Mary, who without intercourse with a man produced the Son of God. Of her it is written: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse.”

Aaron’s rod can also signify the teaching of Christ; the twelve rods signify the sects of worldly things. Others, however, say that the teaching of the twelve prophets is signified by the twelve rods. And just as each person’s name was inscribed on his rod, so the names of the prophets are found in their books and teachings.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Only males shall eat from it, so that only males may understand the mysteries. Women, however—that is, those who are involved in feminine sins—do not desire the sacrament in the Church but are content with the offering, as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content.” After this, the ashes of the red heifer, burned as a whole offering, became an expiation for the people.

## CHAPTER XIX

The red heifer is the flesh of the Savior, rose-colored with the blood of his passion, and of mature age, because Christ suffered at the age of perfection. The fact that no yoke was placed upon it shows that Christ’s flesh was not subjected to sin. Its being driven outside the camp while Eleazar the priest stood by signifies that Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem [Col. 0367C]; the people and the priests consented to Christ’s crucifixion. And just as those who offer the heifer are unclean, so all who crucified Christ are regarded as sinners.

But just as the one who gathers the ashes of purification is unclean, so all are clean who proclaimed Christ’s passion among all the nations and sprinkled them with his teaching. We think that the cedar wood and hyssop signify the cross and baptism. For the vessel was sprinkled with the blood of the lamb by which people used to be cleansed, just as the faithful are now cleansed through baptism.

The twice-dyed scarlet appropriately bears the figure of sacred blood, by which we sinners are washed. It is twice-dyed because through it we are cleansed in heart and body. Through faith in the cross and through the sacred washing of Christ’s blood, we are purified in the sacrament. And just as those people are purified on the third day, so we believe that Christ rose on the third day.

In this manner, one is clean on the seventh day—that is, when the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit arrives.

Morally, the red heifer, whose purification is for the people, is the soul that is not burdened by the yoke of sin and comes to mature manhood. It is called red because it is daily put to death for Christ through martyrdom; and, following its example, others are instructed even after its death, and thus it can be offered in the house of God.

All these things that we have said apply to Christ also apply to every Christian, through imitation of Christ. He is commanded to hand over his flesh to the priest, that is, to Christ, outside the camp of vices, sins, and worldly things, in the sight of all believers or of the good virtues [Col. 0368A]. And dipping his finger—that is, while preaching about the blood of Christ and fulfilling it in action—and sprinkling blood toward the doors of the tabernacle, that is, toward the senses of his heart, through faith in the sevenfold Spirit, so that he may burn it with the fire of compunction, in the sight of all, that is, of believers.

“Even with the hide handed over” [uncertain]. Let him surrender himself wholly to the passion, imitating the Lord.

By the hide, the usefulness of the letter is demonstrated; by the flesh, carnal commandments pertaining to active life; by the blood, martyrdom; by the dung, the integrity of the wretched; by the flames, the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Alternatively, the hide signifies mortality; the flesh, vices or carnal sins; the blood, faith in the passion; the dung, evil suspicions concerning the body of Christ; the cedar wood, faith in the wood of the cross or sublime work; hyssop, humility; the twice-dyed scarlet, the double martyrdom of body and soul; washed garments, clean works; evening, repentance or the killing of prosperity; the clean man, each saint; the ashes, the examples of the saints.

But when these things are referred to Christ, the clean man can be understood as Joseph, who received Christ’s body; the most pure place as the Church; and the corpse of the slain man as sin. He is unclean for seven days—that is, until he has completed his repentance. “From water,” that is, from baptism, repentance, or teaching. “On the third day,” that is, in faith in the Trinity. Water, as was said above, can also mean tears.

Whoever enters the tent—that is, whoever consents to sin. Whoever dies—that is, whoever dies in the teaching of the one who enters the tent, meaning in his teaching. All his vessels will be polluted, that is, the heretics; the whole people for seven days, that is, until they have repented and until they have believed in the teaching of the sevenfold Spirit.

He overturns the covering, that is, the united ones; and the binding, that is, the unity of faith. If he has no covering—that is, if he has sins without defense. If someone touches in a field the corpse of a slain man—that is, whoever consents to the unclean sin of a man slain in sin—or his bones or his tomb, that is, his works or his example.

## CHAPTER XX

At the death of the prophetess Mary, the dead prophets are signified [Col. 0368D]. In Moses and Aaron, the end of the Law and the priesthood is signified.

When Moses struck the rock with his rod, he doubted God’s power, so that the people might see—Moses now representing the one who affixes Christ to the cross—that he gave God’s power to unbelievers. Finally, the Apostle also says: “The rock was Christ.”

The rock is struck twice because Christ was struck first by the tongues of the Jews, when they said, “Crucify, crucify,” and then by the hands of the soldiers who affixed him to the cross. Hence Mark also says that he was crucified at the fourth hour, namely by the tongues of the Jews; but at the sixth hour he was crucified by the hands of the soldiers.

Afterward Aaron dies in the year in which the new people are about to enter the promised land. When the Law ceases, the people of the nations enter and violently seize the kingdom of heaven. And although the priesthood was given to Eleazar on the mountain, and although the Law leads those who fulfill it toward lofty illumination, this exalted state is not beyond the waters of the Jordan; for the Law brought nothing to perfection.

Finally, Aaron is mourned because under the Law there is a descent into hell, whereas in the Gospel there is a passage into paradise. “Hour” is interpreted as “light.” Aaron therefore failed in the light, because as the Gospel flashed forth, the Law failed.

The people wept for thirty days because before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, the synagogue does not receive spiritual joy but, mourning over the letter that kills, remains bowed down.

Others say that Christ is signified by Eleazar, to whom his father’s garments were given, because Christ put on the new garment. They also say that the rock can morally signify each saint, who is struck twice by spiritual teaching—that is, in body and soul—from which good works and souls flow [Col. 0369B].

## CHAPTER XXI

Finally, the Canaanite fought against Israel and, conquering, led away the spoil. Israel then fought again by a vow and conquered. This signifies that, deprived of God’s help, our enemies easily conquer us; but if we turn to the Lord, we may conquer where we were conquered and triumph over our enemies.

The fact that serpents attack the murmuring people, and that the wounds inflicted by the serpents are healed by looking upon the raised bronze serpent, signifies that the wicked serpent poured in the poisons of sin, while they continually look inwardly upon Christ raised on the cross. And those who approached through faith are made [the phrase is incomplete or uncertain]. Concerning this he himself says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent.”

The fact that it is bronze signifies that he died according to the flesh but is eternal according to his divinity. Bronze is customarily more durable than the other metals. The fact that Moses set up this serpent appropriately shows that the Law prophesied Christ. And just as death was introduced among human beings through a serpent, so here salvation is shown to human beings through a serpent.

Adam assuredly consecrated this substance—the body and soul of Christ; so too Mary for Eve; and likewise here he is said to have consecrated the serpent.

Morally, the serpent can signify the saints raised to the height of perfected works and understanding, as the divine Law also sets it forth. The serpents signify vices or sins; the wilderness signifies the Church [Col. 0369D], which possesses a well, that is, baptism. The leaders who dug it are understood as the prophets and apostles: the giver of the Law is Christ; the staff signifies testimonies.

When it says, “Let the well rise, let the well rise,” it signifies Christ and his people desiring baptism to increase without works in teaching.

Finally, Sihon, king of the Amorites, fought against Israel, and Israel conquered. Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes.” He signifies the devil, who disguises himself as an angel of light and through heresies falsely utters plausible things. The Amorites possess this law—being interpreted as “those who embitter”—because they live in the bitterness of vices and resist teachers of the truth. This king is killed in every saint who condemns semblance and loves truth.

Og, however, is interpreted as “conclusion”; Bashan as “confusion.” The devil’s work is always to close off the way that leads to life. Closure goes before as king, and confusion follows like the people, because those whom he shuts off from believing in Christ are confounded when he appears.

## CHAPTER XXII

Next comes the account of Balaam, who, when he went out to curse the people of God, heard the she-ass speaking. What is this she-ass except the brutish Gentile world, which Balaam—that is, every idolater—led wherever he wished, like a brute animal that offered no resistance through reason?

But this animal saw the angel of God, whom the man could not see, so that we might understand that in the future, at the coming of the angel of the great counsel, that Gentile people would, after its natural hardness had been changed and its tongues set free, speak. Although it had been subject to unbelief, it would burst forth in the voice of faith and confession [Col. 0370B].

The angel standing before Balaam and being seen by him on the third occasion signifies that Christ stood in the three Laws but was seen in the third. The two walls surrounding the vineyards demonstrate the two Laws by which souls or Churches are enclosed.

Others say that Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “vain people,” signifies the devil, who struck the she-ass—that is, inflicted blows upon the synagogues of human beings—until Christ came.

Morally, this animal also signifies our flesh, which, touched by the whip, indicates the coming Lord, whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. Thus, when we desire to complete the spirit’s anxiety in this world, it impedes the journey, as it were, until the invisible one who confronts it becomes known [Col. 0370C].

Hence Peter says: “He received a rebuke for his madness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly.” The madman is rebuked by the mute beast of burden when the exalted mind, afflicted through the flesh, is reminded of the good of humility, which it ought to retain.

But Balaam did not deserve the gift of this rebuke [the text reads *domum*, apparently for *donum*, “gift”], because, going to curse, he changed his voice, not his mind.

Who is Balaac, whose name is interpreted as “one who strikes down” and who wishes to destroy God’s people, except the persecutors of the Church, who injure it? And who is Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “vain people,” whom Balaac calls to curse God’s people, except heretics and schismatics, who, devoted to empty teaching, attempt to reproach God’s people?

And the more those men stir up curses and persecutions, the more the saints flourish in virtues and are regarded as blessed and happy. Just as Balaam gave counsel by which the children of Israel were deceived, so through the counsel of heretics many are deceived amid the persecutions endured by the faithful.

## CHAPTERS XXIII–XXIV

Through his seven altars, which he set up for the Lord together with sacrifices that were not accepted, hearts and bodies, or souls, are also said to be signified. They are seven in number because the heretical man performs his work in imitation.

These altars were erected on a mountain because the three things mentioned above are raised through pride. Those who were in a high place were humbled, and those who were in a low place were exalted, as it is said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled,” and so forth.

God placed a word in Balaam’s mouth, and so forth—that is, a blessing. Historically, [this signifies] the meaning or confession of the true faith in the manner of heretics, which would also be a blessing for them if they preserved it.

When he says in a parable, “Son of Seor, a man whose eye has been darkened,” he shows that now we see through a mirror and prophesy in part; or, certainly, that he understood the mystery in ecstasy. The fact that, although he fell, he had his eyes open means the same as above. And when he says, “Water flows from his bucket,” he shows that a great people would grow from Israel.

It follows: “It shall be in many waters.” The many waters are many peoples; or, alternatively, the water is evangelical teaching, which flows from the apostles who were of the seed of Jacob.

What follows, “His king shall be taken away, Agag,” is a prophecy concerning Saul, who, because he spared King Agag, provoked the Lord’s anger.

The statement, “I shall see him, but not now,” and so forth, can also be said of the people, because what was to come was exceedingly glorious in the kingdom of David and Solomon. Nevertheless, it is plainly said of Christ.

It follows: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel,” and so forth.

Some also say that this demonstrates the Church, which historically was spoken of as arising from the people. They understand the statement that it arose “beside the rivers” as meaning beside the teachings of the apostles, like cedars—that is, like saints, because of the loftiness of their virtues. “Near the waters” is to be understood as we explained “rivers” above: water flowing from the bucket signifies teaching or baptism. “It shall be in many waters,” that is, among many believers.

“Like a rhinoceros”: this is the blessing of the unicorn, which is compared to unity because of its size or strength. It is also said to bear the figure of the apostle Paul, who was under one Law before he came into the New Testament.

“Daughter on the way,” that is, wisdom or divinity. “His enemies” signifies holy angels, nations, vices, demons, or heretics. What is said about “their bones” signifies the works or practices of heretics. “With arrows,” that is, with testimonies.

When “lion” is mentioned, it is said from the perspective of Christ or in the person of the people; “lioness” is said in the person of the Church or of a holy soul. “No one dared,” that is, none of the heretics.

The messengers whom Balaac is said to have sent to Balaam signify diabolical suggestions.

“A star from Jacob,” that is, Mary. For the star is situated in heaven, and brightness comes forth from it; so brightness, that is, Christ, arose from Mary. Hence this is said of Christ in Israel on account of his strength. The rod is understood as Christ’s flesh.

Through the star from Jacob, the Church can also be signified as coming from Christ or from the primitive people; and through the rod, the Christian people. This star from Jacob also signifies a soul from a saint; this rod likewise signifies perfected understanding.

The leaders of Moab are the leaders of the devil, or vices and sins. Moab is interpreted as “father of the people.” The children of Seth, whose name is understood as “opposed,” signify here the children of the devil, who is opposed to good.

Edom, that is, “bloody,” signifies the Church, which is Christ’s possession. Seir is interpreted as “hairy” and signifies the devil, whose inheritance will fall to his enemies. Israel signifies the saints who rule—that is, Christ, or his people, or perfected understanding.

“The remnants of the city” signify the Churches of heretics. Amalek, whose name is interpreted as “licking,” also signifies the devil, licking up the sins of human beings; his extremities will be destroyed, that is, at the coming of Christ.

The Kenite also signifies the devil, or the people of the whole world. “Your nest,” that is, your pomp. “Cast out in pride,” that is, in sins. “From the stock of Cain,” that is, from the common people [the source reads *commedio*, an uncertain form].

“Let Asshur capture you,” that is, Christ, spiritually. Asshur is interpreted as “strong” or “conquering,” both of which apply to Christ. These statements above can also apply figuratively to the nations coming to faith.

“Who will survive?”—but would that there were only one when these things come. Alternatively, “Who will survive?” is to be understood as though he had said: “There will be few,” as it is said, “Many are called”; or, “Who will survive?” means, “Which of human beings will survive in the time of Jesus?”

“They come,” that is, the Romans come from Italy. “From the face of the sun,” that is, the saints from the face of Christ. “The Assyrians,” that is, demons. “They themselves will perish,” namely, from carnal life.

## CHAPTER XXV

Then Phinehas the priest put an end to the Lord’s anger by destroying not only idolatry but also every carnal affection. The Lord is appeased when the desire of the flesh is conquered.

## CHAPTER XXVI

After this the people are counted again, and the Levites are also counted [Col. 0372C]. Once the first flesh has been slain, the new people of God are enrolled so that they may receive the heavenly inheritance.

Moreover, the fact that six hundred thousand who went out from Egypt are counted, while only two of them entered the promised land, is likewise written in the Gospel: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” The fact that only two enter shows that people from both peoples attain heavenly life, or that there are two lives: the active and the contemplative.

Then the five daughters of Zelophehad receive an inheritance among their brothers by God’s judgment, because the people of the Law are not excluded from the Gospel’s passion.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Zelophehad is interpreted as “shadow of strength,” because under the shadow of the letter that kills, the spiritual strength of the sacrament lay hidden in the Law.

## CHAPTERS XXVIII–XXX

[Col. 0372D]

After this Jesus succeeds Moses on the mountain; for the Gospel succeeds the Law, in which the commandments of the Law are fulfilled spiritually. We are instructed what we ought to offer every day, because of daily labor; what to offer on the Sabbath, because of the hope of eternal rest; what to offer on the Kalends, because of the invocation of life; and what to offer at Passover, when through baptism we are buried together with Christ and pass from the dead into the newness of life.

We are also instructed what to offer at Pentecost, because of the grace of the Holy Spirit and the forgiveness of sins; what to offer at the new moons of the seventh month, because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; and what to offer during the fast of that same month, when the tabernacles are erected, because this life is not to be loved, since it is brief. This is signified by dwelling in tents and poor shelters.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Next the war against the Midianites is woven into the narrative, together with the death of the divine Balaam, in whose killing the error of unbelief is destroyed. Then comes the division of the spoil taken from the Midianites and the offering from it of souls in the tabernacle of God.

## CHAPTER XXXII

After this the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, possessing innumerable animals, desire a possession on this side of the Jordan and do not wish to have an inheritance in the promised land. They represent the fact that many people are occupied by the entanglements of the world and consequently do not seek a dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTERS XXXIII–XXXIV
The discourse concerning the stations of the children of Israel follows, and it says: “They set out from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover,” and so forth. Rameses is interpreted by some as “turbulent commotion,” or “bitterness,” or “the commotion of the moth”; but we more truly think that “the thunder of joy” is expressed by this city. The people were gathered at the farthest borders of Egypt; and, abandoning the tumult of this world, they were shaken loose from their former vices and from the moth of sins that had often consumed them, turning all bitterness into sweetness, so that they might hear the voice of God on Mount Sinai. That the utterances of the Scriptures call this world’s course “thunder,” the Psalmist declares, saying: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel.” And when we have been changed by the evangelical trumpet, trained by thunder, we go forth into joys.

[Col. 0373B]

“In the first month,” when winter has passed and departed, when the earth has given birth and all things are renewed. We go forth on the fifteenth day of the month, [Col. 0373C] on the following day, in the full light of the month, when the Egyptians surround and bury their dead and do not imitate the example of those who are departing. Setting out from Rameses, they encamped at Succoth. This is the second station, in which they eat unleavened bread and first pitch a tabernacle; hence the place received its name from the event. For Succoth is interpreted as “tabernacles” or “tents,” and this occurs in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the feast of Tabernacles is celebrated.

When, therefore, we have gone out, let us pitch tabernacles, knowing that we must proceed farther; and then let us not eat the leaven of wickedness, but let us feed on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. And setting out from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness. This is the third station, in which God is first seen in a pillar of cloud [Col. 0373D] by day and a pillar of fire by night. Etham is interpreted as “strength” or “perfection.” Great strength is required to leave Egypt and dwell at the edge of the wilderness. From this we understand that Succoth was near Egypt, while Etham was within the boundaries of Egypt and the desert. Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves, so that, illuminated by his fire and overshadowed by his aid, we may be able to reach the promised land.

Setting out from Etham, they entered Phaaroth, which is interpreted as “the mouth of nobles.” Beel-zephon, however, is interpreted as “lord of the north.” Migdol means “greatness” or “tower.” Having therefore assumed strength, let us become noble in the Lord, condemn the secrets of the lord of the north, and avoid his magnificence and tower as pride. [Col. 0374A] He is not from the south, from which the Lord comes, but is the possessor of the north wind, the coldest wind, from which evils blaze upon the earth; although it is the coldest, it is called “right” by name, falsely assuming for itself the title of strength.

Setting out from Achiroth, they crossed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness; and, traveling a three-day journey through the wilderness of Etham, they encamped at Marah, which is interpreted as “bitterness.” After evangelical preaching, after the tabernacles of those who are migrating, after strength has been assumed, after nobility of confession, dangers again arise. Hence we learn that snares must always be avoided and God’s mercy invoked. Therefore, in spiritual baptism, Pharaoh is also drowned for us; and, after we have come out of the Red Sea, we come upon Sur. Traveling there for three days and finding no water, they came to Marah, which received its name because it had bitter water.

And setting out from Marah, they came to Helim, which is translated as “the strong ram.” From bitterness we come to rams and sturdy flocks, to leaders of whom it is said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” The purest springs do not appear except where the teaching of teachers has burst forth.

They set out from Elim and encamped beside the Red Sea. It is asked how, after crossing the Red Sea, and after the strong sea and Elim, they came again to the Red Sea—unless some bay of the Red Sea appeared to them along their route. Crossing the sea is one thing; pitching tabernacles nearby is another. By this we are also warned that, after evangelical discipline and the sweetest food of triumphs, we should sometimes open the sea before us [Col. 0374C] and place former dangers before our eyes, because there is a great difference between crossing the sea and seeing the sea from afar.

This station is not found in Exodus; but it is written concerning it that they came from the Red Sea to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sina. And setting out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the wilderness of Sin. It is the eighth station, although according to the order of Exodus it is the seventh. But it must be understood that every station as far as Mount Sinai is called the wilderness of Sin, and that the place of one station gave its name to the entire region, just as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province.

Sin is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred,” because, after we have come to the place from which the Lord has spoken to us, we deserve great hatred from the enemy. Then we see the bush of the Church burning and being inflamed by persecutions, yet we do not find the Lord speaking in it. Setting out from the wilderness of Sin, they encamped at Dophkah, which is interpreted as “knocking,” in accordance with what the Lord says: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.” And after the eighth number, that of Christ’s resurrection, we begin to knock at the mysteries.

Setting out from Dophkah, they encamped at Alush. Alush is interpreted as “leaven,” which the woman took and mixed into the flour. And setting out from Alush, they encamped at Rephidim, which is interpreted as “the dissolution of the strong” or “the healing of the strong.” Because there she tested the Lord on account of the water of contradiction, the place received the name of testing. Thus Rephidim is called either “the dissolution” or “the healing of the strong”; or it is understood as “scattered,” because Amalek was there; or on account of Israel’s healing. At the same time, it must be noted that after the leaven of Alush and Massan, the demons habitually fix upon us manifold temptations.

Setting out from Rephidim, they pitched their camp in the wilderness of Sinai. They reached this place on the forty-seventh day, as Scripture says: “In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt,” the law was given on the summit of Mount Sinai. Hence the feast of Pentecost is celebrated, and the mystery of the Gospel is completed in the descent of the Holy Spirit.

Sinai is interpreted as “bushes,” not one, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many: there was the beginning, whereas here there is perfection. For it is one thing to possess one grace and another to possess all graces. In this station the giving of the law begins, and so forth. Up to the end of Exodus, and the contents of Leviticus, [Col. 0375B] and a certain portion of Numbers are described.

And setting out from the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped at the graves of craving. There, disdaining the heavenly bread, the people desired the flesh of the Egyptians: “the food was still in their mouths, and the anger of God rose,” and so forth. Hence the place was called “the graves of craving.” From this we are taught that those who have abandoned worldly wisdom and despised the Egyptian pots must not murmur against the heavenly food. Otherwise, if we again desire those things to the point of nausea, we shall immediately be severely tormented by the Lord’s fire. Our desire will be turned into a tomb, so that we become “whited sepulchers,” and so forth.

Setting out from the graves of craving, they encamped at Hazeroth, which is translated as “court.” And observe carefully, prudent reader, that after so much virtue had been brought to completion in the number twelve, Israel became proud and sighed for Egyptian flesh in the graves of craving. Once again he lays another foundation and a court, that is, a vestibule of virtue, showing us that those who stand can fall and those who fall can rise again. For surely one who falls will rise again, will he not?

And setting out from Hazeroth, they pitched their camp at Rithmah. This is the twelfth station. It must be noted that the remaining stations are seventeen, whose catalogue is now briefly described. From Rithmah to Ezion-geber—that is, twenty-two stations—are included under the name of the wilderness of Paran.

Rithmah is interpreted as “the sound of the juniper.” For they say that this wood preserves fire for a long time, so that if coals are covered with its ashes, they last until the end of the year. From this we learn that, after the graves of craving and the vestibules, we should pass on to the wood that retains heat for a long time; or else that we should be fervent in spirit and preach the Gospels with a clear voice.

Setting out from Rithmah, they encamped at Rimmon-perez, which is interpreted as “the division of the pomegranate,” which others call the “granate apple.” This signifies the bosom of the Church, which covers the whole crowd of believers with its rind; or the variety and harmony of the virtues. Hence it is written: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul,” and so forth. Thus the individual ranks were divided in such a way that all were held together by the same structure.

And setting out from Rimmon-perez, they came to Libnah, which we may translate as “brick.” In Exodus we read of the bricks which the people made and over which they groaned. From this we learn that, on the journey of this world, we sometimes increase and sometimes decrease, and that after the ecclesiastical order we often pass over to the work of bricks.

From Libnah they encamped at Rissah. Rissah is interpreted as “bridle.” If, after perfection, we descend to works of clay, we must be bridled, and our wandering and headlong course must be restrained by the reins of the Scriptures.

From Rissah they encamped at Kehelathah, which is interpreted so that the steps of those who run astray may be drawn back by bridles to the Church, and so that they may hasten to enter the doors they previously left behind.

Setting out from Kehelathah, they encamped at Mount Shepher. Shepher is interpreted as “beauty.” See what the bridles accomplish: they draw us away from vices, introduce us into choirs, and make us dwell on Christ’s mountain. According to Daniel, this is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain.

From Mount Shepher they came to Haradah, which is interpreted as “miracle.” What a beautiful order: when, after the work of bricks, we are bridled; after the bridles, we are introduced into the Church; and after dwelling in the Church, we ascend to Christ’s mountain. Placed there, we marvel at those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” and so forth.

Setting out from Haradah, they encamped at Makheloth, which is interpreted as “assembly.” For in this consists the multitude of believers. Hence it can say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together.”

Setting out from Makheloth, they came to Tahath, which is translated as “fear.” You have ascended the most beautiful mountain; in astonishment and wonder you confess the greatness of Christ. Do not be high-minded, but fear. [Col. 0376C] For “the Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Fear is the guardian of virtues, whereas security easily leads to a fall.

Setting out from Tahath, they came to Terah, which some translate as “wickedness” or “pasture.” This properly refers to the leaders of the Churches, or to the guardianship of the soul. If you have fear, you will be watchful; if you are watchful, the lion will not be able to enter the folds of your sheep, and you will be able to escape all the wickedness of the devil.

Setting out from Terah, they encamped at Mithkah, which is translated as “sweetness.” You have trampled the grape, crushed the ambushers, and will immediately obtain the sweet fruits of your labor, so that you may rightly say: “How sweet are your words to our throats,” and so forth.

Setting out from Mithkah, they pitched their camp at Hashmonah, which is interpreted as “hastening”—so that, after we have gathered the sweet fruits of our labor, we should not remain idle or content, but should hasten again toward what lies farther ahead, forgetting what is behind and stretching ourselves toward what is to come.

Setting out from Hashmonah, they encamped at Moseroth, which is interpreted as “bond” or “discipline,” so that we may proceed with hurried step to our teachers and regard the precepts of the virtues as eternal bonds, of which Isaiah says: “Those bound by bracelets walk behind you.”

From Moseroth they encamped at Bareiacha, which is interpreted as “son of necessity” or “son of gnashing.” That these are sons of necessity this psalm teaches us: “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” What is this great necessity that is imposed upon the unwilling, if, contending with adversaries by the shields of truth, you bind them and lead the bound into captivity, and all in the Lord’s temple [Col. 0377A] say, “Glory”?

When we interpret “sons of gnashing,” it refers to this: abandoning the terrors of punishment in that former place where there is “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” the crowd of believers submits its necks to Christ after being freed from the devil’s bonds.

Setting out from Bareiacha, they encamped at Mount Gilead, which is interpreted as “messenger,” or “girded,” or “slaughter.” We cannot otherwise make teachers of disciples and believers into sons of necessity unless we make their instructors thoroughly trustworthy. In the slaughter, let our hand not spare the shoulder or the tip of the ear when extracting it from the lion’s mouth. Hence David says in the morning: “I destroyed all the sinners of the earth.”

Concerning proclamation and girding, we can say this briefly: we should offer great sons of necessity as goads toward virtue when we have announced to them the first things and, girded for battle, taught them these three things. Whatever the teacher does stands upon the mountain.

And from Gilead they encamped at Jotbathah, which is interpreted as “goodness.” When we have come to the perfect man, that is, to the priestly rank and to the fullness of Christ’s age, let us say with David: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be put to shame forever.” For “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.”

From Jotbathah they encamped at Abronah, which is interpreted as “passage” or “crossing.” The true passer-by comes to this place, one who groans daily and says: “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.” Finally, Paul also says: “For the form of this world is passing away.”

[Col. 0377C] Setting out from Abronah, they encamped at Ezion-geber, which is translated as “green tongue,” or “from the doubt of man.” Through this the teaching of an attentive and diligent teacher is shown: he cuts unformed wood, carves it, and makes various vessels in a great house. The woods may signify nations, men of the forests, and every kind of tree, and through them the multitude of the Gentiles.

Thus far extends the wilderness of Paran.

From Ezion-geber they encamped in the wilderness of Sin, which is Cades. It is asked why the eighth station is said to be the thirty-sixth. But it must be understood that the former is written with the letter samekh and is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred.” This one, however, is rendered with ṣade and means “commandment” and “that which is joined.” Cades is not called “holy,” as many think, but is called “changed.” Of it the Psalm of David says: “The wilderness of Cades shall be shaken.”

If it is interpreted as “holy,” it must be understood by antiphrasis, as when something is called “war” that is not at all good, or “grove” though it gives almost no light. In this station Miriam dies, and Moses and Aaron offend the Lord because of the water of contradiction. Where there is a commandment, there are sin, offense, and death.

From Cades they encamped at Hor, which is interpreted as “mountain,” as though it were read, “he ascended the mountain of the mountain,” or “the summit of the mountain.” By this it is signified that we must not be secure concerning our virtues, but must always hasten in a higher degree toward the summits of virtue.

From Mount Hor they pitched their camp at Selmona. Setting out from Selmona, they came to Sinon. These two stations are not found in the historical sequence in place of those listed here. Having gone out from Mount Hor by way of the Red Sea, so that they might go around the land of Edom, they show that the Idumeans were situated at the boundaries of the land.

Selmon is interpreted as “little image,” because there the image of the Savior was plainly represented by the bronze serpent that hung upon the wood. Sinon is interpreted as “mouth,” because after we recognize the passion of the Son of God, what we believe in our heart we proclaim with our mouth.

Setting out from Sinon, they came to Oboth, which is interpreted as “magician” or “female diviner.” This shows that, after the image of God—which is signified by reason in the heart—and the confession of faith, which is conveyed by the mouth, serpents and magical arts arise to provoke us to battle. But let us guard our heart with all vigilance.

Setting out from Oboth, they encamped at Tealzarim, which signifies “heaps of stones of those who cross.” These are the saints who hasten to other stations after this world.

From Tealzarim they came to Dibon-gad, which is interpreted as “a temptation understood with strength.” By this it is signified that we must not be ignorant of the enemy’s cunning. For if they are understood, once understood they are strongly overcome.

From Dibon-gad they encamped at Almon-diblathaim, “contempt of forests,” or “of reproaches.” Through this we learn that all the sweet things and enticements of pleasures in the world must be despised, and that we must not become drunk with the wine “in which is wantonness.” But that reproach is to be despised and produces blessedness, the Savior teaches most fully.

From Almon-diblathaim they encamped in the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo. Abarim is interpreted as “mountains of those who cross.” Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” where the law ends and no memory of it is found. At the same time, consider that the dwelling of those who are passing through is situated on a mountain; but after the mountains we descend into the plains of Moab and to the streams of the Jordan. For nothing is so dangerous as the swollen boastfulness of virtues.

Setting out from the mountains of Abarim, they encamped in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan near Jericho. There they fixed their tents, from the house of anxiety as far as Belsathaim. As we have said, the plains designate humility, the guardian of all virtues.

Abel-shittim is interpreted as “mourning of thorns.” This signifies that we ought to mourn our former sins, which are thorns choking the Lord’s seed. After this the people are taught to destroy the idols and to preserve nothing from their former dwellings. This signifies that, when through faith we enter the land of the holy promise, we must extinguish all vices together with idolatry.

## CHAPTER XXXV

After this it is commanded that cities be given to the Levites for dwelling, together with their suburbs; they are not to receive an inheritance among their brothers. By this those who perform divine service and the priesthood are commanded, according to the Apostle, to be content with food and clothing, so that they may say with the Apostle Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” Nevertheless, they have certain cities and villages in which to dwell. For “the laborer is worthy of his wages.”

# EXPLANATION OF THE FIFTH BOOK OF MOSES, WHICH IS CALLED IN HEBREW *ELLEH HADDEBARIM*, IN GREEK *DEUTERONOMION*, AND IN LATIN *ALTERA LEX* (“THE SECOND LAW”)

[Col. 0379]

## CHAPTERS I–II

[Col. 0379A]

It must certainly be understood that Deuteronomy is a repetition of the preceding four books, and yet contains many things proper to itself. That Deuteronomy is called the second law, or the repetition of the law, signifies that the New Testament would succeed the Old. Nevertheless, it must be understood in what ways this book prefigures the Gospel. It is called this because the book had existed in reality before it existed in writing. It also existed in three books before it existed in one book; this likewise applies to the Gospel, as Paul says: “Set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets.”

Three persons also cooperated in this book: the Father, Moses, and the people to whom it is announced. The Gospel likewise presents the same number of persons: Christ, the four Evangelists, [Col. 0379B] and those who hear.

At this beginning it must also be noted what is indicated by the fact that Deuteronomy is written over twelve days. This shows that, just as Deuteronomy signifies the Gospel because it is the second law, so its testimony over twelve days designates the number of the Apostles. Through them it signifies the twelve Apostles chosen by God after the traitor Judas had been rejected. Or certainly it signifies the fall of the Jewish people, and in the Gospel the transgression of the commandments of the Decalogue.

Moreover, the fact that in it there are four places between which Moses spoke, where they possess much gold, designates the mystery of the Gospel, which is powerful in spiritual meaning.

This Deuteronomy was obscure in two ways, namely in reality and in writing—that is, when it existed separately in four books. But it is revealed when it is extracted from the four books. The Gospel likewise existed through reality and writing until its meaning was proclaimed.

“These are the words,” and so forth. This statement, spoken in the person of Moses—although someone else might have said it concerning Moses, he said it about himself—is spoken in the person of the Holy Spirit and of the translator.

This book is also said to have a certain imperfection because it does not reach the number ten, since Augustine says: “All perfection of numbers lies between ten and thirty, and one hundred and one thousand.” Yet it possesses perfection because the number of the books ends with it.

Deuteronomy was spoken to fathers and sons, which aptly corresponds to the promised land, as in: “Whoever does these things shall live by them.” It is said to the sons: “Hear these things, so that your sons may keep them after you.” He had promised the future reward of the Gospel to souls in the future.

But while this book prefigured the Gospel, each book has its own particular character. The earlier book proclaims the doctrine of the body, that is, the offering of victims, and concerning the letter, because it said earlier: “Whoever kills his neighbor shall be killed.” The second does not preach concerning the letter but concerning meaning; not concerning flesh but concerning soul; not concerning a carnal but a spiritual sacrifice; not concerning present good but future good.

Through history and meaning, through presence and absence, it seems more suitable in other respects if he had said “voices” here rather than “words.” “Words,” however, suit the New Testament, that is, the Gospel. Yet “words” are rightly spoken of this book as well, because they prefigure the Gospel utterances; or because, since the words Moses spoke would not afterward be changed, this shows the dignity of his person.

“To all Israel.” He appropriately said “to all,” because “all” is used only of a crowd, whereas “the whole” applies to either number, whether singular or plural. In what is said, “to all Israel,” those acting are restored in the figure of Christ’s Gospel, to every soul that sees the Lord and the Gospel preaching beyond the Jordan. This signifies that these words were spoken before baptism.

The wilderness signifies the Church, and spiritually there is a wilderness within against everyone, opposite the Red Sea. This signifies that those to whom these words are spoken historically were opposed to baptism, or to the truth of the law that had been given to them.

Between Paran, Tophel, Laban, and Hazeroth—whose interpretations are “increase,” “insipid,” “whitening,” and “courts”—the four minds, as we said above, signify the four Gospels, by which the Church is increased in faith. “Insipid” signifies opposition to vices and the devil; “whitened,” baptism, repentance, and resurrection; “courts,” that is, the Church or the Gospel.

These minds may also signify the fourfold human being, consisting of four elements: moist and dry, cold and hot, to whom the Gospel is preached. The twelve days signify the twelve prophets. Horeb, from which the law begins, indicates the synagogue, from which the law of the New Testament begins.

“By the way of the mountain,” and so forth. This signifies the stability of the Law, because the letter had been changed into meaning; or because the Gospel, whose figure this book bears, announces a life of ascent through faith to heaven.

The Law begins at Mount Sinai and ends at Mount Seir. Seir is interpreted as “hairy,” by which mortality is indicated. For just as the law of the letter had commanded concerning the sacrifice of victims and the killing of those who killed their neighbors, so the Gospel concerns the killing of sins and vices.

The forty years during which the children of Israel laboriously completed their journey and reached the promised land signify the entire time in which the Church lives through labors, preaching the denarius and observing the place of the Law. Four signifies the four Gospels. Four times ten makes forty. Finally, the Lord also fasted for forty days and, while hungry, was tempted, to show us that in the former time we ought to endure temptations.

“On the first day,” and so forth. It was fitting that he should speak the law on the first day. The Law commanded concerning first things, or because the law had been a light to them, provided that they were indeed a people; or because it prefigures the Gospel given on the day of the New Testament. The first day signifies the Old Testament, the second the New.

“Moses spoke,” and so forth. This statement is said of King Jorah, who does not see the one whom he pursues, and it is not permitted to him to come into the king’s presence; rather, the king’s words are sent to him through another. Thus God’s words are sent to Israel through Moses.

Therefore it does not say, “God spoke,” but, “God spoke to Moses,” because the people were unworthy of God’s sight.

“To the children of Israel.” It says not simply “to Israel” but “to the children,” either because they were divided in the worship of idols, or because, of the six hundred thousand who came out of Egypt, only their children reached the promised land, apart from Caleb and Joshua; or it is to be understood in this way: when he says “to the children of Israel,” it is as though he had said, “not to the Gentiles.”

“He had commanded him everything.” This shows that he was to declare to them neither more nor less than he had heard.

“After he struck,” and so forth. It seems appropriate for Moses to announce to the Israelite people, after he had given them victory over Sihon and Og, that they should hear the law well. “He struck” means in body and soul. Sihon, the king of the Amorites, signifies the demon, king of the nations, or the evil sense, king of vices. Moses signifies the figure of Christ, striking the aforesaid powers, or the good sense.

“Moses began to explain the law,” and so forth. This indicates Moses’ dignity: although the law had been plain to him, he himself explains it to the people, in the statement, “The Lord God persuades the people.” “He spoke to us”—in this the dignity of the person is shown.

“It is enough for you to have remained on this mountain,” as if he were saying: You are unworthy to dwell in the land. Or this signifies that they were unworthy to dwell in the law of the Lord.

“Return,” that is, to your sins, to Egypt. Alternatively, “return” means through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, or through history and meaning.

“And come,” that is, you came to the mountain: you came to the pride of the Amorites and of vices. If, however, we announce this in a favorable sense, as when we say, “to the mountain,” that is, to the faith of the Amorites—that is, of sinners—because the Church is adorned by sin in faith, and so forth, then it refers to the other places: to the humbler vices, to the mountains from the law of God, and to the lower places, that is, sins.

“Toward the south,” that is, toward the prosperity of this world. “And beside the shore,” that is, the shore of the sea, he says: “I have given the land to you,” that is, prophecy.

“Enter,” that is, into the Church, or into the faith of the Gospel, or into the kingdom of heaven; “and possess,” that is, as if he were saying, “not for yourselves,” because you did not deserve it, but on account of the love of your fathers.

“Let him add to this number, even as he spoke,” that is: “So shall your seed be as the stars of heaven.”

“Choose from among yourselves,” that is, select from among yourselves men who are wise, that is, in the law, and knowledgeable, that is, in the affairs of the people, and whose conduct has been tested.

A tribune is one who commands a tribe; this signifies teachers who teach faith in the Trinity through the three laws. A centurion, one who is over a hundred, signifies teachers who preach heavenly rewards in the future, or the hundredfold in the present. A fifty-man officer, one who is over fifty, similarly signifies teachers who preach repentance. Each of the five senses is fulfilled in the Apostles. They preached all the things mentioned above.
