A dean commands over ten and signifies one who recounts the ten words of the Law. There is an order of growth in tribunes and centurions, and there is also an order of belief.

The four orders, whose beginning is figured numerically by the four Gospels, taught the four principal virtues: justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude. Moses signifies Christ in the choosing of the rulers. The rulers who are chosen signify the twelve Apostles, chosen by Christ with the four Gospels for leadership over the Church.

“And judge what is just.” This statement judges with equitable judgment and also figures the Apostles, to whom it is said: “You shall sit and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.”

“Ascend,” that is, to the summit of the perfect; alternatively, “ascend and possess,” that is, in rewards.

“As the Lord your God spoke,” that is, he prophesied to you.

“Do not fear,” that is, in your heart; “nor be terrified,” that is, in your mouth.

When the speech had pleased them, the judgment of the people is indicated by this.

“I sent from among you twelve men,” and so forth. These twelve men, by their number, can signify the twelve Apostles. The valley of the grape cluster was spoken of by anticipation. Above we said that the cluster signifies those things that the Apostles carry by preaching on two poles, that is, through the two laws.

“From the north to the right,” that is, from open unbelief to the warmth of faith.

“And you said: ‘The Lord hates you.’” This statement demonstrates an unbelieving people.

“When the Lord heard the voice of your words”: the Lord’s hearing of your words is spoken in human fashion, because I did not hear them in unity, as when it is said, “a crowd not of one will.” Alternatively, one sinner is called “many,” and many righteous people are called “one.”

“Except Caleb,” who represents repentance.

“And I shall give him the land,” as if he were saying, “you shall not call,” as it is said: “Many are called,” and so forth.

“Which your foot has trodden.” Here it is understood that, unless someone considers the kingdom of God through belief in the preaching, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Two are called to the promised land: Caleb and Joshua. Two also enter the kingdom of heaven: those who fulfill the two laws, the innocent and the repentant, or body and soul.

“The Amorite went up, who dwells in the mountains”: that is, heretics dwelling in pride.

## CHAPTER III

Seir is the name of a place, and Hornia likewise; they signify the Church, which sinners persecute.

“Thus the Lord swore,” as he truly said: “No one shall see,” and so forth.

Arbog is a mountain. Aroer is a city. Gilead is a region. Moab is to the west. Bashan is a city from the middle of the tribe of Manasseh. It has a definite division between body and soul, between active and contemplative life, between history and meaning: the region, cities, and all the things of Bashan.

Geshur is a spring, and Magath is a place. Jair and Machir are one man.

“Up to the middle,” that is, the priest up to the torrent. Jabbok, that is, as far as the west, up to the Jordan. They came northward toward the west, and as far as the sea of the wilderness. Westward, toward Mount Sairdas. Passover is on the right-hand side.

“Make ready,” up to this point, the animals.

In this statement three things are shown: beginning in baptism, possession in faith, and willingness in the elevation of the mind to heavenly things.

“And I prayed to the Lord,” that is, that he might enter the promised land.

“You began to show your servant your greatness”: that is, in the garments of the mind bearing Egypt through the sea and the rock; and “in your strongest hand,” that is, in the battles against the Amalekites.

“For there is no other Lord, either in heaven.” He says this because they had seen many gods in Egypt who were unable to save the people except the Lord; or because they had seen on earth the image of an ox.

In this journey fullness is shown: for those who crossed the Jordan, and fullness in those who remained in the land of Moab. They came into the promised land in fullness; this signifies the fullness of the law, which was given to the people in fullness when meaning was lacking.

Alternatively, those remaining in the land of Moab signify those who were in the law before the Law, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; or the Gentiles who reached baptism; or those who oppose baptism; or the people who did not believe in Christ together with the law of baptism.

Those entering the promised land signify those who receive baptism and remain in the Church. Their return, in which battle occurs both before and behind, demonstrates the battle of body and soul. These also, between Moab and the promised land, may represent peoples arriving at the unity of the law of Christ.

“You shall not cross this Jordan.” When this statement is understood otherwise, it appears to mean rest, and that the vision of the Lord will no longer dwell there. Alternatively, “vision” must be understood as vengeance, so that sin would not be avenged in the future.

## CHAPTER IV
Guard yourself, therefore—that is, from worshiping idols—which they saw, that is, in writings. “It burned up to heaven.” He said this hyperbolically. “You heard the voice of its trees,” that is, the law; or here a part is spoken for the whole, and you did not see its form at all. For perhaps, if they had seen its form, they would have made an image: “You saw no likeness whatsoever of the majesty of that God.” “A jealous God,” that is, when we do not exceed the measure of sin. “I call heaven and earth to witness,” that is, as a twofold aid. He terrifies the people—that is, by the word of God and by his own person—[Col. 0383D] heaven and earth, as though he were saying: Heaven and earth will be witnesses of the voice; if you worship foreign gods, you will call upon heaven, it will not rain upon the earth, and the earth will not bring forth its fruit. And you will say, “When will they have worshiped here?” These are the witnesses who have been called against us, if we worship foreign gods. Alternatively, heaven and earth may signify soul and body, or incarnation and divinity, or the law of the letter and the New Testament, which do not see or hear. In this interpretation he takes precautions because they had seen many images of idols among the Canaanites. “By temptations,” that is, as in the manna [Mannaan]. “And among foreigners,” that is, Amalek. “Signs,” that is, figures. “And portents,” such as the serpent. “A strong hand and an outstretched arm,” that is, for battles. Through the three cities Moses conquered [Col. 0384A] before the Jordan, the faith of the three laws, or faith in the Trinity before baptism, is indicated.

## CHAPTER V

“And we saw face to face.” This is said only in the person of Moses. “And I stood between you,” and what follows. So too Christ is mediator between God and human beings. “For you feared the fire.” In this he means his own people. “You shall not usurp,” that is, do not fear in such a way as to sanctify it with sacrifices or by your works. “For six days you shall work the land.” This statement bears the figure of the Old Testament; the seventh day, the Sabbath, bears the figure of the New Testament, in which we offer spiritual sacrifices to the Lord. “We do not turn aside to the right,” that is, to empty glory, “nor to the left,” by worshiping idols.

## CHAPTER VI

“You shall love the Lord your God.” Command and prohibition are shown in this statement. The command is expressed when it says, “You shall love”; the prohibition, “You shall not love foreign gods.” Alternatively, “You shall not love” means, “You shall not love as you loved before.” This statement also takes precedence over the other one where it says, “You shall not worship foreign gods,” which pertains to the work of the wilderness. What is said here pertains to the work of the land of promise. It is also spoken in the person of the Old Testament: “You shall have no foreign gods”; in the person of the New Testament: “You shall love,” and what follows. In the manner of a craftsman, love is placed first, because it is the foundation of all the commandments. For the craftsman first lays the foundation and then builds the house. So it is fitting for us first to lay love as the foundation and afterward establish good works. “With all your heart,” that is, with the part by which the body is animated. “With your soul,” with that part by which one is understood to be above every creature. “And with all your strength,” that is, with the bodily part, so that they might raise the height of creatures to be like the height of the Creator. It was fitting that love should be commanded in three places—in heart, soul, and strength—since they had three dwelling places: Egypt, the wilderness, and the land of promise. Alternatively, “heart and soul” are taken as one, and “strength” as the second. It is fitting that love should be in two places, since all human beings consist of two substances, soul and body; or of two other things, namely, unleavened bread and your hand, that is, your work. “In the light,” that is, in the work.

## CHAPTERS VII–XIII

When the Lord was speaking to Abraham about the future, he counted not seven nations but ten, whose land his descendants would possess. This number is most truly fulfilled when the nations’ idolatry, the Jews’ blasphemy, and the error of heretics are added to it; beneath these, until he recalls Egypt in understanding, the multitude lies subject.

But if someone comes out of Egypt and reaches the wilderness by a spiritual journey of three days, he will be freed from the assault of the nations. These signify the seven principal vices, which each soldier conquers through the grace of God. The reason the numbers are said to be greater is that there are more vices than virtues. What is said, “You shall not go with them,” is to be understood as referring to the worship of idols. “Cut off and strong” [reading uncertain], that is, on the journey of the Jordan or in battles. “May the Lord take away from you,” [Col. 0385A] that is, this fullness and the worst infirmities, namely, the ten plagues of Egypt. “Your eye shall not spare them,” and what follows. In this he takes precautions against their desire. “Do not fear,” because fear belongs to the imperfect. “Your eye shall not spare”—that is, their gods, meaning your desire for their vices. “Hornets,” that is, their evil habits. God is great for drinking offerings and terrible in vengeance.

When he says that the nations are not to be destroyed, lest perhaps the wild beasts multiply against them, he shows that we must beware lest, after sins have been driven from our flesh and suddenly overcome, spiritual beasts approach us—namely, boasting, pride, or certainly empty glory—which, once they have arisen, will be uprooted only with greater labor than bodily vices. Lot, although placed on the mountain, was polluted by an incestuous intercourse, though while living in Sodom he had restrained himself so as not to sin. Therefore, whatever vice we expel, let a virtue immediately be planted in its place, lest the spirit that has been driven out return and find our house empty.

“Dispe” [uncertain reading], that is, a kind of viper, which represents heretics who blaspheme the Trinity; the source is syntactically defective after “what he promised under oath.” The Lord swears by himself because he has no one greater by whom he may swear. “Behold, the heaven of the Lord your God,” as though he were saying: The Lord has power over whether heaven should rain upon us or not. “And the heaven of heaven,” that is, the stars; alternatively, angels are understood by heaven. “The heaven of heaven” means the souls of the saints, as it is written: “Star differs from star in glory,” and so also the resurrection of the dead; or history and meaning; and “earth,” that is, the fruits of the earth; or body and soul; and everything that is in them, that is, Adam with his race.

“God is great,” that is, in Egypt.

“And powerful,” that is, at sea.

“Terrible,” against Amalek.

“He does not accept persons”: here he reproved the people for accepting persons.

“He is your praise,” that is, so that you may praise him.

“The Red Sea” is so called because of its reddish mud.

“You shall set blessings upon the mountain.” This statement refers to the place where it says, “I call heaven and earth to witness,” but two mountains are brought forward as witnesses. As though he were saying: You will have blessings upon you if you keep the law of the Lord, and curses if you do not keep it. Alternatively, the blessing upon the mountains pertains to Israel, while the curse pertains to the Canaanites. These mountains are also said to be in the land of promise, and to be called by other names: Lebanon in the northern region, and Lesser Lebanon on the right side of that same land. Others, however, say that these mountains are not meant so much historically as they are mentioned as witnesses of blessing and cursing.

Mystically, these two mountains may be understood as the two laws. Gebal represents the Old, which administered vengeance; Gazarim the New, which taught mercy. These mountains may also indicate the summit of the perfect and the pride of the wicked, or what is said at the end of life: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you,” and what follows; and: “Go, [Col. 0386A] accursed ones, into eternal fire.” Alternatively, Gebal represents the curse and is assigned to the part of the flesh, just as the apostle Paul says: “I know that no good dwells in my flesh.” Gazarim, together with the blessing, represents the soul in that place, that is, in Shiloh.

In this statement he takes precautions because, if each person sacrificed in his own house, they would make idols, burning their sons and daughters with fire. This was not something the Egyptians had done, but it will be denied that the Canaanites had buried it [or: concealed it], that is, the meaning, through testimonies. “The sons of Eliab went out,” that is, wicked sons, or the sons of sinners.

## CHAPTER XIV

“You shall not make a baldness over the dead.” Historically this is clear. Spiritually it can be understood from what he says: do not shave mortals according to the will of the devil [Col. 0386B] or of the heretic, who divides the hooves into two parts—that is, one who believes in two laws but does not fulfill divine love, or [one who distinguishes] the active and contemplative life, or the incarnation and divinity—and chews the cud in his work.

“You shall eat,” that is, by believing, “of those that chew the cud and divide the hoof,” that is, of those who do not separate in their works what they believe in their hearts. “Feathers,” that is, the commandments of the law; and “scales,” that is, many thoughts; “all clean,” that is, the saints, who are therefore called birds because by clean thoughts and works they fly toward heavenly things. Unclean birds signify heretics. “According to its kind,” that is, if something similar to it in form should occur, it is not prohibited unless it belongs to their kind. All the unclean birds we have mentioned signify the various kinds of heretics.

The fact that Israel’s clothing in the wilderness did not wear out through age can represent the future incorruptibility of bodies, where things that are corruptible will remain without corruption. What is said, “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk,” shows that the one signified by the kid must not be boiled in its mother’s milk; that is, he must not be cleansed by the moderate disciplines of the Church, but his sins must be cleansed by stricter commands. Thus the one who has destroyed himself through the allurements of wantonness may redeem himself by stronger discipline, so that the others, seeing this, may fear.

By the tenth part that the Lord demands from the people, the ten senses are signified, which each of us ought to render to the Lord. “In the third year you shall set aside another tithe.” The command concerning the third year shows that the Lord foresaw the wars they would have in the land of promise. For in the third year he said, “How long did their vineyards grow?” Or this refers to the three years during which, as they said, the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh were in the land of promise in great battles. “You shall set aside another tithe for me,” that is, for the priests—as though by this he were speaking to the priests.

## CHAPTER XV

“When your Hebrew brother has been sold to you.” By “brother,” the meaning is understood. “Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who crosses over.” “Hebrew woman” means the soul of each perfect person from the nations, crossing over to baptism.

The seven years during which he is commanded to serve signify the perfection of the active life.

[Col. 0387A] The seventh year, in which he is released, expresses the active life.

Thus his ear is pierced with an awl, when the mind is struck by the subtlety of fear.

Alternatively, the six years signify the six ages of the world. The seventh year signifies the day of judgment; the awl signifies wisdom, by which the ear—that is, the understanding—is pierced. “The door” means the faith of your house, that is, of the Church. The firstborn signifies a perfect work. When he says, “Whatever is male,” it shows that we must not offer a soft work to God. The male sex also indicates perfect understanding.

When he says, “You shall not work with the firstborn of your ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep,” he shows that if we begin to practice something vigorous—and this is signified by the firstborn of the ox—or when our life begins something innocent, it is fitting that it not be displayed to human eyes, as though the fleece had been removed. This is signified by the words, “You shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep.”

The blind man can signify the gentile people, who could have entered the way of salvation if they had seen. The lame man is one who does not fulfill the twofold love: he sees the way but does not walk in it. The lame man can also signify the Jewish people, believing only the letter and not the meaning. “Like a goat,” that is, the Church; “and a deer,” that is, the people of the apostles.

“Do not eat their blood, but pour it out upon the earth.” This indicates that we ought to interpret their merits with great care, but pour them out into the judgment of the Church. “You shall observe the month,” that is, the fast.

## CHAPTERS XVI–XVIII

[Col. 0387C]

“The solemnity of Tabernacles,” that is, in the month of September. “The solemnity of Unleavened Bread,” that is, Passover. “Of Weeks,” that is, Pentecost.

What is said, “You shall not plant a grove, nor any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God,” signifies that around the faith of the Lord we must arrange nothing in unfruitful words, nothing belonging to secular learning, and nothing alluring. For these things are signified by wooded trees without any fruit. Let us hold fast only, through devotion to the truth, to the knowledge of preaching.

What is said, “God will raise up for you from your people a prophet like me,” although it can be said historically of Joshua, is nevertheless a clear prophecy of Christ, who arose as the true prophet from the people of Israel. And just as Moses was the steward [Col. 0387D] of the Old Testament, so Christ was the steward of the New. Finally, in the Gospel the Lord says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me.” What he says, “Like me,” is to be understood according to the flesh, not according to divinity. When the Lord promises vengeance upon those who refuse to hear the words of the prophet—that is, of Christ—it is a threat against the people who refuse Christ’s words. This is the true Prophet of whom it is said: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country.”

## CHAPTER XIX

“Concerning the man who goes simply with his friend into the forest for cedar wood,” and what follows. We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn our attention toward observing the faults of those subject to us. We go simply when we refer the vices of delinquents to our intention. But the ax lodges in the hand when reproof draws itself into harshness more than necessary. The iron leaps from the handle when a harsher word exceeds the limits of correction. He strikes the one person who kills his hearer from spiritual love by a spoken insult. For the mind of the one reproved rushes into hatred if immoderate reproof adds more than it ought.

But the person who carelessly strikes the wood and destroys his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that he may live protected in one of them, having turned, as it were, to the lamentations of repentance, hidden within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and love. He is not held guilty of the homicide he committed if the person he found was not killed by him. For when the strict Judge comes—he who joined himself to us through participation in nature—he will undoubtedly not demand the guilt of sin from the one whom hope, faith, and love have hidden beneath his pardon.

It follows: “One witness shall not stand against anyone, but every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Although this must be observed historically, nevertheless, whenever we contend against any impious persons or heretics, the holy Scriptures are called into question. The testimony of our understanding has no credibility without these witnesses. Bring forward two witnesses, namely the Old and New Testaments; bring forward also the four Gospels, the prophets, and the apostle, and thus every word will stand. In addition, there are other things in the land of promise: belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the land of the Church after baptism, the priest will stand—that is, the law, or Christ, or each perfect teacher—[Col. 0388C] confirming the truth against heretics, demons, or vices. The leaders are understood to be the prophets or apostles.

## CHAPTER XX

Those who have built a new house are expelled from the battle, as are those who have planted a vineyard or betrothed a wife, because one who serves worldly affairs cannot serve in the divine army. The fearful and timid man will likewise be thrown out of the battle, lest he make the hearts of his brothers afraid. He cannot undertake the battle of spiritual warfare because he still fears earthly works, lest perhaps by his example he turn others back from evangelical perfection. Such people cannot wage war.

“When you approach to attack a city,” that is, the city of the body in water—either a heretic or vices—you shall first offer it peace, that is, Christ for belief. [Col. 0388D] “If it receives you as far as the gates,” that is, of faith or repentance, “and serves you, you shall strike it,” that is, in repentance or vengeance. “Of the male sex,” that is, those who are proud. “Without women, without animals, and you shall not cut down trees,” that is, the saints from whom one may be nourished, namely, by commandments; without souls, soft understandings, and simple ones. Nor should you devastate secular people, that is, penitents.

## CHAPTER XXI

“When the corpse of a man is found,” and what follows. This can be shown to refer to the corpse of Adam with his race; the person guilty of his slaughter is unknown, that is, the devil, among human beings in the good part. The elders and judges signify the prophets and apostles. The place of Adam’s corpse [Col. 0389A] is paradise, the city of the cities of Judah.

The heifer is the flesh of Christ, which did not bear the yoke of sin nor break the earth with a plowshare, that is, it was born without intercourse with a man. They lead it into a rough and rocky valley, that is, the Jews lead it to the humble and harsh suffering of the cross, rocky with the sins and temptations of the world. The valley can signify the humility of souls, which is rough against the devil and has never been plowed, that is, cultivated by teachers with the knife and plowshare of the Old and New Testaments.

When he says, “On the neck of the heifer,” he indicates the preaching of the incarnation. “The priests shall approach,” that is, the sons of Levi or the apostles; or “into the world,” that is, the blood. “They shall wash their hands,” that is, their works through faith in the incarnation, and they shall say: “Our hands have not shed this blood,” as though they were saying: Neither the apostles nor the saints shed Christ’s blood. “And the guilt of the blood shall be removed from them.” Christ’s blood was poured out for the world. “But you will be innocent of the blood of the innocent,” that is, the apostles did not suffer for the world.

It follows: “If you go out to war against your enemies, and the Lord delivers them into your hands, and you take them captive, and you see among the number of them a beautiful woman,” and what follows. The Jews who preserve this history ask what reason there is for the woman’s head to be shaved and her nails to be cut off.

The custom is this: if we find a beautiful woman—that is, a soul created beautiful by God—in gentile conduct, and wish to join her to the body of Christ, after setting aside the worship of idolatry she is to be clothed in the mournful garments of repentance. Let her mourn her father and mother, that is, the memory of this world and the carnal allurements of gentile life; then, by the word of God, let all the sin of her unbelief, which is dead and empty, be shaved away. These are the woman’s hair and nails. Finally, purified through the bath of baptism, she is joined to the saints. When she has nothing superfluous upon her head or hands, that is, when she carries nothing unclean either in her understanding or in her actions, one month, during which he commands her to be taken as a wife, signifies faith and work. Faith is shown by the number three, and the work of the law by the number ten; through faith and the work of the law the soul is rightly joined to God.

Others think that this beautiful-faced woman signifies some rational discipline, found wisely expressed among the gentiles, as though it had been discovered by us. One must first remove from it all the uncleanness of superstition, and then take it up in the pursuit of truth. For among the gentiles there is no wisdom to which some uncleanness or superstition has not been added.

“If a man has two wives,” until “he cannot make a son of the beloved,” and what follows. Here Christ can be understood with the two Churches. He does not bring forth the son of the beloved—that is, the people of the Church of the gentiles—into the division of the substance of the people of the Synagogue, that is, into the commandments of the law; for the beginning is from the people of the Synagogue, that is, from the primitive Church.

“When a man has sinned,” until “he shall be buried on that same day.” Here each baptized person can be understood. If he sins, he must be judged to death, that is, through vengeance or repentance. The corpse must not remain on the gallows for long, that is, in sin. Rather, it must be buried on that same day, that is, renewed through repentance. “You will defile the land with stench,” that is, the land of the heart; “with stench,” that is, sins.

## CHAPTER XXII

“You shall not see your brother’s ox,” until “of your brother who is absent”: this is said to the teacher. Spiritually, the ox demonstrates one who bears the yoke of the law; the sheep, the innocent person; the donkey, the people of the gentiles. Clothing signifies works. Christ is the brother to whom all these things are said through the teaching of the good teacher.

When it says, “She shall not wear a man’s garment,” it shows what the Apostle says: “I do not permit a woman to teach in the Church.” Neither the priesthood nor teaching is granted to women in the Church; nor should a man be clothed in a woman’s garment. For the man who is a man and holds authority in the Church must not have anything feminine or soft in his teaching.

“If, while walking,” until “and may you live for a long time.” The way signifies this world; the tree, pride; the earth, carnal desires; the nest, conduct; the mother, the flesh of each human being lying in sin; the long time, the age to come.

“When he has built a new house,” that is, a soul or a Church, “making a wall,” that is, of faith, “so that blood may not be shed,” that is, the natural good may not be taken by the devil or the heretic—your Church or your soul.

“You shall not sow your vineyard,” that is, the teaching of the Holy Spirit, as though he were saying: You shall not make good and evil occur together. What is said, “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together,” signifies two peoples. In the name of the ox, the people under the yoke of the law are understood; in the donkey, the people of the gentiles belonging to the Gospel. He plows with an ox and a donkey together who receives the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which preceded in shadow and image.

Again, the life of those who work well is signified by the ox, and the senseless folly of fools by the donkey. Therefore, “You shall not plow with an ox and donkey together”: do not join a fool to a wise person in preaching, because they cannot proclaim the word of God equally.

It follows: “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen.” Simplicity is signified by wool, sublimity by linen. A garment woven of wool and linen conceals the linen inside and displays the wool on the surface. Therefore, he wears a garment woven of wool and linen who, under the language of innocence, [Col. 0390D] conceals within the exaltedness of malice.

“You shall make cords on the borders,” that is, the commandments of the law through the examples of the apostles. “On the four corners of your cloak,” that is, through belief in the four books of faith. “Moreover, one hundred shekels of silver,” that is, the integrity of punishments, “because she fornicated in her father’s house,” that is, in the Church of the saints.

“If he sleeps with another man’s wife,” that is, a heretic with the Church, which is called Christ’s wife; or an evil understanding with the soul, which belongs to the good teacher.

Both shall die, that is, through vengeance or repentance. “If a virgin girl,” that is, the Church betrothed to Christ, who has given him her virginity, “and someone finds her,” that is, a Jew, a heretic, or a sinner, “at the gate of the city,” that is, at the end of the Church, “they shall stone them,” [Col. 0391A] that is, through vengeance or through testimonies in repentance. “Because she did not cry out,” that is, she consented.

The field signifies the teaching of the Gospel; what follows should be understood in nearly this same order. “She cried out, and no one was present,” that is, until the coming of Christ. Through the man who took his brother’s wife, the devil or the heretic is shown, taking the Church of his brother—that is, of Christ—so that he might not reveal his covering, namely, faithfulness.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When it says, “The eunuch with crushed or amputated testicles, and with his member cut off, shall not enter the Church of God,” it shows that all who live softly and do not perform manly work cannot remain among the saints or in the assembly.

He who is born of a prostitute is forbidden to enter the Church until the tenth generation. For the one who comes to the Church from a carnal life or from gentile society is to be received when he has kept the commandments of the law spiritually; this is signified by the number ten.

When the Ammonites and Moabites are not permitted ever to enter the Church, this signifies that heretics must always be driven away from the Church. “Avoid a heretical person,” he says, “after one or two admonitions.”

It follows: “You shall not abhor the Edomite, because he is your brother, nor the Egyptian.” By the Egyptian and the Edomite, the present life is signified. Although, renouncing it, we turn away toward the Egyptian land—that is, toward our former worldly conduct and desire—nevertheless, while we are subject to the necessities of this world, we do not utterly destroy the Egyptian nation, although we separate ourselves from it with a certain discernment. We do not think about excesses, but, according to the Apostle, we are content with daily food and clothing.

When it says, “Those who are born from them in the third generation shall enter the Church of the Lord,” it signifies that a secular person can then be joined to God’s saints when he has believed perfectly in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or when he has been adorned with Hope, Faith, and Love.

It follows: “If there is among you a man who is polluted by a nocturnal dream,” and what follows. A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation, through which a dark thought conceives something shameful in the heart but does not complete it in action. To go outside the camp while polluted means that one who is troubled by a shameful assault despises himself in comparison with the continent; he washes with water at evening when, despising his failure, he turns to the lamentations of repentance, so that through tears he may wash away everything that accuses his soul of hidden defilement. But after sunset let him return to the camp, because after the heat of temptation it is necessary for him to regain confidence in the fellowship of the good. Thus he returns to the camp after the setting sun who, after the lamentations of repentance and once the flame of illicit thought has cooled, is restored to confidence in the merits of the faithful.

Moreover, he is commanded to go out when he attends to the necessities of nature, and what follows. Our minds, weighed down by the corruptible burden of nature, discharge certain superfluous thoughts as though under the pressure of the belly. But we must carry a peg on our belt, [Col. 0392A] so that, girded for reproving ourselves, we may have around us the sharp goad of compunction, which continually pierces the earth of our mind with repentance and grief and hides what has burst forth from us as foul.

“You shall cover what has been discharged with earth,” that is, he must obscure his sin by the work of repentance. “You shall not hand over a servant to his master.” This is said to the teacher, so that he does not hand over to the devil the servant whom he has not converted from the servitude of sin. “You shall not grieve him,” that is, by driving him into despair or repentance.

“There shall be no prostitute,” that is, the soul; nor “a fornicator,” that is, the devil who begot the heretic. “Of the brothel,” that is, of the souls. “Nor the price of a dog,” that is, as it is said, “You shall not give what is holy to dogs.” Alternatively, this signifies that we must not offer alms as a sacrifice for sin.

“You shall not lend at interest the fruits,” that is, of the law, “but to a foreigner,” that is, to the gentile people. “Entering the vineyard of your neighbor,” that is, the law of Christ, “eat grapes,” that is, believe the incarnation of Christ. “Outside,” however, means outside the Church.

“If you enter the standing grain of your friend,” that is, into the order of the commandments or the law of Christ, “break off the ears and rub them with your hand,” that is, [break] the letter of the law through the example of your faith. “You shall not reap with a sickle,” that is, do not go beyond it when fulfilling it with understanding.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“If a man takes a wife,” and what follows, until “to reject her.” Here the man signifies Christ, and the wife the synagogue of the Jews, which did not find Christ because it persecuted him and dragged him to the cross. The bill of divorce is the Gospel. His hands, that is, the works of unbelief. The house is the Church, or the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0392C] The second husband signifies the apostle, whose house signifies the Church; or, if he has died, aid to sinners. The first husband—that is, Christ—will not be able to take back the synagogue because it is impenitent. “Nor shall you cause the land to sin,” that is, the body or the Church.

“When a man has taken a wife,” that is, his soul, “he shall not go out to war,” that is, against the persecutions of demons. “For one year,” and what follows, that is, repentance.

“You shall not take the upper or lower millstone as a pledge.” We sometimes use “to take” to mean “to remove”; hence those predatory birds are called hawks [accipitres]. A pledge is the sinner’s confession of sins. A pledge is taken from the debtor when the confession of sin is held from the sinner.

The upper and lower millstones are hope and fear. Hope carries one upward; fear presses one downward. But the upper and lower millstones are necessarily joined to one another, so that one without the other is considered useless. Hope and fear must therefore be joined continually in the breast, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice. He also fears justice in vain if he does not trust in mercy.

Therefore, the removal of either the upper or lower millstone as a pledge is forbidden, because the preacher must arrange his preaching with such careful administration that, without abandoning hope, he does not remove fear, nor, after removing hope, leave a person in fear alone. He removes the upper millstone if, when someone laments his sin, he says, “You will not receive forgiveness for what you have done.” He removes the lower one if he says to the sinner, “Continue to do evil, [Col. 0393A] because the mercy of the Lord is great.”

“You shall not withhold the wage.” This is said to the people of the apostles. “To the native,” that is, to the people of your brother, who are the apostles; or “to the foreigner,” that is, the gentile peoples. “You shall not take away,” until “the garment of the widow,” that is, the faith of the least one, who is a widow because she has died to the devil.

## CHAPTER XXV

The number forty of the blows with which he commanded offenders to be rebuked shows the number forty, in which the Church, spread through the four parts of the world, proceeds under the Decalogue of the law.

We strike the offender with the number forty when in this time we are scourged by the wounds of repentance. For if we are struck because of sins, we are found there without sins.

It follows: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out your grain on the threshing floor.” This aptly signifies what the Apostle says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” For it is written: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain.” Does God care about oxen? Under the name of the ox, the life of each teacher is expressed. Scripture therefore wishes the teacher’s material needs to be provided, so that the hearers may receive spiritual things from him. These are the oxen that tread and separate the chaff and grain on the threshing floor, that is, in the Church.

It follows: “When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without children,” and so forth. What else does this figure demonstrate except that each preacher of the Gospel ought to labor in the Church so that, when his brother—that is, Christ—has died, he may raise up seed, and that what is raised up may receive his name? Understanding this, the Apostle says: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” As though he were saying: “I begot you when my brother had died; you are called Christians, not Paulines.”

But when one chosen for the ministry of the Church refuses the Gospel, he is rightly despised by the Church itself. The command that the woman spit in his face was not without a sign of reproach. For she removes the sandal from one foot, so that he may not belong to the number of those of whom the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace.” Whoever holds the evangelical faith in such a way that he does not refuse to benefit the Church, if he is able, is rightly understood to be shod on both feet. But whoever thinks that it is sufficient for himself to have taken care of what he believes, while avoiding concern for others, throws the sandal of one foot from the threshing floor.

“If men have a dispute among themselves,” until “you shall cut off her hand.” Through these two men the perfect and imperfect teacher can be understood; through the wife, the church of heretics, which wishes to free the heretic from the hand of the perfect teacher, sending the work of heresy against the perfect work of the good teacher. The work of that church must be cut off.

It follows: “You shall not have differing weights in the shekel.” By this we are commanded that there be no double standards in our conscience before the Lord: that is, while living softly ourselves, we should not impose harsher commandments on others and place heavy burdens on human shoulders that we are unwilling to touch with a finger.

## CHAPTER XXVII
What is commanded—namely, that after crossing the Jordan enormous stones be erected on which the words of the Law are to be written—figures the fact that the faithful people, possessing the land of the Church through baptism, ought to establish priests and teachers who are regarded as great and illustrious in their manner of life, and who guard the words of the Law and the divine Scripture. “For the lips of the priest,” he says, “preserve knowledge.” The fact that they are represented as being coated with plaster signifies that teachers ought to shine forth in virtues through all good works. The two mountains, Gazarim and Gebal, on which blessings and curses are pronounced, can signify the two Testaments, because the people placed under the Law were held under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this Law and perform them in deed.” Finally, the Jews, observing the Pharisaic traditions, despised the commandments of the Law. But in the New Testament the blessing of grace overflowed upon the Christian people, when Christ, raising his hand, blessed the apostles. Moses signifies both Testaments, because he has a twofold understanding [the text is somewhat uncertain here]. The Jews, not understanding him, live under the letter that kills them.

[Col. 0393]

ON THE TABERNACLE, ITS VESSELS, AND THE GARMENTS OF THE PRIESTS. (C,S)

BOOK ONE.

CHAPTER ONE. Moses, ascending the mountain of God with Joshua, left Aaron and Hur in charge of the people.

[Col. 0393D]

Since, with the Lord’s help, we are about to speak of the figure of the tabernacle, its vessels, and its utensils, we must first examine and consider more attentively the location and circumstances of the place: how these things were arranged, and when they were commanded to be made. Everything, as the Apostle says, happened to them figuratively; but it was written for our sake (I Cor. X). Everything, that is, not only the deeds or words contained in the sacred writings, but also the arrangement of places, hours, and times, and even the circumstances of the things in which those deeds were performed or those words spoken.

[Col. 0394D]

(Exod. XXIV.) The Lord said to Moses: “Come up to me on the mountain,” etc. Since the Lord was about to give the Law to Moses, he first calls him to the summit of the mountain, so that, dwelling there with him on high, he might hear more freely what he was to teach the people when he returned below. At the same time, from the height of the place he might understand how lofty the Law he was receiving was, how far removed it was from human teachings, and how it could be perfectly understood or kept only by those who had separated themselves from earthly pollution through a life lived more sublimely and perfectly. Hence he also commanded the people to wait below until Moses returned, so as to indicate figuratively that the mysteries of his Law are heavenly and are grasped only by the more perfect; nevertheless, the weak are not deprived of an opportunity for salvation if they humbly strive to listen to the wisdom of their elders.

[Col. 0395A]

Thus also in the Gospel the Lord, calling the new heralds of grace to the mountain, instructed them in saving commandments, so that the very setting of the place might make clear that he was giving them lofty commandments for living and promises of reward, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. XXXIII). After the resurrection, moreover, appearing to these same men again on the holy mountain and sending them to preach not merely to the one people of Israel but to the whole world, he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII). Thus the Lord gave the commandments both of the Law and of the Gospel on a mountain, in order thereby to commend the sublimity of both Testaments. Yet because the text of the Law was then entrusted to one people, Israel, while the grace of the Gospel was to reach all the nations throughout the world through the preaching of the apostles, Moses alone rightly ascended the mountain to learn and receive the Law; but all the apostles together, placed with the Lord on the mountain, heard the teaching of the Gospel while the crowds listened.

[Col. 0395B]

Likewise, at the coming of the Holy Spirit, through which this same grace and truth of the Gospel was more manifestly given to the Church, not the apostles alone but also a very large company of the faithful gathered in the upper room of Mount Zion received it. This occurred through the division of languages, signifying by such a miracle that the Church throughout the world would praise God in the languages of all nations.

[Col. 0395D]

“And I will give you,” he says, “two stone tablets, and the Law and the commandments,” etc. This resembles the Gospel passage quoted above: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” Therefore neither Moses, nor the apostles, nor any teacher ought to teach the people of God commandments other than those taught by the Lord himself and prescribed for us to observe in the eternal decree of his counsel—commandments through whose observance he willed us to have eternal life. Nor ought teachers to omit anything that he commanded to be done; rather, they must necessarily entrust to their hearers everything that he commanded.

He wrote these things on stone tablets because he established that they should be kept fixed and firmly impressed in the hearts of the elect, strengthened by faith. When he sets their examples before us for imitation, he displays the ordinances of his Law as though they had been inscribed and established on stone. For Daniel saw the Lord in the figure of a stone cut from the mountain without hands, crushing the splendor of worldly rule, so that his kingdom alone might remain without end (Dan. II). And Peter exhorts the faithful, saying: “You also, like living stones, are being built into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II).

Moses and Joshua, his servant, arose. Joshua, the servant of Moses, signifies the Lord and Savior both by his name and by his action. He is rightly called Moses’ servant because, appearing in the flesh, he deigned to take upon himself the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law: for he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. He follows Moses’ footsteps in everything, because in all that Moses speaks or writes, Christ is found, if one searches carefully, as his inseparable companion, represented either figuratively or openly.

For this reason he says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (Matt. V).

When Moses ascended Mount Sinai, he said to the elders: “Wait here until we return to you,” etc. Aaron means “mountain of strength,” while Hur is interpreted as “fire” or “light.” Thus Aaron signifies the Lord and Savior, and Hur signifies the Holy Spirit. Isaiah also speaks of this: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains” (Isa. V). And the Holy Spirit appeared over the apostles in the form of fire and light.

Moses, therefore, ascending to the Lord, left Aaron and Hur—that is, the mountain of strength and the light of fire—in the plain to govern the people. And if we cannot follow our teachers to the height of divine contemplation, let us be careful and vigilant lest any temptation draw us away from the vicinity of the mountain of God. Rather, according to our measure, let us devote ourselves to works of virtue, clinging with steadfast heart to the mysteries of our Redeemer with which we have been instructed, and taking care to preserve within ourselves, undefiled, the grace of his Spirit with which we have been sealed.

If any trouble arising from adversity assails us, let us immediately invoke the help of that same Redeemer of ours, who habitually protects his faithful from every evil and delivers them through the gift of the Holy Spirit. We should not doubt that, if we persist in what we have begun, our weakness and humility will be strengthened and exalted through the mountain of strength and will become more powerful against all the assaults of our enemies. Through the light and fire of the Holy Spirit our ignorance will also be illumined, and our spirit will be kindled with love for that same gracious Creator.

When Moses had ascended, the cloud covered the mountain. Just as the mountain on which Moses received the Law signifies the height of perfection that was to be written in that Law, so the cloud by which the mountain was covered signifies the grace of divine protection. Each person enjoys this protection all the more abundantly the higher he ascends, with the eyes of his heart opened, to examine the wonders of God’s Law.

The cloud covered not only the mountain on which Moses ascended; it also overshadowed the people walking through the wilderness, who could not at all ascend to higher things, yet were nevertheless shaded by the cloud sent from heaven.

[Col. 0397A]

Hence it is written: “He spread out a cloud for their protection,” for the Lord truly protects all who fear him, the little together with the great, with heavenly blessing.

And the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, etc. It should be understood that not only the height but also the name of the mountain on which the Law was given figuratively announces the perfection of that Law. Sinai is interpreted as “my measure” or “my amphora.” It was therefore divinely arranged that the mountain on which the Law was to be given should be called “My Amphora,” as though the Lord were signifying through this name that his Law proclaims to everyone a perfect rule of life and renders to each according to his works, in accordance with what he himself says: “With the judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. VII); and, “With the measure you use, it will be measured to you” (Mark IV).

[Col. 0397B]

It is rightly said that, as Moses ascended, the cloud and the glory of the Lord covered the mountain for six days, but on the seventh day he called him to the higher parts of the mountain. For six days we are commanded to labor under the Law and to rest on the seventh. As Moses ascended the mountain, he was covered for six days by the cloud and glory of the Lord, signifying mystically that whoever carries out the Lord’s commandments in righteous works is made worthy of divine protection.

The same Lord who commanded Moses to ascend the mountain also surrounded him as he ascended with his cloud and brightness. For he who grants us the gift of doing good himself enlightens us as we do good, so that we may not fail; and he protects us lest we be burned by the temptations of the ancient enemy, as though by the heat of the sun.

[Col. 0397C]

On the seventh day the Lord calls Moses to the higher parts, because after the perfection of works the Law promises us eternal rest. Thus those who have taken care to stand before the Lord in the height of right action may now deserve to ascend to his vision and conversation, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “Indeed, he who gave the Law will give blessing” (Ps. LXXXIII). “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

It is also established that this has been granted to some of the elect in the present life, so that after the perfection of an active way of life they have ascended to the grace of divine contemplation, insofar as such a thing can be accomplished by human beings still clothed in flesh. This was granted to many patriarchs and prophets, and above all to Moses himself, of whom it is specifically said that he spoke with God face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend (Exod. XXXIII).

[Col. 0397D]

Thus it can also be understood specifically of him that for six days he was protected on the mountain by the cloud and glory of the Lord, while on the seventh day, called to converse with him, he ascended to the higher parts of the mountain. For through the good works he had received by the Lord’s gift, he deserved to be more greatly enlightened by him, to be overshadowed from every attack of evil, and thus to attain the loftier gifts of his vision and conversation.

The “midst of darkness,” from which he is said to have been called, does not mean that any darkness exists in God. Rather, because he dwells in inaccessible light (I Tim. VI), and, as the same Apostle says, “whom no human being has seen or can see” (ibid.), that darkness is the obscurity of heavenly mysteries. It is inaccessible to earthly hearts, but through divine grace it can be entered by Moses and by the other blessed who are pure in heart, to whom it is said in the Psalm: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII).

His light is inaccessible to our powers, yet it is approached through his gifts. To this the text appropriately adds:

The appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire, etc. The appearance of the glory of the Lord was seen as a burning fire because it both illumines the hearts of the elect with the gift of heavenly knowledge and inflames them with the ardor of his love.

The glory of the Lord was therefore seen in cloud, darkness, and fire. In the cloud, because he protects us from the heat of temptations; in darkness, because no creature can fully comprehend the power of his majesty—for “the peace of God surpasses all understanding” (Phil. IV); and in burning fire, because he both irradiates the minds of the faithful with knowledge of heavenly goods and kindles them with hope and love.

[Col. 0398B]

The sons of Israel behold this glory of the Lord from afar and from below, while Moses penetrates it by ascending higher, because the truly perfect see the hidden things of divine mysteries perfectly and sublimely.

As for us, mindful of our weakness and sluggishness, even if we have not been able to enter here by comprehending it, let us at least take care to remain nearby and gaze upon it by believing, hoping, and loving. The sons of Israel, as it were, have their eyes fixed from afar on the mountain of God and on the sight of his glory when the weak members of the Church, earnestly desiring to see God, keep the eyes of their minds diligently fixed on the memory of eternal brightness.

They dwell, as it were, in the vicinity of the mountain of God to which they know Moses ascended when they restrain themselves by that discipline of life through which they never allow the steps of their actions to be drawn farther from imitation of the highest living beings, even though they are not yet able fully to follow their footsteps to perfection.

CHAPTER II. On the seventh day Moses is called to the higher parts of the mountain and remains there with the Lord for forty days and forty nights.

Moses entered the midst of the cloud, ascended the mountain, and was there for forty days and forty nights. Moses entered the midst of the cloud and ascended the mountain when preachers of the divine Law—among whom Moses himself was preeminent—penetrate, at the Lord’s invitation and guidance, to contemplate sublimely the hidden and uncertain things of divine wisdom.

Moses was with the Lord for forty days and nights so that, through this number of days, he might learn that only those could fulfill the Decalogue of the Law, which they had received with their people, who were aided by the grace of evangelical truth, which was to be described in four books. For four times ten makes forty.

Or certainly it signified that a time would come when those same commandments of the Decalogue, which Moses then received with the one people of the children of Israel, would, by the gift of divine grace, be opened to the knowledge of all the nations contained within the four regions of the world, and all peoples throughout the nations would attain eternal salvation through observing them.

But since we have briefly learned by what wondrous ascent Moses reached the point of receiving the Law, let us now turn our ears and minds together to hear what he heard and to expound, according to our ability, the commandments of the Law itself. The text continues:

CHAPTER III. The children of Israel are commanded to offer first fruits to the Lord and to make a sanctuary.

(Exod. XXV.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they take up,” etc. We too offer the first fruits of our goods to the Lord when, whenever we do anything good, we truly attribute the whole of it to divine grace and confess from the depths of our hearts that we can have nothing—not even the beginning of a good action or thought—except from the Lord. We acknowledge, however, that our evil deeds are always begun and completed by us ourselves, at the instigation of the devil, and that they can be forgiven only by the Lord’s grant.

The Pelagians do not wish to offer the first fruits of their goods to the Lord, but retain them for themselves as possessions, because in their foolish presumption they assert that they possess some good from themselves, without the grace of God.

It is rightly commanded Moses to receive the first fruits from the person who offers them voluntarily. For “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). The Apostle also commands us to do good not out of sadness or necessity but from the purpose of the heart (ibid.). Knowing that he did this, the prophet glories in the Lord, saying: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII).

These are the things you shall receive: gold, silver, and bronze, etc. All these things, which the Lord commands the former people to offer materially for the making of a sanctuary, we too, who desire to be spiritual children of Israel—that is, imitators of the people who see God—ought to offer through spiritual understanding. Through such voluntary offerings we may deserve both to make a sanctuary for him within ourselves and for him to dwell in our midst, that is, to deign to consecrate a dwelling for himself in our hearts.

We offer him gold when we shine with the brightness of true wisdom, which is found in right faith. We offer silver when confession proceeds from our mouth unto salvation. We offer bronze when we rejoice to proclaim the same faith publicly. We offer hyacinth when we lift our hearts upward. We offer purple when we subject the body to suffering. We offer twice-dyed scarlet when we burn with the twofold love of God and neighbor. We offer fine linen when we preserve the chastity of the flesh. We offer goats’ hair when we put on the garment of penitence and mourning.

[Col. 0399D]

We offer rams’ skins dyed red when we see the leaders of the Lord’s flock baptized in his blood. We offer hyacinth-colored skins when we hope that after death we shall have spiritual bodies in heaven. We offer acacia wood when, having cleared away the thorns of sins, we serve the Lord alone with pure flesh and soul.

We offer oil for preparing the lamps when we shine with the fruits of charity and mercy. We offer spices, fragrant ointment, and incense when we spread the reputation of our good action far and wide, so that many may take it as an example for living well.

We offer onyx stones and gems for adorning the ephod and the breastpiece when we proclaim with worthy praise the miracles of the saints, by which they adorned thoughts devoted to God and works of virtue. We take up these things for the assistance of our faith whenever there is need.

Because we are accustomed to carry burdens on our shoulders, works of the righteous and pious labors for the Lord are rightly signified by the ephod, that is, the shoulder garment. Because the seat of thoughts is in the breast, the pure thoughts of the elect are rightly expressed in the breastpiece, which is the priestly garment worn on the chest.

The onyx stones and gems adorn the ephod and breastpiece when the signs of miracles are joined to the outstanding deeds and thoughts of the greatest Fathers. Nor does anything prevent us from understanding, in the onyx stones—which are said to be blood-red in color—the merits of martyrdom added to good works. These matters will be discussed more fully in their proper place, with the help of God’s grace.

“And they shall make me a sanctuary,” he says, “and I will dwell in their midst,” etc. The Lord showed Moses the tabernacle on the mountain and the vessels consecrated for its worship, because, while Moses remained with him for so long, the Lord openly demonstrated how greatly the angelic virtues rejoice to obey their Creator in piety, humility, and purity.

These virtues are his perfect tabernacle in all things, since he has never ceased to dwell and abide in them from the time they were created. The likeness of their life and their common dwelling before the Lord is also promised to us in the resurrection, if now, abandoning the pollution of this world, we strive to imitate their life on earth: praising and loving the Lord, loving and helping our neighbor in God, and even urging our enemies toward the love of God through acts of compassion.

Such were those to whom the Apostle says: “But you, brothers, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII).

The tabernacle, therefore, which was shown to Moses on the mountain is that heavenly city and homeland which, at that time, is believed to have consisted solely of the holy angels. After the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of the Mediator between God and human beings, it received a splendid and abundant multitude of holy souls as well.

The individual vessels of that tabernacle are the individual persons of the blessed spirits. From all of them Jerusalem itself, which is the mother of us all, consists in true peace and unity.

It should be noted especially that the children of Israel are commanded to make a sanctuary for the Lord not partially resembling but according to the entire likeness of the tabernacle that he showed Moses, together with all its vessels for worship.

For if we are striving toward fellowship with the angels in heaven, we ought on earth to imitate their life,

[long lacuna]

inasmuch as harmful bodies delay us,

and earthly, dying limbs dull us, always to imitate them. But if you should ask how you, an earthborn human being, can imitate spiritual beings while still in the flesh in this heavenly tabernacle, the answer is: They love God and their neighbors—imitate this. They help the distressed; although the angels are all blessed, they help human beings—imitate this. They are humble and gentle toward one another, peaceful, and obedient to divine commands—imitate this as far as you are able.

They neither speak, do, nor think anything evil, idle, or unjust; tireless in divine praises, they attend to them in word and mind. Imitate this as much as you can, and you will have built a sanctuary for the Lord according to the model shown to Moses on the mountain. Then our Lord and Savior, coming with the Father, will make his dwelling with you; indeed, after this life he will bring you, eternally blessed, into that tabernacle which you imitated. The text continues.

CHAPTER IV. Description of the ark.

Thus you shall make it: join it together from acacia wood. The ark, which is commanded to be made first of all in the tabernacle, appropriately signifies the incarnation itself of our Lord and Savior, in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II).

This ark is rightly commanded to be joined together from acacia wood. Acacia wood is said to be light and incorruptible by nature, not greatly different in quality from white thorn. The ark was therefore made of acacia wood because the Lord’s body consisted of members free from every stain of vice. These same woods are very like thorns, because although he did not come in sinful flesh, he nevertheless came “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” as the Apostle says (Rom. VIII). The text continues:

Its length shall be two and a half cubits, etc. Some customarily ask what measurement should be assigned to the cubit that Moses used either for Noah’s ark or in constructing the tabernacle. If we consult Josephus, the question is easily resolved. For it should not be thought that a man who was Jewish by race and priestly by descent, outstanding in intellect and highly learned in both divine and secular writings, could in any way have been unaware of this.

He says: “The ark was made five palms in length and three in width” (Antiquities, Book III, chapter 8). Hence it is manifestly clear that he designates the cubit as being filled by two palms.

Mystically, however, the length of the ark signifies the long-suffering of our Lord and Redeemer, by which he dwelt among human beings. Its width signifies the breadth of the charity by which he willed to come to us and dwell among us. Its height signifies the hope of future exaltation, because he foresaw either that he himself would be glorified after his passion or that he would glorify others.

Accordingly, the ark’s length was appropriately two cubits, signifying the teaching and works by which he shone in the world. For this reason the evangelist Luke says that he spoke of all that Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts I). And his fellow citizens, wondering, said: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works?” (Matt. XIII). They referred “wisdom” to the things he spoke that were wondrous, and “mighty works” to the things he did.

The fact that, after two cubits, the ark also had an additional half-cubit in length can be referred to the slowness of human weakness, which was not yet able to comprehend the sublime words or deeds of the Savior as it ought. Hence it is openly said of some of his mysteries: “His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus had been glorified” (John XII).

Likewise, concerning his more sublime sayings: “This word was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was being said” (Luke XVIII).

The ark had two cubits in length because the Lord appeared glorious in flesh, in word, and in deeds. It also had half a cubit because he bore patiently the slowness of the disciples, who were not yet able perfectly to comprehend his words or deeds.

The ark was one cubit wide, because of the dispensation of the Lord’s charity by which he took care to unite his elect in God. Thus, praying to the Father for them, he said: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John XVII).

And shortly afterward: “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (ibid.).

After the one cubit it also had a half-cubit, signifying our weakness, because while we are placed in this life we are not yet able perfectly either to love God ourselves or to comprehend the love that God has for us. Rather, as the Apostle testifies, “we know in part and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII); so likewise we love in part.

The ark therefore has one cubit and also a half-cubit, because the Lord loves us with a single act of mercy, intending to associate us with himself and with the Father, and with equally gracious kindness embraces the capacity of our love, whatever it can be in this life, until we deserve to enter into his vision, where we may love him with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength.

The ark’s height was also most appropriately one and a half cubits, signifying the one hope by which either the Lord himself, while he was with us in the flesh, awaited the fulfillment of his future resurrection and subsequent glory, or by which he continually admonishes us amid the adversities of the world to rejoice because of the rewards of future goods.

The ark therefore has a full cubit in height because our Lord and Savior, even while still dwelling in corruptible flesh, knew perfectly what glory was being reserved in the future both for himself and for his members, who are us.

It also has a half-cubit in height because he willingly took upon himself in his body the devotion of our smallness. We love the future homeland with pious intention, but we are not yet able perfectly to grasp what its blessedness is. Nevertheless, whatever we do grasp, we have from him alone.

And you shall overlay it with pure gold, etc. The ark is overlaid inside and outside with pure gold because the human nature assumed by the Son of God was full within with the power of the Holy Spirit and outwardly displayed openly to human beings the works of the Holy Spirit.

A golden crown is rightly commanded to be placed around the top of the ark because the Son of God, appearing in the flesh and coming for the redemption of the human race, awaited the appointed time and hour when he would overcome, together with the author of death, the death he had assumed for us, and ascend victoriously to the Father in heaven.

[Col. 0403A]

The Apostle speaks of this crown: “We see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II). In the Apocalypse John speaks of it: “I saw, and behold, a white horse, and the one sitting upon it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering and to conquer” (Rev. VI).

The white horse is the Church; the rider seated upon it is the Lord, who had a bow because he came to battle against the powers of the air. A crown of victory was given to him because by dying he overturned the kingdom of death.

And four golden rings, etc. The four golden rings are the four books of the Gospels. They are rightly golden because of the brilliance of the wisdom with which they shine; they are rightly compared to rings because the wisdom of God that they proclaim is eternal. The divinity that Christ as a human being received neither began in time nor will cease to exist.

Hence, as the hour of his passion approached, he prayed to the Father, saying: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII).

The ark has four corners because the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation does not cease to be celebrated throughout all the regions of the world in which the holy Church is spread. Four rings were placed at those same four corners because the Gospel of Christ is preached in every part of the world to the hearts of the faithful who are to be saved.

There are two rings on one side and two on the other, either because two evangelists adhered to the Savior’s discipleship while he preached in the flesh and worked miracles, whereas the other two came to faith after his resurrection and ascension into heaven; or because, in the figure of the four living creatures, the two represented by the man and the calf bore indications of his passion and death, while the two prefigured by the lion and the eagle displayed the insignia of the victory by which he destroyed death.

The Lord appeared as a man, made mortal through the incarnation. He was also the calf, offered for us on the altar of the cross. He became the lion by forcefully subduing death, and the eagle by ascending into heaven.

Therefore there are two rings on one side and two on the other, because two evangelists, through their symbolic figures, signify the Lord’s assumption of human weakness, while the other two signify the victory by which he triumphed over that assumed weakness and over death.

The ark had two rings, as it were, on its left side when two evangelists figured the Lord’s incarnation and passion. Likewise, two rings were attached to its right side because two evangelists figuratively express his resurrection and ascension, which pertain to the glory of the future life.

You shall also make poles of acacia wood, etc. The poles by which the ark is carried are the holy teachers, who bring the Lord into the hearts of their hearers by preaching.

These poles are commanded always to remain in the rings because it is necessary that all who preach the heavenly mysteries never withdraw their minds from remembrance of sacred Scripture and never withhold their hands from observing the divine commandments.

The text rightly continues:

[Col. 0404A]

And you shall place in the ark the testimony, etc. We ought to speak and believe concerning the incarnation of the Son of God only those things that the Lord himself has deigned to reveal to us through the authors of sacred Scripture.

If you wish to know what that testimony is which Moses received from the Lord to place in the ark, listen to the Apostle: “Behind the veil was the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold; in it was a golden urn containing manna, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant” (Heb. IX).

The golden urn containing manna in the ark is the holy soul in Christ, having within itself the whole fullness of divinity. Aaron’s rod, which had been cut off and then blossomed, is the invincible power of that priesthood, of which the prophet says: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV).

After it appeared for a time to have been cut off through death, at the dawning of the morning of the resurrection it was found to have blossomed again with greater vitality, and it became known that it would remain forever inviolate and unfading. For “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him” (Rom. VI).

The tablets of the covenant in the ark signify in Christ both the whole knowledge of the Father’s secrets and the power of his judgments. On the tablets of the covenant were inscribed faith in the eternal divinity that created and governs the world; the commandments by which God ought to be served; and the discernment of judgment by which he would justly condemn those who hate him and reward with fitting mercy those who love him.

This, then, is the testimony that the Lord gave Moses to place in the ark, when he signified for us the truth to be confessed concerning Christ’s flesh, soul, and Word. He also showed that the flesh itself, after the suffering of death, was glorified by the resurrection and exalted to the dignity of the eternal King and High Priest. He taught that Christ alone is truly aware of the Father’s secrets and that, possessing the same majesty as the Father, he is the judge of all ages.

CHAPTER V. Description of the mercy seat and the cherubim.

You shall also make the mercy seat, etc. It is customary to ask what is meant by the mercy seat, with which the ark was to be covered. But since he commands that it be made of gold, and of the same length and width as the ark he had ordered to be made, it is unquestionably clear that he wished a golden slab to be made large enough to cover the ark.

This mercy seat signifies none other than the Lord and Savior, and more particularly the depths of compassion within him. Of him the Apostle says: “God put him forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Rom. III). It is also placed above because mercy is exalted above judgment. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

Two golden cherubim also, etc. That “cherubim” is the name of angelic powers the prophet Ezekiel plainly declares; he also indicates that he saw them appear with wings, in accordance with the form in which they are commanded here to be made, saying: “And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the sound of the Lord speaking” (Ezek. X). In the singular it is indeed said *cherub*, but in the plural *cherubim*; it is a noun of masculine gender. Greek usage, however, put *cherubin* in the neuter gender, with the letter *m* changed into *n*. Our translator, following the Hebrew idiom, put it in the masculine gender. “You shall make two golden and beaten cherubim,” not “two golden and beaten cherubin”—which, I believe, has been corrupted through the carelessness of scribes in his translation, so that *cherubim* came to be written *cherubin* according to the custom of earlier writers.

*Cherubim*, or *cherubin*, is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge” or “understanding of knowledge.” This name is all the more appropriately applied to angelic powers because they, being perfectly free from every impulse of impure thought, cling to the vision of their Creator. [Col. 0405B]

Moses is therefore commanded to make wings in the likeness of cherubim, or the prophet testifies that he saw them with wings in their actual form, because painters also commonly imitate this convention, signifying that angels have their seat on high and are able to move everywhere as if with light flight, possessing no slowness that would prevent them from being instantly present wherever they wish. The same promise is undoubtedly made to us once we have been clothed after the resurrection with a spiritual body.

The cherubim therefore spread out their wings and cover the mercy seat, because the angels offer to the service of their Creator all the power of their nature by which they have deserved to dwell on high and to penetrate every place of that heavenly homeland in light and joyful passage. Gazing upon the mercy seat, they overshadow it—that is, they honor it by veiling it—because they attribute the whole state of perpetual happiness that they possess to his grace, from whom they have received that they cannot will any evil.

There are two of them to signify the fellowship of angelic peace, because charity cannot exist between fewer than two. Hence they are also commanded to look toward one another and to have their faces turned toward the mercy seat, since, in the glorification of the divine vision, they harmonize with one another.

Again, the two cherubim may represent the two Testaments, one of which proclaims the Lord’s future incarnation and the other proclaims that it has taken place. They look toward one another because, in their testimony to the truth that they preach, they differ in nothing from each other. They turn their faces toward the mercy seat because they strongly commend the Lord’s mercy, in which alone the world has hope. For this reason they are on either side of the oracle, because they fill with the preaching of spiritual knowledge both the times preceding the Lord’s incarnation and those that follow it.
