The name “multitude of knowledge,” or “knowledge multiplied,” also suits them, because Holy Scripture is full of spiritual and divine knowledge, and this same knowledge, from the time Scripture itself began to be composed, never ceases to increase and multiply. Hence the angel says to Daniel: “Many shall pass to and fro, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII).

The Lord himself testifies that Moses received greater knowledge than the patriarchs. Appearing to him, he says: “I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not make my name Adonai known to them” (Exod. III). Divine knowledge was therefore increased with the passage of time, when the Lord revealed to Moses something concerning himself that he had not made known to the patriarchs.

David, who meditated on the law of the Lord day and night, let us see whether he thought that he had understood something more about the Lord than Moses himself, who wrote the law. “How I have loved your law, O Lord,” he says; “it is my meditation all day long” (Ps. CXVIII). Immediately he adds: “I have understood more than all my teachers.” Elsewhere also he glories in the Lord, saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. L).

The Lord himself also declares that the apostles knew greater things than the prophets, speaking to them as follows: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X). Yet after his resurrection and ascension he promises them an even greater grace of knowledge, saying: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John XVI). He also promises that in the future he will reveal to them more than all that can be known in this life, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

It is therefore rightly said that the cherubim are “knowledge multiplied,” because in both Testaments the knowledge of truth has become increasingly known to the faithful over time. The cherubim of glory are rightly said to overshadow the mercy seat, because, as the Testament grows through time and knowledge is multiplied, they proclaim to us the Lord our Savior as the source of propitiation; and they never cease freely to honor this propitiation with their voices, as if with wings spread for flight. For just as the words of people conversing, flying as it were through the air from the speaker’s mouth, reach the hearer’s heart, so the cherubim may rightly be represented with wings spread and prepared, as it were, for flight. [Col. 0406C]

“From there I shall give commands and speak to you, above the mercy seat,” and so forth. The Lord speaks to Moses above the mercy seat concerning all that he commands through him to the children of Israel, because it happened through the grace of God’s propitiation that, after the guilt of transgression, he deigned to appear to human beings and to show them the way of truth after their error.

He speaks from between the cherubim because God appeared and spoke to Moses through an angelic vision, and not in his own substance, as the Apostle testifies: “The law was established because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made; and it was ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III). Again, the Lord speaks from between the two cherubim because through the words of both Testaments he instructs us with a harmonious voice in the faith of the truth.

Or certainly, he speaks from between the cherubim because through his Only-Begotten Son, who appeared in the flesh between the two Testaments, God the Father deigned to reveal his will to the human race. In this sense also the saying of Habakkuk may be understood: “In the midst of two living creatures you will become known” (Hab. III).

The ark may also be understood figuratively as Holy Church. It is built from incorruptible wood—that is, from holy souls—and, stretched through the four regions of the world in the faith of the holy Gospel, it awaits from God the eternal crown of life. It has within itself the tablets of the Testament, in continual meditation on God’s law; it has the golden urn with manna, in faith in the Lord’s incarnation; and it also has Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed, in participation in the Lord’s kingdom and priesthood, as the Apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II).

It has the mercy seat above, so that it may remember that it received all the good things it possesses from the bounty of divine grace. It also has the cherubim of glory upon the mercy seat: either the angelic protections by which it is always helped by God in his mercy, or the Testaments by which it is instructed how to live and how rightly to seek from divine propitiation the aid necessary for living well.

The cherubim are placed above the mercy seat in the same way that the city of Christ—that is, Holy Church—is said to be established upon a mountain, that is, upon Christ himself. This does not mean that his city can be higher than he is, but that, sustained by his support, it advances. The ark has the cherubim above the mercy seat because either the angelic ministries or the divine utterances assist the Church more truly insofar as they themselves stand firmly established upon the foundation of supreme truth. [Col. 0407B]

## CHAPTER VI. Description of the Table

“You shall also make a table of acacia wood,” and so forth. The table made of acacia wood is Holy Scripture, constructed from the strong words and deeds of the holy Fathers. While it shows us what the joys of eternal blessedness are and how one reaches them, it provides us with food of salvation and life.

It has length when it suggests perseverance in the religion we have begun; breadth when it indicates the breadth of charity; and height when it instills hope of everlasting reward. Its length is rightly two cubits because our active conduct consists chiefly in two virtues, namely mercy and innocence, as the Apostle James says: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world” (James I).

When he commands us to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, he shows all that we ought mercifully to do for neighbors in need; when he urges us to keep ourselves unstained from the world, he expresses all that requires us to live chastely.

The Lord himself also declared that these two cubits of good action are present in the table of his words when he said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII). Girded loins signify that we should remain free from the contagion of this world; burning lamps signify that through works of mercy we should shine brightly before the Lord. What follows—“And you must be like people waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding”—belongs to the height of the same table, that is, to hope of future recompense.

The table’s breadth is one cubit, figuratively declaring the unity of that love which the whole sequence of the Old and New Testaments commends to us. There is indeed one charity, that is, the simple and pure devotion of the mind, by which we are commanded to love God, our neighbors, and even our enemies. Nevertheless, with a very proper difference and distinction in the ordering of this love, we must love God first and our enemies last.

Even among our neighbors, the measure of love to be given should vary according to their merits. Thus, although the patriarch Jacob loved all his sons, Scripture testifies that he loved Joseph more than the others because of his singular innocence. Hence the Church beautifully says to Christ in the Song of Songs: “He brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity in me” (Song II).

The table’s height was a cubit and a half. The cubit, as in its breadth, signifies the unity of our heavenly hope, by which we await our Lord when he returns from heaven to reward the servants whom he finds watchful, with their loins girded and the lamps of good works burning. Although there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house according to the diversity of merits (John XIV), there is nevertheless one kingdom of heaven in which all the elect are received.

The remaining half-cubit indicates the beginning of the contemplative life, which some of the saints were also granted to enjoy while still in the flesh. They were given not only to hope for heavenly rewards but also, by seeing them in part, to taste them beforehand: Isaiah, Micah, and the other prophets who saw the Lord seated on the throne of his glory with the host of angels around him (Isa. VI); Peter, James, and John, who saw the Lord transfigured between Moses and Elijah on the holy mountain (Matt. XVII); and the teacher of the nations, who, before he paid the debt of the flesh, was granted to be caught up into paradise and the third heaven and to hear secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to utter (1 Cor. XII).

In these and similar servants of Christ, the table of the tabernacle—that is, divine Scripture, by which Holy Church is continually refreshed—adds half a cubit in height above the common hope, because it shows that the joys of heavenly blessedness were revealed to them before they were granted. Since this revelation appears to the minds of the saints suddenly and only in passing, it is rightly represented by half a cubit rather than a full cubit. [Col. 0408D]

“And you shall overlay it with pure gold.” The table of the tabernacle is overlaid with gold because Holy Scripture shines brightly with the meaning of heavenly wisdom, and the prophets who composed it were illustrious in life and speech.

“You shall make for it a golden rim all around,” and so forth. A golden rim is made around the table because the teaching of sacred discourse is ministered to us through the most pure mouths of faithful preachers. The speech of those who handed on the divine mysteries never consented to be contaminated by the talk of human conversation; rather, they took care to endure and rebuke not only harmful but even idle human words.

Or certainly, a golden rim is made around the table because, when rightly understood in every aspect of its language, Holy Scripture resounds to us with the brightness of heavenly wisdom. A crown is added to this rim because the tongue of preachers promises their hearers the reward of eternal life.

The crown is rightly commanded to be four fingers high because the loftiness of the everlasting crown is shown to us through the four books of the holy Gospel, or because we must reach the crown of life through the keeping of evangelical faith and practice. The books are beautifully signified by fingers, since the tablets of the law are reported to have been written by the finger of God; and in the Gospel the Lord, tempering the strictness of the law, wrote with his finger on the ground when he said of the adulteress whom the Pharisees and scribes accused: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII).

The finger of God is understood as the Spirit of God. Hence Luke reports the Lord as saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI). Matthew, explaining this more clearly, said, “By the Spirit of God” (Matt.).

Thus a golden crown, four fingers high, is placed upon the table’s golden rim because the purest words of the holy preachers await the hope of heavenly blessedness, which is contained, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, in the four books of the holy Gospel. The preachers themselves receive the reward of their labor in heaven, and by the certain authority of evangelical truth they also promise the same crown of life to all who obey them.

The same crown is rightly commanded to be made with openwork, because the reward of the eternal kingdom is not given indifferently to everyone, but, according to the quality of those who receive it, is distributed individually by divine judgment. The table of the Lord would have a pure, non-openwork golden crown if the splendor of the future recompense of the righteous were displayed equally to all—like the sun of this world, whose brightness God causes to rise indiscriminately upon the good and the evil.

But just as one star differs from another in glory, so will be the resurrection of the dead. The crown of the Lord’s table is adorned with various carvings, yet ones arranged appropriately. Eternal life is promised to all the righteous, but the glory of each person within it is manifold according to the diversity of merits.

After the one crown first described, the text adds:

“And above it another golden crown.” This may rightly be understood of the reward of those who, by voluntarily choosing a life of perfection, surpass the general commandments of Holy Scripture and therefore await a special reward beyond that of the other faithful.

A golden crown four fingers high is placed upon the table’s golden rim when eternal life is promised through the Gospel to those who keep the commandments of the divine law. The Lord says to the rich man: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments. You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XIX).

But another crown, a golden circlet, is placed above that crown when he immediately adds: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (ibid.).

To this crown belongs the new song which, it is reported, only virgins sang before the Lamb—those who were bought from humanity as first fruits for God and for the Lamb. To it also belongs the statement that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. XIV).

Or certainly, the golden crown is placed upon the rim of the Lord’s table when, in the words of sacred Scripture, we say that souls departing from the flesh are received into eternal rewards in heaven. Another golden circlet is added above that crown when the same Scripture repeats that a more exalted glory is reserved for them at the end of the world, when they receive immortal bodies. [Col. 0410B]

“You shall also prepare four golden rings,” and so forth. What we explained above concerning the ark must also be understood here. The four golden rings are the four books of the Gospels, through whose faith it has come about that all Holy Scripture is read and understood throughout the world.

The table has four feet because the whole sequence of divine utterances is distinguished in a fourfold manner. In all the holy books we must observe what is intimated there as eternal, what is narrated as having happened, what is foretold as future, and what is commanded or urged as something to be done.

Again, the table of the tabernacle has four feet because the word of the heavenly oracle is commonly understood historically, allegorically, tropologically—that is, morally—or anagogically.

History is present when some event is reported in plain language as having been done or said according to the literal sense—for example, when it is narrated how the people of Israel were saved from Egypt and made the tabernacle for the Lord in the wilderness.

Allegory is present when, through words or mystical events, the present mysteries of Christ and the Church are signified. Through words, for example, when Isaiah says: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. II). This plainly means: “The virgin Mary will be born from the stock of David, and Christ will arise from her stock.” Through events, for example, when the people saved from Egyptian slavery by the blood of the Lamb signify the Church, liberated from demonic domination by the passion of Christ.

Tropology, that is, moral discourse, concerns the formation and correction of conduct, whether expressed in plain or figurative words. In plain words, as John urges: “My little children, let us not love in word or speech, but in deed and truth” (1 John III). In figurative words, as Solomon says: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil never fail from your head” (Eccl. IX). This plainly means: “At all times let your works be pure, and let charity never fail from your heart.”

Anagogy, that is, discourse leading upward, discusses future rewards and the life that is to come in heaven, whether in mystical or plain language. In plain language, for example: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). In mystical language, for example: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates” (Rev. XXII). This plainly means: “Blessed are those who cleanse their thoughts and actions, so that they may have the right to see the Lord Christ, who says, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life’; and through the teaching and examples of the fathers who went before them may they enter the kingdom of heaven.” [Col. 0411A]

“The golden rings shall be beneath the crown,” and so forth. The rings are appropriately beneath the crown because we use the books of the holy Gospel in this life, while we hope for the crown of the heavenly life in the future.

Through these rings the carrying poles are inserted to bear the table. Thus, in order that holy teachers may refresh the hearts of their hearers with the words of sacred discourse, they themselves must keep their minds fixed in every respect upon evangelical reading, directing every interpretation of it toward the purpose of their teaching according to its faith and meaning. They must diligently take care not to teach in all the Scriptures anything else to be done, hoped for, or loved than what is found in the four books of the Gospel.

When they refer all the words of Scripture to the faith and love written in the Gospel, they carry, as it were, the whole table of the Lord with its bread and vessels upon the four rings. [Col. 0411B]

## CHAPTER VII. Description of the Table’s Vessels and the Bread of the Presence

“You shall also make dishes and bowls,” and so forth. The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of divine discourse, corresponding to the differing capacities of hearers.

The same teaching cannot suit everyone. The wise must be taught one way, the foolish another; the rich one way, the poor another; the healthy one way, the sick another; the old one way, the young another; men one way, women another; the unmarried one way, the married another; those in authority one way, their subjects another.

Yet all these vessels belong to the table of the tabernacle, and all belong to the offering of libations, because whatever a prudent teacher says differently according to the diversity of his hearers is found within the rule of Holy Scripture, and arouses the hearts of hearers to offer the Lord vows of good works.

This appropriate diversity of holy preaching was signified by the Lord’s own mouth when he said: “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matt. XXIV). The faithful and prudent steward gives his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time when a discerning minister of the word observes not only the appropriate time for speaking but also carefully investigates the quality and understanding of his hearers, adapting the manner of his speech according to their differences. [Col. 0411D]

“And you shall place upon the table the bread of the presence,” and so forth. The bread of the presence placed continually upon the table represents the spiritual teachers who, meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, offer the refreshment of heavenly discourse to all who enter the Church.

They are rightly called the bread of the presence because the word of salvation must always be openly available to all the faithful. The Church must never lack for devout hearers the word of consolation, which the Lord, proclaiming it to the world through heralds of truth, desired always to appear in his presence and to abound without ceasing until the end of the age for those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

Concerning these loaves—how many and of what kind they were to be made, and how they were to be placed—Leviticus reports more fully. The Lord says to Moses: “You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it; each loaf shall contain two-tenths. You shall set them in two rows, six in each row, upon the purest table before the Lord. You shall place pure frankincense upon them, so that the bread may be a memorial of the Lord’s offering. Every sabbath they shall be changed before the Lord, received from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant. They shall belong to Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place” (Lev. XXIV).

Here, first of all, the very number of the loaves plainly foreshadows the form of the twelve apostles, whom the Lord, appearing in the flesh, first chose, through whose ministry he would give the food of life to all the nations.

Finally, when the crowds were hungry in the wilderness, he said to those same disciples—our apostles, that is—“You give them something to eat.” After five thousand people had been satisfied with five loaves, they themselves gathered twelve baskets of fragments (Mark VI; Luke IX; John VI), because it belongs to the apostles and apostolic men to grasp the mysteries of Scripture that the crowd cannot comprehend.

The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are therefore the twelve apostles and all their followers in doctrine within the Church. Since they do not cease to nourish the people of God with the food of the word until the consummation of the age, the twelve loaves of the presence never depart from the Lord’s table.

They are rightly commanded to be made not from ordinary flour but from fine flour, because whoever ministers the word of life to others must first devote himself to the fruits of virtue, so that he may commend by his deeds what he urges through preaching, conformed to the example of the one who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John XII).

The same loaves are also rightly commanded to be placed in two rows upon the table, because of the harmony of charity and fellowship. The Lord is also said to have sent his disciples out two by two to preach, figuratively indicating that holy teachers never differ from one another either in their assertion of the truth or in the practice of love.

The frankincense placed upon the loaves signifies the virtue of prayer, because these teachers commend to the Lord both the ministry of their preaching and the devotion of their works. The Psalmist testifies that frankincense signifies prayer when he says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

Frankincense is placed upon the loaves as a memorial portion for the Lord’s offering when pure prayer is added to the holy actions and teaching of the saints, so that, by these two things being rightly joined, the memory of the sacred offering may always appear before the supreme Judge.

The loaves are rightly commanded to be changed before the Lord every sabbath. The loaves that had been placed on the Lord’s table for the six days of work are changed for us on the sabbath when the teachers of Holy Church, having completed the period of their holy labor, are rewarded with eternal rest in heaven and leave others after them to undertake the same labor of ministering the word, under the same hope of reward.

Thus the Lord’s table never remains without bread. As soon as one loaf is removed, another is substituted in its place. As ministers of the word succeed one another in order, the Church never lacks those who display apostolic faith and devotion or purity of conduct, both in words and in deeds. The beautiful saying always remains, spoken in praise of the same Holy Church: “Instead of your fathers, sons are born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV). In other words, one might say to the Lord’s tabernacle: “Instead of your old loaves, new ones have been prepared for you; you will appoint them to refresh the hearts of the faithful throughout the world.”

The loaves were changed for loaves, while the table itself always remained the same in the tabernacle, because teachers of the word depart and come, and as some yield their place, others succeed them in due order. Holy Scripture, however, is established for all ages and cannot be abolished, until, when the Lord appears at the end of the world, we shall have need neither of the Scriptures nor of their interpreters, and the Lord’s most desired prophecy is fulfilled: “They shall no longer teach one another, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jer. XXXI).

Josephus writes that the loaves were baked before the sabbath, divided two by two before the sabbath (Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book III, chapter 13). On the sabbath morning they were offered and placed upon the sacred table, six on each side facing one another, with two golden dishes placed above them, filled with incense. These remained until the following sabbath; then others were carried in their place, while the former were presented to the priests. After the incense had been burned in the sacred fire in which all the burnt offerings were made, other incense was added upon the other loaves.

What is written in the Book of Kings—that David entered the tabernacle and received the holy loaves from the priests—also took place on the sabbath morning. He came to the tabernacle at the hour when the loaves of the preceding week had been removed from the Lord’s table, so that the new loaves, baked the day before, might be set in place. Thus he received the holy loaves, so that the Lord’s table did not remain without bread even for a moment. [Col. 0413C]

It is therefore worth considering more carefully that the loaves were commanded to be changed every sabbath. They were changed in such a way that each sabbath they were placed upon the table, and on the following sabbath they were again removed to serve as food for the priests. They appeared upon the table for six days of work, but on the sabbath—the day of rest—they were placed upon the table and then removed from it on the following sabbath.

What else are we to understand mystically from this order of placement except that the holy teachers—or indeed all the righteous—come to rest after the good works by which they shone in the Church, and are kindled to delight in doing good by the hope of future rest and blessedness?

The loaves were therefore placed upon the Lord’s table on the sabbath, with the intention that, once the sabbath had passed, they would remain there for six days of work. After these had passed and another sabbath arrived, they were consumed as food by the high priest and his sons. This signifies that at the beginning of our life devoted to God, rest and eternal life are promised to us, but on the condition that we must reach them through the labors and good works of the present life.

How the eating of the loaves of the presence by the high priest and his sons relates to entry into the heavenly life will be explained more suitably in its proper place, in the exposition of the following verse.

These loaves were received from the children of Israel because those who are to enter upon the rank of priesthood or teaching must be chosen and ordained from the assembly of God’s spiritual servants.

The concluding statement, “They shall belong to Aaron and his sons,” can be understood mystically in two ways. Aaron eats the holy loaves removed from the table of the tabernacle with his sons when our High Priest introduces his chosen ones, snatched from this life, into the increase of his body, which is in heaven—that is, into the supreme multitude of the elect.

Or certainly, the holy loaves belong to Aaron and his sons when all bishops and the peoples subject to them in the Lord are nourished toward eternal life by the examples of the fathers who preceded them. [Col. 0414B]

## CHAPTER VIII. The Lampstand

“You shall also make a lampstand of beaten work from purest gold.” The lampstand of the tabernacle, like the table, represents the universal Church of the present age. They are before the veil behind which the ark of the covenant has been placed because the Church has not yet deserved to be admitted to the vision of its Redeemer in heaven.

It is a table because it supplies daily heavenly nourishment to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, so that they may not fail amid temptations. It is a lampstand because it shows the way of light to those who wander. It is both table and lampstand because, taught by the holy Scriptures, it has learned both to satisfy the hungry soul with good things and to supply the lamp of the word to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

When it humbly submits itself to this lamp—that is, restraining itself from its own pleasures in order to do what the word of God commands, and lifting itself from visible joys in order to hope for and love what the word promises—it becomes, as it were, its lampstand. For it places the heavenly rule above all its own pleasures and, by both preaching and doing, humbles itself while displaying the brightness of God’s word to all. [Col. 0414D]

“Its shaft, its reeds, its cups,” and so forth. The shaft of the lampstand is to be understood as the one who is the Head of the Church, the Mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, man.

Concerning his body, which we are, the Apostle says—as though of reeds proceeding from the shaft: “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its connections and bonds, grows with the increase of God” (Col. II). For almighty God, our Redeemer, who has no need to advance in himself, nevertheless daily receives increase through his members.

The reeds proceeding from the shaft are therefore the preachers who, established by the Lord, have produced a sweet sound in the world, namely, a new song. The reeds are all the sons of the Church who willingly obey it, as the prophet says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Ps. XXXI), resounding with praise to the Lord and saying: “He made my steps firm and put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Ps. XXX).

Since cups are usually filled with wine, the minds of hearers are appropriately signified by them, for at the voice of preachers they are filled with the wine of knowledge. And because the hearts of the faithful, intoxicated with this same wine of inner love, strive toward God with tireless desire, spherical knobs are rightly made on the lampstand after the cups. A sphere rolls in every direction, and so the minds of the elect can be held back neither by any adversity of the world nor corrupted by prosperity; rather, in all that they encounter, they advance toward God through holy desires.

After the reeds, cups, and spherical knobs, lilies are rightly represented on the lampstand, because after the grace of preaching, after intoxication with spiritual drink, and after the irrevocable course of holy action, the verdant homeland follows—a homeland that blooms eternally for holy souls, who are themselves eternal flowers.

Six branches shall project from the sides, etc. It is clear that the number six, in which the world was made, signifies the perfection of works. But since it is arranged in the description of the branches so as to be divided into two groups of three, more should be said about the number three. For three branches project from one side of the stem, and three from the other, because there were teachers before the Lord’s coming in the flesh who designated the faith of the Holy Trinity in mystical language and proclaimed it insofar as the still unlearned could comprehend it. Hence the Psalmist’s words: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32). By the name “Lord” he means the Father; by the name “Word,” the Son; and the Holy Spirit he calls, by his very name, “the breath of his mouth.” He indicates that this Holy Trinity has one power, will, and operation when he declares that the heavens were established by the word of the Lord and all their host by the breath of his mouth.

There are now teachers who openly proclaim this same faith of the Holy Trinity, so that all who belong to Christ must be consecrated in the same faith. For the Lord said to the apostles: “Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). Hence Paul, praying for the faithful and desiring that they be strengthened by the faith they had received in the Trinity, says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13).

Again, three branches extend from one side of the lampstand, and three proceed from the other, because both before and after the Lord’s incarnation there were three orders of those who faithfully served the Lord in the Church: the married, the continent, and the rulers. The prophet Ezekiel mystically describes their distinction when, at the time of the plague, he foretold that only three men—namely Noah, Daniel, and Job—would be delivered (Ezekiel 14). In Noah, who steered the ark amid the waters, he showed the overseers of the Church; in Daniel, who strove to live chastely in the royal court, the continent or virgins; and in Job, who lived in marriage and offered everyone a wondrous example of patience, he showed the life of the married faithful.

The Lord likewise indicates the distinction among them in the New Testament under the figure of those who will be found in bed, in the field, and at the mill on the day of judgment (Matthew 24; Luke 17). Of these, he says that one of each pair will be taken and the other left. Rest in bed expresses the state of the continent; activity in agriculture, the industry of preachers; and labor at the mill, that of the married. Since in all these degrees some are to be chosen and others rejected, it is rightly said of each: “One of two will be taken, and the other will be left.”

Since among the elect the merit of preachers is higher than that of those who devote themselves only to continence and not also to the work of teaching, and since the way of life of the continent is higher than that of the married, the upper branches that proceeded from either side of the stem rightly signify those who, in both Testaments, devoted themselves to the disciplines of teaching in addition to other virtues. The lower branches, which likewise project from both sides of the stem, rightly represent the life of the continent devoted to God; and the lowest branches, also arising from the single stem of the one lampstand, typologically demonstrate the life of the married faithful, who in the period of both Testaments faithfully served the one and same Lord.

The branches therefore proceed from the stem at different places, yet all, each bent upward in its own place and order, reach a single summit, so that they may maintain the lamps at an equal height above themselves. For the elect, although distinguished by degrees of merit, are imbued with one faith in the truth and will arrive at one light of eternal truth in heaven. The more earnestly each person in this life has striven to cling to Christ, the nearer in the life to come he enjoys Christ’s vision. Thus it is said of certain people, because of the greatness of their virtue: “These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14). Of these, shortly before, as of branches nearest to the lampstand, it was said: “And they sang as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders” (ibid.). This shows that all the saints sing a new song of joy to the Lord throughout the streets of that heavenly city. But those are raised above the others there in the particular joy of song who, in this life, surpassed the common life of the faithful by the privilege of sacred virginity.

Three cups, shaped like a nut, etc. That the nut is customarily set forth as a figure of the present Church is attested by Solomon, who speaks in the person of faithful teachers: “I went down,” he says in the Song of Songs, “to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley” (Song of Songs 6). For just as a nut has sweet fruit within but cannot display it outwardly unless the hardness of its shell is broken, so the present life of the righteous preserves the sweetness of spiritual grace in the innermost heart, but cannot reveal to those near them how great it is until, when the dwelling of the body has been dissolved, their souls freely behold one another in the heavenly light, and it becomes entirely manifest how greatly each shines with the grace of the Holy Spirit and how much each is loved by the others.

Cups are made on the lampstand in the form of a nut when the elect, desiring to be filled with the wine of wisdom, strive to shape themselves according to the example of the righteous who preceded them, whom they know to be filled with the great sweetness and love of invisible goods. The fact that on each branch there were three cups, spheres, and lilies signifies the three divisions of time in which the elect lived devoted to God, both before and after the Lord’s incarnation. There were righteous people before the Law, under the Law, and in the times of the prophets.

Likewise, after the Lord’s ascension, the primitive Church was gathered from Israel; now the Church is being gathered from the nations; and at the end of the world it will be gathered from the remnant of Israel. Thus the first branch on one side had three cups, spheres, and lilies, because among the teachers before the Lord’s incarnation there were three orders distinguished by time. They thirsted for a draught of heavenly grace as though they were cups; they ran most eagerly along the Lord’s way as though they were spheres; and they joyfully awaited the gift of heavenly recompense as though they were lilies, in their whiteness and fragrance—that is, before the Law, under the Law, and under the prophets.

The second branch likewise had three cups, spheres, and lilies, because the continent of that period also had three orders of saints according to the foregoing divisions of time: desiring spiritual drink, running along the way of the Lord’s commandments, and awaiting heavenly rewards.

The third branch similarly had three cups and spheres, and three lilies, because there were many married people before the Law, many under the Law, and many in the days of the prophets who rejoiced to hear the word of the Lord, to run along his way, and to await from him the rewards of good works.

Likewise, on the other side of the stem, the first, second, and third branches each had three cups and spheres, and also three lilies, because in the New Testament as well—among teachers, the continent, and the married devoted to God—there were three orders distinguished by periods of time: in the primitive Church from Israel, in our present election from the nations, and in the final gathering of the remnant of Israel. All of them, each in its own time, desire to be made drunk with the word of life, to hasten along the way of peace, and to behold the radiance of perpetual light.

On the lampstand itself there shall be four cups, etc. We have said that the lampstand itself—that is, the central stem of the lampstand from which the branches proceeded—signifies the Lord the Savior, from whose grace the righteous have received whatever good they possess. Hence, when he had said to his disciples in the Gospel, “I am the vine, you are the branches,” he immediately added: “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John 15).

It is as though he were saying in other words: “I am the lampstand, and you are my branches. Just as a branch cannot raise itself up to support a lamp unless it remains fixed in the stem of the lampstand, so neither can you bear the light of truth and faith within yourselves unless you remain in me.”

Four cups were made on this lampstand because in the four books of the Holy Gospel written about the Lord we find a taste of the new wine—that is, heavenly teaching—which not old wineskins, namely minds still clinging to earthly desires, but only hearts renewed by the Spirit of grace can contain.

On each cup spheres and lilies were fashioned together, because the same Lord who offered us the cup of spiritual wisdom also showed us the course of pious action, safe and ready to be undertaken by us. So that we may possess it, he himself will grant it; and lest we run in vain, he promised us the glory of the heavenly homeland toward which we should strive, and by his grace opened its entrance to us.

Or, since under two branches cups, spheres, and lilies are commanded to be made in three places, we may interpret this mystically as follows: among the three degrees of the faithful of whom we have often spoken—namely, the married, the continent, and the virgins—he both opened the teaching of truth, commanded the course of good works, and promised and bestowed the blessing of an inheritance that is always unfading and incorruptible.

Cups, spheres, and lilies are appropriately commanded to be beneath the branches of the lampstand, not above them, because the hearts of preachers—or rather, of all the elect—are supported by the Lord’s gifts, commandments, and promises, lest they be able to sink down to what is lowest, and are lifted up to love and seek heavenly things.

For this reason the Holy Church, namely Christ’s bride, boasts of him, saying: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 2). The bridegroom’s left hand is placed beneath the bride’s head because, by separating the minds of the faithful from earthly pleasures and desires through temporal benefits, the Lord raises them to hope for and desire eternal goods. “And his right hand shall embrace her,” because the vision of his divine majesty, once revealed, glorifies her without end.

Cups, spheres, and lilies are appropriately beneath two branches because in both Testaments the same devotion to serving the Lord was commanded to the faithful, although the ceremonies differed, and the same glory of the heavenly kingdom was preserved for them.

The fourth cup, sphere, and lily, which were above all the branches near the summit of the lampstand itself, properly pertain to the Lord the Savior. He not only grants his elect knowledge of virtue, the practice of virtue, and its reward; in himself also, as the man Christ, he displayed the figure of a cup when he declared himself full of the Holy Spirit. He presented the form of a sphere when, appearing in the world without any obstacle from surrounding affairs, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18). He displayed the appearance of a lily when, rising from the dead and ascending to heaven, he was glorified with the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17).

This cup, sphere, and lily rightly rose higher than the branches, because the gifts that God the Father bestowed upon the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, transcend every measure of human capacity. “Grace was given to each of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” But in Christ himself, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Ephesians 4).

And rightly the text continues:

[Col. 0419A] “And the spheres and the branches shall be from it,” etc. The entire work of the lampstand—that is, the central stem, the branches proceeding from it, and all their adornment—is made of gold, because the Lord himself appeared in the world uniquely free from sin and altogether illustrious in works of righteousness. His members likewise imitate that same innocence and righteousness in this interim life insofar as they are able; in the future, by clinging truly to him, they will advance.

The same gold was appropriately beaten out, for beaten gold is produced by striking. Our Redeemer, who from conception and birth existed as perfect God and man, endured the pains of suffering and thus reached the glory of the resurrection. “All who desire to live piously in him suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3), because they too, like metal expanded by hammering, advance through the insults of suffering to the grace of immortality.

Hence, in the fourth Psalm, which is entitled “In songs,” the Church says to her Redeemer, speaking in the mystical branches of faith: “You enlarged me in tribulation.” It is as though beaten gold were saying to its craftsman: “By the blows of the smith’s hammer you have enlarged me, and by striking me you have given me greater progress.”

CHAPTER IX. The lamps of the lampstand and the snuffers.

You shall also make seven lamps, etc. The lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These always remained in the Lord and our Redeemer, and they have been distributed among his members, that is, among all the elect, according to his will.

The lamps are therefore placed upon the lampstand because upon our Redeemer, the firstborn from the root of Jesse, rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him (Isaiah 11). And as he himself speaks through the same prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me” (Isaiah 61). What is said—“so that they may shine opposite”—is explained by what the prophet adds immediately afterward: “He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to the captives and opening to those who are imprisoned, to proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord and a day of vengeance for our God.”

The lamps of the lampstand shone opposite and illuminated the Lord’s tabernacle when the Lord, being full of grace and truth, gave to all of us from his fullness, “grace upon grace”; when he entrusted the word of the Gospel to the meek and poor in spirit; when he granted the substance of forgiveness to penitents; and when he declared that the present is a time for pleasing the Lord, but that the future will be the day of universal judgment.

The number and arrangement of the lamps also correspond to what John says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Revelation 5).

If the seven horns or seven eyes of the Lamb there can signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, why should the same seven lamps of the lampstand not rightly be believed to signify them as well? Indeed, just as the horns and eyes rightly signify him because of the omnipotence of his power by which he rules all things and the fullness of his knowledge by which he sees all things, so the same sevenfold Spirit is appropriately expressed by the figure of lamps because of the light of grace by which, in the night of this age, he illuminates the darkness of our blindness.

Hence the text appropriately continues:

The snuffers also, and the places where what has been snuffed out is extinguished, etc. There are certain commands in the divine Scriptures that must always be observed by perpetual right, both in this life and in the life to come, such as: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20); “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22; Luke 10).

There are other commands that are to be observed throughout the whole duration of this life, but whose reward is received eternally in the life to come, such as the Gospel command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). Here almsgiving is to be practiced for a time; there the fruit of almsgiving is to be received forever.

There are also commands that were carefully observed at the Lord’s bidding during the time of the Old Testament. Now, with the Gospel shining throughout the world, they are commanded to be observed in the Church not according to the letter but according to their mystical meaning. Such are the observance of the Sabbath, the rites of sacrifices, the blood of the paschal lamb, and other things of this kind. These were solemnly observed by God’s people in their own time and burned like wicks in the lamps of the lampstand, infused with the oil of pious devotion and kindled by the fire of the heavenly word.

But when the apostles and apostolic men proclaimed that the Lord had brought an end to these and similar observances, all these things were to be observed spiritually in the Church rather than according to the letter. The wicks of the lampstand were, as it were, snuffed so that, renewed, they might shine more brightly, because, understood more sublimely through the Spirit, they offered the Holy Church the light of saving teaching.

Concerning this renewal of the lamps of the tabernacle—that is, the more exalted understanding of the divine Scriptures—the Lord promises his people in Leviticus: “You shall be multiplied, and I will establish my covenant with you. You shall eat the oldest of the old, and you shall cast out the old when the new comes.”

When the children of Israel were multiplied, God’s covenant with them was confirmed. And when the nations were called to the faith, the grace of the New Testament was planted with firm roots in the hearts of the elect.

We eat the oldest of the old when we retain in the sweet memory of our hearts the ancient commandment given to the human race from the beginning: loving the Lord our God with all our heart, soul, and strength, and loving our neighbor as ourselves.

We cast out the old when the new has come upon us when we cease to observe the typological statutes of the Mosaic Law according to the letter, but preserve those same statutes, understood more graciously through the Spirit, in a heart renewed in hope of the heavenly kingdom. This accords with the Apostle’s words: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5). And in the Apocalypse: “He who sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21).

The snuffers by which these things were done are the very words of sacred Scripture, by which it is clearly shown that the letter of the Law must be set aside in many respects and that the Law is to be observed solely according to its spiritual meaning.

An example is found in the Acts of the Apostles, where Gentile believers were forbidden to be circumcised and were commanded to obey the grace of the Gospel without the ceremonies of legal sacrifices.

The Apostle also explains this when, expounding a verse of the Psalm in the Letter to the Hebrews, he first says: “You did not desire sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings for sin, nor were those offered according to the Law pleasing to you”; and then: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10). “He takes away the first in order to establish the second.” By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ.

The snuffers, therefore, and the vessels in which what has been snuffed out is extinguished, are made of pure gold, because the divine words by which the cessation of the legal ceremonies is proclaimed have been illuminated by God’s grace. The hearts in which the figurative shadow of the Law comes to an end are likewise illuminated, so that the succeeding truth of the Gospel might shine more clearly upon the world.

For it is clear that the first apostles set aside the Sabbath in the Gospel before the Lord’s passion and, after the Lord’s ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit, completely brought an end to legal sacrifices, changing many decrees of the letter of the Law through the freedom of the Gospel’s grace.

In these things the wicks that had been snuffed out were extinguished: in them the completion of literal observance displayed the beginning of grace, which shone more clearly upon the world.

Likewise, when mortal life has ended and immortal life has succeeded it, most of the works or gifts of light that we now use will cease, so that the rewards of eternal light may follow in the presence of the divine vision. Those testimonies of Scripture that declare these things to be future are truly golden snuffers, made splendid by hope of the coming glory.

The vessels in which what has been snuffed out is extinguished are, of course, the immortal bodies and hearts of all the righteous. They are therefore most rightly likened to gold, since in them this most desired transformation will occur, so that after temporal benefits from God they may arrive at eternal ones.

Finally, the Apostle provides us with the golden snuffers of God’s lamps and the places where what has been snuffed out is extinguished when he speaks of the difference between present and future goods, saying: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed. For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished.” And shortly afterward: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13).

The entire weight of the lampstand . . . a talent of purest gold. The entire weight of the lampstand, with all its vessels, is the entire body of Christ, together with our head, the Mediator between God and human beings, and all his elect, from the highest to the lowest—from him than whom no one is greater among those born of women to those of whom he says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me” (Matthew 18).

All of these, though in different degrees, ages, sexes, conditions, abilities, and periods, cling in their own time and place to the one and same author and giver of perpetual light, as though fixed by the root of their minds in a golden lampstand, so that they may become partakers of that same light.

This lampstand is rightly said to contain a talent of purest gold, for a talent is a full and perfect weight. “The Lord is just in all his ways” (Psalm 145); and he who in this life grants his faithful the grace to act well himself repays their good works with the crown of righteousness in the life to come.

By contrast, the prophet Zechariah describes iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead (Zechariah 5), because God will also restore to the reprobate according to their deeds in the same just judgment: “For you will repay each according to his works” (Psalm 62).

But it makes a difference whether someone brings gold or lead to the divine judgment. Those who shine with good works like gold advance into the Lord’s lampstand because they become participants in the glory of their Creator. But those who appear burdened by sins at the strict judgment sink like lead in extremely deep water, because by the deserts of their crimes they fall into the abyss of punishing condemnation.

Yet both lead and gold have the measure of a talent, because whether he condemns the wicked or saves and crowns the elect, the judgment of our Creator is just.

Look and make it according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain. The mystery of this command is readily apparent from what was explained above. The pattern of the lampstand that he was to make was shown to Moses on the mountain because, in the height of inward contemplation, he learned openly the manifold mysteries of Christ and the Church.

He did not, however, wish to present these openly to the people whom he was instructing. Rather, he signified them typologically through the figure and workmanship of the lampstand and its vessels, until the Lord and our Redeemer himself came in the flesh and, having given the grace of the Holy Spirit, disclosed to his Church the inner meaning of the same figure.

By dying on the cross he tore the veil of the Temple and revealed the mysteries that had been hidden in the holy places. After his resurrection, appearing to the disciples, he opened their understanding so that, with the eyes of their minds unveiled, they might perceive spiritually these and the other secrets of Scripture.

But when every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is commanded, after learning from the sacred writings about catholic faith or pious conduct, both diligently to follow it himself and to teach it to others, what else is he commanded to do than to look and act according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain?

He carefully examines the pattern that has been displayed and, returning to what is below, acts according to it when he diligently searches his heart concerning what he understands through the sublimity of the divine word to be believed or done within. He continually shows this pattern to his hearers both through the execution of righteous works and through the word of saving doctrine.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0423]

### CHAPTER ONE. A description of the tabernacle and the Temple

[Col. 0423A]

Now the tabernacle shall be made in this way. The tabernacle made by Moses in the wilderness, like the Temple that Solomon made in Jerusalem, signifies the state of the holy universal Church. Part of the Church already reigns with the Lord in heaven; part still journeys in the present life, its members departing and being replaced in turn, away from the Lord.

There is indeed this principal difference between the figures represented by the construction of the two houses: the work of the tabernacle signifies the present building of the Church, in which it is exercised daily through labors; the work of the Temple signifies the rest of the future life, which is brought to completion by the daily reception of souls departing from this world after their labors.

For Moses founded the tabernacle while he and the people of God were still on the road by which they were journeying toward the promised land; Solomon, however, built the Temple after the promised land had been reached and he had obtained possession of its kingdom.

Moses made the tabernacle in the wilderness; Solomon, the Temple in Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace.” For here the Church is built amid the labor and distress of a passing life, in thirst and hunger for the everlasting kingdom; there it is brought to completion in the vision and possession of true peace.

Hence it is rightly said in the construction of the Temple that “the hammer and the axe and every iron tool were not heard in it while it was being built,” since all the stones and timbers had been prepared outside Jerusalem and suitably fitted into their ordered positions. There each was easily and surely placed in its proper location, either joined with cement or fastened with nails.

For in the peace of heavenly blessedness our faith will not be tested by tribulations, nor our life proved by trials. Rather, what in the present age was disciplined and suitably prepared for the heavenly dwelling will there be joined together in the sight of its Creator and King by the bond and ties of mutual charity, so that it can never be dissolved.

When in this life the multitude of believers becomes one heart and one soul, and all things are held in common among them, what else are they than living stones squared for the construction of the Lord’s future house? Transferred from here and there, without any labor or delay, they are inserted into their respective orders and joined to one another by the bond of divine as well as personal love.

The figure of the two sanctuaries may also be distinguished generally in this way. The work of the tabernacle signifies the time of the synagogue, that is, of God’s ancient people; the work of the Temple signifies the Church, that is, the multitude of the elect who came to life after the Lord’s incarnation.

For Moses completed the tabernacle with the Hebrew people alone, whereas Solomon completed the Temple with a gathered multitude of proselytes, assisted also by the king of Tyre and his craftsmen, who were neither Jews by nature nor by profession.

It is clear that among the former people of God the teachers were drawn only from their own nation. In the Church, however, the first leaders were indeed Hebrews, but soon, as the Church grew and spread throughout the world, builders also arose from the nations. Thus the evangelist Luke, as well as Timothy and Titus—apostolic men called from the nations—attained leadership within it.

But if we examine each detail more carefully, the building of both houses mystically describes the state of the entire present Church, which from the beginning of the world’s creation until the last elect person who will be born at the end of the age never ceases to be built. It also depicts, with wondrous truth through its figures, the glory of the future life, which the Church now enjoys in part but will enjoy eternally in all its members after the end of this age.

Therefore, as we are about to say something about the tabernacle, with the Lord’s help, we first invoke him and humbly ask that the eyes of our hearts be opened, so that we may be able to contemplate the wonders of his law and understand that, beneath the beauty of costly metals and garments, the adornment of conduct shining with faith and devotion has been commended to us.

For otherwise the apostolic saying could not apply to us: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6), as God says: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them” (Leviticus 26). So too John heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them” (Revelation 21)—as if we imitate the material adornment of the tabernacle or Temple by the religious worship of a pure heart and body.

But before discussing the spiritual meaning, let us first look briefly at the material text of the letter itself.

The tabernacle was a house consecrated to the Lord, thirty cubits long, ten cubits wide, and likewise ten cubits high, with a roof level throughout, in the manner customary in Egypt and Palestine for building houses.

Its walls on three sides—the southern, northern, and western—were assembled from wooden boards gilded on both sides. On the eastern side there was a single bar, where the entrance was, extending through the middle of the boards from corner to corner—that is, from the upper end of this wall to the upper end of the other wall.

The tabernacle curtain and the roof rested upon it, and there was also a curtain suspended from five columns. The house was covered above and on every side with curtains woven in marvelous variety; this was properly called the tabernacle.

It was also covered on every side with goat-hair cloths reaching to the ground. There was in addition another covering for the roof made of reddened ram skins. Over this again another covering was made of violet skins.

There was also a veil varied with embroidered work, hung upon four columns, by which the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies were divided. Inside it stood the ark of the covenant; opposite the ark, outside the veil, stood the altar of incense.

In the middle of the sanctuary was the lampstand on the southern side. The table stood on the northern side. The altar of burnt offering was outside, before the entrance to the sanctuary; the bronze basin stood between this altar and the tabernacle.

Around all of this was the court of the tabernacle, one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide.

Having briefly set these matters forth by way of clarification, let us examine the actual words of the historical account, so that through them we may arrive more deeply and clearly at the allegorical meaning. When the Lord, with Moses remaining with him on Mount Sinai for forty days and nights, was giving him the ceremonies of the Law and the rule of life, he said among other things:

### CHAPTER TWO. The ten curtains
## Chapter II. Ten Curtains

**[Exodus XXVI.]** “You shall make the tabernacle as follows,” etc.

The Lord’s tabernacle is made from curtains varied by a diversity of colors, because the holy universal Church is built from the many persons of the elect, from the many Churches throughout the world, and from the varied flowers of the virtues. Its entire perfection is contained in the number ten, because the Church is spread throughout the world among diverse nations, tribes, peoples, and languages, and subsists wholly in love of God and neighbor, which is comprised in the Decalogue of the Law. Nor can anyone truly attain membership in the Church unless he has learned to love with an undivided heart both Him through whom the Church is built and those in whom it is built—that is, God and His elect.

The varied beauty of the colors with which these curtains are distinguished signifies the varied grace of the virtues, by which the holy Church, composed through a marvelous and wholly heavenly art, shines in the sight of its Creator. It was by such variety, and, as it were, by embroidered work, that blessed Peter sought to build God’s tabernacle when he said: “As each has received grace, ministering it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (I Peter IV). Paul saw that this was present in the curtains of the tabernacle—that is, in the minds of the faithful—when he says: “To one indeed, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge” (II Corinthians XII), and so forth in that passage.

And indeed, that byssus, which is placed first because it signifies the beauty of the virtues, is attested by John in the Apocalypse, who says: “The marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, and it was granted her to clothe herself in shining, bright linen” (Apocalypse XIX); for “the linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.” Concerning this same wife of the Lamb, that is, the Church of Christ, Solomon says: “Fine linen and purple are her clothing” (Proverbs XXXI).

Yet John, explaining the figure of one color, indicates that the others too are to be interpreted figuratively. Byssus, then, which indeed arises from the earth, but, once pulled from the earth, customarily loses its grassy color through prolonged labor of drying, beating, cleansing, boiling, and spinning, and takes on a white color, signifies bodies made radiant by the beauty of chastity. When such bodies, born amid the enticements of the flesh, through the great labor of continence, as it were sweat out their natural moisture, they attain the beauty of purity worthy of God through diligent fasting and vigils, prayer and reading, patience and humility. Of these the apostolic saying may rightly be spoken: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you?” (I Corinthians VI).

This byssus is twisted into the curtains of the tabernacle because we gird not only the loins of the flesh, but also—as Peter admonishes—the loins of our mind in sobriety (I Peter I), so that we restrain the flesh from wanton movements and the heart from seductive thoughts.

Hyacinth, because it imitates the appearance of the air and the sky, signifies the minds of those elect who seek heavenly things with every hope and desire. Commending to us the mystery of this color, the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians III).

Purple, because it displays the color of blood—and true purple is also dyed with the blood of shellfish—signifies the devoted hearts of those who can say with the Apostle: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts XXI). And with the prophet David: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are considered as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm XLIII).

Scarlet, because it has the appearance of fire, is rightly compared with the most ardent love of the saints. Hence some of them, who had conceived this love in the presence of and together with the Lord, said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV). In contrast, it is said of the reprobate: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV).

This scarlet is, as it were, dyed twice when it burns with love of God and neighbor—when we love Him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves.

Thus, in these four colors of the curtains, four forms of the elect’s righteousness are expressed: in twisted byssus, the flesh retaining chastity; in hyacinth, the mind desiring what is above; in purple, the flesh subjected to sufferings; in twice-dyed scarlet, the mind shining amid sufferings through love of God and neighbor.

### “The length of one curtain shall be,” etc.

In the length of the curtains is expressed the holy Church’s patient long-suffering; in their breadth, the fullness of charity, which is accustomed not only to love the one who loves it, but also to love God and neighbor in return, and even to receive the enemy who hates it into the open embrace of its sweetness, commending its persecutors to the Lord on bended knees in prayer and saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII).

This breadth was appropriately four cubits, because there are four books of the Gospels, in which we are taught by the examples and words of our Lord and Redeemer how this same charity is to be maintained. There are also four virtues in whose practice this charity must be exercised: temperance, fortitude, justice, and prudence. Thus charity toward God is to be kept incorrupt and entire, which belongs to temperance; it is not to be broken by any adversity, which belongs to fortitude; it is to serve no other, which belongs to justice; and it is to remain watchful in discerning matters, lest deceit or trickery gradually steal upon it, which belongs to prudence.

The length of the curtains was twenty-eight cubits. This is the number four multiplied by seven; and by the number seven, on account of the Sabbath day, the eternal rest of the saints is customarily signified. The length of the curtains therefore extended to four times seven cubits, because through faith and observance of evangelical teaching, and through the exercises of the spiritual virtues of which we have spoken, the patient long-suffering of the holy Church advances toward eternal rest.

There is also another mystery in the number twenty-eight, which likewise belongs to the number seven. For if you wish to count all the numbers from one through seven in complete order, you will reach twenty-eight: one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven make twenty-eight. Since, then, the number twenty-eight is found in the parts of the number seven, the length of the curtains is rightly contained in it, because the faith and patience of the saints, distinguished by a variety of virtues, awaits in all that it does or suffers not the glory of human favor but the blessedness of heavenly rest.

For this reason the psalm bearing this number is given the title “On the completion of the tabernacle.” It is clear that the whole psalm was sung about the perfection of the holy Church, especially where it says: “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” And again: “In his temple everyone will say, ‘Glory!’” (Psalm XXVIII).

Psalm XXVIII is appropriately inscribed “On the completion of the tabernacle,” because the perfection of the Church journeying in this world consists in advancing through faith and good works toward the rest of the world to come. Well, then, it follows:

### “All the tent-cloths shall be made of one measure.”

Although the curtains differed from one another in their varied designs, they were all regulated by one measure of length and breadth. Likewise, although the elect have different gifts according to the grace given them, there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

### “Five curtains shall be joined to one another,” etc.

Josephus records (*Antiquities* III.6) that the tablets of the Testimony were inscribed with the Decalogue of the Law in such a way that each tablet contained five sayings. Accordingly, the ten curtains, which when joined together completed the beauty of the tabernacle, were appropriately separated at the proper point so that five remained together on each side. Thus, when the ministers of holy things looked upon them with the people of God, they would be reminded always to observe the Law, which was contained in ten sayings on two tablets, distinguished by the number five on each tablet.

But because of this interpretation, we can also discuss the number of curtains—twice five—in another way: the followers of God were signified in both Testaments. The first five, which protected or formed the front and first part of the tabernacle, bore the type of the ancient people of God, who fulfilled according to the letter the decrees of the Law in the sacrament of circumcision, in sacrifices, and in the various observances of the ceremonies.

The following five curtains, which covered or formed the rear of the tabernacle, signified us, who, born after the Lord’s coming in the flesh, preserve the books and sacraments of the Law spiritually, with Him revealing and granting their meaning.

All the curtains were indeed of one workmanship and depicted in the same colors, but they were joined together in groups of five, because all the worshipers of both Testaments believed in one and the same God and served Him through works of one and the same piety and chastity. Yet in the celebration of the sacraments the two peoples carried out their distinct roles.

For the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, through which both peoples have been redeemed, they celebrate in different ways: they in the flesh and blood of victims, we in the offering of bread and wine. They believed and confessed that the Lord’s birth in the flesh, his preaching, the working of miracles, temptation, Passion, burial, resurrection, ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and the faith of the nations were still to come; we believe and confess that all these things have already taken place and will not take place again.

Nevertheless, at the time when the tabernacle was erected, all the curtains were joined to one another, because, as the entire beauty of the Catholic Church extends from the beginning to the end of the world, so one connection of ten curtains adorns the Lord’s tabernacle.

### “You shall make loops of hyacinth on the sides and at the tops,” etc.

We have said that hyacinth, being of an airy color, corresponds to the signification of heavenly blessings. The curtains are therefore joined to one another by hyacinth loops when the one hope of heavenly blessedness unites all the hearts of the elect throughout the world in one and the same devotion.

These loops are appropriately said to be made not only on the sides of the curtains but also at the tops—that is, at the extreme ends of the corners. For not only do the life and works of the saints hasten toward perfection along the common road of right intention; the very beginning of a good way of life, undertaken through the confession of faith and reception of the heavenly sacraments, is likewise not diverse among them, but is joined together by an equal and undivided grace of truth.

We also possess the end of temporal life as common through the certainty of one and the same hope, when we close our eyes in death with the confidence that, having first received the viaticum of the heavenly mystery, we shall soon be found in the true life and shall remain there forever.

This passage corresponds to the command given in the Book of Numbers to the children of Israel, that they make tassels at the corners of their garments and place hyacinth-colored ribbons on them. The children of Israel have tassels and hyacinth-colored ribbons at the corners of their garments when all the elect, and all who desire to see God, labor to clothe themselves in works of righteousness, placing the end of those works not in the praise of mortals—lest it be said of them, “They have received their reward” (Matthew VI)—but rather seeking in them the eyes of the Judge of hell and eternal rewards.

Therefore, immediately afterward, the text explains: “When they see them, they shall remember all the commandments of the Lord, lest they follow their own thoughts and eyes, committing fornication through various things.” These words must also be used in explaining the hyacinth loops. We should say that the curtains were joined by such loops so that the children of Israel, having these things before their eyes, might then be reminded of the heavenly commandments, and that we, reading them now, might remember that, while living in this life, we are children of the promise of eternity and are separated from one another by times and places; but in heaven there is a homeland that joins its citizens, gathered from the four winds of heaven, in an indivisible fellowship forever.

### “Each curtain shall have fifty loops,” etc.

We read in the Law of the fiftieth year as the Jubilee (Leviticus XXV), which was commanded to be called the year of release, or the year of initiation. In it the whole people rested from all labor of the land, and all debts were to be remitted.

In the New Testament we know that the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon the Apostles at Pentecost—that is, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection (Acts II)—and consecrated by its coming the beginnings of the newborn Church. Hence, in this number, either the grace of the Holy Spirit or the future joy of blessedness may rightly be signified: that blessedness to which one reaches through the gift of the same Spirit, and in whose possession alone one truly rests and rejoices.

The curtains appropriately had fifty loops by which they were joined to one another, because it is only through the gift of the Holy Spirit that the elect are joined together in the fellowship of peace, which is the bond of perfection. It is the hope and remembrance of the fellowship and peace to come that makes the servants of Christ, separated in this life by times or places, one in harmonious devotion.

It is also rightly said that the loops of the curtains were on both sides, so that each curtain might embrace the curtains nearest to it on either side, as though extending arms in both directions.
