For all the faithful must embrace with outstretched arms of sincere devotion both those who preceded us in Christ and those who followed us; both those who instructed us in Christ and those whom, by Christ’s gift, we ourselves have instructed. We must honor them all with one affection in Christ.

We must thus hasten by a good life toward seeing the face of our Creator: we must not abandon the neighbor running alongside us, but strive to arrive with him before the presence of divine glory. For the individual curtains were stretched upward by means of the supports of the boards, and within, in the upper parts, they shone with the varied flowers of their design; yet they did not abandon the curtains that were carried upward with them or that shone beside them in the heights.

Likewise, we ought to assist the faithful who are advancing with us in God’s service by admonitions and examples, and to treat with honor worthy of their virtues those who have been able to advance in any virtue. One loop therefore comes opposite another so that one may be fitted to the other, when the righteous are bound together by harmonious and equal quality of virtues.

### “You shall make fifty rings of gold,” etc.

This passage is explained more fully below, where it says: “He also cast fifty rings of gold, which would fasten the loops of the curtains, and the tabernacle would become one” (Exodus XXXVI).

The number fifty therefore signifies the true rule in the Holy Spirit. Since a circle appears to have neither beginning nor end, while gold, because of its brilliance, is more precious than the other metals, what is expressed by fifty golden rings except the perpetual brightness and bright perpetuity of the highest rest?

The rings fasten the loops of the curtains so that one tabernacle may be made from them all, when the glory of the heavenly kingdom pours itself into the pure minds of the faithful in such a way that, by this bond of saving inspiration, the Church of Christ is perfected as one Church from both peoples—or rather, from all the elect.

## Chapter III. Eleven Haircloth Coverings

### “You shall make eleven coverings of goats’ hair,” etc.

This passage is repeated below as follows: “He also made eleven coverings of goats’ hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle” (Exodus XXXVI).

The coverings by which the tabernacle is covered are the rulers of the holy Church. Through their diligence and labor, the beauty of that same Church is protected and guarded with unceasing care, so that the life and faith of the elect may not be corrupted by heretical seduction, stained by the wickedness of false Catholics, contaminated by the filth of temptations to vice, or driven into sadness by lack of temporal resources.

The more attentively they gird themselves to endure or repel the violence of the temptations that assault them, the greater freedom they grant their subjects to serve the Lord. They provide the curtains, as it were, with room to shine within, while, like haircloth coverings, they endure outside the storms of affliction.

These same coverings are rightly said to be of haircloth, made from goats’ hair, and eleven in number. The holy preachers, the greater they are in merit, must be the humbler in spirit, according to the saying of the wise man: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus III).

The number eleven, which passes beyond ten but does not reach twelve—that is, the apostolic number—signifies transgression of the Decalogue of the Law. In the eleventh psalm the Prophet laments that the saints have failed and that the children of men have exchanged truth for vanity and deceit, saying: “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed,” etc. By this number he also tacitly indicates that such people, being double-tongued and double-hearted, neither keep the legal precepts of the Decalogue nor can receive the apostolic grace of the Gospel.

Haircloth is also the garment of penitents, as the psalmist testifies when he says: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm XXXIV)—that is, I assumed the garment of penance and humility, by which I might either endure calmly the fury of my persecutors or appease it.

For if goats, or goats’ hair and skins, always signified the stench of sinners and never at times the humility of penitents, the animal would certainly not be counted among the clean animals, nor would it be said in praise of the bride: “Your hair is like a flock of goats” (Song of Songs IV).

The coverings, therefore, which signify the holy preachers, are both made of haircloth and numbered eleven, because the more diligently they purify their hearts through faith, the more things they find in themselves for which to reproach themselves. Hence they humbly confess: “We all offend in many things” (James III); and: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John II).

Yet the following words mystically reveal the great perfection of their hearts. They say:

### “The length of one covering shall be,” etc.

Here you have not the number eleven for the length, but ten, and that number multiplied by three. This plainly signifies the virtue of those who perfect the Decalogue of the Law in faith in the Holy Trinity, which works through love. In this perfection, at least in the present life, nothing higher can exist.

You also have four cubits for the breadth, signifying the fullness of sincere charity—that is, the charity which, as we have said, is both commended and given to us in the Gospel through Jesus Christ.

The eleven coverings therefore cover the roof of the tabernacle. They are made from goats’ hair, but are thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, because those supreme preachers, who protect the lives of the faithful through their exhortations, intercessions, daily solicitude, vigils, fasts, and nakedness, humbly regard the excellence of heavenly purity and confess themselves sinners. Yet, insofar as human perfection permits, they appear clean and exalted among human beings.

### “There shall be one measure for all the coverings,” etc.

There shall be one measure for all the coverings, because there is one faith in which the whole Church is saved, and one and the same life toward which it hastens eternally. Hence those who entered the Lord’s vineyard to work at different times are all rewarded with the same denarius.

The division of the coverings into five and six may be understood according to what we explained above concerning the curtains divided into groups of five, because the coverings signify the teachers of both Testaments.

The five coverings may aptly be compared with the ancient teachers of God’s people, either because they preached only the sacraments of the Mosaic Law, although they also proclaimed the mysteries of evangelical truth, or because they lived during the five ages of the world.

In the six coverings, the teachers of the New Testament may suitably be understood, because they take up spiritually, for the aid and example of their preaching, all that divine Scripture reports as done or said during the six ages of the world. They openly proclaim to their hearers that the Lord’s Passion, by which the world was redeemed on the sixth day of the week, must be believed and confessed, and they testify that people can be saved only through this sacrament.

Therefore it is rightly commanded that the sixth covering be doubled at the front of the roof, on account of the confession and imitation of the Lord’s Passion. For it is not enough for believers merely to be baptized and consecrated in the confession of the Lord’s death and resurrection, unless each baptized person also strives, insofar as he is able, to be conformed to the likeness of the Lord’s death by living continually and suffering for Him, so that he may deserve to share in His resurrection.

According to the letter, the front of the roof signifies the entrance of the tabernacle. There, as we briefly said above, boards were not placed, but columns and a bar extending from the corner of the boards to the opposite corner were prescribed. Therefore, as regards the structure itself, a doubled protection of coverings was more necessary there, where the solid strength of a wall was absent.

Mystically, however, the sixth covering is doubled at the front of the roof when all who enter the holy Church are initiated into the faith and sacraments of the Lord’s Passion in such a way that they understand that they must always live in imitation of it as well. The sixth covering is doubled for us, as it were, at the entrance of the sanctuary when we are consecrated through the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion and instructed by His examples.

Concerning reception of the sacraments, Peter says: “According to his great mercy, he has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (I Peter I). Concerning imitation of sufferings, he says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought” (I Peter IV).

### “You shall make fifty loops on the edge of one covering,” etc.

Here too, what we explained above concerning the curtains may be understood: namely, that remembrance of heavenly rest, which is customarily expressed by the number fifty, unites the hearts of the saints in the bond of peace.

Or, if you would like to hear something new, since the coverings signify the humility of exalted men—because they prefer to remember their sins rather than proclaim their virtues, and strive to be more deeply pierced by the virtues they have not yet attained than to glory in those they have already attained—their humble compunction itself may be signified by the number fifty of the loops or clasps.

For the fiftieth psalm is the psalm of penitence. This is fitting, because the gift of repentance is granted only by the Holy Spirit’s generosity, and the gift of forgiveness is bestowed on penitents only through the same grace of the Holy Spirit.

The fifty loops or clasps also rightly join the coverings to one another, because no virtue binds the faithful more firmly into one bond of charity than humility. The more each person recognizes that he is weak, the more diligently he seeks the help of his neighbor by which he may be strengthened.

The clasps are appropriately made of bronze, because bronze is known to be a highly resonant metal; for the humble conscience of the righteous has a great voice before God. Hence the poor David, when he was distressed, did not cry out in the ears of men but poured out his prayer in the Lord’s presence: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Psalm CI).

### “Whatever remains of the coverings prepared for the roof,” etc.

To understand this more fully, it is necessary to discuss at somewhat greater length the entire arrangement of the tabernacle itself.

We said that the walls of the tabernacle, which consisted of boards and columns, were thirty cubits long, ten cubits wide, and likewise ten cubits high. If, then, someone wished to encircle the house across its width with a cord—for example, from the base of one board on the southern side to the base of the board directly opposite it on the northern side—that cord would clearly need to be thirty cubits long: ten cubits rising along the southern wall, another ten spanning the space between the walls, and a third ten descending along the northern wall.

Likewise, if you wished to extend a cord along the length of the house—from the bases of the columns upward, along the entire length of the house to the western wall, and then downward to its bases—that cord would be fifty cubits long: ten cubits rising beside the columns, thirty cubits spanning the length of the house, and ten cubits descending beside the boards of the western wall.

Having considered this, examine the measurements of the curtains with which the house was to be covered, and see how they correspond to the measurements just given. There were ten curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide. Joined together and assembled as one, they filled the tabernacle across its width to forty cubits.

Suspend these curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long, and place them over the house whose transverse measurement is thirty cubits. You will see that, in the span between the walls, the curtains have ten cubits; in the ascent or descent beside the walls, they have nine cubits. Thus the top of the curtains cannot reach the ground but remains one cubit above it.

You will likewise see that, along the length of the house, the curtains have thirty cubits in the span; in the ascent or descent on the eastern and western sides of the house, they have five cubits. Therefore the side edge of the curtains likewise does not reach the ground but remains five cubits above it.

It consequently becomes necessary that those five cubits of the curtains which remain beyond the walls be brought together on both the eastern and western sides and joined to one another, so that the curtains cover the house on every side except for one cubit above the ground.

So much for the curtains. The coverings, however, were thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. Since eleven of them were joined together along their sides, they filled forty-four cubits.

Place these over the house as well. Since the length of the coverings corresponds to the cord with which you measured the house across its width, their upper edge reaches all the way to the ground. They have ten cubits spanning the space between the walls and likewise ten cubits of ascent or descent on each side.

This is what Scripture means when it says that “a cubit shall hang on one side and another on the other,” the excess in the length of the coverings protecting both sides of the tabernacle. For it properly calls the tabernacle the very construction or joining of the curtains, which the coverings exceeded by one cubit on the southern side of the house and by another on the northern side. Thus they reached the ground, because the coverings had thirty cubits of length whereas the curtains had two fewer.

Likewise, along the length of the house the coverings extended forty-four cubits: thirty cubits in the span from the front of the house to the top of the boards on the western side, and seven cubits hanging down at the front of the house and likewise seven cubits hanging down on the western side.

Thus, on the western side, the measurement of the coverings exceeded that of the curtains by two cubits. For, as we also mentioned above, the curtains coming from above covered five cubits of that western wall and left three untouched.

This is what is now meant: “Whatever remains of the coverings prepared for the roof”—that is, one covering, which, beyond half of it, you shall spread over the rear of the tabernacle.

Half of a covering is two cubits in width. With this half, then, the rear of the tabernacle was covered—that is, the curtains properly called the tabernacle—because, as we have said, the final covering extended two cubits below them.

The coverings coming from above covered only seven cubits of the western wall. Yet the remaining three cubits did not lie exposed to the violence of the weather, naked all the way to the ground. Rather, when the seven-cubit coverings that remained beyond the walls were brought together from both sides, the rear of the house was firmly covered with them all the way to the ground.

Nor could these coverings merely reach one another and touch in the middle of the wall like the curtains. Since they were seven cubits long, they exceeded the middle of the wall by two cubits on each side; laid one over the other, they were joined together. We think that the same is to be understood in every respect concerning the eastern side of the house. Hence the instruction given above that the sixth covering be doubled at the front of the roof.

We have briefly explained this very difficult matter as we have seemed to understand it, ready to learn better things concerning it if anyone should wish to teach us. Yet throughout all these matters the meaning of the allegory is perfectly clear.

The coverings protected the curtains above, below, and on every side. Thus, while the curtains shone within with the unhindered beauty of their appearance, the coverings outside made them immune to every assault of storms, rains, and burning heat. For in the same way the perfect leaders of the holy Church habitually watch over the life of the faithful entrusted to them with diligent care, so that they may lack neither bodily support nor the aids of spiritual life.

Let the teachings of heretics and the evil examples of false Catholics be absent. Let saving doctrine be present, so that, strengthened by it, the faithful may wisely repel the words of those who teach evil and patiently endure the deeds of those who inflict evil. Let the leaders’ own heavenly life be present, so that, confirmed by it, the faithful may use it as a living lesson even when the tongue is silent.

The coverings repel the rains, withstand the storms, ward off the sun’s heat, and strongly drive away everything hostile from outside, so that the beauty of the curtains within may remain undefiled. Thus Augustine empties the poisons of the heretics that could disturb the faith; Gregory explains the temptations of the ancient enemy that attack good morals; Cyprian strengthens the weak with pious exhortations so that they do not fall in martyrdom; and other venerable bishops and teachers drive far away whatever could disturb the Church and diligently seek whatever may contribute to the salvation of the faithful.

In this way, the religious life of the faithful, made secure on every side, can devote itself with a free heart to the virtues, shine brightly in deed before its Creator, and direct the eye of the mind toward contemplation of Him.

But since among the holy preachers those are worthy of the greatest honor who, besides serving in the office of preaching and governing the peoples, also pour out their blood for Christ, it is rightly added:

## Chapter IV. The Third and Fourth Coverings of Skins

### “You shall make another covering for the roof from the skins of rams,” etc.

The word “rams” is sometimes used to signify holy teachers, because they are leaders of the flocks that follow the Lord. Hence the Psalmist beautifully says: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm CXXVII).

This plainly means: Bring to the Lord, O angels of God, to whom the care of this office has been entrusted; bring to the Lord in the heavens the spirits of the faithful who, through imitation of the apostles’ life and faith, have deserved to become sons of the blessed apostles.

For this reason the sixth station of the people of God after their departure from Egypt is called Elim, that is, “of rams.” In it there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, so that both by its name and by its appearance it might bear the figure of the apostles and apostolic men.

The skins of rams are dyed red to cover the roof of the tabernacle when the apostles or apostolic men do not cease to devote themselves to the word of teaching even unto the suffering of martyrdom, so that they may protect their subjects more safely from the dangers of approaching temptations, while they themselves do not shrink from enduring persecution for righteousness’ sake even unto death.

The dyed skins of rams cover the Lord’s tabernacle and defend it from the violence of storms when holy preachers, by the example of their own suffering and patience, fortify the hearts of the weak so that they do not fail under the pressures of tribulation.

And because sacred virginity holds an eminent place among the chief members of Christ and the Church, appropriately, after the varied beauty of the curtains, after the protections of the saints made of haircloth, and after the reddened skins of rams, there is added still another covering:
. . . . Another covering of hyacinth-colored skins. For hyacinth is heavenly in color, while the skin of a dead animal is both a part and an indication of death. What, then, is expressed by hyacinth-colored skins except the virtue of those who, having thoroughly mortified all the enticements of carnal desire, in a certain sense lead a heavenly life on earth and, placed among human beings, imitate rather the purity of angels? They strive, while still held by mortal flesh, to anticipate what is promised to all the elect at the time of future immortality: that they neither marry nor give in marriage, but are like the angels of God (Matt. XXII).

Hence such great virtue rightly awaits so great a reward, for, as the prophet bears witness:

> Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be taken away (Isa. L).

Of this place and name, moreover, the evangelist John—who was one of them—reports that he heard them singing a new song before the throne of God (Rev. XIV), a song that no one else could sing. He immediately added:

> These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

The hyacinth-colored skins therefore rightly occupy the highest place in the house of God, and the heavenly color receives a seat nearest to heaven, so that the virgin choirs—who will follow the Lamb with a special nearness of both soul and body—may be designated as singing his praises in hymns.

It is rightly said of the curtains and coverings that, although placed high above, they hung down toward the earth, even though the curtains could by no means reach all the way to the ground. The columns and boards of the tabernacle likewise, although raised upright to a great height, had bases set upon the earth on which they stood. But of the red and hyacinth-colored skins it is said that they covered the roof above; that they were bent down toward the earth is not added. For plainly the other forms of virtue seem to share something with those who are still held on earth, whereas the contest of martyrdom and the glory of virginity dedicated to God, as though suspended above the lowest and earthly things, are shown to be specially joined to the citizens above.

For a martyr placed amid torments directs his whole mind toward nothing else than leaving behind as quickly as possible everything that exists in this world, and the world itself as well, so that, freed from all suffering, he may attain the vision of the Creator of the world and possess the joys that lie beyond the world. Likewise, celibates, while transcending for the sake of a greater reward the common law of the human race, concerning which it was said, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth,” rightly choose for themselves a seat higher than that of the other faithful—indeed, higher than the world itself. Thus they live in the Church in such a way that, by the honor of their greater merit, they surpass the Church’s common way of life.

Therefore John rightly writes concerning such people:

> These have been purchased from humanity as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb (Rev. XIV).

In Latin, such people are rightly called either virgins, as though distinguished by virtue, or celibates, as though blessed by heaven—that is, as imitating on earth the life of the citizens of heaven.

## CHAPTER V. The Boards of the Tabernacle

“You shall make the boards of the tabernacle standing upright,” etc. The acacia wood of which the tabernacle was made is naturally incorruptible, exceptionally white and light, and differs from white thorn only in its greater size. Hence Jerome, both in his *Book of Hebrew Names* and sometimes in his other works, interpreted *setim* simply as “thorns.” For example: *Abel setim*, “mourning of thorns.”

This type of wood, however, is not easily found except in the deserts of Arabia, where the tabernacle was built. Hence the Greek and Latin translators could not give it another name apart from the Hebrew, since they had no knowledge of it among themselves; although some, wishing to express its natural quality, translated it as “incorruptible wood.”

The boards of the tabernacle therefore signify the apostles and their successors, through whose preaching the Church has been expanded throughout the world. The breadth of the boards signifies the expansion of faith and of the sacraments, which had previously lain hidden within the single Israelite people but, through the ministry of these men, reached the fullness of the whole world.

The breadth of the boards may also properly be understood as the expansion of the hearts of the saints. Through this expansion they habitually kindle themselves to despise the world and to desire heavenly things, and through it they rejoice to love not only their friends in God but also their enemies for God’s sake.

Let us finally consider one of the boards of the tabernacle, namely the Apostle Paul, and see how he indicates that he has been expanded in both senses. Of inward breadth, that of the heart, he says:

> Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. I speak as to children: be enlarged yourselves also (II Cor. VI).

He also speaks of that breadth by which he used to contribute to the advancement of the tabernacle, that is, of the holy Church:

> So that from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum I have fully preached the Gospel of Christ (Rom. XV).

Boards of this kind were made from acacia wood, that is, from thorns. According to the Savior’s teaching, thorns are the cares of this age and its deceptive delights and pleasures (Matt. XIII; Mark IV). The pricks of sins may also appropriately be compared with thorns. Hence it is written:

> For thorns are produced in the hands of the drunkard (Prov. XXVI),

that is, sins in the deeds of the foolish.

Because holy preachers therefore strove both to cleanse themselves from the pricks of vices and to strip themselves of all the cares and pleasures of the world, so that with a free mind they might expand in the love of God and neighbor and travel far and wide to preach the word, it is rightly said that the boards of the tabernacle were made from thorn wood. They were indeed made from thorns, but from thorns that had completely shed all their prickly spines and shone only with whiteness.

All the saints, too, radiant with virtues, although conceived and born in sin through the first transgression, nevertheless share in that general condemnation by which God said to Adam after his sin:

> Your earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you (Gen. III).

But by the grace of God through Jesus Christ they have been stripped of the little spines of every sin and, through the worthy practice of virtue, fitted into the structure of his house.

Now each board was ten cubits in length, etc. The length of the boards is their height, which was ten cubits, because holy teachers strive toward perfection through observance of the Decalogue; because they labor in Christ’s vineyard for the reception of the denarius of the day; that is, they persist in the ministry of the word with the intention of restoring, by his gift, in themselves the image of their Creator and King, which they lost when Adam sinned, so that they may recover through right living the name that they had lost by sinning.

For the name and image of a king are customarily contained on a denarius. The fact also that the denarius received its name because it is completed by ten units aptly corresponds to the state of our future blessedness, which is perfected in true love of God and neighbor.

God is often represented by the number three because of the Trinity that he is; the human being is represented by the number seven, because the body consists of the four most familiar elements. The soul, that is, the substance of the inward human being, is customarily comprehended in Scripture by a threefold distinction. Hence we are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

The boards therefore rightly have a height of ten cubits, since the teachers and rulers of the holy Church serve God with the intention of deserving to see him—immortal and blessed in both soul and body—forever, and they strive to urge all their hearers toward this end of life, continually by word and deed, as though lifting them upward.

The boards themselves had a breadth of one and a half cubits. The full cubit that is present signifies the perfection of good works; the remaining half-cubit signifies the beginning of divine knowledge. For in this life the righteous can devote themselves perfectly to almsgiving, persist in prayer, discipline themselves by fasting, and engage in other such religious practices. But for the present we know God by faith, while we hope for full knowledge of him in the future, as God and our Lord Jesus Christ himself says:

> If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth (John VIII).

Again, he says to the Father:

> This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent (John XVII).

The Apostle likewise says:

> We know in part, and we prophesy in part.

Does he perhaps mean that we labor for Christ in part, persist in the word of preaching in part, and serve by good works in part (I Cor. XIII)?

The elect therefore possess in this life a full cubit of good works, but only part of the cubit of blessed recompense, insofar as they can taste in advance, through heavenly desires, the joys of the everlasting kingdom and the presence of their Creator. They will be blessed by the completion of this cubit when the saying is fulfilled that he promised to the whole company of the elect at the end:

> I will rescue him and glorify him; I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation (Ps. XC).

“On the sides of the board let two tenons be made,” etc. The tenons on the sides of the boards signify the virtue of humility in the minds of the righteous, by which they are joined to one another most firmly in fraternal love.

For when each of them, with a contrite and humbled heart, prepares within himself a receptacle for love of neighbor and offers himself to the brothers who are to love him as worthy of their devotion and affection, all the boards of the tabernacle are, as it were, joined to one another through the connection of the tenons.

When the tabernacle is erected and the framework of the boards has been properly arranged beforehand, the form of the tenons cannot be seen. Yet the firm stability of the unshaken wall shows with what strength they have united the boards to one another. For the humility of the hearts of the saints, by which they are bound together, cannot be seen outwardly by human beings; but what it accomplishes within is openly revealed by the most peaceful condition of the holy Church.

Through this remarkable dispensation of divine grace, we who have reached the ends of the ages love with sincere affection even those who were faithful at the beginning of the world. We receive them into the bosom of our love no less than those who now live with us, and we believe that we too are to be received by them through the embrace of charity.

The command that two tenons be made in each board, one on either side, can figuratively be understood in two ways. First, we are to preserve inviolate toward our brothers the rights of charity both in prosperity and in adversity, advancing, according to the Apostle’s example, with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left. Second, we are to hold in the arms of one and the same love both those who preceded us in Christ and those who followed us—both greater and lesser—while striving toward the heights of perfection.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER VI. The Position of the Boards of the Tabernacle

“There shall be twenty on the southern side,” etc. The length of the tabernacle is not expressly stated, but it is indicated by the fact that its walls were made from twenty boards, each of which is said to have had a breadth of one and a half cubits. Twenty cubits together with twenty half-cubits make a total of thirty cubits, which Josephus also writes was the length of the tabernacle.

The length of the tabernacle is rightly comprehended by this number, because there are three virtues on which the whole perfection of the holy Church principally rests—faith, hope, and charity. These are multiplied by ten so that the number thirty may be completed, when good works, contained in the Decalogue, are joined to the virtues of the mind. Thus no one should think that faith, hope, and love of God are sufficient for him without the execution of works.

The fact that the number of the boards is twenty also contains a mystery of the great perfection of the saints, for four times five makes twenty. Since the Mosaic Law is contained in five books, while the grace and truth of the New Testament are contained in the four volumes of the holy Gospels, the holy teachers are rightly expressed by the number twenty. For with wondrous agreement in truth they reveal the hidden things of the Law as disclosed and fulfilled in the Gospel, and they declare that the mysteries of the Gospel were prefigured in the Law.

As they teach that the Old Testament has been elucidated and proclaimed in the New with a broader meaning, and that the New Testament was foreshadowed in the Old and marked out beforehand through the manifold revelation of types, they demonstrate, as it were, in the breadth of their speech, that the number four has been multiplied by five and the number of the five boards by four.

The bases supporting the boards are the words and books of the Law and the prophets, by which the apostles and evangelists proved that what they wrote and preached was true and divine. Hence the statement so frequently repeated in the Gospel:

> Then what was spoken through the prophet was fulfilled (Matt. I),

and:

> All this took place so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled (Mark XIV).

The Apostle Peter also, bearing witness concerning the Lord, added:

> We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it (II Pet. I).

Two bases are rightly placed beneath each board, so that the agreement of prophetic testimony may be shown in everything the apostles said. Or, certainly, two bases are placed beneath each board at its two corners so that, with its corners well supported, the entire board may stand upright and without deviation. For the beginning and the end of all apostolic and evangelical preaching are found prefigured in the prophetic writings.

The entire life of the apostles and their successors, from the beginning of faith to the end of the present life, is shown to be inserted in the same mystical pages of the Old Testament. These bases were rightly made of silver, because of the brightness of the heavenly word:

> The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, etc. (Ps. XI).

“On the second side also there shall be twenty boards,” etc. The southern side of the tabernacle, which extended toward the south, signifies that ancient people of God who, having long since received the light of knowledge of the Law, used to burn with love for their Creator.

The second side, which extended toward the north, represents the multitude of the Gentiles, which had not ceased to lie inert in the darkness and cold of unbelief until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. Concerning their calling the Lord says beautifully through the prophet:

> I will say to the north, “Give,” and to the south, “Do not withhold.”

This plainly means: I will say to the people of the Gentiles, who have long been cold without faith, “Give from among your children those who may come together in faith in and love for my confession.” I will also say to the Israelite people, which was already enjoying the light of knowledge of me, “Do not prevent the Gentiles from being received into the portion of election.”

I will say to Cornelius and his household, “Receive the faith and baptism of Christ.” I will say to the Jews, “Do not compel believers from the Gentiles to be circumcised; for those consecrated in the baptismal font, faith and confession of the truth are sufficient for salvation.”

Both sides had boards of the same number, measurements, and construction, because one and the same faith, hope, and charity are preached to both peoples through the apostles. Both are called to the same promises of the heavenly kingdom, and from both they receive the Savior’s universal command:

> Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark XVI),

that is, both to the circumcised and to the uncircumcised. There also follows, without any distinction:

> Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.

“But on the western side there shall be six boards,” etc. Josephus (*Antiquities* III.7) writes that the tabernacle was ten cubits wide. He also writes that its boards were suspended four fingers above the ground. From this he seems to wish it understood that the bases of the boards themselves were made of that height.

He further speaks as follows about the chapter before us and about the bars of the boards:

> The rear wall was made of nine cubits by six boards, to which two other boards were joined, made of half a cubit, which they placed at the corners in the manner of the larger boards. Each board had golden rings, projecting through the outer faces and fixed in order as though by certain roots, facing one another around the circuit; through them gilded bars were inserted, each having a length of five cubits. They were placed at the joints of the boards, and the end of each bar entered into the end of another bar, as though in the form of a shell. Behind the walls placed lengthwise there was a single row extending through all the boards; by means of hooks, the sides of both walls were held together in the tenons made and inserted into one another. This was devised so carefully that the tabernacle would neither be moved by winds nor disturbed by any other cause, but would remain immovable in secure quiet.

This is Josephus’s account according to the literal text.

According to the allegorical meaning, however, the western side, which receives both walls into itself and completes the structure of the tabernacle, rightly signifies the completion of the entire holy universal Church, which is perfected with the end of this world. To it the faith and righteous activity of both peoples will persevere, reaching as far as the end, like the length of a double wall.

For it is not credible that, before the time of the Lord’s incarnation, there were ever no Gentiles who believed; nor is it credible that now, although the Jewish people have been gravely condemned for their faithlessness, there are none among them—however few—who, living as exiles among Christians, come daily to salvation by believing.

If anyone should dare to deny this, we may say what cannot in any way be denied: that the spiritual teachers and interpreters of both Testaments, who, according to the Lord’s word, bring forth from their treasure things new and old, will remain in the holy Church until the end of the age.

The tabernacle is appropriately completed on the western side, where the sun customarily closes the day and all the stars set, signifying either the death of each of the elect or the universal end of the entire world. The sun seems to set for the one who migrates from this temporal light, through the darkness of passing death, to the joys of eternal light and life.

The sun seems to set for the whole Church in the west so that, when the darkness has passed, it may rise more truly in the east. When the life of the present age has ended at the Lord’s coming, the true morning of the future age will immediately appear, and the true day of eternity will shine upon the righteous.

And because at that time the righteous will reign with the Lord while the reprobate perish forever, it is rightly said below concerning this side of the tabernacle that it faced the sea.

It signifies the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh was drowned with his army and from which Israel was saved by the Lord and went up to Mount Sinai, where he would make the tabernacle. The western side of the tabernacle therefore faces the sea when the holy Church, crowned after the perfection of its works, will behold with free gaze in Christ the vices and punishments of the ungodly, which, with his help, it avoided.

Isaiah bears witness to this, saying:

> For as the new heavens and the new earth that I am making shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name stand.

A little later:

> They shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished (Isa. LXVI).

The deep, bitter, and turbulent waves of the sea may signify the sins in which the reprobate delight wickedly in this life and perish, as well as the future abyss of perdition, when at the final judgment they will be cast into eternal fire with the devil.

Nor should it be passed over that, when the tabernacle was built on Mount Sinai, the Red Sea lay to the west; but when Israel had been led by Jesus into the promised land and settled at Shiloh, the same quarter of the heavens had the Great Sea.

We may understand this mystically as follows: the saints who serve the Lord in this life and make a tabernacle for him in their hearts despise with steadfast mind the proud boasting of the ungodly, as something soon to set. In the future homeland, placed with the Lord, they will behold their perpetual punishment without any interruption of their own happiness, so that they may give him greater thanks because they not only enjoy the good things he bestowed but also behold the evils from which he delivered them.

The western side of the tabernacle, or the side said to face the sea, rightly consisted of six boards. This is either because the number six commonly expresses the perfection of good works—for the Lord completed the adornment of the world on the sixth day, created humanity at the beginning on the sixth day, and restored the human race through his passion on the sixth day—or because there are six ages of this world, in which we must be perfected through good works so that we may attain eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection in the future.

The command that two other boards, apart from the first six, be erected at the corners behind the tabernacle, receiving the wall coming from the eastern side and joining it to the wall of the western side, pertains to the recompense of the future life, which is secure after the labors and ages of this world.

This recompense is divided in two ways: into the Sabbath-rest, that is, the rest of holy souls after the dissolution of their bodies, and into the glory of the resurrection, the reception of incorruptible bodies. Both portions of the recompense are common to both peoples and will never be ended by any limit.

The rest of souls, when the time of the resurrection arrives, receives no diminution but rather increase, and the very union of immortality, by which our flesh and spirit are joined, remains forever inviolate in heaven.

It is rightly added concerning these same boards:

“And they shall be joined together from below to above,” etc. For the entire life of the elect, through one and the same faith and charity, tends toward heavenly things and reaches one and the same end, the vision of God. The speech of all holy preachers agrees in one and the same voice of sound doctrine.

The framework of the boards would gape apart from one another if one prophet or apostle said something that another denied. But because the harmonious speech of the divine utterances raises up the structure of the Church, one joint surely binds together all the boards of the tabernacle and does not allow them to be separated from one another.

“And in the two boards there shall be a similar joint,” etc. The corner boards are joined in every respect to the boards of the walls. This signifies that the future rest and glory of immortality are most firmly connected to our present way of life through faith, hope, and charity.

Indeed, our present way of life remains stable and unshaken for this very reason: it believes, hopes for, and loves the gifts of future recompense. It is continually upheld by the help of the citizens above, lest it fall through the turbulent blasts of unclean spirits.

These boards, which signify either the perfection of our good action or the future rewards for good deeds, are each supported by two bases, because the holy prophets likewise foretold with harmonious voice that all these things would come to pass for the confirmation of evangelical and apostolic preaching.

## CHAPTER VII. The Bars and Rings of the Boards of the Tabernacle

“You shall make bars of acacia wood,” etc. The five bars that hold together the boards of the tabernacle are the five books of the Mosaic Law. Through their protection the holy Church is wonderfully guarded against every assault of tempting sins and of wicked spirits.

This applies to both sides, because the letter of the Law not only instructed the former people of God in faith and good works, but also instructs us, who serve God in the time of the New Testament, when the same letter is understood spiritually, in faith and the practice of virtue through the greater sweetness of grace in the present, and kindles us in hope of eternal recompense in the future.

Bars of the same number are also on the western side, because the Law, rightly understood, likewise proclaims the completion of good works, when we depart from the flesh for future rewards.

Hence, when a rich man asked, saying, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to have eternal life?” the same good Teacher replied:

> If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments (Matt. XIX).

And he gave him no commandments other than those of the Law.

“You shall also overlay the boards with gold,” etc. The boards of the tabernacle shine brilliantly when the whole life and every word of the holy preachers display beforehand the light of heavenly wisdom, and nothing other than the splendor of virtues is seen in them.

The golden rings through which the bars held the boards together signify the blessedness of heavenly life. Because of the glory of its brightness it is rightly compared with gold; because of its eternity, rightly with a circle.

Hence the Apostle says of it:

> A crown of righteousness has been laid up for me (II Tim. IV).

Each board had five circles—not because the heavenly homeland is divided into five parts, but because the same perpetual brightness and bright perpetuity of that kingdom are contained in Genesis, the same in Exodus, the same in Leviticus, the same in the Book of Numbers, and the same in Deuteronomy.

Five golden rings were fixed into each board of the tabernacle because the hearts of the righteous, greatly expanded through love, read in all the books of the Mosaic Law not only the correction of their deeds but also the light of everlasting heavenly recompense.

“And you shall cast for them golden rings,” etc. The bars hold the boards together through the golden rings when the words of sacred Scripture, through the promise of the heavenly kingdom, confirm the stability of the holy Church, so that the less it fears the disturbances of the world, the more certainly it has learned the stability of eternal recompense.

It is rightly added concerning these same bars:

“Whom you shall cover with golden plates.” The bars are covered with golden plates when the superior understanding—shining with evangelical clarity—is shown to be present within the words of the divine Law, which according to the letter seem strong and most suitable for confirming the life of the faithful.

To give one example: when we read the history of holy Noah, how he was wonderfully preserved with his own in the ark and escaped the flood that destroyed the ungodly, it is clear to everyone that God, who loves righteousness and hates iniquity, knows how to rescue the godly from temptation and to punish the ungodly with just severity.

Such a reading therefore holds together the Lord’s tabernacle like incorruptible bars, because it fortifies the minds of the faithful beforehand with words of unfailing truth against the assault of temptations (I Pet. III).

The wooden bars are, as it were, clothed with golden plates when this same reading is shown, through spiritual understanding, to be filled with more sacred mysteries: when the ark is recognized as signifying the catholic Church, the water of the flood baptism, and the clean and unclean animals the spiritual and carnal people in the Church.

The smoothed and pitch-coated wood of the ark signifies teachers strengthened by the grace of faith. The raven that went out from the ark and did not return signifies those who fall into apostasy after baptism. The olive branch brought into the ark by the dove signifies those who were baptized outside, that is, among heretics, but who, because they possess the richness of chastity, deserve through the grace of the Holy Spirit to be brought into catholic unity.

The dove that went out from the ark and did not return again signifies those who, freed from the flesh, fly into the free light of the heavenly homeland and will never again return to the labors of earthly exile.

The bars of acacia wood are therefore surrounded with gold when the most steadfast testimonies of sacred Scripture, through mystical interpretation, prove themselves resplendent with these and similar heavenly and spiritual meanings.

“And you shall erect the tabernacle according to the pattern,” etc. The pattern of Moses’ tabernacle was shown on the mountain because, dwelling in secrecy with the Lord, he saw the sublime life of angelic purity and immortality. According to its likeness, he was commanded to establish human conduct on earth insofar as mortals were able to imitate it, so that, following their example, while on earth we devoted ourselves to mutual love for God, divine praise, unanimous peace, sincere chastity, and other virtues of this kind, we might deserve to become their companions in heaven, according to the Lord’s promise:

> Those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore; they are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection (Matt. XXII).

Moses therefore showed us, through legal precepts, the example of the angelic way of life that he saw on the mountain of contemplation. Through observance of these precepts, we too, though raised from the earth, may attain fellowship with the angels in heaven.

In the figure of the tabernacle and of the priestly and Levitical ministry that he describes, he likewise offered us an example of the more perfect life and of blessed recompense.

The tabernacle is erected according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain when each of the elect orders his work and disposition according to the imitation of the angelic purity that Moses was privileged to contemplate in secret.

Thus far, as the Lord granted, the southern, northern, and western walls of the temple have been explained. In what follows, the eastern side also is shown to have been arranged. But first Scripture judged that it should speak of the middle wall, which divided the holy of holies from the former tabernacle.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Curtains and Columns of the Tabernacle, and the Mercy Seat above the Ark
“Make the veil of hyacinth, etc.” Josephus reports that this veil, by which the tabernacle was divided in the middle, was placed so that twenty cubits in length belonged to the first chamber and ten to the second. This is shown to correspond in every respect with the measurements of the temple later built by Solomon. Since that temple was sixty cubits long and twenty wide, it had one-third of its length—namely, twenty cubits—separated off for the inner chamber, that is, the Holy of Holies, so that the length and width of this inner chamber were equal. Thus the inner part of the tabernacle likewise had equal length and width, namely, ten cubits.

What this same veil expresses figuratively the Apostle clearly explains in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where he also expounds it allegorically. In the first tabernacle, priests continually entered, completing the rites of sacrifice; but in the second, only the high priest entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people.

This veil signifies heaven. The fact that priests entered the first tabernacle daily throughout the year with sacrifices expounds the condition of the present life. Here the saints serve the Lord without interruption and, as true priests of God and of his Christ, atone for the daily faults of their frailty—faults without which they cannot exist in this life—by the daily sacrifices of good works and the daily libations of their tears.

The high priest who entered the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of victims signifies the great High Priest to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). Once offered for our sins, he himself, both priest and victim, entered heaven itself through his own blood, “that he might now appear before the face of God for us.”

Since this same veil was woven with beautiful variety from hyacinth, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen, who would not see that, even according to the literal sense, it corresponds to the beauty of the heavenly vision? If you consider the splendor and flames of the stars, the many forms of the clouds, or the rainbow itself, drawing a thousand varied colors from the sun opposite it, do you not seem to see in heaven paintings of color far more numerous and beautiful than those woven into the tabernacle veil?

The four columns before which this veil was hung signify the heavenly powers of the ranks, distinguished by four outstanding virtues, about which we also spoke above: fortitude, temperance, prudence, and justice. These virtues are maintained by us in one way amid the labors and hardships of this life, and by angels and holy souls in another way in heaven. There, indeed, the present ruling [reading uncertain] appears to be subject to justice. And it belongs to altogether immortal justice to prefer or equate no good with God; to prudence, to cleave most firmly to God; to fortitude, to take delight in no harmful failing; and to temperance [the phrase is incomplete in the supplied text].

Here, however, justice is found in helping the wretched, prudence in guarding against ambushes, fortitude in enduring troubles, and temperance in restraining evil pleasures. None of these will exist there, where there will be absolutely no evil.

These columns are rightly made of acacia wood, either because angelic spirits were created incorruptible by nature and immortal, or because, created without sin, they always preserve inviolate the purity of their creation. Concerning them the text appropriately continues:

“They shall themselves be gilded, etc.”

The columns before which the veil was hung are gilded because the angelic virtues, placed within the veil of heaven, are clothed with the grace of supreme brightness. They have golden capitals because the mind by which they are governed is illumined by the presence of divine knowledge and vision. They also have silver bases because their entire nature rests, as upon a foundation, especially upon this: that they sing hymns of praise to their Creator and proclaim his will to their fellow citizens who are still pilgrims on earth, as though placed outside the veil.

Therefore, while still on earth, we customarily congratulate them in their praises and say, as if with an exhorting voice: “Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who do his will” (Psalm 102). In Scripture, gold often signifies the splendor of wisdom, while silver commonly signifies the brightness of words.

“The veil shall be inserted through rings, etc.”

Because they appear to have neither beginning nor end, circles are sometimes used in sacred Scripture as a figure of eternity. It is therefore appropriate that the veil, which represents heaven, is said to be suspended by rings: either because it was present in the eternal counsel of the Divinity when the world was created, in which the heavenly nature holds the first and highest place; or because the firmament of heaven was made in such a way that its structure will never be dissolved.

For when the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24), this must be understood of the ethereal heaven. Concerning it Jeremiah says: “The kite,” he says, “knows its season in heaven” (Jeremiah 8). That heaven will perish in the judgment by fire which, as is clear, was destroyed in the flood, as Peter testifies when he says: “The heavens existed formerly, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed, being flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been reserved by the same word for fire, for the day of judgment” (2 Peter 3).

Within this temple veil the ark of the covenant was placed, because the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who alone is conscious of the Father’s hidden mysteries, after his passion and resurrection from the dead ascended above the heavens of heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

By this veil the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies are divided, because the Church, which consists of holy angels and human beings, is partly still a pilgrim in the depths below and partly reigns above in the eternal homeland. While the veil of heaven continues to separate its citizens from one another, they remain divided.

“You shall place the mercy seat over the ark of the testimony, etc.”

It is appropriately said that the mercy seat was placed over the ark, because the mediator between God and human beings was specially given by God the Father to be the propitiation for our sins. Hence Paul also says: “Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who was raised—and who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.”

“And the table outside the veil, and opposite the table the lampstand, etc.”

The table and the lampstand of the tabernacle signify the temporal benefits of God, by which we are nourished and illumined in the present life, so that, strengthened and assisted by them while grace and merit increase, we may be able to enter heaven to eat the bread of angels and to see the true light of the world.

Both are outside the veil because in this life alone we need either the sacred Scriptures and teachers or the other mysteries of our redemption. In the age to come, when the Lord will announce the Father openly to us—that is, will openly show us the Father—and when, as John says, “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3), we will no longer need an external aid to salvation. Almighty God, dwelling inwardly in his chosen ones, will illumine them as the light of life and satisfy them as the bread of life, introducing them into the joy of his kingdom and exalting them in everlasting blessedness.

We said above that the southern side of the tabernacle signified the ancient people of God, who first received the light of divine knowledge and the fervor of divine love. The northern part of the same tabernacle, however, signified the Church gathered from the nations, which had remained longer in darkness and in the shadow of death.

Accordingly, by a proper distinction, the lampstand placed on the southern side can signify the grace given to the former people, while the table standing on the northern side can designate the benefits of God granted to us. The lampstand is rightly said to have been placed opposite the table because the Scripture of the Law and the Prophets looks in every respect toward the grace of the Gospel, bearing witness to it and indicating that through it the Scripture itself is to be revealed in the spiritual sense.

## Chapter IX. Description of the tent at the entrance of the tabernacle and of its columns

“And you shall make the tent at the entrance of the tabernacle, etc.”

After completing the account of the veil that divided the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies, he returns to explain the eastern side of the sanctuary. He had seemed to interrupt this subject for a time while describing its other sides, namely, the southern, northern, and western.

The tent at the entrance of the tabernacle, woven with a beautiful variety of colors, signifies the glory of the primitive Church, glorious with the diverse flowers of the virtues. Of this Luke writes: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was no division among them; nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own,” and so forth (Acts 4).

It contained hyacinth because they were accustomed to think of heavenly things and to lead a heavenly life on earth. It contained purple because they were prepared to die for Christ. It contained scarlet twice dyed because they burned with love of God and of their neighbor. It also contained twisted linen because they rejoiced in bodily continence and chastity.

“And you shall gild five columns of acacia wood, etc.”

The columns from which the tent was suspended signify the holy teachers, concerning whom Luke adds immediately afterward: “And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

The more robustly their minds are raised toward heavenly things, the more firmly they are able, by teaching, to lift others toward the love of heavenly things. The apostles and apostolic men can rightly be represented by the boards because of the breadth of their doctrine, by which, going into the whole world, they preach the Gospel to every creature; or because of the love which they extend not only to friends but even to enemies, whom they love and pursue with prayers and benefactions, though those enemies hate them.

Likewise, because of the unconquerable strength of their hearts and their constant intention raised toward heavenly things, they are fittingly represented by the name and form of columns, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were reputed to be columns” (Galatians 2).

These columns are rightly made five in number because of the five books of the Law, with which holy teachers had to fortify their preaching. This was especially necessary for those who established the primitive Church, gathered from the people of the Hebrews, which knew itself to be founded solely upon the authority of the Mosaic Law, since the evangelical and apostolic Scripture had not yet shone throughout the world.

The same columns are rightly commanded to be made of acacia wood but covered with gold, so that holy preachers may be understood to be inwardly sound and deficient in nothing through the strength of their hearts, while outwardly they must be conspicuous through the brightness of their works.

Or, alternatively, the columns of acacia wood are gilded when those same teachers teach that the strength of their actions must always be protected by divine assistance; when in everything they do they seek the glory of the Father who is in heaven; and when in all that they say they rejoice to make Christ resound, saying: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord” (2 Corinthians 5).

Concerning them the text appropriately continues:

“Their capitals shall be golden, and their bases bronze.”

The golden capitals signify him of whom the Apostle says: “All things hold together in him, and he is the head of the body of the Church; he is the beginning and the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1).

It should not seem inappropriate that through the five capitals of the columns one head, Christ, is represented. There were as many capitals as columns because the same Lord Christ is the head of all the saints. He remains in himself always equal and indivisible, yet he distributes the grace of his Spirit to each of the chosen according to the capacity of those who receive it.

Therefore, not only the whole Church generally, but also each of its members individually, may confidently proclaim the prophetic saying: “Now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Psalm 26).

It is fitting that the significance of this head is represented by the fact that the capitals of the columns are commanded to be made golden, not merely gilded like the columns and boards. For all the saints have been made participants in the Holy Spirit and heavenly grace, but he himself was full of grace and truth. As his forerunner said of him: “God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3).

The bronze bases are the prophets, by whose testimony the apostles’ preaching is confirmed. They are appropriately bronze either because of the unconquerable confidence of the prophetic mind, or because their word, even as the world grows old and passes away, can never be consumed by age. For the Lord did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them.

The columns of the tabernacle have bronze bases and golden capitals because the apostles and apostolic men are confirmed in faith by the words of the prophets and raised by their desire for heavenly things to behold the face of their Creator.

Again, they have golden capitals but bronze bases because they have learned that whatever they received through the Lord by heavenly authority had all previously been foretold as mysteries in prophetic speech.

Since we are speaking of the eastern side, it seems appropriate to recall something concerning the interpretation of that singular bar, which, as we have already said, extended from the corner of the boards to the corner of the opposite wall and held the entire structure of the walls together, so that it could not be shaken by the force and pressure of storms or bent this way and that.

It is written in the continuation of the sacred history, where Moses is said to have completed everything that the Lord had commanded.

## Chapter X. The bar that extended from corner to corner

(Exodus 36.) “And another bar, which passed through the middle of the boards, etc.”

This bar should therefore be understood to have extended from the top of the boards on one side to the top of the other side, across the ten-cubit width of the tabernacle. Its two ends were firmly set upon the boards, so that by this means the side of the tabernacle that consisted not of boards but of columns might remain no less fixed than the other sides, even when driven by the wind.

If you also wish to know the mystery of this bar, it figuratively and unambiguously proclaims our Redeemer himself. He reaches, as it were, from corner to corner because, from the Jewish people whom he first chose, he extended himself in mercy to save the multitude of the nations as well.

Therefore, just as in the Prophets he is rightly called the cornerstone, so in the Law the angular bar may likewise rightly be so called (Isaiah 28). He is the cornerstone because of the temple constructed for God from living stones; the angular bar because of the tabernacle built for him from incorruptible wood—that is, from the souls of the elect, free from the stain of corruption.

## Chapter XI. Description of the altar of burnt offering and its vessels

(Exodus 27.) “And you shall make an altar of acacia wood, etc.”

This altar, properly called the altar of burnt offering, signifies the hearts of the elect, which by his gift have been consecrated to offer sacrifices of good works to God. It is appropriately commanded to be made of acacia wood because the hearts and bodies in which the Spirit of God dwells ought to be pure and incorrupt.

It has five cubits in length and the same in width, since each faithful person strives to exercise all the senses of the body in the length of patience and the breadth of charity, so that in sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch he may always remember that he has been devoted to divine service, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God.”

It also has three cubits in height, since the same hearts of the elect reach toward heavenly things through faith, hope, and charity.

“But you shall make horns at its four corners, etc.”

The altar of burnt offering has four corners because the holy Church is spread throughout the four regions of the world. Since the whole multitude of believers is rightly represented as having one heart and one soul, it is also rightly represented by the form of one altar. From this altar four horns arise when the hearts of the righteous are fortified by the four virtues so often mentioned.

Concerning them it is said in praise of wisdom: “For it teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful in human life” (Wisdom 8).

These horns project from the altar itself when the faithful do not display the defenses of virtue merely outwardly and before human beings, but produce them from the innermost root of their hearts, with God as witness.

The horns are four at the four corners of the altar when, throughout all the boundaries of the world, the Church remains inviolable against every ambush of its enemies through the spiritual power of the virtues—indeed, it becomes stronger than all who attack it.

This altar is covered with bronze when the virtue begun by the faithful is steadfastly maintained to the end. Since bronze as a metal commonly endures incorrupt for a long time, it rightly signifies through this the virtue of perseverance.

If anyone is troubled, according to the literal sense, by the question of how the wood of the altar could remain unburned so near such a great fire, let him receive the answer of blessed Jerome concerning this matter. “The wood of the altar,” he says, “which is from the wood of paradise, is not consumed by the nearby fire but is made purer.” Nor is it surprising to believe this concerning the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, and the altar of incense, since even amianton, which is a kind of wood or resembles wood, is found to become cleaner the more it is burned.

“And you shall make for its use pots for receiving the ashes, etc.”

We should understand the various vessels of the altar either as the various persons of the faithful or, certainly, as the manifold actions and thoughts of the faithful, ordered for the service of their Creator.

First, they are commanded to make pots for receiving the ashes. That the ashes of the victims must be understood as a great mystery is attested by the ashes of the red heifer, which, as the Apostle testifies, sanctified those who had been defiled for the cleansing of the flesh (Hebrews 9). In this he understands the sacrament of the Lord’s passion to have been prefigured.

The ashes produced by burning signify the time and reception of Christ’s passion, which purifies and saves us forever. Thus the burning of the red heifer, which was kept for the cleansing of the unclean, signifies the mystery of that passion already completed, through which we are daily cleansed from our sins.

Since all the sacrifices and victims burned upon the altar figuratively proclaim either the Lord’s passion or the devotion of his saints, burning with the flame of charity, the ashes of the burnt offerings appropriately express either the completion of the Lord’s passion or, certainly, the perfection of the virtue of the righteous. They were wholly offered to God’s service through the fire of the Holy Spirit, and they were deemed worthy to bring their good works to completion and to be carried into eternal life to receive the rewards of their works.

To make this clearer, let us see what Moses says concerning the ashes of the burnt offering:

“This is the law of the burnt offering: it shall be burned upon the altar throughout the whole night until morning. The fire shall be from the same altar. The priest shall put on a tunic and linen undergarments. Then, taking up the ashes that the consuming fire has burned, and placing them beside the altar, he shall remove his former garments, put on others, and carry them outside the camp; and in a very clean place he shall cause them to be consumed even to the ashes. But the fire on the altar shall always burn” (Leviticus 6).

The burnt offering is therefore burned upon the altar when, in the heart of any elect person who has vowed himself wholly to God, both in flesh and in heart, a good work is performed with the fire of fervent charity.

It is burned throughout the whole night until morning when someone, throughout the entire period of this life and until he is snatched from the body and deemed worthy to see the morning of the age to come, does not cease to persist in good works.

“The fire shall be from the same altar” because we ought to burn only with the charity that the Lord grants to his Church through the Holy Spirit. Indeed, because the sons of Aaron wished to offer strange fire to the Lord rather than the fire once given from heaven, they were immediately destroyed by heavenly fire. For whoever performs heavenly works not with the intention of a heavenly reward but out of regard for temporal approval or advantage is struck by the sentence of heavenly wrath.

“The priest shall put on a tunic and linen undergarments.” The priest who offers the burnt offering is the Lord, because he himself customarily kindles in us the fire of his charity and through it makes the offerings of our good action acceptable to himself.

In doing this he is clothed in linen garments because, in order to stir us to works of virtue, he sets before us the examples of his incarnation, passion, and death, which, as has often been said, may be signified by linen.

The same priest takes up the ashes that the consuming fire has burned and places them beside the altar when the Lord brings an end to laborious works. He does not command the righteous, snatched from this life, to struggle further for eternal life, but commands them to receive the crown of righteousness in eternal life.

When he places the ashes beside the altar, he removes his former garments by recalling to the righteous the good things they have done and no longer showing them the garb of his passion as something to imitate. Instead, he puts on other garments, namely those of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself and make them recline” (Luke 12). That is, he will prepare himself for eternal recompense and cause them to rest in everlasting repose.

When, clothed in other garments, he carries the ashes outside the camp, the Lord, prepared to reward the labor of his elect, causes whatever good they have done to be seen as something removed from this present life and transferred to that life.

Nor is it without reason that the place outside the camp signifies entry into everlasting life, since the Lord also says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture” (John 10). The Psalmist likewise says: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit” (Psalm 120): entrance, namely, into this life of the Church; exit, into that place where the pastures of eternal fullness are found.

We therefore rightly understand the place outside the camp as that life, especially since it is said to be a very clean place, something that plainly cannot occur fully in this life. The very clean place outside the camp is therefore the soul of the righteous removed from this life and rejoicing in the other life.

In that place the ashes of the burnt offering are consumed even to the last embers when, where the reward of good works is bestowed, all labor is brought to complete fulfillment. This accords with the Apocalypse of Saint John, who, after speaking of the reward of the blessed, says: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them; they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21). Immediately afterward he adds concerning the abolition of all labors: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, neither mourning nor crying; neither will there be pain, because the former things have passed away” (ibid.).

Since, when the labor of good works has ceased, the charity through which they worked will itself never cease, but will burn more intensely when the one whom we love is seen forever, the text rightly continues: “But the fire on the altar shall always burn.”

A little later it says: “This is the perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar.” Once the burnt offering has been consumed even to the last embers, the fire will never fail from the altar, because, when every kind of labor has been perfectly consumed, charity alone will burn perpetually and never be extinguished.

We have spoken at greater length about the law of the burnt offering because of the altar pots that were commanded to be made for receiving the ashes of the victims.

The pots therefore receive holy ashes when the faithful, with devout minds, either carefully recall the examples and mysteries of the Lord’s passion for the preservation of their own souls, or diligently contemplate the departure of the righteous who preceded them. Those righteous, having labored for the Lord in great contests, now rejoice without end in the prize they have received, their course completed. By considering the virtues of their elders, the faithful too may become great, according to the Apostle’s command: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13).

After the pots, tongs, forks, and fire pans were commanded to be made. The tongs should be understood as having been made for tending the fire of the altar. Accordingly, they rightly signify holy preachers, who by their exhortations customarily kindle in us the fire of charity as upon God’s altar.

Like tongs with a double tooth, they arrange the logs on the altar for kindling this fire when they instruct us through the concordant pages of both Testaments and place in our hearts the words of truth by which we may be more greatly inflamed with desire for eternal things.

Or, alternatively, priests tend the fire of the altar with the tongs—that is, with a double instrument of iron—when holy preachers, in everything they teach, pour into us the power of the twofold charity and command us, through its grace, both to burn and to shine.

The forks, which in Greek are called *kreagrai*—that is, flesh-hooks—were kept for the service of the altar so that the flesh of the victims, cooked in cauldrons, could be brought out with them and carried for the nourishment of those who were to be refreshed by it.
