Their use likewise corresponds to the figure of holy preachers, whose ministry is to refresh the souls of the faithful with the word of faith and, according to the rule of apostolic discernment, to offer still inexperienced disciples the rational and guileless milk of simple teaching, while supplying the more mature with solid food of higher doctrine (1 Peter 2).

For all who know how to recognize the mysteries of Christ in summary and receive them for imitation are satisfied as though refreshed by the flesh of the saving victim (Hebrews 5).

Since it is the task of spiritual teachers to discern most carefully which mysteries should be entrusted for hearing to each person, Moses rightly commanded the priests to make forks with which they could arrange the flesh of the victims as appropriate, offering some portions to human beings, but only to the clean, for consumption, and leaving other portions to be consumed by the fires of the altar.

For in the words of God there are some things that he has deigned to reveal to our humility and grant for the nourishment of our feasting. There are also other things of such great depth that they are disclosed only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and entirely surpass the measure of our capacity.

Furthermore, the fire pans were assigned this purpose: by means of them the holy fire was to be carried from the altar of burnt offering to the altar of incense, morning and evening, for the offering of incense. These too plainly represent teachers, who carry fire from the altar of burnt offerings to the altar of incense when they teach their hearers to advance continually from virtue to virtue and, as their merits increase, to penetrate gradually into the higher and more inward mysteries of the divine vision.

All who, seeing the fervent piety of their neighbors, hasten to imitate it likewise become, as it were, fire pans, because they strive to kindle in their own minds the flame of the heavenly sacrifice that they see burning in their brothers.

All these vessels are made of bronze when the devotion of the faithful perseveringly strives to obey the divine commandments. Alternatively, this occurs when they proclaim clearly and diligently, by exhortation, that what they themselves rightly do must also be done by their neighbors. As has often been said, bronze can signify both the perseverance of the faithful because of its long-lasting incorruptibility and the clarity of the teachers’ voice because of the resonance of its sound.

## Chapter XII. Description of the grating of the altar of burnt offering, its rings, and its garments

“And you shall make a bronze grating like a net, etc.”

The whole altar was commanded to be made hollow, as is explained more clearly below. In its middle it had a grating extending throughout it, fashioned like a net, upon which the flesh of the victims to be burned was placed. Beneath it was a small hearth on which the fire burned among arranged pieces of wood, always ready to consume the burnt offerings placed above it.

There was an opening opposite the hearth in the eastern wall of the altar, through which wood could be introduced to feed the fire or coals and ashes removed. We saw this represented in a painting by the senator Cassiodorus, whom he himself mentions in his exposition of the Psalms. In that painting he also gave both altars—the altar of burnt offering and the altar of incense—four feet. We think he learned this, as well as the arrangement of the tabernacle and temple, from Jewish teachers.

The altar of God therefore has a grating in its middle, prepared to receive burnt offerings, because the elect prepare a place for the Lord in the innermost affection of their hearts, where they may place devout thoughts toward him.

It has a hearth beneath the grating to receive the wood and fire of the burnt offerings because those same hearts of the elect prepare within themselves a receptacle for hearing heavenly words. Warmed, indeed inflamed, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, they may offer to God the pleasing vows of devout thoughts.

The priest places wood upon the hearth of the altar when each teacher supplies the minds of the faithful, who desire and eagerly seek them, with testimonies from the holy Scriptures by which they may be more firmly established in faith and love.

He adds fire to the wood when he teaches that understanding of the word and the efficacy of devout action must be sought from God.

The wood burns upon the altar when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

The burnt offering placed upon this fire is consumed when everything we have resolved to do well is, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, made acceptable to God through the power of love.

The grating that bears the burnt offerings is therefore rightly commanded to be made like a net, so that through its many openings the fire placed beneath may freely penetrate to consume every part of the victims.

Thus it is altogether necessary that we not harden our hearts or close them, like the Pelagians, against the grace of God. Rather, we should diligently open them and, as though many gates had been opened at once, earnestly pray that in all the good things we begin or desire to do, as through each individual piece of the sacrificial victims, he may deign to illumine us by his mercy and kindle us with his own love.

The Pelagians, who presume that they can accomplish some good without the grace of God, do not place upon the sacred fire a grating like a net in the altar of their hearts, marked by openings; instead, they interpose something like a solid wall between themselves and the fire of the Holy Spirit, lest they ever be warmed by love.

The four bronze rings, which are commanded to be made at the four corners of the altar, signify the four books of the Gospels. They are appropriately compared with rings because they promise their hearers an everlasting crown of life.

They are appropriately bronze because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.” They are appropriately placed at the four corners of the altar so that they may strengthen the Church of the faithful, spread throughout all the regions of the world, with the word of faith and truth.

They are appropriately fixed beneath the hearth of the altar so that they may raise up the minds of the humble through the protection of their consolation.

“And you shall make two bars for the altar, of acacia wood, etc.”

The bars by which the altar was carried signify the teachers who customarily carry the holy Church, as it were, when they strengthen the faith and the mysteries of truth, either by preaching them to those who do not know them or by confirming them in those who already know and have received them.

Since they preach not themselves but the things that belong to Jesus Christ, they do not follow learned fables but make known to the world the power of our Lord, recognized through the heavenly oracle.

The bars are appropriately inserted into the rings so that they can carry the altar. To carry the Lord’s altar by means of bars through rings is for holy teachers, through the words of the Gospel—which will not pass away even when heaven and earth pass away—to raise and strengthen the hearts of the faithful by exhortation.

There are two bars so that the word may be preached to both peoples, namely, to the Jewish people and to the Gentiles.

The same point is established by the words that follow:

“They shall be on both sides of the altar, etc.”

There will be teachers who call the Jewish people, and teachers who call the Gentiles, with harmonious word and deed, to one and the same grace of faith.

Alternatively, the bars are on both sides of the altar for carrying it when holy preachers teach the minds of the faithful to maintain an unshaken constancy of virtue in prosperity and adversity alike, so that they do not become arrogant through the former or disturbed through fear of the latter.

“Not solid, but empty and hollow, etc.”

The altar was commanded to be made not solid but empty and hollow so that it might have ample space to receive either the sacred fire and the wood for the fire or the burnt offerings that were to be consumed by fire.

Following its example, if you wish to be an altar of God, empty yourself and cleanse yourself of every contagion of worldly things, so that the wood of heavenly words and the victims of virtue may have sufficient room within you.

Receive also the flame of the Holy Spirit, by which these same victims may be consecrated to the Lord and brought firmly to the goal of perfection.

To this the text appropriately adds in conclusion:

As you were shown on the mountain. For all that Moses indicated to us was to be made mystically in the construction of the altar and of the entire tabernacle, he had first seen fashioned by the heavenly citizens during that celestial communion in which he remained with the Lord for forty days, in tireless and perpetual observance. Nor should it be doubted that, before the throne of God, he was able to see that most holy altar which Isaiah was privileged to see, filled with the living coals of inward charity, and the holy tongs (Isa. VI); the same prophet saw these, and with one of them the angel had taken a coal from the altar, by which he might cleanse the prophet’s lips. By that same grace of the Spirit, by which the angels are inflamed continually to love God in heaven, human beings on earth are inflamed to love him; sins are forgiven and gifts of virtue are granted.

Therefore the altar is commanded to be made hollow and empty, just as it was shown to Moses on the mountain; for just as the angels and spirits of the righteous in heaven are empty of sins and full of piety and justice, so we also on earth, according to our measure, must turn away from evil and do good. We are taught to do this both by the heavenly exhortation expressed in clear words and by the mystical figures of the tabernacle, its vessels, and its ceremonies.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Court and the Vessels of the Tabernacle

> You shall also make the court of the tabernacle, etc.

Just as the Holy of Holies designates that part of the holy Church which is in heaven, and the former tabernacle figuratively announces the perfected life of the faithful who dwell only in this present age, so the court of the tabernacle, which was outside, represents the first beginnings of those who are starting out. Accordingly, the curtains of that court were rightly made of twisted linen, because the first concern that must be given to beginners is that they restrain both the enticements of the flesh and those of the spirit, according to what the Apostle added when speaking of the children of adoption: “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (II Cor. VII).

For linen, as has often been mentioned, grows green from the earth; but once pulled from the earth it is dried, beaten, boiled, and twisted, and by great and prolonged labor is brought from green to white. So also, if our flesh is to attain the beauty and excellence of chastity, it must necessarily be subdued by strict fasts, prayers, vigils, and the labors of every kind of abstinence. By these we can dry up its natural and seemingly innate pleasures and kindle it toward that excellence of virtue which we desire. The linen is twisted so that it cannot easily be undone, when not only the lust of the flesh is restrained but its entire memory is utterly uprooted from the inmost heart.

> One side shall be one hundred cubits in length, etc.

It is well established that the number one hundred, which in reckoning with the fingers is transferred from the left hand to the right, sometimes signifies in Scripture the heavenly life, which, like the right hand in relation to the left, is deservedly preferred to the present life. This number’s mystery is frequently found in sacred writings.

Noah completed the construction of the ark in the hundredth year, because the holy Church, which the Lord is building in this present life, he perfects in the future. Isaac, the son of promise, was born to Abraham when he was one hundred years old, because the blessing of the inheritance promised through his offspring to all the families of the earth will be bestowed in the future and heavenly homeland. He himself dwells as a foreigner for one hundred years in the land of promise, because we who become Abraham’s children through faith must lead a pilgrim life in the present Church, in hope of the inheritance above.

Isaac therefore sowed in Gerar, which is interpreted as “sojourning,” and in that same year found a hundredfold harvest, because whatever good the children of promise accomplish while journeying through this life, they receive as soon as they depart from the body in the heavenly life. In the same figure, the seed of the Gospel word that fell on good soil, when it sprang up, produced a hundredfold fruit. Whoever leaves temporal goods for Christ and for the Gospel receives a hundredfold in the present age and, in the age to come, eternal life: that is, now, in hope of the heavenly life, the joy of brotherly fellowship, and then, in reality, the life of the heavenly kingdom.

The side of the tabernacle therefore has one hundred cubits in length, because all who belong to the members of the Church must, for the eternal life in heaven, undertake within themselves the labor of patience and abstinence. The columns on which these curtains are hung aloft are the holy teachers, who draw the hearts of their hearers away from earthly defilements and raise them to desire heavenly things. They carefully stretch out what is like the Lord’s garment, so that no duplicity can exist in it, but so that, with a simple and pure intention before the Lord, it may shine like linen curtains.

These columns were bronze but were covered with silver, as is stated more clearly below. They were bronze because of perseverance in virtue or because of the sound of preaching itself. They were covered with silver because they resound with nothing other than the word of God. Its brightness is often represented by silver; and by their way of life they show in their actions nothing other than obedience to the divine words.

They were not merely silver-plated; their capitals too were entirely silver. This is characteristic of teachers: to submit themselves wholly to the words of sacred Scripture and to devote mind and body to them through meditation, preaching, and action. For just as our limbs cannot exist or live without the head, so those who consider the divine words to be their life never cease to bear them through obedience and to exalt themselves by humbling themselves.

What should we understand more appropriately in the bronze bases of the columns than the beginning of wisdom, the fear of God? Concerning this the son of Sirach says: “The root of wisdom is to fear God.” There he beautifully adds: “For her branches are long-lived,” because the many shoots of virtue which proceed from the bases through the fear of God, like the work and engraving of the columns, will never lack the fruit of their reward.

Why there were twenty columns on one side of the court has already been explained above, where boards of the same number were commanded to be made on one side of the tabernacle.

> Likewise, on the north side, along its length, there were curtains one hundred cubits long, etc.

The same things are repeated concerning the north side that had already been set forth concerning the south, because the heralds of both Testaments raise us with one harmonious voice to heavenly things. Although they had ceremonies of the sacraments differing according to the circumstances of the times, nevertheless, in the present age of the New Testament, all who attain salvation from either people possess not only the same faith, confession, and manner of life, but also the same sacraments for the cleansing of sins and the reception of heavenly life, in the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

> But in the breadth of the court, which faces westward, etc.

The breadth of the court facing the setting of the sun, where, when the day’s labor is finished, the sleep of night and grace succeed, rightly signifies that time when, after active life has ceased at death, the rest of the elect and eternal reward follow. Finally, those who worked in the vineyard of the supreme head of the household, when evening had come, received the rewards of their labor, because each of the righteous, when he reaches the end of this life, then obtains entry into the true life.

Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “I heard a voice from heaven saying: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Apoc. XIV). “From now on,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labors.”

For the sake of this rest, the western side of the court rightly had curtains fifty cubits long and ten columns. For the number fifty customarily signifies the fiftieth year in the Law, which was wholly consecrated to freedom and remission; for this reason it was also commanded to be called the jubilee (Lev. XXV). *Jobel* is interpreted as “releasing” or “changed.”

The number ten likewise clearly signifies the same heavenly rewards, where human nature, raised immortally in both its substances, rejoices in the presence of the divine vision. God is a Trinity. Our body subsists from four elements. Our inner person is comprehended by the number three, since we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. When our fourfold nature is joined eternally to the vision of the Holy Trinity, according to the Psalmist: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII), this is indeed the ten which the workers in the Lord’s vineyard receive as their reward when the day’s labors are completed: the reward signifying that human nature, in its fourfold bodily constitution, is united to the Trinity.

Since the holy preachers promise us that, when this life is ended, we shall have the presence of our Creator and eternal rest, they also raise our desires from the pursuit of earthly things to the seeking of heavenly things through these promises. They are like the ten columns raising and elevating the curtains on the western side of the court, which are fifty cubits long.

> In that breadth of the court which faces eastward, etc.

The breadth of the court that faces east signifies the beginning of our good way of life, which begins from faith. Because it is associated with the first reception of heavenly grace, it is rightly said to face east, according to the words of blessed Zechariah: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to shine upon those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke I).

In this region there will be fifty cubits, because at the very entrance into conversion all who are being catechized are taught to hope for the remission of sins and eternal rest. The number fifty also pertains to the remission of sins. Hence, in the psalm bearing that number, repentance, confession, and the remission of sins are described. The one who had sinned against the Lord and done evil before him, by recognizing his iniquity, was cleansed by the one against whom he had sinned and made whiter than snow; then he received again the joy of God’s salvation—that is, of the Lord Jesus, whom he had offended—and was strengthened by his guiding Spirit so that he might not fall again.

Thus the eastern breadth of the court has fifty cubits, when the first confession of faith rejoices in the remission of sins and in hope of future rest and peace in Christ. Finally, in the Apostles’ Creed we confess that we believe in the holy Church, the remission of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh. The universal synod of the Fathers that followed wished this to be expressed more fully, saying: “I confess one baptism for the remission of sins; I hope for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come.”

The eastern region’s fifty cubits therefore generally designate the beginnings of believers, who are celebrated in the remission of sins and the hope of future blessedness. Yet another particular distinction is immediately added, which, when carefully considered, refers to the same end. For it follows:

> In them, on one side, curtains of fifteen cubits shall be assigned, etc.

The number fifteen, composed of the numbers seven and eight, rightly signifies the joys of eternal life, which begin with the Sabbath-rest of souls and are completed in the resurrection of bodies. For the Lord rested in the tomb on the seventh day of the week and rose from the dead on the eighth, that is, after the seventh day.

The three columns with an equal number of bases on the side of fifteen cubits signify holy preachers who excel in faith, hope, and charity and establish their minds most firmly in the stability of the fear of God. As you enter the court of the tabernacle, you have on either side curtains of fifteen cubits suspended from three columns, because whoever intends to enter the holy Church and learn the sacraments of the faith—whether he turns his mind toward the Synagogue or toward the Church of the Gentiles—will find in either portion of the faithful teachers strong in faith, exalted in hope, fervent in charity, and founded in the fear of the Lord. They promise their hearers the rest of blessed souls and the resurrection of immortal bodies.

They suspend such hearers within themselves like curtains of twisted linen when, by their own example, they teach them to seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth, and to keep their spirit, soul, and body blameless until the day of the Lord.

> At the entrance of the court there shall be a curtain twenty cubits long, etc.

There are four columns at the entrance of the court, because no one can enter the unity of the holy Church except through faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, which are contained in four books. Hence a beautiful custom arose in the Church in ancient times: those who were to be catechized and initiated into the sacraments of the Christians were instructed by reciting the beginnings of the four Gospels and carefully taught, at the opening of their ears, about their figures and order. Thus they would know and remember which books, and how many, were those whose words were chiefly to instruct them in the faith of truth.

At this entrance a curtain twenty cubits long is also commanded to be made. This number is the number four multiplied by five. Our bodily senses are five in number: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

The curtain of twenty cubits is therefore rightly suspended at the entrance of the court upon four columns, because all who enter the holy Church must regulate both their faith and their actions according to the rule of the Gospels, so that, restraining themselves from carnal enticements, they may subject all the senses of their body to the divine commands.

This curtain is not only raised by four columns; in its length it also contains the number five multiplied by four, when humble and devout hearers, having found faith, are not merely imbued with the words of the Gospel but also desire to live the evangelical life themselves, and devote all the senses of their body to the obedience of charity.

This curtain at the entrance of the court is rightly made, unlike those in the rest of the court, not of twisted linen alone, but of four most noble colors—hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen—by the work of an embroiderer. The outward appearance of the Church shines beautifully for those who are being catechized, but its dignity and virtue appear much more splendid to those who are deemed worthy to enter it through the sacrament of baptism.

No one becomes supreme all at once; rather, we must necessarily advance step by step from lesser things to more perfect ones. We have often said that hyacinth signifies hope of heavenly goods, purple tolerance of temporal evils, twice-dyed scarlet the ardor of perfect love, and twisted linen the restraint of carnal pleasure.

These colors are varied among one another by the work of the embroiderer, when each virtue of the faithful shines more brightly through the fellowship of the virtues near it, as though through a kind of kinship. The individual colors mentioned may also correspond to individual persons among the elect. One who is privileged to contemplate heavenly things more deeply is hyacinth; another, because he suffers more for the sake of justice, is purple. The one who burns with a more fervent love of God and neighbor is twice-dyed scarlet. The one who is especially white with the integrity of virginal chastity is twisted linen.

When the righteous rejoice in one another’s virtues within one and the same faith and evangelical piety, they adorn the curtain at the entrance of the Lord’s court, woven with the beautiful diversity of its varied colors.

> All the columns of the court around it shall be clothed with silver plates, etc.

He repeats more carefully what he had said, so that he may diligently warn the reader that no one can be counted among the teachers of truth—the columns, namely, of the heavenly court—unless he has learned to possess, like bronze, unconquerable patience amid adversities; unless he has taken care to protect and adorn himself on every side, as with plates of silver, through the observance and proclamation of heavenly words; unless he has striven to place himself beneath the divine commands in complete submission, as beneath a silver capital; and unless he has stood in the fear of God like a bronze base.

> The court shall occupy one hundred cubits in length, etc.

The Church has one hundred cubits of length, because she raises her arms toward good works for the sake of eternal life. She has fifty cubits of breadth because she hopes for everlasting rest in the grace of the Holy Spirit, which he wished to signify by the number fifty when, by his coming, he deigned to consecrate Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day of the Paschal festival.

Its height shall be five cubits, according to the number of our bodily senses, because then each person will receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. In the court of the house of the Lord, however, only the figure of those who have done good in the body is expressed; for this they deserve to be brought into the rest of perpetual life. Now, in works of righteousness which they perform with chaste body and heart, they shine like twisted linen; then, in the same body raised to the glory of immortality, they rejoice forever after receiving the rewards of righteousness.

In the evangelical parable, however, mention is made of both groups together. Five virgins who had come to the bridegroom with works of light immediately enter the wedding with him; five others, who had practiced works of chastity without a chaste intention, are rejected with their darkness and cast far from the doors of the kingdom (Matt. XXV). There were five and five because both groups were judged according to what they had done in the flesh.

The entire length and breadth of the court therefore extends respectively to one hundred and fifty cubits. It has five cubits of height because those who possess the promise of rest and the heavenly homeland must cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit. They must not merely cleanse themselves from defilement but also perfect holiness in the fear of God, so that when the hour of the promised recompense appears, they may deserve to rejoice in the love of God not only in spirit but also in the flesh.

For this cleansing of both our substances—that is, of soul and flesh—in the fear of God, what had been said above is subsequently repeated so that it may be more carefully committed to memory:

> It shall be made of twisted linen and shall have bronze bases.

Then the text continues:

> All the vessels of the tabernacle for all its uses, etc.

The vessels of the tabernacle, prepared for all its uses and ceremonies, are the people of the Church who serve the Lord in differing merits and ranks. All these vessels are commanded to be made of bronze, as has often been said, as a figure of the mystery: if someone is struck by adversities, he must persevere to the end and not lose through negligence the salvation promised to him; or else he must not fear openly to confess the faith he has learned even when opposed by enemies, but must also remember diligently to sound forth to his friends the gifts he has received. Bronze is resonant and by nature long-lasting.

The pegs of the tabernacle or court were made so that, fixed into the tops of the columns, they projected outward; and ropes of the curtains or tents were placed upon them, by which the curtains were raised and suspended from the ground. Their construction and placement may aptly signify the tongue of teachers, which touches the hearts of hearers through preaching and, by touching them, raises them up.

For Scripture itself is sometimes represented by ropes. Thus it is written: “A threefold cord is not easily broken.” Scripture, which is customarily interpreted in the historical, allegorical, and moral senses, cannot be corrupted by any perversity of heretics or pagans.

The curtains or veils themselves, so that they could receive the ropes, necessarily had loops or rings at their upper edges, through which the same ropes could be inserted. You too, if you wish to become God’s curtain, prepare in your heart a receptacle for his words, by which you may be suspended toward heavenly things.

Let the ropes of the curtains be placed upon the pegs of the columns, so that, spread out and raised aloft, they may complete the beauty of the tabernacle. Let the holy preachers entrust the divine words to the hearts of the faithful and, through them, admonish them to rise from lowly things according to their example.

Let the spread-out veils or curtains, extended by ropes and raised up, display to everyone far and wide the wondrous beauty of their work, which, when folded, they could not show. Let the faithful display the breadth of good action, the beauty of mind, and the inward grace they had received by the Lord’s gift, so that those who see their good works may glorify the Father who is in heaven. Let them say: “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII).

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. The Description of the Offering of Oil for the Lamp

[Exod. XXVIII.]

> Command the children of Israel to bring you oil, etc.

After all the adornment of the tabernacle has been arranged, the light of the lamp is also provided, so that its admirable beauty may be illuminated by the light of the sun during the day and by the flames of lamps at night, lest any place of darkness or any hour of shadows ever creep into the house of God.

According to the mystical senses, the Lord declares in the Gospel what the light of the lamp signifies. After saying in a parable, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house,” he immediately added plainly: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works” (Matt. V).

The shining lamp in the house of God is therefore the works of the righteous, which illuminate the minds of those who look upon them through their examples.

But we must consider more carefully that, so that the lamp may always burn in God’s tabernacle, the children of Israel are commanded to offer oil, while Aaron and his sons are commanded to arrange the lamp itself. What, then, is this distinction—that the people offer oil in the house of the Lord to nourish the light, while the priests arrange the lamp? Unless perhaps this is commanded figuratively, so that the faithful and devout hearers may bring hearts ready for obedience to the faith, while the teachers, by preaching, minister to them the fire of the heavenly word, by which they may be illuminated to recognize God and inflamed to love him.

Through the richness of oil, by which weary and weakened limbs are refreshed and the grace of light is supplied, the inward love of the mind and the work of mercy are often signified. Hence the Psalmist says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God forever and ever” (Ps. LI). It is as though he plainly said: “Because I have shown the fruit of mercy to those in need, I too have hoped that the grace of mercy would be repaid to me by God forever.”

Therefore let the children of Israel offer oil, while Aaron and his sons, having brought the fire, arrange the lamp so that it may burn in the tabernacle of God. Let humble hearers offer the devotion of a devout mind, and let teachers, through their ministry of speech, teach them the secrets of heavenly knowledge. Thus properly instructed, they may burn before the sight of their Creator with the fire of charity and display to those outside the light of good action.

It should be noted that the children of Israel are not commanded indiscriminately to offer oil, but specifically oil from olive trees; and it is further added: “Pure, beaten in a mortar.” Oil is commonly made from nard, radish, nuts, wood, and other kinds of substances, but no oil may be offered to the tabernacle of God except what is made from olive wood. Likewise, no fire other than that which descended from heaven ought either to burn in the holy lamps or to be kindled on God’s altar: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

Let the children of Israel therefore offer oil for the lamp of God—not any kind of oil, but oil from olive wood, and that pure, beaten in a mortar. Let good hearers offer to spiritual teachers a pure conscience, fruitful in the grace of charity and cleansed by the pestle of diligent testing from every admixture of wickedness, rejoicing in the word of God once heard solely from the intention of pleasing and serving the Lord.

Let Aaron and his sons offer not alien fire but fire sent from above to kindle the lamp. Likewise, to complete the burnt offerings and make the incense fragrant, let teachers preach the word—not their own but the Lord’s—proclaiming confidently: “For we are not like so many, adulterating the word of God, but from sincerity, but from God, we speak before God in Christ” (I Cor. II).

They use this fire to illuminate the hearts of their hearers with the knowledge of faith; they use it to perfect and consecrate to God the burnt offerings of their good works; they use it to kindle the incense of holy prayers.

It is rightly said: “So that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony,” because there must never be lacking in the holy Church the light of preaching, nor the pure humility of hearers who willingly receive it and even diligently seek it.

It is rightly added: “Outside the veil that is spread over the testimony.” We do not need the lamp of the Scriptures within the veil of heaven, where the Lord’s ark is and the cherubim of glory overshadow the mercy seat—that is, where the ranks of the heavenly army proclaim with harmonious voice the glory of the incarnate Son of God, whom God appointed as a propitiation for our sins.

The text rightly continues: “And Aaron and his sons shall arrange it,” because it is not everyone’s task to preach the sacraments of faith among the people, but only those who are shown to belong to the sons of the supreme Priest, our Lord and Savior, both by the chastity of their faith and by the execution of good works.

But whoever has strayed from the purity of faith through a wicked doctrine, or has stained the integrity of the faith he has learned and maintained by the wickedness of his works, even if he seems to hold precedence under the name or appearance of a priest, will nevertheless hear from the Lord: “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth? Yet you hate discipline,” and what follows (Ps. XLIX).

James also withdraws such people from the placement of God’s lamp—that is, from the ministry of preaching—by a gracious exhortation, saying: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you assume a greater judgment” (Jas. III). This is the judgment that we earlier set forth, already announced in the voice of the Psalmist.

It is rightly added further: “And it shall shine before God until morning.” When the night of this age has passed and the morning of the future age has shone forth, of which the prophet says, “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see” (Ps. V), we will no longer need the lamp of books, when the true light of the world appears and illumines us. Of this the prophet also says: “But for you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV).

> Its observance shall be perpetual, etc.

This concluding clause, like the preceding statements about the tabernacle, its vessels, and its utensils, must be understood and explained more in a spiritual than in a carnal sense. For how could the observance of the priestly office have been perpetual in the literal sense, when the priesthood itself, the tabernacle in which it was exercised, and the people for whom it was exercised ceased long ago?

It is therefore clear that this word must be fulfilled in the holy Church, where, as teachers and hearers of truth succeed one another in order, there will never be lacking spiritual children of Israel to offer gifts of piety in the house of the Lord, nor sons of Aaron—that is, of our true Priest—to minister to them the light of the word, until, when the order of this age has been completed and the entire tabernacle of God—that is, the whole multitude of the elect—has likewise been transferred to the heavenly kingdom, human beings will no longer be taught by other human beings, since God will be all in all.

## CHAPTER II. The Priesthood of Aaron and His Sons

[Exod. XXVIII.]

> Bring Aaron your brother to yourself, etc.

After the construction of the tabernacle has been described, the priests who are to minister in it are consequently ordained. Their ordination and attire rightly correspond to the priests of the Church, so that everything which there shone outwardly, bright in the ornamentation of the garments, may be understood spiritually as rising inwardly in the minds of our priests and shining outwardly in their actions above the merits of the other faithful.

Accordingly, Moses is rightly commanded to bring Aaron his brother, together with his sons, from among the children of Israel, to perform the priesthood before the Lord. For all who are to be promoted to a higher rank in the holy Church must apply themselves to the law of God with greater mental diligence; that is, they must unite themselves more carefully than others to the observance of the divine commandments.

This is what it means for those who are to perform the priesthood to be brought by Moses from the midst of the children of Israel: the bishops and teachers of the holy Church must rise above the common life of the elect through the singular height of their minds and, by familiar examination, attend to what the law speaks generally to all the elect and what it speaks particularly to the few who are more perfect, so that by the higher excellence of their merits they may attain higher rewards.

For when Moses is commanded to ordain his brother and his sons to the priesthood, what else is mystically commended to us than that all who receive the office of teacher should cling to meditation on the divine law with such devotion and love that they may seem to be joined to it as though by a natural kinship?

Nor does the fact that Aaron’s first sons perished by heavenly fire after their ordination, when they offered alien fire before the Lord, fail to signify the misery of our own time. In it, some who have attained the place of priests and teachers—and this is grievous and deeply lamentable to say—prefer the fire of desire to the fire of heavenly love and are consumed by the fire of heavenly vengeance. Their perpetual damnation was prefigured by the temporal death of Aaron’s sons.

Yet, according to the more excellent figure of the mystery, just as the tabernacle with its ornaments and vessels designates the holy Church, distinguished by the most beautiful variety of virtues and faithful persons, so the high priest of that same tabernacle represents the true Pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered himself as an offering and sacrifice to God for us as a pleasing aroma.

He may rightly be called Moses’ brother. For who is more closely joined to another by a fraternal bond than Christ is to Moses, grace to the Law, and the New Testament to the Old? Moses himself bears such testimony concerning him, saying to the people whom he taught: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; you shall hear him.” A little later, speaking in the person of the Lord, he says: “I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth” (Deut. XVIII).

By his wondrous works, which no other person performed, he is rightly compared to Aaron, whose attire was distinguished by marvelous variety. Or certainly, Aaron’s many-colored garments designate the whole company of the elect, attached to Christ in the various distinctions of their persons and merits, as the Apostle testifies: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

When we understand the Lord and Savior to be figuratively indicated in the person of Aaron, whom else should we say is signified by the sons of Aaron, who themselves were also anointed to the priesthood, except the apostles of Christ, the successors of the apostles, and all the teachers of the faithful?

These matters can indeed be understood principally of the Lord. But it is more fitting for us to consider in them what pertains to the meaning of our devout life in the Lord and what relates to the correction of our conduct. The text continues:

## CHAPTER III. The Priesthood of Aaron and His Sons

> You shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, etc.

The holy garments of Aaron, which Moses made for him, are works of righteousness and holiness that Scripture commends to teachers of the sacred law as necessary, and whose examples it displays for imitation in those who preceded us in Christ.

The wise in heart, whom God filled with the spirit of prudence to make these garments, are the prophets and apostles, together with the other teachers of truth. They show us most plainly how priests ought to live and how ministers of the altar ought to teach, whether by the example of their conduct or by the word of exhortation.

Concerning them the Apostle says to Titus: “For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not irascible, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, continent, holding fast the faithful word that accords with the teaching” (Tit. I).

These, then, are the garments that they shall make, etc. How each of these items was made is explained more fully below. The breastpiece is a garment for the chest; the shoulderpiece is for the shoulders; the tunic and the closely fitted linen garment—that is, the shirt—cover the entire body; the turban adorns the head; and the belt fits both the tunic and the shoulderpiece more tightly to the body. To these six garments a seventh and an eighth are added below: namely, linen undergarments, to cover the flesh of shame, and a golden plate above the turban, which, bearing the inscription of the Lord’s name, rose higher than all the others.

He calls it a closely fitted linen garment because it clung to the body and was so tightly drawn, with close-fitting sleeves, that it had no wrinkle at all. It descended as far as the legs, and hence in Greek it was called *poderēs*—that is, “reaching to the feet.” The high priest was accustomed to put on these eight kinds of garments at the time of sacrifice. Of these, four were also granted to priests of the lesser order: namely, the undergarments, the closely fitted linen garment, the belt, and the turban. For it was fitting that the greater the rank by which someone was distinguished, the more he should shine with admirable acts of virtue.

All these things, however, are made of gold and precious colors, because nothing cheap or filthy ought to appear in a priest’s speech or work. Rather, everything he does, everything he says, and everything he thinks ought to be splendid before human beings and glorious in the sight of the inner Judge.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Shoulderpiece

“They shall make the shoulderpiece of gold,” etc. Since we customarily carry burdens on our shoulders, what is signified by the high priest’s shoulderpiece except the labors of good works, which he must continually bear before the Lord? And fittingly the command is given first concerning the making of the shoulderpiece, because whoever is to be promoted to the priesthood and the governance of God’s people ought first to have his works examined. Once what is outward and visible to everyone has appeared irreproachable, the integrity of his heart and the sincerity of his faith may appropriately be scrutinized as well.

Let us therefore understand the shoulderpiece that the high priest wore on his shoulders as the evangelical burden concerning which the Lord says: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11). Commending this more explicitly elsewhere, he said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Mark 8).

The same shoulderpiece is made of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen. It is made of gold so that, above all, the understanding of wisdom may shine forth principally in the priest’s attire. Violet, which gleams with an airy color, is added to it so that, through everything he penetrates by understanding, he may rise not toward lowly applause but toward love of heavenly things. Otherwise, while he heedlessly feeds on his own praises, he may be emptied even of his understanding of the truth.

Purple is mingled with gold and violet so that the priestly heart may both hope for the supreme things it preaches and, within itself, restrain the suggestions of vices, contradicting them as if by royal authority. Thus it may always contemplate the nobility of its inner rebirth and defend, by its conduct, the character of the heavenly kingdom. Although, as has often been said above, the purple color may also be understood as the outpouring of blood for Christ or the endurance of various afflictions. For this is the cross that we are commanded to bear daily as we follow the Lord. Hence such a color appropriately shines among the others on the priest’s shoulder, teaching him always to be ready to endure adversity.

Twice-dyed scarlet is added to the gold, violet, and purple so that, before the eyes of the inner Judge, all the good works of the virtues may be adorned by love; so that everything that glitters before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Judge by the flame of inward love. This love, by which he loves God and neighbor alike, shines forth as though from a double dye.

But when the mind is directed toward the commandments of love, it unquestionably remains for the flesh to be disciplined through abstinence. Hence twisted fine linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet. Fine linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance. And what is signified by fine linen except bodily chastity, glowing with the beauty of purity? This earth is joined to the beauty of the shoulderpiece, because chastity is led to the perfect radiance of purity when the flesh is wearied through abstinence.

Something similar may not improperly be said of the scarlet, which gleams like fire, because perhaps it was commanded to be twice-dyed for the reason that fire commonly possesses a twofold power: namely, burning and giving light. The bishop ought to imitate its nature in the word of saving doctrine, so that he may both open the light of knowledge to those who desire it and, by rebuking, burn away the rust of sins in those who despise it.

When he explains to his hearers the sweetest mysteries of the Scriptures, whether miracles or the Lord’s evangelical parables, he displays, as it were, the radiance of light in his garment. But when, because of the way of the proud, he strikes them by recalling eternal punishment, he shows those who look on him something like the terror of a devouring flame. For no one who speaks to the people ought to devote himself either solely to rebuking the guilt of the wicked or solely to unlocking the secrets of Scripture. If he speaks only about correcting sinners, he may perhaps be heard less willingly; if he reveals only the hidden things of the mysteries, he may perhaps be of less benefit to those whom he ought to correct. But when he balances his speech between both—opening to his hearers the sweetness of heavenly secrets and urging them toward correction of conduct, by which they may become participants in those secrets—the high priest displays in his garment the radiance of scarlet that has been twice dyed.

“It shall have two edges joined together on each side at the upper ends,” etc. Concerning this it is said later: “So he made the shoulderpiece of gold, violet, and purple.” And shortly afterward: “And two edges joined to one another on each side at the upper ends.” From this it seems likely that, with the garment folded, the edges of both parts were joined to one another on each side from top to bottom, so that half of the garment appeared outwardly to the eyes of observers, while the other half lay hidden inside; but the edges of both sides, joined together, descended toward the lower ends.

What else should we understand figuratively in this except that, when we display good works outwardly to our neighbors, we should preserve those same works inwardly whole before the Lord? Let neither the purity of a chaste thought ever be followed by a lesser perfection of pious action, nor the perfection that appears in an imperfect work be accompanied by an intention of mind that abandons it in part. Rather, the two edges of the shoulderpiece are joined to one another when everything good that we display outwardly we do inwardly with a pure and simple intention of pleasing God. This is to be so on both sides of the shoulderpiece, so that amid adversity and prosperity alike we may always serve our Creator with harmonious action and thought.

For the shorter edge abandons the broader one, and because their measure is discordant they cannot return to unity, if, when we are seen outwardly to do good for the sake of eternal recompense, we are inwardly entangled by the intention of pleasing human beings and seek human favor more than the rewards of invisible life.

“And the whole woven fabric and all the variety of the workmanship shall be of gold,” etc. The gold was not on one part of the shoulderpiece, violet on another, and still other colors elsewhere. Rather, all the colors were woven throughout together with the gold itself. For in priestly action no great virtue ought ever to be interrupted, even for an hour. The priest or teacher of the faithful must always be radiant with the gold of wisdom, always raised toward higher things by the violet of hope, always courageous against the battles of vice through the purple of the heavenly kingdom, always aflame with the twice-dyed scarlet of twofold love, and always shining with the twisted linen of disciplined flesh.

“You shall take two onyx stones and engrave,” etc. Aaron always carried the names of the patriarchs on his shoulders during the sacrifices, as well as on his breast, for three reasons: so that he himself might remember to imitate the faith and life of the patriarchs; so that he might remain mindful in prayers and sacrifices of the twelve tribes that had sprung from them; and so that the same people, seeing the names of their fathers written on the garment of their bishop, might carefully ensure that, by departing from their merits, they did not turn toward the contagion of error.

This is the force of the statement: “And you shall place on both sides of the shoulderpiece a memorial for the children of Israel.” Even now the high priest bears on the shoulderpiece the names and deeds of the patriarchs when every teacher or bishop of the Church considers, in all that he does, the deeds of the fathers who preceded him, strives to direct his life according to their imitation, and endeavors to bear the burden of evangelical perfection.

These names of the fathers were appropriately commanded to be engraved on precious stones. Precious stones are works of spiritual virtues. The priest has precious stones on his shoulders, with the names of the fathers inscribed upon them, when he himself has become admirable to all through the brilliance of good works and teaches that this same brilliance was not newly invented by him but handed down to him through the ancient authority of the fathers.

He bears this on his shoulders for a twofold reason: so that he himself may proceed humbly subject to the Lord’s commandments, and so that he may always place before his hearers heavenly examples—whether his own or those of the fathers—for them to follow. The same stones are also appropriately commanded to be enclosed and surrounded by gold. By gold, as was said above, either understanding or certainly love is signified, because just as gold excels other metals, so love excels the other virtues.

The stones are enclosed and surrounded by gold when the practice of the virtues is watched over on every side by such pure understanding that nothing vicious is permitted to lie hidden in them, and nothing filthy is allowed to remain. The virtues themselves are held together by the bond of love in such a way that, through no change of circumstances, can they fall from their state or, because of the priest’s sluggish mental vigilance, slip away from his character.

Well does it follow:

“And Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord,” etc. The priest bears the names of the fathers on both shoulders for their remembrance when, carefully considering the life of the saints who preceded him at every hour, he is always fortified by the adornment of the virtues in adversity and prosperity alike. Thus, in accordance with Paul’s words, “walking with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left,” when he strives only toward the things that lie ahead, he does not bend in any respect toward lowly love (2 Cor. 6).

“You shall make hooks of gold,” etc. The hooks he mentions were skillfully fastened at the upper corners of the shoulderpiece. The chains he adds, however, seem to have been attached not to the shoulderpiece itself but rather to the breastpiece, that is, to its upper corners, by means of golden rings. Thus, when the high priest was clothed, the chains hanging from the breastpiece could be fastened to the hooks of the shoulderpiece, so that the two garments might hold together firmly.

It is written more explicitly later: “They made on the breastpiece chains joined to one another, of pure gold, and two hooks and an equal number of golden rings. They placed the rings on both sides of the breastpiece, from which the two golden chains hung; these they inserted into the hooks that projected from the corners of the shoulderpiece.” Their significance will be treated more fully in the exposition of the breastpiece.

## CHAPTER V. On the Breastpiece

“You shall also make the breastpiece of judgment in embroidered work,” etc. By “embroidered work” he means workmanship of many kinds. Just as the perfection of works is expressed in the shoulderpiece, so in the breastpiece of judgment, by which the priest’s breast was covered and adorned at the same time, the chastity of his heart and thoughts is expressed.

And appropriately, after the shoulderpiece, the breastpiece of judgment follows, so that when someone has appeared innocent in his actions before human beings, he may strive all the more to stand pure in heart before the presence of the supreme Judge. He should take every care that whatever he does or judges outwardly with regard to his neighbors may shine forth as wholly tested by the rule of inner reason and pleasing to his Creator.

The priest is likewise commanded to carry the breastpiece of judgment on his chest because a ruler must always distinguish good from evil by careful examination and diligently consider what is appropriate, for whom, when, and in what manner.

The breastpiece was made double so that it might more easily bear the weight of the stones. But this doubling of the garment on the breast of the priest under the Law admonishes us that the reasoning of our examination should be approved by the invisible Judge within and should never rightly be despised by human estimation without. Or certainly we carry a double breastpiece of judgment on our chest when both the things that we speak or think concerning the faith of truth and invisible life rest upon sound reason, and the things that we visibly do or plan to do are likewise tested and found balanced by the judgment of just discernment.

The fact that it was a palm’s measure square indicates an indefatigable and perpetual striving of pious intention. For one who measures something by the palm stretches out his hand with the greatest effort, his fingers spread, so that he may grasp fully and without the hesitation of doubt the measure he seeks. Hence, just as action is expressed by the hand, so the unbending striving of good action is expressed by the palm, when each person endeavors to extend his right hand toward all the distinguished works of virtue within his power.

And appropriately the same breastpiece is commanded to have a palm’s measure both in length and in breadth. Whether the mind raises its desire lengthwise toward eternal life or inclines its affection breadthwise toward concern for its neighbor, the priestly heart must in every respect not remain sluggish or idle, but must always be extended with ardent zeal to grasp the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.

“You shall place in it four rows of stones,” etc. This arrangement of various gems in the breastpiece signifies the manifold practice of diverse virtues, which, arranged in harmonious order, ought always to appear in the priest’s heart.

Each stone is inscribed with one of the names of the fathers when the ruler, observing the life of the saints, diligently investigates the virtues in which each of them especially flourished. He strives to gather all these things by meditation in the hidden places of his breast and to bring them forth in action.

Nor was it without a definite sacramental meaning that both garments were so adorned with precious stones and marked with the names of the fathers: the names were inscribed on the shoulderpiece on two stones of one and the same kind, but on the breastpiece with twelve names on stones of different kinds.

The fact that the fathers were engraved on precious stones of one and undifferentiated kind clearly signifies that one faith in God, the same love, and a common hope of heavenly life filled the hearts of all the fathers. But the fact that those same names were inscribed on stones of different kinds figuratively declares that the variety and grace of good works are manifold, and that through these the aforementioned faith, hope, and love of the saints were confirmed and shine forth.

The fact that there were four rows in the breastpiece, each of which had three stones, what did it reveal to us figuratively except that, in the virtues distinguished into four, we should hold a principal and genuine faith in the Holy Trinity? The priest has four rows of gems on his breast when everything he thinks is circumspect through prudence, firm through fortitude, excellent through justice, and set apart from every evil through temperance.

Those same rows have three gems apiece when prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance have been consecrated by faith in the Holy Trinity. Since our life in the present consists in faith and right action, it is fitting that the priest, so as to be outstanding in action, carry four rows of gems on his breast. But so that he may be pure in his works through the sincerity of faith, he has three gems in each row, so that he may always display to all who look upon him both the confession of true faith and examples of good action. Thus they too may become, through imitation of right faith and action, worthy members of the supreme Priest.

We may reasonably understand in the varied beauty of the stones not only the manifold brilliance of priestly action and thought but also the spiritual gifts of virtues and miracles of healings. Concerning these the Lord himself says to the apostles: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matt. 10). And again: “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them” (Mark 16).

But whether the stones signify this, or that, or both, it is rightly commanded that the number in the breastpiece be twelve, so that we may know that the actions and miracles only of those who follow the unity of apostolic faith, teaching, and love are acceptable to God. Otherwise, if someone speaks in tongues, distributes all his possessions to the poor, and hands over his body to be burned, but does not possess the unity of Catholic love, it benefits him nothing (1 Cor. 13).

It is also appropriate that the two onyx stones on the shoulderpiece were engraved with the same twelve-numbered list of the fathers, so that they might signify that the teaching and faith of the apostles would benefit both peoples, namely the Jews and the nations. In accordance with this, the Lord plainly promised the same intellectual Jerusalem—that is, his Church—through the prophet, saying: “For you shall spread out to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations” (Isa. 54).

Since onyx is said to be red in color, having little sparks surrounded by white bands, who would not see that it signifies either the ardor of love or the light of knowledge accompanied by the surrounding band of chastity? The priest bears the names of the fathers inscribed on stones of this kind when, following the example of the righteous who preceded him, he devotes constant effort to love, chastity, humility, teaching, and the other works of virtue.

He bears this on both shoulders so that, whether someone is present from the Jews or from the nations, he may always behold in the teacher of truth and piety the brilliance by which he himself may advance toward better things.

“You shall make chains on the breastpiece,” etc. The order of the work, as it seems to us, was as follows. Two hooks were placed above on the two corners of the shoulderpiece, and opposite them were two rings above on the two corners of the breastpiece. From these hung two golden chains, which, when the high priest was putting on the garments, were inserted into the hooks projecting from the corners of the shoulderpiece, so that, as is written more explicitly later, the shoulderpiece and the breastpiece might be fastened together. The upper connection has been described thus far.

The lower connection now follows, which was beneath the armpits. Scripture continues in this way:

“You shall also make two golden rings,” etc. The statement, “and on the edges that are opposite the shoulderpiece,” does not mean on the edges of the shoulderpiece but on those edges that are opposite the shoulderpiece—that is, on the edges of the breastpiece, which are positioned opposite the shoulderpiece.

The rings that were on the outermost and lowest corners of the breastpiece had opposite them, on both sides of the shoulderpiece, other rings to which they were joined by binding ribbons. Concerning these the text adds:

“And also two other golden rings,” etc. He says, “opposite the face of the lower joining,” because he had spoken earlier of the upper joining, which was above the shoulder blades. There was this difference between the two joinings: the upper one was made with chains, whereas the lower one was made with binding ribbons. Hence it appropriately follows:

“And the breastpiece shall be fastened by its rings to the rings,” etc. It should not be thought, however, that the two garments ended at the same point. The breastpiece, which measured a palm in height as well as in breadth, was sufficient to cover only the breast, and not much more. The shoulderpiece, however, reached as far as the belt, as is shown most clearly later, where it is written: “These, in front and behind, were so joined together that the shoulderpiece and the breastpiece were fastened to one another, tightened to the belt and more firmly joined by rings, which a violet ribbon bound so that they would not hang loose and move away from one another.”

This has been said literally concerning the connection of the shoulderpiece and the breastpiece. But since, as has often been said, the shoulderpiece pertains to the completion of good works, while the breastpiece signifies purity of thoughts, the connection that joins these two to one another rightly figuratively declares that diligence of mind by which the understanding and faith of teachers of the faithful are joined with action.

The joining remains skillfully made, so that the breastpiece and shoulderpiece cannot be separated from one another, because the ruler excels in such great learning and such devoted attention to work that he leaves nothing unfinished of what he has recognized must be done, nor through negligence of heart deprives any of the right actions he is seen to perform of the virtue of uprightness.

The high priest’s garments flow down and move away from one another if either the beauty of good works is stained by lesser vigilance of heart or the integrity of pure thought is not followed by perfected action. But so that these things may not be dissolved from one another, the priest should have two chains of purest gold on the breastpiece—that is, a steadfast continuation of chaste and genuine love firmly attached to his heart—which never permits his hands and tongue to disagree with the justice of a pure understanding.

It is fitting that there are two, so that in matters belonging both to the worship of divine service and to assistance in fraternal need, he may proceed properly adorned. The work of love is plainly expressed by the golden chains, because just as a chain is woven into one from many rods of gold, so love is perfected through the manifold practice of the virtues.

Explaining these rods, the Apostle says: “Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or act wrongly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13).

He should also have golden rings from which the same chains hang: that is, a continual remembrance of the eternal and never-ending brilliance in the heavenly homeland, from which alone the remembrance is customarily formed whereby the bonds of glory can remain continuous for us.

He had two hooks projecting from the corners of the shoulderpiece, into which the chains were inserted. This means that, at the very beginning of every good action, he should have a firm intention of pleasing God, one suited in every respect to receive and retain within itself the love of God and neighbor. Thus, whether prosperity or adversity of any kind should arise, he never loosens the most salutary restraints of pious devotion.

This is what it means for the priest to have on both shoulders hooks that receive the chains of the breastpiece: in prosperity as well as in difficult circumstances, he should maintain a fixed desire to please God, and through the intention of this desire be established in love both of God himself and of his neighbor.

The hooks of the shoulderpiece therefore enter the golden chains that extend from the upper parts of the breastpiece when the eagerness to act well gladly embraces and receives what the mind rationally tastes from the inner light of love. Otherwise, the most beautiful character of the breastpiece might quickly slip from the priest’s breast if the hook of persevering good work, which holds it fast, did not grasp it.

As an aid, violet ribbons are also assigned to the same chains, by which the two garments of the priest may be joined to one another. These are the strongest bindings of heavenly desire, inserted into the golden rings, which draw the shoulderpiece together with the breastpiece. This occurs when, having recognized the light of the eternal homeland, we sigh for that ineffable glory, striving to serve the Lord in the tabernacle of the present Church with harmonious faith and life, work and confession, so that we may deserve to enter it.

The shoulderpiece was tightened by a belt, as is indicated more explicitly below where the high priest was clothed: “And he put the shoulderpiece on him, fastening it with the belt and fitting the breastpiece to it.” Who does not see that the most faithful guardian of good works is the virtue of self-restraint? Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12). Girded loins signify self-restraint; burning lamps signify the practice of the virtues.

“And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastpiece of judgment,” etc. The priest ought always to carry the memory of the fathers on his breast, but especially when he ascends to the altar to minister before the Lord. The more sacred the ministry, the more diligently he should purify himself through every effort and adorn himself with every care of mind and body, looking to the examples of the saints. As their attentive imitator, he should take care to present himself fit for the divine gaze.

Likewise, Aaron carries the names of the sons of Israel as a memorial on his breast before the Lord forever when every faithful bishop never ceases to care for those placed under his authority. Rather, by continually exhorting, rebuking, and consoling them, he strives to strengthen their life himself and to commend them, so that they may be strengthened and protected, to the Lord in frequent prayers.

“But you shall place on the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth,” etc. Doctrine and truth were therefore placed on the breastpiece of judgment, whether impressed in letters or imposed merely through the sacramental significance of the name, so that the high priest, clothed in the same garment, might remember that through the priesthood he had been consecrated to the study and investigation of doctrine and truth, not to the management and probing of worldly affairs. Thus what shone outwardly in symbolic form on the garment might shine inwardly in his heart as a genuine reality.

Doctrine and truth were also placed on the breastpiece so that it might be plainly signified that this garment did not clothe the high priest under the Law alone but also foretold the Gospel—either the Lord himself, concerning whom it is written, “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1), or certainly his apostles, indeed all heralds of that same grace and truth.

“And he shall bear the judgment of the sons of Israel on his breast,” etc. The priest bears the judgment of the sons of Israel on his breast in the sight of the Lord when he examines the cases of those under his authority solely with the intention of the inner Judge, allowing no human consideration to intrude upon what he administers in the place of God.

## CHAPTER VI. The Tunic of the Shoulderpiece

“You shall also make the tunic of the shoulderpiece entirely violet.” He calls it the tunic of the shoulderpiece because a considerable part of it was covered by the shoulderpiece, to distinguish it from the inner tunic, the linen garment. He mentioned both above, saying: “These are the garments that they shall make: the breastpiece and the shoulderpiece, the tunic and the closely fitted linen garment.”

The inner garment was linen, or made of fine linen, which is known to be the most excellent kind of linen. The outer tunic, however, was entirely violet, admitting no other color at all. Its appearance clearly teaches what the uniform life of the priest ought to be: that is, incessantly intent upon heavenly desires alone, having, according to the Apostle, his manner of life in heaven and eagerly awaiting from there the coming of his Savior (Phil. 3).

This tunic, like the linen one, reached down to the feet. Hence both were called in Greek *poderēs*, “reaching to the feet,” to show that nothing low or filthy should remain in the priestly life. Rather, everything he did ought to be most beautiful, as though in an ethereal color, and all his members from head to foot ought to be covered by the grace of the virtues.

Likewise, the priest is clothed in a wholly violet, foot-length tunic so that he may be reminded that the heavenly work must not merely be begun but persevered in until the end by all who wish to be saved. To be clothed in a violet tunic reaching to the feet is to devote oneself to good works until the end of life, as the Lord commands and promises: “Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2).

And because we reach the perfection of good action only through an indefatigable purpose, if we begin it with a fixed intention toward heavenly reward, the following is rightly added concerning the same tunic:

“In its middle above there shall be an opening for the head,” etc. The opening of the violet tunic has a very firm edge, woven from the tunic itself, so that it may not easily be torn. This occurs when the beginning of our good action, supported by the strong root of divine fear, is proven fortified against all the snares of the ancient enemy.

Such an edge clothes and adorns the priest’s neck all around when it gives the ruler the greatest confidence to speak to his subjects and preach heavenly things, because he has not only lived rightly in the course of his life but has also begun from the beginning with uprightness. This accords with the example of the blessed prophets Samuel, Jeremiah, and John, who were filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit from infancy and set apart for the order of teachers.

The voice is in the neck, and therefore the use of speaking rightly is appropriately expressed through the neck. When it was commanded that the edge of the opening for the head be woven all around, the text appropriately added at once: “As is customarily done at the edges of garments.” Just as garments can signify works, so the edges of garments may not improperly signify the completion of works.

Or certainly, the edges of garments are our final concerns, by which each of the faithful, when compelled to bring this life to an end, strives more earnestly than usual to cleanse himself from every stain of evil. With fear and trembling they take care lest, brought before the strict Judge, they be cast out because of the filthy garment of vices and hurled into eternal darkness. Rather, they seek to appear clothed—as God’s elect, holy and beloved—in compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, and above all these, in love, which is the bond of perfection. This is truly the wedding garment that our King and Judge delights to find at his banquet, that is, in the holy Church.

The priest’s violet tunic therefore has a woven edge at its opening for the head, as is customary at the edges of garments, when every distinguished teacher begins the work of the virtues at such a degree of perfection as another person, laboring for a very long time, scarcely reaches at some point. He walked with the Lord his God at every hour with as much fear and devotion, according to the prophet’s word (Mic. 6), as someone who is dying and about to enter the final judgment of his Lord can scarcely manage to possess.

But since the whole perfection of the priest consists in works and the teaching of truth, in accordance with what the blessed Luke says when, in writing the Gospel, he declares that he composed an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1), it rightly follows:

“Below, at the feet of that same tunic, all around,” etc. At the bottom, near the feet of the tunic, pomegranates and bells are made all around when the priest has reached such excellence of devotion to God in his conduct that nothing else is seen in him except brilliance, grace, and, so to speak, the varied flower of good works, and nothing else is heard from him when he opens his mouth except the sweetest sound of these things.

Because many seeds within a pomegranate are covered externally by a single rind, pomegranates rightly signify the manifold practice of the virtues, covered on every side by the single protection of love. The same likeness of pomegranates is made of violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and, as is found later, also twisted fine linen. It has often been emphasized what variety of virtue is indicated by these four colors.

Bells are mingled among them in the middle when the priest’s work never differs from the sound of the word he speaks, nor, frightened by adversity, does the sound of his tongue dissent from the uprightness of his conduct. Hence the text beautifully adds:

“So that one bell shall be golden,” etc. Golden bells are inserted into the high priest’s violet tunic and surrounded on every side when all his speech resounds with the brilliance of heavenly light, and the same sound, firmly fixed in the violet tunic, is commended to the minds of his hearers by the sublimity of his works as well.

Two pomegranates are made around each bell, and two bells around each pomegranate, when everything he says is confirmed by good actions and is fixed more firmly in the hearts of his hearers, while everything he does is shown to be rational by the discriminating sound of his speech.

Well does it follow:

[Col. 0477A] “And Aaron shall put it on when he performs his ministry, so that the sound may be heard,” and so forth. For the priest dies as he enters or leaves if no sound is heard from him, because he incurs the anger of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the sound of preaching. If we wish to attend to Josephus’s words, in which he says that there were seventy-two pomegranates on the high priest’s tunic and an equal number of bells, this agrees with the figures’ mystical meanings: just as he was commanded to bear the apostolic number on his shoulder and breast, so he also bore around his feet the number of the seventy-two disciples. For it is clear that, just as the twelvefold number of the apostles initiated the rank of episcopal dignity, so the seventy-two disciples, who were themselves sent by the Lord to preach the word, signified by their election the lower rank of priesthood, which is now called the presbyterate. Hence their number is figured in the final part of the priestly attire, while the apostles’ number is figured in its first part.
