For it was fitting that those who were destined to hold the higher rank in the body of the supreme priest—that is, in the Church of Christ—should typologically occupy the higher place in the attire of the typological high priest.

But if anyone wishes also to interpret the numbers of both orders mystically, Aaron wore twelve gems on his breast to signify that the time would come when faith in the Holy Trinity would be preached to the human race in all the regions of the four-square world. Or certainly, as we explained above, he wore twelve gems—that is, three groups of four—to admonish all teachers always to possess and commend to their disciples, together with faith in the truth that is in the Trinity, the works of righteousness, which are principally comprehended in the four virtues. [Col. 0477C]

He also carried seventy-two golden bells, with an equal number of pomegranates, to show mystically that the same faith and practice of righteousness would lead the whole world from the darkness of errors into the true light. For three days and nights contain seventy-two hours. And because this visible sun circles through all the regions of the world, traversing those above and below three times in seventy-two hours, this number of bells and pomegranates of different colors was fittingly incorporated into the high priest’s tunic, to teach figuratively that Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, would illuminate the whole world and grant it both the gift [Col. 0477D] of true faith—which consists in the knowledge and confession of the Holy Trinity—and of good works, which are found in the flower and splendor of varied virtues.

We may also understand that this was figuratively expressed in the twelvefold number of the gems: the same Sun of Righteousness would fill all our times and every region of our world with his light, after the example of the worldly sun, which customarily traverses the zodiacal circle through twelve months and encompasses the entire world. Moreover, the fact that the four rows on the breastpiece contained three stones each agrees with the order of the revolving year, which is divided into four seasons by three months each. That the whole period of our salvation, during which we strive for eternal recompense, is called a “year” in Scripture is attested by the Savior himself, [Col. 0478A] who, according to Isaiah’s saying, was sent to proclaim “the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense” (Isa. 61). The Psalmist also sings of this same year, saying: “You will bless the crown of the year of your kindness” (Ps. 64). To those to whom in the present he has given the kindness of right faith and practice, he will give on the day of recompense the crown of everlasting blessing.

## CHAPTER VII. The Golden Plate

“And you shall make a plate of purest gold,” and so forth. The golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, on which “Holy to the Lord,” or “the Holy One of the Lord,” as it is called below, was engraved, was holier than his other garments. And rightly so: just as divine power surpasses all that it has created, so it was fitting that his name, rising above the rest of the high priest’s attire and adornment, should stand out more exalted and, as though sanctifying everything, should occupy an eminent place on his forehead. It signifies the confidence of our profession, which we carry on our forehead, each of us saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6).

And rightly, of the entire high priest’s attire, this one object alone was made of gold, to signify the purity of heart or body in which we ought to conceal or carry the mysteries of our redemption. Or certainly, the priest carries “Holy to the Lord,” inscribed in gold on his forehead, to suggest mystically that we ought to venerate and embrace the passion of our Lord and Savior, through which we were redeemed, in such a way that we also recognize that the radiance of the divine majesty in him, through which we were created, must likewise be confessed: we must confess the death of the humanity he assumed in such a way that we immediately acknowledge that this same humanity rose from death into eternal glory. [Col. 0478C]

The “Holy to the Lord” commanded to be engraved on the plate signifies his holy and venerable name. Among the Hebrews it is customarily written with four vowel letters, whose interpretation in their language sounds ineffable—not because it cannot be spoken, but because no creature can circumscribe it in sense or understanding. And because nothing can be said of him with sufficient dignity, he is therefore most rightly called ineffable, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts” (Phil. 4). And the Psalmist says: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no end” (Ps. 144).

And rightly the same name of the Lord was written in four letters on the high priest’s forehead, because of the corresponding significance of the four parts of the Lord’s cross, which we were to carry on our forehead: the upper, right, left, and lower parts. Again, we carry “Holy to the Lord,” engraved in gold on our forehead, when, cleansed from the defilements of vices that we inherited from our first parent, we receive within ourselves the image and likeness of our Creator, in whose image we were created. We do not conceal that we have received this image in secret, but, making it manifest to all, proclaim it with our voice, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). Addressing the Colossians, he explains this more clearly, saying: “But now you also must put away anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old human being with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him” (Col. 3). [Col. 0479A]

Concerning this “Holy to the Lord,” John too writes in the Apocalypse: “I saw,” he says, “the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand who had his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads” (Rev. 14). Again, describing the glory of the heavenly homeland, he says: “The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will serve him; they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Rev. 22).

Since, therefore, all who follow the Lamb—that is, all the faithful—ought to bear this same name of the most sacred veneration on the forehead of their profession, how much more necessary is it that those who, having received priesthood and spiritual teaching, have been assigned the leadership of the Lord’s flock should display in themselves an example of virtue to all? The text therefore rightly adds:

“And Aaron shall bear their iniquities,” and so forth. For the high priest bears the iniquities of his subjects—that is, he carries them away and removes them—when he either urges them to repent of their offenses by teaching them, or, by entreating on behalf of the penitent, wins for them the grace of the just Judge. He does this through the gifts and offerings that they have presented and consecrated to the Lord, when, on account of the good works they have performed—worthy fruits of repentance, that is, almsgiving and other works of righteousness—he releases the repentant from the guilt of the crimes they once committed.

Divine instruction both mystically represented that these things should be done in the high priest’s attire and openly taught them in the words of sacred speech. But, alas, certain bishops act very differently. They want to receive—or rather, demand—gifts and offerings from the people, yet make no effort to carry away and correct their iniquity so that they may obtain forgiveness. They ought to receive temporal gifts from their subjects for this one reason: that by preaching eternal goods they have corrected them from error and led them to the way of truth, in imitation of the first teachers of the Holy Church, who confidently said to those from whom they received temporal support: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9). [Col. 0479D]

But since every bishop or minister of the word can labor effectively for his subjects—whether by preaching the word or by supplicating the Lord—only if his mind is always furnished with the remembrance of the divine name, the text appropriately adds:

“And the plate shall always be on his forehead,” and so forth. For if the plate inscribed with the Lord’s name is always on Aaron’s forehead, the Lord will be reconciled to the children of Israel. When the teacher himself has faithfully submitted to divine service with a pure mind, his subjects too, inflamed by his example and admonitions, strive to live rightly and to merit the grace of the inward Observer.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Linen Tunic and the Tiara

“And you shall bind the tunic with fine linen.” This is the inner tunic, which he called above the *strict linen tunic*. Why it was called *strict linen*, or why it was commanded to be bound with fine linen, has already been explained above; what should now be added is that soldiers customarily have linen garments, which they call *camisiae*, fitted so closely to their limbs and bodies that they may be unencumbered, whether for running, hurling spears in battle, holding a shield, wielding a sword, or whatever necessity may require. Joab too is read to have worn such a garment when he killed Amasa (2 Kings 20), one tightened according to the measure of his attire.

Priests, therefore, prepared for God’s service, also use this tunic, so that, possessing the beauty of garments, they may move swiftly as though unclothed. Because this tunic, like the hyacinth-colored one, reached down to the feet, it too was called in Greek *poderis*, that is, “reaching to the ankles” or “ankle-length.” Its mystical significance is readily apparent. Since it is established that linen or fine linen signifies continence and chastity of our body, as was explained repeatedly above, priests have a strict linen garment or a tunic of fine linen when they guard their intention of continence with unwavering and undistracted minds. They do so with such complete earnestness that the desirous flesh wages no conflict against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh.

They have a strict linen garment when, as the soul ardently desires and languishes, both their heart and flesh rejoice together in the living God within the courts of the Lord. This linen garment is not only strict but also *poderis*, descending to the feet, when continence is not violently imposed upon a single member but is delightfully perfected throughout the entire body.

This linen garment ought to bind the priest’s hands and arms, so that they do nothing except what is useful; his breast, so that he thinks nothing empty; his belly, so that by desiring delicacies beyond measure he does not presume to make God a glutton; the members beneath his belly, so that by behaving wantonly they do not corrupt the entire beauty of the priestly attire; his knees, so that they do not grow sluggish in constant prayer; and his shins and feet, so that they do not run toward evil. [Col. 0480D]

Let the priest therefore first put on the strict linen garment, so that he may restrain both his body from wicked deeds and his mind from perverse thoughts. Then let him receive the hyacinth-colored garment, so that, after the discipline of salutary continence, he may adorn body and soul alike with the beauty of spiritual virtues.

But since there are five bodily senses—sight, taste, smell, hearing, and touch—the first four belonging properly to the head, while the last is common to the whole body—this tunic, as we have said, signifies especially continence in touch and righteousness. The priestly attire figuratively demonstrates, in due sequence, how the innocence or sanctification of the other four senses must be cultivated or sought, when it says:

“And you shall make a linen tiara.” The tiara, which was also called a *cidaris* and a *mitra*, covered and adorned the high priest’s head, so that through this garment he might be admonished to keep all the senses of his head consecrated to God: so that his eyes might not see vanity; his ears might not, by listening too willingly, receive reproach against his neighbor; his mouth might not overflow with malice; and his tongue might not devise deceit. Nor should his heart be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness, or his sense of smell embrace the bed of a prostitute sprinkled with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. [Col. 0481B]

Rather, let his eyes see equity; let his ears incline to hear words of prudence; let the Lord’s sayings be sweet to his palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; and, while breath remained in him, let him not speak iniquity or depart from his innocence.

Care must also be taken with the fifth sense, which is common to the whole body, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “Depart, depart, go out from there; do not touch what is unclean” (Isa. 52). And as the Apostle admonishes: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing sanctification to completion in the fear of God” (2 Cor. 7).

Josephus explains how this tiara was made (*Antiquities* 3.2), saying: “Upon his head he wears a cap fashioned in the manner of a small reed or helmet. It extends over the crown of the head and projects slightly beyond half the top of the head. It is such that it appears to have been made from woven linen, with bands that are repeatedly wound around and joined together, so that it does not easily come undone.” Josephus reports that another, larger covering was added over this cap, concealing the entire surface of the head. It was fitted carefully so that it would not fall while the priest was occupied with sacrifices; however, he does not indicate what color it was.

This, then, concerns the cap of the lesser priest. Concerning the high priest’s tiara he testifies as follows: “The high priest has a cap similarly fashioned to the first, like the other priests, and another sewn garment variegated with hyacinth. A golden crown also surrounds it, made in three circuits. Above it rises, in the middle of the forehead, something like a small golden calyx, similar to the plant called among us *acharos*, which the Greeks call *hyoscyamon*.” [Col. 0481D]

A little later, after describing it with remarkable variety, he adds: “It has flowers resembling plantain, and the entire crown is engraved all around with these flowers, from the back of the head to both temples. On the forehead, however, it does not have this, but there is a golden plate on which the name of God is inscribed in sacred letters.”

Holy Scripture appears to be silent about this second covering and the high priest’s golden crowns. It does briefly mention crowns later, saying: “They made woven tunics for Aaron and his sons, and linen mitres with their little crowns” (Exod. 39). But it does not say of what material they were made. Since it says, “linen mitres with their little crowns,” it could be understood that both were made of fine linen, if Josephus had not indicated that the crowns were golden. Since he belonged to the priestly family and the Temple was still standing and the legal observances were still being celebrated, he could very easily have learned the entire form of the priestly attire—not merely by reading about it, but by seeing it.

Whether, then, the little crowns were of fine linen or gold, since it is agreed that they were made together with the mitres, let us say briefly what their form signifies. Priests have linen mitres with little crowns when they guard their sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch in the beauty of chastity in such a way that, for this very guardianship, they hope to receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him.

For whoever practices continence or good works in such a way that he neglects to seek eternal rewards in return for them appears indeed to have a linen mitre on his head, but he does not have the little crowns. He presents the image of virtue before human beings, but he does not find virtue’s reward with the Lord. If, therefore, the little crowns were golden, they signify the splendor of perpetual light; if they were of fine linen, they figuratively announce the immortality of our body, which will be everlasting.

And rightly the priest wears crowns added to his linen stoles, so that in continence he may continually meditate on eternal rewards, and in the sanctification of continence or good works may at the same time promise his hearers the same joys of heavenly blessedness. Otherwise, if he imposes the burden of labor without the hope of reward, he makes Christ’s yoke, which is easy, and his burden, which is light, harsh and difficult for his hearers.

When the Lord commanded that the tiara be made, he added:

[Col. 0482C] “And a belt of embroidered work.” Concerning the making of this belt, it is written more explicitly later: “They made the girdle of twisted fine linen, hyacinth, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, in embroidered work.” According to what Jerome writes from Josephus, this girdle was woven in a circle in the likeness of the skin of a serpent that it sheds in old age, so that you would think it a long purse. It was woven beneath a covering of scarlet, purple, hyacinth, and linen thread, for beauty and strength, and ornamented with such multicolored workmanship that you would think various flowers and gems had not been woven in by the craftsman’s hand but added afterward.

It was four fingers wide. The high priest used this belt specifically, and with it the hyacinth-colored tunic and the ephod were fastened. For later there is an explicit statement about the joining of the ephod and the breastpiece: “These fitted together in front and behind in such a way that the ephod and the breastpiece were mutually joined, tightened at the belt and more firmly connected by rings. A hyacinth-colored band joined them, so that they would not hang loosely or move apart from one another.”

No one can doubt that the belt, or girdle, to which the ephod was fastened, encircled the hyacinth-colored tunic, which was also called the ephod-tunic; for everything said up to this point pertains to the high priest’s attire. Next, the belt and the other garments of his sons are explained together, when it says:

“But for the sons of Aaron you shall prepare linen tunics and belts,” and so forth. Nothing is determined concerning their belts, whether they too were to be made in embroidered work [Col. 0483A] or in a single color.

We must therefore first discuss the high priest’s belt, which was made from those four noblest colors, worthy of God. For the high priest appropriately wore such a belt, since he ought always to be girded with the singular beauty of virtues. Appropriately the high priest walked girded with the varied bloom of shining colors, because, just as anyone else must be girded with the discipline of continence lest rebellious flesh disturb the inward peace of the mind, so the high priest and teacher of the faithful, having subdued every desirous movement of mind or body, ought to be surrounded by the glory of virtues. Thus, after the example of the flower that came forth from the root of Jesse—that is, the Lord Savior—“righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the cincture of his reins.”

The linen tunics, belts, and tiaras that were commanded to be made for the sons of Aaron “for glory and adornment” can readily be understood as commending to us an inward beauty and glory from what was explained above. Priests have linen tunics when they dedicate their entire body to the whiteness of chastity. They gird their tunics with belts when they surround that same chastity with vigilant care of the mind, lest through neglect they remain less diligent in the exercise of good works, or lose the merit even of chastity through boasting of chastity.

For whoever walks clothed in an ankle-length tunic without a belt allows the tunic to hang loose, giving wind and cold room to enter once the body is exposed; moreover, it hampers his steps and restricts his ability to walk, or even becomes a cause of falling for those who tread upon it. [Col. 0483C]

Thus, carnal chastity often deprives certain people of chastity of heart, when they take less care to persist in good works because they perceive less clearly that the guardianship of chastity is worthless without an increase in other goods; yet, when joined to good deeds, it acquires great glory for the one who possesses it.

Finally, bodily chastity profited the foolish virgins nothing, since, when the bridegroom came, they lacked the lamp of inward purity. Let the sons of Aaron therefore be girded with linen tunics, so that they may possess chastity. Let priests be girded with belts, so that this chastity may not be lax or negligent; so that it may not provide the wind of conceit an opening to inflate the mind; so that, as iniquity increases, it may not cause their charity to grow cold; so that the progress of good works may not be impeded by the boastfulness of their presumption; so that, when the course of virtues is obstructed, chastity itself may not become cheapened by being polluted with the filth of earthly desire; and, finally, so that by growing proud it may not drive its Author toward ruin.

Once girded, let the priests also receive tiaras on their heads, so that, after vigilant and watchful guardianship of bodily chastity, the sight, hearing, taste, and smell themselves may likewise be held and cared for in a manner worthy of God.

## CHAPTER IX. The Underwear

“And you shall clothe your brother Aaron with all these things,” and so forth. Aaron and his sons were to be clothed with all these garments, but with this distinction: he himself was to use all of them, while his sons were to use the final three, which are specifically assigned to them by name, when it says: “But for the sons of Aaron you shall prepare linen tunics, belts, and tiaras for glory and adornment.” [Col. 0484A]

What follows—“You shall also make linen undergarments,” and so forth—pertains to both together, Aaron and his sons, as the words themselves plainly demonstrate. Thus Aaron himself is clothed in all eight of the garments mentioned: linen undergarments, the linen tunic, the hyacinth-colored ephod, the breastpiece, the belt, the tiara, and the golden plate. His sons, however, use only four of these: the undergarments, the strict linen tunic, the belt, and the tiara.

But since the other garments have been discussed above, these undergarments, which are commanded to be made to cover the shame of the flesh, specifically signify that portion of chastity which restrains the desire for marital intercourse. Without it, no one can either assume the priesthood or be consecrated for service at the altar—that is, unless he has either remained a virgin or dissolved the bonds of a contracted marriage.

This kind of virtue is not imposed as a necessary command upon anyone by God’s law; rather, it is to be offered to the Lord through voluntary devotion, as he himself says concerning it: “Not everyone can accept this saying” (Matt. 19). Yet he immediately invites those who are able by a kindly exhortation, saying: “Let the one who is able to accept it, accept it.” A little later he promises those same people who have left a wife or other relatives and the entanglements of this world for his sake a hundredfold reward in this life and eternal life in the age to come.

Accordingly, as a matter of distinction, Moses is not commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons with this garment, as is said of the earlier garments: “You shall clothe your brother Aaron with all these things, and his sons with him.” Rather, he says: “You shall make linen undergarments, so that they may cover the shame of their flesh.” “They,” he says, “shall cover the shame of their flesh; you shall make the undergarments for the high priest and his sons; you shall teach the rule of chastity; you shall declare to those who are going to exercise the priesthood that they must abstain from marital embrace.”

Yet you shall not impose a violent yoke of this kind of continence on anyone. Instead, whoever wishes to become a priest and serve in the ministry of the altar must of his own accord cease to be slaves to their wives. Once they have done this and, having accepted the commitment to continence, have agreed to be ministers of the sanctuary and altar, divine law will be present. Like the rest of the attire suitable for priests, it will impose upon them abundant instruction concerning how they ought to live and teach. Rejoicing in their voluntary devotion, it will add to their priestly dignity the adornments of wisdom, patience, gentleness, mercy, spiritual zeal, humility, fear of the Lord, and other virtues of this kind. Otherwise they die guilty of iniquity. For the soul most certainly incurs death if anyone, living wantonly, presumes to usurp the priestly rank. This interpretation is also confirmed by the Lord’s subsequent words, in which he adds shortly afterward:

“(Exod. 29.) And when you have washed the father with his sons in water,” and so forth. Here too Moses is not commanded to receive any undergarments. Hence it is plainly established that Aaron and his sons had first clothed themselves in this type of garment, and that they came to Moses ready to be washed, [Col. 0485A] clothed, anointed, and consecrated.

Here we should also note that Moses, when he was about to consecrate them, first washed them with water and then put the attire of the sacred rank upon them. For clearly it is necessary that whoever is to be promoted to the service of the altar should wash himself, at the time of dedication, with a greater-than-usual outpouring of tears or contrition, so that the more cleanly he approaches to receive the rank, the more perfectly he may fulfill what he has received.

This washing could be understood as baptism in the sacred font, if the sequence allowed it—namely, if someone elected to the priesthood were then washed for the first time in baptismal water for the remission of sins. But the Apostle opposes the ordination of such people when he says: “Do not appoint a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil.” Once the high priest has been clothed in the sacred garments, [Col. 0485B] he is immediately drenched with the oil of anointing, so that his consecration may be completed through the grace of the Holy Spirit. This does not mean that we can possess the virtues represented by the garments mentioned earlier apart from God’s grace; rather, it means that a greater assistance of grace must be granted by the Lord when someone has either ascended to a higher rank or been placed over the governance of many.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that, although in this book of Exodus Aaron is said to be clothed in eight garments, in Leviticus a ninth seems to be added: namely, a belt with which the linen tunic was girded before the hyacinth-colored tunic was put on. For it is written: “And when he had washed them, he clothed the high priest in a linen undergarment, and, girding him with a belt, put on him the hyacinth-colored tunic; and over it he placed the ephod, which he fastened with a girdle and fitted to the breastpiece” (Lev. 8). But how this was done is plainly evident from what has been explained, as a figure of spiritual attire.

## CHAPTER X. The Four Colors of the Priestly Garments, the Four Elements, and the Consecration of the Priests

Since, following the statements of the Fathers, we have briefly touched upon these matters concerning the priestly attire, we thought it worth noting that the four distinguished colors from which it was made correspond by an appropriate comparison to the four elements of the world. Fine linen, or linen, corresponds to earth, from which it grows; purple to water, since it is dyed from sea-shells; hyacinth and scarlet to air and fire, because of their similarity of color. Scarlet was twice-dyed because fire possesses a double power: namely, that of giving light and that of burning. The Hebrews say that the high priest therefore bore the representation of all the elements in his attire because he was required to offer sacrifice and pray not only for Israel but for the whole world.

We can perhaps add, not inappropriately, that the representation of all the elements is contained in each human being: fire in heat, air in breath, water in moisture, and earth in the very solidity of the limbs. Hence Greek physiologists call the human being *microcosmos*, that is, “a small world.” If, according to this interpretation, you ask what gold in the same attire signifies, understand in it the rational power of the inner human being. Hence “Holy to the Lord” is specifically written upon it, because no one ascends to knowledge of his Creator except through this power. For the Apostle says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts in the inner human being (Eph. 3). [Col. 0486A]

For this reason Scripture shows us the high priest of the Old Testament clothed in this way, so that the high priest of our own time may know that he ought to intercede for the entire human race, and especially for those who have come to know the truth and carry the sign of that faith on their foreheads. The Apostle admonishes and says: “First of all, then, I ask that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions” (1 Tim. 2).

If in the high priest whom Moses consecrates we understand the Lord Savior, then rightly he possesses in his attire both the representation of the whole world and that of the human being. For he is, as the Apostle says, “the radiance of glory and the exact representation of the substance of God the Father,” and he “upholds all things by the word of his power.” He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; he is the eternal priest, resplendent with every adornment of holiness—not one who, born in the flesh, merited these by the exercise of labor, but one who, having become incarnate in the Virgin’s womb, received them all at once through the arrival of the grace of the Holy Spirit (Heb. 1).

Commending most beautifully the intercession of his priesthood on our behalf, the Apostle says: “But because he remains forever, he has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is able to save forever those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them” (Heb. 7). Commending equally his garments and adornments of virtue, he adds: “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.”

He truly had a golden plate on his head on which “Holy to the Lord” was engraved, because he came in the name of the Father, saying: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me,” and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

Up to this point, the heavenly oracle has indicated what the attire of Aaron and his sons ought to be. From here the manner of consecration also follows, by which they themselves, or the tabernacle with all its furnishings, ought to be dedicated.

“After the calf has been offered to the Lord,” and so forth. All these things figuratively demonstrate that either the devotion of good works and purity of faith, or the grace of divine illumination, is consecrated through priests alone. For who does not know that the immolation and blood of those animals signify the death and sprinkling of the blood of our Lord, through which we are both absolved from sins and strengthened in good works?

The Apostle also teaches what mystery the unleavened loaves of bread contain concerning the Savior, saying: “Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” The cakes and flatbreads were sprinkled or smeared with oil, so that we might be admonished that our works must not only be restrained from the leaven of malice and wickedness, but must also be made worthy of the divine sight through the richness of charity.

Or certainly, we offer a cake sprinkled with oil to the Lord for our consecration when everything we do is enriched by the inward grace of the Holy Spirit in the devotion of our heart. We offer flatbreads smeared with oil when we confidently show people outwardly, as an example for living, that what we do is spiritual. Through these offerings our consecration is completed, while, through good works and pure thoughts, the Lord grants us the merit of holiness.

When these instructions concerning the consecration had been completed, Scripture returns to the construction of the incense altar, on which Aaron was to burn incense daily.

## CHAPTER XI. The Description of the Incense Altar
(Exod. XXX.) “You shall also make an altar for burning incense,” etc. If the altar of burnt offering, mentioned above, generally signifies the life of the righteous—those accustomed daily to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires [Col. 0487B] and to offer it to the Lord as a living sacrifice—what does this altar made for burning incense signify except the particular life of certain perfected people? For it was not without reason that the flesh of animals was burned on the former, while incense was burned on this one. On the former were figured those who do not walk according to the desires of the flesh but, as though sacrificing these desires to the Lord, dedicate all the senses of their body to his will through the fire of his Holy Spirit. On this one, however, is represented the type of those who, with greater perfection of mind, having utterly extinguished and subdued every enticement of the flesh, offer the Lord only the vows of their prayers. They have nothing in the flesh that attacks them, nothing in their conscience from sin by which they may be troubled or afraid, but desire to come [Col. 0487C] and appear before the face of God through the outpouring of sweet tears.

Thus this altar was suitably placed inside, near the veil and the ark, while the other was placed outside, before the tabernacle: for the former shine conspicuously in the sight of holy Church as examples of virtue to all; the latter, through the ardor of a higher desire, draw very near to the contemplation of future blessedness even while still detained in the body. It is fitting that the one is commanded to be clad in bronze and the other in gold: bronze is more sonorous than other metals and long-lasting, whereas gold, to the extent that it yields to bronze in sound, surpasses it in brilliance.

Accordingly, the bronze altar on which the flesh was burned and the blood of victims poured out represents those who, having subdued and as it were sacrificed to God the pleasures of the flesh, steadfastly complete the way of truth [Col. 0487D] that they once began, and frequently proclaim it aloud to their neighbors so that they too may walk in it. The golden altar, on the other hand, appropriately signifies those who are more fully illumined by the grace of heavenly brightness, but disclose less to others what they taste inwardly of secret sweetness. In speaking, they are less able to pour forth how greatly they themselves are refreshed within by the sweetness hidden in the presence of God.

The incense altar was also suitably smaller in size in proportion to its greater metallic brilliance, because the holier people are in the Church, the fewer they are. Both altars were suitably commanded to be made from the same acacia wood, which we have said resembles white thorn and is incorruptible: for there is one steadfastness of unfailing faith by which the hearts of all the elect must be fortified and prepared to receive the fire of love and to offer God the libations of virtue. The Apostle speaks to all alike, the lowly together with the great, saying: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (II Cor. VII). In other words: Let us cut away and remove from ourselves the thickets of vices and the stings of prickling temptations, which the soil of our body, because of the first transgression, habitually brings forth for us; and, as though cutting them down with a kind of double-edged axe of diligent correction, let us vigorously cultivate both our inner and our outer person, so that, having received the fire of the Holy Spirit, it may become worthy to offer a sacrifice of virtues before its Creator.

There was suitably one and the same, not a different, fire that burned the victims on this altar [Col. 0488B] and the incense on the other, because there is one Spirit who gives life to the minds of all the faithful through the varied grace of his gifts.

The incense altar was square, having one cubit in length and another in breadth, while its height was two cubits. Its length signifies long-suffering patience, as was said in the exposition of the altar of burnt offering; its breadth signifies the breadth of love; its height signifies the sublimity of hope, through which we rejoice with sincere hearts amid the endurance of temporal labors and the cheerfulness of love.

The altar’s length and breadth are each one cubit when the highest and most perfect men in the Church endure temporal evils with equanimity, and bestow upon their neighbors whatever good they can through love, with a view to no other thing than eternal reward. [Col. 0488C] For “love is patient, love is kind”: patient, so that it tolerates an injury inflicted by a neighbor; kind, so that it also offers services of compassion to the one whose adversity it tolerates, whenever he has need.

The incense altar is rightly commanded to be square in length and breadth, so that it may be shown that the mind of the perfect, with its virtues joined together, is as capable of loving a brother as it is of bearing with him, and as capable of enduring his annoyance through patience as it is of showing him the benevolence of compassionate love.

It has two cubits in height because the elect hope to receive a twofold reward in the life to come: one, the rest of their souls, when they have laid aside this corruptible and mortal body [Col. 0488D] and entered the heavenly kingdom; the other, when, having received that same body incorruptible and immortal, they exult more perfectly in the presence of their Creator. Then the prophetic promise will be fulfilled: “In their land they shall possess a double portion; everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isa. LXI).

“Horns shall project from it,” etc. In Scripture, horns often signify the eminence of faith and virtues, by which we must blunt and overcome the battles brought against us by the ancient enemy, saying with the prophet to the Lord: “Through you we shall toss our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLVIII). Immediately afterward, explaining what horn he meant, he added: “And in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us.”

Conversely, the battles of vices that attempt to conquer us are sometimes indicated by the name “horns.” Briefly embracing both meanings, the Lord said through the prophet: “I will break all the horns of sinners, but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. XLVII).

Therefore the Law rightly decrees that only animals of the horned kind are clean and edible for the people of God. Animals that chew the cud and divide the hoof are also known to be horned, so that it may be mystically shown that only those can be incorporated into the spiritual Church of God who are proved invincible in the battles against vices through the strength of faith.

Horns project from the incense altar when the elect display works of virtue not merely outwardly, for appearance before men, but exercise them with a firm and immovable affection arising from the inner root of the mind. Hypocrites, by contrast, are like those who have borrowed horns from elsewhere: they possess the appearance of piety but deny its power.

To them the fable of Aesop aptly applies. It tells of a crow adorned with peacock feathers, who vainly gloried in a beauty that was not his own and was nearly deprived both of every power of his feathers and of life itself when the peacocks, blazing with jealousy, attacked him.

The altar is clad in purest gold when the perfect shine with the true inner light of wisdom; when, in all that they do, they display the brilliance of love as though it were the glory of their daily attire; when they show to all who see or hear them that the memory of everlasting brightness is always present to them; and when they make it evident that above all things they think about and seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

It is fitting that both the grating of the altar and its walls and horns are commanded to be covered with gold. The grating was inside, in the middle of the altar, prepared to receive the incense. The walls were visible on the outside, while the horns, also visible externally, projected higher in a special elevation.

The grating is gilded when the grace of Christ shines within our inner person through faith. The walls are gilded when that same grace of the Lord’s love spreads outwardly through good works. The horns are gilded when the confidence of the righteous—the strength by which they have learned either to endure adversaries of the truth bravely through patience, or prudently to refute and correct them through wisdom—flashes everywhere with the brilliance of inner light.

Since such people can rightly say, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (II Tim. IV), the text rightly continues:

“You shall make for it a crown of gold all around.” A golden crown is made around the incense altar when the saints await eternal rewards for the good deeds they remember having done. The crown is rightly made around the altar, so that all that they have done may be taught worthy of heavenly recompense, and so that nothing in such people may remain which, after the dissolution of the flesh, ought to be punished by purgatorial fire.

The incense altar also has a golden crown around it in those who, although lesser in merit and not daring openly to proclaim that the reward of a good fight and a preserved faith has been laid up for them, nevertheless do everything with the intention of pleasing God and with the hope of receiving that same heavenly reward. The text continues:

[Col. 0490A] “You shall make two golden rings beneath the crown,” etc. These rings, by which the altar was carried, may indeed, in accordance with what was explained above concerning the altar of burnt offering, the ark, and the table, suitably be understood as the books of the four Gospels. Through faith in and teaching from these books the saints are carried, lifted above earthly thoughts, and borne through the wilderness of this life toward their heavenly homeland by daily progress in good works.

Yet whereas there the making of four rings is explicitly commanded—two on one side and two on the other—here, without stating the number four, two rings are made on each side. There the number of the evangelists is more plainly evident; here, however, there is also another spiritual mystery, which chiefly concerns the love of God and neighbor.

The altar is surrounded on each side by golden rings, because the hearts of the elect are fortified on either side by love of God and neighbor. Love is aptly compared to rings, because when prophecy has been abolished, knowledge destroyed, and tongues have ceased, love alone will never cease.

There are two rings on each side because the twofold commandment of love is distinguished by a twofold virtue. The love of God is perfected through sincerity of faith and purity of life (Hebr. II): “without faith it is impossible to please God,” and “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II). The prophet embraces both in a single verse, saying: “The righteous lives by his faith” (Hab. II), plainly indicating that a person will come to life only if he possesses works of righteousness together with faith in the truth.

Likewise, brotherly love consists in a twofold virtue, namely patience and kindness, as the Apostle testifies: “Love is patient, love is kind” (I Cor. XIII). Hence the Lord says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI): in forgiving debts, teaching patience; in giving what is necessary, teaching the grace of kindness. In the one, we are to bear bravely the troubles of our neighbors; in the other, we are to share our advantages with our neighbors gladly.

The altar therefore has two rings on each side when the saints, through the twofold perfection of love, gird themselves both for the honor of their Creator and for the care and service of their neighbor.

Into these rings gilded carrying poles are inserted so that the altar may be carried, when such people receive with a prepared heart the most illustrious sayings of the Fathers who preceded them, by which they are lifted ever further above earthly things and swept toward the love of eternal goods. That such people draw near to heavenly things in mind and merit is mystically signified by the words that follow:

“You shall place the altar opposite the veil,” etc. The ark, as explained in its proper place, represents the Lord and Savior; the veil hanging before the ark signifies heaven, which the Lord entered after conquering death, so that, as the Apostle says, he might “now appear in the presence of God for us” (Hebr. IX).

The altar stands opposite the veil hanging before the ark when the entire intention of the righteous is directed toward entering the heavenly kingdom. It stands before the mercy seat that covers the ark when, with purity of mind, they draw near to the vision of their Creator, although enclosed [Col. 0491A] in a bodily way of life, yet dwelling in the heavens.

## CHAPTER XII. On burning incense upon the altar

“And Aaron shall burn incense upon it,” etc. It is clear that incense, or *thymiama*, expresses the power of prayer, as the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). In the Apocalypse of John he saw the saints holding golden bowls full of perfumes. Immediately explaining this, he added: “Which are the prayers of the saints” (Apoc. V).

Since, as stated above, Aaron signifies both the high priest himself in a special sense—namely, the Lord and Savior—and the priests of our own order, Aaron shall burn sweet-smelling incense upon this altar in the morning when either the Lord himself, having illumined the hearts of the faithful, urges them toward the sweetness of prayer with the new radiance of his grace, or when those who share his priesthood rouse the faithful by diligent exhortation to seek the face of their Creator.

The priest burns incense not only in the morning but also in the evening. Incense is burned in the morning so that, at the beginning of every good work that we plan to do with God’s inspiration, we may invoke the help by which we are to complete it. In the evening, however, it is burned so that, when we have completed what we began well, we may return vows of thanksgiving to the one from whom we received it, for the things he has granted.

Or, certainly, the morning and the rising sun allow us to see everything clearly all around, whereas when evening comes our uncertain vision grows dim. Therefore we need the light of a lamp in order to see what we need to see.

Those mysteries or sayings of our Redeemer that, according to the order of human reasoning, we are sufficiently able to discern in some measure, we see as though in daylight. But wherever human reason fails and we must follow only the authority of Scripture, there the eye of our understanding grows dim as though in the night. The lamp of God’s word, however, helps our feet lest they stumble and stray from the way of truth.

Thus Peter, speaking of the mystery of the Lord’s faith, says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (II Pet. I).

It is rightly said, therefore: “And Aaron shall burn upon it sweet-smelling incense; in the morning, when he dresses the lamps, he shall burn it, and when he sets them in place in the evening.” Aaron burns incense upon the altar in the morning when the Lord inflames the hearts of the faithful toward the grace of compunction through those mysteries of truth that they are already able to understand.

He burns it in the evening, when he sets the lamps in place, when, even through those things they cannot yet comprehend, he teaches them to love heavenly things, since they do not doubt that these things too are holy and divine, and that there all mysteries will be revealed.

The incense gives off a sweet fragrance when those who have been suddenly touched by God through compunction find sweetness in devoting themselves solely to tears and prayers. The text fittingly continues:

“You shall burn incense perpetually before the Lord,” etc. For it is necessary that the mind, after prayer and weeping, not turn aside to idle words or deeds, but preserve even after prayer has ended the same strength of devotion that it received in prayer, following the example of Hannah, of whom it is said while she was praying: “Her face was no longer changed toward other things” (I Sam. I).

“You shall not offer upon it incense of another composition.” Later in this book the spices from which this incense must be composed are named: namely, stacte, onycha, fragrant galbanum, and the clearest frankincense. All these clearly pertain to the signification of eternal goods, which must chiefly be sought from the Lord.

Therefore incense of any composition other than what the Lord appointed must not be offered upon the golden altar, because when we pray we ought to seek from the Lord nothing other than what he himself commanded and promised to give, and to believe concerning him nothing other than what he himself taught.

“You shall not offer upon it any victim,” etc. All these things belong to the outer altar, which signifies the life of beginners and of those who are still advancing. The life of the perfect righteous is of such sublimity that nothing carnal can be found in it which they might slaughter for the Lord.

It is true that libations of wine sometimes signify a great power of spiritual grace: either the cup of teaching, or the cup of suffering, or the fervor of exceptional love, or the reception of the Holy Spirit itself, or something of this kind.

But whenever a wine libation is offered together with the flesh of victims, it certainly signifies, according to the tropological interpretation, the holiness of those who still possess something of carnal desire opposed to purity of spirit and destined to be burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit upon the altar of the heart.

The perfect righteous, however, who can say, “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion forever,” as though the libations of victims belonging to the outer bronze altar had ceased, offer the Lord only the spices of heavenly desire upon the inner golden altar. For, having become more secure concerning the forgiveness of sins, they grieve only over the delay of entering the everlasting kingdom, and each night water their bed with sweet streams of tears.

Concerning this altar the text appropriately adds:

“And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns,” etc. Our High Priest offered his blood once a year for the sin of the whole world. It was in that year of which he himself says through Isaiah: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. LXI)—that is, throughout all this period in which he graciously joined the Church to himself.

Once also he granted each believer the washing of the sacred font, as a mystery of his blood, for loosening the bonds of sins. There is a beautiful difference of figures here: once a year the high priest is commanded to make atonement with the blood of the offering upon the horns of the altar, but every day he is commanded to burn sweet-smelling incense upon it.

The Lord and Savior, who daily renews his faithful by kindling them with the inward grace of compunction, redeemed those same faithful once by the sacrifice of his blood, conquering death. The faithful, who are accustomed to wash away their daily sins with daily prayers and tears, rejoice that they have once been absolved from all sins in the sacrament of his Passion.

Aaron makes atonement upon the horns of the altar because he not only prayed for human beings while living among them, but also now, seated at the right hand of the Father in heaven, intercedes for us. Dwelling by faith in the hearts of the elect, and rousing them to pray, he is rightly said himself to pray.

Aaron makes atonement upon the horns of the altar when the Lord commends his elect to the Father by recalling the virtues they have performed. As though touching the horns of the golden altar, he speaks of the devotion of his disciples:

“Those whom you gave me from the world were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you” (John XVII). Praying for them, he added: “I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours” (ibid.).

And because, on account of the merits and intercessions of exalted men, the Lord often has mercy on our weakness, the text rightly continues:

“And he shall make atonement upon it throughout your generations,” etc. Aaron makes atonement upon the incense altar when, on account of the righteousness of the saints whom we seek as intercessors and patrons, the Lord is reconciled to us.

Thus, when Hezekiah was besieged by enemies and invoked the Lord’s help, the Lord said: “I will save this city and protect it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (II Kings XIX).

Likewise, when Moses interceded for the sinning people, he recalled the fathers and, as though praying upon the horns of the altar, sought to appease the Lord:

“Let your anger cease,” he said, “and be reconciled concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I will multiply your descendants like the stars of heaven’” (Exod. XXXII).

We may also interpret these altars in this way: the bronze altar, on which the flesh and blood of victims were burned and poured out, may signify the whole Church of the present age, in which no one is without sin, even if his life upon earth has lasted only one day.

No one who has not been born carnally from the sin of Adam’s transgression can avoid the necessity of being reborn in Christ and purified by the fire of his spirit.

The golden altar, however, may signify the Lord himself, who, through a wondrous and ineffable arrangement, truly assumed flesh from Adam while remaining genuinely free from the sin of Adam’s flesh. Thus both altars were made from wood of one and the same kind, but both were not covered with gold.

Nothing carnal was offered upon this altar; only spices were burned, because when the Lord poured out prayers or tears, he did so not for his own transgressions—for he had none—but for our salvation.

Just as the ark placed within the veil signifies the God-man seated at the right hand of Majesty in the heights, so the altar placed outside the veil but near its entrance [Col. 0494A] can figuratively express the same Mediator of God and human beings: humanly dwelling among human beings, yet penetrating the inner regions of heaven by the power of his divinity.

The incense altar stood in the sanctuary, where the lampstand and the table also stood, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). The ark stood within the veil because the same Lord Jesus, after his Passion and resurrection, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.

Upon the horns of this altar Aaron makes atonement with the blood offered for sin. This signifies that priests, praying for the people of God or for their own ignorance, trust that they will be helped through his only-begotten Son and saved through the sacrament of his Passion, as the Apostle exhorts, saying: “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebr. XII), that is, “the fruit of lips confessing his name.”

This may also suitably be understood of all the elect, who are members of the High Priest and pray to the Father in spirit and truth.

What could more fittingly apply to this altar than the statement: “It shall be most holy to the Lord”? Of this one, destined to be born into the world, the archangel said to the virgin mother: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” etc. (Luke I).

The construction of the incense altar has now been described. There remains the description of the bronze basin, in which the priests entering the tabernacle were to wash their hands and feet. But one command of the Lord is first interposed, which it is fitting for us briefly to mention and explain according to our ability.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the price counted for the souls of individuals among the numbered people

[Col. 0494C]

“When you take the census of the sons of Israel,” etc. David forgot this command when he numbered the people, and therefore brought a plague upon that same people by numbering them.

In the spiritual sense, the census of the sons of Israel signifies the number of all the elect, whose names are written in heaven. Each person gives a price for his soul to the Lord when he offers him the service of diligent obedience through good works.

Otherwise there will be a plague among them when they have been counted, because perpetual vengeance awaits those who, joined in name only to the number of the faithful, refuse to offer the Lord the perfect works of faith [Col. 0494D]. It is said of such people: “They shall not give to God their ransom, nor the price of the redemption of their soul” (Ps. XLVIII).

“For the ransom of a man’s soul is his riches” (Prov. XIII), as Solomon says—whether temporal riches, when he distributes and gives them to the poor, so that his righteousness may endure forever; or spiritual riches, namely the righteousness itself that he has practiced, whether by showing mercy to the poor or by doing other good works.

Everyone who passes into the number shall give half a shekel, that is, ten obols. Nothing more suitably can this signify than observance of the Decalogue of the Law. Whoever knows how to understand it correctly recognizes that it contains both the fullness of faith and works and the promise of future reward.

In the first three commandments the love of God is comprehended; in the following seven, the love of neighbor [Col. 0495A]. As the Apostle testifies: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. XIII).

Nor should another mystery contained in the same number, ten, be passed over. The name “Jesus” begins among the Hebrews with the letter *iod*, and among the Greeks with *iota*; each of these letters in its own language signifies the number ten.

They offer ten obols to the Lord as the price of their soul when, believing in Jesus Christ, they proclaim upon their forehead and in their confession the sign of his name, which begins with the number ten.

Perhaps for the sake of this mystery the Lord testifies in the Gospel that not one *iota* can pass away from the Law (Matt. V), because the power of the Decalogue contained there, together with faith in his name mystically signified there, can never be corrupted by any disturbance among unbelievers.

[Col. 0495B] “He who is counted in the number from twenty years of age and above shall give the price.” The number twenty signifies the conjunction of both Testaments: the Law, written in five books, and the Gospel, which has four books—for four times five makes twenty.

From the age of twenty, therefore, each person is counted among the people of God, because only one is worthy of the fellowship of the elect who, aided by the grace of the Gospel, fulfills according to his measure and capacity the decrees of the Law understood spiritually, and awaits eternal rewards in heaven from the promises of that same grace.

“The rich shall not add to the half-shekel,” etc. Whether someone is great in merit and perfect, or still young and advancing in virtue, the same law of the Decalogue is imposed on all: that they love God and neighbor.

[Col. 0495C] “And you shall receive the money that is contributed by the sons of Israel,” etc. The money received from the sons of Israel is brought in as a memorial of them before the Lord when everything good that we do is preserved in eternal remembrance before our Creator and Judge, so that through the fruits of the good works we have offered him he may graciously become favorable to us.

That same money is kept for the use of the tabernacle when the conduct and actions of later believers in Christ are strengthened by the good deeds of the righteous, and the lesser strive to become such as they recognize those to have been whom they know to reign with the Lord.

It should be noted that the money in question was to be given not according to ordinary popular valuation but according to the measure of the sanctuary. The measure of the sanctuary is the arrangement of the divine Law, which the Lord commands to be observed in his Church and for which he promises eternal rewards in the future.

But if someone strives to serve God according to human preference, then, because he has not offered the money of his devotion according to the measure of the sanctuary, he will be struck by the plague of the final judgment, his offering having been rejected and cast aside.

## CHAPTER XIV. Description of the bronze basin

“You shall also make a basin,” etc. This basin, or laver as it is called below, may principally be understood as the water of baptism, by whose washing all who enter through the doors of the Church must be cleansed.

[Col. 0496A] Yet because it was placed between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar of burnt offering, and because those same priests were commanded to wash in it twice daily—that is, morning and evening—when they entered to offer incense to the Lord, whereas we can be washed in baptism only once, this basin commends to us the washing of compunction and tears, which we always need, but especially when we are about to approach to minister at the heavenly mysteries.

Since the altar of burnt offering, on which the flesh of victims was burned for the Lord, signifies the extinction of carnal desires through the fire of the Holy Spirit, while the incense altar signifies the purity of those who, having subdued every enticement of the flesh and brought the battle against vices to peace, pour out tears solely in expectation and desire of entering heaven, the basin is rightly placed near the altar of burnt offering, so that the priests may wash in it before entering the tabernacle and burning incense to the Lord.

The condition of tears and compunction is distinguished in two ways. First, everyone who turns to the Lord must pray for forgiveness of the sins he has committed, pouring out tears. If he perseveres in this for a long time, accompanied by worthy fruits of repentance, then, having become more secure of the forgiveness he has received, he must await the time when, with longing desires, he may deserve to see the face of his Creator among the most blessed choirs of angels.

Whoever truly does this cannot endure without tears either the length of this life or the delay of the life to come. Concerning this life he says: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. CXIX)—that is, with those who live in the darkness of errors and crimes. The name *Kedar* means “darkness”; he is saying: While sighing for the joys of perpetual light, I have found life exceedingly burdensome. The more I thirst for my heavenly homeland, the more I dread the neighborhood of the wicked among whom I dwell as a stranger.

Concerning the life to come he likewise says: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI). The following words show that he could not bear this thirst without tears: “My tears have been my bread day and night.” It is as though he plainly said: The longer I am delayed from seeing the face of God, for whom I ardently thirst, the more sweetly I am refreshed by the bread of tears that I pour out in his memory.

The altar of burnt offering therefore signifies the tears of penitents over the sins they have committed. The incense altar expresses the weeping of those who rejoice over the good works they have completed with the Lord’s help and who desire the rewards they trust the Lord will bestow.

This weeping surpasses the former to the same degree that gold surpasses bronze and the Holy of Holies, where the Lord’s ark stood, surpassed the former tabernacle, in which the lampstand and the Lord’s table stood.

The basin was placed behind the altar of burnt offering, and those who entered the incense altar washed in it, because no one suddenly becomes supreme. As merits advance, each person must first conquer the battles of vices [Col. 0497A] and then humbly beg his Creator, with compunction and tears, to grant that he may pour out sweet tears for entrance into the kingdom—tears which he once poured out bitterly through fear of punishments.

What could the base on which this basin was placed more suitably signify than the desire for the kingdom and heavenly life itself? For its sake such great things are done, so that perfect and exalted men may wash themselves daily in a fountain of tears and at least taste by sighing the joy of inward rest, which they are not yet able fully to see.

That the tears of the perfect are figured by this washing, placed between the tabernacle and the altar, is testified by the very words: “And Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it with water poured into it.” No one from the ordinary people was commanded to wash there; the high priest himself and his sons were commanded to do so—that is, priests of the lower rank—because in great men, just as life is more perfect, so compunction is usually more exalted.

We do not say this as though only ministers of the altar could possess or ought to possess the virtue of such compunction. Rather, we remember the words of the blessed apostle Peter, who, speaking to all the faithful about the cornerstone, which is Christ, says: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices” (I Pet. II).

And John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ” (Apoc. XX).

We remind all the faithful that they are counted under the mystical name of priests, since they are members of Christ, the eternal Priest. The blessed apostle Paul also shows them what sacrifices they ought to offer, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XII).

Moses therefore placed this basin not only for the ministers of the sacred altar but also for all the perfect, whatever their rank, because the Law of God proclaimed the grace of saving compunction generally to all the faithful.

If we wish to understand the great High Priest, the Lord and Savior himself, in the person of Aaron, it is also clear that he was washed with the water of this basin before entering to offer upon the altar. Before he burned the incense of his most holy body upon the altar of the cross [Col. 0497D] for our salvation, he also shed tears for love of us, as was most famously shown in the raising of Lazarus.

The text fittingly adds:

To offer incense in it to the Lord, etc. For death—spiritual and eternal—is to be feared if anyone chosen for service at the altar neglects to offer to God the incense of prayers. Death is to be feared if anyone presumes to enter the holy mysteries without a special washing of repentance, and to handle the Lord’s holy things with ordinary hands. Let them therefore wash their hands and feet in the water of the bronze basin, and so approach the altar. Let them wash away their actions and their conduct with tears, and then extend their hands to touch Christ’s mysteries, and set their feet within the courts of the Lord.

I judge that this command may equally and very profitably be understood of those who are to be cleansed by receiving these same sacraments: they should first, with more careful diligence, examine, sift, and purify their actions and thoughts, and so proceed to partake of the sacraments of faith, lest they deserve to hear the Apostle’s words:

> For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord (I Cor. XI);

that is, lest with a cautious and attentive mind he fail to distinguish the food of the living bread from the baseness of ordinary foods. These words concerning the basin and the approach to the altar can also be understood in this very useful way, although primarily that altar signifies the inward vows of spiritual prayers.

But we must look more carefully at what is added in conclusion:

> It shall be a perpetual ordinance for him, etc.

For although the basin, or the altar, which Moses made has been removed, and although the priesthood which he established has been changed into the Church’s new priesthood, nevertheless the perpetual ordinance of the washing and of spiritual incense remains in the life of the faithful. This was typologically signified by the incense of that altar and the water of that basin. The same is true of many other things which the law commanded to be done or declared should be performed or celebrated perpetually: literally, their observance has ceased, but according to their typological meaning they will never cease to be observed spiritually by the saints. This is attested by him who did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it:

> For not one iota or one stroke will pass away from the law until all things have taken place (Matt. V).

Our own humility also belongs to that seed of which it was said:

> It shall be a perpetual ordinance for him and for his seed throughout their generations;

not by being born from Aaron’s stock, but by believing in him in whom Aaron and the saints of his age believed. Of this seed it was promised to Abraham:

> In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen. XXV).

Mentioning these families, Isaiah says:

> All who see them will recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed (Isa. LXI).

[Col. 0499]

# ALLEGORICAL EXPOSITION OF THE PROPHET SAMUEL. (C)

## Prologue

[Col. 0499A] Commending to us the practice and constant habit of reading and meditating upon the sacred writings, the Apostle says:

> Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.

And elsewhere:

> All these things happened to them in figure. They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

The blessed Apostle Peter likewise, recalling the times of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and subsequent glory, says among other things:

> And all the prophets, from Samuel onward, as many as spoke, also announced these days.

If everything was written for our correction, instruction, or consolation, and if not only Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the other prophets who signified future events in their words, but also Samuel, Jonah, [Col. 0499B] Ezra, and their like—who recorded past events, whether their own or those of others, in deed or word—make known these days, that is, days radiant with the light of the new grace, then we must apply ourselves with the greatest care and strive, each according to his capacity, with the help of Christ’s grace, lest the things written for our sake pass us by as though they belonged to others because of our sluggishness or negligence.

But let us attend anxiously and watchfully to the sense in which we may obtain correction from them, the manner in which they offer instruction, the understanding by which they bring consolation, and the way in which all of them speak of and announce these days. Let us imitate, according to the ability of our small intellect, that learned scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.

For if we care only to bring forth old things from the treasure of the Scriptures—that is, to follow only the literal figures, in the Jewish manner—[Col. 0499C] what do we gain, while reading or hearing, amid daily sins the correction they provide, amid the increasing afflictions of the world the consolation they offer, and amid the countless errors of this life the instruction of the spirit? Suppose, for example, that, opening the book of the blessed Samuel, we find that Elkanah, one man, had two wives, while our own purpose—especially since the discipline of ecclesiastical life requires us to remain far from a wife’s embrace and to live celibate—would be frustrated unless we also knew how to draw from these and similar statements an allegorical [Col. 0500A] meaning that might vividly restore us inwardly by chastising, instructing, and consoling us.

Therefore, most beloved and most desired of all the bishops who dwell upon earth, Acca, prompted by your frequent and earnest urging and relying upon your prayers, I shall undertake to examine the writings of the aforementioned prophet, who was then called “the Seer,” and, if by the gift of him who granted him the ability to see many spiritual things I am able to perceive anything spiritual and mystical, I shall endeavor to commit it to writing.

After whatever exposition I may give of the words of the blessed Luke, in which he describes the acts of the Gospel—whether those of the Lord himself or of his apostles—I shall also strive to demonstrate that this most holy Nazirite of the Lord from his mother’s womb fulfilled in his writings the office not less of an evangelist than of a historian. For he too designated all the mysteries of the God-man Mediator, Jesus Christ, in the figurative language of a faithful history, yet with the fullest expression.

Finally, to say nothing of the rest: if you rightly consider, in the case of the one David, his place of birth, his pastoral office, the redness and beauty of his appearance, the manner of his anointing, the mark of his virtues, the weight of his tribulations, and the glory of the kingdom once promised him, you will see how many mysteries of evangelical faith and truth have been gathered into each of these details. But these matters will be explained more fully in their proper place. Now I shall undertake the work assigned to me in due order, trusting only in heavenly assistance and following in the footsteps of the Fathers.

And if, as I desire, my labor proves useful and beneficial to many, I hope that the Lord will grant me a great reward together with them. If not, nevertheless my diligence will not be able to prove fruitless, since it does not allow me, for so long a time, to remain idle in this labor or to indulge my mind in pointless matters. Come, then, let us see what the prophet Samuel, who spoke and announced these days, made the beginning of his speaking and announcing. Proceeding in order, with the help of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, who fully taught what things must be adapted to which days, let us seek how each detail is to be fitted to those same days.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0499]

## CHAPTER ONE

One man, Elkanah, in Ramathaim, has two wives: Peninnah, abounding in sons, and Hannah, mourning the reproach of barrenness.

[Col. 0499D]

### Chapter 1

> There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim … Elkanah, etc.

The first reading of the blessed Samuel typologically designates one and the same Lord Christ, who must always be believed to be the Redeemer and Ruler both of the Synagogue and of the Church. One woman boasts of the righteousness of the law and the abundance of her believing offspring; the other mourns, in humble devotion toward the mercy of that same Redeemer, the injuries of her long desolation, and therefore, loving him in return, breathes again through the exalted consolation of her Redeemer.

Ramathaim, as we find in books concerning places, is a city in the region of Thannitis, near Diospolis, from which Joseph came—the man who is called “of Arimathea” in the Gospels. Zophim, however, is a mountain of Ephraim at Ramathaim, which the old edition rendered as Armathem. Ramathaim is interpreted as “the lofty place of them”; Zophim as “watchtower”; Ephraim as “fruitful” or “increasing”; and Elkanah as “possession of God.”

Thus there was one man from “the lofty place of them,” that is, from the watchtower of men, from the fruitful and increasing mountain, and his name was “possession of God.” One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God (Eph. IV), who always possesses as his own and consecrates a dwelling in the spiritual hearts of the faithful. They have passed beyond earthly conduct and desire with the whole effort of their mind to contemplate the heavenly light of wisdom; they possess that mountain which, after the destruction of worldly power, grew through the fruitfulness of believing peoples and filled the whole earth.

Of this mountain the Psalmist says:

> He answered me from his holy mountain (Ps. III),

that is, “He redeemed me through the man whom he uniquely received as holy.” This one man, namely Christ the man, explaining his own name, says:

> The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his ways (Prov. VIII).

This should also be noted according to the literal sense, because it was not written without reason or unnecessarily, “There was one man,” when “There was a man from Ramathaim” might have seemed sufficient—or it might more suitably have been said, “There was a certain man,” as some have dared to interpret it contrary to the truth of the Hebrew text.

But the addition “one” refers to the title of Elkanah’s praise. In accordance with the Apostle’s exhortation (Eph. IV), he was steadfast and immovable, abundant in the work of the Lord, and never carried about by every wind of doctrine. For:

> The wise man remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon (Ecclus. XXVII).

Such men are also most aptly called “possession of God,” since they are placed upon the lofty watchtower of the mind and rejoice in the fruitful summit of virtues.

Not only is any one of the perfected in Christ rightly called “one man”; rather, among the multitude of believers there was one heart and one soul (Acts IV), imitating, according to their measure, him to whom it is said:

> But you are the same (Ps. CI).
