The reprobate, by contrast, are many not only because they are numerous in persons or sin through various errors, but also because each individual among them is many, on account of the many-sided movement of a changing mind. For:

> The heart of fools will be unlike itself, and a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways (Prov. XI; Jas. I).

Hence the cities in whose service they labor are themselves called, in one case, “confusion”—that is, Babylon, of the Chaldeans, meaning “the fierce” or “as if demons”—and in the other, “vision of peace.” The craftsman and founder of the latter is that one man of whom it is said:

> Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one (Deut. VI).

This is the choir of those who are of one mind in the house, singing:

> One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps. XXVI).

And his name, he says, was Elkanah, etc. The names of Elkanah’s fathers disclose the life, faith, virtues, and exalted state of those in whom and through whom the Lord is accustomed to be spiritually born—that is, those through whose action or influence faith and love of him are infused into hearts in which they were not previously present.

For Hieroam means “merciful”; Heliu, “my God is he”; Thau, “sign”; Suph, “watcher”; and Ephrateus, “fertile” or “dusty.”

He taught that the life of the saints is greatly strengthened by mercy when he said:

> Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you (Luke XI).

Those who believe that they have been redeemed through Christ’s incarnation rightly confess him as their God, because his eternal Father, the Lord of heaven and earth, from the time of the assumed humanity also began to be his God. Hence he says:

> From my mother’s womb you are my God (Ps. XXI).

He also testifies that the virtues and works of the saints were signs of the one who was to come, teach, and do what was fitting in the flesh of Christ, when he himself says:

> In the hands of the prophets I was likened (John V).

And speaking of Moses in the Gospel:

> For he wrote about me.

But if the sons of Thau are read as “of the testament” or “of the one who wanders,” this name also suits their virtues, since they know how to say:

> Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you;

and:

> We are fools for Christ (II Cor. V; I Cor. I).

Finally, Paul, standing in chains before worldly judges, because after receiving the ability to speak he was pleading not about the bonds with which he was externally burdened but about the confidence of the virtues in which he gloried inwardly, heard:

> You are mad, Paul; your many writings are driving you to madness (Acts XXVI).

And the Savior himself says to the Father:

> God, you know my foolishness (Ps. LXVIII).

In the Gospel, his relatives wanted to bind him as though he were beside himself, while his adversaries reproached him for having a demon (John XVII).

The mind of the elect, a watcher of heavenly joys, is solitary, and, ignorant of the joy of that life, has learned to contemplate nothing. In the breast, therefore, and from the mouth or work of such people, the Savior is always brought forth in faith, hope, and charity. He deigned for a time to be called and to appear both “dusty” and “fertile,” when, taking upon himself the frailty of the flesh, he bore our sins in his body upon the wood. By the singular fruitfulness of that same sacrifice, he destroyed the kingdom of death and opened for us forever the entrance to life.

But according to the historical sense we must observe that Elkanah is called an Ephratean [Col. 0502D] not because he was from the tribe of Ephraim, but because he was born in a city belonging to that tribe. For the Books of Chronicles report that he was a Levite—that is, from the sons of Isaac, son of Kohath, son of Levi (II Chron. VI).

And he had two wives, etc. Hannah, whose name means “his grace,” signifies the Church; Peninnah, whose name means “conversion,” signifies the Synagogue. Hannah is rightly first and Peninnah second, because the earliest ages of the world possessed saints who, while living a life like ours, pleased God by the righteousness of faith alone, without the ceremonies of legal sacrifices, Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and various purifications. They hoped to be saved solely by Christ’s grace, from the time when his incarnation had been disclosed to the Fathers. Only afterward did the Synagogue’s celebrated conversion from Egypt to the Lord occur.

And Peninnah had sons, etc. From the time when she was betrothed to the Lord, the Synagogue has never ceased to beget spiritual sons for him through teaching. The Gentile world, although it itself never ceased to submit to his grace in certain people, though few, could not beget through preaching children who would live spiritually, because it had not deserved to receive openly either his testament, his prophecies, or the oracles of the angels.

And that man went up from his city on appointed days, etc. The Lord went up from the common life of the faithful. For:

> This is the city of our God, on his holy mountain (Ps. XXVII);

that is, among his saints who advance and ascend from virtue to virtue, so that on appointed days—namely, through each increase of divine knowledge—he might kindle their hearts to offer the libations of good worship and good works. These are offered in the keeping of the divine law, in which alone all sins can be forgiven to the humble, and the feet of those who always keep their eyes upon the Lord can be drawn out of the snare. There alone the one who says, “I am who I am,” must and can be sought and found.

Thus Shiloh is appropriately interpreted as “removal,” “release,” or “where he himself is.” It signifies that very law which, in its justice, rightly commands those who make good progress:

> Seek his face continually (Ps. CIV).

Now there were two sons of Eli, etc. Eli means “my God”; Hophni, “barefoot”; Phinehas is said to mean “mute mouth.” Thus, as the time of the Lord’s incarnation approached, there were priests consecrated to the Lord, good in the law of the priesthood and sons of priests who believed rightly, but deprived of the grace of the action and preaching required of them. They possessed neither an open office of the mouth for teaching nor the adornment of upright steps for walking in the way without blemish.

Then the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed. When the shadow of the law had passed, the light of the new grace came, and the possession of God—namely, Christ visible in the flesh—taught human beings heavenly things and likewise granted them to love, hope for, and believe in them.

For he is said to do what he grants his own to do, as the Apostle testifies:

> For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure.

And the Spirit himself intercedes for us with ineffable groanings (Phil. II; Rom. VIII), because he makes us intercede and groan by his grace.

Therefore, above, when Elkanah ascended, worshiped, and sacrificed, we rightly understood him as the one who established ascents in the hearts of the blessed, in the valley of tears, and teaches them to worship and to persist in good works.

And he gave to Peninnah his wife, etc. The Lord, suffering in the flesh and calling human beings to divine things, gave to the Synagogue and to all within it who believed in and feared him—both the small and the great—various works of virtue and distributions of grace.

To the Church of the Gentiles, however, which at that time existed in only a few believers—for example, the centurion and the Syrophoenician woman, and those others who, going up to worship in the temple on the feast day, said to Philip, “Lord, we wish to see Jesus” (John II)—he granted only the gift of faith. He delayed for a time giving the grace of charismatic gifts.

And she acted sadly, because he knew what sort of church she would become and had praised her faith in the centurion and in the aforementioned woman; he loved her, although by the counsel of heavenly goodness she had still been delayed from receiving the mysteries of that same faith.

Therefore, when the hour of the passion was approaching, he said:

> My soul is sorrowful even to death (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

He did not say “sorrowful because of death,” but “even to death,” because he knew that through that very death he would destroy the one who held the power of death, and after death he rejoiced that he would reach the salvation of the Gentiles.

Her rival also afflicted her, etc. The Synagogue afflicted the Gentile world, reproaching it for having been neglected by God because of its great crimes, and for not having deserved either God’s conversation or the oracles of the prophets, through which offspring of souls acceptable to God might be begotten. Thus the womb of its mind was deprived of the spiritual seed of heavenly virtues and believing peoples.

And so she did this year by year, etc. The temple of the Lord, which remained at Shiloh until those times, is called the tabernacle of testimony. Understand the years as individual virtues by which the Synagogue advanced in the house of the Lord and, accusing the Gentiles of being far from it, provoked them to weeping. Or, certainly, understand them as the long periods of the law that had been given.

When reading the sacred Scripture, you will find that, when Israel went out from Egypt—when the time had come, so to speak, for the Synagogue to be betrothed to God—a considerable crowd of resident aliens also came with it, to be consecrated and joined to the Lord through the legal mysteries. From that time until the time of the Lord’s incarnation, there was never a lack there of those who rightly believed.

But in every respect they were so few and so poor—being resident aliens, strangers, and despised people in comparison with the whole nation dwelling in its ancestral land—that, weeping at the Lord’s feet and being less able to receive the food of spiritual joy and the living bread that came down from heaven, they were content at least to hope for and request, like little dogs, the crumbs falling from the Lord’s table.

Then Elkanah her husband said to her: Hannah, why are you weeping? etc. The ten sons signify those who receive or observe the law of the Decalogue.

The Lord therefore consoles the Church, so that it may not grieve because it has not received, as the Synagogue did, the legislation of the law, its promises and covenant, or the oracles of God entrusted to it. Rather, it should be renewed and rejoice with the greatest joy because it has already deserved to receive, in place of all these things, a greater gift and a better grace: the advent of the Mediator of God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, whom it did not know how to await or hope for.

This reading, however, figuratively expresses not only the differing condition of the two peoples, but also the differing merits of the persons who disagree within each people, and the differing rewards of those merits. For Christ always has loved—and will love—the humble tears of penitents more than the rigid righteousness of the proud. He disregards the Pharisee’s arrogance, by which he exalts himself as fertile with the offspring of ten sons because he has fulfilled the commandments of the law, and instead deigns to look upon the bent-over lamentation of the tax collector.

## CHAPTER II

Hannah, amid prayers and tears, vows to the Lord that, if she receives a son, he will be a Nazirite; and when Eli the priest blesses her, she returns home with her household.

Now Hannah rose, etc. This reading typologically displays the devoted humility of the holy Church. Some of the Jewish teachers insult it, while others assent to the faith; and the Church itself desires either that Christ be spiritually born through faith among its own people, or that its own people be spiritually reborn in Christ.

Now Hannah rose, etc. The Church rose from the long sorrow of its desolation after receiving confidence to entreat the Lord. Once nourished by his most holy body and inebriated by the cup of his precious blood—and while the teachers still remained in Judaism, as though in the soil, and the ministers of the ancient priesthood still sat upon Moses’ chair, guarding the entrance to the kingdom of heaven so that they themselves might enter and teach those who wished to enter—the Church itself began through tears and prayers to seek from the Lord gifts which, before the mysteries of his incarnation were known or received, it had been unable to anticipate.

And Hannah made a vow, etc. The Church vows that, if the word is entrusted to the nations, the grace of faith is granted, and a people strong in virtues arises from them, this people will serve the Lord until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled and will never, after the example of the Jews, bend its knee to Baals, Astartes, or the other idols of the nations.

But if you understand the days allegorically as virtues, the Church gives all the days of its life to the Lord. Whatever honorable thing it lives, whatever radiant thing it performs in mind or body, it does not attribute to itself, but professes with the Apostle:

> By the grace of God I am what I am (I Cor. XV).

And no razor shall come upon his head. The reproach of sin will not violate his conscience. Rather, insofar as is possible for a human being, he strives, like a true Nazirite, to consecrate to Christ all his thoughts, words, and actions, which emerge gradually from the brain of the heart as though from the head.

Finally, because the apostles are holy, not one of their hairs can perish from their heads (Luke XXI). But the unclean leper, the woman captured by enemies, and others of this kind are commanded to shave not only all their hair but also the hair of their entire body, because they are wicked and polluted. Thus, after the superfluous frivolity of mortal actions has been cut away, whatever living perfection is found in them may be consecrated more freely to its author.

We say this not because we believe that any saint passed through this life without the stain of sin, or that the words “Everything he does will prosper” (Ps. I) apply to anyone other than Christ. Rather, we say it because we must all strive to serve the Lord in holiness and righteousness before him all our days (Luke I), according to the one who said:

> I have sworn and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness (Ps. CXVIII).

Nor is it proclaimed without reason elsewhere:

> Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight (Ps. CXLII).

Therefore these words of Hannah may more truly be understood as spoken by the Church about the Lord himself. The Church always desires him to be generated by the grace of a new virtue in the breast of itself and of its members. For he alone truly, since he lived in the flesh without sin, was given to the Lord all the days of his life; he found nothing at all in himself that required cutting away through repentance.

And it came to pass, when she multiplied her prayers, etc. When the Church began to multiply throughout the world, the new signs of its devotion also multiplied. Its praise comes not from human beings but from God, so that the Jewish priests examined its outward deeds to determine whether it lived like a Gentile or like a Jew.

But the Church, gradually abandoning Judaism and following only the mysteries of the faith that purifies hearts, rejoiced to please the invisible Christ through the wisdom of faith.

And only her lips moved, etc. This is plainly an ecclesiastical action, and one most worthy of divine regard; it preceded even the Lord’s exhortation by its devotion:

> Enter into your room and, after closing the door, pray to your Father in secret (Matt. VI).

Therefore Eli thought her drunk, etc. The pride of the Jewish priesthood considered the converted Gentile world still weighed down by the confusion of sins and said to it:

> How long will you remain guilty, held by the bond of original sin? Purify yourself through circumcision, and thus be saved among the number of proselytes.

Hannah answered, “Not so, my lord,” etc. The Church from the Gentiles answered:

> Not so, O priest of Judea. Do not think me burdened with sins, for through the font of baptism and participation in the sacred body and blood I have already been purified and have become inwardly the temple of Christ. I delight in the law of God according to the inner person (Rom. VII). I am no longer sinful, but I am nevertheless your very unhappy handmaid. I rightly call you lord, because you preceded me by so ancient a time of election.

> Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ (ibid.).

For this reason, reclining at his sacred feet, I have poured out before his merciful presence, through tears, my soul melted by the fire of love.

Do not count your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial, etc. Do not compare me with souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. Repenting of my sins with my whole heart, I have renounced Satan and all his works and pomps. Moreover, I have diligently taken up the exceedingly gentle yoke of Christ, which he once proudly threw from his neck; for this reason he deserved to be called Belial, that is, “without a yoke.”

Then Eli said to her: Go in peace, etc. The one whom he had previously branded as drunk he now blesses after accepting the sanctification of her action. The jealous chief priests, mocking the Church’s salutary beginnings as resembling the behavior of drunkards, despised them. Yet some of them later learned the divine will concerning these things, assented to believers, and took care to offer assistance. Many of those who said that the apostles, speaking in the Holy Spirit, were full of new wine (Acts II), after hearing the reasoning of the truth, received in faith the mystery they had previously mocked.

And the woman went her way, and ate, etc. The Church advanced in the hope of heavenly mercy, raised up in faith and love of Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. Nourished by the consoling and strengthening food of sacred Scripture, it could thereafter be changed by no pressures or flatteries into the various errors of those who had once recognized the true God.

> You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me (Ps. XXII).

And they rose in the morning and worshiped, etc. The progress of the growing Church is shown. At first Hannah alone rises to pray, and the hour at which she prayed is not stated. Now, after receiving the priest’s blessing, she rises in the morning, no longer alone but with her husband and her entire household, and persists in prayer.

At first the Church sought the Lord among a few; but when it had received from believing Jewish teachers an increase of faith, the darkness of the Gentile world having been dispelled, it said:

> From the ends of the earth I cried out to you (Ps. LX).

Such an abundance of heavenly grace overflowed that, while praying to the Lord—namely, to her husband—it is not doubted that she has him as an advocate with the Father.

And they returned and came, etc. Ramah is interpreted as “height.” Therefore, once our prayer has been completed, so that we may obtain what we have requested and, after the mournful barrenness of an unproductive mind, may be able to bring forth the shoots of virtues by consecrating them to God, let us strive to return not to pointless outward activities but to dwellings exalted by the faith and truth of our conscience.

Let our face no longer be turned in different directions, but let it persevere in the same expression it assumed in prayer, even after the tears, with the ardor of exhaustion and devotion.

## CHAPTER III

Hannah calls the son born to her Samuel; after he is weaned, she also dedicates him forever to the Lord with gifts and sacrifices.

Now Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, etc. In this reading the Church dedicates its sons, conceived through faith, born through baptism, weaned through instruction, and commended by the gift of sincere conduct, to the fellowship of catholic unity, which derives its origin from believing Jews, and indeed to the Lord himself, who rules the Church, so that they may serve throughout all the days of their life.

Elkanah therefore knew his wife, etc. The Lord took pity on the Church of the Gentiles, to enrich it through his grace. Having sent the seed of his word through preachers, he commanded all the ends of the earth to remember and turn back to him.

And it came to pass, after the cycle of days, that Hannah conceived, etc. After the illumination of abundant spiritual knowledge and the display of virtues with which the apostles flashed throughout the world, the Gentile world conceived through catechesis and gave birth through baptism to a people believing in God—indeed, to a people in whom God was believed.

Both points must rightly be affirmed, not only because of the reasoning of faith and truth, but also because the name Samuel itself makes them clear. For it is interpreted as “there is God himself” or “his name is God.”

“There is God himself” in the people who will be born, whom [Col. 0508A] the Lord made. “His name is God”—whose name, indeed, except that of the one who wished to signify that he would always be born in his own people through grace, when he said:

> Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother (Matt. VII).

Nor should it seem strange to anyone that we have said that both the husband and the son of the same Hannah bear the type of Christ. For the same Mediator of God and human beings is both the bridegroom and the son of the holy Church, which he governs: bridegroom, because he continually assists it to believe, hope, and love; son, because recently he came by grace into the hearts of believers, those who hope, and those who love.

And the man Elkanah went up, etc. Let each person abound in his own understanding (Rom. XIV). The Lord and the Church of the perfected, which is his house and seat, went up to offer to the Father who is in heaven the vows of their works. The Church still remains at home in those who are not yet able to partake of solid food of the word. Some, having received the rudiments of faith, still remain childish in understanding (Heb. V).

But the time will come when they too will be nourished and, with the grace of Christ dwelling with them, will begin to possess trained senses for discerning good and evil. Then they will say with the Apostle:

> When I became a man, I put away childish things (I Cor. XIII).

Then they will be worthy of the Lord’s presence. Remaining in the calling in which they were called before God, they will be able both to attend upon the priests and to eat what belongs to the altar; they will also be able to hear of the summit of the divine nature and, as they read, to discern the mysteries.

Such is the progress of all who believe in Christ. Such were the beginnings of the converted Gentile world among Jews who were learned and teachers, as though among the sons of Peninnah.

And she brought him with her after she had weaned him, etc. The Church brings forward its sons, to whom it had rationally and without deceit given milk, and whom it had advanced by educating them from the childish rudiments of the new human being toward greater perfection.

It brings forward, I say, those whom, with the assisting grace of Christ, it has made strong in understanding, for association with those who had already become the temple of God through observance of the divine law.

It brings them forward in three persons: the married, the continent, and the teachers. By the purity of their lives they are suited to divine sacrifices; they possess bodies prepared to die for Christ, a contrite heart humbled by the millstone of fear and hope, and, already inebriated by a sober cup, they embrace with an undivided mind the fervent love of spiritual grace.

Since an amphora is a kind of measure, it indicates the measure of love by which each person is commanded to love his neighbor as himself. Since it contains three measures, it is rightly applied to the three aforementioned persons, by whom the whole Church is constituted.

But the boy was still very young, etc. The people of the Gentiles had recently been converted to the faith, and they produced not a few martyrs who poured out their blood for Christ with unanimous devotion. They grafted the wild olive onto the good olive. These things were done by the ministers of the word.

And they worshiped the Lord there. The Church carries out under the figure of Hannah the command that the Lord gives to pray without ceasing and not grow weary (I Thess. V). It does not cease to entreat the Lord at the beginning of its vows, in its progress, or in their very completion.

## CHAPTER IV

Hannah, worshiping in the tabernacle with her husband, speaks a hymn of thanksgiving to the Lord.

### Chapter IV

#### “My heart rejoiced in the Lord,” etc.

The Church, once barren but now fruitful, rejoicing in the praise of God, sounds forth a triumphant song over the change from the Old Testament, or priesthood, to the New, by which she herself has also been consecrated. Yet, according to the literal sense, it must be asked how Anna is remembered to have said this while praying, since in her entire song she is found not to have prayed at all, nor even to have addressed words to God except in only two places: “Because I have rejoiced in your salvation”; and below, “For there is none besides you,” and so forth. In all the rest she appears to speak either by teaching, prophesying, or praising the Lord.

It must therefore be plainly understood that all her actions, in which she is engaged in divine service, and all that she does or says according to God, are to be counted as adoration. For if prayer is understood to mean only what we commonly know by that name, Anna will not appear to have prayed in these words, nor will any of the righteous pray without ceasing, according to the Apostle’s command. But if all the actions of the righteous person who lives according to God are considered prayers—because the righteous person unceasingly does what is righteous—then, by this very fact, the righteous person will pray without ceasing and will never cease from prayer unless he ceases to be righteous. Thus Samuel’s mother is not without reason said to have adored even in those things that she rightly speaks to human beings.

Let the joyful mother therefore sing with open mouth, she who earlier spoke with a bitter spirit in her heart; and while she recounts her own present circumstances, let her foretell in advance the future joys of the whole Church.

#### “My heart rejoiced in the Lord,” etc.

Truly her heart rejoices, and truly she has the horn of the spiritual kingdom exalted, since she glories neither in herself nor in things transient and fragile, but in the Lord her God. This agrees with him who says: “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Psalm 74). He does not say, “He himself will break them; he himself has exalted them,” but, “I will break them, and so they will be exalted.”

#### “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies,” etc.

As my heart is enlarged to rejoice in Jesus—that is, in your salvation—so my mouth is enlarged over all the enemies of faith and truth, to confess and proclaim his name. For even in the straits of affliction, your word is not bound, nor is it bound in those who proclaim it.

#### “There is none holy like the Lord,” etc.

We read of angels and human beings as holy and strong. But however much a creature may advance in holiness, and however great a degree of perfection it may acquire, it cannot be so holy and strong as the Creator, because he is the giver of strength and holiness, while the creature receives them. When she says, “For there is none besides you,” and does not add “Creator,” “Lord,” or anything similar, she designates his eternal existence in a singular manner. The Psalmist distinguishes this existence from the frailty of creation when he says: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 108).

#### “Do not multiply lofty words, boasting,” etc.

This is said to Jews and Gentiles: Let it have been enough up to now for you to have taken pride in your supposedly unique glory. Now, having passed beyond the letter of the Law through grace and trampled underfoot the errors of the nations through the truth of the Gospel, receive together the New Testament of Christ, both the faith and the commandment of love.

The same command is given to us: to speak lofty things, but not to multiply lofty words while boasting. That is, we are to think about and seek what is above, not what is on earth; yet we must not think more highly than we ought to think, but think with sober judgment (Colossians 3; Romans 12). Gentiles are commanded to speak lofty things by proclaiming the mysteries of the one true God, and not to multiply lofty utterances by wandering among the many names of deceivers.

#### “For the Lord is God of knowledge,” etc.

Therefore it is necessary for you not to seek things too high for you and not to investigate matters too difficult for you (Ecclesiastes 3), because the Lord is the fountain and treasure of wisdom and knowledge, the one who teaches human beings knowledge: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93).

#### “The bow of the mighty has been overcome,” etc.

The proud intention of the Jews, by which they had always presumed that they could be saved through the works of the Law, has failed. The practice of dialectical art, and the loquacity of secular philosophy—bent, as it were, upon mocking the simplicity of faith—has been enervated. Finally, all the flaming darts of evil spirits have been blunted against the weapons of unconquered truth, because “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 2).

#### “Those who were previously full have hired themselves out for bread,” etc.

The Jews, previously nourished by the living bread of the Scriptures, now hunger within themselves at the banquet of the good father who graciously received back his younger son. While they conceal themselves among the spiritual feasts of the Church, they see former guests of the covenants now tasting and discovering that the Lord is sweet.

#### “Until the barren woman has borne very many,” etc.

Isaiah explains this: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband” (Isaiah 54). The Septuagint Translators rendered it: “Because the barren woman has borne seven.” For *Saba*—a Hebrew word—designates both “seven” and “many.” Yet the meaning of that edition also becomes clear when we recognize the number seven, by which the universal perfection of the Church is signified. For this reason the Apostle John also writes to seven churches (Revelation 1), thereby showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church. Solomon likewise prefigured this earlier in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house; she carved out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9).

#### “The Lord puts to death and gives life,” etc.

He puts the Synagogue to death and gives life to the Church; or he gives life to the very people whom he puts to death, so that we may understand ourselves to be dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus (Ephesians 2). Or certainly this should be understood according to what the Apostle says: “For we who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh” (2 Corinthians 4).

Better still, and without any controversy, we confess that this was fulfilled in the Lord: he died and lived again; descending to the underworld, he rose again.

#### “The Lord makes poor and makes rich,” etc.

Those whom in the present he makes poor and humble in spirit for his sake, he will in the future enrich in himself and raise up.

#### “He raises the needy from the dust,” etc.

He raises Christ from the dead, so that his flesh might not see corruption; and he lifts him to heaven, so that he might not be overcome by the Jewish persecutors, whose traditions the Apostle considers refuse (Colossians 3). For he himself became needy and poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might be enriched (2 Corinthians 8).

#### “To make him sit with princes,” etc.

He himself explains this verse when those whom he was making poor in order to enrich them, and humbling on earth in order to raise them in heaven, asked what reward they would have in the future. He answered: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Solomon likewise says in praise of the valiant woman—that is, the Church or the soul of any chosen person: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Proverbs 31).

#### “For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord,” etc.

He has not only set lofty promontories and rocks in place as a defense of the earthly world against the violence of the sea’s storms; much more, for preserving the stability of his Church, lest any wave of turbulent persecution overthrow her, he has established the firm and strong hearts of his faithful.

He therefore calls these same hinges, which bear up the world, “princes sitting upon thrones.” And rightly so: the more humbly they bear and the more earnestly they defend now, the more exaltedly they will judge then. Blessed Job also remembers that these hinges belong to the Lord and are not fortified by their own strength, saying of the Lord: “Under him those who bear up the world are bent.” In order to be able firmly to sustain the burdens of the weak, they never cease submitting their humble necks to unconquered strength (Job 9).

#### “He has guarded the feet of his holy ones,” etc.

He protects from the snares of the impious the deeds and understanding of the godly, by which they advance step by step, as it were, toward perfection. The impious themselves will perish in the dark contrivances that they spread for the good. Hence one of the saints, giving thanks to the Savior for his feet, sings: “I will rejoice in your salvation; the nations are fixed in the destruction that they made,” and so forth (Psalm 9).

#### “For a man will not be strengthened by his own might.”

This refers back to what precedes. Therefore the impious, who trust in their own strength and disdain to seek divine assistance, must be silent in darkness—that is, having at last been condemned for practicing blind ungodliness. For whoever rightly desires to be called a man will be strengthened not by his own strength but by the grace of his author.

#### “The Lord’s adversaries will fear him,” etc.

He openly foretells the fearful day of the strict and final judgment. Since the Lord’s adversaries will then fear him, it is necessary for us now, before seeing him, to fear him humbly, so that then we may rejoice when his majesty is revealed. Even today the Lord thunders against the obstinacy of the wicked from the lofty and luminous pages of Holy Scripture, which his Spirit has adorned.

#### “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.”

It is certain that the Lord will judge not only the ends of the earth but also the regions lying between them. Thus it is said, “He will judge the ends of the earth,” as though it meant, “Even the ends of the earth,” because “there is no one who can hide from his heat” (Psalm 18).

But it is better understood as referring to the ends of the earth—that is, the final times either of each individual human being or of the whole world—because whatever condition a person has when he departs from the body, in that condition he will be presented for the examination of the strict Judge.

#### “And he will give power to his king,” etc.

After the ordeal of the final examination, Christ’s kingdom—which unbelievers now despise—will be displayed in majesty, with the glory of his divinity revealed. The horn of Christ may appropriately be understood not only as the horn of the only-begotten Son of God but also as that of each of his chosen ones.

Thus, at the beginning of this same hymn, by which throughout she wonderfully commends the grace of God according to her name, she says: “My horn has been exalted in my God.” For we rightly call all those anointed with his chrism “christs.” Yet, together with their head, they constitute one Christ: now, in part, a pilgrim on earth; then, in his entirety, to be exalted in the heavenly homeland. Recall the hymn of blessed Mary (Luke 1), and observe what similar things the prophet, the mother and Lord, the woman and virgin, understood concerning the judgments and grace of God.

## Chapter V

### The sons of Eli profane the priestly office; the boy Samuel ministers before the Lord, girded with a linen ephod; and, with Eli’s blessing, Anna is made fruitful with sons.

#### “And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house,” etc.

This reading teaches that, after the incarnation of the Lord, when the teachers of the Jews had declined into worse things, the great deeds of the same Lord and Savior were to be proclaimed throughout the whole world in the Church.

#### “So Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house,” etc.

Once the Church of the Gentiles had been called to faith—which, we have said, is signified by the birth of blessed Samuel—the possession of God, Christ, who is his coeternal Wisdom, went forth to illumine, as always, the lofty hearts of his holy faithful, angels and human beings alike, which are his houses, erected with greatest strength upon the rock of faith against the gates of hell.

The people themselves, called to faith, while the Jewish priesthood also looked on and marveled, served Christ’s commands humbly, as though they had always been contemplating him.

#### “Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial,” etc.

The sons of the Jewish priesthood—sons of blind light, or “without a yoke” (for both meanings are conveyed by *Belial* or *Beliar*)—were all those who did not know Christ’s teaching and followed not the commands of divine law but the statutes of their own traditions.

#### “Whoever sacrificed a victim, the priest’s boy came,” etc.

Whoever at that time resolved to consecrate his life to the Lord was approached by the disciples of the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests, while the carnal habits of such a person were beginning to be refined by the fire of heavenly devotion. They had a rapacious desire for the world in their actions. Describing its three-pronged bite, the Apostle John says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2).

They thrust examples, and even teachings, of earthly desire into the heart of any listener—whether teachable or of slower and narrower understanding, weak and fragile, enduring adversity, eloquent in speech, or rustic and less sonorous. These differing qualities are compared to vessels of lesser or greater size, whether iron, bronze, or earthenware.

Polluting by their most evil touch the small warmth of divine love that each person had newly conceived, they did not await the reward for preaching established by the Law. Instead, they compelled the people to make for them the offering of obedience that was owed to God. With this thoroughly wicked fork even now those who, after receiving the mystery of faith—or even the ministry of the word—seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, touch the sacred offerings in the Church.

#### “Even before they burned the fat,” etc.

The wickedness of Pharisaic deception advanced so far that, even before they taught that the rich offering of love most pleasing to God should be presented—that offering which, above all other sacrifices of virtue, ought to be immolated uniquely upon the altar of the heart—they placed their own service before divine worship.

They told their wretched hearers to consume not the enticements of their carnal desires with the flame of heavenly charity, worthy of God, but to expend them, insufficiently disciplined and according to their own pleasure, in carnal observances, to the insult of the Creator. These wicked men communicated this to their hearers not by words but by their deeds. Would that we did not know that similar things are done even today by teachers and priests of the Church.

#### “The sin of the boys was exceedingly great,” etc.

The sin of the scribes and Pharisees was exceedingly great before the Lord, although before human beings they justified themselves through hypocrisy (Luke 11). Though they themselves were human beings, they annulled God’s commandment through their traditions. Or, certainly, they took away the key of knowledge: they themselves did not enter, and they prevented those who wished to enter.

But if the boys sinned exceedingly greatly before the Lord by handling the flesh of animal victims unworthily, what punishment do you think those deserve who, with childish folly, trample upon the Son of God and regard the blood of the eternal covenant as polluted (Hebrews 10)? They receive the sacrament but do not discern the Lord’s body (1 Corinthians 11)—that is, they do not distinguish the mystery of heavenly life from the consumption of common and base foods.

#### “But Samuel ministered before the face of God,” etc.

In Hebrew, *ephod* is called in Latin a *superhumerale* or *superindumentum*, an “over-shoulder garment” or “over-garment.” Scripture in Exodus records that a garment of this name, woven from gold, hyacinth-blue, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted linen, was granted to the high priests alone (Exodus 25).

Yet examples testify that the same garment, when made of linen, could be used by priests, Levites, and others: here by Samuel, who was a Levite; later by the priests whom Saul killed; and by David when he danced before the ark of the Lord. For there could not have been eighty-five high priests in succession; priests of a lower rank must also have existed.

In its typological meaning, the ephod of varied color displays in many ways the grace of virtues in a holy man. Linen, however, since it is produced from the earth and reaches its beauty through long cultivation, signifies the most radiant mortification of chaste flesh.

Samuel therefore ministered before the face of the Lord, a boy girded with a linen ephod. Christ, humble in humanity, ministered to our weakness, always bearing a body and soul entirely cleansed from every stain of vice. For he did not sin and did no evil before the Lord: “He was conceived without iniquity, and his mother bore him without sin.” The Christian people minister to Christ by crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires, chastising their body, and subjecting it to servitude.

#### “And his mother made him a little tunic.”

The Lord assumed not only flesh that was chaste and free from every sin, but also flesh humble in every respect. The Church makes this tunic for him, or the person who rightly and healthfully believes him to be such; alternatively, the virgin—who is not an insignificant member of the Church and from whom he himself was born—shines forth in this figure.

#### “Which she brought to him on appointed days,” etc.

The Church, never deserted by Christ, whom she has with her secretly all the days until the consummation of the age, ascends on the solemn days of the Mass to offer sacrifice and carries with her the mysteries of his flesh and blood in wine and bread.

She also makes a garment of humility for the people whom the Church bears to Christ. She brings this garment with her through the growth of individual virtues, advancing with the grace of Christ toward higher things, so that she may return vows of thanksgiving to the Father of lights.

This is the wedding garment which, according to the Gospel parable (Matthew 22), everyone who enters the solemn celebration of the heavenly kingdom must possess. The Son himself of the great King, the author and consecrator of spiritual marriage, first put it on. Coming forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Ezekiel 40; Philippians 2). This tunic, small in outward form but great in virtue, he did not permit those from whom he suffered death to tear even at the time of his death, because he preserved in death the very example of humility by which he reached death.

#### “And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife,” etc.

Priests of the Jews who were converted to the faith blessed Christ and his Church. Of them it is written: “A great number of priests were also obedient to the faith.” The old priesthood, in many of its types, signifies that the Church is to be blessed in Christ and multiplied among the nations through the seed of the word. In a figurative manner it speaks to Christ: “May God the Father grant you believers from the Gentiles.” They are the seed which the Lord blessed.

This is for the interest on the loan that you lent to the Lord—that is, for that uniquely holy man whom, taken from a virgin, you wished to have share with you one person, namely, the name of Christ, which is God. For if the Lord had not received the holy pledge, no one would have thought that seed could be hoped for from a barren woman.

That is: if a human being glorified by God did not sit at the Father’s right hand, wretched Gentile humanity, conscious of its transgression, could in no way have attained the multiplication of Abraham’s seed. But when Christ, the firstfruits of the human race, was lent to God the Father, his example gave believers hope of being saved through him, living in him, dying for him, being raised by him, and reigning with him forever.

It may also be said that the Church earned seed from the Lord as interest on what she had lent him, since, on behalf of the people whom she presented as faithful and devoted to the Lord, she received greater gifts of faith and devotion through preachers sent throughout the world. Those nations, however, which, after hearing the word of God, neglected to obey it could not possess the multiplication of the holy seed, because they had given the Lord no interest on his word, having rejected the teachers from themselves.

#### “So the Lord enriched Anna,” etc.

The Lord gave the Church the Spirit of his grace. Made fruitful by him, she bore spiritual offspring: some capable of investigating or proclaiming the mysteries of the Holy Trinity; others, in the simplicity of perfect love of God and neighbor, despised by the world. For the humility of the incarnation, assumed for a time by Christ, was held in great honor by the Father, by whom everyone who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14). Hence “their sound went out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

## Chapter VI

### The sons of Eli increase their sin, even despising their father’s admonitions; and Samuel, advancing in age and virtue, pleases both God and human beings.

#### “Now Eli was very old,” etc.

In this reading, as Judaism grows old and approaches its end, the fame of Christ increases through the Gospel. Eli’s great age therefore indicates that the time of the legal priesthood was near its completion. For what grows old and ages is near destruction.

#### “And he heard everything that his sons were doing,” etc.

The transgression of Eli’s sons was neither small nor of one kind: it was not afraid to stain both divine religion and love of neighbor. Above we read that, concerning the sacred flesh, they presumed to take not what had been established by the Law but whatever they pleased; that, before the sacred fat was burned for God, they presumed to take a portion of the sacrifice for themselves to eat; that they seized raw meat from those offering it so that they might prepare it more carefully for themselves; that they caused the Lord’s people to transgress; and—what is most horrifying—that they did all these things in contempt of the Creator.

Now a further offense injurious to brotherhood is added: they defiled the women of the people who gathered to pray. Below is attached the culmination of all their evils: even after being rebuked by their father, they did not repent. I have explained these matters more fully so that, reader, you may remember what to avoid in each case.

But what remains must be completed typologically. Priests and teachers must both keep watch in the Lord and rouse others to keep watch, saying: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15). Yet evil teachers sleep, and they sleep with the women who keep watch at the door of the tabernacle. When they entice unstable souls, they neither enter themselves nor permit those who wish to enter the door of life. Such was once the crime of the doomed Pharisaic faction; such it is now among false professors of the Christian religion.

#### “And he said to them: Why do you do such things?” etc.

He rebuked Eli’s delinquent sons, but they did not listen. The institution of the ancient priesthood itself commands its ministers to be perfect. Yet the wicked scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests despised the paternal voice of their Law and priesthood, which was destined to perish.

According to the literal sense, however, we must not overlook the fact that Eli did rebuke his sons; but because they despised his rebuke, he nevertheless failed to cast them out as he should have done, and he perished together with them. What punishment, then, do we wretched people, and those like us, deserve—people who rejoice in vices, who do not dare to correct them, who fear their own conscience, and who pretend not to know what the entire people cries out?

#### “If one man sins against another man,” etc.

Both parts refer to Eli’s sons. The priest sinned against a man when he violated another man’s wife, who had come for the sake of religion. God could have forgiven this, had worthy repentance followed. But not only this occurred: the priest sinned against the Lord in a still greater misery, when, contaminated by fornication, he approached the sacred mysteries of the altar—not merely to handle them unworthily, but as one unworthy to approach them at all.

A terrifying sentence indeed sounds against presumptuous people of this kind from Eli; but much more terrifying is the word of the Judge himself, who says: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12; Luke 12).

#### “But the boy Samuel advanced and grew,” etc.

As Eli grew old and declined, the boy Samuel advanced and grew. Rejection indeed takes place of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness—for the Law brought nothing to perfection—but the introduction of a better hope takes place, through which we draw near to God.

## Chapter VII

### A man of God comes to Eli and declares what will happen to his house because of the guilt of contempt.

#### “Now a man of God came to Eli,” etc.

This reading teaches, not through figurative representations of events but through the explicit words of prophecy, that the entire former priesthood descended from Aaron’s seed is to be changed into the new priesthood of Christ, which is now exercised in the Church.

#### “Was I not openly revealed?” etc.

This does not speak of Eli’s immediate father, who could not have been present during that Egyptian servitude, but of Aaron himself, to whose house he was revealed in Egypt and which, instructed by him, he placed before all the tribes of Israel by the right of the priesthood.

#### “And I gave to your father’s house everything,” etc.

I gave to the sons of Aaron, your father, everything from the sacrifices of the people that priests were permitted to receive, because I chose them for the priesthood.

#### “And you honored your sons more than me,” etc.

Not content with the portion that I granted you, you also attempted to take the firstfruits that were owed to me. This may be understood both of the time and of the portion of the sacrifices, since, before the fat was burned, they presumed to take for themselves the best portions to eat from the victims, as was read above.

#### “Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: Speaking, I spoke,” etc.

It is asked how what was promised to remain forever can be changed. Recall, however, that Aaron’s priesthood was a shadow of the eternal priesthood and that the promise concerned eternity. Understand, therefore, that the change belongs not to the shadow but to the reality represented by the shadow. For, lest you think that the shadow and figure itself was everlasting, its change also had to be prophesied.

The same understanding applies to what was said concerning Saul’s kingdom: “If you had not done this, the Lord would now have prepared your kingdom over Israel forever” (1 Samuel 13). This will be treated more appropriately in its own place.

#### “But now the Lord says: Far be this from me,” etc.

The Lord changes the times but does not change his purposes. He gathers from the Gentiles a spiritual priesthood for himself, and he deprives the sons of Aaron who despise him of the entire order of priestly office.

#### “Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm,” etc.

Those days are already at hand. No priest is now chosen from the stock of Aaron; the glory of the legal priesthood has been cut off—not merely in Eli but in the succession of the entire Levitical race. Thus one should suppose that not even a priest of the lesser order is to be sought there, one whom the Greeks call *presbyteros*, that is, “elder.”

For this reason the Septuagint Translators rendered it more plainly: “And you shall not have an elder in my house.” Countless people of that tribe grow old in bodily age, but in the house of the Lord they are not endowed with the rank of presbyter.

#### “And you will see your rival in the temple,” etc.

Your descendants will see the people of the Gentiles, beloved in the faith, making spiritual use in the temple of the Scriptures and promises of Israel.

#### “Nevertheless I will not utterly remove a man from you,” etc.

The sons of Aaron, although they sin very gravely in the killing of the Lord, are not denied the place of repentance. If any of them wish to come, let them come repentant to the Church and share in Christ’s altar, while the rest remain in the blindness of their faithlessness and envy. This exemplifies a gracious dispensation: although Eli perished with his sons, a man was not utterly removed from his line from the altar of the Lord. For in the days of Saul, Abias, grandson of Phinehas, Eli’s son, is recorded as having exercised the priesthood (3 Kings 13).

#### “And a great part of your house will die,” etc.

A great part of Eli’s house died upon reaching manhood, when, through the betrayal of Doeg the Idumean, eighty-five priests were slaughtered together in Saul’s fury (1 Samuel 22). Even today, when the greater part of the same house reaches the age of understanding, it loses the rewards of life by the sword of its own faithlessness.

#### “And this will be a sign for you,” etc.

These things concern Eli and Samuel. The death of the former’s sons and the election of the latter, who was not of Aaron’s lineage, signify not the death of human beings but the death of the old priesthood and the substitution of the new, in which Christ is eternally priest in the Church according to the order of Melchizedek.

When the Lord says, “who will act according to my heart and my soul,” do not suppose that God has a soul, since he is the creator of the soul. Rather, this is said figuratively, not literally, of God, just as are “hand,” “foot,” and the other members of the body. And lest anyone believe that human beings were made in the image of God according to the form of their flesh, other expressions are added that human beings certainly do not possess, as when one says to God: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16). Thus people may understand that such expressions are spoken of that ineffable nature not through proper terms but through transferred names drawn from created things.

#### “And I will build him a faithful house,” etc.

The faithful house built for the faithful priest upon a foundation of rock by a wise man is the Church. She has walked before Christ throughout all the days of her present life, and the gates of hell will never be able to impede her excellent progress.

Beautifully it says, “She will walk throughout all the days,” because when, after the course of passing days has been completed, one better day in her courts than thousands has come and he who gave the Law has bestowed blessing, this house has nothing further in which to advance as it walks from strength to strength. For it will see the God of gods in Zion, praise him in his blessed house—indeed, it will itself be that house forever.

It is not easy to understand this faithful house as having been built for Samuel, since his sons are reported to have turned aside after avarice and not to have walked in his ways. Unless perhaps his house is to be understood as the people whom he governed, concerning whom it is written: “And all the house of Israel rested after the Lord” (1 Samuel 7). The phrase “to walk before the anointed of the Lord” may be interpreted as referring to the Lord himself before Samuel, or to Samuel himself, Saul, or David [the phrasing is uncertain].

#### “It will happen that whoever remains in your house,” etc.

Every day, some people—not only from the priestly tribe but also from every tribe of Israel—and, at the end of the world, all the remaining people of that nation, come to the Church so that, reconciled to God, they may offer, after rejecting the flesh of victims, the consuming and concise word of saving confession and the bread of spiritual sacrifice.

Silver signifies the word of the confession of faith; the coin signifies the brevity of that same confession, which is contained in the Creed. When this man of God, who is shown by his office to be a prophet, says, “Whoever remains in your house,” this is what Isaiah says: “The remnant will be saved” (Romans 12). Recalling Elijah’s words, the Apostle likewise says: “So also at the present time there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace” (Isaiah 11).

#### “And he will say, ‘Let me go, I beg you, to one priestly portion.’”

This signifies the very people who are glorious under Christ the priest, to whom Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2).

When he adds, “That I may eat a morsel of bread,” he elegantly expresses the very kind of sacrifice of which the priest himself says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world” (John 6). Since above he had said that he gave food from the sacrifices of the Old Testament to the house of Aaron, which had been the sacrifices of the Jews, he therefore says here that a morsel of bread is to be requested for eating: this is the sacrifice of Christians in the New Testament.

## Chapter VIII

### As Eli’s eyes grow dim, Samuel sleeps in the temple of the Lord; answering at the Lord’s fourth call, he learns what will happen to Eli and recounts it to him in the morning, having prophesied after a second divine revelation.

*(1 Samuel 3.)*

#### “Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli,” etc.

In this reading the Lord shows that the ceremonies of the legal priesthood, already corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees even before he completed them through his passion, must be changed in every respect. Soon Judea would believe in him and confess that God had visited his people.

#### “Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli,” etc.

The boy who was born for us in the flesh ministered his gifts to the early Church, in the sight of the Jewish priests, both through himself and through his disciples evangelizing. At that time the word of the Lord was precious because of its rarity, since “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew 9). There was no Pharisee, scribe, or priest who could disclose hidden visions and the sayings of the prophets to the people through clear exposition.

#### “It happened one day that Eli was lying in his place,” etc.

He calls it “the lamp of God” in accordance with Eli’s rank. By a proper symbolism we understand the old priesthood as the lamp: essential during the night under the shadow of the serving people, but destined to be removed as the day of the new grace dawned.

A lamp, shining at night only within closed houses, is unable to spread the rays of its brightness widely; but when the sun rises, it examines everything inside and outside so thoroughly that even the lamp’s own radiance becomes less useful—or rather, capable of being extinguished. Thus the Gospel is appropriately compared with the legal knowledge that shone only within the one house of Judea, as though enclosed inside, while the other Gentiles outside were weighed down by the horror of blind night. After illuminating Judea, the Gospel would also drive away the long shadows of the Gentiles.

The Apostle shows how the rising sun would conceal or even extinguish the lamp when, speaking of letter and spirit, he says: “For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if what is being brought to an end came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (1 Corinthians 3).

Eli therefore lay in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, so that he could not see the lamp of God. Before the dignity of the old priesthood and Law to which he was devoted was extinguished, it should have kept watch, stood firm in faith, acted manfully, and been strengthened in the time of the Lord’s Incarnation. Instead, declining from the vigor of its original condition, it languished as though wearied by old age, and had not yet perceived that its true meaning, fulfilled by Christ’s blood, had already been deprived of light to a very great extent by the *deuterōseis*—the Pharisaic traditions.

[Col. 0520A] “Now Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord,” etc. While preaching and administering spiritual things to mortals, the Lord fixed the mind’s eye, withdrawn from external things, upon contemplation of the highest and innermost light. For they say that the temple is so called from contemplating, since divine and heavenly mysteries are contemplated there; there is the ark of God, that is, the glory of the supreme Trinity, alone conscious of the whole divine secret. Hence he says in the Psalm: “I kept the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken” (Psalm XIII).

“And the Lord called Samuel,” etc. It is a difficult manner of speaking: how the Father, at the appointed time, calls the Son to know the secrets of his judgment, and how the Son answers that he is present—he who, born before time from the Father, says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matthew XI). And: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (John XVI). Yet Scripture often speaks of God in human fashion—or rather, God himself habitually speaks of himself in the Scriptures—according to the saying of the Gospel: “For I do not speak from myself, but as I hear I judge; and all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). Likewise in Genesis God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis I). Thus, when Samuel was called by the Lord, he answered: “Here I am.”

“And he ran to Eli,” etc. Christ, called by the Father—who was always in the Father—to contemplate the perpetual wonders of his majesty, answers that by his eternal presence he remains divinely with the Father. Meanwhile, his humanity suddenly appearing in the flesh speaks to the teachers of the Jews: “I myself, whom you have been seeking for so long, and whose coming in the flesh you desired; I who was repeatedly called by the prayers and vows of the faithful for the salvation of the world—I myself have come, I who was speaking. Behold, I am here.”

“He said, ‘I did not call,’” etc. The scribes and Pharisees deny that they had sought the coming of Christ. When they heard of his birth, not only was King Herod troubled, but all Jerusalem with him. They order him to return to sleep in the temple; having rejected him through their disbelief, they send him back to contemplate the secrets of his Father as a child. Yet they understand him as a young man—that is, after the thirtieth year of his age—to be the Son of God, when some of their number come to believe. This, then, is what Eli understood after Samuel had come to him for the third time: that the Lord was calling him. After the third decade of his years, the Jews recognized and believed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

“And the Lord again called Samuel,” etc. Let us not be reluctant to repeat in our exposition what neither the Lord was reluctant to repeat in speaking nor the historian in writing. God the Father calls God the Son—not as one human being calls another by striking the air with words and summoning him from one place to another, but by showing through visible signs that the Son, who invisibly remains perpetually in the Father, was also carrying the visible form of a man on earth. Since Samuel means “God,” or “his name is God,” we can rightly say that the Lord called Samuel when the Father demonstrated through miracles that the incarnate Son was the true God, and that the Son answered, “Here I am.” [Col. 0521A] The same Son said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV).

“And he said, ‘Here I am,’” etc. Let the attentive reader observe that the order of allegorical interpretation is not always the same as the order of historical truth. Sometimes the two correspond, sometimes they differ, and sometimes they stand in opposition to one another. They correspond when the simplicity of Samuel’s childhood and Eli’s sluggish blindness signify the humility of the Lord our Savior and the faithless folly of the Jews. They differ when Samuel’s uncertain words, “Here I am, because you called me,” foreshadow Christ’s true and certain incarnation. They stand in opposition when, later, David’s sin in the matter of Uriah signifies Christ’s merciful grace, by which he deigned to save the nations.

“Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord,” etc. Moreover, the Savior—whose name means “God”—was not yet recognized by carnal people as knowing all the Father’s secrets. Nor, before he was baptized, did John see and testify that the heavens had been opened to him and that the Father’s voice had come upon him from above. Thus, in accordance with the manner of Holy Scripture, the ignorance of the blessed Samuel in infancy, hidden beneath the appearance of a child, demonstrates the wisdom of the Son of God in the infancy of his flesh. For it was not said without reason: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Colossians II), namely, so that they may be revealed in the faithful and made manifest to believers.

“And the Lord added, and called Samuel again for the third time.” The Lord calls Samuel a third time; rising for the third time, he comes again to Eli and says who has called him. The Father showed the Son visibly in the flesh for the third time, while displaying the invisible God through signs: in infancy, in childhood, [Col. 0521C] and in youth. In infancy, when he shone forth through the testimony of shepherds and Magi, by means of an angel and a star. In childhood, when, having reached twelve years of age, he showed himself in the temple endowed with divine wisdom, where among other things he said: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke II). In youth, when, after he had been baptized, the Father himself marked him from heaven with his voice, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mark I). In each of these instances, when the Son of God is declared by God the Father, the Son himself, offering himself to mortals as a mortal human being, indicated to humanity that he was present—the one who had long been sought, awaited, and desired.

“Then Eli understood that the Lord was calling the child,” etc. At last, after the Lord had performed and spoken many great things, [Col. 0521D] and after John the Baptist had fulfilled his proclamation, the priests, scribes, and Pharisees understood that Jesus—who was truly born for us as a child in the flesh—was himself, in the truth of his everlasting divinity, the supreme contemplator of the Father’s secrets. Immediately, assenting to the faith they had recognized, they desired to seek the heavenly joys, which are never without him, in order to behold them; and they wished to hear from God the Father, by divine revelation, what he ought to relate to human beings in human fashion. Like lovers who, knowing what must be done, urge those things to be done, they themselves admonish him to do them—as we often urge God himself and the angels to do promptly and earnestly what we know they will do, thereby displaying our devotion of mind. For we mortals, born of earth, say: “Arise, O God, and judge your cause” (Psalm LXXIII). “Stir up your power, and come” (Psalm LXXIX). “Bless the Lord, all his angels” (Psalm CII); and countless sayings of this kind.

“And the Lord said to Samuel, ‘Behold, I am doing a deed in Israel,’” etc. What the prophet had earlier foretold to Eli concerning the judgment of his house—that is, its rejection and the substitution of Samuel’s priesthood—Samuel himself learns when God’s oracle is delivered to him, and he reports it to Eli. For what the proclamations of the prophets had foretold in defining the old priesthood and introducing the new, namely, the priesthood of Christ’s Church, Christ himself, dwelling in the flesh, having heard it more certainly from the Father in that hidden place inaccessible to mortals, openly and in a clear voice reveals to the leaders of the Jews.

“Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli,” etc. Literally, the house of Eli could not be purified by the blood of sacrifices, which the wickedness of his sons polluted. Yet it was purified by the blood of martyrdom when so many priests of that lineage were innocently killed in the city of Nob on account of their fatherly hospitality (1 Samuel XXII). According to the progression of the allegory, however, the wickedness of Eli’s house—or rather, of the whole house of Israel—could not be cleansed completely by any kind of sacrifices or gifts of good works, until the Lamb of God came, who takes away the sins of the world. For only the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all iniquity (John I).

“Now Samuel slept until morning,” etc. The Lord remained in secret repose with the Father, with whom he never ceases invisibly to order and govern all things. He awaited the time when, after the night of vices had been driven away, the sacrifice of virtues would be opened; when, as the shadow of the law receded, the lights of evangelical truth would be revealed; and as soon as he saw the radiance of faith arise in someone’s heart through the breath of the Sun of Justice, he would open the greater gifts of his Spirit and promise the hoped-for entrance into the everlasting dwelling in heaven. This happens not only then among the Jews but also in us to this day. For whoever has not yet received the grace of Christ, or has cast it away after receiving it through the merits of his sins, lies in the night of blindness. Christ, who always keeps watch in the saints, sleeps for such a person and closes the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. But when that person receives the light of the forgiveness he hopes for and seeks, the Lord, suddenly awakened as though from sleep, opens the gates of virtue that he had closed when the evening of faithlessness pressed upon him. To this meaning corresponds, though under another figure, the beautiful passage in which the disciples are in danger while the Lord sleeps, but are rescued when he awakens (Matthew VIII).

“Now Samuel grew,” etc. The preaching of the Gospel grew, and God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. The reputation of Jesus grew and spread throughout all Syria. Hence John says: “He must increase” (John III); and immediately, speaking of the passing of the old law as though of Eli’s passing, he adds: “But I must decrease.”

“And none of all his words fell to the ground.” You will find nothing earthly in the Lord’s words; or, no one who savors earthly things comprehends his spiritual sayings. Alternatively, it may be said that while the Lord dwelt in the flesh, he delayed entrusting his word to the Gentiles, who, in comparison with the Jews, were like earth in relation to heaven; yet afterward he deigned to call them to faith through the apostles.

“And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew,” etc. The catholic—that is, universal—Church, namely, spiritual Israel, which was gathered from the beginning of renouncing the devil until it reached the font of baptism, recognized that Jesus Christ was the preacher of the faith, he who is called “God with us.” Dan means “judgment.” It signifies the period of the Church of which it was said: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII). Beersheba, however, interpreted as “the well of the oath,” or “the seventh well,” or “the well of fullness,” signifies the complete reception of baptism: when, after the devil has been exorcised, renounced, [Col. 0523B] and expelled from the heart, a person enters the font of regeneration, to be consecrated by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit and satisfied with the abundance of heavenly gifts.

The very location of these places also significantly alludes to the mysteries of the Church. Dan, the boundary of the land of Judaea, was to the north, while Beersheba was to the south. Their mystical separation by regions is well understood by the one who knows how to sing with the Bridegroom: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs IV). Dan is a village four miles from Paneas on the road to Tyre. The river Jordan also bursts forth from that place and received its name from it. For the Hebrews call a river or stream *Jor*; and this too aptly signifies the beginning of baptism. [Col. 0523C] Beersheba, as we have said, is a city or village in the tribe of Judah, sloping toward the south.

Thus all Israel—that is, the Christian people intent upon the vision of God—recognized, from Dan to Beersheba, from north to south, from the catechumen to the faithful, from those who had recently expelled from themselves the harshest blasts of the ancient enemy to those already fanned by the most radiant warmth of the Holy Spirit, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believers have eternal life in his name.

In this passage the person of blessed Samuel may also, by the merit of pure humility, be referred to the very members of Christ, of whom he himself says: “Whoever therefore humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVIII). While these persons sleep in the temple of the Lord—that is, while they turn away from the external cares of the world and devote the whole light of their heart to contemplating the heavenly will—he teaches how many secrets of heavenly judgments are disclosed to them, though the dim-sighted and rejected old man Eli did not see them. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew X). There too, as an example corresponding to the present passage, the humility of penitents, which must be crowned, and the impiety of the proud, which must be condemned, are set forth beforehand; through these things it is clearly shown which mysteries he reveals to the humble and which he has hidden from the wise of this age.

CHAPTER IX. Israel was defeated and put to flight by the Philistines, and Eli’s sons also were killed; the ark of God was captured. When this was heard, Eli immediately fell backward and died, as did his daughter-in-law, after first giving birth to a son named Ichabod, which means “without glory.”

[Col. 0524A]

“And Samuel’s word came to all Israel,” etc. In this passage it is signified that Israel, having long been deceived through the examples of the nations, would at last receive the faith of the Gospel for a time, but not long afterward lose both that faith and the teachers of truth. When God’s testament was transferred to the Gentiles, the destruction of the legal priesthood together with the Synagogue joined to it is likewise shown to have followed.

(1 Samuel IV.) “For Israel went out to meet the Philistines,” etc. The people went out—that is, after receiving knowledge of the law, they went forth to perform openly the good works they had learned [Col. 0524B] and, as far as they could, to combat the error of paganism, by which the hearts of the impious, intoxicated, were tending toward perpetual death. Hence the Philistines are aptly said to be “falling by drink.” In that conflict, however, Israel was concerned not so much with recalling foreign nations from the pollution of their crimes as with watching over itself, lest it perish by their example.

“And they encamped beside the Stone of Help.” They placed all the confidence of their spiritual warfare in his help, concerning whom he said: “When my heart was troubled, you lifted me up upon a rock” (Psalm LX). And elsewhere: “The Lord is my rock and my strength” (2 Samuel XXI).

“Now the Philistines came to Aphek,” etc. As Israel advanced in the true God, the worshipers of many false gods were immediately seized by a new fury of envy and by the impulse to corrupt Israel. This is what it means for the Philistines to draw up their battle line at Aphek—that is, “in a new fury”—against Israel: the neighboring nations, instructed by unclean spirits, continually set before the people of God examples of perverse religion and conduct in order to cause scandal. From the time the law was received until the grace of Christ made the two peoples one, they never ceased to do this.

“When the battle had been joined, Israel turned its back on the Philistines,” etc. When conflict arose between Israel and the Gentile peoples over words and deeds concerning true religion, with Israel fighting for the worship of the one true God and the others for the defense of idols, Israel’s faith failed. Israel itself was more easily turned toward the error of the nations than the nations could be converted to follow its faith. Nevertheless, a considerable portion of Israel, even while the rest sinned, persisted in returning to defend the camp of spiritual virtues.

Do not think that this has been interpreted allegorically only concerning the condition of the ancient people of God, so that it does not also apply tropologically to you.
