Whenever you strive in spiritual warfare to conquer unclean spirits, relying not on your own strength but on the Stone cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel II), which alone knows how to overthrow the kingdoms of the devil, the same enemies of truth immediately oppose you with a new fury at each beginning of a good work. Take care not to turn your back in sin upon the enemies striking your mind, but rather, as the apostle James admonishes: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” [Col. 0525A] (James IV).

Yet since it is written: “The outcome of war is uncertain, and now the sword consumes one side, now the other” (2 Samuel II), if it should happen that for a time you have yielded and the enemy has conquered,  and if he should boast that he has ravaged the fruitful fields of your good conduct and overthrown prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—as the four most excellent leaders followed by the entire army of virtues—nevertheless you must not abandon the camp of your excellent purpose, which you have pitched beside the firm rock. Rather, through the remedy of humility and repentance, you must renew with a new campaign the ranks of the virtues that have been lost, according to the one who said: “If spirits possessing power rise up against you, do not leave your place, because healing will make great sins cease” (Ecclesiastes XX).

When danger from the adversaries’ battle presses upon you, offer the ark of fervent faith as your helper. But if the wicked should perhaps snatch it away for a time, either by mingling heresy with it or by touching it through some other kind of deceit, the help of heavenly mercy will not fail you. For this mercy often allows its own to fall for a time so that, having recognized their weakness, it may preserve them afterward more cautious in virtues and more perfect for rewards.

Finally, after a short while the ark returns home joyfully and remains for twenty years in the stronghold of the city, because virtue, often recovered through repentance, fills the soul more ardently than before the storm of temptation and accompanies it until the completion of the perfect divine law, the Decalogue, and until it receives forever the joy of the heavenly denarius. But having anticipated these matters in a moral exposition, let us return to the order of the passage and seek new fruits of spiritual allegory in the most ancient woodland of the literal text.

“Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines?” etc. The more learned among the people of Israel at that time consulted together concerning the means of attaining salvation. They asked why, although they had received the law and wished to keep it, they had been unable to perfect or fulfill it; why they had been struck by the Lord before the Philistines—that is, why, with the Lord permitting it and not assisting them by his grace, they had been unable to master desire, although they read and loved the law that says: “You shall not covet” (Exodus II).

At last they found useful counsel: they should seek the grace of Christ, which had often been promised to the fathers as future in the writing of the law (Deuteronomy V); they should discover the grace of Christ signified in the law, through whom they desired to be liberated—that is, they should remember the ark of the covenant placed in Shiloh within the veil of the tabernacle and have it brought from the people to obtain the help of salvation. We explained above in what way Shiloh represents the type of the law.

“So the people sent to Shiloh,” etc. The people sent for the future devotion of their faith, and took to themselves as a helper the grace of God, supreme above all things, which they had learned about through the occasion of the law. It should be noted that throughout the entire time of seeking and bringing the ark to them, Israel’s camp remained at peace; but when the ark arrived, it was disturbed by the enemy. For the same people, who had eagerly sought the faith of the Lord’s future Incarnation, did not hesitate to reject it when it came and, in some of their members, even to persecute and hate it.

“And Eli’s two sons were with the ark of the covenant of the Lord,” etc. Both the name and the merit of Eli’s sons indicate that the failure of the people to believe in Christ in the flesh was greatly aided by the guilt of the priests of that time. For Ophni means “barefoot,” as was said above; Phinehas means “a mute mouth.” The former signifies looseness of conduct, the latter sluggishness in teaching, since even perfect priests ought to be adorned in the manner of their good works and free in the voice of their preaching.

“When the ark of the covenant of the Lord had come into the camp,” etc. When the Lord was born in the flesh, all Israel was troubled. As he was preached, some were moved to believe and others to contradict; and the earthly conscience first resounded with the praises of heaven.

“And the Philistines heard the sound of the shout.” The report of the Lord’s preaching reached even the knowledge of the Gentiles.

“And the Philistines were afraid, saying, ‘God has come into the camp,’” etc. The pagans were afraid when they recognized the coming of the true God into the world to fortify the spiritual camps of his faithful. The worshipers of many false gods, together with their forms of worship, lamented that they were destined to be destroyed, and the faithless encouraged one another to defeat the battle line of faith and truth.

“For there was not such rejoicing yesterday and the day before.” Neither under the law nor before the law had the hearts of believers been so ready to endure, for desire of the heavenly kingdom, whatever earthly beings dread or to reject whatever earthly beings enjoy.

“So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated,” etc. The adversaries of truth—whether human beings or their rulers, the unclean spirits—fought against those who believed in Christ. Some believers, openly attacked by their violence, secretly persuaded, or assailed by examples of wickedness, were struck down either by denial or by martyrdom; others were driven back from the tabernacles of their firm faith, so that they might abandon them more completely.

“And there was a very great slaughter,” etc. More fell after the ark came than before: “If I had not come,” he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” [Col. 0526D] (John XV).

According to the mystical interpretation of the number, we may say that Israel lost four thousand men before the coming of the ark, represented by those who, before the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, rejected the commands of the law by believing, hoping, loving, and acting less perfectly. After the ark had been brought, thirty thousand foot soldiers perished in a greater slaughter: these represent those who refused to receive from the Gospel the mystery of the Holy Trinity together with the promise of the heavenly denarius.

“And the ark of God was captured,” etc. The kingdom was taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits. The order of the priesthood also, because it had not conducted itself rightly, was transferred by the judgment of the Lord.

“Now a man of Benjamin ran from the battle line,” etc. The people that remained after the Jews had perished through faithlessness, hastening to care for their salvation, heard from the apostles: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts II). They came to instruct those who, having been emptied of Christ, still gloried in the law and preserved, as it were, the tabernacle of the Lord at Shiloh without the ark of the covenant. To call their hearers more readily to repentance, the man appeared mournful, his entire old garment completely torn and all confidence in his former strength despised as worthless.

He is rightly said to have come from Benjamin, that is, from the “son of the right hand,” because the Church, in comparison with the Synagogue, stands above it as the heavenly Jerusalem—our mother—surpasses the present one, like the right hand the left. This Benjaminite therefore signifies either the people of the primitive Church, [Col. 0527B] or one of the teachers of that age, a son, namely, of the right hand of faith; or certainly the apostle Paul, who also descended from the tribe of Benjamin and, although he was the last of the apostles, labored more than all in preaching (1 Corinthians XV).

“When he had come, Eli was sitting,” etc. When the teacher of the New Testament appeared in Judaea with the garment of the letter torn, the old priesthood still sat upon the chair of Moses, although it had lost its light, and sat in opposition to Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. For it feared what came to pass: that, once it had been rejected, the grace of Christ might pass to the Gentiles.

“After the man had entered, he announced it to the city,” etc. The teacher evangelized, and the hearer repented. When they heard of the crime they had committed in killing the Savior, the Jews were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” (Acts II).

“And Eli heard the sound of the shouting,” etc. The report of the people’s repentance, prompted by the apostles’ exhortation, reached even the ears of the chief priests, and it was not gladly received. Indeed, while the apostles were speaking to the people, the priests, the magistrates of the temple, and the Sadducees arrived, distressed that they were teaching the people and announcing the resurrection from the dead in Jesus. The apostles did not delay in preaching the Gospel even to them.

“Now Eli was ninety-eight years old,” etc. At that time the legal priesthood lacked two things pertaining to the perfection that leads to life: faith, namely, and works. Therefore its eyes—that is, its heralds—had grown dim in understanding, and they could not see Christ in the law. For a veil lay over their heart, and in Christ it is taken away.

“And the ark of God was captured,” etc. As the apostles’ proclamation and the faith of the repentant peoples spread far and wide, the grace of God was taken away from the Jews. That priesthood, long glorious on the throne of legal judgments, because it did not fear to fall backward—that is, to turn back after itself and return to the sins it had once abandoned—perished with the neck of its singular pride broken. This occurred beside that door of which he said: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). It sat beside that door according to the mystery of the figures, but through the merit of its faithlessness it did not enter it.

[Col. 0528A] “The man was old and advanced in years,” etc. At that time that priesthood had grown old. Once it had been glorified by abundant virtue, and it still functioned through the chief priests, the elders of the people, the scribes, and the Pharisees—who were also called teachers of the law—showing the people of Israel, at the proper time, the judgments of the divine law contained in the Decalogue.

According to the tropology of the law, each of us must likewise keep the ark of the covenant within, in the tabernacle, and, when the time comes to go forth and fight against the Philistines, carry it with us. This means that we must always preserve faith and a firm, chaste conscience; and, when circumstances require, carry it as an aid in spiritual warfare against unclean spirits, whether human beings or demons. It must have two priests as guardians, namely, vigilant dispositions directed toward the twofold commandment of love. [Col. 0528B] For the Apostle does not praise just any faith, but the faith that works through love (Galatians V).

If, while we are fighting, unclean spirits or heretics should perhaps seize the ark of faith and kill its priestly and devout dispositions, then the Benjaminite must immediately arrive in mournful attire. That is, the mind, raised by hope in heavenly mercy, must come humbly and repentantly, bring our offenses and errors back to our awareness, and summon the entire city of our inner ruler to mourning and tears, until, by God’s mercy, the captured ark returns and a better priest in place of those who were lost—that is, a more disciplined and cautious disposition—is granted to us after the labors of repentance.

Nor does the seven-month period during which the Philistines held the ark differ from the form of repentance that it signifies. For the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is handed down as sevenfold, is known both to require repentance for sins committed and to obtain forgiveness; and the judgment of the Fathers declares that the same forgiveness is to be sought in seven ways. Finally, the interpreters of the Psalter transmit seven penitential psalms, through which heavenly mercy is to be implored for obtaining the remission of sins.

Yet there are some who turn the remembrance, recognition, and grief of their sins not toward seeking a remedy but, like Judas, toward increasing their former crimes. Because they have grown old among all their enemies, and because the eye of their mind has been disturbed by the anger of God, they have also lost the light of faith. They suddenly abandon the seat of judicial discernment, intending to turn back and soon to perish; and although for some time they appeared to have lived with discernment and to have conducted themselves well according to the precepts of the law [Col. 0528D] and the Gospel—for this is what it means that Israel judged for forty years—nevertheless, when the critical moment of temptation arrives, they succumb to a wretched death.

“Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant,” etc. The Synagogue, entrusted with governing the sons of the legal priesthood, had received from its teachers the seed of the word and was near to giving birth to the fruit of faith that it had long sought, while the Lord was preaching. Yet after the downfall of its teachers, it too bent away from the uprightness of right living; and although it gave birth to a considerable crowd of people, it itself—because it killed the Author of life—was condemned to death.

“And she called the child Ichabod,” etc. Ichabod is interpreted as “Woe to glory” or “Glory has fallen.” Almost no one will doubt that this name most suitably applies to the Jews of that time. The glory of faith was transferred from Israel to the Gentiles, from the Synagogue to the Church; but at the end of the world it will return to Israel. Let us rejoice that it has been transferred to us; let us fear its transfer from us to the fatherland, to be brought back in the cart of a new way of life.

CHAPTER X. When the Philistines carried the ark of God into the temple of Dagon, Dagon himself was first struck down, and afterward the people and land were punished with a deserved plague; the ark remained among them for seven months.

(1 Samuel V.) “Now the Philistines took the ark of God,” etc. This passage mystically indicates that when the foreskin—that is, the Gentiles—received the testament of faith, the idols first had to be humbled and then promptly overthrown completely; and that those who turned back after recognizing the faith were likewise to be punished with a deserved retribution.

“Now the Philistines took the ark of God,” etc. The nations received the word of the Gospel from Judaea, where the Lord was born bodily, lived, and suffered, leaving behind places that remain sacred to the mysteries of his dispensation even to this day. They carried it by a favorable report into the distant provinces of the world, which until then had been burning with the flame of vices and were being dissolved by the allurements of the flesh. Hence Azotus, which is called *Erdod* in Hebrew, is aptly said, according to its former name, to signify dissolution or effusion, or burning.

“And they brought it into the temple of Dagon.” They brought faith into the world, which lay in the evil one, concerning which the Lord says: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is at peace; but when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (1 John V; Luke XI).

Dagon was strong when he guarded the foolish weapons of paganism in his courtyard. The ark of faith is stronger: it stripped him, the victor, of the spoils of impiety and made those weapons and spoils instruments of piety.

“And they set it beside Dagon.” They raised up churches of Christ among the nations, while the worship of idols still remained in certain places. Dagon, whose name is interpreted as “fish of sorrow,” signifies not only by his person but also by his name the one who, existing from the beginning as the author of our miseries, is called by the prophet king of all that are in the waters. Concerning him the Lord tells blessed Job many things under the figure of Leviathan (Job XL).

Tobias, whose name is interpreted as “good of God,” at the urging of the leader-angel, drags him from the waters when he attacks; he disembowels him, roasts him, eats him, salts him, and carries him with him both as medicine and as provisions. That is, the Lord Savior, by divine power, overcomes the devil who desires the food of his flesh and drags him from the hiding places of his ambushes. He cuts away the members of iniquity from him, seasons them with the salt of wisdom, cooks them with the fire of the Holy Spirit, and transfers them into the members of his body, which is the Church; through some members he provides others with aids to salvation.

For while the Lord saves through those whom he has snatched from the devil, he will save the Gentiles from the deception of idolatry, and at the end of the world he will save the Jews, from whom he assumed flesh, from the error of their faithlessness. Thus it becomes clear what Tobias signifies when, through the entrails of the dismembered fish, he frees both his wife from the demon and his father from blindness.

“When they had risen early at Azotus on the following day,” etc. As signs of miracles shone forth through the heralds of the faith, the worship of idolatry fell among those who were able to convert to Christ. Yet the one who, although exposed and revealed, is vanity, was recovered among those who took up the weapons of faithlessness against the truth.

“Again, rising early on another day,” etc. As the light of heavenly signs gradually increased, they confessed before Christ’s faithful that everything earthly and perishable which they had previously done or believed had been exposed in its shame.

[Col. 0530B] “But the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands,” etc. The head of every sin—the devil’s pride—and the work of idolatry, which was performed as though with two palms through the profession of impiety and through ceremonies of praises and sacrifices, had already been cut away from the body joined to it, namely, from the crowds of those deceived by it, and was about to be cast out as Christ’s triumph increased. He showed that Dagon’s head and hands lay on the threshold when he said: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John XII).

“As for Dagon’s trunk alone,” etc. The people, having rejected and expelled the profession and practice of idolatry and demonic action, remained among those who had advanced in the faith, humble and submissive, as though beside the ark of God. They preferred to remain humble and submissive rather than be cast out with Dagon—that is, anathematized from the members of the Church. Dagon’s former condition is not said to have been restored, because, although many struggles of the Church followed, the defense of false gods ultimately ceased, and victory was given to Christ, the one true God.

Because of this, the priests do not tread upon Dagon, etc. Because the devil is to be cast out and condemned at the end, all who follow him perversely, whether by teaching or by conduct, at his instigation refuse to consider and avoid the time of his expulsion and condemnation. Indeed, before his worshipers repent of their iniquity, he anxiously suspends their understanding—so to speak, the movement of their mind—from foreseeing the future destruction either of himself or of them. And [Col. 0530D] this continues to the present day, that is, until each of them recognizes the light of truth; whoever follows that light, which is perpetually present, will not walk in darkness.

Nor does he fear to tread upon the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod, because he attentively observes and dreads the punishment of the wicked, who burn with earthly desires, and of their head, the devil, at the same time. Moreover, having turned toward better things, he hastens to sprinkle his own threshold with the blood of the paschal Lamb—that is, to fortify his entrance and departure with the mystery of the Lord’s Passion. Thus the severed head and feet of Dagon on the threshold deter his own from touching that threshold. But the blood of the spotless Lamb on the threshold will always make those who remember him safe from the enemy, because the devil removes from those whom he deceives both the consideration of the end that leads to the impious realms of Tartarus and the consideration of his own end. [Col. 0531A] But the Lord continually teaches those whom he has redeemed, by the example of his Passion and resurrection, to hope for life after death.

But the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Ashdodites, etc. Those who, after receiving the ark of God, mourn Dagon’s destruction and raise him up again are struck in their hinder parts, and their land is ravaged by mice. For those who, instructed by the knowledge of faith or even by its mysteries, cannot tolerate either the overthrow of idols or the prohibition of vices, look back and do not abandon the impurity of their former life; instead, they seek again the things behind them, which, with the Apostle (Phil. III), they ought to have forgotten and regarded as refuse. They are punished, of course, by the very things they choose, and what had been their pleasure becomes the cause of punishment for the wretched.

And if such people seem to cause anything good to grow, [Col. 0531B] while they keep the eyes of their mind turned backward, the root of their thought is gnawed away by unclean spirits and the fruit of their activity is consumed. The Lord struck not only Ashdod, where Dagon was, but also all the territory of Ashdod, because he condemns with the judgment of a strict judge not only the conflagrations of capital crimes, in which the devil’s work is plainly visible, but also every minor offense, and those sins that perhaps seem to human beings extreme or trivial. In the end, human beings will give an account for every idle word they have spoken on the day of judgment (Matt. XII).

When the men of Ashdod saw such a plague, etc. The lovers of idolatry, seeing Christ’s power against their gods, do not wish to receive his faith, lest for this reason alone they be compelled to renounce the whole [Col. 0531C] crowd of their gods. False Christians, seeing that because of Christ’s faith the sins they love are forbidden to them, detest the religion of the faith as much as they can, lest on its account they be commanded to extinguish the desires that they serve as God.

The Ashdodites are altogether worthy of the name—that is, of outpouring, dissolution, and burnings—because they do not wish to know the precepts of Sacred Scripture, lest, once they know them, they should have to do what they have learned. And because of the Lord’s saying that those who do not know his will will be beaten less severely, they do not wish to know what they are doing; they do not understand how greatly it differs simply not to know from refusing to know what one has learned ought to be known. And so these people, feeling that their own wills are harshly treated, shamelessly repel from themselves the ark of heavenly knowledge. [Col. 0531D]

And the Gittites answered: Let the ark of the God of Israel be carried around, etc. This carrying of the ark around corresponds to the present age, in which each of the sluggish desires the word of the Lord to be fulfilled by another rather than by himself. Moreover, even barbarian nations—something sufficiently grave—if they have recently received Christ’s faith, are soon weakened by soft desires and judge that it should be given to others rather than practiced any longer among themselves.

While they were carrying it around, the hand of the Lord came upon them, etc. Those who receive the faith transiently and without fixed intention not only earn no benefit by believing, but, wretchedly, also deserve eternal punishment for the price of salvation.

And their protruding entrails putrefied. And [Col. 0532A] the inward meditation of their heart, having fallen backward into the blind and unclean things of the present life, appeared outwardly, filled with stinking filth and the blood of every vice. The madness of heretics may be compared with this kind of striking, as the death of Arius itself teaches. For when his entrails were poured out through his hind parts, he miserably found in this the beginning both of the end of teaching heresy and of undergoing punishments worthy of heretics.

So they sent messengers and gathered all the satraps of the Philistines, etc. Many people today, converted from the nations and now believers, say this, if not in words: “Send away the faith, and let it return to the children of Israel, so that, when we have finally been cut off, they may be grafted according to nature into their own olive tree.” For it is better to perish in ignorance than, together with our other sins, to be condemned for transgressing in the matter of the faith, which we are unable to preserve. [Col. 0532B]

And the wailing of each city rose to heaven. The murmur, impatience, and Sodomitic cry of false believers, conspicuous in whatever places, persons, or bodily senses they may be found—the number of the Philistine cities being five—can never be hidden from the strict Judge, who foretells the time of such things in a terrible sentence: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII).

(I Sam. VI.) The ark of the Lord was therefore in the region of the Philistines for seven months. The number seven ordinarily expresses the totality of any matter, whether of time or number, or certainly the fullness of spiritual grace. The month, however, which varies with the waxing and waning of the moon’s [Col. 0532C] light, signifies the condition of the Church, laboring amid prosperity and adversity but never failing in the Sun of justice.

The ark of the Lord’s faith therefore was, and will be, among the nations throughout the whole age of the world, during which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will deign to fill the Church and illuminate it so that it may shine upon the weak, like the earths subjected to it. But even according to the literal sense, the present reading, which tells that the Philistines were struck by their proximity to the ark of the Lord, teaches that no unclean person should presume to approach holy things. Whoever wishes either to receive the Lord’s body or to handle his most sacred words should examine himself, and then eat of that bread and drink of the cup; let him discipline his body and bring it into subjection, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should become disqualified (I Cor. XI, 9).

## CHAPTER XI

Taught by the priests and diviners, the Philistines send back the ark of God with due reverence; the Bethshemites, receiving it first, offer sacrifices to God.

[Col. 0532D]

And the Philistines called the priests and diviners, etc. This reading teaches figuratively that the faith of the Gospel, now celebrated among the nations, will return at the end of the world to save the remnant of Israel. Taught by the plagues, the Philistines ask their wise men what they should do with the ark of God and how they should send it back to its place.

But they said to them: If you send back the ark of the God of Israel to its place, [Col. 0533A] etc. When we see the vengeance inflicted upon the wicked and wash our hands in the blood of sinners, if we purpose, by urging repentance, to send the ark of heavenly grace back to its place—that is, into the hearts of our neighbors, who once possessed it but lost it through wandering—we must take the greatest care not to attempt this while empty of virtues. Rather, in accordance with the one who said, “His grace toward me was not in vain” (I Cor. XV), let us first hasten to do what is right ourselves, and then instruct others.

In this way we shall be able to escape the plagues of those who, after receiving the gift of knowledge, know how to repay the Giver of grace nothing for the sins they have committed. The Church as a whole must also be watchful, lest at the end of the age the grace of faith, finding no longer the fruit of virtues among the nations, be sent back to save Israel while empty; rather, as it came to us through great teachers, so let it return through great teachers to Israel.

[Col. 0533B]

According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines, etc. According to the number of the five bodily senses, which you polluted by looking backward, and through which you lost all their fruits by handling the faith badly, now, through everything you do by seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, or touching, pay to Christ the clearest tribute of patience, compunction, humility, and the other virtues owed to him.

And you shall give glory to the God of Israel, etc. Confess that God alone is truthful, while every human being is a liar (Rom. III; Ps. CXV), if perhaps he may turn his face away from your sins and blot out all your iniquities, while the merciful Compassionate One lays upon you his lightest burden.

Now therefore take and make one new cart, [Col. 0533C] etc. “Now,” they say, “hasten, and in your own hearts or those of your brothers, strip off the old human being with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth” (Eph. IV). Do this in the unity of catholic peace, in which whatever good one can do is effective for salvation. Yoke noble teachers, instructed by the twofold love—that is, of God and neighbor—freed from the yoke of sin and rejoicing in the offspring of spiritual faithful children, either to the burden of preaching the faith or to that of bearing the needs of the brethren. But keep all the little ones and those still infants in Christ within the measure of their own beds, raising and restraining them until they advance to mature manhood.

[Col. 0533D]

And you shall take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, etc. Place the more hidden things of the heavenly mysteries upon hearts instructed in Christ’s new commandment. Join to them, for all to see and follow, the example of your own correction. Thus, having adorned the Church—that is, burdened both with the mysteries of the faith and with examples of virtues—send it out to seek the remnants of the Israelite people, and never turn the eyes of your mind away from observing its footsteps.

So they did this. They took two cows, etc. The Philistines acted concerning the ark in accordance with the counsel of their priests and diviners. The faithful stewards of the Church have acted, and will act, in accordance with the predictions of the earlier priests and prophets. Let us too act concerning the correction [Col. 0534A] of ourselves or of our neighbor—that is, of the members of the Church—in accordance with the command of our spiritual teachers.

Let no one consider it absurd that, when interpreting the deeds of unbelieving diviners and priests concerning the prophets and teachers of the Church, we have said that these deeds overflow with spiritual mystery. Rather, recognizing the use of allegorical speech, let the reader observe that even those deeds performed not only by unbelievers but also by people openly contriving what was contrary to God have been figuratively referred by excellent interpreters to the service of the most salutary devotion.

It is no less sacred and full of mystical devotion that the impious persecutor clothed the Lord during his Passion in purple or white clothing, crowned him with thorns, gave him vinegar to drink, hung him on the cross, and wrote “King” in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, than that his pious [Col. 0534B] and inviolate mother wrapped him in swaddling clothes at his birth and laid him in a manger; that shepherds praised him and magi worshiped him; and that, after he had been killed, chosen disciples embalmed him with spices, wrapped him in linen cloths, placed him in a stone tomb, and shut it with a great stone. Do not hesitate, therefore, to learn useful things from people of any sort, although they are nevertheless sharers in your nature. Hear what Solomon says: “Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways, and learn wisdom” (Prov. VI).

And the cows went straight ahead, etc. The teachers went straight along the way, Christ, which leads to the kingdom of heaven. The road to Bethshemesh, that is, the house of the sun, is the very one that says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). And elsewhere: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). [Col. 0534C]

They proceeded along one road, going and lowing, etc. They walked along one and the same path of faith and truth, groaning indeed as human beings, as though they were being separated from those whom they loved; nevertheless, whenever necessity pressed, they preferred to hasten more ardently to the sacrifice of Passion rather than abandon the way of justice, and to hurry toward the sacrifice for the ark of the Lord rather than consent to lay down the ark because of the children’s lamentation.

Do you wish to have what we say proved? While Paul was staying in Caesarea, a prophet coming from Judea declared that he would be bound by the Jews in Jerusalem and delivered into the hands of the nations (Acts XXI). Behold, the cow bearing the Lord’s ark is prophesied to be sacrificed. And whatever the calves—whether with dry eyes or not—who await the departure and death of their parent may have done, let the calf nobler than the others, and distinguished by this name among the four great animals, tell us.

“When we heard this,” he says, “we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. But because the mother’s urgency could not turn him either to the right or to the left by the love or tears of her children, see what he says to those who wept as he was about to leave: ‘What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.’”

But the lamentation of the weak—like that of calves shut up at home—which they conceive from the carnal loss of their spiritual parents gradually ceases as they themselves make progress. The same Luke says: “When we could not persuade him, we ceased, saying: ‘The will of the Lord be done.’” [Col. 0535A]

But the Bethshemites were harvesting wheat in the valley, etc. The citizens of eternal light desired to store in the joys of their heavenly homeland the ripe fruits of the virtues that they had produced with humble hearts. And, raising the eyes of their hearts, wherever on earth they saw heavenly things, they rejoiced.

And the cart came into the field of Joshua the Bethshemite, etc. Wherever the Church sees hearts bearing fruit for Jesus Christ, the Lord of eternal glory and the creator of perpetual light, there it immediately prepares to make its dwelling, as though it had found rest after the labor of its search. Such was always the progress of the Church; such was its coming among the nations; and such will also be its return to Israel. [Col. 0535B]

Now there was a great stone there, etc. In the field of the Church there was that uniquely great stone which, cut from the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII)—namely, so that it might make both one.

The persecutors of the Church shattered its structure, which, erected in the likeness of the Lord’s cross, rejoiced in the firmest condition of the new grace. Moreover, they killed as a most pleasing sacrifice to the Lord—even though they did not know what they were doing—teachers and those who were capable of bearing the burdens of the weak, consuming them in the flame of martyrdom.

The wood of the new cart that had carried the ark of the Lord was cut when, [Col. 0535C] after persecution arose in the Church of Jerusalem, all except the apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Samaria and Judea. The cows were made a burnt offering to the Lord when, after all had been pierced by the ardor of inward love and dissolved in mourning and tears, Stephen was stoned and James the brother of John was struck down with the sword. As you read the history of the Church and the innumerable deeds of the martyrs, you will find countless examples of this kind.

More terrible than all these in the times of Antichrist will undoubtedly be the cutting of this cart—that is, the disturbance of the Church. Nor is there anything to prevent us from interpreting these two cows, which carried the ark of the Lord and were given to the Israelites as a burnt offering to the Lord, as Enoch and Elijah, who are believed then to open the grace of faith to the Jews [Col. 0535D] and soon afterward to suffer death at the hands of Antichrist.

Do not be surprised that we have interpreted the good deeds of the Bethshemites in the opposite sense, because it is customary for Sacred Scripture sometimes to represent evil through good and good through evil. Indeed, many kinds of sacrifices in the Law, which were offered with devoted hearts at the Lord’s command, prophetically announce the Savior’s death, which he received from the impious.

But the Levites set down the ark of God, etc. The ministers of the word, receiving the faith and the examples of the lives of the saints who preceded them in Christ, did not place these things in anything lowly, earthly, and base, but in those whom they saw to be firm in Christ.

That great stone may appropriately be referred to the people who glory in the Law—for the Law was written on stone—and the ark may be understood to have been placed upon the stone when the people zealous for the Law received the faith of grace. [Col. 0536A]

And the men of Bethshemesh offered burnt offerings, etc. “All who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V). And elsewhere he says: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. XII).

And the five satraps of the Philistines saw, etc. All who have preceded others in Christ contemplate, as in a mirror, the faith and deeds of those who succeed them in him until they recognize that those people have been strengthened in faith and are making good progress. Then, having become more secure concerning their salvation, [Col. 0536B] they return to the dwellings where they must care for their own manner of life.

This may also be understood of hypocrites, who, although for a time they seem to imitate the way of life, do not deserve to enter the gates of Bethshemesh—that is, of the Sun of justice—because of the instability of their perverse mind.

These are the golden tumors [*ani*], etc. All, small and great, strong and weak, have need to offer the Lord golden vessels for their offense—that is, splendid gifts of compunction and humility, gentleness and chastity, and the other spiritual fruits. For who is clean from filth, even if his life on earth lasts only one day? And “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (Job XV; I John I; Job XX).

Who will boast that he has a pure [Col. 0536C] heart, when he has not at some point turned backward from the path of truth in one of the five well-known senses? Or whose thought or good action has not at some time been gnawed by the tooth of the ancient deceiver, so that he must rightly seek remedies through repentance and must apply himself more earnestly to the practice of virtue because of the memory of the vices he has committed or the temptations he has endured?

This is what it means to return five golden objects to the Lord for the tumors and mice—the corrupters and the corrupted—in which the wanderer was punished, after being corrected. Beautifully, the metropolis of each province, together with the cities and villages adjoining it, is said to have returned one golden mouse and one golden tumor, because we then rightly pay what is owed for sin when we strive that the rich and poor, learned and unlearned—signified by the distinction between the walled city and the village [Col. 0536D] lacking a wall—may all become one in Christ, see one and the same will of the Lord, perceive the same good fragrance of Christ, taste together how sweet the Lord is, and hear and do his words as one.

But those who disdain conversion and refuse to pay the debt of repentance for sin will not themselves escape the hand of the strict Judge. Thrust into the outer darkness, they will not leave it until they have paid even the last penny. Concerning them the wise men of the Philistines, suggesting better things, had said above: “Why do you harden your hearts, as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened his heart? Did he not, after he had been struck, then send them away, and they departed?” This is plainly to say concerning the reprobate: “Did they not, after they had received the sentence of eternal death, only then cease to sin and harm the good?” [Col. 0537A]

And as far as Abel the great stone, etc. Even all those who are strong in faith and capable of supporting and governing the devotion of the wavering Church themselves, conscious of their weakness, say: “For we all stumble in many ways” (James III).

Indeed, the supreme cornerstone, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (I Pet. II), having suffered human things for us, says: “What I did not take by robbery, I then repaid” (Ps. LXVIII). He is most fittingly signified here by that great stone upon which the ark of God was placed, because it was the boundary between Israel and the Philistines. A boundary is shown from which the former exact, as it were, their tribute, and upon which the latter place the ark of the Lord [Col. 0537B] as though it were their own. For by the singular devotion of his virtue he bears the Church’s burden; he is our peace, and he has made both one.

Which was there to that day in the field of Joshua the Bethshemite. This same Joshua, who above is Jesus, signifies the same Lord. For both names are interpreted as “Savior.”

But he struck among the men of Bethshemesh, etc. He did not strike the priests and Levites, whose office it was to carry the ark, but the undistinguished common people, who were not permitted even to look upon it. To prevent this from happening, in Exodus the people stood far away and prayed, while Moses alone went up to the Lord.

For only those perfect in knowledge and action know how to direct their minds in this life toward contemplation of heavenly things. But if someone still imperfect [Col. 0537C] in human matters should presume to handle divine things, care must be taken lest his rashness, lacking understanding, be struck down by heresy, despair, or some other danger.

Perhaps, however, this striking of the people who had looked upon the ark should be understood in a good sense. For the more someone begins to contemplate the secrets of the divine majesty, the more quickly, thinking humbly of himself, he loses confidence in all his own virtues, trembling. He trembled as one struck by this most salutary wound who said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Exod. XVIII). So too the Psalmist, when he says: “My eyes have failed while looking for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII).

This is to say: “The more deeply I behold the most sacred mysteries of your salvation—that is, of Jesus—the more quickly I despise even the deeds I considered strong in myself, struck by a life-giving [Col. 0537D] wound.” He rejoices to have been struck by this wound, and even to have died, who said: “Through the Law I died to the Law, so that I might live for God; I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. II).

The number of those struck—fifty or seventy—also appropriately supports this interpretation, since it principally refers to the rest and grace of the Holy Spirit. For the Law consecrated both the seventh day and the seventh and fiftieth year as times of rest. Moreover, the Holy Spirit, whose sevenfold grace Isaiah records, descended upon the primitive Church on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection.

When people now deny themselves consolation by keeping eternal years in mind and train themselves to delight only in the memory of God, [Col. 0538A] their spirit fails for a little while. Then, raised up by the Spirit of God, they stretch toward eternal rest. Both interpretations are aptly confirmed by what follows:

And the people mourned because the Lord had struck them, etc. The Church labors in tears to restore its weakened or wavering members to their former condition. And, equally inflamed by zeal for its members who are making good progress, whom it sees longing and failing in the Lord’s courts, it pours out the sweet tears of saving compunction. Wounded by love, it says: “I am, and my soul melted away when he spoke” (Song V), and other such words, with which countless passages of Scripture—and the whole text of Psalm XLI—are filled. [Col. 0538B]

And the men of Bethshemesh said: Who can stand? etc. The men of the house of the sun—that is, citizens of the heavenly homeland—wander as pilgrims on earth. If they taste even a little, and that as something snatched away, of the eternal light for which they thirst, they immediately understand how utterly lacking they are in anything of their own, and rightly say in fear: “For no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII).

Even if someone appears to stand in the judgment of human beings, he is nevertheless shown to lie prostrate in the sight of the divine Majesty. After that sublime ardor of love known only to himself and God, he modestly and kindly shares with lesser neighbors gifts of spiritual knowledge sufficient for them to receive. In accordance with this, that great citizen of Bethshemesh said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are of sound mind, it is for you [Col. 0538C]” (II Cor. V).

And this is what follows, when the Bethshemites speak about the ark of the Lord:

And to whom shall it go up from us? etc. Cariathiarim, which is called “the city of forests,” signifies a great perfection of life, though evidently less than Bethshemesh, that is, the house of the sun. The latter signifies the sublimity of contemplation, because “the pure in heart will see God” (Matt. V); the former shows the fellowship of active conduct, in which all the trees of the forest, bearing their own fruits, will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come and makes his dwelling among them.

The ark is sent from Bethshemesh to Cariathiarim because divine grace now inflames the hearts of the great, so that they may contemplate the highest things through faith, and now assists the humble hearts of beginners, so that they may produce many kinds of good works like fruits. [Col. 0538D]

## CHAPTER XII

After some of the Bethshemites are struck because, being less worthy, they presumed to look upon the ark, the Cariatharites receive it and guard it for twenty years. Then, at Samuel’s admonition, Israel abandons the idols and serves the Lord, while Samuel offers a burnt offering. The Philistines are terrified and flee when the Lord thunders. Samuel judges Israel and builds an altar to the Lord at Ramah.

(I Sam. VII.) So the men of Cariathiarim came, etc. The strong members of the Church, fertile in the manifold offspring of spiritual actions, brought to themselves and their own people the knowledge of the divine will that they had received from the lofty contemplators of the faith. They placed it in the elevated hearts of those who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0539A] dwelling in them, were worthy to be the temple of God, to whom he gave power to become children of God, who believe in his name (John I), those whom he voluntarily begot through the word of truth.

Aminadab, whose name is interpreted “my spontaneous father,” signifies the one who, although he is Lord of heaven and earth, has become our Father by grace. Gabaa, which is interpreted “hill,” and which must be understood either as some distinguished place in Cariathiarim or certainly as the citadel of that city, signifies the height of perfect action. The ark of the Lord is brought onto this hill when the divine will is revealed: “These are the ones predestined to eternal life.”

Since no one can attain this manifestation of divine knowledge except the humble, the Bethshemites rightly said to those who were about to receive the ark at Cariathiarim: “The Philistines have brought back the ark of the Lord; [Col. 0539B] come down and take it up to yourselves.” This plainly means that the Jews who believe at the end of the world will say to their neighbors who are being called to the faith: “The nations have brought back to us the knowledge of grace, which they long enjoyed as a gift while we remained unbelieving. Come down from your long arrogance and pride, and humbly receive the humble yoke of faith.”

This interpretation, like the rest of this reading, can also most suitably apply to our daily condition and to the differing merits of different people.

And they sanctified Eleazar his son, etc. They chose certain holy and learned men as teachers, under the name of children of God, to guard the condition of the Church. Eleazar, whose name means “help of God,” figuratively expresses the company of those who can say with the Apostle: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (I Cor. III). [Col. 0539C] And elsewhere: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (ibid.).

And it came to pass, from the day when the ark remained in Cariathiarim, etc. Here too observe the difference between active and contemplative perfection. Behold, the ark of the Lord could scarcely remain for a single day after it had come into the field of Joshua the Bethshemite; it could not only ascend the citadel of Bethshemesh—that is, Gabaa—but could not even clearly enter its gates.

But when it arrived at Cariathiarim and was brought onto its hill, it remained there for twenty years, with its days of virtue multiplied, because contemplation of the heavenly life can scarcely be tasted for a moment by saints who dwell in the flesh. “The corruptible body [Col. 0539D] weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX).

Active life, however, can be pursued tirelessly over a much longer period of time and with the company of cooperating brothers, so that the Law’s Decalogue, doubled by the grace of the Gospel—or certainly completed in body and mind—may be shown, as it were, to be fulfilled by those advancing in good works as the twentieth year of the ark’s dwelling with them.

And all the house of Israel rested after the Lord. This figuratively designates the final blessedness of converted Judea, to which the entire preceding reading especially refers, although it may also be applied generally to the whole Church.

According to the literal sense, some think that the number twenty years, during which the ark remained in Cariathiarim and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord, [Col. 0540A] also indicates the measure and condition of the period during which Samuel presided over Israel. The twenty years during which the ark remained there should not, as some chroniclers are needlessly perplexed, be thought to extend to the eighth year of David’s reign, when it was transferred from there to Jerusalem.

For later, at the beginning of Saul’s reign, we read that it was in Gibeah of Benjamin, when Scripture says: “And Saul said to Ahijah: Bring the ark of God near. For the ark of God was there on that day with the children of Israel” (I Sam. XIV). Therefore we must understand that, although Scripture is silent about it, after this it was brought back from Gibeah of Benjamin to Gabaa—that is, to the hill of Cariathiarim—from which it was transferred to Jerusalem during David’s reign.

Do not believe that the ark of the Lord was moved through these various places without a mystery: now it approaches the Lord of the sun, [Col. 0540B] now enters the city of forests, now appears as a helper among the camps, now returns to the city of forests, and, having abandoned Shiloh—“he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh” (Ps. LXXVII)—finally ascends Mount Zion, which he loved. Yet even from there it does not cease to lead armies out and bring them back.

Indeed, Uriah, speaking with David during the time of the Ammonite war, indicated that it was under tents (I Chron. XVII). This continued until the time of the dedication of the house of God, when it received a permanent dwelling-place in the Holy of Holies.

Understand that these things were not done without purpose, but as a type of the Church. The Church, in the manifold yet most peaceful diversity of its members, now enjoys the sweetest light of the contemplative life, tasting and seeing that the Lord is sweet; now enters the dense realm of active devotion, [Col. 0540C] nourished by somewhat less ardor or light of mind but no less fertile in the fruit of good works; now arms the spiritual militia of virtues against the dangers of the hostile world.

While resisting its adversaries, it does not abandon the practices suited to its fruitful conduct, but carefully guards against seeking, after learning the mysteries of spiritual life, the literal observance of the Law as though it were the tabernacle of Shiloh, through a disorderly choice. Now, in those who have already departed from the body and escaped the labors of the changing world, it ascends toward the vision of eternal peace.

Yet even through those who already reign in heaven, it does not cease to contend in prayer for its members who are still pilgrims on earth and still fighting against the enemy, until, with the glory of the resurrection [Col. 0540D] shining forth—which is its blessed dedication—it is carried up into the heavenly Holy of Holies, forever triumphant over death.

If you return to the Lord with your whole heart, etc. Here it is shown figuratively how the Lord, teaching in Judea, performing miracles, suffering and rising again, ascending into heaven and sending the grace of the Holy Spirit, made not only the Jews but also the nations participants in his mercy.

Thus Samuel, having received the priesthood after Eli’s death, addresses the whole house of Israel, telling them to remove foreign gods from their midst.

And prepare your hearts for the Lord, etc. The Lord, author of the new priesthood, which is according to the order of Melchizedek, appearing in the flesh, teaches the whole house [Col. 0541A] of Israel—that is, the Church of those who desire to see God—to remove from itself the traditions of the Pharisees. He teaches it to prepare not only its works, as the Law also taught, but its very hearts to serve the Lord alone, saying: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: But I say to you” (Matt. V). In this way they can be freed from all enemies in the life to come.

So the children of Israel removed the Baals and the Astartes, etc. These are idols of the Sidonians. Baalim, meaning “those above” or “those ascending,” signifies superior things; Astaroth, meaning “the work of scouts,” signifies the work of explorers.

Therefore, all the children of Israel who served the true God the Father at the preaching of the Savior expelled every profane thought that, rising into the heart from the lowest places, sought to be above good things, rather than descending from the Father of lights among good gifts and perfect presents. They removed from their breasts the whole apparatus of unclean spirits, who go around the folds of the faithful seeking someone to devour.

Samuel said, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah,” etc. The Savior told the apostles that, by preaching the word of the Gospel, they should gather all spiritual Israel at Mizpah—that is, at the watchtower of the new truth and life. From this assembly of the whole, the Catholic Church received its Greek name. All who are established within its unity the Savior himself commends to the Father in prayer. Before his passion, praying through the apostles, he said: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one” (John 17). And now [Col. 0541C] the Apostle teaches that he continues to do this, saying: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8).

And they assembled at Mizpah and drew water, etc. That, while drawing water amid prayers and fasts, they offered it to the Lord is at once a sign and the accomplishment of devout worship. When the Lord preached, the people gathered to hear the word; and, stricken with compunction, they drew from the depths of their hearts a fountain of tears, which they poured out as a most acceptable offering to God by bringing it forth through the vessels of their eyes. In the illumination of heavenly grace they abstained from all the enticements of the world, confessing their former sins and imploring the mercy of Christ.

And Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah. [Col. 0541D] “The heavens are not clean in his sight” (Job 15), and he finds perversity even in his chosen ones. Therefore those also who, rising above all earthly things, came together to Christ at the watchtower of heavenly things—which Mizpah signifies—those who by the name “children of Israel,” that is, “men who see God,” stand preeminent, still have much for which they may be chastised as human beings by the strict Judge. Hence Isaiah says: “And he shall judge the poor in righteousness” (Isaiah 11)—without doubt the very people to whom he says, “Blessed are the poor, because yours is the kingdom of God” (Matthew 5). Judging these same people, he also says: “Are you still without understanding?” (Matthew 15).

And the Philistines heard that the children of Israel had assembled at Mizpah, etc. [Col. 0542A] The enemies of the truth heard that, while the Lord preached the Gospel of the kingdom, the whole people willingly listened to him. Then unclean spirits arose—namely, the rulers of the wicked [and therefore they are called by the Apostle “the rulers of the darkness” (Ephesians 6)]—against the order of the Church, or rather against each of the faithful, whom they sought to attack with their unholy ambushes. We treated above this evil ascent of theirs when explaining the name *Baalim*.

When the children of Israel heard this, they were afraid, etc. [Col. 0542B] Fearing the persecuting Jews, Christ’s disciples kept watch at his command and prayed that they might not enter into temptation. Struck suddenly by the storm of temptations, they cried out: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” They are also frequently remembered as having prayed amid troubles after his ascension (Matthew 8). This same prayer provides us, when we too are tested, with a most salutary protection, so that our soul may be rescued from the fear of the enemy.

Samuel then took one suckling lamb, etc. [Col. 0542C] The Lord took the innocent one—the unique man whom he had assumed for the salvation of the world—and offered him to the Father as a whole burnt offering on the altar of the cross. He is rightly said to have offered a whole burnt offering, that is, something entirely consumed by fire, and to have offered it whole: conceived, born, and living in the flesh without iniquity, he rendered everything he did as man worthy of God through the fire of the Holy Spirit.

The Lord also prayed to the Father for his faithful, that their faith might not fail (Luke 22). He prayed also for those persecuting him, that they might be forgiven the great guilt of their unbelief, into which they had fallen unknowingly (Luke 23). And the Father heard him, strengthening the former in the faith which they had almost lost, and calling the latter to the faith of which they had been entirely ignorant.

And it came to pass, when Samuel offered the whole burnt offering, etc. [Col. 0542D] This happened when the Lord offered himself as a sacrifice to God, as a fragrant aroma: his persecutors sought to blaspheme and mock him even as he hung upon the cross, and, after he had been buried, to obstruct the way to his resurrection, so that, with him condemned—as they supposed—to eternal death, they might take away from his faithful every hope of salvation.

But when the earth was shaken, the rocks split, the tombs were opened, the dead rose, and other heavenly signs shone forth at his cross and burial, the enemies were terrified and scattered in different directions. Finally, the guards at the tomb were terrified and became like dead men. The whole crowd of those who had gathered together to witness the crucifixion, seeing what happened, returned beating their breasts. Likewise, on the day of Pentecost, when the Lord thundered from above and through the apostles—his clouds, as it were, echoing heavenly utterances—the enemies of the faith were cast down. Some, struck down by their words in their impenitence and denial, were crushed.

And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, etc. [Col. 0543A] The apostles went out from Mizpah—that is, from the watchtower of their peaceful way of life—and pursued the wicked by reproving them. They struck them down from their former life, that is, from their life of ungodliness, gradually removing them by the sword of the word, until they brought them to the fellowship of the Church, which is founded upon Christ.

Beth-car, which is interpreted as “house of the lamb” or “house of recognition,” signifies that one who, having died innocently in his humanity, powerfully reveals the mysteries of the Father in his divinity. He found for himself in this house of divine recognition the place of his beloved dwelling, who said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6). He desired to enter it who, humbly knocking and asking, said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14). For they had learned from him that “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke 10). Therefore it is rightly called the house of recognition, because through him alone both the Son and the Father are revealed.

Samuel then took one stone, etc. [Col. 0543B] Above, we read of the stone of help, which in Hebrew is called *Even-Ezer* [“stone of help”]. But there the historian placed the name in anticipation; here he explains both the time and the reason for the name that was given. The stone, a splendid type of the Mediator, is rightly called “one stone,” because there is one Lord Jesus Christ, who justifies the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith.

It is rightly placed between Mizpah and Shen: that is, between the place where the altar of the Lord’s cross was erected and the singular lamb was offered, the one who takes away the sins of the world, and the place to which the victory of the Lord’s word, spread throughout the earth, could reach. That place itself lies most beautifully above Beth-car—that is, above the house of the lamb or of recognition—because Christ’s Church shines throughout the entire world.

Nor is it without reason that the same place is said to be called Shen, that is, “named,” because the people of the Gentiles, who cry to the Lord from the ends of the earth, hear together with Israel: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Of them he also says elsewhere: “And he calls his own sheep by name” (John 10).

The Lord therefore took the precious, chosen cornerstone—that is, himself—and placed it between the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. By the powerful help of his Spirit he would gather both into one and, wondrously rescued from every adversity, raise them up to contemplate the glory of his divine majesty. Since nothing is better than this vision—for when we are found worthy to behold it, we seek nothing greater beyond it, but rejoice in the supreme good—it is rightly said with profound truth: “Thus far the Lord has helped us.” [Col. 0543C]

Therefore in the Gospel the Lord promises the faithful people, as the highest and incomparable good, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14). [Col. 0543D]

And the Philistines were humbled, etc. When we come to that stone of help, to which the Psalmist sings according to the Hebrew truth alone, “Be to me a most steadfast rock and a fortified house, to save me, because you are my rock and my stronghold” (Psalm 30), our enemies will be humbled. They will no longer dare to assail the boundaries of our virtues when, with us glorified before the Lord, they see themselves defeated. For as long as we labor in this world, the battles of temptations will never be lacking.

And the hand of the Lord was against the Philistines, [Col. 0544A] etc. The grace of Christ was brought to crush the enemies of the primitive Church among all those in Judea where the light of the Gospel shone and had not yet been rejected through disbelief and persecution. The souls whom unclean teachers or spirits had deceived were restored and brought back into the fellowship of the Church—from those who had remained sterile in good works to those who had not only persisted fruitlessly for themselves but also sought wickedly to oppress every fruitful soul.

For *Accaron* is translated as “sterility,” and *Geth* as “winepress.” The meaning of sterility is clear: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3). The winepress, moreover, signifies both the persecutors of the good and the Psalms entitled “for the winepresses”; this is also demonstrated by the activity of the winepress itself.

These are pieces of wood cut off at the root, stripped of leaves and bark, and deprived altogether of every hope of bearing fruit, compressed solely for the enclosing and pressing of grapes or olives. When, crushed by the weight, with the grape-seeds broken and the skins emptied, the most joyful must and the richest streams of oil have flowed forth, the fruit of the precious liquid is stored in warehouses, while the inert husks are thrown outside. [Col. 0544B]

The winepresses themselves, empty of fruit as before, wait eagerly for the time when something will begin to be pressed, until at last, worn down by age after a long habit of pressing, they too are handed over to be consumed by flames.

So, truly so, the torturers of the Church lack not only the greenness of faith, the leaves of confession, and the fruits of good works; they also never cease to weary fruitful souls, through their pursuit of mercy, love, and the other virtues, until the liberation of the flesh. [Col. 0544C] After this they have nothing more to do, when the dust has returned to its earth, from which it came, and the spirit has returned to God, who gave it; then those who have always opposed the good will, at the appointed time, be thrust into the perpetual fires of Gehenna.

Yet because some such people recover, through Christ’s mercy, the salvation they lost in the first-created man, it is rightly said that Israel recovered its cities from Accaron to Geth—that is, from sterility to the winepress.

The Accaronite was Sergius Paulus the proconsul; the Accaronite was Dionysius the Areopagite. The Gethite, however, was that young man breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of Christ. Finally, by crushing under the pressure of stones that most noble cluster, crowned by rank, name, and martyrdom and to be offered to Christ as the Church’s firstfruits, he had stripped it of the burden of flesh. [Col. 0544D]

But when the former passed from paganism to faith, and the latter from persecutor even to the grace of apostleship, then, plainly, the cities of sterility and the winepress, once captured by the enemy, were recovered by the Church.

And there was peace between Israel and the Amorite. After the Lord’s ascension, when the Churches had been confirmed in the faith, our peace—“which made both one”—existed between those who believed from the Jews and those who believed from the Gentiles.

There will also be peace in you when, living as a true Israelite—that is, without deceit—you have peace with the former bitter enemy, whose name, Amorite, is interpreted accordingly, once you have taught all the vices conquered within you to favor the virtues and have made the members that had been weapons of iniquity for sin into weapons of righteousness for God. [Col. 0545A]

For in your mind, as long as the grace of the true Samuel lives and reigns, although as a human being you cannot be wholly free from sin, whatever the hands of the Philistines have taken from you through foul thoughts, which as it were lie in ambush against the spiritual virtues, you will recover through his daily help. You yourself will also rescue the boundaries of your good works from the hand of the Philistines, because “the patience of the poor shall not perish forever.” And although you cannot be invulnerable in the midst of battle, once your course has been completed you will nevertheless be awarded the crown of life.

Samuel also judged Israel, etc. The Lord judges the Church throughout all the time in which he gives life to her, wandering on earth, by the light of his divine presence. The days of Christ are the days of the Church. Concerning them he says in the Gospel: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9). Elsewhere, clearly defining them, he says: “And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). [Col. 0545B]

He judges her either by educating her through adversities, illuminating her with gifts, freeing her from an unholy people, or leading her to the heavenly kingdoms. Thus, examining her by his hidden presence in each of the elect, he daily tests their hope, faith, and love, and the progress each has made in the virtues mentioned above—either by himself, who knows what is hidden in the heart, or through spiritual teachers.

That the year represents a human being is also demonstrated by the fact that the four most familiar bodily humors, by which the human body is sustained, correspond to the same number of annual seasons according to a harmonious relation of qualities: true blood to spring, red bile to summer, black bile to autumn, and phlegm to winter. [Col. 0545C]

That the cities mentioned may rightly be compared with the virtues named is shown by their very names: Bethel is translated “house of God,” Gilgal “wheel,” and Mizpah “watchtower.” The house of God signifies those who, having recently received the mystery of faith, have already become the temple of their Creator.

The type of the wheel alludes to those who, strengthened by the certainty of hope, have taken in their minds the swift course of migrating from this world. Those who, perfected by the excellence of charity, though still dwelling in the flesh, have learned by contemplating eternal things to pass beyond the prison of the flesh are expressed by the name “watchtower.”

Indeed, above it was related that Samuel gathered Israel at Mizpah and judged them there, that the Philistines rose up to fight against it, and that, while he was offering the whole burnt offering, they fled in defeat. Now he is said to have traveled around two other cities as though they were companions of Mizpah, because charity is the principal virtue that gathers the Church and protects it from every enemy. Yet in order to reach charity worthily, one must first be furnished with faith, which purifies the heart, and hope, which lifts it toward heavenly things. [Col. 0546A]

And he returned to Ramah, etc. The Lord returned to heaven by ascending bodily once, after completing the work of his dispensation. By his divine presence he returns daily, through which he, wholly present everywhere, reaches powerfully “from end to end” and orders all things gently.

There is the flesh which he assumed and glorified for us; there is the court of the blessed, of angels and human beings; there is the dwelling promised to us by God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens. Hence Ramah is rightly called his “height.” [Col. 0546B]

There, placed bodily, he judges the Church, whether still journeying on earth, chastising her until he leads her to heavenly things, or already dwelling with him, assigning to each the places appropriate to his or her merits. In the house of his Father he has many dwelling places (John 13), knowing that the Father has given all things into his hands and has given him authority to execute judgment (John 5).

There also, within the veil of heaven and the eternal Holy of Holies, he was building for the hearts of the heavenly citizens one altar to the Father. From it, kindled by the fire of his love, the incense of perpetual praise rises fragrantly from those who say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isaiah 6). [Col. 0546C] And again: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7); and other such words, which that beloved disciple, carried away in the Spirit, often heard there to be repeated and always remembered.

Thus far it is enough for the first book of our exposition to have touched briefly upon the transformation of the old priesthood into the new, represented figuratively under the forms of Eli and Samuel. We may now examine more freely, beginning elsewhere, the broader mysteries of the change of kingdom, prefigured through Saul and David—not trusting our own ingenuity, but relying throughout upon the help of him whom the whole prophetic Scripture serves, whose kingdom will have no end, and who is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0545]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0545D]

Since in this little book, the second of our allegorical exposition of the blessed prophet Samuel, we intend, with the Lord’s help, to say what we can about the end of Samuel’s leadership and the beginning of Saul’s kingdom, it seemed appropriate by way of introduction to discuss something about the period during which each of them ruled over God’s people and, since Holy Scripture appears to be silent on this matter, to investigate carefully what may be considered most probable.

There were indeed some who said that neither ruled for more than thirteen years, because it is written: “And it came to pass that, from the day when the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied; for it was already the twentieth year” (1 Kings 7). They thought that the ark had remained at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years and that these years were to be reckoned from the beginning of Samuel’s leadership until after David’s seventh year, when, beginning to reign in Jerusalem, he brought it there. Yet Scripture most clearly testifies that, while Saul was fighting against the Philistines, the ark was with the people in the camp. [Col. 0547A]

It may be much more likely that the twenty years mentioned, if they designate the time the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim, should be counted up to this point rather than only until David brought it away. Some thought that Samuel should be omitted entirely from their chronicles. Some assigned seventy years to him and thirty to Saul. Others, joining the periods of both, asserted that they ruled the people for forty years. But we cannot discover from what basis any of these claims should be affirmed.

How all of them can be refuted and overthrown is very easy to see. Scripture plainly says: “It came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv—which is the second month—of Solomon’s reign over Israel, that he began to build the house of the Lord” (3 Kings 6). [Col. 0547B]

Therefore review the periods of the Judges, and you will find that Othniel ruled the people for forty years, Ehud for eighty, Deborah for forty, Gideon for forty, Abimelech for three, Tola for twenty-three, Jair for twenty-two, Jephthah for six, Ibzan for seven, Hajalon for ten—he is not found in the Seventy Translators—Abdon for eight, Samson for twenty, and Eli for forty. Together these amount to 339 years. Add to them the forty years of the journey from Egypt, the same number of years of David’s reign, and Solomon’s four years: the total is 423 years, namely, fifty-seven fewer than the 480. Those remaining fifty-seven years must be accounted for by the periods of Joshua, Samuel, and Saul; but Scripture does not tell us how they are to be divided. [Col. 0547C]

If we follow the authority of the chronicles and assign twenty-four years to Joshua, the other two have no more than thirty. If we assign forty to Saul, the remaining two have no more than seventeen. Therefore, to open some avenue for inquiry, let us review the writings of Josephus, since apart from the divine words it is difficult to find anyone more learned in such matters.

In the history of his *Antiquities* we shall find that Joshua ruled the people for twenty-six years, Samuel for twelve, and Saul for twenty years. Together these make fifty-eight years. The one year that exceeds the 480 should not trouble us. Either Scripture, following its customary practice of giving a complete total, did not bother to add the one year that remained; or—which is more believable—Josephus’s text, through the carelessness that often accompanies great age, added one year somewhere. [Col. 0547D]

We must not suppose that an error occurred in the letters of Holy Scripture. Although the Hebrew truth and the edition of the Seventy Translators differ in many other places, in the catalogue of the Judges they agree throughout, except for the single case of Hajalon, whom the latter omitted completely. This omission compelled the Greek chronographers, who were ignorant of the Hebrew truth, to assign forty years to Samuel and Saul and twenty-seven to Joshua, disregarding Josephus’s writings.

They saw that otherwise they could not reach the number 480, which they did not know how to complete with Hajalon’s years. To satisfy Scripture, they were permitted to add nine years to Josephus, whom they could by no means have ignored. Why, then, should we, similarly constrained by the calculation, not be permitted to subtract at least one year from his reckoning and assign twenty-five years to Joshua and thirty-two to Samuel and Saul? [Col. 0548A] We should not appear to compromise Scripture by believing the historians more than is proper. Scripture absolutely asserts that the 480th year after the exodus from Egypt was the fourth year of Solomon.
