If it had been written in this way—“It came to pass after 480 years from the exodus from Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign”—there would be no controversy at all, because the additional year would itself be Solomon’s fourth year.

And lest anyone say that we are following a false rule in counting 480 years, as though according to certain manuscripts 580 should rather be reckoned, the translator of the sacred history himself, when he translated the book of *Chronicles* into Latin, upon reaching Solomon’s fourth year and mentioning that the temple began to be built in that year, immediately added—whether from his own learning gathered from the Holy Scriptures or from Greek authority—and said: “The entire period from Moses and the exodus of Israel from Egypt up to the present year amounts to 480 years.” [Col. 0548B]

Let no one be disturbed in the calculation of the period by what we wrote above and already mentioned: “From the day when the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied; for it was already the twentieth year, and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord.”

This verse may also be understood in such a way that it does not indicate that the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years, but rather that, from the day when the ark remained there, the whole house of Israel rested after the Lord for twenty years—rejoicing, of course, over the return of the ark which they had lost because of their sins, but afterward gradually sharing in Saul’s sins and departing from its path. [Col. 0548C]

But since the preface has grown lengthy, let us now begin the very sequence of Scripture that we are examining.

## CHAPTER ONE

Samuel, now old, appoints his sons as judges over Israel. But when they turn aside from the right path, the people ask that a king be established over them. At the Lord’s command Samuel explains the right of the king, yet even so he is unable to turn them back from their most wicked intention.

**1 Kings 8.** “And it came to pass, when Samuel had grown old,” etc., up to “each shall go to his own city,” etc.

Understood literally and typologically, this reading reproves those who, neglecting what they have learned through holy commandment, desire instead to serve their own cravings. It may be understood generally of all who are falsely faithful, and particularly of the Jews: either because, after the Savior’s incarnation, for love of an earthly kingdom they rejected the preachers of the heavenly kingdom; or because, despising the peaceful rule once exercised by the judges, they desired, contrary to the Lord’s counsel, to be exalted by the lineage of a royal scepter. [Col. 0548D]

“And it came to pass,” he says, “when Samuel had grown old, that he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.” In Scripture, when the name “old age” is used mystically, it sometimes signifies the maturity of wisdom and the gravity of counsel, and sometimes the sluggishness of a mind grown cold toward the fresh fervor of an initial virtue.

It is said of the righteous Judge, whose wisdom no conscience can deceive: “The Ancient of Days sat.” It is also said of his members: “The glory of the old is gray hair,” that is, the gravity of wisdom. In the negative sense, the one who felt himself growing lukewarm in the pursuit of virtue said: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Psalm 6).

What is said of Samuel growing old and appointing his sons as judges of Israel may suit both meanings. When faith and love of Christ had grown old among the Jews—some growing cold toward it as toward a very advanced old age, while others had become mature in it as though through a long habit of living—the Lord himself appointed the scribes and Pharisees as judges of that people. They ought to distinguish the right way of life and show it to those subject to them. They were called sons of God, in accordance with what he said in Exodus: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4). [Col. 0549A]

This statement may equally be referred both to the incarnation of the Lord and to the period when judges were first established by the Lord among that same people. For at that time too, as the prophet bears witness, “the righteous person lived by faith” (Habakkuk 2)—without doubt referring to the faith of which Peter says: “But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, just as they were” (Acts 12). [Col. 0549B]

And the name of his firstborn son was Joel, etc. Joel is interpreted as “beginning” or “was of God” (*fuit Dei*); Abijah as “the father was”; Beersheba is called “the well of the oath.” It is a place—as its name also demonstrates—where Abraham and Isaac made a covenant with Abimelech, swearing an oath. It signifies that saving fountain which washes those joined together by the covenant of the one and the same faith, circumcision and uncircumcision. The brothers mentioned above were appointed judges there so that they might both offer and drink from the fountain of life. [Col. 0549C]

Yet, in accordance with their names, they began but did not persevere to the end so as to be saved. Once belonging to God and worthy of the name “fathers of the people,” they have now been changed into the opposite and have preferred their traditions and crimes alike to the law and to grace.

Each of us likewise, when growing lukewarm from the spiritual fervor he had begun and placing lowly, earthly thoughts before his mind, is like Samuel in his old age appointing degenerate sons as judges at Beersheba, because he subjects the mystery of baptism to corrupt perceptions.

Then all the elders of Israel assembled and came to Samuel, etc. [Col. 0549D] After the Lord’s ascension, all the elders of carnal Israel assembled, came against him, and sent a delegation to him in Ramah—that is, to the height of heaven, where everything we do on earth is exposed with swift clarity. They said: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19).

And as though speaking to one whom nothing can escape, they said: “Look, your faith and love in us have grown old, and the sons whom you nourished and exalted have themselves despised you” (Isaiah 1). We therefore prefer, like the nations that did not know you and the kingdoms that did not invoke your name, to remain strangers to your leadership rather than be deprived of the faith, kingdom, and homeland of your grace.

For if, abandoning the skill of warfare, we all follow the simplicity of your teaching, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.

Thus the Jews spoke against the Lord and against his Christ—not with their voice, indeed, but with a reprobate mind and intention. [Col. 0550A]

And the word displeased Samuel’s sight, etc. The unbelief of the Jews displeased the prudent in Christ, who are the eyes of the Church, because by choosing what is lowly in place of what is supreme, they unknowingly said to the Lord: “Give us an earthly kingdom, which will condemn us forever.” As for the heavenly kingdom, which you promise to the poor in spirit, we care nothing for it. For their salvation the Savior prayed to the Father, either directly while he was in the world or through his members after his ascension.

Ecclesiastical history relates this particularly of James, the brother of the Lord (Matthew 5): he supposedly prayed for the people with such persistence and diligence, frequently visiting the temple, that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels. [Col. 0550B]

And the Lord said to Samuel: “Hearken to the voice of the people,” etc. Do not take away their free choice, but grant them the power to become sons of God, to those who refused to believe; and do not grieve that you have become a reproach among human beings through the rejection of the people.

They did not reject your teaching as spoken through a human being, but my divine teaching working through you, lest I grant them an everlasting kingdom in you. To this corresponds what he himself said: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7).

“As they have forsaken me and served foreign gods,” etc. That is: so they will also forsake the grace of the Gospel and serve traditions alien to God—traditions of their own.

“Now therefore hearken to their voice,” etc. [Col. 0550C] These words most appropriately fit the person of the Father speaking to the Son: “Let them go according to the desires of their heart, and they will walk in their own will” (Psalm 80).

Nevertheless, warn them through the Gospel and preach to them what temporal misery before human beings and what eternal torments in the underworld they will suffer because, neglecting service—or rather, spiritual freedom—they preferred to reign over themselves. Say to them: “Days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and your house will be left desolate” (Luke 10), and other such things. Then he said:

“This will be the right of the king who will rule over you.” He does not explain what a moderate and just ruler ought to be, whose perfection is taught in many places of Holy Scripture, especially in Deuteronomy. Rather, he indicates the kind of wicked ruler by whom subjects will be oppressed with severity, in order by these words to turn the people back from their stubborn request. [Col. 0550D]

Figuratively, however, what Scripture says about the good king signifies Christ, concerning whom it is sung under the figure of Solomon: “Give the king your judgments” (Psalm 72). What it says about the wicked king signifies the devil, in accordance with the saying of Ecclesiasticus: “An unwise king will destroy his people” (Ecclesiasticus 10). And rightly so, because the former is the devil’s, while the latter is Christ’s member.

“He will take your sons,” etc. “You have been called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Galatians 5). Whoever uses the freedom to which he has been called as an opportunity for the flesh will soon be crushed under the power of the wicked king—that is, the devil, whom he chose as lord—and will endure in himself all the forms of servitude that Samuel described to the people.

What was once said specifically of one people, but enacted over a long period both historically and typologically, must generally be applied to all mortals who cast off from themselves the Lord’s easy yoke. The wicked king takes their sons and places them in his chariots: the ancient enemy takes their notable deeds—for example, modesty, patience, kindness, almsgiving, and other such qualities—and stains them with hypocrisy, vainglory, pride, or any other destructive vice, binding them to the works of unbelievers. [Col. 0551A]

In the hearts of such people, constrained by the bridle of wickedness, that worst charioteer rides freely everywhere in his chariots, as though they belonged entirely to him, proud and rejoicing. And because the wicked enemy now joins those who are falsely faithful to the faithful through their works, the strict Judge will at the end join those same people to them through punishments. Therefore it is rightly written of such persons: “The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour of which he is unaware; he will cut him in two and place his portion with the unbelievers” (Matthew 24). [Col. 0551B]

“And he will make them his horsemen,” etc. The devil, he says, has subjugated even your stronger pursuits to such an extent that through them he strives to seize and tame others with the bridle of error, turn them aside to the path of ungodliness, and make the offspring of virtue a herald of vices.

Just as, in the good sense, the chariot of virtues is driven by one who brings prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance into the hearts of his neighbors, so conversely the chariot of the wicked king is led by one who displays to his followers examples of vices opposed to these virtues.

[Col. 0551C] “And he will appoint for himself tribunes and centurions,” etc. From your great deeds, as from children born of the womb of a good conscience, the ancient corrupter will appoint some to this office: some, like tribunes, will lead a hostile army against the camps of truth; others, like centurions, will promise those who follow them the great perfection of eternal life.

These are the ones who, sowing in the flesh, will reap corruption from the flesh, in accordance with what Hosea says: “You plowed ungodliness, you reaped iniquity, you ate the fruit of falsehood” (Hosea 10). The fraudulent distributor appoints others who, through dialectical ambushes, strengthen makers of errors and cultivators of perverse doctrines against the truth.

We may also understand as the plowers of the devil’s fields those who cultivate the hearts of the wretched through the labor of false doctrine. The reapers, on the other hand, lead what are, as it were, the perfected fruits of their lesser hearers to the granaries, as though they were purer, so that they may contemplate their more secret mysteries. This is a characteristic invention of heretics, especially of the Manichaeans. [Col. 0551D]

The sons of the rebellious people, whom we have interpreted in relation to the various actions of a single person, may also be referred to different persons, each polluted by a different error from the same one adversary.

Your daughters also he will make perfumers, etc. He will also make your synagogues—or the souls of the deceived, or certainly thoughts once free in native purity—favorably disposed by wicked flattery toward his depraved practices. Detesting this worst kind of perfume, the prophet prays: “May the oil of the sinner never anoint my head” (Psalm 140). Opposed to this is the perfumer of the good king, namely Mary Magdalene, who says: “While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1). He will also make them servants of the hearth of vices, concerning which the prophet testifies: “All of them are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea 7). Opposed to this is the hearth of heavenly love; those who received it when they heard the word of truth said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24). He will also make them bakers, who, calling the foolish to the abominable banquets of heresies, say: “Eat gladly the hidden bread; stolen waters are sweeter, and concealed bread more pleasant” (Proverbs 9, 20). Concerning this bread it is also said elsewhere: “The bread of deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel” (Psalm 103). Opposed to this is the bread of truth, which strengthens the human heart. Since knowledge of it is revealed not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven, it is rightly sung under the figure of the strong woman, representing the Church: “She has become like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from far away” (Proverbs 31).

[Col. 0552A]

He will also take away your fields and vineyards, etc. He will likewise take away your most abundant stores of spiritual virtues, the fruits of your most ardent love, and the exceedingly sweet gifts of radiant mercy, and subject them instead to the pleasures of unclean spirits.

[Col. 0552B]

He will also tithe your crops and the produce of your vineyards, etc. He will also deprive you altogether of your works, already brought almost to the perfection of their nature, and of the hope of your entire life in the heavenly reward marked by the number ten. Through the loss of these, the ancient corrupter will continually feed the ever-insatiable desires of the malignant spirits that serve him—spirits once stripped of angelic virtue and made to hunger for human destruction.

[Col. 0552C]

He will also take your male servants and female servants, etc. He will likewise enslave to his own right the foolish impulses of mind or flesh—for example, anger, rivalry, gluttony, lust, and other such things, which the discipline of the wise must necessarily restrain and curb—as well as the other duties of right intention. Among the rich flocks of virtues in which you long served in vain, but which lack the perfection of the ten, the enemy himself will finally receive the prize of the pasture.

[Col. 0552D]

Thus at last you will groan that you have become servants under the adversary, though formerly you were weary of living as free people under your lord.

And you will cry out on that day because of the presence of your king, etc. This prophecy is clear, and to this day it does not cease to be fulfilled among the Jews. As it is written in the seventeenth Psalm: “They will cry out—and there is no one to save them—to the Lord, and he did not hear them.” To them the Lord says: “I will not hear your prayers. Your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah 1)—namely, the blood for which, at the election of this wicked king, they were invoking a curse upon themselves, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27). Let them wash this away with the water of baptism, and let them cry to the Lord in their tribulation, and “he will deliver them from their distress and their necessities” (Psalm 106).

[Col. 0553A]

Otherwise they hear from the apostle James: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). In the moral sense also, the vices that had oppressed them—while they lay willingly for a long time and deliberately cast themselves down—are conquered only with difficulty and after a long delay.

But the people did not want to listen to Samuel’s voice, etc. This obstinacy of the disobedient people, demanding a king in place of the Lord, took possession not only of the time when grace was preached, but, even before the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation were celebrated, of the Synagogue—indeed, of nearly the whole human race—from the first ancestor, when he preferred the serpent’s words to God. For all the rebellious are always eager to place the freedom of their will before the rule of divine grace. But the good sons, entreating the Spirit of the Father, say: “Not our kingdom, nor our will; but, ‘May your kingdom come; may your will be done, as in heaven and on earth’” (Matthew 6).

[Col. 0553B]

And Samuel said . . . “Let each one go to his city.” Even today the divine word teaches all the obstinate and rebellious against the Lord to return individually from the public forum of stubborn contention to the court of the heart, so that each person, more free within himself, may diligently examine what he has done against the will of the heavenly disposition and what sentence he is to receive from the strict judge.

**(1 Kings 9.)** “There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel,” etc. In Saul the king, in that he was chosen by the stubborn people in place of Samuel; in that he persecuted David while committing other crimes; and in that, after being rejected and dying, he received that same David as successor to the kingdom—in all this he signifies the wickedness of the Jews. They despised and persecuted both the prophets and the Lord, preferring to reign over themselves; therefore they abandoned the kingdom of God, from which they had been expelled, to a nation producing its fruits.

[Col. 0553C]

But in the fact that he was anointed with holy oil and saved Israel from the enemy, he figuratively proclaims the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore the present reading, which recounts the history of Saul’s anointing and contains no mark of reproach, signifies the exalted mysteries of the Lord Savior’s descent from heaven for us human beings and for our salvation, his reception of baptism from John, and the other mysteries of his temporal dispensation.

[Col. 0553D]

First, however, the interpretation concerning the Lord is supported by Saul’s descent from Benjamin and by the report that Saul was chosen and good—whether because Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” or because it was the smallest tribe in Israel. For grace is always accustomed to be generated in those humble in spirit, whose is the kingdom of heaven, through Christ.

“And he had a son named Saul,” etc. “He who is of the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all.” He committed no sin, “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (John 3; 1 Peter 2). The name Saul, moreover, which means “desired” or “request,” most aptly suits Christ, who is always implored with the great longing of the saints and entreated to be present.

[Col. 0554A]

The name of his father Kish, that is, “hard,” also accords with the mysteries—whether it designates God the Father, or David, or Abraham, or any other of the fathers from whom Christ is descended according to the flesh. For that nature is hard which cannot merely be overcome or changed, but cannot even be comprehended by any created nature. It is hard through the severity of judgment for the reprobate, but through the grace of mercy it is sweet for the good. Of the latter it is said: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (Psalm 72). Of the former: “Your almighty word leaped down from heaven, from the royal throne, a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction” (Wisdom 18). And the faithful hearts of the good are hard in temptations; under the figure of Ezekiel they are told: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads. Like adamant and flint I have made it” (Ezekiel 3).

[Col. 0554B]

But the donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, had perished, etc. The souls also belonging to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ had perished, because, even if they lived justly, before the Son of God descended to earth they could not receive the first robe. And God the Father said to his only Son: “Join to your company the noble, harmonious desires of the saints, that they may obediently cling to you; and, with them following you according to their own virtue, enter upon the work of human salvation.”

[Col. 0554C]

If it is preferable to understand by Kish, Saul’s father, the assembly of the ancient fathers, it is clear that he cared for the souls of the faithful and earnestly prayed that Christ would deign to come in the flesh for their salvation, saying: “Lord God of hosts, restore us, and show your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 80), and other words of this kind.

## CHAPTER II

While Saul was seeking his father’s donkeys, he came to Samuel, who welcomed him graciously, told him that the donkeys had been found, anointed him king with holy oil in the morning, and foretold what was to happen to him.

Saul sought his donkeys through five regions but did not find them, etc. These places seem to have taken their names from the ancestors of Saul and of blessed Samuel. The Lord Christ, desiring that the souls of mortals lost in the first-created ancestor should be brought back to the way of life, did not complete his work during the five ages of this world, because until the time of his incarnation he brought no one—even one living perfectly—back into the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0554D]

But when they had come into the land of Suph, Saul said to his servant, etc. Saul is preparing to turn back from the fifth place of his fruitless search. And the Lord seemed, because of the enormity of human transgression, almost to have wished to turn back from caring for the salvation of the wicked, while in the fifth age of the world the oracles of the prophets had been withdrawn, the frequent converse of angels had ceased, and only the criminal deeds of depraved human beings were multiplying.

[Col. 0555A]

Indeed, before the Lord’s coming the world was so weighed down by so many and such great crimes that the Creator of the human race seemed more concerned to preserve the just than to acquire the salvation of the wicked. Yet he, provident for his chosen amid the troubles of adversity, wished both to test their unconquerable patience and, by delay, to sharpen their constant desires more and more. Hence it follows:

“He said to him: ‘Behold, there is a man of God in this city,’” etc. This is the patience and faith of the saints; this is their continual love, their long waiting, looking from afar and saluting the joy of the Lord’s incarnation and of human restoration. This, I say, is that frequent entreaty of saving grace found in Scripture: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us. Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever. Why do you turn your face away?” (Psalms 80, 44), and other such words.

[Col. 0555B]

“Behold,” they say, “he is in the city of worldly conduct, most noble through heavenly grace and, without any doubt, the most truthful chorus of the prophets. Now therefore let us go there, and from contemplating the glory of your divinity—which is visible only to pure hearts—let us come to behold the mysteries of the humanity once promised and long desired. For blessed are the eyes that saw, and the ears that deserved to hear these things” (Matthew 12).

Perhaps, when the praises of the prophets resound there concerning you and assist us by bearing witness to the way of our devotion, the world will begin to believe; and we ourselves, having restored to life those who had perished, shall rest from the long labor of so great a period.

The word of uncertainty is used to show the gravity of human error and the difficulty of curing it, in accordance with the Savior’s saying: “Do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” and: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also” (Luke 18; John 5).

[Col. 0555C]

Something similar is spoken in this place by the wise lover in the song of her love to Christ: “Who will grant that you were my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother, so that I might find you outside and kiss you?” (Song 8). It is as though she were plainly saying: “The invisible God whom I believe, confess, and adore within—I desire also to see and address outside, conformed to my substance.”

Saul said to his servant: “Behold, we will go,” etc. Saul and his servant were mistaken in thinking that they should seek a man of God for the rewards of prophecy. Thus they were needlessly troubled because they had not even brought a small basket that could be given to him, to carry provisions for their journey. Such a basket, woven with beautiful variety from palm leaves, was customarily offered as a gift when one was greeted, even if the bread inside it had run out—unless the holy man was accustomed to speak the truth freely to everyone.

[Col. 0555D]

The order of the allegorical sense, however, does not err. For the Lord urges his chosen servants by frequent compunction not to come empty in mind or deed to hear the word of God and seek his way, which is Christ—for “no one comes to the Father except through him”—but diligently to consider and show what obedience is fitting, what other virtues they possess in relation to their teacher, to whom he ought deservedly to entrust the word.

Moreover, in the Old Testament, whoever desired Christ to come into the world to fulfill the prophecies of the prophets, and desired Saul to enter the city of Samuel and do what Samuel taught, was immediately taught by Christ himself through secret inspiration to persist in good works. In this way they might become worthy to see and hear what many righteous people and kings had previously desired but neither heard nor seen.

[Col. 0556A]

“Behold,” he says, “we will go; what shall we bring to the man? The bread in our bags has run out, and we have no basket.” Behold, the time approaches for the prophecy to be fulfilled in Christ. What good work do we have by which we may commend ourselves to the preachers of that time and deserve to learn from him what we need?

The observance of the Law, corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees—or rather worn away by its own antiquity and almost consumed by long use—has failed in our deeds. Nor could we, through the conduct of the new grace that awaits the kingdom of heaven, possess anything before he comes and teaches, he for whom it has been reserved.

[Col. 0556B]

The baskets woven from palms, which were customarily given as a reward to victors, signify actions worthy of heavenly recompense; the vessels woven from palm leaves signify hearts expanded by hope of eternal joys.

“Behold, a quarter-stater of silver has been found in my hand,” etc. Understand the silver stater as the perfection of human salvation, by which one advances toward praising God. It reaches the fullness of its solidity through the growth of four parts: in the Old Testament it was raised up by faith in the future incarnation of the Lord; in the New it was imbued with the mysteries of that incarnation once received; at the liberation of the flesh it was exalted through the attainment of the eternal kingdom; and on the day of judgment it will also be glorified through the resurrection of the flesh.

[Col. 0556C]

Saul’s servant therefore says to Saul: “Behold, a quarter-stater of silver has been found in my hand; let us give it to the man of God, that he may tell us our way.” The ancient people of the faithful, sighing for the sweetness of the new grace, say to Christ as he exhorts them to good works: “Behold, I have found hope and faith in Christ’s coming in the flesh. Let us confess this to the ministers of the incarnate Word, so that they may instruct us more fully concerning our way, which is Christ.”

It is not without reason that the servant promises to do this together with the same Saul, who signifies Christ. For it is he “who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2).

[Col. 0556D]

“Formerly in Israel each person said . . . ‘Come, let us go to the seer,’” etc. He is rightly called both a searcher-out and interpreter of secrets and a prophet, because he speaks forth—that is, speaks beforehand—the future. He is appropriately called a “Seer” because, with the eyes of the heart purified, he searches out mysteries inaccessible to the less perfect. Hence their writings are called not only prophecies but also visions. “The vision,” it says, “of Isaiah son of Amos”; “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite”; “The word that Isaiah son of Amos saw” (Isaiah 1; Nahum 1; Isaiah 2).

Those who assert, following the Cataphrygians, that God’s prophets spoke in ecstasy, so that they themselves did not know the words of wisdom they uttered, must therefore rightly be refuted. In accordance with the truth of the apostolic judgment, we must hold the Catholic view that the spirits of the prophets were subject to the prophets, so that by reason they knew either how to speak or how to remain silent.

[Col. 0557A]

Thus the Psalmist boasts that he understood more than the elders because he had diligently sought God’s commandments (Psalm 119). And elsewhere he says: “I will sing and understand in the way of the blameless, when you will come to me” (Psalm 100). The one who sings what he sings does not therefore sing like a possessed person who knows nothing; rather, when the spirit of wisdom comes upon him, he understands what he sings.

Moreover, the prophets often inquired from the angels standing by, as though using reason and thirsting for wisdom, about certain things divinely shown to them which, because of their greatness, they could scarcely grasp as human beings. Yet it may be asked how Samuel, who speaks not of events from the distant past but of things present—that is, of the times of his own age—can say: “The one who is called a prophet today was formerly called a seer.” They wish these and similar verses to have been inserted by Ezra the priest and scribe, when he restored the sacred Scripture, as though referring to times already past. For it is clear that long after Samuel’s death, down to the time of Ezra, the name “seers,” just like “prophets,” continued to be applied in the Scriptures.

[Col. 0557B]

And they went into the city in which the man of God was. And the Lord came through the incarnation into the world, where at that time John the Baptist, greatest of the prophets, was present. The saints also came with him—not by being born again into the world, in which they had already lived and into which they desired him to come, but by turning their minds to love him also in the flesh, whom they had always loved spiritually in his hidden divinity.

And as they were going up the slope of the city, they found young women, etc. When the Lord, together with the ministers who followed him in his incarnation and with the first believers, began the lofty commandments of the new life, humble and chaste souls appeared. They had come forth by confessing from the hiding places of their sins and, taught beforehand by John himself, had come to draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior.

[Col. 0557C]

The Lord solicitously asks the women whether the seer is with them, because, examining the consciences of each person who comes to him, he investigates whether they have understood John as a prophet of truth and received his words with love.

They answered them: “He is here—behold, before you,” etc. The simple souls of Christ, to whom whatever individuals think is evident, answer: “Here is John, taught to see heavenly things, made your precursor. We ask you, hasten to follow him in order to save us; for you are our helper and liberator, O Lord—do not delay” (Psalm 40). For he too comes today—that is, he comes with the same grace and faith-giving light as you, its preacher.

[Col. 0557D]

It is time for the entire people of the elect to consecrate a spiritual sacrifice to God on the lofty summit of the new way of life. Indeed, when you, who now stand among us but are not yet recognized, have wished to reveal yourself to the world, you will immediately find him prepared to serve your coming. For even that man of such great grace, before he deserved to see you, could neither climb the highest peaks of virtue nor be nourished by the perfect banquets of spiritual joy.

For the people will not eat until he comes, etc. “The unlearned multitude,” they say, “cannot taste by hope the sweetness of the heavenly life, from which it has long been exiled, until he comes who testifies to penitents that the kingdom of heaven is near. For he first washes those who desire to become a living sacrifice to God by baptizing them, after chastising their former errors, and afterward urges them to rejoice in the hope of an eternal inheritance.”

[Col. 0558A]

And while they were walking in the midst of the city, Samuel appeared, etc. The fame of Christ and of his faithful people began gradually to spread through John’s preaching. When all the people had been baptized, and Christ himself had come to John to be baptized by him, that same John met him with the devoted services of a faithful servant, so that after proclaiming the one who was to come he might also baptize him as one who was now present and show the Lamb to the people of God.

[Col. 0558B]

Advancing in merits and perfected by the blood of martyrdom, he climbed the summit of virtue, so that among those born of women no prophet was greater than he.

But the Lord had revealed Samuel’s ear, etc. God the Father had revealed to John the secrets of his mystery while the Mosaic order still remained, saying: “After you have manifested to the world the day of the new grace, compared in every respect with the legal figures as though by equal intervals of hours, I will send to you a man from the land of the son of the right hand—that is, one who bears flesh conceived not from a man’s seed but made holy by a singular divine work. According to his name, he will save the people who believe in me and desire to see God, from the power of darkness. When you baptize him and see him anointed with the Holy Spirit, you will begin to proclaim him to all as the leader of my people.”

[Col. 0558C]

And when Samuel had looked upon Saul, the Lord said to him, etc. When John saw Jesus coming toward him, instructed by the Holy Spirit he understood that he was the Lamb of God, the one who takes away the sins of the world, the one of whom the prophet Micah speaks: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, little among the thousands of Judah, from you one will go forth for me who is to rule in Israel” (Micah 1).

Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate, etc. The Lord came to John at the boundary between the Law being fulfilled and grace being begun. “The Law and the prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed as good news, and everyone presses into it” (Matthew 11).

[Col. 0558D]

He asks him in what humility and perfection of the other virtues his conscience is established—he who had deserved at that time to see more of the divine contemplation than the other mortals. The house of each individual is his conscience, in which they continually dwell through their thoughts. He questions him not by asking in words, but by granting him his gifts. The other, answering, reveals where his house is, because he shows himself established in the dwelling of humility in all that he does: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3), and other such sayings, to which Samuel’s subsequent answers most aptly correspond.

And Samuel answered Saul, saying: “I am the seer,” etc. John answered, while the Lord bestowed heavenly gifts upon him, saying: “I am the friend of the Bridegroom; I am your precursor; I must be baptized by you, who, coming before me, were made before me.” Indeed, you will now receive baptism from me together with the believing people. Both of us will minister the food of the word while they listen, and we in turn will be refreshed by the faith of those who hear.

[Col. 0559A]

But when the splendor of your grace has shone upon all, once the duty of my precursorship has ended, I will leave you to preach. Joined to the chorus of the preceding prophets, I will undertake to disclose all the mysteries of your temporal dispensation to the crowds of the faithful, who are your members.

“And concerning the donkeys that you lost three days ago, do not be anxious,” etc. “And concerning the souls that began to perish in the third age of the world—that is, at the beginning of the world’s birth—rejoice, because through my preaching they have now learned to repent and, having done penance, to hope for the kingdom of heaven.” Understand three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

“And to whom will belong all the best things of Israel?” etc. “And who will be the giver and author of the grace that I preach, if not you? It is entirely right to confess that all things the Father has belong to you.” The best things of Israel are the gifts of heavenly joys, which he ministers to the house of his Father who is in heaven.

[Col. 0559B]

“Am I not a son of Jemini, from the smallest tribe of Israel?” etc. The Lord, disdaining the lineage of the proud, chose poor parents and those humble in spirit, from whom he would be born; and he himself says of himself: “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8).

Saul is appropriately called the son of Jemini—that is, “of my right hand”—because Christ himself, through the power of his divinity, fashioned the substance of the human being which he was to assume when born of a virgin, in accordance with what is read elsewhere: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9).

[Col. 0559C]

Appropriately he is from the youngest family among all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin, that is, “the son of the right hand.” Christ God is the Son of the right hand, and all the elect belong to his tribe. Yet the more humble each person is among the saints, the more closely he is joined to him, as though by near kinship; for Christ the man, just as he is higher in majesty, is also superior to all the saints in the virtue of humility.

Accordingly Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the dining hall, etc. *Triclinium* is Greek for “banqueting room.” *Triclinos* means “dining room,” so called from the three couches on which the diners reclined. For in Greek they call a couch or reclining place *klinē*. Among the ancients, in the place where the equipment for a banquet was displayed, three couches were spread, on which the reclining guests feasted.

[Col. 0559D]

Thus John, by preaching, inviting many to the banquets of the virtues, placed Christ and his apostles before all these, even though they came later—and rightly so, because the hall of the heavenly kingdom could be opened only through Christ’s baptism, which began to be administered through their ministry. Those whom John instructed were destined to complete the Decalogue of the Law with strong and tireless minds through recognition of the Holy Trinity.

And Samuel said to the cook: “Give me the portion that I gave you,” etc. John spoke to his own tongue, which was accustomed to provide nourishment of life to those who heard: “Proclaim the power of the one whose greatness is unique, which I commanded you to say had been given to no mere human being.”

[Col. 0560A]

Immediately that tongue, obeying the prophetic heart, brought forth words suited only to divine power and majesty. It declared that these words applied to the Mediator of human beings, Jesus Christ, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; and he who comes from above is above all” (John 3). And again: “God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (ibid.).

And Samuel said: “Behold, what remains I set before you,” etc. John spoke to Christ, proclaiming the greatness of his divine power: “I have urged all whom I could call to faith and repentance to devote themselves to virtue. Yet because we were conceived in iniquity and born in transgressions, although we strive greatly, we cannot be entirely free from sin or grasp the citadel of virtue.

[Col. 0560B]

You, who became the Word made flesh” (John 1), feed upon the banquets of perfect victory and teaching in every respect—banquets that our weakness cannot contain. Concerning these banquets the Savior himself said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John 4). John spoke such words to the Lord while also recalling his greatness and the frailty of human condition, saying: “He who is of the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth; but he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3).

And Saul ate with Samuel on that day, etc. The Lord preached with John in the town radiant with grace until John was sent to prison, saying of the peoples who would believe in him: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4). And not only by ascending to the heights of virtue did they teach the perfect, but by condescending to the lowliest they handed down common commandments of life, saying to some: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12), and to others: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery” (Matthew 19).

[Col. 0560C]

And he spoke with Saul on the roof, etc. John spoke with the Lord in the light of his known divinity. The roof (*solarium*)—a name derived from the fact that, because of its height, it first receives the sun’s rays as they rise above the lower buildings—signifies the hearts of those who, suspended from earthly desires by divine fear, are more familiarly visited by the Sun of righteousness.

When both of them—the Lord and John—had begun the work for which each had been sent, and the grace of the new light had begun already to shine upon the world, John confessed that Jesus Christ was the Son of God. He himself had been sent before him, desiring with the whole attention of his mind that Jesus should rise to perform divine works in the flesh and that he should, at the fitting time, rest from the duty of precursorship.

[Col. 0560D]

And Saul rose, and both went out, etc. Jesus manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him. Both went out—namely, Jesus and John—from contemplation of the hidden divine will and proceeded to display outwardly the greatness of their works.

And when they were descending at the farthest part of the city, Samuel said to Saul, etc. While the seated Lord, having assumed humility and poverty for our sake, showed himself despised, the last of men, and the lowest among the citizens of the world, and taught his followers also to be poor in spirit, he did not immediately undergo the setting of death, although the wicked often plotted it.

[Col. 0561A]

Rather, in accordance with the prophecies of the prophets, of whom John is also a part, he commanded his obedient servants to go before him and to pass from vices to virtues and from death to life. He himself remained for a little while in the world as they departed, until he fulfilled for his faithful the Father’s word about him, announced through the prophets.

**(1 Kings 10.)** Samuel took a small flask of oil, etc. John took the grace of the Holy Spirit that was to be preached, and testified that its entire fullness rested in Christ, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him” (Matthew 3; Mark 1). And rightly he poured it out, for it says: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1).

And he kissed him, etc. He joined the figures of prophecy to evangelical truth and the decrees of the Law to the grace of the long-desired peace, and said: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions, so that you may ask of him and he may give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 45).

[Col. 0561B]

“When you depart from me today, you will find two men,” etc. When Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, departed from John at the Jordan, he found peoples long lost through unbelief but already strengthened at that time by faith and action. He found them by recalling them to the way of salvation, while the carnal observance of the Synagogue gradually ceased and seemed as though it were dying and destined for burial—the Synagogue from which he himself deigned to assume flesh.

Rachel was the mother of Benjamin, from the tribe from which Saul derived his origin. The Lord found those whom he would save, as though in the noonday of the new love, shining with the fervor and light of knowledge from heavenly things, at the borders of grace and truth, which in comparison with the Law given through Moses is like the right hand in relation to the left. Hence Benjamin is rightly interpreted as “son of the right hand.”

[Col. 0561C]

Those believing peoples who were mercifully found by Christ confessed to him, giving thanks for his benefits, because their souls, once wandering like brute animals, had now been redeemed by heavenly grace through him who came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19).

They also confessed the mysteries of the faith that they had learned: that the almighty Father, having temporarily set aside—that is, left for an hour—his concern about the stupidity and sluggishness of fools, had been concerned for his Son and for those who believed in him, lest, perhaps, shaken by his Passion, they should fall away from the faith.

[Col. 0561D]

Once the dispensation of that Passion had been completed and the glory of the resurrection celebrated, he would more appropriately command that the unclean souls of either Jews or Gentiles, which he had set aside for a time, be sought and saved, so that those who had already been found in part might be gathered perfectly into the manger of their Lord.

“And when you depart from there and go farther on,” etc. As the Savior’s teaching advanced, he reached the point of revealing to his disciples the mystery of his Passion, through which he would restore to the world the gifts of exalted light.

[Col. 0562A]

Thabor, which is a very high mountain and is interpreted as “coming light,” accords, both in name and in location, with the mysteries of the life-giving cross. As the Lord unfolded its mysteries, they earnestly sought and found strong confessors of the Holy Trinity, ascending through devout progress toward God in the Church, which is Bethel—that is, “house of God.”

According to the grace given to them, some carried offerings of exceedingly rich remedies of repentance for thought, speech, and deed; others carried the strengthening food of holy Scripture, which consists in three modes and was to be revealed to them by divine gift; others carried exceedingly fervent cups of compunctive love, to be dedicated to God in the earthen vessels of their hearts.

[Col. 0562B]

When each of them recognized Christ the Savior in his own degree and desired his incarnation to come for the salvation of the world, they gave him the twofold interpretation of Scripture. After the first reading, namely the historical reading, which was completed through the Law before his incarnation, he himself would disclose through the act of his assumed dispensation the allegorical and anagogical sense as well, corresponding either to the truth of the present grace or to the blessedness of the future life.

He also received the loaves from the hand of those offering them when he opened to the disciples the meaning worthy of their works, so that they might understand the Scriptures. If I am not mistaken, the interpretation of the three loaves agrees beautifully with this: in the Gospel, when the urgency of need presses, the importunate petitioner asks three loaves in equal measure from his faithful friend and receives them (Luke 11). And in Leviticus, the loaves to be offered in sacrifice are commanded to be prepared by three kinds of baking: in the oven, in the frying pan, and on the griddle (Leviticus 2).

[Col. 0562C]

We are nourished by loaves baked on the griddle when we receive for the preservation of our soul those things that are stated openly according to the letter, without any concealment. We are nourished by those fried in the pan when, repeatedly turning over and reconsidering the surface of the letter, we examine what in the mysteries of Christ, in the state of the Catholic Church, and in the correction of individual conduct is fitting allegorically.

Finally, we seek the bread of the word in the oven when, in the anagogical Scripture—that is, with the intention of the mind carrying us upward—we embrace even those things that we cannot yet see but hope to experience in the future.

After this you will come to the hill of the Lord, where the Philistines’ garrison is, etc. Understand “the hill of the Lord” as the city Gabatha, which is interpreted as “hill.” Thus, when the Lord came to the height of his divine majesty, which unclean spirits were brazenly claiming for themselves, in order to disclose it to mortals, he took the company of prophets as his associate, helper, and witness in preaching. This accords with the fact that, after reading one of them, Isaiah, he himself taught thoroughly [Col. 0562D] (Luke IV). Those prophets, harmonious in life and speech, as though in the instrument they played and in the song they sang, habitually returned together, through their deeds and words, from the hidden summit of supreme glory to the common weakness of humanity.

And it is beautifully said that the company of prophets, descending from the heights and prophesying, is described as having had not musicians behind it but before it. For that teacher truly demonstrates that he has been on the heights of divine contemplation who, condescending to speak with the humble and weak, shows beforehand by his deeds, through preaching, everything he is about to say, making his actions accord with his voice, just as it is written of the Lord: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

When the prophets therefore met him, Saul, having received the Spirit of the Lord, prophesied with them, and immediately was changed into another man. So also, after our Lord had disclosed the prophets’ predictions concerning him, he himself undertook the ministry of the spirit of grace with which he was manifestly filled: that is, the ministry of prophesying, of proclaiming future joys. As the minds of believers advanced, he was changed from being a prophet into being Christ—not by beginning to be what he had not been, but by appearing as what he was.

And he will descend before me at Gilgal, etc. The Lord descended before John at Gilgal, that is, “the place of rolling,” namely, those depths of which he speaks to the Father in the Psalm: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no firm ground” (Psalm LXVIII). This does not mean that the Lord underwent the destruction of death before John, but that, before John was killed, the Jews were persecuting Jesus and seeking to put him to death, because he not only violated the Sabbath but also called his Father God, making himself equal to God (John V).

John descended to him because, following his example of humility and patience, he accepted both the rolling-place of imprisonment and death. The Lord offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father and, through his blood, reconciled to himself the things in heaven and the things on earth. But he would await the example of his forerunner until the time appointed for it. The whole of this, according to the customary usage of Scripture, is signified by the number seven, until, namely, John, having suffered death at the hands of the ungodly, should show what the Lord himself was going to suffer.

Thus, when he had turned his shoulder, etc. When the Lord departed from John, he immediately carried out the command of the Father’s disposition and was changed by a new thought, so that he who until then had been subject to his parents and regarded as similar to the rest of mortals might thereafter, as the signs of his virtues became clear, also be revealed as God. Everything, however, that John and the other prophets foretold about him was true.

But when all who had known him yesterday and the day before saw him, etc. While Jesus was teaching in his own country, many who heard him were astonished at his teaching and said: “Where did this man get all these things? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him, and such mighty works that are done by his hands? Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James and Joseph, and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him. And Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country, among his relatives, and in his own house” (Matthew XIII).

He ceased, however, to prophesy, etc. Jesus ceased to be regarded as a prophet and began to be believed to be almighty God, of whom Isaiah said to the peoples persecuting him: “Therefore cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for he is accounted exalted” (Isaiah II).

Saul’s uncle said to him: Tell me, etc. Saul’s uncle who speaks these words with him is understood to be Ner, the father of Abner, who was either the son of Abiel or of Saul. When the Lord’s relatives and brothers were asking what testimony John had given about him, but did not yet believe in him, as the evangelist John bears witness [Col. 0564A], the Lord himself replied and taught that the entrance into the kingdom of heaven had already been preached and promised by his forerunner to those who repented. But he postponed saying that he was the God and Lord whom that same forerunner had proclaimed, and that he was the king to be proclaimed to all nations; he deferred saying this to the ungrateful and proud.

Up to this point we have briefly passed through Saul’s anointing by an allegorical exposition concerning the Lord. But tropologically—that is, according to the principles of moral understanding—each of us guards within the enclosure of his breast simple thoughts, nourished by the word of God to bear the burdens of fraternal need. We pasture, as it were, ready-for-work she-asses for the daily task. If this most salutary devotion of thought should be stolen from us and, as commonly happens at a moment of temptation, slip from its own keeping toward the pursuit of everything external and worldly, escaping after the restraints of continence have been broken, we must immediately hasten with every effort of mind to gather back our wandering thoughts and lead them inward again to the manger of heavenly nourishment.

And because we are not sufficient to do anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves, let us take up the gifts of obedience and humility and climb up to hear the word of God; then, raised up by his modest consolations, let us acquire what our weakness could not achieve. With divine assistance, it will surely come about that we recover not only the observance of mind that had been interrupted, but, enriched by the interest of a more perfect gift, also begin to hope for the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Indeed, while ruling peoples devoted to God in charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, continence, and the other spiritual fruits [Col. 0564C], may we be anointed with the oil of heavenly grace as princes over this inheritance of the Lord. May we also deserve to kiss with the prophetic mouth—that is, in our customary manner to receive the exhortations of Holy Scripture, by which either our own hearts or those of our neighbors may be consoled.

## CHAPTER III

Samuel summons the people at Mizpah, seeks and finds a king for them by lot, and when Saul finally returns, the chosen portion follows him while the rest despise him.

And Samuel summoned the people to the Lord at Mizpah, etc. In this reading Saul signifies both the insolence of the proud and the humility of the Lord and of his faithful people. For in the fact that, after rejecting the Lord who led Israel out of Egypt, who rescued it from the hand of the Egyptians, who is king of all kings and alone saves from every evil, they establish a king, he demonstrates the people either of the Synagogue or of the Church: a people rebellious and preferring to reign for itself in place of God.

Even today many, neglecting the commands of Christ—who led them out of the darkness of error by calling them to faith, who rescued them from the power of darkness through baptism, and who has always saved them from all evils by protecting and chastening them as they proceed—prefer to serve their own wicked corruptions.

Saul indicates the Lord and Savior in that he descended from the tribe of Benjamin, that is, from the “son of the right hand,” because his charity and faith are perfectly generated only in those who belong to the right-hand side of the kingdom. He derives his ancestry from the clan of Metri, that is, “of rain,” namely the rain of which it is said: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth. Let my speech be expected like rain.” Hence the ardent seeker of that kingdom said: “My soul is like land without water to you” (Psalm CXLII). And elsewhere concerning him: “And he descended like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm LXXI).

Saul is called “request” or “requested,” because entrance into the heavenly kingdom must always be desired from him and sought with complete dedication. He is the son of Kish, that is, “of the hard one,” either because God the Father is not a human father who can change, nor the Son of Man who can repent; or because his faithful people, always begotten in that love, cry out with strength amid adversities: “Therefore I have set my face like the hardest rock, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah L).

He was hidden at home when he was to be anointed king, either because, when they were about to seize him and make him king for themselves, he fled; or because he teaches that he must be sought within, that he can be found within, and that what he teaches and the way by which he leads are within.

He was taller than all the people. For who will be like God among the sons of God? He had a house at Gabaath, that is, “on a hill” or “on high.” This is the city set upon a mountain, of which it is written: “And a man was born in it, and the Most High himself founded it” (Psalm LXXXVI).

A portion of the army went with him, those whose hearts God had touched. The sons of Belial, that is, of the devil or of pestilence, are the name given to those who despised him. He pretended not to hear those speaking against him; for he says: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (John VIII).

[Col. 0565C] Samuel spoke to the people the law of the kingdom, etc. John the Baptist and the other prophets spoke to the people the law of the heavenly kingdom, which is given through Christ. Each wrote it in his own book and placed it among the sacred Scriptures, in which alone the divine will is always found.

Strictly according to the literal sense, it must be said that above, where the right of the king is proclaimed, his proud presumption is foretold in order to calm the obstinacy of the people making their demand. Here, however, through the law of the kingdom spoken, written, and deposited before the Lord for the sake of remembrance, it is declared, in accordance with the commands of Deuteronomy, what a good ruler ought to be and what sort of disposition he ought to have toward his subjects.

And Samuel dismissed all the people, etc. Today also, when the sermon is finished, the teacher dismisses all his hearers one by one into their own consciences; and when the page has been completed, the reading does likewise, so that they may reconsider through meditation what they have heard and complete through action what they have meditated upon.

If anyone is troubled by the question why I have presumed to interpret allegorically the deeds of the rejected king in relation to Christ, who is King of kings, let him know that this is the custom of interpreters—or rather, the principle of the Scriptures: according to what the order of the passage requires, they freely take either good from an evil person or an evil allegorical form from a good man. Otherwise black ink ought never to be used, but only shining gold or some other beautiful color, since “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John I).

Blackness does not improperly signify whiteness. Finally, blessed Pope Gregory did not hesitate to apply not only Saul’s anointing to the kingdom of Christ, but also his very death, which occurred because of sin, as an allegorical sign of Christ’s innocent death. For read his exposition on Job, where he said: “Let the day perish in which I was born.” Likewise, in the case of King Jeconiah, who, condemned for his crime, was carried away from Judea to the Chaldeans, he understands the Lord as transferred from the unbelieving Jews to save the nations. The Church refers all the wisdom and deeds of Solomon, although he later sinned most grievously, to the shaping of praises of Christ.

Nor are there few interpreters of the Church who, when the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” understand the rod with which the rock was struck as the cross of Christ, and Moses and Aaron, the holy men who struck it, as the chief priests and teachers of the law—that is, the Pharisees—crucifying the Lord.

And if this rock, although supplying the people with saving drinks, nevertheless, by its natural mass, clinging with its back to the soil, signifies the ineffable gifts of Christ; or if that stone, the patriarch, drenched with holy chrism, proclaims the Son of God anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit; or certainly if Cyrus, that Persian, although a rational human being but entirely foreign to the faith and sacraments of Christ, could rightly be consecrated, because of the appropriateness of the figure, either as a type of Christ or by his name—why could not a man of Christ, consecrated to Christ in his youth by a mystical anointing and illustrious in the sacred name even unto death, by a figure proclaim the future deeds of Christ in the flesh?

It should be noted more carefully that Scripture itself does not approve everything that it takes as an example. For one must not suppose that the wise man was praising the art of the Marsi, which is unquestionably demonic, when he says: “Who will heal one bitten by an enchanted serpent?” The meaning of this saying is: Who corrects a teacher deceived by the devil?

If this too perhaps seems new to anyone—that Saul is said at one and the same time to signify both good and evil—let him observe the holy man Isaac blessing his son but not recognizing that same son at all. He possesses the type of the Jews, who had long sung of Christ the Savior as blessed and destined to come in the name of the Lord, yet did not see him by faith when he was already present in the flesh.

Let him observe the same son, blessed by the angel and at the same time made lame, as signifying the Jewish nation: blessed in those who believe in Christ, but lame in those who persecute Christ. Thus, according to place and time, good things are freely signified through the good, evil things through the evil, and good things through the evil.

Nevertheless, when receiving their rewards, the good take nothing with them except good things, while the wicked take with them none but the evils they have done. Just as, when the same colors are used in writing, a black Ethiopian and a white Saxon—each native to a people of a particular color—can immediately and easily be distinguished without any dispute as to what color each possesses, so it is otherwise in painting: unless each person’s color and clothing are deformed in accordance with his own appearance, the picture is exposed as a thoroughly shameless falsehood, although it promised to be an image.

## CHAPTER IV

The besieged Jabesh-gilead is entrusted to Saul at Gabaath, and when Saul arrives with the army, it is liberated at dawn.

[Col. 0567A]

**(1 Kings XI.)** Now Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight, etc. This reading teaches typologically that the wars of heretics against the Church will rage fiercely, but will always be overcome with the Lord’s assistance.

After Saul had been anointed king, Nahash the Ammonite immediately went up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead. The grace of faith having recently been spread throughout the world, the devil ascended from the abyss—that is, from the hearts of the ungodly—and, drawing with him the armies of the heretics, began to fight against the Church of Christ.

This may be understood generally of all heretics, and specifically of those who, springing up in the times of the apostles, advocated circumcision. Nahash, which is interpreted as “serpent,” is the devil. Ammon, which is translated as “a people of sorrow,” expresses the gathering of heretics—not only because of the name, which signifies the Church mourning over its fall, but also because Ammon was conceived by night and through incest.

Heresy commonly arises in the blindness of wretched thought, from a seed wrongly conceived by a teacher of the word. Jabesh-gilead is a city that cannot be hidden, established on a mountain (Matthew V)—that is, the Church exalted in the faith of Christ.

Hence Jabesh is fittingly interpreted as “dried up” or “dryness,” signifying the Church, or each faithful soul, disciplined away from the flow of vices, so that its ways may not be darkness and slippery ground, and so that, like a stag panting for fountains of water, it may continually thirst in love to see God, the living fountain.

Gilead, which means “heap of witness” or “transmigration of witness,” is the Lord, because he shows us a considerable heap of living stones, established firmly in his faith as a testimony to right conduct; or because he desires us to pass over from the old to the new, from literal testimony to spiritual testimony, and from earthly things to heavenly things.

And all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, etc. Often some faithful men of the Church agreed together, bound by genuine love and humbly obeying teachers whom, through frequent meditation on the Scriptures, they regarded as wise as serpents; yet they also knew that, in guarding ecclesiastical peace, they were to be like doves.

But because nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, the makers of error and worshipers of perverse doctrines soon exposed themselves as having no enlightened eyes of the heart. It could not be said of them, “Your eyes are like those of doves” (Song II). On the contrary, they desired to deprive all their hearers of their right eyes—that is, of the senses of heavenly and higher contemplation—and to turn them toward looking only at leftward and perverse things, rendering them powerless in the daily battle that we wage against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

For this reason Nahash wanted to tear out the right eyes of the men of Jabesh, so that, while they covered the left side of their faces with shields in battle, they could not see what they ought to do against the enemy or for their own salvation. For this reason the ancient enemy tries to deprive the faithful of heavenly light, so as to render them entirely useless in spiritual warfare.

And the elders of Jabesh said to him, etc. The more prudent and more cautious in faith said to the heretics, in whom they recognized the dragon speaking—the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan—as Christ also spoke in Paul and those like him:

“Do not compel us to believe your new doctrine until, seeking the light of the Holy Spirit, who was given to the Church sevenfold, we have passed through the writings of the Fathers by reading them. And if there is no one among them who defends our faith, we shall come out to you. Abandoning the Catholic unity, which is within, we shall join you instead—you who, having once gone out from it, now attack it from outside—and we shall hear that even in it this is read against us: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us’ (1 John II).”

They said this not intending to grant the heretics assent under any condition, but, completely certain of the faith received from the Fathers, intending to defeat them by a just argument. Something similar is found in the Psalmist: “If I have repaid those who rendered evil to me, may I deservedly fall empty-handed from my enemies” (Psalm VII).

And the Apostle says: “For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain, and our preaching is also empty. Moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we bore witness against God that he raised Christ—whom he did not raise, if the dead are not raised” (1 Corinthians XV).

These statements were not made to deny Christ’s resurrection, or to teach that the prophet had repaid those who had done him evil, but so that, through things that could not be proved false, those matters about which there was dispute might also be established as true.

Then messengers came to Gabaath of Saul, etc. Messengers sent because of the necessity of the faith came to Jerusalem, or to some other city noble in faith, in which there could be no doubt that the Lord reigned. They reported that the Church among them had been disturbed by heresy.

When the whole people of those who believed rightly heard this, it testified to the grief of its innermost heart even through tears and weeping. Anyone who has read ecclesiastical history will find that this often happened.

And behold, Saul was coming, following the oxen from the field, etc. [Col. 0568D] Behold, the Lord, the helper in times of need and in tribulation, was coming. He was born as a human being in the world after not a few teachers of the law and doctors of philosophy. Yet by teaching heavenly things he was driving them from the field of external freedom to undertake the defense of the Church’s walls. He was always attentive to the Church’s tears, seeking to wipe them away and console them in compassionate mercy.

And he took both oxen and cut them into pieces, etc. The Lord took both wise men—the one who gloried in the carnal observance of the law and the one who gloried in secular philosophy—and destroyed whatever they thought proudly, through evangelical simplicity, truth, and humility. He sent these pieces throughout all the boundaries of the Church through the evangelists, who rightly receive their name from announcing good news, with works strengthened by his cooperation.

He said: Whoever does not leave behind his former way of life, which belonged to the world, and, following the commands of the Gospel and prophecy in profession and action, girds himself to undertake the spiritual struggle, will at the end find everything that he thought he could govern—whether distinguished by the course of his actions or profitably meditated upon through rumination on the word—destined for destruction, in fulfillment of the words: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” (1 Corinthians I).

Then the fear of the Lord seized the people, etc. When the people of the faithful heard through the Gospel what heretics and schismatics, and what unbelieving Gentiles and Jews, must suffer, they were corrected by a salutary fear. Departing from the enticements of the old man, they returned to the unity of the Catholic Church. Rejecting all the hiding places of the apocrypha [Col. 0569B], they came to be numbered by Christ in the light of the shining Gospel and to give their name in heaven.

Hence Bezek is rightly interpreted as “lightning,” signifying that heavenly light of truth and grace concerning which the Lord, when teaching that heretics must be avoided, said: “They will say to you, ‘Look, here!’ or, ‘Look, there!’ Do not go out, nor follow them.” He added: “For as lightning flashes and shines from one region under heaven to another, so will the Son of Man be in his day” (Luke XVII).

The Psalmist also speaks of this light: “He multiplied them and troubled them” (Psalm XVII). Nor is it without reason that Bezek is also said to signify poverty: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V). And those who leave everything and follow the Lord—why should they not be thought to be numbered by their king at Bezek?

[Col. 0569C] And there were three hundred thousand of the sons of Israel, etc. Among the people of the nations there were those who believed rightly, hoped, and worked through love, most ready to defend the faith. The number three, because of the confession of the Holy Trinity, is referred to faith; the ten and the hundred, because of the choice of the reward at the right hand and the daily denarius to be given to good laborers, are referred to hope.

The thousand, however, because of the solid perfection of the denarius, which by its nature looks toward the immovable and stable activity of perfect love, can rightly be understood in that same Church, whether of Jews or of the nations: through the men of Judah, the strength of those who first confess God; through the sons of Israel, the exaltation of those who have learned to contemplate him more perfectly.

This accords with the Psalm: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.” It should be noted that, according to the literal sense, long before the time of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, the tribe of Judah was counted separately and the others, who were called Israel, separately, although they had not yet been divided either in rule or in religion.

And they said to the messengers who came: Thus you shall say, etc. In former times the defenders of the Church said this aloud in the presence of others; today they say it to us when we consult their writings, and they command that it be conveyed to the members of that same Church who are in danger: Let them never go out to listen to heretics, certain of their salvation wherever the truth of the evangelical sun has shone.

This is also said to all who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, because “the patience of the poor will not perish forever” (Psalm IX). But when the day of judgment inclines toward its fulfillment, eternal salvation will be given.

Then the messengers came and announced to the men of Jabesh, etc. Those who previously feared the trickery of the heretics and the thickets of their arguments now, strengthened by the support of stronger and more learned teachers, promise that they will come out to meet them not in the night of dialectical deception but in the clearest manifestation of truth and virtue. They will no longer be condemned with them by the Church; rather, they will bear arms against them together with the Church.

And you shall do for us whatever pleases you. They spoke joyfully during that night, although conflict was approaching, because they knew with complete certainty that, when the morning of faith dawned, their enemies would soon seek not the contrary sacrileges of false syllogisms, but only the consolations of fleeing and returning to their own darkness.

And when the following day had come, etc. When the grace of God our Savior appeared as help for the endangered Church, he divided it into three parts of the faithful: the married, the continent, and the teachers. The prophet designates these under the names of Noah, Daniel, and Job, carefully commanding that each group sharpen its ranks for the defense of the Church’s peace.

And he entered the middle of the camp at the morning watch, etc. When the Morning Star of sound doctrine rose amid the darkness of heresies, the camps of perfidy were immediately thrown into confusion. When the Sun of justice, the Scriptures, grew hot, those who had been utterly anathematized perished. “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I).

But the rest were scattered, etc. Although the multitude of believers is widely dispersed, it is of one heart and one soul. Heretics, however, who seem for a time to themselves to have escaped the Church’s judgment, having been driven farther away from it, are themselves divided among themselves. As Isaiah says: “I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians” (Isaiah XIX). Sabellius attacks Arius; Eutyches attacks Nestorius; Photinus attacks Manichaeus; and the other impious men raise the weapons of iniquity against other impious men.

And the people said to Saul: Who is this man who said this? etc. When the Samaritans were unwilling to receive the Lord, the sons of thunder said: “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” And Jesus turned and rebuked them: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man did not come to destroy but to save” (Luke IX).

Then Samuel said to the people who were coming: Let us go to Gilgal, etc. When the heretics have been defeated, condemned, or corrected, every perfect teacher says to the Church entrusted to him: “Come, with the face of your heart unveiled, let us contemplate the glory of the Lord.” Gilgal is interpreted as “revelation.”

And the more we are renewed in the spirit of our mind for the knowledge of him who created us, the more clearly we perceive the dangers of those whom we have conquered; for, remaining in oldness, they did not wish to reveal their way to the Lord and hope in him, nor did they earnestly entreat him, saying: “Reveal my eyes, that I may consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm CXVIII).

And all the people went to Gilgal, etc. After hearing the exhortation of their spiritual teachers, the chosen people grew in faith and in knowledge of the truth. In the revelation of their hearts, they humbled and despised themselves, sought the glory of Christ in all things, and exalted his name among themselves. For the peace of the Church they offered before the Lord whatever devotion they were able to offer.
