And Saul rejoiced there, etc. Saul rejoiced at Gilgal, which is called “revelation.” Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent” (Matthew XI; Luke X)—that is, from those who trusted in serpentine wisdom, fighting as though under King Nahash against Israel.

“And you have revealed them to little ones”—that is, to those whom the fear of the Lord gathered, strengthened, and helped both in the radiance of truth and in poverty of spirit, as in the city of Bezek. Again he said: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

## CHAPTER V

After the king has been established, Samuel proves himself innocent and just; and, to strike terror into the stubborn people, he calls down rain from heaven during the harvest.

**(1 Kings XII.)** Then Samuel said to all Israel: Behold, I have heard your voice, etc. In this reading Samuel specifically describes the condition of the Israelite kingdom. [Col. 0571C] Having testified to the people that they had wrongly asked for a king, both although he himself was innocent and although the Lord was always their Savior, he comprehends, under the figure of that same king, the changing periods of their entire kingdom. For what he says about one:

If you fear the Lord and serve him, etc. He indicated that this must be understood of all of them: namely, that because of the demerits they had incurred, just as the rule of the first king, so also the whole kingdom that they had obtained for themselves against God’s will would have later periods worse than the earlier ones. Meanwhile, as long as they feared God, they would be adorned with good kings; whenever they neglected him, they would be punished with evil ones. Finally, as their wickedness grew heavier, they would exchange that kingdom itself, together with their freedom and homeland, for captivity or death. [Col. 0571D]

He also gave a very significant sign of the people’s transgression and hardness of heart—one all the more terrifying because it was unusual in those regions—namely, thunder and rain at the time of the wheat harvest. Such things ordinarily do not come upon the Promised Land during the whole summer except by a great miracle. In this way he clearly signified that all who, after a long recognition of the divine will, neglect its command and desire to reign over themselves and serve their own appetites are behaving in a perverse order. For at the time when, after receiving the watering of the word, they ought subsequently to have borne the already ripened fruits of good works, they still show by their disordered conduct that they need the voice of heavenly correction or exhortation, by which they may be taught the elementary principles of the beginnings of God’s words.

But if anyone should seek an allegorical interpretation of this reading as well, it readily becomes clear what Samuel means when, after a king has been established over Israel and walks before him, he declares that he had already grown old, while from his youth he had lived innocently before them, with the Lord and his Christ as witnesses. For now that the Lord Jesus Christ reigns in the Church according to the prophetic predictions, the books of the Law and the Prophets bear witness to him and affirm everywhere that, as the Father and the Son—and indeed the Holy Spirit—testify, the Law is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.

Let no place therefore be granted to Manichaeus and his associates from which they may criticize either the remaining writings of Scripture, from which not one jot can pass away, or their giver. Nor does anyone who knows that he has been redeemed by the grace of the new light doubt that the figures of the Prophets have grown old. [Col. 0572B]

What of the fact that Samuel also declares that he has taken neither anyone’s ox nor anyone’s donkey? This is because prophetic and legal Scripture has deprived no one, by suggesting anything sinister, either of the threefold practice of rightly conducting oneself toward one’s neighbor or of the seriousness required for correcting and instructing one’s neighbor. The donkey, which by its innate gentleness is accustomed to carry both what human beings need and human beings themselves, signifies love directed toward the benefit of one’s brother. The ox, however, whose custom is not only to carry imposed burdens of flesh but also, by turning the fields, to prepare furrows for seed, represents those who not only endure the weaknesses of their brothers but also, by correction, overturn their sluggish hearts and cultivate them for receiving the seed of the word. In these two persons alone, if I am not mistaken, the whole company of the Church’s laborers is usually comprised. [Col. 0572C]

Samuel therefore took neither an ox nor a donkey from anyone, because the ancient holy Scripture deprived neither the learned of the skill of teaching nor the simpler people of the modesty required for living piously with their brothers.

It is also clear what he means when he says: “If you fear the Lord, you and the king who rules over you will be following the Lord; but if not, the hand of the Lord will be against you.” And what he added in conclusion: “But if you persist in wickedness, both you and your king will perish together.” Whoever rightly preserves the sacraments of faith that he has received will follow the admonitions of that God and Lord of whom Israel’s only true king says: “Just as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and I remain in his love” (John XV).

But whoever hears and does not obey the voice of the Lord has upon him the hand of divine vengeance, held over him until he has done penance. Whoever, however, perseveres unrepentant unto death surely belongs to Antichrist, the worst king, and will be condemned with him to eternal destruction. For we must not think that only those who at the end of the world adhere to that Antichrist, rising up against God, serve his kingdom. Even today very many who have been initiated into the mysteries of the faith, when they plunge themselves into various crimes, are proved to serve impiously in that same kingdom.

The prophetic reading says also to them: “If you fear the Lord and serve him, then you and the king who rules over you”—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—will be “following the Lord God, the Father of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ.” But “if you persist in wickedness, both you and your king”—Antichrist, for then you will have him as your king—“will perish together.”

Yet what he says among other things—“You shall know and see that you have done a great evil against yourselves in the sight of the Lord by asking a king over you”—does not readily seem capable of being referred to Christ the King. Whoever humbly asks that he reign over him does not do some evil, but a great good; indeed, whoever neglects to do this one thing can do no good at all.

Unless perhaps it is said that, as human sin increased, it happened that the Son of God came to suffer in human flesh. If no human being had ever sinned, he would never have fought against the enemy in human nature. Therefore, after angels, patriarchs, and prophets had so often been sent beforehand to educate the human race, he reserved his own coming for the fullness of time, when he foresaw that human beings would sin more grievously, so that, where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more. Accordingly, it may rightly be understood that those did a great evil who refused to listen to Moses and the Prophets, but by the enormity of their crimes compelled the very Son of God to come in the flesh.

Nor does the parable of the evangelical vineyard seem to contradict this interpretation. Its wicked tenants, refusing to return the fruits in due season and impiously beating, stoning, and insulting their master’s servants, caused his only Son to be sent to them.

The report that, on the day of the wheat harvest, thunder and rain were given from heaven can also be interpreted in a favorable sense: we may understand that the voice of evangelical preaching thundered spiritually from heaven at the time when hearts bearing fruit for the Law ought to have been gathered into the storehouses of the primitive Church. It may also be understood in this way: the same apostles who preached were harvesters among those who already knew and practiced the Law, calling them to the grace of the Gospel; but they were waterers among those who did not yet know the words of the Law. Of these it was said: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest” (John IV). Of the former it was said: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III).

It must be understood more carefully, and drawn out for imitation of virtue, that blessed Samuel, although the people despised him and expelled him from the leadership, nevertheless did not cease to offer the help of earnest exhortation and pious intercession. “Far be it from me,” he says, “that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you; and I shall teach you the good and right way.”

O outstanding example of brotherly love! An innocent—indeed, a most holy—prophet and priest is expelled from the leadership, yet he considers it a sin against the Lord if he does not labor, by praying and admonishing together, to raise his very expellers to the joys of eternity.

## CHAPTER VI

Saul and Jonathan choose soldiers for themselves from the people; and after Jonathan has struck the Philistine garrison, the Philistines terrify the sons of Israel with larger forces.

(I Reg. XIII.) “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign,” etc. In this reading, as the Lord provides in manifold ways, various kinds of spiritual warfare against the Church and spiritual defenses on behalf of the Church are disclosed. But first let us examine literally the beginning of the reading, which confuses many inexperienced readers.

“Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign,” etc. The meaning is this: after Saul had been chosen and anointed king with holy oil by blessed Samuel, he remained humble and like a private citizen throughout the first year. He did not concern himself with putting on royal dress or taking up the other insignia of kingship. This was also demonstrated above, during the Ammonite war, when he drove the oxen from the field like a peasant. Josephus states that the beginning of that war occurred one month after Saul had received all his honor.

In the second and third years, however, he assumed a royal mind and presided over the people with royal care. Yet he did not choose soldiers from among the people who would cling more familiarly to his side until the beginning of the fourth year.

Allegorically, however, the “son of one year” is the people of the faithful, whether in the Synagogue or in the Church, when they begin to reign. For each person can belong to the kingdom of faith and be incorporated into the members of the eternal King only after first learning that there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

He reigns for two years and thus chooses for himself three thousand soldiers from Israel, because as soon as he has learned that hope and love must be joined to the unity of faith, he chooses teachers who will diligently teach that same faith, hope, and charity to themselves and to their people and protect them from the enemy’s attack.

This must be understood in two ways. We choose as teachers both the ancient masters of the Church, who once reigned with Christ and who even now are our teachers, whose writings or examples we may follow, and new ones whom we appoint daily in place of their predecessors, judging them worthy to defend believers, those who hope, and those who love against the enemy.

“And there were with Saul two thousand in Michmash,” etc. The Church chooses for itself the stronger ones, those worthy of the number one thousand, so that it may be fortified by the sword of the word and the shield of faith. The weaker in faith it sends back to guard the tabernacles of their own consciences, in which they dwell as exiles from the Lord.

But because Saul and Jonathan both pertain to the kingdom, although their merits are not the same—for, to say nothing of other things, one pursues David, though guilty before God, as an enemy, while the other loves him as his own soul—two orders of believers or preachers seem to be signified in them.

One consists of those who say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” (Matt. VII). The other consists of those who hear: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke XXII).

Hence Saul is properly called “the sought-after one,” plainly referring to him of whom the Lord says to the apostles: “Behold, Satan has sought you, to sift you like wheat” (ibid.). Jonathan, however, is interpreted as “gift of the dove” or “he has given to the dove,” or “gift of the Lord.” He signifies those who attribute whatever virtue they possess to the Spirit of grace and confess that they have received it from him.

They report that Saul remained in Michmash and on Mount Bethel—that is, in humility and on the mountain of the house of God—while Jonathan remained in Gibeah of Benjamin, that is, on the hill of the son of the right hand, together with his soldiers. For even the reprobate sometimes seem to exercise or even teach spiritual virtues, although with a leftward or unstable mind; only those endowed with dove-like simplicity are proved to belong to the exalted kingdom of Christ, who is at the right hand of God.

The fact that two thousand were with Saul but one thousand with Jonathan clearly teaches that the more perfect people are, the fewer they are. Or certainly, the two thousand are those devoted in humility and on the mountain of the house of God, advanced in purity of faith and in the loftiness of hope; while the one thousand are those glorious in the perfection of charity on the hill of the Son of the right hand—a charity that never fails.

“And Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison,” etc. Every humble teacher, aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, conquers the battle line of the wicked spirits by exposing their ambushes, through which they strive to take away from human beings the height of heavenly life.

“And Israel rose up against the Philistines.” When ministers of the word press their hearers either to crush the enemies of their virtue or to rouse their neighbors to the way of virtue with the trumpet of lofty preaching, the minds of those who listen rise up to undertake the spiritual contest and to investigate, avoid, and overcome the wiles of the aerial powers.

“Then the people cried out after Saul in Gilgal,” etc. As the ardor for practicing virtue grows in good people, so also the ardor of the unclean spirits for hindering and breaking that virtue grows. When they see the friends of the faithful rising against them, they strive to assault these hills with forces of various ambushes and deceptions. The Philistines ascend as chariots when, with a most wicked enemy, they bring numerous companies of pagans, assemblies of unbelieving synagogues, or gatherings of heretics against the army of virtue. They sit on horses when they constrain the hearts of wicked individuals, bound by the bridle of perverse error, to oppose the faithful. They advance on foot when they set traps for themselves.

The text aptly adds:

“And the rest of the people were as numerous as the sand on the seashore.” This is the sand exposed to the frequent waves of neighboring vices, and also always unstable and fleeting under the wind of pride. Upon it a house constructed without the foundation of the rock of faith collapses when the moment of temptation arrives, and its ruin is great.

Nor is it without a definite mystery that the army opposed to virtue is represented by the numbers thirty, one hundred, and even one thousand—numbers that usually signify the perfection of faith and works. For Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (II Cor. XI). What wonder, then, if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness? Among their many deceptive disguises, they often present themselves as perfect in faith or in works.

Alternatively, those who love only this present life—which was created in six days—and neglect to strive toward the rest to come are enclosed within the number six and do not know how to ascend to seven. The number thirty also expresses the wicked figuratively, because it is known that the Lord and Savior was sold for thirty pieces of silver not only once by Judas, but daily by many false brothers. Whoever, having neglected the truth of the faith with which he has been instructed, subjects all the senses of his body to the enticements of this world betrays the Lord, as though for five times six pieces of silver.

“And they went up and encamped at Michmash,” etc. As we have said, Michmash signifies humility; Beth-aven means “house of an idol” or “useless house.” Rising from their hidden schemes, the unclean spirits either secretly persuade by themselves, like infantry, or lead people astray through deceived human beings, like riders of horses and chariots. First they try to strip their conquerors of every defense of humility, so that, just as they themselves fell from heaven, they may implant the plague of pride in human hearts. At the same time they strive, whenever they find a house of the mind that is useless and dedicated to themselves, to encamp as though before Beth-aven in the east and, with their intermediary darkness, block every rising of the true light for it.

“When the men of Israel saw that they were in distress,” etc. Whenever the faithful see that the ancient enemy has prepared ambushes to destroy the walls of humility, either in themselves or in their neighbors, or perhaps see some of the weaker afflicted by his frequent attacks, they must immediately seek the defenses of spiritual readings, fasts, almsgiving, prayers, and the other virtues by which they may be defended. In these they must hide from the contradiction of tongues, so that the Father, who sees in secret, may have mercy and help them.

“But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan, into the land of Gad and Gilead.” Whenever the pressures of temptation bear down upon them, the more perfect set aside all worldly concerns, in which the reprobate descend and slip into the world, and by whose snares those who tempt others—or those who are tempted—are accustomed to be caught. They also salutarily bend down and cross over the swelling of pride, because of which Satan descended from heaven with his satellites.

The river Jordan displays these obstacles of vice figuratively not only by its name—for it is called “their descent” or “their apprehension,” namely, that of unclean spirits or human beings—but also by its location, since, flowing down into the Dead Sea, it loses its praiseworthy waters. In this way it signifies that all worldly enticements and the flow of carnal desire are extinguished in the lowest obscurity of perpetual death.

The elect, crossing that Jordan—that is, the apprehension and descent of the wicked—enter the land of Gad and Gilead, that is, “the girded” and “the heap of testimony.” For they ascend to a fertile harvest of good works, possessing a mind equipped by continual exercise of the virtues and bearing from itself the ever-fruitful testimony of good deeds.

Beautifully, those who are said to cross the river opposed to vices are called Hebrews, that is, “those who cross over.” Thus one says: “I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was gone” (Ps. XXXVI). And elsewhere: “In my God I shall leap over a wall.”

## CHAPTER VII

After the people have deserted him, Saul offers a burnt offering; Samuel rebukes him for having acted foolishly and teaches that another is to be anointed king in his place.

“When Saul was still in Gilgal,” etc. This reading presents, under the figures of Saul and David, the Synagogue and the Church: some falling away from the faith, while others receive the promised rewards of the heavenly kingdom. But so that the meaning of the allegory may shine forth more clearly, let us first inquire historically in what Saul sinned and deserved to lose the kingdom.

It is clear, therefore, that when the danger of battle was imminent, as the history of antiquity also reports, Saul sent for Samuel so that in such great need he might be aided by his prayers and counsel. Samuel instructed him to wait there and prepare the sacrifices; he would come to him on the seventh day, so that then, after offering sacrifice, they might assemble for battle.

Saul did wait for the seven days, as Samuel had commanded, but he did not preserve the command perfectly. When he saw that Samuel was delaying while the soldiers were leaving him, he offered the burnt offering. When Samuel arrived and learned what had happened, he testified that Saul had acted foolishly, because he had presumptuously offered the prayers and sacrifices that were to be made for the people according to God’s will.

Saul, therefore, as often happens with the Jewish teachers, signifies the teachers of the Jews. The seven days during which Samuel was awaited signify the time of the Law, which taught the mystery of the Sabbath. Samuel signifies prophecy, or the Lord himself speaking through the Prophets.

Saul in Gilgal—that is, in revelation—is commanded to await for seven days Samuel, who will offer sacrifices and intercede for the people. The Pharisees and the teachers of the Jews, while the Prophets testified to them, were commanded to remain in observance of the Law revealed and given to them until the prophecy became clearer and more open, showing how one ought to live and how the malicious enemies were to be confronted. Indeed, they were to remain until the Lord himself, the head of the Prophets, should come and offer himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the world, to conquer the aerial powers.

“But while Saul was still in Gilgal, the people who followed him were terrified.” While those skilled in the Law remained established in the knowledge of the divine will, the hearers of the Law who followed them were terrified. They began to grow weary of practicing the Law they heard, either because of the attacks of tempting vices, the harshness of the legal commandments, or the examples of those teachers themselves.

The experts in the Law are rightly said to be placed in Gilgal—that is, in revelation—by comparison with the Gentiles, who did not even receive the words of the Law and whose understanding was not obscured by darkness. Yet, by comparison with the brightness of the Gospel, they themselves have a veil over their hearts; only when converted to Christ can they behold the glory of the word with unveiled face.

Nor does the fact that Gilgal, where Saul was, is also said to be interpreted as “a place of rolling” conflict with the significance of the weak heart that has not yet reached the fountain of living water. Of such people it is said: “A sow washed returns to wallowing in the mire” (II Pet. II).

“And he waited seven days according to the time appointed by Samuel,” etc. The company of the teachers of the Law, together with their hearers, waited throughout the period during which the Sabbath was celebrated under the Law for Christ’s coming in the flesh, which they had learned would occur in the final times of legal observance. But because he delayed, so that he might come in the fullness of time that he had predestined, a considerable portion of those hearers fell away and abandoned the camp of the spiritual army.

Concerning those who wait well, the Prophet says: “My righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II). Concerning those who fall away, he adds: “But if he withdraws, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb. X).

“Saul therefore said: Bring me the burnt offering,” etc. Seeing that the people were falling away from him but not seeing Samuel approaching, Saul offered the burnt offering. The teachers of the Law who existed at that time, seeing the people greatly degenerate from the perfection of their ancestors and not knowing that the time of the Lord’s incarnation was near, established their own traditions to be observed, as though these would please the Lord in every respect.

This interpretation is supported by the fact that, when Saul answered Samuel, who rebuked him for his foolish presumption, he said:

“Because I saw that the people were dispersing from me,” etc. The mystical meaning of these words is readily apparent from what has been explained above. He immediately added:

“But the Philistines had gathered at Michmash,” that is, in humility. For unless they had been deprived of humility, they would never have preferred their own things to the Lord; nor, unless the spirits of pride were besieging the gates of their hearts, would they have scorned him who dwells on high and regards the humble.

“I said: Now the Philistines will come down to me at Gilgal,” etc. Fearing that they might either be overwhelmed by demons in the wallowing-place of vices or be rendered useless in the revelation of the Law that had been given to them, the Pharisees and scribes began to have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. As the Psalmist testifies: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. LII).

“And Samuel said to Saul: You have acted foolishly,” etc. The Lord himself in the Gospel, and the Prophets in their respective times, rebuke those who, as though sacrificing without Samuel, worship God without cause, neglecting the help of the divine word and teaching the doctrines and commandments of human beings.

“If you had not done this, the Lord would now have prepared your kingdom,” etc. This must not be understood as though God had established an eternal kingdom for Saul and afterward refused to preserve it for him when he sinned, although he had foreseen that Saul would sin. Rather, he had prepared Saul’s kingdom as a figure of the eternal kingdom.

Moreover, every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasure new things and old, reigns over Israel forever (Matt. XI)—over that Israel which he has made spiritual by teaching and governing it. To such teachers the Apostle says: “For what is our crown or joy? Is it not you before the Lord Jesus?” (I Thess. II).

Hence, to the servant who has labored well and is entering into the joy of his Lord—that is, who has acquired many people through his teaching—it is said: “You shall have authority over ten cities” (Luke XIX). That is, on account of the merits and knowledge of those whom you have spiritually instructed from the Law, you will shine more gloriously in the kingdom.

But if a teacher prefers his own interpretation to the words of Scripture and, through doctrines that he has devised for himself, fires up his hearers rather than leading them to spiritual things, then, like Saul offering sacrifices without Samuel and consecrating his army for battle, the foolish man will lose his authority. If he had not done this, he could have possessed an eternal kingdom over Israel.

Concerning such people the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Such a person is least in the present kingdom of the Church and entirely excluded from the future one.

“But your kingdom shall not continue further.” For, as he says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.”

“The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his own heart,” etc. Under the person of David he signifies Christ and the leaders of the Christian people. Hence he pointedly says “his people” and does not add “Israel,” so that he may also demonstrate that the uncircumcision belongs under this leader’s rule.

The Lord did not seek as though he were ignorant. Speaking to human beings in a human manner, he seeks us even by speaking in this way. For “the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke XIX). We were so well known to him that we existed in him before the foundation of the world.

The Lord therefore sought for himself a man according to his heart—that is, one who would know the purpose of his will with a pure mind and follow it with devout dedication. This is rightly understood of David, who, more discerning than all who taught him, came to know the hidden and secret things of divine wisdom by manifest revelation and sang them with wonderful sweetness (Ps. L).

But it is understood much better and more perfectly of the angel of the great counsel, who alone is the revealer acquainted with the Father’s secrets. We must not believe, with the Anthropomorphites, that the heart of God is a bodily organ of the human body; rather, it signifies inwardly the secret of divine counsel and wisdom.

Accordingly, it was also said above, when the new priesthood of Christ and the Church—and here, likewise, the new kingdom—was prophetically announced as destined to come after the rejection of the old. The man of God said to Eli: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall act according to my heart and my soul” (I Reg. II).

“Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal,” etc. The Prophet demonstrates the same change of kingdom that he had foretold in words by changing his location. The Lord himself, speaking of unbelievers, says: “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV). Leaving the Synagogue, he went up to the hill of the son of the right hand—that is, to the lofty heart of the people who wished to be the son not of some earthly but of a heavenly and eternal blessedness. The prophetic word, illuminated through the Savior’s dispensation, passed from the literal revelation by which unformed minds were instructed to the higher and more sacred mysteries of Christ and the Church, teaching the perfected.

What has been said about the two peoples, however, is also seen daily in individual persons. The people of Saul, established in Gilgal, are terrified whenever the mind of a believer, aware of its own weakness, is less strong either in the revelation of the knowledge it has received or in the wallowing-place of vices into which it has shamefully and feebly fallen. The mind is then disturbed and usefully pierced as it seeks its salvation, lest the spiritual adversary conquer Michmash—that is, the humility he desires above all; lest he take away the revelation of heavenly doctrine; and lest the fraudulent victor break through the walls of the remaining virtues.

Saul waits for seven days according to Samuel’s appointment whenever a person placed in tribulation seeks the Lord’s promised help through attentive faith and action. The seven consist of three and four. Three pertain to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; four pertain to works because of prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice, by which, as if by four corners, the whole structure of spiritual virtues is secured.

When someone has perfectly completed these seven days—that is, the light of sevenfold devotion—in accordance with the Psalm’s admonition, “Wait for the Lord, and act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXVI), the Lord will come into his heart. Making his dwelling there, he will immediately destroy all the ambushes of the hostile army by the illumination of his coming.

But whoever possesses less of this perfection—being less patient in adversity and less confident in the heavenly help that looks upon him, forgetting the words of Ecclesiasticus, “Do not delay in the time of distress” (Ecclus. X)—immediately loses through despair all the battalions of virtues in which he had taken pride.

So it happened with Saul: because the seventh day was not yet fully completed, he despaired of Samuel’s promised arrival and was abandoned by the people who were dispersing. If he had completed the appointed time, he would not have been deprived of the prophet’s promised help: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV).

Saul increased his sin not only by wavering over the prophet’s promises but also by offering the burnt offering himself, although that belonged to the priest. Pelagius increases blasphemy, and so does any other falsely faithful unbeliever, when, being insufficiently attentive to heavenly grace, he trusts that he can be saved by his own virtue and foolishly thinks that he can obtain, by the choice of his own freedom, the gift belonging only to the supreme Priest.

Therefore, according to the Apocalypse of John, another comes and receives the kingdom and the crown of life and blessing promised to such people. Samuel himself signified this change—not a change in heavenly counsels but in human affairs—when, after proclaiming the rejection of the faithless king and the choice of the faithful king, he rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin.

For the word of God sent into the world will not return to him empty, but will do whatever he has willed and prosper in the things for which he sent it (Isa. LV). Leaving behind the hypocritical and crafty, who provoke God to anger, he seeks simple and faithful hearers whom he may raise to the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER VIII

Because Israel has no weapons owing to the scarcity of smiths, the Philistines devastate its land in three divisions while Saul looks on; but Jonathan, crawling among the crags with his armor-bearer, became the initiator both of the battle and of the victory.

[Col. 0581A]

“And Saul reviewed the people,” etc., up to the passage that says: “And a man of Israel joined himself to,” etc. In this reading, as study of the Scriptures becomes scarce through the cunning of the unclean spirits, all the paths of the human heart—which consist in a threefold division—are immediately exposed to be miserably laid waste by them. Yet the miracle of heavenly protection will not be absent from those in danger: through the labor of spiritual teachers and obedient hearers, it will rouse the enemy to hasten his flight and its own soldiers to hope for and obtain the palm of victory. [Col. 0581B]

As the rest fled from fear of the Philistines, only six hundred men remained with Saul. Thus, when various weak people in faith tremble in spiritual combat, and sometimes even fall, only those who perform the right work with the sole intention of heavenly reward continue, together with their teachers, to keep watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened, and devote themselves entirely to charity.

The number six, by which the perfect creation of the world is signified, represents right action. The number one hundred, which is squared by ten decades and passes from the left to the right, signifies the perfection of the right hand—that is, of eternal reward.

“Saul and Jonathan his son, and the people who were with them,” etc. As has often been said, Michmash signifies humility; Gibeah of Benjamin means “the hill of the son of the right hand.” We must therefore ask how, when unclean spirits are besieging the gates of humility, teachers and hearers can pitch their spiritual camps perfectly on the hill of virtues.

We must also observe what is written below: Saul remained with his six hundred men in the farthest part beneath the pomegranate tree. Beneath the pomegranate tree is the people who can say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

For the fruit of the cross, reddened by the Lord’s blood like a pomegranate, encloses many grains of believers within a single rind of charity and hope. But the person who has the same tree of life beneath which to rest at the farthest part of Gibeah is not yet perfectly complete. He complains with the Apostle, saying: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members,” and the rest (Rom. VII).

And three bands went out from the camp of the Philistines to plunder, etc. Every person who serves lawfully in that camp feels that the Church is daily tested by these three bands. For three bands will go out from the camp of the Philistines to plunder when unclean spirits, testing the guard of our inner person, attempt to strip it of the riches of virtues—either its rational part, its irascible part, or its appetitive part; either one part individually, or all of them together. The names of those places, and of the aforementioned bands that went out, aptly correspond to these parts. [Col. 0582A]

The road of Ephraim, that is, “of the one who is growing,” along which the first band proceeded, is the appetitive part of the soul. It is rightly called by this name, because it never ceases to seek increase: an increase of good things, if it is governed by Israel—that is, by the soul that follows the right way and longs for the vision of God—but of evil things if, setting itself against the ordinances of the law, it is ravaged by the wickedness of vices and unclean spirits. And when he said of the first band, “It proceeded along the road of Ephraim,” he rightly added, “toward the land of Saul,” because the first and greatest concern of the most wicked spirits is to turn the leaders of the sacred contest away from the virtues they have begun, by means of desire, whether of soul or of flesh. In this way, when the rulers of justice have been removed, dreadful contagions may spread more freely through the unwary crowd. [Col. 0582B]

The way of Beth-horon, that is, “house of anger,” along which the second band entered, demonstrates by its very name the passion of the mind that it signifies. Israel’s possessor governed this house well when that exceedingly gentle man, gentler than all who dwelt upon the earth, went out from Pharaoh in great anger in order to liberate God’s people. The Philistine was plundering when Cain, who was of the evil one, was offended by the righteousness of his good brother and became violently angry—so much so that, through anger, he destroyed the first laws of brotherhood by murder.

The valley of Zeboim, that is, “of goats” or “of gazelles,” toward which the third band had turned, figuratively indicates the mind’s rational perception. For these animals are said to excel in sharpness of vision; hence the Greeks call them *Dorcades* (Δορκάδες), from their sharp sight. Nor is it without reason that they are so often recalled in the Song of Songs in praise of Christ and the Church. [Col. 0582C]

It is rightly called not a mountain but the valley of the gazelles, and rightly said to be situated opposite the wilderness, because we always need the assistance of humility, and especially when distinguishing good from evil, lest our judgment go astray. The humbler a person is, the more clearly he recognizes that the things of the world are to be loved and sought less.

Thus the road of the boundary overlooking the valley of the gazelles, the road of the one who is growing, and also the road of the house of anger, Israel possesses in peace. The people of God, or each individual believer, while humbly attentive, recognizes what ought to be pursued and what ought to be rejected; and in those things that he has rightly recognized as worthy of pursuit, he strives to grow until the perfect day. But toward whatever things attempt to hinder either his spiritual perception or his progress and advancement, he strives beneficially to become angry and not sin. Thus, whoever foolishly chooses evil instead of good through a corrupt process of reasoning, and wickedly desires to carry out what he has wickedly chosen, and thinks that he ought to be angry with everything that opposes such desire—all the roads and boundaries of that person’s mind are laid waste by the bitterness of the invisible enemy. [Col. 0582D]

Moreover, no blacksmith was to be found, etc. The reason is plainly evident why the enemies were given such great opportunity to ravage the land of promise—that is, the virtues of the Church: namely, if it lacks a teacher and a maker of spiritual weapons, weapons that the Apostle teaches must be taken up against the fiery darts of the most wicked one. For wicked tempters take care, as far as they can, that we not put on the armor of God, and that two-edged swords not appear in our hands for the execution of vengeance upon them (Eph. VI). [Col. 0583A]

Thus all Israel went down to the Philistines, etc. Even today some descend, having abandoned the height of God’s word, to which they ought to have ascended in order to hear it. They listen instead to secular fables and doctrines of demons; and by reading dialecticians, rhetoricians, and poets of the Gentiles, they come unarmed—that is, deprived of spiritual knowledge—to the Philistine smiths, as though to sharpen tools for woodland or rural cultivation, exercising an earthly intelligence.

And when the day of battle came, neither sword nor spear was found, etc. Since the day of battle against the hostile powers presses upon us daily, very few—while the majority are content with their rustic ignorance—come properly armed for this battle through suitable reading or hearing of the Scriptures. Hence, aided by our sluggishness, the spiritual adversary daily does to us what the carnal adversary is then described as having done to Israel. [Col. 0583B]

Now the Philistine garrison went out to advance toward Michmash. Because Israel had no weapons, it betrayed its homeland to the enemies. And we, through our laziness either in reading or in questioning spiritual teachers—through a negligence resembling failure to manufacture weapons or seek out Israelite smiths—give the enemies an opportunity, after they have overwhelmed the humility signified by besieged Michmash, to bring the weapons of ungodliness against the other virtues as well, as though against the boundaries of the holy land. But to repel the weapons of that most hideous enemy, we must seek the exhortation of heavenly teachers, with the aid of the grace of the Holy Spirit, rather than rely upon human skill. Hence what follows: [Col. 0583C]

**(1 Sam. XIV.)** And it happened one day that Jonathan said, etc. Jonathan, whose name is interpreted “gift of the dove,” signifies the aforementioned teachers gifted by the Spirit; his young armor-bearer signifies disciples who obediently carry weapons—not carnal weapons, but weapons powerful through God—whose youth is renewed like that of the eagle (Ps. CII). The particular day on which the contest began signifies their sudden inspiration by the light from above against the assaults of the enemy.

One day Jonathan urges his armor-bearer to cross over to the Philistine garrison, when every perfect teacher, suddenly visited by heavenly grace, stirs the hearts of the devout to the aid of their companions, so that they may overcome the attacks of vices.

But he did not tell this to his father. Jonathan concealed from both his father and the people his plan to cross over to the Philistine garrison. For just as it is always most appropriate to make use of spiritual counsel, so at times it is useful to conceal even those greater works of virtue that have been contemplated or begun by carnal people. Otherwise their fear might, by frightening it, break the still tender desire of our mind; or, by imitating us, they might begin what they are not yet capable of undertaking; or, certainly, the approval of those who praise imperfectly might corrupt the integrity of our spiritual purpose.

For that Saul and the people who were with him were not yet advanced in virtues is disclosed by the words that follow, when it is said:

Moreover, Saul was staying at the farthest part of Gibeah, etc. [Col. 0584A] As an indication of virtue, it is significant that he was staying at Gibeah, that is, on a hill; that he was beneath a pomegranate tree; and that he had six hundred companions. As we have already said above, the hill signifies the height of virtues; the shelter of the pomegranate tree signifies the protection of the Lord’s cross; and the number of six hundred soldiers signifies those perfected in hope and action.

Yet the fact that he was sitting at the farthest part of the hill, and that the tree whose shade covered him stood at Magron, that is, “in the throat,” are signs of a mind not yet fully perfected. This is the mind that has not yet been able fully to enter the walls of the virtues it desires; it holds the mystery of the Lord’s Passion in its mouth but is not yet able to imitate it.

If, following the ancient interpreters, we read *Mageddon* instead of *Magron*, that is, “the tempter,” the meaning remains the same. For there are people endowed with right faith and inflamed with desire for right action who nevertheless do not cease to endure the harsh struggles of temptations to vice. Therefore the perfect athletes of Christ deliberately conceal from such fellow soldiers certain of their more secret battles, which they plan to wage against unclean spirits. [Col. 0584B]

Among the passes there were projecting rocks, etc. For holy teachers striving to ascend against the cunning of malignant spirits, there are frequent snares looming on the right and left—that is, in honor and dishonor, in prosperity and adversity. Just as teeth are accustomed to chew food and send what has been chewed into the stomach, so unclean spirits, long since severed from the fellowship of the blessed, investigate how they may deceive the simple, corrupt the righteous, defile the chaste, and transfer them into the ruinous body of their own wickedness. [Col. 0584C]

The name of one was Bozez, etc. *Bozez* means “he flourished in it”; *Sene* means “distress.” Their interpretation is obvious: whether the world is flourishing or hostile—that is, whether it brings prosperity or distress—the ascent of the saints is hindered, and the tireless enemy attacks them so that they may fail either in body or in heart.

One crag projected toward the north, etc. Gibeah, the hill, signifies the sublimity of the virtues; Michmash signifies the humility of mind from which virtues proceed. Michmash is rightly said to lie toward the north, and Gibeah toward the south, because in the cold of temptations humility is especially both learned and tested; but in the light of the assisting grace of the Spirit it is brought to completion through prosperity.

But because the ancient enemy attempts both to impede the prosperous course of the virtue that has been granted and to take away from teachers and disciples the humility of virtue sought amid adversity, it is rightly said that, for Jonathan and his armor-bearer as they ascended against the Philistines, a crag blocks the way to the north, opposite Michmash, while projecting from the south opposite Gibeah. Nevertheless, when the Lord acts on behalf of his own, all the savage schemes of the enemies soon fail. For, as Jonathan’s words testify, filled no less with faith than with virtue, “It is not difficult for the Lord to save, whether by many or by few.” [Col. 0584D]

The two of them appeared to the Philistine garrison, etc. Although the Philistines speak mockingly, they speak the truth in a mystical sense. For the spiritual Hebrews—that is, those who pass beyond vices—are defended from the attacks of enemies in the safest strongholds of the Scriptures. Refreshed by the consolation of these Scriptures, they advance publicly into works of virtue when the time is favorable, in order to overcome those same most wicked adversaries. [Col. 0585A]

And the men of the garrison said to Jonathan, etc. The proud mockery and contempt of the enemies gives the faithful confidence that they can attain virtue. For “the spirit is exalted before destruction, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. XVI).

Jonathan climbed, crawling on his hands and feet, etc. It is clear that the greater obstacles of temptations must be crossed by a greater exertion of virtue. This is properly accomplished when the humble spiritual hearer, armed against the enemy, follows his teacher’s example in every respect.

But so that the reader may have a clearer understanding of the location, let us examine Josephus’s words (*Antiquities* VI, 7):

> “The enemy’s camp,” he says, “was upon a crag of exceedingly narrow length, projecting in three very sharp peaks, with cliffs running around it and serving, as it were, as fortifications to prevent the attacks of combatants. Consequently, the guards had less concern for the camp, because the place seemed by nature to be fortified against everything and very difficult to capture, since it appeared difficult not only to climb there but even to approach it. When Jonathan therefore came to the camp, he encouraged his armor-bearer.”

A little later he says:

> “When they approached the enemy army, at daybreak, they were seen by the Palestinians.”

Again, after narrating somewhat later the words of the Philistines who were taunting them, he added:

> “Saul’s son, gladly receiving this cry as an indication of victory, withdrew at that time from the place where the enemies had been seen. Changing his position, he came to the rock that lay near the fortifications, deserted by its guards because of the nature of the place. From there, as though crawling and dragging themselves along with great effort, they overcame the character of the terrain, so that they could descend to the enemy camp. Falling upon them while they were asleep, they killed about twenty of them.”

Having recalled these details about the locations, let us return to the investigation of the mysteries of sacred Scripture. [Col. 0585C]

And when the first slaughter took place, in which Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck, etc. The number ten, as is certain, ordinarily signifies either the perfection of good action or the perfection of reward. By contrast, the number twenty—during which Jacob served Laban the Syrian and sent gifts to his brother Esau, whom God hated—demonstrates the duplicity of wicked doctrines. These doctrines strive to take away from the simple and from the members of the Church either their devotion to action or their certainty of heavenly recompense. [Col. 0585D]

Half a *jugerum* of plowed land is the Church, which, while still dwelling on earth among the reprobate, rejoices to be cultivated by the correction of preachers so as to produce the fruits of life.

A pair of oxen plowing in a single day is the harmony of teachers who agree under the same yoke of faith, in the discipline of the Law and the Gospel. In the light of the knowledge commanded, they chastise the hearts of those subject to them and cultivate them to bear for God the fruit of the Spirit. Concerning this Solomon says: “Where there are many crops, there the strength of the ox is evident” (Prov. XIV).

The first slaughter, therefore, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer carried out, was of twenty men in half a *jugerum*. After this, the Philistines, thrown into confusion and scattering here and there, slaughter one another with a very great massacre. First the Church, which is exiled from the Lord, restrains its enemies through spiritual teachers and obedient disciples from besieging and disturbing the faith or conduct of its people, and reveals them as children of death. Then the enemies themselves, representing conflicting errors, stab one another as though with opposing swords, so that, with the Church triumphing, it may plainly be understood of them what is said: “The sword of each was turned against his neighbor.” [Col. 0586A]

And there was a miracle in the camp, throughout the fields, etc. The constancy and virtue of the righteous becomes a miracle to the reprobate, as though they were encamped throughout the fields, possessing a heart that is exercised yet weakened alike by wickedness and by an abundance of pleasures. Hence blessed Peter the Apostle, when describing the licentiousness of those who, as though settled in the open field of pleasure, lead their lives in desires, drunkenness, revelries, drinking, and unlawful worship of idols, added: “In this they are astonished that you do not run with them into the same confusion of licentiousness” (1 Pet. IV).

The spiritual adversaries too, although they are the fiercest plunderers of human salvation, themselves often stand amazed at the deeds of perfected men and yield to the devotion of their perfected prayers and other virtues. [Col. 0586B]

And the land was thrown into confusion, etc. That those who think only of earthly things should be disturbed by the deeds of heavenly men, and that demons, broken in the wickedness of their strength, should recoil trembling and groaning from their attempts against human beings—this is not the work of human virtue but a miracle of divine mercy. Hence, when Paul said that he had labored more than all the others, he immediately added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. XV). [Col. 0586C]

And Saul’s watchmen looked out, etc. Those look out above all others who have climbed the watchtower of sacred Scripture and stand upon the hill of the son of the right hand—that is, established in the lofty fortress of heavenly works, distinguished both by pure knowledge and by simple action. They are the first to see the impending downfall and the flight of the wicked.

For it is not granted to all Catholics, after reading the books of heretics or Gentiles, immediately to recognize what error they contain; nor, after hearing the tricks of dialecticians, at once to discern with an acute mind the ruinous snares of deception. This belongs to those whose senses have been trained, either through long meditation upon the Scriptures or through the grace merited by virtue, for the discernment of good and evil.

The feet of many were almost moved, their steps almost slipped, because they were jealous of sinners when they saw the peace of sinners. But that most noble watchman, wonderfully ascending to the hill of the son of the right hand, saw the impious man exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon (Ps. LXXII). “I passed by,” he says, “and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI).

And this is what it means for the watchmen set on Gibeah to see the multitude fallen: those who are situated below and have not yet climbed the summit of perfect knowledge thought that this multitude stood in prosperity and lived in safety. The wise foresee with complete certainty the punishment of those who live in wickedness. [Col. 0587A]

And Saul said to Ahijah: Bring the ark of God, etc. Ahijah is called “his brother,” or “the brother of him.” Thus the good leaders of the Church speak; so do the faithful who wage daily battles against the powers of the air. They speak to their brothers endowed with the reading of sacred Scripture and who, through greater exercise of virtue, daily offer themselves to God as a living sacrifice through the royal priesthood. Those who see themselves still being driven by temptations, or the Church generally disturbed by heresies, ask such men that, when the secrets of the divine utterances have been disclosed, clearer testimonies may be rationally explained to them—testimonies they ought to use against the makers of heresies and by which they may overcome the other struggles of temptation. [Col. 0587B]

But it often happens that the enemies of the Church—by “enemies” I mean heretics or Gentiles—have so many battles and verbal or doctrinal conflicts among themselves that, through their mutual disposition, they are better shown to be false in what they teach and impure in what they do than by an assertion from the spiritual pages. Then the leaders of the heavenly army must do what Saul is described as having done. When tumult arose in the camp of the Philistines and grew greater and greater, he no longer sought God through the priest; instead, taking the soldiers with him, he hastened to pursue and drive into flight the enemies whom he had discovered were quarreling among themselves.

The priest Ahijah, guardian of the Lord’s ark, may also appropriately represent the very authors of sacred Scripture. Whenever they are devoutly asked, they bring forth for us the ark of the divine oracle that they guard. They also bring forth examples of the good works they performed, as was signified above where that same Ahijah is said to have carried the ephod.

Nor is it irrelevant that he is said to have been in Shiloh: the son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinehas, who had been born of Eli the priest of the Lord. For Ahitub is interpreted “good brother.” Indeed, many of the authors of sacred writings derived their lineage from priests. Taught by good brothers, they nevertheless had some brothers who were not good, as Scripture itself bears witness. Likewise today, its readers, though instructed by the good, cannot avoid the company of those evil ones whom Ichabod—inglorious both in origin and in name—signifies. [Col. 0587C–D]

Then Saul and all the people shouted, etc. Although the Jews, Gentiles, and heretics are all enemies of the Church, each individually strikes the others with the sword of the word. The Jews fight among themselves through the Pharisees and Sadducees. Likewise, heretics and pagans, amid such great disagreement among their various doctrines and sacred practices, wage against one another wars no less serious than those they wage against the Church.

“But one is my dove, my perfect one” (Song of Songs VI): one belongs to her mother, chosen by her who bore her. From her Jonathan, that most powerful leader, received the name of virtue by which he was called “the gift of the dove.” The discord of the wicked serves the perpetual peace of this one. Hence what follows:

But the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, etc. Many had been seduced by heretics and fought with them against the Church. When they recognized the disagreement of their doctrine and saw, through Catholic simplicity—like Jonathan’s deed—that their dialectical crags had been crossed and overcome, they returned so that, through the imposition of the priest’s hands, they might be reconciled to the Catholic Church.

All the Israelites who had hidden themselves on Mount Ephraim, etc. It is rightly a matter of discernment that whoever is able should fight on behalf of the Church by teaching or reproving the reprobate, mindful of the prophetic saying: “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII).

But whoever is not effective in teaching should hide himself in the fruitful height of his mind, lest he be found by the deceitful enemy and stripped of his virtues. For there are people who are not capable of detecting and overcoming the cunning of heretics or the other snares of the ancient enemy. Yet, when these have been exposed by others, they do not cease to pursue them according to their strength and to hate them.

This is what is meant when the Israelites who had previously hidden themselves on Mount Ephraim—that is, on the fruitful mountain—immediately join their own people in battle after hearing that the Philistines had fled. Nevertheless, the Church is always saved not by its own effort but by divine assistance. [Col. 0588B]

The battle reached as far as Beth-aven. Beth-aven is called “house of an idol,” or “useless house.” Thus the Church pursues the heretics by reproving them until it proves that they have blasphemed in many matters no less than the madness of the pagans; and it extends the sword of the word until it restores even the impious and unbelieving to piety and faith.

And an Israelite was joined to his companions on that day. When the enemies have been put to flight in various directions, the Church, spread throughout the whole world, rejoices in one and the same love of brotherhood. [Col. 0588C]

**CHAPTER IX.** Saul adjures the people not to eat before the enemy has been destroyed, and not to eat with blood after the enemy has been destroyed. He forbids the building of an altar, and because of Jonathan’s guilt he does not obtain the oracle of the Lord that he seeks; nevertheless, the people rescue Jonathan from death.

Then Saul adjured the people, saying: “Cursed be the man,” etc., up to the passage written: “But the Philistines had gone away to their own places.” This reading instructs teachers of truth to abstain not only from the other enticements of the world but also from seeking the sweetness of secular eloquence; and it teaches them to slay those whom they instruct upon the rock of faith, separating them from every corruption of their former life. [Col. 0588D]

Saul therefore adjured the people pursuing the fleeing Philistines that no one should eat until victory over the enemy had been completed. Each person, fearing the oath, abstained from bread, though eager for it, and from the honey that he saw flowing in the forest.

The excellent teacher commanded that whoever contends in the contest of faith should abstain from all the enticements of the world. Kindling the others by his own example, he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX).

Whether flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (1 Cor. IX), or a heretic contradicts a Catholic, or a Jew or Gentile contradicts a Christian, or any unclean spirit resists, all the assaults of temptation are better overcome through the discipline of self-restraint. Its power extends so widely that one ought also to abstain from loving and pursuing excessively the sweetness of secular eloquence, through which the proud and uncultivated forest of the philosophers flows.

“For the lips of a strange woman are a dripping honeycomb” (Prov. V). [Col. 0589A]

But Jonathan had not heard when his father adjured the people, etc. He says that their eyes were illuminated—refreshed and renewed for seeing—although they had already begun, as commonly happens, to waste away through prolonged fasting or labor.

Jonathan, therefore, who had earlier overcome the teeth of the crags and the blows of swords, and who, after suppressing the enemy’s audacity, had provided his people with the cause of victory and salvation, is suddenly overwhelmed by an unforeseen fault of flattering gluttony (*gastrimargia*).

Likewise, noble teachers of the Church and victors in great contests often incur a fault that they did not foresee by reading the books of the Gentiles with an excessive delight. One of them even writes that for this very reason he was chastised in a vision, and that the Lord declared to him amid striking blows that he should be regarded not as a Christian but rather as a Ciceronian.

Nor do many faithful hearers, powerful in the grace of virtues, cease to be tested by lesser vices. This is plainly brought about by a divine dispensation, so that those who cannot overcome lesser contests by themselves may learn not to attribute anything to themselves in the great things they possess, but to give thanks solely to the Father of lights.

Jonathan dipped his staff—which he used either for his horse or as support while traveling—into a wild honeycomb, and so brought it from his hand to his mouth. [Col. 0589B–C]

Likewise, any teacher, while seeking by the authority of his power either to govern his subjects or to conduct himself without offense, sometimes believes that he needs the arguments or maxims of the Gentiles for assistance. Thus, as I may put it, his eyes are illuminated by a honeyed mouth drawn from these sources, as though by a honeycomb-like arrangement of words, so that his mind becomes sharper in expressing what he correctly knows. But the progress of that same mind is often delayed when, recalling the vanity of those ideas, he is kept from pursuing the advocates of wicked actions or doctrines.

The Psalmist sings of this, saying: “The wicked have told me stories, but not as your law, O Lord; all your commandments are truth” (Ps. CXVIII). [Col. 0589D]

Your father bound the people with an oath, etc. “He disturbed them,” because he prohibited everything. If he had forbidden some things and permitted others, the matter would seem to have been handled more appropriately.

Yet because in such matters the commands of spiritual fathers must be obeyed, the fact that Jonathan was discovered by lot, and that the oracle of the Lord was withheld from Saul when he consulted it that day, makes this clear beyond doubt. If the command of an earthly king had such force with God, how much force do you think a spiritual teacher’s command has?

In the typological sense as well, earthly hearts are disturbed if someone commands them to pursue only heavenly things, when the Lord testifies that new wine should not be put into old wineskins. The understanding of readers is disturbed and forced to fail if someone judges that they must be wholly prohibited from reading secular literature, even though they may take for themselves whatever useful things they find in it.

Otherwise Moses and Daniel would not have been allowed to be instructed in the wisdom and literature of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, although they abhorred both their superstitions and their pleasures. Nor would the teacher of the Gentiles himself have inserted several lines of poets into his writings or sayings.

But one must gather a sharp rose among thorns with far greater caution than a soft lily among its leaves; and salutary counsel is sought far more safely in apostolic pages than in Platonic ones. For the bees themselves that make such honey present sweet words with their mouths to soothe, but in what follows they preserve poisonous deeds that strike. [Col. 0590A]

You yourselves have seen that my eyes were illuminated, etc. These words suit the person who does not judge the reading of Gentile literature harmful to learned people in the Church, or even to teachers.

“You see,” he says, “that I have become more effective, sharper, and readier to deliver what is fitting because I have tasted a little of the flower of Ciceronian reading. How much more confidently and surely would the Christian people ridicule and refute the errors of the Gentiles, and rejoice more devoutly in their sound faith and give thanks for it to the Father of lights, if they had learned the sects and doctrines of the Gentiles?”

For Moses and Daniel should not be thought to have wished to learn secular wisdom for any other reason than that, once they knew it, they might better destroy and overcome it.

So they struck the Philistines on that day, etc. Michmash signifies humility; Ajalon signifies the plains. In everything the Church rightly does, it strikes the Philistines, because through the good things it does, it weakens the forces of evil spirits. They must be struck from the humility in which virtue begins to the breadth in which virtue is perfected—from the beginning of faith to the fruitful expansiveness of charity.

Concerning this it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII). The universal condition of the Church itself also begins with the humility of a single Jewish nation and reaches, by growing, to the ends of the whole world. Concerning these the Psalmist sings to the Lord: “Your fields will be filled with abundance; the boundaries of the wilderness will grow rich” (Ps. LXIV). [Col. 0590C]

But the people were exceedingly weary, etc. When it is said that the people ate with the blood, one must not think that they ate bloody and raw flesh, which is altogether characteristic not of human nature but of beasts. Rather, after animals had been slaughtered, they cooked or roasted the meat before the blood had been properly drained and before the flesh had been purified, and then they ate it.

This signifies sluggish teachers who, as we see today, often wearied by the lengthy labor of catechizing, slaughter, by instructing them away from Gentile rites, some whom they had rescued through preaching from demonic errors. They have attempted to imitate the one to whom it was said from heaven concerning animals of every kind: “Kill and eat” (Acts X).

But they slaughter and eat, as it were, upon the earth and with the blood, those whom they do not withdraw sufficiently from earthly perceptions and from the enticements of flesh and blood, either by teaching or by their own manner of life. They hasten to incorporate into the members of the Church people still accustomed to vices and not yet instructed in the practice of virtues.

This is contrary to the example of the Church’s first shepherd, who, stationed in the upper room—that is, at the summit of living or teaching—was commanded to slaughter what had been offered and purified by God, and to eat it.

It should also be noted that however complete human perfection of mind may be, it is weak: Jonathan, the performer of so many great deeds and the author of such a triumph, unknowingly fell into the stealthy snare of gluttony. After the appointed period of careful abstinence had been observed, after so many enemies had been struck down in a single day, the entire people too were overthrown by victorious gluttony.

But because the temptation of gluttony is manifold, it drew one person to eat before the permitted time, while it persuaded another, after the permitted time had arrived, to consume things that were less permissible. [Col. 0591A]

They reported to Saul, saying that the people had sinned against the Lord, etc. When the perfect rulers learn of the negligence of careless teachers—that they sin against the Lord by baptizing those whom they have not yet cleansed from carnal thought through complete instruction in the faith—they immediately accuse such people of transgression and order the rule of heavenly life to be publicly set forth with Catholic authority.

They also command the inactive teachers, whom popular ignorance had previously afflicted, to bring all those whom they have undertaken to instruct to the form of life that they themselves had learned from their fathers. By catechizing them according to the firmest model of Catholic perfection, they are to slay them with respect to their former manner of life inherited from paternal tradition, baptize them, and incorporate them into the members of the Church, so that they may no longer sin against the Lord by attaching people ignorant of the faith and of heavenly life to the unity of their body, that is, to the Church of Christ.

Understand the ox and ram seized from the Philistines and slaughtered and eaten by God’s people upon the intellectual rock as signifying any foolish and proud person renewed from a deadly way of life into spiritual life. Likewise, as stated above, the sheep and calves, together with the oxen taken from them, indicate those equally devoted to the irrational movements of soul or flesh and to wantonness, but saved through the Lord. [Col. 0591C]

Saul built an altar to the Lord. He built an altar so that, after a holocaust had been celebrated upon it, he might also intervene on behalf of the people’s sin, which they had rashly committed.

Every perfect teacher builds faith in the Lord’s Passion in the heart of the hearers. Upon the altar of the life-giving cross that precious blood was poured out for the remission of sins. The teacher instructs everyone by an evident example: if the Lord’s death was such, then servants must all the more mortify their members that are upon the earth—“fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is service of idols” (Col. III)—and all similar things. It is perfectly clear that these are works of flesh and blood and cannot be joined to the fruit of the Spirit.

Moreover, whenever we repeat daily the words or deeds of the ancient fathers and wish through them to be spiritually refreshed while struggling with the enemies, all of us who perceive the words of such great authority only according to the letter eat with the blood, as though slaughtering oxen and sheep upon the earth, because we handle heavenly things with a carnal and earthly perception.

But whoever recognizes that all things are recapitulated spiritually in Christ and in the Church may eat what has been slain without guilt upon that great rock which, cut from the mountain without hands, grew after the destruction of the world’s empire and filled the whole earth. Such a person builds for the Lord an altar of devotion and pious understanding that is now pleasing to him. [Col. 0592A]

And Saul said: “Let us attack the Philistines by night,” etc. Saul planned to attack the Philistines by night and destroy them completely. He consulted the oracle of the Lord but did not obtain a response. Seeking the author of the sin, he discovered him by lot; and when Jonathan confessed, Saul condemned him to death. Yet, because Jonathan had accomplished a great salvation in Israel, the people rescued him from the sentence of death. [Col. 0592B]

Good rulers often wish to conquer all the snares of demons and, if possible, to purge completely from the field of this world the weeds sown among the good seed. But they do not receive from the Scriptures the Lord’s answer that this can be done. When they seek the cause, they hear of none more significant than human frailty and ignorance.

For even outstanding teachers and leaders of believers cannot be free from the stealth of sin in the good things they do; rather, “we all offend in many things.” Yet, lest they suffer eternal death on account of these faults, they are aided both by the merits of the good things they have done and by the prayers of the Churches that they have fortified through their struggles. [Col. 0592B]

And Saul withdrew, so that he would not pursue the Philistines, etc. Teachers conscious of their own frailty withdraw, recognizing that they cannot suffice to investigate or abolish all the deceits of demons. But woe to those hearts to which unclean spirits, repulsed and cast out, return as though to their own places. [Col. 0592C]

**CHAPTER X.** Saul conquers the enemies of Israel throughout the surrounding region, renowned for the glory of both his sons and his soldiers.

At Saul, after consolidating his kingdom over Israel, fought, etc., up to the passage that says: “For whenever Saul saw any strong man and fit for battle, he joined him to himself.” In this reading, under the figure of the growing kingdom or house of Saul, the faith of Christ, destined to be proclaimed throughout the world, is described. He fought all around against all his enemies, because Christ, sending preachers from Judaea—which lies in the midst of the nations [Col. 0592D]—subjugated to his name by his word the peoples hostile to him. As the Psalmist foretold: “All who are around him shall offer gifts” (Psalm 75).

“Against Moab and the sons of Ammon, and Edom,” etc. Moab and Ammon, conceived by incest at night with the help of drunkenness, in which there is lust (Ephesians 5), signify heretics: degenerate descendants of the paternal faith, having received its seed in disorder. Edom, who was assigned to serve his younger brother, though he was the elder, expresses the people of the Jews, who throughout the world are subjected to the nations of the Gentiles both by the blindness of an unfaithful mind and by the condition of earthly servitude. “The kings of Zobah, the Philistines, and Amalek,” concerning whom it is said next.

“And having gathered the army, he struck Amalek,” etc. [Col. 0593A] This signifies nations foreign to the faith and sacrament of the blood of the patriarchs. Christ overcomes all of them, as enemies of his peace, in two ways, so that he may rescue spiritual Israel from the hand of its destroyers: either by saving believers through his faith, or by condemning unbelievers through his just judgment.

“Now the sons of Saul were,” etc. Saul’s three sons represent the great leaders of the Catholic faith, which proclaims one God in three persons. Since they are what they are not by their own strength but by God’s grace; since they desire to enjoy the vision of their eternal Creator, of whom it is said, “But you are the same” (Psalm 108); and since they trust that through Jesus Christ, the true King and Savior, they will be saved and reign forever, the first son is rightly interpreted as “Gift of the Dove,” the second as “I Desired” [Col. 0593B], and the third as “My King Is Salvation.” His two daughters indicate the weaker multitudes of the faithful, devoted to God in body and mind; or certainly, the elder daughter bears the figure of the synagogue, while the younger represents the Church. The etymology of their names also corresponds: for since the Synagogue of the elect was gathered not from all the widely spread nations, but from the multitude of the Israelite race alone, whereas the Church was called to the faith from all the Gentiles, the elder daughter is rightly said to be interpreted “from the multitude,” and the second “from all.”

Saul’s wife, Ahinoam, whose name is interpreted “beauty of a brother,” figuratively announces the whole perfection of the Catholic Church. In the Song of Songs she is frequently called both the sister and the beautiful one of her Creator, who deigned to become her brother through the mystery of the Incarnation [Col. 0593C].

Abner, his commander, whose name is said to mean “the father’s lamp,” signifies either John the Baptist, who was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5), or men of virtue who shine forth with singular eminence above the other defenders of the Church.

We have thought it appropriate to admonish the reader that, in the figurative interpretation, the same persons do not always maintain one identical mode of representation. When the circumstances surrounding the events change, the forms and arrangements of the figures likewise change according to time and place.

“Now there was a powerful war against the Philistines,” etc. The principal cause of the powerful war against the Philistines was that Saul joined every strong man and every man fit for battle to himself. For if the king himself [Col. 0593D] were supported by no force of stronger warriors, he would by no means be terrifying to the neighboring enemies or arouse them powerfully to war. Rather, just as in earlier times Israel had served them most shamefully, without any hope of freedom, so indeed—so indeed—in the Church, all of us who are lax in good works and are not equipped with the warfare of spiritual virtues, because we sin in laziness and negligence, pay tribute to hostile enemies through the enfeebling torpor of an evil way of life.

But when we recover from the slavery of sin, we take up again the hope of victory. The enemy rises and attacks us with more frequent and sharper goads of temptation, either to bring us back, if he can, into the service of wicked deeds, or, if he cannot, at least to avenge more grievously, by raging against us, the injury of our having despised him.

But, in order to pass from these moral matters [Col. 0594A] to the contemplation of the deeds of our ancestors in their allegorical sense: at the very beginning of the nascent Church, the more men Christ joined to himself who were strong and fit for spiritual battle, the more numerous and frequent were the spoils of souls that he took through them from unclean spirits. Yet he also endured greater struggles of martyrdom from those same men.

# CHAPTER XI

Saul, commanded to destroy Amalek, orders the relatives of Moses to withdraw so that they may not perish with the others.
