Because he violated the command in part, he hears from Samuel, whose cloak has been torn, that the glory of the kingdom will be torn away from him. Moreover, Samuel, after killing the king of Amalek himself, thereafter refuses to see Saul.

*(I Samuel 15).* “And Samuel said to Saul: ‘The Lord sent me to anoint you as king,’” etc., up to the passage that says, “That he had appointed Saul king over Israel.” This reading teaches, under the figure of Samuel and David, that the kingdom of the Jews would be transferred to the Gentiles on account of unfaithfulness; indeed, it teaches that all who do not hate sins, together with their authors, with a perfect hatred must be uprooted from the kingdom of faith. It also teaches that, although this kingdom is given to their better neighbors, those who practice iniquity must nevertheless be destroyed together with their works.

“Samuel said to Saul: ‘The Lord sent me to anoint you as king,’” etc. The prophetic word says daily to the rulers of the Church that they were chosen to govern his people not by the exertion of their own freedom, but through the Lord’s own ministry; and therefore they must always receive the voice of his command with attentive ear.

It also says to all the children of the Church that they should obey the Lord’s orders, because every person pure of heart who eagerly awaits the vision of God has been anointed king over his people Israel—that is, over the assembly of good thoughts and actions, by whose merits he hopes to attain to God’s vision. For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘I have reviewed,’” etc. This is a suitable preface for one exhorting to spiritual warfare, since it names God, who commands us to undertake this battle, as the Lord of hosts—that is, of the angelic armies, whose assistance must protect us as we fight against the powers of the air.

Egypt, whose name signifies “darkness,” signifies our former sins. They pursued us as far as the sea of baptism, but were drowned there. Amalek, however, who resisted Israel after it had crossed the Red Sea, on the road through the wilderness, and whose name is interpreted “brutish people,” signifies those sins which, after the waters of baptism, assail us daily with their weapons and obstruct us from reaching the promised kingdoms of our heavenly homeland. They try, as though with a deadly tooth, to tear away the fruit of our heart, so that we may not preserve it in sanctification. We are commanded to demolish all of them and spare none of them—that is, to lay aside everything because of which the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, shameful speech from your mouth, and other things of this kind.

“Do not spare them, but kill,” etc. “From man to woman” means from the completed work of sin to carnal thought—that is, its mother [Col. 0595A] and nurse, which gives birth to the unclean offspring. “The little one and the suckling” means the very beginnings and intention of the wicked action, which the evil thought recently brought forth delights in feeding even worse. “Ox, sheep, camel, and donkey” signify, respectively, the dullness of foolishness, the inertness of dissolution, the ugliness of pride, and the wantonness of lust.

“Therefore Saul commanded the people and reviewed them,” etc. So that we too may be able to conquer the battles of our vices, we must gather gentle and harmless thoughts within our heart, imitating that immaculate Lamb who deigned to redeem us by his blood from the Egypt of this world.

These thoughts, obeying the command of a disciplined spirit, truly prevail against the enemy when they proceed along the path of truth fortified by the twofold love of God [Col. 0595B] and neighbor; when, with hope only of the heavenly denarius, they despise all the pleasures and miseries of earthly dwelling alike. Thus the leaders mentioned as foot soldiers are rightly included under the numbers two hundred and ten. For no one doubts that the number one thousand signifies the perfection of the matter or person under discussion.

“And when Saul had come as far as the city of Amalek,” etc. The city of Amalek expresses the compacted battle-line of temptations aroused against the faithful. It rages against us sometimes through demons, sometimes through human beings, and sometimes through our own desire.

Near this city of tempting vices there is a flooding torrent: that is, the turbid assault of wavering thoughts. Falling from the mountains of demonic pride [Col. 0595C], it washes the walls of wickedness more heavily and makes them more impregnable to us in proportion as the winter of persecution, harsher than the former, makes the year of the Lord’s favor more severe.

Yet in this torrent we lay ambushes against Amalek when, through hidden virtues of the soul and through the exercises of devotion known only to the judge of our hearts, we strive to anticipate and overcome the enemy. We confront him in open battle whenever, through almsgiving, prayers, fasts, and other such forms of spiritual armor, we implore the help of our Creator against him.

But when we put on the apostolic weapons of faith, hope, and love, and weapons like these—whose abundance within us is known only by him who gave them, while other people, and even the most wicked spirits [Col. 0595D], remain unaware of them, despite diligently and carefully lying in wait for us—when, I say, we arm ourselves with such invisible weapons against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, even amid the storms of temptation, we lay ambushes against Amalek in the torrent. For where he does not see us, we strike down the adversary raging openly.

“And Saul said to the Kenites: ‘Go away, withdraw,’” etc. Sacred history reports that the Kenites were relatives of Moses, saying: “Now Heber the Kenite had withdrawn from the other Kenites, his brothers, the sons of Hobab, the relative of Moses; and he had pitched his tents as far as the valley called Sennim, which was beside Kedesh” (Judges 4).

Saul therefore commanded the Kenite to withdraw from Amalek. The excellent teacher [Col. 0596A] takes care that, if he finds among the vices he condemns anything belonging to the virtues he embraces, he preserves it unharmed.

For even among pagans you will find many who are gentle, humble, kind, patient, and, after the example of the centurion Cornelius, devoted to almsgiving and prayer. Since these virtues correspond by a kind of kinship to the law of God, and, rising from the deepest darkness of the world, help people to reach the promised rest and light, they must by no means be destroyed among the vices. Rather, so that they may benefit their possessor—for “Kenite” is said to mean “possessing”—they must be separated from the entire catalogue of vices.

The Kenite who is to be saved withdraws from Amalek, which is to be destroyed, at Saul’s command when a strict teacher distinguishes the virtues of those being instructed, which help, from the vices, which burden. Thus, because of detestable vices [Col. 0596B], the virtues that are found to be diligently practiced amid those vices are not also detested. Nor, conversely, should anyone judge that the vices of a good person—vices from which, as a human being, he cannot entirely be free amid his virtues—are to be embraced because of their proximity to those virtues. Rather, with equal discrimination in every case, the wrongs that obstruct the way of salvation must be corrected, and the right things that help must be preserved.

“And Saul struck Amalek,” etc. Havilah, whose name means “suffering” or “giving birth,” signifies the beginning of conversion, which begins neither without pain nor without a certain labor like that of childbirth in the birth of the new person. Sur, which is translated “straight,” designates the perfected goal of correction.

This wilderness is rightly described as lying opposite Egypt, because a person preserves more effectively the uprightness he has received if he always remembers the darkness from whose oppression [Col. 0596C] he was delivered.

Placed in Havilah, he strikes with the sword of the word that says: “Repent, therefore, and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3). The apostle James likewise says: “Be wretched and mourn and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4).

He comes to Sur by striking them—the place that Scripture elsewhere says lies opposite, “in front of,” Egypt—when the apostle Paul says: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Ephesians 4). Even while situated in Sur, he did not neglect to look back toward Egypt, from which he had departed, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God; but I have obtained mercy” [Col. 0596D] (1 Corinthians 15).

He shows that he was struck beneficially, so that he might live better after the slaughter, when he says: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

Not only those who convert, but also those who, after receiving the word of truth, do not care to turn from wickedness, are struck from Havilah to Sur. For, assigned to perpetual sufferings, they endure the just sentence of divine severity, which lies opposite Egypt, because he will repay them according to the wickedness of their pursuits.

Saul also strikes these at Samuel’s command, when the same teacher of the Church, following the teachings of holy Scripture, foretells that those who are obedient he corrects unto life, while those who despise it are justly to be condemned.

“And he seized Agag, king of Amalek, alive,” etc. Up to this point Saul represents an excellent and discerning ruler [Col. 0597A], either of himself or of the people subjected to him; from here onward he is shown as sluggish and rejected.

He rightly spares the innocent relatives of Moses. He rightly demolishes the entire common people and everything lowly and reprobate. But he does not rightly preserve the flocks of sheep and the other animals inclined toward the earth, the garments, and everything beautiful, together with the king himself.

Likewise, the leaders of spiritual warfare ought to exterminate, by the sword of the ruler’s word and life, all who obstruct the servants of God as they flee intellectual Egypt—that is, the darkness of the world—whether those people themselves or their reprobate deeds. But whatever innocent and Mosaic thing they find among them, they ought to preserve unharmed.

Those, however, who strive to eradicate only abominable and unspeakable things—for example, fornication, idolatry, perjury, intercourse between males, thefts, false testimonies, and other crimes of this kind [Col. 0597B]—from their own conduct or that of their subjects, but refuse to destroy banquets and drunkenness, quarrels and rivalries, avarice, hatred, the desire for empty praise or honor, as though these were less harmful or even beneficial, and also refuse to destroy the very king of vices, exceedingly fattened—that is, the swelling of pride—incur the guilt of the gravest transgression.

Because of the merit of this guilt, the kingdom of God once offered to the Jewish people, as an example in Saul, was given to a nation producing its fruits. And many Christians today leave to others the obtaining of the crown of life promised to themselves.

Here too, in the literal sense, we are most beneficially warned that the authority of the divine command must always overcome the human feeling within us. In foolish pity, a person spares a person [Col. 0597C] whom God has commanded not to be spared, as though a human being knew better what should be done with a human being than the one who made the human being (Ecclesiasticus 10).

Agag signifies pride not only by the authority of his kingdom—for “pride is the beginning of every sin”—but also by his very name, which is translated “roof,” because, often content merely with the knowledge of his neighbors, the arrogance of exaltation swells in the hearts of the wicked.

He seizes Agag the king alive and kills the common people when, eradicating the vices of the flesh, he knows how to separate their head, pride, from the virtues by argument and to define how harmful it is, but does not know how to extinguish it in himself by living humbly.

Saul spares Agag, and the people spare him, when the very leader—the mind of the virtues—softly assents to pride lurking within his inmost heart [Col. 0597D]; and the entire host of spiritual works that follows him is corrupted by its assent to that same wicked swelling.

“Now the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying,” etc. God’s repentance does not mean the disturbance of understanding that can occur in human beings when they reconsider some evil they have imprudently committed. Rather, it is called a change in passing things, while the immutable foreknowledge of God remains.

For “not to repent” signifies refusing to change what one has established: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever’” (Psalm 109). That is, what he once established, he never changed concerning the priesthood of Christ.

He is said to have repented of making Saul king because the promise of the kingdom deprives both the unfaithfulness of the entire Jewish people and the faith of false Christians of its royal gift.

[Col. 0598A] “And Samuel was grieved,” etc. These things are not to be expounded allegorically, but rather drawn out for imitation of virtue: for the errors of our brothers, which they themselves are not yet able to understand within themselves, we should not merely grieve over in our hearts, but also cry out to the Lord for them with every kind of earnestness. As soon as place and time permit, we should take care to recall them to recognition and correction of what they have done.

“And when Samuel had risen at night to go to Saul in the morning,” etc. Carmel is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision”; Gilgal as “revelation.”

Many, therefore, who have not yet fully overcome the struggle against vices promise themselves that the crown of righteousness already awaits them, as though their purification had been perfectly completed. This is like erecting for themselves a triumphant sign through confidence in an already completed contest [Col. 0598B], and doing so on the very highest mountain of virtues, which is called “knowledge of circumcision.”

After this they descend into revelation when, after ascending the summit of the virtues and tasting in advance the joy of heavenly recompense, they claim that they are already truly glorious through humility and know, with the face of their heart genuinely revealed, the hidden things. Concerning these the Lord says to the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11; Luke 10).

“And Saul said to him: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord,’” etc. Understand the voice of the flocks and herds as the unformed movements of the soul and the discordant tumult of insolent thoughts. Whoever refuses to subdue and restrain these within himself boasts in vain that he has fulfilled the word of the Lord, by which he was commanded to demolish all vices.

“And Saul said: ‘They have brought them from Amalek,’” etc. [Col. 0598C] Although unwillingly, Saul confesses these things to the prophet with a guilty conscience, since the deceitful hearts of the wicked are open not only to God, before whose eyes all things are naked and exposed, but also to spiritual men. Elisha, too, though Gehazi was far away, was present to him in spirit. And the Apostle, absent in body but present in spirit, rebuked the sinner in Corinth.

“They brought,” he says, “from the examples of the reprobate the many cries of brutish and wanton affections.” The imprudent mind spared these vices because they seemed less harmful and did not take care to destroy them. Indeed, it judged these very things to be virtues, which ought gratefully to be offered to their author: for example, by calling foolishness simplicity; naming the insolent violence of anger the zeal of Phinehas and Elijah; judging the laziness of torpor to be David’s patience; and calling the narrowness of stinginess thrift and discernment.

Equally noteworthy and avoidable is the utterly wicked habit [Col. 0598D] of the depraved, who customarily multiply their offenses by excusing them. For Saul testifies that he and the people killed the things that were killed at the Lord’s command, but that he spared the things preserved against his prohibition, not he but the people.

Many negligent and sluggish people, if they have overcome—or think they have overcome—some vices, attribute this not to the grace of the Author but to their own toil. Whatever they do not wish or are unable to extinguish within themselves, they claim was made dominant by a defect of their inborn nature, so that, indirectly, the cause of human guilt is cast back upon the very Author of nature.

“Then Samuel said to Saul: ‘Allow me [Col. 0599A], and I will tell you,’” etc. Above we read that Saul was anointed king in the daytime; he was foretold to be anointed in the daytime, and now he is shown to have been rejected at night.

This did not happen by chance or without cause, but because day is sometimes called righteousness and night sin. He was chosen in the day and rejected in the night: he deserved to reign because of the restraint of his humility, but deserved to be rejected because of the guilt of his disobedience—not by a change in divine judgment, but by a change in human merit.

And today also, when the Lord says, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20), all who are called are separated from the light of the chosen through works of darkness.

“And Samuel said: ‘Were you not little in your own eyes?’” etc. This rebuke of blessed Samuel also applies to any Christian who transgresses the faith with which he has been instructed. Some spiritual teacher, represented by Samuel, says to him [Col. 0599B]:

“Were you not humbled in your heart concerning your former life, which was without God, when you came to the Church? Having already received the grace of faith and baptism, did you not become a leader in exercising the fruits of the Spirit, through which you ought to reach the vision of divine glory? For Israel is interpreted as ‘a man seeing God.’

“The Lord anointed you with the chrism of his Spirit so that, as a good ruler and governor of your actions, you might belong to the dominion of the eternal King. Sending you also along the path of a new way of life, after the old person with his deeds had been conquered, he commanded you to put to death, member by member, everything that is upon the earth.

“Why then, having despised the evangelical and apostolic word, did you prefer to establish another rule of life for yourself and gather the spoils of vices [Col. 0599C]? In these things, although you may have seemed to yourself to deceive mortal eyes, you nevertheless committed a great evil before the judgment of the inner Judge.”

“And Saul said to Samuel: ‘Indeed, I have heard the voice of the Lord,’” etc. How well this response of rebellious Saul corresponds to the obstinacy of the proud is easily evident from what has been explained above. There are people who, convicted either by the reading of holy Scripture or by the speech of teachers, and reproved for the things they have done, prefer not to humble themselves and seek a remedy, but instead to increase their sins by making excuses.

“And Samuel said: ‘Does the Lord desire burnt offerings or sacrifices?’” etc. These words properly apply to the Jews, who, neglecting judgment, mercy, faith [Col. 0599D], and other such things, thought that they could appease the Lord through sacrifices and burnt offerings.

But even now there are not a few in the Church who are burdened alike by wealth and crimes, and who trust that they can wash away by daily almsgiving the sins to which they do not cease to cling. Others think that they are cleansed from the filth of vices by fasts, prayers, and frequent psalmody, while they do not take care to abstain from the vices themselves. Yet the Lord commands such sacrifices to be offered not by just any sinners and impure people, but by those who abstain from sin.

Finally, the Psalmist does not say, “Do good among evil works,” but says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36). And in the law, a leper or an unclean person was commanded to offer sacrifices to God not while remaining in his uncleanness, but when he appeared to have been cleansed from it.

It should be noted that he says that obedience is better, not that the sacrifices are evil [Col. 0600A], so that he may also show that sacrifices themselves are good in their proper time. He does not condemn the law, but prefers the Gospel. He calls the people of the law worthy of praise because, with pious devotion of heart, they offered burnt offerings from their flocks to the Creator; but he designates as much more praiseworthy the person who, in accordance with the counsel of the Gospel, presents his body as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

“Because you rejected the word of the Lord,” etc. Like the other parts of this reading, Saul’s rejection can, according to the allegory, apply to the synagogue; according to the tropological sense of the law, it can apply to the state of any false Christian, whether teacher or disciple, who was first faithful and afterward became liable to condemnation.

Thus the prophecy of Balaam is fulfilled [Col. 0600B]: “Because of Agag his king shall be taken away, and his kingdom shall be removed” (Numbers 24). For, because of the plague of pride concealed in the heart and not wholly destroyed, both the former Jewish people and now very many Christians are deprived of the seat of the heavenly kingdom.

“And Samuel turned to go away,” etc. Prophetic grace having turned away from the Jews on account of their sins, they did not grasp the whole garment of prophetic reading, by which they could warm their soul with faith and adorn it with works, but only its outermost edge, which lies in the letter. Even this they tore away from the solidity of its spiritual meaning, as though from the integrity of the garment of prophecy.

Therefore, because they did not fear to tear the prophets [Col. 0600C], they deserved that the kingdom of God should be torn from them and handed over to the Gentiles.

Even today, whoever contemptuously rejects the sacred utterances by which he has been instructed and imbued to seek the heavenly kingdom, because he stains with an evil mind the sacred garment that anoints him for the kingdom, leaves the blessedness of the kingdom taken away from himself to a better neighbor.

Nor does the fact that Samuel, after hearing Saul’s pride, is said to have turned away in order to depart fail to signify the misery of such people. For many, while they despise doing the good things they know, finally, by God’s just judgment, deserve not to know what ought to be done.

Hence the luxuriant multitude of heretical tares polluted the harvest of the evangelical seed with its wicked growth. Knowledge, repeatedly rejected from the practice of truth, eventually turned away [Col. 0600D] and withdrew from the mind.

“Moreover, the Triumphator in Israel will not spare,” etc. “He who by his grace made you—and indeed all Israel—triumph while fighting against Amalek will not spare you either when you transgress his word. The more you received the power of conquering not through your own strength but from heaven, the less excusable you will be shown to be in preserving what was placed under the ban.

“For as Moses says: ‘The battle against Amalek belongs to the Lord’ (Exodus 17); and: ‘I will blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven’” (ibid.).

The same must be understood of spiritual warfare, in which we spare our enemies—that is, indulge our vices—with the greater danger in proportion to the greater gift of our Creator that we receive daily in the remission of our sins, both those forgiven and those being forgiven.

We must fear lest, insufficiently concerned even about the heavenly vision [Col. 0601A], we deserve to hear with Saul: “Because the Triumphator in Israel will not spare.” That is: the one who granted you the gift of victory in many things, in order to urge you to thanksgiving and diligence in living, will finally condemn you by a severe examination in the court of his decree.

Some think that the words “Moreover, the Triumphator in Israel will not spare” refer not to the Lord but to the one of whom it was said beforehand, “And he will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you.” They understand this as referring to David, who, having received royal power, would not spare either the house of Saul or foreign enemies whom the Lord had commanded to be slain.

They interpret this morally as meaning that neighbors better than we are will strive with the greatest zeal to extinguish within themselves the vices they see have prevailed over us, lest they themselves fall into the same pit of transgression [Col. 0601B] in which they behold others miserably collapsed.

The following words, “And he will not be moved by repentance,” signify the eternal and immutable sentence of the Lord that he has threatened. The words added, “For he is not a man, that he should repent,” clearly indicate that, above, where God is said to have repented, the reference is not to any passibility of the divine substance—for with him there is no change or shadow of alteration—but to God’s speech accommodated to human beings in human fashion.

God therefore does not repent of any covenant as a human being does; his judgment concerning all things whatsoever is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.

[Col. 0601C] “But he said: ‘I have sinned,’” etc. The obstinate pride of Saul and the ever-humble restraint of blessed Samuel are here made clear.

For what is more arrogant than for someone, after recognizing his crime by which he is shown before the Lord to be a transgressor, indeed even accursed, still to demand that he be honored by human beings and in their presence?

And, conversely, what is kinder than for someone, after recognizing another’s wickedness by which that person is shown to be reprobate before the Lord, nevertheless not to refuse that he be honored before human beings?

Therefore, since even now there are people who, reproved for their crimes either by spiritual teachers or by the sacred pages, are sometimes burdened more by the harmful praise of their neighbors than they rejoice to be healed by their own salutary repentance, we too ought, following the example of blessed Samuel, to act modestly toward such people and not expose those whom we do not doubt are incorrigible and already condemned by divine judgment—especially if we recognize them as marked by some ecclesiastical office [Col. 0601D], which the anointing of that same Saul not unfittingly represents.

“And Samuel said: ‘Bring Agag to me,’” etc. As stated above, Agag means “roof”; Amalek is called “the people of the locust” or “the licking people.”

The prophetic Scripture therefore says—and the ministers and stewards of that same Scripture say to their hearers—that they should bring into the midst by confession the wound of pride [Col. 0602A], long kept covered and badly preserved in the heart.

This pride is the king and head of the other crimes, which proceed from its root. They seek, by flattering the unwary deceitfully, as though by licking them, to deceive them and to gnaw away all the shoots of life-giving grace.

That wicked king is also called exceedingly fat—that is, weighed down by the fattening and pleasurable nourishment of crimes multiplying beyond measure. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “Their iniquity comes forth as from fatness” (Psalm 72).

“And Samuel said: ‘Just as your sword has made women childless,’” etc. Understand Agag’s sword as the most effective fury of pride; the Hebrew women deprived by it of children as faithful souls stripped by victorious pride of the fruit of good works.

“But just as you,” he says, “O proud presumption [Col. 0602B], turned innumerable people away from the way of truth, so at the appointed time, when the one who will justly judge and destroy the whole dominion of iniquity comes, your mother, impiety, taken captive and deprived of her countless crimes, will be deprived of all that wicked offspring of vices and will have no one left whom it may seduce.”

“And Samuel cut Agag to pieces,” etc. Every spiritual and prophetic teacher cuts the king of the licking people to pieces when, exposing the manifold deceptions of pride and carefully laying bare the vice itself, he considers and explains what must be done by himself and his people against each of its deceits.

He clarifies and discloses that within exceedingly fat Agag—that is, within the roof of malice—there are blind receptacles of rottenness and corruption. The teacher does this in Gilgal, that is, in the revelation of manifested truth and faith [Col. 0602C].

Or, in another sense: he foretells that, in the revelation of the final judgment, the entire body of sin—which the reprobate now foolishly spare—will be cut to pieces in every respect and reduced to fragments.

“And Samuel did not see Saul again,” etc. This should be imitated rather than allegorized. Although he detests Saul so greatly on account of the merit of his sin that he does not deign ever again to see him, he nevertheless shows him so much compassion out of regard for their brotherhood that he also bears witness to it with mourning and tears.

Accordingly, the Psalmist’s words are not unfitting for people of such a disposition: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and do I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Psalm 138). The evangelical beatitude likewise applies: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 0602D] (Matthew 5).

For if without any doubt blessed is the person who, with eyes troubled by fear of the coming wrath, washes his own bed—that is, the works of virtue in which he ought to rest—laboring in his groaning and weeping through every night, how much more blessed is the one who, having become more secure concerning his own salvation because God is favorable, weeps and laments before the Lord while praying over the transgressions of his brothers?

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0601]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0601D] Having now completed, with no little labor, two books of our [Col. 0602D] exposition on Samuel—the first containing the birth, life, and leadership [Col. 0603A] of that same most blessed prophet and priest Samuel; the second containing the deeds of Saul, first chosen by the Lord and afterward rejected—we now turn our hand to begin the third under the auspices of blessed David.

We do not rely on our own ability, but in all things place our confidence in the help of the heavenly Helper, together with your sacred prayers, most beloved of bishops. We hope with certainty that he who, amid the many divergent turnings of the historical path—I mean Saul’s deeds, now pleasing to God and now perverse—has preserved our allegorical progress, as we believe, without stumbling, may himself deign, by the grace of his mercy, to accompany us in transferring typologically to the higher mysteries of the spiritual mystery the spiritual deeds of blessed David, who ran along the way of the Lord’s commandments not in a straitened but in an enlarged heart.

Here it should briefly be recalled in the prologue that, since the old things were to pass away and all things were to be made new, the change itself also had frequently to be indicated figuratively.

For just as above Samuel is substituted for the rejected Eli, to signify that the priesthood of Christ, now exercised in the Church, would succeed the priesthood according to the law, so here David, anointed king in place of Saul, signifies that the kingdom of the Jews, which existed through the law, would be changed into the kingdom of Christ’s Church.

In accordance with this, the Lord declares to those same Jews: “Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 22).

# CHAPTER ONE

Samuel, at the Lord’s command, anoints David the Bethlehemite, brought from the pastures, as king; immediately he shines with the perpetual grace of the Spirit, so that he also relieves Saul, seized by an evil spirit, by playing the harp.

[Col. 0603C]

**(1 Samuel 16).** “How long will you mourn for Saul?” and so forth, up to the passage written: “For the evil spirit was departing from him.”

This reading signifies that the Lord and Savior, destined to reign uniquely in the Church, was anointed with the oil of gladness; as his authority shone forth, the shadow of the Law was removed, and the Jews were partly stirred up to persecute him, while others were saved by accepting faith in the Lord’s incarnation and passion.

The Lord therefore said to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him, so that he may not reign over Israel?” God the Father said to the prophets and apostles, who were grieving over the present or even future rejection of the Jews: “How long will you mourn the ruin of this obstinate people, when I, in accordance with their deserved guilt, have rejected them, so that they may not usurp for themselves the singular kingdom of faith and truth, as though they were superior to the other nations and more intimate with God? Rather, let them acknowledge that the nations of the Gentiles, saved by Christ’s mercy, are much higher than they.”

For you may also learn that the ancient prophets were saddened, indeed even lamented, at the future blindness of their own people—a blindness that became for us the cause of illumination. Hear Isaiah, who, after first speaking of the grace of the Lord’s coming, says: “Upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has dawned” (Isaiah 9). Immediately, answering the coming of that same light, he adds: “You have multiplied the nation, but you have not magnified its joy” (ibid.). Elsewhere, recalling the casting away of that same people, he says, among other things: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isaiah 33), clearly signifying the prophets, the messengers of the divine word.

The prophet Jonah also, when commanded to preach to the Ninevites, preferred to flee through the danger of the sea rather than entrust the word of faith to the Gentiles by preaching (Jonah 1), fearing, no doubt, that if the branches of the good olive were broken off through unbelief, the wild olive, grafted in by faith, would become a sharer in the root and richness of the olive.

**“Fill your horn with oil and come,”** and so forth. “Abandon,” he says, “your concern for a carnal kingdom. Instead accept and cherish that rule which is shown to be most rich through the light of the Holy Spirit. Take care to proclaim this—not coming from yourselves, but sent by my Spirit—to that people which, withdrawn from the attractions of the world, longs for the joys of eternal salvation. For I have provided a king for myself among the sons of this people.”

Jesse (*Isai*) is interpreted as “island of holocaust,” or “sacrifice”; Bethlehem as “house of bread.” Every faithful soul is an island; the whole Church of the saints is an island, separated from the waves of this age by seeking higher things. Already purifying herself entirely through the fervor of the Holy Spirit, she offers herself as an acceptable sacrifice to God and makes the dwelling of her breast a home for the living Bread.

**And Samuel said: “How shall I go?”** and so forth. The prophets said to the Lord, and the apostles also said: “How will we be able to preach the kingdom of the New Testament? For the zealous defenders of the Law, the Jews, will hear and kill us. Which of the prophets did they not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of Christ.”

In response, the Lord commanded them to take up and carry his body, separated from the conduct of the people and seized by the hand of stricter self-restraint, prepared to endure death for the Lord; and he also commanded them to kindle in their hearers a desire to attain the glory of martyrdom, as though calling them to Jesse’s sacrifice. For the bearer of death is never overcome more effectively than when death is endured with heavenly love.

“And I,” he says, “will show you, my prophets and heralds of future things—not through human beings for the benefit of others, but through the infusion of my Spirit—what you should say or do, and who Christ is, where he is, and when he will come.”

These things may be understood particularly of John the Baptist. The Jews heard him evangelizing about Christ and killed him; but he, prepared in both body and mind for martyrdom, called his hearers to sacrifice—that is, to the baptism of repentance. No human teacher, but God himself, showed him what he should do; and, by giving him the sign of the Holy Spirit, he instructed him, by the sign of the Holy Spirit that had been given, concerning the one among all those whom he baptized to whom he would bear the testimony of divinity.

**And he came to Bethlehem,** and so forth. When the proclamations of the prophets concerning Christ had arisen in the world, the more discerning people, meeting those prophets with devout minds, already regarded their words as worthy of a miracle. With anxious attention they inquired whether these oracles of the prophets signified that peace would come to the ages, or whether, like the Mosaic Law, they would impose an unbearable yoke upon the necks of the disciples.

The prophets answered, each proclaiming in his own books that they had been sent by God to the city for this purpose: to bear witness to him who would come to reconcile earthly things with heavenly things, and, after the long enmity deserved by human iniquity, to reconcile the world to God through the venerable mysteries of his blood.

The same sequence may also be understood of John, because the people, admiring his life and teaching, thought that he was the Christ and anxiously questioned him about his status. But he, testifying that he announced the peace that would come to the earth,

**“I have come,” he says, “to sacrifice to the Lord,”** and so forth—that is, “I have come to teach and suffer for the Lord. Be baptized and believe with me, so that together we may live in Christ.”

**Therefore he sanctified Jesse and his sons,** and so forth. He sanctified them all, but anointed David alone with the oil of chrism, because the Church has many members but one head. John baptized many, but one dove descended.

[Col. 0605B]

**And when they had entered, he saw Eliab,** and so forth. He presents the first, second, and third sons of Jesse. None of them is found worthy to be anointed, because the Synagogue produced teachers of the Law, prophets, and psalmists; yet all of these are participants, and none among them is found to be the author of human salvation.

**Then Jesse brought seven of his sons before Samuel,** and so forth. The number seven corresponds to the Law because of the Sabbath, just as the number eight corresponds to the Gospel because of the mystery of the resurrection. Therefore none of those who, perfected according to the Law, merely hope for, preach, or receive the Sabbath—whether of the body in the present age or of the spirit in the age to come—can save the world, even though he may be lofty in merits and strong in powers.

[Col. 0605C]

**And Samuel said to Jesse: “Are these all your sons?”** and so forth. After the teachers of the Law had been sent into the world, after the proclamation of prophecy, after the sweetness of psalmody, and finally after the people’s long devotion—for through the Law of Moses the prophets and psalmists had been instructed in divine worship—there still remained the incarnation of Christ, destined to come in the fullness of time.

Of him Jesse rightly says: “There still remains the youngest, and he is tending the sheep.” “For a child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9). He speaks in the Gospel: “I am the good Shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me” (John 10).

Nor is it without a sure mystical reason that this same child is said to have pastured sheep even before he was anointed by the prophet. For that good Shepherd, who came so that they might have life and have it more abundantly, was feeding the ninety-nine sheep in heaven before he sought and found the hundredth on earth.

He fulfilled the number eight, because he gave us both the hope of our resurrection and the example of his own. Indeed, the day on which the Lord rose was the third day from the day of his passion, but the eighth day from the first day of creation. Likewise, after the six ages of this world and the seventh—the Sabbath of souls now being lived in that other life—we hope for the coming of the eighth age, the age of our resurrection.

**And Samuel said to Jesse: “Send and bring him,”** and so forth. The prophets of that time said to the saints: “Send your devoted attention of mind, and by frequent prayers poured out to God obtain the coming of Christ,” saying: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Psalm 34), and other words of this kind.

For even when the sacrifice of present sufferings or good works has been completed, we cannot recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven before the Son of God comes in humility and poverty, breaks the snare of death, and opens for us the gates of life on high.

In the Gospel he himself testifies that we cannot recline—that is, rest in the kingdom—by our own power, but through his grace: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing among them, minister to them” (Luke 12).

**So he sent and brought him,** and so forth. The aged Simeon desired that the Lord should come in the flesh; the other saints of that time desired it as well—and he came.

He was ruddy because of the blood of his passion, for “the good Shepherd laid down his life for his sheep” (John 10). He was also beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Psalm 45; 1 Peter 2).

To him corresponds closely what the bride says in his praise: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song of Songs 5)—white, that is, in action; ruddy, in blood. What follows there, “chosen out of thousands,” is what is signified here: rejected by his brothers, David alone is anointed.

**Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him,** and so forth. The prophet received the task of proclaiming the glory of the true King and said: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God has anointed you,” and so forth (Psalm 45).

Conceived by the Holy Spirit, he never ceased to possess the fullness of that same Spirit from the hour of his conception.

John received the office of bearing witness to Christ. When he saw the Holy Spirit descend upon him in the midst of those whom he baptized, he bore witness: “This is the Son of God.” And Jesus went out in the power of the Spirit into Galilee.

**And Samuel rose and went to Ramah.** Having completed the office of anointing, Samuel returned home, because when the Lord who had been foretold came—the one who was to come—the proclamations of the prophets fell silent. “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Matthew 11); from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed in the Gospel. John himself, in accordance with the office of his forerunning, said: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3).

**But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul,** and so forth. As the proclamation of Christ increased, the hearts of the unbelieving Jews were immediately abandoned by the grace of the Spirit and stirred by an impious plague to persecute his name. This occurred by the Lord’s just judgment, so that the approved might also be revealed in the Church, while the wicked, according to their deserts, were plunged more deeply into the pit of their own malice.

**“Behold, an evil spirit of God is tormenting you,”** and so forth. The apostles, desiring in every way to serve the salvation of the Jews, said to them: “See and recognize how evil is the spirit which, because your guilt has deserved it, has been sent by the Lord into your minds against the name of his only-begotten Son, causing you to assemble and form a plan. Now, having done penance for your errors, flee for help to the life-giving wood, where the innocent members of that immaculate Lamb, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, were stretched out.”

“For we will seek”—that is, we will acquire—“for you, by explaining the faith more clearly if you wish, that man who is very well known to us but still unknown to you. Endowed with knowledge surpassing that of other human beings, he knows how to drive away all the deadly darts of the harmful adversary by the saving wood of his cross. Whenever the devil begins to stir you up to rivalry against the grace of the Gospel by turning the shadow of the Law against you, may the memory of the Lord’s passion be present and immediately restrain your hearts from their mad purpose.”

**“Provide me with someone who plays well,”** and so forth. “I know many,” he says, “who know how to play, but provide and bring me someone who plays well.” This is equivalent to the newly instructed apostles’ agreeing to say to the Jews: “We know that many have been crucified for their sins, but we recognize that they benefited neither themselves nor us. Therefore see to it that you instruct us in his mysteries, and bring his faith and love into our hearts through catechesis—the one who, by mortifying his members well upon the wood, would redeem us from everlasting death.”

**“Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who knows how to play,”** and so forth. “One of the boys” signifies the unity of Christ’s humble ones, agreeing in one and the same heart and soul. When the Jews inquire about the faith and, so to speak, gradually knock at the closed seals of the life-giving cross, this unity immediately makes the mysteries of the faith and of the Lord’s dispensation clearer:

“Behold,” it says, “with the eyes either of the flesh or of faith I have seen and recognized the one born from the root of Jesse, in Bethlehem of Judah: a man who knows how to bear infirmities and undergo the gallows of death; one capable of waging war against the powers of the air; exalted in both strength and prudence; indeed, the very power of God and wisdom of God; beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; and, in the innocence displayed in his life and works, heavenly.

“To come to the highest point, he alone is the one who could say: ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me’; and, ‘Whoever sees me sees the Father also’ (John 14). The glory of his name corresponds to his outstanding virtues. For he is called David—that is, ‘strong of hand,’ or ‘desirable.’ He is strong of hand in the power of his passion, because he cast down his adversaries; desirable in the glory of his resurrection, by which he raised his own to heaven.

“He of whom it is written, ‘The Lord is strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle,’ is the one ‘into whom angels long to look’ (Psalm 23), and who, as the prophet says, ‘will come, the Desired One of all nations, and the glory of the Lord’s house will be filled’ (Haggai 2).”

**Then Saul sent to Jesse, saying: “Send me David,”** and so forth. The Jews, newly catechized, sent words revealing their intention to those who had preceded them in Christ, saying: “Believe us worthy to share in the salvation brought through baptism in Christ. We have learned that he, whom you have always conceived in your hearts through faith, hope, and love, supplies the pastures of eternal life to the blessed, both angels and human beings. Those who had preceded them, assenting to their brothers’ just requests, granted them the mysteries of Christ which they were to receive.”

They did not do these things only in faith, but according to the one who said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28), immediately adding: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (ibid.).

Among the mysteries of faith by which they were instructed outwardly, they also sent examples of virtues by which they might be nourished inwardly: bread and wine signify virtues and spiritual teaching. “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Psalm 104). And, he says, “how splendid is your cup, which intoxicates!” (Psalm 23). The kid from the goats signifies the humble mourning of penitents, separated from the wanton herd of sinners; for in the Law a kid was accustomed to be offered for sins.

Jesse sends these things to Saul by David’s donkey when every wise teacher, instructing his hearers through Christ’s gift, frequently recalls that in simple people and in those despised by human judgment there abounds a grace of virtues worthy of imitation. Note also that at Saul’s anointing—which itself signifies the kingdom of Christ—there were found donkeys, loaves, a flask of wine, and also kids; these have been discussed in their proper place.

**And David came to Saul,** and so forth. The Lord came through faith into the hearts of the believing Jews and stood before them through indefatigable desire for that sweetness which they had recognized and longed for. To those who loved him, he supplied abundant and invincible weapons of faith and truth against every battle with the malicious enemy: “the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6).

**Therefore, whenever the evil spirit seized Saul,** and so forth. The meaning is clear from what has been said above, and it applies not only to believing Jews but also to us. Whenever some temptation of the evil spirit seizes our mind and turns it away from the tranquility of its proper state, any spiritual brother who is present ought to recall for us the humility of the Lord’s passion, earnestly admonishing us that he who, innocent and just, willingly endured the punishment of the cross for us clearly left an example, so that, following his footsteps, we might act innocently in prosperity and patiently in adversity.

Thus, refreshed by fraternal exhortation as though by the hand of David playing the harp, we will bear our troubles more lightly. David always signifies our Redeemer, but sometimes in himself and sometimes in his members. When the impulse of the grim spirit departs, the grace of the Holy Spirit immediately succeeds it and enlightens us.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that the same spirit is called both God’s spirit and evil, let him understand that it is called God’s because of God’s most just permission, but evil because of the spirit’s own most wicked will. God uses evil spirits for the testing, condemnation, correction, or even preservation of certain people who are good.

For testing, as when the Lord tested blessed Job by allowing Satan to tempt him; for condemnation, as when, because of his former crimes, the lying spirit deceived King Ahab, with the Lord’s permission, so that he might perish in battle; for correction, as when the Apostle handed over the sinner in Corinth to Satan “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 5); and for the preservation of virtues, as when the same apostle received “an angel of Satan” to buffet him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians 12).

Josephus, in his history of the *Antiquities*, recalls that passage in these words: “Certain afflictions and demons suddenly seized Saul, inflicting suffocations and distresses upon him”; and shortly afterward: “They ordered,” he says, “that whenever the demons invaded and troubled him, someone should stand over his head, play, and recite hymns.”

For it must not be thought that the harp, however sweetly it resounded, could possess such power as to drive out unclean spirits. Rather, the figure of the holy cross and the passion of the Lord that was sung were already breaking the devil’s boldness.

So too, the angel who destroyed Egypt did not pass over the houses because of any power in the blood placed on the doors (Exodus 12), but because that blood was a type. The place of the middle lintel, the upper lintel, and the two doorposts, on which it had been applied, also expressed the figure of the saving cross. The houses of the Hebrews that he saw marked he passed over unharmed, divine providence foreshadowing that he would come in the flesh who, through the cross and by his blood, would free us from eternal death.

# CHAPTER TWO

The camp of Israel is terrified by Goliath, who for forty days demands single combat; at last he is overcome by David with a sling and a stone.

[Col. 0609C]

**(1 Samuel 17).** “Now the Philistines gathered their forces for battle,” and so forth. . . . “But all Israel loved David,” and so forth.

This reading mystically teaches that the long-standing and repeated snares of the ancient enemy against the human race were conquered solely by the power and endurance of Christ incarnate.

The Philistines therefore signify the opposing powers, while Israel signifies the people of the faithful—indicated not only by the merit of their conduct but also by the meaning of their name. For Israel means “seeing God,” or is interpreted as “a man” or “a mind seeing God”: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

“Philistines” is interpreted as “a twofold ruin.” Evil angels or evil human beings first fall into sins and afterward fall into the punishment of eternal fire.

**Now the Philistines gathered their forces for battle and came together at Socoh of Judah,** and so forth—that is, in the humility of praise or confession—when evil spirits come together with one accord against the Church and shake her with various temptations of vices.

They do not lead one army against Israel, but many, when, according to the divided character of their wickedness, some spirits attempt to strike down the elect with the weapons of anger, others of envy, others of pride, others of vainglory, others of lust, others of gluttony, others of discord, and others of avarice.

All of these labor to take away from wicked human beings the humility of devout confession and praise toward God, which they themselves lost through pride. For this humility is that noble foundation on which the house built of virtues and faith knows no fall from the assault of any storm.

**And they encamped between Socoh and Azekah, at the borders of Domim,** that is, between humility and strength, in the borders of blood, when with the whole intention of their wicked conflict they strive to deprive the faithful either of strength in action or of the humility that guards their strong works.

For although they are exceedingly proud and weak, they themselves cannot ascend the lofty ramparts of humility or virtue. Rather, while laying their snares between these things, they work to destroy and steal Judah—that is, the confession of the devout.

They themselves are placed in the borders of blood, that is, they continually seek to inflict the wounds of evil suggestion upon the elect.

But the men of Israel draw up their battle line in the Valley of the Terebinth against the Philistines, when the strong in the Church, harassed by the temptations of demons, seize the protection of true humility.

This valley is most appropriately called the Valley of the Terebinth. The terebinth is a tree that pours forth a most excellent resinous tear; when dissolved by the physician’s skill, it joins what has been separated and glues together what has been torn apart.

Such indeed is the humble and tearful conduct of the saints. By restraining the fluid movements of vices, it restores the loosened members of the soul by holding them together. Concerning this valley the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; he has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which you appointed for them” (Psalm 84). For, with the Lord’s help, one ascends through tears of humility all the way to the place of the heavenly kingdom.

The terebinth may also suitably be understood as the very tree of life in paradise—that is, Wisdom coeternal with God the Father. In order to overshadow us with the branches of her gifts, or rather to raise us from the valley of tears into the place appointed for us, and to open more fully the fragrance of her knowledge, she first came to this valley of tears, destined to arise from the earth a second time, so that she might exalt us to see the God of gods in Zion.

Therefore that same Wisdom, which is the tree of life to those who embrace her, speaks in Ecclesiasticus: “I also spread out my branches like a terebinth, and my branches are branches of honor and grace” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

**And the Philistines stood on the mountain on one side,** and so forth. To this day unclean spirits, fighting against the Church, stand raised up by proud boasting, after the example of that first proud one, of whom it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “And like a great mountain burning with fire, it was cast into the sea” (Revelation 8).

The soldier of righteousness also stands—not trusting in his own weapons, but exalted by the aid of him who says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 3).

**And there was a valley between them.** The place where both sides fight is temporal life itself. As good and evil battle one another in it, the tree of life in the midst helps and refreshes the worthy, but condemns and expels the wicked.

The righteous also pass through this common life of the world, hoping in Christ, the highest mountain, with attentive minds, saying: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Philippians 3). The reprobate, swelling through the devil, rise above it while scorning the fellowship of their neighbors. Against this the Apostle warns the faithful: “Do not aspire to high things, but associate with the humble” (Romans 12).

The Philistines signify perverse human beings no less than angels, all serving the one and same kingdom of the devil.

**And a man came out from above . . . named Goliath,** and so forth. This notable man is the devil, who each day comes out from the camp of the Philistines—that is, from the hearts of the wicked—prepared to rebel against God, and does not cease to challenge the devout.

Goliath is rightly called “the revealed one” or “the one who migrates.” For a long time he terrified Saul and the men of Israel while concealed from mortals, as though for no reason; and he arrogantly boasted to the minds of the wicked, as though they were the camp of the Philistines, that he was exceedingly strong. But now he has been revealed to those who can say: “For we are not ignorant of his designs.”

For a long time he dwelt proudly in the hearts of the wretched, but now he has been made to migrate by that same Strong of Hand—that is, the Lord and Savior—who says: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12).

Or he is suitably called “the one who migrates” because he once migrated through pride from angelic blessedness to hell. If we understand the term actively, as meaning one who causes others to migrate—that is, transfers them from one place to another—the name should be referred to this fact: he strives to make all his followers migrate from the land of promise to the land of perdition, from life into death.

He is rightly said to have been six cubits and a span tall, because he who boasts that he is like the Most High promises, through his philosophers, that he possesses perfect works and a blessed end.

God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh; and through the Law he established for mortals six days of work and a seventh day of rest.

Finally, Ezekiel saw, in the hand of the man measuring the new city, a reed six cubits and a span long. The Lord measures the perfection of work in his elect as though it were six cubits, while he contemplates the hope of eternal rest, which will be perfected in the future, as though it were a portion of the seventh.

Since, therefore, what the Lord truly provides the devil falsely promises, the height of the fallen Goliath is asserted to resemble the Lord’s measure.

His city, Gath, which is interpreted as “winepress,” most aptly reveals the multitude of the wicked—the city of the devil—ever exercised in tormenting the good in this world.

It should certainly be made known to those who do not know that a person is called illegitimate (*spurius*) when born from an ignoble father but a noble mother; conversely, one born from a noble father but an ignoble mother is customarily called illegitimate (*nothus*).

**And a bronze helmet was upon his head,** and so forth. If you ask what a coat of mail made of linked rings was, read Virgil:

> A coat of mail joined with hooks, and triple-woven with gold.

**And he had bronze greaves on his legs,** and so forth. The helmet, coat of mail, shield, and greaves are different kinds of arguments or argumentative devices by which the devil, rebelling against the Lord, attempts to defend the folly either of his own head—that is, of all the wicked—or of his most wretched body.

He covers the head of sin when, even though condemned, he does not fear to call himself God and to be believed so. He also covers the body when he inclines the heart of the wicked toward an evil word, “to make excuses for sins” (Psalm 141). He covers it when he fortifies every side of the human mind against the darts of truth.

All these forms of defense are said to be made of bronze, a metal more resonant than the others, because whether it is a wicked deed or a perverse doctrine, he customarily defends it not by recognition of invincible truth but by the fabulous sweetness of secular eloquence.

It is rightly said that the weight of his coat of mail was five thousand shekels of bronze, because through the sweetness of persuasive but misleading speech he does not protect all the senses of his soldiers from the enemy’s attack, as he himself promises; rather, he blocks all their senses—which are famously five—from receiving the word of truth by which they might be saved.

He arms his right hand with a spear when he also strives, through certain men of more cautious intelligence, to disturb or even overthrow the faith of the Church.

With a helmet, coat of mail, shield, and other such things, we protect ourselves from a wound; with a spear or sword, however, we customarily strike an adversary. Therefore, when the Philistine carries weapons that serve combatants as defensive armor, these signify the persons or speeches by which the wicked cover their crimes. Those weapons by which an adversary is customarily wounded signify the speeches or people through whom even the virtue of the good is torn and disturbed.

Concerning these it is rightly added:

**“Now the shaft of his spear,”** and so forth. The work of those whom the devil brings forth to battle against the Church appears to the eyes of the foolish to be perfectly suited to weaving a garment of righteousness and holiness.

Their very skill in argument knows how to see and discuss nothing beyond the limits of this world, which endures through six ages. Although they possess such great intelligence that they can estimate the age of the world, they cannot discover its Creator.

Yet in truth their threads are not in a garment that can warm the soul, because, as Isaiah said: “They have woven spiders’ webs” (Isaiah 59).

As the Psalmist, the victor over that same Goliath, testifies in Psalm 143, which is written specifically against Goliath: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Psalm 144).

**And his armor-bearer went before him.** As Goliath goes out against Israel, his armor-bearer precedes him, when examples of the reprobate, clothed in the weapons of iniquity, precede and assist the devil as he strives to deceive the faithful.

**And he stood and shouted against the ranks of Israel,** and so forth. The ancient enemy’s pride presumed that he could not be overcome by any mortal until the incarnation and passion of the Lord and Savior.

For it was not without reason that it was said to blessed Job: “There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him who was made to fear no one” (Job 41). Until the end of the present age, through Jews, Gentiles, and heretics, he disturbs the Church. With a wicked armor-bearer going before him, he stands against the armies of Israel and shouts.

[Col. 0613A]

Nor is it surprising that all the Israelites, fearing him, flee. For how can flesh fight against an archangel unless the Lord is present? But in order that flesh might prevail against a spirit without flesh, God must first triumph over that same spirit while hidden in flesh.

Of this it is symbolically added:

**“Now David was the son of an Ephratite man,”** and so forth. David, as always, is Christ the Lord. He is the son of an Ephratite man—that is, a fruitful man—because he deigned to assume flesh from that ancient people of the Hebrews, which produced many fruits of righteousness by believing. Yet he also never ceases to be born and nourished through love in the fruitful breast of his faithful ones.

Not only the mystical names of places, whose interpretations are well known, but the place itself—Ephrata or Bethlehem—bore witness to Christ, who was to be born there.

It is rightly recalled that this very old man—that is, the people already mature in knowledge of the Law—had eight sons, because after proclaiming the Sabbath and the Old Testament, he also prophesied the grace of the Gospel and the faith in the resurrection that would come through Christ.

**Now his three older sons had gone away,** and so forth. The teachers of that people, whose three orders we explained above, either girded themselves against the attractions of their flesh and mind or were solicitous for the instruction of others; they continually waged spiritual warfare.

**Now David was the youngest.** The Lord should be understood as the youngest among the brothers, completing the number eight—that is, the one who would entrust the mysteries of the Gospel to those perfected in the Law—for two reasons: namely, in time and in humility.

In time, because “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Galatians 4).

In humility, because “the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many” (Matthew 20).

The Gospel’s mustard seed, which he himself sowed in his field—that is, in the hearts of believers—is indeed the smallest of all seeds in the humility of its teaching, but outstanding in the fervor of spiritual grace.

**So, when the three older brothers had followed Saul, David went away,** and so forth. Because “we all offend in many ways,” only the one who was conceived in sanctification (James 3)—the *Anamartetos*, that is, the Sinless One—could live in the flesh without sin.

God is therefore rightly understood here. While the teachers and legislators of a definite Law in Judea, the prophets and psalmists—or, as some interpret it, the high priests, scribes, and Pharisees—struggled in spiritual combat against the law of sin that opposed the spiritual law of their minds, our Creator and Redeemer alone returned free from every conflict with assailing guilt.

Moreover, although humble and a little child in mortal flesh, he refreshed the faithful flock of his Father through the abundant mercy of his eternal divinity. He agreed with mortals in the truth of his nature, but differed from them in the power of sinning: he filled human beings with spiritual gifts, yet committed no vice among them.

David is rightly brought forth by the Psalmist to heal Saul, but to conquer the Philistines he returns from the enemy as though secure from harm. Indeed, as the good Shepherd, while the others stand ready for battle, he himself free from warfare calls his gentle lambs at Bethlehem to the pastures.

The Philistine came forth morning and evening, etc. The number forty, the number of days during which the Philistine came forth and stood against Israel, expresses the whole period of the Church, during which it fights in this life and, with the grace of the Gospel assisting, strives to fulfill the law’s Decalogue amid the snares of the ancient enemy. He comes forth each day morning and evening to tempt it, because he seeks either to corrupt the beginnings or the end of each of the works we perform. Morning and evening he terrifies the weak, whom he labors to overcome either through adversity or prosperity. This same period of the laboring Church was specially represented in its Head when, having been in the desert for forty days, he was tempted by Satan. But the cunning tempter, who had long exulted that he had conquered the first Adam, mourns forever that he was conquered by the second.

[Col. 0614B]

Then Jesse said to his son David, etc. The whole faithful people of the Hebrews was saying to the Lord, who was to be born from its stock, earnestly longing and sighing for his coming:

“Take, I beg you, to refresh and assist your people Israel, who are your brothers, in spiritual battle—for you have deigned both to become human and to be born from them according to the flesh—take, I say, as you appear bodily among their camps, weary with daily warfare, the form of perfect humility; and deign voluntarily to undergo the observance of the law, though you owe it nothing.”

For polenta signifies a troubled spirit and a contrite and humbled heart. The measure of an ephah, which contains three amphorae, represents either the spirit, soul, and body of the Lord Savior himself, or those of each of the elect, perfected and united in a fitting practice of humility. This polenta of humility appeared in the Lord, by his own power, in whatever measure he himself willed, in order to instruct us. But in all of us it can be prepared only by the millstone of what is lower and higher—that is, of fear and hope.

The ten loaves brought by David plainly demonstrate the nourishment by which the Decalogue is perfected, a nourishment that we possess not from ourselves but as the gift of the giver. After he himself was made subject to the law, he also made the burdens of the law bearable for us; and by his undeserved humility he taught us to be humble because of such great debts as we were wholly unable to repay.

“But,” he says, “turn from the same Decalogue’s milky tenderness, so to speak, suited as it is to little ones, toward the strength of spiritual understanding, by which it can refresh and strengthen even the great and distinguished commanders of the heavenly army.”

For this happened when our strong-handed and desirable one, after giving loaves to his brothers, also carried cheese-curds to the commander: after displaying to the Jewish authorities an example of patience and humility, and after showing that the commandments of the law and the prophets had not been abolished but fulfilled, he opened the understanding even of his disciples, whom he was appointing as rulers of the Church by instructing them more intimately, so that they might understand the Scriptures.

[Col. 0615A]

And you shall visit your brothers, etc. The Lord himself, in the flesh, carefully attended to his own, to see whether they were acting rightly. Wherever and with whomever he found them, he took care to visit and summon them; and even now, through his members, he diligently continues to do the same, distinguishing the good from the evil, distributing his gifts to the former and sending the latter away empty-handed.

Jesse commanded David to do this, as he commanded him to do the other things, when all the faithful in Israel, whether in their own words or in prophetic utterances, urgently implored the Lord to come quickly and redeem the world, saying: “Lord God of hosts, turn now, look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine, and direct it” (Psalm LXXIX), and other such things.

[Col. 0615B]

So David rose early, etc. When the shadow of the law had declined, truth arose from the earth—that is, the Lord appeared in the flesh, to provide the light of the Gospel to the world. Although he became human in the world in order to seek the one straying sheep, he did not abandon in heaven the ninety-nine elect in his divinity. He came full of grace and truth, and from his fullness we have all received “grace for grace” (John I)—the one whose coming all the prayers of the godly hoped for, believed in, proclaimed, and loved.

And he came to the place Magala, etc. Appearing in the flesh, the Lord found both the saints contending for the faith and the unclean spirits plotting to destroy the defenses of faith. Such was the condition of the world at the Lord’s birth, and such it continues to be until the end of this age.

[Col. 0615C]

Therefore, David left behind the vessels that he had brought, etc. The Lord left in the remembrance of his faithful followers heavenly things, or signs of his earthly birth, which he had brought when he was newly born into the world, so that these too might be carefully preserved among their good stores, as it were, of virtues. He himself did not delay hastening to battle the prince of the world; but, concerned for the salvation of his own, by doing and teaching works of righteousness he openly inquired about his brothers, as though asking whether their works were upright or still appeared in need of correction.

While he was still speaking with them, that man appeared . . . named Goliath, etc. While the Lord Savior was speaking to human beings, and they were carefully investigating through his deeds and words whether his works pleased him as rightly performed, the ancient enemy appeared, rising from the hearts of the impious and, through their wicked deeds and tongues, hurling against the elect the dreadful poisons of his proud malice—as he does even today. No deception of the wicked man escaped him, just as their strength did not frighten him. Hence the text openly continues:

Now all the Israelites, when they saw the man, fled, etc. “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans III). Christ alone could say: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John XIV). Therefore David alone despises and regards as nothing the pride of the Philistine, whom all the others avoid and flee in fear.

And one of the Israelites said: Have you seen? etc. One of the Israelites asks whether David or the Philistine has been seen. This signifies the unity of those who, while awaiting Israel’s redemption, as the Lord’s birth was already becoming manifest through miracles, anxiously sought to know whether that same Lord had been caught in any snares of the ancient enemy, who habitually reproaches all the faithful, or whether he was free among the dead—whether he owed death anything at all, or anything to him who held the power of death. For it was not immediately and easily clear to everyone that he was the Son of God, conceived in sanctification, born without sin, and destined to conquer in the world.

The king will enrich the man who strikes him, etc. “The whole people of Israel,” they say, “confesses that the man who will overthrow the devil’s kingdom is the one distinguished above all nations by a royal as well as priestly mystery, the possessor of all the riches that are in heaven and on earth—that is, the Lord of the whole world.”

It also bears faithful witness that the primitive Church, certainly sprung from his flesh, will be joined to this man, preeminent above all others, by the bond of a bride, in chaste and faithful love; and that all his elect will be released from slavery to sin and exalted in the freedom of the Holy Spirit. Whether you wish to understand by this the Father of Christ the Lord or the people of the saints, from whom Christ is according to the flesh, the interpretation will reach the same conclusion. For there is one house of all the faithful, living by the same faith, hope, and charity; and this same house belongs to the one of whom it is sung: “Let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult forever, and you shall dwell in them” (Psalm V).

Such was the faith of the ancients concerning Christ who was to come in the flesh, and such also is ours concerning him whose coming we now celebrate.

[Col. 0616C]

The people repeated to him the same report, etc. While the Lord was teaching openly and proclaiming the expulsion and overthrow of the prince of the world, the whole people, as the evangelist recalls, was in suspense, listening to him. But the law-teachers and chief priests, envious of him and seeking how they might extinguish his saving beginnings—or even destroy him himself—marked him with accusations of pride and fury, since he plainly showed himself to be the author of sobriety and humility.

Why, he says, have you come? etc. Let the Jews rage against Christ and blasphemously reproach him for the mercy of his coming and incarnation; let us instead render him the thanks we owe, because, seeking us on earth, he deigned to leave in heaven those most blessed cohorts of angels. Although they are innumerable, with their many choirs of spiritual hosts, they are nevertheless not improperly called a few sheep, until the hundredth sheep that had gone astray is brought back and they rejoice with us, joined to them in the fullness of their perfect number.

Let us rejoice that, bending his heavens, in which peace and justice reign, he willingly descended in order to see our battle. For he descended so that, engaging the enormous enemy, he might win the battle for his own; and so that he might crown in his kingdom his own, for whom he had won the victory, as they rejoiced with him.

[Col. 0616D]

The words that David had spoken were heard, etc. The words spoken by Christ concerning the glory of the kingdom to come, which was to be claimed, were believed and, as rumor spread, reached even the rulers of the Jewish empire. When not a few of them themselves gathered to hear the word, he spoke to them, so that they would not be disturbed by the power of the ancient deceiver, soon to be weakened, or by his fraud, soon to be emptied; and so that they would not lose faith in the salvation of the human race, which was already about to arrive.

“I,” he says, “who for this very reason have assumed the form of a servant, advancing to greater works of virtue, will conquer the ancient conqueror of the world, the devil.”

And Saul said to David: You are unable to resist this Philistine, etc. This is the trembling of the weak, or even the resistance of the proud. “Can this man do battle with the devil’s power, a task belonging solely to divinity, since he is human—or rather clothed in humble flesh? His adversary, meanwhile, is immensely powerful in spiritual nature; moreover, ever since he was created he has learned to bear arms against the Creator and against our race.”

For “he was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John VIII): a murderer, first of himself through pride, and then of humanity through seduction.
