Through this double murder he fell farther from the truth, from which he had long ago been banished; indeed, he does not cease accumulating sins and falling still farther until the end of the age.

[Col. 0617B]

David said to Saul: Your servant was tending, etc. The Lord strengthens those who are weak in faith and summons unbelievers to faith, gently exhorting them to recognize, amid the frailty of his humanity—in which he received our sufferings—the exalted divinity by which he is sufficient to heal those very sufferings.

“I,” he says, “now deformed in the guise of a servant, was tending, for the sake of your salvation, the hearts of all the faithful with heavenly nourishment throughout the ages—the flock of my Father, that is.”

And there came one of the unclean spirits, either overwhelmingly powerful in force or cunning in ambush. For although both the lion and the bear excel in strength, the bear has more deceit, while the lion has more force; and therefore the former figuratively expresses the demons’ deceit, the latter their violence, and both their wickedness.

“They came,” he says, “and by deception carried away one of the strong leaders of the Church, drawing him through sin from the midst of the brotherly fellowship.”

But I, either by openly bearing witness through angels or human beings, or by inwardly pricking them invisibly through myself, recalled such people to the way of salvation after conquering the evil spirits. The spirits themselves, grievously resenting that the souls of the faithful had been snatched from their darkness, immediately turned the fury of their madness toward tearing apart and blaspheming the worship of my name. By bringing their blasphemy into the light and exposing it through my prophets, I completely reduced the whole rite of idolatry to nothing, “catching the wise in their own craftiness” and silencing the mouths of their wicked profession.

saying: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm XCV). And: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak,” and so forth (Psalm CXIII). Another prophet likewise says: “The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from those things that are under heaven” (Wisdom XV).

For I also powerfully emptied the whole strength and wisdom of the profane, which they habitually display through themselves or through human beings deceived by them. I remain forever the power and wisdom of God in divinity, yet I appeared for a time in humanity to serve the salvation of human beings.

This discoverer and origin of every evil, therefore, will himself be caught, as though in the snares of one of his own followers. He dared once to incite angels in heaven and later human beings on earth to curse their Creator. He also continually seeks unjustly to aggravate with the arrows of his curse those who persist in faith in their Creator, as though the worshipers and servants of that Creator did not truly serve God. Of him it is said: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V). Through Gentiles, Jews, and heretics, he will never cease saying this to them.

[Col. 0618B]

Then Saul said to David: And may the Lord be with you. At last, in those who were able to come to faith, the Jewish people assented to the Lord’s beginnings. Truly recognizing his two natures in one person, they wished that, confronting the proud devil’s weapons with the humility of humanity and with divinity as his aid, he might obtain the palm of victory.

And Saul clothed David in his garments, etc. The Jewish people applied to the incarnate Lord the figures of legal observances: circumcising him on the eighth day, then bringing him to the temple on the thirty-third day, offering a sacrifice for him, teaching the carnal Sabbath, and providing each year the examples of sacrificing the paschal Lamb, along with other practices of this kind. In their proper time these were highly beneficial, and they armed very usefully against all the fiery weapons of the wicked one the spiritual teachers of the Jewish people in the law, as Saul’s head, and the people themselves as his body.

[Col. 0618C]

So David girded Saul’s sword over his garment, etc. Saul’s sword is the law given through Moses; David’s garment is the work of grace and truth, which came through Jesus Christ. Thus David, girded with Saul’s sword over his garment, began to test whether he could walk while armed. For, he says, he had no practice in it.

For a time the Savior observed the carnal commandment of the law, while the gift of spiritual grace remained hidden within and had not yet been proclaimed among the peoples. He gradually began to show that his body, which is the Church, could not suffice for spiritual combat if burdened with the ceremonies of the law—especially among those from the nations who were to be called to the faith and who had no practice whatsoever in bearing the heavier decrees of the law.

Finally, the apostle Peter testifies against and rebukes those who wished to burden the members of David, about to advance against the giant in battle, with Saul’s weapons, saying: “Now therefore, why are you testing God by placing upon the disciples’ necks a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were.”

[Col. 0618D]

And he put them aside and took his staff, etc. The Lord set aside the sacraments of the law, which, to show that they were good in their proper time, he had deigned to assume for a short while; and he freely exercised his judicial authority, by which he had always governed all things, even with regard to the ordering of the law.

He laid down Saul’s weapons when he said: “The Son of man is also Lord of the Sabbath” (Matthew XII). He took up his staff, which he always held in his hands, when he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees. He put on Saul’s weapons when he was about to go to single combat, as his passion drew near, and said to his disciples: “With desire I have desired,” etc. (Luke XXII). He laid them aside when he added: “For I say to you, I will not eat it from now on until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God,” and so forth (ibid.). In the same way he foretold that the cup of the legal Passover was no longer to be observed carnally.

He took up the staff that he always held in his hands when, with the mystery of his cross—which was destined to benefit the salvation of the world, and which may itself appropriately be understood under the figure of the staff, since he always had its time and measure in his power—instructing his disciples, he “took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body,” etc.

And he chose for himself five very smooth stones from the torrent, etc. Having shown the rejection of the preceding commandment—for it was weak and useless—the Lord taught that he preferred the law itself, written in five books, to be observed spiritually: he drew it out from the turbid perceptions of those who, having a veil over their hearts, could not look upon Moses’ face, and raised it into the free breezes of evangelical light.

[Col. 0619B]

For this reason he also took care to entrust that same spiritual elevation of the law’s understanding to the hearts of the spiritual shepherds whom he kept with him as close companions. To it he added the assistance of the allegorical, moral, and anagogical senses, woven together as though into a sling with three strands. Armed suitably with such weapons, he attacked the prince of the world, destined to be the victor.

When the Philistine looked and saw David, etc. When the devil had looked very carefully and saw the Son of God in the world doing and teaching things contrary to himself, as though advancing against him, he detected that he was humble. Himself knowing nothing but pride, he despised him. For he was full of new virtue and grace, red with the blood of sufferings and beautiful in the performance of mighty deeds.

And the Philistine said to David: Am I a dog? etc. Whether you understand this as referring to the Savior’s power or to the wood of the cross, it points to the same meaning. The exceedingly proud enemy denies that he is like a dog—that is, contemptible in deed and weakness, unclean in work and infirmity. He denies that the Savior’s patience can overcome him, and denies that his power can subdue him, though he pursues all who pass through the life of this world with dreadful, insane, raging barks and tears them with his bites.

But let us see what the strong-handed one himself, coming with the staff of the cross, thinks of the adversary who confronts him. He says to the Father: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog” (Psalm XXI). Elsewhere also he marked the members of that same adversary as comparable to dogs, when he said: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matthew XV). Yet by giving the children’s bread to many of these most shameless or rabid dogs, he changed them into chaste and gentle sheep.

[Col. 0620A]

And the Philistine cursed David by his gods, etc. The devil curses the living and true God when he does not fear to give to mortals as gods the spirits whom he has deceived and who, for this reason, have been condemned or are to be condemned to eternal fire. Moreover, accusing the spiritual men of the Church of carnal living, he boasts that its members can be overcome by his own followers and that they ought to be transferred to his teachers, some of whom are heavenly by angelic nature and some mortal through earthly flesh.

He also curses the body of the true David through heretics and their gods when he teaches that they should prefer to evangelical truth notions fabricated from their own hearts and molded in the worst fire. These people, though teaching carnal things, presume that they can refute the words and deeds of the spiritual.

Such notions are more fitting for the proud philosophers of the pagans or for certain barbarians—for birds of the sky and beasts of the earth can be suitably compared with these—than for ecclesiastical learning and humility.

[Col. 0620B]

Then David said to the Philistine: You come against me with a sword, etc. The Lord aptly showed, both to all whom he was helping and to the powers whom he was overthrowing, that the devil of the air was clothed only with the weapons of pride and deceit, with which he either defends and protects his own petty possessions or shatters the perceptions of truth. He also showed that he himself was the one of whom the Psalmist had sung beforehand: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXVII). Finally, reproaching certain unbelievers, he said: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John V).

And the Lord will deliver you into my hand, etc. “You will be overcome,” he says, “by the power of my divinity, you who, seeing in me the lowliness of flesh, rise up proudly. I will remove you, who are the head of all evils, from the mortal members unjustly joined to you; and I will give the fallen members—your members and those of your followers, that is, people separated from you and humbled by my power or grace—to be instructed by my ministers and joined to them. Some of these ministers are heavenly by angelic nature, while others are mortal through earthly flesh.

“Thus, when the Gospel has been proclaimed throughout the whole world, every human being will know that there is one true God, whose great name is now known in Judah and in Israel” (Psalm LXXV). Then he will be celebrated with catholic—that is, universal—praise, as people from the ends of the earth cry out to God and say: “Lord our God, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Psalm VIII)!

Let no one think it absurd that we have said that the lowest things of the flesh, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the earth signify teachers who first seize and capture carnal souls through faith. For the Lord himself is most plainly called the lion from the tribe of Judah, and the Church is figuratively called a lioness—not only on account of strength, but also to suggest the Church’s diligent zeal for holy capture.

The patriarch Jacob says of the Lord: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son” (Genesis XLIX). The Lord himself says of the Church to Job: “Will you capture the prey of the lioness and fill the souls of her cubs?” (Job XXXIX).

The Savior is also represented through four living creatures. Through the man and the calf he wished to indicate the humility of his incarnation and sacrifice; through the lion and the eagle, the strength and loftiness of his resurrection and ascension into heaven. He himself also speaks of the Church to blessed Job, saying: “Will the eagle be raised at your command and set its nest in high places?” (ibid.).

So that you would not think that only the height of its nesting or flying, or even its keen ability to gaze at the sun, and not also its act of devouring, was being commended figuratively, he added at the end: “And wherever the carcass is, there it is immediately present.”

Wherever it sees someone fallen from a proper way of life, it hastens to rebuke him immediately with biting words, to bring him into the members of the life of its body, and, as though raised from death, to restore him to catholic life.

We thought it appropriate to give two examples, so that whoever reads this may also know what he can understand without danger to the faith concerning the other birds or beasts.

[Col. 0621B]

And he put his hand into the bag, etc. Above we said that the pastoral bag signifies the hearts of pastors, who cling more closely to Christ’s side. Why, then, should the conscience or soul of the supreme and uniquely good Shepherd not rather be called the pastoral bag? It contains five very smooth yet exceedingly powerful stones with which to overthrow the enemy, because Christ alone was able perfectly to know and fulfill the purest knowledge of divine law, by which every error is defeated. Its fullness is expressed in the stone, while its breadth is spread through the five books.

Putting his hand into this bag, he took one of the five stones that he had placed there, when, undertaking the work of speaking from the ark of his sacred heart, he armed himself with one of the five books of Moses, of all of which he was both author and fulfiller. This was Deuteronomy, which he took as testimony for himself in repelling the temptations of the ancient enemy.

He also taught us, instructed in the sacred writings, to overcome the snares of that same enemy through the unity of faith and charity. And he cast the sling well, because with the spiritual sense of the Scriptures, which we showed above to be threefold, he broke the enemy’s pride and gave us spiritual understanding as weapons against him.

He struck the Philistine well on the forehead, because by the very audacity of his presumption he laid the devil low and, from the ostentation of his own profession, revealed the worshipers of perverse doctrines to be foolish. For just as the hand indicates the strength of action, so the forehead indicates the acknowledgment expressed in profession.

Therefore, whoever fears being struck on the forehead should arm that very forehead with the sign of the saving cross, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI).

David himself, because he knew how to say, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV), brought down the forehead of the Philistine, which was covered by the helmet of boastful loquacity but by no means marked with the light of heavenly grace.

The stone is rightly said to have been fixed in his forehead, because the devil will never be able to dislodge the sentence of the divine word that he receives from Christ the Savior or from his members, whether against himself or against his followers. Condemned, he will pay the penalty of accursed Gehenna without end.

Isaiah gives a similar testimony to his irrevocable condemnation, saying: “And there shall be a passage of the rod established, which the Lord God will cause to rest upon him” (Isaiah XXX). That is, he will not be released from torments to be saved forever, nor will he pass back and forth among punishments according to changing periods of time. Rather, like a person under punishment, we lift a rod or whip from the back of one being beaten at frequent intervals for a moment, so that we may strike again; but he, without any interval of rest, will groan, subjected to perpetual vengeance.

This is directed against those who, on account of Isaiah’s testimony, in which he writes concerning the wicked, “They shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited” (Isaiah XXIV), promise the devil and his angels, and all the reprobate, remission of their immense crimes and eternal life with the Lord after long and innumerable ages—contrary to the sentence of the Lord and Judge himself, who foretold that at the final judgment he would say: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew XXV).

Struck by the stone, the giant fell to the ground, because, struck by God’s word, the devil’s error was shown to be not lofty, as it had long boasted, nor heavenly but earthly—and indeed most lowly.

[Col. 0622B]

Although David had no sword in his hand, etc. When the Lord had no one as a minister of his word through whom he might shatter the devil’s pride by teaching—unless it was someone whom he had first rescued from the devil as victor—for all are by nature children of wrath, all conceived in iniquities and born by their mother in transgressions (Ephesians V; Psalm L), he arrived unexpectedly and, like one stronger, overcame the enemy who had long been wickedly strong. He took away all the weapons in which the enemy trusted.

Thus, through those by whom the enemy had previously slaughtered the souls of the wretched as though through his own weapons, the Savior later, having converted them into weapons of righteousness, cuts off the head of iniquity from its body. That is, he compels sinners converted to the faith to anathematize Satan and renounce all his works and pomp.

David is rightly said first to have taken the sword with his hand and drawn it from its sheath in order to kill the Philistine. For whenever the Lord receives some great champion of the devil’s empire through the visitation of his mercy, he draws him out of the dark hiding places of error into the light of liberating grace; and through him he also permits others to be rebuked and corrected.

We too, when confronting the madness of heretics in debate, convict them of being fabricators of falsehood and worshipers of perverse doctrines by using no other proofs of argument or testimonies of Scripture than those which they themselves had presented for bringing us over. With their own sword, therefore, we bring down the insolence of the presumptuous giant.

[Col. 0622D]

When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, etc. When the unclean spirits saw that their strongest champion had been conquered and struck down through the Lord’s incarnation and passion, they fled from the hearts of believers.

Then the strong men of the Church, gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, rose up, raised the dreadful voice of divine preaching and praise against the wicked, and pursued them until they recognized that they must be humbled by Christ and, as though submerged in a valley, sunk in defeat—those who had previously boasted that they had set their camp against him on the mountain of pride.

As fugitives they returned to the hearts that they had formerly inhabited wickedly, stripping them entirely of every fruit of piety and faith. For the fleeing Philistines approach the gates of Accaron—that is, of sterility—when the evil spirits, driven back from the minds of the faithful, return again to the teachers.

They enter the walls of that city of vanity and falsehood when they constrain even the ignorant populace to increase a fruitless work, worthy of the fire. They also reach Geth—that is, the winepress—when they draw the hearts of the deceived toward torturing the good through wicked persecution.

All these things can likewise be understood, in the same order, of perverse human beings.

[Col. 0623B]

And the children of Israel returned, etc. It is fitting that teachers of the truth first drive every unclean spirit from the hearts of their hearers by exorcising and catechizing them; then, having instructed with saving mysteries those who had been the camp of demons but have now become the possession of spiritual Israel, they should gather them into the strong fellowship of the saints.

And David took the head of the Philistine, etc. In the literal sense, I think it should be understood that David arranged for the severed head of so powerful an adversary to be brought to Jerusalem, a rebellious city still inhabited by Jebusite citizens, for no other reason than to terrify those who, trusting in the impregnable strength or height of their walls, presumed that no one could overcome them.

Indeed, in the conquest of that city, which was accomplished by David himself, we read that they rose to such pride that they said that even if they stationed on the battlements no others than the blind and lame who might happen to be found in the city, those men alone would suffice to preserve it by both number and strength.

Therefore, the victorious boy hung the head of the vanquished giant against the hostile city, so that its citizens, however savage, would not doubt that they too could be conquered by him.

According to the laws of allegory, however, we should say that the Lord hastened to display to the still faithless nations, through the apostles who proclaimed the victory received over the ancient enemy and performed miracles, the victory by which he would convert them through this sign to the mysteries and doctrines alike of life and truth. He also placed the enemy’s weapons in his tabernacle, because he joined to the holy Church human beings rescued from the devil and exposed the enemy’s snares—for these too may be understood as weapons.

No one doubts that David’s tabernacle signifies the house of Christ, which is the Church of the faithful.

### CHAPTER III

Jonathan and David enter into a covenant; and the women who meet the returning army create in Saul the fuel of everlasting hatred and envy because they place David before Saul in their praises. Finally, Saul, seized by an evil spirit, attempts to strike him; but since he cannot do so, he removes him from himself and appoints him commander over a thousand men.

[Col. 0624A]

At the time when Saul had seen David going forth, etc. This reading figuratively signifies Christ’s victory, by which he overcame the devil, honoring the devout and humble with the honors of due service; but also signifies that the obstinate and proud envied his glorious triumphs. Yet, although they seized the weapons of impiety for rebellion, they could not resist heavenly grace, which continued to shine throughout the world.

It is asked how Saul, ignorant of David’s lineage, sought information about his own minister, who had for so long been both exorcist and armor-bearer. Some think that the evil spirit by which he was driven sometimes hindered his mind from recognizing even a familiar person. They fail to notice that Abner himself, a man of such gravity and prudence, does not testify that he knew David’s ancestry. The text continues: “And Abner said: As your soul lives, O king, if I know.”

It therefore seems more credible that David had not merely been absent from Saul’s side during those forty days in which the battle against the Philistines was fought in the Valley of the Terebinth, but had returned long before for the purpose of tending his father’s sheep. At the age of adolescence, as commonly happens, growth in the other limbs may alter even the appearance of the forehead, so that one is not easily or quickly recognized by those to whom one had previously been familiar.

But whatever the reason may have been, let us pass over the foundation of the history and climb toward the fragrant fruits of spiritual allegory. As David went out against the Philistine, Saul asked about his lineage; but because he did not ask David himself, he could not learn what he sought. After the Philistine had been struck down, he asked David himself and heard:

I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite. Before his passion, while the Lord was preaching and healing all those oppressed by the devil—going forth against the Philistine in order to strike him down with the staff of the cross and with the fulfillment of the Scriptures that concerned him—some Jews asked among themselves who he was: Elijah, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, or some other distinguished prophet.

But, although they were asking what was necessary, they could not know it, because, by coming to faith, they did not know how to ask him himself. After the triumph of his passion, resurrection, and ascension, however, when the apostles were preaching, many of them believed and truly recognized him as Christ, who had come forth from Bethlehem of Judah and from the root of Jesse in accordance with the prophecies of the prophets, and who by invincible power had conquered the kingdom of the prince of the world. This is what it means for the strong-handed young man to hold in his hand the head of the slain giant.

(I Kings XVIII.) And it came to pass, when Saul had finished speaking to David, etc. When the Savior, through the apostles, had fulfilled the preaching of the gifts of his incarnation in Judea, many indeed believed after hearing the word. But all the more perfect among them, overflowing with spiritual grace—which, as has often been said, is signified by the name Jonathan—were bound to him by such great love that they did not hesitate even to give their lives for him. Others, however, and especially those who rejoiced in the summit of earthly power, whether they had cast it aside or desired it, received him with less ardent love but with the same acknowledgment of faith; they too firmly believed and confessed his mystery, judging that he was by no means to be compared with the merits—however exalted—of the fathers from whom he took his flesh, but following the Apostle’s statement: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, blessed forever” (Romans IX).

Now Jonathan and David made a covenant, etc. Christ and the Church entered into a covenant of mutual love and peace. The Church loved him in her more perfect members, so that she was ready to die for him, rightly deeming it just to give both body and soul for him who, for her redemption, although he was true God from true God, deigned to put on human flesh and a soul. For “the Word became flesh” (John I), and “the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Psalm LIII). Finally, in the martyrs she stripped off the flesh with which she had been clothed and gave it in service to Christ; and whatever else she possessed—intelligence, virtue, and works—she devoted to his will, even to the sharpness and skill of speech, and to the diligence of bringing forth arguments true in faith and reason against the subtleties of those who think wrongly, and even to preserving, for love of him, the glory of chastity and spotless modesty.

David also went out to everything, etc. Whether the Jewish people preferred to believe in Christ or contradict him, whether to make him king or fasten him to the cross, he prudently conducted himself as the coeternal Wisdom of the Father, powerfully rewarding the devout and patiently enduring the impious. That same people set him over the men of spiritual warfare: in some cases by believing and confessing that he alone assists those who fight for the salvation of their souls, so that they may conquer; in others by crying out that he was guilty of death, by which death, finally accepted according to the desire of the impious, he overcame the author of death and granted us also an example of fighting and triumphing together with him.

And he was pleasing in the eyes of all the people, etc. The Lord was pleasing to all who possessed those eyes of which he himself says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Matthew XIII). He was especially pleasing in the pure heart of the apostles, who by special providence were commanded to serve the salvation of the Jews by preaching. For those to whom the Lord was not pleasing must not be thought to have possessed such eyes open; rather, they belong among those of whom it is said: “Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (Matthew XV).

But when David returned after striking down the Philistine, etc. When the Lord, having conquered the ancient enemy through his passion, returned and appeared to his elect in the glory of his resurrection, the glory of this triumph was spread throughout Judea. Then humble souls, conscious of their own weakness, came forth from all the cities of Israel, rejoicing in Christ, whom they recognized as the author of life and victor over death. Through the many Churches that make one catholic Church, they celebrated him with united praise, each in the diverse gifts of virtue given by the one same Spirit. As devoted members, consecrating themselves to their Lord through fitting services of humility, they proclaimed above all with eager faith, as though in a triumphal song, that although the institution of the Law, by commanding works of righteousness, had inflicted no small slaughter upon the enemy’s army and had rescued from it no few spoils of souls, yet the grace of Christ, with incomparable power, by granting the denarius of heavenly life, had victoriously destroyed even the gates of death. Thus it confidently declares that those who have received the eternity of life will insult death and say: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians III).

It should be noted that it was not all the women of Israel who went out, but women from all the cities of Israel. Faith does not belong to everyone, yet from every kind of person, condition, place, and age those who receive faith are chosen by him who said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). He did not say “all people,” but “all things,” signifying that believers would come from every human class.

It should also be noted that the women are said to have met Saul, but to have raised their voices in praise of David. The souls of those who devoutly believed in Christ were openly telling the people zealous for the Law what judgment should be formed concerning the shadow of the Law itself and concerning the light of the Gospel, so that by preaching they might summon this people also to the way of grace and truth.

We may also say that, when the Lord Christ returned to heaven with immortal flesh, angelic hosts came forth to meet him from all the seats of the heavenly ranks, whatever and of whatever kind they may be, and received the victor over the enemy and the giver of life to us with the joyful celebration of fitting, shared praise.

But Saul was exceedingly angry, etc. The people who gloried in the Law became angry against the heralds of grace, and the saying that, as the Gospel shone forth, brought an end to the shadows of the Law displeased them. Raging against the Lord and against his Christ, they said:

“Behold, the followers of this teaching insist that, while I perform the commands of the Mosaic Law, I serve shadows and figures, whereas their Jesus has brought the light of truth and life to the world. Through the Law, earthly goods have been promised to me, though they cannot endure; through the grace of his Gospel, he gives his faithful the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom. Since everyone is now rushing together to hear this doctrine, neglecting the ritual of altar and sacrifices, what remains for him except that he has not also taken the summit of the kingdom from me? For although Christians surpass us in number, they have all been cast down by a new and unfamiliar humility and poverty.”

Therefore Saul did not look upon David with a right eye, etc. The Jewish people did not receive the words of the Gospel with right understanding from the time when, inflamed by the torches of envy, they began to hate its teachers and hearers, fearing that the glory of their Law would be taken away and that the fame and faith of the Gospel would instead reign throughout the world.

After another day the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, etc. As the light of the faithful gradually increased, the madness and blindness of the treacherous Jews also increased. Moved by an unclean spirit in the midst of their synagogue against the Lord, they sang with frenzied mouth the words of prophecy that they did not understand. But the Lord, to calm and soften their wickedness, repeated daily through the apostles the example of his patience and passion. For he played the lyre for them with his hand when, through the outstanding instrument of his body, he said: “Therefore let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made both Lord and Christ this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts II).

And Saul held the spear, etc. The Jewish people held the power of the kingdom and exercised it against the Lord and Savior, thinking that by persecuting him they could extinguish his faith and glory, as happens with other mortals, whose praise and memory, love or hatred, often perish together with life itself. Against such people he himself prays to the Father in the Psalms: “Let him not become like those who descend into the pit” (Psalm CXLII).

For as much as David surpasses a wall—being a living, feeling, and discerning human—without nature, life, sensation, or reason, so much does the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, differ from mere human beings, however holy they may be. He too is represented, in suitable passages, under the name of a stone, but not merely any stone in a wall, according to the words: “You also, like living stones, are being built up” (1 Peter II). Rather, he is the highest, cornerstone, chosen, precious stone, laid in the foundation. Carrying and protecting the whole structure of the rising Church, he joins circumcision and uncircumcision in unanimous peace.

It may also be understood, not inappropriately, that Saul thought he could fasten David to the wall: the Jews thought they could remove the name and memory of Christ and erase him from the land of the living if, by killing or driving away from themselves the apostles who preached his resurrection—those who were the portion of his household nearest to him, that is, the Church—they repelled them. But David could not be fastened to the wall, nor could Christ’s glory be diminished, nor could the impious, however much they struggled, be made like those who descend into the pit—that is, those buried in the tomb and not to be raised before the day of judgment.

And David turned aside from his face a second time. Christ withdrew from the heart of the impious, although he never abandons devout hearts without dwelling in them. But the word “a second time” is not added without reason.

The first time David departed and returned to Saul, going out to battle against the Philistines; later, when he arrived, he alone quickly struck down the enemy whom all the others had long been unable to defeat. Now, the second time, he turned aside from the face of one attempting to kill him. This accords with the mystical meaning. For the first time, as was explained above, while all mortals were struggling against vices, the Lord appeared in the flesh and lived freely in the world, exempt from this conflict; yet, after they had long labored in vain, he came upon those same mortals with a wondrous visitation of his grace and helped them.

But—and this must be recalled with sorrow and corrected with groaning—many drive away from themselves their life-giver and protector by despising his words and transgressing. What we condemn the Jews for doing by unbelief, we ourselves are not afraid to do while professing belief, through evil living.

David unwillingly turns aside from his face a second time, so that he may not free him from the enemy by playing the lyre, although earlier he had voluntarily returned in order to fight the enemy with him. Thus, when our merits demand it, the almighty Savior hides from us the light of his knowledge and removes the grace of his protection, so that he does not guard us by the daily aid of his cross from the ambushes of our enemies—he who deigned to take flesh for our salvation, so that he might fight with us in our weakness and enable us to conquer in his holiness.

Therefore God, having lived among human beings, first withdrew from their company in this respect: he did not fight with them against the law of sin, which in no way resisted him. Secondly—and here too, not from everyone, but from the proud—he withdrew his fellowship, so that he would not entrust his gifts to them; for “he resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter V).

And Saul feared David, etc. The Jewish people feared the Church of Christ because, seeing themselves abandoned, they beheld in her the grace of divine power. For it is written: “Many wonders and signs were done through the apostles in Jerusalem, and great fear was upon all. All who believed were together and held everything in common” (Acts II). That fellowship of mutual love is itself a sign of the heavenly grace then present.

And elsewhere: “Through the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people, and they were all together in Solomon’s portico. None of the others dared join them, but the people magnified them” (Acts V).

Therefore Saul removed him from himself, etc. Just as men who command fifty soldiers are called quinquagenarians, and those who command one hundred are called centurions, so in Greek those who are in command of a thousand soldiers are called chiliarchs. Latin usage prefers to call them tribunes rather than millenarians, from the fact that they preside over a division.

The Jews, therefore, removed Christ from themselves by despising his faith, and caused him to provide the leadership of spiritual warfare to believers more fully. For “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles.” Above all, the Lord reigns over those who, firm and immovable, always abound in the work of the Lord, knowing that their labor is not in vain in the Lord.

The number one thousand displays, so to speak, their squared and stable way of life, subject to no fall. For one thousand is the solid square of ten. The number ten usually signifies either the perfection of a work or the perfection of a reward. But in order that this same perfection may increase the breadth of fraternal love, multiply ten by ten until you reach one hundred. According to arithmetic, this sum has equal sides like a square, but it is still flat; therefore, by its figure, it is appropriately applied to love of our neighbors, whom we see on earth.

But in order that the very square of fraternal love may also be strengthened by the height of divine love, multiply each part of the number one hundred by ten until you can ascend to one thousand. Thus you understand the number ten not only as equal through fourfold firmness but also as solid, completed, and perfect. For such a number suits those over whom Christ presides, both in most steadfast height and in highest stability. However you turn a square, it stands solid; whatever confronts the righteous proves them altogether firm and immovable.

And all Israel and Judah loved David, etc. All who believed from among Jews and Gentiles loved, love, and will love Christ. He went forth by appearing in the flesh and entered by returning to the Father; he went before them so that he might give hope and a model both to those who remain outside while living rightly and to those who enter into blessed reign. Even today he goes before us when he protects those who fight on earth by assisting them. He enters when, after the struggle is ended, he leads those who are to be crowned into eternal life.

We thought it necessary to admonish the reader that the order of allegorical fulfillment cannot always be preserved in the same way as the order of historical prefiguration. For example, Joseph is first stripped of his tunic, then thrown into the cistern, and afterward sold at Judah’s instigation; but when Judah’s action is placed first, he signifies Christ as sold, then stripped of the garment of his body and buried. The same practice is found not only in prophetic events but also in prophetic words.

Isaiah first said: “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, him the nations will seek” (Isaiah XI). Then he added: “And his tomb will be glorious” (ibid.). Yet it is clear to all the faithful that first, when the Lord rose from the dead, his tomb was glorified, and afterward, when the apostles exalted the sign of his cross among the peoples, he became one whom the nations sought. Those skilled in Scripture customarily call this in Greek anakephalaiosis, that is, recapitulation.

This too should be noted: one and the same person does not always indicate one and the same portion of the person or thing represented. For example, David signifies Christ—sometimes in himself, sometimes in his holy preachers, sometimes in other believers, and sometimes in the righteous who fall seven times but rise again through repentance. All these, as many members of the same body, are clearly joined to Christ, their uniform head.

Likewise, Saul, figuratively representing the Jewish people, sometimes signifies the people reigning, sometimes teaching correctly, sometimes believing in Christ, sometimes neglecting Christ’s commands, sometimes envying and persecuting Christ, and sometimes inflicting threats, ambushes, slaughter, and death upon his faithful. In each case he indicates a portion of the same people.

Likewise, Goliath, who bears the type of the devil, represents him sometimes in the head of all the impious and sometimes in his members—namely, pagans, treacherous Jews, heretics, and false brothers. Yet from these members the Savior has graciously deigned to cut out some of his own members from that most wicked head. To prove all these points with examples would be a greater undertaking than suits this place.

## CHAPTER IV

Saul gives his elder daughter, whom he had promised to David, to Hadriel [the Molathite], and gives him the younger, betrothed to the foreskins of the Philistines.

And Saul said to David: “Behold, my elder daughter Merab,” etc., up to the passage written: “And Saul became David’s enemy all his days.” This reading figuratively designates the following: although the greater part of the Synagogue loved the Pharisees and the lesser part loved Christ, leaders moved by envy sought a pretext in that kingdom by which they might hand him over to the authority and power of the governor. But, although the Jewish leaders were unwilling, with many called to faith—including many from among the Gentiles—he desired to join the Church to himself in heavenly nuptials.

Then Saul said to David: “Behold, my daughter Merab,” etc. Above, where Saul, through the anointing of sacred chrism and the governance of the kingdom, represents Christ, we understood Saul’s two daughters as the peoples begotten for salvation through faith in and love of Christ, perfected by a twofold discipline, namely of body and mind; or certainly as signifying the greater Synagogue and the lesser Church.

Here, however, because the order of the surrounding events has changed, David represents the Lord Christ, while Saul represents the Jewish people who envy him. The elder daughter, who was promised to David but not given to him, rightly signifies that portion of the same people which was greater in number and power. It was promised as though to be joined to the strong-handed and desirable bridegroom, since the leaders of that portion—scribes, priests, Pharisees, and elders of the people—flocked to hear him and called him a good teacher. Not only that: as though he were a teacher uniquely learned, they questioned him repeatedly, whether to learn or to test him.

But she was not given to him; she was given to another, when those same teachers, seeking to be called Rabbi by human beings, compelled as many as they could to listen to them instead.

The younger daughter, whom David merited to receive because of her love, is plainly that portion of the Jewish people which, inferior both in number and in contempt, preferred to follow, love, and hear the Lord Savior rather than the scribes and teachers of the Law, hearing from him: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII).

Therefore the Pharisees and the other leaders of the Jews said to Christ: “Behold, we entrust to you for teaching the greater part of the Synagogue subject to us. Only see to it that, being strong in spirit, you fight in word for the freedom of the people, who have been commanded to keep God’s Law and serve him alone. For we know that you are truthful and care for no one; you do not regard the status of any person, but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or shall we not pay it?” (Matthew XXII; Mark XII).

They said this in the presence of Herod’s servants, so that, if he forbade the payment of tribute and they punished him, they themselves might appear innocent of his death.

But David said to Saul: “Who am I?” etc. He does not confess himself unworthy to become the king’s son-in-law; rather, he proposes to that king that he should recognize and remember who he is, what his life is, and what his father’s kinship is in Israel, and from these considerations infer whether he is worthy to receive his daughter.

He is the strong-handed and desirable one in his deeds and appearance: his life is to feed his father’s sheep and, for their protection, to confront and kill lions and bears; and, for the salvation of his people, to go out against a giant armed with bronze and iron and give his life to danger.

His father’s kinship in Israel is that to which Israel, while blessing him, says among other things: “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent” (Genesis XLIX).

The same order may be interpreted concerning the Lord, since he did not deny himself worthy to join to himself, in a covenant of unanimous peace and love, the people generated through the instruction of the Law from a royal lineage. Of him his herald proclaimed: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III).

For those coming to his faith, he also indicated that they should seek who he is, what his life is, and what his Father’s kinship is in Israel, so that from this they might recognize that he, indeed he alone, is worthy to join the Church of the faithful to himself by the right of a bridegroom.

He is the one of whom John writes: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I), and so forth, up to what he says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

His life is the life of which he himself speaks: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V). His life is the one whose imitation the Apostle Peter urged upon his hearers when he said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten,” and so forth (1 Peter II).

His Father’s kinship in Israel is that of which it is said: “The Lord swore truth to David and will not withdraw from it: ‘I will set the fruit of your womb upon my throne’” (Psalm CXXXI). His Father’s kinship is also that of which he himself testifies: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew VII).

The Lord therefore does not deny that he is the bridegroom of the Church, that is, Christ; rather, he teaches that he must be sought and understood as such. Finally, by proposing the testimony of the Psalm, he teaches the Pharisees how Christ is at once David’s son and David’s Lord. In asking them, he does not deny that he is the Christ; he stirs them to seek, ask for, knock upon, and recognize the truth.

Elsewhere, when someone called him a good teacher and asked what good he should do, he replied: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark X). There too he did not signify that he was not good, but that God must be believed to be good.

But when the time came for Merab to be given, etc. When the greater part of the Jewish people ought to have believed in Christ teaching in the flesh, it instead believed and adhered to the scribes and Pharisees. Another portion of the same people, itself royally educated through the Law of the Lord, loved the coming of the Savior.

The very name is also appropriately understood as signifying the teachers of the Law: Hadriel the Molathite. Hadriel means “flock of God”; Molathite is said to mean “from the one giving birth.” The assembly of teachers of the Law, selected from ordinary activity and rusticity and commanded to devote itself to divine matters, to meditate upon, practice, and preach divine things, rightly shines with the distinctive designation “flock of God.”

Nor is it the fault of the good shepherd if some portion of the flock, leaping away from his care, prefers to submit to a wolf’s tooth rather than to a shepherd’s rod. This assembly of teachers, having rightly received through the letter the beginnings of a life made pregnant with the new grace, is beautifully called the city Hadriel, “from the one giving birth.”

And whom else could the one giving birth signify except him whose mysteries the whole Old Scripture served to represent? The entire knowledge of the Law and the Prophets had long held him hidden, but after a long period resembling childbirth, at the proper time it brought him forth for us to behold.

And it was reported to Saul, and it pleased him, etc. The envious leaders of the Jews learned that the Lord loved the crowd and that people flocked eagerly to hear him. What they condemned in other cases, they began to approve in this one, because they thought that through the abundance of his teaching they could find fault with him in speech and catch something from his mouth, so that they might accuse him and hand him over to the Gentiles to be killed. They even thought that God’s wisdom was subject to the saying: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs X).

And they said: “Let us permit him to teach, so that it may become a stumbling block for him and so that we may be innocent of his blood. Let the hands of the Romans be upon him, while we accuse him of having found him subverting our nation, forbidding tribute to be paid to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ.”

Then Saul said to David: “Today you shall be my son-in-law in two matters,” etc. Setting aside Saul’s words, which clearly signify through their deceit and fraud the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees by which they tried to ensnare the Lord, let us turn rather to examine the mighty deeds of blessed David. He became Saul’s son-in-law in two matters: by killing the giant and by bringing the foreskins of the Philistines whom he had struck down.

He signifies the one who, in order to adopt the Church from the Jews as his own, first nullified the ambushes and strength of the ancient enemy and brought her into the light; afterward he offered her examples from the Gentiles converted to the faith for imitation.

The one whose faith the Lord showed the Jews they should follow was from the Gentiles, when he said: “Truly I tell you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matthew VIII). The woman who heard from Christ, “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matthew XV), was from the Gentiles. Those who, among others, went up to worship on the feast day and said to Philip, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus” (John XII), were from the Gentiles. The centurion too was from the Gentiles: when the Lord gave up his spirit, he alone, together with his century, while all the Jews present remained silent, feared and glorified God, saying: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark XV).

It is fitting that, when Saul was weaving his deceit, he said:

“Speak to David in this way: The king has no need of bride-price,” etc. Thus we may understand truthfully that this was figuratively spoken of the proud: they did not think they needed Christ’s gifts, but only that he should be handed over to the Gentiles and killed.

And after a few days David arose and went, etc. A few days after the leaders of the Jews had decided to hand Christ over to the Gentiles to be killed, the Lord himself arose with the apostles who were with him to work the salvation of the world. He shone with such virtue and grace of teaching that, against the efforts of the impious, he called not a few Gentiles also to the grace of faith, as we have shown above.

David struck the men of the Philistines when the Lord shattered the proud impurity of the Gentiles by the word and example of humility and chastity. He brought their foreskins and counted them out to the king in order to become his son-in-law when he showed the Jewish people the dead members of sin among the Gentiles converted to God, so that in this way he might finally receive even those who would follow the conversion of the Gentiles.

Nor was it without reason that David brought Saul, who had requested one hundred foreskins, two hundred. The Jews presumed that the Lord could not impose even the profession of bodily chastity upon the Gentiles; but he cleansed them from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God.

The number one hundred, as it always pertains to the indication of great perfection, signifies what he began in himself before the triumph of his passion and completed in them after the glorification of his assumption, through the apostles and the confirmation of his mysteries.

So Saul gave him his daughter Michal as wife, etc. The unbelieving people could not prevent those predestined to life from among their own nation from believing. For they saw and understood that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. As love for him increased among believers, so fear of him increased among the treacherous.

Some apply the foreskins taken from the Philistines by David to the state of the present age, since the grace of Christ operates among the Gentiles. They refer the marriage of Michal, delayed for some time but celebrated at last, to those Jews who will believe at the end of the world: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

## CHAPTER V

Saul seeks to kill David, but Jonathan intervenes and appeases him.

And the leaders of the Philistines went out, etc., up to the passage that says: “Jonathan brought David to Saul,” etc. This reading figuratively shows that, when persecutions were stirred up in Judea as though to remove the Christian name from the earth, many even among the persecutors themselves, through the apostles’ persistent efforts, were not only brought back from persecution but also led to believe in Christ.

Thus unclean spirits went out against spiritual Israel, that is, the Church—not once but repeatedly—namely, the rulers of the darkness, that is, the leaders of wicked people. From the beginning of their advance, Christ conducted himself more wisely in his members than all the zealots for the Law; and the fame of Christianity and the Church became exceedingly widespread, so that the Church’s faithful were called Christians throughout the world.

(I Kings XIX.) Saul spoke to his son Jonathan, etc. The leaders of the Jews, the elders, and the scribes spoke to the apostles and strictly commanded them not to speak at all or teach in the name of Jesus.

But Jonathan, Saul’s son, loved David greatly, etc. The apostles loved Christ greatly. Recounting the insults of the treacherous, they asked him to defend his Church himself and to preserve the faith of his name in the Church himself—remaining secretly in the hearts of believers, but hidden from the disturbance of human beings.

“We,” they say, “while you dwell within the fruitful mind of the devout, are a field full of fragrance and grace, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis XXVII). We will speak and teach this people in your name, and we will announce to your holy Church those among them who have preferred to believe rather than disbelieve, so that, having learned the condition of each person, she may know how to join herself to the faithful and preserve herself from the unfaithful.

Then Jonathan spoke good things about David to Saul his father, etc. The apostles spoke good things about Christ to the Jews, recalling that he was a man approved by God among them through the mighty works, signs, and wonders that God performed through him in their midst. Not only could he not be accused of sin, but, diligently performing mighty works, he went throughout all their cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity.

And he placed his soul in his hand, etc. “The Lord,” they say, “commended his love toward you—the greatest love anyone can have—by laying down his soul for you, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who throughout their whole life were subject to slavery. Many from our number saw the glory of his resurrection and his ascent into heaven, and rejoiced” (Hebrews II).

Why, then, do you sin against innocent blood? etc. Why do you sin by attempting to extinguish his faith and remove his love from the Church, since he alone among mortals was able to live without guilt?

When Saul heard this, he was appeased by Jonathan’s voice, etc. When the Jewish people heard the voice of the apostles preaching, they were appeased from the anger of their ancient fury. They testified with true affirmation of faith that the Church of Christ could never be exterminated from the midst of the world and that the memory of him—who existed before the ages and remains forever—could never perish.

That same people spoke these words in those who, through spiritual understanding, are signified by Jonathan in his merits, and who heard the voice of the teachers. Wherever this people did not say such things, they are those of whom it is written: “They heard heavily with their ears” (Acts XXVIII). And elsewhere: “Who is deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers?”

And Jonathan brought David to Saul, etc. Jonathan speaks good things about David to Saul and is heard when the apostles, evangelizing about Christ, catechize the Jews who entrust themselves to the faith. He brings him in when, baptizing those same people, they refresh them with the flesh and blood of Christ, instruct them in Christ’s commands, and strengthen them with Christ’s love.

He becomes before them as he had been yesterday and the day before, when the hearers of this age received him with the same faith, hope, and love with which those who saw him in the flesh and recognized him as God received him, or with which those who hoped from of old that he would come in the flesh received him.

## CHAPTER VI

Saul attempts to strike David but cannot; he orders the house into which David has fled to be guarded. David, having placed an image in his stead, descends through the window and comes to Samuel. When Saul hears of it, he sends three groups of messengers ahead and then comes himself, and prophesies with the others before Samuel.

Now the war was stirred up again, etc., up to the passage written: “The proverb arose: Is Saul also among the prophets?” In this reading, the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation are recapitulated from the beginning. His birth, mighty works, teaching, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven are described in figurative language, together with the faith of those who followed him and the treachery, madness, and destruction of his persecutors.

When the war of temptations had been stirred up by unclean spirits, the strong-handed champion of the human race went forth from the Father’s bosom into public view among us—he who said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI).

Concerning him the Psalmist, expressing the same matter under the figure of the sun and in other words, says: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course reaches to its highest point” (Psalm XVIII).

Directing the whole force of his temporal activity against the temptations of the wicked, he restrained them to a great extent at once from deceiving and harassing mortals. They fled, and to this day flee, from his face, because wherever the grace of Christ who helps is recognized, the wickedness of the deceiving devil is immediately driven away.

And the spirit of the Lord became evil in Saul, etc. As the Son of God flashed forth in the flesh through miracles, a spirit of envy was kindled against him in the minds of the Jews, the Lord abandoning them to the desires of their hearts because of the merits of their preceding offenses. Yet they still sat peacefully in their kingdom and homeland, and, trusting in the insignia of that same kingdom, did not fear to prepare death for their Savior. But he strove to recall those who contradicted him—or rather, who were driven mad even by blasphemy—to moderation of spirit and sobriety, by the example of his gentleness and patience, as though by the sweetness of a harp [Col. 0635D].

And Saul tried to pin David with a spear, etc. The Jews tried, by killing Christ in the flesh, to kill the whole person who is God, soul and flesh. But he commended his spirit into the Father’s hands and, bowing his head, surrendered it. The wound of death, however, touched the body alone; he escaped bodily, and his soul was saved from the sword and from the hand of the single dog (Psalm XXI), while the executioners were overwhelmed by the night of their own perfidy.

Therefore Saul sent his agents to David’s house, etc. The chief priests and Pharisees sent their agents to the Lord’s tomb to guard it, so that, by denying the truth of the resurrection, the memory of his name might be erased for the future. When the frequent groaning of the Church had announced this to him—for “the desire of the poor the Lord hears” (Psalm IX)—and, trembling at the conspiracy of the faithless, had in a sense said: “Unless you rise from the dead, the faith and confession of those who believe in you cannot remain firm; unless by conquering death you abolish the vigilance of the guards, all faith in the future resurrection will be removed from the world,” at last it was learned that he had left no place in the tomb for his guards. He went away and fled from his executioners and lying guards; and by appearing after the resurrection to those who loved him, he restored their hope and faith, safe and complete in every respect.

More particularly, David’s harp may figuratively signify the Lord’s cross; Saul’s spear, the nails of the cross in the wall, or the very spear of the soldier by which his side was opened. David’s house, as we have said, is the Lord’s tomb. His leap through the window [Col. 0636B] signifies the hidden and sudden swiftness of his rising again. The wife by whose aid he escaped is the Church of the believing Jews, which both desired the Lord Savior to rise and taught that he had risen.

But Michal took a statue and placed it on the bed, etc. The history is clear concerning the hairy hide, the hide of goats: a cushion had been sewn from goatskin, and, with its unshorn hair, it could make the head of the person wrapped in it seem to be lying on a man’s bed. A statue, however, is an imitation of what is true and living; a dead goatskin is the hide stripped from a dead animal. Thus Michal took a statue and placed it on David’s bed, from which he had escaped through the window and had been secretly saved. The Church learned that the Jews judged the Lord, who had been placed in the tomb, not to be Christ, life, and truth, but rather a kind of imitation of truth [Col. 0636C] and life, claiming to be Christ the king.

Yet she herself is said [to proclaim him alive] by his true resurrection—for Scripture uses this manner of speaking when the Church is said to do what the impious do or have done—in the same way that it is written in Leviticus: “Behold, the priest shall contaminate her” (Leviticus XIII). This does not mean that he could bring leprosy upon the clean, but that he could reveal the leprosy already present in the unclean.

Michal also placed a hairy goatskin at the head of the statue. At the beginning of its existence the Church discovered even the perfidy of those who not only deny that the Lord Savior is Christ, but also assert that he was burdened with sins and was neither raised from the dead nor truly resurrected. It is well established that the goat often represents the type of the sinner, just as the sheep represents that of the righteous. The hairs too, which are fragile and grow externally beyond the body, signify dead works, already becoming manifest to all because of their dense profusion [Col. 0636D]. They place a hairy goatskin at the head of the statue substituted for David on the bed: they assert that the Savior’s flesh is bristling, as it were, with capital sins and impure, and they say that, with the time of the resurrection postponed, it continues to occupy the little bed of the tomb into which the dead man descended. Michal, however, covers this statue with clothing when the Church, after recognizing such perfidy, rejects it; after displaying it to her faithful, she immediately shows that it has been condemned in every respect by the principal works which no other could perform, and that it has been defeated.

But Saul sent attendants to seize David, etc. Immediately after the Lord’s resurrection had been celebrated, the unbelieving Jews sent scheming agents, who, examining the hearts of the faithful, might snatch Christ’s love from them either by flattery or by threats. But they, still silent through carnal fear and remaining hidden until Pentecost, seemed to wish to return to those who asked only this answer: that faith in them was sick and had not yet flourished properly, being strengthened by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Again Saul sent messengers to see David, etc. When the Church began to preach Christ from the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Jewish leaders sent men to investigate more carefully what was believed about Jesus: whether he was Christ or a prophet; whether he had risen or still rested in the tomb. They said: “Announce to us in our presence that he has not risen from the dead, but still lies on the bed of the earth awaiting the day of the universal resurrection, so that the faith which is in him may be uprooted [Col. 0637B] completely and removed from the world.”

When the persecutors began to contend with the Church, while the faithful rejoiced in Christ’s triumph, the impious encountered nothing else but “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” for those who stumbled at the word and did not believe, thinking him to be like a leper, “struck by God and humbled” (Isaiah LIII). But the prophet immediately added concerning him: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes.”

And Saul said to Michal, “Why have you thus deceived me?” etc. The unbelieving Jews said to the primitive Church: “Why, neglecting our traditions, did you prefer to believe in Jesus and confess that he escaped our guards by rising again?” She answered: “Because he himself,” she said, “threatens me—or rather, all who do not wish to believe in him and confess these things—with eternal death.”

But David, fleeing, was saved, etc. Ramah means “exalted”; Naioth means “beauty,” and is a place in Ramah. When Saul’s messengers saw only an image and a goatskin on David’s bed, David himself escaped by fleeing and was saved. Likewise, when the Jews, at the time of the Lord’s death, mutually claimed that the Lord had been an impostor, not truly innocent and righteous, but crucified on account of his own crime and held shut in the tomb, the Lord himself, rising powerfully from death into the heights of life, appeared to the disciples in immortal glory, saying: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead” (Luke XXIV). He went away and dwells in the beauty of the everlasting kingdom [Col. 0637D], which is in heaven. After him the Church also went away in hope, both in soul and in flesh, and thus she will always be with the Lord.

Now it was reported to Saul by those who said, “Behold, David is in Naioth in Ramah,” etc. The same things concerning the second messengers and also the third are related in the same order. The apostles and the apostles’ disciples announced to the Jews that the Lord Jesus Christ, after his passion, resurrection, and ascension, reigns in heaven on high, seated at the Father’s right hand. But they immediately sent three messengers—once messengers of their faith and religion, but now of their impiety and perfidy—namely priests, scribes, and Pharisees, so that they might take away his confession from the faithful persecuting them. Although all of these bore the disposition of persecutors and unbelievers, as soon as discussion reached the words of the prophets—over which Christ’s apostles preside through the revelation of spiritual understanding—they too, testifying that these words had been written by the divine Spirit, both sang them with the faithful in love and belief, though not also in understanding [Col. 0638A].

He himself also went to Ramah, etc. When Jewish teaching had proved powerless against Christ, weapons were added to words, to persecute on earth the Son of Man seated at the right hand of God the Father. But when their earthly leadership went to search the hidden Scriptures concerning Jesus and his disciples, it could find no other answer in them than that he himself, together with his followers, dwells in Naioth in Ramah—that is, in the beauty of the Father’s kingdom, in the heights of heaven. Thus all the house of Israel must know with absolute certainty that “God has made him both Lord and Christ.”

And rightly is a cistern mentioned as situated in Socho, that is, in humility, since by the depth—or breadth—of the waters it corresponds to the abyss of the Scriptures. Holy Scripture, existing as a teacher of humility contrary to the custom of worldly teachings, was produced by humble writers and is open only to humble hearers or readers. But the proud, having heard through it of Christ’s heavenly glory, whom they did not wish to follow by the steps of the body, nor to attain by the steps of love, began to pursue him by the steps of their wicked conspiracy. Thus, concerning one whom he was saving from such people and restraining from his perfidy, he himself testified from Naioth in Ramah—that is, from the most beautiful height of the heavenly seat—and said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX) [Col. 0638C].

And the spirit of the Lord also came upon him, etc. The Jewish persecutor of the Church knew that holy men of God spoke when inspired by the Holy Spirit. Yet, although he knew how to utter their words with his mouth, he did not know how to understand them correctly, and he did not fear to advance in his fury against the one by whom or concerning whom those words had been spoken. The madman prophesied—or rather, he prophesies to this day: without understanding the truthful words of the prophets, he sings, reads, and loves them, and prolongs the office of such prophecy until, making a sound without a mind, he reaches the exalted mysteries that recount the beauty above, which we hope for in heaven.

He himself also stripped off his garments, etc. These are plainly the actions of a madman and a deranged person: to strip himself, fall down in torment, and lie naked on the ground all day and night [Col. 0638D]. Yet even through the anger of such people something mystical can be spoken, for the anger of these people is not beyond divine power, for the sake of those who listen and discern.

He who, through Balaam, who was opposed to him in mind, foretold so many mysteries beforehand; who through Caiaphas, the impious persecutor, caused the secrets of his saving passion to be prophesied; who, speaking in a human voice through a mute beast of burden, forbade the prophet’s folly: he himself, through Saul when possessed, in the presence of Samuel and the other prophets, disclosed whatever mystical things he wished, so that David, innocent, might thereby take hold of the way of salvation; so that the madness of Saul, his persecutor, might everywhere be evident to all; and finally so that it might be understood how much the presence of the perfected contributes to the prayers of the humble, since it could even raise up the proud through the power of prophecy.

In this way too was marked beforehand the distorted condition of the persecuting people that was to arise: by pursuing Christ with hatred, it would deserve to be stripped of the adornment of its unique kingdom; it would fall from its former state of uprightness amid the prosperity and adversity through which the Church advances; stripped alike of heavenly and earthly glory, it would cling miserably to worldly desires alone; and amid all this it would retain the words of prophecy in writing, to strengthen the Church’s faith, though only verbally.

And it is rightly said that he prophesied with the others before Samuel. For even now the unbelieving Synagogue meditates upon and reads aloud with the Church the words of the Law and the prophets: the Church recognizes that everything in them is to be understood concerning the Lord, whereas the Synagogue lacks spiritual understanding.

[Col. 0639B] Hence the proverb arose: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” The Jews became a proverb to the Church: although they are present among the faithful intent upon sacred readings, they too use the Scriptures while empty of faith and understanding, but with a perverse mind. A proverb also are those who on the last day will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?” etc. (Matthew VII). And when you see unlearned people in the Church presumptuously taking for themselves the teacher’s chair and, under the guise of a faithful teacher, imposing upon deceived hearers not God’s commandments but their own traditions to observe and their own doctrines to follow, say: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

## CHAPTER VII. Jonathan and David renew their covenant; and when Saul plans to kill David, Jonathan signals to him to flee by shooting arrows.

[Col. 0639C]

**(I Kings XX.)** David fled from Naioth, etc., up to the passage that says, “But Jonathan also entered the city.” In this reading the Lord, having suffered persecution from the Jews, confirms by his grace the Church gathered more fully from among them, signifying what ought to be done with those same Jews and what with the Gentiles who were to be called to faith. But those reprobate Jews also plan to destroy the Lord, together with his distinguished members, namely the apostles, while celebrating the feasts of the Scriptures without the faith of Christ; and, having driven him away, they compel him to hasten to save the Gentiles.

We have said that Naioth, which was in Ramah—that is, “beauty” which was in the heights—typologically signifies the joys of the heavenly kingdom, which the Lord, by ascending bodily, deigned to promise and open to us. We have said that the words of Holy Scripture, in which that same kingdom was foretold, point to it. Yet in both these lofty beauties the Lord both remains always with his faithful and appears to them; from the unbelieving and proud, however, he turns and withdraws himself, because they neither believe, when they hear from a teacher, that he reigns in heaven, nor understand, when they themselves read in the prophet, that “ascending on high he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Psalm LXVII; Ephesians IV), or, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Psalm CIX), or other such things spoken concerning him.

This, then, is what it means for David to flee because of Saul’s ambushes. The Lord Savior, who is at God’s right hand, is not believed by proud hearers to have ascended into heaven from the beauty set on high. Although all Scripture of prophecy overflows with his mysteries, when the impious seek him, he cannot at all be found in prophetic reading. Though he always remains wholly present everywhere, when he is absent from the unrighteous and withdraws from them, let us see where he comes and is present [Col. 0640A].

And he came and spoke before Jonathan: “What have I done?” etc. Since the Lord is expelled from the reprobate by their unbelief, he is accustomed to revisit more sweetly the hearts of those who love him and to remind them more frequently of his incarnation, his blameless life, and his unjust persecution, so that, rejoicing in him, they may confess the memory of his holiness.

“Nevertheless, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives,” etc. He was separated from death by only one degree—that is, by the wall of the house in which he was staying—when, as the title of the fifty-eighth psalm also records, Saul sent men and guarded him in order to kill him. But he was soon rescued from that death by slipping through the window; and, fleeing, he was saved completely, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, what had been stated at the beginning of that title might come to pass: “For the end; do not destroy David,” in the inscription of the title.

This must likewise be understood concerning the Lord Savior, because, as far as human recklessness was concerned, he was separated from death by only one degree when the chief priests sent men and guarded his monument, so that, by denying the possibility of resurrection, they might supposedly block his way of rising again, remove from the faith the disciples who clung to him, and, once the disciples had been withdrawn from the faith, erase every memory of his name [Col. 0640C]. But in accordance with the testimony of the inscription just mentioned, just as the title written by Pilate—“This is the King of the Jews”—could not be nullified, so neither could the rule of that same king ever be corrupted.

And Jonathan said to David: “Come, let us go out into the field,” etc. The order of speech is remarkable: it seems to begin as though addressed to God, yet he completed it by speaking to a human being. This was because of the incomparably ardent affection of the young men, mutually commended to one another by their virtue; and it served as a sign of the faith that, with God as witness, was always and everywhere to be preserved.
