Grammarians call this figure in Greek *paraprosdokia*, that is, an unexpected ending.

First, therefore, Jonathan and David, having kept themselves hidden in the city, then going out into the field, made a covenant of the Lord: Jonathan would not conceal from David anything good that his father might be contemplating concerning him; he would not bring him before his father unless perhaps his father had turned toward piety; and Jonathan himself, if he lived, would receive mercy from David, but if he died, David would show mercy to his household forever.

The primitive Church, at its beginning judaizing to no small extent but soon going out into the fruitful breadth of Christian liberty, entered into a covenant of perpetual love with the Lord. It was agreed that if any of the Jews who persecuted Christ wished to recognize his goodness and turn to him, their faith and conversion should immediately be disclosed to his faithful members—that is, to the Church herself—so that through fellowship with her they might obtain complete salvation. It was not to pigs that pearls were to be given, nor were his mysteries to be profaned for unbelievers; rather, they were to be received piously by all who rejoiced to live in peace.

And if the Church’s whole condition and life remained intact among the Jews, those who believed would nevertheless be crowned not by their own merit but by the compassion and mercy of their Author. If, however, while they despised him, the way of life turned toward him, the entrance of mercy would nonetheless not be denied either to those individuals from that people who believed until the end of the age or to all the remnant who would be converted together at the end.

And Jonathan said to him: “Tomorrow is the new moon,” etc. Holy Scripture does not mean by “new moons” those unequal beginnings of months that the Romans have twelve times each year, but the new moons called by the Greeks *Neomenia* (“new moon”). In accordance with the institution of the Law, the Hebrews celebrated these solemnly with sacrifices, feasts, and the sabbath’s leisure, that is, rest [Col. 0641B].

By this the Holy Spirit signifies that whenever Christ sprinkles the Church, or any faithful soul, as though it were the moon, with the new light of his grace, then sacrifices of spiritual life are to be offered to God with greater solemnity; then one is to delight more sweetly in the nourishment of the divine utterances; and then one is to rest in blessed leisure from all the tumult of external care. Hence Jonathan now tells David that he will come on the following day at the new moon.

“Therefore you will go down quickly,” etc. That is, he was to go on the day on which it was permitted to work up to the new moon, so that during the new moon, when he said that all should be silent, he might sit at rest. Jonathan therefore tells David that the new moon will be the next day and that Saul will seek him until the day after tomorrow.

The primitive Church, already taught by Christ himself what she should say to him, says to Christ that the time is approaching when the believers—or those who will believe—from the Jews will be renewed by the light of truth, through the Sun of righteousness. The unbelievers will seek him both at the rising of this new light, which comes through hearing the word, and as that same light increases, which takes place through the practice of the word heard.

For those hearing in the Church and those practicing the commandments of the Gospel, the men of whom the Lord speaks were devising plots: “Let my enemies be confounded and ashamed, those who seek my soul” (Psalms XXXIV, XXXVI, and LXIX). Jonathan warned David to go down quickly and come to the place where he would be hidden, and this on the day when it was permitted to work; and he was to sit beside the stone of Ezel, which means “going away” or “proceeding.”

The elders of the primitive Church asked the Lord, through the grace of his inspiration, to descend quickly into the hearts of the faithful—the place, namely, where he would always be received in love—of which it is sung in the Psalms: “His place has been made in peace” (Psalm LXXV). There he would be hidden through faith from those who resisted Christian peace by their unbelief and, devoted only to outward things, were not worthy to behold the inner mysteries of their Creator.

The devout also prayed that, when he came, he might deign to make his dwelling with those strong in faith, who were ready in spirit either always to advance toward lofty virtue or, having perfected their virtues, to depart to behold the joys of heavenly life. They desired these things in the present light of grace, namely, in the time for working good toward all and for running along the way of light, lest anyone be caught unawares by the outer darkness [Col. 0642A]. These are the desires that the saints, both then and now, and for as long as the present age is called “today,” wish the Lord Savior to fulfill with insatiable prayers.

“And I shall shoot three arrows beside him,” etc. “I,” says the Church to the Lord, “with you dwelling in the hearts of the perfected, shall send preachers of the holy and undivided Trinity. Flying on the wings of virtues, piercing through the sharpness of their speech, driven from the bow of diligent reading, they shall strike with the word of faith those who are still more fragile and, as it were, earthly, though remaining near the strong through shared love. Thus, touched by the saving wound of charity, they will be compelled to bear all visible things with fortitude, to rest in the memory of their Author alone, and to regard only his vision as sweet [Col. 0642B].

“I shall send them not as though they were to bring the course of the word to an uncertain end, but as though I were training myself toward the mark of true and unique salvation; as though, directing all the blows of my teaching toward the single vision of the divine will, I pursued them toward the appointed goal, toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.

“I shall also send hearers eager to obey the faith. Carefully seeking out everything said or done by the spiritual teachers, they shall refer it piously, by following it, to the glory of my condition. To these hearers, if I show that they have attained the teachers nearest to them and placed among them by living well, I shall show that, if you deign to visit me, the customary blessing from the Jews is to be increased, because peace is yours while the weapons of those who hate are for the moment at rest.

“But if I tell them that my humble teachers have been shaken beyond their former place and driven away from Judea by persecution, go and turn your attention to visiting all the nations. For this is the eternal will and providence of the Father: when blindness has come upon Israel, the fullness of the nations should enter through the gates of life.

“Concerning the one Word of the Father, of which we shall speak—I by confessing and you by teaching—let God the almighty Father alone be the eternal witness between you and me. And rightly so, because the Father alone knows the mysteries of the Son, and only those to whom the Father has deigned to reveal them. Concerning them the same Son says to the Father: ‘You have revealed these things to little ones’ (Matthew XI), those whom he ordained to be saved by that same incarnation at the end of the ages, when he himself, begotten before the ages, was to become incarnate at the end of the ages.

“Yet by saying these things the Church does not instruct the Lord as though he were ignorant, nor does she teach him as though he were ignorant what she herself is to do. Rather, she has learned from him what he mercifully intends to do through her. She desires by devout prayers that he accomplish these things more quickly; and the things she has received from him as right for her to do, she does not cease to confess with thanksgiving and praise.”

Therefore David was hidden in the field, etc. Christ was hidden in Christians through faith, so that he would not be seen by those who had learned to know, believe, and love only earthly and temporal things. The times came when the splendor of the Church, through the touch of the new Sun of righteousness, increased more and more; and the Jewish people sat among those who preferred to take pride in an earthly kingdom rather than humble themselves for the sake of a heavenly one, in order to taste the feast of sacred readings.

[Col. 0643A] And the place of David appeared empty, etc. To unbelieving readers, Christ’s place appears empty in the Scriptures. For although they review the entire sequence of the Old Testament, they do not deserve to find anywhere the one whom the learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven knows how to discover in almost every page of the divine writings.

Finally, Saul, as a type of the Jews, sat down to eat the bread of Scripture but could not have Christ present, since by hating him he had driven him from his table. Cleopas, however, called him to the table with his companion—not yet fully recognized, but already loved—and therefore immediately recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke XXIV).

We too do both of these things today when we read. Some of us try to twist even clear statements about Christ toward something else in perversity; others, bringing forward dishes of the divine writings [Col. 0643B], begin, by seeking Christ there piously and soberly, to have him present, although not recognized at once, until he gradually unseals for us the mysteries that he had previously closed, and we recognize him, as it were, in the offering of the bread that he himself has broken for us.

Yet not everyone who cannot understand Christ in the Scriptures he reads is immediately able to raise questions or persecutions against Christ, since the human mind is accustomed gradually to decline into vices, just as it advances toward virtues.

It may also be understood in this way: while Saul was feasting, David’s place appeared empty because the Lord called his members—namely, the Church—from celebrating the carnal sacraments of the Law to the practice of spiritual things. What follows agrees with both interpretations:

“For he thought that perhaps something had happened to him,” etc. The Jews thought that Jesus was not clean and had not been purified from sins, since he had violated the sabbath and had both done and taught other things contrary to the decrees of the Law—or rather, of their own traditions. Therefore, they thought, nothing marked concerning him could rightly be found in the Scriptures.

They thought that Christ’s disciples were not clean, because they saw them placing the righteousness of faith before the works and purifications of the Law. Thus they did not greatly care that those whom they detested with all their heart because of their difference in conduct, or whom they had even expelled from the Synagogue, had not come with them to the sacrifices.

And when the second day after the new moon had dawned, etc. When the radiance of new grace, happily increasing in the hearts of the faithful, had come after the silence of hearing the word to the time for practicing what was taught, the insolence of the unbelievers nevertheless celebrated their empty, Christless nourishment from the Scriptures and the blind rites of carnal worship. The faithless parents asked their elect children in Christ—of whom it is said, “Your children, in what do they cast them out?” (Luke XII)—why Christians did not come together with the others either to hear or to perform the many carnal works of the Law: circumcision, sacrifices, and the various solemn observances.

Why, they asked, could Jesus himself, whom they believed to be Christ and God, incarnate from the root of Jesse, dead, and risen again, nowhere be found in the prophetic reading?

And Jonathan answered Saul: “He earnestly asked me to go to Bethlehem,” etc. According to the literal sense, it seems strange why David or Saul should think and inquire in this way, or why Jonathan should answer as he did, since the unmistakable cause of the king’s jealousy had preceded, and David had good reason to take thought for his safety, indeed for his life. Unless perhaps Saul should be thought to have done or said many things when the demon repeatedly attacked him, which, like those possessed, he could neither deliberate beforehand nor remember afterward. Among these things, therefore, this too should be believed to have been done by Saul in a mind raging against David rather than listening to him.

Scripture itself seems to support this interpretation. When David was absent from Saul’s table, it does not say that Saul recalled the earlier insult, but only that he thought David might perhaps be unclean, whether through nightly sleep, sexual intercourse, or contact with some funeral matter or other defilement by which, according to the decree of the Law, he would be excluded from association with the clean. The statement written at the beginning of this entire reading also supports it: “And the spirit of the Lord became evil in Saul” (I Kings XIX) [Col. 0644B].

However these matters may stand, the mystical sense is readily apparent. The dove-like simplicity of Christ’s elect answered the persecuting authority of the Synagogue: “Jesus Christ, concerning whom you ask, is my God and Lord. He earnestly asked me, by sending teachers for this very purpose and in all directions, to bring him into the heart of those who rejoice in the grace of the New Testament, where not the blood of sacrifices, nor Mosaic manna, but the living bread that descended from heaven is celebrated as a mystery, with the priesthood enacted according to the order of Melchizedek.

“Therefore the gathering of such people is most rightly called by the sacred name Bethlehem, that is, ‘house of bread.’ Let me go to such people,” she says, “believing in the mystery of that same baptism and in the fellowship of your catholic peace. And, as is fitting first and last, let the safeguard of the word by which they are to be catechized and continually strengthened be entrusted to them, since the solemn sacrifice is the very life of those converted in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Psalm XLVII).

“The Unity of God—the unity of my elect, who are my brothers and have been made co-heirs by grace—entreats me with frequent prayers to deign to multiply their number continually by the new offspring of believers. Therefore, if you love me with all your heart, I shall now visit and win for myself other future brothers through you, for this reason.

“He no longer took care to seek the typological table of the Law with its contents, nor do you find in the Scripture that you do not understand by reading it carnally the one who must be sought spiritually.”

But Saul, angry against Jonathan, etc. The leaders of the Synagogue, angry against the assembly of the spiritual, brand its mother, the Church, with the name of adulteress, because she had accepted for governance, in place of Moses, Christ; in place of the bridegroom’s friend, the bridegroom; in place of the servant, the Lord—accepting those nobler figures as her rulers.

“Do we not know,” they say, “that you love Jesus to your own disgrace and to the disgrace of Christian teaching? It is rightly called disgraceful, since, though bearing the sacred Law, it gladly abandons of its own accord the venerable and widely celebrated attendance at the temple and prefers to gather its despised assemblies in hidden places.

“As long as faith in Jesus remains on earth, you will not be stable, nor will your kingdom. Therefore send teachers now, and send to us for instruction those who still believe and confess that Jesus Christ is both God and Christ; for the assembly of those who serve this name is a son of death.”

The faithless were indeed saying these things, but what happened was altogether different from what they had demanded. Those who, for love of an earthly kingdom, persecuted citizens of heaven while themselves wandering on earth lost both the kingdom of earth and the kingdom of heaven. They could have possessed both if they had chosen not impiously to repel the one Lord of both, but piously to follow and receive him.

And Jonathan, answering Saul his father, said, etc. The assembly of Christ’s faithful answered the unbelievers: “Why does the Christian religion die? Why is Christ himself torn by your swift tooth, when even the governor who handed him over to death first confessed him innocent and righteous? Even the thief, who received the sentence of death along with him, testified that he had done nothing wrong?”

But while Christ’s co-heirs persisted in defending the faith, the faithless rushed to arms with which to defeat them. Since they could not reach Christ after the glory of the resurrection, nor lay hands on him a second time, they struck his members in his place.

Therefore Jonathan rose from the table in anger and fury, etc. Once persecution had been stirred up because of the word, the apostles and the first teachers of the Church gradually withdrew, even from the custom of judaizing, which for a time they had maintained in order to avoid giving scandal to their persecutors, as the Epistle to the Galatians and the Acts of the Apostles testify more fully.

They had not refused to take part in hearing the words of the Law as they sounded carnally—which, as we explained above, is the beginning of the intellectual new moon—but they were entirely unwilling either to assent to these things in their carnal observance or to remain absent from them. For they had great sorrow and continual pain in their hearts concerning Christ, because their brothers and fellow countrymen had not listened to them when they taught them to believe in him. Although he is God blessed above all forever, he deigned to be born from them according to the flesh in all things and, in order to free us from the curse of the Law, to become a curse for our good.

And when morning had dawned, Jonathan came into the field, etc. [Col. 0645D] When, after doctrine and glorious works, the manifestation of virtues also—like the third day of the Kalends—began to rise in the Church, there came the harmonious fellowship of spiritual teachers. Having left the table of literal observance, they entered into the fruitful freedom of grace, according to the arrangement of the Lord and Savior. The choir of humble hearers followed, and to it she herself gave this instruction:

“See that you grow by the steps of good deeds, and understand that all the ministers of the word whom I scatter near and far are to be preserved in my catholic peace. Do not let yourselves be disturbed by anyone’s apparently harsh outcome in the present, even if untimely death snatches him away, even if the black Indian, the savage Scythian, or the barbarian raider separates them from one another. The integrity of my order joins them all in one heart and soul, and has granted them one and the same reward of life in heaven.” [Col. 0646A]

Or, certainly, the passage may be understood in this way: the boy gathers up the arrows and brings them to Jonathan, signifying that good disciples carefully learn all the sayings and deeds of their teachers alike, and that these are to be brought back for pious and sober reconsideration, to strengthen the universal Church.

And when the diligent hearers had persisted equally in speaking and in putting the word into practice, that dove-like unity of the saints, customarily called the Church, sent other teachers. These advanced beyond the first hearers and entrusted the word even to foreigners—that is, to the cities of the nations. Thus the humility of the learners came to behold the deeds and teachings of those whom the afflicted Church had sent; for, from that very sending, a new voice of the fervent Church suddenly resounded, which the humility of the lesser ones had not known how to foresee. It showed that those who, like arrows, would healthfully wound hearts with the sharpness of the word were destined for the nations. The first and foremost arrow, striking the inmost heart of Cornelius the centurion, expelled the deadly corruption and wounded him so as to receive new life more effectively. [Col. 0646B]

And the Church cried out to her hearers, who were still ignorant of the heavenly arrangement: “Behind the boy”—that is, let no one delay to travel the way of virtue during the time of growing grace.

But the boy gathered Jonathan’s arrows, etc. The humble and devout discipleship learned in due order the deeds of its teachers; it also learned the words of its instructors, and referred everything to the praise of the Church. Or, according to what we explained above, it saw the disciples of Christ, some still vigorous in life, others already taken away by death, dispersed far and wide from Jerusalem, whence the word of the Lord went forth, and it recognized that all were to be gathered again into the one heavenly Jerusalem. Yet it could not know the secret of the divine will: that repentance was to be granted to the nations for salvation. Only the greater ones in the Lord—those to whom it is said, “But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV)—and he himself, strong of hand and desired by all nations, knew the hidden matter.

Therefore Jonathan gave his weapons to the boy, etc. The Church gave her disciples the examples of teachers and the patterns of her own good conduct for imitation, and said to them:

“Go forward, progressing from virtue to virtue; compare these things with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, and see that we do nothing under Christ’s teaching other than what Moses and the Prophets foretold would come to pass.” [Col. 0646D]

And when the boy had gone, David rose from his place, etc. When the disciples, obeying the command of their elders, had gone to compare the deeds of their own times with the writings of the ancients, the grace of Christ appeared more abundantly, shining forth in the virtues of the saints—namely, of those who, in order to receive the fervent gifts of charity given through the Holy Spirit, had always learned to open the recesses of their hearts in humble submission.

This is that most splendid diversity of the advancing Church which Psalm 44 sings: some, flashing with miracles, manifest Christ’s presence in themselves; others, still intent upon the sacred writings, examine how the old and the new agree with one another; others perform one service and others another in the same faith. Finally, in others there is accomplished what the following words indicate: when divine love’s regard, as it were, “falls”—that is, suddenly arrives—in earthly hearts once alien to it, it summons them to adore the glory of the Holy Trinity more fervently through assiduous compunction. This is said to be done by him who is strong of hand and desirable, our Lord, when he kindles his saints inwardly so that they may act.

Accordingly, it is also said of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit helps our weakness, for we do not know what we ought to pray for; but he himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings” (Rom. VIII)—that is, he causes it to happen. This figure of speech, extremely common in the Holy Scriptures, is called by Greek grammarians metonymia, that is, “transnaming” (*transnominatio*), when what is accomplished is understood through the one who accomplishes it. So too in the Lawgiver’s statement: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him or not” (Deut. XIII)—that is, “to cause it to be known.”

“And kissing one another,” he says, “they wept.” Nor was this without reason. The stronger their mutual love—which the virtue of each had nurtured—the more sweetly those most holy young men were moved to embraces and kisses; and the more sharply the lasting separation, which they saw now to be imminent, provoked them to tears and lamentation.

The typological meaning must also be stated: our Lord bestowed the sacred gifts of his mouth upon those among the Jews who believed in him; but for those who did not believe and who cast him out by persecuting him, he did not refuse to weep, saying, “If you also had known” [Luke XIX.42]. For David and Jonathan kissing one another signify the Lord granting the Church the saving gifts of his word, and the Church responding to the Lord with devoted confession or teaching of that same word.

Their weeping together signifies the Lord, in our flesh, shedding tears of compassion either for the chosen whom he raises to life or for the reprobate who remain in eternal death. One of these was demonstrated in the raising of Lazarus, the other in the sight and lamentation of the destruction of Jerusalem. Even now he moves his saints to mourn many of those who persist in sin and have not taken care to return to salvation through repentance.

For those who believed could not see without pain and mourning the Lord Christ leave their fellow tribesmen in unbelief and turn to the salvation of the nations. “They wept together,” he says, “but David wept more,” [Col. 0647D] because whatever the Church undertakes for her growth, in which she rejoices, or for her decline, over which she grieves, is altogether small in comparison with what God was able to do for her in the flesh.

Then Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace,” etc. The Lord rose from the midst of the unbelieving Synagogue, saying:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you—how often I have wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

And he went away to seek the Church for himself from among the nations.

Moreover, all the more perfect returned to the teachers in the primitive Church, from contemplating the aforesaid change of the right hand of the Most High, in order to complete the beginnings of the new city descending from God out of heaven. If, as was explained above, it is pleasing to understand the city as the fortification of prophetic reading, concerning which it is said, “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. I), then it is also pleasing to understand that the afflicted and sorrowful enter it—not a little—so that within its protection each person may either devote himself more sweetly to tears or wipe away tears more wisely.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The priest Achimelech gives David and his companions the consecrated bread and the sword of Goliath, while Doeg the Idumean spies out treacherous plots from his hiding place

(1 Sam. XXI.) “David came to Nob to Achimelech,” [Col. 0648B] etc., up to the passage written: “There is none like it; give it to me.”

In this reading, David principally shows that the Lord and Savior was to be born from his line as both king and priest. He takes the consecrated bread, edible only by priests, to eat for himself and his companions, and, by royal right, arms himself boldly with the sword unlike all others.

Nothing, however, prevents us from understanding the bread as nourishment of the word, and the sword as those who strike the wicked with the word of truth. Therefore, in this reading the Lord is understood to have commanded the apostles, while keeping themselves from the filth of vices, to entrust the Gospel to the nations; and to make those who had been weapons of the strong man of iniquity into weapons of righteousness—fit by the strong and desirable hand not only to assent to the truth but also to resist false doctrines. The passage also shines with a twofold argument, one which the Lord himself deigned to mention in the Gospels.

David therefore, fleeing Saul’s plots, came to the city of Nob, whose name means “barking,” to the priest Achimelech, whose name is interpreted “my brother.” The King—that is, the Savior—avoids the plots of the Jews and comes among a gathering of faithful teachers. Devoted through the long nights to watchfulness, they habitually give, so to speak, great barks of preaching for the Lord and shrewdly defend the household of faith, in remembrance of inward refreshment, against the attacks of the wicked.

They too are rightly indicated by the name of the priest Achimelech, since they are ministers of the new priesthood in Christ, who deserve to hear:

“And I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII).

Elsewhere the Lord shows that, having turned aside from his persecutors, he wished to seek them, beseeching the Father in these words:

“But you, O Lord, do not keep your help far from me; look to my defense. Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns. I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI).

And Achimelech was astonished, etc. The ancient elect were astonished, and the modern are astonished as well, whenever in simple faith they receive the arrival of the Lord’s visitation—[Col. 0649A] not only struck with awe by the majesty of his appearance but also troubled by the rarity of those who desire to follow the grace of such compassion.

Thus it is said: “Why are you alone, and no one is with you?” And elsewhere he says: “All refuge has fled from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Ps. CXLI). Yet it is certain that at the time of the Passion many saints, although very few in comparison with the crowd of persecutors, lovingly sought the soul of Christ.

But just as, among those of whom it was previously said, “They hid traps for me, those who seek the soul of Christ” (Ps. XXXIV), he was not present, so here there was no one among those who drove Christ away who would follow Christ’s faith. Elsewhere, when he says, “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII), [Col. 0649B] to show that he did not mean absolutely all human beings but all those whom he had undertaken to discuss, he added below:

“They devour my people like food of bread; they have not called upon the Lord. There they trembled with fear where there was no fear, because God is in the generation of the righteous.”

And in the Gospel the Lord says: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII). Yet it is clear that even before the mortification of his Passion many of the faithful had clung to that same grain in service.

But it is said to remain alone, without the company of those who had previously been unbelieving and were to be called to faith through that very Passion. Why, then, he says, “are you alone, and no one is with you?” Why are you alone—that is, with your faithful members—and why, outside the number determined by the Father, could no one from so great a multitude be saved? This was said in astonishment, rather than as though the elect were reasoning against the proud counsel.

And David said to Achimelech the priest, “The king commanded me concerning a matter,” etc. The Lord said to the apostles, heirs alike of the everlasting kingdom and of the priesthood:

“The people of persecutors and unbelievers compelled me, insofar as it had power, and commanded me not to call them to faith by teaching them. It said, as it were, in my hearing: ‘Let no one know the reason for the hatred and plots because of which, leaving me, you have been sent to bring salvation to the nations, nor the kind of commands, overflowing with unjust hatred, by which I have sought to expel you from my borders.’”

To this is similar the Psalmist’s statement: “They conferred together to hide traps; they said, ‘Who will see them?’” (Ps. LXIII)—though he saw them, the God who also searched the kidneys and hearts of those who conferred (Jer. XVII).

“For I have also distinguished the peoples of the nations who will believe and obey me in various regions of the world. To them, I ask, if you have at hand anything of perfected work, offer it as an example for conversion; or offer the nourishment of the sacred Law, which shines forth in the five written books of Moses; or whatever else you can provide from yourselves, take care to offer it for their salvation.”

Some, either seeking to excuse their lies or hunting for grounds to criticize Scripture, boast that David did not hesitate to seek the salvation of himself and his companions by lying. They must be answered that David himself elsewhere, and many saints frequently, offended God by sinning; indeed, no living person is justified in his sight, as that great apostle says—he who, because of his exceptional love, was worthy to recline upon the breast of his Creator and Lord:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I).

The words of Holy Scripture were not given to us for this purpose, that we might learn to sin through the examples of the good. Rather, the sins even of good people were inserted into Holy Scripture so that, when they sinned, we might learn not to presume upon our own righteousness, and, when they repented, might learn to trust that through repentance we can obtain pardon for our guilt.

In this passage, however, I readily think that blessed David can be defended as having told no lie but, under pressing necessity, having concealed the truth in more cautious words. He does not say that the king was his friend, nor does he deny that he was fleeing the king’s plots. Rather, he says: “The king commanded me concerning a matter, and said: ‘Let no one know the affair for which I have sent you away from me.’”

This statement can, without any false coloring, reasonably bear the following meaning: “I have come alone and without the company of the others because the king gave me such an urgent command to flee that none of my enemies must know that I have been here, lest he betray me.”

But if anyone wishes to know whether a just man’s steadfastness may at some time demand the necessary support of a lie, let him read Saint Augustine’s book *On the Eight Kinds of Lying*, composed with marvelous and salutary discernment. Let him also read the Conferences of the Fathers, where Joseph, a man of no small standing among the Fathers, arguing exceptionally well that nothing should be defined, fully takes up part of this little question as well.

I have raised the matter only so that, for the present, it may suffice to say this briefly: although truth must always unquestionably be preferred to a lie, nevertheless, because of the circumstances of a matter, a lie may sometimes be usefully employed for a time, while the truth may, on the other hand, be salutarily concealed.

Finally, was Rahab the prostitute not justified by her works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? Without temporarily assuming the aid of a lie, she could not have fulfilled the merit of justification. But Doeg the Idumean—whose exploration is contained in the present reading and whose betrayal follows—because of his manifest knowledge of the truth deserved, as a type of Judas Iscariot, to be destroyed at the end, uprooted, removed, and eradicated from the land of the living.

And the priest answered David and said to him, etc. Since *laos* in Greek means “people,” *panes laici*—“lay loaves” or “people’s loaves”—signifies loaves not consecrated by offering, but ordinary loaves prepared for common use.

Thus the sacred order of spiritual leaders answered Christ: “I possess no secular wisdom for the work of righteousness, but only the word of the Gospel, which I shall entrust to pure hearers. Nor do I judge this to be entrusted to the nations unless perhaps they have been turned from the various enticements of error to the chastity and devotion of the one virgin Church. For it is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. XV; Mark VII).

And David answered the priest and said to him, “Indeed, if the matter concerns women,” etc. He answered the apostles who were being sent to teach the nations:

“What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X).

The Church, with my assistance present, kept herself from idolatry and the other crimes from the time when, through confession, she came out of the ancient hiding place of blindness until she approached the light in which the holy Trinity—which is God—is known. The hearts of the humble were holy through their renunciation of Satan.

But this way of life, by which one lives among the nations, is polluted—not yet cleansed, sanctified, and justified by the bath of regeneration and the grace of the Spirit in those receiving catechetical instruction. Yet even this way of life will be sanctified by the present light of reconciliation in those who receive baptism with devoted hearts. [Col. 0651B]

It should certainly be noted, according to the literal sense, with what cautious care either the priest questioned David or David himself answered the priest about the purity of himself and his companions. The priest does not merely inquire whether the men are free from women so that they may receive the holy bread; he examines whether they are clean from every pollution that can befall mortals, asking particularly about the contamination of sexual intercourse with a woman, as though he considered it greater than the others.

In fact, this is the greatest of those impurities which do not make people guilty through fault, but nevertheless deter them from contact with holy things through some kind of uncleanness—for example, contact with a carcass or a creeping creature.

David too, examining himself and his companions with discernment, asserts that he has abstained from his wife’s embrace and carefully explains the period of that abstinence. He testifies that all the boys’ holy vessels—that is, their weapons, clothing, and the vessels they happened to carry for conveying provisions—were clean from contamination by every kind of filth.

And because he knew that what had been consecrated to divine ministries could not be transferred to common use without the greatest discernment, he did not conceal any aspect of his condition from the priest who administered these things. He says only that the road by which they had come was polluted, because some corpse or other inherently unclean object was lying upon it.

“But,” he says, “it will be sanctified today in the vessels”—that is, “nevertheless I do not believe that we could have been defiled by walking along that very road, in which something unclean might be present, since we carefully kept both all our vessels and our bodies from contact with the same contamination.”

Therefore the priest gave him the consecrated bread. Because he heard that those who were to receive it were clean, he consented to give it to them; he would in no way have dared to do so had he not recognized them as clean in every respect.

If such careful purity was required of the one who tasted the typological bread consecrated by the hands of Moses, how great a concern for purity must be shown by the one who is about to receive, for the assistance of eternal life, the bread taken into the holy and venerable hands of Christ, consecrated as the sacrament of his body and entrusted to mortals in remembrance of his death?

He must surely always retain in mind the apostle’s words:

“Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. XI).

Therefore the priest gave him the consecrated bread.

For there was no bread there except, etc. The apostles gave the word of the Law and the Prophets, sanctified by the grace of the Gospel, to those from the nations who believed and were baptized.

For the apostles and the disciples of the apostles possessed no literal knowledge except the prophetic books. These books, which had formerly been publicly set before that ancient people for reading, had recently been fulfilled through the Lord’s Incarnation, so that they might no longer be preserved for the saying of them, and so that the books of the New Testament might be written to refresh priestly souls—that is, souls joined to the members of the eternal Priest and warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

It should also be noted that David is said to have asked for loaves, but he is not reported to have received five or twelve—the number of the showbread—but to have received the consecrated bread in the singular. Similarly, he is remembered above as having put five stones into his bag, but as having struck down Goliath with one.

There are five books in which the elements of legal teaching are contained. But, as the apostle says, “The whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Matt. XXII; Mark XII).

The consecrated bread may also properly be understood as spoken of in the singular because of the unity of faith and love, but understood in the plural because of either the manifold works of virtue or the abundant multiplicity of the divine Scriptures by which we are instructed in virtue.

Thus, although it is written in the Psalms in the singular, “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. LXXVII), no one doubts that it must be understood in the plural, especially since the Lord in the Gospels, affirming by this example of the reading that mercy is to be preferred to sacrifice, asserts that loaves were given to him in the plural (Matt. IX):

“Have you not read,” he says, “what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the showbread, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?” (Luke VI).

Here, according to the interpretation by which we said that our Lord and Savior was figuratively shown in this reading as both priest and king, we must understand it as prefiguring that, when the Lord came, priestly food would no longer be distributed to the tribe of Levi or to the one people of the children of Israel, but would be divided among all the nations called to faith.

For to all who hunger for righteousness and all who wish to belong to the company of the true David it is said:

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Pet. II).

Since we have spoken about the mystery as far as our powers allow, Josephus’s words (*Antiquities* III.13) concerning the showbread should also be examined briefly, for clarifying the literal sense more plainly. When we reached the commemoration of this passage in the exposition of blessed Luke, we thought it useful to insert them into our treatment for the benefit of readers.

While the religion and condition of Jerusalem and the Temple still continued in his own time, Josephus, himself a priest, could very easily know and disclose to his readers what was performed by the priests through ancestral succession. He says:

“They were accustomed to make twenty-four loaves from fine flour, without leaven, and to bake them.”

He adds:

“For two and two they are baked, divided before the Sabbath; and on the morning of the Sabbath they are offered and placed upon the sacred table, turned toward one another, with two golden bowls filled with incense set upon them. They remain until the following Sabbath, and then others are brought in their place. The former are presented to the priests, and, after the incense has been burned in the sacred fire in which all burnt offerings are made, other incense is added upon the other loaves.”

[Col. 0653B] “There was there a man among Saul’s servants . . . and his name was Doeg,” etc. Among the apostles preaching there were false brothers; their leader was Judas. They were established within the Church through the mystery of faith, but shaken from the firmness of their stability and bloodthirsty toward betraying the peace of fraternity—for Doeg the Idumean is said to mean “blood-moved.” He was among the most powerful of the Jewish persecutors, since he had recently received him.

Nor should it be passed over, I think, that among the Septuagint interpreters this Doeg is said to have been not simply a shepherd but a muleteer, a shepherd of a sterile and fruitless flock.

We know that the mule, being of mixed breed from a mare and a donkey, as conversely the *burdo* comes from a stallion and a jenny, customarily seeks the pleasure of coupling without the fruit of generation. Such are the fruitless works of darkness, produced from a kind of unclean seed of lustful or deceitful thought. Both animals are equally lustful.

Hence it is said of certain people: “Their flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and their discharge like the discharge of horses” (Ezek. XXIII). But the race of donkeys is also especially intent, with a sharper sense, upon deceits and ambushes. When anyone, himself moved away from righteousness and ready to weave frauds for the righteous, is appointed with impious diligence to accumulate such wicked works, Doeg the Idumean is, as it were, preferred by herding the flock of mules.

And David said to Achimelech, “If you have a spear or a sword at hand here,” etc. The Savior exhorts the apostles to train their hearers not only to learn but also to teach the word of life, by which he himself can conquer the world. He delayed sending throughout the world the angelic powers through which the Law was ordered in the hand of the Mediator and which would always keep watch and fight for the Church against the powers of the air.

“For,” he says, “the king’s word pressed”—that is, the enormity of human perversity, which, neglecting God, preferred to reign for itself. It compelled me to send not angels, whose spiritual glory they could not see because of their habit of carnal life, but mortal human beings, equally like them, to instruct them—those who would announce to them that they should turn from vanity to the living God. If they had never sinned, they would now rejoice in the household fellowship of angelic light.

[Col. 0654A] And the priest said, “Behold, the sword of Goliath the Philistine,” etc. The apostles said to Christ, who was seeking teachers against the kingdom of the world:

“Behold, those accustomed for a long time to fight for the devil through perverse doctrines are entangled in the wrappings of the first transgression and are far from the clothing or ornaments of the priesthood—that is, from works worthy of the divine presence. If you wish to release them from those same wrappings and advance them to the rank of proclaiming the truth, it is clear to us that this is the work of your power, not of ours or of our devotion.

“For no mortal on earth exists who was not, from the moment of birth, assigned to the service of this kingdom, since a corrupted root, once corrupted, had no power to produce branches of offspring other than corrupt.”

And the Lord said:

“No one knows better how to overthrow the doctrines of vanity than those who were once steeped in them and accustomed to defend them against the Church. From their number—those whom I already know to have shaken themselves free from the devil’s hands—I shall make, by teaching and baptizing, future teachers and bishops of the Church.”

The title of Psalm 33 fittingly recalls this election. It reads:

“A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he let him go, and he departed.”

For he changed his countenance by stating that the reason for his journey was something it was not, and concealing what it was.

This can be interpreted concerning the Lord as follows: he changed his countenance before the apostles either by appearing immortal after the glory of his resurrection to those accustomed to seeing him mortal before the struggle of his Passion, or by commanding them, “Go and teach and baptize all nations” (Matt. XXVIII), although shortly beforehand he had commanded them, while preaching only to Judea, to refrain from entering the roads of the nations and the cities of the Samaritans.

He “let them go” when they departed to preach everywhere, with him cooperating and confirming the word by the signs that followed (Mark X); and he himself “departed” through the triumph of his Ascension, returning to heaven.

In the same Psalm, the Lord himself speaks. In its first part he testifies that he always blesses the Father, admonishing his meek ones—namely, the apostles—to persevere with him in proclaiming his praise, since he delivered him from the tribulation of Passion and death.

In the second, he declares the rewards of those who have earned well by the conversion of the faithful, especially urging them to the feasts of that most sweet bread which, to be eaten with his own in the kingdom of the Father, he receives as consecrated in the present reading.

In the third, he admonishes his boys, as sons, from what contaminations they must abstain as they approach this bread.

In the fourth, he says that the righteous will be delivered from all tribulations and that the wicked will suffer their deserved punishments.

These matters have been stated briefly by way of digression, so that every reader may recognize how beautifully Scripture always and everywhere corresponds with itself.

If anyone should object that the priest to whom David came was called Achimelech, not Abimelech, we answer that he had two names—not on our own judgment, but on the testimony of the inscription of another Psalm, where it is written:

“When Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul, and said to him: ‘Behold, David is in the house of Abimelech’” (Ps. LI).

By this name too the glory of the saints is not inappropriately displayed. For it is interpreted “the kingdom of my father.” They are the ones concerning whom the Lord spoke the parable of the kingdom:

“A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return” (Luke XIX).

That is, Christ the man, coming forth from the bosom of the Father, went to human beings who had withdrawn far from his grace by sinning, in order to make them worthy to be those in whom he would reign, and to return with them to the joys of eternal rest.

And concerning these, when the apostle had proclaimed the glory of the resurrection and said, “Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s at his coming, then the end,” he added:

“When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. XV)—that is, when he has led the saints whom he redeemed to the vision of the Father, there to be glorified.

## CHAPTER IX  
### David comes to Achish and, when recognized, escapes by pretending to be insane; fleeing to the cave of Adullam, he receives four hundred men who gather around him, and from there he entrusts his parents to the king of Moab

[Col. 0655B]

“So David rose and fled that day from Saul’s presence,” etc., up to the passage written: “David departed and came to the forest of Hareth.”

In this reading, the Lord, because the leaders of the Jews persecuted, envied, and despised what he had begun to do and teach, departed from there and came into the hearts of the humble. Having gathered around himself no small crowds of believers, he became their leader.

Without delay he also came to the nations to be saved, making his dwelling among them, and at some time to return to God the Father and to the Church, the mother of us all, according to the prophecies of the prophets, when even the remnant of Israel would be saved at the end of the world (Isa. X).

For throughout many pages of Holy Scripture (Hos. I; Rom. IX), and through the repeated deeds of the saints, one and the same dispensation of our incarnate Savior is repeated under varying figures. This is rightly so, because what the saints always desired and hoped for ought always to have been prophesied by them and marked out as future.

David, therefore, fleeing from Saul’s presence, came to Achish, king of Gath. The Lord, fleeing from those who despised his word lest he be understood by the unworthy, came through teaching to others, in case they might hear and perhaps become quiet. He did not cease this activity until he found those who were willing to receive him humbly.

Achish means “my brother” or “brother”; Gath is interpreted “winepress.” Because Christ the man deigned to become incarnate from the Jewish people, he had as his brother the very people whose persecution he endured.

Hence he says in the Psalm:

“I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother” (Ps. LXVIII)—that is, to the Synagogue or to mortal nature.

That people is not improperly called the king of the winepress, since it first devised tribulations and pressures for Christ and for the Church against the other nations: seeking to kill the Lord himself as an infant, killing him as a young man, and afterward persecuting the Church and expelling it from its borders.

I think that this is the mystical difference between Achish and Saul: Saul signifies those within that people who were imbued with knowledge of the Law, while Achish signifies the ignorant among the same people. Although they differed in education, they united in equal hostility against the Lord. For this reason, in the reversed order of the Law, the more knowledge they had received, the more insanely they persecuted the giver of that gift.

“Is this not David, the king of the land?” etc. The scribes and Pharisees, serving wickedly the Jewish kingdom of evil, said:

“You see that we are accomplishing nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII).

They were the ones who sang to him in choirs, saying:

“Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that has come! Hosanna in the highest!” (Matt. XXI; Mark XI).

His faithful glorify him with harmonious rejoicing, exalting him because more people have been called through his teaching to earn the denarius of heavenly life than have been called through ours to observe the commands of the Law.

David, however, kept these words in his heart, etc. In his wisdom the Lord saw the unbelieving and deceitful hearts of certain Jews; and, as Scripture customarily speaks of God in human fashion, he feared exceedingly the people who were his brothers through the common frailty of humanity but the authors of persecution through the impiety of their conspiracy against the Lord. Therefore he spoke to them of his mysteries or admonitions more through parables and riddles than in plain light, lest he should entrust what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine (Matt. 7). For just as David, who was always accustomed to present himself as sober before his own people, altered his behavior before the Gittites, so the Lord, speaking in parables before the proud—who carried hearts ready to torture him and his followers—reserved the full explanation of everything for his own disciples. Indeed, he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures.

Some wish to say that the Lord “altered his mouth” when he said, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, but I say to you” (Matt. 5); or when, with the priesthood transferred, he also wished the transfer of the law and its ceremonies to take place. But they should observe that he displayed this kind of change not specifically to his enemies, but rather to those who were receiving the mysteries of his faith; and therefore the alteration of the mouth which blessed David, as a type of him, displayed so that he would not be recognized by his enemies must instead be referred to the understanding of those who, seeing the signs and teaching of the Savior, did not see, and hearing, did not understand.

And he collapsed in their hands, etc. The hands of the Gittites signify the works of the Jews; the doors of the gate, the beginnings of revealed heavenly grace; saliva, weakness; the beard, strength. David collapsed in the hands of the Gittites: to the blind, the Lord seemed to fall into sin when compared with the works of the Jews, who said that he not only violated the Sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God (John 5).

David struck against the doors of the gate: the Lord encountered the fall of death amid the beginnings of the new salvation he proclaimed—a salvation which, in the place of doors, he preferred at one time to open to the worthy and at another to close to the unworthy. Rather, he made those very doors of life an occasion of death, either because the Jews who persecuted him killed him through the grace of evangelical preaching, or because he himself, in order to open for us the thresholds of paradise, deigned to extinguish with the blood and water flowing from his side the flaming and turning sword that stood in the way. Hence the Psalmist, seeing him, in order to lead us to announce his praise in the gates of the daughter of Zion, first showed him striking against the doors of that gate, after he had spoken of the hope of our salvation, saying:

> Our saving God will make the journey prosperous for us; our God is the God of salvation, and the Lord, the Lord, has the exits from death (Ps. 67).

David’s saliva flowed down into his beard, and the Lord, despised and blasphemed on the cross among thieves by the impious, endured everything patiently, concealing for a time the strength of his divinity beneath the appearance of human weakness. Thus the prophet Habakkuk, commending the trophy of the glorious cross, says:

> His splendor will be like the light; horns are in his hands, where his strength is hidden (Hab. 3).

For it is not without reason that in the Song of Songs, where the mystical members of Christ—and likewise those of the Church—are described with such great skill and such careful repetition, we find nothing said about the beard alone, which above all suits a man. For, like saliva clothing the beard, the weakness of the flesh temporarily concealed the perpetual strength of the Word.

Thus he altered his mouth, concealing the mysteries of the kingdom of God which he disclosed to the faithful from those who preferred to remain outside. He collapsed in their hands, appearing sinful to those who gloried in the works and righteousness of the law. He struck against the doors of the gate, undergoing the humiliation of his passion amid the first signs of the revealed heavenly entrance. He let saliva fall upon his beard, the power of his divine majesty hidden for a time amid the vices and mockeries of his enemies, dying at that time an ignominious death—that is, the death of the cross.

And Achish said . . . “You have seen a madman,” etc. David, suspected by the Gittites because of his reputation for valor, deliberately imitated the behavior of a madman, so that, being thought possessed, he might be released unharmed by those who saw him out of pity. But their king, unaware of his deliberate transformation, drove him away from himself as truly mad and denied him entrance to his house as an insane man.

Nor does the truth of allegory depart from the shadow of the historical account. For the Lord, in order to heal the eyes of the hearts of those who could not see the glory of his divinity, applied the ointment of human humility. Yet some of the impious accused him in his sufferings as a man of weakness, and in his mighty acts they regarded him as possessed and as performing miracles by a power opposed to God.

Finally, as the Gospel relates, we learn not only what his adversaries thought and said about him, but also what was thought and said by some of his own people, who were not yet strengthened by complete faith:

> And they came to the house, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread. When his own people heard this, they went out to seize him; for they were saying, “He has lost his mind” (Mark 3).

His own, still carnal, did this because of the immeasurable quantity and quality of his continually increasing miracles. But consider what outsiders said as well:

> And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He has Beelzebul,” and, “By the ruler of demons he casts out demons” (Matt. 12; Mark 3).

Even after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, while the apostles were preaching the truth of the Gospel, certain madmen mocked and rejected it as a fabulous insanity. Hence the apostle, who was indebted to the wise and the foolish, bearing witness to Christ, heard:

> “You are mad, Paul; much learning is turning you to madness” (Acts 26).

Therefore, whoever accuses Christ of frenzy and madness should not be surprised if, by madly despising him, they reject him from the house of their own mind.

## (1 Samuel 22)

David therefore departed from there and fled into the cave of Adullam. Adullam is interpreted as “their testimony.” And the Lord, fleeing from the hearts of the proud, enters as a welcome inhabitant into the breasts of the humble—those who possess nothing of earthly eminence or beauty. Their very humility is a faithful testimony that they are worthy to receive Christ.

Or certainly, those from whom God flees because of their pride are called “the humble” as their testimony, so that by this testimony they may be convicted that they too could have pleased God and received God, had they been willing.

When his brothers heard this, they came down, etc. While Christ remains among the humble, all the elect descend to him by humbling themselves—whether human beings, who are his brothers because he became human, or angels, who are especially members of his Father’s household and the dwelling-place of his glory.

All those also come together who, weighed down by the consciousness of their sins, desire to be cleansed by the bitter tears of repentance and to be freed from debt—that is, from the interest of sin, which the devil imposed. With Christ as their leader and ruler, they hope to be raised to the joys of the kingdom.

And there were with him about four hundred men. Those who stand fast in faith cling to the Lord, acting manfully and having their hearts strengthened by the teaching of the Gospel, which is marked by the most beautiful unity of its four books. They are called to hope for, seek, and obtain the heavenly kingdoms.

The number one hundred, which, after all the numbers that run toward the left, is accustomed to be the first to seek the right, as has often been said, opens the entrance to the heavenly kingdom after the lowly labors have been completed.

It should be noted, however, that what took place in the cave of Adullam and what we have explained as best we could can be referred to the primitive Church in such a way that it may also appropriately be applied to the condition of the whole Church. For what follows pertains specifically to our Church, that is, the Church of the nations.

And David departed from there to Mizpah, etc. “From Zion the law went forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2), and, growing, it reached the Church of the nations, established upon the highest watchtower of faith and virtues.

Mizpah is translated “cave.” He also went to reconcile to himself orators, dialecticians, philosophers, and the very rulers of earthly affairs. To these as well Christ, until the times of the nations should be fulfilled, commended the faith of God the Father and the piety of the Church for careful and religious protection.

And the prophet Gad said to David: Do not remain in the stronghold, etc. Prophecy speaks to Christ, which omitted none of his mysteries, so that, when the fullness of the nations had entered, it would not strive to protect its faith any longer with the weakest believing Church against the ambushes of the Jews, but would instead deign to save the remnant of the Israelite people according to the election of grace.

In fulfillment of the prophets’ predictions, at the appointed time he will come to the long-uncultivated—but now destined through him to be exalted—hearts of the proud people, whose name, Hareth, that is, “custom” (*more*), is not unfitting.

It is therefore to this people that its author speaks through the prophet, as a bridegroom to the virgin betrothed to him, but long delayed from the joys of marriage:

> You will wait for me many days; you shall not commit fornication, and you shall not belong to a man, but I shall wait for you (Hos. 3).

How the same prophet intended this to be understood, he explained in what follows:

> For the children of Israel will sit many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without ephod, and without teraphim. Afterward the children of Israel will return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; they will fear the Lord and his goodness in the last of the days.

## CHAPTER X

While Saul seeks David, Doeg, becoming both traitor and executioner, strikes down the city of Nob with its inhabitants; Abiathar alone escapes to David.

And Saul heard that David had appeared, etc., up to what David said to Abiathar: “Remain with me; do not be afraid,” etc. This reading figuratively signifies what Judah, returning at the end of the age to its end, will suffer from its fellow tribesmen; and what reward it will obtain from the Lord—indeed, with the Lord eternally—for steadfastness in the same faith even amid the tribulations of Antichrist. The same interpretation can also suitably apply to the beginnings of the nascent Church and to the times of the apostles.

Saul therefore heard that David had appeared, together with the men who were with him. Near the end of the world, unbelieving and impious Jews will hear that Jesus Christ is being preached, believed in, and confessed among them after their long denial. There is no doubt that when the Savior appears to the hearts of the Jews through the preaching of Enoch, Elijah, and the other ministers of the word who will exist at that time, the persecution of Antichrist will soon follow.

But while Saul remained in Gibeah, etc. When the persecuting people from the Jews remain at that time in Gibeah—that is, on the hill of prophetic understanding, not of interpretation but merely of reading—and delight in the shadowy language of the law and the prophets, which is in Ramah, that is, in the height of spiritual meaning incomparable with the other Scriptures; when, lifted up by the glory of the earthly kingdom, which is undoubtedly destined to exist among them in the time of Antichrist, they are surrounded by all the associates of that persecution, keeping watch, standing in unbelief, and acting with force in order to overthrow every defense of faith and charity—

then, exhorting his followers with words of this kind, he will stir them to battle against the faith and steadfastness of the good:

> Hear, sons of Jemini—that is, “of my right hand,” those who are destined with me to be blessed with the better life and joy.

For I think that those who prefer to be condemned with the Nazarenes, according to your number, rather than to reign and live with Christ, who has appeared to us, should be designated by the name of the left hand.

> Is Jesus, who is undoubtedly said to have come from the root of Jesse, not able to give all of you in this age the fruit of perfected works and the wine of saving wisdom, which gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103), and in the age to come make you all sit upon thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel, as he has frequently promised (Matt. 15)—that is, as I am able to do?

For I can teach perfect wisdom together with good works, and I can bestow a blessed reward upon those who act and think rightly, since you have all conspired in allegiance to his name. Yet there is no one who shows me where those who worship his faith—and who deserve punishment—are hidden, especially since a man instructed by me to no small degree in the law has joined a greater covenant with Jesus the Nazarene, believing and confessing that he is the Son of God.

He appeared much more contemptible than I did, disfigured in a servant’s appearance, and taught him, to my injury, that God must be worshiped—a man who attempted to corrupt the legal statutes through his Gospel by stealth, and who has not ceased to do the same through his ministers down to the present day.

It is not unknown that Antichrist’s ministers will blaspheme Christ and speak countless things of this kind in order to make the hearts of Christ’s strong believers recoil. In response to their wicked efforts, those who persist in the faith will soon reveal what the troop of the impious harbors within itself. For it follows:

And Doeg the Edomite answered, etc. As we said above, Doeg is interpreted as “moved” or “anxious”; Edomite, “bloodstained”; Nob, “barking”; Ahimelech, “the kingdom of my brother”; Ahitub, “my good brother.”

The assembled company of evil associates, moved to shed innocent blood, will therefore answer the Jews persecuting Christ. While others openly attack the faith, this one habitually plots inwardly, more anxiously investigating and, at the time of persecution, betraying the gatherings of Christ’s faithful. Saul fittingly introduces him first among the servants, because the more perverse and insensitive someone is toward the good, the greater his position among the impious.

There is no doubt that false brothers, who oppress the Church from within, weigh upon her more heavily than open enemies who attack her from without.

I say that the enemy of the final conspiracy against Christ will answer, just as it is written of Judas:

> Night declares knowledge to night (Ps. 18).

What he recognized as sober, just, and pious he will wickedly betray, saying that he had seen the faith of the Lord Jesus in the teaching of those who, like the sharpest and most vigilant dogs, bark against the wickedness of the impious as against thieves and robbers, and who, following the example of the good brothers who went before them, also await possession of the eternal kingdom.

They will also beseech the Father for the kingdom of Christ and continually refresh him in his members with spiritual bread. They will rescue from the devil’s hands all whom they can, and urge, command, and assist them to fight rather for the peace of their deliverer.

The king therefore sent to summon Ahimelech, etc. When the priests consecrated to the service of the Lord had been summoned, Saul called David’s friendship and reception of him a crime of conspiracy conceived against himself. When impious Jews seize those consecrated to Christian piety, they will regard whatever they see done for the faith of truth as having been done against themselves, and will immediately prepare to avenge it—and deservedly so, for religion is an abomination to the sinner.

And Abimelech answered the king and said: “Who is there,” etc.? The sacred order of the commandments that serve the kingdom of Christ will respond to the people of the Jews, who regard faith in and love for Christ as a crime:

> Who among all the prophets and saints, who plainly served your interests greatly by their words, prayers, and examples, could be compared with the apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to the one who made him (Heb. 3), just as Moses was in all his house?

For this man has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself. He joined to himself, by the covenant of marriage, the Church of the nations, sprung from the ancient faith of your fathers.

He is not shown to have appeared in the flesh to do or teach anything other than what you yourselves had learned from the prophetic utterances—or rather, what you had always desired Christ to do when he came.

Did we only today begin to have this faith in him and to seek divine oracles of the word for the condition of his Church? Or did we not rather receive it as something given and entrusted to us through the ancestral tradition of the patriarchs and prophets, and therefore venerate and worship it?

For your servant did not know, etc. He replied to the accusation that he had helped David while knowing that David was weaving fraud and ambushes against Saul, because at that time he had known nothing of this affair.

Christian faith likewise denies that it knows that the Lord Jesus ever corrupted the legal statutes through any fraudulent ambushes. This openly confesses that it has learned Christ Jesus to be not a plotter and coveter of another’s praise, but the true messenger of the Father’s will; and for that reason the prophet rightly calls him “the angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9).

Such is the apostle’s statement:

> “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest” (Acts 23),

instead of saying, “I knew that he was not the high priest,” since the priesthood of that one had already appeared and been glorified—he who, with his chosen sons, is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

And the king said to the guards, etc. We always observe a different condition among the wicked, and a different condition among the good.

Some, ascending to the highest summit of wickedness, become the authors of persecution; Saul himself represents these by persecuting David. Others submit to wicked authority by openly and evilly supporting the fury of that same persecution; Doeg the Edomite represents these.

Others, as though of milder disposition, seem to keep their hands innocent from teaching their neighbors or extorting obedience from them through punishments, though not from actively committing impiety. The servants of Saul, who restrained themselves from injuring the Lord’s priests, are fittingly applied to these.

Among the faithful, who are tested by the temptations of the wicked, some struggle for the truth even to the point of bloodshed; these are prefigured by the priests of Nob, who were destroyed with their own people. Others possess equal faith and love but less strength to endure tribulation, and therefore seek refuge in flight, knowing that “the high mountains are for the deer, but the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs and hares” (Ps. 103). The one priest who escaped the blow of Saul’s hand is figuratively compared with these.

Since we have seen this difference in merits and dispositions in the past, we believe that it will also exist in the final persecution, although that persecution will be greater than the others. Thus, even while the authors of impiety rage and command unspeakable deeds, and while those who are mute obey evil, there will not be lacking people who preserve themselves unharmed from injuring the good. Yet even such a small measure of restraint will not be able to remove them from the heat of the most savage tribulation. For it follows:

And the king said to Doeg the Edomite: “Turn yourself,” etc. The impious persecutors said this to their most wicked ministers, who had been moved away from every state of uprightness and stained with the blood of the innocent and steadfast:

> Turn yourselves to evil, and, after the crime of betrayal, increase the severity of punishments against Christ’s faithful, by which they are compelled either to die or to deny him.

And he slaughtered, etc. The eighty-five men slaughtered on that day signify those who come out of the great tribulation and wash their robes in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 22)—those who are strong in their works and perfected alike in the spiritual observance of the Gospel and the law.

For five times the sum of ten and seven makes eighty-five. Few will doubt that the five pertain to the five well-known senses of our body, while the ten and seven pertain to the law and the Gospel: ten because of the Decalogue of the law, and seven because of the grace of the Holy Spirit, poured out more abundantly upon all flesh and shining forth in the times of the Gospel.

Therefore, whoever with a courageous spirit applies whatever he is able to do by seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching to fulfilling the commandments of the law and grace and obtaining their promises—such people, multiplying ten and seven by five, complete the number of eighty-five men.

They are rightly also said to be clothed in the ephod, that is, in the linen shoulder-piece, so that all their works—for shoulders are usually understood to signify works—may be shown to have been commended and adorned by the mortification of the flesh before the glory of martyrdom, and perfected with greater splendor.

But he struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, etc. After Antichrist has slaughtered Christ’s teachers, he also strives to defame and utterly eradicate the reputation of their teaching—the teaching by which they were accustomed to contend against impious doctrines as though barking, and in which they habitually fortified their own lives by inhabiting it through their works.

He does not fail to compel the strong in action, fruitful in begetting and nourishing children for Christ, the little ones in Christ, and those who still lovingly and chastely suck the breasts of their mother, as well as those who bear his easy yoke and light burden and hear his voice innocently and follow him to the eternal pastures of heavenly blessedness, either to deny his faith or to undergo death for him through impious tortures.

But one of the sons of Ahimelech escaped . . . Abiathar, etc. Just as Doeg the Edomite, the one who struck down the priests, represents the entire hand of executioners, so Abiathar, the one who escaped the sword of the striker, represents all the confessors of Christ who are able to survive that most savage persecution.

Abiathar is therefore rightly interpreted as “the superfluous father,” since he signifies those who, glorious by the name of father within the Church, will survive such a great storm.

He fled to David and announced to him that Saul had killed the Lord’s priests. This signifies the pious devotion of those who remain after the slaughter has been completed, turning more ardently toward the Lord and commending to him the memory of the slain brothers under his covenant, whether by praying or offering sacred sacrifices.

Christ himself responds in his Gospel that he knew beforehand and predestined that all who desired to live piously in him would suffer persecution for his name. Therefore, as though he were a debtor of certain interest, he will lead all souls released by such a death to the joys of eternal life.

> I knew that, since false brothers would never be lacking in the Church, they would certainly help external enemies through internal scandals. I knew that, since the wicked would never be lacking in this whole age—wicked people through whom the wisdom of those who dispute and the patience of those who struggle would be exercised and at the same time tested—the Church, journeying here, would certainly always be met by tribulations and temptations. But I am the one who, after each soul of the elect has labored through its struggles on earth, will bestow upon it the heavenly crown forever.

Remain with me; do not be afraid, etc. “Remain,” he says, “in my love; do not fear those who kill the body. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. But where I am, there also my servant will be; if anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (John 15; Matt. 10; John 12).
