This betrayal and slaughter by Doeg the Edomite can be understood both in the times of the Lord and the apostles—in Judas Iscariot and the other false brothers—and at the end of the world in Antichrist himself, who will be greater than the others. Thus Psalm 51, which is sung with reference to him, is appropriately applied to both enemies. Its title says:

> For the end; understanding for David, when Doeg the Edomite came and announced to Saul and said, “David has come to the house of Abimelech.”

The phrase “understanding for David” is placed at the beginning for no other reason than to signify that, amid the afflictions he innocently suffered, David understood what the wickedness of evil people would devise against the true David who was to be born from his seed.

For he came boasting in wickedness, powerful in iniquity, thinking of injustice all day long, and so forth, as the Psalm continues.

Judas, who understood through the Spirit that these things would happen, burdened both by the weight of sins and by the punishments he was to bear, announced it to the Jews and said:

> “Behold, Jesus regularly goes with his disciples into the garden on the Mount of Olives.”

How this title should be understood of the final tribulation is perfectly clear from what has been discussed above.

But because we have drawn out the discourse at length, and have composed this third book as longer in its exposition of blessed Samuel than the second and the first, we have decided to bring it to an end with the martyrdom of the victorious priests and to cease from our labor for a while in order to recover strength through silence.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0663]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0663C]

Having completed the third volume on blessed Samuel, I thought that, after my pleasure in meditating and writing had been restored by a period of rest, I would at last apply my hand to beginning the fourth. Yet this same rest—if indeed an unexpected anxiety of mind may be called rest—has lasted much longer than I had intended because of a new change in the circumstances surrounding us, especially the departure of my most reverend abbot.

After a long observance of monastic care, he suddenly planned to go to Rome and, among the holy places consecrated by the bodies of the blessed apostles and martyrs of Christ, to give up his final breath in old age. This greatly disturbed the minds of those entrusted to him, and all the more because the event was unforeseen.

But the one who, when long-lived Moses was taken from human affairs, substituted Joshua the son of Nun as leader, and who substituted Eleazar for his father Aaron in the priesthood, himself substituted the young Huetbert for the aged Ceolfrith, who was hastening to the sacred thresholds of the blessed apostles. Huetbert had long ago received the surname Eusebius because of his love and zeal for piety; he was appointed, in the place of an abbot, to govern the souls of the faithful through priestly and spiritual leadership.

After the fraternal election, I confirmed the rank of this substitution by the blessing given through your office, dearest bishop.

As the condition of the times returns to greater tranquility, leisure and pleasure have likewise returned to me, so that with my whole soul and careful attention I may investigate the marvels of Holy Scripture.

Therefore, beginning the fourth little book of allegorical exposition on Samuel with the victory of blessed David by which he saved the inhabitants of Keilah and defended them from the assault of the attacking Philistines, and beginning it with your prayers, most loving of bishops, I shall endeavor to communicate to readers whatever I am able to disclose, through him who holds the key of David.

## CHAPTER ONE

David saves Keilah when it is attacked by the Philistines; and when Saul is about to come against him with an army, he flees with his six hundred men to the mountain of the wilderness of Ziph.

[Col. 0664D] (1 Samuel 23). And they announced to David, saying: “Behold, the Philistines are attacking Keilah,” etc., up to what is written: “Nevertheless Saul sought him every day,” etc.

This reading, under the figure of the men of Keilah—saved by David from the enemy but soon preparing to hand that same David over to the enemy—marks the fickleness of those who hear the word and immediately receive it with joy (Luke 8), but have no root in themselves and are temporary; when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, they immediately fall away.

Those who knew that the Philistines were attacking Keilah therefore announced to David that, after all the inhabitants had been driven within the walls, the threshing floors that happened to be found outside could be plundered and devastated.

The elect truthfully announce this to the intellectual David, strong in hand—not instructing him through speech as though he were ignorant of human affairs, but reporting the dangers of the wretched to him as the merciful one through supplication—when they see either one soul or a multitude of souls together occupied by the unclean spirits, whether weighed down by the bundles of vices or still enslaved to pagan rites.

If such a soul possesses anything of naturally implanted virtue, or anything resembling a life-giving seed, all of it, because it is found outside—that is, because it has been employed only for worldly advantages—is plundered by the wickedness of those spirits.

They announce these things to the intellectual David, who, contemplating the common misery of humanity, complains and entreats against the kingdom of unclean spirits, saying:

> We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and contempt to those around us. How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name. For they have devoured Jacob (Ps. 79), and so forth, to the end of the psalm.

Shall I go and strike these Philistines, etc.? Since David, whenever he is understood mystically in Scripture, almost always signifies the Lord Christ—sometimes in his members, sometimes in himself—it is rightly understood that this passage, where he consulted whether the Lord should attack and conquer the enemies, must be referred to the person of his members, that is, his faithful.

These faithful, grieving at times over the destruction of the faithless made known by those near them, inquire through the oracles of divine Scripture what should be done about it.

Likewise, above, when David was told that the Philistines were attacking Keilah, it can not improperly signify that faithful people frequently show to more perfect Christians, who are likewise faithful to Christ, the dangers of temptations in the world which they perceive themselves unable to overcome.

Those more perfect and stronger-handed teachers of the Churches, immediately examining the testimonies of Scripture, discover that the oppressed must be pitied and assisted and that, after the assault of the evil spirits has been broken, the multitude afflicted by prolonged temptation must be saved.

But when the weaker are often afraid because persecution is imminent, the reading of the divine utterances, consulted again, quickly makes the answer clear: they must not fear those who kill the body (Matt. 10), but must rise from their torpor by doing what is right, go to the oppressed by preaching what is useful, and attack the oppressors through exorcism.

There are some who, when the storm of persecutions bears down upon them, scarcely dare to profess publicly the faith with which they have been instructed. How much less, then, would they presume to call others to faith or to strengthen them in the faith and undertake battle against the armies of malignant spirits?

And what does it mean typologically for David’s men to say to him, “Behold, while we remain here in Judah we are afraid; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?” It means that weaker hearers, while spiritual teachers prepare themselves for the work of the word, openly respond in fear:

> Behold, we are afraid to defend freely within the household walls of the Church the confession of the faith of the Father, which Judah signifies. How much more, if we go to those who have either never known the way of truth or have abandoned the truth they knew, in order to instruct them with the word of salvation, and begin to provoke the powers of the air to battle, do we recognize that we shall be exposed to greater dangers?

But the Lord does not cease to raise up their weakness and fear through the frequent words of his Gospel and to strengthen them for confidence in prayer. This is what follows:

> I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.

> In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage: I have conquered the world (John 16).

David and his men went to Keilah, etc. The Lord went in his preachers to heal the brokenhearted. He fought against the spirits of falsehood and unbelief by revealing the light of truth and faith. Through a just separation he drove away from them the souls of the redeemed, which those spirits had previously held bound by the bridle of error, as though riding upon them, and had subjected them to their own right and power.

The spirits had been accustomed to plunder and subjugate these souls; the Lord caused them to anathematize the spirits with a great curse. Thus the Lord saved those who, recently avoiding the spirits’ temptations, had earnestly sought his protection.

Few indeed doubt that these things have often happened from the beginning of the nascent Church and continue to happen daily in various places.

Moreover, at the time when Abiathar fled, etc. As we mentioned above, the ephod is a priestly garment, distinguished by four notable colors shining with gold, sacred through the two precious stones on each shoulder and the names of the twelve patriarchs. It most appropriately signifies the understanding of exalted men.

Those who flee to proclaim the glory of Christ ever more fully—those who have escaped the hands of executioners and persecutors after many have suffered martyrdom for him—carry with them hearts and minds exalted by four outstanding virtues shining with charity. In adversity and prosperity these virtues are tempered by precious discernment, and they are both taught and fortified by the word and example of the Fathers who went before them.

It is fittingly recorded that the priest, fleeing to David with the ephod, did not ascend but descended, in accordance with what is written:

> The greater you are, humble yourself in all things (Eccles. 3).

But because, as devotion to the faith grows, the hatred of unbelievers also grows—God from above arranging that temptation, testing those sound in faith, may make them more illustrious and at the same time expose the fickleness of pretenders—it is rightly added:

And Saul commanded all the people, etc. As the condition of the Church increased, there were never lacking adversaries in their respective times who, by the Lord’s permission, would test her patience and wisdom by assailing her with the gravest struggle.

They likewise sought to capture and remove from the midst the Lord himself in her, together with his men—that is, the strong defenders of his Gospel—by an impious siege. Yet they never succeeded in achieving the wicked desires of their unbelieving malice.

When David learned that Saul was secretly preparing evil against him, etc. After Abiathar had brought the ephod, David consulted the Lord whether Saul would come to destroy Keilah and whether its inhabitants would deliver him up. From this we may infer the manner in which he consulted the Lord: the priestly garment was brought to him, and thus an answer was sought from the mouth of the Lord’s priest. This was apparently the practice of those who consulted God at that time, at least of those who could not approach the ark of the Lord. For concerning it we read: “There I will speak with you,” namely, “from above the mercy seat and between the two cherubim” (Exod. XXV).

When David discovered both that the enemy was about to arrive and that the city, which had received him as a guest, offered him no trustworthy refuge, he went out with his men, about six hundred in number, and wandered here and there, uncertain where to turn. The saints—namely, the members of the supreme King—through men distinguished in virtue and in the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, inquire how the condition of the Church will be in the last times. Through the Scriptures they learn that the rule of the Jewish people will come to overthrow it, and that the men of Keilah—that is, those of restless mind who wish to live for themselves and not for the Creator—will soon betray the faith into which they were initiated. Christ will depart from such people and will not make his dwelling among them. Teachers who are perfect in hope and conduct also depart. For six signifies works, while one hundred [Col. 0667C] signifies the hope of eternal things; together, six hundred signifies perfect men. They abandon the lukewarm, lest by speaking further to those who will not be preserved they should harm them, as the historical account, describing what happened to David, adds:

“So David arose,” etc.

Woe to that soul, woe to that city, when the word of God, abandoning it, wanders here and there, uncertain where it may find a dwelling and rest, or in whose breast. “Foxes,” he says, “have dens, and the birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII). This is also what he says elsewhere: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII).

It should indeed be noted that these words can be referred typologically to the whole period of the Church, which is never without false brothers, but especially to the last times, when such people will abound more greatly. Their fickleness and treachery are aptly signified even by the name Keilah. For it is said to mean “cast onto a sling,” or “raising it,” or “taking it up for oneself.”

A wise woman explains why the soul of a false Christian, plainly unstable and erring, is called “cast onto a sling.” In the figure of the Church, she speaks with a strong and desirable hand, saying: “The soul of your enemies shall be whirled about in the force and circle of a sling” (1 Sam. XXV).

Why “raising it” is said of one who is unfaithful while appearing faithful is clearly demonstrated by that traitor who, added from the number of Christ’s disciples to the number of his persecutors, continues to have heirs of his wickedness in the Church. Those who claim the knowledge of faith especially for themselves and do not fear to separate themselves from Catholic unity show in what sense Keilah is said to mean “taking it up for oneself” [Col. 0668A].

“It was reported to Saul that David had fled from Keilah,” etc.

The enemies of the faith pretend not to burden with persecution those whom they see voluntarily abandoning the faith. But the ancient adversary himself also wearies with harsher blows of temptation those whom he sees resisting him bravely in faith and action. Those whom he sees either sluggish in faith or wholly unbelieving or apostate, he is more eager to possess as his own, subject to him in every respect, often troubling them with no—or at least fewer—temptations of anger, pride, fornication, envy, and the other passions of this kind.

“David remained in the wilderness,” etc.

Christ, leaving those who receive the faith only in word, dwells rather in the firmest breasts of those who, amid the aridity of the present world, thirst for God, the living fountain, asking when they may come and appear before the face of the Lord. He gladly remains in those whose exalted heart, removed from the enticements of the world and secluded in a blessed solitude, rejoices in the failing growth and flower of virtues. For Ziph is interpreted as “flower” or “sprout.”

“Saul sought him all the days,” etc.

From the beginning of the Church’s birth to its end, the wicked strive to take Christ away from the hearts of the righteous, while he himself defends the righteous so that they may never be overcome by the wicked. He promised to remain with them all the days until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII). Elsewhere he says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers shall not overwhelm you” (Isa. XLIII).

## CHAPTER II

Jonathan and David make a covenant before the Lord; and when the Ziphites betray him, Saul comes against David, but is prevented from capturing him by the more urgent necessity of confronting the Philistines.

[Col. 0668C]

“David saw that Saul had gone out,” etc., up to the passage written as follows: “Therefore they called that place the Dividing Rock.”

This reading mystically signifies, while the wicked persecute the Church, with what devotion the faithful assist Christ’s companions, with what impiety brethren under God assist the adversaries of the faith, and finally by what miracle Christ, the merciful Redeemer, sometimes rescues his own from the very crisis of death. “David saw,” it says, “that Saul had gone out to seek his life.”

“David was in the wilderness of Ziph, in the wood.”

The Lord, before whose eyes all things are naked and open (Heb. IV), saw that a gathering of the wicked had gone out from its inward security to seek the faithful who were persecuted by it—those whose heart and soul are one (Acts IV). He himself remained in the wilderness, in the Church gathered from the Gentiles. This Church, pregnant with the fruit of varied virtues, like trees, regularly produces fruitful growth. Concerning these trees the Psalmist sings of the house of remission and life to be built after the captivity: “Then,” he says, “all the trees of the forest shall rejoice before the face of the Lord, for he has come” (Ps. XCV).

These trees of the widely fruit-bearing Church are spiritually made fruitful with so much greater height by the flower or sprout of good works—for Ziph is said to be interpreted in both ways—as they more diligently abandon all the joys of this world.

“Jonathan son of Saul arose and went to David,” etc.

As persecution advances, the dove-like and simple spirit of the elect, often called from the very number of the persecutors to the grace of faith, draws near to Christ by the steps of its growing virtues and strengthens the laborers—that is, the teachers of his word—with the divine aid that is always present in times of need (Ps. IX).

“He said to him: Do not be afraid,” etc.

Although Jonathan, being human and ignorant of the future determined by fate and destiny, uttered falsely concerning himself that he would reign under David, nevertheless, in accordance with the mystical sense, he reveals the joys of Christ and the Church. He bore witness to that inviolable kingdom, to which he himself also belongs, by asserting that the enemies were not to be feared, since they could in no way reach the extinction of the rule of faith and truth. Rather, he affirmed that Christ himself, whose dominion was to increase and whose peace would have no end, would reign forever over the elect angels and human beings; and that those who faithfully loved him with their whole heart would in every respect be near him in the citadel of that same kingdom.

Their enemies having been overthrown and defeated, and being wholly subjected to the feet and rule of Christ, Paul says: “He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet” (1 Cor. XV; Ps. CIX). When he says, “All things are subject to him,” there is no doubt that this excludes “the one who subjected all things to him” (Ps. VIII).

From this it is clear that Christ will render powerless and empty the powers that have defected from him, and will set up trophies as the victorious sign against the enemies of our salvation—those whom he had already defeated long before by his death, as it is written: “Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death” (Heb. II), that is, the devil.

Text: “Thus he struck,” and so forth.

“Then both of them made a covenant before the Lord,” etc.

The Lord and the faithful make a covenant with one another: they are to follow him, and he is to give them eternal life. This takes place before the sight of his divinity, in whose faith he commands us to live and whose vision he encourages and helps us to desire. The Lord remains in the Church, thickly crowded with the forest of many peoples, all the days until the consummation of the age (Matt. VIII).

Each of the faithful, after completing the duty of prayer, exhortation, or any other devotion offered to the Lord, returns to his own conscience. Thus, free for a time from outward activity, he may more freely consider all that he has done or must do, cleanse himself more freely from what was badly done, and gird himself more perfectly for what must be done well.

Such people, knowing how to say with the prophet, “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Ps. LIV), may deservedly be called, with Jonathan, the gift of the dove; indeed, with the apostle Peter, they may be surnamed “sons of the dove.”

“The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah,” etc.

False brothers often ascend, having abandoned the sprout and flower of their virtues, to proud enemies of the faith, in order to assist them against the Church. Detesting the simplicity of the faithful, they say in a manner to the persecutors: “Does Christ not dwell among us through faith in the safest hearts of the Gentiles?”

Nor is it without significance that this is said to occur on the hill of Hachilah, that is, “of the one who receives it.” Where should the Spirit of Christ be thought to dwell more graciously than in the elevation of a mind that firmly receives its faith? This hill is on the right side of the wilderness, because it abandons the splendor of the world for what is on the right hand—that is, the joys of eternal life.

For one who avoids worldly enticements with an eye to a temporary and earthly reward should be said to have turned not to the right side of the wilderness but rather to the left, where our desirable King does not dwell, but the detestable enemy habitually resides [Col. 0670B].

The Ziphites say all this to Saul when some falsely faithful people betray either the mysteries of the faith or its worshipers to openly hostile persecutors. Although they differ from those persecutors in their recognition of the faith, they agree with them in hatred of the same faith. The more deeply they have come to know the secrets of Christ, like David’s hiding places, the more wickedly they assist those who seek to attack the Church from outside.

“Saul said: Blessed are you by the Lord,” etc.

The Jews and their supporters promise themselves that a blessing will come to them from the Lord when, possessing zeal for God but not according to knowledge, they pursue the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, either with hatred or with weapons. As the Lord says elsewhere concerning them and their accomplices: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John XVI).

But woe to their blessings! They investigate ambushes against the Church, or at least against any single member of the Church, and are shown to grieve in the manner of persecutors when they cause one of Christ’s little ones to stumble.

Woe to those who, reaching in name only the flower that ascends from the root of Jesse, now seek with all the mind’s attention the advantages of the present life—things that quickly wither and perish. They have forgotten that blessing which is to be regarded and hoped for by all, concerning which it is written: “The Lord has remembered us and has blessed us. He has blessed the house of Israel; he has blessed the house of Aaron” (Ps. CXIII).

While blessing both, he blessed all who fear the Lord. You ask: “Which two?” The answer is: “The little with the great”—that is, the house of Israel with the house of Aaron. These are those who from that people believed in Jesus the Savior, because God was not well pleased with all of them. Yet if some of them did not believe, did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not.

“For not all who are of Israel are Israelites, nor are all the descendants of Abraham his children. But, as it is written, ‘A remnant shall be saved’” (Isa. X).

By this oracle of Isaiah, some Jews are foretold as attaining this heavenly blessing in such a way that the greater part of them is blinded. Saul, rejected by God, prefigured and represented them, while the Gentiles were substituted in their place: “For sheep that were not of this fold were added, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

The faith of all the nations joined them, and the number grew not only of wise bishops but also of obedient peoples. To them many blessings of God were promised, as it is said: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. I).

God blessed us not with one blessing but with all. This does not mean that we all attain everything; rather, while individuals possess one or several of all these blessings, through the individual blessings we all possess the whole.

And these are not earthly blessings, after the manner of the Jews, concerning whom Isaiah said: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isa. I), but spiritual blessings. Earthly blessings include having children, abounding in wealth, and enjoying honor and health. Such an earthly blessing descends even to irrational beasts, for it was said of them: “The Lord blessed them and said: Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. I).

But spiritual blessings are in the heavenly places, because the earth cannot contain a spiritual blessing. Even those blessings promised in Leviticus to those who observe God’s commands—for example, lending to foreign peoples, having storehouses full of grain, being blessed in the cities and blessed in the fields, and things of this kind—we do not see fulfilled in the prophets. They wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, and oppressed; the world was not worthy of them, and they wandered in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the ground [Col. 0671C].

Everything must therefore be understood spiritually, and spiritual blessings must be awaited not in earthly places but in heavenly ones.

“But if he should hide himself even in the land,” etc.

The land is the mind of the elect, made fruitful by works of faith. God visits, waters, and multiplies it, yet the most arrogant investigator boasts that he will search it out, because he may be able to take Christ away from his worshipers not only in the public sphere of work or confession but also in the very secrecy of their inward faith and love.

“But if he should hide himself even in the land,” he says, “I will search him out among the thousands of Judah.” It is as though he said openly:

“If through us the Christian people should be reduced to such smallness and poverty that, with confidence to preach, celebrate their solemn rites, call public assemblies, or even openly profess themselves Christians taken away, they should scarcely dare to worship Christ, hidden as it were, in the innermost recesses of their breasts, I will gradually drive him out from there also, as the number of persecutors and informers increases together. For I have countless thousands of Judah—that is, armies of divine praise or confession—with which I can easily extinguish all the rash undertakings of those who think otherwise.”

This may also be understood simply, since Christians have sometimes been dragged from crypts and hiding places and brought forth to suffer death for Christ.

“But they arose and went to Ziph before Saul.”

The Ziphites are rightly said to have gone before Saul to Ziph while lying in wait for David. Schismatics and heretics, the closer they are to Jews or pagans—for they have been admitted within—the more wickedly they wither the Church’s fruit, as though they were the first to do so.

Would that we did not know that this would happen especially in the time of Antichrist, when the Jews would inflict greater persecution than all the others, and that it happens daily. In the end, the more Judas had been received inwardly, and the more he had become the Lord’s companion and acquaintance, eating sweet food with him, the more powerfully he lifted up his heel against him.

“David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon,” etc.

Maon is interpreted as “habitation.” Jeshimuth means “bringing death.”

The faithful, under Christ’s leadership, often rejoice in thirsting for their eternal homeland; this is signified by the waterless places of the wilderness. They sigh with ardent desire for the habitation of heavenly blessedness, which is suggested by the name Maon, that is, “habitation.” They know to hope for eternal life from the death inflicted for God, which the right side of Jeshimuth figuratively expresses.

Yet they are not still able to cross perfectly the vast fields of earthly thoughts. But when the storm of persecution breaks upon them, the mind immediately abandons all things of this world, humbles itself, and gathers itself together at the most strongly fortified rock of faith. Setting its feet upon that rock and directing its steps, it now burns with a sweeter desire to roam in spirit through the heavenly places and to sing more ardently the song of new hope and joy. This is what is signified when David and his companions remain in the wilderness of Maon after taking refuge in the protection of the rock.

That same wilderness of Maon, the same habitation, signifies not only the desire for an everlasting dwelling, because of the heights scorched by heat, but also, because “wilderness” derives its name from “abandoning,” indicates the very dwelling of heavenly rest which man had previously abandoned.

Finally, in the parable of the Gospel, the Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness and goes to seek the one that had gone astray (Luke XV). In this wilderness, under David’s leadership, dwell those endowed with the grace of Christ who can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

“When Saul heard this, he pursued David,” etc.

These words refer especially to the Jewish persecutor. Having heard of the faith and devotion of believers, he persecutes on earth those who gaze toward heaven with the whole intention of their minds. He himself believes that Christ is still to come in the flesh, while they have learned that he has already come.

This is what is signified by Saul walking on one side of the mountain and David and his men remaining on the other side. The former, empty of Christ, hasten with perverse hope as though Christ were still to be incarnate; the latter, through the grace of Christ their author, have long ago received the sacraments of the Christian faith by which they would be saved.

This is the mountain of the house of the Lord, prepared on the top of the mountains, upon which a city set on a hill cannot be hidden (Isa. II). Nor is it surprising if they despair of being able to escape their enemies in the flesh, since it was not said to them: “Do not fear, for you will not be killed by your enemies” (Matt. X). Rather, it was said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

Nevertheless, those who had despaired were sometimes rescued from their enemies in the present life: the three young men from the furnace, Daniel from the lions’ den, Paul and Silas, and the chief of the apostles himself (Acts V). Elsewhere, all the apostles together were rescued from prison; and finally, many martyrs thereafter were delivered to great praise and glory in Christ and in the Church. Hence it is rightly added:

“So Saul and his men surrounded David like a crown,” etc.

For when the Lord and Savior protects his faithful, those who, because of the fear of God, would not have wished to do so are very often compelled, for the sake of human peace or some advantage, to desist from tearing them apart.

For this reason the faith of Christ, upon which his Church is built and against which the gates of hell do not prevail (Matt. XVI), is most rightly called the Dividing Rock. It often wonderfully protects its own, even when they have despaired in the present; and in the future it separates those who hope from the disturbance of human beings through an everlasting reward.

Whether we believe that these things happened in our own times or that they are to happen in the future under Antichrist, let the reader judge. Let him not contemplate without tears a matter worthy of tears: how the condition of the Church daily declines toward worse things—or, to put it more mildly, toward undertaking weaker things.

The city of Nob suffered martyrdom because it received David and all his companions. This means returning good soil’s fruit through patience. Keilah, with its inhabitants, was saved by David from the enemy; but when persecution was imminent, because it was not afraid to betray its savior, it lost him. This is what it means to receive the seed of the word with joy, but, when tribulation arises because of the word, immediately to fall away (Matt. XIII; Luke VIII).

When the Ziphites discovered that David was staying nearby, they not only did not invite him to themselves but voluntarily betrayed him. Nor did they investigate his paths and devise the overthrow and tripping-up of his steps in order to avoid danger; rather, they did so to obtain Saul’s friendship. These are the people who, according to the Lord’s aforementioned parable, hear the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.

I have not pursued these matters as though I did not believe that many people exist today, and that many will always exist, perfect in faith and truth. Rather, I have done so because I have already seen, in large part, the times approaching that were foretold long ago, when, because iniquity abounds, the love of many will grow cold (Matt. XXIV).

The title of the fifty-third Psalm remembers this reading and the betrayal of the Ziphites. It reads as follows: “For the end, in songs, an understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden among us?’”

To explain it briefly: “For the end” signifies that the psalm was spoken in the person of Christ. For “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X). “In songs,” in great distress, nevertheless declares the same song’s joy, in accordance with the one who said: “We also glory in tribulations” (Rom. V). For, unless I am mistaken, psalms bearing the title “in songs” always announce the singer’s rejoicing amid adversity.

“An understanding of David” shows that David, surrounded by anguish but unexpectedly delivered, understood that the body of the true David, of whom he too was a member, would suffer at the hands of the wicked; yet, through the grace of its Redeemer, it would often be delivered in the present and always crowned in the future.

What is said at the beginning of the same psalm—“O God, save me by your name, and deliver me by your strength”—is what David in this reading does when he seeks refuge in the rock. For this indication of deliverance the place is called the Dividing Rock. “Our fathers drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.”

## CHAPTER III

David cuts off the edge of Saul’s cloak in the cave of the wilderness of Engedi and, by showing it to him, moves him to confess his crime. Samuel dies, and David descends into the wilderness of Paran.

(1 Sam. XXIV.)

“Then David went up from there,” etc., up to the passage written as follows: “David arose and descended into the wilderness of Paran.”

In this reading the Lord reveals his hidden gifts to little ones rather than to the wise and prudent. Entering the barriers of death, he immediately destroys them by rising again. After taking away part of the Jews’ earthly kingdom, he calls them to repentance through the disciples. Soon, when the shadow of the law has failed, he is brought in to be worshiped in the truth among the long-abandoned and savage hearts of the Gentiles.

David, fleeing Saul’s ambushes and abandoning the feeble protection of the Ziphites, ascends and dwells in the safest places of Engedi, which is interpreted as “the Fountain of the Kid.” The Lord, fleeing the proud hearts of unbelieving Jews, and also abandoning those who do not hesitate voluntarily to leave behind the beginnings of virtues they have undertaken, ascends to what may be called higher places and dwells in the hearts of the humble in spirit. These hearts had already confessed the crimes of their own shamefulness and washed them in the life-giving fountain of the Savior, so that they might pass from kids to lambs through a blessed transformation.

The Church remembers this place when it speaks in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me in the vineyards of Engedi” (Song I). It says plainly:

“For just as the cluster of the island of Cyprus is superior to others, so the grace of my Redeemer commonly makes the mind it begins to possess drunk with incomparable ardor for spiritual pursuits.”

This occurs only among those peoples who, renewed in the remission of sins by the fountain of baptism, know how to propagate the joys of fruitful good works. It calls these the vineyards of Engedi—the trees of balsam, for which that place is fertile. When their bark is cut, the liquid that drips from it, beautiful with its tear-like drops and most suitable for preparing chrism, clearly shows how appropriate it is for signifying virtues.

“When Saul had returned,” etc.

Saul is suddenly recalled from pursuing the Philistines to seek out and kill David with an evil intention. He turns his weapons from the just conflict in which he was confronting enemies to the unjust conflict in which he also strikes a fellow citizen.

So unbelieving Jews, although endowed with the word of Holy Scripture and often contending in debate against idols and the various errors of the nations, suddenly, in their misery, turn the darts of unbelieving words against Christ and the Christian religion. When they learn that he has admitted to himself publicans and sinners cleansed through the washing of saving water and already withdrawn from the enticements of the world—for this is typologically signified by David’s remaining in the wilderness of Engedi—they immediately conceal snares against the innocent, vainly seeking to swallow him as hell swallows the living, as though he were descending whole into the pit. Hence it is appropriately added:

“Saul took three thousand chosen men,” etc.

Just as the number three is customarily placed in a good sense because of a definite mystery—signifying those who are glorious through confession of the Holy Trinity, devoted through faith, hope, and charity, perfect in thought, speech, and action, or something similar—so, when it is placed in an evil army, it rightly announces those who are proved to act in every respect contrary to these things.

Therefore, in this passage, the three thousand armed men with whom Saul goes out to pursue David and his men are to be understood mystically as those who, arrayed in a threefold battle line against the Lord and against his Christ and meditating vanities (Ps. II), namely, departing into the counsel of the ungodly, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of pestilence, did everything contrary to the blessed man whose delight is in the law of the Lord and who meditates on his law day and night.

Saul proceeds to seek David even over the most precipitous rocks, accessible only to ibexes, when the Jewish kingdom sets the snares of deception and ambushes for the Lord, even in the loftiest of his sayings, which remain scarcely comprehensible except to perfect hearers.

Ibexes are small four-footed animals that know how to remain and give birth only among rocks. If they ever fall from the high peaks of the rocks, they catch themselves unharmed on their own horns. They signify humble hearers of the word of God. The more they recognize themselves as lacking in merit, wisdom, and virtue, the more they seek, as ibexes seek refuge among rocks, the strong defenses of the Holy Scriptures in which they ought to dwell in mind and bear the offspring of good works. Whatever temporal ruin comes upon them, they sustain themselves upon the testament of the heavenly words and are saved as though caught by their horns.

The Lord mentions this animal and indicates that its figure is not to be despised when he speaks mystically to blessed Job: “Do you know the time when the ibexes give birth among the rocks?” (Job XXXIX).

“He also came to the sheepfolds,” etc.

While Judea was pursuing the great Shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, it extended the force of its wicked questioning even to the gatherings of his faithful disciples, who offered themselves as sheep to raging wolves, in case it might find in them something with which to accuse their teacher. Hence the saying: “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful on the sabbath,” and so forth (Mark II).

“There was a cave there,” etc.

This cave is a figure of the Lord’s tomb. Saul entered its opening to relieve himself, just as the rulers of the Jewish kingdom, departing from Pilate, fortified the tomb and sealed the stone with guards. In their attempt to close the way of resurrection to the author of life, they displayed outwardly to everyone the stench of their faithlessness, which had long been conceived and inwardly fermented in their minds.

The Lord, buried in the inner part of the tomb, lay hidden there. His men also lay hidden there—that is, his disciples, strong at that time and destined to become stronger. Wherever they were bodily within the city of Jerusalem at that time, it is certain that in the whole intention and desire of their minds they occupied the tomb, where they grieved that the one whom they loved lay buried.

They were hidden in the cave because they absolutely did not wish those who had killed him unjustly to know what devotion and love they held toward him.

Or certainly David’s men are to be understood as having been hidden with him in the cave, indeed as having risen with him and gone forth from the cave, according to the apostle’s saying: “Our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. VI).

As he said earlier: “Whoever among us was baptized into Christ Jesus was baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

“David’s servants said to him: Behold, the day,” etc.

His disciples, still fleshly and servile in spirit, said to Christ when they saw the power of the crucified man and the madness of those crucifying him:

“Behold, the time is here of which God the Father spoke to you through the mouths of his holy prophets from ancient times: that he would place all your enemies as a footstool under your feet” (Ps. CIX).

All those who wished to destroy the people who, after releasing the robber, condemned the Savior to death, said this with their whole heart, although not in words. This was demonstrated in the one who cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant, unwilling that the Lord should drink the cup which the Father had given him.

It was demonstrated in those who wished fire to descend from heaven upon the wicked, not knowing whose spirit they possessed, since “the Son of Man did not come to destroy lives but to save them.”

But he, with an appropriate moderation of his mercy, did not utterly destroy the wicked. Rather, he took away from them no small part of the royal apparel, so that, thus confounded, they might come to recognize and correct their madness.

“After this David’s heart struck him,” etc.

The Lord grieved, with compassionate affection, for the human race from which he took flesh, because, as its merits demanded, he was compelled to remove some royal adornment from it. He preferred that, while the divine law was preserved, it should always possess a perpetual kingdom both in this age and in the age to come.

Finally, when he saw the sinful city, he wept over it, saying: “If you too had known,” and so forth (Luke XIX). With human compassion he lamented the detestable cutting off of the kingdom which, in accordance with divine severity, he justly decreed would take place.

“He said to his men: The Lord be merciful to me,” etc.

David is shown to have restrained his hand from killing Saul, although Saul was pursuing him with the greatest hostility, for two principal reasons: he remembered that Saul was both his lord and one anointed with royal chrism.

First, therefore, he reverences with fitting honor the kingdom or anointing, which he knew also to prefigure the Lord’s own inviolable kingdom and spiritual anointing.

Next, he instructs us in moral discipline, so that we may not presume to stain with the sword of harsher speech those set over us—especially those distinguished by sacred orders—even when they persecute us unjustly. Nor should we tear away, by condemning it, what is like the fringe of their garment, meaning some final and superfluous action of theirs.

But if it should happen that we have done something of this kind through carelessness, we should immediately strike our heart with grief and strive by repentance to correct our rash deed.

According to the order of the interpretation begun above, in which we said that Saul signifies the Jewish people or kingdom and David Christ, we may understand that Christ called that same people or kingdom his lord because he deigned to take from it the form of a servant. He called it “the Lord’s anointed” because, above the other nations, it had anciently received the anointing of spiritual grace.

Therefore he did not wish to raise his hand against it and destroy the wicked utterly. Rather, as though their royal cloak had been cut off, he divided them from the earth and overthrew them during their lifetime.

As another psalm says: “Do not kill them, lest they forget your law. Scatter them by your strength and bring them down, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. LVIII).

“David restrained his men by his words,” etc.

The Lord restrained the harshness of his disciples, by which they desired the wicked to perish, saying: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Matt. VII). “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned” (Luke VI). Elsewhere: “God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John III), and other words of this kind.

He did not permit them to love the immediate punishment of wrongdoers; rather, he taught them to love the life of those who had been corrected.

[Col. 0677C] Moreover, Saul, rising from the cave, etc. The guards of the Lord’s tomb, who had been thrown prostrate by fear of the approaching angel and had become like dead men, and who fled from the tomb, nevertheless continued along the paths of their wicked conspiracy against the Lord, saying that his disciples had come by night and stolen him while they were sleeping. This may rightly also be understood of those who had appointed guards over the tomb (Matt. XXVIII): although, while guarding the Lord’s tomb, they departed groaning and confused, they nevertheless did not turn their steps away from the purpose of their raging pursuit of his faith. When both groups had been driven away from guarding the tomb, the Lord himself did not delay gradually to reveal to his own the glory of his resurrection, which he had concealed. Once this truth had been confirmed and [Col. 0677D] thoroughly taught, he soon thundered through the same men with the free proclamation of preaching, kindly calling his persecutors, who had turned away from him, back to repentance and to his love. While reconciling some of them to himself through his first words of humanity and compassion, he taught them to look back after him—that is, to repent of the crime they had committed against God.

And David bowed himself forward upon the ground and worshiped, etc. And the Savior, displaying through the ministers of his word the forward-bowed heart of his compassion, ready to pity and assist earthly and infirm hearts, himself first offered an example of worship and reconciliation to God for those who had long before offended him. Through the heralds of the Gospel he said to the Jewish people: “Why do you listen to the words of the wise men among men, the scribes and Pharisees, who say: ‘Jesus seeks evil against you; if we let him continue in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation’” (John XI). Behold: at the time of my Passion, when so many miracles appeared, all who were able to see truly saw in you that the Lord had delivered you into my power. At the single, most gentle word of my answer, when I said, “I am he,” such a great armed band trembled and fell; when I was crucified, an extraordinary darkness covered the whole sky at midday; when I breathed out my spirit, the whole earth was shaken, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and countless corpses of the dead were raised. Finally, when the angel appeared as witness to my resurrection, an immense earthquake likewise occurred, and your guards were made like terrified and dead men. Indeed, I considered killing you if you did not repent; but the regard of my mercy, acting patiently, spared you, preferring that, after repentance, you should merit pardon and salvation. For I said: “I will not strike them down completely or remove from the midst a nation, sinful and hostile to me though it is, from which I took the form of a servant, in which I would win the whole world, and which long ago, in its ancestors, divine generosity had covered with the blessing of singular grace.”

“Rather, my father, look,” etc. “Rather,” says the Lord, “my people, from whom, in order to confirm the promises made to the fathers, I was called and became the Son of Man, and I did not disdain to become incarnate: look and recognize [Col. 0678C] the end of your royal state, which lies in my power. For when I cut off the summit of your earthly kingdom, calling many away from its defense—which is carried on through weapons, disputes, and wars—to the simplicity of my faith and religion, and delivering many, because of the guilt of their faithlessness, into the hands of enemies, I did not wish to extend over you the hand of open vengeance. Observe and see that there is nothing evil or unjust in my work, and recognize that I am the one of whom the prophet testifies: ‘He committed no sin,’ he says, ‘nor was deceit found in his mouth’ (Isa. LIII). ‘Who among you will convict me of sin?’ (John VIII)—you who, by plotting, are trying to erase the memory of my name from the land of the living.”

“Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing?” [Col. 0678D] etc. Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” “Whom, then,” he says, “are you pursuing, my people, who were chosen before all other nations to behold the glory of divine brightness? Whom are you pursuing? Is it that great and most vigilant guardian of the holy sheep, whom you did not hesitate to hand over to death, and whom even after death you do not cease to pursue with hatred? He who, modest in the appearance of humanity but swift in the leap of resurrection, escaped your hands while you were trying to seize him—do you, foolishly, suppose that you can now seize him again as he thunders from heaven? Indeed, I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

Let no one think it absurd that a dead dog or a flea should signify the Lord, since elsewhere, because of the weakness of the flesh which he received from virginal flesh without the seed of a man, he himself says of himself: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXII). And because of the glory of the resurrection, which he accomplished suddenly and most swiftly by leaping, as it were, from death to life: “And I was shaken,” he says, “like a locust” (Ps. CVIII).

And Saul raised his voice and wept, etc. And, with the Lord teaching through the apostles, the Jewish people, in those who had been predestined to eternal life, raised their voice in confession of the faith which they had previously suppressed in the lowest depths by denying it, and washed away the contagion of their former guilt by pouring forth fitting tears of repentance. They confessed alike the Lord’s justice and goodness, while also recalling the errors of their own wickedness: they themselves, indeed, had savagely handed over to death the author of all goodness, whereas he, unjustly delivered to death, although omnipotent, preferred to preserve those who killed him for life rather than destroy them.

“And now, because I know that you will certainly reign,” etc. This is the voice of the repentant Jewish people, seeking from Christ, whom it has recognized, an entrance to salvation. “And now, because I know with certainty that you are the one of whom it was said: ‘His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace’ (Isa. IX), possessing in your power that kingdom in which those who are pure in heart will see God without end in blessedness, confirm, I beg you, the faith you have bestowed through the generosity of your sacraments, and increase that faith in me through your heavenly gifts, so that, having received the pledge of the Spirit, I may have confidence that you will save from eternal destruction the offspring of works begotten from my heart after the dissolution of the body. Do not remove my name from the house of heavenly dwelling, which you deign to grant to my fathers, who faithfully and lovingly awaited your coming through the Law.”

When some of the Jews poured forth these and similar words of confession, the Lord assented to their just petition and, having imbued them with the sacraments of the Gospel, made them believers from catechumens and candidates for baptism.

“Saul therefore went to his house,” etc. The Jewish people, in those who were able to repent of their faithlessness through the apostles’ teaching, went to attend to the working out of their inward salvation. But the Lord himself and his preachers, knowing that many from the same people would stir up wars against the faith, left the low and earthly places and soon ascended to safer and higher regions—that is, illuminating the hearts of the Samaritans and of the neighboring nations, who would believe rightly and persevere bravely [Col. 0679D] in the faith.

The title of the fifty-sixth psalm recalls this reading and teaches that it is to be referred spiritually to Christ. It is written thus: “For the end: Do not destroy David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” This title seems to have been written about David on account of two words, but by two others it reveals that it truly signifies Christ in its entirety. For what it says, “Do not destroy David,” seems to forbid the destruction by a lurking enemy of the one who had been promised by the Lord and prepared for the kingdom. And what it adds in the closing phrase, “When he fled from the face of Saul into the cave,” fits the very moment when he was thought capable of being destroyed. But the words placed at the beginning, “For the end,” forewarn us that everything must be referred to him who remains for us the perfection of all good things, because when we have come to him we shall have no need to seek anything further. And what is inserted next, “In the inscription of the title,” expresses the title of the Lord’s Passion, which Pilate wrote in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; and that title itself, as a figure of an inviolable kingdom, could in no way be destroyed, not even by the one who wrote it.

The sense of the whole title, then, is this: it commands the Jews not to imagine that they can take away the glory of Christ, whether of Christ himself or of Christ who was killed and buried. Understand a psalm to have been sung: “For the end: Do not destroy David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave”—that is, concerning him who is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Do not seek to destroy Christ by removing [Col. 0680B] or diminishing his kingdom, which has been marked by the inscription of the true title, even when you see him, under pressure from the wicked, to have entered through death the barriers of the tomb. Indeed, he fled through the barriers from the face of his persecutors, so that they would no longer have the power either to persecute him or at least to see him.

The psalm itself, in accordance with the meaning of this reading, sings openly and with suitable testimony of the Lord’s Passion, burial, and resurrection, as well as of the faith of the nations, which is likewise mystically contained at the end of the present reading. Among other things, concerning his triumphant Passion: “He made those who trample me an object of reproach” (Ps. LVI). Concerning the burial and resurrection: “He rescued my soul from the midst of lion cubs; I slept troubled.” This troubling, however, is better understood in his members, who had not yet fully believed in his resurrection while he slept in the tomb. Again, concerning the resurrection: “I shall rise at dawn.” But concerning the nations that would believe through his inspiration and cooperation: “I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing a psalm to you among the nations.” The psalm also describes the condemnation of the Jewish people, which Saul’s cutting off of the cloak signifies in this reading: “They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it.”

(I Reg. XXV.) “Samuel died,” etc. As the Gospel flashed forth, the shadow of truth that had formerly proclaimed the future came to an end, and the people could not be withdrawn without sorrow from the customs of the familiar ceremonies which it did not doubt had been bestowed through the institution of the divine Law. Hence James, speaking to the apostle Paul, says: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts XXI). Nevertheless, as the custom of Judaizing gradually ceased in the Church, the prophet’s limbs, as though grown cold and withdrawn from human sight, were buried in his own house at Ramah—that is, in a high place—because, when the sacraments of the Law had ceased to be celebrated outwardly, all things began to be sought, understood, and recognized inwardly in Christ and the Church. The prophet’s house is the Church of believers, and it is situated in that height of which it is written: “And he himself founded it, the Most High” (Ps. LXXXVI). And elsewhere: “For he himself has been regarded as exalted” (Isa. II).

But David rose and went down into the wilderness of Paran. Paran is interpreted as “wild ass,” or “fruitful,” or “their ferocity.” Thus, when the prophetic type had ceased and had been completed in Ramah—that is, in Christ—and in the Church, the truth of the faith, leaving Judea, deigned to approach the nations, long wild and untamed in spirit but now destined to be made fruitful by the fruit of righteousness. Paran is most suitably applied to signify the nations not only because of the name’s reference to something wild or savage, but also because of its harsh and fierce inhabitants. Scripture tells us that Ishmael, from whom the Saracens derived their descent, lived in the wilderness of Paran—he of whom it was said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. XXI). Shuddering at his turbulent proximity, the son of the free woman—that is, the people renewed by spiritual grace—complains, saying: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. CXIX), and so forth to the end of the psalm. These words describe the Saracens in particular and all enemies of the Church in general.

But so that Christ might also call the sons of the slave woman—that is, peoples enslaved to this world—to freedom, and make them, like Isaac, sons of the promise, he went down into the wilderness of Paran: that is, into the humbled hearts of the Gentiles, pouring into them the grace of his compassion.

## CHAPTER IV

When David was preparing to strike Nabal of Carmel, who had despised him, he was appeased through the intervention and gifts of his wife Abigail. After Nabal died ten days later, David took Abigail as his wife; he also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, while his wife Michal was given to Phalti son of Laish.

“There was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon,” etc., [Col. 0681C] up to what is written: “Saul gave Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Phalti son of Laish,” etc. This reading teaches figuratively that the Synagogue, condemned through the wickedness of its rulers and teachers, was saved by the Lord, but afterward, when the Gentiles had been called to the faith, was rejected to a considerable extent. It indicates salvation in some persons, the humble, and rejection in others, the proud.

There was therefore a certain man in the wilderness of Maon—that is, of habitation. There was a company of scribes and Pharisees occupied with the study of Holy Scripture. Scripture, endowed with a singular excellence beyond the other writings, teaches all its readers to become solitary from the world—that is, to be separated from its desires and spectacles—and to make themselves a dwelling worthy of God. “His possession,” it says, was in Carmel—that is, in the knowledge of circumcision—because the discourse of the Law which he proclaimed taught true correction to be understood, but did not grant its accomplishment. For what the letter, by commanding, displayed was accomplished not by the letter itself but by assisting grace. The Pharisee and the legal scribe therefore possessed not the perfection but the knowledge of completed correction: “For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I).

That man was called very great, because although the teacher in question was, to a considerable extent, earthly-minded, he nevertheless greatly surpassed all teachers of secular philosophy, who, being wholly ignorant of the divine Law, relied only upon themselves as masters in the matters they taught.

“And he had three thousand sheep,” etc. Innocent and penitent souls were entrusted to the scribes and Pharisees for instruction: the former perfected in faith, hope, and charity; the latter following the first rudiments of faith, which begins from fear.

“And it happened that his flock was sheared in Carmel.” It happened that the more perfect hearers of the scribes, in their knowledge of chastity, laid aside the legal acts of the outer person, so that the inner person might be renewed day by day. It happened that the whole people subject to them offered to the Lord the fleeces of their firstfruits and tithes, as though these were superfluous to them and could be lost without pain.

“The name of that man was Nabal,” etc. Nabal means “fool”; Abigail is said to mean “the father’s joy.” He was a foolish teacher of the Law who, possessing the key of knowledge, did not enter himself and prevented those who wished to enter. The Synagogue is rightly called “the father’s joy” in those of whom it is said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). In such matters it was exceedingly prudent for understanding the word of faith, and beautiful for doing what it was able to understand. But its teachers were harsh through unbelief, most wicked through evil living, and malicious in plotting against the Lord.

“He was of the family of Caleb.” The teachers of the Synagogue were from the discipleship of the Lawgiver. “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII). Since at that time they surpassed the other mortals both in human and in divine wisdom, Caleb—that is, “whole heart”—may rightly be applied to them. Or, because we read that the patriarch Caleb was powerful in faith and virtue, we may say that the life of the faithful, from which the unbelievers had degenerated, increases the condemnation of unbelievers through the contrast with their ancestors.

“When David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his flock,” etc. When the Lord, having lived among men in the world, heard that those learned in the Law were preparing their hearers, as though with suitable shears, either to rid themselves of vices or to offer their possessions to the Lord, he sent his strongest disciples, namely, heralds of the attainment of the heavenly denarius, whose youth had been renewed in baptism like that of an eagle. He said to them:

“Ascend to the knowledge of circumcision. Through the evident advances of virtue and teaching, show that you truly know and have climbed the stronghold of spiritual chastity. By doing this you will come to the teachers of the Law themselves, and you will also proclaim salvation to them in my name, who am called and am the Savior, announcing in peace the future things above. Say: ‘Peace to all who, by believing in the name of God the Father, wish to become brothers of Christ; peace also to you who have been converted to the same faith in holy fellowship; indeed, peace to all whom you have instructed and to everything you do.’”

This is the peace “which made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, abolishing hostility in his flesh” (Eph. II).

“I have heard that your shepherds are shearing,” etc. The Lord also spoke these words through his apostles to the leaders of the Jews:

“I have heard that your disciples are teaching the people who used the same pastures of Holy Scripture as we did. We were never troublesome to them, but lived peaceably toward all; moreover, we preached the easy yoke of humility and the light burden. At no time did anything perish from their teaching or their practices. At all times they were with us in the knowledge of circumcision—that is, they recognized, as we did, spiritual circumcision in the loftiest words of the divine utterances.”

Here we should understand that something could have perished from the possessions of those who were without David in Carmel—that is, the superfluous and unprofitable reading, for the salvation of the soul, of those who, while reading the Scriptures, did not know how to understand Christ in the Scriptures.

“Ask,” he says, “all the innocent and truly and knowingly humble among your people, whose is the kingdom of heaven; and they will tell you that the grace of the Gospel is not opposed to the letter of the Law, but that in both Testaments the righteous person lives by faith.”

“Now therefore, let the young men find favor in your eyes,” etc. “Since,” they say, “you teach the people—that is, shear the intellectual flock—take care that the disciples of Christ, who are preaching, also find in you the grace of faith and good action. For we have come preaching good things in the light of grace, uniquely good things indeed, so good that we proclaim to mortals the kingdom of heaven, previously unheard of, and call the whole human race to it. From this very goodness the Gospel received its principal name in Greek. Whatever your virtue of faithful obedience has found, offer it willingly to the teachers who rejoice to serve your salvation and to Jesus Christ, begotten from your stock, truly with strong and desirable hand.”

But Nabal answered David’s young men, etc. The foolish rulers of the Jews answered the disciples of Christ who were preaching to them: “We are disciples of Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John IX). The disciples of Jesus advanced to the presumption of teaching, so that they could not be overcome by anyone, having fled while despising the teachers of the Law, who were far their superiors in knowledge.

“Therefore we shall take for ourselves the words of Holy Scripture entrusted especially to us for teaching—some of which can be read and understood simply, which is, “I drank water”; others of which ought to be treated more carefully so that they may be understood, which is to eat bread by breaking and chewing it. [Col. 0683D] We shall also take the deeds of our predecessors, which we have prepared in teaching for the assistance of life and virtue for our hearers, and give them to teachers wholly separated from our religion and faith, who have perversely fled to the meanings of their own dogma.”

Then David said to his men, “Let each one gird on his sword,” etc. This may indeed be understood as the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. With it the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (Eph. VI), was girded to defeat unbelievers whenever he disclosed the Father’s word to the world through his Gospel. His disciples were also girded when they preached the same message.

But since it is read below that, through Abigail’s intercession, David was prevented from striking the wicked, and since the Church never asks Christ not to inflict the saving wound of his word upon unbelievers, this passage is better understood as referring to the sword of the vengeance of destruction that threatened the Jews after the Lord’s Passion. The Lord himself and the ministers of his word were girded with this sword—not to impose punishment upon sinners themselves, but to proclaim that such punishment would come upon sinners unless they repented. Because of fear of this sword, the Church, coming to meet the Lord, suspended its blow through intercession for more than sixty years.

“And about four hundred men followed David,” etc. All who could be found perfect in prudence, courage, temperance, and justice followed the Lord in the ministry of preaching. Others, content with the perfection of the twofold charity, preferred to live quietly with those already brought close to Christ rather than gird themselves for spiritual wars in order to acquire others.

[Col. 0684B] “One of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife,” etc. While the leaders of the Jews were scorning the word of faith, the unity of Christ’s disciples announced it to the Synagogue subject to them and said:

“Behold, Jesus Christ sent the apostles, messengers of truth instructed in the divine Scriptures, to announce eternal blessing to our ancestors, and they rejected them. These men—that is, Christ’s apostles—were good, exceedingly good for us, preaching the kingdom of heaven, and not troublesome, since they no longer imposed the burdens of the Law upon our necks. Nothing of what we had done perished at any time while we lived in the faith that they teach, in a life deserted from the allurements of the world and, as it were, solitary. At all times—that is, whether while the rites of the Law were still observed or now that the revealed grace is celebrated in its mysteries—everyone who has joined himself to the faith of Christ has been saved from every kind of destruction. They were our assistants in teaching on all the days when, according to their truly evangelical meaning, we instructed our hearers, both in investigating obscure passages of the Scriptures and in openly proclaiming what was clear.”

“Therefore consider and reflect on what you should do,” etc. “I have explained,” she says, “what usefulness and grace the faith of Christ possesses, and with what great hardness our rulers resisted it. Therefore consider and reflect by what course, turning aside from and avoiding the wickedness of the proud—who refused the blessing, and from whom it will be kept far—you may merit not only to escape his anger but also to receive the blessing of an inheritance. For the wickedness deserving vengeance has been completed against the rulers of your people and against your people itself. After formerly killing and stoning the prophets, they did not fear, to complete the wickedness of their sin, to lay hands even upon the Lord of the prophets, who was uniquely strong in hand. They are themselves sons of the devil, choosing the robber Barabbas for Christ the Savior, and so hardened in understanding that they cannot grasp the words of any spiritual teachers.”

So Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves, etc. Pierced by the apostles’ preaching, the Synagogue hurried to be reconciled to Christ, whom it recognized as having been offended by its rulers. It took its hearers, already instructed in the letter of the Law, and placed them upon the humble and simple dispensers of the evangelical word, through whose ministry or intercession they might be brought to Christ—namely, upon those who could say: “We became like beasts before you on earth, and we are always with you” (Ps. LXXII); and: “We are fools for Christ” (I Cor. IV).

The two hundred loaves are those who, through their fellowship in the same faith and action, are bound together with one another by such a mutual bond and strengthened by the fire of heavenly devotion that they cannot in any way be separated from one another.

The two skins of wine are those who, made drunk with the virtue of twofold love, desire to be put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit, and to be renewed inwardly day by day, so as to receive and contain the new wine of spiritual grace.

The five cooked rams signify whatever they discover in their own understanding to be proud and, as though badly horned, hostile toward weaker neighbors. They habitually boil and subdue all of it in the flame of a devotion appropriate to God’s mortification.

The five measures of parched grain signify those who know how to subject the aforementioned bodily senses to the spirit and to tame them, as with a millstone, through the necessary discipline of humility. Since this humiliation or mortification of the flesh must be practiced moderately—neither less nor more than is right—the parched grain is appropriately described as being measured by a *sata*, which among the Hebrews is a fixed measure containing one and a half *modii*.

The hundred clusters of raisins signify those who rejoice in virginal continence and are also bound to one another by the unbroken bonds of charity, tasting, even while remaining in the flesh, the most perfect beauty of angelic chastity. A raisin, cut from the vine that produced it while still full of its wine, is customarily kept uncrushed, as a gift of greater grace. Likewise, virginal flesh, separated from the fellowship of the universal Church by the stricter discipline of continence, embraces within itself the sweetness of mature chastity, cherished by the Lord for the grace of the whole Church. The meaning of one hundred is widely evident to all, since it signifies the mystery of heavenly and angelic perfection.

The two hundred cakes of figs are souls that impart to their neighbors, through teaching, the sweetness of their spiritual and perfect fellowship, so that, through doubled virtue, they may merit a double palm.

All these things were sent by Abigail to David as provisions when the Synagogue sent to Christ men instructed through the teaching of the Law in various virtues, to be baptized and instructed in the sacraments of the Gospel.

And she said to her young men, “Go on ahead of me,” etc. Many individuals came from Judea first to the faith; the Synagogue followed them. For it was said earlier: “The Lord added daily those who were being saved to the same community” (Acts II). Later, “the Church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, and it was built up, walking in the fear of the Lord and filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit.” But the Synagogue of believers, so as not to provoke its foolish rulers to worse things, hesitated to disclose the mystery of its faith.

“When she had mounted the donkey,” etc. When the Synagogue confessed to all that it had hitherto served a foolish understanding and descended to the beginnings of the Christian faith—which, beginning from the weakness of the Lord’s incarnation, ordinarily leads upward to the heights where his divinity is recognized—Christ and his disciples went down to meet it. By aiding its efforts through preaching, they would raise it from the very mysteries of his humanity, with which it was to be instructed, to the highest summits of his divinity.

And David said, “Truly I have guarded all this in vain,” etc. The Lord, condemning the long folly of the proud Jews, says: “Truly, for so long I offered the gifts of my grace in vain to the mad, before all other nations, and they repaid with the evil of faithlessness, persecution, and the cross the good of the grace I had given. Therefore I will remove the wicked from the earth, so that until the morning of universal judgment no one from the perverse offspring may remain unpunished.”

This was said not to show that all unbelieving Jews would die before the day of judgment, but to teach that they were wholly deserving of death and condemnation. A similar statement occurs when Korah stirred up sedition in the wilderness and the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation, so that I may suddenly destroy them” (Num. XVI). Yet when they interceded and said, “Most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh, shall your anger rage against all because one has sinned?” the anger was suspended and the grace of mercy was bestowed.

Again, on the following day, when the whole multitude murmured against them, he said: “Withdraw from the midst of this multitude; even now I will destroy them.” But what he showed the wicked to have deserved by just judgment was changed into mercy through the intervention of the righteous. So here too, under the figure of David, the Lord declines to judge what the faithless deserved, as the spiritual meaning of what follows in this reading will show. For it continues:

“When Abigail saw David, she hurried and descended from the donkey,” etc. When the Synagogue recognized Christ—or rather, when it itself was recognized by Christ—it hastened to renounce its former manner of life, which had zeal for God but not according to knowledge. By most devoted humiliation, declaring itself to be earth and ashes, it began humbly to worship the footsteps of the Lord’s incarnation, entreating either for itself in repentance, that it might be received by the Lord, or for its people and unbelieving rulers, that they might not be struck down bodily. It now openly confessed that the wicked had been reserved for eternal punishment and that Christ’s kingdom would endure in perpetual peace, while beseeching with every desire of its soul that it might itself be able to belong to this kingdom.
