“Let not my lord the king, I beg, set his heart against this wicked man Nabal,” etc. Moved by devout humility, the Synagogue of believers asks the Lord not to destroy its wicked teachers and leaders before the final punishment of judgment, so that those whom eternal destruction awaits because of the folly of their faithlessness may at least be permitted to enjoy, for a short time, the pleasure of temporal happiness. At the same time it humbly excuses—or rather tearfully accuses—itself, because it too recognized so late the heralds of such great goodness, namely, the apostles whom he sent.

“Therefore receive this blessing,” etc. “Since,” she says, “it is not hidden that the wicked will perish by just judgment, I beg you kindly to receive those whom I have offered to you, so that, having been converted in holiness, they may be dedicated to you, consecrated by you, and blessed through you; and join them to your servants who went before them in ecclesiastical fellowship.”

“Take away the iniquity of your handmaid,” etc. “Wash me more thoroughly from my injustice, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. L). For without any doubt I believe and confess that, when the plots of the persecutors have been restrained and defeated, God the Father will multiply far and wide the people consecrated by your faith; you alone are sufficient to save and defend the world from the evil ruler.

“And when the Lord has dealt well with my lord,” etc. “When God the Father has placed all your enemies beneath your feet and you have entered into an eternal kingdom with your elect, I beg you to establish me at the right hand of your throne and deign to make me a participant in that same kingdom.”

And David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel,” etc. The Lord refers the grace of the believing Synagogue to the glory of the Father, indicating that he must always be blessed and praised by us. He also rewards the believing Synagogue, which even prays for unbelievers, with a fitting blessing. At the same time he shows how pleasing he regards prayer that is poured out with goodwill for adversaries.

David therefore received from her hand everything that she had brought him, etc. The Lord received the devotion of all believers, which the hand—that is, the activity—of the preaching Synagogue had brought to him through its sons. In his kindness he instructed it, after receiving the grace of heavenly peace from him, to return to its conscience and carefully discern how it ought to live.

Then Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he had a banquet in his house, etc. After displaying to the Lord the affection of its devotion, the Synagogue of believers came to observe the life and mind of the unbelievers, perhaps hoping to call them also to the faith. When it saw them filled with the feasts of legal sacrifices, rejoicing that they were a royal race above the other nations, and—what was more serious—swollen against the word of the Gospel with a kind of madness like drunkenness, it was silent for a while about the danger of the crime committed. Meanwhile, strengthened more and more by the light of the Holy Spirit, it would proceed more freely to rebuke them, so that they themselves, as the glory of Christ shone openly, might recognize more clearly the sin they had committed against him at that time; recognizing it, they might grieve; grieving, they might wash it away.

But although they recognized their guilt, they preferred not to wash it away through repentance but to increase it through pride. For the apostles themselves, and all who were recovering from the snares of the devil, are unquestionably understood to belong either as companions or as gifts to Abigail—that is, to the person who represents the Father’s joy.

“When ten days had passed,” etc. The death of Nabal can be understood in no better way than as the extermination of the kingdom of the most arrogant Jews, the overthrow of the Temple, and the cessation of the observances of the Law. Finally, when ten days had passed, what occurred clearly pertains to the completion of the Law, which was given in the Decalogue; no one can doubt this.

[Col. 0688A] David therefore sent and spoke to Abigail, etc. The Lord sent preachers so that, after the leaders of the Synagogue—faithless with their followers—had been destroyed by the sword of the Romans, they might invite the Synagogue itself, in those remnants who survived, to its spiritual marriage.

She, rising, prostrated herself in worship upon the ground, etc. Rising for the exercise of good works, the synagogue of believers at that time first gives an indication of its faith: to worship Christ as God. Then it promises, in the humblest service, to cleanse away the earthly filth polluting the works of his servants—first in the water of baptism, and afterward in the most gracious fountain of its intercession and exhortation. In accordance with what he himself intimates by washing his disciples’ feet: “How much more,” he says, “ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John XIII).

[Col. 0688B] And she mounted the donkey, etc. The faithful synagogue, having followed the messengers of the Lord’s word, recognizes its own stupidity, slowness, and uncleanness with increasing certainty the nearer it comes to receiving the gifts intended for it. This can rightly also be understood of every faithful soul, which, having mounted the donkey, brings five maidens with it to David. For, once it has recognized its natural sluggishness and dullness, it rejoices to devote entirely to fulfilling the commands of its author whatever it is able to do by seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching.

Alternatively, when Abigail comes to David, she has five maidens as companions, because the synagogue, which is to be joined to the mysteries of Christ, brings with it souls imbued with no other rites than those of the Law, which was written in five books. If anyone doubts that the Church was gathered from their number after Vespasian and Titus inflicted slaughter upon the Jews, let him read ecclesiastical history. He will find that, once the destruction of Jerusalem had been completed, Christians who lived in that region—especially those from the circumcision who, by the Lord’s revelation, had escaped the Roman sword—immediately returned. For more than sixty years, until the final overthrow of that people under Hadrian, there did not fail to be Jews who faithfully served the Lord in the Church, so that throughout that entire period the bishops of Jerusalem were elected from no other group than the circumcision.

[Col. 0688C] Thus Abigail, bearing the figure of the faithful synagogue, signifies not merely persons of one particular period. At one time she signifies those who began to believe in the Lord while he was present in the flesh; at another, those who, after his ascension, did penance at the apostles’ preaching; at another, those who, from among their number, were able to advance even to the office of preaching; and at another, those who came to the faith after the persecutors of Christ and the Church had been killed, sold, and scattered.

Since all of them learned to have one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father, they are all rightly signified by the same Abigail, a most prudent and beautiful woman whose name is translated “the Father’s exultation.” She signifies, of course, the one whom that same rejoicing Father, seeing her standing at his right hand in gilded clothing—that is, radiant with the glory of works of charity—addresses: “Hear, daughter,” he says, “and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, because the King has desired your beauty” (Psalm XLIV).

But David also took Ahinoam from Jezreel, etc. Ahinoam is interpreted as “the beauty of a brother,” and Jezreel as “the seed of God.” Therefore the Lord chose not only from the synagogue of the Jews those whom he would join to himself in inward love, but, having shown mercy, he also took from the nations a people to be imbued with his sacraments and strengthened by his love.

She is rightly called “the beauty of a brother,” insofar as she delights in seeking the glory of her Redeemer rather than her own. For he deigned to become our brother, either because of the humanity of our nature, like which he assumed, or because “to as many as received him, he gave power to become the sons of God” (John I). Finally, in the Song of Songs, the Lord himself is called the brother of the Church because of their sharing in one and the same nature, and she herself is called his sister. Hence the words: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart” (Song IV).

And she, among the ancient faithful, eagerly awaiting his incarnation, says: “Who will grant you to me as my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you?” (Song VIII)—that is, so that I may deserve to see and address you in human form, you whom, in the invisible nature of your divinity, I have always been accustomed to believe in, love, and worship.

[Col. 0689B] This “beauty of a brother” is most fittingly said to have originated from Jezreel, that is, from the seed of God: from that seed which “went out to sow,” the one who sows (Matthew XIII), namely, from the word of faith. After committing it first to the Jews through himself, the Lord also arranged for it to be preached by his apostles to the nations, so that, according to the Gospel parable, “there might be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

But Saul gave Michal, his daughter, as David’s wife, etc. Phalti means “my savior”; Lais means “a lion,” or “he fears for himself”; Gallim is said to mean “those who migrate.” After the leaders and teachers of the Jews saw that the Gentiles had come to believe in Christ, they withdrew from him the people of the synagogue subject to them. They taught them instead to believe in Antichrist, whom they await as their own kind of savior, destined to come at the end: the son, clearly, of the devil, who was made so that he would fear no one and who “went about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he might devour” (1 Peter V).

He belongs to the number of unclean spirits who once migrated from heaven to Tartarus and who daily do not cease to make their followers migrate from virtues to vices and from bad things to worse.

## CHAPTER V

When the Ziphites betray him, Saul goes down against David. David, going down to his camp by night while everyone is asleep, takes away both the spear and the cup of water, and, awakening him, urges him to acknowledge his error and guilt.

(I Kings XXVI.) And the Ziphites came to Saul at Gabaa, etc., up to the passage that says: “Saul returned to his house.” This reading teaches that Judea, because of the guilt of its faithlessness toward the Lord, lost the kingdom which it ought either to have hoped to receive from him in heaven or to have preserved after receiving it from him on earth. It also teaches that it entirely lost the observance of the legal ceremonies, which, if it had been willing to believe in Christ, could have been transformed into a spiritual understanding and preserved spiritually in its own right. Nevertheless, if it should consent—even late—to conversion and repentance, the heavenly kingdom promised by the Lord will be granted to it.

The Ziphites, whose name is interpreted as “flourishing,” represent the teachers of the Jews, who boast of a flower—and indeed a fragrant one—that is, of the rudiments of legal knowledge, while wholly ignoring the fruit of the righteousness of faith. Saul, whose name means “desired,” prophetically signifies their kingdom, which they asked the Lord to give them. Gabaa, his city, whose name is translated “hill,” reveals the proud elevation of that same kingdom. Achila, which is interpreted as “receiving her,” represents the steadfastness of those who received the faith of Christ in Judea with devout hearts.

[Col. 0690B] Thus, while David dwelt in the desert, the Ziphites came to Saul at Gabaa, saying: “Behold, David is hidden on the hill of Achila, which is opposite the wilderness.” Concerning this it is written below that it was “opposite the wilderness on the road.”

While the Lord was preaching in Judea, hypocritical scribes and Pharisees came to their royal authority, swollen with pride, to arouse it to jealousy, saying that the love of Jesus was hidden in the heart of the crowd which had received his faith, believing him to be Christ the King who had come into the world. The place is rightly said to be “opposite the wilderness on the road.” For the city on whose hill David is hidden lies opposite the wilderness when the company of the righteous, blessed by the presence of Christ, strives to avoid the tumult of earthly desires and to make itself solitary, withdrawn from worldly enticements.

This is the one road to attaining that most perfect solitude of mind: to receive Christ’s coming in the height of that same mind, as upon a hill. He is the one of whom Christ himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

And Saul rose and went down to the desert of Ziph, etc. Understand “Gabaa of Achila” not as Gabaa, Saul’s city, but as the hill of Achila, which is called Gabaa in Hebrew. At the prompting of perverse teachers, the kingdom of the Jews was stirred up to persecute the Lord, having in its army those who would fight against faith, hope, and charity, advancing to battle as though in a threefold battle line of unbelief, despair, and hatred.

With such soldiers armed, the camp of iniquity hastened to pitch itself in the midst of the crowd that had received Christ in its heart, hoping either to destroy him if he could be found bodily or to drive him spiritually from the love of his faithful.

Thus, while David dwelt in the desert, Saul came after him into the desert: once Christ had taken up his dwelling in the hearts of those who strove to abandon the world, persecution immediately appeared. It tested the believers and, by bringing on the struggle, provided an opportunity for earning the palm of victory. This continues to happen today and throughout all the ages of the Church. But let us see what David did when Saul came after him.

And David rose and came to the place where Saul was. While the Jews were persecuting him, the Lord did not abandon the region or withdraw the benefits he had ordained. Rather, he always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where everyone had gathered, and he healed their sick (John X).

And David said to Achimelech the Hittite, etc. While the Lord was preaching in the flesh, many from the Gentiles and many from the Jews flocked to the faith. But he chose the first ministers of his word, by whom he would overthrow and conquer the camp of the persecuting kingdom, from among the Jews who adhered to him with a closer love and likewise through the reception of the sacraments.

Achimelech the Hittite, whose name is interpreted “my brother, the severed king,” represents by nationality the people of the Gentiles, and by his name and faith that same people, severed from the rites of idolatry and joined and united to the kingdom of Christ.

Moreover, Abishai, son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab—that is, “incense of my father,” “son of distress,” “brother of the enemy”—figuratively represents the chosen disciples from the Jews, fervent in the love of Christ, sons of repentance, and brothers by nature of the persecuting people.

David and Abishai therefore came to the people by night, etc. The Lord and his disciples came to visit the people who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death. They found that its entire kingdom, with all its kindred, was being forced down into the depths and lay inert in a blind stupor. All the defenses of virtue with which it ought to have been armed against spiritual enemies had been devoted to earthly desires; and all the teachers and hearers alike were languishing under the same plague of sloth as their rulers.

And Abishai said to David: “God has today shut up your enemy,” etc. The disciples, already endowed with spiritual faith, understood that all things had been delivered by the Father into the hands of the Savior. Yet, still impeded by carnal ignorance, they thought that the proud and contemptuous should be sought out and consumed by fire sent down from heaven.

He immediately recalled them from this intention and determined that patience should rather be exercised, saying: “The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke IX).

What David adds—“For who has stretched out his hand against the Lord’s anointed?” etc.—according to the exposition begun above, shows that no one is free from the crime of sacrilege who attempts to violate the kingdom of the Jewish people, specially given to him by the Lord and consecrated with holy oil, or, having cast away the fear of God, to profane the city and temple dedicated to divine worship.

[Col. 0691D] But according to the suppliant sense of the speaker, it teaches how great a reverence must be shown to the divine sacraments, even when they are administered through the hands of evil men; how great an honor must be given to persons devoted to the service of the sacred altar; and how far every presumption against them, however badly they may live, must be restrained because of the distinction of their rank.

David himself, an exile and innocent, refrained from killing the man who most unjustly persecuted him because of the sole fact that he had received the oil of holy anointing as a figure of Christ, of his name, or of the kingdom, though he would not preserve it. By divine fear he restrained both his soldier by command and himself.

Therefore we must beware lest we presume indiscriminately to tear apart and defame the reputation of bishops, priests, and deacons.

[Col. 0692A] Now therefore take the spear that is at his head, etc. The spear signifies either the power of the kingdom itself or the weapons of spiritual virtues by which the kingdom could have been strengthened. It may also be understood of the earthly kingdom they possessed and of the heavenly kingdom they hoped for—at least by those among them who knew how to hope for it. Both, it is clear, were deservedly taken away from the faithless.

The cup of water signifies the observance of carnal types. In comparison with evangelical perfection, this is like a cup of water compared with a cup of wine, and it is not inappropriately understood in this way. Hence above Nabal refused to give David the water he requested. Abigail, however, gave him wine, because the people of unbelievers refused to ascribe even the letter of the Law to Christ, whereas every faithful person recognizes that everything must be referred to him and that these things boil over with spiritual savor.

Thus Saul’s spear and cup of water are taken away when, because of their guilt of faithlessness, the entire kingdom and the literal observance of the Law are removed from the Jews. This is done through Abishai at David’s command, when, at the Lord’s command, each of the apostles, preaching the rights of the Gospel, teaches that all ancient things are passing away.

When David added, after the spear and cup had been taken, “And let us go,” he signified that Christ would depart from the Jews and pass over with his preachers to save the Gentiles. As he himself, when he was about to come to his Passion, announced in nearly the same words: “Rise, let us go from here.”

And there was no one who saw or understood, etc. There was no one among the reprobate who, while the Lord or his apostles preached the future desolation of Judea and the erasure of its ancient state from the earth, understood either its past crimes or its future condemnation and awoke to repentance. Rather, they persisted entirely in ungodliness, because the Lord, in accordance with the merits they had previously incurred, blinded their understanding.

Alternatively, the sleep of the Lord fell upon them—that is, a sleep heavier than usual, which the Lord inflicted upon them specifically because of David’s arrival, not allowing them to awaken until he himself had returned and departed.

And when David had crossed over to the opposite side, etc. When Jesus had passed from this world to the Father and remained undisturbed in the height of his Father’s kingdom, far removed from the sight of mortals, there was indeed a great distance between him—the immortal victor over death, God in the flesh, seated at the right hand of the Father—and those mortals who, wretched and impious in this world, strove to fight against him.

[Col. 0692D] Through his apostles he cried out by preaching to the people of Israel and to their teachers of the Law, compelling them to rise from the sleep of their harmful torpor and to answer him by believing in him.

Abner, whose name is interpreted as “the Father’s lamp,” represents those who at that time ought to have supplied the people with the light of truth. His father Ner, whose name is translated “lamp,” figuratively represents the teachers who preceded them in kindling the light of legal knowledge spiritually and making it known to them and to the people.

And Abner answered and said: “Who are you, who cry out?” etc. The Pharisees and scribes replied that they did not know the disciples of Jesus who were crying out as they taught the people and disturbing the kingdom of the Jews, as though it were guilty of Christ’s blood. “Do you wish,” they said, “to bring upon us the blood of this man?”

And David said to Abner: “Are you not a man?” etc. The apostles say: Are you not scribes learned in the Law, chief priests, and Pharisees, surpassing the people alike in rank and knowledge? Why did you not preserve the rule of your people intact by maintaining vigilance in perfect works and teaching?

For one of the crowd entered in order to kill the king, your lord. According to the literal sense, this is said of Abishai, who entered the camp with the intention of killing the king if he could in any way do so [Note: Perhaps it should be read: “so that, if he could in any way, he might kill the king.” Editor.]. According to the allegory, it is understood of the apostles, who diligently proclaimed the future destruction of the wicked kingdom on account of its sins.

[Col. 0693B] Now therefore see where the king’s spear is, etc. “See now,” they say, “where the scepter of your rule is—both the one you have lost on earth and the one you have ceased to hope for in heaven. Where is the shadowy observance of the Law, for which you thirsted with all your heart, in which you boasted that the hands of your actions could be washed clean from every stain of sin?”

All these things alike have gone, because you lost Christ; the temple itself also has departed. Although none of these things had yet been completed in the time of the apostles, anyone who reads the history of earlier times will find that they had begun to a very great extent both before the apostles’ time and while the apostles were still alive.

Herod the Great and his sons, among the countless calamities they inflicted upon the Jews, also stripped the priests of the sacred vestment and never again granted them permission to minister in it. Having abolished the legal order, they changed the succession of the high priesthood according to their own will.

Pilate polluted the temple by secretly introducing images of Caesar during the night, following the impiety of Herod, who had previously profaned it by setting up a golden eagle there and ordered the young men who attempted to remove it for religious reasons to be burned in the flames.

Gaius ordered the temple itself and all their synagogues to be profaned with sacrifices to the Gentiles and filled with statues and images, and he commanded that he himself be worshiped there as God.

These matters concern religion. As for the deterioration of the kingdom until it perished completely, there is no end to what could be said.

Saul recognized David’s voice, etc. Once Saul recognized David’s voice and was moved by his humility, innocence, and justice, he confessed that he had sinned and promised that he would not sin against him again; he ordered him to return.

Many among the leaders of the Jews, having recognized the voice of Christ through the apostles’ exhortation, confessed in repentance that they had sinned and implored him, with many tears and great prayers, to return by the grace of forgiveness to their hearts, which he had abandoned because of their faithlessness.

“If the Lord stirs you up against me,” etc. “If,” he says, “you persecute me under the guidance of God’s Spirit, I must appease the divine mercy with sacrifices and prayers. But if, not by the Lord’s command, but deceived and corrupted by the wicked persuasion of men against his will, you have thought that you should rage for a time against an innocent man, it is certain that those who by evil counsels drive me away from his tabernacle and from the holy land and compel me to live among idolaters, whom I especially detest, are held worthy of a curse in the divine judgment.

“And if, as I have said, this fire of persecution has arisen from men, it is altogether just that my blood should not be poured out by the ungodly, since the hands of my persecutors have continued until now unjustly to seek it.”

According to the mystical understanding, this is the voice of the members of Christ, that is, of his faithful, who, afflicted by the persecution of the wicked, habitually examine their hearts carefully.

If they recognize that, on account of their sins, the Lord has imposed upon them through such people the punishment of correction, they immediately strive to cleanse themselves of it by the sacrifices of due compunction. But if they see that they are suffering unjust injuries or deaths at the hands of the wicked in order to be called away from the way of truth, they understand that those who do such things will be punished by the Lord with an eternal curse, because they have wished to turn Christ’s faithful away from the inheritance of the Catholic faith toward the idolatry of the Gentiles or any kind of heresy.

But those who suffer these things innocently rejoice that the Lord will save them from every death and corruption, and indeed that they will receive the palm of their patience.

We may also understand it as spoken by the apostles to their Jewish persecutors: If the Lord stirs you up to persecute us, let his anger be appeased by our prayers. But if—as is more true—the sons of men have done this, cursed before the Lord are those who drove us out while we preached divine things, so that we would not live in Judea and Jerusalem. They said: “Depart,” and, because you believe Jesus to be God, “serve him instead among the Gentiles, who are accustomed to worship foreign gods.”

And Saul said: “I have sinned,” etc. David had proposed two causes for his exile and asked Saul which one was true. Saul, conscious of his own mind, replied that he had persecuted him not at the Lord’s prompting but at the command of his own folly. Now, however, he begged him to return home, promising that he would suffer no further harm from him.

Many of the Jews likewise, after confessing their crimes, took care to call back by faith the Lord whom they had driven away through unbelief.

And David answered and said: “Behold, let the king’s spear pass over; let one of the servants come,” etc. The Lord, answering through his teachers to the Jews who were repenting and turning away from the crime of persecution, says: “Behold, the power of your kingdom is with me. Let the unity of the faithful pass into the unbelieving hearts of the proud, and let it quickly carry back the spiritual weapons of the heavenly kingdom once promised to you.”

This was fulfilled to no small extent in the time of the apostles, and it remains to be fulfilled more fully in the times of Elijah, who preaches and turns the hearts of the fathers toward their sons.

He is silent about taking away the cup of water, because the Lord does not teach that the shadow of the Law should be observed any longer.

The title of Psalm LIII recalls the betrayal of the Ziphites, although it seems to refer more to the earlier betrayal, since there the title says: “Is not David hidden among us?” Here, however, it says differently: “Behold, David is hidden on the hill of Achila.”

## CHAPTER VI

David comes to Achish with his six hundred men and, after receiving a dwelling at Ziklag, devastates the neighboring inhabitants of the wilderness.

[Col. 0695A]

(I Kings XXVII.) And David said in his heart: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands,” etc., up to what Achish says about David: “He has done many evil things against his people Israel,” etc.

This reading signifies the present state of the Church, which, after the long struggles of the martyrs, now enjoys as much peace among the nations as can exist continually among human beings.

David said in his heart: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands. Is it not better that I flee and be saved in the land of the Philistines?” and so forth.

The Lord said in his wisdom, in which he makes and orders all things: Behold, the Jews persecute the Church of the saints, that is, my members. Once their rage for violence has been kindled, they never know how to lessen it. Therefore, lest they overturn her state by a sudden assault and remove her from the midst, it is better that, always guided by me, she withdraw to save the Gentiles. When those nations have been converted to her faith and love in such numbers, let the Jews despair that they can erase her steadfastness. Let them also cease to persecute with threats and murders in Judea the one whom they will see shining with heavenly grace among the Gentiles.

And David rose and departed, he himself, etc. The Lord leaves the dwelling that he once habitually possessed in the hearts of the Jews and goes to acquire the Gentiles for his faith, he himself and the ministers of his word. These are marked by the number six hundred, that is, presently intent upon perfect works and suspended in mind by an unwavering hope of heavenly things to come.

And David dwelt with Achish in Geth, etc. Geth, which is translated “winepress,” signifies the pressures and tribulations by which the faith of the Church is tested in this life. The Psalms entitled “For the winepresses” also declare this.

Achish, whose name means “brother of a man,” signifies the people of the Gentiles, who, by believing in Christ, rejoice to be his brother through grace and to act manfully.

His father Maoch, whose name is translated “emasculated,” that is, deprived of manly action, mind, and strength, represents the Gentiles of earlier times, who, serving idols, remained empty both of virtuous work and of its reward.

[Col. 0695D] Thus the Lord first dwelt among the Gentiles amid the greatest persecutions and pressures, until they themselves learned to receive his faith. This means both the Lord and his apostles, and every pastor with the Church entrusted to him, which he governs and instructs [Note: Perhaps “instructed” should be read]. Christ himself is the one shepherd of two kinds of sheep: those whom he brought from the Gentiles and those whom, scattered among the nations on the day of darkness and cloud, he does not cease to preserve and feed among the Gentiles.

David’s two wives may also be understood as the chaste souls of the faithful who adhere to Christ while living in the two forms of life, namely the active and the contemplative.

Ahinoam the Jezreelite—that is, “the beauty of my brother,” deriving her origin from the seed of God—may signify the soul whose eyes, enlightened in mind, burn with all their strength to see the King in his beauty.

[Col. 0696A] Abigail, however—that is, “the exultation of my father,” the wife of Nabal of Carmel, that is, of “the fool” or “the soft”—may signify the soul over whom the Father in heaven rejoices with the angels, just as he rejoices over the one recently saved by repentance from the flatteries of a foolish teacher, more than over the ninety-nine righteous who do not need repentance.

And Saul did not continue to seek him any longer. This signifies the present time of the Church, when the Jews, although they do not cease to hate her, have nevertheless entirely lost all hope and intention of overcoming her, seeing her glorified among the Gentiles and protected even by the favor of secular kings.

And David said to Achish: “If I have found favor in your eyes,” etc. The Lord said through his disciples to the people of the Gentiles: If the doctrine of truth that I preach and the life that I promise please you, let a humble heart of hearers be given to my words within the firm unity of the faithful, where I may dwell through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore Achish gave him Ziklag on that day, etc. Ziklag is interpreted as “the purification of the utterance that has been brought near.” To purify an utterance means, with attentive discernment, to inquire of a word brought all the way to oneself which speech gives off the scent of truth and which of deceit.

Thus the believers from the Gentiles, in order to dedicate their dwelling to Christ—which is understood as the Church—gave him companies of souls that knew how to distinguish rationally the voices of preachers when they came to them and to separate the purity of the apostolic voice from the dregs of philosophical or pagan speech.

For this reason the assemblies of such Gentile souls, rescued from pagan rites, were made permanently subject to the authority of the apostles.

If I am not mistaken, the history of Josephus’ Antiquities also supports this interpretation (Book XVI, chapter 13), where it says: “The king gave him a certain village called Ziklag. He loved that village so much that, when David had become king, he himself and his servants honored it as their own possession.”

And the number of days that David dwelt in the region of the Philistines was, etc. There was, is, and will be a period of Christ’s dwelling in the Church of the Gentiles until he floods the four regions of the world with the full light of his heavenly grace, until he pours into the believing hearts of the Gentiles the lightning of the Gospel, which is contained in the harmonious diversity of four books.

Notice that when David came to the Philistines, he began to dwell in Geth; but soon, with Achish’s permission, he turned aside to Ziklag. For when Christ came to the Gentiles in his disciples, he was first trodden in the winepress of pressures by unbelievers. At last, after many grapes of the martyrs had been pressed, he approached those who were to be instructed in discerning the various meanings of intellectual vintners—that is, of teachers—amid the dregs and wine.

And David and his men went up, etc. Sur means “rock”; Egypt sounds like “darkness.” Thus, through the efforts of Christ’s disciples, the Church advanced and rescued souls from pagan rites. These souls had clung to earthly desires, following the examples not of the new but of the old man. All went toward hardness of heart and arrived at a land of darkness covered by the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness where the shadow of death, no order, and everlasting horror dwell.

And David struck the whole land, etc. The Lord strikes with the sword of his word whatever he finds low and earthly in unbelievers. He does not permit any of those who truly receive the faith to live any longer, either in spirit or in flesh, according to their former way of life. Rather, he makes them all say with the Apostle in a true confession: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians II).

And taking sheep and oxen, etc. Christ hastens to gather for himself from the Gentiles souls of diverse ways of life and to unite them all into the unity of the Church that preceded in him.

And Achish said to him: “Against whom have you made your raid today?” etc. Although, literally, he appears to be deceiving him—when, rising against the Palestinians and devastating their nearby province, he said to their king, who was stirring himself up, that he had attacked his own people—the figure of the speech is nevertheless not false. For while Christ draws the Gentiles to the faith, he attacks the Jews’ open and fervent blasphemy.

By his just judgment, “a partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans XI). Therefore, while he brings in the Gentiles, he attacks Judea. He broke off not a few branches of the good olive because of their pride, so that, grafting in the wild olive, he might make it share in the root and richness of the good olive.

He is rightly said to make a raid, because: “Whoever falls upon this stone,” he says, “will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Luke XX).

David did not keep alive either man or woman, etc. Christ forbids those who are converted to him to live for sins. Thus, showing this first to the teacher of his Church, he commands the crowds of unclean hearts, saying: “Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts X). Paul teaches that they are dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus (Ephesians II).

Yet he does not command believers in this age to undergo martyrdoms and deaths for his name at the hands of the ungodly.

Saying: “Lest they perhaps speak,” etc. For this reason he did not keep them alive, lest they speak against him. A hearer gives testimony against his teacher when he proves, by either his actions or his thoughts, that he has been less perfectly instructed in believing or doing and less thoroughly put to death with respect to wicked conduct.

Therefore Achish believed David, etc. The entire brotherhood of the Gentiles believes in Christ, saying that he abandoned the people among whom he was born because of their unbelief. Because of their unbelief, he cast down so many branches of the good olive, so that it might itself be grafted in by believing, and committed them to the fire to be burned.

Now that I believe, hope, and love, he will be my debtor for eternal life, so that, without whom I can do nothing, he may provide me in the present with the pledge of the Spirit and in the future with the everlasting grace of his protection.

Concerning this perpetual service provided by God the Lord to his faithful servants, the Lord himself says: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, minister to them” (Luke XII).

## CHAPTER VII

When the Philistines have gathered against him, Saul seeks through the witch at Endor the oracle of Samuel, who has been raised, and learns what adversities are about to come upon him and his people.

[Col. 0698A]

(I Kings XXVIII.) It happened in those days, etc., up to the passage that says: “When they had eaten,” etc.

This reading signifies that the Jews, because the entire ministry of prophecy had been fulfilled in Christ and the faith of the Gentiles had been confirmed and spiritually raised up against the faithlessness alike of the Jews and the heretics, would no longer frequent the Church of the Lord to be saved, but would frequent the synagogue of Satan in order to perish. They would hope for and believe not in the dispensation of Christ come in the flesh, but in the future kingdom of Antichrist.

First, it must be noted that the same things or persons do not always retain the same significance. Sometimes evil things can be represented through good persons, and good things through evil persons.

The Philistines, who are accustomed to be placed almost always in an evil sense, here signify believers from the Gentiles because they have David with them. Conversely, Israel, the people of God, because it had driven him away by persecuting him, figuratively announces either the faithlessness of the Jews in the present age or the wickedness of the heretics.

And conversely, Israel prepares for battle against the Philistines when, with councils of teachers assembled, believers from the Gentiles propose to overcome either the cunning of the heretics or the faithlessness of the Jews, so that they may either be corrected entirely or be less able to prevail in argument against the good.

If this seems absurd to anyone—that unbelieving Philistines should represent the faithful—and if he thinks they represent only the type of the Gentiles, let him know that the Gentiles themselves, worshipers of many gods, commonly fight against both Jews and heretics, since the Jews glory in the worship of the one true God and the heretics in the name of Christ.

Nevertheless, he should understand with complete certainty that Achish, whose name is interpreted “brother of a man,” who kindly receives David in exile, gives him a place to dwell, and trusts so greatly in his strength and friendship that he asks him to go out with him to battle, signifies believers from the Gentiles.

Thus the passage continues:

And Achish said to David: “Know now and know certainly,” etc. This openly represents Catholics who, when they propose to overcome error by rebuking, reasoning, or recalling the words of Scripture, say to the Lord: “God, you know our foolishness and weakness” (Psalm LXVIII). For without you we can do nothing. Give us assistance while we fight; let your saints provide us with the help of their intercession; and let all those who, with you as their author, composed the holy Scriptures supply us with the secrets of spiritual knowledge by which we may overcome the carnal.

David said to Achish: “Now you shall know,” etc. Literally, it is clear that, while David promises the king assistance, the king in turn promises that he will make David guardian of his own head, whether in the struggle of battle or after victory. But according to the spiritual meaning, Christ is the head of strong and manfully acting brothers. To him, when he says, “And behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. [Col. 0699A] 28), they reply: “And we have learned that we are to have no guardian of the grace by which you govern us, through which you remain in us, other than you yourself—not only throughout all the days of this age, but also in the age to come, where one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83).

Now Samuel had died, etc. Josephus reports that this occurred two years before Saul’s death, writing as follows (*Antiquities* VI.14): “Saul therefore reigned eighteen years while Samuel was alive, and two more after his death.” Above, in the historical sequence, Samuel’s death and burial are described in almost the same words. Here, however, the account is recapitulated so that readers may be reminded of the urgent necessity that led Saul to seek a woman possessing a pythonic spirit. Mystically, Samuel’s death signifies the cessation, after the Lord’s Passion, of the legal figures, and likewise of the prophets who foretold his future incarnation. Israel’s mourning declares that carnal people could not be torn away from the ancient institutions of the Lord without exceedingly great grief. I believe that all Israel who were able to see the desolation of the temple of Jerusalem and of the Promised Land—for these too had been given to the fathers as figures of heavenly grace—were utterly unable to restrain their mourning and tears.

The burial that followed death and mourning signifies the time when the faithful Jews ceased entirely from observing the shadows of the Law. For it is well known that the primitive Church remained Judaizing for a considerable time, until, as evangelical teaching gradually prevailed, it too restrained itself completely from legal observance. And Samuel is rightly buried in his own city, Ramah, where he was born and whose name means “lofty”: for that same Church of Christ, which once poured forth the beginnings of nascent prophecy, enclosed the completed figures of prophecy—like the dead limbs of Samuel—with reverent honor.

And Saul removed all the magicians, etc. The magicians and diviners—the first of whom are commonly called sorcerers, use blood and sacrifices, and often touch the bodies of the dead, while the latter (whom other translations call “enchanters”) accomplish their work by words—mystically signify all the prophets of the Gentiles and their idolatries. At this time the Jewish people removed these completely from their midst, although it has a taste for earthly things more than for heavenly ones. For now no one dares to worship Baalim, Astaroth, or any other monsters of the Gentiles, although neither does anyone submit to the Lord with perfect faith.

And the Philistines assembled, etc. In this passage the Philistines, insofar as they desire the assistance of David and his men, signify the faithful from the Gentiles; but insofar as they despise and reject them, they signify the unbelievers who resist Christ. For both groups—the unbelieving Jews and the badly believing heretics—are opposed by both Catholic Christians and pagans. Hence the Philistines are rightly said to have encamped at Shunem, whose name means “scarlet.” Scarlet has the appearance of fire. Both the faithful, burning with love for Christ, and the pagans, raging with the fire of persecution, do not hesitate to attack their respective adversaries.

The good and the wicked fight among themselves; the wicked and the wicked fight among themselves; but the good and the good can in no way fight among themselves. Israel, however, because it assembled for battle under Saul, who was about to die and was impious, and not under David, who was just and about to reign, signifies either, as was said above, the present blindness of that same people, or heretical perversity. Therefore it is rightly described as having assembled at the mountain because of the proud destruction of its faith—for this is what the name Gilboa signifies—and as having fallen there.

And Saul said to his servants: “Seek for me a woman who has a pythonic spirit,” etc. Since the Lord had denied him an answer, Saul sought a woman who possessed an unclean spirit, through whom he might inquire. And when, after the Lord’s Passion, the figures of the ancient prophets and ceremonies had ceased, the Jewish people consults and frequents the synagogue of Satan—such as their synagogue is today—which possesses a pythonic spirit; in their language, this means “the mouth of the abyss.” Nor can its entrance be understood in any better way than as an entrance into everlasting punishments. The familiar name itself also corresponds to the meaning of the faithless faction. For it is said to have been derived from Apollo Pythius, who was an assiduous practitioner of these arts; he himself is also said to have borrowed this sort of name from the fact that he struck down the serpent Python in vengeance for his son killed by it.

And his servants said to her, etc. The pythoness—whom some call a ventriloquist—is rightly said to have lived at Endor, that is, “at the spring” or “eye of generation,” so that the very place of her dwelling might also bear witness against the already ruined Synagogue. Deceived by a serpentine conversation, it falsely claims to give its hearers the light and cup of wisdom.

Therefore he changed his appearance, etc. The Jewish people, having changed for the worse the appearance of its earthly kingdom, or of its faith and works—by which it ought spiritually both to have been adorned and loved—came to hear such a synagogue, signified by the pythoness, in the blindness of an obscured heart, together with those who, transgressing the unity of right faith or charity, had never learned to attain knowledge of the Holy Trinity. For one who knows how to understand rightly the innumerable passages of Scripture of this kind also knows that the dual number is sometimes used in an evil sense: why, at the creation of the world, the work of the second day alone did not merit the blessing of divine approval, and why unclean animals entered the ark in this number, along with countless other examples.

And the woman said to him: “Whom shall I raise up for you?” etc. The Jewish people, having entered its synagogue, desires that the prophecies once recapitulated and fulfilled in Christ be raised up for it, as though from the dead, by acting so as once again to serve sacrifices, the Sabbath, new moons, leprosy in houses and garments, and the other literal shadows.

And the woman said to Saul, etc. Seeing one, she calls him in the plural, following the very common usage of Scripture, by which many are often designated in the singular and individuals in the plural. Thus, after making one calf, the people said: “These are your gods, Israel” (Exod. 32). Nor was it one frog or one fly that was sent upon the wicked, yet it is said: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. 77); and there are countless other examples of this kind.

And Samuel said to Saul: “Why have you disturbed me?” etc. The books of the Old Testament, themselves full of the grace of prophecy, openly testify to readers that after the Lord’s Passion they ought not to be raised again for the figurative observance of the letter. Rather, the ministers of prophecy themselves are disturbed when they see that what they wrote is understood differently from what they themselves intended.

And Saul said: “I am greatly distressed,” etc. The Jews, abandoned by God, not deemed worthy to possess the gift of prophecy, and attacked by all the nations, follow beneath the blind night what may be called the dead shadow of the Law and the prophets. Beset by these troubles, they think that this shadow should be consulted concerning what they ought to do. But the very legal ceremonies, now celebrated uselessly and in hidden places, signify the same thing that they once displayed publicly at God’s command and with his gracious acceptance: namely, that the old things would pass away, that all things would be made new, and that the kingdom of the Jews would be utterly destroyed while that of the Christians would be extended throughout the whole world. Samuel, dead but raised by impious art, foretold this in every respect concerning the change of kingdoms, just as when he was alive he had previously foretold it.

If anyone is troubled by the question of how the woman could, by demonic art, disturb and raise up a prophet after his death, let him know with certainty either that the devil then showed those who were seeking it a false shadow, or, if Samuel truly appeared, that the devil was permitted to do these things only to the extent that the Lord allowed. Nor is it surprising that such things should be permitted to the evil spirit for certain more hidden reasons, since he even placed the Savior on the pinnacle of the temple, and asked for and received Job to be tested.

But if we believe that what appeared was rather a phantasm of the unclean spirit, this too ought not to trouble us: how could such a spirit have spoken true and prophetic things? For we know that the devil can often foresee or proclaim many future events that he has learned from holy angels. Yet the less should one listen to his words, since everything he says or does among human beings he does with the aim of deceiving them.

As for what was said among the rest:

“Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me”—whether Samuel said this or an evil spirit—it is best understood as meaning “without the body,” that is, in the other life. For wicked Saul could not have been received there after death where the good Jonathan could be received; rather, a great chasm has been fixed between them. One was received with Samuel in Abraham’s bosom, while the other was buried with the devil in the flame of hell. Both, however, were taken away from the conduct of this life, which the devil had always lacked.

Nor does anything prevent us from understanding that, if we believe these words and appearances to have been produced fantastically by the devil, the evil one wished to mingle deceit among the truths he spoke. By saying under Samuel’s name to the impious man, “You and your sons shall be with me,” he secretly persuaded sinners that, once even their greater sins had been lulled to rest and dismissed after death, they too could then live in blessedness with those who had lived well before death.

And immediately Saul fell stretched out upon the ground, etc. The Jewish people, reading the words of the prophets and celebrating sacrifices that are ineffective, does indeed suffer terror in its misery; but it does not possess the strength of faith by which it might be blessed, because, while the grace of evangelical preaching has shone throughout the world for so long, it has not learned to eat the living bread that came down from heaven.

Then that woman entered to Saul, etc. And that faithless people, now oppressed by such great calamities among the nations, is troubled on every side, so that it takes no pleasure even in perceiving through reading or hearing the words of sacred reading—which it nevertheless apprehends amid the darkness of ignorance—although its own synagogue compels it to do so.

[Col. 0702B] Now that woman had a pasture-fed calf in the house, etc. The very tender and excellent calf, and the cakes of fine flour that Abraham and Sarah prepared to refresh the Lord beneath the burning midday sun (Gen. 18), signify faith in the Lord’s incarnation and the perfection of devoted humility. With these, the holy Church, burning with the light of love and wisdom together with its spiritual teachers, shows that it seeks to appease the Lord.

By contrast, this fattened calf and the flour that the demonic woman baked for Saul, who was about to die, and his servants in the dead of night, and set before them to eat, express the birth and kingdom of Antichrist and the contrition of heart of those who serve him with foolish humility. The synagogue of Satan, wrapped in the darkness of impiety, suggests to its miserable hearers—condemned to eternal death—that these things are to be believed and hoped for, refreshing them as though with sweet banquets from the fear of the surrounding troubles. Having been fed with this food, their hearts advance toward worse things, and they go about in darkness, beneath the single night, through the shadow.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Philistines, about to fight against Israel, order David to return from the camp and go home

*(I Reg. 29.)* Then all the forces of the Philistines were gathered at Aphek, etc., up to the statement: “But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.” This reading, in which the princes of the Philistines expel David from their camp, signifies that time of which the Lord says: “And because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24).

The forces of the Philistines therefore gather at Aphek, which means “new fury.” The faithlessness of the nations rages against the Jews; it rages against the heretics. In this passage Israel signifies both groups, and the enemy never ceases to increase its ancient attacks against them with ever-new ambushes: against the former, because they proclaim one God alone; against the latter, because they proclaim Christ; against both, because they mock idols, engaging them in savage conflicts.

But Israel also encamped above the spring, etc. The spring that was in Jezreel—that is, in “the seed of God”—signifies the baptismal washing by which the children of the Church are regenerated through the grace of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, you understand unbelieving Jews or heretics worse than unbelievers to be represented by the name Israel, both set up faithless camps above the spring of renewing grace: the one by despising it through pride, the other by violating it through heresy.

And the satraps of the Philistines advanced by hundreds, etc. Understand the rearmost group either according to the merit of humility or according to the order of time. For while the nations of the Gentiles, throughout the whole age of the world from the time that that people was established, stand in battle formation against the Jews and strive to defeat them by hand or by word—and while they likewise rage against the heretics, because the heretics are a portion of the Church, with a similar mind through envy of Christ’s name—the Lord is present in his elect, humble and despised by worldly people. For “the children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16).

He also, when he became incarnate in his own time and in the fullness of time, appeared humble to the world, displaying outwardly to his followers examples of humility, rejection, and poverty. Yet inwardly he taught them how mighty he is in overthrowing the proud and how desirable in blessing the submissive.

And the princes of the Philistines said: “What do these Hebrews want?” The pagans despise the life, fellowship, and teaching of the faithful of Christ, who are rightly called Hebrews—that is, “those who cross over”—because they know that they must now cross from vices to virtues, hope in the future for a passage from death to life, and transcend the lowest desires of the flesh, together with all the adversities of the world, by the heights of an uplifted mind.

And Achish said to the princes of the Philistines, etc. Achish praises David’s friendship, but the angry princes of the Philistines avoid having him as a companion in battle, fearing his valor as the fame of his fighting spreads. Accordingly, among other things they say:

“Is this not David?” etc. While the Church of the nations praises the faith of Christ, through which eternal life may be deserved, the angry philosophers and priests of idols fear to believe in him. They grieve that by his word their worship and wisdom alike have been destroyed. They see his triumph over the ancient enemy to be such as no one else could merit, and see it celebrated in the unanimous choir of the holy Church; yet they shrink from being joined to his members, from being subjected to his rule, and from receiving faith in him.

And Achish called David and said to him, etc. Achish himself confesses David to be upright, innocent, and good, “like an angel of God”; yet, so as not to offend the eyes of the satraps of the Philistines, he orders him to withdraw from the battle and remain at peace amid their anger.

The multitude of the faithful from the Gentiles praises, loves, and proclaims the justice, mercy, and holiness of Christ, as one sent by God for the salvation of the nations. But it begs that the Word not be entrusted to the blasphemous and proud leaders of idolatry, lest, hearing without believing, they incur a greater judgment. It is as though it exhorts the Lord to be content to rest in the calm and serene heart of believers rather than, by being preached to those who will not believe, provide an occasion for the scandals of persecution to arise.

“I know that you are good in my eyes,” etc. And the Church, outstanding in the praises of the Lord, makes this prayer also:

“I know indeed, and with the open eyes of faith I understand, the goodness of your heavenly grace, and that you yourself are he of whom the prophet foretold: ‘And his name shall be called the angel of great counsel’ (Isa. 9), that is, the messenger of the Father’s will. But the princes of pagan doctrines and cults, having rejected the help of your protection, trust that they ought to be saved by their own strength and ingenuity.”

But the Philistines had gone up to Jezreel. When David departed with his men, the Philistines went up to fight at Jezreel—that is, at “the seed of God”—where they had previously assembled while he remained with them at Aphek, that is, “in new fury.”

Often, too, after driving the stronger teachers of the Church away from their vicinity, the reprobate exert all their strength to corrupt the more vulnerable. Out of reverence or fear for their superiors, they had previously not dared to touch or disturb these people, although raging in their minds. Moreover, not only those who bear weapons in combat or arguments in debate against the good, but also those who display examples of wickedness under the name of brothers before the eyes of the pious, try to infect Jezreel—that is, the seed of God—with the tares of this diabolical seed.

We see and hear the mysteries of this reading fulfilled in countless places even today by those who drive the Lord from their hearts and oppress his elect. But as the end of the world approaches, and the heaps of evil increase, we fear with trembling expectation that these things will be fulfilled more and more.

## CHAPTER IX. With an Egyptian boy as guide, David defeats the Amalekites who had struck Siceleg, recovers the spoil, and distributes gifts to his friends

[Col. 0704C]

*(I Reg. 30.)* When David and his men had come to Siceleg, etc., up to the statement: “David sent some of the spoil to those who were in those places where David himself and his men had stayed.” This reading figuratively shows that those seduced by heretics can easily be restored to the faith by the grace of Christ through teachers of truth, so long as they have not lost the love of unity; and that all alike—whether the teachers themselves or the simpler people content with their own salvation—will be rewarded with the one and same denarius of eternal life. It also shows that the heresiarchs themselves are partly to be corrected by the Lord and partly to be punished with everlasting retribution.

Amalek means “the people of the locust” or “the people who lick.” The Amalekites make an attack from the south against Siceleg when heretics, who customarily seduce the hearts of the innocent through flattering speeches and blessings, and maliciously gnaw away all the fruits of spiritual knowledge with their tongue, set ambushes for the simple from the very words of sacred Scripture that holy men, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke and composed.

And they struck Siceleg, etc. Siceleg means “the purification of the brought-forth word.” Those strike and burn it who confuse the discernment of the preaching they have heard by the battering ram of their arguments and cast down the tranquility of ecclesiastical faith by the malignant fire of their error. The fire with which the proud king burned the books of the prophet Jeremiah was very much like this fire. By contrast, there is the fire that the Lord sent upon the earth and desired to be kindled intensely.

And they had killed no one, etc. Heretics take captive but do not kill. Although they can rob the less instructed of the simplicity of faith, they nevertheless cannot take away the fervor of charity, which is the life of the virtues.

And when David and his men came to the city, etc. When the Lord comes in his elect and in Catholic teachers, and sees the towers and roofs of the Church, once resplendent, leveled to the ground by heretical teaching, he first—as is fitting—implores the Father with tears and prayers for its restoration, and then immediately sets about its restoration.

The teachers mourn the Churches entrusted to them and the souls whom they had begotten and nourished for God, but who, while Christ’s help was delayed for a time, had been corrupted from the simplicity of faith. This is signified by the delay of David’s arrival, while the wives and children of his men were carried away captive. If his grace, which brings help, had been present, they could not have been corrupted at all.

Indeed, David’s two wives had also been taken captive, etc. It has already been said above that David’s two wives signify the two forms of life of the holy Church, by which it rejoices to serve the true king in the present: namely, the active and the contemplative life.

But such a storm has often enveloped the Church through heretics among the nations—as was especially clear in the great Arian uprising—that not only does the beauty of the contemplative life, which, in accordance with the name Jezreel, God himself, the author of graces, sowed in the hearts of the quiet and humble in spirit, appear to perish, but also the steadfastness of the active life, which is usually exercised more by those who have recently escaped the hands of the ancient enemy, when the persecutor’s rage drives it away.

And Abiathar brought the ephod to David, etc. Whatever the saints do under the inspiration of the Lord, Scripture’s manner is to say that he himself does it, because he helps them to do it. Thus it is also said of the Holy Spirit, whose power and operation are one with those of the Father and the Son: “For he himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings,” because he makes those whom he has filled groan and plead with the Lord for their salvation.

David therefore, after the priestly robe had been brought to him, consults the Lord about whether he should pursue the raiders. So the pastors of the Church, inwardly taught by the grace of their author, seek the counsel of heavenly will through reading sacred Scripture—the garment with which teachers ought always to be clothed in their ministry of the word—in order to learn how they should act toward those who are in error.

The Lord answers that the raiders are to be pursued by David and that, once they have been captured, their spoil is to be recovered. In the same reading he teaches that the heretics are to be pursued by the teachers and masters of the Church through debate, captured by overcoming them, and stripped of their spoil by restoring to the Church the souls whom they had previously seduced by their fraud.

So David himself went, and the six hundred men who were with him, etc. The torrent Besor, whose name means “announcement,” or “flesh,” signifies either the carnal sense of heretics, exceedingly difficult to correct, or the overflowing abundance of secular eloquence, likewise rushing in a violent stream and not easily crossed except by teachers of the greatest perfection.

Our desirable king, therefore, truly mighty in hand, went to fight the obstinacy of those in error with the word of truth. He was accompanied by his elect, proven both by the integrity of their works and by the certainty of their hope. This is clearly indicated by the number six, with which the Lord completed his works, and by the number one hundred, which in counting first reaches the right hand of the little finger.

Indeed, in the hundredth psalm the crisis of the final judgment is openly described, in which the hope of all who hope rightly burns. After mercy and judgment have been sung, the faithful of the earth and those who walk in the blameless way are to be brought through mercy to the seat of perpetual blessedness and to the service of their Redeemer. But all the sinners of the earth are to be slain in the morning by just judgment, when their deeds—previously hidden for a long time—are revealed, and are remembered as being destroyed from the city of heavenly peace.

As the saints accompany the Lord on the way of truth, when they come to the point of debating and refuting heretics, some men who are often otherwise great—though not wearied in the purity of their belief, yet exhausted in their skill of speaking—remain behind. For not all who know how to believe rightly also know how to defeat by reasoning those who hold opinions contrary to right faith.

Their carnal sense, which is unable to grasp spiritual things, or their impulse to proclaim the carnal things they feel, often obstructs them like a torrent of announcement or flesh. Those who are less skilled do not know how to cross it, break through it, and scatter it by the power of their discernment, like Elijah or Elisha. This was especially evident at the Council of Nicaea. Although so many and such great teachers had been gathered from throughout the world, at first scarcely anyone could be found—apart from Athanasius, deacon of the Church of Alexandria—who knew how to engage Arius and immediately detect, expose, and defeat his evasions and frauds.

There a certain pagan philosopher, heavily armed with many Aristotelian arguments, repeatedly challenged the Christians. He could not be overcome at all by any of the teachers, even those distinguished in the art of dialectic, until one bishop of remarkable holiness arose. Completely ignorant of sophistical speech, but illustrious in the wisdom of divine faith, he nullified all the philosopher’s many-branched stratagems by a simple yet wholly truthful argument.

Teachers therefore do not suffice to cross such a torrent by instruction unless they are either strengthened in faith by an exceptional grace of the Spirit or thoroughly trained by greater diligence in debate. Since they excel sublimely in prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice, and since they rejoice to fight for the Gospel, they are rightly said to have been four hundred, pursuing the raiders. The two hundred who remain behind in weariness are also rightly numbered, because there are people who, although they do not know how to defend the faith and the life of action by debate, nevertheless know how to practice them by living.

And they found an Egyptian man in the field, etc. As Catholic teachers hurry to engage in battle with the heretics, they often find men abandoned by them, marked by the dark blackness of their sins and, because of the tenderness of their intellect, unable to follow the teachers of error in laying waste to the Church.

They bring these men to hear the Catholic faith and give them the bread and water of the word. They also add the sayings of earlier teachers, who, once cut down from the beautiful fig tree of the present Church—as it were at the point between life and death—do not cease throughout the whole year of this present age to preserve the mature memory of their teaching for the refreshment of the minds of the faithful.

They rightly give him a fragment of a cake, because they do not offer such people complete works, but provide as many sayings of the fathers as they judge sufficient. They rightly give him two clusters of raisins, because they show that such people are to be joined to Christ and to the Church by the bonds of the twofold love.

And when he had eaten, etc. When he had received nourishment from right faith, he also received confidence of mind, by which he hoped to obtain the grace of mercy.

Therefore David said to him: “Whose are you, and from where?” etc. It is the rule of the Church that, through its teachers, it inquire of those fleeing to it from the heretics what they believed concerning the faith before they fled and toward what they intend to direct their minds in the future.

When the teachers have discovered that such people wholly resist the heresies and favor the Catholic faith, only then do they apply to them the sacraments of that faith for their reconciliation, lest they appear indiscriminately to cast holy things before dogs and pearls before swine.

“Whose hearers are you,” he says, “and from which sect, or to which sect, do you now intend to come?” Anyone seeking to escape the snares of the heretics must answer:

“I confess that I am darkened by my sins; until now I have been devoted to listening to heretics. But the teacher who imbued me with errors abandoned me, because, when battles were being fought against the Church, he saw that I was not sufficiently capable in tongue or intellect for this contest, and he no longer wished to take me with him into such a conflict. For when we came forth from the south—that is, from light—promising that our doctrine was perfect and life-giving through the breath of the Holy Spirit, we brought not a few of the Gentiles over to our sect and disturbed the faith of the Church to no small degree.”

And David said to him: “Can you lead me to that band?” etc. David is advised to use as a guide for finding and defeating the raiders the man who had been left sick by the Amalekites. For there are some who, having lived among heretics, lack the power to harm the good because of sluggishness of intellect. Then, suddenly visited and touched by heavenly grace, they receive from God sufficient strength to resist the perverse. Indeed, through those who know the secrets of the heretics, their wandering words are refuted much more effectively and certainly once they have been converted to Catholicism.

As for his asking him to swear that he would not kill him or hand him over to his master, and only then promising to reveal the hostile band to his pursuer: this is precisely what he asks of the spiritual teachers—that he reveal the secrets of the heretics to them only on the condition that they show him, without any doubt, the faith by which he can avoid eternal death, and that they not allow him to be subjected again to empty doctrines.

When he had led him, behold, they were reclining, etc. Heretics recline upon the face of the earth, eating and drinking. Whether they read obscure passages of Scripture or clear ones—for this is the difference between eating and drinking—they seek through them not heavenly things but always earthly things, and they cannot say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

They celebrate a feast day, as it were, over the spoils they had taken from the land of the Philistines and Judah. For they regard their discoveries—by which they had either taught some pagans to fall into worse error under the pretext of Christ’s name, or turned the faithful away from the way of truth—as the most excellent light of knowledge. Rejoicing, they say: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117).

And David struck them, etc. Christ strikes heretics in two ways: by chastising them so that they may receive the faith, or by anathematizing them so that they may undergo everlasting punishment. Both blows extend from evening to evening, because they reach from the recognition of the error that darkens the heart to either the repentance that makes the same error bitter for a time or the punishment that lasts forever.

The four hundred men who, having mounted camels, escaped by flight the sword of David and of an equal number of his soldiers are surely those who, despising the voice of Catholic teachers, neither consent to be corrected by them nor fear to be condemned. Trusting in the height of their virtues—or rather, in the height of their pride and boasting—as though upon the hump of camels, they boast that they possess no less the name and number of evangelical perfection and that they hope for and will attain the things on the right, that is, the joys of heavenly life.

So David recovered everything, etc. After defeating the founders of heresies and their impious doctrines—whether by correction, punishment, or exposure—the Lord rescues the souls whom they had deceived and restores them to the unity of Catholic peace.

And David came to the two hundred men, etc. After his complete victory over the raiders, David likewise enriched with a portion of the spoils those who had remained behind in weariness, together with those who had fought.

“Let the wise man not glory in his wisdom” (Jer. 9). “We cannot all do everything.” Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Nevertheless, all who labor at different times in the cultivation of the same vineyard of the Lord will receive one and the same denarius of life while contemplating the image of the supreme King.

And he sent gifts from the spoil to the elders of Judah, etc. The Lord loves and commands the members of his Church, in their various persons, conditions, and ages, always to rejoice in his victory and in the perpetual enlargement of his kingdom. Whenever they see souls previously corrupted by diabolical rebellion restored to the Church, he wants them to glorify and bless the Father who is in heaven.

He especially rejoices when they do this who, as he has seen, preserved his love in a pure heart even amid the bitter snares of persecutors and retained the sayings or examples of the saints in the diligent memory of a chaste conscience. This is the true David rejoicing and giving his men lodging or shelter in a hiding place.

Likewise, every Catholic teacher, when he investigates, exposes, and attacks the thickets of heretics, must not delay in revealing these things to other brothers—whether by conversation or by writing—so that they may know how to avoid and overcome such things.

And note that heretics fall far short of Catholic perfection, and Gentiles of Christian perfection, not only in believing in God but also in loving their neighbors. The Amalekites abandon their exhausted and dying companion on the road and expose him to be torn apart by wild beasts and birds. But David prepares his exhausted companions for battle in a safe place and, returning with rich peace, enriches them with blessing.

The title of the fifty-second psalm also recalls this reading. It runs as follows: “For the end, concerning Amalek, an understanding of David.” By this it signifies that, concerning Christ—who is “the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10)—the understanding of the figurative David, on behalf of the adversaries of the Church, whether to be corrected or condemned, understood what the city of the true David would suffer from the faithless and what he himself would repay them by enduring, pursuing, and fighting against the Amalekites.

The text of the psalm itself also rejoices in the meaning of this reading through all its mysteries, because it begins with the faithless undertakings of the wicked: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 52)—either considering in his foolish heart that there is no God who cares for human affairs, or that some person of the Holy Trinity is not the true God—and it ends with the triumph of the true David [F. Davidis]: “When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob rejoiced and Israel shall be glad” (Ps. 13).

## CHAPTER X. In the battle that follows, Israel flees and falls before the Philistines; after Saul’s sons have been killed, Saul himself throws himself upon his sword and dies. The Philistines carry off their bodies, and the men of Jabesh bury them honorably and seek relief from their troubles from the Lord through fasts.

(I Kings XXXI.) “The Philistines were fighting against Israel,” etc., up to the passage that reads: “And they took their bones,” etc. In this reading it is shown figuratively that the leading men of the Jews, corrupted by the examples or sayings of the nations, and turning to their own destruction—through neglect—the weapons of their spiritual knowledge, with which they ought to have been armed against the enemy, also left the lesser encampments of good action to the nations that succeeded them in their place. When evil men rejoice at their fall, let the good instead, if they find in them any useful example or discover any of them to have been chosen, bring forward the memory of such people; but let them leave the end of the reprobate to the judgment of the heavenly Judge. Everything here can likewise be understood of heretics and, in the same order, of false Catholics.

As the time of David’s kingdom was approaching, the Philistines, as always, were fighting against Israel.
