As the time of the new grace drew near, the Gentiles, as they had been accustomed to do before, attacked the chastity of the Israelite faith by examples of wickedness: now through perverse practices destined to perish, now by displaying the worship of idolatry, following the example of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to fornicate (Numbers XXIV).

“And the men of Israel fled before the Philistines,” etc. Those who seemed strong in contemplating the will of God—which is what the name Israel signifies—were deceived because they followed too carelessly the works and teaching of the Gentiles; and, corrupted by luxurious pride, they perished in the manner signified by the name of Mount Gilboa, that is, “slippery.” Secular wisdom also greatly aided the destruction of the heretics. Hence one of our own writers aptly said: “The philosophers, patriarchs of the heretics, stained the purity of the Church with perverse teaching.”

“And the Philistines fell upon Saul and upon his sons,” etc. The surrounding nations attacked with all their determination in order to destroy the kingdom of Judea and remove its sons from their midst; and by their corruption they perverted the priests, scribes, and Pharisees—the sons, that is, and teachers of that kingdom. They also prevented the heretics from preaching or worshiping the grace of the Holy Spirit with a simple heart. This is what it means to strike Jonathan, that is, “the gift of the dove”: they prevented them from praising the Father, who made us his sons not by nature but by adoption, with a worthy confession. This is signified by the killing of Abinadab, that is, “my spontaneous Father.” They hindered them from believing that salvation would come to the world in the kingdom of Christ; this is indicated, I believe, by the slain Melchisue, whose name is said to mean “my king is salvation.” The philosopher who seduced Arius, as though he were Melchisue, killed him; the one who seduced Macedonius, Jonathan; and the one who seduced Manichaeus, Abinadab. The teacher of corruption taught the first to deny the omnipotence of the true King Christ, the second to detract from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the third to blaspheme the goodness of the supreme Father.

“And the whole weight of the battle turned against Saul,” etc. The Gentiles acted with all their strength to remove the kingdom of Judea. Men most skilled in the deceptions of trickery drew near to it, and the leaders of that kingdom were powerfully seduced and corrupted by those who, having snatched simplicity from their hearts, inflicted upon them a many-sided wound of fraud and cunning. For just as an enemy’s sword indicates open persuasion toward idolatry and more serious crimes, so an arrow signifies the subtler arguments of deception. Saul did not perish by the sword of the Philistines but by their arrows, because the leaders of the Jewish kingdom did not perish with the kingdom through manifest crimes—whose deadly character no one would doubt—but rather through acts carried out under the cloak of piety that brought the most impious poison of death. For example, when God said, “Honor your father and your mother,” they taught their hearers instead to say to their parents: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,” and thus to cease entirely from honoring them. Likewise they said: “Whoever swears by the temple is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound,” and other things of this sort, which the Lord sets forth against them with repeated reproach in the Gospel—especially the fact that they killed the Lord of the Law and of the Gospel himself as though he were a transgressor of the Law.

The Gentiles imitate all these arguments of wickedness when they bend an intellect trained in philosophical studies toward sinful arts; they fall, plainly, wounded by the arrows of the Philistines’ archers. There is nothing, however, to prevent us from understanding the archers as unclean spirits, by whose deceits those men were imbued and perished.

“And Saul said to his armor-bearer, ‘Draw your sword,’” etc. Saul’s armor-bearer signifies the teachers of the Law. For just as the weapons and arrows of the Philistines signify the deceptions of the wicked, so, conversely, the weapons of the Israelites are to be understood mystically as nothing other than the words of spiritual teaching, by which the people of God ought to have fortified themselves against every danger. But Saul, wounded by the archers almost to despair, preferred to perish by the sword of his armor-bearer rather than by the sword of the uncircumcised. The leaders of the Jewish kingdom, having once resolved to die in their sins, preferred to be destroyed by teachers who dissolved the commandments of the Law and taught them in this way rather than by association with the Gentiles, whom they called common and unclean, which they regarded as polluting them. Accordingly, they were afraid to enter the Gentile praetorium, lest they be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover (John XVIII). Yet they did not fear to defile that Passover, by turning the Law they had received to their own destruction, with the blood of the innocent.

“And his armor-bearer was unwilling,” etc. There is no doubt that among the reprobate teachers of the Law there were some who did not wish to twist the sharp point of the word through a sinister interpretation in order to kill their hearers. Nevertheless, the hearers themselves—either by despising what they had rightly received from their teachers or, worse, by blaspheming it—turned it to their own destruction. When their spiritual death was seen, that is, their obstinacy in sinning, the ministers of the word themselves also deteriorated over time, and the testimonies of the Law, which they had feared to interpret wrongly, became for them an occasion of ruin because they had wrongly despised them. Would that we did not know that these things also happen among us today.

Heretics too, wounded by the darts of their own sins, turn their weapons against their own breast when they change the words of the divine utterances into arguments for their error. And any brother who remains within Catholic unity, when he has learned some skill for the common benefit of the Church and of those among whom he lives, but pollutes it with the contagion of pride, vainglory, avarice, or any other vice, miserably pierces himself with his own sword; for what ought to have been defended against the enemy has instead aided the enemy.

“And when the Israelite men saw,” etc. The unlearned, who knew neither the remedies of true humility nor the bath of saving baptism, saw the learned men and their teachers in Judea defeated in spiritual combat, with sin triumphing over them. They also saw no small part of the common people, formerly close to their teaching, driven by the pursuing adversary from the seat of their ancient steadfastness. Shaken at once by the fall of their elders, they too lost all the works of virtue and safeguards of spiritual knowledge that they had possessed. The sins of the Gentiles came and corrupted all the pursuits of virtue among the unbelieving Jews through a perverse inhabitation; unclean spirits came and occupied the hearts that the constancy of faith had abandoned.

Or certainly, the Gentiles came and made the former excellent pursuits of the Jews their own by believing. For even then they caused the divine utterances—which the Jews had already abandoned in no small part—to be interpreted for themselves; and now they have received the faith in Christ contained in divine Scripture, which the Jews cast away together with those utterances, and, as though inhabiting it, possess it.

Since the phrase “across the valley and across the Jordan” is to be understood more clearly in its mystical sense, the location itself should be briefly described. There is a great valley around the Jordan, itself level and extending an immense distance, called in Hebrew Elon or Aulon. It is surrounded on both sides by mountains that follow and join one another. They begin at Lebanon and extend beyond it as far as the desert of Paran. In this Aulon, that is, in the level valley, are famous cities: Scythopolis, Tiberias, and the lake near it; also Jericho, the Dead Sea, and the surrounding regions. Through these the Jordan, as we have said, flows midway, rising from the springs of Paneas and emptying into the Dead Sea.

Since it is clear that the valley signifies the abasement of humility and the Jordan, in which the Lord deigned to be baptized, signifies the water of baptism, the Jordan is rightly enclosed by the valley, so that the location itself may admonish us humbly to seek entry into the saving fountain and, after emerging from it, to live humbly. Therefore all who were not in the valley of the Jordan but across the valley and across the Jordan fled; for those who neglect either to receive the remedy of humility and baptism or to preserve it once received are wholly unable to stand against the evil spirits. This may generally be understood of Jews and pagans, of heretics and wicked Catholics.

“And they cut off Saul’s head,” etc. The corrupters—or the demons—persecuted Judea with the weapons of impiety until they completely tore away from it the very foundation of its kingdom and seized the safeguards of the sacred Law by which it had prevailed against every adversity. Immediately they hastened to spread the news of its overthrow far and wide among their accomplices, as a sign of their own triumph and a cause of their own joy. As an increase of their crime, they also sought to lead into the infernal dwelling places—their own household—the armor of God that blessed Paul commands us to put on as we wage war against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians VI), and that he himself first put on when he fought the good fight, completed his course, and kept the faith, receiving from the Lord the crown of righteousness (II Timothy IV). This, I say, the armor of heavenly warfare, taken from the Jews, the impious—both deceived and deceiving—tried to bring into the dwellings of hell, that is, to equate the divine utterances with the teachings of demons.

It is clear that they did and do this in two ways: either by interpreting spiritual sayings carnally and understanding them perversely, or by bandying about the same divine writings as though they were common and supported by no heavenly authority, treating them as they wish. They openly set up the nation itself, deprived of the citadel of the kingdom of Judea, reduced as though to nothing, and handed over to the power of its enemies, as a mockery and a public proverb for themselves. Figuratively, this means that Saul’s mutilated body was hung with impious hands on the wall of Bethshan, that is, “the house of the enemy,” to be displayed.

They also deprive heretics, struck down by the arrows of their preceding sins, of the protection of charity, which is the citadel of all virtues. Unclean spirits cut off Saul’s head when they persuade them to follow their own sense rather than that of Scripture. They strip away his weapons when they twist the divine utterances to their own—that is, demonic—meaning. They place Saul’s weapons in the temple of Astaroth. Astaroth signifies the teaching of evil spirits, not only because it is an idol but also because its name is interpreted as “the work of scouts”: these spirits daily circle around the folds of the faithful, scouting whether they can devour anyone. When they violently transform the very works by which people had served God into services of their own wickedness, they hang members deprived of light and life on the wall of the enemy’s house.

“And when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard,” etc. Jabesh, which is interpreted as “dried up,” designates the Church. The fervor of the Sun of righteousness—that is, the aspiration of divine love—restrains it from every flow of carnal desire and every defilement of flesh and spirit. Hence it is rightly described as situated on a mountain. Gilead itself is called “a heap of testimony,” signifying that the most refined life of the saints is fortified by suitable testimonies of Scripture so that it cannot turn aside into error.

This is the city that Saul, at the beginning of his reign, while he still served the Lord with humble devotion, freed from the siege of its enemies. When, therefore, the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the strongest men arose.

“And they traveled all night,” etc. When the inhabitants of the city situated upon the mountain of Christ heard that Judea—whence they remembered that heralds and ministers of salvation had come to them through the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles—was despised by the nations and held up to ridicule, they all rose courageously to the work of the word. Walking themselves along the path of virtue amid the darkness of those who had gone astray, they prevented people from rejoicing, through public insult, at the fall of those whose offense had brought salvation to the nations, who had seemingly belonged to the house of the devil.

“For if the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches. But if some of the branches were broken off, while you, though a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive, do not boast against the branches” (Romans XI), along with the rest of what the Apostle set forth to the Romans in wondrous and varied speech.

“They came to Jabesh and burned them there,” etc. The corpses, or the carnal bones, signify the stronger people and the works of virtue. They therefore burned the corpses of Saul and his sons, leaving the weaknesses of the Jews to the heavenly judgment, so that they might recognize that these things had been done or permitted according to the incomprehensible counsel of God’s will, “the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Romans XII).

In this passage we should understand the burning according to what is commanded concerning the reception and examination of the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion under the figure of eating the lamb: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exodus XII). They buried the bones in the forest of Jabesh when, if they found anything of virtue and strength among the weak, they preferred not to despise it as worthless but to add it to the fruitful works of the saints. If they recognized any among the carnal and fragile who pursued the virtues of the soul, they took care to number them among the company of the saints.

The forest aptly expresses the fruit of good works. Anyone who reads in Genesis what kind of forest Abraham planted at Beersheba can rightly understand this.

Alternatively, Saul, dead because of his sins and exposed to ridicule, is publicly rescued from disgrace by the men of Jabesh, whom he had saved. The corpse is burned and the bones are buried in the forest, because it is surely fitting that if any of the faithful and great men, overcome by sin, has incurred spiritual death, those whom he benefited through goodness should especially help him so that he may come back to life. Through their fervent prayers of compunction, they should uncover what is carnal in him and commend to its worthy author the spiritual things he achieved.

“And they fasted seven days.” Literally, it is rightly the practice to fast for the dead for seven days, so that they may reach rest. After the six ages of this world, in which we labor in the flesh, the seventh age in that world is the age of rest for souls separated from the flesh; in it they await that blessed and glorious time when they may deserve to rise again. The Law typologically foreshadowed this figure of rest and resurrection through the seventh day and through the seventh or fiftieth year, in which rest from works was granted.

The Lord himself displayed the example of this hope and faith in the divine dispensation: crucified on the sixth day, resting bodily in the tomb on the seventh, he rose from the dead on the eighth, which is the first day of the week.

But in the allegorical sense, when the faithful citizens and fellow countrymen of the Jews rightly retain sadness and continual grief in their hearts over the blindness of the Jews who have until now observed the Sabbath carnally, they fast, as it were, for seven days. Because their brothers and relatives remain established in error, they cannot have complete joy. But when those Jews themselves have perfectly come to know the mystery of the eighth day—that is, both the Lord’s resurrection and their own—then, with the grace of Christ assisting both peoples, they will rejoice together in perpetual celebration.

[Col. 0715]

ONE BOOK OF THIRTY QUESTIONS ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS. (C)

EPISTLE TO THE PRIEST NOTHELM CONCERNING THE THIRTY QUESTIONS

[Col. 0715A] Bede to his most beloved brother Nothelm, greetings!

Most beloved brother, concerning the matters in the book of Kings that you sent for elucidation, I immediately endeavored, with the Lord’s help and insofar as I could, to explain them. I made only this distinction: thirty of the propositions that perhaps seemed more difficult I included in this volume, separated into brief chapters so that they might be found more easily. But the remaining names or words that you had noted miscellaneously, which could be resolved more easily and briefly, I had collected separately on other sheets and sent at the same time to your brotherhood.

Although I myself knew that in the same book there were many matters far more obscure than those which you judged should be asked of me. Yet I was also aware that it often happens that someone who has already understood certain more obscure matters well—because he had found them sufficiently explained in the treatises of great authors—still remains uncertain and doubtful in the sense of certain easier points, which those treating deeper matters perhaps did not consider worth investigating. It also happens that not all that has been written by the Fathers can be possessed by everyone, and that questions of Scripture are unknown to readers, not because they have not been expounded by teachers, but because either the questions themselves are not available, or, though available, are not understood by those who inquire; as is evidently the case with many of those matters whose answers you both sought from me and received.

Since in these answers I have endeavored, following the footsteps of the Fathers, to satisfy your requests, I ask that, rendering the due return to our devotion, you remember to intercede, together with the brothers who serve the Lord with you in those places, for the well-being of both our heart and body. And if you find anywhere a more suitable exposition of anything that I have written—which can very easily happen—do not hesitate to send it to us promptly as well. Farewell, brother ever most beloved in Christ.

THE BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0715B] 1. (I Sam. II, 35.) “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart,” etc. What the prophet says, speaking to Eli in the person of God—“And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart and my soul; and I will build for him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Christ all his days”—must, under the figure of Samuel, be understood of the Lord Savior, namely the supreme and true high priest. For just as Samuel succeeded the deceased Eli in the priesthood, chosen not from the stock of Aaron but from another Levitical family—for he was the son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Thou, son of Suph, son of Elkanah, son of Maath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel (I Chron. VI), as the words of Chronicles relate—so the Mediator of God and men, in order to be our high priest, took the origin of his flesh not from Levi but assuredly from another tribe, namely Judah. He offered the Father for us a sacrifice other than the legal one, that is, his own flesh; and he left heirs of his high priesthood other than those of Aaron’s line, namely the sons of the grace of the new covenant, gathered from the whole race of the Gentiles.

As for God’s saying, as though in human fashion, “who shall do according to my heart and my soul”: of Samuel it can rightly be understood that in all things he obeyed God’s will as a human being obeys God; but of the Lord Savior, that as the only-begotten Son he is in all things privy to the Father’s secret counsels, as he himself plainly testifies concerning himself: “I do nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, these things I speak. And he who sent me is with me, and does not leave me alone, because I always do the things that please him” (John VIII). The Father builds him a faithful house—“whose house we are, if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope.” And this house will walk before his Christ, namely that supreme high priest, all its days; that is, the holy Church will never cease to advance, through the increase of its members, until the end of the age.

Otherwise, how can it be understood of Samuel that a faithful house was built for him which should walk before the Christ of the Lord, that is, before Samuel himself, all its days, when we read later that his sons turned aside from his ways after avarice and perverted judgment? Unless perhaps by his house here we understand the people of Israel, who served the Lord throughout all the days of his priesthood. Of them it is written: “And all the house of Israel rested after the Lord.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore the children of Israel put away the Baals and Astaroths, and served the Lord alone” (I Kings VII).

What is further added—“And it shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house shall come to pray for him and offer a silver coin and a cake of bread” (I Kings II)—is customarily fulfilled to some extent in the present time and will be fulfilled perfectly at the end of the world. For although few, still some daily flee to the Church from the Jewish people, not only from the common stock but also from the priestly line; and “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans II). Whoever among them is to be saved is precisely the one said to be remaining in the house. With Eli’s priesthood passing away, he must offer for himself to a Christian priest the coin of confession devoted to God which is contained in the Creed—brief in words, indeed, but outstanding in power. It is established that silver often signifies the brightness of the heavenly word, just as gold signifies the radiance of spiritual wisdom. Let him also offer the bread of the saving sacrifice, setting aside the flesh of legal victims, and say: “Dismiss me, I pray, to one priestly portion” (I Kings II), that is, to that people made glorious by Christ the priest, to whom Peter says: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (I Peter II). When it adds, “that I may eat a morsel of bread” (I Kings II), it also elegantly expresses the kind of sacrifice of which the priest himself said: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI). For what he had said above—that he had given food to the house of Aaron—concerned the victims of the Old Testament, which were the sacrifices of the Jews; therefore here he said that one must ask to eat a morsel of bread, which is the sacrifice of Christians in the New Testament.

2. (I Sam. III, 19.) “And not one of all his words fell to the ground.” What is said of Samuel after he had reported to Eli in the morning the words of the divine oracle received by night—“And not one of all his words fell to the ground”—means that none of what he spoke was ineffective, but all that he said was fulfilled in events. Superfluous words fall to the ground; they are to be counted as nothing and trampled under the contempt of all. Thus blessed Job also said: “And the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground” (Job XXIX), because he was accustomed to maintain such gravity of expression that he was never relaxed into contemptible merriment; but whenever he showed himself more cheerful to those present, he always did so for some definite benefit to them.

3. (I Sam. VI, 19.) “And he struck of the people seventy men and fifty thousand of the common people.” What is said of those who dared to look upon the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines, though they were not of Levitical stock—“And he struck of the people seventy men and fifty thousand of the common people”—uses people and common people indifferently for one and the same thing. For both are customarily translated from the single Greek word laos. But this seems to be the distinction: in the first clause of the verse, “men” is added. For your codex’s reading, “seventy-two,” is altogether erroneous; “men” signifies the elders, so that the sense is that seventy were struck from the leading men of the people, but fifty thousand from the common multitude. To prevent this in Exodus, the people stood at a distance and prayed; Moses alone went up to the Lord (Exodus XX).

[Col. 0718A] 4. (I Sam. VII, 2.) “From the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days were multiplied,” etc. What is said, that from the day when the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim the days were multiplied—for it was already the twentieth year—and that all the house of Israel rested after the Lord, must not be understood as though the twenty years during which the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim were to be counted down to the eighth year of David’s reign, when he brought it to Jerusalem with a gathered multitude of the people. For it is found later that in Saul’s time it was taken from that city and brought into the camp when he was fighting the Philistines. For it is written: “And Saul said to Ahiah: Bring the ark of the Lord near, for the ark of God was there that day with the children of Israel.” Since it is established that David brought it to Jerusalem, taking it from the house of Abinadab, into which it is reported to have been brought, it remains to be understood that in Saul’s days it was brought back from the camp and taken into the aforesaid city, whence it was again brought to Jerusalem during David’s reign. Therefore the sense of the statement mentioned is that it was the twentieth year from the time that the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim when it happened to be moved from there in Saul’s time because of war (Book of Antiquities VI, ch. 13). Or certainly, it was the twentieth year when all the house of Israel still rested after the Lord, having put away idols and serving him alone. No careful reader of sacred history is ignorant that it did this throughout the whole time of Samuel’s leadership—which, according to Josephus’s testimony, lasted twelve years—and in the first period of Saul’s reign, which, as the same historian affirms, lasted twenty years. For afterward, when the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit tormented him, especially in his persecution of the innocent and righteous David, it was necessary that a considerable part of his army or people should have become complicit in his wickedness.

5. (I Sam. XX, 14.) “If I live, you will show me the mercy of the Lord,” etc. Jonathan, grieving that David was harassed by his father’s unjust persecutions, said to him: “If I live, you will show me the mercy of the Lord; but if I die, you will not take away your mercy from my house forever, when the Lord has uprooted David’s enemies, every one from the earth.” When Scripture added, “Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David,” it immediately inserted, saying, “And the Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies.” This was done by anticipation: the narrative inserts beforehand what occurred much later, when, after Saul was slain, the kingdom was transferred to David’s house and those who had unjustly persecuted him in his innocence were punished by just divine vengeance. For then the Lord required from his enemies why they had afflicted the holy man; then they were compelled to render an account of the hatred with which they had raged against him for so long. This may also be understood of Absalom, Sheba son of Bichri, and David’s other enemies.

Alternatively, if you wish to know what the Lord required from the hand of David’s enemies, it may, unless I am mistaken, be clearly understood from the preceding statement that Jonathan made a covenant with David’s house: namely, that he required this from David’s enemies—why they too had not wished to enter into a covenant of peace with the one with whom they saw that the Lord was. Scripture seems to insert this statement by anticipation in order to prove true Jonathan’s testimony, “When the Lord has uprooted David’s enemies, every one from the earth,” because David’s enemies were indeed uprooted from the earth, not because David himself took vengeance on hostile opponents, but because the Lord judged on his behalf. It is fittingly added: “And Jonathan continued to make David swear, because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul,” so that the man who embraced David with such perfect love according to God’s law might be shown exempt from the destruction of David’s enemies. Although, snatched away by death in this manner, he could not share with David, as he had hoped, the earthly kingdom, without any contradiction he received fellowship in the heavenly kingdom with the one whom he loved for so long because of the glory of his virtues, being himself also full of virtues.

6. (I Sam. XXV, 29.) “For if at any time a man rises up pursuing you,” etc. Abigail, interceding for herself and her household with David, whom her husband, numbed by folly and drunkenness, had offended, said: “For if at any time a man rises up pursuing you and seeking your life, the life of my lord will be kept as in a bundle of the living with the Lord your God. But the life of your enemies will be whirled about as in the rush and circuit of a sling.” By a most beautiful comparison she distinguishes the state of the righteous from the lot of the reprobate. She calls the souls of the former living, thereby implying that the latter have, by contrast, been overtaken by spiritual death, according to the prophet’s saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel XVIII). She likens these to a bundle and those to a sling-stone: a bundle is bound together so that it may remain whole and be preserved, whereas a stone is placed loose in a sling in order to be cast away. Thus the elect in this world are hemmed in by the pressures of tribulations, so that, warned by them, they may bind themselves more closely to one another in mutual love and, united together, may be preserved forever in the hand of their Redeemer. But the reprobate, the more freely they are let loose in this life, as though free, to their own pleasures, the farther they are cast in the future from the glory of the divine vision, so that it may rightly be said of them: “Indeed, they have been driven out from your hand.”

She also wonderfully describes the omnipotent providence of the heavenly protector when she says that the soul of a holy man must be kept with him as in a bundle of the living. For just as it is very easy for anyone to preserve in his own hand a little bundle of grass or hay that he is holding, so the power of our Lord and Savior protects without labor all the elect throughout the world from the beginning to the end of the age, lest any one of them perish in any way. As he himself says of them in the Gospel under the figure of sheep: “They follow me, and I give them eternal life; and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John X). Just as a single bundle is bound with whatever ties, so the whole company of saints is bound together by one and the same faith, hope, and love, surrounded by the one defense of divine protection. The literal sense is plainly that David’s life, though enemies pursued him, was always kept in the lot of the living. But his enemies, with adversities pressing upon them, were to be disturbed by an unstable motion, like a stone whirled about in a sling, and driven from their territories or even removed from human affairs.

7. (II Sam. I, 18.) “And he commanded that the children of Judah should be taught the bow,” etc. What is written of David when he mourned Saul and Jonathan after they had been killed—“And he commanded that the children of Judah should be taught the bow”—he did because he had already learned that the Philistines abounded in archers, and that Saul had chiefly perished by their blows; thus his own soldiers also might learn the same art of warfare in order to defeat them in return. What follows, “As it is written in the book of the just,” refers to a book which they affirm cannot today be found anywhere, even among the Hebrews themselves, just as neither can the book of the wars of the Lord, mentioned in the book of Numbers; nor Solomon’s songs; nor his most wise discussions of the nature of trees and all herbs, and likewise of beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish; nor that of which the book of Chronicles says: “The rest, however, of the former and latter acts of Solomon are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam son of Nebat” (II Chron. IX); and many such volumes, which Scripture proves did exist but which are evidently not extant today. For when Judea was ravaged by the Chaldeans, the library that had been assembled in antiquity was also consumed by hostile fire among the other treasures of the provinces. From it, the few books now contained in sacred Scripture were afterward restored through the industry of Ezra, priest and prophet. Hence it is written of him: “Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a swift scribe in the law of Moses” (I Ezra VII)—swift, namely, because he discovered more ready forms of letters than the Hebrews had possessed up to that time. And in the Persian king’s letter: “Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven, greetings” (ibid.).

### 8. (II Samuel 8:2) “And he struck Moab, and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground,” etc.

What is written about David—“And he struck Moab, and measured them with a line, making them equal with the ground”—must be understood hyperbolically. It could not have happened that human beings living on the earth were so completely humbled that, with a line stretched over them along the surface of the ground, they appeared equal to the very earth itself. Rather, Scripture wished by this expression to intensify the immense humiliation of the captured and oppressed nation: it says that they were made equal with the ground, as though they had been unmanned and despised by God, so that human beings dwelling on the earth could have no more power than the earth itself, which had no human inhabitants. Scripture contains many examples of this kind of expression, such as the Gospel passage:

> “But there are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” [John 21].

How could the world not contain books that might have been written in the world? Scripture used such language to suggest the greatness and multitude of the Lord’s works. Likewise, in David’s lament: “Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions” [2 Samuel 1]. Closely similar is this passage from secular literature:

> “Who would outstrip the snow in brightness and the winds in speed.”

When it says that he measured them with a line, it uses “line” allegorically for a lot, because the extent of fields is customarily measured with a line. Hence it is written: “And by lot he divided the land among them, by the line of distribution.” It signifies that David divided the regions of the Moabites among whatever heirs he wished with as free a disposition as any landowner might, at his pleasure, mark off his own fields by drawing a line here and there. He measured two lines: one for killing and one for giving life. This too is said allegorically, signifying that David had such authority in his own power, with no one contradicting him, that he could assign some of them, as rebels, to death, while he spared others who submitted.

### 9. (II Samuel 23:8) “He is like the tenderest worm of wood.”

This is said of David’s wisest prince among the warriors, whose name is omitted in the Book of Kings, but who is called Jesbaam in the Book of Chronicles and is recorded as having been the son of Hachamoni [1 Chronicles 11]. “He is like the tenderest worm of wood” [2 Samuel 23:8]. The man’s civil character—that is, his gentleness—is indicated together with his military strength. Just as a woodworm is indeed tender and fragile throughout its body, and also very small, yet consumes the strongest substance of wood by eating through it and makes it rotten—for this reason it receives its name from wearing away wood, *teredo*—so that man appeared at home affable to everyone, quiet, and humble; but in public combat he showed himself a lion, powerful and unbearable to his enemies.

### 10. (II Samuel 23:20) “He went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern.”

This is said of Benaiah: “He went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern on a snowy day” [Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book VII, chapter 12]. Josephus explains more clearly how this happened. The cistern was exceedingly deep; in winter, when everything was covered with snow, it too had been leveled by a great accumulation of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, came upon it and fell in, remaining trapped there and roaring loudly, people hurried to see what had happened. When Benaiah also arrived with the others to witness the spectacle, he immediately leapt into the cistern, attacked the lion amid the snow, and struck and killed it.

### 11. Why the Book of Kings (II Samuel 6) says that the temple was thirty cubits high, while the Book of Chronicles (II Chronicles) gives one hundred twenty

What is said in the Book of Kings about the construction of the temple—that it was thirty cubits high—while the Books of Chronicles state, “The height was one hundred twenty cubits” [2 Chronicles 3], should not be thought contradictory; both statements are true. For, as Josephus’s *History* relates:

> “Thirty cubits extended from the pavement to the middle story, and another thirty from the middle to the third, where the height of the porticoes that adjoined the temple on its southern, western, and northern sides reached—that is, sixty in all; then another sixty to the highest roof of the building. Thus its entire height amounted to one hundred twenty cubits” [*Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3].

### 12. (III Kings 6:8) “The door of the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house.”

The statement, “The door of the middle side-chamber was on the right side of the house,” does not mean, as some think, that the door by which one entered the temple was made on the southern side, that is, in the middle of the southern wall. Otherwise Scripture would simply have said: “The door of the house was placed toward the south.” [Col. 0722B]

The door by which people entered for the temple’s daily services was actually toward the east, as Josephus reports. A portico stood before it, also open toward the east, so that the rising equinoctial sun, without any obstruction, might send its rays through the doors of the temple and the sanctuary directly onto the ark, which was in the Holy of Holies. The staircase leading to the upper story, and from the upper story to the third, was constructed secretly on the southern side of the temple—for this is the right side of the house—with a very small lower door from the east, in the very corner of the right-hand wall. Hence the text continues: “And by a spiral staircase they went up to the middle story, and from the middle to the third.”

The arrangement of this ascent commends to us a deeply memorable mystery. It is clear that this temple, which Solomon built, figuratively signifies the body of Christ, the King of Peace—not only that body which is his entire Church, but also that body which he received from the Virgin, holy and sanctified, to be the head of the Church.

There was a door of the middle side-chamber on the right side of the house, through which one ascended secretly from the lower levels to the middle story and from the middle to the third. When the Lord had suffered on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his right side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out: the blood of our redemption and the water of our cleansing. By these mysteries we are purified and consecrated, and from this life that we lead on earth we journey toward the future rest of the spirit, as though toward the upper house. When, released from the flesh, we have ascended to the rest of the spirit, we await, by receiving our flesh again on the day of resurrection, an ascent as though to the highest story.

### 13. (III Kings 6:9) “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings.”

The statement, “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings,” refers to paneled ceilings: these are wooden boards fixed with nails beneath the beams, whose painted decoration customarily displays a remarkable beauty to those who behold it.

There were three such ceilings in the temple. The first reached thirty cubits from the pavement; the second reached sixty cubits, opposite the top of the porticoes; and the third reached one hundred twenty cubits, at the summit of the whole building. For in Palestine, as in Egypt, roofs do not have pitched ridges; rather, the roofs of houses are generally built flat, suitable for sitting or walking upon. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you have heard in the ear shall be proclaimed upon the roofs.” Such a place is most suitable for proclaiming a word, whether to those sitting there or to hearers below.

Solomon also says in Proverbs: “It is better, he says, to dwell in the corner of a roof than with a quarrelsome woman in a common house” [Proverbs 21]. What is called *tectum* in Latin is called *doma* in Greek.

The porticoes themselves around the temple also had three levels of ceilings. The first reached twenty cubits from the ground; the second forty; and the third sixty. Their roofs too were flat. There were thirty porticoes below, thirty in the middle, and thirty above. They were separated not by walls from one another but by paneling, so that each of the ninety porticoes was five cubits in width and length and twenty cubits in height. These porticoes are frequently mentioned in the Book of Chronicles. Josephus explains more fully the order in which they were arranged.

The following statement—“And he built a paneling over the whole house, five cubits high”—refers to what Moses commanded in Deuteronomy: “When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become guilty when another falls and plunges down” [Deuteronomy 22]. This paneling stood at the very top of the temple walls, functioning as a railing, so that anyone climbing to the upper levels, when he reached the edge of the roof, would not fall headlong through careless movement. We find later that King Ahaziah suffered this very fate: he fell through the railing of the upper chamber and was stricken with a fatal illness.

Such paneling, walls, or railings, when placed for the protection of a walkway, were commonly called *luriculae*. The further statement, “And he covered the house with cedar wood,” indicates the covering at the summit of the entire structure: that is, the paneling laid above the beams to which the highest ceilings mentioned above were attached underneath.

### 14. (III Kings 8:8) “And when the poles projected, their ends appeared,” etc.

When the ark had been brought into the Holy of Holies, the text says: “And when the poles projected, their ends appeared outside the sanctuary, before the oracle; they did not appear farther outside.” The matter is expressed more clearly in the Book of Chronicles:

> “The ends of the poles by which they carried the ark, since they were somewhat longer, could be seen before the sanctuary. But if anyone had been a little farther outside, he could not see them” [2 Chronicles 5].

Here it must be noted that, although the ends of the poles could be seen before the sanctuary by those who came nearer and looked more attentively, it could not be that the ends themselves projected beyond the sanctuary. Once the sanctuary had been closed and a veil hung before its doors, the poles too, together with the ark and the cherubim, necessarily had to be hidden inside. This would have been impossible if the poles had projected so far that they left no room for the doors to be drawn shut. [Col. 0724A]

Scripture has taken such care to explain the position of the poles not without reason, but because of the greatness of the mystery. It is established that the outer structure of the temple signifies the Church journeying on earth, while the Holy of Holies signifies the inner happiness of the heavenly homeland. The ark brought into the Holy of Holies signifies Christ’s assumed humanity, brought within the veil into the royal heaven. The poles by which that ark was carried signify, in type, the preachers of the word, through whom Christ himself was made known to the world.

In the ark there was a golden urn containing manna, signifying that in the man Christ dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity. There was Aaron’s staff, which had been cut off and then flowered again, signifying that all power of judgment belongs to him whose judgment seemed to have been taken away in the humility of his passion. [Col. 0724B] There were also the tablets of the covenant, because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

The poles by which the ark was carried adhered to it, because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice in the glory of Christ through the vision of his presence. For what one of them said about himself—“I desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Philippians 1]—he left to be understood of all his fellow laborers.

The ends of the poles appeared outside before the oracle, not always, but whenever it happened that the doors of that same oracle were opened. Nor were they visible to everyone, but only to those who came nearer and earnestly sought to see what was inside. The ark itself, and the manner in which it was placed, could be seen only by those who had entered the oracle. No saint still living in this present life, even if he raises his mind greatly toward the heights, sees it; only the citizens of that homeland fully behold there the glory of their Redeemer.

The poles too were stored with the ark in the sanctuary. This signifies that all the perfected elect who preceded us from the world are even now hidden in the secret place of God’s face, away from the disturbance of human beings. Yet the ends of their poles are sometimes seen by those who draw near, when divine grace grants the more perfect, who cleanse the eye of their heart with complete devotion, some final glimpse of the joy of the heavenly citizens. Such contemplation, however, is not granted to those who have withdrawn a little farther away; the more they remain outwardly with an empty mind, the less they see what the inner joys are.

### 15. (III Kings 8:65) “Solomon held a solemn festival,” etc.

The statement that Solomon held a solemn festival, and all Israel with him—a great multitude “from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt” before the Lord—designates by “the entrance of Hamath” the northern region of the Promised Land, and by “the Brook,” or “Torrent,” of Egypt, as the Book of Chronicles calls it, the southern region.

I think it will be pleasing to the reader if I set down at somewhat greater length some passages from the words of Saint Jerome. It is written in the Book of Numbers, where the whole Promised Land is divided in brief terms according to its four regions:

> “The southern region shall begin from the wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and shall have its boundaries opposite the east, at the Salt Sea. These shall go around the southern region by the ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass through Senna and reach southward as far as Kadesh-barnea. From there the boundaries shall go out to the village called Adar and extend as far as Asemona. Then the boundary shall go around from Asemona to the Torrent of Egypt, and shall end at the shore of the Great Sea.”

In the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel the same region is described as follows: “The southern region, toward the south, shall extend from Tamar to the waters of Meriboth” [Ezekiel 47], that is, “of contradiction.” Kadesh and the torrent extend as far as the Great Sea. This refers to the vast wilderness of Zin beside Edom, whose boundary turns around at the Red Sea, proceeds by the ascent of the Scorpion and through Senna and Kadesh-barnea, then through the court or village of Adar, and from Asemona reaches as far as the Torrent of Egypt, which flows into the sea near the city of Rhinocorura. [Col. 0725B]

The boundary of the southern region begins at Tamar, a city in the wilderness, which Solomon also built with remarkable works and which is today called Palmyra. In Hebrew it is called Tamar, a word that in our language means “palm.” It extends as far as the waters of contradiction at Kadesh, which is certainly in the wilderness. The torrent flows into the Great Sea, the sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine.

The Book of Numbers continues:

> “The western region shall begin at the Great Sea and shall be closed by the same boundary” [Numbers 34].

That is, it extends from sea to sea: from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, to the place where Hamath, a city of Syria, is located. Ezekiel also gives the name of this region:

> “The region from the sea to the Great Sea shall extend directly from the boundary until you come to Hamath” [Ezekiel 47].

Hamath is now called Epiphania, its name having been changed by Antiochus, the most savage of tyrants; for his title was Epiphanes.

The text continues concerning the northern region:

> “The boundaries shall begin from the Great Sea and reach as far as the highest mountain. From there they shall come to Hamath, as far as the borders of Sedada. The boundaries shall go as far as Zephrona and the village of Enan. These shall be the boundaries on the northern side” [Numbers 34].

The Hebrews say that the northern region begins at the Great Sea, which extends along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria—which is called Coele-Syria—and Cilicia, and runs through Egypt toward Libya.

When the text says that the boundaries reach as far as the highest mountain, those same Hebrews think that it signifies either Mount Amanus or Mount Taurus, which seems more likely to us. “The boundaries shall go,” it says, “as far as Zephrona.” This city is today called Zephyrium, a town of Cilicia.

The following phrase, “and the village of Enan,” corresponds in Hebrew to *Haser Enan*, which is interpreted as “the court of the fountain.” It is the boundary of Damascus. Hence Ezekiel says:

> “The boundary shall be from the sea to the court of Enan, or Haser Enan, the boundary of Damascus, and from the north toward the north, the northern region” [Ezekiel 47].

“From there,” the text says, “the boundaries shall be measured toward the eastern region, from the village of Enan to Sephama; from Sephama the boundaries shall descend to Riblah, opposite the fountain. From there they shall reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth, and extend as far as the Jordan; and finally they shall end at the Salt Sea” [Numbers 34]. [Col. 0726A]

Thus, from the end of the northern region—that is, from the court of Enan—the boundaries extend to Sephama, which the Hebrews call Apamea. From Apamea the boundaries descend to Riblah, which is now called Antioch in Coele-Syria.

To show that this Riblah signifies the city that is now the most celebrated in Coele-Syria, the text adds: “opposite the fountain.” This clearly refers to Daphne, whose fountain supplies the city mentioned above with an abundance of water.

“From there,” it says, “the boundaries shall reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth,” that is, the Lake of Tiberias. It is called a sea, although its waters are fresh, according to the idiom of Scripture, by which gatherings of waters are called seas.

“And the boundaries shall extend,” it says, “as far as the Jordan, and finally shall end at the sea,” either the Dead Sea or, as others think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated.

### 16. (III Kings 16:34) “In his days Ahiel of Bethel built Jericho.”

What is written concerning the time of King Ahab’s reign—“In his days Ahiel of Bethel built Jericho. In Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and in Segub, his youngest, he set up its gates”—has this clear meaning: when the aforesaid builder began to lay the foundations of the city, his firstborn, whose name was Abiram, died; and when, after the city had been built, he attempted to fortify its gates, he lost Segub, the youngest of his sons.

Joshua had foretold that this would happen when, after destroying the city, he devoted it to destruction, pronouncing this curse:

> “Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up and builds this city of Jericho. In his firstborn shall he lay its foundations, and in his youngest child shall he set up its gates” [Joshua 6].

Ahiel, however, means “living to God,” and Bethel means “house of God.” Ahiel of Bethel restores the walls of Jericho, destroyed and devoted to destruction by Joshua, whenever someone who has assumed the religious way of life in the Church returns to the sins from which the Lord Jesus freed him on the day of baptism, and luxuriantly resumes the pomps of the devil, which he himself had renounced; or whenever he places the teachings of heretics or the fables of the pagans above the ecclesiastical truth in which he was instructed. By going out from Bethel, as it were, he raises up again the ruins of Jericho.

Such a person is rightly cursed before the Lord, and loses both his firstborn in the foundation of the wicked city and his youngest in the setting up of its gates. For he loses the foundations of faith, from which he ought to have begun the building of good works, and the house of good action by which he ought to have brought it to completion.

I have explained these matters also in an allegorical sense, so that you may remember how true is the apostle’s statement: “All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us” [1 Corinthians 10].

### 17. (I Kings 20:10) “May the gods do this to me, and may they add this,” etc.

When Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was besieging Samaria and beginning his attack, he said:

> “May the gods do this to me, and may they add this, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me.”

The meaning is as follows. Samaria, in accordance with the custom of cities, had earth inside, close to the walls and nearly level with them, so that blows from a battering ram, repeatedly applied by the enemy, would not overthrow the walls standing without the support of the adjoining earth. On the outside, however, the height of the walls rose far above the level of the ground, especially since, as Scripture reports, the city itself was situated on the summit of a mountain.

The proud king, therefore, terrifying the besieged city, claimed that the army accompanying him was so numerous that, even if each of his soldiers brought only one stone, clod, or stake to construct a mound against the city, so high a mound could be raised from these materials that it would seem level with the surface of the city inside the walls. Thus the attackers would be able to hurl weapons or torches against the city from the same level.

The king of Israel restrained this rash arrogance with a measured saying: “Tell him: Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself.”

There is a difference between one who is girded, one who has ungirded himself, and one who is not girded. A girded man is one who goes about wearing a belt. One who has ungirded himself is one who has recently removed his belt—for example, to enter a bath, climb into bed, or perhaps put on another tunic. One who is not girded is a man who is about to put on a tunic but has not yet secured himself by fastening a belt around it.

Likewise, in a military expedition, the man who has taken his position is properly called girded, that is, armed. The man who has completed the battle and returned home victorious is rightly called ungirded, because, having laid down his weapons, he enjoys the leisure of the peace he desired. But the man who has not yet fought or begun to prepare himself for battle is rightly said to be not girded.

Thus the king of Israel said to the king of Syria, who boasted that he had already captured Samaria, although he had only begun to besiege it: “Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself.” As though he were saying openly: Do not boast as though you were already victorious in the dangers of war, when you are still stationed in battle and do not know which side victory will follow.

He was speaking the truth. For as soon as the battle began, Ben-hadad did not return home in triumph over defeated enemies; he returned fleeing after his army had been slaughtered.

### 18. (IV Kings 11:6) “A third of you shall enter on the Sabbath,” etc.

The high priest Jehoiada said this to the priests and Levites when he brought forward Joash, the son of Ahaziah, whom he had secretly raised in the temple during the six years of Athaliah’s reign:

> “A third of you shall enter on the Sabbath and keep watch over the king’s house; another third shall be at the gate of Seir; and another third at the gate behind the dwelling of the shield-bearers. You shall guard the watch of the House of Mesha. The two parts of you, all who go out on the Sabbath, shall guard the watches of the house of the Lord around the king. You shall surround him, each of you holding weapons in your hands,”

and the other things said and done there.

These instructions are better understood if some fuller account is given of the places in the temple where these events occurred. The temple itself, apart from the porticoes that surrounded and adjoined it on every side, measured within its walls—for this is the first measurement, which the Book of Chronicles mentions—sixty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width.

Its entire court was surrounded by a wall three cubits high, with an entrance on the eastern side. Scripture refers to it in the Book of Kings as follows: “He built the inner court with three rows of dressed stones and one row of cedar wood” [III Kings 6]. It calls this the inner court because other outer courts had been built around it.

In the Book of Chronicles it is written: “He also made the court of the priests, the great basilica, and the doors of the basilica, which he covered with bronze” [II Chronicles 4]. It calls it the court of the priests because it had been made to keep others from entering the temple and to indicate that only priests were permitted to enter it.

This same court was nearer to the temple wall on the southern, western, and northern sides. On the east, where it also had its entrance by means of steps, it extended a great distance away from the temple. In that part it had the altar of burnt offering; in another part, ten basins in which the victims were washed; in another, the bronze sea in which the priests who were about to minister washed themselves; and there the choirs of Levites for the priests offering sacrifice and singing psalms.

This court was surrounded on every side, at some distance, by a very large building arranged in a square. Its inner wall—that is, the wall facing the temple from the four regions of the world—was constructed below entirely in arches, while the outer wall was founded with solid masonry. It had bronze doors, as we have recalled above, and “doors in the basilica, which he covered with bronze.” It was also strengthened by very large porticoes and divided by suitably placed chambers.

Outside this building there was again another structure arranged in a similar form, in a circle. A third was likewise built around the others in the same order and surrounded all the inner structures far and wide. It differed from the earlier buildings only in that its eastern and northern walls had no doors, since both belonged to the walls of the city.

These are the courts of which the Psalms sing: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” [Psalms 113, 134].

Because the house of the Lord had been built on higher ground, the farther outward the courts were, the higher their walls had to be, since they had foundations at a lower level. Thus the outermost courts reached four hundred cubits in height, yet did not come close to matching the height of the temple.

All these structures are mentioned generally in the Book of Chronicles:

> “David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico and the temple, the storerooms, the upper chamber, the rooms in the inner parts, and the house of propitiation, as well as the plan of all the courts and chambers around the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the holy things” [*Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3].

Josephus’s written account, or the illustration handed down from ancient times, distinguishes more fully the order in which all these were constructed.

Once these arrangements had been made, only the high priest could enter the Holy of Holies once a year, with the blood of the sacrifices. Only purified priests entered the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary; all the priests and Levites entered the inner court. Around this court, in the open air—or, if the weather prevented it, in the surrounding buildings—Israelite men customarily gathered to pray or to hear the word.

In the third row of courts, Israelite women stood to pray in the open air; if the weather did not permit this, they took shelter under the nearest roofs of the surrounding buildings. The Gentiles who happened to come together to pray entered the outermost row of courts. After the time of the Dispersion, those who had recently come from the nations and had become Israelites were also purified there for seven days, and only then approached the inner holy places.

The pavements between the courts and within the courts were all laid with variegated stone. The doors of the buildings were placed opposite one another in such a way that even those standing in the outermost courts could see the temple.

There were twenty-four courses of priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, succeeding one another in order over an equal number of weeks. A new group entered upon its service on the Sabbath, while the group that had ministered during the preceding week returned home after the Sabbath.

On this occasion, however, the high priest, because it was necessary to increase the forces around the new king, retained both those whose week of service was beginning and those who had completed their week of ministry, preventing them from departing. As the Book of Chronicles relates, he had also gathered to Jerusalem other Levites from all the cities of Judah, together with the heads of the Israelite families, sending centurions for this purpose [II Chronicles 23].

When he was about to bring them out, he arranged the king’s son in the following way. All who had completed their Sabbath duty and were about to depart were divided into two groups, and, armed, surrounded the king in the inner parts of the court. The remaining multitude—that is, those who were not of the tribe of Levi—guarded the outer doors of the courts against the queen’s fury, in case she attempted any hostile action.

The priests, Levites, and doorkeepers who had recently come for the Sabbath were divided into three groups. They kept watch over the king’s house—that is, the palace—so that the queen could not defend it against the king by gathering an army. They also guarded the gate of the dwelling of the shield-bearers, through which one descended from the temple to the palace, as the text says below:

> “They brought the king out of the house of the Lord, and came by way of the gate of the shield-bearers into the palace, and he sat upon the throne of the kings.”

The gate of Seir and the House of Mesha, which are mentioned together with the gate of the shield-bearers, also appear to have been located there.

The shield-bearers are called the king’s protectors, as the Book of Chronicles testifies. After relating that Rehoboam had made bronze shields in place of the golden ones, it adds: “And he entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers, who guarded the vestibule of the palace” [II Chronicles 12].

In that same book all these matters are set out more distinctly:

> “A third of you who come on the Sabbath, of the priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, shall be at the gates. Another third shall be at the king’s house, and another third at the gate called the Foundation. Let all the rest of the people remain in the courts of the house of the Lord. Let no one else enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those Levites who minister; only those who have been sanctified may enter. Let all the rest of the people keep the watches of the Lord. Let the Levites surround the king, each holding his own weapon” [II Chronicles 23], etc.

### 19. (IV Kings 11:12) “He brought out the king’s son and placed a diadem and the testimony upon him.”

The following statement concerning the same event—“He brought out the king’s son and placed a diadem and the testimony upon him”—signifies by the diadem the royal insignia of the head, and by the testimony the decrees of God’s law, which instruct the king what he ought to do and how he ought to live.

Accordingly, the Book of Chronicles expresses it more clearly:

> “They placed the diadem upon him and gave him the law to hold in his hand” [II Chronicles 23].

This was certainly a wise and salutary arrangement: after the death of the tyrannical and impious queen, when the son of the legitimate king succeeded to the throne, the discipline of God’s law was entrusted to him together with the royal insignia, so that the man who saw himself set over the people for their governance would remember that he himself must be governed by submission to the divine laws.

### 20. (IV Kings 12:15) “No account was required from the men who received the money,” etc.

When the aforesaid King Joash was restoring the temple of the Lord, the text says: “No account was required from the men who received the money to distribute it to the craftsmen, but they dealt with it in good faith.” This demonstrates the devotion of those about whom the passage speaks. They had such zeal for religion that no one doubted they would handle the Lord’s money without any suspicion of fraud, faithfully taking it from the treasury and offering it to the craftsmen for repairing the house, according to the needs of each.

### 21. (IV Kings 14:7) “He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand,” etc.

The statement concerning Amaziah, king of Judah—“He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand, and captured Petra in battle, and called its name Joktheel”—means that the Valley of Salt was the place where salt was produced. This could have been done either from a salt spring, after it had been cut off, dried, and burned in many places, or by heating the salty waters of wells and boiling them until they reached the consistency of salt, or by any other process by which salt is customarily made.

Joab is also said to have struck twelve thousand Edomites in this same place.

It should not be passed over that, instead of “Valley of Salt,” the Old Edition gives *Gemelach*, apparently as the name of a region.

Petra is a famous city of Arabia, in the same land of Edom. In the Book of Numbers it is called Rekem, and it is still called this by the Syrians [Numbers 31]. Joktheel, the name Amaziah gave it after his victory, means “assembly of God” or “help of God.” By acting faithfully, he ensured that it would be remembered forever that he had captured it either through the assembly of God’s people or with God’s help.

### 22. (IV Kings 14:25) “He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath,” etc.

The statement concerning Jeroboam, king of Israel—“He restored the boundaries of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Wilderness”—means that Hamath, now called Epiphania, was the northern boundary of Israel.

The Sea of the Wilderness, called *Arabah* in Hebrew, designates the Dead Sea. It extends lengthwise for 580 stadia as far as Zoara of Arabia, and across for 150 stadia toward the vicinity of Sodom.

### 23. (IV Kings 17:29)

“And each nation made a god.” This is said of the nations brought into Samaria by the king of the Assyrians:

“And each nation made its own god, and they placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritans had made, each nation in its cities in which they lived. For the men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; and the men of Hamath and Hama made Ashima. Moreover, the Hivites made Nibhaz and Tartak.” [Col. 0731A]

In the *Book of Places* it is read that Benoth and Nergal were cities that the Samaritans who had migrated from Babylonia built in the region of Judah. Asima, likewise, was a town built by those who had come from Hamath. Nibhaz and Tartak were cities that the Hivites founded in that same land of Judea.

Yet, in accordance with the context of the passage, it also seems possible to understand these as the names of the idols that these nations had previously worshiped in their own land. When it had been said, “And each nation made its own god,” the statement was completed by what follows: “For the men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth,” that is, “the tabernacles of Benoth.” And, if I am not mistaken, the translator would have done better to render *Succoth* in Latin as *tabernacula* (“tabernacles”) and to leave the name of the idol, *Benoth*, standing by itself. [Col. 0731B]

Likewise, when it is expressly said later: “Those who were from Sepharvaim burned their sons with fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim,” it is shown that Adrammelech and Anammelech were the idols of the city of Sepharvaim. Accordingly, it seems to follow that Nergal was the idol of the Cuthites, Asima that of the Hamathites, and Nibhaz and Tartak those of the Hivites.

### 24. (IV Kings 18:34)

“Where is the god of Hamath and Arphad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim?”

This is what the Rabshakeh said among the other things with which he blasphemed God, crying out against Jerusalem:

“Where is the god of Hamath and Arphad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim, Ana, and Ava? Have they perhaps delivered Samaria from my hand?” [Col. 0731C]

He showed that the Samaritans had served the gods of all these cities or nations, and that, since they were not gods but idols, their worshipers—appropriately people devoted to vanity—had deservedly been overthrown.

Hamath is a city of Coelesyria, now called Epiphaneia, near Emesa, as we noted above. Arphad is a city of Damascus, which Hieronymus also records was conquered by the king of the Assyrians (Jeremiah 40). *Sepharvaim*, which in the plural signifies “books” or “letters,” is the name of the places from which the Assyrians migrated and settled in Samaria, as we find in the *Books of Places*. Yet in Isaiah this word also appears to be the name of a city, where it is expressly said: “Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim?” (Isaiah 37), although it is expressed in the plural, like *Thebae* and *Athenae*. [Col. 0731D]

For *Ana* and *Ava*, the Old Edition placed what appears to be the name of a single city, *Aneugava*. Indeed, it is written that way in Hebrew. But because the syllable *u*, placed in the middle of the name, signifies the conjunction “and” among them, it can also be divided so that one reads *Ane et Gava*, as Aquila translated; or *Ana et Ava*, as our translator rendered it.

### 25. (IV Kings 20:9)

“Do you want the shadow to rise ten lines, or to return by the same number?”

This is what the prophet Isaiah said to King Hezekiah:

“Do you want the shadow to rise ten lines, or to return by the same number of steps?”

The expression “steps” means the same as “lines,” namely, the divisions of the hours—twelve during the day—that we usually mark on a sundial. Or, as Hieronymus says, the steps had been constructed by mechanical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended along each one, it marked off the intervals of the hours. [Col. 0732A]

It was the tenth hour of the day when the Prophet spoke these words to the king:

“Do you therefore want,” he said, “the shadow to rise ten lines, while the sun proceeds above the earth through the northern regions toward the east—a course which it was daily to make beneath the earth according to its customary movement? Or do you want the shadow to return by the same number of steps, with the sun’s face turned backward and the sun itself returning toward the east through the southern region?” [Col. 0732B]

But the king replied:

“It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines. I do not want that to happen, but for it to return backward by ten steps.”

For he saw that it could be a greater miracle if the sun followed a course contrary to its own path than if, proceeding according to its customary movement, it advanced—although in that case it would have to fly toward the east much higher, that is, raised above the earth, as though it were bringing the morning of a second day without the intervening night.

Indeed, those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain, or in the remotest regions of the Scythians, see something like this happen for several days every summer. While the sun is below the earth and at setting for the rest of the world, it nevertheless appears above the earth to them throughout the whole night; and it can plainly be seen returning low from the western part toward the east, until at the appointed time it is restored to the whole world by its common rising, as both the histories of the ancients and our contemporaries who come from those regions report most fully. [Col. 0732C]

But those who inhabit the interior parts of the south never see the sun return from the west toward the east through the southern regions.

### 26. (IV Kings 22:14)

“She who lives in Jerusalem, in the Second.”

This is said of the prophetess Huldah. What the phrase signifies is explained in the *Book of Chronicles*, where it is written concerning the aforementioned King Hezekiah:

“He also built, acting diligently, the entire wall that had been destroyed; he raised towers above it and constructed another wall on the outside” (II Chronicles 32).

Zephaniah mentions this place when he says:

“A voice of crying from the Fish Gate, and wailing from the Second” (Zephaniah 1).

For this, the Old Edition translated *in Masena*, as though it were the proper name of a place. *Masena* means “the second.” Therefore, when it is said that the prophetess lived “in the Second,” understand this as referring to the section of the second wall.

[Col. 0732D]

### 27. (IV Kings 23:10)

“He also polluted Topheth…”

This is said of King Josiah:

“He also polluted Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son, or his son through fire to Molech.”

These places are frequently mentioned in Scripture, especially in the *Book of Kings* and in the prophet Jeremiah.

The valley of Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem, toward the east. In it there is a most beautiful grove watered by the springs of Siloam. Topheth, or Tapheth—for both forms are written—was a place in that same valley, near the Fullers’ Pool mentioned in Scripture, and near the field of Acheldama, which is still shown on the southern side of Mount Zion.

In Topheth, a most pleasant place that even today provides the delights of gardens, they used to sacrifice to demons at an altar set up there, consecrating their children to the impious fire or offering them as a burnt offering, as it is written in the *Book of the Words of Days* concerning King Ahaz: [Col. 0733A]

“He is the one who burned incense in the valley of Ben-hinnom and caused his sons to pass through the fire.”

*Ben-hinnom* signifies “the son of Hinnom.” The valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew *Gehinnom*. From its name, the punishment of the underworld is called *Gehenna* in the New Testament, because, just as those who served idols perished in the valley of Hinnom, as the prophets testify, so sinners will be punished with eternal condemnation for the things they have done.

Finally, when Jeremiah reports that the Lord commanded him and said, “Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate,” he shortly afterward says:

“And this place shall no longer be called Topheth, or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. And I will destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword” (Jeremiah 19). [Col. 0733B]

Isaiah also most clearly calls Topheth the underworld. When he described the everlasting destruction of the devil under the name of Assyria, saying:

“For at the voice of the Lord Assyria will be terrified, struck with the rod, and there will be the passage of the rod established, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him” (Isaiah 30),

he immediately added how and where Assyria would perish:

“For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king—deep and broad. Its fuel is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulphur, sets it ablaze.”

He aptly says, “And broad,” because *Topheth* means “breadth.” “Its fuel,” he says, “is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulphur, sets it ablaze.”

Josiah polluted Topheth either with the bones of the dead, as we read that he did with other places of idolatry later in the passage, or by scattering various other unclean things there, so that the place might appear to all who saw it suited to abomination rather than delight. [Col. 0733C]

### 28. (IV Kings 23:11)

“He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given…”

What follows is said about the same King Josiah:

“He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord.”

And shortly afterward:

“He burned the chariots of the sun with fire.”

This shows that the Jews had always been enslaved to every form of idolatry and superstition, so that, in honor of the sun—which they believed, in the manner of the nations, to be a god—they had placed chariots and horses beneath the image they had made, and this in the courts of the temple of the Lord. [Col. 0733D]
