For the gentiles commonly depict or fashion the image of the sun by placing a boy or young man in a chariot and harnessing horses to him, as though they were making for heaven at a run. They attach the image of a boy to it because the sun, as though born each day in a new rising, never grows old throughout the ages.

John, bishop of Constantinople, believes that their attribution of chariots and horses to the sun was taken from the miracle of the prophet Elijah, who was carried up into heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses.

For the sun is called *Helios* in Greek—as Sedulius also shows when he sang of Elijah’s ascent:

> How fittingly the path of lightning-flashing heaven, shining before him,  
> accords with Elijah, who deservedly shines even in his name.  
> He was worthy of this aid; for if in Greek speech  
> one letter is altered by an accent, it is “sun.” [Col. 0734A]

When the Greeks heard from the Israelites—whose possession of divine writings was widely proclaimed—that Elijah had been carried into heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses, or when they saw this very event depicted among other scenes on a wall, they were deceived by the similarity of the name and believed that the sun’s passage through the heavens was being represented. They transformed a miracle wrought by divine power into an argument for an error invented by human folly.

The Jews themselves, imitating them, took pains not to appear in any respect less foolish than the most foolish of the gentiles.

### 29. (IV Kings 23:13)

“He also destroyed the high places that were in Jerusalem…”

A little later the same king is said to have done this:

“He also destroyed the high places that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense …”

The passage continues:

“The king polluted them and broke the statues.”

It is as clear as daylight that Scripture usually calls “high places” sites situated on wooded hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the pleasantness of the places, offered victims even to the Lord, abandoning the altar that had been established in the temple in defiance of the prohibition. [Col. 0734B]

Thus, in this book, it is often said of kings who were not perfectly just:

“Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.”

He calls the Mount of Offense the mountain of the idol, because it is customary in Scripture to call idols “offenses”: either God is offended through them, or they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers. This is indicated in the very sentence that follows:

“Which Solomon the king had built in Israel for the idol Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the sons of Ammon.”

Here, if I am not mistaken, this too is openly shown—although one could wish it had not been shown: namely, that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry that he had committed. [Col. 0734C]

For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built should be removed from the holy city. He would not have left, as a scandal to fools, the things that he himself, although he had been the wisest of men, had made in error, as though they had been wisely and rightly made.

Scripture also mentions this place earlier, saying:

“Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain that is opposite Jerusalem, and for Molech, the idol of the sons of Ammon” (III Kings 11).

It should not seem contradictory that the mountain on which these idols were made is there said to be opposite Jerusalem, while here it is asserted to be in Jerusalem. [Col. 0734D] For it was situated so close to the city that it appeared to belong to the city itself and to defile it also with the filth that was gathered there.

### 30. (IV Kings 24:14)

“And he transferred all Jerusalem…”

In recounting that Nebuchadnezzar transferred all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty warriors—ten thousand persons—into captivity, Scripture added:

“And every craftsman and *clusor* [incloser].” [Col. 0735A]

This is what is said above to have been done to the same people of Israel when the Philistines ruled over them:

“There was no ironsmith to be found throughout Jerusalem and in all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews make a sword or a spear” (I Samuel 13).

Just as the Philistines had then taken precautions to prevent the Hebrews, if they possessed ironsmiths, from making weapons with which to resist, so now the Chaldeans, after destroying Jerusalem and laying waste the whole land of promise, took pains that no craftsman and no *inclusor* [incloser] should remain there who could repair the city’s defiled walls or mend what had been broken. Rather, whatever skilled workmanship they found among the exterminated people, they transferred entirely to Babylon, so that it might either no longer be of any use or might serve the needs of that city.

Since the allegory of this deeply lamentable history is very relevant to the negligence of our own times, I do not think it should be withheld.

It is clear that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church; while Babylon and the Chaldeans or Philistines signify the city of the devil, that is, the entire multitude of evil human beings or angels. [Col. 0735B]

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when the faithful, although remaining in name within the Church, are deceived by unclean spirits or human beings and submit the necks of their minds to avarice, lust, or any other sin.

Nebuchadnezzar leads Israel, all the princes, and the mighty warriors—ten thousand persons—into captivity when he suddenly subdues teachers of peoples and those who seemed, with unconquerable spirit, to serve the Lord and faithfully preserve the law’s Decalogue in love of God and neighbor, either by the allurements of the world or by adversities, so that they pollute themselves with greater crimes or, turning aside into heresy, incur the mark of open apostasy. [Col. 0735C]

What weapons are there other than the words of Scripture with which, resisting the devil, we defend the freedom given us by God? In these, through the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, we learn with utmost clarity the order by which the battles against vices must be overcome.

The Philistines deprive the sons of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits hinder the souls of the faithful from meditating on sacred reading by inserting worldly occupations into their lives, so that they may neither gain confidence to resist through this exercise themselves nor approach others who do not know how to read by encouraging or correcting them to resist vices. [Col. 0736A]

They remove the weaponsmiths when they overwhelm those who know the sacred words with such crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they had learned.

They transfer every craftsman and *inclusor* from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn aside from their purpose those who used to benefit many through the manifold practice of the virtues and fortify the city of God against the attacks of temptations, compelling them instead to devote the skill that they ought to have expended in protecting the holy Church to the will of the king of vices.

If, however, we wish to understand *inclusor* here not as one concerned with doors or walls but rather as one who sets gold and gems, the spiritual interpretation reaches the same end. [Col. 0736B]

For it is said of wisdom that it is gold and an abundance of gems (Proverbs 20). Therefore we can understand no one more appropriately by those who set these than teachers, who, so long as they live and teach rightly, devote the industry of their art to the adornment of the holy city.

But if they should happen to fall into error, what else happens except that they are taken captive by the nation of the Chaldeans and transferred to Babylon? And since for the craftsman and *inclusor* to migrate from Jerusalem to Babylon is to bury in the earth the talent of the word received from heaven, that is, to turn spiritual knowledge toward the works of sin.

I beseech you, reader, that if I have said anything agreeable to you in these little explanations, you refer it to the praise of God the Giver. But if not, grant pardon to my ignorance or presumption in such a way that you yourself, together with all whom you can, may devote yourselves to frequent meditation, continual observance, and timely preaching of the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0736C]

Let us strive by common labor to be found faithful merchants of the Lord’s money; craftsmen and setters of spiritual gems or walls; defenders of the holy city; and makers of heavenly weapons. May the supreme Master of the household, returning from the wedding feast, deign to say to us:

“Because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

Amen.

[Col. 0735]

## BOOK ON THE TEMPLE OF SOLOMON (C)

### LETTER TO THE SAME ACCA, ON THE TEMPLE OF SOLOMON

[Col. 0735D]

The chosen vessel and teacher of the nations urges us to read the divine words, bearing witness with truthful voice that “whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15).

Here he very aptly declares that, in order to obtain hope of heavenly goods, we must possess patience and attend to the consolation of the Scriptures. Patience, namely, so that we may endure whatever adversities arise with a humble and submissive mind, as scourges inflicted by a just judge and loving father—whether we are struck for the glory of the virtues and the increase of our merits, if we are just and innocent, or for the correction of our conduct, if we are entangled in vices. [Col. 0736D]

The consolation of the Scriptures, on the other hand, is given so that by frequent meditation on them we may recall how much those supreme fathers and illustrious lights of the Church often endured in the present life amid dark affliction; how much glory they deservedly received with the Lord in the life to come because of their devotion and patience; and how much unfailing praise and honor they left among all the faithful even in this life.

As Scripture says: “The memory of the just is with praises” (Proverbs 10); and again: “The bodies of the saints were buried in peace, and their names will live through generations and generations” (Sirach 44).

The apostle James also says: “Behold, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord” (James 5). [Col. 0737A]

It was not without reason that, after recalling the afflictions of the just, he added, “And you have seen the end of the Lord.” For neither did the one who lived here without sin depart from this life without a scourge. He who appeared in the world to heal the sick and raise the dead himself chose to return from the world through the weakness of death, in order to show us an example of patience.

Therefore, when the Psalmist had said, “Our God is the God of salvation” (Psalm 67), he immediately added, in wonder—or rather in amazement:

“And the Lord God’s exits are toward death.”

Thus, “through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures,” let us have hope that we too will be consoled after the afflictions of our own trials, when we have been patient in tribulation and have brought to mind the deeds of those who not only preceded us by the merit of their righteousness but also endured far greater struggles of adversity than we do. [Col. 0737B]

They often suffered persecutions from the unjust because of the righteousness in which they excelled, so that, together with the practice of righteousness, they might receive the crown of unconquerable patience and leave behind for all who followed them the glorious traces of their perseverance.

We, however, are more often chastised by the mercy and providence of our Creator for our errors, so that, returning to our conscience through salutary compunction, we may carefully punish with cleansing tears what we have committed through deceptive allurements and negligence. Thus, corrected with the Lord’s help, we may become worthy of belonging to the fellowship of those who were afflicted though innocent, and of attaining the hope of life.

For we also find this in the consolation of the Scriptures: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, both small and great” (Psalm 113). [Col. 0738A] He has also declared that there are many dwelling places for us in his Father’s house.

By the consolation of these promises, I do not doubt that you too, most beloved of bishops, daily alleviate the present anxieties of temporal affairs and are nobly encouraged to behold the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (John 14), once the evils of human beings who reign in the land of the dying have been overcome. You are well supplied not only with the pages of the divine Scriptures but also with their devout interpretations, which the venerable writing of the fathers has handed down to us.

But because new things sometimes give greater pleasure, I thought it appropriate to send for your holiness to read through a little work that I recently composed allegorically concerning the construction of the temple of God, following in the footsteps of great interpreters. [Col. 0738B]

As you attend to its reading, the more sacraments of Christ and of the Church you find embedded in the ancient pages, and the greater gifts of God you perceive to have been given to us in the present or promised for the future, the lighter, I believe, and less worthy of concern you will judge all transitory things, whether adverse or prosperous.

You will follow the example of blessed John, who, when he had been confined by a wicked emperor within the narrow limits of a tiny island and seemed to be deprived of the help and companionship of human friends, was immediately introduced by the loving Creator, through the Spirit, to contemplate the boundless mysteries of the heavenly dwelling places. [Col. 0738C]

Where he was thought by his deceived enemies to have been deprived of the help and society of human friends, there he deserved to enjoy the sight and conversation of angelic friends. Taught by them, he learned all the more to despise the enticements and bitterness of the world, the more sublimely he contemplated those things which, by reason of their greatness and eternity, are plainly either to be feared or loved far more.

Farewell always, most beloved, and intercede for us.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0737]

### CHAPTER ONE. That the building of the tabernacle and of the temple signifies one and the same Church of Christ

[Col. 0737C]

The house of God that King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church, [Col. 0737D] which, from the first elect person to the last, who will be born at the end of the world, is built day by day through the grace of the peaceful King, namely, its Redeemer.

Part of this house is still journeying away from him on earth; part, having escaped the hardships of pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven, where, after the final judgment has been completed, the whole Church will reign with him.

The elect angels belong to this house, whose likeness is promised to us in the future life, as the Lord says:

“Those who will be considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they can no longer die. They are equal to the angels and are sons of God, since they are sons of the resurrection” (Matthew 19).

The Mediator himself, the man Christ Jesus, between God and human beings, belongs to this house, as he himself testifies when he says:

“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). [Col. 0738C]

Explaining this, the evangelist added:

“But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

The Apostle says of us:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (II Corinthians 6).

Therefore, if he became the temple of God through the humanity he assumed, and we become the temple of God through his Spirit dwelling in us, it is clear that the material temple bore the figure of all of us and of him himself—namely, of the Lord and of his members, who are us. [Col. 0738D]

It represented him as the uniquely chosen and precious cornerstone, laid in the foundation; but it represented us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, that is, upon the Lord himself (Ephesians 2).

This will become clearer from consideration of the temple’s very order of construction. In some respects, its figure pertains to the Lord himself; in others, to all the elect. In some features it describes the undefiled blessedness of the angels in heaven; in others, the unconquered patience of human beings on earth. In some it signifies the angelic assistance granted to human beings; in others, the struggles of human beings rewarded together with the angels. [Col. 0739A]

The same spiritual house of the Lord was also represented by the tabernacle once made in the wilderness through Moses (Exodus 25).

But the former house was built on the journey by which Israel was coming to the land of promise, whereas this one was built in the land of promise itself and in the city of Jerusalem. The former was carried repeatedly from place to place through the ministry of the Levites, so that it might finally be brought into the land of the promised inheritance; the latter was constructed immediately in the homeland itself and in the royal city, so that it might remain forever on an unshakable foundation until it fulfilled the function of the heavenly figures entrusted to it. [Col. 0739B]

In the former, therefore, the labor and exile of the present Church may be signified; in the latter, its future rest and blessedness.

Or, certainly, because the former was made by the sons of Israel alone, while this one was also made by proselytes and gentiles, the fathers of the Old Testament and that ancient people of God may be expressed figuratively in the former, while in the latter the Church gathered from the gentiles may be represented.

Although, when the construction of both houses is examined more carefully in a spiritual sense, it is shown in many ways to suggest through its figures the daily labors of the present Church, the eternal rewards and joys of the heavenly kingdom in the future, the election of the first Church from Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ.

Since, with the Lord’s help, we are going to discuss the building of the temple and seek the spiritual dwelling of God within its material structure, it seems appropriate first to say something about its workers—who they were and from where they came—and also about the material from which it was made. [Col. 0739C]

For the Apostle testifies that these things too are pregnant with spiritual mysteries when he says:

“All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us” (I Corinthians 10).

### CHAPTER TWO. How King Hiram assisted Solomon in the work

The history of Kings relates that Solomon, when he was going to build a house for the Lord, sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre. Hiram had been David’s friend at all times, and, after Solomon had obtained the kingdom, had also begun to maintain peace with him.

Solomon immediately found Hiram ready to assist him in everything, so that Hiram supplied him with craftsmen, timber, and gold according to the needs of the work. In return for this service, Solomon gave him every year a very large quantity of wheat and oil for the food of his household (III Kings 5). [Col. 0739D]

There is no doubt that Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” signifies both by his name and by the most peaceful condition of his reign the one of whom Isaiah says:

“His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of his peace” (Isaiah 9).

Hiram, however, whose name in Latin means “living on high,” figuratively expresses believers from the gentiles, glorious in both life and faith.

Nothing prevents us from understanding Hiram, since he was a king and assisted Solomon in the construction of the house of the Lord with royal power, as typologically signifying those rulers of earthly affairs who have been converted to the faith. Through their help, the Church has often been assisted, nobly increased, and raised up against heretics, schismatics, and pagans by the decrees of rulers.

Solomon therefore asks Hiram for assistance in the work of the temple because, when the Lord came in the flesh and planned to build the house he loved—namely, the Church—he chose fellow workers not only from the Jews but also from the gentiles. From both peoples he appointed ministers of the word. [Col. 0740A]

Hiram sent Solomon cedar and fir timbers cut from Lebanon to be placed in the house of the Lord, because the gentile world, once converted, sent to the Lord men who had once been distinguished in the world but had already been cast down and humbled from the mountain of their pride by the axe of the Lord’s rebuke. Instructed according to the rule of evangelical truth, they are placed in the building of the Church, each according to his merit or appointed time.

He also sent craftsmen, because the gentile world offered to the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, by reason of their learning, could rightly be placed in charge of governing peoples. Such were Dionysius the Areopagite in the times of the apostles; and later the gentle and powerful teacher and martyr Cyprian; and many others. [Col. 0740B]

He also sent gold, which is understood in the same sense, since it signifies men distinguished for wisdom.

For all these offerings the gentile world expects gifts of heavenly grace from the Lord: the wheat of God’s word, the oil of charity and anointing, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

It is entirely appropriate to the affairs of the Church that Solomon earnestly said to Hiram in requesting assistance for the holy work:

“Command, therefore, that they cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants.”

The servants of Hiram who cut cedars from Lebanon for Solomon are teachers chosen from the gentiles. Their duty is to correct and lay low those who rejoiced in the possessions and glory of this world because of the pride of their arrogance, and to transfer their desires to the service of their Redeemer. [Col. 0740C]

With these servants there were also Solomon’s servants, and together they devoted themselves to the work mentioned. For the first teachers from the gentiles necessarily had to be instructed in the word of faith by the apostles themselves, who had learned from the Lord, lest, if they began to teach without masters, they should become teachers of error.

For this reason Solomon wanted Hiram’s servants to cut the timber from Lebanon for him: they were more skilled at cutting than his own servants. And for this reason he wanted his own servants to be present with them, so that they might show the cutters what dimensions the timber ought to have.

The meaning of this figure is obvious. The apostles knew how to preach to others the word of the Gospel that they had deserved to hear from the Lord with greater certainty. But the gentiles, converted from error and transformed into the truth of the Gospel, knew the errors of the gentiles better; and the more thoroughly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to overcome and abolish them. [Col. 0740D]

Paul knew the mystery of the Gospel better, because he had learned it through revelation. But Dionysius was better able to refute the false doctrines of Athens, since from childhood he had known their errors, their syllogisms, and all their arguments.

This interpretation fits what follows:

“For you know that there is no man among my people who knows how to cut timber as do the Sidonians.”

There was no one among the Jewish people, where the Lord was teaching bodily present, who knew how to refute the errors of the gentiles as learnedly as those gentiles who had themselves been converted to the faith and had become Christians from among the nations. [Col. 0741A]

The Sidonians and Tyrians, since they belonged to gentile peoples, are rightly understood as a figure of the gentiles.

### CHAPTER THREE. How many workers Solomon had in the work of the temple
How many servants, then, our Solomon sent to this work is indicated in the following passage in mystical language:

> “Solomon chose workmen from all Israel, and the levy was thirty thousand men. He sent them to Lebanon ten thousand each month in rotation, so that they would spend two months at home.”

Here we must first observe that Solomon did not choose workmen from all Israel without reason, nor was there any portion of the people from which men worthy of so great a task were not taken. For now those who are to be chosen are not to be sought from one stock—that of the priest Aaron; rather, they must be sought from the whole Church: men able to build the house of the Lord either by their example or by their teaching. Wherever they are found, they are immediately promoted to the office of teachers, without respect of persons.

When such men are appointed to instruct unbelievers and summon them into the fellowship of the Church, they are nourished like vigorous and chosen men for cutting the timber of the temple in Lebanon. The number of thirty thousand, by which these woodcutters were counted, can appropriately be referred to the figure of those who are perfected in faith in the Trinity, something especially fitting for teachers.

[Col. 0741C] But because the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand attended to the holy work each month, we ought rather to consider the mystery of the number ten. Ten thousand men from Israel are sent to cut timber for the Lord’s work because all who are to be appointed teachers and instructors of the ignorant must themselves observe in every respect the Ten Commandments of the Law, and must show their hearers that they too are to observe them. They must also hope for the rewards to come in heaven, which are customarily represented by the denarius, and must constantly declare to their hearers that they too should hope for them.

The three-month intervals imposed upon the individual woodcutters figuratively proclaim the perfection of the three Gospel virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. For when the Lord had said in the Gospel, “Take care not to practice your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI), in developing the same point he mentioned nothing other than almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. These were to be practiced not for the display of men but solely for the glory of the inner observer; otherwise they would remain empty of eternal fruit.

By these words he plainly taught that all the fruits of the virtues are signified by these three branches, as it were, growing from one root of charity. By almsgiving are understood all the things that we benevolently do for our brothers in order to fulfill love of neighbor. By prayer, everything through which we are joined to our Creator by inward compunction. By fasting, everything by which we guard ourselves from the contamination of vices and the enticements of the world, so that with a free mind and a chaste body we may always be able to cling to the love of both our Creator and our neighbor.

[Col. 0742A] These, then, are the three months of the temple’s workmen. Since a month is completed by the full number of days in the lunar cycle, it reveals the fullness of each spiritual virtue, in which the minds of the faithful are daily illumined by the Lord, as the moon is illumined by the sun.

The one month during which timber was cut for the temple’s work is almsgiving—that is, the work of mercy by which we labor for the salvation of our neighbor, so that they may make good progress and arrive at unity with the holy Church: by teaching, correcting, providing temporal necessities, and offering examples of life.

The other two months, during which the men were permitted to remain in their homes and attend to their own needs, signify prayer and fasting. Through these, apart from what we do outwardly for the needs of our brothers, we turn inwardly in mind toward the Lord and care for our own salvation.

And because only those care perfectly for their own or their brothers’ salvation who humbly submit themselves to the scrutiny of divine grace, the text rightly continues:

> “And Adoniram was over such a levy.”

Adoniram, whose name in Latin is said to mean “my exalted Lord,” whom does it better signify than the one whom the name imitates—namely, the Lord and Savior? Adoniram is placed over the temple’s workmen so that, by his provision, it may properly be arranged in which months each man should go out to work and in which he should return again to care for his own house.

So our Lord and Savior, by a more intimate illumination, instructs the minds of holy preachers to discern when it is appropriate to begin the work of building the Church through preaching or by performing other works of piety, and when it is appropriate once more to return, as if to inspect their own house, to examine their conscience and make it worthy of the heavenly Visitor and Inspector through prayers and fasts.

> “[Col. 0742C] Solomon therefore had seventy thousand of those who carried burdens, and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, besides three thousand three hundred overseers who directed the people and those who performed the work.”

He calls them *latomi*, “stonecutters.” These stonecutters figuratively signify the same thing as the woodcutters: holy preachers who exercise the minds of the ignorant through the labor of God’s word, striving to transform them from the shame and deformity in which they were born, and carefully making them, once instructed according to the rule, suitable for the unity of the faithful—that is, for the building.

The fact that both timber and stones are cut in the mountain, and that both kinds of material, once cut and prepared, are transferred to the mountain of the Lord’s house, makes the meaning clear: all human beings are born on the mountain of pride, because we derived the origin of our flesh from the transgression of the first man, which pride caused.

But whenever those predestined by God’s grace for life are cut down through catechesis and the reception of the mysteries of faith, we are transferred from the mountain of pride to the mountain of the Lord’s house. For, rescued from the power of darkness, we reach the citadel of the virtues, which is found in the unity of the holy Church.

It should also be noted that these workmen were distributed so that some cut stones in the mountain, while others carried burdens. The gifts of the Spirit are diverse. Some possess greater steadfastness for speaking and rebuking the insolent; some are gentler in comforting the fainthearted and supporting the weak; and some, endowed with both virtues, come together for the Lord’s work. Such men the Apostle wished those to become to whom he says:

> “Correct the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone.”

The overseers who presided over the individual tasks are the authors of sacred Scripture. Under their instruction we are taught in every respect how it is fitting to teach the uninstructed, rebuke the contemptuous, and bear one another’s burdens through our works, so that we may fulfill the law of Christ.

[Col. 0743B] The more each person labors either in supporting the needs of his neighbors or in correcting their errors, the more certain are the rewards he awaits in the future—whether the rest of souls after death or the blessed immortality of bodies. Hence the aforementioned workmen are rightly said to number seventy thousand and eighty thousand.

The seventy signify the sabbath-rest of souls, for the seventh day was consecrated as the Sabbath, that is, as rest. The eighty signify the hope of the resurrection, which took place in the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath; and which is likewise awaited by us on the eighth day and in the eighth age.

The overseers numbered three thousand three hundred (2 Chron. II), plainly on account of faith in the holy Trinity, which the sacred Scriptures preach to us. The fact that, instead of three thousand three hundred overseers, three thousand six hundred are recorded in the book of Chronicles refers entirely to the perfection of the same exalted men.

Since the Lord completed the adornment of the world in the number six, good works are rightly customarily represented as perfected in it. And since Holy Scripture teaches that works of righteousness are to be joined with faith in the truth, the temple’s overseers are rightly said to have numbered three thousand six hundred.

[Col. 0743C] Nor should it be passed over that these seventy and eighty thousand burden-bearers, and the stonecutters with their overseers, were not Israelites but proselytes—that is, resident foreigners living among them. For it is written in the book of Chronicles:

> “Solomon counted all the proselyte men who were in the land of Israel, after the census that David his father had taken; and they were found to number one hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred. He made seventy thousand of them carry burdens, and so forth.”

Proselytes were called *proselytae* in Greek: those born from other nations who, after receiving circumcision, passed into the faith and fellowship of the people of God.

Thus there were workmen for the house of the Lord from the children of Israel, from the proselytes, and from the Gentiles. From the children of Israel there were thirty thousand, who were sent to cut cedars from Lebanon. From the proselytes came those of whom we have now spoken, the stonecutters. From the Gentiles came Hiram himself and his servants, who cut timber from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants.

Thus every kind of human being through whom the Church was to be built was represented beforehand in the construction of the temple. Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build the one and same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or by teaching.

## CHAPTER IV. Of the kind of stone from which the temple was made

> “The king commanded that they should bring great and precious stones for the foundation of the temple,” and so forth.

[Col. 0744B] The foundation of the temple is to be understood mystically as nothing other than what the Apostle indicates when he says:

> “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III).

He can rightly be called the foundation of the Lord’s house because, as Peter says, “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

Great and precious stones are brought to this foundation when men distinguished in deeds and holiness cleave to their Creator through the familiar holiness of their minds, so that the more firmly they place their hope in him, the more strongly they may be able to direct the lives of others—which is to bear the breadth.

The stones placed in the foundation of the temple to support the entire building are properly the prophets and apostles, who received the word and sacraments of the truth from the Wisdom of God itself, whether visibly or invisibly. Therefore the Apostle says that we, who strive according to our ability to imitate their teaching or their life, are “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II).

More generally, all the perfect who have learned faithfully to cling to the Lord himself and courageously to bear the burdens of their brothers laid upon them may be signified by these great and precious stones.

[Col. 0744C] They are rightly commanded first to be squared and then placed in the foundation. Everything square customarily stands firm, fixed whichever way it is turned. The hearts of the elect are likened to this figure: they have learned to stand so firmly in the stability of faith that no adversity among the things that occur—not even death itself—can incline them from the rectitude of their position.

The Church has received many such teachers not only from Judea but also from the Gentiles. Hence, concerning these great, precious, and squared stones, it is appropriately added:

> “Which Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons hewed.”

Precious stones are hewn when all the elect among believers, through the instruction and earnest effort of the saints, abandon whatever harmful or useless thing they possess within themselves and display before the sight of their Creator only the rule of their innate righteousness, as though it were the form of a square.

[Col. 0744D] The stones were hewn not only by Solomon’s masons but also by Hiram’s masons, because from both peoples of God there were men who rightly became teachers even of those exalted teachers and prepared them, as it were, as squared stones to support the building of the Lord’s house.

For it was not only Jeremiah, Isaiah, and the other prophets from the circumcision who supplied later teachers with the greatest model of life or patience and the most splendid proclamations of saving doctrine. Blessed Job too, with his children who were from the Gentiles, supplied them with this model, so that, once empty words, deeds, and thoughts had been cast aside, they might become worthy and fit to bear the burden of the holy Church.

> “The Giblites prepared timber and stones for building the house.”

Giblos is a city of Phoenicia, which Ezekiel mentions, saying:

> “Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots, the elders of Giblos and its wise men” (Ezek. XXVII).

In Hebrew the name appears as *Gobel* or *Gebel*, which is interpreted as “defining” or “separating.”

This word aptly applies to those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building constructed from the virtues of the soul. They are able to teach their hearers faith and works of righteousness only because, first instructed in the sacred pages themselves, they have learned with careful and definite discernment what faith is to be held and by what path of virtue one must walk.

For one who does not know the distinction of the catholic faith vainly assumes the office of teacher. They build not a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for themselves if they try to teach others a rule that they themselves have not learned.

[Col. 0745B] In building the Lord’s house, timber and stones must first be cut from the mountain, because those whom we seek to establish in the faith of the truth must first be taught to renounce the devil and to be rescued, through rebirth, from the lot of the first transgression in which they were born.

Next, great and precious stones must be sought and placed in the foundation of the temple. We must remember, after abandoning our former way of life, to examine in every respect the life and conduct of those whom we know to cling especially to the Lord through the virtue of humility, and to propose them to our hearers for imitation. We must observe those whom we see persisting, as it were squared, through an invincible stability of mind, immovable against every assault of temptation, and whom we find to be precious and great in reputation and merit.

After the foundation has been composed of such great stones, the house must be built with timber and stones carefully prepared and placed in fitting order, having been removed from their former position or root. For after the rudiments of faith, and after foundations of humility have been laid in us according to the example of exalted men, the wall of good works must be raised high, as though successive courses of stones were placed one upon another, while we walk and advance from virtue to virtue.

Or certainly, the great, precious, and squared stones of the foundation are, as I said above, the first teachers of the churches, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The courses of stones or timber laid upon them are the priests and teachers who follow in their respective times, through whose preaching and ministry the structure of the Church grows, or is ordered in virtues.

The color of the stones from which the temple was made is clearly explained in the book of Chronicles, where David says to Solomon, as he showed him the expenses for the temple that he had prepared:

> “I have prepared in great abundance every precious stone and Parian marble.”

By Parian marble he means white marble, such as that island customarily produces. Hence the poet says:

> “Olearos, and snowy Paros, and the Cyclades scattered across the sea,  
> and we sail through the straits stirred by frequent winds.”

He calls Paros “snowy” because it produces marble of the whitest kind. It is one of the Cyclades, and Josephus indicates that the temple was made from this stone, saying:

> “He raised the temple as far as the vaulted roof, constructed of white stone; its height was sixty and one hundred cubits” (*Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3).

The mystical meaning is not hidden. It is clear to anyone that the white marble from which the Lord’s house was built signifies both the pure conduct of the elect and their conscience, chastened from every blemish of corruption. The wise architect wished those whom he placed upon the foundation of Christ to be precious stones redeemed with gold and silver:

> “Beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.”

## CHAPTER V. When and where the temple was built

[Col. 0746B]

> “It was therefore in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt,” and so forth.

The statement that it was in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv, means that Ziv was the second month of King Solomon’s reign over Israel. The order of the sense is: in the fourth year of King Solomon, in the month of Ziv, which was the second month.

He calls the second month May. For April, in which Passover is celebrated, was the first of the months and the beginning of the year’s months among the Hebrews. It is therefore plainly evident that, immediately after Passover had been completed, he began to build the Lord’s house, and that the people, consecrated by the mystical solemnity, set their hands to the mystical work.

[Col. 0746C] The departure from Egypt is mentioned when the tabernacle began to be built so that the reader might be reminded how many years elapsed between the building of the two houses and might recognize the spiritual mystery contained in this total period.

For four times one hundred and twenty make four hundred and eighty. Four aptly corresponds to evangelical perfection, on account of the number of evangelists. One hundred and twenty corresponds to legal instruction, on account of the same number of years belonging to the Lawgiver. In this same number the primitive Church visibly received the grace of the Holy Spirit, showing that those who use the Law lawfully—that is, those who recognize and embrace Christ’s grace in it—are rightly filled with the grace of his Spirit, through which they burn more fully with his charity.

[Col. 0746D] We have said that the tabernacle made in the desert by Moses and the children of Israel can signify the synagogue, while the temple built by Solomon and the children of Israel with the assistance of proselytes and Gentiles can signify the Church of the Gentiles.

The worship and religion of the tabernacle continued for four hundred and eighty years, and then the temple began to be built, because the writing of the Old Testament is so full of perfection that, if anyone understands it well, he will find that it contains within itself all the mysteries of the New Testament.

Many fathers of the Old Testament also attained such a height of perfection by their lives that they should in no respect be considered inferior to the apostles and apostolic men. The tabernacle remained among the people of God until the construction of the temple for four hundred and eighty years—that is, one hundred and twenty multiplied by four—because from the time when God’s Law was given until the Lord’s incarnation and the time when grace was revealed, there was never a lack of men who, established within the Law, observed evangelical perfection in every respect in mind and deed. Nor was there a lack of Scripture that proclaimed the grace of the New Testament in the prophetic utterances of the Old.

The fact that the Lord’s house began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon can be referred mystically to this: after the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, which is written in the four books of the Gospel, had been completed, the structure of the Church began when the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven.

[Col. 0747A] The fact that it began in the second month can refer to the election of the Gentiles, who, coming after Israel, received into themselves those who were to be built. Hence the second month was also permitted by the Law for celebrating Passover by those who were unclean in soul or far away on a journey and could not come to celebrate Passover in the first month.

Here we are most clearly signified: unclean because of the death of our soul and still far away from the people of God, we could not celebrate the first Passover, which was performed in the flesh and blood of the Lamb. But today we celebrate the second Passover, which was accomplished in the body and blood of our Redeemer, by whom we were sought and cleansed.

The place where the temple was built is shown more clearly in the book of Chronicles, where it is written:

> “Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, at the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (2 Chron. III).

The house of the Lord is therefore built on a mountain, in the vision of peace, because the Church, spread throughout the world, stands in one and the same faith and fellowship of catholic truth. “God is not in the division of minds, but his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV).

[Col. 0747C] It is built on a mountain—namely, on the Lord and Savior himself—of whom Isaiah says:

> “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. II).

And he himself says of himself in the Gospel:

> “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V).

For he is the mountain of mountains, who arose from the earth through the origin of the flesh he assumed, yet by the singular height of his dignity surpasses the power and holiness of all earthly beings.

On this mountain the city or house of the Lord has been built, because if our hope and faith do not fix their root in him, they are nothing. He is rightly called Mount Moriah, that is, “of vision,” because he deigns to see and assist his elect, whom he preserves for the eternal vision of his glory, while they labor in this present life.

It is the place where Abraham offered his son Isaac to the Lord and, through the devotion of his obedience, merited to be seen by him; hence the place received its name. Thus, where the Lord says, “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go to the land of vision and offer him there as a burnt offering” (Gen. XXII), the Hebrew has “the land of Moriah” in place of “the land of vision.”

And because Isaac’s sacrifice was a type of the Lord’s passion, the temple is rightly built at the place of that sacrifice, because through faith and the mysteries of the Lord’s passion the Church, dedicated, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.

Concerning this mountain it is appropriately added:

> “Which had been shown to David his father.”

The Lord who was to come in the flesh had been shown to David, as also to the other prophets. Through the mysteries of that same incarnation he would cleanse the Church called from the Gentiles of its sins and consecrate it as a faithful and beloved house for himself.

It is rightly added:

> “At the place that David had prepared.”

David had prepared the place for the Lord—the true Solomon—by singing psalms, and the other prophets had prepared it by prophesying, so that he might build his house there. They instructed the hearts of their hearers in faith in the truth, carefully admonishing them to receive with faithful and devoted minds the Son of God who was to come in the flesh.

Therefore the Lord says to his disciples concerning the peoples prepared to believe in him:

> “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest; and the one who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together” (John IV).

It is as though he were saying in other words concerning the building of the temple: “Lift up your eyes and see the place, for it is already prepared for the building of the Lord’s house. The one who builds by teaching receives his reward and gathers precious stones for eternal life, so that the one who prepares the place for the building may rejoice together with the one who builds”—that is, the prophet who foretells the Lord’s coming and the apostle who proclaims the Lord who has come may together receive their reward in him.

[Col. 0748B] The same place was rightly the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, because the Church is customarily signified by the term “threshing floor.” John says of the Lord:

> “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. IV).

Ornan, whose name means “illuminated,” was by nationality a Jebusite. His nationality signifies the Gentiles; his name, however, shows that they were to be illuminated by the Lord and changed into children of the Church. The Apostle rightly says to them:

> “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

[Col. 0748C] Jebus is the same city as Jerusalem. Jebus is interpreted as “trampled down,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” As long as Ornan the Gentile ruled there, it was called Jebus. But when David purchased the place of the burnt offering there, and Solomon built the temple of the Lord there, it was no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem.

For as long as the Gentiles remained ignorant of divine worship, they remained [alternative reading: continued] trampled upon and mocked by unclean spirits, being led after mute idols wherever they were driven. But when the grace of their Creator looked upon them, they immediately found peace within themselves, as well as a place and a name. Concerning them the Lord says:

> “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V).

Thus, while Ornan still held kingship in that city, it was called Jebus. But when he sold his threshing floor, with its oxen and threshing sledges, to King David, it received the name Jerusalem. The Gentiles, still persisting in their obstinacy, were trampled down as vile and rejected by the evil spirits.

But when they learned to sell all that they possessed and offer it to the true King, they could no longer be trampled down by demons and vices; rather, they became more fully established in the inner peace they possessed with their Creator.

## CHAPTER VI. Of the measurements of the temple

> “The house that King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long,” and so forth.

The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the holy Church, by which, in the exile of this pilgrimage, it patiently endures every adversity until it reaches the homeland for which it waits.

Its breadth signifies charity. With the bosom of the mind enlarged, charity rejoices to love not only friends in God but also enemies for God’s sake, until the time comes when, those who have been converted to its peace or entirely destroyed, it rejoices with its friends alone in God.

Its height proclaims the hope of future recompense. In view of this hope, it willingly despises all lowly things, whether pleasing or hostile, until, having passed beyond both, it deserves to see only the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

Thus the length of the house is appropriately comprehended by the number sixty cubits. The number six, in which the world was made, customarily signifies the perfection of good works. We must therefore bear the troubles of our pilgrimage through long-suffering in such a way that, by the merit of good works, we may be able to enter the promised homeland when it appears.

The breadth is determined by the number twenty, on account of the twofold dimension of the same charity, by which we love God and neighbor.

The height is determined by the number thirty, on account of faith in the holy Trinity, who [or, *which*] is one God, to whose vision all the desires of our hope are suspended.

Thus six pertains to the perfection of works, two to love of God and neighbor, and three to hope of the divine vision. Each number is rightly multiplied by ten, because our patience is profitably exercised, our charity usefully kindled, and our hope sublimely carried toward eternal desires only through faith and observance of the Law’s Decalogue.

It should be noted that the thirty cubits of height did not reach to the roof of the temple but only to the lower upper chamber. For it is expressly written in the book of Chronicles that the height was one hundred and twenty cubits (2 Chron. III). The mystery of this matter will be treated more suitably below, when the order of the reading reaches as far as the middle upper chamber and the third.

[Col. 0749D] There was a porch before the temple, twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the temple, and ten cubits wide before the front of the temple. Concerning this porch it is written in the book of Chronicles:

> “The porch before the front, extending lengthwise according to the width of the house, was twenty cubits.”

It is therefore clear that this porch was made on the eastern side of the temple. The temple faced east, as did the tabernacle, and the entrance of the porch was to the east, opposite the entrance of the temple. The Jewish historian Josephus teaches this most clearly:

> “Thus the equinoctial sun, rising in the east, could pour its light upon the ark of the covenant through the straight lines of its rays passing through the three entrances—namely, those of the porch, the temple, and the sanctuary” (*Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3).

Since the temple signifies the holy Church, what more aptly can the porch that stood before and nearer to the temple, and customarily received the sunlight, typify than that part of the Church which preceded the time of the Lord’s incarnation? In it are the patriarchs and prophets, who first received for this world the rising Sun of Justice and bore witness to the Lord born in the flesh—by living, preaching, being born, and dying.

The door of the temple is therefore the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him. Elsewhere he says:

> “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

[Col. 0750B] The door of the porch is the prophetic word, which led those entering by a straight path to the Lord’s door, because it proclaimed the grace of the Lord and Savior by which he was to redeem the world.

The whole structure of the porch therefore signifies the faithful of that time. The door in the porch signifies the teachers who opened to others the light of life and the entrance by which they might come to the Lord.

There was rightly one door, on account of the agreement in faith and love of the truth found among all the saints. This porch was twenty cubits long, according to the width of the temple, because the ancient righteous waited with great patience and long-suffering for the time when the Lord, appearing in the flesh, would bring the new grace of the Gospel to the world. They did not receive the promises themselves, but saw and greeted them from afar.

Its length therefore equaled the length of the temple, because through the long-suffering of a devoted mind they desired the coming of the Church’s expansion in the charity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Although they were still separated in time from the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, they were near through faith and preaching.

At the first front of this most sacred porch were blessed Abel, the first martyr, and Seth, and Enoch, and the other righteous men of the original world. In its innermost recess, as if near the mystical wall of the temple, were the parents of the Lord’s Forerunner, Simeon, Anna, and the others.

[Col. 0750D] Although they were worthy to see his birth, they could not reach the hearing of his teaching or the reception of his mysteries. The porch was rightly ten cubits wide, because although such men had not yet received the words or mysteries of the Gospel that were to be delivered by the Lord, they nevertheless observed the commandments of the Decalogue, having been enlarged in the Lord by perfect love of heart.

## CHAPTER VII. Of its windows and its surrounding chambers
He made slanting windows in the temple. The windows of the temple are the holy teachers and all the spiritual persons in the Church, to whom, when they are lifted beyond themselves in God, it is granted to see more distinctly than others the hidden mysteries of heavenly secrets. When they disclose publicly to the faithful what they see in secret, they are said to be like slanting windows that admit the sun’s light, that is, wider within; for plainly, whoever has received even for a moment the radiance of heavenly contemplation must immediately enlarge the bosom of his heart through greater self-discipline and prepare himself by diligent practice to undertake greater things.

[Col. 0751A] “And he built chambers against the wall of the temple all around, against the walls of the house, around the temple and the sanctuary, and he made side structures all around. The upper chamber had a breadth of five cubits, the middle chamber a breadth of six cubits, and the third chamber a breadth of seven cubits” (Matthew IV).

These chambers were called the pinnacles of the temple in the Gospel, where the Lord was tempted by the devil. We also read that James, the apostle and brother of the Lord, was lifted onto the pinnacle of the temple, from which he might preach to the people (Hegesippus, Book V). We nowhere find in the Scriptures, however, whether it was customary for teachers to sit in these chambers and address the crowd standing below.

The sacramental meaning is therefore clear: these three chambers signify as many degrees among the faithful—namely, the married, the continent, and virgins. They are distinguished by the height of their profession, but all belong, through the fellowship of the same faith and truth, to the house of God and cling to it with steadfast mind.

It is beautifully said that the upper chamber had a breadth of five cubits, the middle six, and the third seven. The uppermost chamber was therefore narrower than the others, the middle one wider than the uppermost, but the lowest was made narrower than the middle, because a higher profession of virtue ought to maintain a higher standard of life [perhaps *ritum … vivendi*, “a manner … of living”]. For all who, having renounced the bond of marriage, have consecrated their virginity to the Lord ought also to display conduct worthy of virginity. Let them abstain from idle speech, anger, quarrels, detraction, immodest dress, feasting, drinking, contention, and rivalry; and, conversely, let them devote themselves to holy vigils, prayers, sacred readings, and psalms, to teaching and almsgiving, and to the other fruits of the Spirit, so that those who hold in their profession the state of the future life—in which they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven—may strive, as far as mortals can, to imitate that state in the present.

But the lowest chamber had greater breadth, because the command is not given to the married, “Go, sell what you have and give to the poor,” but rather: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth (Matthew XIX).

The continent occupy the place between these two: they are as much higher than the married as they are lower than virgins. The most glorious portion of these built the primitive church in Jerusalem, as blessed Luke writes: “The multitude of believers were of one heart and one soul,” and so forth (Acts IV). The history of Saint Stephen testifies that the greater part of them had abandoned marital embraces; for, when it speaks of women who were distinguished by the same religious observance, it calls them not their wives but their widows.

Each chamber had side structures all around it—that is, little towers—so that no one standing or sitting in those chambers could fall to the lower level (Acts VI), as we read happened to King Ahaziah in Samaria. These side structures appropriately signify the daily defenses of divine protection toward us. Concerning them the Psalmist says:

[Col. 0752A] “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm XXXIII).

King Ahaziah of Samaria, who had separated himself from the house of David, did indeed ascend to the upper room, but fell through the latticework. Thus, although heretics or schismatics may seem to climb some height of good action, because they lack the framework of the Church’s unity, they are like those whose side defenses are open and unsolidified: they continually fall back to the lowest depths of vice, and, deprived of divine help, perish through the arrogance of their obstinacy.

By what construction the aforesaid chambers were fastened to the walls of the temple is explained when it is added: “He placed beams in the house all around on the outside, so that they would not be attached to the walls of the temple.”

The beams, then, which strengthened and adorned the house within, were of such length that [Col. 0752B] their ends projected outside—seven cubits in the lowest row, six in the middle, and five in the uppermost. The chambers were assembled upon these projecting ends; they were not fixed into the walls of the temple, but were placed beside the walls upon the beams that extended from them.

Who, then, are typologically signified by the beams of the house that carried the chambers, if not preachers? While they themselves hold an exalted and honorable place in the Church of God, by their preaching they raise the weaker and more fragile from the desire for earthly things and lift them toward the desire and hope of heavenly things. By their intercessions also they help them to persevere in what they have begun.

[Col. 0752C] We read in the book of Chronicles that the beams of the temple, like its other interior parts, were covered with gold. This was plainly done in such a way that those portions of the beams which were inside the temple were covered with plates of gold, while those visible outside were not gilded at all but displayed to everyone the appearance and form of cedar. Upon them the chambers were placed and carried.

The portion of the beams that projected outside signifies the life of the saints insofar as it has been possible for us below to know it. What shone, gilded, inside the temple figuratively announces that glory in which they rejoice in the heavenly homeland, in the sight of their Creator. This golden brightness of the beams was visible only to those who had entered the temple, because only those who have deserved to enter the heavenly kingdom know how great is the abundance of God’s sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him and hope perfectly in him.

[Col. 0752D] Yet when, seeing or reading in the Scriptures about the life, sufferings, and teaching of the saints, we are stirred by their example to do good, we are lifted from the earth as though by the projecting ends of the beams. Although we are not yet able to perceive the saints’ inward glory, nevertheless, from what we have been able to see outwardly, we cling faithfully to the exalted members of the Church.

We may also understand these things of the saints who are still living in this life, whose purity of love, by which they shine secretly in their hearts before the Lord, we cannot behold. Nevertheless, from what they display outwardly by speaking, acting, or suffering, we find assistance for our salvation.

“And when the house was being built of hewn stones,” [Col. 0753A] and so forth. These words properly concern that part of the Church which, after the labors and struggles of this world, has deserved to be brought into eternal rewards. For there only the perfect and spotless enter, those purified from every stain of iniquity. “Nothing unclean, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, will enter that city,” as John wrote in the Apocalypse.

Hammer, axe, and every iron tool are not heard there, because here we are struck by adversities and exercised by the discipline of truth, so that there we may be arranged in places suited to our merit. When chastisement has ceased, we shall be filled with one Spirit and suffused with it, joined to one another solely by the bond of love.

[Col. 0753B] Although it is said, “Noah was a perfect man in his generations,” and, “Blessed are the spotless in the way,” and other statements of this kind, no one can truly walk perfect and without blemish while he remains on the road of this life. “There is no just person upon earth who does good and does not sin.” Nevertheless, according to the measure of the present time, those who will then truly be perfected are called perfect and spotless when, released from the bonds of the body, they have reached that immortal beauty of the house of the Lord and ascended to the place of his glorious dwelling. Then only the perfect and spotless, purified from every stain of iniquity, will enter that city.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the ascent to, or construction of, the middle and third chambers

“The door of the middle side was on the side of the right-hand part of the house,” [Col. 0753C] and so forth. Some, misunderstanding this passage, think that the door of the temple was on the south, failing to observe that, if Scripture had wished to signify this, it would not have said, “The door of the middle side was on the side of the right-hand part of the house,” but would rather have said simply, “The house had a door toward the south.”

It now signifies something quite different. It calls the right-hand part of the house the southern side of the temple. In its eastern part there was a door made at the very corner, close to the ground. Those entering through it immediately ascended by degrees to higher levels, having a route of ascent through the interior of the wall, until by that path they reached the middle chamber, and from the middle chamber the third.

This must be understood to be so, although Scripture does not say it, because those ascending in this way had frequent windows on the south, by whose light they could travel the entire route with certainty and without stumbling.

This place properly refers to the Lord’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. The door of the middle side was on the side of the right-hand part of the house because, after the Lord died on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear. And rightly it was on the side of the house’s right-hand part, because the holy Church believes that his right side was opened by the soldier.

The Evangelist also used an apt word: he did not say “struck” or “wounded,” but “opened,” as though it were the door of the middle side through which a way to heavenly things would be opened for us. Accordingly, he added: “And immediately blood and water came out”—water, by which we are washed in baptism, and blood, by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice.

[Col. 0754A] Through this door there is an ascent for us to the middle chamber, and from the middle to the third. Through faith and the mysteries of our Redeemer, we ascend from our present life in the Church to the rest of souls after death; then, on the coming day of judgment, we shall ascend again from the rest of souls to the immortality of our bodies, entering, as it were, the third chamber by a more exalted advance, so that we may live forever in the great blessedness of both body and soul.

This journey took place invisibly, so that only those who entered knew it, although those standing outside could see the door itself. For the deeds of the faithful in this world, and the celebrations of the sacraments, can also be observed by the reprobate; but no one recognizes the secrets of faith and the inward grace of love unless, with the Lord as guide, he ascends through these things to heavenly realities.

[Col. 0754B] “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.”

It should certainly be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above extended to the middle chamber. Another thirty cubits were then added up to the third chamber, until it reached the portico around the temple, roofed on the south, north, and west, as we learn from Josephus. From there sixty further cubits were counted up to the highest roof of the temple, and thus the entire height of the house, according to the book of Chronicles, was completed at 120 cubits.

The portico before the front of the temple toward the east likewise had the same height of cubits, according to the testimony of the aforesaid volume. This book calls the porticoes around the temple that we mentioned storehouses and chambers.

[Col. 0754C] “David,” it says, “gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico, the temple, the storehouses, the upper chamber, the inner chambers, and the house of the mercy seat.”

There it also mentions the outer buildings that were outside the priests’ court around the temple, when it immediately adds: “and also the plans of all that he had conceived for the courts and chambers around, for the treasuries of the house of the Lord and for the treasuries of the holy things.”

[Col. 0754D] The fact that the entire height of the temple was 120 cubits refers to the same mystery: after the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the primitive Church in Jerusalem received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men.

The number fifteen, composed of seven and eight, is sometimes taken as a sign of the future life, which is now carried on in the Sabbath-rest of faithful souls but will be perfected at the end of the world through the resurrection of immortal bodies. When fifteen is multiplied in triangular form—that is, when all its parts are added together—it produces 120. Therefore the great blessedness of the elect in the future life is fittingly signified by the number one hundred and twenty.

The third chamber of the house of the Lord is fittingly completed in this number, because after the present labors of the faithful and after the future rest received by souls, the complete happiness of the whole Church will be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0755A] The same mystery is equally signified, as we have said, by the fact that, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, the Lord sent the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire to this number of men. Those who had been divided from one another by the diversity of languages he caused to have one speech, through the kinship of their languages, in the common praise of God.

So also the Church, rising in its own time from death and ascending bodily into heaven in incorruption, will be fully and perfectly illumined by the gift of the Holy Spirit, when, according to the Apostle’s promise, “God will be all in all.” Then there will be a full uniting of languages in all for proclaiming the mighty works of God, because with harmonious mind and voice all will praise together the glory of the divine majesty, which they will see present before them.

## CHAPTER IX. That the walls should be covered with cedar and the pavement with fir

“And he built the house and completed it,” and so forth. The ceilings are the chambers, arranged and adorned with great beauty, which are fastened from below to the beams. Since the house of the Lord had been made with three levels of height, it likewise had three ceilings.

[Col. 0755B] What more suitably can we understand by the ceilings than the more exalted righteous in the holy Church? Their work and teaching, set before all as an example, stand out like something raised higher in the distance; and by their intercessions and exhortations they protect the minds of the weak, so that they do not fail in temptations.

These ceilings are rightly described as cedar. Cedar is a tree of entirely imperishable nature, of pleasant fragrance and shining appearance; when burned, its odor drives away and destroys serpents. These qualities correspond to the perfect, whose patience is unconquerable, whose reputation for virtue is exceptional, whose presence is most pleasing to all good people, and whose authority is most steadfast in refuting and confounding those who resist the truth. Both in this life and in the future, they shine with a distinction surpassing that of the other saints.

[Col. 0755C] “And he built a chamber over the whole house,” and so forth. This signifies the little towers that were made around the highest roof of the house, so that no one reaching the higher places might suddenly fall to the depths. Moses commanded that this be done on every house anyone built: “When you build a new house,” he said, “you shall make a wall around the roof, so that blood may not be shed in your house and you become liable when someone falls from it and plunges headlong.”

These chambers or little towers were above called side structures. When it had been said, “He built chambers against the wall of the temple all around, against the walls of the house, around the temple and the sanctuary,” it was immediately added, “And he made side structures all around.”

[Col. 0755D] In these side structures we understood divine protections to be signified. As we still labor in this world and strive upward according to our capacity, they help us daily so that we do not fail. We should understand this passage in the same way, with the distinction that in this life, amid the frequent or continual assaults of the relentless enemy and the obstacles of our frailty, we are repeatedly—or rather constantly—defended from falling by the gift of heavenly mercy.

In the life that the highest roof of the temple signifies, as we have shown above, we are protected by such abundant present grace that we neither wish nor are able to sin any longer, and we are afflicted by no fear of death, pain, or the attacking adversary.

[Col. 0756A] Concerning the Lord’s present helps, as though concerning the side structures of the chambers, the Lord himself says, speaking of his people: “He called upon me, and I will answer him and glorify him.”

Concerning his future grace, by which that heavenly city is illumined, the prophet says to the same city: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem,” and so forth, up to: “He makes your borders peace.”

It is rightly recorded that this chamber on the roof of the house of the Lord was five cubits high, because in that homeland the presence of the divine glory so fills us that our sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch find nothing sweet except loving the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and loving our neighbor as ourselves.

[Col. 0756B] “And he covered the house with cedar wood.” Here he means the highest roof of the house itself—that is, the chamber placed upon the uppermost beams. The temple did not have a ridge at the top, any more than the tabernacle did; rather, it was level, as is customary for all who build houses in Palestine and Egypt.

This same chamber, by which the house and the ceilings were covered, signifies the most distinguished men in the glory of the resurrection, those who by singular holiness have reached the very summit of virtue. Of one of them it is said: “Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew XI). If you wish to know the measure of his greatness, hear what the angel said to his father: “He himself will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke I).

[Col. 0756C] “And he built the walls of the house within with cedar chambers, from the floor of the house to the top of the walls, and he covered them with wood up to the ceilings.” Within, the house was clothed with cedar. Outside, however, the stone itself of which it had been made shone with such brightness that it seemed to be covered with white stone.

According to the mystical meaning, the walls of the temple are the peoples of the faithful, from whom the holy universal Church is constituted. Their extension throughout the world is signified by the breadth of the walls, while their hope and every intention, raised toward heavenly things, are signified by their height.

[Col. 0756D] Or certainly, the height of the wall, which consists of rows of stones placed one upon another, signifies the present condition of the Church. Here the elect are all built upon Christ the foundation; over the course of time they succeed one another in ordered ranks, bearing one another and fulfilling the law of Christ, which is love.

Those who are now instructed by earlier teachers in turn instruct others, like rows placed one upon another. As living stones in the house of God, they are borne by others with such steadfastness that they themselves are also sufficient to bear others, all the way to the last righteous people who will be born at the end of the world. These are placed, as it were, at the summit of the house of God. They are taught and borne by others, but have no others to teach or whose weakness to endure.

They are covered within with cedar chambers when the hearts of the faithful overflow with love of virtue. For just as the nature of cedar, as we have explained above, typologically announces perfect people, so in suitable passages it also appropriately signifies the height of the virtues by which that perfection is reached.

[Col. 0757A] Everything is covered with wood, from the floor of the house to the top of the walls and up to the ceilings, when the elect, from the first rudiments of faith to the perfection of good action and to entry into the heavenly homeland, never cease to labor at good works. From the first righteous to the last, at the consummation of the age, all devote themselves to virtues, so that they may rightly declare: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place.”

“And he covered the floor with fir boards.” How this was done is explained more fully in the book of Chronicles, where it is written: “He also laid the floor of the temple with the most precious marble, with great splendor” (2 Chronicles III).
