[Col. 0757B] It is therefore clear that he did not place the fir boards with which he was to cover the floor directly upon the ground. First he covered it with marble, then placed boards upon it, and added a third covering of gold over these two, as is read in what follows.

Just as the height of the wall, rising upward and reaching to the ceilings, signifies the progress of virtues by which the elect reach the heavenly kingdom—or certainly the choirs of the elect succeeding one another through changing times—so the levelness of the pavement appropriately demonstrates their concordant humility, by which, while they still live in this temporal life, they conduct themselves toward one another socially under the direction of charity.

That pavement was laid with the most precious marble, with great splendor, and the marble was immediately covered with fir boards. This signifies that the life of the righteous must first be fortified in the heart by the firmness of faith and then adorned in action by the breadth of spiritual virtues.

[Col. 0757C] Otherwise, what benefit would the beauty of the most precious marble have, hidden beneath wooden boards, unless it silently signified something mystical and taught that the abundance of good works must be supported by the strength of undefiled faith?

Fir, because of its height and enduring strength, appropriately represents the minds of the elect, who disdain every low desire of the mind, remain always intent upon contemplation of heavenly things, and excel in the virtue of patience.

[Col. 0757D] The sheets of gold placed over the marble and the fir boards signify the breadth of love—love proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. As gold is more precious than other metals, so love, surpassing the other virtues, shines in the temple of God with a singular radiance.

Accordingly, when the Apostle was enumerating, as though the adornment of the pavement, the many good virtues that should be preserved by the humble in heart—“Therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, patience, and gentleness, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another; just as Christ forgave us, so also do you” (Colossians III)—he suddenly added, as though laying a covering of gold on top: “Above all these things, put on love, which is the bond of perfection.”

## CHAPTER X. On the distinct measurement of the temple itself and the sanctuary

“He also built twenty cubits [lacuna] with cedar chambers,” [Col. 0758A] and so forth. He means the western rear part of the temple. The temple had its entrance from the rising of the sun, and at the setting of the sun it had the inner house, that is, the holy of holies.

When he says that the chambers separating the inner house from the outer one were built from the floor up to the higher parts, he does not mean up to the ceilings, which were suspended thirty cubits above the floor, as has already been said, but only up to a height of twenty cubits, as is made clear in what follows.

Above the chambers there remained an open and empty space up to the ceilings, ten cubits in height and twenty cubits in length, corresponding to the breadth of the house. Through this opening the smoke of the incense used to ascend and enter the holy of holies, reaching even to cover the ark of the Lord (Hebrews IX).

[Col. 0758B] In this arrangement of the house of the Lord the mystical figure is evident, and, with the Apostle explaining it, it is clearer than daylight. The first house, into which the priests continually entered to complete the services of sacrifice, is the present Church, where, daily persisting in good works, we offer sacrifices of praise to the Lord.

The inner house, which had been made at the rear of the temple, is the life promised to us in heaven. It is “inner” in relation to this exile-life of ours, because there, in the presence of the supreme King, the perpetual solemn assembly of blessed angels and human beings is celebrated. Therefore the deserving servant is rightly told concerning it: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew XXV). It is later in time, because after the labors of this world we are brought to enter it.

[Col. 0758C] The chambers that divide the two houses from one another are the barriers of heaven. We sigh daily for their opening and, insofar as the Lord grants it, continually knock with devout persistence until they are opened and we may enter. Although we are not yet permitted to enter before the dissolution of our bodies, we nevertheless have an open door of divine mercy through which we may send ahead the incense of our prayers, almsgiving, fasting, and other works.

For this reason the cedar wall of the inner house had a door above, extending throughout it, through which the smoke of the incense could enter. The eyes of the Lord are open over his house night and day, and his ears attend to the prayers of his servants; this extends throughout the breadth of the Church spread across the world.

[Col. 0758D] The altar of incense, which stood in the outer house but near the door of the inner house, was a type of the perfect righteous. They are still held in the world in the flesh, but in every desire they are suspended toward heavenly things. Like incense sending up rising smoke into the holy of holies, they, burning with heavenly love, strike the ears of their Creator with frequent prayers.

The smoke of the incense found a broad open door above, because the purer people are on earth, and the closer they dwell, as it were, to the heavenly homeland, the more quickly they receive from the Lord all that they ask.

The inner house was rightly made twenty cubits long because of the mystery of the twofold love of which we spoke above. In this present life that love illumines the minds of most of the elect only in part; in the homeland, when the works of the other virtues have ceased, it alone will reign forever.

[Col. 0759A] Moreover, the temple itself was forty cubits, before the entrance to the sanctuary. We have said that the temple itself bore the type of the Church; hence it was rightly forty cubits, since this number often signifies the present labor of the faithful, just as fifty signifies future rest and peace.

The commandments are contained in the number ten, and through their observance one reaches life. The same number ten signifies the everlasting life that we desire and for which we labor. The world in which we struggle to obtain that life is square. Thus the Psalmist, foreseeing the Church gathered from the nations, said: “He gathered them from the regions, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm CVI).

Ten multiplied by four makes forty. Therefore the people liberated from Egypt, as a figure of the present Church, were exercised for forty years in the wilderness through many labors, while at the same time they were refreshed with heavenly bread, and thus at last reached the homeland promised long before.

[Col. 0759B] They are exercised by temptations for forty years, so that the bearers of the Church—those who labor throughout the whole world in observing God’s law—may be represented. They are fed with manna from heaven for those same forty years, so that it may be shown that the sufferings the Church endures are to be lightened by hope of the heavenly denarius, that is, eternal blessedness [Latin *levigandae*; perhaps *levandae*, “made lighter”]. There those who now hunger and thirst for righteousness will be satisfied. As that same Church sings to her Redeemer God: “But I, in righteousness, shall appear before your sight; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI).

Thus the people of God are both afflicted by adversities and refreshed by manna, so that the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans XII).

[Col. 0759C] In this figure our Lord also fasted for forty days before the death of his flesh (Matthew IV). For forty days after the resurrection of his flesh he feasted with his disciples, appearing to them with many proofs, speaking about the kingdom of God, and eating with them.

By fasting he showed our labor in himself; by eating and drinking with the disciples he showed his consolation in us. Fasting, he seemed to cry out: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke XXI). Eating and drinking, he seemed to cry out: “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII). Again he said: “I shall see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

[Col. 0759D] For as we travel along the way of the Lord, we both fast from the vanity of the present age and are refreshed by the promise of the future: here we do not set our heart on earthly things; there we feed the heart raised above.

## CHAPTER XI. That the whole house should be clothed with cedar and gold
And the whole house was clad within with cedar, etc. We have said concerning cedar that it signifies the unsurpassable beauty of the virtues. By this wood, then, the whole house of the Lord is clothed within, when the hearts of the righteous shine only with the love of good works. The house of the Lord has its turned moldings and skillfully made joints in cedar boards, when all the elect are joined to one another by the most beautiful bond of charity, so that, although the multitude of the faithful is countless, they are rightly said to have one heart and one soul through the fellowship of a common faith and love (Acts III). For the turned moldings that were applied to the joints of the boards, so that one panel might be made from all of them, are the works of charity by which holy brotherhood is joined together and throughout the whole world is formed into one house of Christ.

This house also has raised carvings, when the works of the virtues of the saints do not conceal themselves, but by open manifestation set before everyone what sort of people they are and what they do, as an example for living. Thus the apostle Paul showed how eminent he was not only by preaching Christ to the nations and suffering for Christ, but also by declaring in the letters sent to the churches how many dangers he had endured for Christ and by how many revelations he had been exalted by Christ. He did so with glorious acknowledgment, and did not hesitate to say to his hearers: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI). What does he display in the house of the Lord except raised carvings, since by the singular height of his virtue he presented himself to all as one to be imitated?

Everything was clothed with cedar boards, and no stone could appear at all in the wall. The stones of the wall or pavement, the boards, and the gold all signify the life of the saints in the Church. Yet they do so with this distinction, when they are placed together: the saints are living stones, cemented to one another by the strength of faith according to one and the same rule; the cedar or fir boards are the saints who, through the breadth of diverse virtues according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, are mutually joined together in one and the same faith; the sheets of gold are the saints who excel above others, possessing the love of knowledge and rejoicing with one another in its most pleasing radiance.

The blessed apostle embraced these three in one sentence when he said: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision is of any value, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. V). The stone represented invincible faith; the cedar, fragrant action; gold, love transcending all things.

The stone wall is clothed with cedar boards when the profession of faith is adorned with good works, so that it may not be judged idle or dead without works. But because the law was written on stone, while the teaching of the Gospel was confirmed through the wood of the Lord’s passion—for this reason also the people were circumcised in the foreskin with stone, whereas we are consecrated on the forehead by the sign of the cross—the stone walls of the temple, or the pavement laid with most precious marble, may suitably represent those who lived faithfully and perfectly under the law. The cedar or fir boards, however, may indicate the righteous of the New Testament, who, wishing to come after the Lord, deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him daily.

And because the righteous of both periods await the common glory of heavenly recompense, a threefold kind of golden sheets is added to the precious stones and woods. Nor should it seem contradictory that above we said that the portico before the temple bore the figure of the faithful of ancient times, that the temple itself represented those who came into the world after the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, and that the inner house signified the joys of the heavenly kingdom, which are given to the righteous of both groups. Now, however, let us say that the stone walls signify the ancient people of God, the cedar paneling the new people, and the golden sheets the rewards of both in heaven, since the same walls of the temple—in the portico, in the temple itself, and in the holy of holies—were constructed in the same manner from stones, wood, and gold. For the same figures are repeatedly presented in diverse things.

It must also be said that both under the law and before the written law there were many who served the Lord according to the law: they did not kill, commit fornication, steal, or bear false witness; they honored father and mother and loved their neighbors as themselves. These belonged to the stone walls of the portico.

There were others who pursued greater perfection: abandoning the affairs of the world, taking up their cross, and following the Lord. As the apostle says: “They experienced mockeries and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were sawn apart, they were tested; they died by the slaughter of the sword; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, distress, and affliction—people of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI). Those who led an evangelical life before the times when the Gospel was revealed—what were they but cedar paneling shining in the portico before the entrance to the temple?

Because the heavenly kingdom receives both groups together, although in distinct dwellings, it is as though the portico of the temple, after the stones and cedar, is covered within with gold. There are now many who are content with the legal commandments mentioned above and believe that it is sufficient for them merely to deserve to come to life. There are others who strive toward perfection: selling everything they possess, they follow the Lord, remembering his promise that such people would receive at the resurrection not only life but also a special honor: “Amen, I say to you,” he said, “that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

The latter belong figuratively to the walls of the temple made of white stone; the former to the cedar paneling. Both await from the Lord the everlasting rewards of light, like sheets of gold with which they may be adorned. In the hidden parts of the temple there are precious stones and boards of aromatic wood, both covered with gold, because both those who walked blamelessly in the law of the Lord and those who perfectly received the grace of the Gospel enjoy eternal life together.

He made the inner sanctuary in the middle of the house, so that he might place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord. This was explained earlier in anticipation, namely, that the inner secret house signifies the homeland of heaven, and the ark of the covenant the Lord the Savior, in whom alone we have the covenant of peace with the Father. After his resurrection, ascending into heaven, he placed at the Father’s right hand the flesh that he had assumed from the Virgin.

The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. It signifies the cedar wall that separated the inner sanctuary—that is, the holy of holies—from the outer building, as we said above. The inner sanctuary, therefore, where the ark was, had twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height—that is, it was square—because in that heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints behold the King in his beauty, only the divine and fraternal grace of charity shines everywhere. This is also asserted by the words that follow: “And he covered it and clothed it with purest gold.” This is plainly to say that the walls of the heavenly city were filled with the grace of charity.

## CHAPTER XII. That the altar of the inner sanctuary should be covered with cedar and gold

He also clothed the altar with cedar. He means the altar of incense that stood before the inner sanctuary, concerning which he adds shortly afterward: “He also covered the whole altar of the inner sanctuary with gold.” From this it may be understood that the same altar was made of stone, clothed with cedar, and then covered with gold.

Figuratively, it signifies the life of the righteous who are perfect, placed as it were near the inner sanctuary, because, having abandoned lowly pleasures, they devote all their care to entering the heavenly kingdom. Hence on this altar the flesh of victims was not burned, but only incense, because such people no longer need to slaughter within themselves the sins of the flesh and the enticements of thought. Instead, through the fire of eternal love, they offer before their Creator the fragrances of spiritual prayers and heavenly desires.

What the stone, cedar, and gold signify on this altar can easily be understood from what was said above. He also covered the house before the inner sanctuary with purest gold and fastened sheets with golden nails.

We have said that the house before the inner sanctuary represents the present Church, where we burn with love for our Redeemer but are not yet able to see him face to face. Accordingly, this house was suitably covered with excellent gold, yet was separated from the inner sanctuary by an intervening wall. The inner sanctuary is called an oracle when either a divine address to human beings or an angelic address is granted together with the revelation of hidden things. Hence the inner sanctuary was rightly made in a hidden place, that is, in the inner house, because in the heavenly homeland both the vision and address of angels, and the very presence of God, will be revealed to us, according to what the Truth himself promises to those who love him: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). And again: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will openly announce to you concerning the Father” (John XVI).

The house before the inner sanctuary is covered with gold because all the perfect righteous in this life—where they cannot yet hear openly about the Father, that is, cannot yet see him openly—adorn faith and the work of righteousness with divine love, through which they may deserve perfect vision and full knowledge of God.

The golden sheets with which the house is covered are the manifold works of piety that pure love displays in service either to its Creator or to the needs of its brethren. The golden nails by which the sheets were fastened are the commandments of charity, or the promises of eternal glory, by which, through the practice and pursuit of virtue, we are held fast by the grace of Christ so that we do not fail.

Accordingly, it is rightly written concerning these same nails in the Book of Chronicles: “He also made golden nails, so that each nail weighed fifty shekels” (II Chron. III). In Scripture the number fifty commonly represents the remission of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal rest: the fiftieth Psalm concerns repentance and remission; the fiftieth year is the jubilee; and on the fiftieth day after Easter the Holy Spirit came and consecrated the primitive Church.

Each nail by which the golden sheets were fastened to the walls of the house of the Lord weighed fifty shekels, because the heavenly words by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works promise us forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal Sabbath-rest in the future.

These, then, are the nails of love. There are also nails of fear, by which beginners and those who have not yet attained perfection mortify the enticements of vices and carnal pleasures. These are the words of truth by whose instruction we learn to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. The prophet wished to possess them when he said: “Pierce my flesh with nails through your fear, for I feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII). Then, having reached perfection, he says concerning the nails of love: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII).

And there was nothing in the temple that was not covered with gold. He also covered the entire altar of the inner sanctuary with gold. The altar has been discussed above; the matter is explained more fully in the Book of Chronicles, where it is stated that the portico before the front of the temple was also gilded within and that the upper chambers were roofed.

The meaning of the mystery is evident: the whole Church, both in this age and in the age to come, abounds above all in the virtues pleasing to God with the gift of charity, and charity alone appears here as uniquely preeminent. The portico before the temple was gilded because the fathers of the Old Testament pleased God through charity. The temple was gilded because that same charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. The inner house was gilded because in the heavenly homeland charity alone reigns.

There it reigns more truly and securely because God himself, who is charity, is seen there; more certainly because the Mediator of God and human beings himself, who alone knows the Father’s secrets, is always seen there as the ark of the covenant.

That the upper chambers were also covered with gold refers to the same meaning. For just as the inner house of the holy of holies, where the ark of the covenant was, signifies the life of the saints in the presence of their Creator and Redeemer, according to the Psalmist’s words, “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX), so the upper chambers signify that this same life is above, that is, in heaven, and not in this world, as the apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God; set your mind on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the making of the cherubim

And he made two cherubim in the inner sanctuary, etc. Cherubim, as the prophet Ezekiel clearly declares, is a term for angelic rank; in the singular it is Cherub, and in the plural Cherubim. Accordingly, in the figures of the cherubim that were made in the inner sanctuary, the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven may rightly be understood.

They are properly said to have been made of olive wood, because the angelic virtues have been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they may never wither away from the love of God. For together with us they share in the one of whom the prophet says in praise of Christ: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV).

Figuratively, they were rightly made of olive wood, since their Creator immediately filled them with the light of heavenly wisdom. Hence he wished them to be called Cherub, which in Latin is interpreted as “multiplied knowledge” or “a multitude of knowledge.”

They were ten cubits high because they enjoy the denarius of eternal life, possessing within themselves the inviolate image of their Redeemer and preserving forever the holiness, righteousness, and truth that they received from their first creation. The denarius consists of ten obols and customarily bears within it the name and image of Caesar. Therefore it most suitably corresponds to the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the holy angels always remain in the image of their Creator, according to which they were made, and where the elect receive again his image, which they had lost by sinning.

“For we know,” he says, “that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits—that is, together they measured ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.

When wings are presented in the figure of holy human beings, they signify their virtues, by which they continually fly toward heavenly things and delight to have their way of life among them. When they are presented in the symbolism of angels, what is more appropriate than the grace of their perpetual and unfailing blessedness, by which they always remain in the heavenly places in the service of their Author? Or certainly, because they are endowed with the lightness of spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish they immediately arrive, as though flying, they are represented here with wings and have also been shown with wings by the prophets.

It is rightly said that one wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other five cubits, because the angelic virtues guard the law of God, which was written in five books, with tireless devotion: loving God and their Lord with all their strength, and loving their neighbors as themselves. “The fullness of the law is love.” Their neighbors are the angelic spirits themselves and the elect human beings who are equally their fellow citizens.

Hence each wing is said to have the same measure, because by the very devotion with which they love one another in God, they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them. Thus the wings together make ten cubits, when the angels rejoice in the presence of their Creator in the manifestation of the twofold love.

The second cherub also measured ten cubits, and the two cherubim were one work. Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of the same charity of which we are speaking, because charity cannot exist among fewer than two. Hence the Savior also took care to send his disciples in pairs to preach, so that he might quietly teach that those who preach the word of faith must hold the virtue of love before all other works.

The two cherubim were of one measure and one work because there is no difference of wills or thoughts in that heavenly homeland, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of the God who is present.

And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple. The cherubim stretched out their wings, and one wing touched one wall, while the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall. Their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple.

It is clear from what has been said above why the cherubim were placed in the middle of the inner temple, since their dwelling is always in heaven. The cherubim stretched out their wings as though to fly because angelic spirits always have their mind prepared for the service of the divine will.

That one wing touched one wall and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall pertains to the ministry of charity that the angels offer us. That their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple expresses the grace of love with which they embrace one another.

It rightly follows: “He also covered the cherubim with gold,” because their Creator both exalted their nature by immortal charity and filled their minds with the light of true love and humility.

It should be noted that when Moses made the tabernacle, he also made two golden cherubim and placed them on the mercy seat above the ark. Solomon added two other, larger cherubim, which he placed in the temple, and beneath whose wings he placed the ark in the middle, together with the mercy seat and the earlier cherubim. Thus it came about that there were two cherubim in the tabernacle but four in the temple.

Both groups, however, belong to one and the same meaning. The work, magnificently executed, was repeated and enlarged by Solomon, so that it might be taught figuratively that, through the Lord’s Incarnation, the Church had multiplied and that the sublimity of the citizens of heaven was to be more widely revealed to the nations. They praise their Creator for the gift of blessedness bestowed upon them in such a way that they also rejoice in our deliverance and introduction into the same blessedness.

They extend their wings toward one another over the ark when they refer every good thing they have received to the praise of the Lord the Savior. They extend their other wings toward the walls of the inner sanctuary when they rejoice to see holy human beings with them and touch, as it were, with the tips of their wings those whom they celebrate as having been companions and imitators of their purity in this life.

They touch the two opposite walls with their wings because they have with them as possessors of the heavenly palace the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. This does not mean that there is a local distinction between the two peoples in that homeland, but that the inward festival of blessedness becomes greater through the fellowship of united brotherhood.

The cherubim therefore extend their wings toward both walls of the inner sanctuary because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they also stir up the righteous of both peoples to praise their Creator by the vision of their glory.

The heavenly hosts rejoice not only in the blessedness of those righteous human beings whom they have within with them; they also diligently care for us, who are still placed outside and cry to the Lord from the depths. Hence it is rightly written concerning these same cherubim in the Book of Chronicles: “They stood upright on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the outer house.”

The cherubim stood upright on their feet because they never departed from the way of truth in which they were placed as soon as they were created. The angels have their faces turned toward the outer house because they desire us, delivered from the misery of this pilgrimage, to come to their fellowship.

Thus they stood upright on their feet and extended their wings toward the walls of the inner sanctuary covered with gold, while keeping their faces turned toward the outer house. The angels preserve their own innocence perpetually and rejoice in the blessedness of holy souls in heaven, yet they do not cease to bring aid to those elect whom they see still wandering on earth, until they also introduce them into the heavenly homeland. For “all are ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. I).

The two cherubim may also signify the two Testaments. These cherubim were made in the inner sanctuary because, in the counsel of divine providence, inaccessible and incomprehensible to us, it was determined before the ages when, how, and through which authors sacred Scripture would be composed.

They were made of olive wood because the divine books were written through men of mercy, whose works of piety were not lacking, and through men enlightened by the anointing of the Holy Spirit. They were made of olive wood because they give us the light of knowledge with the flame of the love of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

They were ten cubits high because they preach that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue, and because they show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the denarius of the everlasting kingdom.

They have two wings, which declare that the Testaments, through adversity and prosperity alike, have continually reached toward heavenly things and arrived there with tireless purpose, and that this is what they show their hearers must do.

One wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other wing of the cherub five cubits, because amid every variation of passing days the saints extend all the senses of their body in the service of their Creator. They keep their eyes always toward the Lord; they desire to hear the voice of his praise and to recount all his wonders; they hold his words sweet in their throats, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to their mouths; they run in the fragrance of his ointments; and, while breath remains in them and the Spirit of God is in their nostrils, they do not speak iniquity with their lips or utter folly with their tongue.

Thus, walking with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, they reach the heavenly denarius that the supreme householder promised to the workers in his vineyard.

The two cherubim were one work because the writers of both instruments served God with one and the same purity of life and devotion of charity, preaching with one harmonious voice and faith of the Lord.

The New Testament narrates the Lord’s Incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the calling of the nations, the rejection of the Jews, and the manifold tribulation of the Church. The Old Testament, if rightly understood, truly foretold that these things would happen.

Both Testaments prove with harmonious truth the coming of Antichrist, the end of the world, the day of the final judgment, the eternal glory of the good, and the punishment of the reprobate.

Therefore the inner wings of the cherubim touched one another over the ark because both Testaments agree in giving equal testimony concerning the Lord. Likewise, their outer wings touched one wall and the other touched the other wall, because the Old Testament was written particularly for the ancient people of God, while the New was written for us, who came to the faith after the Lord’s Incarnation.

We are rightly compared with the second wall, that is, the northern one, because after the cold and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth. For although the primitive Church blossomed chiefly from the Jews, and it is believed that all Israel will be saved at the end of the world, nevertheless very many of the faithful of this time are gathered from the nations to receive the mysteries of the Gospel. To them it has also been divinely granted, with the eyes of their hearts unveiled, clearly to recognize that the letter of the Old Testament is full of the mysteries of evangelical grace.

The faces of the cherubim are turned toward the outer house because the divine books were composed for us who still stand outside and have been saved not in reality but in hope. Their writers, already reigning with the Lord and praising him together in heaven, care for our salvation and intercede with his mercy for our errors.

The cherubim are surrounded with gold because the authority of the Testaments is confirmed by the glorious works of their writers.

When the divine Scriptures became known throughout the world—or when the inner glory of the heavenly hosts became known, since, as we have said, the cherubim signify both angels and the Testaments—many immediately began to convert to the faith and abound in good works. Hence it suitably follows:

## CHAPTER XIV. That the walls should be carved and the pavement clothed with gold

And he carved all the walls of the temple all around, etc. All the walls of the temple all around are all the peoples of the holy Church. Set upon the foundation of Christ, they have filled the whole circuit of the world, and the building of faith, once begun, does not cease daily to increase through a new generation of its members, as though by the addition of precious stones.

These walls are carved with various engravings when “to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of words.”

And, to come to the virtues that we can all possess—love, joy, peace, patience, endurance, kindness, goodness, faith, modesty, self-control, and the other fruits of the Spirit—what are these except the carvings of the temple walls, since they are the ornaments of the minds of God’s people?

The same walls are carved by a lathe when the faithful possess a ready spirit for doing everything that the Lord commands and enduring everything that he permits, saying from the heart in every circumstance that arises: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. XXXIII), and, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Ps. LVI).

They are carved by a lathe when they devote themselves so diligently to virtue that no dangers arising around them and no enticements can turn them from its path. Because turning on a lathe surpasses other crafts in speed and itself supplies the rule by which the work may be completed without error, it suitably signifies the holy life of the saints, which is always ready for the service of the divine will and, trained by long practice in virtue, has learned to fulfill that will without straying into error.

Hence the holy Church, admiring the virtues of her Bridegroom and Redeemer in the Song of Songs, said: “His hands are turned gold, full of hyacinths” (Song V). His hands are turned because, appearing in the flesh, the power and wisdom of God accomplished whatever holiness and miracles he willed without any sluggish delay or winding paths of error. They are gold because what he commanded outwardly by word, divine power brought fully to pass inwardly. They are full of hyacinths because he referred everything he did to the glory of the Father and, through the works he performed, lifted our minds toward the pursuit of heavenly things.

All the walls of the temple, therefore, are carved around with various engravings and by a lathe when the Church throughout the world applies herself with ready devotion to carrying out spiritual virtues, entirely without error. It is rightly said: “And he made in them cherubim and palm trees and various pictures, as though projecting from the wall and emerging from it.”

Solomon makes cherubim on the walls of the temple when he grants his elect to direct their lives according to the rule of the holy Scriptures, in which there is a multitude of knowledge. He makes cherubim when in this world he teaches them, according to their measure, to imitate the chastity of an angelic way of life, which is practiced especially through vigils and divine praises and through sincere love of the Creator and neighbor.

He makes palm trees when he impresses the memory of eternal recompense upon their minds, so that they may deviate less from the stronghold of righteousness, which they always keep before the eyes of their hearts. He makes various pictures, as though projecting from the wall and emerging from it, when he grants the faithful manifold works of virtue: compassion, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, bearing with one another, forgiving one another, and above all having charity, which is the bond of perfection.

When these virtues have become such a habit in the elect that they seem to be naturally implanted in them, what are they other than pictures of the house of the Lord projecting as though from the wall? For they no longer learn the words and works of truth from others externally, but, rooted within, they always bring forth from the depths of their hearts what must be done or taught.

He also covered the pavement of the house with gold within and without. “Within and without” signifies in the inner sanctuary and in the temple itself. We said above that the evenness of the pavement signifies the humble concord of holy brotherhood, where Jews and nations, barbarians and Scythians, free and enslaved, noble and ignoble, all glory in being brothers in Christ and in having one and the same Father, who is in heaven.

No one may doubt the profoundly harmonious humility of the citizens above. Solomon therefore covered the pavement of the house with gold within and without, because our peaceful King filled both angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven perfectly and completely with the gift of love, and separated the citizens of the same heavenly homeland, while they are still pilgrims in this world, from the baseness of the other mortals by the mark of love: “By this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII).

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the entrance of the temple, or of the inner sanctuary
And at the entrance of the inner sanctuary he made little doors of olive wood, etc. What he had first said—“He made little doors of olive wood”—he seems to have wished to explain more clearly when he added: “And two doors of olive wood.” For there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary, but that same entrance was closed by two doors. When they were opened again, the entrance was opened, just as the temple and the portico before the temple had one entrance and no more. This was certainly for a definite mystery: there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God; one entrance is to be hoped for into the present Church through baptism, and one into the heavenly kingdom through the works of faith.

That there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary is attested by what is written below concerning the ark: “And when the poles projected, and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they did not appear any farther outward” (3 Kings 8). Here, unless I am mistaken, it is plainly shown that there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary, directly opposite the ark, which stood in the middle of that same sanctuary. The little doors of its entrance can be understood symbolically in many ways.

For they very clearly signify the angelic spirits, through whose ministry we are introduced into the dwelling of our heavenly homeland. They likewise signify apostolic men, who bear the figure of the apostles and to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given. Having received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, they admit the worthy within the gate of the kingdom, while by excommunicating or anathematizing the obstinate, impure, and proud, they exclude them from entry into eternal life.

The works of righteousness also, through whose merit one reaches the heavenly kingdom, may rightly be symbolically represented by the doors through which one entered the holy of holies, according to what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The keeping of the laws is the perfection of incorruption; and incorruption makes one near to God. But the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom” (Wisdom 6).

All these interpretations fit appropriately with the fact that the same little doors were made of olive wood. For angels and perfected human beings alike display themselves gloriously in the house of God through the fruit of mercy and works of light. Indeed, all the elect open for themselves the entrance to their heavenly homeland through the weapons of light and piety.

There are two little doors, either because holy angels and human beings love God and their neighbors, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love; or because the same gate of life is opened to both faithful peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

The doorposts have five angles, because the palace of heaven will receive not only the souls of the elect, but will also open its doors at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory. For there are five senses of our body, which we also mentioned above: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

Or certainly, each doorpost of the tabernacle was made five cubits high because the entrance to the heavenly homeland is opened only to those who have striven to serve the Lord with all the senses of their body and heart. They serve him with the senses of the body when they do something for him through those same senses; with the senses of the heart when they think soberly, justly, and piously about what they have decided to do through the bodily senses.

“And he carved upon them cherubim, and representations of palm trees, and highly projecting reliefs, and overlaid them with gold.” In Greek, γλυφή is called in Latin caelatura, “carving” or “engraving.” All these things, placed above together with the cherubim in the decoration of the walls of the temple, have already been explained according to our capacity.

There is no need to labor in proving that those who have been entrusted with the care of the faithful and have been given the keys of the kingdom of heaven ought to devote themselves with every diligence to works of virtue, which the Church throughout the world exercises in her holy and perfected members, so that, insofar as they excel others in rank, they may likewise surpass them in the merit of good action.

They bear within themselves the image of the cherubim, that is, an angelic life on earth, insofar as this is possible for mortals, both imitating it in mind and practicing it in deed. They also bear representations of palm trees when, with steadfast intention, they meditate upon the gifts of heavenly reward. For the palm is the adornment of a victorious hand.

They have highly projecting reliefs when they display before all who look upon them the most certain proofs of good works, which no one can interpret in a sinister sense. All these works are covered with golden plates when—as has often been said and must always be said—the radiance of love shines more specially among the great members of the Church than do the other flowers of virtue.

The Books of Chronicles also report that a veil was added to these little doors: “He also made a veil,” it says, “of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and embroidered cherubim upon it.” This was done for the sake of beauty, so that even among the gilded walls silk cloth might gleam. But it was also hung before the ark and the entrance to the inner sanctuary as a sign of the same mystery as the little doors, so that, just as the little doors were opened at appropriate times, the veil too might be unveiled whenever the occasions arrived on which one was to enter the holy of holies.

The continual unveiling of this veil signifies the opening of the Law and of the kingdom of heaven, which has been given to us through the incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Hence, when he was baptized, the heavens were opened, to show that through the baptism which he himself consecrated for us we should enter the gate of our heavenly homeland.

And when he died upon the cross, that same veil was torn in two from top to bottom, so that it might be plainly taught that the legal figures had then reached their fulfillment, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and entry itself into heaven—no longer merely to be foretold prophetically and signified figuratively—were now about to be opened immediately to all who, from the beginning of the world until that time, had passed from the world in faith in the truth.

For on the fortieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, they all ascended to heaven with him; and, with every veil removed, each received mansions of many kinds in the Father’s house according to his merits. For us also, who were still to come, the entrance into that heavenly city and the Father’s house was opened at that same hour.

One ascends into that city only through inward desires for eternal goods, through faith and the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion, through the fervor of sincere love, through the putting to death of carnal desire, and through the daily assistance of the angels.

Accordingly, it is fittingly remembered that the same veil beneath which one entered the inner sanctuary was made of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and that cherubim were woven into it.

Hyacinth, which imitates the color of heaven, is appropriately compared with desire for heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and displays a bloodlike appearance, not improperly signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion. We must be initiated into this sacrament and imitate it by carrying our cross.

Scarlet, which glows with a red color, fittingly expresses the virtue of love. Concerning this, the disciples who had walked with the Lord said in astonishment: “Was not our heart burning within us, while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

Fine linen, which arises from the earth through green growth and, through the long labor of artisans, sheds its natural greenness and is brought to a white appearance, appropriately indicates the chastisement of our flesh. The Apostle Paul commands its innate moisture, as it were, to be dried up when he says: “Put to death therefore your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3).

He shows to what degree of whiteness he wishes this to be brought when he says: “I beseech you, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; let your service be rational” (Romans 13).

Cherubim are woven into the veil and are made from these same four splendid colors when, by the protection of the angels and by the Lord’s gift, we are shielded from the poisonous darts of demons in everything we piously do.

Cherubim are woven into the veil when, in the good things we do, we continually employ the abundance of knowledge, always looking to the divine utterances; and, lest we stray from the path of virtue, we regulate our steps by keeping our eyes fixed upon them.

“And at the entrance of the temple he made doorposts of olive wood, square, and two doors of fir wood on either side; and each door was double, and opened while holding the other.”

Just as the entrance to the inner sanctuary, by which one reached the cherubim at the Lord’s ark, signifies the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, where we hope and desire to be introduced to the vision of our Creator and of the citizens of heaven, so the entrance into the temple symbolically demonstrates the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter the present Church.

The former signifies our entrance into faith; the latter, our entrance into vision. Accordingly, the doorposts of this entrance were appropriately made square, on account of the four books of the holy Gospel, through whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of the truth; or on account of the same number of four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice, upon whose most firm foundation the whole structure of good actions rests.

Prudence is the virtue by which we learn what it is fitting for us to do and how we ought to live. Fortitude is that by which we carry out what we have learned ought to be done. The prophet briefly embraces these virtues in a single verse when he says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Psalm 26). Illumination means that he teaches us what we ought to do; salvation means that he strengthens us to accomplish it.

Temperance is the virtue by which we discern that we must not be found to devote more or less effort than is right to prudence or fortitude. And since everyone who uses prudence, fortitude, and temperance is, without any contradiction, proved to be just, the fourth virtue—justice—follows prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The two doors made for this entrance are the love of God and of one’s neighbor. They are rightly said to have been made on either side because they face one another, so that one can in no way be possessed without the other: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves him who begot him loves him also who has been born of him” (1 John 5). And again, as he says: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (ibid., 4).

Accordingly, the outer door is rightly understood as fraternal love, and the inner door as divine love, because the former comes first in time, while the latter is higher in dignity. One enters through the former into the latter, because from love of one’s neighbor one learns how the Creator ought to be loved.

Each door was double, and opened while holding the other, because in each love there are two things which we must observe above all.

In the love of God, we must have the faith of the truth and the purity of good works. Without faith it is impossible to please God, and faith without works is dead. In brotherly love, however, patience and kindness must be preserved, as the Apostle Paul says: “Charity is patient; it is kind” (1 Corinthians 13). Patient, namely, in bearing the annoyances and injuries of one’s neighbors; kind in forgiving from the heart and doing good to those whose injuries one endures.

The Lord showed what sort of love he wished us to have when he said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6). Forgive the injuries inflicted by those who harm you; give acts of mercy to those whose injuries you release.

He himself desires us to offer such love when he commanded us to say in prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

Each door was double, and each love is perfected in a twofold order. They opened while holding one another because the virtues are joined together and cannot be separated from one another.

For neither can faith exist without works, nor can good works please without faith. Nor is it sufficient merely to endure injuries if the one who endures them, although able, refuses also to provide what the person he tolerates needs. Nor is it enough for someone who possesses the world’s resources to give to a needy neighbor if he does not sincerely forgive the annoyances that neighbor may perhaps have inflicted upon him.

What is said of both doors—that one opened while holding the other—does not signify a separation of spiritual virtues from one another. Rather, it indicates that through the joining of these virtues the entrance into the holy Church is opened more widely for us, so that the more abundantly we possess them, the more truly we are associated with the assemblies of the saints.

Similarly, the division of the Red Sea, through which God’s people escaped the pursuing Egyptians, did not signify the division of the one baptism, but rather the opening by which, after all sins had been extinguished, we pass over to the shore and into the solitude of the virtues.

Or the door that held the other is opened when, through the ministry of the preacher, it is discerned what properly pertains to knowledge of the faith and what pertains to purity of life—although neither of these can be separated from its connection with the other. There is indeed a distinction between enduring the evils of one’s neighbors and commending our good things to them, even though these qualities most certainly remain inseparable in one and the same heart of the perfect.

It should be noted that, at the entrance of the inner sanctuary, two doors are said to have existed, but they are not said to have been double. At the entrance of the temple—that is, of the former house—there were two doors, and each was double, because in the present Church we must enter and live a life in which we preserve love of God and neighbor through faith and action, through patience and kindness.

In the future life, however, where we shall see God and our neighbors in the light of eternal blessedness, we shall enjoy that same twofold love without any labor at all, indeed in great rest, amid an abundance of divine sweetness.

Accordingly, the entrance of the inner house appropriately had two doors, but these were simple. Faith is not necessary there, where we shall see in manifest light all that we now believe and hope. The labor of works is not necessary where we shall be given an everlasting reward for the things over which we labor here. Patience is not necessary where no one inflicts any adversity. Nor is generosity of kindness necessary where no one lacks what is needed.

We have discussed these matters concerning the figure of the doors according to our limited ability, following in the footsteps of the Fathers. In truth, according to the form of the structure, provision was made for the sake of beauty that there should be two doors in one and the same entrance to the temple.

For it was necessary that the walls of the house, which were twenty cubits high, should also have some thickness. The doors were attached at the outer edge of this thickness, so that each door was level with the wall; and whether someone stood inside or outside the temple and looked at the door, it would appear to him to be in every respect a single wall.

Likewise, since the cedar wall was twenty cubits in length and height, it too necessarily had considerable thickness. Therefore, two doors were made at its entrance, so that on either side—that is, inside and outside—the door would be level with the wall. And because the door had the same pictures as the wall, the wall would truly appear to be one continuous expanse in every respect: one part presenting the beauty of the structure, the other prefiguring the dispensation of the mystery.

What follows after the description of the temple doors—“And he carved cherubim and palm trees and highly projecting carvings, and overlaid everything with plates of gold, fashioned square and according to the rule”—has already been explained. For paintings or carvings were made both on the walls of the house and on the doors and in the interior of the Church.

The reason for the figure is clear: why the first door of the temple receives the very same pictures and carvings, and the same cherubim, as the inner door. It is because the same mysteries of faith, hope, and charity are received in an exalted manner by all who are exalted and perfected. And all the elect fully perceive these mysteries in heaven through the divine vision; yet they are handed down to catechumens and beginners through their respective teachers, to be learned and confessed, so that, having been initiated into the sacred mysteries, they may eventually attain to receiving what they have piously believed.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the courts of the house of the Lord

“He built the inner court with three courses of hewn stones,” etc.

He speaks briefly of the inner court and seems entirely to pass over the outer court. Yet in the Books of Chronicles mention is made of both, where it is written: “He also made the court of the priests and the great basilica, and doors in the basilica, which he covered with bronze” (2 Chronicles 4).

The inner court, which is called the court of the priests because the priests and Levites ministered there, was surrounded on every side by the temple. But on the eastern side, where the entrance to the temple was located, it was separated from the temple by a much greater distance than on the other three sides, because it was on that side—that is, at the front of the temple—that the sacred ministries were performed.

There stood the bronze altar for offering sacrifices to the Lord; there were the ten basins for washing those same sacrifices; and there stood the bronze sea for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they entered to minister.

This court, as Josephus relates, was three cubits high, so that it might prevent outsiders from entering the temple and signify that only priests were permitted to do so. There was also a gate on the eastern side, as far as which the people brought their sacrifices and offerings, to be received from there by the priests and carried to the altar.

Concerning the outer court, which the Books of Chronicles call the great basilica, Josephus writes as follows:

“Outside this temple he built another court, made in the form of a square, raising very large and broad porticoes; and he established in it lofty and spacious gates on the four quarters of the world, each of which faced one of the four winds at the four corners, and there he placed bronze doors” (Book 8).

A little later he says:

“Into this sanctuary all the people who possessed purification and observance of the lawful rites entered.”

Cassiodorus the senator distinguished these porticoes in the Pandects, as he himself records in his exposition of the Psalms, in three tiers.

He placed the first tier outside the court of the priests, extending in a square on every side; the second in the same manner outside the inner porticoes, running all around in a circle; and the outermost likewise on every side around the earlier porticoes.

Thus the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold protection of buildings. A pavement of marble was laid under the open sky between the individual buildings, while the inner walls of the structures—that is, those facing the temple—were made between the columns, and the outer walls were solid.

In this way the whole structure of the temple was rationally divided according to the variety of its levels. When the high priest entered the holy of holies, the priests who had been purified were in the temple itself; in the court of the priests were the priests who had not been purified, together with the Levites and singers; in the innermost court of the great basilica stood the purified Jewish men, praying under the open sky if the weather was clear, and taking refuge in the nearest porticoes if there was a storm; in the outer court were the purified Jewish women; and in the outermost court were Gentiles and Jews who had recently come from among the Gentiles, until the sixth day of purification.

We have briefly noted these matters, as we found them distinguished in Cassiodorus’s account, since we believe that he learned them from the ancient Jews and that so learned a man would not have wished to set before readers as an example something which he had not first recognized as true.

These are the places mentioned by the final Psalm of Degrees, which begins as follows: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 113).

In these porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets preached the word to the people; in these the Lord and the apostles preached. In one of them the Lord was sitting and teaching when the adulterous woman, whom the Pharisees who were testing him had brought to be judged, was presented to him.

In these he found those who were selling and buying oxen, sheep, and doves, and he drove them from the temple with their merchandise. In these Peter and John found a lame man and healed him, then led him inside with them to pray.

In these the whole multitude of the people was praying when the angel appeared at the altar of incense to Zechariah, who was offering incense, and instructed him fully concerning the birth of the Lord’s forerunner.

Yet these courts, together with their porticoes, could not conceal the view of the temple from those looking at it from a distance, because the place where the temple stood was much higher than the place where the porticoes had been founded. For Josephus writes:

“The outermost structures of the courts, although they had been raised to four hundred cubits, nevertheless reached as far as the summit of the mountain on which the temple had been built” (ibid.).

We have thought it right to make this account of the temple’s structure known to the diligent reader. But wherever sacred Scripture has seen fit to report something concerning these matters, let us seek the figures of the mysteries; in the remaining details, let us make simple use of historical knowledge.

The building of the temple within the court of the priests expresses the life of perfected and exalted men in the holy Church—those, namely, who both draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and customarily show the way of salvation to others by word and deed.

The priest receives his Latin name from the fact that he ought to provide sacred guidance to those who are lesser. In Scripture, this name is understood mystically to refer not only to ministers of the altar—that is, bishops and presbyters—but to all who, through the height of an upright way of life and the excellence of saving doctrine, benefit not only themselves but themselves and many others, while presenting their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.

For the Apostle Peter was speaking not only to bishops or presbyters, but to the whole Church, when he said: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (1 Peter 2).

The ancient people of God were also marked by this honor of dignity, when he himself said to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the house of Jacob, and you shall announce it to the children of Israel” (Exodus 19). And a little later: “And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.”

The great basilica, however, which stood outside the court of the priests, where the whole multitude of the people used to worship or gather to hear the word, figuratively indicates the life and conduct of carnal people in the holy Church, concerning whom the Apostle says: “And I, brethren, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They are appropriately represented by the great basilica because, without any doubt, the number of such people in the holy Church is much greater than the number of the perfect. But to the extent that they surpass the others in number, they fall short of them in merit.

Accordingly, although this great basilica receives many, it does not admit them into the inner parts of the gilded temple, nor to the service of the altar, nor even into the court of the priests. For although all who are still carnal and weak in the Churches belong, on account of the merit of a chaste faith and piety, to the lot of the elect, they are nevertheless far from equaling those who confidently say: “For I dare not speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed” (Romans 15). And again: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4).

The common people did indeed approach as far as the court of the priests. They brought their sacrifices to its gate, where the priests received them, and they followed with their eyes the sacrifices offered upon the altar. When the temple was opened, they also directed their gaze toward it from a distance, but they did not have permission to enter the court of the priests.

Nevertheless, from below they cried out to the Lord, because the simplicity of carnal people in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer the vows of piety that they are able to offer.

They direct their eyes from afar toward the temple of God when they diligently rejoice in learning and imitating the life of exalted people, and when they embrace those whom they cannot follow in virtue with the affection of pious reverence.

They see the sacrifices of the priests consumed upon the altar by the sacred fire because they recognize that the Lord graciously receives the great rewards of works through the Holy Spirit.

They also bring their own sacrifices to the court of the priests to be offered to the Lord through them when, by doing the good things of which they are capable, they are strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and teachers and commended through their intercession.

They likewise offer their sacrifices to the priests to be commended through them to the Lord when, with a view to the highest reward, they give to the holy poor what they themselves possess in abundance, as the Lord admonishes and says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

And he says: “Whoever gives one of these least ones of mine a drink, even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matthew 10).

Thus one and the same fire of God’s altar consumes the sacrifices of both when the Lord, by his own judgment and reward, deems worthy the almsgiving of the rich, by which they have ministered to the saints, together with the great virtues of those same saints.

The multitude of believers who, having abandoned their possessions, served the Lord with one heart and soul is itself the temple of God, and the place specially consecrated to him within the court of the priests.

The great basilica, moreover, and those praying in it in a circle around the court of the priests, bear the figure of those who at that time were believing from among the Gentiles in Syria, Antioch, and the other provinces and cities. The apostles and the elders who were in Jerusalem imposed no greater burden upon them than that they should abstain from sacrifices offered to idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from fornication.

Yet they wished the poor among the saints who were in Jerusalem to be sustained by their offerings, so that, by ministering their material goods to them, they might become participants in their spiritual goods.

Barnabas and Paul, together with their companions, who received their offerings and carried them to Jerusalem, are the priests who received the offerings and brought them to be consecrated upon the Lord’s altar, because they brought the devotion of those donors so that the saints might pray for them.

The court situated between the place of the common people and that of the priests signifies the division which distinguishes carnal people in the holy Church—those who have only recently begun the way of righteousness—from the citadel of the perfect, not by the lot of election but by the measure of their merits.

The carnal believe that it is enough for them to possess faith, hope, and charity, together with purity of works. The perfect possess these things as well, but in addition they labor in preaching the word; they give all their possessions to the poor; they devote themselves to vigils, fasts, hymns, spiritual songs, and sacred readings; they endure persecutions and dangers for the sake of righteousness; and they carry out with willing devotion the other things which Paul boasts that he did with his companions.

Accordingly, it is fittingly remembered that the court of the priests was built with three courses of hewn stones and one course of cedar wood.

The three courses of hewn stones are faith, hope, and charity. They are rightly called hewn or polished because careful instruction is certainly necessary, so that each person may discern how he ought to believe, what he ought to hope for, and what he ought to love.

The one course of cedar wood is good action itself, displayed without the corruption of pretense. Without this addition, faith, hope, and charity cannot be genuine.

As has often been said, cedar wood signifies perseverance and the reputation of pious action on account of the excellence of its fragrance and the incorruptible strength of its nature.

All the elect who desire to please God through faith, hope, love, and action ascend as far as this court. The perfect rise above it through the excellence of their merits when they advance to such a height of virtue that they can say to their hearers: “Be imitators of us, as we also are of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4). And they glory and say: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more worldly matters?” (1 Corinthians 6).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### How many years the temple was built

“In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded,” etc.

The meaning of the allegory is clear as to why the house of the Lord was built over seven years. The holy Church is constructed from the souls of the elect throughout the entire period of this world, which is completed in the course of six days; and at the end of the world it brings its own growth to completion.

Or certainly, it is built over seven years to signify the spiritual grace through which the Church receives the very gift of being the Church. Isaiah enumerates seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11), without which no one can become faithful, preserve the faith, or arrive through the merit of faith at the crown of righteousness.

But the statement that in the seventh year, and in the eighth month of it, the house of the Lord was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings pertains to the future age and the day of judgment. Then the holy Church will have reached such perfection that nothing further can be found which could be added to it.

For then it will possess what that pious suppliant desired and asked of the Lord when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

It is established that the day of judgment is often expressed figuratively in Scripture by the number eight, because it follows this age, which runs through seven days. Hence the prophet gave the title “For the eighth” to the psalm which he sang out of fear of that same strict Judge, beginning as follows: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury,” and so forth (Psalm 6).

But a question arises which should not be dismissed: how can the house of the Lord be said to have been completed in the eighth month in all its work and in all its furnishings, when it is read below that its completion and dedication were finished in the seventh month?

It is not incredible, however, that Solomon, building the temple over seven years, completed it in the eighth month of the eighth year, or that he deferred its dedication until the seventh month of the ninth year.

Rather, it seems more plausible that the house was built over seven years and seven months, so that the solemnity of the dedication was celebrated in that seventh month and, as the Books of Chronicles report (2 Chronicles 7), Solomon dismissed the people to their tents on the twenty-third day of that month. Thus, after one week, when the eighth month arrived, the house of the Lord was found to be complete both in all its works and in its dedication, which had previously been completed.

Unless perhaps we should think that, after the temple had been dedicated, some additional furnishings for its ministries were added until the beginning of the eighth month, the king hastening the work so that the temple might be dedicated entirely in the seventh month, which was wholly solemn. In this way both statements would prove true: the temple was completed in all its work and furnishings in the eighth month, and it was dedicated in the seventh month.

“King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre, the son of a widow woman from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian, a worker in bronze, and full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, to perform every work in bronze. When he had come to King Solomon, he performed all his work” (3 Kings 7).

This too was done for the sake of a mystery. The Tyrian craftsman whom Solomon took as his assistant signifies the elect ministers of the word from among the Gentiles.

He is aptly called a craftsman because he was the son of an Israelite widow. In this person the Church of the present age is sometimes signified. Her husband, namely Christ, tasted death, rose again, and, ascending into heaven, meanwhile left her as a pilgrim on earth.

There is no need to labor in explaining how the holy preachers are sons of this widow, since all the elect individually confess that they are sons of the Church. Moreover, a special promise concerning these preachers of the New Testament is made by the prophet, who says: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them as princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44).

Hiram performed all the work for Solomon because, while the holy preachers faithfully devote themselves to the ministry of the word, they perform the work of God. By speaking outwardly, they open the way of truth to those whom God himself, by illuminating them inwardly, has predestined to eternal life.

“I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

He performed the work in bronze because the diligent teacher seeks to entrust the word to those who desire to receive it piously and guard it perseveringly, and who also rightly strive to spread more widely among others, by preaching, whatever they themselves have learned.

For it is well established that bronze is an extremely durable metal and altogether resonant.

## CHAPTER XVIII
### On the bronze columns
And he cast two bronze columns, etc. These are the columns of which Paul says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Galatians 2). By these words he seems, as it were, to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they signified and why two were made. For they signify the Apostles and all spiritual teachers, strong indeed in faith and works, and raised upright through contemplation toward heavenly things. They are two so that, by preaching, they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church [Col. 0780A].

They stood in the portico before the temple doors, and by their ornament and beauty wonderfully adorned its entrance on either side. The door of the temple is the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him; and as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). The columns stand before this door, placed on either side, when the ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, so that whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of knowledge of the Law or from the harshness of paganism, he may have teachers ready to show him the way of salvation both by word and by example.

Or certainly, because the following is written about these columns in the book of Chronicles: “He placed the columns in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left” (2 Chronicles 3) [Col. 0780B], two columns were made and arranged in such a way that they teach us to keep before the eyes of our mind the entrance into our heavenly homeland both in prosperity and in adversity. For this reason Paul—truly a most excellent pillar of the house of the Lord—earnestly urges us by his own example and that of his companions to be protected on the right and on the left by the weapons of righteousness, so that, neither delighted by prosperity nor broken by hardships, we may in no respect turn aside from the royal road of life, by which we must journey toward the heavenly inheritance promised to us (2 Corinthians 6).
