It should certainly be noted in the passage from Chronicles that I have cited that the same portico of the temple was also called the vestibule of the temple; and that where we read in the prophets, “The priests prayed between the vestibule and the altar,” it should be understood as “between the portico and the altar” [Col. 0780C].

It is rightly recorded that each column was eighteen cubits high. For three times six makes eighteen. That three pertains to faith, because of the Holy Trinity, and six to action, because the world was made in that number of days, is perfectly clear. Three is multiplied by six when the righteous person, who lives by faith, increases the knowledge of pious belief through the execution of good works. A column before the temple doors is eighteen cubits high when every outstanding preacher openly makes known to all that we can attain the joys of the heavenly life only through faith and works of righteousness.

This may also be understood more profoundly: the name Jesus among the Greeks begins with this number [Col. 0780D]. For the first letter of the name Jesus signifies ten among them, and the second signifies eight. The columns of the house of God are appropriately eighteen cubits high because the holy teachers—or rather, all the elect—direct their good lives toward this end: that they may deserve to see their Creator face to face. For they will have nothing further to seek when they have reached him who is above all things.

And a measuring line twelve cubits long surrounded each column. The twelve-cubit line is the standard of apostolic teaching. It surrounds both columns when every teacher sent to preach either to Jews or to Gentiles takes care to do and teach only what the holy Church has received and learned through the Apostles. For if anyone wishes to live or preach otherwise, and prefers either to disregard apostolic decrees or to establish new things according to his own will, such a person is not a column suited to the temple of God. By refusing to follow apostolic statutes, he fails to correspond to the twelve-cubit line, as though through the thinness of his sluggishness or the thickness of his swollen pride.

The Lord surrounded the columns of his temple with these lines when he said to the disciples sent to teach and baptize all nations: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28). Whoever observes and teaches everything that the Lord commanded the Apostles, adding nothing else and omitting nothing of it, is truly a column in the house of God, which is the Church, and a pillar of the truth, such as the Apostle Paul warned Timothy that he should be [Col. 0781A].

But because the life or speech of teachers cannot be firm [Col. 0781B] without knowledge of the Scriptures, it is appropriately added: “He also made two capitals to be placed upon the tops of the columns, cast in bronze. One capital was five cubits high, and the other capital was five cubits high.”

The heads of the columns—that is, their uppermost parts—are the innermost thoughts of faithful teachers. By the thoughts devoted to God, all their works and words are directed, just as the limbs are directed by the head. The two capitals placed upon these heads are the two Testaments, to whose meditation and observance holy teachers submit themselves entirely in mind and body.

Thus it is fitting that each capital was five cubits high, because the Mosaic [Col. 0781C] Law is contained in five books, and the whole sequence of the Old Testament encompasses five ages of the world. The New Testament proclaims nothing other than what Moses and the prophets had foretold would be proclaimed. Hence the Lord said to the Jews who clung uselessly to the letter of the Old Testament and rejected the grace of the New: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5).

Moses wrote about God in many things figuratively, and most plainly when he recounts the promise made by the Lord to Abraham: “In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” He also says directly to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him according to everything that he will speak to you.”

The voice of the Father from heaven reminded the disciples of this prophecy when, as the Lord appeared to them in glory between Moses and Elijah on the holy mountain, it resounded, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Luke 9) [Col. 0781D].

Thus, through the wondrous harmony of divine working, the grace of the New Testament was first hidden within the veil of the Old, and now the mysteries of the Old Testament have been disclosed through the light of the New. In this way, the capital of each column is five cubits high, because it is evident that within the Old Testament—whose mysteries are prefigured either in the five books of the Law or fully encompassed in the five ages—the grace of evangelical perfection is also implanted.

Thus every outstanding preacher, whether sent to the Jews or to the Gentiles [Col. 0782A], confirmed by the harmonious testimony of the divine words, preserves without error the contest of faith and uprightness of conduct, and knows how, while teaching, to bring forth from his treasure things new and old.

Not only do the Testaments sing in harmony with one another through their account of the divine mysteries, but all the elect whose names are contained in the books of those Testaments, endowed with one faith and joined to one another by the same love, are also united. Hence the account of the capitals’ construction appropriately continues: “And each capital was cast in the form of a net and chains wonderfully woven together.”

This is written in the book of Chronicles: “He also made something like chains in the sanctuary and placed them upon the tops of the columns” (2 Chronicles 3). The appearance of chains [Col. 0782B], the likeness of a net in the capitals, is the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints, of which it is sung to the Lord in the Psalms: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44)—that is, clothed in the splendor of love and enveloped in the variety of diverse spiritual gifts.

Or certainly, the manifold interweaving of chains and the spreading out of the net indicate the many different persons among the elect. When they faithfully listen and obey the words of the holy preachers and cling to them, they offer to all who see them the marvelous sign of their unity, like little chains placed upon the tops of the columns.

These chains were wonderfully woven together because it was accomplished by the astonishing grace of the Holy Spirit that the lives of the faithful—so greatly separated from one another in place and time, rank and condition, sex and age—should nevertheless be united with one another by one and the same faith and love [Col. 0782C].

That this fraternal union of the righteous, separated in place and time, is effected through the joining of spiritual gifts is also shown by the words that follow, when the account of the capitals’ construction adds: “Seven network panels on one capital, and seven network panels on the other capital.”

The number seven ordinarily signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as John attests in the Apocalypse. After saying that he saw a Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes, he immediately explained: “These are the seven Spirits of God, sent into all the earth” (Revelation 1). The prophet Isaiah explains this more openly when, speaking of the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, he says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah 11) [Col. 0782D].

Thus there were seven network panels on each capital, and the fathers of both Testaments received the grace of the one and the same sevenfold Spirit in order to become elect.

“And he made the columns and two rows around each network, to cover the capitals.” There were indeed two rows of network around the circumference of the capital, but each row proceeded with a sevenfold number of panels until, after circling the capital, it returned to itself again, forming a circle.

The meaning of this mystery is not hidden: the reason there were two rows of network is that the virtue of love has a twofold distinction, since we are commanded to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves [Col. 0783A]. But each of those rows has seven network panels because neither God nor our neighbor can be loved without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The truthful saying remains: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts,” not through our merit, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” Wherever the love of God is present, there the love of our neighbor is also poured into the hearts of the faithful, because one can in no way be possessed without the other.

These networks were made to cover the capitals—that is, to surround them on every side and all around—because every page of Sacred Scripture, when rightly understood, proclaims throughout the grace of love and peace. The capital is the divine utterances; the networks are the bonds of mutual love. The capitals are covered by the networks when the sacred words are, so to speak, shown on every side to have been restored through the gift of love. For love is also widely evident in those passages of Scripture that we do not understand [Col. 0783B].

It is fittingly added concerning these networks or capitals: “Which were above the top of the pomegranates.” Pomegranates, whose nature is to enclose many seeds within a single outer rind, are aptly placed as a figure of the holy Church, which, protected by the unity of Catholic faith, customarily gathers within itself countless hosts of the elect.

They may also signify the righteousness and character of each individual, who, like one enclosing many seeds within a single rind, takes care to surround the many signs of spiritual thoughts and virtues with the firm protection of faith and humility, lest they scatter [Col. 0783C].

It was entirely appropriate, according to the mystery, that the tops of the columns were surrounded all around by pomegranates, because holy teachers must recall the lives of the faithful who came before them and always fortify their own actions and words on every side by their examples, lest they err by living or teaching in any way contrary to their rule.

Just as the remarkable joining of the networks signifies the unity of the faithful, which exists in the bond of peace, so the pomegranates also typologically proclaim that same unity, which restrains countless peoples throughout the world within the one rule of the Catholic faith.

Or certainly, the marvelous interweaving of the networks demonstrates the visible harmony of all the faithful, while the arrangement of the pomegranates expresses the inward virtues of the soul, which cannot be seen by others at all: patience, humility, kindness, modesty, and other qualities of this kind [Col. 0783D]. The beautiful outer surface of the fruits is visible, but the abundance of seeds enclosed within is not, just as the pious activity of the saints is openly displayed to all, while the grace of faith, hope, love, and the other good qualities of the soul that exist within cannot be seen.

Since it was said that the networks covered the capitals that were above the top of the pomegranates, the order of the work seems to indicate that the pomegranates were made around the capitals on their lower side, and that the networks arose from those same pomegranates, covering part of the capitals. The symbolic meaning is clear: the networks were attached above the top of the pomegranates [Col. 0784A], and both belong almost to one meaning, whether of spiritual persons or of virtues.

For we know that virtues arise from virtues, and that the saints go from strength to strength until the God of gods is seen in Zion. Hence the Apostle says: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Romans 8).

Within the universal fellowship of the elect, too, the persons of the righteous succeed one another in various ways. The lesser gladly cling faithfully to the footsteps of their elders and predecessors, and rely upon their words or writings, lest they should fall into error.

The networks are therefore placed above the top of the pomegranates when the harmony of love is added to perfected works. And when the life of the saints shines through both gifts of virtue—namely, action [Col. 0784B] and love—the chainwork of the networks, added above, accompanies it like a circle of pomegranates around the capitals of the column.

And because all the gifts of present virtues look toward the glory of eternal reward, which has been promised and bestowed upon us through the Gospel, it is appropriately added: “The capitals that were above the tops of the columns were fashioned in the portico like the work of a lily, four cubits.”

What is signified by lilies if not the brightness of the heavenly homeland and the loveliness of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of immortality? What is signified by four cubits if not the evangelical proclamation, which promises us entrance into that eternal blessedness and shows the path by which it may be reached?

Thus, when the holy teachers display to us the promised thresholds of the heavenly kingdom in the four books of the holy Gospel, they exhibit, as it were, upon the tops of the columns a lily-work of four cubits [Col. 0784C].

Here it should be noted according to the literal sense that, when the lily-work on the capitals is said to be four cubits, without adding whether this refers to breadth or height, it is left to the judgment of the reader to understand whether it should be taken as height or breadth.

It is nevertheless completely certain that the column surrounded by a twelve-cubit cord had a thickness of four cubits. For every circle has three times as much circumference as it has space across its diameter. Accordingly, since the bronze sea had a diameter of ten cubits, as we read below, it consequently had a circumference of thirty cubits [Col. 0784D].

But since the lily-work is said to have been four cubits, whether it indicates breadth or height, the symbolic meaning is nonetheless clear: it was only through the Gospel that the world heard that greatly desired voice saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (Matthew 3).

What follows—“And again, there were other capitals at the tops of the columns above, according to the measure of the column, facing the networks”—means by “according to the measure of the column” that they were of as much height as the column, although the precise height of the column is not reported.

Whatever the nature and size of these capitals may have been—for Scripture does not clearly specify their measure—they appear to have been fashioned in the manner of lilies. If one wishes to seek a mystical meaning in their construction, they may appropriately signify the exaltation of the everlasting kingdom, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” which God has prepared for those who love him [Col. 0785A].

After the four-cubit lilies, other capitals were placed, whose height is not stated, because in the Gospel we read many things about heavenly blessedness: that the pure in heart will see God; that they will be equal to the angels of God; that they will neither marry nor be given in marriage; that they will no longer be able to die; that wherever Christ is, there his ministers will also be; that he will reveal himself to them; that he will openly announce the Father to them; and that no one will take their joy in seeing him away from them.

But the actual appearance of the things we have mentioned, and the actual condition and way of life of that heavenly homeland, is evident only [Col. 0785B] to those who have deserved to enter it, its citizens. Thus it is fitting that the construction or height of these capitals above the lily should be incomprehensible to earthly beings, thereby suggesting the character of the heavenly dwelling.

Yet this is by no means hidden: all there enjoy the common happiness of the divine vision, while each person enjoys it more sublimely in proportion as he has purer eyes of heart with which to see God.

The one who said, “He blessed all who fear God, the small together with the great,” also said, “For you will repay each one according to his works” (Psalm 113). There will therefore be a common blessing for all the elect. Nevertheless, according to the differing quality of their works, there are many dwellings of the blessed in the one and same eternal house of the Father in heaven.

I believe that this was also mystically signified in the structure of these columns [Col. 0785C] when it is said: “And again, there were other capitals at the top of the columns above, according to the measure of the column, facing the networks.”

Capitals are made above according to the measure of the column when the holy teachers—or rather, all the righteous who follow in the footsteps of those teachers—receive the rewards of heavenly recompense according to the merits of their pious activity.

The same capitals are also made facing the networks because, in proportion to the manner of the love by which the holy brotherhood was joined to one another in this life, so also it will be joined in heaven, in the presence of its Creator, through the fellowship of the citizens above.

That this same fellowship of the heavenly citizens is granted to the faithful of both peoples is rightly added: “There were two hundred pomegranates arranged in rows around the second capital” [Col. 0785D].

We have said that the pomegranates represent the whole of the holy Church. The number one hundred, which is the first number reached by the right hand, is sometimes accustomed to signify the life of eternal blessedness.

Here this number of pomegranates around the second capital is doubled, to signify mystically that the people of both Testaments, to be united in Christ, are to be brought into the crown of eternal life.

The following passage concerning the Apostles who were fishing after the Lord’s resurrection accords with this figure. When they saw him standing on the shore, it is written: “They were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits, dragging the net of fish” (John 21).

By the two hundred cubits, the disciples draw toward the Lord a net full of large fish, showing on the shore the effect of his resurrection, when the holy preachers entrust the word of faith to both Jews and Gentiles, and lead the elect of both peoples—drawn out from the waves of the present age—to the future glory of peace and immortality [Col. 0786A].

The circuit of the second capital therefore has two hundred pomegranates arranged in rows when the sublimity of the heavenly kingdom gathers the elect of both peoples into one citadel of blessedness.

“And he set up the two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the column on the right, he called it by the name Jachin, that is, ‘firmness.’ Likewise, he raised the second column and called its name Booz, that is, ‘in strength.’”

As we said above, the right-hand column represents those teachers who established the primitive Church in Jerusalem; the second represents those who were appointed to preach to the Gentiles [Col. 0786B].

Or certainly, the right-hand column signifies those who foretold in prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second signifies those who testify that he has already come and redeemed the world by his blood.

The two columns were appropriately designated by similar names: one was called “firmness,” the other “in strength,” so that all teachers might be shown to possess the one strength of faith and action. At the same time, the sluggishness of our own age is reproved: some wish to be seen and called teachers, priests, and pillars of God, although they possess no firmness of faith for despising the pageantry of the world and desiring invisible goods, no strength for correcting the errors of those over whom they have been set, and not even the diligence required to understand those errors [Col. 0786C].

CHAPTER XIX. On the bronze sea.

He also made a molten sea, etc. This molten sea was made as a figure of the saving bath by which we are cleansed for the remission of sins. For the priests washed in it, as the Book of Chronicles plainly testifies. It is established that in Scripture all the elect are called priests figuratively, because they are members of the supreme Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ. And Scripture rightly gave this vessel the name “sea,” evidently in memory of the Red Sea, in which the figure of baptism first preceded through the destruction of the Egyptians and the liberation of God’s people, as the Apostle explains, saying: “For all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” [Col. 0786D]. The sacrament of baptism acquires for us the purity of life in this world and promises us the glory of eternal life in the world to come (I Cor. X).

Both of these are signified in one statement by this bronze sea, when it is said to be ten cubits from rim to rim. For by the ten commandments the Lord expressed in the Law everything that we ought to do. Likewise, he signified by the denarius the reward of good works when he declared that it was to be given to those laboring in the vineyard. Thus the sea was ten cubits from rim to rim because, from the first person baptized in the name of Jesus Christ to the last, who will believe and be baptized at the end of the age, the whole chorus of the faithful must enter upon one and the same way of truth and hope from the Lord for the common crown of righteousness [Col. 0787A].

It was round all around, so that the whole world might be shown as being cleansed in the circle of the bath of life from the filth of sins. Concerning this it is aptly added: “Its height was five cubits,” because whatever we sin by sight, whatever by hearing, whatever by smell, whatever by taste, whatever by touch—all this the grace of God releases for us through the washing of the life-giving font.

But the remission of past sins is not sufficient if each person does not thereafter strive to persist in good works. Otherwise, when the devil who had gone out from a person sees that person empty of good actions, he returns with greater force and makes that person’s final state worse than the first. Hence it is aptly added: “And a cord of thirty cubits surrounded it all around.” By the cord, the discipline [Col. 0787B] of the heavenly commandments by which we are restrained from our pleasures may aptly be signified. Scripture bears witness that “a threefold cord is difficult to break,” because the observance of God’s commandments, which is strengthened in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, and love of the heavenly reward, cannot be dissolved by any obstacle of temporal things.

The cord surrounds the sea when we strive to strengthen by pious works the sacrament of baptism that we have received. This cord is aptly said to be thirty cubits long. For five times six makes thirty. By the number six, in which God made the human being when he did not exist and remade him when he had perished, our good work is rightly figured. And six is multiplied by five so that one reaches thirty when we humbly subject all the senses of our body to the divine commands [Col. 0787C].

We may also, not inappropriately, understand this mystical number thirty of the sea in another way: three times ten makes thirty. After the Flood, the human race filled the breadth of the whole world through the offspring of Noah’s three sons. The lineage of Shem possessed Asia, the descendants of Ham Africa, and the offspring of Japheth Europe and the islands of the sea. And because the mystery of baptism, together with the performance of good works and hope of heavenly rewards, was to be administered to all nations, aptly a cord of thirty cubits surrounded that sea in which the baptismal water was prefigured.

It should also be said that the Lord, when he was thirty years old, came to the Jordan to be baptized by John. Since by his baptism—received when he was thirty—he consecrated for us the water of the saving bath, rightly a cord of thirty cubits encircled the sea that figured our baptism, so that it might be signified that, by the gift of him who underwent baptism without sin, baptism was consecrated for the remission of sins for all of us who believe in him [Col. 0787D].

“And sculptured work beneath the rim surrounded it, encircling the sea for ten cubits. There were two rows of sculptured work representing histories, cast in one piece.” Since it was stated above that a cord of thirty cubits went around the sea, and it is now added that this sculptured work placed beneath the rim encompassed it for ten cubits, it is clear from both statements that the vessel was spread and expanded in the form of a lily, narrowing from the circumference of thirty cubits that it had at the rim to ten cubits [Col. 0788A].

Sculptured work representing histories is work that imitates certain narratives of events. Thus, rightly, by the historical sculptures with which the sea was surrounded, examples of earlier times were signified. We must carefully contemplate them, so that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning; with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in crimes; with what iniquity the reprobate perished on account of their crimes; how, at the beginning of the world’s birth, Cain was condemned for the malice of envy, while Abel was crowned for the merit of righteousness; how Lamech was cursed for adultery and murder, while Enoch was taken back to paradise because of the grace of his piety; how, after the Flood, Ham was hated by his father because of his impiety, while the peoples of Shem and Japheth were granted perpetual [Col. 0788B] blessing for their dutiful reverence; how Abraham, because of the merit of his faith, was made heir of the divine promise, while the rest of the multitude of the nations was left in ancestral unbelief; how, when the Lord came in the flesh, Judea was rejected for the guilt of its faithlessness, while the Gentiles were brought back to salvation through the grace of faith; and other matters of this kind, which, when diligently and devoutly considered in both Testaments, greatly benefit all who are studious.

And so perhaps two rows of historical sculptures were made in the bronze sea, so that those who had been imbued with the baptismal font might diligently attend to the histories of both Testaments. They were ten cubits in circumference so that, whenever they perceived people devoted to these histories, obedient to the heavenly commands, and wholly intent upon heavenly rewards, they might strive to imitate them [Col. 0788C].

Then follows appropriately: “And it stood upon twelve oxen, of which three looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east.” We understand from the Apostle’s teaching that the oxen signify the apostles and evangelists—or, indeed, all ministers of the Word. Explaining the commandment of the Law in which it is said, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading grain,” he asks: “Is it really oxen that God is concerned about?” (Deut. XXV). “Or does he certainly say it for our sake? For our sake it was written, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes ought to partake of the fruit of his hope” (I Cor. IX).

The twelve oxen, therefore, are the twelve apostles and all those who, in their place, have undertaken to govern the holy Church. These oxen carry the sea placed upon them when the apostles and the successors of the apostles earnestly strive to fulfill with ready devotion the office of evangelizing that has been entrusted to them [Col. 0788D]. They look three toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east when they preach the faith of the Holy Trinity in all the regions of the four-sided world.

The apostles were also chosen as twelve—that is, four groups of three—so that, evangelizing throughout the four quarters of the world, they might baptize in the faith and confession of the Holy Trinity, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” We can readily see in the present, or learn by reading, the words, deeds, and sufferings of these apostles and their successors; but what glory of recompense awaits them in the future, we cannot yet see. Hence it is aptly added: “Their hindquarters were entirely hidden within” [Col. 0789A].

All the hindquarters of the oxen are hidden within because the reward by which the holy preachers will be endowed forever has already been determined in the judgment of the inward Judge; but for us, who are still outside, it remains entirely concealed. Yet this cannot be wholly hidden from those who receive the bath of baptism for salvation, because everyone who receives it must possess life, faith, hope, and charity. Without these three virtues no one can now accomplish anything, nor can anyone enter into life. Hence it is rightly added: “The thickness of the basin was three unciæ.”

The thickness of the basin signifies the firmness of virtue in baptism. Its thickness is three unciæ when the reception of baptism is strengthened by the power of faith, hope, and love. Nor is baptism shown to be beneficial to those who receive it in any other way, unless the firm certainty of these virtues confirms both the minds of the recipients and their works [Col. 0789B].

The bath of baptism is received and celebrated in the likeness of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection from the dead, according to the Apostle’s explanation: “For whoever among us was baptized into Christ Jesus was baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been grafted into the likeness of his death, we shall also be so into the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. VI).

This too was figuratively signified in the form of the bronze sea when it is subsequently added: “Its rim was like the rim of a cup, and like the leaf of a spreading lily.” By the rim of the cup, [Col. 0789C] the taste of the Lord’s Passion is expressed; by the leaf of the spreading lily, the revealed glory of his Resurrection.

That a drink in a cup signifies the Passion, the Lord himself indicates when, as he approaches his Passion, he prays to the Father, saying: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me” (Luke XXII). The lily, which, accompanied by the grace of a most pleasing fragrance, displays a white color on the outside and a golden color within, aptly suggests the glory of his Resurrection. For he showed the disciples the immortality of his body outwardly, and at the same time taught that he possessed within himself a soul radiant with divine light.

The spreading lily may also, not inappropriately, be understood as the Mediator between God and human beings, crowned after the Passion of his death with glory and honor. Before his Passion [Col. 0789D] he was like a lily still closed, when, as a glorious human being, he shone forth through the signs of the miracles he performed. But after his Resurrection and Ascension he displayed himself as a spreading lily to the citizens of the heavenly homeland, showing in the humanity he had assumed the power of the divine glory that he had with the Father before the world existed. Hence in the Song of Love he also wished to designate himself by the name of the lily, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II).

The rim of the sea in which the priests washed was therefore like the rim of a cup, and like the leaf of a spreading lily, because the saving bath by which we are made members of the supreme Priest purifies us from every stain of sin through faith in his most holy Passion and, once purified, admits us to the vision of his everlasting glory [Col. 0790A]. In this bath, the two peoples—the people of circumcision and the people of uncircumcision—are made one in the Lord through faith, hope, and love. He himself bears witness to this. Preaching concerning circumcision, he says among other things: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

This too was figuratively represented in the sea, for it follows: “It held two thousand baths.” The number one thousand is commonly used in Scripture to signify perfection, because it makes the number ten solid and square. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred. This figure is already square, but is not yet complete. But so that it may rise in height and become solid, one hundred is multiplied by ten, and the result is one thousand [Col. 0790B]. By this number the stable, unconquerable, and, as it were, squared conscience of the righteous is signified. Whichever way you turn it, the square stands firm. So too the mind of the elect does not know how to be bent from the state of its uprightness by any assault of temptations.

A bath is a Hebrew measure, which they themselves call *bath*, containing three *modii*. It is also the *ephah*, which they call *epha*. But the *ephah* belongs to the measure of dry crops—wheat, barley, and legumes—whereas the bath is used for liquid substances: wine, oil, and water. Thus the baths, which are a measure of a fixed standard, signify works of equity and righteousness, in which those who are baptized for the remission of sins must necessarily be instructed.

The sea held one thousand baths when, washing the people of the Jews with the water of baptism, it conveyed them to the heavenly kingdom. It received another thousand when it also made the multitudes of the nations, reborn from the same font and strengthened by works of righteousness, participants in that same everlasting kingdom [Col. 0790C].

This should certainly be noted here, because there are people who think that the Law of God prohibits us from carving or painting likenesses of human beings, animals, or any other things in a church, on a wall, or in any other place, on the grounds that the Decalogue says: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or of what is in the waters under the earth” (Exod. XX).

They would by no means think this if they had recalled the work of Solomon, who made palms inside the Temple, and cherubim with various carvings; on its columns, pomegranates and latticework; and in this bronze sea, twelve oxen and historical sculptures. On the bases of the basins, as is read below, he also made lions with oxen, palms, axles, and wheels, together with cherubim and various kinds of paintings. Or certainly they would have considered the works of Moses himself, who, at the Lord’s command, first made cherubim on the mercy seat and afterward made a bronze serpent in the wilderness, by looking upon which the people were saved from the venom of wild serpents [Col. 0790D].

For if it was permitted for a bronze serpent to be lifted up on wood, so that the children of Israel might live when they looked upon it, why is it not permitted to recall to the memory of the faithful by painting the exaltation of the Lord the Savior on the cross, by which he conquered death, or his other miracles and healings by which he marvelously [Col. 0791A] triumphed over that author of death? The sight of these things often produces great compunction in those who behold them, and for those who do not know letters it unfolds, as it were, a living reading of the Lord’s History.

For a picture is called in Greek ζωγραφία (*zōgraphia*), that is, “living writing.” If it was permitted to make twelve bronze oxen, carrying the sea placed upon them and looking in groups of three toward the four quarters of the world, what prevents us from depicting the twelve apostles as they went forth teaching all nations and baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—designating, so to speak, a living writing before the eyes of all?

If it was not contrary to the Law for historical sculptures to be made around that same sea in a circumference of ten cubits, how will it be thought contrary to the Law if we carve or paint historical representations of the saints and martyrs of Christ on panels, since through their observance of the divine Law they deserved to attain the glory of eternal recompense [Col. 0791B]?

But if we attend more carefully to the words of the Law, perhaps it will become clear that it is not the making of images of things and animals that is forbidden, but that making them for the sake of idolatry is altogether prohibited. Indeed, when the Lord was about to say on the holy mountain, “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness,” he first declared: “You shall have no other gods before me.” Then he added: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or of what is in the waters under the earth”; and he concluded: “You shall not worship them or serve them.”

By these words it is plainly declared that those likenesses are forbidden to all which the impious customarily make in honor of foreign gods, and which erring paganism devised for service and worship [Col. 0791C]. But to make such things simply, no letter of the divine Law, as I think, forbade; otherwise the Lord, when the Pharisees tested him concerning the payment of Caesar’s tribute—in which they said that Caesar’s name and image were represented—would by no means have answered in this way: “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). Rather, he would have corrected their error by saying: “It is not lawful for you to make an image for Caesar by striking your gold, because the divine Law prohibits such a carving.” Nor would he have spoken thus after being shown the coin of the tax, if Caesar’s image had been formed upon it for the sake of idolatry and not rather as an indication of royal authority [Col. 0791D].

## CHAPTER XX. On the ten bases and the basins.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Ten Bases and Lavers

“And he made ten bronze bases,” etc.

The sacraments of our salvation are prefigured in one and the same way through many figures and in many forms. For the same apostles and apostolic men who are represented by the oxen carrying the Sea are also represented by the bases prepared for carrying the lavers, just as the lavers themselves represented the same spiritual washing as the Sea. For, as the Books of Chronicles recount, they washed in them everything that they were going to offer as a burnt offering (2 Chronicles 4). The Lord’s burnt offering, therefore, may generally be understood as the entire multitude of the elect, which, according to the voice of the Forerunner, was baptized by him in the Holy Spirit and fire.

Thus, just as the priests who were washed in the Sea represent those who through baptism are made companions of the supreme priesthood that is in the Lord Jesus Christ, so too the burnt offerings most clearly prefigure these same people, since through the washing of baptism they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. The victim is washed in the laver when one of the faithful is drenched with water; it is offered as a burnt offering when, through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit.

When the evangelist Philip was preaching in Samaria, what else was he doing but washing the Lord’s victims in the laver of the temple? But because the Holy Spirit had not yet descended upon any of them, and they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, they were like washed victims that had not yet reached the fire of the most holy altar. When Peter and John were sent there, however, and laid hands on those who had been baptized, and they received the Holy Spirit and spoke in tongues, the victims had already reached the altar’s fire, so that they might become a burnt offering—which in Latin is called *holocaustum*, “wholly burned”—because the grace of the Holy Spirit, filling their consciences, made them burn with divine love.

Since ten bases were made to carry the lavers, this could be interpreted mystically to mean that the ministers of the life-giving washing support by the work of their example those whom they instruct by their preaching, leading them toward the joys of eternal blessedness, which is commonly represented by the number ten. Yet because it is written distinctly below that five of these lavers were placed on the right side of the temple and five on the left, the mysteries of the number five are more particularly to be discerned in them.

For bases of lavers were placed on both sides of the temple, so that it might be signified that the grace of the sacred font was to be opened to both peoples of God. There were five on each side so that, just as in the interpretation of the Sea—which, as we have already said, was five cubits high—it might also be shown typologically through the five bases of the lavers that everything in which the faithful had sinned through the five bodily senses was to be remitted through the washing of baptism.

Thus, just as the one Sea placed upon twelve oxen expresses the unity of baptism, which was to be preached throughout the whole world by the apostles, so through the two rows of lavers it is mystically shown that the Gentiles and the Jews were to be gathered into one fellowship of faith through the water of baptism. For although victims were washed in twin sets of lavers—some on the right side of the court and others on the left—all were nevertheless consumed by one fire of the altar, so that they might become a burnt offering. Whether someone received Christ’s washing on the side of circumcision or on that of the foreskin, all are sanctified by one Spirit so that they may become children of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father.” You have received, he says, one Spirit, in whom all of you are made children by adoption; in that Spirit, namely, we cry, “Abba, Father”: “Abba,” that is, we who have come from the Hebrews to the faith; “Father,” we who have come from the nations. Though we invoke one and the same God as Father in various languages according to the diversity of nations, we do so because of the gift of the one Spirit.

As for the fact that each base was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high, its meaning is readily understood. Length pertains to the patience of long-suffering; width, to the expansion of love; height, to hope of heavenly recompense. There are four principal virtues, upon which the rest of the structure of the virtues rests: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Thus the bases were four cubits in length and width, because the holy preachers—whether they endure outwardly the adversities of the world and the length of exile and present labors, or expand their hearts in the love of their Creator and their neighbors in eternal rejoicing—always strive to practice the virtues: discerning prudently between good and evil, enduring adversity bravely, restraining the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in their conduct.

The bases are three cubits high when, through the practice of the virtues—which they exercise with patience toward evils and love toward good things—they continually strive to attain the vision of the Holy Trinity.

“The work of the bases was in relief, and there were sculptures between the joints.” By the joints he seems to mean those places where the panels of the lavers were joined together, so that one base was made from four or five panels. What sort of sculptures they had between these joints—that is, on the sides themselves, front and back, right and left, and also above—is explained by what follows: “Between the wreaths and braided work were lions, oxen, and cherubim, and there were joints likewise above.”

That surface of the bases, therefore, was not smooth on any side, but was everywhere carved with mystical figures, because the minds of the saints—or rather, their entire manner of life—display the grace of the virtues in every respect. No hour passes them by empty and vacant in which they cease to devote themselves to pious works, words, or at least thoughts.

They have wreaths carved upon them when they pant with tireless longing for entry into eternal life. They have braided work when, amid their desires for the life above, they never loosen the bonds of brotherly fellowship that is near at hand. Between the wreaths and the braided work they have lions when they raise their minds toward heavenly hopes and enlarge them toward love of their neighbors in such a way that they do not delay exercising the fervor of stern rebuke against sinners entrusted to them.

Along with the lions they have oxen when they offer that same rebuke with a spirit of gentleness; when, in the fervor of correction, they never cease to distinguish the cloven hoof of discreet action; and when they continually roll the words of divine reading in their mouths, as if chewing the cud.

Thus blessed Stephen, an outstanding base of the Lord’s temple, seemed to display the fierce teeth and claws of a lion when he said to his persecutors: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7), and so forth. Yet by saying this he showed how much piety—and, so to speak, the gentleness of an ox—he carried within his heart, when, kneeling, he said for those same persecutors who were raging against him even unto death: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

But because we cannot possess either hope of eternal things in heaven, love of our neighbors on earth, the fervor of biting zeal, or the gentleness of compassionate moderation without knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, it is fittingly said that cherubim were carved between the wreaths and braided work, and the lions and oxen.

Scripture establishes that the cherubim hold the figure of sacred Scripture, either because the two cherubim over the mercy seat of the ark represent the two Testaments singing harmoniously of Christ, or because the very name signifies an abundance of knowledge. The more diligently someone applies himself to reading the pages of the divine utterances, the more necessarily he must fear, in everything he does or judges, the scrutiny of the inward witness or judge, lest by exacting more than justice from sinners, or again by forgiving without the restraint of proper discretion, he incur the anger of the just Judge. “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1).

Therefore, besides the sculptures of the cherubim, this is appropriately added: “And above the lions and oxen, as though reins hanging from bronze.” Reins hang above the lions and oxen when holy teachers, both in the severity of strictness with which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of leniency with which they forgive the penitent, fear the judgment of their Maker, lest perhaps, by binding unjustly, they deserve to be justly bound by him whose judgment cannot err.

“And four wheels for each base, with bronze axles, and cast supports beneath the laver on its four sides, facing one another.”

The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels. They are most aptly compared with wheels, because, just as the rolling wheel runs with very swift motion wherever it is driven, so the Gospel message, with the Lord’s help, quickly filled all the regions of the world through the apostles. Just as a wheel raises the cart placed upon it from the ground and carries it, once raised, wherever the driver directs, so evangelical preaching lifts the minds of the elect from earthly desires toward heavenly aspirations and leads them, thus lifted, either toward progress in good works or toward the ministry of preaching, wherever the assisting grace of the Spirit wills.

For it is said below: “The wheels were of such a kind as wheels are customarily made for a chariot.” We read of the saints: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands upon thousands rejoicing” (Psalm 68:17). What, then, does it mean that the wheels of the bases resemble the wheels of chariots, unless it is that one and the same Gospel message makes some of those whom it instructs into the chariot of God and others into bases?

All those teachers who were sent throughout the world, far and wide, to evangelize were certainly chariots of God, and exceedingly swift ones, because, running through every region, they brought God to the hearts of believers. But those who remain in one place, announcing the word of salvation to their neighbors and kindling them toward the washing of life—which is celebrated either in baptism or in the compunction of tears—are like the bases of the temple, which carry the lavers for washing the victims. They provide the ministry of salvation to the faithful placed under their care, but do not undertake the labors of traveling farther afield to acquire new peoples.

The wheels of the bases, therefore, resemble the wheels of chariots because the same books of the Gospels send some teachers to preach the faith of truth, while commanding others to remain among the teachers in order to strengthen the faith further after they have already been imbued with the heavenly sacraments.

The four wheels supported the base of a laver when the Gospels ordered James, the Lord’s brother, to remain in Jerusalem to strengthen the Church. Wheels like those of the chariot of God, placed beneath it and prepared for movement, were present when the same Gospels willed Paul and Barnabas to travel everywhere preaching to the nations. Wheels placed beneath the bases raised the laver-bearing bases from the ground when, in our own times, blessed Pope Gregory, strengthened by the Gospel utterances, governed the Roman Church. Those same wheels, attached to the chariot of God, stood far away when the most reverend fathers Augustine, Paulinus, and their other companions, strengthened by the same Gospel oracles, came to Britain at his command and entrusted the word of God to peoples who had previously been unbelieving.

If, then, the bases of the lavers are holy teachers who minister to us the washing of life, and the four wheels of the bases are the four books of the Gospels, what are the axles of the wheels that bear the bases, unless they are the hearts of those same teachers? For, while they diligently attend to the commands of the Gospel and lift their hearers away from desire for the lowest things, they are like axles inserted into wheels, raising the base higher from the ground.

The supports placed before the wheels, so that they could not slip from the axles, are the proclamations of the prophets, by which evangelical and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, lest anything in it perhaps come into doubt for any reader. Hence the Apostle Peter, speaking of the Lord, says: “And we have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention” (2 Peter 1:19).

All the evangelists and apostles, moreover, were accustomed to mention the Law and the Prophets in what they wrote. Thus Mark says: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet”; and Matthew: “All this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Mark 1), and other statements of this kind.

It is rightly said that the supports, which were placed beneath the laver on its four sides, faced one another, because all prophetic Scripture agrees with itself, having been composed by one Spirit. There were four supports for each base, corresponding to the number of wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because in everything the prophets and Moses spoke, they bore witness to the words of the four evangelists, so that, through the agreement of both, one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all.

“The opening of the laver was within, at the top of its head; and what appeared externally was one cubit, entirely round, and it had a circumference of one and a half cubits.”

The opening of the laver was one cubit, because of the unity of confession and faith by which we are all baptized in the confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.” The opening itself was at the top of the head (Ephesians 4), to show that through baptism a path to the heavenly kingdoms has been opened for us.

The laver itself was one and a half cubits in breadth, because of the perfection of action and the beginning of contemplation. The complete cubit in the laver signifies the perfection of good action. Without any doubt, this was possessed by the man of whom the Lord said to the ancient tempter: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a blameless and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 1).

There is, moreover, another cubit, of the vision of God, which is customarily granted in part even in this life to the faithful who still remain here. Thus Job, after defeating his adversary, says while speaking with the Lord: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42); thus the Lord appeared to Moses face to face; thus he appeared to Isaiah, seated upon the throne of his kingdom, with the citizens of heaven surrounding him and giving due praise; thus he often appeared to the other prophets; thus, at the moment of his passion, when the gates of heaven were opened, the glory of God was shown to blessed Stephen; thus the mysteries of the entrance into paradise and of the third heaven were disclosed to Paul.

Yet all these things are only partial in comparison with the glory that is to be revealed in the future. Therefore, after the cubit of good action that can be completed in this life in the saints, the cubit of heavenly contemplation begins—the contemplation that in the future life will already be fully completed in all the elect.

This measure of one and a half cubits was present not only in the lavers but also in their wheels and bases. For it is written below: “One wheel was one cubit and a half in height.” A little later: “At the top of the base there was a rounded projection of one and a half cubits, made so that the laver could be placed upon it.”

The lavers measured one and a half cubits because we are washed in the font of life by that faith through which we deserve to enter eternal life by works of righteousness, although, while we live here, we cannot be without sin. In this present life we are able only partly to taste and love the sweetness of heavenly life; we cannot see it perfectly in any way.

The wheels too were measured at one and a half cubits, because the study of evangelical reading shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live. It also displays to us in the present the hope of eternal recompense, while promising that the nature of that recompense will be disclosed and granted to us in the future.

The bases themselves had one and a half cubits of breadth at their tops, where they received the lavers, because those supreme teachers and ministers of the saving washing shone in this life through the perfection of their works, but enjoyed the light of contemplation only in part. Hence they say: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away” (1 Corinthians 13).

“In this manner he made ten bases, cast in one mold, of one measure, and with similar sculpture. He also made ten bronze lavers” (1 Kings 7; 2 Chronicles 4). Why the bases were made, and an equal number of lavers placed upon them, has already been explained above. But the fact that there was one casting and one measure, and similar sculpture on all the bases and lavers, was not done to signify that the merits of all teachers could be equal. Rather, it signified that there is one faith of the Gospel by which they are instructed, one sacrament of baptism by which they are washed, and one and the same Spirit by whom all the elect are consecrated, although they possess different gifts in that Spirit, who distributes to each one as he wills.

“One laver held forty baths.” The number forty commonly represents great perfection, because four times ten make forty. There are ten commandments by which all our conduct has been established in the divine Law; and there are four books of the Gospels, through which, by the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, the entrance into our heavenly homeland has been opened to us.

Because all who belong to the mystery of sacred baptism ought, with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, to display the fruit of right action, it is fitting that each laver in which the burnt offerings were washed held forty baths.

What follows—“It was four cubits”—whether it signifies height or width, makes the meaning of the mystery clear. One laver was four cubits, either because of the books of the holy Gospel, in which the pattern of baptism has been established for us; or because of the four cardinal virtues, in which every faithful person, if faithful not in vain, must be instructed; or certainly because of the four regions of the world in which the washing of salvation is administered. The Psalmist says: “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, whom he gathered from the lands, from the rising of the sun and from its setting, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm 107:3).

When he said above, “It also had one cubit and a half,” without indicating whether he meant height or breadth, he seems to have intended the bottom of the laver to be understood as one measure in breadth. This can very easily be inferred from the measure of the base upon which each laver was placed, which is described as follows: “At the top of the base there was a rounded projection of one and a half cubits, made so that the laver could be placed upon it.”

The breadth of the bottom of the lavers, therefore, was one and a half cubits, while the capacity of the lavers was four cubits. But whether he speaks of height, length, or both, who can know?

“And he placed ten bases, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.”

By the right and left sides of the temple he does not mean inside the temple itself, but before the temple toward the eastern region, namely in the inner court, which was properly called the court of the priests.

He placed five on the right side of the temple because of the Jews, who had anciently been accustomed to use the Sun of righteousness for the teaching of the Law; and five on the left because of us, who for a long time had clung in blind-hearted servitude to him who said: “I will place my seat toward the north.” This is plainly to say: “I desire to rest in those hearts that I perceive to be alienated from the light of truth and the flame of divine love.”

He placed the Sea on the right side of the temple, toward the east and the south. It too was placed in the same court, toward the east. What he says—“on the right side of the temple”—he repeats when he says, “toward the south.” For those entering the court from the east had first to turn toward the south, where the Sea stood in the very corner, prepared for the priests to wash in. Then, as they proceeded farther inside, they encountered the lavers for washing the victims, placed on both sides. Between them stood a bronze base five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple. Then, as they proceeded farther, they encountered the altar of burnt offering toward the south side of the court. After that came the portico of the temple, or vestibule, where the bronze columns stood around the entrance to the temple.

The placement of the Sea on the right side of the temple signifies that through the washing of baptism we must reach the heavenly kingdom, which is rightly represented by the name “right hand”: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.”

When the right and left are both taken positively, they signify either the Jews and the Gentiles, as we said above in the interpretation of the bases; or the present life of the Church and the future life; or the joy of the saints and sorrow; or something of this kind. But when “right” is used positively without qualification, it more often signifies eternal joys.

The placement of the Sea toward the east refers nearly to the same meaning: through the washing of the sacred font, the splendor of inward clarity is opened to us. Its placement on the southern side of the court signifies that the faithful, through receiving the Holy Spirit, are accustomed to be kindled toward the fervor of true love. For in Scripture the heat of the noonday sun commonly signifies the ardor of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom that same love is poured into the hearts of the elect.

## CHAPTER XXI. That the Vessels of the Lord’s House Were Made in the Region of the Jordan

“All the vessels … were of bronze,” etc.

The vessels of the Lord’s house were appropriately cast in the region of the Jordan, in the river in which our Lord deigned to be baptized and, having been immersed in its waters, transformed the element of water for us into a means of washing away sins. For every baptism of the faithful, by which they are consecrated to the Lord, is celebrated as an imitation of the baptism by which he himself sanctified the waters.

Rightly, then, the vessels of the Lord’s house were made in the region of the Jordan. For we cannot become vessels of election and mercy in any other way than by looking toward the baptism that he underwent in that river and striving to be washed ourselves in the life-giving stream.

It should be noted that he says the same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but also in its plain country. This signifies the multiplication of the faithful, which was to take place not only in Judea but also across the breadth of all nations, fulfilling the prophecy: “The plains shall rejoice, and everything in them” (Psalm 96:12).

Something similar is found where the same Psalmist, speaking of the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation—from which they came to faith—says: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephratha; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 132:6). We heard of the Lord’s mysteries in Ephratha—that is, in Bethlehem—because we learned that Christ would come in the flesh from the fruit of the Virgin’s womb, the Virgin who was from that same city, as had been revealed through the prophets. We found them in the fields of the forest because, once revealed throughout the breadth of the nations across the world, we ourselves came to know them, we ourselves saw them, and we ourselves became participants in them.

Thus the king cast the vessels of the Lord’s house in the plain country of the Jordan, because the Lord extended throughout the breadth of the world the baptism of salvation through which he would make vessels of mercy.

What can the clay soil from which the molds were made for casting the vessels of the Lord’s house better signify than sacred Scripture, from which we receive the rule for living well? As clay hardened by fire presents the form of the Lord’s vessel, showing how great and what kind the vessels ought to be, so Scripture shows us the rule of righteousness that we are to follow, and sets before us the examples of the saints who remained invincible in the fire of tribulations, to be followed in all things.

If we desire to be chosen and precious vessels in the Lord’s house, then, just as bronze melted by fire enters the clay molds so that the vessel may become suitable for heavenly services, so we too, profitably humbled and softened either by the flame of divine love or by human adversity, enter the way of the fathers by doing good works, so that by running well we may reach the rewards of the fathers.

For it is not always necessary for us to be fitted to the rules of good action. Once good action has been completed, the palm of blessed recompense is to be hoped for. The vessels were not always kept enclosed in the clay molds; rather, when they had reached perfection, the restraints of the molds were broken, and they were brought into the light and each was arranged in its proper place in the Lord’s temple.

We say this not because the works of the saints will ever perish, but because, once they have received the crown of righteousness that they earned by doing good, all the duties of laborious action will then cease. Who would suffer martyrdom for the faith of Christ in that life, when the adversaries have been driven out and all the elect rejoice in the presence of Christ (Revelation 7)? Who would bury the dead there, where the land belongs only to the living? Who would console the grieving, where God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints? Who would open his house to a traveler and guest, where all the elect together have from God a dwelling, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens? Who would bring bread to the hungry or drink to the thirsty there, where the Lord will feed me and I shall lack nothing?

When, therefore, the molds once necessary for the vessels have been broken apart, the vessels themselves already shine splendidly in the Lord’s house, because, when at the end of the age not only the persecutions that the elect endure for righteousness but also the laborious works of righteousness through which they willingly toil for eternal blessedness have ceased, they will rejoice in the sole vision of their Creator, in the brightness of immortality.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Both Altars
Solomon made all the vessels in the house of the Lord, etc.

The golden altar signifies the hearts of perfected righteous people, flashing with the light of inward radiance and purity; and the position of that same altar is also fitting for signifying their exalted state. For it stood before the entrance of the Holy of Holies, as we read plainly in the account of the tabernacle’s construction. [Col. 0800A] On this altar, indeed, neither the blood of sacrifices nor libations was burned, but only incense; its smoke, rising upward, covered the ark and filled the oracle with the fragrance of sweetness. In this it represented the saints who, while neglecting temporal desires and seeking heavenly things with undivided purpose, are placed, as it were, within, near the oracle, and are not far removed from the veil by which the temple and the Holy of Holies are separated. In body alone they inhabit the earth; in their inner person, however, they have their entire way of life in heaven.

Smoke from incense of this kind ascended from the altar into the Holy of Holies, where the ark was kept hidden, when the prayers of the saints, kindled by the flame of love, reach all the way to heaven, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. [Col. 0800B] For on this altar the blood of sacrifices was not burned, but only incense, because such men do not possess works of flesh and blood which they slaughter as sacrifices to the Lord upon the altar of their hearts; rather, they offer him only the vows of tears and prayer, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.

Yet because no one suddenly becomes supreme, but one ascends toward heavenly desire through the surrender of carnal pleasures with an attentive mind, Scripture did not omit, in the mystical construction of the Lord’s house, to represent those who still labor to burn away, by the flame of heavenly exertion, the carnal desires that wage war against the soul. Thus, when these have been uprooted from heart and body, they may subsequently ascend to greater things and offer God the spiritual incense of prayers and compunction. [Col. 0800C]

Another altar was made for offering victims. It was much larger, but in proportion to the extent by which it surpassed the other in size, it was inferior in the position of its site and in the kind of metal. For it was made of bronze and placed before the doors of the temple. In it were figuratively represented those who serve the Lord with such devotion that their flesh still desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh (Rom. 7), and who are accustomed to say: “In mind we serve the law of God, but in flesh the law of sin.” When they strive to subdue the incitements of the flesh, restrain the fluidity of lust, and draw near to God worthily toward the tranquillity of chastity through frequent fasts and prayers, vigils and almsgiving, and the other fruits of the Spirit, what do they offer him except the victim of their devotion, fulfilling the Apostle’s appeal that we present our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God (Rom. 12)? [Col. 0800D]

Because they burn with the fervor of spiritual love but have not yet attained the triumph of conquered carnal desire, the altar of burnt offering has indeed the most holy fire from heaven, but it displays the appearance of bronze, not gold. Yet because there are more carnal people in the holy Church than spiritual ones—more who restrain themselves by curbing the allurements of vice than those who, after overcoming and quieting the struggle with vice, rejoice in the security gained through virtue—it was rightly asserted that the altar of burnt offering was much larger than the altar of incense.

For it is written of it in the Book of Chronicles: “He made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, [Col. 0801A] twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high” (2 Chron. 4). The altar of incense, however, Moses made in the wilderness, one cubit in length, another in width, and two cubits in height. How large Solomon made this one, Scripture does not say; it merely says that he made a golden altar. It is clear, however, that he could not have made it as large as the altar of burnt offering, because if it had been twenty cubits long, it would have filled the entire width of the temple.

Therefore, by as much as the altar of burnt offering was placed farther out than the altar of incense, and by as much as it was inferior in the kind of offering and the baseness of its metal, by that much it surpassed it in the size of its dimensions and in the frequency of sacrifices. For there are far more to whom it is said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” than there are those who delight to hear, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor” (Matt. 19). [Col. 0801B]

Nevertheless, the measurement of this altar is not without mystical significance or numerical meaning. It has twenty cubits in length, the same number in width, and ten cubits in height; concerning this number we have spoken in our exposition of the temple and its vestibule. But now it must be said briefly that the altar of burnt offering represents the elect in the Church, who seek to consecrate their body and soul to God through the fire of his love. Their perseverance in good works is signified by the altar’s length; their breadth in love of God and neighbor, by its width; and their hope in expectation of the divine vision, by its height.

[Col. 0801C] The fact that the altar’s length and width were each twenty cubits signifies a great perfection of that tireless perseverance and sincere love which is granted to us through observance of both Testaments. For four times five makes the number twenty. There are five books of the Mosaic Law and four of evangelical freedom. When, enlightened by the grace of the Gospel, we attain spiritual understanding and observance of the Law, we complete the number twenty.

The same number twenty appears in the length and width of the altar when the hearts of the elect, instructed by both Testaments and aided by the one Author of both Testaments, preserve perseverance in good works even amid persecutions and display the joyfulness of love toward those who persecute them. [Col. 0801D]

The number ten is customarily used to signify hope in heavenly rewards, as the Lord affirms when he declares that those who labored in the vineyard of the great householder would be rewarded with a denarius (Matt. 20). It is fitting that eternal reward is represented by this number, in which our nature is joined forever to the divine vision, because in this number the divine and human natures are mystically signified together. God is a Trinity. Humanity, however, is comprehended by the number seven: by four because of the body, which consists of four elements, and by three because of the threefold distinction of the inner person that Holy Scripture shows us when it commands us to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength.

Thus, in the Decalogue of the Law there are three commandments that arouse us to the worship of divine love, and seven that commend love of neighbor. Those, therefore, who keep the Decalogue in love of God and neighbor rightly receive the reward of this observance in the vision both of God and of neighbor. Those who in this life love both the neighbor whom they see and God whom they do not see will in the life to come see both God the King in his beauty and their neighbor glorified and adorned.

For this reason the altar made as a figure of the elect, signifying their perpetual life, was ten cubits high. When it had been said that Solomon made a golden altar, it was immediately added: “And the table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed, golden.” [Col. 0802A]

The golden table is Holy Scripture, fruitful in the radiance of spiritual understanding. [Col. 0802B] Concerning it the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You have prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me” (Ps. 22). So that our troubling adversaries might not bend us toward error, our Creator prepared for us the table of heavenly knowledge, by which we might be strengthened in the faith of truth.

The bread of the Presence is the holy teachers, whose works or saving words, set before us as examples of life, anyone who seeks rightly will always find in the divine books. Hence, appropriately, twelve loaves were commanded to be made in Exodus, on account of the twelve apostles, through whose ministry both the writing of the New Testament was composed and the mysteries of the Old Testament were revealed by the Lord’s gift (Exod. 25). [Col. 0802C]

By this number not only the apostles themselves were signified, but also all who, by preaching the word, minister the nourishment of life to the faithful, because all follow the very form of teaching that the apostles received from the Lord.

We read concerning these loaves in Exodus that they were to be changed every Sabbath and that new ones were to be placed on the Lord’s table in place of the old; they were always to be prepared according to one measurement and of similar form. In all this, the mystical meaning concerning inward nourishment shines forth more clearly than light. The old loaves are removed and new ones restored when, after some faithful teachers have been taken from this life, the holy Church appoints others in their place.

This occurs only on the day of the Sabbath because whoever has fought the good fight, completed the course, and kept the faith will, at the time of his release, enter the rest of blessed eternity. [Col. 0802D] The loaves were always made of one measurement and not unequal, because the form of truth and faith is one and the same: first the apostles showed it to their hearers, and afterward their successors and all devout teachers in the churches of Christ throughout the world have not ceased to preach it, down to the faith of the age.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Ten Golden Tables

As for what we read in the Book of Chronicles—that Solomon made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, and also one hundred golden bowls—it is credible that these were made not so much for the bread of the Presence as for the vessels of the Lord: namely, the bowls, which Scripture reports were made in equal number, the incense vessels, censers, and the other objects read of in what follows. [Col. 0803A]

For when a little later in the same book of Chronicles it adds, “He made all the vessels of the house of the Lord, and the bronze altar, and the tables, and upon them the bread of the Presence,” either it used the plural for the singular, as is extremely common in Scripture—as in Joshua: “The children of Israel transgressed the commandment and appropriated what was devoted to destruction” (Josh. 7), although Achan alone, and not several children of Israel, had done this—or else the reason is that the bread of the Presence was customarily baked before the Sabbath so that it could immediately be placed on the table of the Presence on the Sabbath.

It could have happened that newly baked loaves were immediately placed on those tables and kept covered there during that night, until, early in the morning, the old loaves had been removed and the hot ones placed on the table of the Presence. [Col. 0803B]

These ten tables, however, do not differ in their symbolism from that of the single table of the Presence. For just as the table laden with twelve loaves signifies the unanimous harmony of all Scripture, fortified by apostolic authority, so too the ten golden tables rightly signify the words of the divine Law and of the prophets. These either offer us the refreshment of God’s word, as though the bread of the Presence, or set before us examples of the faithful, as though vessels of the Lord placed upon them, displaying the Lord’s glory and miracles.

The tables are rightly five and five, not only because the lawgiver wrote five books, but also because the entire sequence of the Old Testament embraces five ages of the world. [Col. 0803C] The number of the tables is doubled—five being placed on the right and five on the left—when, after the Lord’s Incarnation, the same Scripture is entrusted either to both peoples of God, namely Jew and Gentile, or is shown to be full of evangelical figures, whereas formerly it was thought that the ancient people of God were to understand it only according to the letter.

When, for example, as we read Holy Scripture, we take Abel, crowned through martyrdom; Enoch, translated from the world; Noah, wondrously saved while the world perished; hospitable Lot, sublimely rewarded after the wicked had been destroyed; Abraham, made father of all nations through the merit of obedience; and Joseph, after his sale, taken as an example of virtue because of his chastity and innocence—what do the five golden tables, or the vessels of the Lord, or the bread of the Presence still on the left side of the temple signify except that the divine writings, according to the historical sense, open for us the door both to living rightly and to hoping for eternal rewards from the Lord?
