[Col. 0803D]

But when, understanding the same writings more deeply, we see them proclaiming either the dispensation of the Lord’s Incarnation or any of the other mysteries of the holy Church, we find, as it were, another five tables on the right side of the temple, for carrying the vessels of election and the nourishment of spiritual life. We recognize that these same words of sacred history open to us an entirely new flash of heavenly wisdom and new meanings from ancient things. In this same figure, five lampstands were made in the temple.

When Scripture had said that King Solomon made a golden table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed, it subsequently added and said:

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Ten Lampstands

[Col. 0804A]

“And five golden lampstands, etc.”

These tables are rightly set forth as a type of Holy Scripture, because they supply the bread of the word to those who hunger for righteousness and bear the vessels of heavenly ministry—that is, they set before us the deeds of the righteous as an example. Likewise, the same divine utterances are most suitably represented by the lampstands, because they bring the light of wisdom to those who wander.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet” (Ps. 118), etc. Hence Solomon says: “For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light” (Prov. 6).

[Col. 0804B] Why the lampstands were placed five on the right and five on the left is readily clear from what we have discussed concerning the tables. When he had said, “Five on the right and five on the left,” it is appropriately added, “opposite the oracle.” The oracle, where the ark was, as has often been said, signifies the entrance to the heavenly homeland, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, aware of the Father’s secrets.

Alternatively, the golden lampstands of the temple were placed opposite the oracle because the divine utterances always look toward the dwelling of the heavenly city, so that they may pour the knowledge and desire of it into our hearts and kindle those who have their origin in the earth according to the flesh to seek and merit the seat of perpetual dwelling in heaven.

There are some, however, who think that what is said of the lampstands—five on the right and five on the left—is to be understood in this way: five were on the right of the lampstand that Moses made in the desert, and five on its left, although both groups were toward the southern side, where the one lampstand that Moses made was commanded to stand. [Col. 0804C]

They understand the same arrangement concerning the ten tables: all of them were placed toward the northern side, but five on the right of that Mosaic table and five on its left.

Yet if you consider the words of Holy Scripture, which say, “Five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the oracle,” it is evident, unless I am mistaken, that the two groups were placed lengthwise along both sides of the temple. For if all the lampstands had been placed lengthwise along the southern side of the temple, they would not have been said to be placed opposite the oracle, but rather opposite the north—whether opposite the tables or even among the tables, where they stood. [Col. 0804D]

This is what was said in Exodus about the one lampstand in the tabernacle of testimony: it was “opposite the table, on the southern side” (Exod. 25). Likewise in the Book of Numbers: “When you set up the seven lamps, they shall shine toward the side on which the lampstand is to give light” (Num. 8).

There were lampstands on both sides of the temple, and tables on both sides, because Holy Scripture was composed for the illumination and refreshment of both peoples of God. In prosperity and adversity, in sad and joyful circumstances, whether they come upon us or happen around us, it refreshes us so that we do not fail and enlightens us so that we do not remain blind. It also sets before both of us the vessels of mercy placed upon it—that is, the written deeds of the righteous—through which we too may be strengthened in the practice of righteousness.

[Col. 0805A] If you ask what typological distinction there is between the lampstands and their lamps, we may rightly understand the lamps to be holy men who, infused with the oil of the Holy Spirit, themselves burn with the fire of love in their hearts and bring the light of knowledge to their neighbors through their speech.

The lampstands that raise these lamps aloft, so that they may be seen far and wide in the Church, are Holy Scripture, which through its reading displays to us the virtues and teaching of the saints. The Lord’s statement concerning John supports this interpretation: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5).

We may also say, very appropriately, that the lamps are the divine utterances, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying, which we quoted above: “Your word is a lamp for my feet” (Ps. 118). The lampstands of these lamps, however, are all the saints, who humbly and continually submit their hearts and [Col. 0805B] bodies to bear the Lord’s commandments.

Whoever does not seek to follow his own will in anything, but attends in all things to what Holy Scripture says and strives to submit himself to its commandments and to listen to its promises, carries its golden lamps like a golden lampstand in the house of God. For he strives to submit the chaste members of his body and the pure thoughts of his mind to doing what God commands.

[Col. 0805D] And just as a lampstand must stand firmly upright toward heavenly things, so he must preserve the lamps placed upon him not only without falling but also without any alteration of his position, with such steadfast intention.

When Scripture had said, “Five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the oracle, of pure gold,” it added: “And like lily flowers, with golden lamps above.” [Col. 0805C] According to the literal sense, it appears that the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the shape of an open lily, as we read was done in the lampstand of the tabernacle. Its central shaft and the branches proceeding from it, with their cups and spheres, are written to have borne very many lilies.

The flowers of the lily, as has often been said, signify the loveliness of the ever-green land of the living. Concerning it blessed Peter says that we have been regenerated by the Lord into a living hope, for an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven.

The golden lily flowers were fittingly made on the lampstand of the Lord’s house, because Holy Scripture, scorning temporal joys, habitually urges us to seek the good things of the heavenly homeland. And just as the lampstand, raised up on high, has golden lily flowers and lamps at its summit, so all the elect who are contained in the same sacred Scripture are shown, with their minds raised toward heavenly things, to have sought and received heavenly goods from the Lord.

We have spoken more fully of the table and the lampstand, and of both altars and the foundation of the Lord’s house, in the books that we wrote concerning the construction of the tabernacle and priestly attire. Therefore, if anyone desires to know about these matters according to the capacity of our understanding, handed down from the tradition of the Fathers, let him seek it in that work.

The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Hinges of the Doors and the Completion of the Lord’s House

“And the hinges of the doors of the house of the Lord, etc.”

If the doors [Col. 0806A] of the inner house, the Holy of Holies, are the angelic mysteries that unlock for us, once we have departed from the body, entrance into heavenly life, and the doors of the temple-house are the holy teachers and priests who, by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, open for us the first lights of the present Church, what are the hinges of both sets of doors except the minds and hearts of those angels or saints, by which they adhere immovably to contemplation and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the ministry divinely entrusted to them, since they never turn their eyes away from the will of the one whom they serve?

The doors are opened and closed at the proper time, but they never at any time leave their hinges, because angels and holy human beings, whether they receive the faithful and elect in [Col. 0806B] this life of faith or in that life of sight, always keep their minds fixed at the root of inward love. Hence these hinges are rightly said to have been made of gold, on account of the merit of their own radiance.

“And he completed all the work, etc.”

Solomon completes the work he was doing in the house of the Lord when our peaceful King glorifies all the elect with the immortality of the resurrection on the last day. Otherwise, as long as the condition of this age continues, Solomon does indeed make the work of the Lord’s house, but does not yet complete it, because the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good works. Yet he does not grant anyone who remains in this life to be without sin, for he reserves this gift for the blessedness of the life to come.

He completes [Col. 0806C] all the work of his temple and makes it fit for dedication when he leads those who have been transferred from this life into the eternal kingdom. This is aptly signified by the fact that the temple was built in seven years but completed and dedicated in the eighth. For this entire age revolves through seven days. The eighth is the day of judgment and the future resurrection, concerning which the sixth and eleventh Psalms were titled. To that time what follows appropriately applies:

“And he brought in the things that his father David had consecrated, etc.”

Silver pertains to the brilliance of eloquence; gold to the splendor of wisdom; vessels in general to rational creatures. David, Solomon’s father, sanctifies silver when God strengthens eloquent people [Col. 0806D] of every kind through the grace of the Holy Spirit to speak the word of the Gospel. He sanctifies gold when, filling those endowed with natural intelligence with his Spirit, he enlightens them to contemplate the wonders in his Law. He sanctifies vessels when, having generally bestowed the grace of the same Spirit upon all the children of the Church, he inflames them to love and seek the gifts of perpetual salvation.

Solomon brings this silver, this gold, and these sanctified vessels into the temple when, after universal judgment has been completed, our Lord introduces all the elect—the teachers as well as the gathered company of the other faithful—into the joy of the heavenly kingdom. He places vessels of different kinds, whether silver or gold, in the treasuries of the Lord’s house when he hides those who have deserved to enjoy the abundance of his sweetness in the secret place of his face, away from the turmoil of human beings. [Col. 0807A]

There are fittingly many treasuries in which the vessels of election are stored, but there is one house of the Lord in which those treasuries have been made, because there is one Church in which all the elect are contained, however much they differ in merit. There is also one, and not several, heavenly homeland promised to all the elect, although, as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead.

The Judge and Dispenser of rewards himself demonstrated both truths in one statement [Col. 0808A] when he said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.”

Solomon therefore made one house of the Lord, but prepared many treasuries within it for receiving vessels of different kinds, all sanctified by one blessing. This house of the Father, not made by hands, is eternal in heaven, but in it are many dwelling places for receiving all who fear and love him, those whom the Lord has blessed, the small together with the great.

Amen.

[Col. 0807]

# ALLEGORICAL EXPOSITION OF THE PROPHETS EZRA AND NEHEMIAH (C, S)

## PREFACE

[Col. 0807B]

The distinguished interpreter and teacher of Holy Scripture, Jerome, when he briefly reviewed the books of that same Scripture in a letter to a friend and touched summarily on what each contained, says:

“Ezra and Nehemiah, namely the helper and the comforter from the Lord, are related in one volume, and they restore the temple, build the walls of the city, and all that crowd of people returning to their homeland, together with the description of the priests, Levites, Israelites, and proselytes, and the division by each family of the work on the walls and towers, present one thing on the surface and retain another in the marrow.”

Therefore, most reverend [Col. 0808B] Bishop Acca, diligently complying with your exhortations, I devoted myself to considering that volume. Trusting in the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ as our helper and comforter, I hope that in his mercy he may grant us, once the bark of the letter has been laid open, to find something deeper and holier in the marrow of its spiritual meaning—namely, that it designates the Lord himself, and his temple and city, which we are, by prophetic figures but with manifest meaning.

In this work the aforementioned teacher of the Church, Jerome, was of the greatest assistance to us in his explanation of the prophets. For what Ezra and Nehemiah write as having happened, he had himself foretold, under the figure of Christ and the Church, as things that were to happen.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0807]

[Col. 0807C]

It is clear to all readers that in Holy Scripture the house or temple of God is customarily called both each individual of the elect and the whole Church together, that is, the universal body of the righteous. This is because God deigns to dwell in the hearts of those who believe and hope in him and love him, in accordance with what he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Hence the Apostle also says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3). And in the Letter to the Hebrews: “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house, which house we are, if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope” (Heb. 3).

As a figure of this spiritual house or temple, King Solomon built a temple for the Lord in Jerusalem. For Solomon himself, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” aptly represented the one of whom the prophet sings: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. 9).

Concerning him the Apostle, writing to the Church from the Gentiles, says: “And coming, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2). [Col. 0808C]

The fact that he built this temple in seven years but completed and dedicated it in the eighth signifies that throughout the entire time of this age, which revolves through seven days, the Lord builds the Church from the faithful gathered for the heavenly structure. In the future life, however, when the glory of the resurrection appears, he completes it wholly and raises it into the joy of immortal life, in the eternal vision of his glory.

Because he himself rose from the dead on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day, the time of our resurrection is rightly expressed by the number eight.

The fact that later, as the years passed, certain structures of the temple began to collapse through excessive age, but were soon restored and raised again [Col. 0808D] to their former condition through the diligence of the kings and priests who lived in those times, signifies the daily and very slight falls of the faithful, concerning which Solomon says: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24). By the Lord’s gift, these are likewise corrected daily through the examples or exhortations of the righteous who came before them, as though by the diligence of God’s kings and priests.

For kings and priests are rightly called all the perfect in the Church, since they are members of the supreme King and Priest, once they have learned to govern themselves well and to present their bodies to the Lord as a living sacrifice. [Col. 0809A]

The fact that later, as wickedness increased, the temple itself was polluted with the filth of idols and finally destroyed and burned by the Chaldeans signifies the more serious falls of those who, although joined to the members of the holy Church through confession of the right faith and the sacrament of saving baptism, are afterward cast down from the state of faith by the deceit of evil spirits and consumed in the fire of vices.

When the temple had been destroyed, and the city of Jerusalem likewise laid waste, its citizens were transferred to Babylon; but after seventy years, having done penance for their evils, they were sent back to their homeland by the Lord’s mercy and restored the same temple and holy city again with great labor. This figuratively designates those who, [Col. 0809B] deceived by the devil, lose not only the sincerity of faith and the integrity of good works but also, through the bitterness of their crimes, appear to be made like the Gentiles and publicans, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a publican” (Matt. 18).

Nevertheless, some of these, recovering through the regard of divine grace, return to the Church. Struck with compunction by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, they begin again to hear and keep the commandments of the divine Law that they had abandoned.

For there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah enumerates with clear distinction. The whole sum of the divine Law is contained in ten commandments. Seven multiplied by ten produces the number seventy. Hence, with fitting significance, those who had been taken captive to Babylon through wicked works are liberated after seventy years and rebuild the house of God and the holy city. [Col. 0809C]

For sometimes those who, through their sins, had been separated from the communion and fellowship of the holy Church and joined to the lot and number of unbelievers again devote themselves, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, to the practice of good works, and through this fellowship of the faithful—the house and city of the Lord—from which they had been expelled, they are received back.

It must be noted that one and the same penance is [Col. 0809D] typologically signified by the return to the Church, the rebuilding of the Lord’s house after the fire, the restoration of the city of Jerusalem after its destruction, the people’s return to their homeland after captivity, and the return to the house of the sacred vessels that had been carried away.

But since the prophet Ezra sufficiently explains how all these things happened, let us recall something from his book and, insofar as the Lord grants, expound it in a spiritual sense. Thus it may become more evident how those who have perished through negligence or error ought to return to penance; with how great grace from God and with how great exertion on their part forgiveness for their offenses must be sought or obtained; how these penitents, together with those who have recently come to the faith, build one and the same house of Christ; and how together they await the solemnities of its future dedication.

## CHAPTER ONE. Cyrus, at the beginning of his reign, released the people of God from captivity and, returning the sacred vessels, commanded them to go up to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple

[Col. 0810A]

In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, etc. Ancient histories relate—and the Scripture of the prophet Daniel agrees with them—that Cyrus, king of the Persians, together with Darius, king of the Medes, destroyed the empire of the Babylonians, killing their last king, Belshazzar, and razing and devastating the city itself.

Cyrus, knowing that the kingdom had been handed over to him by the God of Israel, as soon as he had conquered that kingdom which had taken the people of Israel captive and oppressed them in servitude, granted that same people permission to return to their homeland and rebuild the house of their God, which had been burned there. He made this decree of liberty known not only by word to those present, but also by letters sent to those who were farther away throughout all the provinces of his kingdom. In a public declaration he confessed that the one who is the God of Israel is truly the Lord and God of heaven, and the author of all kingdoms.

All these things the holy prophets—and Jeremiah in particular—clearly foretold as future events. Jeremiah even predicted the number of years they would serve in Babylon and when they would be recalled to their homeland. Isaiah, moreover, openly disclosed, without any riddles of prophetic speech, the name of King Cyrus, through whom they were to be freed from servitude and recalled to their homeland, and with whose permission they were to restore the temple.

For Jeremiah says:

> Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: “Build houses and dwell in them,” etc. Thus says the Lord of hosts: “When the seventy years in Babylon begin to be fulfilled, I will visit you, and I will raise up for you my good word, and I will bring you back to this place” (Jer. 25; 29).

Isaiah, in turn, says:

> Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer and your Maker from the womb: “I am the Lord, who make all things.”

And a little later:

> I say to the deep, “Be desolate,” and I will dry up your rivers. I say to Cyrus, “You are my shepherd, and you shall fulfill all my will.” I say to Jerusalem, “You shall be built,” and to the temple, “You shall be founded” (Isa. 44).

> Thus says the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subdue nations before his face and turn the backs of kings, and open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut. I shall go before you, and I shall humble the glorious ones of the earth. I shall shatter bronze doors and break iron bars. And I shall give you hidden treasures and secret storehouses, so that you may know that I am the Lord, who call you by your name, the God of Israel, for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel. I called you by your name; I made you like [my Son], and you did not know me. I am the Lord, and there is no other; apart from me there is no god. I girded you, and you did not know me (Isa. 45).

From this prophecy of Isaiah we should believe that Cyrus, the king, especially loved the children of Israel, released them from captivity, sent them back to their homeland, and ordered them to rebuild the temple of the Lord because he had heard that their prophets, through the Spirit of God, had foretold his kingdom and the destruction of the Babylonians.

For the same prophets had specifically described the very manner of conquest by which Babylonia began to be destroyed. Isaiah says:

> I say to the deep, “Be desolate,” and I will dry up your rivers.

Jeremiah, moreover, says:

> That very broad wall of Babylon shall be utterly undermined, and its lofty gates shall be burned with fire.

The histories relate that, after the Euphrates—which flowed through the middle of Babylon—had been divided and drained into numerous channels, the enemy entered the city through its dried-up and desolated bed.

This is what we have briefly said about the historical sense. According to the mystical senses, however, King Cyrus signifies the Lord and Savior both by his name and by his deeds. We say this not from our own conjecture, but on the basis of Isaiah’s most explicit words, spoken in the person of the Lord:

> I made you like [my Son], and you did not know me (Isa. 45).

For God likened him to his Son, although he himself did not at all recognize the God who likened him to the Son. First, this is shown by the fact that God deigned to surname him “his Christ”; then by the fact that he determined, long before Cyrus was born, that he should be called Cyrus, a name interpreted as “heir.” This designation rightly suits the one to whom the same God the Father says:

> Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance (Ps. 2).

The Apostle likewise says of him:

> Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages (Heb. 1).

And when he appeared in the flesh, his enemies who were pursuing him said:

> This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt. 21; Mark 12).

God the Father also likened him to the Lord and our Savior in that he subdued nations before Cyrus’s face, turned the backs of kings, shattered bronze doors, and broke iron bars—namely, those of Babylon and of the other cities he captured—and in that he gave him hidden treasures and secret storehouses, that is, the unknown wealth of various provinces.

So too, through the apostles preaching throughout the world, he likened him to the Lord and our Savior, who subjected to himself the necks of all the nations, and also brought under his rule the very lords of worldly affairs and the authors of secular wisdom; who destroyed the gates of hell, so that he might bring his elect, rescued from there, into the liberty of their heavenly homeland; who crushed the errors of the nations and overthrew doctrines fortified by human reasoning through the mouths of the humble, so that, once these had been corrected, he might open the light of his faith and truth to them, in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Our Lord possessed these treasures eternally from the Father in the nature of his divinity; but in the humanity he assumed he received them in time, from the moment when he himself began to be human.

Thus the Lord likened Cyrus to his only-begotten Son, our God and Lord Jesus Christ. Just as Cyrus, after destroying the empire of the Chaldeans, freed God’s people, sent them back to their homeland, ordered the burned temple in Jerusalem to be rebuilt, and took care to make this same decree known in writing so that the words of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, in which he foretold that this would happen, so the Mediator between God and humanity, after destroying the devil’s kingdom throughout the world, gathers into his Church his elect, who had been scattered and recalled from the devil’s tyranny.

In the present, justified by faith, this Church has peace with God through him; in the future she hastens toward the vision of perpetual peace—for Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” He also causes the burned temple to be restored when, bringing back to salvation those who had lost the faith through the snares of the ancient enemy, he makes them worthy of his indwelling.

He also sent the Holy Scriptures throughout the whole world, through which the faith in his name and the hope of salvation might be proclaimed to all who belong to his kingdom, that is, to all the elect. This was foretold not by Jeremiah alone, but by all the prophets in common agreement, in accordance with what he himself said to his disciples:

> It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled (Luke 24).

The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians, so that, having recognized the power and providence of the God of Israel, he might do what Scripture relates about him. And in the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews:

> When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself; but just as the Father taught me, so I speak (John 8).

Now, when the same Cyrus says in his decree:

> The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth,

he rightly confessed that the God of Israel is the Lord, the God of heaven, and recognized that he possesses all the kingdoms of the earth and can give them to whomever he wishes.

But it seems to sound less truthful when he says that all the kingdoms of the earth had been handed over to him, unless perhaps this is to be understood as meaning that, at the time when he wrote these things, he had no adversary to his kingdom; or else that, after conquering, destroying, and exhausting the powerful and ancient empire of the Chaldeans, he believed that no kingdom anywhere in the world could resist his own.

This statement, however, truly suits the majesty of the one who said:

> All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matt. 28).

The same Scripture of Cyrus continues:

> Who is there among you of all his people? May his God be with him, etc.

Great faith in these words of the king is evident, and great piety. His faith is shown by his understanding that the people of Israel, above all other nations, were God’s people. His piety is shown by the fact that, without excluding anyone, he permitted all who wished to return freely to their homeland.

His faith is shown again by his confession that the same Lord God both dwells in heaven and is present in Jerusalem, and that he can ascend with each of those returning from Babylon to Jerusalem. Is it not clearer than daylight that he believed this God not to be corporeal or confined to a place, but to be Spirit and present everywhere? He confessed that God has a place in Jerusalem and in the temple while not doubting that he simultaneously presides over the kingdom of heaven. He believed that God reigns in heaven while nevertheless being with his faithful on earth and directing both their minds and their hands toward the things that should be done for salvation.

Moreover, all the words of this Scripture breathe a spiritual sense. For whom would it not readily become clear that only those with whom God is present can pass from the confusion of sins to works of virtue, as from Babylonian servitude, into the liberty of Jerusalem? For:

> Without me you can do nothing (John 15).

Who would not see that an ascent is rightly named in the same sentence? For all who sin and serve the cares of the world are in the depths. Those who desire to please God must raise their minds to higher things, long for heavenly realities, and transcend all the world’s pomp and allurements through love of eternal things.

It is also mentioned that Jerusalem is in Judea, that is, in confession, so that we who, through forgetfulness of God, deserved to be taken captive by the Chaldeans—who are interpreted as “demons,” that is, to be enslaved to evil spirits—may return through confession of divine mercy to the vision of free peace and light.

There let us build a house for the Lord God of Israel, that is, in the unity of catholic peace, in confession either of our own iniquity or of divine mercy and grace. Let us prepare our hearts, in which the Lord himself may graciously deign to dwell and illuminate them by his presence. Let us also take care to kindle the hearts of our neighbors to praise their Creator and to works of piety.

In both ways we build a house for the Lord: either when we exercise ourselves in works of righteousness, or when, by our examples and words, we encourage those whom we can to undertake the path of righteousness.

The remaining words of the same Scripture of King Cyrus follow:

> And let all the others in all the places wherever they dwell help him, etc.

The distinction in the wording should be noted. Although the king released everyone from the injury of captivity, he gave permission—and indeed ordered—that anyone who wished to ascend under the Lord’s guidance to build the temple should do so. Yet he did not order everyone to go there.

For if there were some of the same people of God who preferred to enjoy the freedom granted them in their various localities rather than elsewhere, he ordered these people to assist those who were ascending, each from his own place. He provided them with money or livestock for the necessities of so long a journey.

He also desired them to give and entrust other gifts to them, which those who reached Jerusalem were to offer in the temple of the Lord as a memorial of those who remained.

Thus all were freed from Babylonian captivity. All devoted themselves to acts of piety; but the more perfect ascended to build the temple of the Lord, while the others assisted those who had gone up.

For although all the elect, rescued from the power of darkness, belong to the liberty of the glory of the children of God, and all rejoice to be counted among the fellowship of the holy city, that is, the Church, nevertheless it belongs not to all but only to the perfect to labor for the building of that same Church by preaching to others.

Therefore the Apostle considers such people worthy of a double honor above the other faithful (1 Tim. 5). Likewise the angel says to Daniel:

> Those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars forever and ever (Dan. 12).

These teachers of many, the more they instruct their helpers to seek and love heavenly things, the less concern they themselves show for acquiring or possessing earthly things. Indeed, they very often abandon everything temporal that they have acquired for the hope of eternal things.

Therefore their poverty must be supported, so that they can continue preaching, by the generosity of the wealthy who cannot preach, so that the wealthy themselves may also share in that preaching.

In their person John says to Gaius:

> For they have gone out for the sake of his name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles (3 John).

Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.

For this reason it is now said that those who were ascending to build the house of the Lord were to be assisted by gifts of money from their friends wherever they lived—that is, whether in Chaldea or in other places to which they had fled for fear of the Chaldeans.

This was excepted, he says:

> Apart from what they voluntarily offer for the temple of God, which is in Jerusalem.

For those who abound in temporal wealth ought not only to provide what is necessary for Christ’s poor from their resources, but also willingly to perform for themselves the good works they are able to do, so that through the merit of this voluntary offering they too may deserve to have a share in the temple of God, which is the Church.

This brief account of the decree of King Cyrus should suffice. No one will doubt that his words abound in spiritual mysteries, since it was foretold that God would stir up his spirit so that he would understand that these things ought to be written or commanded, and since the prophet Ezra himself reminds us that he issued these commands to the peoples in order to fulfill the words of the prophets.

For how could a king, instructed by divine inspiration, be unable to write heavenly mysteries, when he is shown to have known God, confessed him, loved the true beauty of his house, and undertaken to restore it? Even the faithless governor, the enemy and murderer of our Redeemer, wrote the greatest mystery of true faith when he placed above his cross:

> This is Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.

He persisted so firmly in his intention concerning the inscription that he could not be induced to alter it by the Jews, although they strongly demanded this. He also wrote it, for the sake of a certain sure mystery, in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

For, plainly, all the divine law possessed by the Hebrews, all the worldly wisdom in which the Greeks gloried, and all the earthly power in which the Romans then especially excelled bear witness that Christ is king of all the saints and of all who confess God.

If, therefore, the writing of a ruler hostile to God is laden with so many and such great mysteries, how much more could a king who loved and practiced divine worship, inspired or stirred up by the Lord—as the prophet says—both proclaim and disclose in writing the mysteries belonging to the Lord?

What fruit his decrees or writings produced is shown by the following text of Sacred Scripture in its sequence.

> And the heads of the fathers’ households of Judah and Benjamin rose up, etc.

After proclaiming his decree and sending letters throughout his entire kingdom, Cyrus permitted—or rather commanded—that, from the whole people of Israel, which consisted of twelve tribes, those with whom God was present should ascend to Jerusalem to build the house of the Lord.

Yet not the whole people wished to go up, but only those from Judah and Benjamin, together with the priestly and Levitical tribes, to whom Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord had formerly belonged.

For the other ten tribes had long before, under King Jeroboam, been alienated from the temple of the Lord and from the worship of piety. Because of the merit of so great a transgression, they had been taken captive by the kings of the Assyrians and deported beyond the mountains of the Medes; nor are they ever said to have been entirely sent back to their homeland.

The two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, on the other hand, held Jerusalem and the regions of Judah surrounding it. Together with the priests and Levites, whose responsibility was the service of the temple, they too had imitated the sins of the ten tribes, but they never abandoned residence in the city of Jerusalem or the rites of the temple.

Therefore they were the last to be captured by the Chaldeans and the first, under the rule of the Persians, to be permitted to return home. This was fitting, because our Lord arose from the tribe of Judah, while his mother Mary was also related by kinship to the tribe of Levi. Hence Elizabeth, the wife of the priest Zechariah, is called her kinswoman by the angel (Luke 1).

The tribe of Benjamin had also joined itself to them in religious faith, especially because the city of Jerusalem itself had fallen within its allotment. For this reason it deserved to share in the mercy bestowed upon them.

It is beautifully said that the heads of the fathers of the aforementioned tribes rose up in order to ascend to build the temple of the Lord. For it belongs to heads and fathers—that is, to teachers and preachers—to undertake the contest of pious labor, building the minds of those who are in error by exhorting, rebuking, and correcting them in the practice of good works and instruction.

They are rightly also said to have risen in order to ascend to Jerusalem, because those who refuse to care for their own salvation or that of their brother lie, as it were, prostrate in mind, weak and inactive.

They rise when they hear the king’s decree—or rather, when the Lord stirs up their spirit—so that they ascend to build the house of the Lord. Instructed by the words of the Holy Scriptures and inflamed by the grace of their Creator, they shake off the old lethargy of their former negligence. Taking up the resolve to adopt a better way of life, they strive through daily progress in good works, as though by steps of ascent, toward the heights of virtue that exist in the vision of eternal peace.

Among these steps, the first is that each person restrain his own life from vices by living well. The second is that he also turn his neighbors away from their errors or negligences by teaching them well. The highest is that, after good works and instruction, he await the joys of everlasting reward.

As for the fact that all those who ascended to build the house of the Lord were assisted by everyone around them with silver and gold, goods and livestock, we have explained above briefly how this should be understood mystically: the poverty of preachers ought to be supported by the abundance of wealthy believers.

This can also rightly be understood in another way. The hands of those who build the temple are assisted by their companions, who cannot build, through gifts of money, when secular men entrust their children or household to holy preachers to be educated for the Lord. What they cannot offer to the Lord by themselves, they offer through those who are able to accomplish it.

They give silver vessels when they entrust men resplendent with eloquence. They give golden vessels when they entrust those distinguished by natural intelligence. They give beasts of burden when they entrust people slower in understanding but gentle in bearing the light yoke and easy burden of the Gospel.

They give sheep when they entrust humble and meek persons who are accustomed to give freely to the poor from their resources, as though from milk or wool. They also give possessions and various furnishings when they entrust to the holy teachers of the Lord men or women—parents or masters—distinguished by many different blossoms of good works, so that through them they may be consecrated to the Lord and advance the building of his house.

For many possess by natural gift chastity, patience, modesty, generosity, self-restraint, and kindness. They reject both the honors and pleasures of the world; they love righteousness no less than wisdom; and perhaps, like Cornelius, they devote themselves to prayers and almsgiving. Concerning such people the Apostle says:

> Because those who do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, etc. (Rom. 2).

When such people are offered to holy preachers in Christ in order to be reborn or more fully confirmed in the faith, they are assigned to the heads of the fathers as varied furnishings brought for the building of the house of the Lord.

> King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the temple of the Lord, etc.

Nebuchadnezzar took the vessels of the Lord from Jerusalem when any unclean spirit, snatching certain faithful people from the Church, deprives them of the joy of inward peace. He places them in the temple of his god when he joins them to the fellowship of the reprobate, who are the temple and city of the devil, the head of all evil angels and human beings.

But King Cyrus brings them out and counts them for the prince of Judah, to be returned to Jerusalem, when our Lord, who is the heir of all things, rescues from Satan’s power those whom he predestined to eternal salvation and offers them to the priests of the Church to be reconciled through repentance.

He rightly says that the vessels were counted for the prince of Judah, because the Lord knows the number of his elect, and none of his sheep who confess his great and terrible name perishes. For Judah is interpreted as “confession.”

> And this was their number: thirty golden bowls, etc.

The different kinds of vessels signify different persons or activities among the faithful. Thus we read in the Apocalypse that the twenty-four elders held golden bowls full of incense (Rev. 5); and the Scripture explains by adding:

> Which are the prayers of the saints.

The bowls, therefore, which are open and shining vessels, signify the hearts of the simple, who do not know how to conceal within themselves any deceitful thought, but ordinarily express with a pure tongue what they hold in their minds.

Hence it is rightly said that such vessels contain spices—that is, prayers acceptable to God.

By contrast, the impure breasts of the reprobate are deservedly compared with sponges, which are dark with blind and winding recesses. For this reason the Jews also offered the crucified Lord a sponge full of vinegar (Matt. 27; Mark 15; John 19), signifying by this service that, when their Creator came to them in the flesh, they offered him from a deceitful heart bitter thoughts and words, degenerate and far removed from the purest flavor of their fathers.

The knives with which they used to cut and divide the limbs of the victims according to due order—so that, once everything had been properly distinguished, one part might be consumed by the sacred fire on the altar, one part assigned to the priests, one to the Levites, and one to the use of those who offered them—represent in the Church those distinguished by the grace of discernment.

They know perfectly how to distinguish, concerning the saving sacrifice that is Christ, what should be said to everyone, what only to the more perfect, and what exceeds the limits of human thought and must be entrusted to the fire of the Holy Spirit. At the same time, all who are devoted to God in faithful service are God’s victims.

The knives by which the limbs of the victims are divided into pieces are to be understood figuratively as the scribes instructed in the kingdom of heaven. Examining carefully the merits and understanding of their hearers, they know how to judge rightly whom they ought to promote to which degree of ecclesiastical ministry.

The cups, which are vessels for drinking, figuratively express those who are accustomed to be intoxicated by the more fervent ardor of inner charity.

The fact that some vessels are reported to have been golden and others silver signifies that the golden ones represent those who shine with the greater splendor of spiritual wisdom, while the silver ones represent those who, bright with the beauty of speech, know how to explain more eloquently what they understand.

Distinguishing these from one another, the Apostle says:

> To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit (1 Cor. 12).

The fact that the number of the vessels is mentioned both individually and generally in the total number reminds us that the Lord keeps the total number of his elect written in the book of eternal remembrance—not only those who persevere in the purity of the faith they have received, but also those who, after going astray, return to the faith through repentance.

An appropriate figure of these people follows:

> Sasabasar carried away all of them, etc.

For none of those predestined to life can perish forever. All who belong to the Lord, even if for a time they seem to have been carried away to Babylon—that is, into the confusion of sins—are, through divine providence, restored in some manner to the peace of the Church through the fellowship of the righteous.

The vessels which the army of the Chaldeans is said to have captured in Jerusalem, broken, and carried broken into Babylon represent those who are captured by the victorious devil in such a way that, before they are saved through repentance, they are taken away from human affairs and carried off to everlasting punishment.

## CHAPTER II. The number of those who returned to Judea under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua; also the total amount of money offered by the heads of the fathers for the restoration of the temple.

[Col. 0817D]

> These are the sons of the province who went up from the captivity, etc.

He calls them sons of the province of Judea, not of Babylonia. For those belonged to Judea not only who had been deported from it to Babylon, but also those who had been born in Babylon from their descendants.

Although they had been born bodily in Babylon, they longed with their whole mind for Judea and Jerusalem. Their figure was represented by their distinguished leader Zerubbabel, whose very name shows that he was born in Babylon, while his purpose and actions reveal that he was a citizen of Jerusalem.

In another sense, however, they are sons of the Church, sons of the heavenly homeland—not only those who have already been imbued with the Church’s sacraments, but also those who, although for a time they wander outside, that is, among the ungodly, have nevertheless been foreordained by divine election before the ages to life and are, at the proper time, to be consecrated through the mysteries of divine grace.

Concerning them it appropriately continues:

> And they returned to Jerusalem and Judah, etc.

For when those who had been freed from Satan’s power—those who had strayed from the faith—return with those who had recently learned the faith to Jerusalem, the desired peace, and to Judah, devoted confession or praise, each soon enters again into his own city. That is, each devotedly carries out the guardianship and practice of the virtues that divine generosity has granted him according to the measure of faith.

After saying generally that they had returned to Jerusalem and Judah, the text rightly adds immediately:

> Each to his own city,

because they dwelt individually in their own cities while all generally belonged to Jerusalem and Judah.

Jerusalem therefore signifies the universal state of the holy Church throughout the world. The cities belonging to it signify the individual virtues of the faithful, in which, as though within the defenses of cities, they are protected from the temptations and attacks of evil spirits.

The cities in which those who came from captivity to Jerusalem and Judah dwelt can also be understood as the various Churches of Christ throughout the world, from all of which the one catholic Church is completed. Whoever dwells in them professes individually to be a son of the catholic Church, as a citizen of Jerusalem.

They were led, moreover, by Zerubbabel and Jeshua before the others. Many places in Sacred History show that one derived his lineage from the royal family and the other from the priestly line. Both signify one and the same person: our Redeemer, the true king and supreme priest.

For he alone is the one through whom we must come to salvation. Hence he says:

> No one comes to the Father except through me (John 14).

Through himself, by hidden inspiration, or through open instruction by holy preachers, he gathers each of the elect from the confusion of the present life to the vision of perpetual peace and the confession of divine praise, as from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah.

This vision of peace and confession of thanksgiving begins in the present, by his gift, but is perfected in the future.

> The number of the men of the people of Israel: the sons of Phares, two, etc.

After the catalogue of the leaders, the number of the people follows; after the total number of the people has been recorded, the various orders of God’s ministers follow in sequence.

By “the people of Israel” he means the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and anyone from the other tribes who had once escaped the hands of the Assyrians but had subsequently been captured by the Babylonians and carried into captivity with them.

It should finally be noted that in the actual sequence of the catalogue—and even more so where the same catalogue is repeated in the second part of the book, that is, in the words of Nehemiah—the names of nearly fifteen cities are inserted which, unless I am mistaken, are found exclusively in the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

It is therefore likely that in this passage “the people of Israel” should be understood especially as referring to those tribes, together with the priests and Levites who had received their allotment among them.

The Nathinnei, who are listed after the priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, were those who are now called subdeacons in the Church. They attended to the duties of the Levites and received the offerings of the peoples in the temple.

The sons of Solomon’s servants were called the temple’s craftsmen. They were responsible for repairing the sacred buildings or restoring, from the sacred funds, whatever had been damaged.

What we said above about the vessels must now also be said about the people: Scripture made such a careful distinction in recording how many from each generation of captives had been released and returned to their homeland so that we might be reminded with what certainty the Lord writes the total number of his elect in the book of life and records it, as it were, in the register of heaven—how many souls each of the faithful has converted from error, either by preaching or by displaying examples of good works—and rewards those who converted them with a definite recompense for each one.

> And those who went up from Thelmela, etc.

In this passage even according to the literal sense the grace of God is shown, by which Gentiles were also received into salvation in the Old Testament.

After the catalogue of those whose true membership among the people of God was established had been given, some others were added whose origin—whether from Israel or from proselytes—was unknown; their number was nevertheless set out together with that of the children of Israel.

Although, because of the long separation of their fathers from the temple or people of God, they could not show how they belonged to that people, nevertheless, since a general permission had been given, they had come up from captivity and were hastening with those who certainly descended from Israel to build the temple of God, they were received by them as companions.

They rejoiced to have them as brothers and acquaintances because of their love for the common faith and religion, even though, because of uncertainty about their physical origin, they seemed to know them less well.

In the spiritual sense, however, these people belong among the penitents who, freed from captivity to vices, ascend to build the house of the Lord either in themselves or in others.

There are often some bound by more serious sins who seem so estranged from every act of piety and chastity that no goodness or religious devotion received from holy teachers appears to have remained in them.

What else can be said about such people except that they cannot show whether they were born from Israel—that is, from the holy Church—through believing? For by sinning they have become as though they had never belonged in any way to the holy seed.

Nevertheless, through repentance they are sometimes so thoroughly corrected and turned toward a better life that their number is rightly written in heaven among the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit (John 1).

> And concerning the sons of the priests: the sons of Thobia, etc.

The children of the transmigration exercised the same caution concerning the priests that they are said to have exercised concerning the people. They took great care that it should be clear without confusion who truly belonged to the people of Israel or to the priestly line, and who was suspect or certainly descended from proselytes, that is, from foreigners.

Accordingly, they removed the suspect priests from the service of the altar until their origin became more certain. Nevertheless, they preserved them among the community of the returning exiles in unanimous peace with themselves.

According to the mystical sense, the sons of the priests who ascend from Babylonian captivity seek the record of their genealogy. When they do not find it, they are expelled from the priesthood.

This occurs when ministers of the altar fall into such great crimes or such abominable doctrines that, even if their souls return to salvation through repentance, they cannot be considered worthy to be promoted again to the sacred rank they lost or to resume the office of teaching in the Gospel or administering the sacraments.

Although such people await eternal life among the faithful, they do not find, among the perfect priests, the record of the rank they cannot resume.

> The whole assembly was as one, etc.

Observe that the grace of the primitive Church, in which the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts 4), is also found in this assembly of returning exiles. Although the army was so large that it amounted to nearly fifty thousand, and although it consisted of various ranks and conditions, nevertheless the whole multitude, because of the same faith and love, seemed to be one human being, by the gift of him who makes people dwell together in unity in one house.

The male and female servants of those returning from Babylon to Jerusalem represent in the Church those who strive, through progress toward a reformed life, to overcome vices and ascend the summit of virtue, but who are not yet sufficient in themselves to provide for the path of a disciplined life. Rather, they still need the diligence of those who have gone before them in Christ to restrain them and direct them along the path of the truth they desire.

It follows:

And with them were two hundred male and female singers (2 Chronicles XXV). Not only were singers found among the order of the Levites, together with the temple gatekeepers and the Nathineans, but these same people, accompanied by female singers from among God’s own people, hastened to restore the buildings of God’s house.

Literally, he calls singers those who resounded the psalms with sweet melody; the Books of Chronicles testify that the Levites were accustomed to do this in the temple of God during the daily sacrifices. But it is credible that at that time many from the common people likewise did this, each in his own place. In the mystical sense, however, singers in the temple or people of God are those who, with greater sweetness of soul, both keep the heavenly commandments themselves and, through frequent exhortations, commend them for observance to their hearers.

Female singers are appropriately joined to the singers, namely on account of the female sex, among whom many persons are found who kindle the hearts of their neighbors to the praise of their Creator not only by their way of life but also by preaching, and who, as if by the sweetness of a holy voice, assist the labor of those building the Lord’s temple [Col. 0821A].

The title and text of Psalm CXV correspond to the ministry of all these people. Its title is: “When the house of the Lord was being built after the captivity, a song for David.” Literally, this appears to refer to the restoration of the temple, about which the present book writes. In the anagogical, that is, higher, sense, however, it signifies the building of the holy Church, which is made from souls saved from demonic captivity and recalled to the knowledge of their Creator. In this building, each chosen person ought to resound a song of praise and confession through the strong and desirable hand, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, understanding truly that without his grace he can do nothing good.

To this title the psalm also corresponds: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord and bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples” (Psalm XCV), and so forth.

First, then, we are commanded, in the building of the Lord’s house, to sing a new song to the Lord himself—that is, to retain his love inwardly in the heart and to display the observance of his commandments outwardly. This is not to be done by a few, but by all the earth, through which the holy Church has been spread.

Next, we are commanded to evangelize his salvation, namely Christ—for this is what *bene nuntiare* means in Latin. And this is not to be done to a few hearers, but to all the peoples of whom the Church consists, spread throughout the whole world. This does not mean that one individual can evangelize among all nations; rather, all of us, each in his own time and place, can do so among all peoples, and each both ought and can wish for everyone the joy of perpetual salvation, saying: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples. For his mercy has been confirmed upon us” (Psalm CXVI), and so forth.

Their horses numbered six hundred and thirty-six, and so forth. A male mule (*mulus*) is born from a donkey and a mare; a female mule (*mula*) from a horse and a she-ass. Thus, among the people who came up from captivity, the animals by which their journey was aided are also described, and their number, like that of the people, is recorded in the prophetic book.

For there are many in the Church who are slower in understanding or even carnal in spirit, yet who obey their spiritual teachers with submissive devotion. They humbly offer the back of their minds for bearing the burdens of fraternal necessity, and they themselves, together with the other chosen, rescued from the confusion of diabolical captivity, advance toward the walls of the heavenly city.

Their number, like that of the more perfect, is certainly preserved whole in the eternal memory of the inward Witness. Hence it is said to God in the person of the holy universal Church: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and all shall be written in your book” (Psalm CXXXVIII). And in another psalm: “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord; how greatly you have multiplied your mercies, O God” (Psalm XXXV). But immediately afterward, concerning the more perfect: “The children of human beings will hope in the protection of your wings” (ibid.), and so forth.

And from the leaders of the fathers, when they entered the temple of the Lord, and so forth. It is a great indication of devotion when someone offers to the sight of the divine majesty not only the offerings that are owed—that is, those commanded by the law of the Lord—but also, of his own accord, other gifts about which he has received not a command but counsel.

The commandment is: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XIX).

The voluntary offering is: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor.” And the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Corinthians VII). And concerning himself: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these things” (1 Corinthians IX) [Col. 0822B]. He also says to the Thessalonians: “We did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but in labor and toil we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you—not because we lacked authority, but so that we might give you an example of ourselves for you to imitate” (1 Thessalonians IV).

It is therefore rightly reported that the leaders of the fathers voluntarily offered gifts for constructing the house of God, because the more each person abstains, together with forbidden things, even from things permitted, the more effectively he builds the Church of God. For all who have come to know the examples of their perfection fear falling into illicit things all the more because they observe that these men do not use even permitted things in every respect, but rather say: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Corinthians VI).

It is rightly added that they gave according to their means for the expenses of the work [Col. 0822C]. For this is the measure of human perfection: that each person should labor for the Lord according to his strength and should strengthen the state of the holy Church, first through his own upright conduct and then through the correction of his neighbors.

Those who live in this way among God’s people are rightly called “leaders of the fathers,” because through the perfection of their life and teaching they preside even over those who, through devoted concern, have deserved to be called fathers in the Church. They live more sublimely and transcend the general commandments of the law.

They gave a voluntary offering—gold, silver, and priestly garments. Gold signifies the brightness of wisdom; silver, the splendor of eloquence; and priestly garments, works of righteousness greatly surpassing the customs of the common people and worthy only of priestly hearts consecrated to God. “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise”; “the sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire”; and “let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalms XI, XVII, CXXXI).

Thus the leaders of the fathers offer gold, silver, and priestly garments, according to their means, for the expenses of the temple’s works, when holy men contribute to the building up of Christ’s faithful by making good use of whatever wisdom, eloquence, and good action they possess.

A definite weight of gold and silver, and a definite number of priestly garments, are contained in the sacred history, so that, in accordance with the preceding exposition concerning the number of vessels, people, and animals, we may remember that the Lord is always able to weigh all our thoughts, words, and deeds [Col. 0823A] and to reward them with a worthy recompense.

Among these things, however, we should note how much the injury of captivity and prolonged servitude benefited God’s people. Those who had been taken captive in very small numbers—that is, human souls, as Jeremiah writes, four thousand six hundred, while the rest had either been killed, scattered far and wide through fear of the enemy, or certainly left in their homeland through the mercy of those same enemies—now, having multiplied among their enemies, returned as men to their homeland in a number approaching fifty thousand.

They had been stripped of their wealth and carried away subject to every kind of servitude; now they return not only liberated but enriched with gold, silver, garments, servants, possessions, and animals.

And, most importantly, those who had lost their homeland because of the multitude of false gods, so that the prophet rebuked them with the words, “According to the number of your cities were your gods, Judah” (Jeremiah II), now returned to that same homeland rejoicing not only in faith in the one true God, but also worshiping that faith with one accord and devotion of soul, and submitting themselves with religious mind and tongue to singing its praises. Thus those who were once designated by the divided names Israel and Judah on account of their differing religion were now all called by the ancient name Israel on account of the unity of their piety.

The devotion of piety that they had despised in the holy land, despite the protests of the prophets and the examples of righteousness they displayed, they recalled to mind in a foreign land, among enemies serving idolatry.

What, then, should we observe in these events and commit to memory, except that those whom freedom and abundance of every possession had made negligent in their homeland and forgetful of the heavenly commandments were brought by servitude abroad and poverty to obey their Creator and Liberator?

It is a familiar fact that the human heart is loosened by wealth and freedom, but gathered back to itself by hardship and poverty. Thus, what once happened to one people is daily enacted concerning all who repent after sin: those who through negligence fell into temptations and the snares of the devil rise again with the help of God through the diligence of repentance. Those who were stripped by the ancient enemy of the riches of the virtues and withdrew from the fellowship of the Church often return to its communion after being exercised in greater virtues than those they previously lost [Col. 0823D], because the more seriously they remember that they went astray, the more ardently they strive in good works.

The priests and Levites, and those of the people, dwelt there, and so forth. By “all Israel” he does not mean only the ten tribes that were once called Israel, in distinction from the two tribes called Judah, but generally all who came up from captivity, whether descended from Judah and Benjamin or from the other tribes.

For after the ten tribes had been carried away into Assyria and the Samaritans had been settled in their land, those who remained destroyed and broke all the idols together and began to serve the Lord with an undivided heart and to offer their sacrifices in the temple. The Books of Chronicles clearly prove this, where it is written: “Josiah removed all the abominations from all the regions of the children of Israel and made all who remained in Israel serve the Lord their God. Throughout all his days they did not depart from the Lord, the God of their fathers.”

A little earlier, under the same king, when the restoration of the house of the Lord was being discussed, it says: “They took the money that had been brought into the house of the Lord, which the Levites and gatekeepers had gathered from Manasseh and Ephraim and from all the remnant of Israel, and also from all Judah and Benjamin and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and they delivered it into the hands of those who were supervising the workers in the house of the Lord.”

These remnants, together with the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, to which they had been joined, were taken captive together to Babylon and sent back together to their homeland. Each entered his own city, which he found vacant, together with its fields and villages [Col. 0824B].

They had not entered those cities while they themselves were serving in Babylon, just as no colonist had entered the lands of the two tribes. Scripture says: “Whoever escaped the sword was carried away to Babylon, and he served the king and his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power, and the word of the Lord from the mouth of Jeremiah was fulfilled, and the land kept its sabbaths. Throughout all the days of its desolation it kept sabbath, until the seventy years were completed” (2 Chronicles XXXVI).

When this very long sabbath had been completed, the land of Judea received back its inhabitants together with the rest of Israel. But the greater part of the ten tribes, which had been carried away by the Assyrians beyond the mountains of Media, never returned home. Even if it had returned, it could not have entered its cities, since the Samaritans had taken possession of them.

Concerning these people, the Jews today make a very Jewish and faithless promise to themselves: when their Christ comes and reigns, they too will return to Judea with the other people of their nation and will reign throughout the whole world. They do not understand the words of the prophets, who promised the kingdom and riches of Jerusalem, the city of God, not carnally to the Jewish nation alone, but spiritually to all nations in Christ—as is now being enacted throughout the world.

Let this suffice concerning the surface meaning of the text. In the spiritual sense, the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and Nathineans dwell in their cities, and all Israel in its cities, returning from Babylon, when the ministers of the holy altar, the teachers, and God’s own people each faithfully serve God in their respective ranks. This applies either to those who, after their rank had at some time been stained or lost through vices, were corrected through repentance, or to those who, recently coming from the kingdom of the devil to the Church, acquired for themselves a good rank by serving well.

The Levites or children of Israel entered their cities—not only those who had once lost the same cities when they were taken captive, but also those who, born from the stock of captives, learned through paternal succession that they belonged to those cities.

Likewise, in the spiritual sense, a Levite receives his own city, from which he had been carried away by the Chaldeans, when a deacon of the holy Church, by the Lord’s gift, restores the perfection of virtue that he had lost after being deceived by the devil.

For example, someone who through drunkenness, lust, or pride became unworthy of the rank he had received returns to it more worthily through continence, moderation, humility, and the other marks of a corrected life [Col. 0825A].

Again, a Levite born in Babylon enters his city when he comes into the land of Judea, whenever someone regenerated in Christ puts off the guilt of his first transgression and, well instructed in the Church, preserves with regular discipline the rank of the diaconate that he once received.

For just as he was liberated from Chaldean servitude through the grace of his Redeemer, so also, through the performance of good works in which the predecessors of that same rank lived, he ascends as if to the walls of his own city.

Those of the children of Israel who were carried away captive in such a way that they never returned to their homeland, but left their cities and fields to others to possess, signify the errors of those who depart from the Church by sinning in such a way that they never recover through repentance. Instead, they leave to others who are worthy the rewards promised to them.

Persuading one person—or rather the whole Church—to repentance, the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen, and repent, and do your first works. But if not, I am coming to you and will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (Revelation II).

Again, urging another who perseveres in the faith not to fall, he says: “Behold, I am coming quickly; hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Revelation III).

## CHAPTER III

The people gather in Jerusalem in the seventh month, and, after building the altar, celebrate the Feast of Booths and the other solemnities of the Lord that follow.

The seventh month had now arrived, and the children of Israel were in their cities, and so forth. The seventh month, which we call October, was more solemn than the other months in legal observance; in it the dedication of the temple was also celebrated.

It was therefore fitting to the devotion of the faithful who had come up from captivity that, after each had first entered his own city with his animals and the money he had brought, and had provided suitable dwellings there for himself and his household, they should all immediately gather together in Jerusalem and build an altar there for offering holocausts to God. This was to take place at that season of the year when the temple itself, with its altar and all its vessels, had formerly been consecrated, and when they had been accustomed to come annually on the day of its dedication [Col. 0825D].

In a deeper sense, however, the seventh month signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is described as sevenfold in the prophet Isaiah and in the Apocalypse of Saint John.

In this month, after the captivity, we come together from our cities in Jerusalem when, after our stains have been washed away and the errors of our vices removed, and after we have begun the defenses of good works, we are illuminated by a greater grace of that same Spirit. Thus we are kindled with love for the heavenly peace that is contained in true unity; for Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.”

It is rightly said that all Israel was gathered in Jerusalem in the seventh month as one man. This happens daily in spiritual Israel, when all the chosen throughout the world worship God through one and the same faith, and with one, undivided love yearn for the joys of perpetual peace and faithfulness. To the extent that they are able, they imitate this even in the present by loving and enduring one another.

It is rightly added:

And Jeshua son of Jehozadak rose, and so forth. For the work of divine worship he employed the leaders Jeshua and Zerubbabel, who, as we said above, together complete one and the same figure of the Lord and our Savior: Jeshua in relation to the priesthood, and Zerubbabel in relation to the kingdom, because the former descended from a priestly line and the latter from a royal line.

Our Lord is the true king of Israel—that is, of all who see the Lord—and the true high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. He is high priest because through the offering of his body he washes us from our sins, and even after his passion and ascension he intercedes for us at the right hand of the Father (Romans VIII).

He is king because in the present he girds us for spiritual battle and helps us to conquer, while in the future he grants an everlasting kingdom to those who conquer.

Not only Jeshua and Zerubbabel, but also their brothers presided with them over the building for the people. These are the brothers whom our same king and priest, after the glory of his resurrection, appeared to the women seeking him and addressed: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matthew XXVIII).

These brothers—namely, those who are greater in the Church and cling more familiarly to their Redeemer—build his house with him when, with his help, they strengthen the hearts of the faithful by their words and examples.

It is rightly said that he calls Jeshua’s brothers priests. The Apostle Peter says to the whole Church: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter II). John likewise says in the Apocalypse concerning the whole Church: “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ” (Revelation XX).

Since all the chosen are members of the supreme priest, when they present their members as a living sacrifice and offer their contrite spirit as a sacrifice to God, they are rightly reckoned by the dignity of both brotherhood and priesthood.

With great religious foresight, the children of the transmigration built God’s altar first of all. Since the temple of God had not yet been founded, they nevertheless had a place where, by offering holocausts and sacrifices, they could display the devotion of their minds.

We too do this spiritually in the Church today, when above all we place in our hearts faith in the Lord’s incarnation and passion, and when we deliver this faith to our hearers as something to be received before all else and rooted in the depths of their hearts, in accordance with the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians, who were still inexperienced in Christ: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians II).

On this altar we ought to offer our holocausts—that is, our perfect thoughts and works—because the vows of our actions can be pleasing to God the Father only if we participate in the sacraments of our Redeemer and are kindled by the power of his Spirit as though by the fire of the most holy altar.

A holocaust is called a “whole burning,” and by this name they called those sacrifices or offerings from which nothing was permitted to pass into human use, but everything was to be given to God and consumed by sacred fire.

These sacrifices mystically portrayed the life of the faithful who seek nothing of their own and devote everything they live to the service of the inward Judge. They rejoice not only in trampling underfoot, for the Lord’s sake, the pleasures of soul or body, but also in laying down their very lives for him. They can say with the apostles: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matthew XIX).

In answer to them he himself says: “And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

This holocaust of a more chaste and sacred life must be offered on the altar of the God of Israel, because, as we have said, our good works can be acceptable to God the Father only through faith in our Redeemer.

For Diogenes and those like him, followers of foolish philosophy, although they abandoned their possessions and lived a naked and poor life in the world, did not follow the Lord. They appeared to make a holocaust, but they did not make it on the altar of the God of Israel, because although they removed themselves from their own pleasures, they did not know Christ Jesus as their advocate with the Father.

Concerning this altar it is rightly added:
