They placed the altar upon its bases, and so forth. The bases of the altar are the hearts of the chosen, prepared to receive the sacraments of the Lord’s faith by the commandments of preceding teachers, as though by the tools of craftsmen [Col. 0827C].

It is rightly one altar, but there are many bases that bear it, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God (Ephesians IV), but there are many hearts of the faithful. Established by one rule of truth and gathered, as it were, into an equal fold, they bear the common burden of the heavenly sacraments with shared devotion.

Otherwise, whoever entrusts the sacraments of the faith to people who are less instructed and have not yet taken care to abandon their former vices places the Lord’s altar upon the ground without bases, because he entrusts heavenly things to minds that are still earthly.

The Lord’s saying in the Gospel is appropriate here: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matthew V).

Just as the Lord is rightly called an altar because he cleanses us from our iniquities and, receiving the vows of our prayers, commends them to the Father, so he may also appropriately be called a lamp, because in the vessel of his assumed humanity he placed the light of eternal divinity.

The bases are placed beneath the altar, and the lampstand beneath the lamp, when all the faithful humbly submit their hearts or bodies to putting into practice through their works what they believe.

When it was said that they placed the altar upon its bases, it was rightly added that the peoples of the lands around them terrified them. For whenever the devout beginnings of the faithful are made to God, opposition immediately appears from wicked spirits or human beings who strive to prevent the good work from being completed [Col. 0828A].

Such peoples are rightly called “peoples of the lands,” in distinction from those who say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III).

Although the peoples of the lands terrify them, the citizens of the heavenly city must persevere in the virtuous works they have begun. For it follows:

And they offered holocausts to the Lord upon it, morning and evening.

We offer a holocaust to the Lord upon his altar when, with firm faith established in our hearts through complete devotion, we devote ourselves to good works. We do this morning and evening when we remember with certainty both that we received the beginning of our saving intention from him and that we can bring the good things we have begun to completion only through the help of his grace. Therefore, with burning desire for a godly way of life, we return vows of thanksgiving to him in all things.

Again, we make a holocaust in the morning when, for the light of spiritual knowledge we have received, we repay our Creator by living well. We make a holocaust in the evening when, in expectation of the everlasting rest that we hope to receive from him after our good works, we burn with unceasing zeal.

In the literal sense also, we rightly understand ourselves to offer a holocaust to the Lord morning and evening, when we take care to please the sight of the divine majesty at all times. Rising at dawn, we do not proceed to the necessities of human frailty before, kindled by the fire of divine love, we commend ourselves to the Lord in devoted prayers, according to the one who said: “And in the morning my prayer will go before you.”

Likewise, after completing the works of the day, we do not give sleep to our eyes or slumber to our eyelids before we consecrate a place for the Lord within us through more diligent persistence in prayer, in accordance with what the same prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands as the evening sacrifice” (Psalm CXL).

And they celebrated the Feast of Booths, and so forth. The Feast of Booths, which in the Gospel is called in Greek *Scenopegia*—that is, the “fixing” or “setting up of booths”—was a festival of seven days. It began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. During those days the Lord commanded the entire people to make booths for themselves from foliage and branches of beautiful trees, and, leaving their houses, to remain in those booths for seven days, daily searching out the decrees of the divine law and offering holocausts to the Lord in fire [Col. 0828D].

They were commanded to do all this in memory of the time when, after once leaving Egypt, they lived in booths in the wilderness, while Moses proclaimed the law and the divine presence appeared to them repeatedly. They were to await for a long time the permission to enter the promised land, so that the grace of so great a benefit would never slip from their minds.

Therefore, when those who had come up from Babylon arrived in Jerusalem, burning with great devotion to carry out all the Lord’s commandments, they took care to celebrate this feast after gathering on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, performing on each day of that week what the law had commanded.

We too ought to perform all these things spiritually with equal devotion [Col. 0829A]. We too have gone out through the blood of the Lamb from Egyptian servitude, so that we might come to the promised land, when, baptized into the sacraments of the Lord’s passion, we cast off the heavy yoke of transgression, so that, adopted into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, we might be heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

We lived in booths and tents, traveling through the wilderness for a long time until we came to our homeland, when in baptism we renounced not only Satan, as though he were the king of Egypt—that is, of darkness—but also all the pomp and works of this world. We promised that we were pilgrims and travelers in this world, but citizens of another life, which we hoped to receive from the Lord.

In memory of this hope and promise, we must remain in booths during the seventh month [Col. 0829B]. That is, as the grace of the Holy Spirit, described as sevenfold, illumines us, we must abandon this world entirely in mind as something foreign and oppressive, and hasten with fixed intention toward the unfading joys of paradise.

We must do this for seven days—that is, throughout the whole period of the present life, which revolves through the same number of days—without ceasing. On each day of this week we must offer a holocaust and perform the work of the day on its own day.

The holocaust is the offering wholly consumed in matters that properly pertain to divine service, such as prayers and fasts. The work of the day on its own day consists in those things that pertain to the service of fraternal love: giving bread to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold, lodging to the traveler, visitation to the sick, burial to the dead, instruction to the one who has gone astray, and consolation to the sorrowful [Col. 0829C].

When he said that they were to offer a holocaust each day according to the commandment of the law and perform the work of the day on its own day, he rightly inserted the words “in order,” because whatever is done in the services of either divine or fraternal love without order loses the merit of its perfection.

“Judgment loves the honor of the king” (Psalm XCVIII). Whatever we devoutly do in honor of the supreme King must necessarily be distinguished by the discernment of judgment, so that we know when and to what extent it should be done. Otherwise, if we perform a right work with insufficient order, we distort the norm of its righteousness.

Paul indicated that these solemnities of the booths, that is, *Scenopegia*, should be celebrated mystically when, while preaching, he practiced the craft of tentmaking (Acts XXVIII) [Col. 0829D].

For he made *scenomata*, that is, booths, so that he might teach both that he himself was an inhabitant and pilgrim of the world, and that those whom he instructed should live as pilgrims in this life while awaiting and hoping for their homeland in the future.

We customarily use tents when traveling or journeying. The same Apostle testifies that the saints live in this way in the present life when he says: “While we are in this body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians V). And to the Hebrews: “For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews XIII).

Since he wished those who completely alienate their minds from the world and faithfully confess themselves citizens of the homeland that is above to open the entrance immediately to all virtues within themselves, it is rightly added:

And after these things, the perpetual holocaust, and so forth. He calls the perpetual holocaust that which was offered morning and evening.

He calls the beginnings of the months “Kalends,” that is, the rising of the newborn moon. The Hebrews always began their months from this point, since they had no months except lunar ones. Hence the Greeks more appropriately call the Kalends *neomeniai*, that is, “new moons.”

If the month, because it is completed by thirty days, signifies the fullness of works of light—when we fulfill the commandments of the Decalogue in faith in the Holy Trinity—what do the beginnings of the months signify, when the moon is said to be newly kindled by the sun so that it may shine for us again, except the beginnings of each good work? These we receive, through the grace of our Creator, as though from the presence of the Sun of righteousness.

To signify this divine illumination, without which we can neither begin nor complete anything good, the Lord commanded all the Kalends—that is, the beginnings of the months—to be celebrated and the ceremonies of sacrifices to be observed.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Psalm LXXX). This means plainly: “Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord and in the word of teaching sounding forth to your neighbors, as soon as you perceive that you have been regarded by him for the performance of a good work in the notable light of inward inspiration.” Through this inspiration it is fitting for you to be drawn away from desire for this world and to devote yourselves more deeply to divine things.

It is therefore rightly said that, after completing the Feast of Booths, the children of the transmigration offered a perpetual holocaust both at the Kalends and at all the solemnities of the Lord that had been consecrated, and in all the occasions on which a gift was voluntarily offered to God [Col. 0830C].

For after the mind has once renounced this world completely, it ought continually to devote itself wholly to the service of the divine will, which we have said is signified by the holocaust. It should do this both at the beginning of every good action and in the devout performance of the virtues that the Lord has commanded, as well as in those matters through which the pious mind, beyond the general commandments, gladly serves the Lord of its own accord.

Concerning such matters the Lord himself, not commanding but giving counsel, says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess” (Matthew XIX). And when discussing the refusal to marry, he says not by commanding but by advising: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (ibid.).

Paul too gloried in those things that he had offered to the Lord as a voluntary gift, saying: “Do we not have authority to eat and drink? Do we not have authority to take along a believing sister as a wife?” (1 Corinthians IX), and so forth, in the same passage.

From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings, etc. It has often been said that the seventh month signifies the sevenfold illumination of spiritual grace. Hence it is rightly said here: “For from the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord,” because, plainly, from the very beginning of divine inspiration the human conscience must be changed; and, neglecting the lowest pleasures, it must burn only with desire for those things that belong to the Lord. From the first day of the seventh month—that is, from the first illumination of heavenly grace—they offered the burnt offerings of virtues to the Lord. When the Holy Spirit came upon them in tongues of fire, they were immediately changed, as it were, from what they had been, and began to burn with new flames of inward love and to proclaim the mighty works of God in the languages of all the nations. They devoted themselves so completely to this burnt offering—or rather, they themselves became a burnt offering—that they could more readily be killed by those who held contrary opinions than be recalled from their purpose.

Therefore, among the Hebrews, the same seventh month is rightly called the new year. By its name it indicates to us that the Holy Spirit is given to the faithful so that, through this gift, they may fulfill the new commandment of mutual love and may resound with a new song of heavenly praise in the building of the Lord’s house. Concerning the observance of this month the Lord gave the following mystical command:

“In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, there shall be for you a sabbath of remembrance, with the blowing of trumpets, and it shall be called holy. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord” (Lev. XXIII).

The sabbath of remembrance—that is, rest—will be on the first day of this month when the mind, kindled by divine power, has abstained from temporal allurements and has striven to contemplate the will of God. The priests blow the trumpets when the faithful endeavor to proclaim even to their neighbors the fervor of inward sweetness that they have begun to feel. No servile work is done on such a sabbath when the mind has kept itself, insofar as possible in this life, free from every pleasure and contagion of sin by pleasing God. For servile work is sin: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII).

And thus a burnt offering is rightly offered to the Lord on that same sabbath, because the person is truly freed from slavery to sin whose whole heart is set ablaze by the fire of love.

It should be noted, according to the literal sense, that the people are reported to have assembled in Jerusalem in the seventh month; and that, after everyone had assembled there, Joshua and Zerubbabel with their brothers built an altar; and that from the first day of that same seventh month they offered a burnt offering to the Lord. From this it is inferred that this altar was composed very quickly of unworked stones, and was not, as formerly, made of wood and covered with bronze plates. For otherwise, even with a very large crowd of builders laboring on it, it could not have been begun, completed, and prepared for the offering of a burnt sacrifice on one and the same day. In the Book of Maccabees too it is shown to have been made of stones, when it is recorded that, after it had been profaned by the Gentiles, it had to be restored by Judas Maccabee after six years (1 Macc. IV): “They took whole stones according to the law and built a new altar like the former one.”

It should also be noted that the beginning of the fifth age of the world, like that of the four preceding ages, is consecrated by burnt offerings offered to the Lord. In the first age, the blessed protomartyr Abel, the first of all the elect, offered God burnt offerings from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat. He consecrated the entrance of the newly arising world, first with the victims of animals and finally with his own blood.

Noah consecrated the beginning of the second age by offering God burnt offerings from all the clean living creatures that the ark had contained. The third age was sanctified by Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, and by the patriarch Abraham: the former by offering bread and wine, the latter by offering his own son to God. He also consecrated the very beginning of that age—that is, the time when he received the promise and entered the promised land—by building an altar there and invoking God’s name.

King David consecrated the fourth age to the Lord by building an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and offering burnt offerings to God, by which he might appease His anger, incurred when he numbered the people (2 Sam. XXIV). Abraham is also said to have once offered his son at that place; and afterward, when Solomon built the temple, the altar of burnt offerings was established there.

Now Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel consecrated the beginning of the fifth age. As soon as they returned to Jerusalem after the yoke of their long captivity had been shaken off, they built an altar in the same place and offered burnt offerings to God. Thereafter they took care to appease the Lord on their behalf each day with the continual burnt offering.

All these things went before as a figure of the one who was to come in the flesh in the sixth age and, by the sacrifice of his own flesh and blood, redeem the whole world.

After the altar had been built and burnt offerings had been offered to God, Scripture continues:

But the temple of God had not yet been founded.

The foundation of God’s temple here typologically represents those who, recently converted to the faith, prepare a dwelling and habitation for the Lord in their heart and body, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you?” (1 Cor. VI). And again: “That Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (1 Cor. VI).

Those who had been freed from captivity and had come to Jerusalem therefore resolved to build the temple, which they later completed by their work. But first, after building the altar, they commended themselves to the Lord through daily burnt offerings, so that they might deserve to approach the building of the temple in a more purified state.

The same is necessary in spiritual building: whoever decides to teach others must first teach himself. Whoever intends to instruct his neighbor in the fear or love of God must first make himself worthy of the office of teacher by serving God more earnestly, lest he hear from the Apostle: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Rom. II). Hence the Apostle says of himself: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (1 Cor. IX).

Therefore the sons of the transmigration are appropriately found to have offered God no other victims or sacrifices than burnt offerings—that is, wholly consumed offerings. For everyone who wishes, by teaching, to restrain another from unlawful acts must surrender his entire self to his Creator by living well and even abstaining from what is lawful. Thus, both by the merit of good action he may obtain more abundant heavenly assistance in preaching, and by the example of that same good work he may more effectively urge his hearers to follow what he teaches.

This may also be interpreted mystically in the following way: those who have recently turned to the Lord offer burnt offerings to God after building an altar, but do not yet build the temple. Once they have recognized the faith, they burn with such love for Him with their whole heart that they can already be counted among the perfect, even if they have not yet received the time or opportunity to undertake and complete the good works they desire.

The blessed Abraham offered such a burnt offering to the Lord even before the temple had been built, when he had already become perfect in faith but had not yet carried out the works of faith. Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XIX). When he added to the perfection of faith the fullness of good work, offering his son Isaac upon the altar, he offered more perfect burnt offerings to God, as though the temple too had been built. For each act or step of pious devotion is like a row of hewn stones by which we construct in our heart a house and dwelling beloved by God.

How, then, the sons of the transmigration proceeded to the building of the temple after constructing the altar and offering burnt offerings to God is shown below.

They gave money to the stonecutters and the masons, etc.

Stonecutters are those who cut stones. Hence it is written in the Book of Chronicles: “David commanded that all the resident foreigners in the land of Israel be gathered, and he appointed from among them stonecutters to cut stones” (1 Chron. XXII). Masons are those who make mortar from gypsum or lime for joining stones together. Thus another translation has “stonecutters and craftsmen” instead of “stonecutters and masons.”

The people’s devout diligence should therefore be noted: they spared none of their resources, but from what they themselves needed and from which they lived, they either bought materials for building the temple or hired workers.

Joppa is a coastal city of Palestine, lying approximately forty miles from Jerusalem. Sidon and Tyre were the most renowned cities of Phoenicia, with Mount Lebanon nearby. Accordingly, the sons of the transmigration, obtaining their assistance, asked that cedar trees be cut from Lebanon and transported by rafts across the sea as far as Joppa, so that from there they could be carried overland to Jerusalem for the work of the temple. The same procedure is known to have been followed in the first construction of the temple. For this reason Solomon, by royal power, received whatever he wished from his friend King Hiram without any labor of his own. These exiles, however, returning to their homeland after many years, because they did not possess royal power, obtained everything required for the desired work at a price.

In the spiritual sense, the stonecutters in the construction of God’s house are those who instruct the hearts of their neighbors by teaching or rebuking. While teaching them to stand firm among the participants in the same grace, they fit them together like squared stones arranged around one another. For a square will stand whichever way it is turned. When the minds of the elect remain unmoved amid all the circumstances of the world, whether adverse or prosperous, they show that they possess, as it were, the form of a square—invincible virtue. In this sense Noah’s ark too is described as having been made of squared wood (Gen. VI). For the same Church that is signified by the temple made of stone was also prefigured by the ark joined together from wood. The same Church was also represented by the tabernacle composed of boards and curtains (Exod. XXXVI).

The masons in the Lord’s house, however, are those same holy preachers. While they bind together by the bond of charity those whom they instruct in good works, they join them, like squared and polished stones, with an infusion of mortar, so that they do not abandon the order of their composition. They say: “Be prudent and vigilant in prayers, and above all have continual mutual charity among yourselves” (1 Pet. IV). The Apostle Paul, after commanding us to possess compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, and other such qualities—as though they were stones of the heavenly building—immediately adds: “Above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. III).

Sidonians and Tyrians, who cut cedar trees from Lebanon for the structure of the temple, also figuratively signify the same holy preachers. By the axe of God’s word they cut down from their former way of life people who were once exalted and splendid in the glory of this world, so that, beneficially cast down and, as it were, purged by fire from the corrupt moisture of their inborn disposition, they may correct them from every crookedness of vice and raise them up as an adornment and defense of the holy Church.

Of this it is said figuratively in the psalm entitled “At the dedication of the tabernacle”: “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars” (Ps. XXVIII). The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars so that the tabernacle may be completed, when, through heavenly inspiration, the hearts of the proud are humbled, so that, once these too have been corrected, the number of the holy Church may be brought to completion.

Hence Sidonians are rightly interpreted as “hunters,” and Tyrians as “the distressed” or “those brought into straits.” The holy preachers are hunters when they catch and subject to Christ, in the nets of faith, the wandering and errant thoughts of the wicked, as He Himself says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV). They are also “the distressed,” because they experience affliction in the world, although they are confident because the Lord has conquered the world (John XVI).

The stonecutters and masons, therefore, preparing stones and mortar; and the Sidonians and Tyrians, transporting cedars from Lebanon for the work of the temple, signify the holy preachers who, by instructing their hearers, train their minds for fellowship with the Church.

The heads of the ancestral families—namely Joshua and Zerubbabel and their brothers—give money to these stonecutters and masons to make them more ready for their work. So, when they preach the word, those teachers who have preceded them in age, merit, and learning offer, with Christ as their source, either examples of their virtues or the pages of divine writings. Strengthened by their exhortations and promises, the workers become less weary in the heavenly labor.

They also give food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and Tyrians so that they may transport cedar wood from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa. This occurs when they commend to those same teachers, so that they may be capable of preaching, the spiritual gifts to be desired, among which charity is greatest (2 Cor. XII).

Or certainly it occurs when our Lord—whom we have taught is represented by both Joshua and Zerubbabel—distributes spiritual gifts to these ministers of His word. Enlightened inwardly by them, they become stronger in preaching to overthrow the arrogance and foolish wisdom of the proud.

There is no need to explain how food, drink, and oil signify the inward refreshment of our mind for one who rightly recites the Psalmist’s saying to the Lord: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me. You have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, intoxicating, how splendid it is!” (Ps. XXII).

Money is therefore given to the stonecutters and masons, and food, drink, and oil are given to the cutters of wood, so that they may prepare materials for building the Lord’s house. This occurs when divine generosity confers an abundance of virtues upon preachers of the truth, by which they may be helped sufficiently to correct the hearts of the wicked and make them fit to receive heavenly blessings.

They transport the cut wood across the sea—not to be submerged in it, but to be carried across it to Joppa, whose name means “beauty.” This occurs when these same teachers declare to their hearers, called to the faith, that the temptations of the world will confront them but must be overcome by faith. First they must endure the savage waves of vices or wicked people, and then reach the most beautiful walls and harbor of the virtues.

We may also understand the wood destined for the temple’s construction to be carried by sea to Joppa in this way: first we renounce the devil, who is called by the prophet the dragon, king of all that is in the waters—that is, of the ungodly, whose way of life is not in heaven but in the disturbances of the sea of this fluctuating world. We renounce all his pomp and works, and then arrive at the beauty of faith, by which we confess the holy Trinity, the one true God; the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation; the unity of the holy Church; the remission of sins; and the resurrection of the flesh.

Hence Peter rightly raised Tabitha, a woman devoted to God, from death in this city (Acts IX). For plainly, in the perfection of this faith, the whole Church in general is raised from the death of sins through baptism. And when, after baptism, we again incur the death of sin, it is necessary that through the same faith we come back to life by repentance and, through reconciliation by the priests, be restored once more to the assembly of the faithful.

## CHAPTER IV

In the second year after their arrival the house of the Lord is founded, but the people of the land prevent its completion.

[Col. 0835D]

In the second year after their arrival, etc.

He says that they came to the temple of God, not because they found the temple already built—for it was stated above that it had not yet been founded—but “to the temple of God” means to the place of the temple of God, to the work by which they wished to rebuild the temple.

The Jews of the present day are mistaken when they commonly say that the walls of the temple were never overthrown by the Chaldeans, but only its roof. For Ezra plainly writes that the sons of the transmigration built the temple from its foundations.

Since it was said above that they came to Jerusalem in the seventh month, while it is added here that in the second year after their arrival, in the second month, they began the work of the temple, it is perfectly clear that during seven months they prepared stones, mortar, wood, and the other necessary materials. At the beginning of the eighth month they began to devote themselves to the desired work.

There were six months of the first year and the seventh month of the following year. Anyone learned in such matters will easily recognize that this occurred in a great mystery. For seven belongs to the sabbath, on which day the Lord either rested from all His works after creating the world or, after redeeming the world through His passion, rested in the tomb. Eight refers to the first day after the sabbath, on which He rose from the dead. Seven refers to our hope of sabbath-rest after death; eight looks toward the joy of our eternal blessedness after the resurrection.

Since, therefore, all the activity of the elect, who are the temple and house of God, both begins and is completed through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and is carried out with every regard and intention toward the future rest and immortality, the builders of the temple rightly begin, from the seventh month, to prepare the expenses needed for the building by offering burnt offerings to God; and, having made preparations during seven months, they undertake the work itself in the eighth.

No other number at all is found in the preparation for so great a work except the number that figuratively signifies either the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit by which we who labor are assisted, or the rest of souls, or the resurrection of bodies, for which we labor in good hope.

What the period of forty-six years signifies—the time during which the temple was built, as the Gospel too testifies—will be explained in its proper place.

The great devotion of that whole people, which we too must diligently imitate, is shown when not only the elders—namely Zerubbabel and Joshua, together with the remaining priests and Levites—but all who had come from captivity to Jerusalem, from the greatest to the least, appointed Levites to hasten the work of the Lord.

They rejoiced that they had returned from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem. To the degree that they detested the idols and crimes of the proud city from which they had escaped, they desired to see the beauty of the city consecrated to the Lord, to which they had deserved to come. To the degree that they abhorred the temples of idols in which they had long participated, they wished the temple of their Creator, whose destruction they mourned and from which they had long been exiled as captives, to be restored as quickly as possible.

In the same way today, bishops and priests ought not only to build by teaching the people of the faithful, that is, the house of God, but also to appoint as leaders, by giving counsel, those teachers who diligently fulfill the most holy work of the word. The people themselves, called from the captivity of vice to the vision of true peace, must demand the ministry of the word from those who know how to speak.

These ministers of the word, that is, the Levites, are reported to have been appointed from twenty years of age and upward. For those are to be placed before the people for preaching God’s word who show the Decalogue of the law as an example to their hearers not only through the execution of works but also preserve it undefiled before their Creator through purity and integrity of heart.

There is no doubt that the Church prospers and advances where the bishops, properly preserving their rank, regularly appoint teachers of truth for the people to be instructed by, and where the people themselves compel the teachers given to them not to cease speaking by listening attentively and obeying their words.

But alas, what a sorrow! The carelessness of our times harms both the greater and the lesser: it hinders some from preaching the word, others from listening, and both from acting. We consider too little either how severe was the bitterness of the devil’s captivity from which we were delivered, or how great is the solemnity to which we have been called—the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all—whose pledge we have already received in the present Church.

Let us, however, contemplate the outstanding works of the Fathers, so that we may be more deeply ashamed of the smallness of our own conduct. The text continues:

Then Joshua and his sons stood, etc.

Here Joshua does not refer to the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, but to one of the Levites concerning whom it had previously been said that they had been appointed from twenty years of age and upward to hasten the work of the Lord. Among them were also Kedmiel and the sons of Henadad, who are said, together with their sons and brothers, to have applied themselves to the same work entrusted to them. Indeed, in the preceding catalogue of the people of Israel, these are named first among the Levites after the priests: “The Levites: the sons of Joshua and Kedmiel, of the sons of Hodaviah, seventy-four” (Ezra II).

From both passages it is therefore inferred that they were the leaders and patriarchs of the Levites of that time. It is appropriate that the sons of Judah are placed among the Levites, since they jointly devoted themselves to restoring the Lord’s temple; and, because of this same agreement in piety, they are said to have stood as one.

This is the order of virtue that, as we said earlier, we must always imitate: each person, according to his own measure, should build the holy Church, all the ranks dedicated to God, and the devotion of the entire common people.

It should be noted and frequently recalled how much good the evil of captivity brought to the people. Once delivered from it, they are shown to have devoted themselves to the service of heaven with an intensity such as they had never shown before.

Even today it has benefited many who had lived negligently in the peace of the Church to fall suddenly into error and into certain crimes. After being raised up through repentance following their fall, they began to serve the Lord more vigilantly. Those who had seemed sluggish and careless in remaining innocent were warned by the ruin that befell them to gird themselves more diligently for their own protection against all the snares of the ancient enemy. Thus those who had offended by failing to care even for their own lives afterward also took care, through their own restoration, for their brothers’ salvation.

All the people returning from Babylon to Jerusalem therefore took charge of restoring the temple, but especially the Levites and the sons of Judah, on account of the priestly and royal dignity of the holy Church taken together. The royal and priestly tribe in particular builds the temple, because all who instruct the hearts of the faithful either by teaching or by living well belong to the body of the eternal king and priest, that is, to our Lord and Savior.

Hence the founders of the work themselves came from both tribes: Jesus from the priestly tribe and Zerubbabel from the royal.

After the temple of the Lord had been founded by the masons, etc.

The devotion of all the persons is greatly displayed when, after the temple of the Lord had been founded, the priests, the Levites, and the entire people, each according to his rank, praised the Lord’s mercy.

The priests, clothed in holy garments as they had been accustomed to be while the temple still stood, sounded the trumpets and kindled the people’s hearts to the sweetness of heavenly praise. The Levites sang hymns to the Lord on well-sounding cymbals. The people, with a common shout, displayed the affection of their hearts in praising the Lord.

The Levites praised the Lord “by the hand of David,” either by singing with the instruments that he had made, or by singing the psalms that he had instituted, or because, when he placed the ark, David appointed Asaph and his brothers as leaders to give thanks to the Lord, as the Book of Chronicles testifies. Of them it says again: “His sons were under his direction, prophesying according to the king” (1 Chron. VI).

Rightly, then, in this passage, when the sons of Asaph praised and gave thanks to the Lord “by the hand of David”—that is, according to his arrangement—they are to be understood as having done so.

According to the mystical sense, after the temple of the Lord has been founded by the masons, the priests stand in their vestments with trumpets. When sinners have been converted from error and faith in and love of Christ have been founded in their hearts, all the teachers of the Churches who hear of it rejoice with them. They adorn themselves more diligently with good works and sound forth the trumpets of salutary doctrine, so that both by the example of their virtues and by the encouragement of their words they may assist the good beginnings of those who have recently come to the grace of Christ through repentance, or who have recently converted others to the grace of Christ by teaching.

The Levites too stand to praise God on cymbals when ministers of the second order serve their Creator through pious actions for the instruction of beginners in the faith, and do so in the sweetness of mutual charity. Cymbals, which strike one another in order to resound, most appropriately express works of charity, by which the saints rouse one another to praise their Creator.

They also praise Him “by the hand of David, king of Israel,” when they diligently consider the works that the same Lord and Savior performed in the flesh and strive to imitate them insofar as they are able.

[Col. 0838D]

Many also of the priests and Levites, etc.

Those who had seen the temple formerly founded and this temple before their eyes raised, in part, cries of weeping and, in part, shouts of joy. They rejoiced because the temple of the Lord, which had been destroyed, had now begun to be restored. They wept because, when they saw it, they mourned how far the wall begun in their own time fell short of the magnificent power of Solomon, by which the former temple had been founded.

They rejoiced greatly because, released from captivity, they had received the opportunity to rebuild the temple. But they wept with a loud voice because they knew that the former temple had been destroyed on account of their sins, and they were utterly unable to equal either its size or its beauty.

For the prophet had said: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than that of the former” (Hag. II). This pertains to a greater glory not with respect to the size or adornment of the house, but with respect to the matter itself. It was a greater miracle and a clearer manifestation of divine power that a small remnant of captives, even while their enemies resisted them, was able to complete so great a work than that the wealthiest king, having no adversary at all—but rather having the most powerful and richest king of Tyre as his helper—accomplished this work with the most skilled craftsmen, according to his will.

Again, the glory of that latter house would be greater than that of the former because, in the former house, the worshipers of the Old Testament proclaimed the writings of the law and the prophets to the people. In the second, Christ and the apostles proclaimed the grace of the New Testament and the entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

In the rebuilding of the spiritual temple too, weeping and joy arise together among its leaders. Holy teachers rejoice in the salvation of penitents; they mourn because they once committed things requiring repentance and did not always persevere in the will of their Creator. Those who have risen from the death of the soul through repentance themselves exult in their salvation; they mourn because they once lost the life of the soul by sinning.

The newly converted also rejoice that they have been gathered by the grace of their Redeemer. They grieve that, together with the whole human race, they perished in the first parent, and that, as though the temple of God—the state of the immortal body and soul—had been corrupted by enemies, they had been carried away to Babylon, that is, to the confusion of the present exile.

But because, as good works increase, the envy of the wicked increases equally, and because amid the growth of the devout there will never be a lack of attacks by the wicked—who try to harm the saints either by falsely displaying goodness or by openly inflicting evil—the text rightly continues:

(1 Ezra IV.) When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard, etc.

The history is well known. By the enemies of Judah and Benjamin it means the Samaritans, whom the king of the Assyrians transferred from various peoples during the captivity of the ten tribes into their cities and lands. Afterward they accepted the law of God and observed it in part, while nevertheless continuing to serve the same images as before.

Because these people detested true worshipers of God, they promised assistance with the work so that, once admitted into the community, they might bring harm.

It is easy for anyone to see that such peoples figuratively represent false brothers—that is, heretics and bad Catholics. They are enemies of Judah, that is, of the confession and praise that the Church now offers to the Lord through true faith and works worthy of faith. They are also enemies of Benjamin, that is, of the sons of the right hand, since they separate from the lot of the faithful people those who listen to them—the people who in the future will receive blessing and the eternal kingdom at the Judge’s right hand.

Such people therefore say to Zerubbabel and the heads of the ancestral families: “Let us build with you.” Heretics seek the authority to preach to be granted to them equally among Catholics, claiming that they seek your God just as you do and promising that they hold and love with them one and the same right faith and purity of conduct. They do this so that, once granted the power to teach among the good seed—from which the Apostle Paul received the name *spermologos*, that is, “a sower of words”—they may secretly insert the weeds of their doctrine.

Some did this at the Council of Nicaea: they subscribed to the orthodox faith among the Catholic Fathers, but not with a Catholic mind, so that the more familiarly they were mixed with the faithful, the more freely they might prepare a place for the acceptance of Arian treachery.

Pelagius did the same at the council in Palestine. He anathematized his own heresy—which fiercely opposed the grace of God—in confession and writing, but not sincerely, lest, if he were himself anathematized by the Catholic priests, he should lose his place for teaching in the Church and his opportunity to sow his error.

“Behold,” they say, “we have sacrificed victims since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who brought us here.”

You have sacrificed victims, but unclean ones, because you have not renounced idols. “For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. VI).

You entered the land of the sons of Israel without being brought in by Joshua and without being subject to the rule of Jerusalem. You were brought into his land by a faithless king, an enemy of God’s people—not to serve the Lord in it, but to serve that king who was His adversary.

So too heretics and false Catholics, when they attack the peace of the Church either by living perversely or by teaching, are entirely foreign to the kingdom of Jerusalem. They belong instead to the lost lot of the Gentiles, whose sins they do not abandon. Indeed, to speak more plainly, such people enter the boundaries of the holy Church not under the Lord Jesus but under the leadership of the devil, whom King Esarhaddon of Assyria represented.

For what else is happening except under the devil’s instigation when someone receives the sacraments of the Church, not so that he himself may be consecrated to God and healed through them, but so that, having been consecrated, he may corrupt others through familiarity and become deserving of harsher condemnation?

Simon Magus did this (Acts VIII). He received baptism in the Church not out of concern for his own salvation, but so that he might more certainly learn, through proximity, the affairs of the Church. He made this clear by the outcome itself, when he most bitterly disturbed the Church—not in the person of a feigned brother, but in the person of an open enemy.

The text continues:

It is not for you and for us to build a house for our God, etc.

It does not belong to heretics to build the Lord’s house, which is the Church, from which they are proved to be alien. It belongs only to those who, adhering to Christ, the true king and priest, have deserved to be called the heads of the ancestral families, because of the pious care they have for those who desire to see God—which is what Israel means.

And so it happened that the people of the land hindered, etc.

He rightly calls them “the people of the land,” those who troubled the workers of truth and attempted to impede the work of the Church.

By “the people of Judah”—that is, those who confess and glorify Him—he means the people who sought to build for the Lord God with an undivided mind, that is, to do His will and seek His glory, and to turn toward Him the minds and mouths of all whom they could.

Would that we did not know how often heretics have hindered the doctrine of true confession, not only in individual cities but also throughout entire provinces, either by teaching perversely or by raging with hostility.

To say nothing of the teacher of the nations, who, after being imprisoned for two years in Caesarea because of the persecution of the Jews (Acts XXIII), was restrained from the ministry of building God’s house by the silencing of his tongue: behold, through the plots of succeeding heretics, the blessed Athanasius was an exile from his homeland for many years; Ambrose was besieged in his own city; Hilary was banished into exile; Eusebius suffered martyrdom; many bishops in Africa had their tongues cut out and were expelled from their province; and others were afflicted or killed by various punishments.

They left the house of God, which they had built, to be profaned by the people of the land—that is, by people seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ—until, at a divinely appointed time, the opportunity was again supplied by wise architects to rebuild that same house after its captivity. That is, until the Catholic Fathers were given the means to restore the Church after the heresies had been exposed and overcome.

[Col. 0841B] **But they hired counselors against them, etc.** The distinction of the words should be noted: he says that they hired counselors, having paid them, against the restorers of the temple, so that their plan might be destroyed; yet he does not say that their plan was destroyed, or that they ceased from the work, before they prohibited them by the authority of the letter of accusation sent to Artaxerxes, at his own command, as Scripture says, “by force and power.” For it follows:

“Then the work of the house of God in Jerusalem was interrupted, and it was not carried on until the second year of Darius king of the Persians” (I Esdras 4).

From this it is gathered that throughout the whole period of Cyrus, once the work had begun, they continued to press on with it, although more slowly than was proper; but after his death they were not hindered by secret counsels, but were driven away from the work by open opposition. For while Cyrus, who had ordered that work to be done, was still alive, the enemies did not dare openly to resist his decrees, though they did so by covert suggestion and counsel.

The allegorical meaning is readily apparent: heretics pursue the Church, as the opportunity of the time permits, now with the counsels of malignant doctrines, now with a more bitter struggle of the sword; and sometimes they do not fear to harass her even with the support of gentile rulers. They impede the hands of the people of Judah when they hold back the Church, in her weaker members, from the works of pious confession. They strive to destroy the plan of working when they endeavor to turn their minds away from the very intention of good action. They accuse them before kings when they seek even the assistance of earthly rulers against the Church. How greatly this harms the faith became clearer than daylight during the period of Arian treachery.

## CHAPTER V. The Samaritans write letters of accusation to the kings of Persia and, by a royal decree, prohibit the work of the temple.

**In the year of the reign of Ahasuerus . . . they wrote an accusation, etc.** Josephus (*Antiquities* XI, 2, 3) considers this Artaxerxes—the one who, receiving the letter of accusation from the Samaritans, forbade Jerusalem and the temple to be rebuilt—to have been Cambyses, the son of Cyrus. Cambyses himself reigned for eight years after his father had held the empire for thirty years; after him the Magi reigned for one year, and Darius son of Hystaspes succeeded to the kingdom.

[Col. 0842A] In the second year of this Darius, in whose reign he permitted the temple to be built, the angel, intervening on behalf of the people, said through the prophet Zechariah: “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year” (Zechariah 1).

As for Ahasuerus, to whom the letter of accusation is likewise said to have been sent, perhaps the reason why it is not said whether he wrote back or gave any reply is either that, dying in the same year in which he began to reign, he left the height of kingship—and the care of these matters—to Artaxerxes; or that, although he was Artaxerxes’ contemporary, he allowed him, as the more powerful, to handle and decide these matters.

**This is the copy of the letter, etc.** Artaxerxes, to whom the appeal is made and who, persuaded by it, ordered that Jerusalem should not be rebuilt, represents either some gentile ruler, certainly an enemy and persecutor of the Church; or the ancient enemy of all good things, the adversary of the Jews who accused ecclesiastical men before the king. The Samaritans who brought the accusation signify heretics, as always. Accordingly, in a fitting expression, they call Jerusalem a rebellious and utterly wicked city. For heretics judge the Catholic unity, which they attack, to be such.

In reality, however, she is rebellious, and she builds her walls and ramparts with stones of right faith and heavenly testimonies against the weapons of attacking errors. Isaiah says of these walls: “Salvation shall occupy our walls, and praise your gates” (Isaiah 60). Yet she should be called wicked only by those who are wholly alienated from the best judgment.

Among these things it should be noted that from this time the people of God began to be called by the name “Jews,” because those who first came up from captivity and restored the walls of the city of Jerusalem and the work of the temple were chiefly from the tribe of Judah; after overcoming the enemies who held the neighboring regions, they again took possession of the province, which had been emptied of its inhabitants.

**Now therefore let it be known to the king, etc.** Thanks be to God, because the enemies of the city of the Lord, which is the Church, confess the truth about that city. For if it was built after the captivity, and if its walls were raised from living stones—that is, from holy souls—against the pride of this world, then the citizens of that city, that is, the people of the elect, will no longer pay the tribute of impious servitude to evil spirits by sinning.

Indeed, the building of piety harms the rulers of the power of the air, since every day, through the washing of regeneration, many who had been born into the service of that kingdom because of the guilt of the first transgression are taken away from the devil’s kingdom. Through the action of the grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, they now pay to the enemy no unjust but to their Creator a just tribute of due service. They return to the giver from whom they received them the annual revenues of their firstfruits and tithes—which are produced through the beginning and perfection of good works—both by living well and by giving thanks.

**We therefore, remembering the salt that we ate in the palace, etc.** The Samaritans eat salt in the palace when heretics instruct themselves with the flavor of worldly philosophy, the sweetness of rhetoric, and the cunning of dialectical art. They also deem it impious to see harm inflicted on the king, since they cannot tolerate anyone attempting to assail the devil’s kingdom by pious faith or action. They fear that wars may be stirred up in the Church, lest its defenders wage battle against their heresies and deceits together with the doctrines of the gentiles, under the leadership of the one who says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10); and again: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke 12).

He means the sword of his word, with which he strikes down adversaries, and the fire of charity, with which he kindles the hearts of his own people and burns all the weapons and shields of the opposing sect.

**We announce to the king that, if that city is built, etc.** He calls the river the Euphrates, within which Syria lies. This aptly signifies the stream of holy baptism, either because it is one of the four rivers which, issuing from the one source of Paradise, water the whole world—an image of the four evangelists, who, inspired by the one source of life, namely, the Lord and Savior, proclaim the bath of salvation to all nations with harmonious voice—or because “Euphrates” is interpreted as “fruitful.” This name most appropriately suits that sacrament by which the world, washed and sanctified, customarily brings forth for God a thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit of souls.

The king of Persia—whose name is interpreted as “those who test”—therefore seeks possession beyond the river when the ancient enemy, stirring up assaults of temptation, tries to invade the boundaries of the Church and to subjugate even those who have been redeemed by the sacred font.

[Col. 0843C] The Samaritans help him when heretics attacking the Church fight on behalf of the devil’s kingdom. They are said to grieve, as though saying: “If that city is built and its walls are restored”—through the true faith, certainly, and the religious works of the righteous—then he who is beyond the river, that is, in the hearts of those who have already been reborn to God through baptism, will no longer be able to possess a place or a dwelling.

This is also understood of those who do not understand the true faith: light and darkness, iniquity and righteousness, Christ and Belial cannot possess one and the same mind.

**The king sent a message to Rehum Beelteem and to Samsai the scribe, etc.** The literal meaning is clear, and so is the allegory: the profane king, namely the ancient adversary, most willingly favors the wishes of those who persecute the Church and prohibit her from being built.

The enemies of Jerusalem dwell in Samaria, which is interpreted as “guardian”—not because they can in any way preserve the commands of faith and truth, since they are shown, with obstinate mind, to oppose the vision of true peace, but because they boast that the guardianship of the virtues remains with them when they fight against the walls of peace through heresy.

**And so the copy of the decree of King Artaxerxes was read, etc.** The order of the history is clear: first the enemies of the people of God hindered the holy work by persecuting it; then they tried to scatter the plan of their right intention by wicked counsels. Yet they were still unable entirely to withdraw them from the work of the house of the Lord, until, supported by royal assistance, they opposed them with public authority.

Their fraud in making the accusation should be noted. They charged those who were building the house of God with building a city against the kingdom of Persia. When the king ordered that the city should not be built, they immediately used the authority of the royal letters to resist, with harmful force, the building of the temple—although they themselves had accused them of nothing concerning the construction of the temple, but only concerning the city, and although the king had prohibited nothing except the construction of the city.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0843]

## CHAPTER VI. At the exhortation of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel and Joshua build the temple of God; and Tattenai, governor of the region beyond the river, asks Darius what should be done about them.

[Col. 0843D]

**(I Esdras 5.) Now the prophet Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, etc.** These matters are written more fully in the books of those same prophets. In their words they either rebuked the negligence of those who had been too indifferent toward the work of the temple, or, by promising God’s assistance, stirred them to work. With similar devotion, at their exhortation Zerubbabel and Joshua, or the whole people, girded themselves for the work of building the house of the Lord.

The prophet Haggai begins as follows:

“In the second year of King Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Say to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and to Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come to build the house of the Lord.’ And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: ‘Is it time for you to dwell in paneled houses, while this house lies deserted?’” (Haggai 1).

A little later:

“And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Jesus son of Jehozadak the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. They entered and worked on the house of the Lord of hosts, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius” (ibid.).

And later, the passage quoted above:

“Great shall be the glory of this latter house, greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts” (Haggai 2).

Zechariah likewise begins:

“In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo the prophet” (Zechariah 1).

From this heading it becomes clearer how Ezra calls the same prophet “son of Iddo”: namely, he was his grandson. Iddo himself is to be understood as having been a noble prophet; since Zechariah was distinguished among the prophets, he could rightly be called his son.

Among these matters it should be noted how great was the spirit of these prophets: against the edict of so great a king, and against the Samaritans and all the surrounding peoples who were hindering the building of the temple, they ordered that the temple should be constructed.

Zerubbabel and Jesus, together with the people who were with them, are likewise shown to have possessed no less faith, since they listened rather to the prophets commanding them than to the authority of the king who prohibited the work.

But because we have often spoken in this volume of Zerubbabel and Joshua, or Jesus—for it is one name—and of how they signified the Lord Savior, the king and high priest, both in origin and in action, it seems useful to explain their very names and how they signify him.

Zerubbabel therefore means “garden in Babylon,” or “master of Babylon”; Shealtiel means “God is my petition”; Jesus or Joshua means “savior”; Jehozadak means “the righteous Lord.”

Indeed, plainly, as does the son of Nun, the name signifies the Lord Christ Jesus. Thus each of the two led the people into the promised land: the former from a long dwelling in the wilderness, the latter from the still longer servitude of captivity. This prefigures the true Jesus, who rescues his elect from every evil and leads them into the joys promised by the heavenly kingdom.

He is the son of Jehozadak, that is, of the righteous Lord, of whom it is sung in the Psalm:

“The righteous Lord shall cut off the necks of sinners; let all who hate Zion be confounded and put to shame” (Psalm 128).

Zerubbabel, who is called “a garden in Babylon,” pertains, according to the history, to Zerubbabel himself, because he was born there, although he was of the line of David, who was born in Bethlehem.

According to the allegory, however, the name pertains to the Lord, who, in order to rescue the world from the confusion of errors, deigned for a time to arise and dwell in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this world.

He is also called “master of Babylon,” not because he teaches the things of Babylon, that is, of this world, but because he educates those whom he finds oppressed beneath the yoke of the Babylonians in the grace of liberty, and leads those whom he has educated to the walls of the heavenly homeland.

His father is Shealtiel, that is, “God is my petition.” He himself says in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2).

Moreover, each of the faithful, when invoking the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and seeking nothing else from him but God himself, may rightly be called Shealtiel, that is, “God is my petition,” in accordance with the Psalmist:

“For what remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72)

—and so forth, until he says:

“But for me it is good to cling to God.”

God is therefore our petition when we seek from him only himself, so that we may deserve to enjoy his eternal vision.

**At that time Tattenai came to them, etc.** The literal meaning is clear: strengthened by the words of the prophets, the leaders of the Jews were no longer able to be hindered from the holy work by the attacks of their enemies, though earlier, while the prophets were still silent, they had ceased from it through fear of those enemies.

The same order of events now takes place in the holy Church. Those who, delayed for a time by the snares of wicked men or spirits, had remained lukewarm toward good work are suddenly corrected by the words of faithful teachers or of the divine Scriptures. They then begin to burn with such zeal for good pursuits that no machinery of temptation can conquer them or recall them from the purpose of their intention.

It is reasonably asked how it is said, “To whom we replied,” as though the writer himself had been present at that time, since Ezra is said to have written this book, yet is found not to have been in Jerusalem during those days but to have come there much later, under Artaxerxes.

Either he really was there at the time when the temple was being built and, after the temple had been completed, returned to Babylonia in order to bring more of the children of Israel back to Jerusalem; or, even if he was not yet there when the temple was being built, he nevertheless joins himself to those who were building it, because he considered everything that was being done among his brethren, or by them, to be as though it were his own.

Thus the Apostle also, for the sake of fraternal harmony, in a certain sense associates himself with the saints who will exist at the end of the age:

“We who are alive, who remain until the coming of our Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4).

**And it pleased them that the matter should be referred to Darius, etc., through the end of the letter.** This letter, which Tattenai writes to Darius, is very different from the letter that Rehum and Samsai wrote to Artaxerxes. The former is full of accusation against the people of Jerusalem; this one is full not only of praise for the people but also for almighty God.

It begins as follows:

“To Darius the king: complete peace. Let it be known to the king that we went to the province of Judea, to the house of the great God, which is being built with unhewn stone, and timber is being placed in the walls. The work is diligently constructed and advances in their hands. Therefore we questioned those elders and said to them: ‘Who gave you authority to build this house?’” etc.

In these words it should also be noted how it is said that the house of God was built with unhewn stone, although it is clear that so great a work could have been made only from dressed stones. “Unhewn stone” should be understood as new stone: they found it unhewn, but by dressing it made it suitable for the building of the house of the Lord.

Even if some of the old stones remained—those which, as Jeremiah shows in his lament, had been scattered at the head of all the streets (Lamentations 4)—there is no doubt that the stones from which the work of the temple could be completed were new stones requiring dressing.

The mystery of this matter is immediately apparent when we see that the Church of God is built not only from those who, through repentance, return to the life of holiness that they had formerly lost by sinning, but also from those who have recently been called to the faith and, shaped by the instruction of teachers as though by the craftsman’s rule, are placed in the building of the house of the Lord in an order appropriate to them.

It may also rightly be understood that the temple was built from old and new stones—from those dressed long ago and those that had remained unhewn for a long time—since the one Church of Christ is gathered from both peoples, namely the Jews and the gentiles.

One of these peoples had long existed, as though dressed, through knowledge and observance of the law of God; the other, enslaved to idolatry, had not cast off the deformity of its rustic and earthly mind through any skill of spiritual architects or any practice of piety.

What follows in the same letter is: “And timber is placed in the walls.” The timbers attached to the walls of the temple for their support or adornment signify the same life of the saints, for the adornment of the holy Church, as the stones signify, according to what we taught above.

The prophet mentions these timbers in the Psalm in which the house of the Lord is built after the captivity:

“Then all the trees of the forest shall exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth” (Psalm 96).

The hearts of those who were once proud exult because they have been cut down from the impious mountain of ancestral tradition and have deserved to be transferred into the building of the house of the Lord.

They exult before the face of the Lord because he has come to judge the earth. By salutarily fearing the severity of his judgment, they anticipated it; and although once they could have feared his coming as sinners, now, corrected and justified, they eagerly desire him to come to them.

That former letter was therefore written in treacherous terms, while this one was written in friendly terms—and rightly so. The former came from the Samaritans, who were everywhere enemies of the Jews; this one was sent by the governor of the region beyond the river, that is, of lower Syria and Phoenicia, and by his associates. They had no private hostility against the Jews; they merely sought to know and carry out the will of the king from whom they had received the authority of the governorship.

Accordingly, the Samaritans, who in writing the first letter inflamed the king’s anger against the builders of the temple, are appropriately compared with heretics. They often defile the Church with such a foul plague that they make her hated even by gentiles and stir up their fury against her.

This governor of Syria, however, who does not incite the king against the work of the house of God by accusing it but asks him for guidance, rightly represents those who, while still living among the gentiles, admire the faith and works of the Church. They do not deny that they will believe if they can understand that this is the true and righteous worship of the divinity.

After hearing the elders of the Jews explain the reason for their building, he heard them say:

“We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are building the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel had built and completed. But after our fathers provoked the God of heaven to anger, he delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the Chaldean, and he destroyed this house also,”

and the rest of what they replied concerning the restoration of the same temple, which had been commanded by Cyrus.

After hearing this, he did not wish to contradict them further with his associates or to hinder the builders. Rather, with a simple intention, he inquired whether Cyrus had ordered the temple to be built and whether Darius himself wished it to be built.

Once the will of both kings was known, he himself, together with his associates, carefully provided assistance for the building of the temple, so that the whole work might be completed, as is written in what follows.

All these things correspond to the mind and action of those who, previously situated in gentile life, are suddenly astonished when they see the conduct of the holy Church. Then they strive to hear and learn the reason for that religion; and finally, once they recognize that it originated from the God of heaven and earth, who alone is the true God, they rejoice to believe in his mysteries, to share in them, and to assist his building.

But let us see what King Darius did after receiving the letter of the governor and his associates.

## CHAPTER VII. After reviewing the letters of Cyrus, Darius orders the temple to be built; it is completed in the sixth year of his reign.

**(I Esdras 6.) Then King Darius commanded, etc.** Josephus (*Antiquities* XI, 3) gives the name of the place in which these letters of Cyrus were found in this way:

“And a scroll was found in Ecbatana, in a tower constructed in the region of Media.”

Another translation reads:

“In Ecbatana, in a very secure building in the region of the Medes.”

It therefore seems likely that the name “Medena” signifies nothing other than Media.

As for what follows:

“And let them lay foundations that support, etc.,”

we have no need to explain it, since neither in the earlier building of the temple nor in the later one is anything of these dimensions or of this kind of work found.

It is therefore inferred that Cyrus produced this from his own understanding and recorded the measure or arrangement of the work as it seemed appropriate to him. For, according to the *Books of Chronicles*, the temple, in its first measurement—that is, within the inner walls—had sixty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width.

As for its height, the history of the Kings records that it was thirty cubits up to the upper chambers, then another thirty cubits up to the upper chamber, where the height of the porticoes rose, as Josephus testifies (*Antiquities* VIII, 3); then another sixty cubits up to the top of the roof. Thus the total was one hundred and twenty cubits, as the *Books of Chronicles* teach.

How, then, does he say that there should be three courses of unhewn stones and then courses of new timber, when the whole interior of the temple was covered with cedar? Perhaps it was the custom of the Persians to construct temples in alternating work, so that three courses of stones formed the walls and the fourth was made of worked timber; and he thought that this should also be done in the temple of Jerusalem.

Or perhaps he was speaking of the priests’ court, which surrounded the temple. Around it, there were three courses of dressed stones and a fourth of cedar timbers; it was as high as the breast of those standing nearby.

Or perhaps the house of the Lord in front of the temple is intended—the one of which Scripture, when describing the construction of King Solomon’s palace, says:

“He also made the great court, round about, with three courses of hewn stones and one course of dressed cedar; and likewise the inner court of the house of the Lord and the portico of the house” (3 Kings 7).

**But also the golden and silver vessels of the temple, etc.** When he says that the vessels were then placed in the temple of God, he means the temple of the Babylonians, where Nebuchadnezzar had placed them, as is read more explicitly above. Cyrus had ordered them to be taken from there and brought back to Jerusalem.

Thus far extend the letters of King Cyrus, which had been found in Ecbatana. To them, suddenly and in a new and unusual manner, the following was added in the person and authority of King Darius:

**Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of the region, etc.** The continuity of the text is therefore as though Darius himself had read the letters of Cyrus and, immediately after reading them, confirmed them by his own authority. Thus, restraining all their adversaries, he ordered the temple of God to be built in its place according to what he had read, and he himself helped God's worshipers in every respect, with the most devoted willingness to serve him.

Artaxerxes, therefore, who above forbade the house or city of God to be built, represents those rulers who opposed the building of the holy Church through persecutions unto death. Amid these disturbances the same Church flourished especially through the victory of the martyrs.

Darius represents the pious devotion of those kings who, once they recognized the will of the Christian faith, took care not only not to resist it but also to assist it with their own resources. Many of them, when the earlier persecutions had been prohibited, wished to consecrate themselves, together with the peoples subject to them, to the mysteries of the same faith.

Their persons are aptly represented by what is subsequently added in the words of King Darius:

**But it is also commanded by me, etc.** Who could explain how greatly the Church throughout the world has either been aided or enriched by the generosity of royal gifts?

The passage may also be understood allegorically: expenses for the work of the temple are supplied from the king’s treasury when some members of secular ruling families come to the faith of Christ with the favor of those same rulers. They were, as it were, in the king’s treasury because they were entrusted with royal secrets.

They are given to the priests, that is, to the elders of the Jews, for the expenses of the temple’s work when those who have preceded in the confession of Christ—teachers who instruct them and unite them to the members of the Church—are entrusted with them.

Such was Cassiodorus, once a senator and suddenly a teacher of the Church. In the excellent exposition of the Psalms that he produced, he carefully considered what Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, Cyril, John, and the other brothers had said. He thereby demonstrated that he had unquestionably been taught by the elders of the Jews, that is, by those who confess and praise.

A similar meaning is found in what follows:

**And if it should be necessary, calves, etc.** Who does not know that calves, lambs, and kids—which are clean animals—as well as grain, salt, wine, and oil, all of which were offered to God according to the law, are frequently understood in the sacred Scriptures as signifying good people, perfect works, or spiritual gifts?

All these are now offered in burnt offering to the God of heaven at the king’s command. This happens when, with the authorities of this world favoring it, the affairs of the holy Church grow, and the peoples subject to them are gathered from every side to be consecrated to Christ in one and the same faith of truth. Whatever good each person has heard naturally from God, and whatever salutary teaching he has learned from the men of the Churches, he devotes entirely to the service of divine worship.

It is appropriately said that these things should be given according to the rite of the priests who are in Jerusalem, because the vows of those who offer are acceptable to the Lord only when they are offered according to the order of Catholic peace.

Whatever good is mixed with pagan superstition or heretical contention should in no way be considered good.

The same priests offer these things for the life of the king and his sons, in accordance with the Apostle’s words:

“I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life” (1 Timothy 2).

**Therefore the decree has been established by me, etc.** The literal sense is clear: he wished anyone who attempted to alter the decree of his religion to perish under the gravest punishment—namely, the loss of all that he might possess and of his own soul, which, after he had been fastened to the wood amid the torment of prolonged suffering, he would lose.

The spiritual meaning is also clear, since all our works are compared with wood: good works with fruitful wood, but evil works with barren wood fit for burning.

The wood is taken from the house of the one who tried to oppose the Lord’s burnt offerings, and it is raised up, and he himself is fastened to it, when the works of those who resist the peace of the holy universal Church are openly shown to everyone as useless and perverse. They are proved to have sought for themselves in those same works not the joy of life but rather a snare of death.

The house of such people is also made public—that is, entered in the public register—when even their bodies, in which they remained longer in this life, are handed over to the most savage exactors, namely spirits, to be punished forever at the resurrection.

Darius rightly and faithfully desires that his decree be confirmed by the help of divine power, when he suddenly adds a prayer, saying:

“But may the God who has caused his name to dwell there destroy every kingdom and every people that stretches out its hand to oppose and destroy that house of God which is in Jerusalem.”
