**I, Darius, have established the decree, etc.** As a man temporarily endowed with a temporal kingdom, he does everything he can by public law for the peace of the house of God and, insofar as he can, crushes those who oppose it.

Because God possesses eternal and omnipotent power, Darius truthfully asks him and piously desires that he accomplish the same thing: that his name may remain forever in his house, and that whoever presumes to attack it may themselves be deprived of the eternal kingdom and life.

The same order of events now occurs in the holy Church when earthly powers, converted to the faith, issue public edicts on behalf of the Church’s security. With the Lord’s help, they desire that she have perpetual tranquility and peace, and that all her enemies be placed beneath her feet.

**Therefore Tattenai, governor of the region beyond the river, and Shethar-bozenai . . . carried it out so carefully, etc.** Even now, when peoples stream to the faith and sometimes those who are outside favor its peace, the elders of the Jews—that is, those worthy of the teaching office—build up and prosper their Church daily by word and example.

Although the ancient enemy attacks for a time, the word of God nevertheless finds some in whom it prevails; once the adversaries have been driven away, it builds the walls of truth.

**And they prospered according to the prophecy, etc.** The same prophets had foretold that, if they persisted in building the temple, then, with the Lord’s gift, they would soon complete the work itself and would also abound more generously in every good thing as the reward of their devotion.

Among these prophecies is that of Zechariah:

“The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands shall complete it; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you” (Zechariah 4).

That is: when you see that the temple has been completed by Zerubbabel himself, by whom it was founded, then you will understand that he was sent by the Lord and that I spoke what I said at his command.

Haggai likewise says:

“From the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day on which the foundations of the temple of the Lord were laid, set your hearts upon it: Is the seed yet in the bud? And has neither the vine, nor the fig tree, nor the pomegranate, nor the olive tree blossomed from this day?” (Haggai 2).

The outcome of events itself showed that this had truly been foretold.

All the prophets, indeed all the sacred authors of Scripture, promise prosperity to the builders of the holy Church—that is, to its teachers—if they themselves, worn down by adversity, do not cease from the holy labor.

Divine assistance will be present, by which the house of the Lord begun in the hearts of its hearers will be completed through believing and living well.

The same architects will receive the blessing of the fruits of the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive—that is, a more abundant supply of spiritual gifts. Without any doubt, the Lord will grant these to us more generously the more diligently we strive to build his dwelling of glory, either in ourselves or in the hearts of our neighbors.

No one should think that Haggai’s statement that the foundations of the temple were laid under King Darius contradicts the sacred history we are explaining, in which it is written:

“In the second year of King Cyrus, the temple was founded by the masons, while the people rejoiced greatly and praised God” (I Esdras 3).

For in that passage the foundation of the temple itself is described, that is, of the inner holy house, whose dimensions are specifically reported both in the history of the Kings and in Chronicles.

Here, however, the foundations of the buildings surrounding that house on every side are narrated together with the building of the house itself: the porticoes and treasuries which encircled it. Chronicles mentions them in this way:

“He also made the priests’ court, and the great basilica, and doors for the basilica, which he covered with bronze” (1 Chronicles 4).

In this basilica surrounding the temple, the people used to stand for prayer, and the guards and gatekeepers of the temple used to keep watch in their turns, day and night, as the book of Chronicles teaches at great length.

Sometimes this structure is counted generally as part of the house together with the temple itself, as in the Gospel. When the Pharisees and scribes brought to the Lord, while he was teaching in the temple, a woman caught in adultery (John 8), they could not have brought her anywhere except into one of the temple’s porticoes.

At other times it is named separately as the treasuries, chambers, porticoes, or courts. Hence the Psalmist says:

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

[Col. 0852A] “And they built and constructed,” etc. He calls Artaxerxes the one who reigned after Darius, during whose reign Ezra went up from Babylon to Jerusalem. It is asked, however, how it can be said that the house of God was built at the command not only of Cyrus and Darius but also of Artaxerxes, when it is immediately added that, while Darius was still reigning, it was completed and dedicated. Unless, perhaps, we should believe that Artaxerxes too, having sent to Jerusalem a very large weight of gold and silver, ordered that if anything remained unfinished in the construction or adornment of the temple or its vessels, it should be completed from the money he had sent and donated. For when Ezra was hastening there, it is written that the same king, together with his princes and counselors, sent a great quantity of gold and silver and precious vessels to the temple.

[Col. 0852B] Among other things, the king’s letter contains the following in its copy: “And whatever else shall be needed in the house of your God, as much as may be necessary for you to spend, you shall give from the treasury and from the king’s fiscus” (I Esdr. VII). The month of Adar, on whose third day the house of the Lord was completed, is the month which we call March; Scripture is accustomed to call it the twelfth month according to the course of the moon.

Nor is it without a mystery that the house of the Lord, which was begun in the seventh month with the construction of the altar, was completed in the twelfth month. For it was begun at the start of the seventh month because we begin every good work with the grace of the Holy Spirit going before us, and, with that grace accompanying us, we strive toward perfection. It was completed in the twelfth month because of the symbolism of perfection contained in this number, especially [Col. 0852C] on account of the total number of the apostles, in whose faith and teaching the Church is perfected.

Likewise, the number twelve signifies the perfection of right faith and action because, whether you multiply three by four or four by three, you arrive at twelve. Three is rightly referred to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; four, to good works, because of the four more excellent virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. The Book of Wisdom mentions these in its praises of wisdom, saying: “For she teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful in human life” (Wis. VIII).

Rightly, therefore, the house of the Lord was begun in the seventh month and [Col. 0852D] completed and dedicated in the twelfth, because the mind of the elect is illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit so that it may attain the perfection of good works together with faith in the holy and undivided Trinity; and thus, rejoicing, it awaits the dedication of blessed recompense.

And since this recompense itself—our future solemnity—is fulfilled at the time of the universal resurrection and in the vision of that same Trinity in which we now believe, rightly the house of the Lord is remembered as having been completed not only in the twelfth month but also on its third day. For because the Lord rose from the dead on the third day, our resurrection may rightly be signified by the number three. Concerning it the prophet says: “For he has wounded us, and he will heal us; he will strike us, and he will cure us; he will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. VI).

The construction of the [Col. 0853A] temple began in the first year of King Cyrus and was completed in the sixth year of Darius. According to the testimony of the Chronicles, these years amount to forty. Cyrus reigned for thirty years; after him, his son Cambyses for eight years, whom Josephus asserts is called Artaxerxes in this book; after him, the Magi who killed him for one year; and after them Darius for six years, until the completion and dedication of the temple. These are, as we said, forty-five years.

It is asked, however, how, when the Lord said to the Jews under the figure of the temple, concerning his passion and resurrection, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” they replied, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” (John II), when no more than sixty-five years are found [Col. 0853B] between the first year of Cyrus and the sixth year of King Darius.

But if we read Josephus’s History, in which he adds three further years after the completion and dedication of the temple—years during which the *peribolos*, that is, the construction of the fortifications surrounding the temple, and certain other things that had remained unfinished, were completed—we shall see that the total of forty-six years could rightly be reckoned for the temple’s construction, during which all its more prominent buildings were completed.

Yet, instructed by this Gospel passage, we must keep in mind that the temple which was built by Solomon and rebuilt by Zerubbabel and Jesus has several meanings. For it signifies each individual elect soul, which, because Christ dwells within it, is rightly called Christ’s house and his temple; [Col. 0853C] it signifies also the whole Church, that is, the gathering of all the elect, angels and human beings; and it signifies the Lord’s own body, which was born of a virgin, lived in the world without sin, was put to death by the ungodly, and was raised by him on the third day to life.

The statement that the temple was built in forty-six years is especially suited to this last figure. For natural philosophers report that, in the womb, the human body reaches complete formation of its bodily features by growing over this number of days from the time of conception. It was entirely fitting, therefore, that the house which was to bear the figure of the Lord’s body should be founded in Jerusalem in the same number of years as the number of days in which the Lord’s body was to be formed in the virgin’s [Col. 0853D] most holy womb. That virgin, most truly, is to be called Jerusalem—that is, “the city of the great King” and “vision of peace”—namely, the one of whom it was said: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

Likewise, the statement written concerning the same temple—“The door of the middle side was on the right side of the house, and by a spiral staircase they went up to the upper chamber, and from the upper chamber to the third” (III Kings VI)—especially prefigured the Lord’s body, of which it is written: “But one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX).

The door of the middle side was on the right side of the house: that is, beginning on the ground at the eastern corner of the southern side and leading gradually, by a hidden route through the interior of that same side, to the higher chambers [Col. 0854A]. For our Lord and Savior wished to open for us the door of salvation in the right side of his body, so that, washed and sanctified through its mysteries, we might enter the higher court of the heavenly kingdom.

We ascend through the door of the middle side to the upper chamber when, consecrated through the water of baptism and the cup of the Lord’s chalice, we pass from this earthly way of life to the heavenly life of souls. From the upper chamber, moreover, we penetrate into the third chamber when we increase the blessedness of souls by receiving immortal bodies.

## CHAPTER VIII. The children of the transmigration dedicate the house of God and celebrate the solemnity of Passover.

[Col. 0854B] “And the children of Israel, the priests and the Levites, made,” etc. The children of the transmigration rightly rejoice that they themselves have been found worthy both to cast off the yoke of captivity and to build the house of God that had been destroyed. Like devoted servants of God, they offer very many sacrifices for the dedication of his house. As lovers of brotherhood, they also offer sacrifice for the sin of all Israel—that is, not only for those who were able to be present there, but also for those who, situated either in Babylon or in other provinces, were still living among enemies outside the promised land. They ask God also to be gracious to these people: either to protect them from evils among their enemies or, having rescued them from their enemies, to call them back to their desired homeland.

But because the rebuilding of the house after their captivity, as has often been said, signifies the correction of those who, after making a small beginning on the way of truth, wandered from it by sinning, this kind of restored temple is fittingly dedicated by the priests, Levites, and the rest of the children of the transmigration with joy. For when those who have sinned are corrected, great joy is produced in heaven before the angels of God (Luke XV). It is produced also for the teachers who labored for the salvation of the erring, and for all who have migrated from Babylon—that is, from the confusion of sins—to the citadel of the virtues, the promised land, in mind and deed.

The priests, therefore, and the Levites, and all the people rejoice at the dedication of the restored house of the Lord, because all the orders of the holy Church must rejoice together when those who have sinned are reconciled through repentance. They offer sacrifices at this dedication [Col. 0854D] when, through the conversion of the erring, they render vows of thanksgiving to God; when many, seeing their life devoted to God, gird themselves for works of greater virtue, unwilling to be less diligent in good works than those who, by sinning less, had remained more innocent.

The same may equally be understood of those who have recently come to faith and to receive the sacraments of Christ: often many of those who went before them in faith imitate the more fervent zeal of beginners and perfect their own efforts in goodness by their example.

Not only did the priests, Levites, and people offer sacrifices for the dedication of the house of the Lord that they had renewed, but they also offered them for the sin of all Israel. For surely we ought to favor the good of those who are with us in such a way, and by imitating their good make it our own, that we may also pray to the Lord with diligent care for the condition of the whole Church that exists throughout the world, following the example of the Lord’s Prayer itself. In it no one is commanded to ask specially for his own daily bread, or for his own sins to be forgiven, or to be delivered specially from temptation and evil; rather, he is commanded to pray for all who have the same Father in heaven.

Likewise, after the temple has been built, dedication follows when, at the end of the age, the full number of the elect has reached the grace of heavenly rewards. At this dedication, sacrifices highly acceptable to God are offered—namely, those of which the same house of God, the holy Church, rebuilt after the long captivity of mortal suffering through the glory of immortality, sings to its Creator and [Col. 0855B] Redeemer: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV).

And because this sacrifice of praise is to be offered to God not only for the gifts of virtue bestowed but also for the filth of vices cleansed and removed, rightly, after calves, rams, and lambs have been offered for the dedication of the temple, goats are also said to have been slaughtered for the sin of all Israel. For the grace of God, which bestows the benefits of virtues, itself removes the wickedness of sins. Nor does Pelagius have any place in the house of God, for he persuaded himself and others that by the freedom of their own will they could either be delivered from evils or be strengthened in good.

In this life goats are offered for sin when the elect beseech heavenly mercy that they may be delivered from sins. They are offered also in the future life, when the same people give thanks to him because, by his granting it, they have been delivered from sins. Therefore they will sing the mercies of the Lord forever (Ps. C), because they never forget that they were once wretched and were made blessed through his gift.

“And they appointed the priests in their orders,” etc. The order of devotion required that, after the house of the Lord had been built and dedicated, priests and Levites should immediately be appointed to minister in it, lest the erected house shine to no purpose if those who would serve God within it were lacking.

This should be impressed repeatedly upon those who build monasteries with magnificent workmanship but make no provision in them for teachers who might exhort the people of God to the works of God; instead, they serve their own pleasures [Col. 0855D] and desires there.

When it says that the priests were established in their orders and the Levites in their divisions, it signifies the weekly rotations. The whole assembly of both ranks was divided into twenty-four groups, so that each order served in the temple during its appointed week for eight days, namely from Sabbath to Sabbath; after that, freed from the temple’s duties for twenty-three weeks, it took care of its own household, as the Books of Chronicles relate.

They had also already made porticoes around the inner sanctuary of the temple, at whose doors the Levites kept watch in their rotations, as is likewise read there.

But when it says, “As it is written in the book of Moses,” this refers not to the Levites’ rotations but to the works of God. Moses wrote what the priests and what the Levites were to do in the house of God; but the rotations of the Levites and the orders of the priests, divided by the twenty-four lots of which we have spoken, were described not by Moses but by King David together with the prophets, priests, and Levites of his time.

Now also, when Christ’s Church has been built and dedicated, priests and Levites ought to be established in their orders and rotations over the works of God through the regeneration of peoples newly brought to faith. The people should be initiated not only into the sacraments of faith but also instructed, through the examples and teaching of those righteous in Christ who preceded them, to undertake the things that belong to God—and this not according to the capacity of human ingenuity, but “as it is written in the book of Moses.”

To this agrees the Lord’s command: “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0856B] teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII). Therefore, if we desire to reach, together with our hearers, the rewards that the Lord promised, we must teach them not our own ideas but the commandments of the Law and the Gospel.

“And the children of the transmigration kept Passover,” etc. What relevance did it have to the historical account to report the celebration of Passover after the house of the Lord had been built, since it had long before been promised that, from the first day of their arrival in Jerusalem, they would offer the lawful sacrifices and burnt offerings at all the solemnities of the Lord? Unless perhaps he wished to give a special account of the Passover for this reason: to remind the reader that the children of the transmigration completed the building of the temple with the same devotion of mind with which they had begun it.

For it had previously been stated that the people gathered in Jerusalem as one man, and that Jeshua son of Jehozadak and his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his fellow Israelites, built the altar of the God of Israel in order to offer burnt offerings upon it (I Esdr. III).

Now, with the temple dedicated and the forty-sixth year already approaching, the same religious devotion is said to have existed in the minds of all, when it is stated that the priests and Levites had purified themselves as one, all of them clean, to sacrifice the Passover.

For what greater perfection can there be in this life than the unity of a clean multitude? There were many thousands of priests and many thousands of Levites, yet all had been purified and were clean [Col. 0856D] to sacrifice the Passover.

Nor did this unity arise from differing intentions of soul but, as Luke writes concerning the primitive Church of the New Testament, from being “one in heart and soul.” Thus a true unity of faith and love toward God, and an undivided unity of love and chastity among the people, are found.

When it says that the Passover was sacrificed for all the children of the transmigration, their fellow priests, and themselves, it immediately adds:

“And the children of Israel ate,” etc. The Passover, therefore, was sacrificed for all the children of the transmigration, and all the children of Israel ate—not only those who had returned from captivity, but also all who had previously been settled somewhere else and had at that time prepared themselves by separating from the impurities of the nations of the land.

This may rightly also be understood of proselytes. Though by nature they were Gentiles, they were converted to the people of God, receiving circumcision and being purified by the legal sacrifices, so that they too might be worthy to share in the saving sacrifice.

It should be noted that he calls “the nations of the land” those who serve what defiles, so that, by contrast, he might teach that the nations of heaven are those who, separated from them, serve the Lord in unity and chastity and celebrate his solemnities with a sincere heart.

Nowhere else, if I am not mistaken, is the same people of Israel found to have shown such devotion with the priests and Levites, their teachers, from the time when they came out of Egypt through Moses. But this devotion was produced by divine chastisement: because of their sins they were handed over to be afflicted by enemies; afflicted by adversities, they turned away from sins through repentance; through the merit of repentance and their way of life they were delivered from [Col. 0857B] their enemies; and, destined to serve God better, they were brought back to their homeland.

Even now we very often see those who, by repeatedly sinning, have profaned the temple of their body and thereby been taken captive by the devil return to the Lord through repentance. Rightly, with greater earnestness than before, they labor at good works, by which they prepare a dwelling within themselves anew for their Creator.

It should be noted that Solomon completed the first temple swiftly and with the greatest ease, during the peace of his kingdom, with no one resisting in any way. But now, because this temple had been destroyed on account of sins, the children of the transmigration, laboring under great contrition of heart, persevering in prolonged toil, and very often delayed by enemies, finally restored it with divine help.

It is easy for anyone who has been converted to faith and knowledge of the truth to renounce the devil, confess the living and true God, receive the sacraments of Christ, and, having been initiated into them for the remission of all sins, become his temple and preserve the innocence of life that has been received with his grace accompanying it.

But it requires much labor for one who, after receiving the sacraments of faith, has scorned them by sinning to recover his former dignity. For cleansing through the water of baptism cannot easily be given to such a person again; rather, the defilement of crime must be washed away through prolonged labor of repentance, abundant streams of tears, and the more rigorous sweat of self-restraint. In this cleansing, the very habit of vices also resists like the hostile crowd of the Samaritans; it is all the more difficult to overcome because it had possessed the soil of the heart, empty of virtue, for so long.

It may also be said that Passover is specially mentioned as having been celebrated after the house of the Lord was rebuilt and dedicated, although no one doubted that people of such religious devotion would wish to celebrate Passover at the proper time, so that it might be mystically indicated that this is the summit of all perfection: having passed beyond all the desires and enticements of the world, we continually devote the whole intention of our mind to meditating on entry into the other life.

For Passover (*pascha*) means “passing over.” It receives this name either because, through the sacrifice of the lamb, the children of Israel passed from Egyptian slavery to the joys of freedom, or because the immaculate Lamb himself—that is, the Lord Christ, sacrificed for our redemption—passed from this world to the Father.

We imitate this when we pass from lowly pleasures [Col. 0858A] to the pursuit of heavenly things. We truly complete the passage when, released from the prison of the flesh, we enter the heavenly kingdom. The following accordingly agrees well with this meaning:

“And they kept the solemnity of Unleavened Bread,” etc. The Apostle teaches how we ought to keep this solemnity spiritually, saying: “Let us therefore celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V).

This solemnity is to be celebrated for seven days because throughout the whole period of this age, which runs its course in that number of days, our life must be conducted in sincerity and truth—indeed, in the sacrifices and burnt offerings of every good work.

Since our Lord, at the Paschal season, overcame the death he had tasted only temporarily through the eternal power of the resurrection, the celebration of Passover in this passage may typologically be referred to the time of our resurrection. Thus the building of the temple signifies the present state of the holy Church, dedication the future life, which is experienced in the rejoicing of holy souls when they depart from the body.

The sacrifice of Passover signifies the glory of the resurrection, when all the elect are nourished by the flesh of the immaculate Lamb—that is, of our God and Lord—not believing any longer in sacrament alone but seeing him in reality and truth.

Therefore, in this Passover, all the priests and Levites, the entire assembly of the people, and all who had come to them from the nations are said to have been clean and to have been present as one, because then the Lamb of God truly takes away the sins of the world. And as the apostle John says: “The blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin” (John I).

Then there will be true unity, when God is “all in all” (I John I; I Cor. XV). Then the true solemnity of Unleavened Bread will be celebrated in joy, when no leaven of malice and wickedness remains among the elect, and all adhere to the divine vision in truth and sincerity of heart—not during the seven days of the passing age, but in the one day of eternal life, in the courts of the Lord, which are better than thousands, in the light of the Holy Spirit, whose sevenfold grace the prophet commends to us (Ps. LXXXIII).

“They kept the solemnity of Unleavened Bread for seven days,” etc. This is the greatest joy of the righteous in this age and in the age to come: that the work of the Church is perfected, with even the Gentiles who once resisted being converted to assist its condition and to confirm throughout the whole world the peace of the Christian Church’s religion.

Up to this point, the return from Babylon to Jerusalem of the people who had been taken captive; the restoration of the vessels that had been carried away; the rebuilding and dedication of the temple that had been burned; the celebration of the solemnities; and the singing of the songs of the Lord, which could not be sung in a foreign land, are described under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua.

All these things contain one and the same understanding of humanity’s salvation in Christ: either those who entered the world with the sin of the first transgression are saved after being purified through the sacraments of faith, or those who, by sinning, corrupted the faith they had received recover their senses through repentance. Both groups, through one and the same Savior, true King and Priest, celebrating as it were the most blessed Passover, pass from this world to the Father and from death to life.

But because, when the temple had been burned and the city of Jerusalem overthrown, the holy Scriptures that were kept there had likewise been consumed by the hostile disaster, they too had to be restored through the Lord’s mercy and his return to his people. Thus, since they had restored the ruined buildings, they might have the means by which, admonished themselves, they could learn to be restored inwardly in faith and love of their Creator. Hence the following fittingly comes next:

## CHAPTER IX. Ezra the priest goes up from Babylon, bearing the honorable letter of King Artaxerxes to all the guardians of the public treasury beyond the River; by it he also honored the temple of the Lord itself.

[Col. 0859B]

(I Esdr. VII.) “After these words, in the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,” etc. Josephus (Antiquities XIII, 5) thinks that this Artaxerxes, under whom Ezra went up from Babylonia to Jerusalem, was Xerxes, son of Darius, who reigned after him.

The Books of Chronicles, however, judge that the successor of this same Xerxes—who among them is also called Artaxerxes—is intended here. Darius, under whom the temple was built, reigned for thirty-six years; after him Xerxes for twenty years; after him Artabanus for seven months, which the chronographers counted as a year; and after him Artaxerxes for forty years.

Ezra, the swift scribe in the Law of Moses, restored the Law because it had been consumed. He restored not only the Law but also, as the common tradition of our ancestors relates, the entire sequence of sacred Scripture, which had likewise been destroyed by fire, rewriting it insofar as seemed sufficient for readers.

They say that in this work he added certain words that he considered useful. Among these is the following: “And there arose no prophet again in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face,” and so forth. Clearly, only someone who lived long after Moses could have spoken these words.

Likewise, in the Book of Samuel: “Formerly in Israel, when anyone went to consult God, he would speak thus: ‘Come, and let us go to the seer.’ For the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer” (I Kings IX).

But he left intact certain complete volumes that had once existed among the people of Israel. For this reason, in sacred Scripture there is now nothing more than a memory of their names, as in the Book of Numbers: “Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord” (Num. XXI). And in Joshua: “Is this not written in the Book of the Just?” (Josh. X).

The Books of Kings and Chronicles likewise mention historical books of the prophets Ahijah the Shilonite, Shemaiah, Jaddo, and Nathan, as well as Isaiah and Jehu son of Hanani (III Kings XVI; II Chron. IX). Of the latter it is said that he wrote the Book of the Kings of Israel. There are many other such books, of all of which, they say, no trace can now be found anywhere.

The Hebrews also report—and among them there is no doubt about this—that Ezra devised lighter letters under the names of those which they had possessed until then, so that he might restore with the greatest speed the vast quantity of books that had been destroyed. Hence he is called not only “scribe” but also “swift scribe.”

The earlier letters, however, remained among the Samaritans, and with these they used to write the five books of Moses, which alone they accepted from sacred Scripture.

“And they went up from the children of Israel,” etc. Because he began to go up from Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, he anticipates the narrative by saying that they had come to Jerusalem. In what follows, he describes more fully and in order how they came and where they gathered their army.

It should be noted that at the beginning of this book it is written that they went up from Babylon in accordance with Cyrus’s promise, under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua, all from the children of Judah and Benjamin together with the priests and Levites whose spirit God had raised up. It is also added that they were from the captivity which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had transported to Babylon.

Here, however, under Ezra’s leadership, there is no mention of Judah and Benjamin, nor of the transmigration carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, but only of the children of Israel and of the priests and Levites who went up with him.

Hence it seems probable that those who were then recalled to Jerusalem were from Judah and Benjamin, who had been transported to Babylonia by Nebuchadnezzar. But those who are now said to have been brought back by Ezra may have come from the ten tribes, which were specially called Israel after the division of the kingdom. The kings of the Assyrians had captured these tribes long before Nebuchadnezzar’s time and made them dwell beyond the mountains of the Medes.

At that time, therefore, the two tribes returned home for the most part and restored the temple through severe labor. But the ten tribes, which had shown less concern for the temple and religion, although commanded by the king, neglected to return to their homeland, since, after the Chaldaean empire had been destroyed, they lived freely under the kings of Persia, who favored their people.

But when they learned that the temple had been rebuilt and that the Samaritans’ hostility had been aroused, they finally agreed that some of them too should return home, although more remained there. Their descendants are said to remain in those regions to this day and to serve the Persian people.

Just as Zerubbabel and [Col. 0860D] Jesus, as has often been said, signify the Lord and Savior, who loosens the captivity of the human race by his grace and himself builds his house in us by sanctifying and possessing us, so Ezra the priest and swift scribe clearly announces the same Lord, who “did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V).

For this reason he could rightly be called the scribe of the Law of God, or the swift scribe in the Law of Moses: he himself gave the Law to Moses through an angel; he himself taught the holy prophets all truth through the grace of his Spirit; and he himself, as soon as he touches the minds of the elect with his love, kindles them to understand and accomplish the will of God the Father.

Therefore, promising the grace of the New Testament, the prophet said: “And this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts” (Jer. XXXI; Heb. XV).

The Psalmist beautifully recalls this scribe, saying: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV). The prophet’s tongue was the pen of a swift scribe, because what the Lord taught him by inwardly enlightening him without any delay of time, he declared outwardly to human beings through the ministry of his tongue.

Ezra also openly demonstrates him by his own name, which means “helper.” For he is the one through whom alone the people of the faithful are accustomed to be delivered from tribulations and brought, as it were, from Babylonian captivity to the freedom of Jerusalem, from the confusion of vices to the peace and serenity of virtues, as the steps of their merits advance.

In the second *Anabathmon*, that is, the Psalm of Ascents, he cries out to all who strive toward the heights, indicating under whose leadership they ought to strive and arrive: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXX).

Ezra also bore a figure of him in his actions, when he brought back a considerable part of the people from captivity to Jerusalem, and at the same time brought money and vessels consecrated to God for the glory of his temple, and when, by priestly authority, he purified the same people from foreign wives.

What all these things signify as having been done—or as still to be done—in the holy Church by the Lord is evident to the learned reader. But we shall also labor to make them clear to the simpler.

The fact that Ezra went up from Babylon, and that the children of Israel, together with the children of the priests [Col. 0861C] and Levites, went up with him, signifies the gracious dispensation of our Redeemer. Appearing in the flesh, himself free from the world’s confusion and from the confusion of vices, he entered it so that, returning with us, he might lead us, freed from every confusion, into the tranquility of heavenly peace.

We have received the pledge of this eternal peace in the present Church, as the Lord says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV)—that is, “I leave temporal peace to those journeying on earth; I give perpetual peace to those who arrive at the heavenly homeland.”

He is blessed because he began to go up from Babylon in the first month and came with the children of the transmigration whom he was leading in the fifth month to Jerusalem. The journey from Babylonia to Jerusalem is completed in four months because, through the four books of the holy Gospel, we learn the faith and mysteries of truth by which, with the Lord as our guide, we ought to be rescued from the captivity of the ancient enemy and ascend to the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

Those same four books contain commandments concerning works, by which, as though by daily steps, we may reach the heavenly promises.

Nor did it happen without a figure of mystery that he began to ascend from Babylon on the first day of the month and again arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of a month. For the beginning of the month, when the moon is believed to borrow new light from the sun, signifies the new beginning of a heavenly gift.

Appropriately, Ezra ascended from Babylon with those whom he was saving from captivity on the first day of the first month, because the beginning of holy conduct, in which we renounce Satan and his kingdom, is effected in us through the illumination of divine mercy.

On the first day of the fifth month he likewise arrived in Jerusalem, because this too is brought about in us not by the freedom of our will but by the inspiration of heavenly light, so that, having heard the oracles of the Gospel, we may be incorporated into the members of the holy Church.

A beautiful and salutary custom has grown up in the Church: the teaching of the fathers has established that the mystery of the four Gospels be explained to catechumens and that their beginnings be recited.

Likewise, he came to Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month with those who had been freed from their enemies. For when, having fulfilled the commandments of the four holy Gospels, we enter the heavenly kingdom, we celebrate, as it were, the beginning of a new month, because we behold the joys of new light in the Sun of justice; and, as it were, after four months of luminous action, which we pass as pilgrims on the path of life, we keep the fifth month of everlasting recompense in the light of the heavenly homeland.

“And on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem,” etc. That is, strengthened by divine grace and protection, because he completed the journey he had begun successfully.

In the mystical sense, the mediator between God and human beings came into the Church according to “the good hand of his God upon him”—that is, according to the disposition of divine power that was in him. “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V).

This hand of God was upon him according to the fact that he became human. Hence he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV). For greater than Christ’s humanity is divinity—not only the Father’s but also that of Christ himself and the Holy Spirit, which is one.

By this same hand of divine power, exalted in his passion, he ascended to the walls of the heavenly city; and by it he showed the way of ascension to his faithful, who humbly followed him.

Ezra had prepared his heart, etc. Oh, what power there is in this statement, what exalted merit: to prepare one’s heart for obedience to the divine will, and to be able to say, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Psalm 56)! That is: “With my whole heart I will rejoice in the Lord, and by carrying out my works I will fulfill what he has commanded.” Thus he prepared his heart to investigate and rewrite the law of the Lord, which the devouring flame had consumed. He also prepared himself to fulfill it first by doing it himself, and thus to open his mouth for instructing others. The same may readily be understood of the Lord Jesus: he prepared his heart to investigate the law of the Lord, because by divine providence he provided for himself such a man as he would assume—one who would be not only without sin but also full of grace and truth. Since no law of sin opposed him, he kept God’s law without any contradiction of mind or flesh. Hence he says in the Psalm: “In the beginning of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will, O my God; I desired it, and your law is in the midst of my heart” (Psalm 39).

The Lord likewise investigated the law of God because, having rejected the traditions of the Pharisees, he taught how Holy Scripture was to be understood mystically and what secrets of the spirit it concealed beneath the covering of the letter. He showed that the ordinances of the Gospel which he himself brought to the world were more perfect and more acceptable to God the Father than those for which he had previously sent Moses. Hence he himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy’; but I say to you, ‘Love your enemies,’” and other sayings of this kind.

“This is a copy of the letter of the decree,” etc. Artaxerxes, who with most devout intent, according to his capacity, venerates the temple and priests of God and offers them ready service, signifies Christian rulers, just as his predecessor Darius did. Nor is it surprising if we say that the successors of Cyrus—who caused the Lord’s temple and city to be built, and who loved and assisted his servants and his law—bear the figure of Christian kings, since the Lord himself said through the prophet that Cyrus would come as a figure of his Son and deemed him worthy to be honored by his Son’s name, saying: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, to Cyrus” (Isaiah 45), together with the other matters concerning him that we have set out more fully above.

“Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest,” etc. He calls him “the most learned scribe of the law of the God of heaven,” because the fame of the divine power by which Ezra had renewed the Law burned by the Chaldeans, using the same words as before though in a different written character, had reached the king himself. He too calls him “the God of heaven,” to distinguish him from those gods whom he knew the foolish madness of wretched men had established from dead human beings, or at least from certain individuals. I ask, however, that it not be burdensome for the reader briefly to pass through the text of the letter and observe how well it corresponds to Christian rulers.

[Col. 0863C] “By me it has been decreed,” etc. He grants permission to all who wish to go to Jerusalem; he compels no one to go. Likewise Christian rulers, compelling no one—for otherwise the will of faith would be uncertain or doubtful—allow all who wish to worship Christ within their realm to do so.

“For you have been sent from the presence of the king and his seven counselors,” etc. In the book of Esther also we read that it was the custom of the kings of Persia to employ the counsel of seven wise men in all matters that had to be done or decided. The faithful employ seven counselors when, in everything they do, they follow the commands and decrees of divine Scripture. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11). That is, it is perfected by the sevenfold illumination of the Spirit.

If this seems incongruous to anyone—that the counselors of the Persian king, by whom the people and prophet of the Lord are released from captivity and sent back to their homeland, could signify anything good in the holy Church—let him read the works of the Fathers, who said that the deeds or circumstances of the wicked kings Saul and Jeconiah figuratively represented the most holy works of our Redeemer. They interpreted Saul, anointed as king but killed on account of his crimes, with reference to the innocent death of Christ the King. They likewise referred Jeconiah’s transfer from Judah to Bethlehem, where he was held because of his sins, typologically to the grace of our Redeemer, who, having left the Jews on account of their faithlessness, graciously transferred himself to save the nations throughout the world.

They also taught that the words and deeds of Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar were to be understood typologically of the enemies of the Church. For example, Pharaoh commanded that the male infants of God’s people be killed in the river, while the females were to be preserved, because the devil desires to extinguish what is strong in us and nourish what is weak and fleeting. Likewise Nebuchadnezzar ordered all the peoples subject to him, when they heard the sound of instruments and musicians, to fall down and worship his statue. So too the devil strives, through the sweetness of earthly pomp, to bend the human race away from uprightness of mind and to corrupt the hearts of the deceived so that they follow desire, which is the worship of idols.

If, therefore, the evil deeds of the wicked went before as figures not only of evil but also of good things, why could not the good deeds or words of good people contained in the prophetic book prefigure the deeds of those who would follow what is good? Let us also consider the works of Saint Augustine, who said that even the seven men of one woman who died childless—concerning whom the Sadducees, denying the resurrection, tested the Lord—possessed a clear figure of an ecclesiastical mystery, as did the woman, her barrenness, and her death. He taught that the deaths of those men too were figures of memorable realities, since neither the Lord himself nor any of the evangelists narrated this story in his own person; rather, the evangelists inserted in their writings, on account of the Lord’s most sacred response, what the impious had uttered against him with profane mouths.

Ezra, then, is sent “from the presence of the king and his seven counselors” to visit Judea and Jerusalem. The rulers of this age, converted to the faith and strengthened also by the exhortations of the holy Scriptures, desire the Lord Christ to come for the salvation of his Church and for the daily gathering of the nations into it—an aid signified by the name Ezra—and they earnestly proclaim: “Lord God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vineyard” (Psalm 79).

“To visit,” he says, “Judea and Jerusalem according to the law of your God, which is in your hand.” The law of God was in Ezra’s hand because he proclaimed it not only with his tongue but also fulfilled it in deed. Our Lord likewise, appearing in the flesh, had the law in his hand—not only because he followed the precepts of the law in everything, but also because he held the decrees of the law in his power. He himself had once established it through Moses as he willed, and now he altered and transferred the same law to more perfect things through himself, as he willed. Hence he said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, but I say to you.”

It is remarkable that the word which the prophets commonly used is found in the letter of Artaxerxes, so that he says the law of God is in the hand of his servant. For it is written: “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet”; and, “The Lord did what he spoke by the hand of his servant Elijah”; and, “The Lord testified in Israel and Judah by the hand of all his prophets” (Haggai 1). Since the prophets proclaimed everything belonging to God no less by their deeds than by their words, the text continues:

[Col. 0865A] “And that you may carry silver and gold,” etc. The faith and wisdom of the king and his counselors deserve notice: the gifts they wished to offer to the Lord, they understood should be offered through the one who had the law of God in his hand—that is, who fulfilled it in deed. It is remarkable how faithfully and learnedly the king says that the one whom he had earlier called the God of heaven had a tabernacle in Jerusalem. We use a tabernacle on a journey, and the God of heaven has a tabernacle in Jerusalem, because he who has his eternal dwelling in heaven deigns to dwell for a time with the saints who are pilgrims in this Church. Hence the statement in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings” (Revelation 21).

But blessed Ezra bore the figure not only of the preachers of the holy Church, one of whom he himself was, but also of the Lord and Savior, whose members he was. Thus, as it were, through him we offer our gifts, since in everything we need his assistance, so that the good things we do may be acceptable to God the Father. For no one, he says, comes to the Father except through me (John 6). And John says of him: “For he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2).

“And all the silver and gold that you find,” etc. The historical meaning is clear: the king and his counselors gave Ezra money to bring to the temple of the Lord, and they also wished others to contribute from it so that victims, sacrifices, and libations might be purchased and offered upon God’s altar; and if any money remained, it was to be distributed only according to God’s will. It should also be noted that when he says that the priests will offer in the house of their God, he plainly teaches that, although some priests and Levites went up to Jerusalem with Ezra, others still remained in Babylonia with the rest of their people.

The allegorical meaning is also clear: the faithful desire their good works to shine in the holy Church so that they themselves may deserve to share in the company of the saints through them, and so that others may advance through their examples. Our sacrifices, libations, and victims are purchased, as it were, from silver and gold when our neighbors, seeing the brightness of our works, are converted to the practice of piety, by which they too, living well, are consecrated to the Lord.

But if any silver or gold remained—money from which offerings were not to be purchased—he commanded that this too be arranged according to God’s will and pleasure. There are indeed certain exceedingly bright virtues of the saints that cannot be displayed to everyone as examples of conduct, but may be recounted only to glorify God’s grace. Such are the facts that Daniel and Jeremiah prophesied while still boys; that John received the Spirit while not yet born; and that Cornelius, though not yet baptized, received the Holy Spirit together with his household. Such too are the countless miracles of the saints, which shine in the house of the Lord like silver and gold. Yet offerings to be placed upon the altar cannot be purchased from that same silver or gold, because when we hear such things we ought indeed to marvel at them as divine, but we cannot imitate them as though they were within our power.

Sacrifices, properly speaking, were those offered from the fruits of the earth, such as bread, fine flour, and ears of grain; libations were those made from wine and other liquid substances.

“And the vessels that are given to you for the service of the house of your God,” etc. Ezra is given not only silver and gold of various weights but also vessels to be carried to Jerusalem. Our Lord too, represented figuratively by Ezra, delivered before God the Father in the heavenly Jerusalem all the vessels entrusted to him by human beings—such as Paul, the vessel of election—and those of whom Paul speaks as “vessels of mercy” (Romans 9).

He speaks of these vessels himself in the Gospel: “Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and seize his vessels, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house” (Mark 3). The king of Babylon was indeed strong—that is, the devil, ruling wickedly over the reprobate. But when he was conquered and bound by the Lord, he lost the vessels he unjustly possessed, namely, the hearts of the elect. He could not resist the one who took these away and restored them to the heavenly city, to which they properly belonged.

“And I, Artaxerxes the king, have established and decreed,” etc. Christian rulers likewise command all their subjects to give without delay whatever our Lord and pontiff asks of them, holding nothing back, but swiftly fulfilling the commands of the divine will. Let them give him gold in confession of the true faith, grain in the display of good works, wine in the fervor of love, and oil in the exercise and cheerfulness of mercy.

All these things are commanded to be given, under the number one hundred, to the great priest and scribe of the law of the God of heaven—that is, to the Lord Jesus Christ, who brings us heavenly commands from the Father and promises heavenly rewards in the Father’s house to those who follow what is heavenly. Let us persist in good deeds for no grace other than that of heavenly recompense. The number one hundred, which in counting on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, generally signifies joys belonging to the right hand—that is, to eternal life.

A talent, it is said, has three measures: the smallest, fifty pounds; the middle, seventy-two pounds; and the largest, one hundred twenty pounds. A corus is thirty modii; a bath, also called an ephah, is a tenth of a corus, that is, three modii.

“But salt without measure. Whatever pertains to the rite,” etc. Everyone recognizes that salt signifies wisdom; hence in ordinary speech dull people are called “unsalted” (*insulsi*), that is, stupid. Yet the kind of salt matters. The Lord commanded through the law that salt be offered with every sacrifice (Leviticus 2), and in the Gospel he says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9).

Nor is it without significance that David is read to have struck the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, for we are commanded to offer in all the sacrifices of our works the salt of heavenly wisdom with which catechumens are initiated. David strikes the saltworks of the valleys together with their inhabitants because Christ destroys worldly and feeble wisdom together with its followers.

It is therefore fittingly commanded here that salt without measure be carefully supplied in the house of the God of heaven, since whatever wisdom anyone possesses must be offered wholly in the service of his Creator. We should also recall that earlier in this book the Samaritans are said to have written to another Artaxerxes that they remembered the salt they had eaten in the palace and therefore could not tolerate the temple and city of God being built against his interests.

Here, however, this Artaxerxes commands all the keepers of the public treasury to supply his salt, as much as is needed, to the house of the God of heaven along with the other gifts. There it is shown that heretics are sometimes encouraged to attack the Church by a deceitful taste of human wisdom. Here it is suggested that those converted to the faith, while also becoming wise, often assist that same faith through the discipline of secular wisdom, by which they overcome its adversaries more powerfully.

“And we make known to you concerning all the priests,” etc. This privilege, by which priests, Levites, and the other ministers of the house of God are made exempt from taxes, clearly shows that the rest of the people of Israel, upon reaching their homeland, paid tribute to the king. The king evidently acted with entirely judicious foresight, so that those who were always occupied in divine service would be free from his service, and so that those who possessed nothing of their own on earth but lived from the tithes of the people would not be required to pay tribute.

From all this it is most plainly proved that the king had not only loved but also thoroughly learned what the worship of divine service required.

[Col. 0867C] “But you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God,” etc. The king repeats what he had said and confirms by repetition the truth he had recognized. Earlier he said that the law of his God was in Ezra’s hand. Now he says that the wisdom of his God is in his hand. For the law of God is wisdom, as the Psalmist says: “The mouth of the righteous meditates wisdom, and his tongue speaks judgment. The law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 36).

The righteous person has the law of God and wisdom in his hand when, in everything he does and says, he shows himself mindful of the divine will. The literal meaning is clear, and so too is the spiritual understanding: our Lord and Savior has the wisdom of God in his hand. He is himself the power of God and the wisdom of God, and it belongs to him alone to appoint judges and overseers of the Churches, who judge everything according to his will and preach his faith to the unlearned throughout the world. Everyone who despises the decrees of his law will be punished—either by a present penalty or by a future one—according to the measure of his error.

Thus, when Artaxerxes wrote these things to Ezra and committed to writing the love he had for the practice of religion, he clearly expressed what devotion Christian kings would possess in future times and what they would do for the faith of truth. For this reason we have briefly recalled his letter, omitting whatever could be omitted, so that the reader might recognize how closely it corresponds to what Christian rulers, after the grace of the Gospel was revealed, did for the peace of the holy Church.

We may properly refer the person of Ezra figuratively not only to the Lord Christ but also to some bishop or teacher of the Church, to whom kings and rulers often sent letters concerning the welfare of the faithful. And Ezra himself, to whom this letter was given, rightly breaks forth afterward in praise of God, saying:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of our fathers,” etc. Who would doubt that he should confess these sacred and mystical words of his, which the prophet records as divinely inspired in him, by whom he also asserts that the house of the Lord was glorified?

## CHAPTER X  
### The number of those who went up with Ezra, and how they obtained the Lord’s help for their journey by fasting and praying

“And I, strengthened by the hand of the Lord my God,” etc. He calls the hand of God the power of God, which accomplishes all things. It was fitting, therefore, that he should gather those whom he was to bring from Babylon to Jerusalem, since he recognized that he himself possessed within him the hand of God by which he was strengthened. For each person becomes capable of gathering others to God through his teaching only when God’s grace has first strengthened him inwardly in his mind against everything that hinders holy work.

“These, then, are the heads of the families,” etc. He carefully enumerates the heads who went up with him from Babylon to the end of the genealogy, and explains their ancestry. He also strives to add their number, which reached 1,440, thereby suggesting that the names of those who ascend from the confusion of this world are inscribed in the Lamb’s book of life.

Teachers likewise—the heads, that is, of the families of God’s people—receive increases of eternal reward in proportion to the number of souls they acquire for the Lord, according to that parable of the Gospel in which the good and prudent servant says: “Lord, your mina has acquired ten minas” (Luke 19). His master answers him: “And you shall be over ten cities”—that is, because of the life of those whom you have taught, you will appear more glorious in the heavenly kingdom.

“And I gathered them at the river that flows toward Ahava.” I do not remember ever having read the name of this place elsewhere. Since it is written later, “And I proclaimed a fast there beside the river Ahava,” and afterward, “So we set out from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month,” it seems likely that Ahava itself is a river and that another river flows into it, and that Ezra gathered those who went up with him at their confluence.

Josephus, however, gives the Euphrates for this name. Thus Ahava may appropriately be understood as some tributary of the Euphrates.

“And we remained there three days,” etc. Ezra acted wisely in making careful provision for the ministers of the house of God before beginning so great a journey, so that when he reached Jerusalem he would have those through whom he could accomplish what was necessary for the temple’s use.

“And I sent them to Iddo,” etc. Orosius writes that the Caspian Sea rises from the ocean beneath the northern region. Both of its shores near the ocean, and the surrounding places, are regarded as deserted and uncultivated. From there it extends southward through long narrow passages until, spreading out over great distances, it ends at the roots of the Caucasus Mountains. From the east toward the ocean it has many peoples of Hyrcania and Scythia, wandering widely because of the barren expanse of the land. On the west it has many peoples. In general, however, the region beyond Albania, beneath the Caspian Sea and mountain, is called Amazonia.

Here it should be noted that while historians write “Caspian,” Ezra names it “Casphian” in this passage. The Hebrews do not have the letter *P* and therefore use the letter *Ph* in Greek or foreign names in its place, as in *Phetrus* and *Philatus*. Thus it is also proved that the children of Israel reached the regions of Casphia during the captivity of the Assyrians or Chaldeans, since Ezra sent there to bring him ministers of the house of the Lord—namely, Levites and Nathinneans, whom Josephus calls sacred servants.

It should be noted concerning them that they lived in considerable freedom and peace among foreigners, since they were able, immediately at Ezra’s command or request, to send so large a contingent of the army. The following catalogue shows that 258 chosen men were on that expedition; with Ezra added, he is found to have had an army numbering nearly 1,700 men.

“And I proclaimed a fast there,” etc. This provides an example of fasting and praying when we wish to undertake some work of great virtue. Since faithful hope in the Lord never deceives, and since it cannot happen that we fail to obtain what we seek from a merciful and just helper through abstinence and prayers offered in faith, the passage deserves careful attention.

Fasting is placed first, and prayer is then taught to follow. First he says, “And I proclaimed a fast, that we might humble ourselves before our Lord.” Then he adds: “And that we might ask him for a straight way for ourselves and our children,” and so on, up to the conclusion: “We fasted and entreated our God concerning this, and it went well for us.”

It is entirely necessary that whoever approaches to implore the Lord’s mercy should first, by living with greater self-restraint, make himself worthy to be heard. Then, while entreating the Lord, he should not doubt that what he requests will turn out well for him.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Ezra weighs the gifts of the king and his counselors and entrusts them to the chief priests to carry to Jerusalem; when they arrive there, they offer burnt offerings to the Lord

[Col. 0869D]

“And I separated twelve from the chiefs of the priests,” etc. It has often been said that the silver and gold and vessels sent from Babylon to Jerusalem signify souls that are converted from the confusion and errors of this world to the Lord. Ezra therefore appropriately entrusts such vessels to priests to carry to Jerusalem, because those who desire to reach fellowship with the holy Church must necessarily be washed in baptism by the hands of priests and consecrated to the Lord.

Likewise, through the ministry of priests those who had withdrawn from the fellowship of the holy Church by sinning, and who through perseverance in their sins had fallen into the service of the devil, into the captivity of the king of Babylon, must be reconciled to the Church by repentance.

There are appropriately twelve priests to whom this responsibility is entrusted, on account of the twelve apostles, through whose teaching the Church was first established throughout the world and, through their successors, does not cease to be built up until the end of the age. The following words of Ezra to these priests are fitting:

“You are holy to the Lord, and the vessels are holy,” etc. The teachers of the Church must never forget the holiness by which they themselves were consecrated to the Lord through the Holy Spirit on the day of redemption. They must also instruct their hearers to receive that holiness, so that those who have already been offered to the Lord through the beginnings of faith may be strengthened more and more by the examples and admonitions of those who preceded them in faith, and may become worthy to enter the heavenly city.

They must be vigilant in every respect and take care that none of the souls entrusted to them—those vessels of the Lord—perishes, but that they lead them in their full number to the thresholds of the holy city.

“Watch and guard them until you weigh them,” etc. We weigh the silver and gold and the vessels that we have received from Ezra before the chiefs of the priests and Levites and the leaders of the families of Israel in Jerusalem, and into the treasury of the house of the Lord, when we present those whom heavenly providence has entrusted to us, after instructing and teaching them, as people found blameless and fit for the treasury of the heavenly palace—that is, for the seats of inner peace and light.

We do this not by the judgment of just any human beings, who can easily be deceived, but by the examination of the blessed apostles and the other exalted men who are with the Lord and will judge our deeds with him. These are rightly understood as the chiefs of the priests and Levites and the leaders of the families of Israel—that is, of the men or souls who see God.

Concerning them the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You shall establish them as princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44). Solomon says of them in praise of the Church: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31). By “at the gates” he means at the judgment of the final examination.

“So we set out from the river Ahava on the twelfth day,” and all the rest is full of mysteries. Earlier it is written that they began to go up from Babylon on the first day of the first month; now it is said that on the twelfth day of the same month they set out from the river Ahava.

Thus, on the first day of the month they went out through the gates of Babylon, but they waited beside the aforementioned river until the twelfth day, until they had summoned the Levites and Nathinneans to themselves from the regions of Casphia, and until, because of the dangers of the long journey, they had commended themselves more carefully to the Lord by fasting and praying at the appropriate time.

So when we teach new peoples of the Church to renounce the devil and to believe in and confess the true God, we go out from Babylon, as it were, at the beginning of the first month, carrying money to be consecrated to the Lord. For we show them the beginning of a new way of life, which will lead those rescued from the devil to the heavenly kingdom. Hence this month is usually called in Holy Scripture the month of new things or of new crops.

In the same month, with the same meaning of a new way of life, the fathers were led out of Egypt through Moses. But when we hand on to these same hearers of the new life the symbol of faith, which was ordered through the twelve apostles and is comprised in an equal number of articles, we remain, as it were, for twelve days at the first station. Then we undertake the journey begun toward the promised land, showing them that, through the knowledge of faith they have received, they must enter upon the path of virtues by which they may reach life.

During those days Ezra devoted himself, together with the children of the captivity, to fasting and prayers and to gathering Levites and Nathinneans. For when we propose to acquire new peoples for the faith, it is necessary that we ourselves devote the greatest attention to the pursuit of virtues, by which we may commend ourselves more intimately to the Lord and offer those whom we teach an example of good action. We should also summon to our aid a devout company of brothers, so that, assisted by them, we may transfer the souls of the faithful more effectively into the fellowship of the elect and to the stronghold of more perfect life, like holy vessels to the temple of the Lord.

It is also appropriately added that those who had gone up from Babylon, when they arrived in Jerusalem, remained there for three days, and that afterward the silver and gold and vessels they had brought were offered and weighed in the house of the Lord.

There are three days of remaining in Jerusalem, namely, the outstanding virtues that all the faithful must possess: faith, hope, and charity. Teachers must first display these in themselves and then offer those whom they have taught and instructed in these same virtues for examination by the fathers who preceded them in Christ.

When the holy Church finds those whom we catechize upright in faith and action, it will discover them, as vessels offered into the temple and weighed by the priests’ hand, to be of pure metal and perfect weight. This examination is carried out daily in this Church by the elect as the lives of believers are tested, and it is likewise completed more perfectly in the heavenly Jerusalem, as we have said above, in those who have deserved to enter it.

In this life, the holy teachers, remaining in Jerusalem as if for three days, offer to the priests on the fourth day the silver and gold that they had brought to be weighed. They show themselves strong in faith, exalted in hope, and fervent in love; and they demonstrate that their hearers too shine like tested silver through confession of the right faith, gleam like the finest gold through purity of an uncorrupted understanding, and excel like vessels consecrated to God through the reception of spiritual gifts within themselves.

In the heavenly homeland these same teachers receive the grace of recompense first for their own faith, hope, and charity, and then also for those whom they have taught. As though after the joy of a three-day stay in Jerusalem, they are honored more greatly for the precious and God-worthy gifts and vessels they have brought.

There is, however, a distinction between these vessels that Ezra offers with the priests in Jerusalem and those which are reported above to have been offered by Zerubbabel and Joshua. The former had been transferred from the temple of the Lord to Babylon and were afterward brought back to Jerusalem. The latter were made in Babylon itself but sent to Jerusalem out of devotion by the king or princes of the Persians, or even by the people of Israel who lived in those regions.

Those vessels therefore signify people who, after receiving the knowledge and sacraments of faith and beginning works of virtue, are deceived by the ancient enemy and carried off into the confusion of errors, but are recalled to salvation through Christ’s merciful grace. These signify those who were born subject to death because of the sin of the first transgression, but who, cleansed through the bath of regeneration by the ministry of priests, were added to the children of the holy Church.

The former signify penitents returning from their errors; the latter, nations persevering in the virtue they have begun. Concerning them it is appropriately added:

“And the whole weight was recorded at that time.” The priests record in the temple the entire weight of the silver and gold and vessels offered to the Lord when diligent teachers carefully examine the lives of those subject to them, investigate precisely how far each person has advanced in faith or in works, and assign each one a place in the house of God according to the measure of his capacity and the degrees appropriate to him.

Even if the negligence of those set over them now lies dormant, and they either do not know the lives of those entrusted to them or pretend not to know them, there is an inner judge who preserves intact on the scales of his examination the number of believers and the weight of each person’s soul, so that he may repay each according to his work.

It may also be understood in this way: when the holy preachers reach the heavenly Jerusalem with those whom they have instructed, the entire weight of their good action is recorded at that time in the book of life, and they are granted a worthy recompense in heaven.

“But the sons of the captivity who had come from the exile,” etc. Great devotion and religious seriousness are shown by those who, having come from captivity and reached the temple and altar of the Lord, first of all offered burnt offerings—not only for themselves but also for all Israel, that is, both for those who had already returned home and for those who still remained exiles from their homeland—so that the mercy of the Creator of all might protect everyone.

The spiritual meaning is also clear: those truly and perfectly escape the captivity of the ancient enemy, in which they were held by sin, who submit themselves with fixed purpose to divine service and, wholly drawn away from earthly desires, kindle themselves toward heavenly things with the flame of longing.

This is what it means to offer burnt offerings—that is, wholly burned sacrifices or victims to the Lord: to think and do nothing in every matter except his will. It is also a sign of a perfect mind when someone sacrifices for all Israel—that is, for the general safety of all the faithful—and, mindful of unity and brotherhood in everything, pleads with heavenly piety.

“And they delivered the king’s edicts to the satraps,” etc. Another edition has: “And they honored the people and the house of God.” They exalted the people when they made the royal authority by which Ezra had been elevated honorable to everyone. They also exalted the house of God by adorning it more magnificently with the vessels and gifts that the king, his counselors, and his princes had sent to it, and by making its ministers and priests free from taxes and tribute, save for service to the Lord alone.

Mystically, the people and the temple of God represented one and the same figure, that of the holy Church. Ezra and the children of the captivity raise it up with the sacred vessels brought from Babylon when holy preachers, gathering into it companies of believers through the Lord’s gift, make it honorable to all—even to outsiders—and awe-inspiring.

Likewise, these same preachers raise up the people and the house of God when they advance those whom they instruct by their examples or words in good conduct all the way to the reception of heavenly rewards. For they bring great joy both to the elect who remain in the heavenly homeland and to those who are still pilgrims on earth.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Ezra hears that the people of Israel have been polluted by foreign wives, assumes the clothing of a mourner, and prays to the Lord for pardon of their guilt
## (I Esdras IX)

After these things had been completed, etc. The guilt of this transgression is also plainly described and censured with prophetic authority in the prophet Malachi. For those who had returned from the Babylonian captivity—the leaders, priests, and Levites as well as the rest of the people—cast aside their Israelite wives, who had been worn down by poverty, want, and the hardships of a long life, and who, unable to endure labor because of the weakness of their sex, had become exhausted and had acquired bodily weakness and deformity, and contracted marriages with foreign women who were either in the flower of their age, more beautiful in bodily appearance, or daughters of the powerful and wealthy.

This should not be understood of the Israelites who were then with Ezra, but of those who had come up from captivity long before with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. For those who had come with Ezra could not so quickly despise the teaching of so great a leader and prelate—as we must understand him—that, after dwelling in their homeland for not yet five months, they would abandon their wives and take foreign ones. Rather, those leaders are to be understood as belonging to the earlier group, who, when they reported this crime to Ezra, took care that it should be punished.

Nor should it be surprising that the people of Israel, together with the priests and Levites, are said to have committed this crime, although that migration had consisted more of Judah and Benjamin than of the ten tribes called Israel. For it must be known that, after Israel—that is, the ten tribes—had been carried into captivity, the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, were also indiscriminately called Israel by their former name. Therefore, in this passage “the people of Israel” should not be taken to mean the ten tribes, in distinction from Judah and Benjamin. Rather, the people of God in general is intended, in distinction from the peoples of the earth: a people that had polluted the dignity of its heavenly name through association with earthly things.

The same prophet Malachi—whom the Hebrews affirm to have been Ezra himself—also recalls this transgression in his prophetic book:

“Judah has transgressed, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has profaned the holiness of the Lord, which he loved, and has taken as his wife the daughter of a foreign god. May the Lord cut off from the tents of Jacob the man who does this, teacher and disciple, and the one who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

By speaking of Judah, he plainly indicates that the people of the first migration had been polluted by this crime.
