When he adds, “May the Lord cut off the man who does this, teacher and disciple, from the tents of Jacob,” by the terms “teacher” and “disciple” he teaches that both the leaders and the people polluted by this transgression must be uprooted from the fellowship of the saints if they do not correct themselves. By adding, “the one who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts,” he warns that those offer sacrifices to the Lord in vain who, by sinning, do not fear submitting themselves to the devil.

Amid all this, one must marvel at the faith and excellent purpose of the people rescued from captivity. They call themselves “the holy seed,” while they call other nations “the peoples of the earth,” in order openly to indicate that, although they themselves were born from the earth, their citizenship was not on earth but in heaven. For, more than other nations, they believed in the God of heaven and hoped to receive heavenly benefits from him. They therefore rightly grieved that their holiness had been defiled by people of the nations; and, what is more serious, they confessed that even the leaders, by whom they ought to have been corrected, had been the first to go astray.

It should also be carefully noted and drawn into an example for our conduct that the sins committed by the leaders, who caused the people entrusted to them to sin, were diligently corrected by other leaders who lived more holy lives. Yet because they could not accomplish this by themselves, they referred the matter to the high priest—that is, to their archbishop—so that, by his authority, so grave, so widespread, and so longstanding a crime might be expiated.

No one doubts that, figuratively, foreign wives represent heresies and the superstitious sects of philosophers. When these are carelessly admitted into the Church, they not only contaminate the holy seed of Catholic truth and pure conduct with their errors, but also produce all the sins by which the pagans are accustomed to be polluted, when Christians are not ashamed to imitate them. Thus, through foreign wives, they generate a degenerate offspring from the holy seed of the word of God by which they had been begotten, as the apostle James says: “For he begot us voluntarily by the word of truth” (James 1). And, following the enticements of those who go astray, they produce a profane offspring from the daughters of foreigners, bringing their perverse deeds into the knowledge of everyone.

### “When I heard this report, I tore my cloak,” etc.

Ezra reveals the innermost grief of his heart: he tears his clothing, pulls out the hair of his head and beard, and sits mourning. By this dishonoring of his body and clothing, together with the sorrow on his face, he more quickly stirs everyone’s minds to repentance for their own guilt and that of their brothers. For clothing commonly signifies our deeds, with which a person is clothed either for glory, if they are clean, or for destruction, if they are polluted and are not proved splendid by nuptial charity.

The hairs of the head signify thoughts, which arise from the hidden root of the heart, as from the innermost recesses of the brain. If they are upright, they should be preserved; but if they are wicked, they must be cut off. Hence, concerning Samuel, who was destined to be holy, his mother says: “No razor shall come upon his head” (Luke 21). And the Lord says to the apostles: “Not a hair,” he says, “of your head shall perish,” because all the thoughts of the saints are worthy of eternal remembrance with the Lord.

But the sinner, if he is to be cleansed from his iniquities, must cast away from himself rejected thoughts—the origins and sources, that is, of evil deeds. Hence, when the leper in Leviticus had received healing, he was commanded, among the other rites of purification, to shave off all the hair of his body, so that, cleansed in this way and having offered sacrifices, he might deserve to enter the camp (Leviticus 14). For we are then completely cleansed from the foulness of vices when we strive to drive away from ourselves not only harmful deeds but also harmful thoughts.

The beard, moreover, which is an indication of male sex and maturity, is commonly placed symbolically for virtue. The high priest tore his cloak and tunic to signify that the people he governed possessed works that were less than perfect, and that this people, because of its own hardness, needed to be rent through repentance and renewed into a better condition.

He pulled out the hair of his head to make clear to that same people that evil thoughts had to be uprooted from its heart, and that room had to be made for useful thoughts to grow again. He also pulled out the hairs of his beard so that they might humble themselves even in the virtues they seemed to possess, and remember that these were small or worthless in the judgment of the inner judge, since it was evident that they were mixed with vices. He sat mourning to teach that forgiveness for so great a guilt had to be earned through the laments of repentance.

Nor is it surprising that so many beginnings made by a good prelate soon produced great fruit of virtue among his subjects. See what follows:

### “And all who feared the word of God gathered around me,” etc.

O what a great change of circumstances! It was said above that many followed the perfidy of the leaders and magistrates into luxury; but now, when the good leader has been turned to mourning and, through his grief and tears, has shown sinners what they ought to do, all who feared the word of God—which threatens punishment for transgressors—are said to have gathered around him.

O how greatly pious examples assist good teachers! Ezra said nothing at all; rather, merely hearing of the crime, he is recorded to have turned to tears and lamentation, and to have drawn a crowd of the faithful to himself not by shouting but by mourning. It continues:

### “At the evening sacrifice I rose from my affliction,” etc.

Through contrition of heart and bodily affliction alike, Ezra had prepared himself to become worthy of hearing the compassion of heaven, and thus he burst into words of prayer. He bends his knees, spreads out his hands, and pours forth prayers to the Lord at the time of the sacrifice. He has no doubt that a sacrifice offered in a spirit of humility and with a contrite soul is more pleasing to God than one offered with the flesh and blood of animals.

Typically, however, the fact that, with his clothing torn, he bends his knees and spreads his hands toward God, and that through prayers and tears he turns the minds of many to repentance, reveals—as is written later—the Lord and Savior. For he deigned to pray for our crimes both before his passion and at the very time of his passion. With his hands extended on the cross, he willed that the garment of his flesh should, for a time, be torn and put to death by wounds for our restoration, so that he who, as the Apostle says, “died because of our sins” might “rise again for our justification” (Romans 4).

This occurred appropriately at the time of the evening sacrifice, either because, at the end of the age, the Lord offered the sacrifice of his flesh and blood to the Father and commanded that it be offered for us in bread and wine; or because, as the legal sacrifice was coming to its end, he freed us through his passion, separated us from the peoples of the earth, made us heavenly, and granted that those pure in heart and body might cling to him.

The prayer itself, by which, although he was just, he associated himself with a sinful people, begins as follows:

### “My God, I am ashamed and embarrassed,” etc.

This accords with the humility of our Redeemer, who appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh in order to take away the sins of the world. Hence, in the Psalms—which, as the Gospel bears witness, were written in his person—he plainly calls the sins he had taken upon himself his own, saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21). And he adds: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (ibid.). Again: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my sins are not hidden from you” (Psalm 68). This is not because he himself could possess sin or foolishness—for, as the Apostle says, he “became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption”—but because, taking upon himself the cause of those whom he had come to save, he also deigned to transfer to himself those things that truly belonged to their weakness.

## CHAPTER XIII  
Ezra prays and weeps; the people likewise turn to repentance, and by unanimous decision separate themselves from foreign wives.

### (I Esdras X)

Thus, while Ezra was praying and imploring, etc. The extent to which Ezra’s prayer, weeping, and lamentation profited is shown by the fact that a very great gathering of people of both sexes and every age is immediately said to have assembled and flowed toward him.

Those who had sinned were weeping, practicing repentance for their guilt; or those who had remained chaste were grieving over the transgression and fall of their brothers. But whether the former, the latter, or both groups wept, all are shown to have been deeply disturbed by the prayers and lamentations of their high priest, since women and children are also reported to have been present.

It may also be understood as a matter of order that the innocent and upright first came to him, when it says: “And all who feared the word of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the transgression of those who had returned from captivity” (above, chapter 9). Now, however, those who had sinned with their wives and children also gathered to practice repentance.

### “And Sechenias answered,” etc.

Josephus says that this Sechenias was the first among the Jerusalemites. He too, as was fitting for a leader, immediately assisted Ezra with the greatest authority, both by confessing that the people had sinned together with him and by urging that they should practice repentance, rejecting their foreign wives together with the children born from them.

### “And now, if there is repentance in Israel concerning this,” etc.

“If the people,” he says, “truly repent of this transgression, let us first turn to the Lord, promise amendment, and ask forgiveness. Then, having returned to ourselves, let us uproot from among us both the root and the branch of the crime we have committed—that is, let us expel the unlawful wives together with all their offspring. For this is what it means to repent truly: to turn inwardly, in the heart, wholly toward the Lord, and outwardly to cut away every occasion of sin from its very origin.”

What he adds is:

### “Rise; it is yours to decide,” etc.

He teaches most appropriately how one should act in a council among one’s elders: each person should state, according to his own judgment, what he understands—or thinks he understands—to be best, while nevertheless leaving the place of decision to the one who has authority, and being ready to obey everything that person determines should be done according to the will and law of God.

### “And Ezra the priest arose before the house of God,” etc.

Eliashib was the high priest of that time. After Jeshua son of Josedec, his son Joiakim held the rank of high priest, and after him Eliashib, his son, as is demonstrated by what follows in this sacred history and by the Jewish history of Josephus.

### “He ate no bread,” etc.

Here they receive an outstanding example not only of weeping and praying but also of fasting on behalf of those who have sinned. If those who mourn their own sins are blessed, because they are consoled when they receive forgiveness, how much more blessed should we believe those to be who mourn the errors of their brothers—so much so that they are unwilling even to touch bread and water, the nourishment of those who abstain, or to enter their own house or ascend to the bed where they sleep, but rejoice instead to spend the night praying in the courts of the Lord’s house.

For the priest’s house was there, and Ezra is said to have entered it when evening came. Indeed, another edition has, instead of “the chamber of Johanan,” “the portico of Johanan.” Scripture often uses this name for the porticoes by which the Temple was surrounded on every side and in which its ministers and guards were accustomed to remain.

Even now they mourn the transgression of those who had returned from captivity: they grieve that those who had recently been rescued from sins through repentance have again fallen into them by sinning, through which they may once more be taken captive by the devil. Concerning their seducers, as though they were the parents of unclean wives, the apostle Peter says: “For speaking proud words of vanity, they entice through the desires of the flesh and luxury those who have escaped for a little while” (2 Peter 2). Shortly afterward he speaks of those who, though they had come up as if from captivity, were nevertheless captured through luxury: “For if,” he says, “after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in these things and overcome, the latter condition has become worse for them than the former” (ibid.).

### “And a proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem,” etc.

When the sons of Judah and Benjamin are said to have gathered, it is plainly evident that those polluted by marriage with foreign wives belonged to the first migration, which consisted of these two tribes and was brought back to its homeland through Jeshua and Zerubbabel, as we also said above.

### “It was the new month, on the twentieth day of the month,” etc.

The ninth month is the one called Kislev by the Hebrews and December by the Romans. Surely no one is unaware that it comes in the middle of winter and is rainy and stormy. It should therefore be carefully noted that, when the people gathered in midwinter, they are said to have trembled because of their sin and because of the rains.

When they saw rain falling at that very season of rain in greater abundance than usual, they returned to their consciences and understood that this had happened because of their crimes. Warned by the very disturbance of the air, they feared that heavenly wrath was about to come upon them. For this reason they did not presume to conduct their business in private houses, but sat in the square before the house of the Lord, having assumed the posture of repentance and humility.

This is written for those who, although the elements have been disturbed, and although by the roar of winds, the overflowing of rains, heaps of snow, the heat of drought, or even the destruction of human beings or animals, a calamity from above grows heavier and the Judge himself threatens the force of his anger through evident signs, seek nothing at all concerning the correction of their conduct by which they might please the Judge and escape the impending blow. Instead, they diligently consider only by what strategy they might avoid or overcome the external adversities that rage because of their sins.

The people sat in the square before the house of God—that is, around the priests’ court, by which the house of God was surrounded on every side, as we explained above. Around it, on all sides in a square, were extensive buildings belonging to the courts, in which the people could stand when rain made this necessary, while still being able to see what was being done at the Temple gates or around the Temple. Their inner walls, near the ground, were constructed on columns, while the outer walls were solid.

### “And Ezra the priest arose and said,” etc.

This passage corresponds to what was said above: “And Ezra arose before the house of God, went to the chamber of Johanan son of Eliashib, entered it, ate no bread, and drank no water, for he was mourning.”

Here we should note the devotion of the high priest, who, mourning, praying, and fasting for the transgression of the people, remained for three days in the Temple courts. He did not wish to enter his own house before he saw the people, with one heart, repentant and converted to the Lord.

The other leaders also appear to have shared in this devotion, since they too are said, after the assembly had ended, to have gone to the houses of their fathers. For if the sacred historian did not intend to signify this by his wording, why was it necessary to write that, when the conference was completed, Ezra and the heads of the families left the Temple enclosure and went to their ancestral houses, when everyone would know that they would do this even if Scripture had not said so? Why add, “and all according to their names,” when this too was well known to everyone—unless he wished them to be understood as men whose names and deeds deserved to be kept in memory and handed down for posterity to know?

### “And they sat on the first day of the tenth month,” etc.

Note that the number three is extremely common in mystical figures. It was said above that all the sons of the migration were to come to Jerusalem within three days; now, over three months—namely, the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth—they are chastened and separated from their foreign wives.

There are three virtues without which we cannot attain life: faith, hope, and charity. The Lord came into the world in the third age and bestowed upon us the grace of the Gospel. The first age, before the Law, was given in the patriarchs; the second, under the Law, in the prophets; in the third, he himself came with grace. Redeeming us through his passion, he rose from the dead on the third day.

By his grace we are joined to the fellowship of the holy Church and cleansed from the enticements of vices. Thus it is fitting that the sons of the migration gathered in Jerusalem within three days to be corrected for their errors, and that they completed the work of their correction over three months.

In the literal sense also, the heads of the families and the Levites worked with sufficient appropriateness and salutary care so that, before the beginning of the first month, all who had been defiled by an unholy marriage might be brought to completion—that is, cleansed from such a crime. Thus they would enter, clean, the first month in which the Passover was to be celebrated; celebrate the Passover festival clean; and bring to its end, clean, the year they had begun clean.

This is also fitting for us to imitate every year during the Lenten season before Easter: as the solemnities of the Lord’s Resurrection approach, we should cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we too may be able to share in the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XIV  
A summary of those who expelled the foreign wives whom they had married.

### “And among the sons of the priests who had married them were found,” etc.

The Hebrews apply to this passage the words of the prophet Zechariah:

“And the Lord showed me Jeshua the great priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zechariah 3).

A little later:

“And Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the angel. And he answered and said to those who stood before him: ‘Take away the filthy garments from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you, and I have clothed you in changing garments. And place a clean turban upon his head’” (ibid.).

“Rightly,” they say, “Satan stood at his right and at his left to oppose him, because the accusation was true: he too had taken a foreign wife along with the others.”

The statement that Jeshua was clothed in filthy garments is interpreted in three ways: either because of the unlawful marriage, because of the sins of the people, or because of the squalor of captivity.

The angel before whose face Jeshua stood commanded the other angels, speaking on the Lord’s behalf, to remove from him the filthy garments of which we have spoken. When they had carried out the command, the same angel again addressed Jeshua: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you.” These are the filthy garments. “And I have clothed you in changing garments”—that is, I have joined an Israelite woman to you in marriage.

What follows—“Place a clean turban upon his head”—which many call a *mitre*, is understood by them to signify the dignity of the priesthood: after the filth of his sins had been washed away, he would possess a clean priesthood.

Yet it should be observed that Ezra does not write that Jeshua himself married a foreign woman, but says that some of his sons and brothers were polluted by this crime. Nevertheless, the guilt of sons also reflects upon their father, and no one can be perfectly just who neglected to correct his delinquent sons when he was able to do so.

Hence some say that the prophecy about Jeshua mentioned above should be referred not to the son of Josedec but to the Lord and Savior. Although he is “the radiance of glory and the likeness of God’s substance,” he temporarily received filthy garments out of compassion for our weakness, as Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our iniquities and weakened for our sins” (Isaiah 53). Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him, always seeking to resist his right-hand side and his virtues, as the sacred history of the Gospel relates.

The Apostle also says: “He is in all things made according to likeness, without sin” (Romans 8). His filthy garments are removed and he is clothed in changing garments when he washes us from our sins in his blood, so that the Apostle’s words may be fulfilled: “Therefore, all of you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

Alternatively, he who had filthy garments in his passion received changing garments in his resurrection, so that we can truly say of him: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (1 Corinthians 5).

He also received a turban upon his head, because he was proved to possess an everlasting priesthood, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 109).

When Ezra says that the brothers of Jeshua son of Josedec also married foreign wives, “brothers” should not be understood as his natural brothers but, according to the custom of sacred Scripture, as his relatives. For his actual brothers could not have continued to live in the flesh and devote themselves to pleasure, since a hundred years and more had passed from the time when Cyrus, beginning to reign, sent Jeshua and Zerubbabel with the migration of Judah and Benjamin back to Jerusalem to build the house of the Lord.

It continues:

### “And they gave their hands to expel their wives,” etc.

First they reject their unlawful wives, and then they offer a ram for themselves, so that, having removed their crime, they might approach the altar clean. For it is difficult for the victim of one who does not first strive to abandon the guilt for which he offers it to be acceptable to God, as Isaiah says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah 1).

And because these men were sons or brothers of the high priest, who had been the first to sin, they rightly offer a ram from the flock as punishment for their crime. By such a victim they signify that they have determined to put to death their former life, to cleanse themselves, and to offer worthy repentance to God through a better life—those who seemed to be the teachers and leaders of the people, like shepherds guiding their flocks.

We should note how skillfully the devil always attacks the faithful in battle, leaving them no time ever secure from combat. For behold, those who could not be overcome by adversities are overcome by enticements. They conquered public enemies by building and dedicating the Temple of the Lord, but they were conquered by love of foreign women, so that they would not preserve the temples of their hearts or bodies as worthy for God to inhabit.

This has been most clearly represented in our own times, when we see the minds of the faithful now being tempted inwardly much more dangerously, drawn away and enticed by their own desire, than they were once tempted outwardly when the savage adversary raged against their steadfastness with sword and fire.

But the Lord’s mercy will be present. Just as then he granted them the strength of patience against the open attacks of the raging enemy, so may he grant us the protection of vigilance against the snares of creeping enticements.

Finally, when the diligent high priest and all those who feared the Lord took action, those who had sinned were pierced in heart and expelled their foreign wives. Thus, when the disgrace of luxury had been driven out, the beauty of chastity returned; and in the city of the Lord, once the rubble of vices had been removed, the flowers and fragrances of virtues were scattered abroad.

Here end Ezra’s words, in which he described first the deeds of Zerubbabel and Jeshua and afterward his own. Ezra himself also clearly prefigured the Lord and Savior in that he renewed the sacred Scripture, brought the people back from captivity to Jerusalem, raised up the house of the Lord with greater gifts, appointed commanders beyond the river Euphrates and governors who knew the law of God, and chastised the sons of the migration by separating them from foreign wives.

The Lord restored sacred Scripture because the scribes and Pharisees had either defiled it through their traditions or taught that it was to be understood only according to the letter; he himself showed that it was full of spiritual meaning, just as it had been written by Moses and the prophets. He also caused the New Testament to be written down through the apostles and apostolic men after sending the Holy Spirit from above.

He led the people out of Babylonian captivity and brought them, freed, into Jerusalem and the promised land, because, having suffered once on the cross, he redeemed the world by his blood. Descending into hell, he found there whatever true Israelites—that is, the elect—were present, brought them from there to the walls of the heavenly city, and granted them the joys of the inheritance promised long ago.

Every day, too, he gathers the faithful from the disturbance of this world and summons them to fellowship with the holy Church and to the everlasting kingdom.

He increased the adornment of the Temple with gold, silver, and precious vessels, which either the people of Israel or the princes of Persia had sent through him. For, bringing believers from both peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile—into the Church, he never ceases to adorn and glorify her with the radiance of their faith and works.

He appointed commanders and governors over all the people beyond the river who knew and taught the law of God. For in the holy Church—which has been washed by the river of sacred Baptism and, through the sincerity of faith, has crossed the Babylonian river, that is, the turmoil of the fluctuating world—he placed apostles, evangelists, pastors, and rulers.

He chastised the sons of the migration by separating them from foreign wives because he prohibited those who had renounced the world by their profession of faith from continuing to serve the world’s enticements.

He also expelled the children of such mothers from the assembly of the migration, lest, when grown, they should follow their mothers’ unbelief rather than their fathers’ faith. By this he taught that even our works, which appear good to human beings, are to be rejected if they are mixed with carnal pleasures or have arisen from the contagion of human approval; they are not worthy of the fellowship of those who, completely abandoning the world, pass over with their whole mind to heavenly things, who are not weakened by temporal flatteries but rejoice to be exercised by adversities and prepared for eternal rest.

If someone should object that Scripture does not say that they expelled the children of adulterous women, but only the women themselves, although above Sechenias had suggested this when he said, “Let us make a covenant with our God and expel all the wives and those who were born from them,” and it immediately adds: “Then Ezra arose and adjured the leaders of the priests and the Levites and all Israel to act according to this word, and they swore”—let that person understand that, if the sons of the migration did not expel the children whom the foreign women had borne to them, the reason was that they taught them to renounce their mothers’ unbelief and, having been consecrated to the Lord through circumcision and the saving sacrifice, made them participants in their own faith and chastity.

The mystery of this matter is plainly evident: good works performed with regard to temporal advantage, human approval, or pleasure must either be counted among evil works or be set apart from their base intention; they must be done solely for heavenly reward.

For example, one who fasts, prays, or gives alms with the intention of being seen and praised by human beings has produced, as it were, offspring of a good action from an unclean mother—offspring born to a defiling conscience. Therefore, such offspring cannot have a share in the assembly of those who migrated from Babylon and ascended to Jerusalem, because righteousness—or rather, the pretense of righteousness—which has received its reward in the present will lack a future reward in heaven.

But if the author of such a work turns his mind toward better things and begins to do for the sake of heavenly reward what he had done out of a vain desire for praise, then, consecrating his offspring to the Lord even though it was unworthily born, he makes it a citizen of Jerusalem. For by correcting in time a work badly begun, he renders it worthy of an everlasting reward in heaven.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER XV  
Nehemiah, cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, hears of the affliction of those who were in Jerusalem, fasts and prays, and seeks mercy from the Lord.

### (II Esdras I)

### “The words of Nehemiah son of Helkiah,” etc.

Nehemiah is interpreted in Latin as “the Lord is a consoler” or “a consoler from the Lord.” Since he renewed the walls of Jerusalem and, having freed the people of God from the assaults of their enemies, raised them up in observance of the divine law, it is plainly evident that, by his name, work, and person, he appropriately signifies the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.

He indicates that he was sent to console the poor in spirit when, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to his disciples: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” that is, “another consoler” (John 14).

The Psalmist shows that the city of God, namely the holy Church, is to be built and that those who mourn are likewise to be consoled, when he says: “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel. He heals the brokenhearted” (Psalm 146), etc.

The figure of Nehemiah corresponds to the holy preachers, through whose ministry heavenly consolation is granted to us. After the fall of sin, they promise penitents the hope of divine forgiveness and reconciliation and, as though restoring the walls and ramparts of Jerusalem that had been demolished by enemies, rebuild them.

The month of Kislev is the month we call December. Among the Hebrews it is the ninth month; among us it is the last month of the year. Its name, which is interpreted in Latin as “his hope,” most clearly accords with the hopes of the man who was directing his mind toward raising up the ruins of the holy city.

For the first foundation of a good action is that we possess an unwavering hope in the Lord’s help to accomplish what we desire.

This is the month in which our Lord was born in the flesh. By its name it beautifully prefigured for us long beforehand that, in this month, the true Nehemiah—namely, the consoler from God the Father, long awaited by the elect—would come into the world for the building of the holy Church.

When Nehemiah writes that he was in the fortress of Susa when men arrived to report concerning Jerusalem, Susa was the capital of the Persian kingdom, as we read in the history of Esther (Esther 1). Not only Nehemiah but also the prophet Daniel calls it a fortress (Daniel 8). He does not do so because the city was actually a fortress, since, as we have said, it was a capital city, great and powerful, but because it had been built with such strength that it appeared to be a fortress.

“Susa” is interpreted as “riding” or “returning.” This name appropriately applies to the stronghold of the minds of the faithful, especially those who care for the captivity of Jerusalem—that is, for the salvation of those who were once snatched from the Church by the devil’s snares but, through repentance, have been restored to the Church by God’s grace.

Such people are in the returning fortress, that is, in the strength of a mind recalled from weak pleasures to desire for the heavenly homeland, from which they had fallen in the first parent.

They are also in the firmest cavalry of holy hearts, which carry God as their rider, according to the prophet’s words: “You who mount, mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.”

The Lord mounts upon his horses when he enlightens with the grace of his mercy the hearts of preachers whom he governs. His riding is salvation because he advances to eternal salvation those over whom he presides by governing them, and through them makes others also share in that same everlasting salvation.

When Nehemiah therefore asks about those who had remained from the captivity of Jerusalem, let us see what follows:

And they said to me: “Those who remained and were left behind,” etc. The literal sense is clear: although those who had remained from the captivity appeared to be living in peace—for the king of the Persians was their friend, and had even earlier sent Ezra the scribe with letters granting him authority throughout the region beyond the River—they were nevertheless in profound distress of mind, because their enemies reproached them that the holy city still lay destroyed. But even now, in the holy Church, those rightly suffer and are pierced by salutary sorrow who, recovering from their own former crimes, observe that their neighbors still remain subject to vices, so that, through the negligence of those who could have benefited many by correcting them, the devil has, as it were through the walls of a ruined city, free access into the Church. This must be all the more grievous if those who ought to benefit others by teaching or example themselves display, by living corruptly, an example of destruction to those who see them. This is what it means for the gates of Jerusalem to have been burned through by hostile flames: those who ought, by living and teaching well, to admit the worthy into the assembly of the elect and to exclude the unworthy perish in the fire of avarice, lust, pride, contention, envy, and the other vices which the malignant enemy is accustomed to bring upon them. What, then, appears to be required of us in these circumstances, and what ought to be done, is shown when the text immediately adds:

“And when I had heard words of this kind, I sat down and wept,” etc., up to “And direct your servant,” etc. If the holy man, hearing of buildings of stone and wood that had been destroyed, rightly mourned, fasted, and prayed, sitting in sadness for a long time, how much more must we persist in continual mourning, tears, and prayers over the destruction and ruin of souls caused by sin, so that, through the Lord’s mercy, those who lay in disgrace to religion, while the enemy triumphed, filthy and squalid with the long accumulation of vices, may be raised again to their former well-being?

## CHAPTER XVI

Nehemiah, having received permission and letters from the king, comes to Jerusalem to rebuild the city. From this year the seventy weeks of years foretold by the angel to Daniel are reckoned, and they extend to the time of the Lord’s Passion.

### (II Esdras II)

Now it came to pass in the month of Nisan, etc. [Col. 0885A] Nisan is the first month of the year according to the Hebrews, in which they always used to celebrate Passover; we call it April. What he said above—that he had mourned, fasted, and prayed for many days—therefore plainly shows that for four consecutive months, namely the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth, he devoted himself to this most sacred observance, awaiting a suitable time when he could make his desire known to the king. He was indeed chief cupbearer and presented the king with his drink; outwardly he performed an office of gladness, but inwardly he was weighed down by deep sorrow, remembering that the holy city had been destroyed and that the people of God had been made a reproach and object of contempt to the enemies of God. Hence, speaking in the Psalm, he protests together with those like him: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion” (Psalm 136).

And the king said to me: “Why is your face sad?” etc. Just as we have clearly learned from Isaiah that Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, prefigured the Lord and Savior, because he released the people of God from captivity and ordered the Temple to be restored, so also we may rightly understand his successor in the same empire, Artaxerxes, who with the same devotion commanded Jerusalem to be rebuilt, as a type of the Lord, who through the ministry of preachers builds for himself a city from living stones—that is, one Church from all the elect. Accordingly, Artaxerxes is aptly interpreted as “testing the light in silence.” For the Lord is the light of life, and he tests the hearts of his faithful in silence, sometimes illuminating them with the sweetness of heavenly grace, sometimes clouding them with the pressures of the present life, so that, instructed by temporal adversity, they may desire eternal goods more ardently.

This memorable year, in which Jerusalem was permitted to be rebuilt, had long before been prefigured in the prophet Daniel’s mystical writings. The angel said to him that seventy weeks had been shortened for his people and for his holy city. A little later: “From the issuing of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” And shortly afterward: “He will confirm a covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease.”

These weeks therefore begin with the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, when he granted permission to rebuild Jerusalem. At that time, as Julius Africanus writes, 115 years of the Persian kingdom had elapsed, and an equal number of years remained incomplete until Alexander the Great, when he killed Darius. It was the 185th year of Jerusalem’s captivity. The weeks extend to the time of the Lord’s Passion, through which an end was imposed upon the legal sacrifices and offerings.

Each week contains seven years, making 490 years, according to the course of the moon—provided only that, in this new and unusual reckoning, each year has no more than twelve lunar months. Hence the angel deliberately says that the seventy weeks were not counted but shortened for his people [Col. 0886A]; they amount to 475 solar years. I have taken care to discuss the entire meaning of this prophecy as fully as I could in the book *On Times*.

And Sanballat the Horonite heard, etc. Heretics are also distressed, as are all the enemies of the Church, whenever they see the elect laboring either for the Catholic faith or for the correction of morals, by which the walls of the Church are renewed. We must observe the difference in persons and circumstances. Above, those who had remained from the captivity in Judea were said to have been in great affliction and disgrace; Nehemiah too was said to have prolonged his fast with weeping and prayers because the walls of Jerusalem had been destroyed and its gates consumed by fire. Now, conversely, the enemies of the same holy city are distressed and placed in great affliction because they understand that its buildings are to be restored and its citizens, at the same time, rescued from the attacks of the enemy.

From this we may conclude that even in this life the Lord’s saying can be fulfilled. After saying, “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful,” he immediately added: “But your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16). When the world that had rejoiced is weeping, the sorrow of the righteous will be turned into joy when the affairs of the holy Church are seen to increase and those who had gone astray by sinning are known to return to her through repentance.

## CHAPTER XVII

Nehemiah, arriving at Jerusalem, inspects the ruin of the walls by night; then, revealing the reason for his journey in the morning, he strengthens the hearts and hands of the people for rebuilding.

[Col. 0886C] And I came to Jerusalem and remained there three days, etc. He travels around inspecting the various places of the ruined city and carefully examines each one to determine how it ought to be repaired. So too it belongs to spiritual teachers frequently to rise at night and, with diligent inquiry, inspect the condition of the holy Church while the others rest, so that they may watchfully seek out how to correct and raise up by discipline whatever in it has been stained or cast down by the wars of vices.

The wall of Jerusalem lies destroyed when the conduct of the faithful is sullied by earthly and base desires. The gates are consumed by fire when those who ought, by teaching others, to open the entrance to life themselves, abandoning the teaching of truth, grow torpid in common indolence with the rest and serve temporal concerns [Col. 0886D].

And I said to them: “You know the affliction in which we are,” etc. These words are plain and exceedingly appropriate in their spiritual meaning. Holy teachers—or rather, all who burn with zeal for God—are in the greatest affliction as long as they see Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace which the Lord left and entrusted to us, laid waste by the wars of dissension. They see the gates of the virtues, which according to Isaiah ought to have been occupied by praise (Isaiah 60), thrown down and held in disgrace as the gates of hell prevail. Therefore, gathering the ministers of the word into a single enterprise, they strive once more to build by faith and good action what had appeared to be destroyed.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The wall, towers, and gates of Jerusalem are built, beginning with Eliashib the high priest.

[Col. 0887A]

### (II Esdras III)

And Eliashib the high priest rose up, etc. This Eliashib, the high priest of that time, was the son of Joiakim, who himself had exercised the office of the high priest for no short time after his father, Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest. The restoration of the city rightly began with the high priest and his brothers, so that those who preceded others in rank might themselves become examples to all in good works. It is fitting that priests are mentioned among the builders.

And up to the tower of one hundred cubits, etc. Priests build to the measure of one hundred cubits when they kindle in all whom they instruct love and desire for eternal things. For the number one hundred, which in counting on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, signifies heavenly goods, which in comparison with temporal and lowly goods are, as it were, the right in relation to the left. They are also said to have sanctified the gate which they built. It belongs to priests to make their works especially worthy through sanctification and to act diligently so that all who join themselves to them may sanctify the Lord’s name in themselves by living well.

According to the literal sense, it appears that the first gate was called the Sheep Gate either because it was built by priests or because it was sanctified by them, since it was near the Temple and properly belonged to them. It also seems reasonable that the building of the city should begin from the Temple [Col. 0887C]. For it is necessary first of all that we preserve within ourselves steadfast faith and love toward God, then add works of mercy relating to love of our neighbor, and third—that is, last of all—attend to those things concerned with the general provision of this life. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, with these let us be content” (1 Timothy 6).

It may also plausibly be held that it was called the Sheep Gate because through it the animals that were to be offered in the Temple were customarily brought in. The priests therefore build the Sheep Gate at the beginning of the city of God’s construction when holy preachers first instruct their hearers in the truth of faith working through love, through which they are to bring in victims of good works [Col. 0887D] and offer them to God on the altar of their hearts. They sanctify the building of this gate, extended for one hundred cubits up to the Tower of Hananel—that is, the grace of God—when, from the beginning of faith to the steadfastness of good action, which can be accomplished only through God’s inspiration and help, they persevere with the sole intention of eternal reward.

It should certainly be noted that our manuscripts read: “And they built the Sheep Gate.” The Old Translation reads: “And they built the gate and the Sheep Pool.” John mentions this name in his Gospel: “Now there is in Jerusalem a pool of the sheep, which is called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porticoes; in these lay a great multitude of the sick” (John 5), etc. Nor does anything prevent us from understanding this very place to be designated here [Col. 0888A]. The name *probatica* is not far removed from the name “sheep”: in Greek, a sheep is called *probaton*. Jerome also mentions this place in his book *On Places*, writing as follows:

“Bethesda is a pool in Jerusalem, which is called the Sheep Pool and may be interpreted by us as ‘of cattle.’ It once had five porticoes; and twin pools are shown, one of which is usually filled by winter rains, while the other, strangely red as though with bloody water, bears witness in itself to the signs of an ancient work. For they say that victims were customarily washed in it by the priests, and from this it received its name.”

From all this it appears that the Sheep Gate was near the Sheep Pool, so that through it the victims to be washed in the pool might be brought.

And the sons of Asnaah built the Fish Gate. [Col. 0888B] He calls the gate the Fish Gate because it faced Joppa and Diospolis—that is, Lydda—and was nearer to the sea than any of Jerusalem’s other roads. It is now said to be called the Gate of David and to be the first of the gates west of Mount Zion. This opinion seems to agree with the *Books of Chronicles*, where it is written concerning Manasseh, king of Judah: “After this he built a wall outside the city of David, westward toward Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the Fish Gate, around as far as Ophel, and raised it exceedingly high” (2 Chronicles 33).

Figuratively, however, just as the Lord’s faithful are customarily called a flock, so they are also called fish. Thus, just as he said to Peter, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), so also to him, with Andrew and the other apostles, he promised, saying: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matthew 4). Concerning these fishermen he likewise said in a parable: “They gathered the good fish into vessels, but the bad they threw out” (Matthew 13).

The Fish Gate is therefore built in Jerusalem when offices of rank are ordered in the Church through which the elect are brought into the fellowship of perpetual peace, separated from the reprobate like good fish from bad. The Fish Gate is built when the faithful serve through works of virtue by which those who see them are rescued from the waves of worldly disturbance and desire and brought into the tranquility and peace of the spiritual life.

The prophet Zephaniah mentions this gate, saying: “A sound of crying from the Fish Gate, and wailing from the second” (Zephaniah 1). The addition “from the second” signifies the gate of the second wall in the same quarter. For the *Books of Chronicles* relate that in the time of Hezekiah the city wall was doubled, where it is written: “He built up, acting diligently, the whole wall that had been broken down, and constructed towers upon it, and another wall outside” (2 Chronicles 32).

This is the literal sense. According to the allegory of the Law, however, Zephaniah heard a sound of crying from the Fish Gate and wailing from the second because he foresaw that both would be cast down by enemies. For he saw that both the faith and the works of teachers—through which others ought to be rescued from the waves of corruptible life and brought into the holy Church—would be laid low by the snares of the ancient enemy, that is, deprived of heavenly joys through the desire for earthly pleasures.

He rightly heard a sound of crying and wailing from both gates, the first and the second, the outer and the inner, because he saw that both outward works and the inward hearts of the negligent would be overthrown through the devil’s attack. Yet because “the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Psalm 44), Nehemiah relates that this same Fish Gate was restored after its long ruin. For even if some preachers should at times fall through sin, there will nevertheless be people until the end of the age who, succeeding to the place of their predecessors, will, with the Lord’s help, open the gates of righteousness to the faithful by preaching and living well. Appropriately, the text adds concerning those who destroyed this gate:

They covered it and set up its doors, etc. When he returns to the other things said to have been built, the gate is mentioned repeatedly, because it is necessary that all who have begun the structure of good action should carry it through to the roof of perfection by persevering in what they have begun, and should establish, with vigilant care even over the smallest safeguards, doors, bolts, and bars.

Doors are set in gates so that, when opened at the proper time, citizens may have the opportunity to enter or leave. Bolts and bars are set so that, when the doors are closed and secured, the enemy cannot enter. Thus in our good works we must also set up doors of benevolent foresight, so that our fellow citizens—that is, our neighbors—may see these things, glorify our Father who is in heaven, and themselves learn through our examples to walk and enter with us within the walls of the virtues.

Bolts and bars must also be set against the snares and attacks of enemies, so that we may be carefully fortified on every side and the ancient enemy, admitted through carelessness, may not conquer the stronghold of our virtue. Hence Proverbs says aptly: “A brother who is helped by his brother is like a fortified city, and judgments are like the bars of cities” (Proverbs 18). When both peoples—the Jews and the nations—agree with one another in fraternal love in Christ, they build one Church, namely the city of their Creator. And just as the bars of cities fortify their gates, so doctrines of truth defend the Churches throughout the world, which together constitute the one Catholic Church, against the assaults of unbelievers.

Likewise, we set bolts and bars on our gate when we diligently take care lest we expose the secrets of our faith to swine and dogs—that is, to unclean minds—or, for the sake of human approval, make a display of our righteousness and admit to viewing our good works those who, by praising us, bring us more danger than they return salutary assistance by seeing them.

And they built the Old Gate, etc. This is the old gate of which John speaks: “Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning” (1 John 2). “The old commandment is the word which you heard.” The Old Gate is therefore built in Jerusalem when the word of faith and love, handed down from the beginning of the holy Church, begins either to be restored among those who have gone astray or to be established among those who have recently come to faith.

And they left Jerusalem, etc. The wall of the Broad Street in Jerusalem is the firmness and defense of perfect love in the hearts of the elect. Its builders reach it by constructing when, advancing in works of charity, they can say to their Creator and Helper: “We ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged our heart” (Psalm 118). This is the enlargement of an enlightened mind that can love both a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake.

And Hanun built the Valley Gate, etc. We know that the Valley of Jehoshaphat, which was also called Gehenna—that is, the Valley of Hinnom—lay on the eastern side of the city of Jerusalem. Through it the torrent Kidron, mentioned in the Gospel (John 18), flows from the northern side toward the south whenever it receives rainwater or melted snow. But we also read of the Valley of Gihon on the western side of the same city, where the book of Chronicles says concerning Manasseh, king of Judah, as we quoted above: “After this he built a wall outside the city of David, westward toward Gihon in the valley” (2 Chronicles 33). Gihon is the name of the spring where Solomon was anointed king outside the city.

Whether Ezra means this valley, that one, or any other valley of the same city, the mystery is clear: the Valley Gate is built in Jerusalem when the virtue of humility is prescribed, among other things, either to the elect newly instructed through knowledge of the faith or to those who had strayed and have been restored by teachers of truth to the purity of faith, so that they may deserve to be exalted by the greater grace of God. Holy Scripture says: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5). And in the Psalm: “The valleys will abound in grain” (Psalm 64), that is, the humble will abound in gifts of heavenly nourishment.

The Valley Gate is rightly built after the Old Gate and the wall of the Broad Street, because after the foundations of the Catholic faith, which works through love, it is necessary for humility—the guardian of the virtues—to be held fast and commended to us, so that, according to the command of the wise man, “the greater we are, the more we humble ourselves in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

And one thousand cubits of the wall as far as the Dung Gate, etc. They report that the site of Jerusalem is arranged on such a gentle slope, slanting at once toward the north and the east, that rain falling there never remains, but flows away like rivers through the eastern gates, carrying with it all the filth of the streets and swelling the torrent Kidron in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Hence it seems likely that the Dung Gate was so called because through it filth and refuse were customarily removed.

It is by no means a lesser virtue or benefit to carry unclean things out of the city of the Lord than to gather clean things within it. Those who appoint people to the ministry of the holy Church through whom the filth of vices may be cleansed from the minds of the elect therefore build the Dung Gate in Jerusalem. They also exclude corrupt-minded people from the boundaries of the Church, with the heavenly shower of grace helping them and weakening every impurity, so that, according to the Psalmist, “all those who work iniquity may be destroyed from the city of the Lord” (Psalm 10).

Since it is a sign of great perfection when someone advances so far through the merit of humility that he can clearly inspect his errors and effectively cleanse those he has discovered, it is rightly said that those who built the Valley Gate also constructed one thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate. The number one thousand signifies perfection, while the cubit signifies work, which is performed through the hands and arms. Those therefore reach, by building one thousand cubits in the wall of the holy city from the Valley Gate to the Dung Gate who, having received the grace of humility, devote themselves with such zeal to the good works of perfection that they cast out from themselves every kind of refuse—not only harmful action or useless speech, but even superfluous thought.

And Shallun built the Fountain Gate, etc. *Pagos* in Greek means “village” in Latin. Writers report that from that side of Mount Zion which, with its precipitous cliff, faces the eastern region, the spring of Siloam bursts forth within the walls at the foot of the hill. Its waters flow southward with an alternating movement: it does not bubble forth continuously, but at uncertain [or: regular] hours and days, and it is accustomed to come through hollows in the earth and caverns of very hard rock with a great roaring. The city is said to make use of this one spring, and even of this one not perpetually.

Understand, therefore, that the Fountain Gate designated here is this one, especially since the text plainly adds:

And the walls of the Pool of Siloam toward the King’s Garden, etc. Siloam, interpreted as “sent,” where the man blind from birth was healed and illuminated, signifies the Lord and Savior, who was sent by God the Father for our illumination. The Father himself, from whom the Son was born, may most appropriately be understood as the source of this fountain. Of him the Psalmist says well: “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35).

The Fountain Gate is built in Jerusalem when teachers are appointed in the Church to preach to the peoples the faith of divine eternity. The walls of the Pool of Siloam are also built when the firmest and unconquerable testimonies of Scripture, by which the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is signified, are rooted in the minds of the faithful.

These walls of the divine utterances reach the King’s Garden when, having understood the mysteries of the Lord’s dispensation, we begin, with the supreme King, the Lord our God, giving aid, to produce shoots of virtue. They also reach the steps that descend from the City of David when someone learns to advance from the common life of the faithful toward heavenly things through spiritual desires.

For the steps that descend from the City of David to the lower parts of the city of Jerusalem are aids of divine inspiration or protection, by which we are gradually stirred up so that we may be able to reach the walls of the heavenly kingdom. David made steps by which we ought to ascend to his city when divine goodness taught us the order of the virtues by which we should seek heavenly things and granted us the gift of practicing those same virtues.

Concerning these steps the Psalmist said: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord; he has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears, in the place which he established,” etc., until he says: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Psalm 83).

The builders of the holy city therefore reach these steps, after the walls of the Pool of Siloam and after the King’s Garden, by building when, after the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation have been revealed—through which the Gentiles, blind from birth, were cleansed and illuminated—and after the shoots of good action begun through faith, the holy teachers diligently show their hearers, in due season, the progress of the virtues. Through these they may ascend to the vision of their Creator, who is designated as strong of hand and desirable, which is what the name David signifies.

The most reverend father Benedict, in name and life, understood that these advances consist chiefly in humility. Interpreting the ladder of the patriarch Jacob, on which angels were seen ascending and descending, as signifying our path to heavenly things, he distinguished the steps of that ladder through the increases and advances of good works performed by humility, with the most diligent and devout inquiry.

According to the literal sense, the City of David is called Mount Zion. It lies to the south and rises above the city as its citadel, while most of the city lies below the mountain, situated on the plain of a lower hill. Hence it is written in the Book of Kings: “David captured the stronghold of Zion; this is the City of David.” And shortly afterward: “David lived in the stronghold and called it the City of David” (1 Kings 25).

After him Nehemiah built, etc. Note that King David was buried not in Bethlehem, as some suppose, but in Jerusalem—and not without a certain reason in the mystery. Just as, being born in Bethlehem and anointed king there, he prefigured that the Lord Christ would be born there from his lineage and worshiped by the Magi in the person of a king, so, having died and been buried in Jerusalem, he signified that the Lord himself would suffer and be buried in that same city, but would rise quickly from the tomb.

After the Fountain Gate and the walls of the Pool of Siloam—which reach the King’s Garden and as far as the steps that descend from the City of David—the extent of the holy city is likewise extended as far as opposite David’s tomb. For one who preaches the faith of divine eternity, who declares to faithful hearers the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation and the fruitfulness of the Church clinging to Christ—of which he himself says, “My sister, my bride, is a garden enclosed” (Song of Songs 4)—must not merely imitate the steps of good works by which they may ascend to their eternal homeland. He must also continually impress upon their memory the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, so that they may understand that through him who died and rose for them, they too are to be raised from the region and shadow of death to life and are to ascend to the heavenly kingdom. The text rightly continues:

And as far as the pool, etc. The pool, constructed with great labor, may not improperly be understood as divine Scripture, which, fashioned through the work of the Holy Spirit, supplies us with a bath for cleansing sins and at the same time a cup of salutary taste. If it is changed by the Lord into wine—that is, if it is transferred into spiritual meaning—it intoxicates us with the more delightful sweetness of truth.

There too is the House of the Mighty, because all who have become accustomed to being refreshed by hearing and practicing the frequent streams of the divine utterances are made strong and unconquerable against all the snares of the ancient enemy. After David’s tomb, therefore, a pool constructed with great labor is placed in the holy city, next to which is the House of the Mighty, because through the Lord’s Passion the abyss of Scripture has been opened to us. Through its abundance, the hearts of the faithful are strengthened, and the city of Christ is made unconquerable by all enemies.

For when its waters fail or have been seized by the enemy, a city is easily captured. And if the ancient enemy takes away from us the fountain of the word of God, nothing prevents the fierce destroyer and attacker from immediately climbing into the stronghold of our mind.

After him his brothers, the Levites, built, etc. Up to this point the first wall of the city is constructed; from here the second measure begins—that is, the inner wall, about which we spoke above. Hence this description says that many of the builders built opposite their own houses, since many houses of the city were either near or joined to the inner wall.

After the construction of the outer wall, the measure of a second wall follows in our city as well, when, after the perfection of works and speech—which can also appear to human beings—we strive more earnestly to please God in the inner regions of our mind, lest we presume to conceive anything under a veil that would offend the eyes of the inner Judge.

It is fittingly said that the second measure was built opposite the ascent of the firmest corner. For the firmest corner is the Lord, who united the people of the Jews and of the nations in his faith and love. Hence in the Psalm (Psalm 117) and in Isaiah (Isaiah 28) he is called the cornerstone.

The second measure is built opposite the ascent of this corner when, through the purity of pious thought, we strive to arrive at the vision of our Creator, and when, still held in this life, we sigh frequently with desire for his vision. From this point onward many orders of builders follow, who are said to have built the second measure, because the greatest structure of the holy Church lies in the defense of inner virtue, when we guard our heart with all vigilance, since from it life proceeds. To discuss these one by one and draw everything toward spiritual understanding would be excessively lengthy.

Now the Nethinim lived in Ophel, etc. The Nethinim are understood to be the Gibeonites, who served with faithful devotion in the ministry of the house of the Lord, according to the arrangement of Joshua son of Nun. Ophel was a tower not far from the Temple, of extraordinary height. Hence it received the name Ophel—that is, “of darkness” or “cloudy”—because it raised its head as far as the clouds.

Thus, where it is written in Micah, “And you, tower of the flock, cloudy one of the daughter of Zion” (Micah 4), the Hebrew has, instead of “cloudy tower,” “the tower of Ophel.” The Book of Chronicles also mentions this tower and shows in what part of the city it was situated, reporting concerning Manasseh, as we quoted above, that he built a wall outside the City of David westward toward Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the Fish Gate around as far as Ophel (2 Chronicles 33).

It was therefore appropriate, according to the situation of the place, that the ministers of the Temple should live in the tower near the Temple. According to the mystical sense as well, the Nethinim live in Ophel—that is, in the cloudy tower—when those who have dedicated themselves to God by a profession of more perfect life do not cease to dwell continually in the defense and height of virtues and actions, and in thought, saying with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Concerning them the crowd of ordinary people may also testify with wonder, saying: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isaiah 60). Likewise, the Nethinim live in Ophel when those distinguished by the habit of religion learn to penetrate the hidden things of Scripture—of which it is said, “Dark water in the clouds of the air”—that is, mystical knowledge in the prophets, with an enlightened heart, and to meditate on these things in their reading day and night.

The text aptly continues concerning their dwelling: “As far as opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the projecting tower.” The Water Gate is the Lord, who waters us daily with the grace of his mercy, lest we fail amid the hardships of the present life. The Psalmist desired to enter this gate when he said: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, God” (Psalm 41).

This gate is fittingly said to be toward the east, because the same Lord who refreshes us with the torrent of his delight so that we do not thirst also illuminates us through the gift of his visitation, so that we do not grow blind in the darkness of error. As Zechariah says: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1).

He also defends us through the protection of his guardianship, so that we are not touched by the enemy. Hence the text rightly continues: “And as far as the tower that projected.” Understanding this, the same Psalmist said: “You have led me, because you became my hope, a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60).

The Nethinim therefore dwell in Ophel, as far as opposite the Water Gate toward the east and the projecting tower, when all the faithful devoted to sacred reading rejoice in being refreshed and illuminated by the grace of divine goodness and in being continually protected from the enemy by his help. And because after the present gifts of the virtues one ascends to behold the glory of the Lord’s humanity, the text rightly adds:

After them the Tekoites repaired a second section, etc. The wall of the temple, to be sure, is the body of the Lord and Savior, concerning which he himself said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). His persecutors destroyed the temple of his body in death, but, once it had been raised and exalted to the heavens, those who love him saw it in glory and do not cease seeing it forever.

Thus the construction of the holy city extends from the great and lofty tower to the wall of the temple, when the just, from the height of contemplation by which—even in this life, having despised temporal things—they suspend their minds in desire for heavenly realities, ascend in the life to come to behold the splendor of the Lord’s incarnation, once it has been revealed, and also the eternity of divine glory. Since *Thekua* is interpreted as “trumpet” or “horn,” and *Tekoites* as “trumpeters,” it is appropriately said that the Tekoites built this section. For it belongs to teachers—those whose sound has gone out into all the earth—to disclose either the gifts of God present among us or those that are to come in his city, that is, among the people of the faithful.

Above the Horse Gate they built, etc. Jeremiah mentions this gate and indicates that it was situated on the eastern side of the city, writing figuratively about the holy Church: “And the city shall be built for the Lord from the Tower of Hananel” (Jeremiah 31). A little later he says: “As far as the brook Kidron, and as far as the corner of the eastern Horse Gate” (ibid.).

Horses, when taken in a favorable sense, as are also asses, camels, and mules, sometimes signify the peoples of the Gentiles converted to the Lord, and sometimes the concerns of temporal matters rightly subjected to the Lord of the soul. The priests built the wall of the city of God at the Horse Gate when, after the calling of the Jewish people, the holy teachers advanced by scattering the word as far as the introduction of the peoples of the Gentiles into the holy Church.

They likewise build at the Horse Gate when they provide adequate examples of conduct for those who enter the gates of the holy Church in order to restrain the unruly movements of their flesh or soul. Or certainly they build there when they so arrange their own thoughts—thoughts that necessarily concern their sustenance and clothing and that of their dependents—that these thoughts in no way impede the freedom of mind by which they had resolved always to seek heavenly things.

Here the text appropriately adds concerning those who were working: “Each one opposite his own house.” This statement is repeated frequently in the construction of the holy city. There is no need to labor over explaining how, in the holy Church, each person ought to build a wall of virtues opposite his own house and fortify his mind against the snares of the devil, lest he who “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5) be able to break in anywhere, while each person has fortified his body and mind with strong faith in the Lord.

Each person also builds opposite his own house if he protects those entrusted to him with careful observance of regular discipline, lest they be deceived either by the assault of vices or by heretical persuasion.

It would be a long task to discuss individually, in a spiritual interpretation, the buildings and builders of the holy city; even without our speaking, an experienced reader readily understands them. This alone should be noted: those who build the gates and towers through which the citizens enter or the enemies are kept out are the prophets, apostles, and evangelists. Through them the form and order of faith and right conduct have been supplied to us, by which we ought to enter the unity of the holy Church; and from their words we learn how to refute and repel the adversaries of truth.

Those who build with the remaining words are the pastors and teachers whom the Apostle placed second. Through their diligence, the Catholic faith—built by the great architects of the Church—is preserved throughout the whole world to this day. And just as Nehemiah, enumerating all the builders of the city in order, makes their memory perpetual, so the Lord, the consoler of our poverty, inscribes in heaven the names of all who build his Church among the elect. But let us examine what follows.

## CHAPTER XIX. Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders but are despised; they wage war but are driven off by prayers and weapons.

*(2 Esdras 4.)* Now it happened, when Sanballat heard, etc. Clearly, this is the anger of heretics; these are the words of those who falsely call themselves Samaritans, that is, “guardians of the law of God,” although they are utterly opposed to God and his laws. They have long since been separated from the house of David—that is, from the unity of Christ and the Church—through heresies, schisms, or evil works. They fear the building of the walls of faith lest their own impiety perhaps be attacked and excluded.

This mockery belongs to all who say that they know God but deny him by their deeds. For the Samaritans served the Lord in such a way that they did not renounce their ancient gods. Those who imitate them figuratively today are people who are Christians in such a way that they make their belly their god and pursue greed, which the Apostle expressly calls the service of idols; enslaved also to the other enticements of the world, they serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

Such people, like the heretics, do not want the walls of the Church renewed, lest, as the condition of piety grows, they be forced to abandon their own impiety. They customarily call the weak “Jews,” that is, confessors of the faith, and say that they can easily be overcome by the Gentiles, while in the daily contest of souls they prefer vices to winning the palm of victory in virtue.

Since among the heretics there are also those who deny that forgiveness should be granted to penitents after their fall, the text appropriately continues in their person:

“Can stones be built?” etc. Stones, burned out of heaps of dust, are built and restored to the work of the holy city when those who had either denied the faith after being overcome by the fire of persecutions, or had lost the purity of their conduct after being subdued by the pleasures of vices, recover through the Lord’s mercy. Thus they recover the integrity of the catholic faith through steadfast confession and attain the adornments of virtue after reforming their conduct.

But Tobiah the Ammonite, his near associate, also said: “Let them build,” etc. Both the person and the words of this Tobiah suit the heretics. His person does so because his ancestor Ammon, the patriarch of that people, was conceived through incest and drunkenness, at night and in a cave. It is readily clear to anyone how all these things may be applied to the founders of heresies: their entire origin arose from carnal pleasure and impurity, from the darkness of error or crime, and from private gatherings, not from the public creed of the holy Church.

As for the fact that this same Tobiah—whose name, supposedly, is interpreted as “good of the Lord”—says, not from merit or truth but from arrogance and pride, that the wall of the holy city could be leaped over by a fox, it is obvious that heretics are called foxes. Hence the saying in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2). This openly means: “Detect and bring into the light, exposing them, the foul and deceitful tricks of the heretics by which they strive to corrupt the fruitful minds of the faithful.”

“If a fox climbs up,” he says, “it will leap over their stone wall.” If some heretic rises against the assertion of their faith, he immediately grows arrogant and will trample under his feet all confidence in their teaching, which they boast is fortified like a strong stone and founded upon Christ.

But what the sacred writer of this history adds by way of imprecation will come upon such blasphemers:

“Hear, O our God, for we have become despised,” etc. [Col. 0897B] Similar is the Psalmist’s statement about the enemies of the elect, speaking as though through the person of a single wicked man: “His sorrow shall return upon his head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his crown” (Psalm 7).

“And we prayed to our God,” etc. This is the sole refuge against all the enemies of the Church: prayer to God, together with the diligence of teachers who, meditating on his law day and night, fortify the hearts of the faithful through preaching, consoling, and exhorting them against the snares of the devil and his soldiers.

Then Judah said: “The strength of the bearers has failed,” etc. “Judah” means the tribe of the sons of Judah. The complaint that the wall could not be built because too much earth had been heaped up at the site of the wall—earth that first had to be carried away so that the foundations of the wall could be laid upon living ground—agrees with the parable of the evangelical house, whose builder dug deeply. After removing the raised heap of earth, he laid its foundations upon rock, so that no force of waters or winds could overthrow it (Matthew 7; Luke 6).

First, then, the earthly soil of desires must be removed from our heart; afterward, a firm and unconquerable wall of good works must be built upon the foundation of faith. For whoever tries to raise the building of holy conduct upon the soil and rubble of weak thoughts is deceived; and instead of a house or city, as soon as the storm of temptation breaks upon him, he will discover that he has built a ruin.

“Our enemies said: Let them not know or understand,” etc. [Col. 0897D] These things are always enacted in the spiritual building as well. The indefatigable enemy remains with his attendants—namely, unclean spirits and wicked men—who, caring little for the works of faith and virtue, always strive to obstruct them and, as far as they can, to overthrow them. They endeavor to kill the minds of the faithful with the sword of wicked suggestion.

Against these things, however, we must take up the armor of God, according to the Apostle, so that we may be able “to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things” (Ephesians 6). It was rightly said that he stationed the people with weapons behind the wall all around, so that the builders, surrounded by a column of armed men, could devote themselves to building with freer hands and a more secure wall.

The ranks of the faithful are distributed: some, adorning the Church within by good works, build it; others, armed with the weapons of sacred reading, keep watch against the heretics who attack that same Church. The former strengthen their neighbors in the truth of the faith through religious devotion; the latter engage in the necessary struggle against the darts of the devil or of vices, by which the enemies labor to overthrow that same faith, and with pastoral concern drive away the wolves lurking near the Lord’s sheepfold.

Now it happened, when our enemies heard that it had been reported to us, that God dispersed their counsel, etc. In the spiritual building also, if we are always clothed in apostolic weapons, the counsel of the devil and his angels, who desire to wage war against us, will be dispersed.
