## CHAPTER XX. All the builders, armed and prepared for battle, apply themselves in this way to building the walls.

[Col. 0898B] From that day onward, half of the young men performed the work, etc. It must be noted that not only did half of the young men perform the work and the other half stand ready for battle, but those same young men who performed the work were also girded with swords.

Such is the cunning of the ancient enemy, and such the fury of his army fighting against the Church, that not only the preachers of truth but even the people of God themselves must always keep watch against his devices and stand as though in battle formation.

The builders are girded with swords at their loins when those who devote themselves to good works and take care to regulate and govern those entrusted to them according to an orderly rule—that is, to place the living stones in the building of the holy city in their proper order—strive to restrain the looseness of luxury within themselves with the sharpness of the word of God.

Nor should it be passed over that, when David or Solomon built this same city, nothing is reported about armed builders or attacking adversaries. But when the city, destroyed because of their crimes, is restored with greater labor and diligence, this is because such is also the spiritual building accomplished for the salvation of souls: in baptism, those reborn through faith and confession of the Holy Trinity become his city and house by God’s grace, without any labor of ours.

If, after the washing of the sacred font, we relapse into sins because the devil has deceived us, and our victorious enemy casts down the battlements of our virtues with the fire of vices, then we must necessarily repair the buildings of good works that we have lost through more strenuous efforts of prayer, affliction, vigils, almsgiving, and a stricter way of life. For we rid ourselves of the allurements of vices, once experienced, with greater difficulty than of those unknown. It requires less labor to avoid an unknown pleasure of the flesh than to reject one that is known.

“Let each one remain with his servant,” etc. Observe how much zeal they had in their work, since they persevered in labor even at night. So did the Apostle, who worked with his own hands night and day, lest he weary any of the believers by seeking his livelihood (1 Corinthians 4). Unless, perhaps, we should understand that they took turns working in such a way that some labored during the day on the wall, while others kept the night watches against the incursions of the enemy.

The builders of our city likewise do both things at once. The very people who build the Church by instructing the faithful also drive unbelievers and contradicters away from harming the Church by rebuking them.

## CHAPTER XXI. When the people are stirred into an uproar because of hunger and want, Nehemiah adjures the nobles and magistrates not to exact interest from their brothers but rather to give money on their behalf.

*(2 Esdras 5.)* A great cry arose from the people and their wives, etc. The people desired to build the wall of the city, but the severity of the famine hindered them from the holy work. This famine had been caused not only by a scarcity of crops but also by the avarice of the rulers, since they demanded from the same people greater taxes than they could pay. We see the same order of things occurring among us every day.

For how many there are among the people of God who gladly desire to obey the divine commandments, but are held back from fulfilling what they desire by want of temporal goods, by poverty, and by the examples of those who appear to be endowed with the religious habit—while they themselves demand from those over whom they appear to preside an immense burden of worldly possessions and tribute, yet contribute nothing to their everlasting salvation, whether by teaching, by providing examples of conduct, or by performing works of piety.

Would that in our days some Nehemiah—that is, a consoler coming from the Lord—might restrain our errors, kindle our inmost hearts to divine love, and strengthen us by turning our hands away from our own desires toward establishing the city of Christ.

But let us consider the literal sense: the wretched cry of the afflicted people was increased in three distinct ways. Some, compelled by hunger, were preparing to sell their sons to the wealthy for food. Others, sparing their children, wished instead to give their fields and houses for food. Others, conversely, forbidding the sale both of their children and of their fields, persuaded them only to borrow money for the king’s taxes, giving their fields and vineyards as pledges until, when the abundance of fertility and crops returned, they could repay the lenders what they had borrowed.

He rebuked the nobles and magistrates, etc. Like an excellent leader of the heavenly army and a wise architect of the city of God, he declared that he had first done himself what he wanted the nobles and magistrates of the people to do: namely, to give alms to the poor and ask nothing from them except the keeping of God’s law and the building of his city.

In this passage, we ought not to seek the allegorical meaning while neglecting the text of the letter; rather, we must preserve it diligently in our conduct. Thus, in addition to the daily fruits of almsgiving, whenever a general time of famine and want afflicts the people, we should take care to lend to the needy what we can and also relinquish those taxes that we had been accustomed to demand from our subjects as though they were justly owed, insofar as our Father may likewise forgive us our debts.

A very dreadful conclusion is imposed upon this passage when it says:

“Moreover, I shook out my lap and said,” etc. Whoever refuses either to show mercy to the poor or is not ashamed to demand from them, as though justly owed, what they do not possess is shaken out of his house—that is, expelled from the assembly of the holy Church, in which he believed he would remain forever. He is also shaken out of his labors, deprived of the fruit of good works in which he thought he had laudably labored. For labors performed without piety cannot become fruitful before the Lord.

How greatly this rebuke or imprecation of Nehemiah moved the hearts of all is openly shown when the text immediately adds:

“The whole multitude said, ‘Amen,’” etc. When, after hearing his solemn declaration, they all answered “Amen,” praised God together, and did what he had commanded, it is evident that they accepted his words not under compulsion of fear but from the innermost affection of their hearts.

## CHAPTER XXII. Nehemiah explains how much piety he himself had shown toward the people.

“From the day when he commanded me to be governor,” etc. Explaining this figuratively, the Apostle says: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel; but I have used none of these rights” (1 Corinthians 9).

For twelve years Nehemiah lived in the governorship with his brothers in such a way that they did not eat the rations owed to governors. Through this, he mystically indicated that it is an apostolic work when someone promoted to govern the people of God nobly exercises the work of a ruler by building up the Church, yet does not seek the profit of his office by expecting earthly advantages from those whom he governs through preaching and a good life.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Sanballat and his companions attempt to draw Nehemiah away from building the wall, even employing domestic conspiracies against him; but when he detects them, the wall of the city is completed in full.

*(2 Esdras 6.)* Now it happened, when Sanballat and Tobiah heard, etc. The enemies of the holy city urge Nehemiah to descend to the plains and enter into a peace treaty with them, slaughtering calves together as a testimony to the compacted treaty. But he, lest the religious work be neglected, remains in the mountains.

So heretics and false Catholics also wish to have fellowship in peace with true Catholics on the condition that they themselves do not agree to ascend to the citadel of ecclesiastical faith or conduct, but instead force those whom they see dwelling at the summit of virtues to descend to the depths of evil practices or doctrines.

They rightly wish to make a pact with Nehemiah in one field, because they desire all whom they can seduce to be dissolved into the same freedom of a more luxurious life that they themselves pursue. They likewise rightly wish to make the pact with him through calves slaughtered together, because false brothers are eager to offer sacrifices of their prayers or actions to God together with true Catholics, so that, being themselves regarded as truly faithful, they may corrupt the true Catholics through the proximity of communion.

But Nehemiah, representing the teachers of the faithful, does not agree to descend to the profane or to be defiled by their sacrifices. Rather, he persists devotedly in the virtues he has undertaken. The more fiercely the enemies tried to terrify him, the more he strove, by acting well, to become terrifying to those same enemies. Hence the following is also said:

“All these men were terrifying us,” etc. Therefore, in the spiritual structure also, since the cunning enemy always tries to impede our hands, let us always take care, with divine assistance, to strengthen those hands in good action.

“And I entered the house of Shemaiah,” etc. Assailed by the enemies’ ambushes, Nehemiah enters Shemaiah’s house as though that of a friend and brother. But he finds him to be an ambusher and enemy, corrupted by the gifts and friendship of outsiders. The elect always have struggles outside and fears within; not only the apostles but also the prophets led lives made suspect by dangers from their own people, dangers from the Gentiles, and dangers from false brothers.

The wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Elul, etc. According to the Hebrews, the month of Elul is the sixth month of the year, which the Romans call September. It is rightly in the sixth month of the year that the wall of the holy city is completed, so that even in this final period the perfected action of the faithful—whether penitents or innocent—is signified.

The number six commonly signifies the perfection of a good work, either because the Lord completed the creation of the world on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, or because he wished us to labor in good works during the six ages of this world and to hope, in the seventh—which belongs to the life to come—for the Sabbath-rest of souls.

It is rightly completed on the twenty-fifth day of that month because the body has five senses, through whose service good works must be performed outwardly. Just as the number five in its simple form commonly represents these senses, so the same number, multiplied by itself and brought to twenty-five, displays those same senses in greater perfection.

We therefore complete the wall of Jerusalem on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month when, diligently dedicating all the senses of our body to divine service, we bring the practices of virtue that we have begun to a firm conclusion and, with the Lord’s effective help, complete what we have faithfully begun to do for the fortification of catholic peace.

This wall is also rightly said to have been completed in fifty-two days. For the fiftieth psalm is the psalm of repentance and remission, in which the Prophet also prays specifically for the building of this city, saying: “Deal favorably, O Lord, with Zion in your good will, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Psalm 51).

On the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, the Holy Spirit came upon the primitive Church. Through him the devotion to repent is infused into us, and the gift of forgiveness is bestowed upon penitents. There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. By these, we are commanded to labor for the reception of eternal life, after the forgiveness of sins has been granted to us through the Holy Spirit.

Therefore it is most fitting that, rebuilding the wall of the holy city that had been destroyed by enemies, its citizens restore it in fifty-two days. For this is truly the perfection of the righteous in this life: that they chastise through repentance whatever offenses they have committed, by the grace of divine inspiration, and thereafter adorn themselves with good works in the love of God and neighbor.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Once the city of Jerusalem has been completed, the Gentiles are terrified; Nehemiah lists the singers and appoints guards at the gates.

Now it happened … that all the nations were afraid, etc. Those who had previously tried to terrify the builders of the holy city in order to hold them back from their work now fear themselves and lose heart when the construction of that same city has been completed, recognizing that the building had been begun and completed with God as its author.

So also in the holy Church, when the structure of charity, continence, peace, and the other virtues has risen firm, unclean spirits are afraid; their temptation is driven away and repelled by our strength, and it contributes instead to our victory. The same may be understood equally of heretics and false Catholics: by the steadfast faith of the good, working through love, they are either corrected and reformed or, once exposed, avoided and expelled from the boundaries of the Church.

*(2 Esdras 7.)* After the wall had been built, etc. In the spiritual sense also, wherever the wall of the Church has been built through the gathering of new peoples into the faith or the correction of those who had gone astray, the doors of regular discipline must immediately be put in place, lest the ancient enemy, who “prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5), be able to break in anywhere into the sheepfold of the faithful.

Gatekeepers, singers, and Levites must be appointed to guard these same gates; it is clear that their persons correspond to all the holy teachers. Gatekeepers are those who have received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that they may receive the worthy and humble but keep the proud and impure from entering the heavenly city, saying: “You have neither part nor share in this matter, for your heart is not right before God” (Acts 8).

Singers are those who proclaim the sweetness of that same heavenly homeland to their hearers with devout voice. Levites are those who are always vigilant in the service of divine worship.

Nehemiah commanded that the gates of Jerusalem should not be opened until the heat of the sun—that is, throughout the whole time of night—so that either the enemy might not break in under cover of darkness or, certainly, some careless citizen going out might be captured and perish by the enemy.

Throughout the night of this present age, the guardians of souls must likewise act diligently, lest, when the observance of devout conduct is neglected, the devil enter to disturb the company of the faithful, or seize and destroy one of their number. When the Sun of justice appears and the light of future blessedness shines forth, there will no longer be any need for the enclosures of continence, because the adversaries will no longer be given the power to attack or tempt the faithful, having been condemned, together with their prince, to everlasting punishment.

Therefore John says in his Apocalypse concerning the future glory of that same holy city: “Its gates shall not be shut by day, for there will be no night there” (Revelation 21).

“And I appointed guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem,” etc. The guardians of souls are not to be chosen from the newly converted or from the common crowd, but from those who, by God’s grace, have been freed from the contest with vices and have already become accustomed to possessing their minds in Jerusalem—that is, in the tranquil vision of peace—who can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

It is rightly said of them that he appointed each one at his post, so that when some, having completed their course, are taken from this light, others might immediately be placed in their position to govern the faithful. At no time are there lacking those who strive to keep watch for the peace of the holy Church because of the terrors of the night. The truth of the prophetic word continually runs to the end of the age, when it says to that same Church: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 45).

It is also rightly added: “Each one opposite his own house.” The guardianship of the holy Church is properly fulfilled if each person cares for all the faithful in such a way that he is especially responsible for those over whom, by God’s authority, he has been placed to exercise more diligent care.

## CHAPTER XXV. To find inhabitants worthy of the city, Nehemiah rereads the census-register of those who first came up from Babylon into Judea.

Now the city was very broad and large, etc. These things correspond figuratively to that period. When, through the apostles, the word of God had been scattered far and wide and the whole world had received the new shoot of faith, the peoples were still inexperienced, since the Church had not yet been built but had been imbued only through hearing and through the sacraments of the word.

“God put it into my heart,” etc. Therefore, after gathering to himself not only the nobles and magistrates but also the entire common people, he carefully took account of their number, so that he could distinguish the complete total: who ought to dwell in the city of Jerusalem itself and who in the other cities.

## CHAPTER XXVI. In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem, and when Ezra reads the Law of Moses, they listen attentively.

*(2 Esdras 8.)* The seventh month had come, etc. While Nehemiah was seeking to provide for and arrange who ought to dwell in the city they had built, the seventh month arrived; for they had been far away. Since the wall had been completed on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, no more than five days remained before the beginning of the seventh month.

From its first day through the twenty-second, that seventh month had been wholly consecrated to lawful ceremonies. After these had been duly celebrated, he returned with the leaders and the people to arrange the inhabitants of the established city.

Here the devotion and concord of the people should be noted: like one man—that is, with one and the same faith and love—they came together at the temple of the Lord. They themselves asked their high priest, when the book had been brought, to repeat the commands of the law that had been given to them and that they ought to perform, so that, together with the built city, a structure of conduct pleasing to God might also arise, lest, as before, the city’s ruin follow from negligence in religion.

The city was rightly built in the sixth month and the people gathered into it in the seventh to hear the law. The sixth day is for working according to the law, while the seventh is for resting. This is our rest after our good work, most beloved and acceptable to the Lord: that, abstaining from servile work—that is, from sin—we devote ourselves more diligently to hearing and fulfilling his commands.

Hence, at the beginning of that seventh month, the solemnity of trumpets had been established, by whose sound the people, amid prayers and sacrifices, might be stirred more fervently to remember the divine law. Now also, in spiritual understanding, after the holy city has been built, divine reading must follow and the trumpets must sound more frequently. For it is necessary that the people initiated into heavenly sacraments also be instructed, through sacred words at the proper time, in how they ought to live.

When it says that the people gathered at the square before the Water Gate, I think the Water Gate means the gate in the priests’ court. The temple was surrounded on every side by this court in a square, especially on the eastern side of the temple, where the bronze sea stood for washing the hands and feet of those entering the temple, and where there were ten bronze basins for washing the sacrifices. The altar of burnt offering was also there; between it and the temple, Zechariah son of Barachiah was stoned (Matthew 23).

The people were not permitted to enter within this gate of the court; only the priests, the ministers of the Lord, had that privilege. The people customarily stood outside this gate, especially in the square on its eastern side, to hear the word or to pray. The people were therefore rightly gathered before the Water Gate, since through their high priest they were spiritually to be watered by the streams of Scripture.

Ezra the scribe stood upon a wooden platform, etc. Scripture appears to recall this passage in Chronicles, where it says: “Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, opposite the assembly of Israel, and stretched out his hands.” For Solomon had made a bronze platform and placed it in the middle of the basilica. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and he stood upon it (2 Chronicles 6).

“In the middle of the basilica” means in the middle of the priests’ court, by which the larger basilica was surrounded on every side within the outer courts of the temple. Concerning these, it was written above in the same book: “He also made the priests’ court and the great basilica” (2 Chronicles 4).

Solomon, as a king, made a bronze platform; Ezra, being of lesser power, constructed a wooden platform for speaking. Likewise, Solomon and Moses made the altar of burnt offering from bronze, whereas the children of the transmigration replaced it with stone.

But one should not think that the wooden platform possesses a sacrament of lesser perfection than the bronze platform. As has often been said, bronze suitably pertains to the divine sacraments because of its endurance through the ages or the sweetness of its sound—sacraments that do not fail through any length of time, and whose sound has gone out into all the earth. In the same way, wood is also most appropriately suited to them because of the trophy of the Lord’s passion.

The high priest therefore rises above the whole people when the person who receives the teacher’s platform surpasses the common people by the merit of a more perfect life and conduct. He stands upon the wooden platform that he had made for speaking when, through singular imitation of the Lord’s passion, he makes himself higher than the others. Hence he rightly possessed the confidence to preach the word of God freely.

For whoever scorns to imitate the Lord’s passion according to his own measure has not yet ascended the wooden platform by which he might rise above the weak. Therefore such a timid scribe must preach God’s commands with trembling, fearing or feeling ashamed to propose to others what he himself has not done. Hence the text appropriately adds what follows:

“The people, however, stood at their stations.” When rulers strive to surpass their subjects in good works as much as they excel them in honor, then those same subjects, stirred by their good examples, devoutly follow the course of their own lives. Warned by their pious exhortations, they also take delight in shedding frequent tears for their transgressions, or even from longing for the heavenly homeland.

Hence it is also appropriately added here:

“All the people were weeping when they heard the words of the law.” But since those same holy teachers, who stir the minds of their hearers to tears both through sacred readings and through their own devout exhortations, also console those tears by promising that everlasting joys will follow them, the text rightly continues:

And he said to them: “Go, eat rich foods,” etc. For the day of the Lord is holy for us when we devote ourselves to hearing and fulfilling his words. On that day, although we suffer outward afflictions, we ought to rejoice in hope, according to the Apostle’s words: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (II Cor. VI). On that day we are also commanded to eat rich foods and drink sweet wine—that is, to rejoice in the abundance of good works bestowed upon us by God, and in the sweetness itself of hearing the word of God. Sweet wine is wine sweetened with honey; hence in Greek it is called *oinomeli* (οἰνόμελι, “honey-wine”). But we are also commanded to send portions of these most health-giving feasts of our mind to one who has not prepared anything for himself: that is, we must take care to strengthen the weaker consciences of our neighbors either by the example of pious action or by the sweetness of devoted admonition, so that their souls too, according to the Psalmist, may be filled with the abundance of heavenly generosity “as with marrow and fatness,” and that “with joyful lips” they may praise the name of the Lord (Ps. LXII). We ought also to imitate this passage literally: whenever, on feast days, after prayer, reading, and the completion of our study of the psalms, we plan to refresh the body, we should remember to give a portion also to the poor and to strangers.

## CHAPTER XXVII. They celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles, while Ezra reads the law of God to them each day.

“And they found written in the law that the Lord had commanded,” etc. These matters are written more fully in Leviticus, including the fact that they were commanded to be done in memory of that very long journey during which, after bringing his people out of Egypt, the Lord caused them to dwell in tents for forty years in the wilderness, daily declaring to them through Moses the precepts of his law (Lev. XXIII). The erection of tabernacles—called in Greek *Scenopegia* (σκηνοπηγία, “the setting up of tents”)—was commanded every year for seven days, namely, from the fifteenth day of the seventh month to the twenty-second. The sacramental meaning of this observance rightly deserves to be examined through spiritual inquiry, especially since the Lord deigned to be present at this same feast in the Gospel (John VII), and, addressing the people who had gathered, consecrated it with his sacred words.

Our fathers, therefore, were freed from Egyptian servitude through the blood of the Lamb and led through the wilderness for forty years, so that they might come to the promised land. This took place when, through the Lord’s Passion, the world was freed from slavery to the devil, and through the apostles the primitive Church was gathered, being led, as it were, through the wilderness for forty years until it came to the homeland promised in heaven. In imitation of the forty-day fast, which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself completed, it was accustomed to live a life of great self-restraint, always thirsting for the eternal homeland; completely separated from the enticements of this world, it conducted its life as though in seclusion, through daily meditation on the divine law.

In memory of this, we too must remain in tabernacles at the same time, leaving our dwellings—that is, abandoning worldly pleasures, confessing that we are strangers in this life and that our homeland is in heaven, and desiring to reach it more quickly. This takes place on the solemn day of the seventh month, that is, in the light of heavenly joy, when the grace of the Holy Spirit, commended by the prophet as sevenfold, fills our heart. We are commanded to remain in these tabernacles for seven days because, throughout the whole period of this life, which we pass through over so many days, we must retain in our minds that we are “inhabitants with God on earth, and strangers, as all our fathers were” [sentence incomplete in the supplied text].

“Go up,” he says, “into the mountain,” etc. Let us too go out from a certain dwelling-place of general thoughts and ascend into the heights of sacred Scripture, to meditate on it more frequently. From there let us bring ourselves, as it were, olive branches—the fruits of mercy—with which, by refreshing the poor, we may at the same time shade ourselves from the heat of vices that tempt us. Let us also bring branches of the most beautiful tree, which the Jews call cedar: namely, the fruits of charity, which is the most beautiful and outstanding among all the virtues, and through which our Lord also climbed the wood of the cross for our salvation. As we imitate his Passion, insofar as possible, we are indeed protected by the branches of the most beautiful tree.

Let us also bring branches of myrtle, in the mortification of lust and every vice. For the Magi too, when they offered myrrh to the Lord, taught symbolically in their gift that those who belong to Jesus Christ ought to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires. Whoever can say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God, in every place” (II Cor. II), also brings branches of myrtle to make himself a shelter.

Let us also bring palm branches, which are the adornment of a victorious hand, so that we may always carry a mind victorious over gluttony, anger, greed, and the remaining vices, and may always strive to prove stronger than all our enemies, so that we may deserve in the future to be companions of those concerning whom John says in the Apocalypse: “They stood before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms were in their hands” (Apoc. VII).

Let us bring also branches of a leafy tree—that is, the adornments of the remaining virtues. From all these we make mystical tabernacles for ourselves when, delighting in good works, we withdraw our whole mind from worldly enticements.

“And the people went out, and they brought,” etc. He says “on the roof,” that is, on the roof of the houses. For in Palestine houses do not have pitched roofs; rather, the upper surfaces of all the houses are level, with beams and planks laid across them. Hence the law commands that whoever builds a new house should make a parapet around the roof, lest someone fall from it and incur the danger of death (Deut. XXII).

Thus each one of us, having gone out, makes tabernacles on the roof—that is, on the roof of his house—when, transcending in mind the dwelling-place of his flesh, he tramples its harmful desires through diligent meditation on heavenly light and freedom. We do the same in our courtyards when, with our mind burning toward heavenly things, we stand, as it were, outside the world, whose dwelling we desire to leave more quickly.

We also make them in the courtyards of the house of God when, although we are not yet permitted to enter the hall of our heavenly dwelling, we place the whole memory and seat of our thoughts in its vicinity. We make them in the square of the Water Gate when, with our heart enlarged in the way of God’s commandments, our soul longs for the living God as a servant longs for fountains of water (Ps. XLI). We make them in the square of the Gate of Ephraim—that is, of the fruitful or growing gate—when, in the same breadth of a free heart, we make such progress that, with the gate of righteousness opened to us by the Lord, we may continually grow in him unto salvation and deserve to abound each day in greater fruits of good action.

“And he read in the book of the law of God,” etc. As far as the literal sense is clear, the Feast of Tabernacles itself used to be celebrated for seven days, namely, from the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the moon is full, to the twenty-first. Then, on the eighth day—that is, the twenty-second day of the month—the people gathered again for a distinguished celebration of greater solemnity. For it is written in Leviticus: “From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered all the fruits of your land, you shall celebrate the festival of the Lord for seven days. On the first day and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath,” that is, a rest. “And on the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruits of a most beautiful tree,” etc. (Lev. XXIII).

Ezra therefore read to the people from the book of the law of God for seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles, because this is truly the solemnity of our mind in this life: that each day—that is, in all good works by which we are enlightened by the Lord—we devote ourselves with attentive heart to reading, hearing, and doing his words.

This solemnity begins on the fifteenth day of the month, when the moon is fullest at night, when all the darkness of our mind is dispelled by the clearest light of Christ. The eighth day of rest follows it—that is, at the time of the resurrection in the future life. In the meantime we are lifted by hope toward its joys; then we shall enjoy them in reality, when that most desired gathering—the entire assembly of the saints, angels and human beings alike—has been gathered in the presence of its Creator and rejoices, never again to be separated.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. After completing the Feast of Tabernacles, they assemble again to confess, read, and pray to the Lord.

“Then the sons of Israel assembled in fasting and sackcloth,” etc. We should note the devotion of the people corrected after the captivity: when they had duly completed the solemnity commanded by the law of the Lord, after only one intervening day they immediately assembled of their own accord in fasting and penitence. What they had heard was to be done during the days of sacred readings and rejoicing, they now diligently performed without delay, separating themselves in mind and body from the company of those proved to be strangers to the Lord and to his worship, lest through association and the examples of the reprobate they should again fall into the evils of captivity and distress, from which they saw that they had scarcely escaped after the long passage of times, or even centuries.

And what should we understand mystically from these things, except that, following such examples, we should again discuss among ourselves by mutual conference whatever we have learned must be done in the public assembly or lecture hall, and diligently inquire how we may complete each of these things through the correction of our heart and body? Their greatest diligence in a reformed life is especially demonstrated when it is added:

“And they rose to stand, and they read,” etc. Who would not marvel that the people possessed such exceptional care for piety, that four times each day—early in the morning, at the third hour, the sixth, and the ninth, the times when they were to devote themselves to prayer or psalmody—they gave themselves to hearing the divine law, so that, with their mind renewed toward God, they might return purer and more devoted to imploring his mercy? Moreover, four times during the night, shaking off the sluggishness of sleep, they rose to confess their sins and ask forgiveness.

I think that from this example the custom arose in the Church that at each hour of the daily psalmody one reading from either the Old or the New Testament should be delivered by heart to all who were listening; and thus, strengthened by apostolic or prophetic words, they should bend their knees for earnest prayer. During the night hours too, when work has ceased, their ears are freely given over to hearing the divine readings.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Ezra’s prayer or confession, in which he asks the Lord to remember the covenant he made with their fathers.

“And Ezra said: You alone, Lord,” etc. What was said above—“For they confessed their sins and the sins of their fathers”—is shown more fully in the account of Ezra’s prayer, which explains how this was done. At the conclusion he says: “Therefore, because of all these things, we ourselves make a covenant and write it; and our princes, our Levites, and our priests seal it,” and so forth. It is shown more clearly how great was the grace of devotion with which all their persons made a new assembly after the Feast of Tabernacles, in order that, having cleansed themselves with complete intention from the contagion of crimes, they might join themselves to the divine covenant, confirming the condition of the holy covenant both by speech and in writing. Thus, separated from the company of the ungodly, they might carry out more securely the work they had begun long before: namely, establishing suitable citizens of the newly built city from among the pious.

## CHAPTER XXX. The princes, together with the people, make a covenant and write that they will observe all the Lord’s commandments and assist in the rites of his house.

(II Esdr. X.) “The signatories were Nehemiah the Athersatha,” etc. Another translation has: “Nehemiah, who was Athersatha.” For this same Nehemiah had two names. Hence it is added separately: “son of Hachelai.” The same point is indicated more clearly above, where it says: “Now Nehemiah, who is Athersatha, and Ezra the scribe, and the Levites interpreting for all the people, said: This day is sanctified to the Lord our God” (Neh. VIII).

“The peoples of the land, who bring merchandise,” etc. For us too a spiritual sabbath must always be observed: we must always cease from servile work—that is, from sin—always rest and see that the Lord himself is God, so that, after such a sabbath, freed from the sins of conscience, we may reach the sabbath of future glory in heaven.

But the peoples of the land seek to profane our sabbath by bringing all kinds of merchandise to us on the sanctified day. For unclean spirits strive to stain the purity of our heart and, having received the price of our consent, thrust the enticements of vices upon us, so that they may defile the day of the greatest sanctification—that is, obscure the light of our pious thought or action by introducing errors. We must wholly avoid such commerce, shut within the walls of our city, that is, within the guardianship of a more perfect life.

“And we shall establish commandments over ourselves,” etc. Everything contained in this chapter concerns the care of the house of the Lord and of its ministers and ministries. It presents an excellent order of religious conduct, which we too must now imitate spiritually: first, the sons of the transmigration chastised themselves from the defilements of the nations; then they were sanctified through the observance of the sabbath, which held a foremost place among the commandments of the law; and thereafter they turned all their care toward carrying out the service of divine worship.

First we must be cleansed from evils, and only then adorned with good works. It would take a sufficiently long treatment to discuss allegorically, in their proper order, how all these things ought spiritually to be performed by us for the worship of the Lord; and this is better done in the actual book of the law.

## XXXI. Princes from the sons of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi dwell in Jerusalem, together with a tenth of the remaining people.

(II Esdr. XI.) “The princes of the people dwelt in Jerusalem,” etc. The arrangement begun as soon as the city was built has now been completed. Yet it could not be brought to an end until the number of the people had been recorded and the solemnities of the seventh month had been completed, determining who should dwell in the holy city itself and who in the other cities.

The fact that the princes of the people are reported to have dwelt in Jerusalem accords with the figures of the sacraments. The leaders of the holy Church ought, to the degree that they surpass the people in the height of their power, to surpass them equally in the merits of their life. The other cities of Israel signify the devout manner of life of God’s people. The dwelling in Jerusalem, moreover, specially represents the conduct of those who, having overcome the contest with vices, draw near with a free mind to the vision of heavenly peace, according to the Psalmist’s words: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. XXXVI).

Consequently, a tenth of the people was chosen by lot to receive a dwelling in Jerusalem, while the remaining nine tenths stayed in their own cities. For it belongs to the perfect—namely, to those who keep the commandments of the Decalogue completely in love of God and neighbor—to draw near in mind to heavenly mysteries and, so to speak, to imitate the peace of supreme blessedness amid the storms of passing life.

Nevertheless, the door of entry into eternal life is also open to those who keep God’s general commandments, as the Lord declares in the Gospel to the rich man who questions him. Such people dwell, as it were, in cities entrusted to them by the Lord, because they diligently watch over themselves, fortifying themselves against the snares of the ancient enemy through the guardianship of the divine law.

But those who, wishing to be perfect, sell all they possess and distribute it in alms to the poor, and thus follow the Lord—these dwell, as it were, in the fortress of Jerusalem, close to the temple of God and the ark of the covenant, because they draw nearer to the grace of their Creator on a higher level. It is rightly said that their dwelling in the holy city came to them not through human choice but through the outcome of the lot, just as the possession of the other cities was assigned by lot to the children of Israel in the days of Joshua. For small and great goods alike are received by the small and the great not through their own freedom or ingenuity of choice, but through the gift of the hidden Judge and Giver.

“And the people blessed the men,” etc. We too ought to make the lofty life of the elect, which we cannot follow by imitation, our own through rejoicing and reverence.

It should be noted, in accordance with the faith of sacred History, that those said to have dwelt in Jerusalem were from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, together with the Levites. The text clearly continues:

“Each one dwelt in his own possession,” etc. These words plainly teach that all Israel—that is, the ten tribes—dwelt in their own cities, in which the priests and Levites also held the portion assigned to them by the law. From the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, those whom the lot chose dwelt in Jerusalem, together with members of the priestly and Levitical tribe.

The tribe of Benjamin had dwelt there from ancient times, because that city had fallen to it by lot. The tribe of Judah entered there in the days of David, when he made it the capital of the entire Israelite kingdom. The tribe of Levi was added to them once the ark of the covenant had been brought there and the altar and temple of God had been built.

Examine the following passages of this book and you will find that it counts only these three tribes among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and also carefully adds the total number of them all. After completing this catalogue, Scripture took care to add in which cities the remaining members of those same tribes had dwelt. For it continues:

“Of the sons of Judah they dwelt in Kiriath-arba,” etc. Beersheba was the boundary of Judah on the southern side, while the valley of the sons of Hinnom lay to the north, near Jerusalem on the east. The cities of the sons of Benjamin are then listed in a similar order.

When these have been enumerated, the text adds:

“And portions for the Levites of Judah and Benjamin.” This signifies that in the possession of the sons of Judah and Benjamin the Levites received their lot according to the decree of the law.

These points may suffice concerning the history. If anyone takes pleasure in hearing an allegorical meaning applicable to our actions, Judah is interpreted as “confessing,” Benjamin as “son of the right hand,” and Levi as “taken up.” The tribes of all these dwell partly in Jerusalem and partly in the dependent cities given to them by God, because the progress of the faithful is many and varied, and for this reason there are also many dwellings in the house of the Father in heaven, as we have shown above.

Some are content to observe God’s general commandments: not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to give false testimony against their neighbor, to honor father and mother, and to love their neighbors as themselves. Others strive to seize the narrower way of a perfect life. Yet all of them, each according to his vocation, praises and confesses the grace of his Creator, and they are sons of the everlasting kingdom, which is at his right hand. They are taken up by him into life when the decisive moment arrives, at which “two will be in the field; one will be taken; two will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken, and one will be left” (Matt. XXIV).

(II Esdr. XII.) “These are the priests and the Levites,” etc. Here the chief priests are described together with their brothers, that is, the lesser priests, and with the Levites—those who ascended from the Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak. After these have been explained, those who from that time succeeded one another in the chief priesthood up to the beginning of the Macedonian kingdom are also added. The text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXII. The lineage of Jeshua the high priest, and those who in those times were the chiefs of the priests and Levites, is set forth.

“Jeshua begot Joiakim,” etc. Finally, Josephus writes that Jaddua, who is placed last in this list, was high priest in the time of Alexander the Great and, when he met him with his brothers, was received by him humbly and honorably (Antiq. II, 8). Josephus calls him Jaddus and says that he was the father of Onias the high priest, of whom the Book of Maccabees speaks. This does not mean that Nehemiah, the author of this book, could have remained alive in the flesh until those times, but that he knew Jaddua in his infancy; Jaddua could nevertheless have reached the priesthood long after Nehemiah’s death.

At the end of this little book there is also mention of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib, one of whom was the son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite, although the name of this son-in-law is not given. But since Joiada was the grandfather of Jaddua, it is clear that the son-in-law in question was either Jaddua’s actual father or his paternal uncle. Thus he could have been born while Nehemiah was still alive.

“In the days of Joiakim there were priests,” etc. After the succession of the chief priests has been described, there is also added a catalogue of the lesser priests and Levites who lived in their times, so that we may know that, once a large number of citizens had been gathered in Jerusalem, there was also an exceptional and noble company of priests and Levites sufficient for the ministries of the temple and altar, for confessing and praising God, for guarding that temple and city, and for educating the people.

Nor did it happen without a deeper sacramental meaning that, once Jerusalem had been rebuilt, the city deserved to have such a multitude of citizens in every rank and order, as it is read never to have lost while the enemy was pressing upon and destroying it. Thus the holy Church often received greater growth from its losses: when one person through carelessness falls into sin, many, frightened by his example, become more cautious about persevering in the purity of faith.

Often those same people who sinned begin, after performing penance, to bear greater fruits of good works than they had been accustomed to bear before they fell into sin. Often, after the Church has been devastated by heretics, once it has received the light of truth through the diligence of Catholic teachers, it brings forth more sons of that same truth by recovering the means of knowing and defending it.

Indeed, the blessed Fathers Athanasius, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, and others like them would never have composed so many magnificent treatises on sacred Scripture if such a manifold error of heretics had not arisen against the true faith. But while the heretics attempted to support their falsehood with testimonies from Scripture, they were compelled, in opposition, to refute them by the authority of those same Scriptures and to explain how their statements should rightly be understood.

When we read their writings today, we receive them as more vigilant guardians at the gates and vestibules of the holy city and temple, and as more numerous ministers for the service of the altar and the Lord’s sacrifices, because through their sermons we are instructed in the guarding of the faith and of good action, so as to serve the divine majesty more earnestly.

This may also be understood mystically of the persecution of the Gentiles, by which the holy Church was very often shaken. On account of the martyrs, it seemed destined to be utterly destroyed, but while they were crowned in secret, it was built more strongly. After their deaths, as their miracles became renowned, a greater people flocked to confess the faith, until the very summit of worldly imperial power consented to submit its neck to the most gentle yoke of Christ. Thus the state of the holy city—that is, the Church of Christ—which had long been attacked by unbelieving kings, was again strengthened and extended through the zeal of believing kings and rulers of the world.

In the same way, the kings of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as “fierce,” or as “demons,” overthrew the city of Jerusalem; but the kings of the Persians, who are said to be interpreted as “tested,” restored it through friendly providence and exalted it with due honor.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The city of Jerusalem is dedicated with solemn joy, and the guardians over the treasury chambers for the offerings of the holy things are listed.

“At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem,” etc. The city had been built some time before, but it was not fitting for it to be dedicated until inhabitants had been gathered, suitable ministers for the temple appointed, and guardians assigned to the gates and vestibules.

The holy city is dedicated when, at the end of the age, the number of the elect has been completed and the universal Church is brought into heaven to behold its Creator. Whenever in this life we are lifted up by desires for that life, we rejoice as though at the dedication of the figure of our city. Thus this same dedication can be understood in two ways: for the present, in the hope of those who desire and purify the eyes of their heart so that they may be able to see God; and then in reality, when blessed human beings, possessing spiritual bodies amid the ranks of angelic spirits, enjoy the divine vision.

“They sought the Levites from all their places,” etc. Spiritual Levites too—that is, those taken into the lot of the kingdom from all their places—are sought when the Son of Man sends his angels and gathers his elect from the four winds, from the extremity of earth to the extremity of heaven.

They make the dedication with joy, song, and thanksgiving, and with various musical instruments, when, upon receiving eternal life, they rejoice together, giving thanks to him by whose gift they have deserved to enter that city. The cymbals, psalteries, and citharas may then be understood as the bodies of the saints, already immortal, in which they will return the sweetest sounds of their praise to the Lord.

In the present life, however, the Levites are gathered in Jerusalem when the faithful, inflamed by the memory of heavenly peace, place all the delight of their mind in it, and rejoice in the eternal inheritance in heaven that they hope to receive. If they cannot yet behold it, they rejoice at least by desiring it, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and confess the memory of his holiness” (Ps. XCVI).

They make the dedication in song and thanksgiving when, with a mind rejoicing in the Lord, they receive whatever adversity or prosperity arises in the world. They make it also with cymbals, psalteries, and citharas when they cause the pleasing sounds of good works to ascend to the ears of their Creator, and when through these works they kindle the hearts of their neighbors to love that same Creator and Savior.

“Then the sons of the singers were gathered,” etc. The sons of the singers are imitators of those who served the Lord with devout and cheerful minds, or who strove to make his word resound by preaching it to others. They make villages for themselves around Jerusalem when they dwell with lofty hearts near the heavenly homeland, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

They make these same villages in the plains around Jerusalem when, the more sweetly they touch the glory of his sublimity by tasting it, the more they humble themselves with a heart expanded toward God. All of these are now gathered toward the heavenly homeland through progress in good works, and at the time of the dedication—that is, of perpetual reward—they are found together there.

“And the priests and Levites were purified,” etc. The order is entirely just: those teachers and leaders who desire to purify the people must first purify themselves. First they must chastise their own body and subject it to servitude, lest, while preaching to others, they themselves be found reprobate (I Cor. IX).

The priests and Levites were purified by prayers and offerings of victims, and also by abstaining from wives; through preaching that same continence, they purified the people. They also purified the gates and wall with trumpets and psalm-singing, going around them with the people accompanying them. Together with the people, they purified the people, the gates, and the wall, completing the circuit and offering great victims for the condition of the citizens and of the city alike.

Even now, those who preside over the peoples under sacred leadership and have been taken by the Lord into spiritual ministry strive all the more earnestly to cleanse and sanctify both themselves and those entrusted to them, the more deeply they retain the memory of our dedication, which will take place in the future resurrection. They do this lest anyone, found in a filthy condition of mind, should be cast out from the common joy of the holy solemnity and, with hands and feet bound, be sent into the outer darkness.

“And I brought up the princes of Judah upon the wall,” etc. The princes of Judah—that is, of confession or praise—are the more advanced teachers of the holy Church, who ascend upon the wall at the dedication of the city, because when the time of retribution appears, they will be proved to have surpassed the general manner of life of the holy Church by the height of their own life.

They are those to whom the Lord promises through the prophet concerning the same Church: “I have appointed watchmen upon your walls” (Isa. XXVI). It is therefore right that those who now serve as the wall of the holy Church and have been placed over it as watchmen should then also surpass others in the glory of their reward.

Two great choirs of those who praise are stationed there, because from both peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—those who praise God together in the heavenly homeland come forth. This is also recognized by the knowledgeable person as occurring daily in the present life.

These choirs go to the right upon the wall because, by living rightly, the just hasten toward eternal life in the present and reach it in the future. They go to the Dung Gate: in the present, so that by living more correctly and correcting those who err they may purge the filth of sins from the Church; in the future, so that by judicial authority they may expel from the city of the Lord—that is, from entry into the heavenly homeland—those who refused to be corrected.

Or certainly, the choirs of those who praise go to the right upon the wall as far as the Dung Gate when they proclaim as worthy of praise those who took care to eliminate every impurity from the Church by preaching, reproving, excommunicating, and anathematizing.

“And of the sons of the priests with trumpets, Zechariah,” etc. In the present life the sons of the priests blow trumpets at the dedication of the city of God, because by preaching they kindle the hearts of their hearers in remembrance of the heavenly homeland. They do this with the instruments of the song of David, the man of God, when they rely neither on their own understanding nor on their desires, but follow in every respect the life of the fathers and prophets and devote themselves to doctrine and the word of preaching.

Ezra, the scribe of the law of God, precedes them to the Fountain Gate when, in everything they do, they keep the words of sacred Scripture before their eyes; through those words, which lead them, they may arrive at the entrance to eternal life. Concerning this the Psalmist says to the Lord: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV).

“And opposite them they went up by the steps of the city of David,” etc. Earlier, when the city was being built, it was said that those who built the Fountain Gate brought the measure of their work as far as the steps descending from the city of David (Neh. III). There, while the city was being built, the descent of the steps was mentioned; here, when the city is dedicated, an ascent is named.

There, labor and conflict were being carried on against the enemy; here, after the enemy has been conquered, joy is celebrated, because all the saints who in the present are humbled beneath the powerful hand of God will in the future be exalted by him. Those who now build the walls of the Church on earth from living stones—that is, from holy souls—in affliction and danger and through many vigils will then, once that building has been completed and raised into the kingdom of heaven, ascend joyfully to contemplate its glory.

The house of David—that is, of the strong and desirable hand—comprises all the righteous, whom the grace of their Creator fills and in whom he is accustomed to dwell. The sons of the priests ascend upon the house of David when holy preachers or martyrs, just as they now surpass the general life of the righteous either through the ministry of the word or through the contest of martyrdom, so then surpass its general rewards by gifts of a higher recompense.

The parable of the faithful servants aptly applies to them. To one who said, “Lord, your mina has acquired ten minas,” the same Lord replied: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.” To another who said, “Lord, your mina has made five minas,” he said: “And you, be over five cities” (Luke XIX).

For however many people someone now instructs unto life by word or example, so many will then make him more glorious in the reception of life and honor him with a greater reward.

The priests also reach the Water Gate toward the east when those who in this life desired to appear before the face of God as the deer longs for fountains of water attain the object of that desire and deserve to see, without setting, the rising of the Sun of righteousness.

The statement, “And opposite them they went up,” does not signify opposition in distance, but an encounter in harmony: the elect kindle one another to love their Author once in this life, and in that life praise him more perfectly, rejoicing together in one another’s blessedness, always without weariness, after the example of the seraphim who, as the prophet testifies, crying out to one another, celebrate the holy Trinity together in shared exultation (Isa. VI).

And the second choir of those giving thanks went from the opposite side, etc. It would be tedious to discuss each gate or tower individually. It is enough to say that those who completed the gates, towers, and wall of the city amid great labor, distress, hunger, cold, daily vigils and also nightly ones, while the tireless enemy resisted and lay in ambush, then, after the enemy had been repulsed and confounded, walk through the gates, towers, and buildings of that same city and, with songs and hymns, psalteries, cymbals, lyres, trumpets, and thanksgiving, rejoice together with those who were the authors of the work and teachers of God’s law.

There is no doubt that the same order is also observed in the spiritual building. When the time of the final recompense arrives, as though at the long-desired dedication of the city of God, eternal faith receives the rewards due for its works. Then, like Nehemiah and Ezra and the other priests and Levites, each bringing forth his own workers, all the teachers of the faithful peoples introduce those whom each has acquired for the Lord as hearers to the walls of the heavenly homeland. Then, among the other walls of the holy city, Nehemiah also proceeds over the Tower of the Furnaces, in whose earlier construction he had labored, while the teachers of truth rejoice over the exalted rewards of those whom they taught.

For if the furnace-baked loaves, which are baked in concealment, signify the inner devotion of the faithful mind, strengthened by the fire of love—and therefore such loaves were commanded by the Law to be offered in the sacrifice of the Lord (Lev. II)—then they are more suitably represented by the furnaces in which those loaves are baked than by the hearts themselves, which are always accustomed to burn with the flame of inward love and to bring forth deeds or words of virtue. Of these the prophet beautifully says: “Your Lord is a fire in Zion, and his furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI). And Luke himself says of himself: “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

By contrast, the hearts of the reprobate also burn, but with the fire of their crimes. Hence another prophet says of them: “They are all adulterers; their hearts are like a furnace” (Hos. VII). Therefore the builders of the holy city build, among its other structures, the Tower of the Furnaces when teachers form the hearts of their hearers in faith and in the practice of truth, so that they may be made worthy to receive greater gifts of the Spirit and to bring forth each day new banquets of virtue for the joy of God’s people.

They proceed rejoicing and singing praise to the Lord over the Tower of the Furnaces on the day of the dedication of Jerusalem when, at the time of the future recompense, they rejoice with eternal blessedness over the glory of those whom they instructed through the disciplines of life. The furnaces, therefore, are the hearts of the elect, in which love is poured out through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them. The Tower of the Furnaces is the exaltation and protection of good works. These same hearts must always be fortified with vigilant caution and solicitude, so that they cannot be harmed by evil spirits and so that the flame of virtue cannot be inflated or disturbed by the wind of self-exaltation.

And two choirs of those giving praise stood in the house of God, etc. Having gone before along the walls and gardens of the city with songs of joy and musical instruments, they return to the temple of the Lord, so that there too, standing, they may offer praise to the Lord with harmonious trumpets; there, by offering victims, they may fulfill the vows of the dedication.

The one and the same homeland of the future life is mystically the house of the Lord, which is also signified by the city of the Lord. So too, in the Scriptures, the present Church is customarily called both the house of Christ and the city. The difference, however, is that they are said to have ascended the buildings of the city while praising with songs of thanksgiving and instruments, whereas in the house of God they are said to have stood in praise and sung aloud.

The elect ascend the walls of the city which they themselves built when they enter the joys of the heavenly homeland, which they themselves made theirs through the diligence of good works. They behold the diversity of the gates, the towers, and the height of the buildings when, entering the house of the Father, they contemplate the differences among the many dwelling places there, according to the various merits of human beings. They stand in the house of God and sing more clearly when, each received into his own dwelling place, they continue in stable habitation in the perpetual vision of their Creator and celebrate his praises forever with undivided voice.

Where there are two choirs giving praise, this may mean either those from each of the two peoples, as we interpreted above, joined and united in one harmony of divine praise; or those formed from angels and human beings, when the Lord’s promise is fulfilled that human beings will be equal to the angels of God (Mark XII).

But even in this life the righteous ascend into the city of the Lord with hymns of dedication when, yearning with their whole heart in remembrance of the future reward, they advance more and more each day in good works, according to the Psalmist’s words: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. LXXXIII). And again: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). For he calls those who walk in the law of the Lord undefiled in the way because they hold to such innocence of heart and conduct that they strive to increase still further toward higher attainments of virtue.

They stand in the house of the Lord with praises because they persevere indefatigably in the progress of good works, according to the saying of blessed Elijah: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (III Kings XVII), that is, “in whose will I remain with an unwearied mind, so that it may be fulfilled.” The text fittingly continues:

And they offered great sacrifices on that day, etc. On that day of perpetual light—of which Zechariah said, “There shall be one day, which is known to the Lord, neither day nor night,” that is, removed from the customary succession of passing times—the elect offer great sacrifices to the Lord, namely those sacrifices which the Psalmist, tasting them in hope of future things, said: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV).

He also aptly showed where he hoped to offer this sacrifice when he immediately added: “I will pay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem.” In the midst of Jerusalem we pay our vows to God in the sight of all his people when, in the heavenly homeland, with the whole multitude of the saints gathered together, we offer him the praises for which we now groan and which we thirst to offer through our daily desire of thanksgiving.

For God had made them rejoice with great joy, etc. These words truly pertain to the building of that holy city which is in the future, in which God is the king who makes his citizens rejoice by his presence, with great joy indeed. Hence, when that King was born in the flesh, an angel appearing to the shepherds said: “For behold, I bring you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke II). This is clearly distinguished from human joy, which is both small and transitory and therefore should be regarded as nothing by the wise.

It is fitting that, in the joy which God grants to his city, the wives of the citizens, and likewise their children, are also said to have rejoiced. For at the time of the resurrection, not only those who built up the Church either by proclaiming the word or by persevering courageously in works of faith receive the great fruit of their great labor; every one of the weaker members who share the same faith also rejoices with them in the one and the same reception of eternal life. For the Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small together with the great (Ps. CXIII).

This dedication may also be understood figuratively, appropriately, in certain elect persons even in the present life. After the eye of the heart has been purified, they are sometimes permitted to contemplate in part the joys which the Church will altogether receive in the future: Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the other prophets; the apostles (Matt. XVII), who rejoiced to see the Lord glorified on the holy mountain; Paul (II Cor. XII), who was granted to be caught up into paradise and into the third heaven; and John in his Apocalypse, who saw that the higher they entered the lofty places of the heavenly city, the more clearly they took care to sing the praises of the Lord and always offer him the greatest sacrifices of good works.

They also appointed men over the treasury chambers of the treasure on that day, etc. While everyone rejoiced over the building and dedication of the city, every effort was made to ensure that the worship of religion within it—which had been established through ceremonies, and especially through the teaching and duties of the priests, Levites, singers, and doorkeepers—would be preserved and increased.

Therefore able men were appointed to collect carefully into the treasury of the temple the money contributed by the people and to guard it, for the use of those same ministers of the temple and altar. They were also to preserve with diligent care the first fruits of the crops, tithes, wine, and drink offerings that were brought to the temple, so that, with an abundance of what was to be offered to the Lord or from which the Lord’s ministers could live, the multitude of those ministers might more willingly consent to make their dwelling in Jerusalem, since a flowing crowd of people was to be taught and sanctified by them.

Because Judah rejoiced in the priests and Levites standing there, etc. This was the reason why the people loved having the priests, Levites, and other holy ministers dwell in Jerusalem: they rejoiced in their good works, through whose devoted diligence the people themselves were corrected from their errors, the city was built up, and it was dedicated with great praise and joy.

The allegorical exposition of this chapter is readily available to us, since the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (I Cor. IX). But woe to those priests and ministers of holy things who gladly receive from the people the expenses owed to them, yet make no effort for the salvation of that same people: who do not provide them with sound sacred guidance by living rightly, do not sing anything sweet to them by preaching something of the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven, and do not open for them the gate of the heavenly city by possessing citizenship in heaven, but rather are proved to shut it by acting perversely. Since the people place no confidence in their works and cannot praise the Lord because of them, they are compelled to suffer even greater distress.

It should certainly be noted that the Judah who earlier, while the city was being built, spoke almost in despair—“The strength of the bearers has failed, the rubble is abundant, and we cannot build the wall” (Neh. IV), and the rest of that passage—had now recovered strength of mind and body to carry away the rubble that impeded the rebuilding of the fallen wall and to overcome the ambushes of the enemies that threatened them.

Therefore he rightly rejoiced in the priests, Levites, singers, and doorkeepers, through whose labor and exhortation he escaped such great danger and affliction and found such great glory in his restored prosperity. So too, if you perceive that the rubble of vices weighs down your heart, so that you cannot build within it a city worthy of divine indwelling; if you see that the evil enemy is trying to hold you back from clearing away the ruins of vices and building the walls of virtues, listen to the comfort and counsel of the priests. Be constant in hearing and observing the divine readings. Stand in such a way that, after the ambushes of demons have been driven out, God the victor may enter the dwelling-place of your heart [the source reads *praetorii tui*, apparently an OCR error for *pectoris tui*], as though to sanctify his own city and make his dwelling there.

And they sanctified the Levites, etc. The people sanctified the Levites by giving them tithes, as to the holy ones of God; and the Levites sanctified the priests by offering them a tenth portion from their own tithes, as to those who were higher in rank.

## II Esdras XIII

On that day the book of Moses was read, etc. It is clear that the Moabites and Ammonites, since they were born of incest, represent heretics. Their founders, by corrupting through faulty interpretation the teaching of the fathers by which they themselves were instructed, use it improperly, as though the daughters of Lot secretly and in darkness had used their father’s seed, and not lawfully. Therefore the offspring of such people—that is, the followers of heresies—can never have any part in the Church of the Lord. For whoever among them is corrected will no longer be the offspring of such mothers.

They met the children of Israel as they came out of Egypt with bread and water if, living rightly themselves and dwelling in Catholic peace, they brought the consolation of God’s word to those who, recently rescued from slavery to sins through the water of baptism and the waves of the sea, long for the freedom of the heavenly homeland. This is what Barzillai the Gileadite did (II Sam. XIX), who brought provisions to David and his army when they were fleeing from Absalom, so that by refreshing them and assisting them he might make them stronger against the new tyranny of the king’s son. He thus signified those who strive to strengthen the Church, scattered by heretics, with the resources of the heavenly word and to animate it for the destruction of their madness.

But when those same heretics strive to destroy the newly converted by means of their leaders, by examples they display, or by wicked words, they attack Israel coming out of Egypt—the people born of incest—with their own weapons and with the counsels of Balaam the diviner, whose name is interpreted as “vanity of the accursed people.” Yet God turned Balaam’s curse into a blessing for his people and protected them from the weapons of hostile nations, because “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. VIII).

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### All foreigners are separated from Israel, and the portions of the Levites and the priests’ first fruits are placed in the treasury of the house of the Lord

When they had heard the law, etc. After hearing the law concerning the two hostile nations that were to be anathematized, the faithful people immediately separated every foreigner from themselves. For we must attend to the hearing of truth in such a way that, whenever divine reading forbids us any single vice, we immediately cleanse from our conduct and conscience not only that particular vice mentioned in the passage, but everything sinful and defiled that we discover within ourselves.

Therefore Eliashib made for himself a great treasury, etc. This statement, in which Nehemiah writes that he had not been in Jerusalem, seems to refer not to what he had narrated above up to this point, but only to the present passage. For the earlier events and statements appear to have taken place at the time when the city was built and dedicated, while Nehemiah was still living in Jerusalem. After these matters had been vigorously completed, he returned to the king. During his absence, Eliashib made a great treasury in which the things necessary either for the service of the house of the Lord or for the use of its ministers were to be stored.

He did not hesitate to place certain unlawful things there in the treasury of the house of the Lord. When Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem, he immediately set about putting an end to this. For the text continues:

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### Nehemiah, having returned from Babylon to Jerusalem, again cleanses the treasuries of vessels belonging to foreigners and restores to them what was appropriate to the house of the Lord

And I came to Jerusalem, and I understood the evil, etc. We read above that Tobiah was an Ammonite servant and an enemy of the people of God. Thus Eliashib the priest acted very wrongly: although Tobiah was related to him, he made a treasury for him in the vestibules of the house of God, in which he could place his vessels, having removed from there the vessels of the house of God and the other things required for its service. “For what partnership has righteousness with wickedness? What fellowship has Christ with Belial? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? What communion have heretics and schismatics with the orthodox and peaceful children of God?” (II Cor. VI).

And I threw out Tobiah’s vessels from the treasury, etc. You too, whatever infidelity and uncleanness you find among the faithful, immediately throw it out, so that the vessels of the Lord may be brought into the cleansed hearts of believers—which are the treasuries of the Lord—when they have been filled with the riches of virtues. That is, let those very hearts which shortly before were vessels of error through guilt become vessels of the Lord again through correction; and there let the sacrifice of good works and the incense of pure prayer be found, where previously there was a den of thieves.

Those also throw Tobiah the Ammonite’s vessels out of the treasury of the temple and restore there the vessels of the house of God, together with sacrifice and incense, who, after excommunicated or anathematized heretics or false Catholics have been expelled from the Church, appoint Catholics—servants of Christ—in their place, so that they may serve him through faithful deeds and prayers.

This should also be compared with Nehemiah’s zeal as a type of the Lord Savior, when, finding sellers and buyers in the temple, he made a whip from cords and drove them all out (Mark XII; Luke XIX). Thus Nehemiah, in this action as in his others, appropriately bore the type of the true Consoler and Cleanser of God.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### Nehemiah diligently insists that the Sabbath rest not be violated by the commerce of foreigners

In those days I saw in Judah men treading winepresses on the Sabbath, etc. For six days the Law commands us to perform the necessary work, but on the seventh we are commanded to rest. The general mystery of this command is clear: all the elect in this age, which unfolds through six periods, must labor for eternal rest; but on the future day, as though on the seventh day, they must hope from the Lord for everlasting rest.

According to the tropological, that is, moral, sense, the elect also keep a Sabbath consecrated to the Lord in this life when, for a time separated from the cares of this world, they devote themselves to prayer and suspend their purified minds in contemplation of heavenly things. When we sincerely perform what the care of the flesh rightly demands, and not in desires contrary to the Apostle’s command, we labor as though on the six days in which necessary things are done, because we are occupied with those things that we need on account of this age.

The Sabbath observance of our prayers and devotion, in which we refrain from temporal activities so that we may taste the joys of eternity more sweetly, is rightly assigned to the seventh day, because it imitates the future rest and blessed praise of life. But foreigners seek to profane the Sabbath day when earthly thoughts improperly disturb us during the time of our prayer and, through the memory or pleasure of temporal things, strive to draw us away from inward love.
