They load asses with wine, grapes, figs, and every kind of work, and bring them into Jerusalem when they burden the foolish movements of our mind with carnal pleasures and, through these and similar temptations, attempt to violate the repose of our heart dedicated to God. But Nehemiah opposes these disturbances of wicked thoughts, lest they disturb our Sabbath, when, with strict diligence and the Lord’s help, we exclude useless and foolish fantasies from our heart during prayer.

He protests against them, telling them to sell such merchandise on the day when selling is permitted, when the soul devoted to God imposes this limit upon its thoughts, so that during prayer it abstains from the cares of passing things. Yet at other times, whenever opportunity dictates, it should not entirely withdraw its diligence from the things pertaining to food and clothing, but should distribute them with suitable moderation whenever necessity requires.

And Tyrians lived there, bringing fish, etc. Just as a good fish signifies pious faith—for one who asks the Lord for it certainly does not receive the serpent of unbelief—so an evil fish signifies a lowly thought, which is accustomed to immerse itself beyond measure in the cares of this world. The Tyrians, whose name is interpreted as “the constricted,” seek to sell this to us on the Sabbath when unclean spirits improperly attempt to overwhelm the rest of our pious way of life with the deep cares of the world.

But because of such commerce Nehemiah rebukes and chastises the nobles of Judah, when divine inspiration mercifully cleanses those who strive to serve the profession of piety from such thoughts.

And it happened that, when the gates of Jerusalem were at rest on the Sabbath day, etc. If our conscience, cleansed from vices, rejoices in God as its inhabitant, it can rightly be called Jerusalem. What are the gates of this Jerusalem except the senses of our body—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch? Through these, things done outside reach the awareness of our mind, as though entering through the gates. We are commanded to close them on the Sabbath day, so that when we seek to devote ourselves to God through psalms or prayers, everything that is being done externally may be cast far from the mind, and we may pray to and praise our Judge alone in secret, with a free mind.

And because no one suddenly becomes perfect, but must reach the perfection and peace of mind of which we speak through the long progress of holy conduct, with the help of Christ’s grace, the text rightly adds:

He also told the Levites to cleanse themselves, etc. Those who wish to guard the gates of their senses against every turbulent intrusion of thought must necessarily be cleansed through the daily exercise of good works. Whoever wishes to sanctify the Sabbath—that is, to make the leisure of prayer, psalmody, holy reading, and tears beneficial to himself—must cleanse his conscience with great diligence, so that he may bring the intention of good action to completion.

This may also rightly be understood allegorically of the teachers of the faithful. Whoever desires to guard the gates of the holy Church—that is, the faith and works of their hearers, through which alone one enters the Church—from the contagion of heretics and vices that assail them must first purify his own heart and conduct from every stain of error.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### Nehemiah cleanses the Jews from foreign wives, establishes the orders of priests and Levites, each in his own ministry, and finally commends himself to God’s memory for good

And in those days I also saw Jews taking wives from Ashdod, etc. Even now, in the holy Church, people take foreign wives whenever they stain their conscience with the pleasures of crimes, which properly belong to the Gentiles.

The sons born from these women do not know how to speak Jewish, when the works that have proceeded from a corrupted mind display nothing of a pious profession but rather sound of Gentile folly than of ecclesiastical chastity. Ashdod, which is called *Asdod* in Hebrew, is interpreted as “the word of fire.” Therefore, according to the tropological sense, the sons born of foreign wives speak the language of Ashdod when works generated through wantonness await the punishment of eternal burning.

Thus Nehemiah rightly not only rebuked and cursed the parents of such children, but also struck some of them. For those who err must be restrained more sharply by teachers of truth, so that from the word of avenging fire they may learn, through a blessed transformation, to pass to the word of divine praise.

Heretics likewise, when they devote themselves more to the studies of Gentile philosophy, dialectic, and rhetoric than to ecclesiastical simplicity, should not be surprised if their hearers speak according to the language of the people and of the people: they turn the Holy Scriptures over in their mouths, but interpret them with an erring and Gentile sense.

Therefore I cleansed them from all foreigners, etc. This is in every respect a fitting and worthy conclusion to the building of the holy city and the temple of the Lord: once the citizens have been cleansed from every stain of external pollution alien to God, the orders of priests and Levites are properly maintained in their ministry. Thus the teachers of the Church, established in royal order, may continually exhort a people disciplined from every sin to remain in the good and to grow ever further.

That people, among other things, offers wood to the Lord for feeding the fire of the altar when it performs works of virtue worthy of divine consecration. For if wood did not sometimes signify something good, the prophet would not say: “Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice before the face of the Lord” (Ps. XCV). The wood burns and is consumed on the altar of burnt offerings when works of righteousness are brought to perfection by the flame of love in the hearts of teachers.

Therefore, after many labors of devotion, such a builder and dedicator of the city rightly commends himself to the memory of his Creator and of the Giver of all good things. And you, highest Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends; you who have given me, the lowliest of your servants, both love and the help to consider the wonders of your law; you who in the treasury of the prophetic volume have graciously allowed one unworthy as I am not only to embrace the old things, but also to discover new gifts through the raising up of the old and bring them forth for the use of my fellow servants: remember me, my God, for good (Jas. I).

[Col. 0923]

# ALLEGORICAL INTERPRETATION OF THE BOOK OF THE BLESSED FATHER TOBIT (C)

[Col. 0923C]

The book of the holy Father Tobit is plainly beneficial to readers even on the surface of the letter, since it abounds in the greatest examples and admonitions for moral life. And if anyone also knows how to interpret it allegorically, he sees its inner meaning surpassing the simplicity of the letter as much as fruit surpasses leaves. For, when understood spiritually, it is shown to contain within itself the greatest mysteries concerning Christ and the Church.

Tobit himself signifies the people of Israel, who, while all the nations were devoted to idolatry, served God in the true faith and through righteous works, as is read concerning Tobit.

## Tobit I

Because, when everyone was going to the golden calves, etc. Jeroboam, who fashioned golden calves for the deception of his subjects, expresses the author of idolatry.

And Tobit had indeed been taken captive … he did not forsake the way of truth. This captivity carried out by the king of the Assyrians signifies that captivity of the human race by which it was cast out from the dwelling of the heavenly homeland and transferred into the wandering of this exile by the king of all wickedness, that is, the devil.

Tobit distributed daily among his captive brothers everything that he was able to possess, etc. The people of Israel, through their teachers, dispensed the alms of God’s word not only to the inexperienced hearers of their own nation but also to those from the nations who wished to be converted to their manner of life. Whatever natural good it was able to possess, which had not been taken away by the enemy who held it captive, it displayed entirely to its own people as an example of virtue.

It also always gave some portion of saving knowledge to the Gentiles. This is what it means for Tobit to distribute a tithe of his substance to strangers.

After Tobit had become a man, he took Anna as his wife from his own tribe, etc. In the same way, after the people had grown and increased in Egypt, it received the synagogue established by Moses with legal ceremonies.

He begot a son by her, etc. For he knew that Christ would be born from his race, as Moses said: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him” (Deut. XVIII). And the Lord said to David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne” (Ps. CXXXI). He gave him his name by believing and confessing what the Father says concerning him: “I will make him my firstborn” (Ps. LXXXVIII), just as he says concerning that people: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV).

He taught him to fear God from infancy, etc. By believing and confessing that he would commit no sin and that deceit would not be found in his mouth, but that the spirit of the fear of the Lord would fill him.

Tobit gave ten talents of silver to his needy kinsman Gabael under a written obligation. The people of God entrusted the nations, through the Seventy Interpreters, with knowledge of the divine law contained in the Decalogue, so that through this knowledge it might free them from the poverty of unbelief.

He gave it under a written obligation, that is, under the condition that it be repaid after he himself had grown rich or after the one who had given it demanded its return. The nations received the word of God from the people of Israel through translation. After the Lord’s incarnation they now understand it spiritually and exercise themselves in seeking the riches of virtues.

They repay the lender when, at the end of the age, they receive believing Jews into the unity of the Church, entrust them with the mysteries of Christ for their salvation, and also disclose the hidden things of the Scriptures.

Tobit was ordered by the king to be killed and all his property taken away because of the good things he had done, etc. The devil strove through idolatry to destroy the people of God by spiritual death and to take away all their riches of virtue, but he could not, because there were many holy teachers among them who cared for their life and salvation.

But he fled with his son and wife. The enemy could not take away either faith in the Lord’s incarnation or the stability of the synagogue, although he pressed violently against it, as became especially evident in the struggles of the Maccabees.

But after the king had been killed by his sons, all Tobit’s possessions were restored. After the devil had often been overcome and condemned together with his crimes, which he had begotten as a most wicked offspring, prosperity returned to the people of God. We see the condition of the Church likewise wavering through such conflicts after the Lord’s incarnation.

## Tobit II

Exhausted from burying the dead, Tobit came into his house, [lacuna], and became blind. Do not be surprised, reader, that things which are sometimes good signify evil figuratively, and at other times the evil deeds of human beings signify good. If this were not permitted, God would never be written in black ink, but always in shining gold, because he is light. Likewise, even if you write the name of the devil on a white pebble, it nevertheless signifies profound darkness.

Tobit’s blindness therefore signifies what the Apostle says: “A blindness in part has happened in Israel” (Rom. XI). He was exhausted from burying the dead and became blind because one who persists tirelessly in good works is never deprived of the light of faith. Spiritually he lies down and sleeps, exhausted, when he neglects to keep watch and stand firm in faith, to act courageously, and to be strengthened.

The apostolic saying aptly applies to him: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V). Swallows, because of their light flight, signify pride and the lightness of the heart; their impurity immediately blinds those whom it dominates. For one sleeps as though placed beneath a swallow’s nest when, without caution, he submits his mind to levity, wantonness, and pride.

This blindness prevailed especially over the people of Israel as the Lord’s coming in the flesh drew near, when they were both oppressed by the yoke of Roman servitude and grievously violated the precepts of the divine law by their evil way of life.

Tobit’s relatives mocked him, and his wife reproached him, as though he had served God in vain. Rebuking and instructing them, he turned to God in prayer. There were certain people among that nation who, with foolish presumption, mocked the miseries of the wretched people, which had already become far removed from the ancient blessedness of the holy fathers who had once served God among them in a lofty manner.

That same people, through its teachers and elect members, diligently sought to correct them and turned itself toward imploring God’s mercy for the reception of eternal life. It should not seem inappropriate that Tobit is said to signify both the reprobate and the elect, since he is at once blind and proclaims the word of God.

The patriarch Jacob likewise became both lame and blessed when he wrestled with the angel: in his lameness signifying the unbelievers of his nation, and in his blessing the faithful.

## Tobit III

Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, was in the city of the Medes. She had been given to seven husbands, and the demon killed them as soon as they entered to her. This figuratively announces the multitude of the nations, all of whose teachers knew only the life of this world, which revolves through seven days, and knew nothing to say about eternity.

Therefore they were all seized by the devil, being enslaved to idolatry, until the true bridegroom, our Lord, came. Having overcome the enemy, he joined this multitude to himself through faith. Thus Tobit, after binding the demon, received Sarah as his bride, at the command and with the cooperation of the archangel. Through the archangel the divinity of our Savior is not unfittingly signified, just as his humanity is signified through Tobit.

No one will be surprised that we say two persons—namely, the angel and the human being—signify the one person of the Mediator between God and human beings, if he has read in the expositions of the venerable Fathers that one person of Christ, suffering for the salvation of the world, was figured both in Isaac, who was offered by his father on the altar, and in the ram that was sacrificed.

In his humanity he was killed like a sheep; in his divinity he remains impassible with God the Father, just as Isaac, alive with his father, returns home with him. If the ram suitably signifies the humanity of Christ and the man signifies his divinity, why should a human being not much more suitably signify his humanity and an angel his divinity?

Therefore the holy angel of the Lord, Raphael, was sent. His name is interpreted as “medicine of God,” because he was sent to free both Tobit from blindness and Sarah from the demon. The Lord was sent into the world, of whom he himself said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke IV). He was sent to redeem both the Jewish people from the darkness of unbelief and the Gentiles from the slavery of idolatry.

Concerning him the prophet said: “And his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. IX).

[Col. 0927A]

## Tobit V

The angel appeared to Tobit and offered himself as his companion, through whom Tobit would accomplish great things for the people to whom he had been sent. In the same way, the Son of God assumed a human being, in whom he lived visibly among human beings and saved the human race.

Tobias introduced the angel to his father, who greeted him, saying: “May joy always be with you.” When the father replied, “What joy can I have, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?” he answered: “Be strong in spirit; it is near at hand that you should be healed by the Lord.” And our Lord, through the miracles that he performed in the flesh, showed the Jewish people—from whom he had assumed the flesh—that he himself is the Son of God and the angel, that is, the messenger of the Father’s will. To them also he proclaimed the joy of everlasting salvation, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near [Col. 0927B]” (Matt. III). And to those despairing of obtaining heavenly light he said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

The angel promises Tobias to lead his son to Rages, a city of the Medes, and to bring him back to him. The Lord promises believers from the Jewish people—even though that people has been blinded in large part—that he will disclose to the Gentile people the mysteries of his incarnation, and that again, at the end of time, he will open them more fully to the same people from whom he assumed the flesh, with the faith of his divinity accompanying and accomplishing everything everywhere. He himself speaks of the journey to the Medes: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these too I must [Col. 0927C] bring in,” and so forth (John X). The Apostle speaks of the return: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

When Tobias asked the angel where he was from, he replied: “I am Azariah, the son of the great Ananias.” Azariah is interpreted as “the Lord is helper,” and Ananias as “the grace of the Lord.” And the Lord makes known to those who believe in him that he is the one whose coming the prophet desired and sang of: “Be my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay” (Ps. LXIX). Of him the evangelist also says: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

Then, when everything that had to be carried on the journey had been prepared, Tobias bade farewell to his father and mother, and the two of them set out [Col. 0927D] together. When the Lord appeared in the flesh, everything necessary for the redemption of the world, and by which the faith and life of the holy Church would be nourished and strengthened until it completed the journey of this age, was prepared: his virtues, teaching, temptation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the sending of the Holy Spirit, the faith of believers, and the persecution of unbelievers. When these things had been accomplished in Judaea, the Mediator of God and human beings himself proclaimed through the apostles to the people and synagogue from which he had received the origin of his flesh the joys of heavenly salvation and peace. To those who wished to believe and receive them, he himself bestowed them, and thus he came to the salvation of the Gentiles in those same teachers of his.

*(Tob. VI.)* Tobias therefore set out, and the dog followed him. When the Lord came to save the Gentiles, [Col. 0928A] the holy preachers followed in his footsteps, because they fulfilled what he commanded: “Go and teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII). Indeed, the Lord himself first filled the house of Cornelius with the Holy Spirit, and then Peter sprinkled it with water (Acts X). Teachers are called dogs because they defend the house, the substance, and the spiritual sheep of their Creator from thieves and wild beasts—that is, from unclean spirits and heretical human beings.

Tobias remained, having set out under the guidance of the angel, at the first stopping-place beside the river Tigris. He went out to wash his feet, and behold, an enormous fish came out to devour him. Here again the mystery of the Lord’s passion is signified more clearly. The enormous fish, which the angel instructed Tobias to kill when it sought to devour him, designates the ancient devourer of the human race, [Col. 0928B] namely, the devil. While he sought the death of the flesh in our Redeemer, he was captured by the power of the divinity. The river Tigris, which received its name from the tiger, the swiftest of beasts, because of its extremely rapid current, indicates the course of our death and mortality. In it the enormous fish lay hidden, because the invisible seducer of the human race held the power of death. Tobias remained beside the waters of the Tigris because, appearing in the world, the Lord led his life among sinners and mortals; yet neither did the flood of sin touch him, nor did the prince of darkness, when he came, find anything of his own in him. Tobias went out into the river to wash his feet; and the Lord accepted a death to which he owed nothing, so that he might wash all the faithful—who are, so to speak, his members—from the contagion of sin and death. The fish came upon Tobias, desiring to devour him; and when the Lord was suffering on the cross, the devil came, he who had taught others to crucify him, [Col. 0928C] seeking whether he might perhaps find some crime in his soul.

Terrified by the fish, Tobias cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Lord, it is attacking me.” And the Lord, when the moment of death was imminent, began to be afraid and distressed—not fearing the devil, but dreading death, which entered the world through the devil’s envy (Wis. II), with the natural frailty of the flesh; hence he prayed that, if it could be, the hour might pass from him (Mark XII). And he said: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup from me, but not what I will, rather what you will” (Luke XXII).

The angel said to Tobias: “Grasp the fish by the gill [Col. 0928D] and pull it toward you.” The Lord grasped the devil and, by dying, captured and conquered the one who had wished to seize him in death. He grasped its gill so that, by the right hand of his power, he might separate the most wicked head from the deceived body: that is, so that he might take away the wickedness of the ancient enemy from those whom he had wickedly joined to himself and had made, as it were, one body with him, and so that the merciful Redeemer might insert them into the body of his Church. A fish has its gill at the boundary between its head and body. Just as our Lord is the head of his Church, while the Church is his body, so the devil is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are his body and members. The Lord therefore grasped the gill of the enormous fish, pulled it toward himself, and threw it onto dry land, because, crushing the devil’s power, he made a public display [Col. 0929A] confidently and drew out of the power of darkness those whom he had foreknown to be sons of light.

When he had done this, the fish began to writhe on the dry land before his feet. When the Lord overcame the wickedness of the evil enemy and brought it into the light, making it manifest to all, the enemy, still swelling with pride, attempted to stir up persecution against his elect, who are his feet, because through them the Lord, who reigns over all in heaven, walks upon the earth.

Then the Lord’s angel said to him: “Eviscerate this fish,” and so forth. The Lord eviscerated the fish when he disclosed the devil’s wickedness more fully to the holy ones and, as it were, disemboweled the hidden chambers of his snares. He kept its heart because he enclosed his cunning in the holy books; concerning it Scripture says: “Now the serpent was more cunning than all the animals [Col. 0929B] of the earth” (Gen. III). Paul also said of this heart: “We are not ignorant of his thoughts” (II Cor. II). He also kept the gall because, for the sake of caution, he wished it to be written down and preserved how violently, in the fury of his malice, he raged against the human race. He also kept the liver because he graciously made known to us through the teachers of truth the malignant maturity of his plans against us. For they say that by the heat and power of the liver the hidden substances of food that has been eaten are cooked and brought to digestion. When we carefully investigate in what order the things we intend to do should be carried out, we are like people cooking in the stomach, through the heat of the liver, the food they have taken in.

These things are indeed useful and necessary for medicines. The cunning and malice of the ancient enemy, once known to us, [Col. 0929C] benefit us for healing; for the more certainly we examine them, the more cautiously we avoid them.

Tobias roasted the fish’s flesh, and so forth. Whatever they took from the fish signifies those who are transferred from the devil’s members into Christ’s members—that is, those who are converted from unbelief to faith. Whatever they left behind, on the other hand, represents those who, after hearing the word of God, prefer to remain among the dead and rotten members of their deceiver rather than return to the fellowship of the Savior. He roasted its flesh in those whom he found carnal, but through the fire of his love he made them spiritual and strong. Indeed, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles in the appearance of fire. “The rest,” he says, “they salted,” which pertains spiritually to the teachers, to whom it is said: “You are [Col. 0929D] the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). Tobias and the angel salted them because the same Mediator of God and human beings taught the apostles humanly by speaking, and divinely bestowed upon their hearts the salt of wisdom.

They took with them whatever was sufficient for them, and so forth. For the Lord gathered from Judaea so many people into the faith that they would suffice as examples of living or for the ministry of preaching, until he also established the foundations of the Church among the Gentiles.

The angel suggests to Tobias that, after entering Raguel’s house, he should ask for his daughter Sarah as his wife. Raguel indicates the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord graciously visited through his preachers, so that he might take a bride for himself from their stock—that is, make the Gentile people themselves into his Church. The name Sarah also suits the Church because of Sarah, the wife of Abraham the patriarch, who bore Isaac, the son of promise, that is, the free people of the Church. The [Col. 0930A] name Raguel, interpreted as “God is his nourishment” or “God is a friend,” designates that people who, having overcome the devil’s deceit, joins itself and its own to the Lord’s fellowship, and knows how to say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXXII). It deserves to hear: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV).

“All his substance is owed to you.” And the Father says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,” and so forth (Ps. II).

*(Tob. VII.)* They entered Raguel’s house, and he received them with joy. Through the teachers of his word, the Lord approached the people of the nations, who willingly received him in many [Col. 0930B] places, as the Acts of the Apostles testify.

When Raguel’s daughter was requested, he was initially afraid, knowing what had happened to the seven men; but when the angel explained that the unclean spirit could not possess her, while Tobias, who feared God, could, he immediately consented to give her.

When the people of the Gentiles heard the word of faith and were admonished by the apostles to establish throughout the world the Church of Christ from their own offspring, they could not receive the law and rule of the new faith without careful examination. They knew that in former times they had had many teachers, all of whom, as though included in the number seven, knew only the joys of this life and said nothing certain about eternal things; therefore destruction would have snatched them away without hope of immortal life and into eternal death. But when the truth itself, speaking inwardly through what sounded outwardly from the mouths of the teachers, [Col. 0930C] instructed them, they at last understood that it was necessary for fools to speak foolishly, and that those who did not know the true Lord should perish; whereas the Creator of the world, rightly coming into the world, should take up the governance of the world. Having confessed the faith of Christ, the people rejoiced to be sanctified by his mysteries.

*(Tob. VIII.)* When Tobias had been brought to Sarah in the chamber, he took from his satchel a portion of the liver, and so forth. And the Lord, about to receive the Church from the Gentiles, commands her, at the very beginning of her ordering, to renounce Satan in each of the faithful, together with all his works and all his pomps; then to confess the faith of the holy Trinity for the remission of sins. This is to burn the innermost organs of peace with living coals.

[Col. 0930D] When these things had been done, the angel seized the demon and bound him. For after the renunciation of the devil and the confession of right faith comes the remission of sins, with the demon expelled through the water of baptism. He bound him because he restrained him from harming the faithful. Although the devil is sometimes permitted to tempt them so that they may be tested, he is nevertheless forbidden to overcome them, lest they fall away from the faith.

He bound him in the desert of upper Egypt. Both the desert and Egypt signify the hearts of unbelievers, which are deserted—that is, abandoned by God—and are unworthy of his indwelling. These same hearts are also, according to the interpretation of the name Egypt, darkened by the darkness of their faithlessness. Nor is it without reason that the one abandoned by the grace of divine light is filled by the prince of darkness. The angel therefore seized the demon who wanted to kill Tobias and bound him in the desert of upper Egypt, because the same Lord and Redeemer of ours, restraining him from snatching away the faithful who are members of their Redeemer, [Col. 0931A] permits the devil to rule only over unbelievers. He also keeps him bound among them, because he does not permit him to harm even the impious whom he possesses as much as his insatiable fury desires.

Meanwhile, at about the time of the cockcrow, Raguel, fearing that Tobias might perhaps have been killed by the demon, dug a grave with his servants; but as soon as he learned that Tobias was safe, he ordered the earth to be put back. The crowing of the cocks is the sound of preachers, who sang that the true morning and day of faith would come into the world after the darkness of error. Yet there were some among the people of the Gentiles who doubted whether [Col. 0931B] the Lord had truly conquered the ancient enemy, and who therefore thought it better to bury and conceal the faith in his name. Later, however, when they recognized the light of truth—as dawn advanced and the cockcrow grew louder, that is, through the voice of the teachers, who are accustomed to raise themselves toward heavenly desires on the swift flight of an eager heart—they drove every cloud of doubt from their minds and truly recognized Christ, with the enemy struck down, as the bridegroom of the holy Church.

Raguel rejoiced at Tobias’s life and at the union and marriage of his daughter. He had two fat cows and four rams killed, and prepared a feast for all his neighbors and all his friends. Rejoicing in the faith of Christ and in the calling of the Gentiles to God, the people of the nations progressed so greatly in the Lord that teachers [Col. 0931C] even arose from their number, and these same teachers afterward also became martyrs.

They are cows, certainly, because they bear the light yoke of the Gospel; and because, by preaching, they beget and nourish those who may likewise advance toward bearing that same yoke. They are also rams because they are fathers and leaders of peoples, concerning whom it is said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII). The cows are fat because the teachers are filled with the grace of heavenly delight. Concerning this the Psalmist prays: “May my soul be filled as with the fatness of richness” (Ps. LXII). Two cows were killed because all who suffer for Christ either willingly mortify their own bodies so that they may become a living sacrifice, or hand them over to unbelievers to be killed. Such people have learned to stand against the enemy by the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left—that is, in [Col. 0931D] prosperity and adversity. Four rams were killed because holy teachers and martyrs preserve the four books of the holy Gospel in faith and action; because they are fortified by the four chief virtues—prudence, courage, temperance, and justice; and because throughout the whole world, which is divided into four regions, they establish Christ’s flock.

Raguel had the cows and rams killed because the people of the Gentiles taught that those who had come to the faith from their own stock were such people: their excellence of virtue would cause the enemy to desire to tempt them, but he would not overcome them when tempted; rather, he could make them martyrs who conquered. Or certainly he himself had them killed, since he taught them to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires for Christ’s sake. By their slaughter he prepared a feast for all his neighbors, because the progress, life, [Col. 0932A] passion, and crown of the saints bring joy to many, and people receive them like a feast, being refreshed by their examples.

Raguel adjured Tobias to remain with him for two weeks. We too adjure our Lord, praying that he remain with us until, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we attain the perfection of holy rest: that we may rest from servile deeds, that is, from sins in the body, and from evil thoughts in the mind; and that he himself may rest in our heart and body, he who says: “Over whom will my spirit rest, if not over the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

*(Tob. IX.)* Tobias asks the angel to take the animals or servants, go to Gabelus in Rages of the Medes, [Col. 0932B] return his bond to him, receive the money from him, and ask him to come to Tobias’s wedding; and the angel agrees. The faithful, who are his members, ask the Lord to take some of the believers and entrust to them the work of preaching the word, and that he himself may come in them to gather into his faith the nations that have not yet received the mysteries of faith but have merely heard the report of them. They ask him graciously to grant those nations that they return, through obedience to faith, the talent of the word that they learned by report, and that they too may be joined to the wedding of the holy Church, whose bridegroom is Christ, and in which he made new wine from water—that is, gives the spiritual understanding of the Law—by believing and living rightly. The Lord does not refuse, but, graciously receiving the prayers of those who ask well, daily gathers new peoples into the [Col. 0932C] Church. As was said above, this may spiritually be understood of those nations that received the letter of the Law through the seventy translators; therefore they were able to accept the faith more quickly, since they possessed it in books familiar to them.

Raphael therefore took four of Raguel’s servants and two camels and went to Rages of the Medes. He told Gabelus everything about Tobias, received the money, and made him come with him to the wedding. Raguel’s servants and camels are preachers chosen from the Gentiles, through whom the Lord gathers others also. They are servants because they serve the needs of those to whom they preach the Gospel. They are camels because they bear the burdens of their weakness through the fraternal submission of charity. Why there are four servants and [Col. 0932D] two camels was shown above, where two cows and four rams are killed. With Raphael’s help, such men bring Gabelus to Tobias’s wedding when the holy preachers, with divine assistance, gather new peoples into the unity of Christ’s Church.

*(Tob. X.)* Because Tobias delayed on account of the wedding, his parents were saddened that he did not return to them on the appointed day. And now, while Christ remains through faith in the Church gathered from the Gentiles, whatever individuals from the Jews are converted to his faith are deeply grieved in spirit, because the Lord delays coming to save them, detained among the Gentiles. His mother, poor and deprived, as it were, of both husband and son, spoke to them fittingly and with great sorrow:

“Alas, alas, my son! Why did we send you away to wander [Col. 0933A]—you light of our eyes, staff of our old age?” and so forth. And when Tobias consoles her, replying: “Be silent, and do not be troubled; our son is well,” and so forth, this applies to those same people who now believe from among the Jews. They console themselves and their own with the assurance that the time will truly come when the Lord will return to them, and then all Israel will be saved, knowing that the Lord who promised this is entirely faithful. For, as we have taught above, this same Tobias designates unbelievers by his blindness and believers by his faith, in the manner customary in Scripture.

Raguel asks Tobias to remain with him for a longer time, but he is not heard, for Tobias says: “I know that my father and mother are now counting the days, and their spirit is tormented within them.” And when the fullness of the Gentiles [Col. 0933B] has entered, no one will be able to prevent God from granting salvation to Israel and removing its blindness, which has happened in part. For divine clemency remembers that there is great sorrow and continual pain of heart among believers from the Jews because of the blindness of unbelievers who are their kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites.

Raguel therefore sent Tobias back to his parents, giving him Sarah with much property. At the end, the teachers of the Church send Christ back with the Church itself, filled with the riches of virtues, to enlighten the Jewish people and enrich it with the substance of good works—the people from whom he assumed the flesh.

*(Tob. XI.)* The angel and Tobias went ahead to his parents; afterward his wife followed with her possessions and [Col. 0933C] household. After the father who enlightens had gone ahead through divine grace to illuminate the blindness of the Jewish people, and after they recognized in their Scriptures that Christ is true God and human being, then, after recognizing the right faith, they rejoiced greatly, as though seeing the angel and their son whom they had not seen for a long time. Thus at last they joined themselves to the holy Church, which has been gathered from the Gentiles, by participation in the heavenly mysteries.

As they approached the house, the dog that had accompanied them on the journey ran ahead and, like a messenger arriving, rejoiced while wagging its tail. The figure of this dog, who is the angel’s traveler and companion, must not be dismissed. As we have taught above, it expresses the teachers of the Church, who often engage the heretics in combat and drive grievous wolves away from the fold of the supreme Shepherd. It [Col. 0933D] fittingly corresponds to dogs’ natural quality of returning gratitude for benefits and keeping careful watch for the safety of their masters. The dog therefore runs ahead because he first proclaims salvation to the household, and then the Lord who enlightens the hearts of the world does so. It is beautifully said that he arrived like a messenger, since every faithful teacher is indeed a messenger of truth. It is also beautifully said that he rejoiced by wagging his tail: the tail, which is the end of the body, signifies the end of good action—that is, perfection—or, certainly, the reward that is bestowed without end. The dog therefore rejoiced by wagging his tail when he revisited the dwelling of his masters, from whom he had long been absent. Teachers rejoice in the effect of their work when they understand that Judaea is to be gathered back to the Lord through their ministry. [Col. 0934A] They rejoice in receiving the reward of eternal life, and by this same reward, shared by all the elect, they gladden the hearts of those to whom they preach, promising them the grace of Christ, which will soon come.

When the dog announced that Tobias had come, his blind father rose and began to run toward him, stumbling with his feet. After hearing from the teachers the word of salvation, the Hebrew people rose from the long slumber of their faithlessness and ran toward the Lord in love, although stumbling in the steps of their works, until, regenerated and instructed in Christ, they should receive the light through the fullness of faith and good works.

He gave the boy his hand and went out to meet his son. The blind man gives his hand to the boy so that he may meet the Lord with an unimpeded step of action. Although he himself does not yet fully understand the way of faith, he strives to give [Col. 0934B] assent to the one who has come to know the light of truth well, so that through him he may reach the Lord.

He and his wife received him and kissed him, and they wept for joy. At the end, Judaea receives the union with Christ with joy, but joins weeping to it: rejoicing because it believes, grieving because it has come to the Lord so late.

Then Tobias took some of the fish’s gall and anointed his father’s eyes. And the Lord reveals more clearly to believers how great is the malice of the ancient dragon, who once eagerly sought to devour him in his passion; but through this act he himself was instead killed and lost his members, that is, those whom he had previously held.

A kind of membrane, the white of an egg, began to come out of Tobias’s eyes after they had been anointed with the fish’s gall, and he regained his [Col. 0934C] sight. So the Jewish people, after recognizing the exceedingly bitter malice of the wicked enemy, will recover the light it had lost. The white substance that had covered his eyes signifies the foolishness of self-satisfaction. “They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X). And again he says: “Desiring to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (ibid.). The black pupil sees, whereas the white part grows dark. And those who seem wise to themselves, saying, “Are we also blind?” (John IX), do not possess the truth. But those who know their own frailty and ignorance and know how to say, “My God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII), will enjoy the light of life in the Lord.

The white substance was appropriately like the membrane of an egg. Through eggs hope is signified, because an egg is not yet alive, not yet animated; it is separated from the bird that laid it until it comes alive, emerges, runs, and flies. [Col. 0934D] The Apostle says: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Luke XI). Hence, in the Gospel parable, under the names of bread, fish, and egg, the three highest virtues—faith, hope, and charity—are expressed.

The Jewish people therefore still have a veil before the face of their heart, so that they do not understand the grace of Christ. They have the white substance because they appear righteous and pure to themselves above all others. But they have that same white substance like an egg’s membrane because they endure a blindness of mind under the most foolish and vain hope that Christ will be born in the flesh, liberate them, and give them a great kingdom throughout the world. [Col. 0935A] But when the darkness of error has been removed from any of them, they will recognize that Christ has already come and redeemed the world by his blood. What follows suitably applies to them:

When his sight had been restored, Tobias glorified God with his wife and all his acquaintances, saying: “I bless you, Lord God of Israel, because you chastised me and you saved me,” and so forth. The seven days signify the light of spiritual grace, which is understood as sevenfold. After the seven days, when Tobias has been enlightened, his son’s wife enters, because after Judaea has been enlightened through faith and has received the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Church will enter into it, so that there may be one fold and one shepherd, and one house of Christ, firmly established upon one cornerstone.

[Col. 0935B] The livestock, the camels, and the wife’s much money also entered. Many faithful people and many virtues of the Church will then be gathered into the Jewish people.

So too the money that he had received from Gabelus. The knowledge of the Scriptures, which they once lent to the Gentiles, will then be returned to the same people.

Tobias’s cousins came, congratulating him on all the good things that the Lord had done for him, and they feasted with him for seven days. This is what Moses said in the song: “Rejoice, Gentiles, together with his people” (Rom. XV). They feast together for seven days because they rejoice in spiritual gifts and virtues. As the angel is about to return to heaven, he explains to them more openly who he is, why he came, and that he will return to God. And the Lord then discloses more fully the gifts of his knowledge to that advancing [Col. 0935C] people, opening and showing to all that he is in the Father and the Father is in him. The angel therefore returns to God, while Tobias remains with his father. And the Lord is understood by the elect to be equal to the Father in divinity and consubstantial with us in humanity.

*(Tob. XIII.)* Then the elder Tobias opened his mouth and blessed God. Having confessed both God’s severity and his mercy, and at the same time admonished his faithful to proclaim his benefits always and fear his scourges, he sang at length in praise of the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, filled with the spirit of prophecy. And the Jewish people, converted to the faith at the end of the age, will have many teachers and prophetic men who kindle the minds [Col. 0935D] of their neighbors toward heavenly desires while proclaiming repeatedly the everlasting joys of the heavenly homeland.

*(Tob. XIV.)* At the hour of his death, the elder Tobias called his son Tobias and the latter’s seven sons—his own grandsons—to himself, and told them that the destruction of Nineveh and the restoration of Israel were near. And then, in Judaea, the faithful and just teachers, seeing these things and about to depart from the world, admonish their relatives that the world is already approaching its end and that the goods of the future life are near to come. They especially warn those whom they see to have been reborn by the Lord’s grace and filled with the gift of the sevenfold Spirit. This is what it means to be the sons of the younger Tobias in the number seven, and to be young men—that is, strong in faith and victorious over the evil one.

[Col. 0936A] “Direct your steps, so that you may depart from Nineveh. For I see that its wickedness will bring it to an end.” This is what the faithful say to their hearers: “Direct the intention of your heart, so that you may abandon the desires of earthly life and of this age, and seek heavenly things with your whole mind.” It is clear that the multitude of the wicked and the transgression of God’s commandments throughout the world are so great that they cannot end in any other way than through the destruction of the world itself, just as once through the Flood and the abolition of the whole human race.

Tobias therefore departed from Nineveh with his wife, his sons, and his sons’ sons, and returned to his in-laws, whom he found in a good old age. The Lord does this daily, and will continue to do it until the end of the age: abandoning those whom he recognizes as not being his own, he turns to visit and enlighten the hearts [Col. 0936B] of those whom he predestined for eternal life. He finds them in a good old age when he rejoices that, by his gift, they have long devoted themselves to good works. Otherwise he sees them in an evil old age, and therefore passes them by: living [far from] divine things, they are not mature in counsel, nor venerable through the whiteness of good action like gray hair, but are bent beneath the burden of vices. Concerning such people Isaiah says: “A child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV). He will rightly lie under a curse for his sins, because although he has lived many years, he has never taken care to abandon the light-mindedness of a childish spirit.

He found them safe in a good old age, and so forth. Our Lord and Savior also cares for those [Col. 0936C] whom he knows to persevere in the safety of good works. Closing their heart’s gaze to the delight of the present life, he raises it to the contemplation of everlasting light. He himself leads them to heavenly things after the end of this life. His is the inheritance of which the prophet sings to him: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations” (Ps. LXXXI).

After completing many years in the fear of the Lord with joy, all his relatives buried him. The burial of Tobias signifies the faith of the whole world, when our Lord enters eternal rest with his entire body, which is the Church that he redeemed, while the angels rejoice over the fellowship of redeemed human beings, [Col. 0936D] and place each of them—namely, the members of their Creator—in the various dwellings of the heavenly homeland according to the diversity of their merits.

And all his generation remained in a good life and holy conduct. This is the one generation, throughout the whole world and throughout the entire time of the age, of those who seek the Lord and seek the face of the God of Jacob (Ps. XXIII). Of it he likewise says: “The generation of the upright will be blessed” (Ps. CXI). What life is better, what conduct is holier, than to remain forever in the glory of its Creator?

Thus they were acceptable both to God and to all the inhabitants of the earth. Once led to the heavenly homeland, human beings will be acceptable to God, by whose grace they were redeemed; they will also be acceptable to the angels, whose number they will complete, [Col. 0937A] and to whose fellowship they will be joined forever as brothers. For these are the inhabitants of that earth of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall [Col. 0938A] possess the earth” (Matt. V). Desiring to see it, the Psalmist said: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXV).

[Col. 0937]

## COMMENTARIES ON JOB

This was the place of the commentaries on the Book of Job, which some have attributed to the Venerable Bede; but since we have assigned them more properly among the works of St. Jerome, see there, we ask you, reader, in volume XXIII of the *Patrologia*.

[Col. 0937]

## ALLEGORICAL EXPOSITION ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON (C)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0937B]

## Allegorical Exposition of Solomon’s Proverbs

### Book One

### Chapter One

**“The Proverbs of Solomon,” etc.** *Parables* in Greek are called *similitudes* in Latin; Solomon gave this book its title for the purpose of teaching us to understand what it says at a deeper level, rather than according to the letter. In this respect he signifies that the Lord would at some time speak to the crowds in parables. Likewise, by his proper name and by the peaceful condition of his kingdom, he proclaims the everlasting kingdom of Christ and of the Church, concerning which it is written: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace, upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom” (Isaiah 9). By the construction and dedication of the Temple, he also suggests the building of the holy Church, which will be dedicated eternally at the time of the resurrection. For he himself is also the son of David and the spiritual king of Israel, as is declared even by the testimony of the crowds, who are said to have gone out to meet him as he entered Jerusalem, with branches of palms and praises (Matthew 21).

It should be noted, however, that the Vulgate edition, in place of *Parables*, which are called *Mishle* in Hebrew, uses *Paroemias*, that is, “proverbs.” Yet even this name does not depart from the truth. For what are rightly called parables, because they contain hidden things, may also appropriately be called proverbs, since they are such sayings as rightly ought to circulate frequently on the lips of those conversing and to be retained in memory. Proverbs, too, are often spoken so obscurely that, not without reason, they may likewise be designated by the name of parables, as the Lord bears witness when he says: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John 16).

What benefit, then, Solomon’s Proverbs provide is shown in the expansion of the title, when it adds:

**“To know wisdom,” etc.** To know wisdom and discipline is to learn how one ought rightly to believe, how one ought to live, and, for each person who has truly learned, to know where to direct the intention of the heart and what it is fitting to undertake in action. When it adds:

**“To understand the words of prudence,” etc.,** it admonishes those whom it instructs not merely to embrace the wisdom they have once received and to know how to serve the virtue of discipline they have recognized, but also willingly to listen to the words of prudent people, through which they may advance toward perfection, and to take care diligently to understand them.

**“Justice and judgment,” etc.** Justice consists in the good works we perform according to the rule of truth; judgment, in the things we do rightly with our neighbors through sound discernment. Equity consists in striving, with a sincere intention, to please God alone in the things we rightly do or judge.

**“That cunning may be given to the simple,” etc.** By “the simple” he means those who have recently begun to lend an ear to wisdom; by “the young man,” one who has already made some progress in listening to it. Perhaps he therefore calls the simple by a plural name and the young man by a singular one because the teaching of wisdom receives people devoted to different movements of the soul and different ways of life, and advances them by instructing them in the more perfect way of virtue. Of these it is rightly said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

“Let cunning,” he says, “be given to the simple.” For this is necessary to the untrained and those who are beginning, so that they may recognize and avoid the craftiness of sophisms, lest they be led away from the simplicity of true wisdom, which leads to life, by the deceit of false arguments. “Knowledge and understanding” are given to the young man, because one who prudently avoids falsehood will consequently receive knowledge of the truth.

Thus far belongs to the prefatory title; from this point the text of the Proverbs itself begins.

**“The wise man hearing shall be wiser.”** Because Solomon was a lover of wisdom—when given a choice, he asked for and received wisdom—he fittingly begins his Proverbs with wisdom. By saying that the wise man, when he hears a word, becomes wiser, he shows that no one in this life can become so wise that his wisdom cannot increase, and that it is always characteristic of the wise to listen to the sayings of their elders, and sometimes even of their juniors, and to apply to themselves whatever benefit they hear in them, remembering it in their hearts.

Indeed, the younger wise person heard the elder: the queen of Sheba heard Solomon and returned wiser (1 Kings 10). Moses heard his much-inferior father-in-law and returned more exalted and wiser (Exodus 18). The disciples heard Christ and were found worthy to receive the spirit of wisdom. Nicodemus heard; Gamaliel heard; his disciple heard—then Saul, now the apostle Paul. They were wise in the word of the Gospel and were made wiser. Paul himself, after being caught up to the third heaven and hearing words that it is not permitted for human beings to speak (Acts 22), nevertheless, when he had returned to earth, said: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13).

**“And the one who understands shall possess the means of direction.”** Let no one boast of his own knowledge, because whoever neglects frequently to hear and understand the words of the wise does not know how to direct his life properly. How much less can one be placed over the governance of another who has refused to submit himself to the discipline of his fathers!

Therefore, when it says, “The wise man hearing shall be wiser,” it refers to knowledge of the things that are known through wisdom. But when it adds, “And the one who understands shall possess the means of direction,” it refers to the uprightness of life that is learned or taught through that same wisdom. And fittingly the beginning of the Proverbs corresponds to the beginning of the title, which reads: “The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, to know wisdom and discipline.”

**“He shall understand a parable and its interpretation,” etc.** Wisdom itself, which instructed the disciples humbly listening to it when it appeared in the flesh, granted them this gift: that they might spiritually understand and explain to their hearers both its own parables, which the crowds could not understand, and the riddles of the prophets and the Law—that is, their obscure sayings. To the subsequent teachers of the Church, too, it opened the same mysteries of spiritual understanding when they piously sought and knocked.

**“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”** There are two fears of the Lord. The first is servile and is called the beginning of knowledge or wisdom; the second is friendly and accompanies the perfection of wisdom.

Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom because whoever begins to become wise after the error of sins is first seized by divine fear, lest he be led to punishments. But perfect love casts out this fear (1 John 4). In its place comes the holy fear of the Lord, enduring forever and ever (Psalm 13); charity does not exclude it but increases it. This is the fear by which a good son fears even slightly to offend the eyes of his most loving father. For in the initial fear, the still-servile soul fears that it may be subjected to punishment by an angry master.

Both fears, however, will cease in the life to come; but charity will never fail (1 Corinthians 13). Rather, it will remain forever in the fullness of wisdom, which is to know the true and one God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17).

**“Fools despise wisdom and discipline.”** He had said of the wise man that, after hearing a word, he would become wiser and, understanding, would learn to govern his actions properly. Conversely, he says of fools that they not only fail to attain the wisdom of sound doctrine and the discipline of pure conduct, but also scorn to know them.

Indeed, when Wisdom itself was preaching in the flesh, all the wise hurried to him with joy; but the Pharisees and the chief priests rejected both his saving words and his deeds. It should also be noted that he describes “the wise man” in the singular but “fools” in the plural, because fools are more numerous than the wise, and the company of the wise keeps to one uniform path of piety. The dissimilar doctrine of those who err is accompanied by a dissimilar order of life.

**“Hear, my son, the discipline of your father,” etc.** Up to this point he has discussed both parties proverbially; now he begins diligently to admonish every believer to prefer the discipline of divine law to the flatteries of the reprobate, since the keeping of the former is followed by a crown, while the crimes of the latter are followed by eternal death. Thus he rightly calls him “son,” because a father carefully takes responsibility for instructing him.

This may also be understood as spoken in the person of God the Father, while “mother” is understood as the Church, which at that time was called the Synagogue. It should be noted that he commands us to hear the discipline of the Father in such a way that we do not abandon the Law for any reason, because it is not enough for someone to say that he loves the Lord and obeys his commandments if he does not follow the unity of the Church in fraternal charity. Nor is there any obstacle to understanding the mother herself as the grace of God by which we are saved. For among the Hebrews, the spirit that bestows grace is also named with a feminine gender.

**“That grace may be added to your head,” etc.** It was the custom among the ancients for those who competed lawfully to receive a crown upon the head and a necklace around the neck. Therefore, if we keep the discipline of our Creator and the ordinances of the mother Grace, the splendor of spiritual virtues is thereby increased within us.

Grace is added to the head when charity, which adorned the chief part of the mind, is inflamed more ardently. A necklace is added to the neck when the word of preaching, which proceeds through the neck, is strengthened by the radiance of perfect action; and, so that it may not be despised by its hearers, it is taught with an unbroken connection of virtues.

Grace was also added to those who kept the decrees of the Mosaic Law when the Lord came: the grace of the New Testament, together with the hope of the heavenly kingdom. Its exceptional splendor, like that of a crown or necklace, will never be closed off by any end.

To us, too, when eternal light is granted for the deeds which divine grace has beforehand bestowed upon us, grace is certainly added to the head and a necklace to the neck, according to the saying of the Gospel: “We have all received from his fullness, grace for grace” (John 1)—that is, the grace of blessed recompense for the grace of right action.

**“My son, if sinners entice you,” etc.** Sinners entice those whom they deceive in two ways: either they lure them by flatteries into committing crimes, or they exalt deeds already done by favor, as though they had been performed laudably. In both respects Wisdom urges its hearers not to yield to such people.

**“If they say, ‘Come with us,’ etc.”** This passage may generally be understood of robbers who inflict either the snares of death or losses upon the innocent. It may also be understood particularly of those who handed over the very author of life to death.

**“Let us hide snares against the innocent without cause.”** They did this when they said: “Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Mark 12), along with countless other things of this kind. For he was truly innocent, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. Truly they laid snares against him without cause: they had been harmed by him in nothing; rather, they had experienced his many benefits.

**“Let us swallow him like the underworld,” etc.** The ungodly desired to extinguish the Lord in such a way that every memory of his virtues and teaching would be removed, and even the fact that such a person had ever lived among them would be consigned to oblivion.

**“We shall find every precious substance,” etc.** They were speaking about the people whom they saw clinging to Christ. For they thought that, if they killed him, they could separate from his love and following everyone who had believed, and fill the meeting places of their houses with such spoils of living beings. The saying in the Lord’s parable is similar: when the king’s son came to them, they said, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (ibid.).

**“Cast in your lot with us,” etc.** A purse is a small bag of money. It is evident that this concerns robbers, since, in order to acquire more partners in crime, they promise them a share in the spoil they have seized. The persecutors of our Redeemer likewise joined to themselves everyone they could. But those whom they saw following him they drove away from the Synagogue and deprived of their fellowship.

**“My son, do not walk with them,” etc.** He forbids those who believe in Christ from associating with the Jews who persecuted Christ. Indeed, all who believed were together as one. Peter, speaking to these same people, said: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts 2).

**“For their feet run to evil,” etc.** They hasten not only toward the evil they perform temporarily, but also toward the evil that the ungodly will suffer forever, whenever they hurry to commit murder or perpetrate some other crime. For to the extent that, seeing clearly, they are led toward completing the crime, to that same extent, without seeing it, they draw near to enduring punishment for the crime.

This may be understood particularly of those who plotted against our Savior. The following verse, however, is inserted generally concerning his faithful, who likewise endure the wickedness of evil people.

**“The net is spread in vain,” etc.** For the snare of persecution or death is spread in vain against the elect, who have the wings of hope and charity and of the other virtues. By these wings, while they live, they desire heavenly things, so that after death they may deserve to attain them. They also have the eyes of the mind, by which they foresee that the evils they endure from the ungodly will quickly pass away, while the good things they have merited will remain forever.

With these same eyes they perceive both the pride of the reprobate, which will soon be consumed, and the punishments that follow, which will remain forever. This may also be understood in the following way: he rightly calls pernicious the teaching of the wicked, which he connected with the place where he said, “If sinners entice you, do not consent.”

Such a net, then, is spread in vain before those who contemplate heavenly things with pure eyes of heart and know how to say with the prophet: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters.” For the one whose manner of life is in heaven easily avoids the snares spread upon earth.

Thus the wicked prepare both nets in vain for the good: if they persuade them to wickedness, they are overcome by the wisdom of the righteous; if they inflict adversity, it is despised through endurance. Moreover, the tempters themselves are destroyed by their own plots. Hence it is rightly added:

**“They themselves also lie in wait against their own blood,” etc.** “Against their blood,” so that they may be punished by temporal death; but he says “against their souls,” so that they may also be condemned to eternal destruction of soul.

Although this applies to all who lie in wait for blood and think that they must live by deceit, it nevertheless applies especially to the Jews, who hid snares against the innocent Lord and strove by treachery to entrap his apostles, supported by the wings of virtues. They were acting against their own blood and their own souls: fearing that they would lose an earthly kingdom, they killed the King of heaven and earth and persecuted the citizens of heaven on earth. Therefore they lost both what they possessed on earth and the kingdom they could have acquired in heaven.

In general, however, it must be said that whoever has the eyes of faith opened and receives from the Lord wings like a dove, by which he may fly to eternal rest, finds that the wicked spread snares in vain against such a person; by presuming this, they destroy themselves instead.

**“If the paths of the covetous seize the souls of those who possess,” etc.** By the paths of the covetous he means his subtle thoughts, by which he diligently investigates how he may increase his money. Such paths seize for destruction the souls of those who possess—that is, of those who devote themselves beyond reason to the possession of wealth.

Thus, he says, not only do those who, because of their love of money, devote themselves to the robbery and slaughter of the innocent lose themselves by doing this, but, in the same manner, though with lesser guilt, all the thoughts of the covetous that prefer gold to God drag the covetous person to destruction.

Alternatively: “Thus the paths of every covetous person seize the souls of those who possess.” By such an end, as I have said, every covetous person destroys or strips those who abound in possessions, so that he himself perishes by doing this instead. For why should he kill the poor, whom he sees to possess nothing? He finds no one whom he can strip.

Up to this point the persecutions that the Jews inflicted upon Christ have been described. From here onward they report what he himself, after his Passion, speaks to those same persecutors through the apostles.

**“Wisdom preaches outside, in the streets,” etc.** The Wisdom of God is Christ, who lived in the world and revealed the mysteries of his divinity to a few. He commanded them not to preach before his Passion and Resurrection that he was Jesus Christ, nor to tell anyone of the glory they had seen on the mountain. At that time he showed the power of his majesty more through works than through words, fulfilling the prophecy that said: “No one shall hear his voice in the streets” (Isaiah 42).

But after the Resurrection Wisdom preached outside (Matthew 12), because, after the Spirit had been sent from above, it declared through the apostles that it was opening and revealing itself to the world. It raised its voice in the streets because, openly and in the broad gathering of the peoples, it repeated what it had previously taught to a few, fulfilling the word that it spoke to those same heralds: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10).

It cried out at the head of the crowds because it also openly brought back to the memory of the rulers who seemed to have prevailed over it so that it might be crucified the guilt of the homicide they had committed, and called them to the remedy of repentance.

**“At the gates of the entrances of the city she utters her words.”** The city of the Lord is the Church, united from both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. Its gate-entrances are the teachers, who introduce believers into it by preaching the word.

Wisdom uttered its words at the entrances of its gates when it spoke with its apostles. One of them said: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13).

The gate-entrances of the city may also be understood as the leaders of the Synagogue, among whom Wisdom disputed when, speaking through the apostles, it recalled the lawyers, Pharisees, and priests to its grace, so that, as Luke says, “a great number even of the priests obeyed the faith.”

What Wisdom cried out is added:

**“How long, you simple ones, will you love childishness?”** How long, being childish in understanding, will you love the ceremony of the Old Testament while the New Testament is shining forth? How long will you prefer Moses to Christ and the Law to the Gospel? How long will you place the decrees given through a servant to peoples still untrained above those things that the Son himself, when he came, conferred upon those perfect in understanding?

“How long,” he says, “will you do these things? You have already seen Christ in the flesh; you have not merely despised him performing miracles and teaching, but have also killed him. At least now love him, raised from the dead and presiding in heaven, and he will forgive you the crime you committed.”

**“And fools will desire the things that are harmful to them,” etc.** The words must be supplied from the preceding “how long”: How long will they desire? How long will they hate? They desired harmful things and hated knowledge because they followed the surface of the legal letter and refused to receive the mysteries of the Gospel, which were signified by that very letter.

**“Turn to my correction.”** Through the mouths of the apostles he reproved the Jews because they had refused to believe, and even then, after he had risen and ascended, he admonished them to turn.

**“Behold, I shall pour out my spirit to you,” etc.** “If,” he says, “you still neglect to turn, I shall pour out upon you the vengeance you deserve, and I shall show that the words I foretold concerning your destruction are true.”

He calls his spirit the power of vengeance, about which Moses said: “You sent your spirit, and the sea covered them” (Exodus 15). And in the book of blessed Job it is said that the wicked perished at God’s breath and were consumed by the spirit of his wrath (Job 4).

**“Because I called, and you refused.”** He said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matthew 11).

**“I stretched out my hand,” etc.** First by doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil; afterward, by suffering upon the cross.

**“You despised all my counsel.”** He said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3).

**“And you neglected my rebukes.”** He said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered” (Matthew 23). And, in general: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3).

**“But I shall laugh at your entrance,” etc.** The same is expressed in the psalm concerning these people: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them.” This does not mean that the Lord laughs with his lips or mocks with his nose. Rather, the force designated by this expression was given to the apostles, so that they might foresee that the ungodly could accomplish nothing whatever by their plots against him, above whom he himself permitted them to act; instead, they would foresee that all their undertakings would be brought to nothing, while his glory would be spread throughout the world after his Passion. Therefore, even when they saw the pride of the ungodly at its greatest strength, they were to despise it as nothing.

**“When what you feared comes upon you.”** They conferred with one another, saying: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11).

**“When sudden calamity rushes upon you,” etc.** He refers to the sudden siege of Jerusalem and the conquest of the entire province carried out by the Romans, which the Lord himself foretold in the Gospel when he saw the city and wept over it (Luke 19).

**“When tribulation comes upon you,” etc.** The Jews are not recorded as having called upon the Lord during that siege; rather, they trusted only in weapons, although they witnessed the desolation of their homeland and the ruin of the Temple with the bitterest anguish. If some of them did call upon him at that time, because they did not wish to understand the guilt for which they were punished and thus truly repent, they cried out in vain to the one whom they had despised.

Hence they are rightly said to have endured tribulation together with distress. Tribulation was in them because they were oppressed outwardly; distress lay in the fact that inwardly they found no consolation from God.

The saints, by contrast, when they are outwardly oppressed by adversities, are inwardly enlarged by a sure hope of salvation, knowing that they are heard by the one whose words they remember hearing as he commanded them. Therefore the prophet says: “When I called, you heard me, O God of my righteousness; in tribulation you enlarged me.”

This entire correction of Wisdom may also be understood generally of all the reprobate, because on the day of judgment they will cry out to the stern Judge, asking that the door of the kingdom be opened to them, yet they will not deserve to be heard. For what follows also clearly designates the time of the final examination: “They shall rise early and shall not find me.” At that time some will rise to eternal life, while others will rise to everlasting disgrace.

**“Because they hated discipline,” etc.** They are rightly deprived of salvation who not only fail to possess the fear of the Lord and discipline, the beginning of wisdom, but also pursue them with hatred. But the son of salvation says: “I hated the wicked, and I loved your law.”

**“Therefore they shall eat the fruits of their way.”** He calls their way the one of which he had said above: “For their feet run to evil.” Because, he says, they did not wish to enter my ways in order to live, they will receive the reward of their ways, so that they may perish forever.

But concerning those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways it is said: “You shall eat the fruits of your labors; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

**“And they shall be filled with their own counsels.”** Because they refused to yield to my counsel, by which I had determined to save them, they shall be filled with their own counsels—the counsels by which they said, “Let us hide snares against the innocent without cause,” and by which, instead of the Savior, they chose a robber for themselves, so that they might be ravaged by robbers and condemned among robbers.

This, like the other statements, may also be understood of all who despise the word of God.

**“The turning away of the simple shall kill them.”** He calls them “simple” not in age but in understanding. To them it was said above: “How long, you simple ones, will you love childishness?” They could have been not simple but perfect in understanding if they had not turned away their hearing from the counsel of Wisdom. By turning away, they were assigning themselves to eternal death.

**“And the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.”** When, without any adversity holding them back, they have accomplished in deed what they conceived when they said, “We shall find every precious substance,” then the turning away of the simple will kill them and the prosperity of fools will destroy them. For often a soul turned away from fear of the Creator suffers, because of the anger of that same just Creator, the appearance of enduring no adversity in the things it does wrong.

But, as blessed Job says: “Let him spend his days in good things, and in a moment let him descend to the underworld” (Job 21).

**“But whoever hears me,” etc.** This may be understood both in the present life and in the future. For whoever serves the Lord perfectly is frightened by no adversities; rather, he rejoices in adversities, and even in death itself he rejoices as though entering into life. With the assistance of the grace of the Holy Spirit, he always carries a breast quiet and free from superfluous thoughts and the disturbances of temptations, which the rest of the seventh day mystically signified in the Law.

When he has passed from this world, he will likewise rest not only without fear of evils but also in great joy at the resurrection he hopes for, like Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom.

**“And shall enjoy abundance,” etc.** In the present life, abundance consists in good works, once the fear even of those who kill the body has been removed; then it will consist in an abundance of joys as a reward.
