For how great is the abundance of all good things there, where one may behold the glory of him from whom all good things come, with the fear of everything that could thereafter bring adversity completely removed!

### Chapter Two
My son, if you receive my words, etc. He hides [Col. 0945C] God’s commandments with himself who, hearing them, stores them carefully in his heart, in accordance with the one who says: “I have hidden your utterances in my heart, that I may not sin against you.” For we must take the greatest care lest, according to the Gospel parable, demons carry these away from us like seed cast beside the road and snatched up by birds.

—So that your ear may hear wisdom. A person is shown not to hear wisdom with the ear who, perceiving God’s words only through the bodily sense of hearing, refuses to retain them in his memory so as to put them into practice. If, therefore, you receive God’s commandments with a fixed desire to learn and preserve them, first keep to the way of humility. This is what is added next:

—Incline your heart to know prudence. To incline is to humble the heart so that it may know prudence, and to cleanse the heart so that it may become worthy of receiving the mysteries of truth [Col. 0945D]. Hence the same Wisdom, speaking to the Father, says: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI; Luke X)—that is, “You have hidden them from the proud and revealed them to the humble.”

—For if you call upon wisdom, etc. We ought to call upon no one— that is, summon no one to us through prayer—except God. When, therefore, he teaches that wisdom must be invoked, he plainly shows that he is proposing for us to attain not just any wisdom, that is, knowledge of heavenly or earthly things, but the very knowledge of the Godhead. For in the apprehension of this wisdom lies the highest apprehension of blessedness, as Wisdom herself testifies when she intercedes with the Father for us: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true [Col. 0946A] God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

It should be noted that he urges us both to invoke wisdom and to incline our own hearts toward knowing prudence, because it is plainly necessary both to implore divine assistance in everything and, with the Lord himself helping us, to do the good that we are able to do. For we can do nothing without him; yet, without some effort of our own, however small, we should not suppose that we can be saved by him.

—If you seek her as money, etc. If you seek wisdom with as much care as the greedy seek money—or certainly if you seek wisdom itself so earnestly, as though through it you were going to acquire boundless and ineffable riches—you will receive the rewards that are explained below. Whoever digs out treasures casts away the earthly rubble, makes a deep [Col. 0946B] pit, and diligently persists in his labor until he reaches the treasures he seeks. Likewise, whoever desires to find the treasures of wisdom must purge whatever earthly thing he discovers within himself, cut away carnal enticements, make within himself a pit of humility, and not cease from action before he recognizes that he has found the way of truth.

—Then you will understand the fear of the Lord, etc. If you seek with an attentive heart, you will attain experience of the Lord’s lovable fear, which in this life is not only the beginning but also the perfection of heavenly wisdom. Therefore perfect love does not cast it out (1 John IV), but makes it remain forever and ever. You will also find knowledge of his divinity, which makes one blessed forever.

—For the Lord gives wisdom. This verse refers to what he said [Col. 0946C] above: “For if you call upon wisdom,” and so forth, until he says, “And you will find knowledge of God.” Wisdom—that is, the Lord—is to be invoked in order to receive wisdom because wisdom cannot be possessed from ourselves, but is given by the Lord. Let Pelagius be silent, refuted by the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. IV). And the Apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God” (James I).

—And from his mouth come wisdom and prudence. In this verse one may understand the ineffable and coeternal birth of Wisdom from God the Father, of which she also says elsewhere: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn” (Ecclus. XXIV). The Lord’s mouth may also be understood as his saints; hence it is often said in the prophets, “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken [Col. 0946D].” “And from his mouth come knowledge and prudence”: unless he himself sanctifies the human mouth, unless he graciously makes it his own, it cannot speak perfect wisdom in any way.

—He will guard the salvation of the upright, etc. Uprightness and simplicity are kindred virtues and cannot be separated from one another. Hence wisdom does not seek one of them without the other; rather, wherever both are found together, it guards and protects those people. Thus it is said of blessed Job that “that man was simple and upright” (Job I): simple through the innocence of gentleness, upright through the caution of discernment. Simple, because he desired to harm no one, but rather to benefit everyone; upright, because he allowed himself to be corrupted by no one.

—Preserving the paths of justice, etc. By “the ways of the saints” he means God’s general commandments; by “the paths of justice,” the stricter practices of heavenly [Col. 0947A] life, which are accessible only to the perfect. Wisdom preserves both, so that at whatever level of virtue they may be found, she may assist the upright and the simple.

—Counsel will guard you, etc. “The evil way” means wicked deeds; “a man speaking perversely” means teachers of wicked conduct. “The evil way” is the way into which those who say, “Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood,” invite others. “The one speaking perversely” signifies the author of this persuasion.

—Those who abandon the straight path, etc. He beautifully set dark ways against the straight path, because the course of right action is carried out in the light and leads to the joys of the heavenly light. But, as the Lord says: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John III). Such a person meets his end in outward darkness.

—Those who rejoice [Col. 0947B] when they have done evil, etc. Those who do evil exult because they walk through dark ways and do not know where they are going. If they saw that they were heading toward punishments, they would certainly restrain their steps and chastise their harmful joy with saving tears.

—So that you may be delivered from the foreign woman, etc. This verse depends on what came before, where it had been said, “Prudence will preserve you.” The meaning is: Prudence will preserve you so that you may be delivered from the foreign woman. Since Solomon had first warned his hearer, whom he was striving to teach wisdom, not to join himself to robbers, and, if he saw a thief, not to run together with him, but to walk uprightly and simply, he now warns him not to place his portion among adulterers.

This may also be understood specifically [Col. 0947C] of those concerning whom it was said above, “So that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the man who speaks perversely,” for what speech is more perverse than persuasion to sexual immorality? This chapter begins at the place where he says: “My son, if you receive my words and hide my commandments with yourself.”

The foreign woman may also be understood as the depravity of heretics, alienated from the members of Christ and the Church, which is accustomed to deceive the hearts of the innocent through the softness of eloquence and the blandishments of speech. Hence the Psalmist says: “They have softened their words more than oil, yet they are darts.”

—And she has abandoned the guide of her youth, etc. This is clear concerning the adulteress, because she abandons her first husband and forgets the covenant of her God—namely, the covenant which, with God as witness, she made with her husband at the time of marriage, that they would preserve faithfulness to one another.

It is also clear concerning the heretical mind, because it abandons the teacher from whom [Col. 0947D] it had learned the faith of the Church and forgets the covenant of its God—that is, the faith of the Lord contained in the Creed, which it had promised on the day of baptism that it would preserve.

—For her house has inclined toward death, etc. The whole manner of life of the adulteress leads to destruction, and although it may appear gentle and mild, in the end she will suffer no lighter vengeance than those who serve open impiety through robbery. The adulteress’s house may also be understood as her flesh, beneath which she subjects herself to shame and lust; at the time of the final judgment it will rise not to life but to everlasting death.

The house of heretics, too, because it is built upon sand, tends toward collapse even when it appears to stand. Through its own growths, as through various paths, it advances toward the fellowship of the impious—that is, toward the torments [Col. 0948A] of evil spirits.

—All who enter to her do not return, etc. By “to her” he means “to death,” not “to the woman.” For one who has joined himself to an adulteress can, with the Lord’s help, return and obtain life through repentance; and one who has been defiled by heresy can, by recovering his senses, return to salvation. But whoever has once been seized by eternal death will never return to the way by which he might seek the life of the blessed.

This is directed especially against the Origenists, who promise heretics, prostitutes, and every crowd of the dissolute—and even the devil himself and his angels—that after innumerable ages, once the universal judgment has been completed, they will receive remission of sins, life, and a kingdom in heaven. They badly understand the words of Isaiah: “And they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited” (Isa. XXIV). They act as though he had said that the impious would be released and saved after the long period of judgment had [Col. 0948B] ended. On the contrary, he grants them no salvation, but signifies only that those who have died in this time and, because of the enormity of their crimes, deserve to be shut up in the prison of punishments will be visited for a short time at the resurrection, so that, once they have received their bodies, they may be condemned more severely at the judgment and, immediately after the judgment, be confined forever in still harsher punishments.

The words may also rightly be understood in this way: “All who enter to her,” that is, to the prostitute or to her house, “will not return,” because, insofar as human nature has been corrupted by its own wicked will, it has no return by itself; it returns only through the grace of God, by which it is helped and restored so that it may grasp the paths of life. This saying, therefore, indicates the weight of iniquity, so that when [Col. 0948C] someone returns, he may not attribute it to himself but to the grace of God—not from works, lest he should boast.

—So that you may walk in the good way, etc. By “the good way” he means the unity of right faith, of which the Lord says, “I am the way” (John XIV), and again, “No one can come to the Father except through me” (ibid.). By “the paths of the righteous” he names the many examples of the saints. This verse depends upon what was said above: “Prudence will preserve you,” just as does the statement, “So that you may be delivered from the foreign woman.”

—For the upright will dwell in the land, etc. Here too he joins the upright with the simple, just as above when he said: “He will guard the salvation of the upright and protect those who walk simply.” Simplicity without uprightness is lax and foolish, while uprightness without simplicity is [Col. 0948D] severe and harsh; but the two virtues joined together make a perfect person.

There is, however, a difference between the two verses: in the first, the Lord is shown to assist the righteous while they struggle in the present; in the second, to crown them as victors in the future. The name “land” designates the Church, which habitually brings forth spiritual fruit for God. The righteous dwell and remain in it because not even death separates them from its fellowship; when this life has ended, they reach that part of it which reigns with Christ in heaven.

—But the impious will be destroyed from the land, etc. These words may be understood not as spoken generally of all the reprobate, but specifically of those who seem to belong to the Lord’s land—that is, the Church—and yet, because their merits demand it, will be removed from it. Some are removed openly by the judgment of the [Col. 0949A] Church, such as Simon, Arius, and Porphyry; others secretly by the judgment of the invisible Judge, including countless people who also appear good to human beings.

He calls the openly impious “apostates,” but calls all who act wickedly those who, having received the sacraments of faith, in some way degenerate from its purity. Both groups will be destroyed in the future retribution from the land of the living, because “the wicked shall not dwell near the Lord, nor shall the unjust remain before his eyes.”

And rightly so: since he had said much about the ways of the good and the wicked, he added at the conclusion what would be the end of both, just as in the preceding parable, in which he forbade association with robbers. Of the end of the wicked he said: “The prosperity of fools will destroy them”; of the end of the good: “But whoever listens to me will rest without fear.”

The verses we have most recently [Col. 0949B] discussed may be understood with reference to the ancient people of God: when they lived rightly, they remained happily in their land; but when they sinned, they were driven out by their enemies.

## CHAPTER III

My son, do not forget my law, etc. Here he teaches that we must devote ourselves to works of mercy and must not rely on our own strength, but must implore help from God. He arranges all these matters in a sufficiently fitting order: after restraining the person he had undertaken to instruct from cruelty, and after correcting him concerning lust, he adorns him with good deeds.

—For length of days and years of life, etc. So that the hearer would not be disturbed by the burden of keeping the commandments, he first set forth definite rewards and then enumerated the commandments. By “length of days” he signifies everlasting light; by “years of life,” passage beyond this [Col. 0949C] mortality; by “increase of peace,” the very state of blessedness attained. Concerning this Isaiah says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. IX).

It was also granted to the earlier people of God, and is granted in the present, that when they obeyed God’s law they might live for a long time in peaceful rest.

—Let mercy and truth not abandon you. Let truth, which must be spoken, never depart from your mouth; let mercy, which must be shown to your neighbors, never depart from your deeds. Thus it comes about that God’s mercy and truth always accompany you: mercy, by which he wipes away your sins; truth, by which he fulfills his promises.

—Bind them around your throat, etc. By “the throat,” the organ of the voice, and by “the tablets of the heart,” he suggests the breadth of thought. Therefore let the virtue of mercy [Col. 0949D] and truth be fixed at the root of the mind, and let it be brought forth by the voice of the speaker, so that both the hidden intentions may please God, the hidden observer who alone searches hearts and reins, and the neighbors may be helped by the service of speech.

He rightly teaches that the virtues should be bound around the throat, although the voice of the speaker is usually produced within the throat, because the voice of preaching proceeds from inward things but extends outward, spreading over many hearers at once. For insofar as it arouses others to live well, it also teaches them to do good, and the hearers should read the preacher’s deeds, lest his action fall short of his speech and his life contradict his voice.

—And you will find grace and good discipline, etc. A person finds grace and good discipline before God when, through continual practice of the virtues, he continually earns the Lord’s favor, so that day by day he becomes more perfect and better than himself. He also finds grace and good discipline [Col. 0950A] before human beings when his works are of such a kind that he is rightly praised and at the same time offers his neighbors an example of living.

—Trust in the Lord with all your heart, etc. Do not fear that, because of your own weakness, you cannot keep the divine commandments; nor imagine that you can fulfill them by your own strength or know them through your natural understanding unless you are instructed by his law. Rather, seek his frequent help both in learning and in acting, and he himself, in his mercy, will grant you the ability to fulfill what he has commanded.

—Do not be wise in your own eyes. It may seem to someone that this is the same commandment as the one stated earlier, “Do not rely on your own prudence,” but there is a great difference. A person relies on his own prudence when he places before the decrees [Col. 0950B] of the fathers those things which seem to him ought to be done or said. But a person is wise in his own eyes when, in matters that he was able to understand correctly through the teaching of the fathers, he exalts himself above others as though he were more learned.

He next shows what true human wisdom is:

—Fear the Lord, etc. As it is written in Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job XXVIII). All who are perfect ought to restrain themselves from every evil in such a way that they continually remember, with fear, the presence of the divine majesty.

It should be noted that above he urged us to trust in the Lord with all our heart and not to rely on our own prudence, while here, conversely, he urges us with equal concern to fear God. There is no contradiction. There he strengthens the minds of the weak, so that they may not despair, by promising God’s help; here he restrains the stronger, so that they may not presume upon themselves, by recalling the fear of [Col. 0950C] God.

—For it will be health to your navel, etc. By “the bones” he signifies the solid works of virtue; by “the navel,” which is in the middle of the body’s inner region, he signifies the still weak and imperfect action of the good. If, therefore, you fear God and, trusting not in your own strength but in heavenly protection, strive to abstain from evil, there will be health for your navel and refreshment for your bones. Through these things the weakness of your works grows strong toward perfection, and your stronger deeds receive from them the means by which they may be strengthened further.

—Honor the Lord from your substance, etc. Many give much to the poor, but from another person’s substance and from crops which they had seized by force or fraud. Many give from what is their own, but do not honor the Lord by giving, because they do so for human approval and not from love of the heavenly [Col. 0950D] Observer.

Whoever, therefore, desires almsgiving to become a fruitful benefit for himself should give both from his own possessions and in honor of the Creator, who in his gracious kindness has deigned to bestow abundance, so that human beings—who are his creation and made in his image—may be refreshed, and we may be found to be his true and faithful stewards of his goods.

It should also be noted that we are commanded to honor God not only from the substance of money that we extend to the poor, but also from the substance or fruits of every good work that we perform and of all the heavenly grace that we receive. That is, in everything we are to seek his praise, not our own.

The person also honors the Lord from his substance and from the firstfruits of his crops who attributes everything good that he [Col. 0951A] does not to his own strength and merits, but to heavenly grace, remembering the saying: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

—And your granaries will be filled with abundance, etc. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Luke XII). If the righteous can have treasures in heaven, because they find true riches there, then they can certainly have granaries and winepresses there as well, because they will hunger and thirst no more.

“And your granaries will be filled with abundance.” “For I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI). The winepresses will overflow with wine because the inward sweetness of eternal things kindles the hearts of all the faithful in praise of their Creator. Hence he says: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII).

In the present life as well, the Lord sometimes grants a teacher, who ministers the bread of the word and the cup of grace [Col. 0951B] spiritual to the needy, greater gifts for ministering as his reward. The one who distributes earthly support to the poor is made richer by giving and is repaid with heavenly recompense.

—My son, do not reject the Lord’s discipline or grow faint, etc. Some serve the Lord in prosperity but fall away in adversity. Therefore Wisdom, having taught the person to live well in prosperity, also urges him not to fail under correction, lest, when weakness, poverty, or human persecution comes upon him, he lose the devotion that he seemed to preserve in tranquility.

—For whom the Lord loves, he corrects, etc. The less we ought to murmur against the scourging by which we are disciplined, the more certainly we hold in it the pledge of paternal love. Hence he himself also says: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. [Col. 0951C] III).

It should be noted that for this saying the translators of the Septuagint gave: “But he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). It is remarkable why the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews in Hebrew, preferred to follow that wording.

—Blessed is the person who finds wisdom, etc. Since he was consoling those placed under discipline and correction, he adds to what he had begun, indicating that true human blessedness consists not in being free from adversities in the present, but in rejoicing in the perception of eternal wisdom. This means knowing God’s will in the present life and enjoying his vision in the future.

It is fitting that after saying, “Blessed is the person who finds wisdom,” he immediately added, “And the one who abounds in prudence.” For there are some who find wisdom by receiving the teaching of [Col. 0951D] truth with the ear, but neglect to abound in prudence because they are unwilling to enlarge their heart’s chamber so as to receive its fullness.

—Her acquisition is better, etc. Whoever has acquired the riches of wisdom need not fear correction through poverty, because the heavenly gift incomparably surpasses earthly treasures.

—Her first and purest fruits. If, according to Ecclesiasticus, the root of wisdom is the fear of God, what are the fruits of wisdom except seeing God? They are “first and purest,” either because God, who exists from the beginning, is seen and nothing defiled enters into his vision; or because the human being was created first for contemplating him.

Thus the younger son, although he had squandered all his substance by living luxuriously, is nevertheless said to have received his first robe when he returned penitently [Col. 0952A] to his father (Luke XV). Or they are first and purest because raw and unworked gold is usually the purest, and our first blessedness alone is truly to be called blessedness—the blessedness that the Lord promises to restore to us more perfectly in the resurrection.

—She is more precious than all riches, etc. Not only earthly riches, but even heavenly riches—and indeed the very sight of the angels—are surpassed by the splendor of this wisdom. Hence the prophet says: “What remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” and so forth to the end of the psalm (Ps. LXXII).

—Length of days is in her right hand, etc. By the vision of his divinity he grants the elect perpetual light, and in the present life he enlightens and strengthens them through the mysteries and gifts of his incarnation. To those who, for his sake, [Col. 0952B] sell all that they possess in order to acquire him, he gives a hundredfold in this time and, in the age to come, eternal life.

At this point, according to the ancient translation, there follows a passage that our manuscripts do not contain:

> From his mouth proceeds righteousness;  
> he bears law and mercy upon his tongue.

I thought this ought to be noted because these verses are often found inserted in the works of the Fathers.

—Her ways are beautiful ways, etc. His actions and teachings contained in the Gospels are beautiful because they are divine and pure, far surpassing human measure, and all his commandments lead to eternal peace. Everything he did in the flesh pertains to reconciling mortals to God, making the human race peaceful with the angels, and showing his own people examples [Col. 0952C] of preserving peace and love toward one another.

—She is a tree of life to those who possess her, etc. Just as Moses testifies that the tree of life was placed in the middle of paradise, so the Church is given life through the wisdom of God, namely Christ. Through the sacraments of his flesh and blood she now receives the pledge of life, and in the future she will be blessed by the sight of his presence.

—The Lord founded the earth by wisdom, etc. God the Father created all things through the Son. In a figurative sense, he founded the earth by wisdom when, through him, he established the holy Church in the firmness of faith; he established the heavens by prudence when, through that same one, he enlightened the exalted hearts of preachers.

—By his wisdom the abysses burst forth. This refers either to the time when, in the days of Noah, all the springs of the great abyss were broken open, or to the daily course by which springs and rivers flow from the abyss through the [Col. 0952D] veins of the earth.

Alternatively, “By wisdom the abysses burst forth” when, through the generosity of Christ’s grace, the depths of the heavenly mysteries become known to the faithful.

—And the clouds grow thick with dew. This is clear according to the literal sense. Allegorically, however, the clouds are the teachers of the Churches, exalted through contemplation and life, watering the hearts of their hearers through instruction as though they were the earth placed beneath them. They grow thick with dew because, with the most refined discernment, they examine their virtues—what may benefit others, what may lead them to seek higher things, and what they should show as an example to those of lesser ability.

—My son, do not let these things slip from your eyes. Take care lest, wearied by temporal discipline, you lose the grace of wisdom, which is so great.

—Keep the law and counsel. The law of wisdom is expressed when he says: “If you wish to enter into life, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, [Col. 0953A] you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth (Mark X). The counsel of wisdom is expressed when he immediately adds: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have,” etc. (ibid.).

—And it will be life to your soul. Your soul has life with God if you keep his decrees, even though the flesh is weighed down by the discipline of correction or even by death.

—And grace to your throat. “How sweet are your utterances to my throat,” the psalm says (Ps. CXVIII). The mind’s senses therefore have their own throat, by which they judge the words they hear and examine through discernment the deeds and affairs of individuals that they observe, embracing some and rejecting others.

When we keep the law and counsel of the Lord with these throats, grace is multiplied, because the more diligently [Col. 0953B] someone obeys the divine commands, the more sweetly he conceives love for God. The Psalmist desired grace to be present in our throats when he said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII).

—Then you will walk confidently in your way. We walk confidently in our way when, trusting in God’s grace, we make progress in our good manner of life. If we humbly submit to his commands and attain the taste of heavenly love more sweetly in the throat of the mind, we will always obtain an increase of good action. In temptations too, with his help, we are defended so that we do not fail.

This is what follows:

—And your foot will not stumble. “For all things work together for good for those who love God.”

—If you sleep, you will not fear, etc. This is clear [Col. 0953C] according to the literal sense: the person who remembers that he lives innocently and justly before God sleeps and keeps watch, rests and walks, in security. The righteous person, when he sleeps in death, not only fears no power of the evil spirits, but also rests in peace and safely awaits the day of resurrection, because he has God everywhere as his protector and guardian. So it is in the psalm: “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Ps. XXII).

—Do not prevent doing good to one who is able, etc. Since above he had carefully urged that the law and counsel of the Lord be observed and had promised eternal rest to those who observed them, he now repeats in various ways what must be observed. First, returning to what he had interrupted, he teaches that mercy must be shown to one’s neighbor and that one must live justly with [Col. 0953D] him; then he warns that one must also beware of the enemy.

“Do not,” he says, “prevent doing good to one who is able. If you are able, do good yourself.” Do not hear the Lord say to you, together with the Pharisees: “You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke XI).

—Do not say to your friend, “Go and come back,” etc. This command is given not only concerning someone who asks for a monetary alms, so that we may be willing and ready to give, but also concerning all Christ’s commandments. When he says, “You are my friends,” we are commanded to do them immediately and not postpone them until tomorrow.

—Do not contend without cause against a person, etc. He does not forbid contending against someone who does wrong in order to correct him, because what a definite necessity compels us [Col. 0954A] to do is not done without cause. Indeed, the one who says, “If your brother sins, rebuke him” (Luke XVII), wants you to strive, insofar as you are able, to recall the person who has gone astray to the way of truth.

—For every mocker is an abomination to the Lord. “Every mocker,” he says, because a mocker is one who either scorns fulfilling the words of God that he knows or corrupts them by interpreting and teaching them perversely. A mocker is also one who despises his promises as though they were insignificant and regards the severity of his anger as though it could easily be endured; likewise, one who wickedly insults the simplicity or poverty of his neighbors. Therefore divine justice rightly abhors every such mocker.

He rightly adds:

—And with the simple is his conversation. The proud often mock the simple and, while doing so, judge themselves wiser than those whom they ridicule. But their [Col. 0954B] wisdom, as James says, is “earthly, natural, demonic” (James III). The Lord’s conversation is with the simple because he illumines with the secrets of heavenly wisdom those whom he sees to possess none of earthly arrogance. Hence he says: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Mark XI; Luke X).

—Poverty comes from the Lord upon the house of the wicked. This may be understood from the example of the rich man dressed in purple, who lacked spiritual goods in this life and in the future came into such poverty that he asked for a single drop of water from the finger of Lazarus, once a poor man, and did not deserve to receive it (Luke XVI).

—But the tents of the righteous will be blessed. As the Apostle says to the faithful, speaking of God: “He has blessed us with every spiritual [Col. 0954C] blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. I). They will also hear from him at the time of recompense: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV).

According to the literal sense as well, it often happens that those who seize the possessions of others for a long time are finally consumed by poverty, while those who distribute what is their own abound even in earthly goods.

—He himself will mock the mockers, etc. The Apostles James and Peter, according to the ancient translation, placed these verses in their writings, saying: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV; 1 Pet. V).

—The wise will possess glory, etc. The Lord also says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV and XVIII).

## CHAPTER IV
Listen, my son, to the discipline of your father, etc. Here, as he is about to exhort him to philosophy, he explains how he himself was taught wisdom by his father. [Col. 0954D]

For I too was my father’s son, tender, etc. Nothing raises the mind more toward hope of attaining wisdom than remembering that those whom we now admire as already illustrious in wisdom were once themselves small and unlearned. “And he taught me and said: Let your heart receive my words.” David, Solomon’s father, gave such admonitions to Solomon, as one who has reread the *Books of Chronicles* discovers. But why does Solomon call himself an only child before his mother, when Scripture testifies that a brother born of the same mother preceded him, unless it is because that child, born without a name, died soon afterward as though he had never existed?

And in all your possessions acquire prudence. In all the good things you possess, remember to act wisely; or, “in all your possessions acquire prudence.” Despise everything earthly that you possess, provided that you attain wisdom. Solomon himself did this when, given a choice, he preferred love of wisdom to all other things (III Kings III); and in the Gospel, the man who sought the precious pearl, once he had found it, sold everything he possessed and bought it (Matt. XIII).

He will give increases of grace to your head, etc. This is clear in the case of Solomon: because he despised everything for the sake of wisdom, once wisdom had been received he shone with a still greater elevation of glory. But also for our head—that is, for the ruling faculty of the mind—if it embraces wisdom, the greater grace of the Spirit is increased, and, in addition, the crown of life will be given in the future. Having set out what he had received as words from his father, he returns to teaching his hearer the wisdom with which he had begun.

Listen, my son, and receive my words, etc. That is, so that you may receive the gifts of eternal life.

I will lead you along the paths of righteousness, etc. The paths—that is, the actions—of righteousness seem narrow and confined when they are first begun; but when they make progress, they already seem spacious and broad through habit. The Psalmist bears witness to this: when, at the beginning, he said to the Lord, “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. XVI), later, as he progressed, he sang, “I ran along the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. CXVIII). Therefore, when you begin to enter the paths of righteousness, they seem narrow to you; yet, once you have entered them, the steps of your mind will not be confined. Rather, you will find what the Lord says: “His yoke is easy and his burden light” (Matt. XI). Indeed, the reprobate enter upon the broad way in this life, but on the last day they will be cast, with hands and feet bound, into darkness (Matt. XXII); whereas the feet of the elect will be directed into the way of peace.

And when you run, you will not have a stumbling block. The more eagerly you run to fulfill God’s commandments, the less you will fear the adversities that might impede you. For all who toil in wicked action encounter a stumbling block in the middle of their course, because, while they do not foresee it, they are suddenly carried away to punishment.

They eat the bread of wickedness, etc. By their wicked deeds, the unrighteous take delight in crimes as though in dishes set before them. Or certainly they drink the wine of the condemned, and rejoice in taking away ears of grain from the hungry, as Holy Scripture testifies is the custom of the wicked.

But the path of the righteous proceeds like shining light, etc. The works of the righteous are performed in the light of knowledge and lead to eternal life, which is the perfect day.

The way of the wicked is dark, etc. The apostle John also says of them: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him; but whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II). In contrast, the wise person is told above: “When you run, you will not have a stumbling block”—that is, a scandal.

With all vigilance guard your heart, etc. There are people who seem to live rightly in the eyes of men; but because they do not act with right intention, their life—which was believed to be good—is rejected by God, who sees what is crooked. Therefore, with every diligence guard the purity of your heart, because the standard of your life will be judged according to its examination.

Remove from yourself a perverse mouth, etc. This should be understood in two ways: guard your own mouth, so that it does not say anything perverse, and your lips, so that they do not become accustomed to slander; and flee from others whom you know to be subject to this vice, lest they corrupt you.

Let your eyes see what is right, etc. Carefully learn the way of justice on which you ought to enter, and in everything you intend to do, diligently foresee the end toward which it will come. This is what it means for the eyelids of your seeing eyes to precede your steps: to anticipate by careful thought the good work you are about to do, and, by meditation, to foresee that it is according to God’s will.

Direct your path with your feet. So that you may not go astray either in your actions or in the faith. And all your ways will be made firm. So that you may not be moved from your good purpose by fickleness of mind. Hence the Apostle also says: “Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding more fully in the work of the Lord” (I Cor. III).

Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. The right way is understood as the good way, and the left as the way of the reprobate. We are therefore forbidden not to walk on the right way, but to turn aside toward the right. He turns aside to the left who is unjust; he turns aside toward the right who wants to claim for himself what belongs to the just; he turns aside toward the right who presumes upon his own strength; he turns aside to the left who, because of his weakness, despairs of being able to be saved; he turns aside to the left who serves folly; he turns aside toward the right who wants to be wiser than he ought to be. The same understanding applies to the other virtues and vices.

Turn your foot away from evil. That is, do not deviate from what is straight either this way or that, because virtues require discernment, and every excess is a vice.

For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right. That is, he has chosen them, and they please him. Therefore he will say to those whom he rejects and condemns, “I do not know you” (Matt. VII), which is to say, “I have not chosen you; you do not please me.”

But he himself will make your steps straight, etc. If you turn your foot away from evil, and if, with the Lord’s help, you strive to do the good things I have taught, he himself will be favorably present to your efforts, so that both now you may walk rightly and then be able to reach everlasting peace.

## CHAPTER V

My son, attend to my wisdom, etc. Up to this point he had corrected his hearer in general terms; here, under the figure of a prostitute, he forbids the wickedness of heretics.

So that you may guard your thoughts, etc. The thoughts by which you believe rightly; the lips by which you profess that faith in simple, customary, and ecclesiastical words. But literally: whoever clings to a prostitute also defiles his lips or mouth, whether by kissing or by speaking shameful things.

For the lips of a prostitute drip with honey. When, in the mouths of heretics, the sweetness of eloquence sounds not merely sufficiently but excessively, falsehood, because it is seen to be skillfully expressed, is consequently judged by fools to be truth.

And her throat is smoother than oil. Catholic faith is consecrated by the oil of the Holy Spirit; those who prefer their own opinion to the faith of the Fathers display their throat as smoother than oil. The literal meaning concerning the prostitute is clear, since she seeks both sweetness of speech and bodily beauty in order to capture the wretched.

But her end is bitter, etc. A draught of wormwood grows bitter within the bowels, while outside the limbs are struck by the sword. Thus, to show that the wicked at the final vengeance will be filled inwardly and surrounded outwardly by everlasting punishments, he affirms that they will be tormented by the bitterness of wormwood and slaughtered by the sword. But why is that sword called two-edged? The Lord explains when he says: “Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X).

Her thoughts are wandering, etc. The thoughts of heretical deception are wandering, because some deny that Christ is God, while others deny that he is human; some deny that he assumed flesh, others that he assumed a soul; some forbid confessing that he was born of a virgin, others the Holy Spirit, others the Father as God, and others that forgiveness should be granted to penitents. This plague spreads into so many innumerable paths that it is impossible to investigate completely how many there are. Catholic truth, however, is neither wandering nor unsearchable, because throughout the whole world it is acknowledged as one and the same by all the faithful.

Keep your life far from her, etc. The Apostle also says, “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI). For the first remedy for this vice is plainly to remain far from those whose presence either entices one toward vice or cooperates in it. It is likewise beneficial for weaker hearers to be entirely separated from listening to heretics.

Do not give your honor to strangers, etc. Do not subject the honor by which you were created in the image of God to the will of unclean spirits, nor spend, at the adversary’s pleasure, the allotted span of life you have received. For whoever is subjected to any crime thereby surrenders dominion over himself to the malign spirits.

Lest strangers be filled with your strength, etc. Do not assist the deeds of demons by applying either the intelligence of your mind or the powers of your body to the commission of crimes; and do not increase another’s house—that is, the number of the lost—by adding yourself to it. He aptly says, “Let your labors be in another’s house,” because there are those who, according to the prophet, labor in order to act wickedly. And if only it were hidden how much labor heretics have undertaken against the Church.

And you groan at the end, etc. “Lest perhaps” should be supplied from what precedes. The sense is: Keep yourself chaste for this reason, lest you be forced to groan amid punishments when not only bodily attractions have passed away, but, once the body itself has been abandoned, the soul—which acted through the body—is compelled to render an account of everything. Yet in this life it often happens that those who, living luxuriously in youth, have squandered their possessions waste away in poverty in old age. When the heat of the flesh has cooled and the flower of youth has withered, they see others using the possessions they had sold for their wantonness, and in their groaning they say, with tardy repentance, what follows:

Why did I hate discipline? etc. By “discipline” he means the faith of the Church; by “reproofs,” the rebukes by which heretics are admonished concerning why they have withdrawn from the Church. The literal meaning concerning fornicators is also clear.

I was almost in every evil, etc. *Ecclesia* and *Synagoga* are Greek names that signify one and the same thing in Latin, namely, an assembly of many people together. If they are distinguished more precisely, *ecclesia* means “convocation,” while *synagoga* means “congregation.” In former times the people of God were called by both names. Now, however, for the sake of distinction, their assembly is called the Synagogue and ours the Church—rightly, on account of the greater faith and knowledge, since an irrational creature too can be gathered together. Thus God said, “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.” But only a rational and sentient creature can be summoned.

Yet these names sometimes signify assemblies of wicked people. Hence the words, “The fire blazed up in their synagogue” (Ps. CV), and, “I hated the church of the wicked” (Ps. XXV). Therefore, when the contemptuous person, repenting too late, says, “I was almost in every evil, in the midst of the Church and the synagogue,” it seems that, as the wretch weighs the magnitude of his damnation, he is saying that there was almost no crime in which he was not entangled, since he deserved to undergo such torments. And this was added to the accumulation of his misery: he was not the least among sinners, but rather stood in the middle, almost as their leader. Or certainly, although bodily present in the midst of the gatherings of the saints, he did not fear living a life alien to them. This should also be understood specifically of heretics, since they could not be recalled from error either by the words or by the examples of the ancient or the modern Fathers.

Drink water from your own cistern, etc. Enjoy the desire and services of your own wife, and cherish her with devoted care.

Let your springs flow out, etc. Give your son and daughter in marriage to others, and do this openly, with many people aware of it.

Keep them for yourself alone, etc. Retain alone within your power the kinds of marriages into which you join your children, and do not let fornicators or prostitutes share in your offspring.

Let your spring be blessed, etc. Preserve such temperance with the woman whom you took as a young man even when you grow old, so that you may deservedly obtain the blessing of faithful chastity in your offspring.

A most dear doe and a most pleasing fawn. Let that wife always be most dear to you who, like a doe pursuing serpents, pursues prostitutes and drives them from her own house. Let a son be born from her, himself a most serious lover of chastity.

Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, etc. He is not teaching that one should always devote oneself to marital intercourse; rather, he warns you neither to take another wife while the first is alive nor ever to join yourself to a prostitute.

Alternatively, by the words, “Drink water from your own cistern and the streams of your well,” he teaches that one must avoid heretics and attend to the guardianship and reading of the Scriptures. “Keep,” he says, “the knowledge that you preach to others yourself, and pour it out through the irrigation of your speech. Let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets.” Once you have kept it yourself, preach it also to others, and distribute the divine words among a great multitude of hearers, according to each person’s condition.

Keep them for yourself alone. We divide the waters in the streets and yet possess them alone when we pour our preaching widely in public, while having no desire whatsoever to gain human praise through it.

Let strangers not share in you. Unclean spirits share in a teacher if, while he is preaching, they corrupt his mind either through the pride of arrogance, through heresy, or through any other vice. But he alone possesses the waters when, faithfully joined to the members of the Church, he keeps himself free from the companionship of strangers.

Let your spring be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth. Let your teaching be blessed, and let all who are born from it be in the blessing of the Church; and rejoice with her to whom you have been joined from youth—that is, from the first time of believing.

A most dear doe and a most pleasing fawn; let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, and delight continually in her love. The most dear or most pleasing doe—as some books have it—is the holy Church, which habitually hates and crushes the serpent’s doctrine. The most pleasing fawn is the people, delightful through the variety of its virtues and always inflamed by the same zeal for chaste faith. We are intoxicated by her breasts when we are instructed against the frauds of heretics by the pages of both Testaments. To delight continually in her peace and love is a great opportunity for practicing the virtues.

Why are you seduced, my son, by a stranger? etc. This should be understood both of the prostitute and of heresy.

The Lord watches the ways of a person, etc. Let adulterers not think that they can be concealed by the darkness of night beside a wall, nor heretics that their schemes can be concealed, because darkness will not be darkened before the Lord, and night will be illumined like day.

His own iniquities capture the wicked, etc. There is a difference between a sinner and a wicked person. A sinner is anyone who falls into either small or great crimes; a wicked person is one who either never receives the faith or, through the enormity of his crimes, has been made accursed from the faith he received—such as heretics or Catholics entangled in notorious offenses. They are bound by the ropes of their sins and perish amid the continual increase of their depravity. For whoever makes a rope, by continually twisting it and wrapping thread around thread, increases it. Such is the strength of evil deeds; such are the books of heretics, in which they join perverse things to perverse things and, by writing nothing other than what binds them more tightly, carry out their work.

He himself will die because he did not possess discipline, etc. Since he had discussed much concerning adulterers or heretics, he shows at the conclusion, in his customary manner of narrating, what the end of such people is: namely, that they advance toward eternal death because they hated the discipline of life. He speaks of “the multitude of folly” when heretics claim to be wiser than the holy Fathers, or when the wicked, doing works of darkness, either think that the Lord does not see them or suppose that they can easily endure his anger.

## CHAPTER VI

My son, if you have become surety for your friend, etc. The literal sense is obvious: he advises the person who has become surety for a friend to warn that friend diligently, so that, once the money he owes the creditor has been repaid, he may free both himself and his friend. Allegorically, however, in this section he instructs the teacher; in the following section, he instructs anyone who is wandering, teaching each how he ought to conduct himself cautiously.

He says to the teacher: “If you have become surety for your friend, you have struck hands with a stranger.” This openly means: If you have accepted the soul of a brother into the danger of your way of life, you have already bound your mind to a care of vigilance that previously was absent.

You have been ensnared by the words of your mouth, etc. Since, by what has been entrusted to you, you are compelled to speak good things in preaching, you must first keep for yourself what you have said.

Do therefore what I say, my son, etc. Run, hurry, rouse your friend. Remember not only to keep watch by living well yourself, but also to separate through preaching the one placed under your authority from the body of sin.

Do not give sleep to your eyes, etc. He gives sleep to his eyes who completely neglects the care of his subordinates. He merely nods off who recognizes their blameworthy actions but, because of weariness of mind, does not correct them with the rebuke they deserve.

Rescue yourself like a doe from the hand, etc. As a doe seeks to escape from the hand of one who is trying to capture it, strive with all your strength so that, once your hearer has been soundly instructed, you yourself may be freed from the obligation arising from his life.

Or certainly, because the doe is an animal pure by nature, swift in running and extremely sharp in sight—for which reason in Greek it is called *dorcas* (δορκάς), from δέρκειν, “to see”—and because a bird is accustomed to seek the altar by flying: when you are occupied in teaching those under your authority, strive to be pure from all sins, energetic in good works, perceptive in detecting the plots of the wicked, and supported by the wings of virtues. Thus, when the work of preaching has been completed, you may deserve to fly to the heights and enter the pastures of heavenly life.

Go to the ant, O sluggard! etc. Here he exhorts anyone who is wandering that, if he is not sufficient to instruct others, he should at least not neglect to care for himself; and if he cannot learn the wisdom of teaching from a human being, he should learn from an ant the wisdom of working.

Although it has no leader, etc. If such a tiny creature, lacking a ruler and devoid of reason, foresees the future for itself under the guidance of nature, how much more ought you, created in the image of God, called to behold his glory, assisted by the teaching of teachers, and having the Creator himself as your guide, to gather in the present the fruits of good works by which you may live forever.

This life is compared to harvest and summer because now, amid the heat of temptations, it is the time for gathering the rewards of future good things. The day of judgment is likened to the cold of winter because then no opportunity remains for laboring for life; instead, each person is compelled to bring forth from the storehouse of his former conduct whatever he has stored there. Hence the Lord also commands, saying: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV). In winter the opportunity, and on the Sabbath the permission granted by the law, to gather the fruits of life and escape everlasting want is absent.

How long, O sluggard, will you sleep? etc. How long will you sleep in vices, when you can rise to do good, you who, weighed down by harmful torpor, always say, “Let me lie down a little longer, and afterward I will rise through repentance”? For when you are always postponing the good work, suddenly the Judge who observes your evil deeds is present. This is what follows:

And poverty will come upon you like a traveler, etc. Poverty and want are the final punishment, in which the condemned deserve none of the riches; they will come like a traveler because they are unforeseen and sudden, and like an armed man because they cannot be defeated permanently. The literal meaning is also clear: laziness is the nurse of poverty and want.

But if you are not sluggish, etc. The earthly fruits that we harvest are compared not to a spring but to a cistern, because they nourish the one who gathers them only for a time and fail in due season. But for the one who is not sluggish in laboring for heavenly riches, the harvest will come like a spring, because it will bring his reward for his labors to completion without failing.

And poverty will flee far from you. For, he says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.”

An apostate man, a worthless person, walks with a perverse mouth, etc. He had spoken of heresies and other kinds of vice; he had instructed the teacher and roused the sluggard, but now he rebukes the schismatic. Here it should be noted that the person whom he intended to describe as sowing quarrels he first called an apostate, because unless, after the manner of the proud angel, he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of the Creator through an aversion of mind, he would not afterward have come forth to sow quarrels.

He is rightly said to wink with his eyes, scrape with his foot, and speak with his finger. There is an interior guard that keeps the external members in order. Therefore, whoever has lost the stability of his mind flows outward into instability of movement and, through outward restlessness, reveals that he has no inner root.

There are six things that God hates, etc. He indicates by sowing discord the same thing that he had explained above more fully: how hateful it is to God. When the Lord speaks of his soul, he does so in human fashion, to signify that he hates such people with full and not superficial intent. The same appears in Isaiah: “My soul has hated your new moons and your feasts” (Isa. I).

Haughty eyes, a lying tongue, etc. He lists six capital crimes, yet sets them down as comparatively lesser in relation to the sower of discord, because the crime by which the unity and brotherhood joined together through the grace of the Holy Spirit are broken apart is plainly greater. Anyone may lift his eyes boastfully, lie with his tongue, defile himself with murder, plot evil against his neighbor, subject his members to other crimes, or give false testimony against someone. This should not be thought identical with what he calls above “a lying tongue.” For a lie can be told without being told against one’s neighbor. Blessed Augustine also teaches that there are eight kinds of lies in the book he composed *On Lying*. Anyone, I say, may inflict such evils either upon himself or upon others while the peace of the Church remains intact. But what Donatus and Arius and their followers did was more serious: by sowing discord they tore apart the harmony of fraternal unity.

Keep, my son, the commandments of your father, etc. Now, under the figure of an adulterous woman, he forbids listening to heresy.

Bind them continually upon your heart, etc. Keep the Lord’s commandments fixed in your thoughts, and fortify your speech on every side with the sweetness of these commandments, lest you stumble in your tongue.

When you walk, let them walk with you, etc. Let your meditation on the Lord’s law be so great that, when you have done anything while awake, you recall it attentively in your mind; when you wish to sleep, you rest in its remembrance; and when you wake, you first bring it back to mind. Thus it will happen that neither will you offend while awake nor will you be harmed by nocturnal fear.

Alternatively: When you walk in progress along the way of justice, let God’s commandments walk with you to instruct you; when you sleep in death, let them guard your soul so that the enemy may not snatch it away; and when you wake in the resurrection, speak with them by seeking the rewards that they had promised you if you kept them.

Do not be captured by her gestures. The literal meaning concerning the adulteress is clear. But although heretics may seem to live and act well, beware lest you be seduced by their doctrines.

For the price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread. Remember that the pleasure of fornication is brief, while the fornicator’s punishment is everlasting. Just as one loaf drives away only the day’s hunger, and afterward the person who left satiated after eating the bread becomes hungry again, so the one who enters a prostitute’s house dispels lust for an hour, but after a short time it returns more fiercely.

Can a person hide fire in his bosom, etc.? Only one who has been so firmly established in the Catholic faith that he cannot be separated from it by the sweetness or cunning of words is permitted to read the books of heretics.

The guilt is not great when someone has stolen, etc. Theft is said not to be a great guilt not in itself but by comparison with the greater sin—that is, adultery. So Jerusalem, which sinned more gravely, is told: “Sodom has been justified in comparison with you”; not because Sodom sinned nothing or little, but because Jerusalem sinned more.

For the jealousy and fury of a husband will not spare on the day of vengeance, etc. This is also to be understood of the Lord: although he now spares the reprobate, he will not spare them on the day of death. He will not heed the prayers of those who cry out to him too late, nor will he accept gifts, since there will then be neither time nor opportunity for them. He is jealous when someone presumes to corrupt his bride—that is, the Church—or any faithful soul.

## CHAPTER VII

My son, keep my words, etc. This section too concerns the same matter that above is explained more fully under the person of a prostitute.

And my law as the apple of your eye. Guard what I teach with such care as though you were unable to see anything right without it.

Bind it upon your fingers, etc. By “fingers” he means actions; by “the tablets of your heart,” the breadth of your thought. Indeed, another translation says: “Write it upon the breadth of your heart.”

Say to wisdom, “You are my sister,” etc. Join the wisdom of ecclesiastical teaching to yourself with sisterly affection, so that it may preserve you from heretical pollution, which is shown to be alien to the chastity of the Church.

For from the window of my house, through the lattice, I looked out, etc. Solomon appropriately says that he looked out from the window of his house through a lattice in order to judge the actions of the immature. For one who looks through a lattice from a window is indeed able to consider fully what is happening outside, but those who are outside cannot see the person who is reading within. This is what the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

“From the window,” therefore, and so forth. The literal meaning is clear: the gaze of wise teachers carefully observes the actions of the weak and the strong; but the eternal Wisdom of God looks down from heaven and sees all the sons of men.

I see an inexperienced young man, etc. He calls the adulterer a young man not because of virtue but because of instability. He passes through the street because he has abandoned the narrow way that leads to life. He is near the corner because he turns aside from straightness.

And he walks along the way toward her house. Whoever has turned away from the way of truth rightly approaches the way to the prostitute’s or the heretic’s house. As we have explained, this way is properly situated both in the street and near the corner.

In the darkness, as the day was growing toward evening, etc. Such a person, already blinded in heart, is hastening toward the darkness both of sin and of damnation.

And behold, a woman meets him in prostitute’s attire, etc. All this is plainly applicable literally to the works of prostitutes. But heretical teaching, whenever it finds someone careless and inexperienced, attempts to deceive him. It appears in prostitute’s attire because it shines with unclean eloquence. It is prepared to capture souls because it kills by spiritual death all whom it can associate with itself.

Talkative and restless, etc. She desires to disturb the peace of the Church.

Unable to keep her feet still in her house. No heresy is content with its first disciples—for they are its house—but it is always seeking new people whom it may deceive.

Now outside, now in the streets, etc. Outside, when it seizes pagans; in the streets, when it seizes the pleasure-loving; near the corners, when it encounters other heretics.

And, having seized the young man, she kisses him. She tests the unstable person with the blandishments of deceptive words.

And she flatters him with an impudent face, saying, etc. The literal meaning is clear: the prostitute claims that she has prepared a very splendid banquet. But heretics assert and eagerly desire that, in everything they do, they are offering to God sacrifices for their own salvation. The Lord likewise says to his disciples: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God.”

I have woven my bed with cords, etc. Beds woven from cords—or, according to another translation, from bands—are usually softer than those laid upon wood, leather, or any other material. In a bed woven from cords, therefore, the prostitute signifies the softness of repose. In embroidered coverings from Egypt she also attempts the enticements of the eyes; once these have been ensnared by a sinful gaze, she more easily penetrates the secret places of the mind in order to seduce them.

Since cords sometimes symbolize the divine commandments, which restrain us from our pleasures by binding us back, heretics promise that, through a woven fabric of heavenly words, they will prepare for their hearers a salutary bed on which they may rest with a free heart, released from the turmoil of vices. But in truth they construct for them, with the cords of sins, a pit of perdition, where, with feet and hands bound forever, they will be condemned.

Concerning this the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her will be in great tribulation” (Apoc. II).

In the embroidered coverings from Egypt, the ornament of eloquence and the subtlety of dialectical art are understood—an art that took its origin from the pagans. Through it, the heretical mind, like a prostitute, boasts that it has woven itself a bed of crime from the meaning of its pernicious teaching.

I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh, etc. Such people promise that they possess the fragrances of heavenly virtues, with which they may consecrate their own hearts and those of their followers as beautiful beds, so that they might say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (II Cor. II).

Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts, etc. Heretics boast that they will mutually satisfy one another with draughts of holy teaching and be joined together by the grace of virtues, until eternal light follows their deeds.

The man is not at home; he has gone away, etc. “Christ,” she says, “is not bodily present in the Church. Having risen from the dead, he ascended into heaven and left us the ministry of governing the Church, which is his house.”

He took a purse of money with him. He carried away with him the glory of resurrection and the splendor of immortality, by which he might gladden and enrich the citizens of that homeland.

He will return to his house on the day of the full moon. At the time when the Church has completed the number of his elect, he will return for judgment.

At once he follows her, etc. That is, like a fool, not knowing that he is being led, he is conducted to destruction.

And all the strongest have been slain by her. Solomon himself, the wisest of men; Samson, the strongest; David, the gentlest—all were ensnared by the trap of women. Likewise Origen was ensnared by heretical teaching. Whoever denies that, for as long as he taught rightly, he was a teacher of the Church after the apostles is in error.

Her house is the way to the underworld, etc. But concerning the Church he says: “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). By “the innermost places of death” he means the harshest torments of Gehenna, as though they were more severe and darker, into which heretics and fornicators are known to be plunged. So it is said of the saints who suffer adversity for the Lord in this life: “He sent them into the inner prison”—that is, a prison more painful, more hideous, and darker.

## CHAPTER VIII
Has not Wisdom cried out? etc. Has not the Lord spoken openly to the world, and spoken nothing in secret (John XVII)? Why, then, neglecting his Gospel, do wretched people flock instead to listen to heresy or to the persuasion of lust, which whisper in a corner?

—On the highest and loftiest summits above the way, etc. On the mountain he taught his disciples amid the crowds; but he also often preached along the roads to those who gathered, and healed those who needed healing. At the very gate of the city of Nain, too, when he raised the dead man, he commended by the example of the miracle the words he had taught. And why do you follow those who in hidden places sharpened their tongues against him (Luke VII)?

—At the very doors she will speak, saying: O men, etc. She cries out to men—that is, to vigorous hearers of the word of either sex. For those who are effeminate, that is, weak-minded, cannot receive the words of wisdom.

—Understand, little ones, shrewdness, etc. This is plainly about the Lord: when he himself was in the world, he spoke the word to every age, sex, and condition; indeed, he even cried out while standing in the temple, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII). And now, through the teachers of the Church—for they are its city gates—he preaches alike to men and women, to the wise and the foolish, to the very old and the little ones. False teaching, by contrast, seeks out privately and in secret those whom it may be able to seduce.

—Listen, for I am going to speak of great things. Great indeed, because he both promised and gave the kingdom of heaven, taught faith in the Holy Trinity, and many other things without number which the prophets left him to speak.

—And my lips shall be opened, etc. His lips are the two Testaments, joined in harmony as witnesses to the truth; when he himself appeared in the flesh, they were opened throughout the whole world through the gift of the Holy Spirit to proclaim salvation.

—Receive my discipline, etc. “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Luke XVI).

—I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, etc. “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII).

—Arrogance and pride, etc. Arrogance and pride are found in those who consider themselves better than others; a crooked way in those who openly do evil; and a double-tongued mouth in those who have nothing steadfast in the good pursuits they undertake, but change their words according to the inclination of their hearers.

—Mine is counsel and equity, etc. Let human presumption not exalt itself: the fullness of virtues belongs to God’s Wisdom alone, and from her human weakness receives whatever virtue it possesses.

—By me kings reign, etc. By “kings” he means the apostles, or other saints, who know how to govern first themselves and then the Church entrusted to them. By “lawgivers” he means the authors of both Testaments and the subsequent writers of the Church; by “princes and mighty ones,” the other teachers and rulers of the faithful. All of them, in fact, possess whatever they are only through Wisdom, so that they may be something. For he says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

—I love those who love me, etc. The Gospel says the same: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). For they rise early in watchfulness toward Wisdom who, by the ever-renewed zeal of their minds, strive to attain the vision of Christ.

—With me are riches and glory, etc. He calls them proud riches and lofty riches, signifying heavenly gifts. For in Greek, “proud” is *hyperiphanos*—that is, “appearing above” or “surpassing.” Therefore Wisdom rightly says that *hyperiphana* riches are with her, because whatever gifts are given from heaven to the faithful are shown to be superior to all the riches of the world. She makes this still clearer by adding “righteousness”: for the unjust often possess earthly riches and glory, whereas we await, as Peter says, “new heavens and a new earth,” and his promises, “in which righteousness dwells” (II Peter III).

—The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways. The ways of the Lord are his works, through consideration of which a person arrives at faith or knowledge. “His invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world.” His ways are also the illuminations through which he reveals himself both to angelic spirits and to human minds. He possessed Wisdom at the beginning of these ways because, at the beginning of the creation that was coming into being, he had the Son who arranged all things with him. But lest anyone suppose that the Son began at the beginning of these ways, or at some earlier time, he prudently added:

—Before he made anything from the beginning, etc. The Gospel has a similar statement: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him” (John I). Let those, then, perish who deny that God’s power and God’s Wisdom—namely, Christ—was begotten from the beginning, indeed before every beginning that can be spoken or conceived, by the Father himself.

Another translation begins this passage as follows: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, in his works.” The Fathers understand this as spoken of the Lord’s incarnation, saying that he used the expression “The Lord created me,” and not “The Father created me,” for the sake of the certainty of the mystery. “The flesh,” they say, “acknowledges the Lord; glory signifies the Father. The creature confesses the Lord; love names the Father as the beginning.” Or, “at the beginning of his ways,” as he himself says, “I am the way”: for, rising from the dead, he made a way for his Church to the kingdom of God and to eternal life. “In his works,” because he was created from the Virgin to redeem the works of the Father, assuming flesh in order to free the Father’s works from the service of corruption. For Christ’s flesh exists because of the works, whereas the Divinity existed before the works.

—And I rejoiced every day, etc. By “playing,” he means “rejoicing.” Thus he was playing before the Father every day because, as the prophet says, “From the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Micah V), he rejoiced to be one with the Father. He was always playing in the world, because when the times of the world and of creation began to exist, he himself, who was in the Father, remained the Son he had been. This is said lest anyone claim that he began together with creatures and times. And his delights are to be with the children of men, because he desires to rest in our hearts and to bring us, through the grace of good merits, to see him.

—Blessed is the person who hears me, etc. She calls her doors and the posts of her doorway the Holy Scriptures and their teachers, without which we cannot enter the life she promises.

## CHAPTER IX

Wisdom built herself a house. Since he had sufficiently spoken of the eternity of Christ’s divinity, he adds a statement about the humanity he assumed: Wisdom therefore built herself a house, because the Son of God himself created the human being whom he was to assume in the unity of his person.

—She hewed out seven pillars. Throughout the world he raised up Churches through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. These Churches, his house—that is, the mystery of his incarnation—contain it, as though supporting it, by believing, honoring, and proclaiming it, so that its memory may not be destroyed by the wickedness of the faithless.

Or certainly, the house of Wisdom is the Church of Christ, while the pillars are the teachers of the holy Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, such as James, Cephas, and John. Wisdom hewed out these pillars because, separating them from love of the present age, she raised up the minds of preachers to bear the structure of that same Church.

—She sacrificed her victims. She consecrated the Church by her own sufferings, or allowed the lives of preachers to be sacrificed in persecution. The victims opposed to these are the harlot’s victims, to which she invites fools, as was read above when she said, “I owed victims for my welfare; today I have paid my vows.”

—She mixed her wine, etc. To those unable to grasp the mysteries of his divinity, he disclosed the sacraments of his assumed humanity and prepared nourishment from Holy Scripture for us by opening it up.

—She sent out her maidservants, etc. He chose weak and despicable preachers to gather faithful peoples for the buildings of the heavenly homeland above.

—If anyone is little, let him come to me, etc. By “little ones” he means the humble; by “foolish,” those who have none of the arrogance of worldly wisdom. He calls such people in order to make them wise and exalted through his teaching.

—Come, eat my bread, etc. In the bread, the divine utterances are expressed; in the mixed wine, the natures of his divinity and humanity, joined in the one person of Christ, are signified, as stated above. Or certainly, in the bread the sacred mystery of his body is shown, and in the mixed wine that of his blood; with these we are satisfied at the altar, his table.

—Leave childishness and come, etc. After offering the feast, he adds instructions for life, so that those whom he has refreshed with the mysteries of his incarnation may also be instructed by the words of his teaching.

—Whoever instructs a scoffer, etc. It is as though you asked why Wisdom invited little ones and fools to her feast before others. “I did so,” she says, “because he labors in vain who tries to press the word of wisdom upon one who scorns hearing it, believing himself wiser and greater than his teacher.”

—Do not rebuke a scoffer, etc. One must not fear that a scoffer, when rebuked, will heap insults upon you; rather, one must take care that he not be drawn into hatred and made worse. Therefore, at times you must refrain from correcting him—not because of your own timidity, but for his benefit and out of love for him.

—Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you. By “wise” he means one who is making progress, that is, a lover of wisdom, whom above he called little because of his humility. The perfectly wise have no need to be rebuked.

—A foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements, etc. This woman is heresy, directly opposed to Wisdom, which earlier sang of her own mysteries. She too sits at the doors of her house—that is, in teachers of falsehood—who introduce wretched people into the inner chambers of faithlessness to be deceived. She sits upon a chair because she usurps for herself the teaching chair. This is the chair of pestilence, on which the blessed man refuses to sit (Psalm I).

—In the high place of the city. He says of Wisdom that she gives her voice on the highest and loftiest summits; but Wisdom is raised up in the loftiness of virtues, whereas the other woman is raised up on the brow of arrogance.

—To call passers-by along the way, etc. Heresy often calls Catholics to faithlessness when it sees them traveling the straight road, wishing to cross more quickly through the way of this world and hurry toward the eternal homeland.
