—Whoever is little, let him turn aside to me, etc. Wisdom too appears to invite the little and the foolish to her banquet in almost the same words. But the difference is that Wisdom simply calls them to come to her, whereas the other urges those whom she calls to turn aside to her. Wisdom calls those whom she sees wandering back to the straight path of action; the other teaches those walking rightly to stray from their road and turn aside to her.

—Stolen waters are sweeter, etc. Wisdom openly set out her table and mixed her wine; but the foolish woman, possessing nothing pure, gathers everyone she can to stolen waters and hidden bread. The Catholic Church openly spreads before the world the banquets of the divine utterances and commands that the mysteries of Christ’s divinity and humanity be celebrated. Or certainly, in the mixed wine she serves her hearers historical and allegorical knowledge together, refreshing each person with the cups of life according to that person’s capacity.

The teaching of heretics secretly places its decrees above the public faith and confession. Since it possesses nothing spiritual, it boasts that it teaches the Catholic pastors a more pleasing knowledge, so that people may more willingly hear and practice what is forbidden to be said and believed openly in the Church. Thus folly, which is thought to be knowledge, is drunk more sweetly, and its forbidden hearing is stolen.

The “stolen waters” may signify the baptism of heretics, and the “hidden bread” their sacrifice. But according to the literal sense, the adulterous woman asserts that forbidden and illicit unions are sweeter in stolen waters and hidden bread.

—And she did not know that giants are there, etc. The adulterous woman does not know, nor does the heretic know, that unclean spirits inhabit their houses, and that those who suffer eternal punishments in the depths of hell take delight in the very actions of the licentious and in the very doctrines of heretics, as though in rich banquets.

But when the sacraments are rightly celebrated in the Church of Christ, and the word of Christ—which is the Wisdom of God—is heard and preserved, it is clear that angelic powers are there, and that in the heights of heaven they are companions of the faithful. “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm LXXVII).

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0967]

## Proverbs of Solomon

He introduces a new title because a new kind of discourse begins: instead of arguing at length, as before, about the individual parts of good and evil, he describes the actions of both in alternating verses.

## CHAPTER X

A wise son makes his father glad, etc. Whoever faithfully preserves the mysteries received in faith makes God the Father glad; whoever pollutes them by evil conduct or heresy saddens the mother, the Church.

—Treasures of wickedness will not profit, etc. Righteousness often delivers even from temporal death, as in the case of Daniel and the three youths, and always delivers from everlasting death. But treasures gathered through wickedness, although they sometimes seem to rescue a person from bodily death, bring more evil because of the wickedness by which they were acquired than benefit through the life for which they were given.

—The Lord will not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger, etc. And if the wicked sometimes afflict an innocent person with hunger or even kill him, they will not harm his soul, since the Lord consoles him in the future life with the visitation of his glory. He also justly turns the same plots of the wicked back upon them in judgment.

—The slack hand produces poverty, etc. Whoever lives negligently in this age will lack good things in the future; but whoever serves the Lord courageously will be rewarded with the riches of eternal blessedness.

—Whoever gathers in the harvest is a wise son, etc. Whoever gathers the souls of the faithful for Christ is a wise son. Indeed, “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke X). Whoever grows sluggish in caring for his salvation during this acceptable time will be put to shame on the day of tribulation.

—The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous, etc. At the judgment the righteous will be told, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matthew XXV). But the mouth of the wicked, which served gluttony, drunkenness, and evil conversations, will be condemned for the iniquity it committed. Finally, iniquity covered the mouth of the rich man who, placed in torments, sought refreshment for the tongue through which he was punished more severely for his many crimes (Luke XVI).

—The memory of the righteous is with praises, etc. In this life as well, the good raise both the living and the dead to praise; but they detest both the deeds and the name of the wicked. In the future life the righteous live in God’s praises, while the honor, name, and praises of the reprobate are exchanged for the rotting punishments of Gehenna, where “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah LXVI).

—Whoever walks simply walks confidently, etc. Whoever knows that he lives simply easily despises all adversities, because he trusts that through them he will come to joys, saying with the prophet, “The Lord is the protector of my life; whom shall I fear?” and the rest (Psalm XXVI). But whoever walks in crooked ways is exposed, whether he wishes it or not, and receives what his deeds deserve. “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Luke XII).

—Whoever winks with the eye will cause pain. Whoever mocks someone with gestures of the eyes will not escape without the pain of punishment and remorse. The Psalmist speaks of such people: “Those who hate me without cause and wink with the eye” (Psalm XXXIV). Or certainly, “Whoever winks with the eye will cause pain,” because a foolish son is his mother’s sadness.

—A fool will be beaten by his lips. Either by his own lips, by which he deserved to be condemned, since “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs XVIII); or by the lips of those from whom he received a sentence of condemnation because he could not be corrected. Thus the Psalmist, saying, “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm CXIX), asks the Lord for both things: that he himself may not have lying lips and a deceitful tongue, and that he may not be deceived by the wickedness and treachery of others.

—The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life. The Lord says of teachers, “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII).

—But the mouth of the wicked covers iniquity. The wicked are those who conceal and cover either their own errors or those of their neighbors, preventing them from reaching healing. The prophet abhors this and prays that the Lord will not incline his heart to an evil word, “to excuse excuses in sins” (Psalm CXL).

—Wisdom is found on the lips of the wise, etc. “The rod on the back” is vengeance in what comes afterward, that is, in the next life; the famous blow by which the Philistines were struck on the buttocks expresses this well (I Samuel V). Therefore, whoever does not want to carry the rod on his back should carry wisdom on his lips. Let him speak the praises of Christ and preach his commandments.

But because it is fitting always to praise God, though not always to teach, and because it is not appropriate for a wise person to teach everyone everything he knows, it is rightly added:

—The wise conceal knowledge. They know, of course, that “there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes III). Hence the prophet says, “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII). And the Apostle says, “I judged myself to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Corinthians II).

—But the mouth of a fool is near confusion. For he will either speak good things disorderly or openly speak evil.

—The substance of the rich is his fortified city, etc. The rich trust in riches as in a fortified city; the poor therefore fear, because they know themselves to be needy. Spiritually, whoever is rich in God trusts in him through good works as in an impregnable city that no enemy can overcome. Those who are cramped by poverty of virtues, however, lack heavenly riches because they fear with harmful fear to endure hard labors for the Lord.

—Lying lips conceal hatred, etc. Therefore, if you desire to be truthful and wise, conceal hatred neither in the secrecy of your heart nor by uttering insult with your mouth. Let both your heart be filled with love and your mouth with truth.

—As though in laughter a fool works evil, etc. Prudence takes its name from foreseeing. A fool, therefore, is one who rejoices in wickedness (Proverbs XIV). It belongs to the wise, and to one worthy of the name “man,” to foresee that laughter will be mingled with sorrow and that the joys of sinning will be followed by the punishment of retribution.

—What the wicked fears will come upon him, etc. He speaks of the wicked person who sins knowingly. The wicked therefore fears to see the strict Judge; the righteous desire to depart and be with Christ: the former fears being deprived of earthly joys and punished with everlasting retribution; the latter fears that their sojourn may be prolonged and desires to receive the rewards for which they have struggled. For both, what they fear in their hearts will come upon them.

—Like a passing storm, the wicked will not be, etc. He speaks of the persecutors of the Church, who seek to overthrow the house of faith. But because that house is established on the true foundation, namely Christ, it remains, while they suddenly perish.

—As vinegar to the teeth, etc. As the faithlessness of heretics generates trouble and tears for good teachers, so a Catholic who lives badly is burdensome through his inertia to those who have commanded him to demonstrate his faith by his works. The eyes and teeth are preachers of the holy Church, who are accustomed to foresee the right paths for her and supply spiritual food.

Vinegar, which degenerates from wine, and smoke, which rises from fire and vanishes, figuratively announce those who withdraw from the sweetness and charity of the Church through pride or negligence and then attack it even with their words. John speaks of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us,” and the rest (I John II).

—The fear of the Lord adds days, etc. Those who faithfully serve God will be given eternal light; but those enslaved to wickedness lose, together with this life, the goods they loved.

—The expectation of the righteous is joy, etc. It is clear that the righteous rejoice in expectation of the coming life, although they are saddened by the affliction of present distress. Hence the words, “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me; you are my exultation” (Psalm XIII). But the wicked, who think that they will find rest in the future—or else that there will be nothing after death—are deceived.

This does not conflict with what was said above: “What the wicked fears will come upon him.” For there are people who, knowing the judgment of future goods and evils, nevertheless sin through negligence, despair, or even deliberately. The destruction they fear will therefore come upon such people. There are others who think that the evils they do will never be punished, or that their good deeds deserve a good reward; of them it is rightly said that the hope of the wicked will perish. Of those who sin knowingly he subsequently adds:

—The way of the Lord is strength to the upright, etc. If, he says, you cannot grasp the hidden things of Scripture, do not despair of salvation; rather, walk in the way of the Lord, do the good things you know, and you will be counted among the strong. But those who disdain to do the right things they know should rightly be afraid, because certain evils remain for them to suffer.

## CHAPTER XI

A deceitful balance is an abomination before God, etc. A deceitful balance is used not only in the measuring of money but also in judicial discernment. Whoever hears the case of a poor person one way, the case of a powerful person another way, the case of a friend one way, and the case of a stranger another way, weighs with an unjust balance. So too does the person who judges his own good deeds better than those of his neighbors and his own errors lighter. Likewise, the person who places unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders but himself refuses to touch them with one finger (Matthew XXIII). So too the person who does good things in public and evil things in secret will be detested by the Lord for the iniquity of his deceitful balance.

But whoever acts sincerely in all things, who judges one case and another with an equal scale, plainly conforms in will and action to the desire of the just Judge.

—Where there is pride, etc. Because proud and insulting people behave contemptuously or through ignorance of discipline, they heap insults upon their neighbors; or certainly because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, XVIII).

—But where there is humility, etc. “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI; Luke X)—that is, to the humble.

—When the wicked person dies, there will be no hope afterward. Alas, wretched man! Origen passed beyond this sentence: after the universal and final judgment, he believed that life would be given to all the wicked and sinners.

It should be noted, however, that although there is no hope of forgiveness for the wicked after death, there are nevertheless some who can be absolved after death from lesser sins in which they died bound—either by being chastised with punishments or by being released through the prayers, almsgiving, and celebrations of Masses offered by their own people. But whenever such things occur, they concern lesser offenses and occur before the judgment.

Those who think that they will be freed after the judgment, however long a time afterward, are deceived; perhaps the following applies to them:

—And the expectation of the anxious will perish. There is one kind of anxiety by which the good are always girded to fulfill God’s commandments; there is another by which the reprobate, while knowingly sinning, anxiously fear that they may at some time be seized for eternal punishment. Therefore it is rightly said that the expectation of those who serve God with an anxious mind will be crowned, while the expectation of those who despise God and, before his judgment, are condemned by their own accusing conscience will perish.

The ancient translation has this verse quite differently: “The hope of the righteous person who has died will not perish, but the glory of the wicked will perish.”

—The righteous person is delivered from distress, etc. Every martyr is delivered from the distress of suffering after death, while the persecutor who afflicted him will be handed over to punishment on his account. James was crowned by martyrdom; Peter was saved from prison; and Herod, who persecuted them, was visibly consumed by worms and invisibly carried to the place where “his worm shall not die and his fire shall not be quenched.”

—The pretender deceives his friend with his mouth, etc. A heretic pretending to teach Catholic doctrine deceives his hearer; but those who rightly follow the truth of the Gospel will be freed by Catholic knowledge, lest they be seized by a heretical snare.

—Whoever despises his friend is lacking in heart, etc. We must not despise or ridicule someone who is not found to love sincerely, even if through inertia he does something foolishly; whoever does this is unworthy of wisdom. But a prudent person remains silent publicly about such people’s faults and corrects them privately. The same point is pressed more closely in the verses that follow:

—Whoever walks deceitfully reveals secrets, etc. In the Gospel too the Lord says, “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone; if he listens to you, you have gained your brother,” and the rest (Matthew XVIII).

Hence the following is rightly added:

—Where there is no governor, the people will fall, etc. Lest you think that, if you cannot correct your friend, you ought to conceal his faults any longer, he rightly says that a people falls without a governor but is saved where there are many counselors. He shows that what you are unable to correct alone should be disclosed to several, so that the united diligence of all may bring about correction.

—He will suffer harm who gives security for a stranger. The literal sense is obvious. But someone is a stranger to the lot of the saints if he refuses to correct his sins through repentance. Whoever grants such a person the grace of communion or promises him eternal life, because he has given security for a stranger, has certainly made himself worthy of punishment before the eyes of the strict Judge.

—But whoever avoids snares, etc. He will be secure in the future who is rightly fearful at that time, diligently cures his errors through repentance, and keeps himself free from association with the unrepentant.

—The evil person who joins hand to hand will not be innocent. Whoever joins hand to hand is doing nothing. But “the evil person who joins hand to hand will not be innocent,” because even if he withdraws his hand from wicked action for a time, an evil person cannot possess innocence of heart. Hence it is prefaced: “A heart that is small is abominable to the Lord.”

—But the offspring of the righteous will be saved. This is what was said above: “For the one who sows righteousness there is a faithful reward.” Or certainly, “the offspring of the righteous will be saved,” because those who follow the examples of the righteous who came before them also follow their footsteps to see the joys of eternal salvation. Isaiah speaks of them: “All who see them will recognize them, because they are the offspring whom the Lord has blessed.”

—A golden ring in a pig’s snout, etc. If you insert a golden ring into a pig’s snout, it nevertheless turns the earth with its nose and hurries to plunge into a mud wallow. So too a foolish woman, even if she has received beauty of face or dress, delights in inclining her face toward low things, carrying her attractiveness everywhere to overturn the blossoms of chastity, and defiling herself with the filth of pleasure.

Alternatively: whoever acquires the ornament of the divine utterances through meditation but pursues it with evil living has a golden ring in his snout; yet, after the manner of swine, he does not cease to subdue the earth, because he has befouled by filthy action what he received through the fragrance of knowledge. Therefore such a soul is considered a beautiful and foolish woman: devoted to carnal enticements, she is beautiful through knowledge but foolish through action.

Alternatively: whoever sees heretical teaching shining with every polish of eloquence but nevertheless does not find it to agree with a sound understanding of wisdom has, as the saying puts it, a golden ring in a pig’s snout—that is, beautiful and elaborate speech in the thoughts of a foolish mind. Gold hangs from its eloquence, but because of the weight of its earthly intention it does not look upward, after the manner of swine.

He explained what follows accordingly, saying, “A beautiful and foolish woman”: that is, heretical teaching—beautiful in its words, foolish in its understanding.

—The desire of the righteous is wholly good, etc. The righteous always desire righteousness to reign everywhere. The wicked, by contrast, even when they seem to rest from carrying out their wickedness, nevertheless, according to the purpose of their savage minds, remain intent on inflicting violence and fury upon anyone. This is what was said above: “The evil person who joins hand to hand will not be innocent”; likewise, “The expectation of the wicked is fury,” because anger often confined in silence burns more fiercely within the mind.

—Some distribute their own possessions, etc. Because they receive a hundredfold in this time and in the age to come eternal life (Matthew XIX).

—Others seize what is not theirs, etc. “Always in poverty,” he says—not only in torments, where they do not receive even a drop of water with which to refresh themselves for a moment (Luke XVI), but also in the present, where, however many things the miser seizes, he is always needy.

—The soul that blesses will be made fat, etc. Whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives inwardly an increase of spiritual richness. And while he does not cease to intoxicate the minds of his hearers with sacred speech, he grows, intoxicated by the abundant drink of the gift.

—Whoever hides grain in time, etc. Whoever keeps within himself the words of holy preaching will be cursed among the peoples, because he is condemned for the guilt of silence alone, on account of the punishment of the many whom he could have corrected. He is the lazy and wicked servant who, for retaining the talent he received, was cast into outer darkness (Matthew XXV).

Those who sell grain are those who impart the word of life to their hearers, from whom they receive the price of faith and confession, as the Lord says, “Trade until I come” (Luke XIX). Blessing comes upon their heads when, as each returns from such business, the Lord says, “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid.).

—He rises early to seek good things who seeks what is good, etc. To seek the good things that you ought to do, by which you may reach heavenly goods, is to rise early in the right way—that is, as the light of knowledge increases, to gird yourself for good work.

Or certainly, he rises well—that is, rises to life—at the time of the resurrection who now seeks good things in the time of action. But whoever now diligently searches out what he may say or do that is evil will then be held back by the weight of those things, so that he cannot reach the higher things of the kingdom.

—Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, etc. Whoever longs for present goods and does not consider the future will finally lose both. But those who do good in hope of future rewards receive justly in the present what they hope for.

A green leaf on a tree signifies fruits that are destined to appear but have not yet appeared. The righteous, like a green leaf, put forth shoots because, saved in hope, they do not cease to progress in faith and in the grace of virtues until they reach the fruit of the desired recompense—that is, the heavenly homeland.

—Whoever troubles his house will possess winds, etc. Whoever does not fear that his mind will be troubled by great tumults of thought opens it to the blasts of evil spirits, by which it may be overwhelmed. And when a fool persecutes a wise person, he serves him even by ruling over him in this way, because by pressing upon his patience he makes it more proven, so that, while the fool is condemned, the wise person receives the prize for which he contended.

—The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. The reward of the righteous is the vision of Christ. For he himself is the Wisdom of whom it was said, “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Proverbs III). And in the Apocalypse he says, “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Apocalypse II). The righteous now await this fruit, because for a long time, as was said above, they put forth shoots like a green leaf.

—And whoever receives souls is wise. Whoever undertakes the care of souls for the Lord, so that he may teach those who are wandering, console the sorrowful, support those lacking temporal goods, draw the resistant toward the remedies of salvation, or govern those deprived of a shepherd, and thereby bring many with himself to the Lord—whoever, I say, receives souls in this way is wise, because through these things he makes abundant provision for his own soul, so that he may reign more gloriously with the Lord.

—If the righteous person is scarcely saved on earth, etc. If the holy martyrs, who were righteous, suffered so much, what torments do you think await those who unjustly afflicted them? If Job and Tobias and the other elect of God received so many adversities in this life, why are you troubled if an affliction that tests you touches you briefly, when you lie so far beneath their footsteps?

Indeed, although you ought not to call or believe yourself wicked, you ought not deny that you are a sinner—that is, that you possess some sins, whether small or great, open or hidden. Rather, you ought to confess this, lest you deceive yourself and the truth be unable to exist in you (I John I).

If, then, the righteous received such things on earth—Abel the crown of martyrdom, and Job the model of patience—how much more did the wicked receive them, Antiochus and Herod! And the sinners in the Gospel, such as the paralytic, could be healed by the Lord only after their sins had first been forgiven.

It should be noted that Peter placed this saying in his Epistle according to the ancient translation: “And if the righteous person will scarcely be saved, where will the wicked and the sinner appear?” (I Peter IV).

## CHAPTER XII
He who is good will receive grace from the Lord, etc. The connection between these verses is as follows: He who is good does not trust in his own thoughts, but seeks the Lord’s grace and through it receives the ability to live piously. He, however, who trusts in his own thoughts cannot be good. For whoever does not take care to seek the grace of heavenly Help rightly persists in impious action.

—A diligent wife is a crown to her husband, etc. The literal sense is clear: a good and chaste wife honors her husband in all things and, by managing the household well through her own virtues, adds something like grace to the crown. An adulteress, however, though she may appear beautiful outwardly, defiles her members inwardly with the stench of lust. Spiritually, however, the Church offers Christ a crown, none other than herself.

—For all who are around her, etc. The son of Sirach likewise says of the high priest: “He stood beside the altar, and around him was a crown of brothers.” But the bones—that is, the virtues—which the faction of heretics is seen to possess are corrupted by the rottenness of their perverse doctrine.

—The thoughts of the righteous are judgments, etc. The righteous carefully examine their deeds to see whether they please the Lord, lest, because of their insufficient vigilance, the heavenly Judge should invisibly arrange adversity against them, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI). The reprobate, however, forgetful of divine fear, form their plans around the fraud they practice.

—Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more, etc. When the wicked are turned from this life, they will no longer be what they had been, because after death they do not find what they had believed would be there. Deprived of their hope, they receive torments instead of rewards. But the house of the righteous—that is, the Church—which is partly a pilgrim on earth and partly reigns in heaven, never fails. Whatever members of it reach that place, they find there the joys they had hoped for.

Alternatively: “Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more,” because great impiety existed among the gods of the nations, great impiety among the sects of heretics, great impiety in the magic arts, and great impiety in the persecutions of the pagans. But when these were overthrown by the Lord’s gift, the memory of their impiety was likewise removed: even the foolish letters themselves and the doctrines themselves were snatched away by fire, as we read happened at Ephesus in the time of the apostles. The house of the righteous, however, will remain, because such a long span of time has never been able either to hide or remove the holy Church, to corrupt anything in her Scriptures, or in any respect to violate her faith.

It may also be understood in this way: “Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more”: convert them from impiety, and they will no longer be wicked but righteous. For this another translation says: “Wherever the wicked turns, he will be destroyed.” In contrast, it is said of the saints: “For those who love God, all things work together for good.”

—By his teaching a man will be known. Scripture commonly calls those men who are endowed with divine virtues. Hence the Apostle says: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully” (I Cor. XVI). A man, therefore, is known by his teaching, because if he teaches what is right and fulfills it in his works, he is understood to be holy.

—But whoever is empty and senseless, etc. This is because he has refused to possess the strength of a manly spirit.

—Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself, etc. Better is the unlearned and simple brother who, by doing the good things he knows, merits life in heaven than one distinguished by learning in the Scriptures, or even one who has exercised the office of teacher, yet lacks the bread of love. Concerning the aspect of that love which pertains to one’s neighbor, he subsequently adds:

—The righteous man knows the souls of his beasts. That is, he shows mercy and compassion toward the condition and weakness of those entrusted to him.

—But the inward parts of the wicked are cruel. They not only fail to have compassion on their subjects, but also, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “They strike boys and maidservants, saying, ‘My master is delaying his coming’” (Luke XII).

—He who works his land, etc. He who exercises his soul in spiritual pursuits will be satisfied now with virtues and then with the banquets of rewards. But he who refuses to labor for the salvation of his soul will then be rejected among the foolish, even though he may now appear glorious in either divine or human wisdom.

—The desire of the wicked is a memorial of the worst men. The wicked desire to imitate the evil who came before them and to speak about their life and deeds. Or certainly: “The desire of the wicked is a memorial of the worst men,” because all his desire tends toward this—even though he does not know it—that he be shut up with the earlier unrighteous in the prison of eternal death. Since such people meet an end they by no means foresee, he says in contrast concerning the good:

—But the root of the righteous will prosper. For the faith and charity of the elect, by which they have been rooted in Christ, do not deceive them in any way. Rather, ever increasing toward greater perfection, it will receive in the future more than it knows how to hope for.

—Each person will be filled with good things from the fruit of his mouth. The fruit of the mouth is a good word. For whoever speaks evil does not produce the fruit of his mouth but loss. Everyone, therefore, who speaks good things will be endowed with eternal goods, provided that he does not contradict by his conduct what he says. He adds this carefully when he says:

—And he will be repaid according to the works of his hands. A teacher’s speech does not become fruitful in any other way unless he himself first does the good things he teaches.

—A fool immediately displays his anger, etc. Whoever desires to take revenge in the present is a fool; whoever disregards an injury for the Lord’s sake is wise. Another translation has this verse as follows: “The fool declares his anger at the same hour, but the crafty man conceals his disgrace.”

It does not, however, decree that the shameful passion of anger should be hidden by the wise in such a way that, while blaming its swiftness, it fails to forbid its delay. If anger should burst forth because of human weakness, it judged that it should for this reason be concealed: so that, while wisely covered for the moment, it may be removed more wisely and destroyed forever. For this is the nature of anger: when delayed, it grows weak and dies; when expressed, it blazes ever more fiercely.

—There is one who makes promises, etc. Some promise that they will obey the truth, but when a frightening or flattering temptation presents an obstacle, they abandon what they began, yet are pricked by the consciousness of their promise as though by a sword.

—But the tongue of the wise is health. By fulfilling the good things they promise, they themselves attain life, and by preaching they show others what they should follow.

—The lip of truth will be firm forever, etc. The faith of the Church will always remain. Whoever suddenly introduces new doctrines of falsehood is the servant of a heretic.

—A crafty man conceals knowledge. Here “crafty” is understood in a good sense: that is, wise and prudent. Such a man sometimes deliberately conceals his knowledge, for two reasons: either because he is unable to speak to weak hearers as to spiritual people, but must speak to them as to carnal people; or because he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before swine.

—And the heart of fools provokes folly. This happens either when they themselves, desiring to know more than they ought to know, advance so far in their reflections that they regard folly as wisdom; or when, attempting to teach others what they are not yet able to understand, they provoke them to greater folly. They are like people who thrust sunlight into small eyes: they take away the little light that the eyes seemed able to perceive.

—The hand of the strong will rule, etc. The perfect not only overcome the battles of vices but also exercise authority over elect brothers through a greater grace of virtues. Those who are slack in spirit and do not fear becoming entangled in sins pay daily a tribute of vices to the devil, the worst of exactors. If, while alive, they do not escape his dominion through repentance, then, after death, having been handed over to him, they are sent by him into the prison of eternal punishments, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel parable.

Nor should one despair of the correction of such people, since he immediately adds:

—Sorrow in a man’s heart humbles him, etc. It is necessary first that the sorrow of repentance healthfully humble the sinner; afterward, through the judgment of the priest, the word of reconciliation that has been granted makes him joyful.

—He who disregarded loss for the sake of a friend is righteous. If this is rightly said of the general distribution of money and of a true human friend, how much more worthy of the crown of righteousness is the one who, for the sake of him who said, “I say to you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body” (Luke XII), either sells what he possesses and gives it to the poor, or joyfully accepts the seizure of his goods, or indeed gives over his very flesh to be mortified or killed in his passion!

—But the way of the wicked will deceive them. This happens when they rejoice either in retaining their own property or in seizing what belongs to others. Hence it is rightly added:

—The fraudulent man will not find profit, etc. Money acquired by fraud adds more loss to the soul than profit to the treasury. Whoever knows how to distribute his own possessions for the Lord’s sake will, with the Lord as his rewarder, receive heavenly gifts in exchange for earthly things.

Alternatively: “The fraudulent man will not find profit,” etc. Whoever, with a deceitful mind, pretends to be good while living wickedly in secret will not find the goods of the life to come. But whoever truly acquires the substance of spiritual virtues will purchase from it the splendor of the eternal kingdom. This he stated more clearly in the verses that follow: “In the path of righteousness there is life, but the wandering way leads to death.” The path of righteousness acquires the substance of virtues, by which the splendor of eternal life—more precious than gold—is purchased. But the crooked way on which the fraudulent man walks, having lost the temporal profit he seeks, moves toward the everlasting death he refused to foresee.

## CHAPTER XIII

—A wise son is the instruction of his father, etc. There is this much difference between the wise and the foolish: the former may at some time progress through the benefit of instruction to the point of teaching the one who had taught him, while the latter does not know how to listen when he is reproved.

—The lazy man both wishes and does not wish, etc. The one who wishes to reign with God but does not wish to labor for God is rightly marked by the name “lazy.” Rewards delight him when they are promised; struggles deter him when he is commanded to undertake them. James speaks of such a person: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James I). The son of Sirach likewise says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways!”

Those who perform the Lord’s commands do so because their perfected souls are refreshed by the sweetness of heavenly things, in accordance with the one who implores the Lord, saying: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII). Or certainly, the soul of those who labor will be enriched, because those who sweat through pious labors for the Lord will, after their labors, be endowed with a heavenly and unfading reward.

—He is like a rich man when he possesses nothing, etc. The man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day seemed rich to himself; but because he did not possess God, he discovered at the end that what he had possessed amounted to nothing. Hence it is said of such men: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV).

Lazarus, by contrast, who lay at the rich man’s gate covered with sores, seemed poor; but he possessed great riches, since he had the virtue of humility and carried in his heart the Creator of all riches, namely, God. What true riches are worth and what true poverty accomplishes, he makes clear by adding:

—The redemption of a man’s soul is his riches, etc. Whoever wishes his soul to be redeemed from future wrath should gather the riches of good works. For whoever lacks such riches cannot endure the rebuke of the strict Judge. Concerning this the Psalmist asks, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury.” Otherwise, those who are poor in spirit are not rebuked there by the Lord but receive the blessing of an eternal inheritance.

—The light of the righteous brings joy, etc. The light of the righteous, which brings perpetual joy, is hope for future things; the lamp of the wicked, which is suddenly extinguished, is the happiness of the passing world.

—Among the proud there are always quarrels, but those who do everything with counsel are governed by wisdom. Heretics are always quarreling among themselves, as are the other reprobate, because they do not know the unity of faith and truth. The faithful, however, who do not cease to enjoy the counsel of the divine words, are governed by the moderation of wisdom, which does not permit them to quarrel.

—Substance gained hastily will diminish, etc. Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, and they do not possess forever even the riches they acquire or desire. But whoever applies himself to righteous labors in order to receive the substance of heavenly rewards will receive manifold gifts of heavenly blessedness. Concerning this he aptly adds:

—Hope that is deferred afflicts the soul, etc. As long as hope for eternal things is deferred, the souls of the faithful are afflicted, either because the goods they love are delayed or because of the evils they endure. But when what they desire has come, they easily forget what they had suffered, because they begin to live forever with their Redeemer, whom they had sought with complete devotion. He is the tree of life for those who embrace him.

—He who detracts from any matter, etc. Whoever detracts from a good thing binds himself for the future, because by doing what he ought not to do, he prepares for himself the punishment by which he will be constrained. But the one who detracts from an evil thing also binds himself for the future—not so that he may suffer punishment for such detraction, but so that after his criticism he may conduct himself more cautiously. What he rightly condemns in others, he himself does not admit with impunity, as the Apostle cries out: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. II).

—But he who fears the commandment, etc. It is therefore better for each person to fear because of his own weakness, lest he transgress the divine commands, than to tear apart the faults of others with a foolish mouth. The Apostle says: “If a man is overtaken in any trespass, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI).

—The astute man does everything with counsel, etc. By teaching that everything should be done with counsel, he understands divine counsel, clothed as it is in the sacred words, rather than human counsel. For he is a fool who lives outside this counsel, even though he may naturally appear astute and prudent. Concerning such a person it is rightly added:

—The messenger of the wicked will fall into evil. He calls Arius and Sabellius, and the other angels—that is, messengers of Satan—by this name, because, having neglected the counsel of the divine Scriptures, they fell into the evil of the punishments of Gehenna.

—But a faithful ambassador is health. That is, every Catholic preacher acquires eternal health for himself and for his hearers.

—When desire is fulfilled, it delights the soul, etc. Every desire, whether good or evil, delights the soul when it has attained fulfillment. But fools, who rejoice only in carnal desires, detest those who, for love of heavenly things, despise earthly pleasures.

—Whoever walks with the wise will be wise, etc. To go with the wise is to imitate the deeds of the wise. Therefore, however simple or rustic a person may be, even if he is unable to comprehend the secrets of wisdom, if he nevertheless follows the examples of the wise in his manner of life, he will rightly be numbered among the wise.

But whoever loves fools—not because of their nature, since they are human beings, but because of their folly, since they are mimics, actors, or people of that sort—not in order to correct them by instruction but in order to make them worse by encouragement, such a person, even if he appears wise in ability and learning [the reading is somewhat uncertain], will be held deserving both of the mark and of the condemnation of fools.

—The good man leaves sons as heirs, etc. We often see good men die without children; indeed, the Lord promises greater rewards to those who place the chastity of virginity before the begetting of children. Yet the substance of the righteous is also taken away by sinners. The Apostle, moreover, praises those who joyfully accepted the seizure of their goods.

This should therefore be understood spiritually: the good and righteous one is the Lord, who, after his Passion, ascending into heaven, left as heirs of his teaching the apostles and their successors. To his faith was converted the multitude of the nations, which had been the substance of the devil. For he entered the house of that wicked and strong adversary, crushed him by greater strength, seized his weapons in which he trusted, and distributed his spoils, as he himself testifies in the Gospel.

Or certainly, the substance of the sinner is guarded for the righteous when the kingdom of God was taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits.

—There is much food in the fallow fields of the fathers, etc. He acts without sound judgment who diligently devotes himself to gathering riches and, after accumulating them, does not distribute them himself to the poor for the redemption of his soul but reserves them for others to distribute after him. In the preceding verse, according to the literal sense, it is said: “And the substance of the sinner is kept for the righteous,” especially when he has an abundant livelihood from the right of his paternal inheritance and no necessity presses upon him to gather money. This is what he means by saying: “There is much food in the fallow fields of the fathers.”

According to the spiritual sense, there is much food of heavenly nourishment in the words and examples of venerable fathers. He acts without reason who, by laboring to read, meditate on, and expound these things, serves through them not his own salvation but rather that of others, while he himself departs from what he reads either through reprehensible actions or through the impiety of heretical understanding. Such a person, in the fallow fields of the fathers—that is, in works or words of the fathers cultivated by excellent instruction—acquires support not for himself but for others, namely, for those who, reading his treatises, discover through them the secrets of the spiritual sense by which they may be inwardly refreshed.

Both senses are aptly suited to what follows:

—He who spares the rod hates his son, etc. A good father diligently instructs his son, and a Catholic teacher his disciple, so that he may not turn aside to iniquity. The ancient interpreters translated the preceding verse as follows: “Righteous men will enjoy riches for many years, but the wicked will perish quickly.”

—But the righteous eats and fills his soul, etc. The righteous receives the food of wisdom that is shown to have arisen in the fallow fields of the fathers—that is, in the works and words of the righteous who came before—and transfers it into the advancement of his soul by living well.

But the belly of the wicked—that is, the capacity of the heretics’ understanding—is insatiable, because, as the Apostle says, “They are always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth” (II Tim. III). Why do they not deserve to be filled with knowledge, unless because they themselves have never been nourished by the food of their fathers’ teaching, while they gather it for others without judgment?

## CHAPTER XIV

A wise woman builds her house, etc. Every faithful soul, and the Catholic Church throughout the world, builds for itself by good works a dwelling in the heavenly homeland. The reprobate, however, by living badly and sometimes even openly resisting, scatter what has been rightly ordered by the good.

Why fools tear apart the deeds of the wise is shown by the words that follow:

—He who walks on the straight path and fears God, etc. Religion is an abomination to the sinner. It seems foolish to unbelievers that the faithful, out of fear of God, not only cast away fear but even mock the torments of those who kill the body.

Concerning them he aptly adds:

—In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride, etc. Through empty speech, fools afflict the humble whom they despise. Those same humble in spirit, however, fortify themselves through the teaching of wisdom so that they may not be deceived.

—Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, etc. This follows from what was said above. The oxen signify Catholic teachers; the manger, the assemblies of hearers; the crops, the fruits of good works.

The proud man therefore swells up in vain, and unlearned eloquence beats upon the ears and hearts of those subject to him, because where there are no learned preachers, the crowd of the common people gathers to hear in vain. But where very many works of virtue appear, it is entirely clear that no heretic chattered uselessly, but that the one who labored for the fruit of the word worked there—the one who knows both how to ruminate upon the word itself with a chaste mouth and how to walk along the way of truth with the upright foot of discernment.

Nor is it surprising that we have said that hearers are signified by the manger, since an ox is fed from a manger, while a teacher customarily nourishes his hearers with the word. Yet one must observe that the manger is filled by the labor of the ox, and that the ox itself is refreshed by its own fruit from the manger. For the faithful preacher both refreshes his hearers with the word and is himself refreshed before the Lord by that same refreshment. This is represented in the deed of Elijah, who fed the widow of Zarephath and was himself fed by her.

—The scoffer seeks wisdom, etc. Caiaphas said to the Lord, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ.” Because he sought badly, he did not deserve to find what he sought. The disciples, however, who had humbly submitted themselves to hearing the truth, after receiving the grace of the Spirit, deserved not only to recognize Christ as the Son of God but also to understand the hidden things of Scripture.

At that time the teaching of the prudent was easy, when Cornelius with his household and others like him humbly heard the word, immediately believed, and, having received the Holy Spirit, spoke in every language. Even now, while being catechized, a prudent person readily grasps the teaching of the Catholic faith. Heretics, however, because they seek perversely, never find it at all.

—Go away from a foolish man, etc. The scoffer does not find the wisdom he seeks because, even if you proceed openly against his folly by disputing with him, he does not know how to understand what you say. Thus Arius claimed that the word “consubstantial” could nowhere be found in Scripture, even when these passages were clearly brought against him: “I and the Father are one”; and, “The Word was God,” etc.

The teaching of the prudent is easy because the lips of prudence are wisdom: that is, whatever lips are governed by the guidance of prudence delight in speaking and hearing only about wisdom and eagerly devote themselves to meditation upon it.

—The heart that knows the bitterness of its soul, etc. The elect possess bitterness of soul as long as they are kept from eternal joys; the reprobate possess it when they are afflicted by perverse desires. But the elect, because they walk in the light, foresee how greatly their bitterness will be changed into joy. The reprobate, on the other hand, blinded by their own will, do not see what they suffer in the present and do not foresee what they will suffer in the future.

Therefore they will remain strangers to the future joys of the good, because they have not known how to share in their present bitterness. Hence it is aptly added:

—The house of the wicked will be destroyed, etc. A house is ordinarily used for a dwelling, tents for a journey. The house of the wicked will therefore be destroyed because, at death, the reprobate will lose the habitation of the present life in which they had always desired to remain; and they will undergo the perpetual exile of damnation, something they had not foreseen.

But the tents of the righteous will flourish, because their present way of life—in which they are dwellers with God and pilgrims—will, as their merits continually increase, reach the sweetest fruit of the heavenly homeland.

—The innocent believes every word, etc. John both forbade this innocence and taught the possession of this prudence when he said: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (I John IV).

—The wise fears and turns away from evil, etc. Just as it is foolish to trust in one’s own agility and attempt to leap across a rushing torrent or a broad chasm, while it is wise to turn aside to level ground or a bridge, so the person who avoids sins as far as he can, fearing that he may become entangled in evils, is wise.

The fool, however, sins contemptuously, flattering himself either that he will later repent of his offenses or that, if he should suddenly die, he will bravely endure the punishments of hell.

—The impatient man will work folly, etc. An impatient person is certainly blameworthy, but much worse and more hateful to God is the crafty person, even though he may be judged better by human beings. The former openly displays his folly to everyone; the latter, though perverse in heart, often pretends to be simple and just and delights in being called holy by human judgment, while by divine examination he is judged among the reprobate.

—The wicked will lie before the good, etc. At the final judgment, the reprobate who oppressed the righteous in the present will be condemned while the righteous are crowned. What he says—“before,” that is, before the good and before the gates of the righteous—does not refer to proximity of place but to the vision of the good, because they will always see the torments of the wicked, so that they may render unending thanks to their Deliverer.

Hence Isaiah says of them: “They shall go out and see, he says, the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched; and they shall be, even to the satiety of vision, a spectacle to all flesh” (Isa. LXVI).

What he says, “They shall go out,” does not signify the movement of feet but the gaze of the eyes: those who are placed within the kingdom send their sight outward whenever they wish to behold the punishments of the wicked.

—The crown of the wise is riches, etc. The wise do not possess any earthly profit as their riches, but only the crown that they will receive in the future for their virtues. The greatest folly of fools, however, is this: careless of eternal things, they rejoice only in present advantages. “Imprudence” is so called as though it meant lack of foresight.

—A faithful witness delivers souls, etc. Christ delivers souls. He is the faithful witness, as we read in the Apocalypse, and, as the Apostle says, “He bore witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession” (I Tim. VI).

The devil utters lies. He is rightly called “crafty,” because he declares that the evils he suggests should be done are good, and promises eternal joys to those whom he prepares for the torments of hell.

Again, the Catholic teacher delivers souls when he faithfully—that is, rightly—proclaims the testimonies of Scripture, while the heretic utters lies. Or, as another edition expressly translates it: “But the deceitful man kindles by lying,” with “souls” understood—those whom he has deceived by his error.

—In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength, etc. Fear of the Lord grants confidence of strength, because our mind despises the terrors of temporal things with that much greater power, the more truthfully it submits itself in strength to their Creator.

The sons of the fear of the Lord are those who are governed by divine fear, just as there are sons of virtue and sons of resurrection: either those who devote themselves to virtues or those who belong to the joys of the resurrection. They will have hope, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “Let those who fear the Lord hope in the Lord” (Ps. CXIII). Concerning this hope he adds:

—The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, etc. This, then, is the hope of those who fear the Lord: that, turning away from the ruin of death, they may deserve to reach him who says, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Earlier it says, “The law of the wise is a fountain of life, that he may turn away from the ruin of death,” and now it says, “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, that he may turn away from the ruin of death.” From this it is clear that there is no earlier law of the wise by which one ought to avoid death and acquire eternal life than possessing the fear of the Lord. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

—In the multitude of the people is the dignity of the king, and in the smallness of the populace is the disgrace of the prince. Where there is a multitude serving God, there especially is the glory of Christ. Where only catechumens, candidates for baptism, or newly born infants are still held under the rule of the devil—although at the proper time they hasten to be reborn in Christ—there the manifest disgrace of the prince of this world is evident.

Or certainly, in the assemblies of heretics, which are always fewer than the churches of Catholics, the disgrace of those who have separated them from ecclesiastical unity is clear.

—The life of the flesh is the health of the heart, etc. By “flesh” certain weak and tender things are signified; by “bones,” strong deeds. It is therefore rightly said, “The life of the flesh is the health of the heart,” because if innocence of mind is guarded, whatever is weak outwardly will eventually be strengthened.

It is rightly added, “The rottenness of the bones is envy,” because through the vice of malice those things perish before God’s eyes that appear strong to human eyes. For the bones to rot through envy is for even certain robust things to waste away.

—An intelligent servant is acceptable to the king. This is the one to whom it is said: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV).

—An unprofitable servant will endure his wrath. This is the one of whom the same Lord says: “And cast the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV
Soft answer turns away wrath, etc. Whoever humbly receives words of reproof is already drawing near to pardon for the guilt he has incurred; but whoever proudly resists the one reproving him provokes greater wrath against himself from the strict Judge.

—The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, etc. The tongue of the catholic Fathers adorns the knowledge of divine utterances by explaining more fully what canonical Scripture either presented obscurely or left written only in historical form.

—And the mouth of fools pours forth folly. This happens when they understand the sayings of sacred Scripture perversely and prefer their own opinions to its authority. It may also be understood of pagan philosophers, as in the saying, “The mouth of fools pours forth folly.” Such were Porphyry and Julian, who poured out the streams of their folly against the teachers of the Church.

—A soothing tongue is a tree of life, etc. The tongue of a catholic teacher leads to the fruit of everlasting life; but a tongue that does not know the measure of ecclesiastical discipline will, by speaking wrongly, crush both its own spirit and that of those who listen to it.

—The house of the righteous has abundant strength, etc. The house of Christ, that is, the Church, possesses very great strength, so that it can in no way be destroyed by the frequent rain, winds, and floods of temptations. But confusion continually rages in the works of the devil, because he attempts to overthrow this same house of Christ through false brothers or open adversaries.

—The lips of the wise will disseminate knowledge, etc. The lips of Catholics will disseminate, by preaching, the knowledge of right faith. The heart of heretics will be unlike this, because it conceives faithlessness in place of knowledge in order to teach. It may also be understood in this way: the heart of those who worship will be unlike itself, since through the mutability of various thoughts it shows itself changeable and never remains what it was. In contrast, concerning Anna, when she was entreating the Lord with attentive mind, it is said: “Her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel 1:18).

—The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, etc. The Lord abhors the prayers, works, and sacrifices of heretics, but accepts the vows of those who affirm the catholic faith by righteous works.

—The teaching of one who abandons the way of life is evil, etc. Evil is the teaching of those who abandon the way of truth. Concerning them the Lord says: “Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). Yet if such people repent after being reproved, the way back to pardon remains open; but if they do not heed ecclesiastical correction, certain destruction already awaits them.

—All the days of the poor are evil, etc. All the time of God’s people, so long as they are poor in the present life, is filled with afflictions and hardships, because they have not yet reached the riches of heavenly goodness and eternal dwelling. Hence the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5). But the reprobate, who lack fear of God and enjoy the world in security, are refreshed as though by continuous banquets of folly. Therefore he rightly adds:

—Better is a little with the fear of the Lord, etc. As it is said in the psalm: “Better is the little that the righteous man has than the great riches of sinners” (Psalm 36). It is therefore better, while preserving the fear of God, to lack wealth or even daily food than to abandon the fear of God through the desire to acquire more.

—Better is one invited to herbs with love, etc. Everyone who displays to his neighbors examples of good works for them to imitate invites them, as it were, to a banquet at which they may be refreshed. It is better, however, to be invited to herbs with love than to a fattened calf with hatred, because it is far more beneficial to preserve the innocence of a simple life together with charity than to shine outwardly with greater miracles of virtue while failing to cleanse the interior of the mind from the filth of hatred. Hence the Lord will say to certain people who professed faith: “Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name? And in your name cast out demons? And in your name done many mighty works?”—“I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

—The way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns. He calls slothful those who are reluctant to practice righteousness. When they desire the way of God, the suspicions arising from their fears prick them like thorns set against a resisting hedge. Since this does not usually hinder the elect, he adds:

—The way of the righteous is without stumbling. The righteous do not stumble in their conduct, whatever adversity may meet them, because by leaping over it they pass beyond the obstacles of temporal adversity toward eternal hope and inward contemplation.

—A man rejoices in the judgment of his mouth, etc. It is human to rejoice in one’s own opinion when it seems wisely expressed. But the truly wise person carefully considers not only the matters about which he speaks, but also the suitability of the place, time, and person to whom he speaks.

—The path of life is above the learned, etc. By “learned” he means one perfected not only in knowledge but also in action. For such a person the paths of life are rightly opened above; for him the gate of heaven stands open. But the lowest hell, from which he is delivered, is the final punishment of condemnation. The first hell is the blindness of the sinful soul, lacking knowledge of the true light. Concerning this it is said in the Psalms: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Psalm 54), that is, let those who know descend into sin.

—The Lord demolishes the house of the proud, etc. The Lord demolishes the gatherings of heretics and of the other persecutors of the Church, and makes firm throughout the world the boundaries of that same Church, his bride, for whose life he deigned to die.

—The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord, etc. The Lord abhors the thoughts of heretics—indeed, all thoughts opposed to piety—and the pure speech of right faith will be established by him, when in the judgment he will render fitting rewards not only for all deeds but also for all words. He abhorred the thoughts of those who said, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (Mark 2). And he established as most beautiful the pure speech of the one who said, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God”; to him he replied: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17).

—The light of the eyes rejoices the soul, etc. The human mind is rightly delighted when it recognizes that, through the Lord’s revelation, it has received the light of heavenly mysteries. Another translation states this more clearly: “The eye that sees good delights the heart”—namely, the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Whoever contemplates these with the eye of the mind is rightly delighted in heart, even though outwardly he may appear sad because he is afflicted by the enemy.

We also know that most blessed report by which we learn that not only our deeds and words but also our thoughts are laid open in heaven, carried there by the angels. It supplies our virtues with the richness of love and faith, lest they dry up through failing. For the more certainly we hold that the secrets of our heart, together with our deeds, lie open to the divine gaze, the more we ought to strengthen our good action with the oil of his charity, so that it may not grow weary.

—The ear that hears the reproofs of life, etc. A disciple who obediently accepts the reproofs of his teachers often advances through progress until he reaches the seat of honor. Thus Paul, who humbly submitted himself to the reproof of his Creator, afterward reached the throne of apostolic dignity in exaltation.

## CHAPTER XVI

—It belongs to man to prepare the soul, etc. It is certain that we can neither prepare the mind nor govern the tongue nor do anything good without divine grace, for he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). How, then, does it belong to man to prepare the mind and to God to govern the tongue, unless this specifically signifies the time of persecution? Concerning that time the Lord says: “When they deliver you up, do not think how or what you shall speak; for it shall be given you in that hour what you shall speak” (Matthew 10:19).

—All the ways of a man are open to his eyes, etc. The Lord sees the ways—that is, the actions—of all, both good and evil, so that with a true balance he also discerns the spirit of each person and what each thinks in secret. Hence he rightly adds:

—Reveal your works to the Lord, etc. We reveal our works to the Lord when, knowing that nothing is hidden from him, we recall him in everything we do and seek his help in all things. When we do this devoutly, it follows that not only those works themselves but also our inward thoughts proceed under his direction.

—The Lord has made everything for himself, etc. The Lord had no reason for creating an invisible or visible creature except his own will, namely, to display his goodness to a rational creature whom he would make blessed forever. He also, with just severity, condemned the one who by his own choice abandoned the goodness of his created condition—that is, the devil together with his followers.

—Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord, etc. Whoever attributes to himself the good he does, even if he seems to perform no evil with his hands, has already lost the innocence of his heart, in which he has placed himself above the giver of gifts. Therefore his Creator abhors him as guilty, seeing him to be ungrateful for his benefits.

—When the ways of a man please the Lord, etc. The holiness of divine religion is so great that often even those outside it hold it in reverence. When they see people serving God perfectly, they begin to live at peace with them, although they differ in religion. Thus, because the ways of Daniel and of the three young men pleased the Lord, he converted even their enemies—those who had cast them into the fire or exposed them to beasts—to peace. Because the ways of the holy preachers pleased the Lord, he converted many of their persecutors not only to peace but also to the same unity of faith and religion.

—Better is a little with righteousness, etc. The Lord also says: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Matthew 5). And again: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6). It may also be understood in this way: it is better to serve God devoutly in a simple way of life than, while abounding in many virtues—for example, almsgiving, prayers, fasting, teaching, and chastity—to despise the deeds of one’s neighbors and boast of one’s supposedly unique exaltation.

—Divination is on the lips of the king, etc. He signifies that king of whom it is said, “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Psalm 17 [18]). For which temporal king never errs in judgment? Divination is on his lips because he directs not only the words and deeds of his own people, but also determines inwardly what the gentile prophets—commonly called diviners—should answer those who consult them. The prophet Micaiah testifies to this: for the deception of Ahab, the most wicked king, he declares that a spirit was sent from the throne of the heavenly Judge to fill the mouths of his prophets and arm them to persuade him of what would bring about the wicked king’s ruin.

The mouth of the eternal King did not err in this judgment. Rather, what the impious king deserved to hear because of his preceding sins, he permitted the erring prophets to speak to him. Ezekiel likewise says to the sinful and doomed people of Ammon: “When you saw vain things and divined lies” (Ezekiel 21:29). This is not the divination of demons but the judgment of God, who gave them over to the end of their perfected wickedness.

Another translation presents this verse more clearly concerning the Lord: “Nothing false shall go forth from his mouth,” because he can neither be deceived by any liar nor ever lie himself.

—Weight and scales are the judgments of the Lord, etc. He calls the righteous and strong in faith “stones of the world,” such as the apostle Peter desired those whom he instructed to be: “You also, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses.” No one, therefore, is chosen from the beginning of the world by his own strength and made fit for the heavenly building. Rather, this is accomplished by the work of him who, establishing all things in weight, measure, and number, distributes to each person the measure of faith and of graces as he wills.

—The will of kings is just lips. By “kings” he means the saints, who are accustomed to rule principally over vices and to be surrounded by the virtues of the soul as by ranks of obedient companions. Concerning such people the Lord says: “Many prophets and kings desired to see the things that you see, and did not see them” (Matthew 13). Earthly kings, on the other hand, very often hate just lips, as Herod hated those of John, for which reason he punished him by beheading him.

—Whoever speaks what is right will be directed. That is, he will reach eternal life by the upright steps of his works. But in contrast, “a man of a talkative tongue shall not be directed upon the earth.” This does not conflict with what is said of Antiochus: “Deceit shall prosper in his hand.” Scripture did not say that the man himself would be directed, since it foresaw that he would be perverse and exceedingly wicked. Rather, it says that deceit would prosper in his hand, because the frauds and crimes he planned reached the outcome he intended without any hindrance. Yet after accomplishing them, he himself perished eternally, as he deserved.

—The king’s indignation is a messenger of death. The messengers of death are the angels of Satan—that is, heretics and vain philosophers—or rather all who announce to their neighbors words by which they may be snatched away from eternal death. The more devotedly they serve the author of death, the more gravely they offend the giver of life; yet the way of repentance is not closed to such people. For he adds:

—And a wise man will appease him. By recovering his senses, he can appease God, whom he happened to offend by speaking foolishly.

—In the gladness of the king’s face is life. Whoever is deemed worthy to see the joyful face of Christ will be granted to live with him forever. Otherwise, on the day of judgment, as it is written, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” But then the reprobate will see him angry, while the righteous will see him peaceful.

—And his mercy is like the latter rain. In Judea the latter rain has continued to fall until the present after the harvests have ripened. There the Lord also promises the early rain, saying through the prophet: “I will give you the early and latter rain of the land” (Isaiah 30). The early rain, or “seasonal rain,” as it is called elsewhere, falls when we first receive the seeds of faith in Christ. The latter rain falls when, having been taken from this life with the fruits of virtue mature, we are stored in the Lord’s granary.

The king’s mercy is rightly compared with the latter rain, because the fruit of life that we receive by doing good is produced not by the freedom of our will but by the watering of heavenly grace.

—The learned in the word will find good, etc. Not only will the person learned for preaching the word of the Lord find good with him, but also the person who has learned to place his hope in the Lord. Even if he is not capable of preaching to others, he becomes a participant in the blessedness of that same God.

—Whoever is wise in heart, etc. Whoever preserves undefiled in his heart the wisdom of the catholic faith that he has learned rightly receives the name of prudent. But whoever also knows how to preach that wisdom learnedly and defend it against heretics will receive greater rewards for his greater labor.

—The fountain of life is the instruction of its possessor, etc. When he says “of its possessor,” he does not add what the possessor possesses. What, then, should we understand him to mean except instruction itself? The complete sense would therefore be: “The fountain of life is the instruction of one who possesses his own instruction.” This plainly means that the preacher truly opens the ways of life to his hearers when he himself practices what he preaches, possessing firmly in his heart the love of the word by which he teaches others, rather than merely retaining it in memory and scattering it like seed gathered into his lap upon the earth.

The teaching of fools is therefore folly, because even if through habitual instruction they have learned to say certain good things, they nevertheless despise in their foolish hearts the very good things they say.

—A honeycomb is composed speech, etc. Through eloquence many people can speak sweetly to those who love and favor them of good things that they themselves neither love nor take care to do. Only those words contribute to the health of your bones—that is, to the spiritual growth of your virtues—which proceed from the inward sweetness of your soul.

—The soul of one who labors labors for itself, etc. In the literal sense it is clear that, after being expelled from paradise, man performs daily labor so that he may not perish. He compelled his mouth when he spoke with the serpent and when he touched what was forbidden, so that he might endure a long exile through labor and eat his bread in the sweat of his face. But the teacher also compels his mouth to labor, because he must do the good things that he says.

—An ungodly man digs evil, etc. The prophet also says: “They labored to do iniquity” (Jeremiah 9). This may be understood particularly of a heretic, who tears up with the noxious plowshare of his tongue the beautiful and flourishing fields of divine utterances, so that he may extract from their inner recesses impious meanings that are not there. Fire burns on his lips, by which he destroys himself and his hearers forever. Hence James says: “The tongue is placed among our members; it defiles the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by hell.”

—An iniquitous man entices his friend, etc. This may be understood of a heretic and of every perpetrator of evil. “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who does iniquity is blessed” (James 1).

—Whoever thinks of evil with staring eyes, etc. To complete evil is worse than to do it. Nor does only the person complete evil who performs something perverse and harmful through the members of his body; the person who deliberately plans to commit evil also completes it. The proud, enraged, are accustomed to bite their lips; they are accustomed to keep their eyes fixed and not to see what is before them while for a time they silently ponder the matter with attentive mind. Hence it may be inferred that “to think of evil with staring eyes” refers to one who investigates the evils he is about to do in such a way that he does not see the punishment that will follow evil deeds in the future.

—Better is the patient man than the strong, etc. It is a lesser victory to conquer cities, because what is conquered lies outside oneself. But greater is what is conquered through patience, because the mind itself is overcome and subjects itself to itself when patience lays it low in the humility of endurance.

—Lots are cast into the lap, etc. Just as lots are publicly cast into a lap and kept concealed within it, while it belongs to the divine Judge to determine whose lot will come forth and who will hold the prize, so human deeds are open to one another in the present life, but the merit belonging to each will be disclosed in the future, when the judgment of each person is brought forth and made manifest, as though from the lap of divine examination.

## CHAPTER XVII

—Better is a dry morsel with joy, etc. It is better to perform small good works with charity without the knowledge required for preaching—that is what it means for the morsel to be dry—than to shine with great virtues mixed with discord.

—The crown of the old is the children’s children, etc. By “the old” he means the patriarchs and prophets, who are celebrated with worthy praise by the children’s children—that is, by the successors of the apostles. It is also the glory of the preachers of the New Testament that they were found worthy to be sons of the ancient fathers.

—The most welcome jewel is the expectation of one who waits, etc. Whoever faithfully awaits future rewards rejoices as though in possession of a most splendid jewel. For in the Gospel the wise merchant sold everything he had in order to acquire the precious pearl, that is, heavenly desire. Whether adversity or prosperity befalls such a merchant, he is not diverted from his purpose, wisely understanding that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

—The wicked always seeks quarrels, etc. The cruel angel is an unclean spirit sent by the Lord against sinners to afflict them in the present, as he sent against the Egyptians “the anger of his indignation, indignation, wrath, and tribulation, sent by evil angels”; or even to seize them after death for eternal destruction. In contrast, the Lord sends an angel around those who fear him and delivers them.

—It is easier to meet a bear robbed of her cubs, etc. It was easier for the holy teachers to confront the fury of paganism after some peoples had been snatched away from it and converted by preaching from its bestial savagery to the piety of faith than to confront a heretic confident in the false doctrine of his own faithlessness.
