For in the former case they were fighting against outsiders, but in the latter against their own members.

The name “bear” may also signify the malice of the ancient enemy. We snatch away her cubs when, by catechizing and baptizing those who were sons of the devil, we join them to the fellowship of the sons of God. This is often accomplished with much less labor than when one attempts to recall a heretic to right faith or restore a Catholic who is acting wrongly to the practice of good works.

—Whoever releases water, etc. To release water is to let the tongue loose into flowing speech. In a good sense, however, it is said: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man.” Whoever therefore releases water is the beginning of quarrels, because whoever does not restrain his tongue destroys peace. Hence, in contrast, it is written: “Whoever imposes silence upon a fool calms anger.”

—What does it profit a fool to possess riches, etc.? What does it profit the Jewish people to possess the riches of Scripture in unbelief, when they cannot understand Christ in it? What does it profit a heretic to abound in those same riches, when he cannot learn unity of faith from them? What does it profit an evil Catholic to possess the riches of true faith, when he has neglected to possess the wisdom of devout action?

—Whoever is a friend loves at all times, etc. Whoever truly loves the Lord preserves his love for him at all times. He does not abandon in the distress of suffering the one whom he confessed in the tranquility of peace.

—A foolish man claps his hands, etc. A man is foolish if, when he undertakes to govern his brother’s soul, he boasts of his own deeds instead of offering him, with humble compassion, whatever salutary assistance he can.

—A joyful mind makes a flourishing age, etc. Whoever rejoices in the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit is also adorned with the flower of good action and awaits the fruits of heavenly rewards. But whoever is troubled by worldly sorrow, which produces death, may seem to exercise the richness of divine charity in the strength of his virtues, yet he cannot truly possess it. Rather, he withers like bones dried up, because he has lost the grace of love in the good works he performs.

—Wisdom shines on the face of the prudent, etc. On the face of the Lord and Savior the wisdom of divinity shone forth. Appearing in the flesh, he demonstrated it by the testimony of his virtues and teaching. But the eyes of the unbelieving Jews were directed more toward fulfilling earthly desires than toward attending to his saving admonitions.

More generally, prudent people often display the gravity of their understanding even in their outward appearance. Yet fools do not lift the eyes of their minds to admire and follow it; instead, they seek with complete attention how they may reach the end of carnal pleasures.

—It is not good to harm the righteous, etc. This may be understood of the very Prince and Judge of the ages, who willed to be struck for our salvation, and generally of all the rulers of the Church, who have either been stripped of their possessions by the wicked or consumed by death itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII

—When the wicked has entered the depths of sins, he despises, etc. Whoever, enveloped in the long darkness of sins, despairs of the light, then, out of despair, loosens the reins of sinning and gives himself over to it without restraint. Such a person cannot in any way escape the reproach of future condemnation, since no remembrance of divine fear restrained him from the practice of his iniquity.

—Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man, etc. The words of the wise are compared with water because they both wash the minds of hearers and water them, lest they remain disfigured by the filth of sins or waste away from lack of heavenly teaching and perish through a harmful dryness.

And because in the same words of teachers certain mystical and hidden meanings lie concealed, to be grasped by more diligent effort, while others flow forth openly and are easy for all hearers to understand, he rightly calls them both deep water and an overflowing torrent. It may also be distinguished in this way: because the Scripture of the Old Testament was expressed typologically, the words “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man” may be said of it, since the Lord and the apostles openly disclosed to the world the mysteries of both Testaments. He then adds concerning them: “And an overflowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom.”

—Whoever is lax and negligent in his work, etc. Whoever does not strictly carry out the good things he has begun imitates, through the dissolution of negligence, the hand of one who destroys.

—The substance of the rich is his city of strength, etc. Earthly substance cannot always defend anyone; indeed, many have been captured or killed because of their riches. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Riches preserved to the harm of their master; for they perish in the worst affliction.” It is therefore better understood as praising the substance of virtues. Whoever abounds in these virtues repels all the ambushes of enemies as though with an impregnable wall.

—Whoever answers before he hears, etc. Whoever desires to be a teacher before learning does not avoid the guilt of folly. Whoever hastily seeks to judge the deeds of his neighbors before fully discerning the case of both parties shows himself worthy of shame.

—The spirit of a man sustains his weakness. The man himself says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26). It may also be understood of any holy man who, by the strength of his mind, sustains the weakness of the flesh so that he may not yield in temptations.

—But a spirit easily moved to anger, etc. Whoever is quick to anger cannot sustain himself, so that when angry he often says things of which he later repents once calm, and frequently does not know what he has said. Yet his madness is sometimes very easily endured and immediately quieted by the restraint of the wise.

—A man’s gift enlarges his way, etc. The gift of charity, or of the other virtues that the faithful receive from the Lord, enlarges the way of their action. The more they are filled inwardly with the grace of the Spirit, the more broadly they multiply the steps of good works outwardly, and in the future they attain a height of honor among the great rulers of the Church.

Alternatively, the spiritual gift of the Savior, which he brought to the world, enlarged his way by reaching the many nations of the earth through the presence of his faith and love. It caused not only peoples but also the very rulers of the world to renounce their desires and willingly obey him.

—The righteous man is the first accuser of himself, etc. Whenever someone is truly righteous and sees the faults of sinners, he first turns the eye of consideration toward himself. After carefully accusing himself of his own weakness, he then kindly extends his tongue to correct others. But the one who deigned to say to his faithful people, “I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15), enters his heart through the presence of divine contemplation. He recognizes how pure it is from the stain of iniquity and rewards its humility with a fitting recompense.

—A brother helped by his brother, etc. When both peoples—the Jews and the nations—agree with one another in fraternal love in Christ, they build one city, the catholic Church. Just as bars secure the gates of cities, so the doctrines of both Testaments defend the churches throughout the world, which together constitute the one catholic Church, against the assaults of unbelievers.

—The poor man will speak with supplications, etc. The humble in spirit humbly adore the Lord, like that publican in the Gospel; the proud boast of their merits, like the Pharisee.

—An amiable man is inclined toward companionship, etc. The believing people from the nations were more beloved by the Lord than the Jewish people who continued without faith, among whom he was born according to the flesh. This may also be understood of the apostles born from Judah, since they loved believers from the nations more than the unbelievers of their own people.

## CHAPTER XIX
“Better is the poor man who walks in his integrity,” etc. A simple hearer of the word of God is better if he completes in practice whatever he has been able to understand in the Scriptures than any learned man who turns his lips, in the matters he has cleverly understood, toward preaching heresy.

“Where there is no knowledge in the soul, there is no good,” etc. Knowledge of heavenly life is indeed necessary for the human soul, since without it the soul cannot be blessed forever. Yet whoever, with unrestrained senses, desires to know more than is fitting often incurs the offense of heretical folly through rash interpretations. This was mystically signified in the first parents of the human race: while, driven by a desire for greater knowledge, they hastened to touch what was forbidden, they turned aside from the state of blessedness in which they had been created and fell into the punishment of misery and mortality.

“The folly of a man overturns his steps,” etc. It is the habit of fools that, when by sinning they abandon the way of truth, they do not admit that they have gone astray but refer the origin of their guilt back to the fault of their Creator, as though he had given them an opportunity to sin by making man fragile or by sending a crafty enemy to test him. Thus the first parent of our race, after his transgression, when rebuked by the Lord, immediately fled to the defense of excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave as my companion gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III). The woman herself said: “The serpent deceived me” (ibid.). Both of them turned back upon the Creator the blame for what they had done: the man, because he had received from the Lord as his companion the woman through whom he perished; the woman, because the Lord had placed in paradise the serpent that would deceive her.

By contrast, the Wise Man prays the Lord not to incline his heart toward an evil word, “to make excuses for sins.” The man, too, who overturns his steps and rages against God is burning with anger in his heart: he despises the divine commands through his own laziness and, in his insane mind, even reproaches God himself, as though he had imposed burdens impossible for human beings to bear.

“Riches add many friends,” etc. The riches of the heavenly kingdom, which the holy teachers preach must be bestowed upon the faithful, bring many friends both to those same preachers and to the Lord who grants them. But because philosophers and the other teachers of the nations know nothing certain to promise concerning future blessedness, those whom they had acquired are separated from them—namely, those who have been converted to the faith and to the firmest hope in the Lord’s promise.

“Whoever pursues words alone will possess nothing,” etc. The Apostle also says: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II).

“A false witness will not go unpunished,” etc. He had reproved the man who pursued knowledge merely in words, without the effectiveness of action; now he reproves the man who corrupts the very words of divine authority by interpreting them wrongly. The fact that many things are repeated so often is an indication of their certainty, as Joseph said when interpreting the king’s dream: “Because the word of God will come to pass, and will be fulfilled more quickly” (Gen. …).

“Delights do not suit a fool,” etc. The delights of the Scriptures do not suit a heretic, because he does not know how to use them well. Nor should one who is still shown to be a servant of sin be preferred to the just in governing the Church.

“The teaching of a man is known through patience.” The perfection of ecclesiastical teaching is demonstrated through the patience of its teachers. Since they preferred to subject their bodies to afflictions and death rather than cease from the duty of teaching, they plainly showed how salutary their teaching was, since they took such pains to defend it.

Alternatively: “The teaching of a man is known through patience,” because the less patient a person proves to be, the less learned he shows himself to be. For no one can truly offer good things through teaching if, in his life, he does not know how to tolerate the faults of others with equanimity.

Appropriately, the text adds:

“And his glory is to pass beyond iniquity.” For it is the mark of a perfect teacher to endure the wickedness of others patiently while also carefully guarding his own weakness against sinful action. Neither purity of one’s own conduct without tolerance of external disturbance, nor the strength to endure adversity outwardly while inwardly still weakly favoring evil habits, is sufficient.

“As the roaring of a lion, so is the anger of a king,” etc. He speaks of God the King, who will appear cheerful and gracious toward the righteous in judgment but terrifying toward the unjust.

“A foolish son is the grief of his father.” God is always impassible and tranquil in his nature, yet he is said, in our manner of speaking, to grieve when he sees human beings—whom he created to believe in and praise him—serving the malicious enemy rather than himself. Thus Moses says of him: “It repented him that he had made man on the earth.” And, touched by grief deep within his heart, he says: “I will destroy man, whom I created, from the face of the earth” (Gen. …).

“And continually dripping roofs, a contentious woman.” Just as roofs that continually drip receive rain from heaven but do not distribute it for any useful purpose, instead channeling it to the annoyance of those who live beneath them, so the church of heretics turns the heavenly gifts of words, by interpreting them wrongly and quarreling against Catholics, not toward the salvation of souls but toward the use of its own wickedness. Dripping roofs receive clean drops of rain but make those beneath them in the house filthy; likewise, a heretic takes in the clearest words of the heavenly oracle through bodily hearing, but once he has touched them with a polluted heart, he supplies them to his hearers mixed with filth.

“Sloth brings sleep.” The slothful person is one who, while apparently awake through right belief, grows numb by doing nothing. But sloth brings sleep because even while believing rightly, a person gradually loses his vigilance when he ceases striving to do good.

The text appropriately adds: “And the slack soul will hunger.” Since it does not direct itself toward higher things by restraining itself, it spreads itself downward through its desires. And because it is not constrained by the strength of disciplined pursuits, it is wounded by hunger for base desires; to the extent that it refuses to be bound by discipline, it scatters itself hungrily through desires for pleasures.

“He lends to the Lord who has mercy on the poor,” etc. The Lord himself proves the truth of this saying when he declares that he will say to those who give alms: “As long as you did it for one of these, the least of my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV).

“Educate your son, and do not despair; but do not set your soul on his destruction.” If you see anyone subject to you going astray, take care to correct him diligently. If he refuses to be corrected, act toward him with such prudence and moderation that he finds absolutely nothing in your words or actions by which he might sin further.

The following saying supports this interpretation:

“Whoever is patient will endure loss,” etc. If, provoked by the hardness of the brother whom you have begun to instruct, you yourself fall into the vice of impatience, you plainly suffer loss in your virtue. And if, by rebuking him perhaps too harshly, you take away the hope he had of attaining salvation and practicing repentance, you will render an account to the strict Judge because you have scandalized your brother.

The literal sense is clear: whoever, through impatience with poverty, gives himself over to theft or robbery harms his own soul; and when he takes away another’s property, even if he does not have to render an account to a human being for this, he certainly must render one to the eternal Judge. Hence another edition translated this verse as follows: “A man who devises evil will be afflicted with great loss; and if he is destructive, he will stake his own soul,” since, when he has violently seized money, he will unwillingly give his soul in exchange for it.

“A needy man is compassionate.” By “needy” he means the humble person who continually remembers that he is in need of everlasting goods. Such a person, in order to obtain mercy from the Lord, never refuses to show mercy to his neighbor.

Concerning him he adds immediately:

“And a poor man is better than a lying man.” Better is the man humble in heart, who trusts nothing in his own works, than the man who, because of the excellence of his virtues, considers himself worthy of the name “man” and is deceived—unaware that, by transferring God’s glory to himself, he loses through pride the good things he has done.

“The slothful hides his hand beneath his armpit,” etc. No one is so lazy that he would consider it labor to bring his hand to his mouth in order to eat. Yet for the slothful it is labor to extend his hand to his mouth, because every negligent preacher refuses to practice even what he says. To bring the hand to the mouth is to make one’s work agree with one’s voice.

“An unjust witness mocks judgment”—that is, the judgment expressed in the command, “You shall not bear false witness.” Or perhaps it refers to the future judgment, concerning which it was said above: “A false witness will not go unpunished”; “he who speaks falsehood will perish”; and “the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.” As a hungry man longs to be refreshed by food, so the wicked man eagerly seeks to be satisfied by an excuse for his iniquity.

“Judgments are prepared for mockers,” etc. Although the reprobate, as was said, mock the judgment of God’s command or threat, judgments of condemnation nevertheless await them, striking them without end in the furnace of Gehenna as hammers strike red-hot iron.

## CHAPTER XX

“Because of the cold the slothful would not plow,” etc. Whoever now neglects to labor in God’s service through laziness will beg on the coming day of the kingdom, and it will not be given to him, because “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” The kingdom of God is therefore rightly compared with summer: then the clouds of our sorrow pass away, the days of eternal life shine with the brilliance of the everlasting sun, and the fruit of labor is received in joy.

“The righteous man who walks in his integrity,” etc. This cannot always hold according to the literal sense. Blessed Samuel, a righteous and simple man, left behind sons unlike himself; and Ahaz, an unjust and reprobate king, left behind him the blessed son Hezekiah. But by “sons of the righteous” he means those who follow the righteous man’s example. Thus now all the elect are called sons of Abraham on account of their faith, according to the Apostle, who says: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed.” Blessedness is promised to them not in this age but in the age to come.

Hence the text rightly continues:

“A king who sits on the throne of judgment,” etc. Although the elect suffer evils in this life, when the day of universal judgment appears, all the evils of the reprobate will be destroyed; and when the righteous have been crowned with the Lord, only the unjust will undergo punishment. This also happens now in part, whenever one of the saints departs victorious from the world and the persecutor who troubled him receives what his deeds deserve.

This verse may also be understood of the elect, who sometimes have hidden evils in their minds that cannot be seen by other human beings, but which the Lord himself perceives when, through a hidden visitation of grace, he destroys them. The witness to this is the one who says: “The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord,” etc. (Luke XXII).

“Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” It should be noted that he does not say, “Who can have a clean heart and be pure from sin?” but rather: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?”

For there are people who, by the gift of divine grace, can possess, according to human measure, purity of both heart and conduct. Hence the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V); and in the Psalm: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. XXIII). For if no one has a clean heart and no one is pure from sin, it necessarily follows that no one ascends the mountain of the Lord and no human being stands in his holy place. But since it is certain that many will ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in his holy place, it remains that there are many pure in heart and, according to the measure of human possibility, pure from sin.

Nevertheless, no one should declare without presumption that he himself is pure in heart and free from sin. The boastful display of one’s own praise is foolish; it is presumptuous for anyone to glory in his own innocence or righteousness.

And since there are people who praise their own deeds as though they were strong while condemning the deeds of their neighbors as worthless, the text rightly continues:

“A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure,” etc. A person who has one weight in his own house and another measure—who measures himself in one way and his neighbor in another—searches constantly in his own actions for what can be praised, but in the actions of others for what can be blamed. The Lord therefore rightly abhors such a person, since the more he pleases himself without merit, the more deservedly he displeases the heavenly Inspector.

But because it is dangerous for anyone to judge another person’s conscience, whose intention he cannot know, the text gives advice about the signs by which we should direct the judgment of our heart concerning our neighbor. For it follows:

“And by his pursuits the boy is understood,” etc. Whoever you see devoting himself to virtues—to modesty, chastity, listening to the wise, observance of God’s commandments, and especially humility and simplicity—understand that his works are pure and upright. But if you discover someone following the opposite path, take care either to correct and chastise him as a man of impure and distorted heart or, if you cannot do so, to avoid and shun him, lest you yourself be corrupted by him.

It should not seem contradictory that this passage testifies that the works of a diligent boy are pure and upright, while above it says: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” In the present verse it recommends the pursuit of right living; in the other it discourages presumption about one’s own purity. Here it teaches that purity and uprightness such as the righteous can possess in this life are to be maintained; there it warns that the subtlety of the divine examination, by which God judges human deeds and intentions, must always be kept before our eyes.

Thus the ancient interpreters translated that passage as follows: “When the righteous King has sat upon the throne of judgment, who will glory in having a pure heart? Or who will glory in being clean from sin?”

They also rendered the verse that we are explaining more plainly, saying: “The young man who is with the righteous will have his way made straight. He who walks with the wise will be wise. Conversely, the friend of fools will become like them.”

“An ear that hears” means a hearer obedient to the word; “an eye that sees,” an educated teacher. Let no one who sees himself trained in knowledge of the Scriptures and fit to proclaim the word of God despise the simplicity of his brother. Although the brother may be less learned for preaching, he is not less ready to learn or to fulfill the good things he has learned.

Let him remember that the one who gave him the greater grace of knowledge himself bestowed upon his brother the spiritual gifts that the brother possesses. He gave him these gifts not solely for his own sake but also for the benefit of his brother, giving each person grace “according to the measure of his gift” (cf. Eph. IV).

“Do not love sleep,” etc. Do not love the sleep of sin and inactivity, concerning which the Apostle says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII), lest, if you are unwilling to keep watch well now, that most grievous poverty seize you in the future, where, though thirsty, you will be unable to find even a single drop of water. Open the eyes of your heart to holy vigils, and by living well acquire for yourself the fullness of heavenly joys.

“‘It is bad, it is bad,’ says every buyer,” etc. Therefore the man who desires to purchase eternal rewards in heaven says that what he must endure in the present is bad, but when he has departed from the world he will then rejoice, clearly perceiving that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (…).

“Gold and a multitude of jewels,” etc. This is the boast of the wise buyer, who, while he is making his purchase, says that what is happening to him is bad. But when someone has offended or injured God’s saints and, as though they were a cheap slave, has not refrained from treating them according to the pleasure of his own desire, he will rejoice that he has bought wisely.

So also the buyer of the heavenly kingdom, once he has departed from this world, will exult when he discovers that the lips of knowledge—that is, the spiritual teaching he used in purchasing heavenly things—are to be compared with gold, jewels, and precious vessels.

“Bread obtained by deceit is sweet to a man,” etc. Whatever member a person has sinned against most, in that member he will suffer greater torments in punishment. Hence it is rightly said that whoever has sinned more with his tongue will burn more in it, since his mouth is said to be filled with a stone, which is a burning stone.

This is known to have happened to the rich man who feasted splendidly every day: while burning in hell, he asked Lazarus to cool his tongue. Because he had indulged in superfluous speech and in feasting, he burned more intensely in his tongue.

“And whoever reveals secrets,” etc. If someone wishes to join your circle of friends and you see that he reveals the secrets of a former friend, beware of him as of a faithless man.

“An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning,” etc. Those who desire to multiply their possessions in this life through the wickedness of greed become disinherited from the eternal inheritance in the future.

Alternatively: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end.” Whoever rashly accepts a position of governance before learning to be subject will lack at the end the reward of blessing owed to good rulers. Whoever approaches the ministry of the altar ignorant and presumptuous will himself lose on the last day the grace of reward promised to those who minister well.

It may also be understood in this way: whoever in the present wishes to avenge his own injuries will lack the crown of patience in the future.

This interpretation seems especially suited to what follows:

“Do not say, ‘I will repay evil,’” etc.

The following verse also confirms it, saying:

“An abomination to the Lord is a weight and a weight,” etc. A person has a double weight and a deceitful balance in his heart when, after sinning, he himself asks forgiveness from the Lord but nevertheless refuses to forgive the person who has sinned against him and repented of what he did.

He strives by prayers to bend God, who is divine, toward mercy, while, although he himself is human, he can be bent toward mercy by no human prayers. Such a person will rightly be abhorred by the Lord as an unjust measurer, because he measures his own injuries as more serious than those of the Lord—for example, when he refuses to forgive the man who violated his wife, yet asks that he himself be forgiven for having perhaps defiled a virgin betrothed to Christ; or when he has polluted by some stain of vice the soul consecrated to God in baptism.

“By the Lord a man’s steps are directed.” Whenever human beings walk along a straight path, this does not happen through the freedom of human choice but through the governance of the one to whom Isaiah says: “For you have accomplished all our works in us” (Isa. …).

“But what human being can understand his own way?” This, he says, makes it plainly clear that whatever good anyone possesses, he does not possess from himself but by the grace of God. Nor, through the freedom of his own will, can he understand what he will be, or how or for how long he will live.

“It is the ruin of a man to devour the saints,” etc. Since it is a sin to harm any human being, how much more serious is it when he has feared? [The surviving Latin is uncertain here.] Thus in the Acts of the Apostles forty men vowed that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. And, as we often read, pagans vowed the blood of Christians to their gods.

An ancient edition rendered this verse according to another sense, saying: “It is a snare for a man to consecrate something of his own in silence; but after he has made the vow, he repents.”

And because eternal condemnation awaits both groups—those who persecute the saints in order to fulfill their vows and those who otherwise devour them—the text rightly adds:

“A wise king scatters the wicked,” etc. It was customary among the ancients, after gaining victory over an enemy, to erect arches for themselves on which they inscribed the praises of their valor, as we read in the account of Saul. Therefore our Lord and King not only destroys the wickedness of the impious but also perpetually celebrates with his elect the great glory of that same triumph.

Another translation has this verse as follows: “A wise king is a winnower of the wicked, and he will send a wheel of evils upon them”—that is, a punishment that will never come to an end. Opposed to this wheel is the crown of eternal life that God has promised to those who love him.

“The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man,” etc. When the illumination of the divine breath enters the human mind, it illuminates it and reveals it to itself: before the Holy Spirit’s coming, the mind could carry perverse thoughts but did not know how to weigh them.

“The exultation of the young is their strength,” etc. By gray hair he means wisdom. The cities of each people are then well ordered, and the affairs of the holy Church are rightly conducted, when those who are strongest in bodily power devote themselves to necessary works and the elders, endowed with greater prudence, give sound counsel concerning what must be done.

“The bruise of a wound wipes away evils,” etc. When we are struck outwardly, we are recalled silently and sorrowfully to the memory of our sins. Through what we suffer outwardly, we grieve more deeply over what we have done inwardly. Thus, amid the open wounds of the body, the hidden wound of the belly cleanses us more thoroughly, because the secret wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of an evil deed.

The mind is often understood by the term “belly,” because just as the belly consumes food, so the mind, by pondering, digests cares.

## CHAPTER XXI

“As the divisions of waters,” etc. Why does he say that the heart of the king, rather than the hearts of all human beings, is in God’s hand, when it is written, “For all the ends of the earth are in his hand” (Ps. XCIV)?  Perhaps he calls every holy person a king—one who knows how to conquer the battles of vices within himself and uproot the shoots of wickedness.

Just as the Lord fills the ends of the earth and the expanse of the air together through the manifold divisions of waters, and also covers the heights of the heavens with waters, so he inclines the king’s heart wherever he wishes. For just as, according to his will, he grants the divisions of grace to angels and human beings, so also he makes the hearts of the saints worthy of whatever gifts he wishes to bestow. No place therefore remains for the Pelagianist where anyone could be saved without the grace of God.

“A man’s perverse way is alien,” etc. To live rightly before the Lord is proper to the human condition. Hence he says elsewhere: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is every man” (Ecclus. XII). But whoever lives perversely plainly walks in a way alien to human nature. A perverse action is therefore alien and contrary to nature. Whoever is pure in conduct rightly carries out what he originally received by nature.

“It is better to sit in the corner of the housetop,” etc. It is so true that it is better for you to sit in the corner of the housetop—that is, in the hidden height of a more restrained life—than in a house shared with an evil woman, that even if the opportunity to marry an excellent woman is offered you, it is better to reject marriage and lead a celibate life for the companionship of the Lamb.

“Whoever stops his ear to the cry of the poor,” etc. This saying should be understood generally, not merely of the needy or of one who is physically ill. Whoever, when confronted with the sins of others, prefers to maintain the severity of a judge rather than grieve with compassionate feeling shows that he has not yet been cleansed of the offspring of vices and is not worthy to hear the divine mercy.

“A hidden gift extinguishes anger,” etc. Whoever desires to appease the anger of the strict Judge, which he has deserved by sinning, should give alms to the poor—not out of any pleasure in human approval, but solely out of love for the Creator, who sees what is hidden in hearts. In this way the gift is hidden; in this way it helps to lessen the Creator’s anger, if it is offered with no regard for external recompense. Thus what he himself commanded is fulfilled: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

“It is joy to the righteous to do judgment,” etc. The righteous man rejoices when he labors at good works, because he hopes that for these works he will be rewarded with everlasting good things. The reprobate, however, while doing the evils they know God has forbidden, may experience bodily pleasure in the indulgence of their lust, but they cannot be free from inward fear of mind, since they do not doubt that they will suffer everlasting evils for the temporal evils they have committed.

“A man who wanders from the way of instruction,” etc. By “giants” he means unclean spirits, concerning whom blessed Job says: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them” (Job XXVI, 5)—that is, the proud and wickedly powerful spirits of demons are tortured under punishment together with the human beings whom they have deceived.

Those who have wandered from the way of truth will be joined to their assembly, as the Judge himself testifies when he foretells that he will say to them: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

“An impious man is given in place of a righteous man,” etc. The righteous and the upright appear to be the same, but there is a difference between the impious and the wicked. All the reprobate are wicked; the impious are those entangled in greater crimes, who either never received the mysteries of the holy faith or, after receiving them, returned to apostasy.

Thus in this passage “impious” may be understood as referring to all persecutors of the faithful, while the word “wicked” generally designates all evil people.

“An impious man is given in place of a righteous man” when the persecutor who delivered a martyr to death is punished in place of the martyr. “The wicked in place of the upright” refers to those who saw the righteous life of the upright but were unwilling to imitate it.

Herod is condemned not only because of the innocent children whom he impiously delivered to death; he also received an additional basis for condemnation because he refused to follow the faith of the Magi in seeking the Lord, although he was among the Jews and knew the statements of the prophets. Hence the Lord says: “The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it,” etc. (Matt. XXI). She will not condemn it by her own virtue and power; rather, those who, knowing her devotion, nevertheless pretended not to care for wisdom even though they could have done so much more easily, will be condemned in comparison with her.

“A desirable treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the righteous,” etc. The readiness of good works, always pleasing to God, and the richness of love shine forth in the church of the saints.

Blessed Pope Gregory placed this verse in his Homilies on the Gospels according to the ancient translation: “A desirable treasure will rest in the mouth of the wise.”

The reprobate, however, hasten not only to fail to attain virtues but also to persecute them and, as far as they can, to overwhelm them in the good.

This verse may certainly be understood of any martyr, in whose dwelling—that is, in whose body—the holy soul, God’s treasure, is preserved, and the anointing of spiritual grace abounds. The imprudent persecutor may break open such a dwelling, but he cannot touch the treasure held within it or the oil. Hence the Lord teaches us not to fear those who kill the body and, after that, have nothing more they can do (Luke XII).

“A wise man ascends the city of the strong,” etc. By “the city of the strong” he means the world, which once, subdued by the foolish tyranny of evil spirits, served them, placing its confidence for life in the worship of those who are not gods but the works of human hands (Ps. CXIII).

The one born in the flesh who is the power of God and the wisdom of God entered this city (1 Cor. I). Through his preachers he destroyed the worship of the gods in whom those people had trusted while ignorant of the truth, and he taught them to place their confidence in faith in heavenly things—a confidence that could never be destroyed.

Every day, too, the wise man ascends the city of the strong and destroys the strength of its confidence whenever a faithful teacher refutes and tears apart through the assertion of faith and the discipline of ecclesiastical correction the arguments of philosophers or heretics, or even the stubborn contradictions of carnal brothers, by which they try to defend and excuse their crimes.

“A lying witness will perish,” etc. Whoever testifies that he serves God but does not carry out his words in his deeds will perish. But whoever faithfully submits to the divine commands as he promises will bring his speech to victory. While striving through obedience to conquer his own desires, he will later receive the palm of victory through the justice of the Judge.

“An impious man boldly hardens his face,” etc. Judas was impious in heart: although the Lord himself rebuked him, he was unwilling to restrain the evil he had begun. Peter, however, was upright in heart—that is, a lover of uprightness—and when the Lord looked upon him, he immediately corrected through repentance what he had done wrong by denying him.

“There is no wisdom, there is no prudence,” etc. Whatever heretics deliberate and consider wise is nothing—vain and useless.

“A horse is prepared for the day of battle,” etc. It is indeed the human being’s task to prepare a mind devoted to God during persecution and to offer his body to danger. But it belongs to divine assistance that success should follow the labor undertaken: victory in the struggle and salvation.

## CHAPTER XXII

“Better is a good name,” etc. By “a good name” he means not one praised by the crowds of the ignorant populace but one commended by the testimony of the faithful, even if they are few. He did not refuse to have a good name; he sought only to be praised by the good, as the one who said: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I).

A good name is therefore the name of religion, rightly preferred to worldly riches. Even if someone were to gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it merely so that his name might be written in heaven and his memory established eternally among angels and holy human beings.

“Good favor is above silver and gold.” He signifies the favor one receives when praised for a good work by good people; indeed, through the gifts of merits bestowed upon him, the Father who is in heaven is glorified.

“The rich and the poor meet one another,” etc. Do not despise the rich because of his wealth and honors, nor the poor because of his poverty. Rather, honor what is worthy of honor in both, because both are God’s work, having been made in the image and likeness of God.

“The prudent saw the evil and hid himself,” etc. Many of the rulers believed in the Lord, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they be expelled from the synagogue. Because they were prudent, they saw the evil of the persecution that threatened and hid the faith of devotion that they had begun to conceive, at least for a time.

But the innocent apostles passed along the straight road of the confession they had begun, and they were afflicted with blows, imprisonment, chains, and even death.

Many people continue to follow the example of both groups, both in the struggle of faith and in ordinary conduct.

The ancient interpreters translated this verse more plainly, though in another sense: “The clever man, seeing the wicked punished, himself receives much discipline; but fools, passing by, are afflicted with loss.”

“The end of modesty is the fear of the Lord,” etc. By “modesty” he means constancy in good works; by “the fear of the Lord,” the fear that endures forever and ever.

For the perfection of virtues is to rise to this state of mind: to fear offending the grace of the Creator even in the smallest matter, putting absolutely nothing before remembrance of him. Elsewhere this remembrance is called love, which “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV)—namely, slavish and beginning fear, by which a person fears that, if he sins, he may deserve to be subjected to punishments.

What he adds—“Riches, glory, and life”—signifies the future. Thus the end of modesty is the fear of the Lord, and riches, glory, and life: the perfection of virtues in this life is to fear the Lord with holy fear, that is, to worship him with sincere love. The end of virtues in the future is to receive from the Lord the riches of the promised inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, glory, and life without end.

Hence Peter says: “When you see him, you will exult with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (1 Pet. III).

“Weapons and swords are on the way of the perverse,” etc. This should be understood in two ways. The perverse are always armed and prepared to harm their neighbors by wicked word or deed, and the vengeance of divine judgment always awaits them. Whoever takes care to save his soul eternally keeps far away from such weapons and swords: he restrains both mind and hand from harming his neighbors and, lest he himself be struck by the sentence of the strict Judge, takes careful precautions with attentive mind.

“It is a proverb: ‘A young man according to his way,’” etc. It is clear that many people, by the Lord’s gift, are changed in old age from the vices they had as young men; conversely, when the Lord abandons some people, they abandon in old age the virtues by which they had seemed to shine in youth.

But because a person much more often continues throughout the rest of his life the habits with which he was formed from adolescence, he calls it a proverb: whatever each person begins as a young man, he ordinarily does not change in old age. He does not, however, affirm that this always happens.

He introduces this proverb in order to persuade his hearers to devote themselves to virtues from their earliest age, lest in old age they be unable to learn the disciplines to which they had refused to devote themselves in their tender years.

For also:

> “What has once been imbued while fresh will retain the scent.”

[Testa diu: reading uncertain] [Col. 1003A]

And Greek history relates that Alexander, the most powerful king and ruler of the world, could not free himself, either in character or in bearing, from the faults with which he had been infected when still a little boy under the tutelage of his teacher Leonidas.

—“The rich rules over the poor,” etc. This is clear according to the literal sense; but, allegorically, the rich in virtues also exercise authority at the judgment over those who lack the riches of virtues—or rather, they become their future judges. And whoever receives the word of saving doctrine from a teacher is that teacher’s servant, that is, bound to fulfill everything which that master, by right of his heavenly teaching, commands him. [The manuscript has *ille* for *illī*?]

—“Whoever sows iniquity,” etc. It is certain that the one who teaches iniquity either by word or by example will receive punishment. But because it follows, “And with the rod of his anger he will be brought to an end,” he seems especially to mean that iniquity which is carried out with a cruel and impious mind: practicing robbery, oppressing people with servitude, tearing them apart with tortures, killing them, taking away a widow’s ox as a pledge, and refusing, when able, to avenge her against her adversary. Such a person will rightly be brought to an end by the rod of his anger; for, as the Lord says, “Everyone who takes up the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI, 52), that is, those who rage unjustly against others bring destruction upon themselves by that very rage.

But because he had spoken of the impious, he next speaks, by contrast, of the godly:

—“Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed,” etc. Similar is the saying of that same Judge, who, distinguishing the merciful from the impious, says: “Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. [Col. 1003C] XXV, 34–35). The bread given to the poor may be understood not only as bodily food but also as spiritual doctrine, by which the soul is refreshed.

—“Cast out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him,” etc. Cast the heretic whom you cannot correct out of the Church; and when you have taken away his freedom to preach, you provide assistance to catholic peace.

—“Whoever loves purity of heart,” etc. Whoever preaches rightly with a pure heart will be counted among those of whom the prophet said to that same King and Creator of the ages: “But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honorable” (Ps. CXXXVIII). For if someone displays the grace of his lips by preaching what is right, but neglects to preserve purity of heart, he must in no way be thought capable of enjoying the friendship of the eternal King. [Col. 1003D]

—“The eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge,” etc. Heavenly inspection always preserves within the Church the knowledge of the truth which He taught. The words of heretics—or rather, every speech contrary to piety and justice—are not preserved, because the Lord governs; together with their author, they are overthrown.

—“The sluggard says, ‘There is a lion outside,’” etc. The one who is lazy in performing good works and fearful of confessing openly the faith he holds in his heart often says within himself: “I dare not profess openly the faith I hold, lest the impious persecutor kill me when he hears that I am faithful. I am afraid to come forth publicly to practice the works of virtue, lest perhaps either the more severe hostility of the ancient enemy test me, or some perverse person, together with his crowd, mock me, disgrace me with insults, harm me with injuries, or, like many righteous people who disagree with his way of life, destroy me with torture and death.”

“There is a lion outside,” he says; “I will be killed in the middle of the streets.” This is plainly to say: As soon as the words and works of virtue begin to be displayed publicly, persecution by human beings or by unclean spirits immediately accompanies them. Nor can I resist temptations; rather, I will be overcome in the very beginnings of my good purpose.

—“A deep pit is the mouth of a strange woman,” etc. Whoever willingly embraces the words or kisses of a prostitute is, as it were, already knocking at the gate of the abyss of Gehenna, and will quickly be submerged unless he cautiously withdraws his foot, unless he restrains his other members from the vices of the penal pit, into which absolutely no one falls except a son of wrath.

—“Folly is bound up in the heart of a child,” etc. We know many children endowed with wisdom; for Jeremiah, while still a child, undertook the ministry of prophecy. Daniel writes that “God gave knowledge and discipline in every word and wisdom to the abstinent children” (Dan. II). We must therefore understand that in this passage “children” signifies not those young in age but those who are little in understanding—people whom the Apostle forbade to be such when he said: “Do not become children in your minds, but be infants in evil” (1 Cor. XIV). Such children—that is, minds devoted to folly, wantonness, or sluggishness—must necessarily be corrected by youthful discipline and brought, through the vigor of the prudent, onto the right path of life.

—“Whoever slanders the poor,” etc. It is clear that rapacious people lose everything alike: both what they take from the poor and what they appear to possess justly, when, at the examination of the strict Judge, they receive punishment for what they have done. The same is true of those who slander a poor brother in spirit by disparaging his virtues, so that through denigrating him they may increase the riches they desire—that is, greater human praise, as though they were more holy. Such a slanderer rightly loses whatever good action he seemed to possess and will remain empty of the fruit of virtues at the end.

Thus far extends the heading “The Proverbs of Solomon,” which was placed above. From this point he is shown to have adopted a new manner of speaking, so that what he says appears to be addressed not to another whom he is teaching, but as though he were reasoning alone with himself. The first verse of these Proverbs is: “A wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is his mother’s sorrow.” The last is the one whose exposition we have now reached. From here he returns to the earlier manner of speaking, so that he addresses specifically the person whom he is instructing. It begins as follows:

—“Incline your ear,” etc. He makes a most beautiful beginning to the new discourse, commanding the person he is teaching to apply his ear to hearing and his heart to understanding what the wise say.

—“It will be beautiful for you when you keep it within your belly,” etc. The teaching of wisdom often appears harsh and unpleasant to the foolish. But once they have grasped its power in their inmost heart, learned to preserve it in their works, and learned also to offer it to their brothers with their lips, they will discover it to be more beautiful than all other doctrines.

—“Behold, I have described it to you three times,” etc. He has described his teaching to his hearer in three ways, because he commanded him to think it, speak it, and practice it in his works. If one considers it carefully, this whole little book shines forth as full of this threefold description.

—“Do not use violence against the poor,” etc. This may be understood of any poor or needy person, concerning whom it is said: “For the poor man is left to you; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. XIX). But because it follows, “And he will pierce those who pierced his soul,” it is better understood of Him who, although rich, became poor for us (2 Cor. VIII); He not only consented to become poor in order to enrich us, but also consented to be crucified in order to redeem us. Wisdom therefore forbids its hearers to inflict violence and death on the Lord preaching in the flesh, since certain destruction awaits those who were not afraid to lay hands upon the author of life.

—“Do not be a friend to an angry man,” etc. These words can generally be understood of every angry or furious person. Nevertheless, nothing prevents their being understood of those who raged with deranged minds against the Savior and His disciples. All who believed in Him and were concerned for their salvation are forbidden their friendship and company, lest they too perish through proximity to the wicked. The case of Judas Iscariot proved that this could happen.

In general, however, it must be said that just as perfect men ought not to flee from perverse neighbors, because they often draw them toward righteousness and are themselves never drawn toward perversity, so all the weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils which they frequently see but cannot correct.

—“Do not be among those who drive in their hands,” etc. Do not associate with those who, though free and devoted to themselves, fix themselves in concern for the salvation of wicked people, promising that they will render an account to the Lord for their souls. For if the one for whom you made this promise has no good works by which to make you free and secure from your pledge, what benefit is it to you that on the day of judgment you should yourself be judged for his soul and lose the garment of righteousness with which you seemed to be clothed? Hence also the Lord says: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX).

—“Do not move the ancient boundaries,” etc. Do not cross the boundaries of the faith which catholic teachers established from the beginning.

—“Have you seen a man swift in his work?” etc. Whoever you see swift in his work—that is, diligent and attentive in the good work which it was his duty to do—know that he will stand on the day of the final examination before the apostles, who will sit with Christ to judge the world, because he has kept their commands. He is not to be placed among the ignoble teachers whose error he avoided—that is, on the left hand of the Judge.

## CHAPTER XXIII

—“When you sit down to eat with a ruler,” etc. Everything is said allegorically: when you sit down to read with a teacher, so as to be refreshed by the bread of the word, carefully understand what is written, and preserve the discernment of sacred reading in your speech—provided, however, that you are such a person and so instructed that you have your soul in your own power, and are not, like one untaught, subject in mind to your teaching. For he used “throat” for speech, because the voice is in the throat; and “knife” for discernment, because when we are refreshed we prepare food by cutting it with a knife. And one who sits down to eat sets a knife to his throat when the person who diligently meditates on the divine utterances brings forth discriminating words from his mouth and turns over on his tongue nothing more frequently than the sayings of the heavenly oracle. This belongs to one who has his soul in his own power, that is, who has learned to preserve the steadfast condition of a wise mind amid the errors of deceivers. Hence he rightly adds:

—“Do not desire his foods,” etc. That is plainly to say: Do not desire to listen to the words of one who is accustomed to deceive his hearers by the sweetness of false doctrines.

—“Do not labor to become rich.” He means riches of knowledge, which we are forbidden to seek beyond the measure of our capacity.

—“Set a limit to your prudence.” Namely, the limit of which it was said above: “Do not cross the ancient boundaries which your fathers established”; that is, the boundaries of the faith handed down by the fathers.

—“Do not lift up your eyes toward riches,” etc. Do not raise your mind to investigate the mysteries of divinity which you cannot penetrate. These are open only to heavenly citizens.

—“Do not eat with an envious man,” etc. Do not discuss the Scriptures with a heretic, because he envies human salvation and prefers to deceive rather than correct. For just as a diviner and interpreter of dreams supposes what he does not know, so the heretic presumes to interpret the things he does not understand in the Scriptures as he pleases.

—“He will say to you, ‘Eat and drink,’” etc. “Learn and do without anxiety what I teach,” he says, although he himself has no sure faith in what he teaches, knowing that he has fabricated in his own heart what he teaches.

—“You will vomit up the foods which you had eaten,” etc. The perverse meanings which you learned from heretics you must either abandon, correcting yourself through repentance, or after death be compelled to pay penalties for them; and you will lose the words of confession by which, while they preached, you had thought one ought humbly to support them.

—“Do not speak in the ears of fools,” etc. Similar is that saying of the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine,” and so forth (Matt. VII, 6). Therefore, just as above he warned you not to listen to the doctrines of heretics, so now he urges you not, seduced by love of empty glory, indiscriminately to offer the mysteries of truth to unclean people.

—“Do not touch the boundaries of little ones,” etc. He calls the Lord the kinsman of little ones and orphans, because when He was in the flesh He deigned to be a sharer in the faith of the poor rather than of the rich. Otherwise, the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon Him. The name of orphans and little ones may also fittingly designate those of whom the Lord says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me. For I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Whoever touches their fields and boundaries—that is, injures their good way of life by troubling it—will not escape the Lord’s judgment.

—“Let not your heart envy sinners,” etc. If throughout the day, that is, throughout the entire time in which you remain in the light of this world, you strive both to avoid the examples of sinners and to fear the Lord, you will have the hope of blessed recompense at the last, that is, when you reach the end of this life; as He Himself testifies: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. II).

—“Do not be among drinking parties,” etc. To contribute meats for eating is, in a conversation of detraction, to recount in turn the faults of one’s neighbors. Of their punishment he immediately adds:

—“For those who spend their time drinking and give contributions,” etc. *Symbolum* is a Greek word and means “a contribution.” There is a contribution of words, as commonly occurs in deliberations; and there is one of money or other things, as the present passage also shows. Those spend their time drinking who become intoxicated by the reproach of another’s life. To give a contribution is, just as each person contributes food to eat according to his share, to contribute words in a conversation of detraction. But those who spend their time drinking and give contributions will be consumed, because, as it is written, “Every detractor shall be rooted out.”

—“Drowsiness will be clothed in rags.” For death will find despised and destitute of all good works the one whom here the languor of detraction has occupied in searching out the crimes of another’s life.

—“Let your father and your mother rejoice,” etc. Let God the Father rejoice in your righteousness, and let the Church, your mother, rejoice; and let the priest who regenerated you through the grace of baptism and instructed you from childhood rejoice over your good works.

—“Who has woe? whose father has woe?” By disputation he asks for what crimes of men the greatest punishment is reserved by the Lord. He himself answers by reasoning: without any doubt, it is for those who through drunkenness descend into lust. “Who,” he says, “has woe? whose father has woe?” By “woe” he means eternal destruction. Of it the Lord says: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII). By the father of one over whom woe hangs he means either the person from whom anyone received outward examples of wicked conduct, in order to sin; or indeed the devil, who inwardly pours the poison of pestilential suggestion into the heart. Of him it was said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII).

—“Who has quarrels? who has pits?” Quarrels, because one whom drunkenness has made incapable of sense does not know how to preserve the concord of peace; pits, because one who, as if deranged, does not know how to distinguish good and evil does not fear to fall everywhere into the mire of every vice. And the drunkard very often falls into that pit of which it was said above: “For a prostitute is a deep pit, and an adulteress a narrow well.”

—“Who has wounds without cause?” etc. Wounds without cause: because many, filled with wine beyond measure, receive fearful wounds in their limbs which they have suffered for no cause of the sword. Bloodshot eyes: because the immoderate draught of wine produces both dimness of bodily sight in very many and blindness of the inner sense.

—“Are they not those who linger over wine?” etc. He does not forbid drinking wine for necessity, but lingering over wine beyond the proper time and use, and competing with one another in emptying cups, as Isaiah says: “Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. V).

—“Your eyes will see strange women,” etc. After the poisons of drunkenness have been poured into the heart, it is a customary and almost natural vice to follow female desire, accompanied also by perversity and obscenity of speech.

—“And you will be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea,” etc. He sleeps in the midst of the sea who, placed amid the temptations of this world, neglects to foresee the onsets of approaching vices as though they were threatening waves; and, like a sleeping helmsman, loses the rudder when the mind loses its attentive care for steering the ship of the body.

—“And you will say, ‘They struck me, but I did not hurt,’” etc. The voice of one struck and sleeping is expressed. For the mind sleeping from lack of attentive care is struck and does not hurt, because just as it does not foresee impending evils, so it does not recognize what it has committed. It is dragged along and does not feel, because it is led through the enticements of vices and nevertheless is not roused to guard itself. It wishes to awaken in order to find wines again: although it is oppressed by the sleep of stupor and neglect of itself, it nevertheless strives to wake for worldly concerns, so that it may always be drunk with pleasures. And while it sleeps in that in which it ought diligently to have kept watch, it desires to keep watch for that in which it might laudably have slept.

## CHAPTER XXIV

—“Do not envy evil men,” etc. Do not desire to imitate those whom you see entangled in the vices which I have mentioned; rather, take care to devote yourself to wisdom.

—“The storehouses will be filled with teaching,” etc. The storehouses are the hearts of the righteous, which will be filled with the gifts of virtues only through the teaching of wisdom.

—“A wise man is strong,” etc. Not everyone who is strong and wise is to be called wise; but every wise person is to be called strong, because even if he is weak in body, if wisdom is present he conquers all the contests of the strong adversary, that is, the devil.

—“Wisdom is too high for a fool,” etc. The fool cannot attain wisdom; for it is high above one who lies in the lowest vices. Even if in the present he thinks himself to know something, at the gate of the city—that is, at the departure from this life—he will find that what he thought he knew was nothing.

—“He who thinks of doing evil will be called a fool.” Lest you think that one whom you see dull and slow in intellect ought to be considered a fool, he plainly shows that the one to be called a fool is the person who consents even in thought to the suggestions of sin, although he seems sharp in intellect; not one who, though he appears dull in understanding, has resolved to obey God’s commands which he has been able to learn.

—“If you despair when weary in the day of distress,” etc. Nothing is more execrable than despair. Whoever possesses it loses steadfast courage both in the general labors of this life and, what is especially harmful, in the contest of faith.

—“Rescue those who are being led to death,” etc. This may be understood mystically. Rescue those deceived by heretics by preaching the right faith; show examples of good works to those drawn to destruction by Catholics living badly. And if you see any who have fallen, or are about to fall, in the contest of persecution, strive to restore them to life by earnest exhortation. If you see some about to perish from hunger or suffering from cold, refresh them by providing food and clothing.

—“Eat honey, my son, because it is good,” etc. It is very clear why he compares the teaching of wisdom to honey and honeycomb: just as honey surpasses other foods in sweetness, so wisdom surpasses other teachings. But there is this difference between their meanings: honey, readily available to eat, signifies the moral surface of the letter; the honeycomb, in which honey is pressed out from wax, figuratively denotes allegorical discourse, where, after the veil of the letter has been drawn aside, the sweetness of spiritual meaning is perceived with some labor or delay.

—“Do not lie in wait and seek wickedness in the house of the righteous,” etc. Do not seek any occasion by which to disparage a righteous person. If he falls, he quickly removes his foot, so that he may be free of a vice not repeated in action. But the wicked fall so as not to return thereafter, as he adds next:

—“For the righteous man falls seven times,” etc. But how is one who is said to fall—that is, to sin—called righteous? Unless he speaks of light and daily sins, without which no righteous person could be in this life. For through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, surprise, necessity, and the frailty of the flesh, daily, whether unwillingly or willingly, we frequently incur guilt. Yet the righteous rise again, precisely because they are righteous; nor does the fall of human frailty prejudice their righteousness. Thus, when speaking of the righteous person’s fall, he rightly did not add “into evil,” because though it is evil that they fall, they nevertheless hasten to rise and cannot remain in the evil into which they have fallen. But of the reprobate, on the contrary, it is said: “The wicked will fall into evil,” because when the wicked have fallen—or, what is graver, have utterly fallen, as Scripture says, that is, when they have committed capital crimes—they so consent to their fall by delighting in it that they disdain to be raised from it by repentance.

—“When your enemy falls, do not rejoice,” etc. Above he forbade laying snares for the righteous; now, in order to make one perfect in all things, he forbids insulting even enemies when they sin or incur some adversity, lest perhaps, if through the Lord’s mercy they return to repentance and the salvation of their souls and begin to have faithful friendship with you, you may then be ashamed because you once despised those whom divine grace had preserved for life. But, as far as you can, grieve with those who lie fallen and help them to rise; and if your prayer and effort are followed by success, you will rejoice over one healed whose illness had grieved you; otherwise, you will nevertheless not lack before God the fruit of your goodwill. Or it may certainly be said thus: Do not rejoice at your enemy’s fall, lest the Lord, humbling you by bringing down in this manner your pride—which undoubtedly displeases Him—cause you to fall into sin while your enemy, coming to his senses, is healed.

—“Fear the Lord, my son, and the king.” This is in accord with His saying: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII). Nor is there any obstacle to understanding the Lord and the king as signifying the Father and the Son, who are to be worshiped with one and the same honor of divinity. “For whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V). “And do not mingle with detractors.” Namely, with those who, saying that they knew God the Father, refused to receive the Son of God appearing in the flesh.

—“For their destruction will arise suddenly,” etc. He speaks of both: the detractor and the person mingled with him by supporting him; the rulers who disparaged Christ and the people deceived by them; the founders of heresies who tear apart the faith and the hearers who listen to them.

—“These things also are for the wise.” It is understood: it is unknown when any of the reprobate will be suddenly snatched from the world by death. Or: these things too, which I have taught—that they should not mingle with detractors—are to be observed by the wise, because almost the whole human race is endangered especially by this vice. Wishing to remedy this same vice, blessed Father Augustine had these verses inscribed on his table:

> Whoever loves by speech to tear apart the life of one absent,
>
> let him know that he is unworthy of this table.

The old edition states this verse more plainly: “I say these things to you who acknowledge wisdom,” which can suitably be the beginning of the following sayings.

—“To recognize a person in judgment is not good.” Above he taught that the king should be feared, and now he forbids recognizing a person in judgment. From this it follows that subjects ought to render rulers the temporal obedience due to them, but never depart from the way of truth out of regard for, or fear of, them.

—“He will kiss the lips,” etc. A kiss is a sign of peace and love. Therefore, the person who answers rightly will kiss lips, because whoever, disregarding respect of persons, follows only the words of justice will find many prudent people with whom he may have peace and many who embrace his words with love, even though he may perhaps seem burdensome and harsh to fools. He will often also receive as friends and companions those whom he had endured as opponents of his right assertions, when they afterward turn to better things.

—“Prepare your work outside,” etc. What is it to cultivate the field diligently after preparing the work, except, having uprooted the thorns of iniquities, to cultivate our action for the fruit of recompense? And what is it to return to building a house after the cultivation of the field, except that we often learn from good works how great a purity of life we should establish also in thought? For he builds the house of the mind well who first clears the field of the body from the thorns of vices, lest, if the thorns of desires grow in the field of the flesh, the whole structure of virtues within be destroyed by the growing hunger for good.

—“Do not be a witness without cause against your neighbor,” etc. These matters too concern the cultivation of our field—that is, the practice of good action: not to harm an innocent neighbor by false testimony; not, by flattery, to grant anyone who sins greater confidence in sinning; not to repay evil for evil. Thus it comes about that, when you have first ordered your outward actions well, you afterward attain also to cultivating the purity of the inner person and, as it were, after tilling the field, begin to adorn and establish more deeply the dwelling of the mind with godly thoughts. Since the reprobate neglect to do this, he rightly adds: “I passed by the field of a sluggard,” etc. To pass through the field and vineyard of a sluggard and fool is to inspect the life of any negligent person, which nettles and thorns fill because in the heart of the negligent the itching desires of earthly things and the pricks of vices spring up. As it is written: “Everyone who is idle is given over to desires.” And the wall of stones in the vineyard or field of the fool lies destroyed when every negligent person loses the defenses of virtues once begun, either deceived by the wickedness of evil people or by the crafty persuasion of unclean spirits.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1011]

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 1011A]

These, too, are Solomon’s proverbs, etc. Here he begins to speak in a new order, so that he no longer addresses the hearer of the word as before, but examines by discussion with himself what the reasoning of truth contains. Yet in these passages every reader or hearer may recognize with complete clarity what he ought to desire and what he ought to avoid.

These proverbs are said to have been collected by the men of Hezekiah, because perhaps until his time they had remained scattered among many people, just as they had received them once spoken from the mouth of the wisest king. Through Hezekiah’s diligence, however, they were gathered into one collection and inserted into the body of this little book. It should certainly be noted that these proverbs contain far more allegorical interpretation than the others, namely, through the comparison of things that appear suited to serve as figures.

### “The glory of the Lord is to conceal a word,” etc.

[Col. 1011B]

The glory of the Lord is to display to mortal eyes the humanity of his appearing in the flesh more than his divinity, and to confess himself as the Word—that is, the Son of God—rather through miracles of his works and mystical sayings than through explicit assertions. Hence in the Gospel he very often customarily calls himself the Son of Man rather than the Son of God.

The glory of his faithful disciples, on the other hand, is to investigate his saying diligently, by which he mystically signifies God even where he does not state this openly. Such is the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and others of this kind. Finally, concealing the eternity of the Word and displaying the weakness of the flesh, he says: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16). The foremost of the apostles, having investigated his saying—which he had often heard before—answered him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.). By this investigation he earned no small glory, for immediately he heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” and so forth (ibid.).

### “Heaven above and earth below,” etc.

[Col. 1011C]

Just as human beings cannot comprehend the height of heaven or the depth of the earth, so the knowledge of the prophets and apostles—who, through the revelation of the Spirit, came to know the divine mysteries—surpasses the capacity of our weakness.

### “Take away the rust from silver,” etc.

Remove the surface of the letter from sacred eloquence, and you will find the purest meaning hidden beneath the subtlety of the letter, and discover that spiritual mysteries have lain concealed beneath the carnal figures of ceremonies.

### “Take away wickedness from before the king,” etc.

[Col. 1011D]

Take away from Saul’s mind—or from that of any other zealot of the Law—the wickedness of persecuting Christians. When they begin to preach Christ, the throne of justice will be established as the seat of their teaching, whereas wickedness had previously driven it toward its ruin, so long as, resisting the justice of God, they strove to put their own justice first.

Again, “take away wickedness from before the king, and his throne will be established by justice.” Those who rule peoples, if they wish their throne to remain firm, should always present faces full of cheerfulness and grace, lest, becoming too rigid through arrogance, they incur the grumbling of the people.

### “Do not appear glorious before the king,” etc.

[Col. 1012A]

Above he instructed the ruler; now he addresses the subject. For just as he said there that the ruler should show cheerful faces to his subjects, so now he admonishes the subordinate not to appear arrogant in the presence of his superiors, but rather, being placed in a modest position, to deserve to be summoned higher.

The Lord’s saying is similar: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place,” and so forth (Luke 14). We may also understand the king and prince as signifying the Lord, in whose presence we must always humble ourselves, as the apostle Peter admonishes when he says: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5).

### “What your eyes have seen, do not quickly bring forth in a quarrel,” etc.

[Col. 1012B]

In the Gospel, too, the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone,” and so forth (Matthew 18).

### “Golden apples in beds of silver,” etc.

[Col. 1012C]

Sacred utterances are most fittingly compared with silver beds—beds, indeed, because they provide rest for the souls of those who hear them; silver, because they shine with the virtues of the fathers. Hence it is written: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested in fire” (Psalm 11).

Whoever, by explaining those same divine utterances as full of spiritual meanings and mysteries, displays golden apples in addition to the adornment of these beds, supplies their ornament. These meanings are aptly called apples because they have come from the tree of life, that is, from the wisdom of God. They are aptly called golden apples because they pour the knowledge and love of perpetual brightness into minds.

“Golden apples in beds of silver” is one who speaks a word in its proper time, because whoever knows how to preach the word of God opportunely, according to the capacity of his hearers, sometimes repeats literally the examples and sayings of the fathers, through whose guardianship eternal rest is reached; at other times he removes the veil of the letter and opens within them the sweeter fruits of spiritual meanings, by which he nourishes the pious desires of his hearers.

### “A golden earring and a shining pearl,” etc.

[Col. 1012D]

The humble hearer is rightly compared to a golden earring, because, while willingly lending his ear to one who rebukes and teaches, he is already preparing himself to receive the brightness of heavenly wisdom and drawing near to the vision of the light above.

The learned teacher is rightly likened to a shining pearl, because, while he displays the correction of conduct and the knowledge of heavenly things to minds that desire and piously seek them, he fastens upon golden adornment the greater and more pleasing radiance of a burning gem.

### “Like the cold of snow on the day of harvest,” etc.

[Col. 1013A]

It seems entirely inappropriate for it to snow during harvest.
