For later we read: “As snow in summer and rain in harvest, so honor is indecent for a fool.” Yet in the extremely hot regions of Palestine it is very pleasant for harvesters if a sudden cold arrives, as it does with snow: it somewhat cools the burning of the sun, wipes away the laborers’ sweat, and moderates their burning breath.

A faithful messenger is rightly compared to this cold, because by acting prudently he gives rest to the mind of the one who sent him. Mystically, however, the faithful messenger is the catholic teacher, and the one who sends him is the Lord. The day of harvest in the heat is the time of preaching amid the fury of persecutors, concerning which it is said: “The harvest is indeed abundant” (Matthew 9).

### “Cold of snow in harvest,” etc.

[Col. 1013B]

This signifies a brief respite for preachers from the persecution of their opponents. It is rightly said, therefore: “As the cold of snow on the day of harvest, so a faithful messenger makes the soul of the one who sent him rest.”

For just as it is desirable for preachers of the word to receive some relief from the rage of unbelievers, while the opportunity to teach is not denied, so it is pleasing to the Lord who sent them to preach when they faithfully fulfill the commission they received from him even amid the opposition of adversaries.

Finally, as Luke reports, when the disciples returned from their preaching mission, he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and gave thanks to the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” and so forth (Luke 10).

### “Clouds and wind,” etc.

[Col. 1013C]

This seems similar to what he said above: “Do not flatter anyone with your lips.” That verse specifically teaches that one should not receive a person by making promises and then deceive him by failing to fulfill them. This verse, however, may contain both that meaning and what the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3).

### “By patience the prince will be appeased,” etc.

Although you have offended the Lord by sinning, you can still earn his clemency if you patiently endure the adversities inflicted upon you for your sins and, by humble satisfaction, atone for the hardness of your former disobedience.

### “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you,” etc.

[Col. 1013D]

You have found the sweetness of heavenly understanding, which has been supplied to you through the labor of spiritual fathers, as though through the work of exceedingly wise bees. Take care, therefore, not to desire to know more in it than one ought to know, lest, while you seek to understand what is too lofty for your strength, you also lose what you had understood well.

This verse may also be understood figuratively as referring to what is suitably added in the following verse:

### “Withdraw your foot from your neighbor’s house,” etc.

Even if you find the conversation or visit of any neighbor sweeter than honey, it is nevertheless better to make him always love your arrival by coming less often than either to remain with him for too long on a single occasion or to visit him so frequently that he grows weary of seeing you and begins to wish that you would not return.

### “A rotten tooth and a weary foot,” etc.

[Col. 1014A]

Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being and makes flesh his arm” (Jeremiah 13). Such a person is rightly compared to a rotten tooth and a weary foot, because whoever does not know that humanity’s one true good is to cling to God and place one’s hope in the Lord God can neither take in the food of life nor reach the dwelling of the salvation desired.

Such a person also loses his cloak on a cold day. For although in the serenity of the present life he may appear clothed in the habit of religion, when the strictness of the just Judge arrives he will appear altogether naked of the adornment of justice and unworthy of the company of those concerning whom it is written: “Blessed is the one who watches and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.”

### “Vinegar on nitre,” etc.

[Col. 1014B]

Nitre takes its name from the province of Nitria, where it usually grows in greatest abundance; it does not differ greatly from the kind of ammoniac salt. Just as the sun’s heat on the seashore produces salt by hardening seawater into stone—after the greater force of the winds or the heat of the sea itself has cast it farther onto the shore—so in Nitria, where the summer rains soak the broad earth, the heat of the stars becomes so intense that it cooks the rainwater itself throughout the expanse of the sands into a stone resembling salt or ice in appearance, though possessing neither icy hardness nor salty taste.

Yet, according to the nature of salt, it remains solid in the heat and flows and melts in cloudy weather. The inhabitants collect and preserve it, and when necessary use it for washing. Hence the prophet says to sinful Judea: “If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply for yourself the herb called borith, you are stained by your iniquity, says the Lord God” (Jeremiah 2).

[Col. 1014C]

It crackles in water like quicklime; it itself disappears, but makes the water suitable for washing. Observing its nature and the figure to which it is suited, Solomon says: “Vinegar on nitre, and one who sings songs to a very wicked heart.”

For if vinegar is poured onto nitre, it immediately boils up. So a perverse mind, when corrected by rebuke or encouraged toward good by the sweetness of preaching, becomes worse through the correction and is thereby inflamed into the wickedness of murmuring—by the very means through which it ought to have been restrained from wickedness.

### “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” etc.

This may be understood both of bodily food and of spiritual nourishment.

### “You will heap burning coals upon his head,” etc.

[Col. 1014D]

He is not speaking of the fire of punishments. Wisdom would not teach you to supply good things to an enemy as a cause of his destruction. Rather, the burning coals upon his head signify the ardor of charity in his heart.

It sometimes happens that an enemy, overcome by repeated benefits and having the harshness of his hatred softened, receives the warmth of charity in his mind. From being an enemy he begins to become a friend and to defend the one whom he had unjustly hated.

### “The north wind drives away rain,” etc.

If you listen to a slanderer with a cheerful face, you give him fuel for slander. But if you listen with a sorrowful face, then, as a certain man said, he learns not to say willingly what he has learned is not willingly heard.

### “It is better to sit in the corner of the roof,” etc.

[Col. 1015A]

A *doma* is both an elevated and a secluded place. For what is called *doma* in Greek is called *tectum*—“roof”—in Latin. Accordingly, in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter ascended to the upper place to pray, the Greek text uses *doma* for “the upper place.”

It is better, therefore, for someone to remain elevated in virtue, free from the bonds of a wife and secluded from the desires of this world, than to suffer daily insults from a wicked woman while engaging in carnal pleasure.

### “Cold water to a thirsty soul,” etc.

The Psalmist says: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs,” and so forth (Psalm 41). Cold water, therefore, which quenches the thirsty person’s heat, is compared with a messenger who comes from far away bearing unexpected and unfamiliar joys.

The sweetness of the divine vision consoles a soul that has long desired it and frees it from the heat of present tribulations. Likewise, angels come daily from a distant land—that is, descending from the heavenly homeland into the world—and strengthen the righteous amid temptations through hope of heavenly things, or lead the righteous through the trials of temptation toward the palm of everlasting reward.

### “A fountain troubled by a foot and a corrupted spring,” etc.

[Col. 1015B]

The fountain and spring of life are the mouth and tongue of the righteous person who meditates on wisdom and speaks judgment. If it should happen that the devil overcomes such a person and brings him into a fall, the fountain is rightly called troubled when the adversary tramples it, and the spring corrupted.

It often happens that those who shone with greater knowledge finally fall into the pit of foolishness, desiring to know more than human frailty has been permitted to know. Hence what follows:

### “Like one who eats too much honey,” etc.

The sweetness of honey, if taken in excess of what is necessary, kills the life of the eater by the very means through which it delights the mouth. The investigation of majesty is also sweet. But whoever desires to scrutinize it more than human understanding permits is crushed by its very glory; like honey taken immoderately, it tears apart the mind of the investigator because it cannot be grasped.

A wise person must attend not only to avoiding the search for things higher than himself and the scrutiny of things too difficult, but also to ensuring that he does not make the things he could know rightly and usefully less useful to himself through immoderate speech. Hence the following is suitably added:

### “Like a city lying open and without a circuit of walls,” etc.

[Col. 1015C]

If it does not have the wall of silence, the city of the mind lies exposed to the arrows of the enemy. When a person casts himself outside himself through words, he shows himself openly to the adversary; and the adversary overcomes him with as little effort as the one who is conquered fights against himself through excessive speech.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 1015D]

### “As snow in summer,” etc.

This verse also warns that the honor of teaching should not be entrusted to the unlearned. Snow in summer and rain during harvest are the persecutions of unbelievers during the time of evangelical preaching. When these become especially severe, they both hinder the warmth of love in many people and spoil the fruits of good works.

The glory bestowed on a fool is rightly compared to harvest, because if the teaching chair is granted to an unlearned person, the Church is harmed by this just as surely as by the persecution of unbelievers. The calamity of the Arian storm proved this to be entirely true.

### “For just as a bird flying across to the heights,” etc.

Words are rightly compared with birds, since they fly through the air by sound, from the mouth of the speaker all the way to the ears of the hearer. They differ in this respect, however: a bird flying wherever it will may settle in a place where it has no definite necessity or advantage.

[Col. 1016A]

The words we speak, by contrast, do not simply scatter into the wind and vanish. Everything returns to its author, and words spoken well help the speaker, while words uttered badly burden him, so that we shall be compelled to give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word.

How much more, then, do curses oppress not another person but the one who curses—not only those hurled with malicious intent against the innocent, but also those casually uttered against anyone through the habit of the negligent. “For those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

He does not say without reason “a curse uttered in vain,” because there is also a curse uttered not in vain but issued against the impious in the just anger of divine strictness. Such is blessed Peter’s word against Simon Magus: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8). The same applies to the ban—anathema [variant: anathemata]—pronounced against apostates and heretics by ecclesiastical judgment, concerning which the Lord says to that same Church: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16 and 18).

### “Do not answer a fool according to his folly,” etc.

[Col. 1016B]

“Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself.” These two sayings should not appear mutually contradictory: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly,” and “Answer a fool according to his folly.” Both agree according to the diversity of circumstances and persons, since the fool is both disregarded because he does not receive wisdom and foolish pride is struck down by another kind of folly. Thus the Apostle also says: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12).

### “Lame in his feet and drinking iniquity,” etc.

[Col. 1016C]

It may happen that a wise person sends a fool as a messenger, unaware that he is a fool; yet he does not thereby lose the glory of his wisdom, since he believed in an unknown good that he had heard about.

But whoever knowingly sends a heretic to preach to the people is lame in his feet and drinks iniquity: he has lost the outward gait of good works and intoxicates the inner parts of his understanding by drinking in folly.

### “Like one who throws a stone onto the heap of Mercury,” etc.

[Col. 1016D]

Whoever grants the honor of teaching to an ignorant person—that is, to a heretic—sins no less than one who reverences the gods and shrines of the pagans through empty worship.

### “As when a thorn is produced in the hand of a drunkard,” etc.

A thorn is produced in the hand of a drunkard when the pricks of crimes arise in the works of one who serves carnal enticements. The proverb that a fool proposes is rightly compared with these pricks. For even if a fool knows how to speak words of prudence, he does not know how to avoid in them the pricks of vices by which he might wound either himself or his neighbor.

Often the imprudent person, even while saying good things, secretly seeks either his own praise from other people or the condemnation of others.

### “Like a dog that returns to its vomit,” etc.

[Col. 1017A]

When a dog vomits, it certainly casts out the food that had weighed down its chest. But when it returns to its vomit, it is burdened again by what had relieved it.

Likewise, those who mourn their sins certainly cast out through confession the wickedness with which they had been badly filled and which weighed down the innermost parts of their mind. But after confession, when they desire it again, they take it up once more.

### “Have you seen a man who appears wise to himself?” etc.

Explaining this, the Lord says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

### “The lazy person says, ‘There is a lioness on the road,’” etc.

Many people, when they hear words of exhortation, complain about the devil. They say that they indeed wish to begin the way of righteousness but are prevented by Satan from completing it. Thus, through such excuses, they always turn in the bed of their sluggishness like a door on its hinges, sometimes proposing to go out to work and sometimes to return to rest, yet never ceasing to lie in their wickedness.

### “The lazy person appears wiser to himself,” etc.

[Col. 1017B]

He calls “seven men who speak opinions” those who, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, have supplied us with knowledge of sacred Scripture.

The fool considers himself wiser than these, because some people so contemptuously turn their minds away from doing what the Lord commanded that they even argue that none of these things can or ought to be fulfilled by a human being. As though wiser than those who wrote the divine utterances, they assert that a person cannot do what those writers, under the direction of the Holy Spirit, commanded human beings to do—or rather, what they showed many people to have accomplished with the help of that same Spirit’s grace.

### “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears,” etc.

[Col. 1017C]

The Apostle says: “Do not quarrel over words, for they are useful for nothing except the subversion of the hearers” (2 Timothy 2).

Therefore, whenever someone simple in understanding catches an earful of the biting speech of two people quarreling with one another, he himself quickly begins, like a dog, to bark and generate disputes. The wise person avoids this completely.

### “The words of a whisperer are like simple things,” etc.

He calls the whisperer an instigator of strife and double-tongued: he feigns praise in his words while seeking to hear something from which he can sow quarrels.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### “Do not boast about tomorrow,” etc.

[Col. 1017D]

Do not ever be secure about the future. Even if today you see yourself serving the Lord, you cannot foresee at all what kind of person you may be in the future or how you will end your life. “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28).

### “A stone is heavy,” etc.

It is certainly sufficiently burdensome for someone to be weighed down by even one capital crime, as though by the weight of a stone, or to be loaded with innumerable lesser sins, as though with grains of sand. Yet the anger of a fool is heavier than either, because the more clearly these things are shown to be evil, the more sharply they pierce the soul so that it may be chastened.

[Col. 1018A]

Since this is not a bodily but a spiritual vice, it weighs all the more heavily the less it is detected. Hence he does not simply say “anger,” but “the anger of a fool,” which he declares heavier than stone and sand. The wise, by contrast, diligently strive to examine and correct not only their acts and words but also the movements of their minds.

### “Anger has no mercy,” etc.

This is not said of every kind of anger. For it is written of the very gentle and moderate man Moses that “he went out from Pharaoh exceedingly angry” (Exodus 10). But he speaks of the anger of the fool, whom he had mentioned in the preceding verse. When this anger has flared up, it immediately loses the inner organs of compassion and knows only how to loosen the reins to its own fury.

Otherwise, anger that is useful and necessary is praised in the saying: “Anger is better than laughter” (Ecclesiasticus 7), because through sadness of face the mind of the delinquent is corrected.

### “Open rebuke is better,” etc.

Here he calls hidden love illicit love, such as adulterous love, which wise people rightly conceal because of its shamefulness, lest it be reproved. Open rebuke is rightly preferred to it, because it is better to rebuke someone openly with the desire to correct than secretly to love him with a shared intention to sin, without any contradiction.

### “The wounds of a lover are better,” etc.

[Col. 1018B]

It is better to endure wounds and affliction from the Lord, who as a father is accustomed to educate us as sons, than to be deceived by the flatteries of the devil. The devil, wishing to deprive us of our heavenly inheritance, usually favors our errors, as though the evil we commit were insignificant and the tribulation inflicted upon us for our sins were excessive—though we endure it by the Lord’s dispensation.

### “A soul that is satisfied will trample the honeycomb,” etc.

The soul of the rich, who have their consolation and to whom the Lord says, “Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger” (Luke 6), despises the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom when it hears it.

But the souls of those who hunger and thirst for righteousness find it sweet to endure even the adversities of the world for the Lord, indeed even death itself, knowing that through the cup of bitterness they will come to the everlasting joys of salvation.

### “Like a bird migrating from its nest,” etc.

[Col. 1018C]

As a bird that neglects the eggs or young it had brooded over and abandons them to the plunder of other birds or animals, so the person who abandons the guardianship of the virtues in which he was progressing becomes himself a betrayer of those same virtues he had seemed to possess, handing them over to unclean spirits.

Hence elsewhere he says: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place.” This plainly means: if the temptation of the ruler of the world—that is, of the devil—should perhaps assail you, be watchful lest you desist from the good work to which you had devoted yourself.

### “A neighbor who is near is better,” etc.

A neighbor who joins your spirit to himself in brotherly fellowship is better for you than a blood brother who neglects to share with you the obligations of faith and piety.

The Lord plainly demonstrated this in the parable of the man wounded by robbers as he descended from Jerusalem to Jericho, and of the Samaritan who cared for him.

### “Whoever blesses his neighbor in a loud voice,” etc.

[Col. 1018D]

A person blesses his neighbor in a loud voice when he exalts him with excessive praise, either by favoring his evil actions against justice or by praising his good deeds beyond what is appropriate.

Such a person is likened to one who curses, because he greatly harms the one to whom, by praising him, he grants confidence in an evil action or diminishes the simplicity of a pure heart in a good work—so that the good work he had begun with a view to heavenly reward he completes out of love for passing praise.

### “Iron is sharpened by iron,” etc.

The fellowship and counsel of the wise are very good. When they instruct one another by taking counsel together, iron is sharpened by iron.

### “The underworld and destruction will never be filled,” etc.

[Col. 1019A]

The torments of hell will not be filled by reaching an end. Similarly, the intentions of those whose minds are set on human things are insatiable in their desire to sin. They therefore suffer punishments without end because they possessed a will to sin without end, if only they had possessed a nature capable of living without end.

### “Know well the face of your flock,” etc.

This is said to the shepherd of the Church: diligently care for those over whom it has happened that you preside. Recognize the dispositions and actions of each person, and if you find in them any vice that soils them, remember to correct it quickly.

For you will not always have the power to feed the Lord’s sheep, but the crown you will receive is eternal if, in your appointed time, you have faithfully administered the office entrusted to you.

### “The meadows are open,” etc.

[Col. 1019B]

The pastures of the heavenly sacraments, which had long been closed by the typical rites of the Law, are now open. The newness of evangelical truth and grace has appeared. The writings of the ancient fathers have been gathered as food for the Lord’s flock; they were taken away from the proud Jews by the sickle of divine judgment and given for the spiritual support of the humble peoples of the Church, according to the Lord’s saying to them: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21).

### “Lambs for your clothing,” etc.

He calls the innocent “lambs” and the penitent “young goats.” You will be clothed in the fleece of lambs when, as a shepherd, you yourself advance through the good conduct of obedient disciples. Seeing their praiseworthy deeds, you will become more glorious in the adornment of virtues and in the warmth of love.

You will acquire a field through young goats when, by calling sinners to repentance, you gain for yourself a higher place in the land of the living.

### “Let the milk of goats be sufficient for your food,” etc.

[Col. 1019C]

Feed the flock entrusted to you with such constant diligence:

> “May fresh milk not fail you in summer or in cold weather, but always suffice for you and yours.”

That is, devote yourself so diligently to teaching that you may even advance former penitents to the office of teaching, so that through those who, because of the foulness of their vices, once seemed destined to be placed on the Judge’s left, rational and guileless milk of the word may now be supplied as nourishment to the little ones.

Milk of goats becomes food for maidservants when those who do not yet serve the Lord with perfect love but still with slavish fear are refreshed with the life-giving banquets of the word by the example or words of those who have been saved through repentance, and are united so that they may progress toward greater growth in virtue.

[Col. 1019D]

Some have interpreted the passage, “The meadows are open, the green herbs have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains; lambs for your clothing and young goats for the price of the field,” in this way:

> “The tombs have been opened; resurrected bodies have appeared; sinners have been separated from the saints; hay has been gathered from high places for burning. The lambs have been separated to the right, the young goats to the left: lambs for the king’s clothing, because he himself said, ‘I will dwell in them’; young goats are sold for fire as the price of the saints whom they harmed [or killed?].”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### “The wicked flee when no one pursues him.”

[Col. 1020A]

Whoever is not strong in faith sometimes abandons the faith voluntarily, even when no persecutor is pressing upon him, when through robbery, perjury, fornication, poisoning, or other crimes of this kind he makes himself resemble an unbeliever.

### “But the righteous man is confident like a lion,” etc.

A lion does not tremble when wild beasts confront it because it knows that it prevails over them all. The security of the righteous man is therefore rightly compared with a lion, because when he sees anyone rising against him, he returns to the confidence of his mind. He knows that he overcomes all who oppose him, because he loves only the one whom, being unconquered, he can in no way lose.

### “Wicked men do not consider judgment,” etc.

The elect take notice of everything: both that the universal judgment will come and that eternal rest or punishment will be repaid according to particular works.

### “Whoever deceives the righteous on an evil way,” etc.

[Col. 1020B]

Whoever deceives lovers of righteousness through heretical teaching so that they turn away from the truth incurs the punishment he deserves for his evils. Yet whatever good he may have done—whether by writing useful things or by living chastely—benefits others: namely, those who, reading or hearing these things, take examples of salvation even from one whom they know to have perished.

### “In the exultation of the righteous there is much glory.”

They rejoice not in present riches but in future and eternal goods. They rejoice not in the world’s possessions, which they see, but in the Creator of the world, whose vision they hope for, as the Psalmist says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Psalm 31).

Or certainly, much glory is produced in the exultation of the righteous, because whenever the elect happen to rejoice in this life over prosperous events affecting the Church, much glory is given by the Lord through the faith and pious works of many.

### “When the wicked reign, people hide.”

[Col. 1020C]

Just as many begin to give glory to God when they see the righteous rejoice in their progress in virtue, so whenever the reprobate hold power, they show many to be accomplices in their faithlessness. This can rightly be understood both of pagans, heretics, and bad Catholics.

### “Blessed is the person who is always fearful,” etc.

The coming anger of judgment will be endured then with all the greater severity because it is scarcely feared now amid sins. Hence it is said elsewhere: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils; and in the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclesiasticus 11). Both, therefore, must be joined, so that each may always be supported by the other.

### “A roaring lion and a hungry bear,” etc.

This can also be understood of pagan and heretical rulers, who often test the patience or wisdom of the poor people—that is, of the holy Church—with beastly savagery.

### “A man who commits violence unto blood,” etc.

[Col. 1020D]

Whether one cultivates the soil of a field or the soil of his own body, he will be satisfied: the former with grain, the latter with virtues. Whoever despises both will be filled with poverty.

### “A person who hastens to become rich,” etc.

Certainly, whoever desires to increase his wealth does not heed sin. Like a bird caught by bait, when he greedily begins to pursue food consisting of earthly things, he does not recognize the noose of sin by which he will be strangled. When he desires whatever goods belong to the present world, he does not understand what losses he will suffer in the future.

### “When the wicked rise up, people will hide,” etc.

[Col. 1021A]

He calls the same people righteous whom he had called human beings—those, namely, who preserve the just and established order of human existence given by God. Hence in the book of blessed Job it is said of a certain penitent who had gone astray: “He will look upon human beings and say, ‘I have sinned’” (Job 33).

This means plainly: he will look upon those who rightly preserve the nature of human creation, and he will recognize that by sinning he has made himself like the beasts.

The meaning is therefore clear: while the persecution of the wicked rages, the faithful will often hide, either not daring or not being permitted to appear in public. The Lord says: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matthew 10).

When, however, the persecution has ceased after its leaders have been destroyed, glory shines more brightly after the pressures endured by the faithful. Many unbelievers also, seeing the condemnation of unbelief, receive the grace of faith, according to what is written: “When the pestilent person is scourged, the simple will become wiser” (Proverbs 19).

You will be proved to stand naked of the adornment of virtues, because you were unable to fulfill what, as the Lord’s witness, you promised.

[Col. 1021B]

This is not said to mean that you should refuse to undertake the care of governing souls when it has been regularly imposed upon you, but that you should not rashly usurp for yourself the office of teacher and ruler indiscriminately, without anyone commanding you.

## CHAPTER XXIX
A man who speaks to his friend with flattering and deceitful words, etc. Whoever praises his neighbor with deceitful words prepares snares for him, by which he may fall into danger through a cautious undertaking, once he has been made more secure by the word. But let us see whether the nets of the fraudulent entangle the one at whose feet they are spread, or rather the one by whom they are spread. It follows:

“A sinful and wicked man will be caught in a snare,” etc. The snare of sinners therefore does not harm the righteous, even if it kills him bodily. But the plots that the wicked prepare for their neighbors [Col. 1021C] condemn the wicked themselves forever, while the righteous rejoice and praise the Creator’s just judgment, both for their own deliverance and for the destruction of the wicked. Finally, the ancient edition clearly gives the closing words of the preceding verse: “He surrounds his feet with nets.” For from the ambiguity of the Greek word αὐτοῦ (“his”), either interpretation is possible. Thus, “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it himself,” as it is said elsewhere.

“A wise man, if he contends with a fool,” etc. If a wise teacher contends with an unbelieving and obstinate person—whether he tells of the punishments of the wicked or the joys of the good—he labors in vain with one who lacks understanding. Whether he urges the coverings of repentance or speaks of the rewards that belong to good works, the fool does not listen. Hence the apostles also said to the Jews: “We lamented [Col. 1021D] for you, and you did not mourn; we sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matthew 12).

“The fool pours out all his spirit.” Impatience drives him to pour out his whole spirit outwardly. Agitation expels it all the more quickly because no discipline of wisdom encloses it within.

“But the wise man delays and reserves it for the future.” When he has been injured, he does not desire to avenge himself at once, because, even while enduring, he wishes to suffer patiently; yet he does not fail to understand that all things will be avenged at the final judgment. The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “The wicked man pours out all his anger, but the wise man distributes it in portions,” because the fool is inflamed by agitation to avenge himself, whereas the wise man gradually diminishes and drives out his anger through maturity of counsel and moderation.

[Col. 1022A]

“The poor man and the creditor meet one another,” etc. The poor man is the humble hearer of the word of God; the creditor is the one who entrusts to him the money of that same word by preaching it. They meet one another when they come together in one and the same grace of piety. God is the illuminator of both, because neither could preach without divine mercy, nor could the other believe without it. For the truthful saying of Truth remains: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

“A king who judges the poor in truth,” etc. The Psalmist also says of Christ the King: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom” (Psalm 44).

“The rod and correction give wisdom,” etc. Concerning this rod, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Do you wish me to come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4). The child whom he very frequently urges to be corrected and instructed is the people of God. If that people is not disciplined by the continual admonitions and rebukes of priests, it produces disgrace for the Church, as those outside revile the religion of the Christian faith. Hence it is rightly added:

[Col. 1022B]

“When prophecy has failed, the people will be scattered,” etc. For when priestly instruction has ceased, the discipline of divine law will immediately be dissolved, by which the people ought to have reached the rewards of blessedness.

“Have you seen a man who is quick to speak,” etc.? Folly is indeed a grave vice, but talkativeness is no lighter. It often happens that some dull person, ignorant even of letters themselves, accepts the words of salutary correction more quickly than one endowed with an abundance of speech, who strives more eagerly to proclaim boastfully what he knows—or thinks he knows—than to hear the words of the wise.

[Col. 1022C]

“Whoever delicately nourishes his servant from childhood,” etc. Whoever delicately nourishes his body from childhood, although he ought to have subjected it to the mind, will find it wanton and ungovernable when it reaches the years of adolescence. Another translation beautifully renders this verse: “Whoever indulges himself from childhood will be a slave; at the end he will also be grieved.” For he will be late in repenting of the evils within him, remembering that, while still of tender age, he had been unwilling to restrain himself from his pleasures according to the rule of the prudent.

“An irascible man provokes quarrels,” etc. Anger is the doorway of all vices. When it is closed, rest is given to the virtues within; when it is open, the mind is armed for every crime.

“Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul,” etc. Wisdom teaches its helper not only to abstain from sins but also to restrain himself from the companionship of sinners, lest perhaps he deserve to hear from the strict Judge: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Psalm 49). For not only the thief is held guilty, but also the person who, knowing of the theft, refuses to identify it when the owner seeks the money he has lost, although he is able to do so. But lest anyone plead fear of a more powerful person as an excuse for being unable either to separate himself from the company of thieves or to disclose what he knows, the text plainly adds:

[Col. 1022D]

“Whoever fears a man will quickly fall,” etc. To this corresponds the Gospel saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 1023A]

“The words of the Gatherer, son of the Vomiter (*Vomens*).” Up to this point we have had the Proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, transcribed. From here, the words of Solomon begin again. He is called by the name that in Greek is *Ecclesiastes*, now rendered into Latin as “Gatherer.” For *ecclesia* means “assembly” or “congregation.”

“The vision that the man who is with God spoke,” etc. He says “the vision that he spoke” because what he saw with God while contemplating more secret things, he disclosed to human beings by speaking outwardly. Whoever is strengthened by the Spirit of God speaks what follows with a humble heart.

[Col. 1023B]

“I am the most foolish of men,” etc. “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16). And the Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3). Of himself and those like him, in whom God is present, he also says: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1).

“I have not learned wisdom,” etc. Solomon did not learn wisdom from a human being; rather, he received it when God freely offered it, so that he might know the knowledge of the saints. The Apostle too, after saying, “We are fools for Christ’s sake,” says again: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 2).

“Who has ascended into heaven and descended?” This is the knowledge of the saints, which the wise of this age consider foolishness. The Son of God, having assumed flesh, ascended into heaven after his death and resurrection, and at the time of our resurrection he will descend from heaven to judge the living and the dead.

[Col. 1023C]

“Who has held the spirit in his hands?” Every spirit—human and angelic, and that of animals and storms—is held by God’s power so that it does not perish.

“Who has gathered the waters as though in a garment?” “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.”

“Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth?” The Lord, who now arouses life and growth in all living creatures and plants. On the day of judgment he will also raise the entire human race from death from the four winds of heaven.

“What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?” He speaks of the name of God the Father and of the Son, whose mystery worldly wisdom cannot naturally know. It can, however, understand that there is one God who made all things, through the things it sees to have been wonderfully made. “If you know,” he says—“you,” that is, the one who, boasting of your own wisdom, presume to call the mysteries of our faith foolishness.

[Col. 1023D]

“Every word of God is a fiery shield to those who hope in him.” The whole Church of Christ knows this, and especially those who, because God dwells with them, despise earthly wisdom. For every divine word both kindles the hearts of the elect with the fire of charity, enlightens them with knowledge of the truth, consumes the filth of vices, and protects them from the snares of enemies and from every adversity.

But we must look more carefully at the fact that the Latin translation does not express in a single word the precise meaning of the Greek term *pepyromenon*. Hence it is rendered at one time “ignited” and at another “tested by fire,” as in: “Your word is greatly ignited” (Psalm 118), and: “Silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11). Both are expressed in Greek by the one word *pepyromenon*. Similarly, the statement that sounds most like this saying of Solomon—“The words of the Lord are tested by fire” (Psalm 17)—is *pepyromena*.

[Col. 1024A]

*Pepyromenon*, therefore, means something like metal that has been melted and purified in fire. Just as metals melted in fire contain no foreign or useless impurity within themselves, but everything that remains in them is genuine and perfect, cleansed from every stain of vice, so the word of God bears witness within itself to faith in eternal goods. Hence comes the Lord’s saying: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished” (Matthew 5). For all things are true, and, having been kindled, they stand beyond every ambiguity of empty excess.

“Do not add anything to his words,” etc. Do not corrupt the sayings of the holy Scriptures, as certain heretics are known to have done so that they would not be convicted by them.

[Col. 1024B]

“I asked you for two things; do not deny them to me,” etc. The man who is with God, still radiant with the fire of his word, now speaks to the Lord himself, turning his voice toward him. He begs that he may never prefer either the vanity of this age or lying words to heavenly truth in Scripture, and that he may not, through either the abundance or the scarcity of transient things, fall into forgetfulness of eternal realities.

“A generation that curses its father,” etc. Earlier he had asked the Lord to grant him purity of life. Now, suddenly turning his attention to contemplate the wickedness of the evil, he indicates how many miseries surround it and how far it stands from the truth: namely, because such people do not honor their parents.

“A generation that seems pure in its own eyes,” etc. For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves.

[Col. 1024C]

“A generation whose eyes are exalted,” etc. The Psalmist says of it: “Lord, my heart is not exalted,” and so forth (Psalm 130).

“A generation that has swords for teeth,” etc. Concerning this generation the Psalmist says: “The teeth of the children of men are their weapons and arrows,” and so forth (Psalm 56). These are the persecutors of the Church of Christ.

If you wish to consider the matter more carefully, you will find that these generations are the most wicked assemblies of Jews and heretics. Thus the generation of the Jews curses its Father—that is, the one who said, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4)—when it denied his Son living in the flesh. It did not bless its mother—that is, the Synagogue—whose former faith concerning Christ, received from the fathers and prophets, it disparaged.

[Col. 1024D]

The generation of the Novatians seems pure to itself, saying, “It has no need of repentance.” Yet it cannot be pure from the stains of sins, since, by denying pardon to sinners, it closes off the fountain of repentance.

Likewise, the generation of the Arians has exalted eyes and eyelids raised above God, asking who existed beforehand, whether there was a time when the Son did not exist, and what power the Holy Spirit has, whether equal or unequal.

Again, the generation that has swords for teeth is that assembly of the wicked which strives to communicate its unbelief to others. Just as bodies are accustomed to be struck down by swords, so it strives to subject the souls of its hearers to eternal death by the poison of its perverse speech.

[Col. 1025A]

“A leech has two daughters,” etc. The leech is the devil, who is incessantly inflamed by a thirst for committing sins and persuading others to sin. He has two daughters, because there are two particular enticements of the human race that imitate the ardor of the ancient enemy: lust and avarice. For the more freely the reins of lust are loosened, the more harmfully it delights; and, as one of the poets says:

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.

“There are three things that are never satisfied,” etc. The fire never says, “Enough”; hell is never filled. Likewise, the harlot’s body is not satisfied with pleasures, and the avaricious person never says, “Enough.” Some interpret hell as the devil, because he is insatiable in seducing human beings. The mouth of the womb and the earth, which are not satisfied with water, have been discussed above. The fire that does not say, “Enough,” is the burning of Gehenna, which never ceases but consumes with infinite heat those who have refused to put an end to their sins.

[Col. 1025B]

“The eye that mocks its father and despises the birth of its mother,” etc. The wicked mock the Father when they criticize divine judgments. Heretics, when they ridicule and despise the preaching of the holy Church, despise the birth of their mother, because those who speak against her have come forth from her. “They went out from us,” he says, “but they were not of us” (John . . .).

When Catholic preachers, proceeding from the streams of the divine Scriptures, refute their purpose by reproving them, they are, as it were, digging out the wicked eye of the raven from the torrents, and the young of the eagle eat it. Holy teachers are called ravens because, through the grace of humility, they confess the blackness of sin within themselves. They are called the young of the eagle because through the grace of the one who, in the form of assumed flesh, flies up to heavenly things, they have been reborn. Hence elsewhere they are also called the children of the Bridegroom.

[Col. 1025C]

“Three things are difficult for me,” etc. As far as the historical sense is concerned, the passage is as it is written. But because he speaks in parables, the eagle’s way in heaven is difficult to discern; that is, it is difficult to detect the subtlety of the enemy as he flies around the hearts of heavenly men. Likewise, the serpent’s way upon the earth is difficult to discern: that is, the cunning of the poisonous enemy, who never ceases to lie in wait for those whom he sees to be founded upon the rock of faith.

So too is the way of a ship in the midst of the sea: that is, the way of iniquity, which travels with such subtlety through the bitter waves of this age, driven by the winds of unclean spirits, that its course can scarcely, or not at all, be detected. That the eagle signifies the evil enemy is testified by the prophet, who says: “Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations 4). This means that the people who persecuted us were so savage that they seemed more cruel than the demons themselves.

[Col. 1025D]

That the serpent often signifies the devil was proved both in the transgression of the first man and when a certain wise man said: “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent” (Sirach 21).

That a ship signifies the fickleness of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine is demonstrated by the prophet, who says: “And the Chaldeans glorying in their ships” (Isaiah 43). This means that unclean spirits exalt themselves through the frailty and instability of the human mind and rejoice as victors over its ruin.

[Col. 1026A]

Therefore, just as those things are so hidden that they cannot be discovered, so it is difficult to conceive where the young man who has abandoned the way of truth continually turns during all his hours, wandering through the thoughts of a foolish mind.

Such also is the way of an adulterous woman, who eats, touches her mouth, and says, “I have done no evil.” The adulterous mind, like the things mentioned above, is always unstable and wandering. When it has been able to conceal the shamefulness of its conduct, it denies having committed any wrongdoing.

“Four things are among the smallest upon the earth,” etc. The righteous often appear smaller upon the earth than the reprobate—that is, more humble and more despised by this world. Yet they are wiser than the wise of the world, because they savor eternal and heavenly goods and, in their desire to obtain what the worldly do not know, they willingly endure every adversity of this age with courage.

“The ants are a people without strength,” etc. The people of the Church also, in order to preserve strength of mind, show themselves temporarily weak while adversaries rage. The Lord says through the Gospel: “But I say to you, Do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). In this life they prepare for themselves the fruits of good works, by which they may deserve to possess eternal life.

[Col. 1026B]

“The little rabbit is a weak people,” etc. Here too he signifies the people of the Church, which is called weak either because, as we said above, it does not seek to avenge its own injuries, or because it has learned to place no trust in its own strength but to hope for salvation in the help of its Redeemer.

This is to place its dwelling in the rock. Under the Lord’s protection against the assaults of life, it says with the Psalmist: “Be for me a very strong rock and a fortified house, that you may save me; for you are my rock and my fortress” (Psalm . . .).

[Col. 1026C]

In place of “little rabbit,” the ancient translation has *chyrogrillus*. This is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling both a mouse and a bear. It is very abundant in the regions of Palestine and is accustomed always to live in caves in the rocks and in holes in the earth.

It should be noted that in the psalm where we sing, “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Psalm 103), we find in some manuscripts “for rabbits,” and in others “for *chyrogrilli*.” In some copies of this saying of Solomon too, “hedgehog” appears in place of “little rabbit.” Likewise, in the book of Hebrew names we find the same Hebrew word, *sapham*, in Jeremiah, translated by Saint Jerome as *chyrogrillus*, “rabbit,” and “hedgehog.”

[Col. 1026D]

“The locust has no king,” etc. Some interpret the locust as the populace of the Gentiles, who once existed without a king—that is, without Christ, without a prophet, and without a teacher—but who, now gathered into the unity of faith, hasten to spiritual battle against the devil.

The locust may also be understood as the harmonious community of anchorites. Although they are governed in their hiding places by no human master, they nevertheless serve Christ with tireless zeal, each in his own place, and habitually destroy the shoots of carnal pleasures as they spring up evilly.

“The lizard clings with its hands,” etc. The lizard clings with its hands because it does not have wings by which it might be carried. That it dwells in kings’ houses signifies the humility of those who, although by nature slow-witted, nevertheless by the careful skill of their diligence attain either knowledge of the divine Scriptures or the grace of the virtues by which they may deserve entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 1027A]

Very often birds, which feathers lift into flight, remain below. But the lizard, which has no wings for flight, holds fast to the king’s building by clinging with its hands. Thus it often happens that the clever, while growing sluggish through negligence, remain in wicked actions, whereas the simple, whom no wing of cleverness assists, are lifted by the virtue of their works to obtain the walls of the eternal kingdom.

“There are three things that proceed well,” etc. Here the lion is mentioned, concerning whom it is written: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5). He is called the strongest of beasts because in him “what is weak of God is stronger than men” (1 Corinthians 1). He fears no one’s approach, for he says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

[Col. 1027B]

The rooster girded at the loins signifies the holy preachers announcing the true dawn amid the darkness of this night. Their loins are girded because they restrain the flowing excesses of lust from their members.

“And the ram, and there is no king who can resist him.” Whom else should we understand here as the ram except the first order within the Church, the priesthood? Concerning them it is written: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28). By their example they draw along the people who walk after them, like a following flock of sheep. When they live spiritually and rightly, no king is able to resist them, because, whatever persecutor may confront them, he cannot impede their purpose.

And because after these things the Antichrist will also appear, he added the fourth, saying:

“And the fool who appears after he has been exalted on high,” etc. He will indeed be lifted up on high when he falsely claims to be God. But, though lifted up on high, he will appear a fool, because in that very exaltation he will fail at the coming of the true Judge. If he had understood this, he would have placed his hand over his mouth; that is, if he had foreseen his punishment when he began to grow proud, he, though once well created, would not have been lifted up in such an outburst of arrogant boasting.

[Col. 1027C]

This should not trouble anyone because it was said above, “The fourth proceeds prosperously.” He said that three proceed well and the fourth prosperously. Not everything prosperous is good, nor in this life is everything good prosperous. The lion, rooster, and ram proceed well, but not prosperously here, because they endure the battles of persecution. The fourth proceeds prosperously but not well, because the Antichrist walks in deceit; yet, for the brief span of the present life, that deceit prospers for him.

[Col. 1027D]

“Whoever presses the breasts firmly to draw out milk,” etc. We press the breasts firmly when we weigh the words of sacred eloquence with subtle understanding. While seeking milk through that pressure, we find butter, because, while seeking nourishment through a modest understanding, we are anointed with the richness of inward fullness. This must not be done excessively or constantly, lest, while milk is sought, blood should flow from the breasts. For when the words of sacred eloquence are examined more than they should be, they fall into a carnal understanding. The one who milks violently draws out blood, because what is perceived through excessive spiritual analysis becomes carnal.

[Col. 1028A]

“And whoever provokes anger,” etc. The preceding parable explains what this means according to the literal sense. Whoever addresses his neighbor in moderate speech receives a gracious response, as though he were expressing butter from the breasts in which he had sought milk. But whoever provokes anger and discord from a brotherly heart by an inept word is like one who milks beyond measure and finds blood instead of milk.

## CHAPTER XXXI
Words of King Lemuel, etc. Lemuel is interpreted as “in whom is God.” He is the one of whom it was said above, with the same name rendered into Latin: “The vision which the man spoke, with whom is God.” The mother who taught him this vision is best understood as divine grace, which invisibly instructed him in his heart with the understanding of wisdom that he himself would outwardly provide to human beings. Yet it may also rightly be understood as Solomon’s physical mother, who taught him these things when he was a child. Since he recognized that they had been wisely spoken, he wished to incorporate them into his book of Proverbs. And therefore, after the title says, “The words of King Lemuel,” it immediately adds, “The vision with which his mother instructed him,” because, when he was anointed king and received the spirit of wisdom, he saw through that same Spirit how wisely his good mother had instructed him.

“What, my beloved? What, beloved of my womb?” You should supply: “What shall I say to you, my son, who, born from my womb, have been chosen for kingship?”

“What, beloved of my vows?” That is, “You who have been chosen for that which I desired with complete devotion.”

“Do not give your substance to women.” The literal sense is clear; but we are also forbidden to pollute the substance of our virtues with the corruptions of vices.

“And your riches to the destruction of kings.” He gives his riches to the destruction of kings who corrupt human hearts with earthly pleasures, so that they do not seek the heavenly goods in which they may reign forever with Christ. Kings are destroyed by riches when those who have been joined through faith to the body of the supreme King nevertheless deserve, through the allurements of the world, to be uprooted from the land of the living.

“Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings.” The following words are clear according to the literal sense. Allegorically, however, he commands that wine—in which there is sensual indulgence—not intoxicate the minds of the faithful, who are members of the eternal King. There is no secrecy where drunkenness reigns; nothing concerning hidden things is considered where carnal pleasure reigns; such people investigate only those carnal things that are visible.

“Lest he drink and forget the judgments,” etc. Lest, intoxicated by earthly enticements, he forget the poor of Christ, who himself was made poor for our sake.

“Give strong drink to those who are sorrowful,” etc. “Let them drink and forget their poverty, and let them remember their pain no more.” Here he calls strong drink and wine the heavenly consolation of divine wisdom, which is to be offered to hearts that refuse to be consoled by things below and receive whatever happens in the present with a bitter spirit, cleaving with their whole mind only to joys they do not yet see in heaven—according to the one who said, “My soul refused consolation; I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Psalm 76).

Again: “Give strong drink to those who are sorrowful, and wine to those who are bitter of heart,” and so forth (Proverbs 31). Pour abundantly into those who are weighed down by sorrow and sadness because of the fullness of their former deeds the delight of spiritual knowledge, like wine that gladdens the human heart; refresh them with the wholesome intoxication of the word, lest those who are such, sunk in continual grief and deadly despair, be swallowed up by an even greater sadness.

“Open your mouth for the mute,” etc. Remember to speak on behalf of the poor, who cannot speak for themselves at the judgment, and take care to defend those who, looking toward their heavenly homeland, hasten to pass more quickly through the way of this life. Alternatively, by “opening your mouth for the mute” he commands that the word of faith be preached to the Gentile peoples, who previously did not know how to utter the divine words, and that care for salvation be extended not only to the Jews but also to all nations throughout the world.

“Open your mouth; judge what is just,” etc. Just as in the preceding verse he commanded that the mouth be opened on behalf of and for the rescue of the poor, so here he admonishes us to correct and judge the poor person justly when he has gone astray. In accordance with this Moses also says, “You shall not pity the poor in judgment” (Exodus 23). The prophet indicates that the Lord does both of these things when he says: “He shall judge the poor in justice, and shall reprove in equity for the meek of the earth” (Psalm 71).

Thus far the words of Lemuel. From this point the wisest of kings, Solomon, sings the praises of holy Church in a few verses, but with the fullest truth. For this song consists of twenty-two verses, according to the order and number of the Hebrew letters, so that each verse begins with a different letter. Through the most perfect order of the alphabet, this figuratively indicates how fully the virtues and rewards either of every faithful soul or of the whole holy Church—which is formed as one catholic Church from all elect souls—are described here.

“Who will find a strong woman?” etc. The catholic Church is called a strong woman: a woman, because she is accustomed to beget spiritual children for God from water and the Holy Spirit; strong, because for faith in her Creator she despises all the adversities and prosperities of the world alike. When he appeared in the flesh, he found her weak, but by his finding her—that is, by his loving visitation—he made her strong. Therefore, returning to heaven after her redemption, he said joyfully to the citizens above: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke 15).

Seeing, therefore, that the human race was entangled in innumerable errors, and that no patriarch, no prophet, and indeed no one among the elect, except the sole Mediator between God and human beings, was sufficient for its salvation, Solomon says: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the remotest ends.” As though he were openly proclaiming with wonder the future grace of the Lord: “Who has such great virtue, who has such merit, that he could gather for himself one Church of the elect from the many unbelieving and criminal nations of the world, and by his grace make her strong and unconquerable against all adversaries?”

Certainly, this one is not like us, nor is he to come in our time; but at the end of the ages God, made human, will descend from heaven, and by his passion redeem us from death. This is what he says: “Her price is from afar and from the remotest ends.” “From afar,” namely, in the temporal order, because the time extending from the days of Solomon to the Virgin’s childbirth lay in between. “From the remotest ends,” because “his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Psalm 18), and he offered himself as the only price for our redemption. Hence the Apostle says: “He loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Ephesians 5).

It may also rightly be understood that the price of holy Church was placed far away, because the incarnation, the Word of God’s life among human beings, his passion, and his resurrection were altogether distinct from the condition of our nature. For he was born when he wished and from the mother whom he wished; he lived in the world without sin; and when he wished, and by whatever death he wished, he departed from the world. He also held the time of his resurrection and ascension in his own power, and other things of this kind—in all of which he was as far from us as heaven is distant from earth.

Since the Lord, who redeemed the Church, granted her not only to receive the word of salvation but also steadfastly to fight for it and preach it throughout the world, he rightly adds:

“Her husband’s heart trusts in her,” etc. By the husband of holy Church he means her Lord and Redeemer, who also deigned to become her price. Thus the Apostle says to believers: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

Therefore, when he says, “Her husband’s heart trusts in her,” the expression is taken from human custom. Just as one who has a strong, faithful, and chaste wife trusts her completely, because she can do nothing against his will, cannot be defiled even by an adulterous thought, willingly bears every adversity for his love, and desires to convert to his friendship as many as she can, so indeed our Lord and Redeemer trusts in the Church. For he knows the spirit of grace that he gave her; he knows the power of charity that he infused into her heart. Therefore he does not doubt that she can in no way be corrupted from the integrity of her faith, and that she will persevere in gathering many into the unity of that same faith.

This is what follows: “And he shall have no need of spoils.” The Church despoils the devil when, through her preachers, she recalls to the way of truth those whom he had deceived. And it is rightly said, “He shall have no need of spoils,” because the Church will never cease restoring to the faith of Christ the souls liberated from diabolical deception, until, when the course of the world has been completed, the predetermined number of her members has likewise been fulfilled.

But because whatever good holy Church, or any faithful soul, does is received from above, it is rightly added:

“She shall render him good, and not evil,” etc. A soul renders good to Christ when, having received from him the gifts of life, it responds by living rightly; and when it strives to make known to others whatever, with his help, it is able to know or do. But after saying, “She shall render him good,” he immediately adds, “and not evil,” because there are indeed people who, after receiving good things from the Lord, repay him with evil: either by defiling the mysteries of faith they have received with heretical filth, or by blaspheming the faith they preserve in their profession through wicked works, or by corrupting through evil conversations the good morals with which they serve together with right faith.

Nor do those return to the Lord the good things they received who do not take care to persevere until the end of this present life in the things they have begun well. Therefore, after saying, “She shall render him good, and not evil,” to show that perseverance in goodness is necessary, he adds, “all the days of her life.” Similar is the Gospel saying: “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness before him, all our days” (Luke 1).

The works, and especially the fruits of righteousness or holiness, to which the person who strives freely to repay the good received from the Lord must chiefly devote himself are subsequently indicated when it says:

“She sought wool and flax,” etc. The beginning of this verse, “the strong woman,” may also be understood and observed according to the literal sense by holy Church, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah 58). She does not work with useless and blind labor, but with the specific purpose of deserving to hear from her husband, namely the Lord Christ, at the judgment: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matthew 25); and, “Whatever you did to one of these least, you did to me” (ibid.).

She works by the counsel of her hands—that is, through those persons by whom she distributes alms to the poor. In their devoted work she most beneficially follows the counsel that, when she scatters and gives to the poor, she herself should not be praised by human beings for a time, but that her righteousness should remain forever and ever, and her horn be exalted in glory (Psalm 3).

Mystically, wool, which is the covering of sheep, may signify all the works of simplicity and piety that we perform for our neighbors. In flax, which grows green from the earth but through long and repeated labor loses its natural moisture and reaches the grace of a new whiteness, the chastisement of our flesh may be signified. While by continence we burn away its innate filth of vices, we make it worthy to be clothed with Christ, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3).

Thus the strong woman seeks wool and flax and works by the counsel of her hands when holy Church diligently seeks with what fruits of piety she may exercise herself and how she may cleanse herself from carnal enticements. And she does both with the wisest counsel—that is, solely with a view to the reward above. The following verse also speaks more clearly of this reward:

“She became like a merchant’s ship,” etc. By a merchant he means a trader, who was so called by the ancients because he diligently applied himself to acquiring and multiplying merchandise. The strong woman therefore became like a merchant’s ship, because just as a merchant’s ship, loaded with wares that are more abundant in its homeland, crosses the sea to foreign lands, so that after selling what it brought it may carry home more valuable goods, so holy Church, and every perfect soul, rejoices to be laden with the riches of virtues, by which it may purchase greater gifts of divine grace.

For this is an excellent exchange: when, by doing the good things we are able to do, we first receive from the Lord this reward—that we may always advance toward doing greater things—and afterward also receive eternal life.

Thus the holy soul became like a merchant’s ship, which crosses the waves of the present world through desire, hopes to receive in heaven alone, meditates on eternal joys, and, in order to attain them more abundantly, strives earnestly to do whatever it can and bravely to overcome whatever adversity may arise. Of it it is rightly said that “she brings her bread from afar,” because in all the temporal good that she does she expects only an eternal reward; she desires only the satiety of the living bread, namely that of the one who lovingly and powerfully promises his hearers: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

On the other hand, the person who receives his bread nearby, rather than carrying it from afar across the seas, is the one who, while seeming to live justly, seeks only the rewards of human favor. He does not strive, with any thought of enduring life, to overcome and trample upon the things that pass away. Concerning such people he himself thunders terribly: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” [printed: “suamc”].

“And she rose while it was still night and gave prey to her household, etc.” Just as the entire course of the fleeting world is varied by the perpetual alternation of day and night, and day was naturally created for work, not for rest, so the whole period of the present Church is distinguished by a kind of twofold condition of rest and work.

She rests, as it were, at night when some of her faithful, having for a time interrupted their external anxieties, begin to devote themselves to themselves and to care for themselves spiritually, exercising themselves more privately in sacred readings, prayers, tears, or other such pursuits. But she rises at night when, in those same faithful, she girds herself diligently to care also for her neighbors. She customarily performs this work of fraternal service in two ways: she calls those who are wandering outside to the grace of faith, and she never ceases to awaken those who have already been instructed in the sacraments of faith to devote themselves more fully to good works.

Hence it is rightly said: “She gave prey to her household and food to her maidservants.” She gives prey to her household when, by teaching, she is able to rescue them from the ancient enemy and reconcile them to the fellowship of those who preceded them in faith. She gives food to her maidservants when she refreshes the humble, who preserve themselves in due fear, with the remembrance of the heavenly reward, lest they grow weary under their pious labor.

“She considered a field and bought it,” etc. By the field he means possession of the heavenly inheritance. Of this the patriarch Isaac speaks when blessing his son: “Behold, the odor of my son is as the odor of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27). The odor of the saints is like the odor of a full field that the Lord has blessed, because they gaze with the whole intention of their minds upon what the fullness of blessing is in the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

The Church therefore considered a field and bought it, because she diligently learned what the joys of eternal life are and strove to labor for their attainment with whatever strength she possessed. She also planted a vineyard from the fruit of her hands, because from the fruitful deeds or words of her faithful she established holy Scripture, through which she might intoxicate the minds of her hearers with faith and love of their Redeemer.

Nor is it unreasonable if we understand the Church herself, who is represented by the strong woman, to be figured under the name of the vineyard, and those who are the woman’s children to be the branches of the vineyard. The woman planted a vineyard when the primitive Church, sending preachers throughout the world, scattered the seeds of faith more widely.

She considered the field when she saw that the whole world, bristling with the thorns of vices, needed a spiritual cultivator. She bought it when, sending teachers everywhere, she entrusted the talent of the word to her hearers, so that by believing she might subject them to the most blessed service of Christ. She planted a vineyard in that same field when, among new peoples of believers, she strengthened the Church through instruction in the fullness of evangelical truth.

She planted that vineyard from the fruit of her hands because the apostles and their successors instructed the peoples whom they taught not only by word, but also joined testimony of good works and signs of miracles to their words of doctrine.

Even today, indeed until the end of the world, the strong woman considers the field and buys it, and plants a vineyard from the fruit of her hands, because holy Church is always anxiously seeking those whom she may convert to the faith. Whoever she finds teachable, she buys for the service of Christ with the money of the word that has been given; and she strives to plant Christ’s vineyard in them, or rather to make them Christ’s vineyard.

And because anyone who desires to teach another must first abstain from evil himself and exercise himself in good works, it is rightly added:

“She girded her loins with strength,” etc. The Church girded her loins with strength when, intent upon the desires of heavenly things, she disdained to succumb to carnal enticements; she strengthened her arm when she prepared herself for the performance of virtuous works.

It is rightly said first that she girds her loins with strength and afterward strengthens her arm, because the action of a good work cannot be acceptable to the Lord if a person does not first restrain the flow of lust from both flesh and mind. Hence the prophet says: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah 1). And the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12). Let your loins be girded, so that you may not be subjected to lust; let your lamps burn, so that you may shine with good works.

“She tasted and saw that her commerce was good,” etc. By “her commerce” he means that field of which he said above, “She considered a field and bought it.” Holy Church therefore tasted, and every perfect soul tasted—that is, through the innermost desire of the mind it understood—that the commerce of imperishable life is good, by which, after abandoning temporal enticements, we merit the eternal life of heaven.

She tasted—that is, she learned openly—that it is good, through persevering preaching, to lead to the way of truth all whom she can. Therefore no darkness of tribulations, not even death itself, can extinguish the lamp of her devotion.

The lamp of those people is extinguished at night, although it appears to burn during the day, who, as the Lord says, “believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8). The lamp of those others is extinguished in the middle of the night who, when the Judge comes, are found not to have had the oil of charity in the vessels of their hearts; when the reputation of their false virtues has been lost, they suffer the true torments of their dark deeds.

But if we wish to understand “night” here as rest, in accordance with what is said above, “She rose at night”—that is, “after resting, she prepared herself for work”—then it is appropriately said that the lamp of holy Church is not extinguished at night. For when she rests from the business of action, she is more freely occupied with the light of heavenly contemplation. When she ceases from public works, she takes greater care to devote herself either to hearing holy reading or to divine praises, following the example of the industrious woman, who is accustomed not only to devote herself to necessary labors during the day, but also, with the lamp frequently lit at night, to exercise equal care for her household.

“She put her hand to strong things,” etc. By “strong things” he means perfect works in the love of Christ, to which the Church joyfully subjected herself in the sure expectation of a heavenly reward. For example: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy’; but I say to you, ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,’” and so forth (Matthew 5). And concerning the preservation of virginity: “Let him take it who can take it” (Matthew 19). And concerning the contempt of riches: “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell all that you have,” and so forth (ibid.).

The people of the Synagogue, to whom it was said, “If you are willing and will hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1), were so much weaker in the work of righteousness as they were less uplifted by hope of eternal recompense. But the Church, which heard from the Lord, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3), rightly endures all hard things with patience for the sake of attaining it. Hence he says again of her strength: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

“And her fingers,” he says, “have grasped the spindle.” Women commonly hold the spindle in the right hand and the distaff in the left. Wool is wound around the distaff so that it may pass from there, drawn out and spun, onto the spindle.

In Scripture the right hand often signifies perpetual life, while the left signifies God’s present gifts: the abundance of worldly things, temporal peace, bodily health, knowledge of the Scriptures, and the understanding of heavenly mysteries. When, with the Lord granting them, we receive these and similar goods, we carry them in the left hand, as wool wound around the distaff.

But when we begin beneficially to exercise ourselves in them for the love of heavenly things, we transfer the wool of the spotless Lamb from the distaff to the spindle, from the left hand to the right. For from the gifts of our Redeemer and from the examples of his works we make for ourselves a robe of heavenly glory and a garment of bridal charity.

The fingers with which she is said to grasp the spindle signify the very intention of discernment by which each person acts. This is indicated by the fact that none of our bodily members is divided into more joints or suited to more flexing than the fingers. Whoever can truly say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3), from which also we await “the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,” has learned, through careful discernment, to grasp the spindle with the fingers of the right hand—that is, to labor for eternal goods.

It is rightly said, “They have grasped,” so that it may be more vividly emphasized with what zeal and haste we ought to work in this uncertain life for the rewards that are certain with the Lord.

What the strong woman—that is, holy Church or every perfect soul—has worked with the intellectual spindle is explained next:

“She opened her hand to the needy,” etc. This may be understood of the works of almsgiving that are generally performed for the poor; but it is better understood of the word of the Lord, which grants the garment of salvation to souls. Concerning this blessed Job boasts, saying: “I was clothed with justice, and I clothed myself with it as with a garment and a diadem; with my judgment” (Job 29).

The Church opened her hand to the needy when, through the workers of truth, she revealed the mysteries of faith to those ignorant of them. She extended her palms to the poor when she scattered preachers far and wide to instruct the needy nations in eternal salvation.

“She shall not fear for her household because of the cold of snow,” etc. The cold of snow is the hearts of the reprobate, stiffened by the chill of their unbelief. Concerning them the Lord says: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).
