They are also weighed down by that most wicked snow which, having fallen from heaven into the depths of darkness because of the merit of its original pride, nevertheless presumes to display itself to the foolish as an angel of light and to present the appearance of its merits as resembling the whiteness of snow to those unaware of its frauds. It is proper to the Lord and his angels to signify the brightness of their virtue by a snowy appearance.

The Church, however, will not fear for her household because of the cold of this snow, because, with the Lord’s promise, she believes that the gates of hell will not prevail against her. All her household are clothed in double garments: in wisdom, to expose the heretical teachings of false brothers; and in patience, to endure the battles of open enemies.

Or certainly they are clothed in double garments because they have the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come. Now, during their temporal pilgrimage, they are aided by divine assistance so that they do not fail; then, in the perpetual dwelling of the homeland, they are lifted up by the vision of divine grace so that they may live forever in happiness.

Again, her household are clothed in a double garment: one of works, the other of the faith of the mind. They have the coverings of deeds and are instructed and formed by the mysteries of their Redeemer and by his examples. Thus is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever among you has been baptized in Christ has put on Christ” (Galatians 3).

The cold of snow may also be understood as the eternal torments, which we read are associated with both fire and cold, when it is said: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8). Fire and smoke produce weeping in the eyes, while cold commonly produces gnashing in the teeth. Hence blessed Job, speaking of the eternal punishments of the reprobate, says: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24).

But the Church will not fear these things for her household, because whoever perishes did not belong to her household and was not clothed in her spiritual garment, even though such a person may for a time have appeared to be instructed in her mysteries. Finally, we read in the Gospels that a man was cast out of the house of that banquet because he had presumed to enter it in filthy garments of works, and was thrown into the outer darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth. He was rightly bound in the cold of punishment, because he had neglected to possess the garments of piety.

“She made herself a variegated garment,” etc. A variegated garment, which is customarily made very strong through its varied weave, signifies the strong works of the Church and the various adornments of her virtues. Concerning these the prophet sang in praise of the supreme King, that is, of that man: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied colors” (Psalm 44).

Her clothing is also fine linen and purple: fine linen in the whiteness of a pure conscience and manner of life; purple in the pouring out of precious blood. Fine linen is white in color; purple is made from the blood of a living creature called purple and itself has the appearance of blood. Hence the Fathers beautifully said that holy Church, blooming with the flowers of the elect, has lilies in peace and roses in war.

Again, fine linen grows green from the earth, but through long and varied exercises, after losing its natural moisture and greenness, it is brought to the beauty of a white garment. Purple, however, is royal attire. The Church is clothed in fine linen when the elect chastise their bodies and subject them to servitude; she is clothed in purple when they practice that same continence not for popular approval but to obtain the blessedness of the eternal kingdom.

In the present, this garment of virtues appears contemptible to those who do not understand it; but in the future what it has been will be plainly revealed. Hence John beautifully reports in his Apocalypse that he heard the voice of the saints saying: “Let us rejoice and exult, because the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, and it has been granted to her to clothe herself in shining, white fine linen” (Revelation 19). For the fine linen is the righteousnesses of the saints.

“Her husband is noble in the gates,” etc. The husband of holy Church and the Lord of every faithful soul is the one who appeared ignoble when he stood bowed before the governor’s tribunal, when he received insults, scourging, spittle, and the death of the cross itself. But he will appear noble when he comes to judge the world in justice, and all his angels with him. “Then,” he says, “he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another,” and so forth (Matthew 25).

“Her husband is noble in the gates,” because in ancient times people customarily sat at the gates to judge, so that those arriving at the city from elsewhere might immediately receive the judge’s prepared response. In this way neither peasants nor shepherds would be bewildered by the unfamiliar buildings of the city, nor would the inner peace of the city be polluted by the frequent disputes of litigants.

The Lord, therefore, will be noble in the gates of his city, because he who is now thought worthy of contempt by many will appear sublime to all when the end of the world has arrived and the entrance to the heavenly homeland has appeared to the elect.

“He will sit,” he says, “with the senators of the land. Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

“She made and sold a linen garment,” etc. In the linen of the sindon is signified the fine weaving of holy preaching, in which one rests gently, because in it the mind of the faithful is refreshed by heavenly hope. Hence animals are shown to Peter in a linen cloth, because the souls of sinners, gathered together mercifully, are contained in the soothing rest of faith.

The Church therefore made and sold this sindon, because she learned through speaking the faith that she had woven through believing, and receives from the faithful the life of right conduct. She also gave a belt to the Canaanite, because through the strength of demonstrated righteousness she extinguished the loose works of paganism. Thus what is commanded may be maintained in life: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12).

The name Canaan, which both produced the Gentile people and is interpreted as “changed,” appropriately signifies the Gentiles converted to the faith. Through a most blessed change, paganism migrated from vice to virtues and from the devil to Christ.

Therefore Psalm 44 was also written in his praise, whose title is: “For the end, for those who will be changed, a song for the sons of Korah, for the beloved.” The sons of Korah are interpreted as “sons of Calvary”; they are the children of the Lord’s cross, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

How they are changed is taught by the following verses of that same psalm, where the beloved himself—that is, the Lord of the Church—says: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44). He desires her to be changed, whom he commands to forget the house of her former father—that is, of the ancient enemy—so that she may be called a daughter.

“Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day.” Strength is for enduring the wickedness of the perverse; beauty is for exercising the grace of virtues. Beauty is present because she practices righteousness; strength, because she suffers persecution for righteousness (Matthew 5).

Therefore she shall laugh on the last day—that is, she shall rejoice in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom, though she grieved in the struggle of the present life. It is the custom of Scripture to use laughter for joy, as the Lord says: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6). And blessed Job says: “The mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter” (Job [reference incomplete in source]).

The prophet likewise placed a similar statement concerning the Lord and Savior of this strongest woman, saying: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength,” and so forth (Psalm 92). When he preached the Gospel of the kingdom, some were pleased and others displeased; some spoke well, while others slandered, tore at, bit, and reviled him. To those, therefore, who were pleased, he put on beauty; to those who were displeased, strength.

Imitate your Lord, then, so that you may be his garment. Be beautiful toward those who are pleased by your good works; be strong against those who slander.

“She opened her mouth to wisdom,” etc. She opened her mouth only for this purpose: to teach wisdom, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4).

Or certainly she opened the mouth of her heart in order to learn inwardly from wisdom itself the truth that she might teach outwardly to others. Since the Church does both, what follows appropriately agrees with both senses: “And the law of clemency is on her tongue,” namely, that she should not immediately punish sinners according to the manner of the Mosaic law, but mercifully call them to the remedy of repentance.

From the very Wisdom of God, our Lord and Savior, she clearly received an example of this clemency when a sinful woman was brought before him: “Let him who is without sin,” he said, “be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8). Thus he mercifully absolved her from the crime she had committed, on the condition that she sin no more.

“She considered the paths of her household,” etc. She considers the paths of her household because she carefully investigates all the thoughts of her conscience. She does not eat bread in idleness because she demonstrates through works, before the eyes of the eternal Judge, what she has received by understanding from sacred Scripture.

Again, the house of the strong woman is the dwelling of the heavenly homeland; the paths of that house are the precepts of righteousness, by which one reaches the dwelling of eternal life. The soul considers these paths well when it carefully examines by what actions one must reach the things above, and does not cease diligently practicing what it has learned must be done.

Nor does it eat bread in idleness when, receiving the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, it strives to imitate in action what it celebrates in the ministry. It is very careful not to eat the Lord’s bread and drink the cup unworthily and thereby eat and drink judgment upon itself, but to follow as far as it can the example of his passion by suffering for Christ, shedding tears, and devoting itself also to good works.

It is possible
and may be understood simply to mean that the strong woman does not eat her bread in idleness, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (II Thessalonians 3). He likewise says of himself: “These hands ministered to my needs and to those who were with me” (Acts 20). Therefore, rightly rebuking widows who live wantonly, he adds: “At the same time they also learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome” (I Timothy 5).

—“Her sons rose up,” etc. What he knew would certainly happen, he reports prophetically as though it had already occurred. For the sons of the Church—namely, all the elect—will rise at the end, endowed with the immortality of the flesh. Then they will proclaim blessed their mother, who gave them birth to God from water and the Holy Spirit, and who is now despised by unbelievers as wretched. Indeed, as the Apostle says: “If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (II Corinthians 15).

But because in the present life we strive for the life to come, rightly, when what we shall be has been revealed, we will proclaim blessed our mother, who, gathered from all the righteous, is called the one dove, bride, and friend of Christ. Her husband, too, will rise and praise her, saying in the judgment: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matthew 25). He himself indeed rose from the dead as “the firstfruits of those who sleep”; but on the day of judgment he will demonstrate more openly to all those whom he judges worthy of his praise how great is the glory of that same resurrection of his.

What is said—“Her sons rose up and proclaimed her most blessed”—may also appropriately be understood of the present time, whenever one of the faithful, having passed beyond the sufferings of the world, is brought to the heavenly kingdoms. For to sit sometimes pertains to humiliation, while to rise pertains to glory. Hence it is said: “Would that those sitting in ashes and sackcloth had repented” (Luke 10), that is, had been humbled. And the prophet says: “I alone sat because of the threat of your hand, for you filled me with indignation” (Jeremiah 15). The Psalmist likewise says: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm 126).

This is plainly to say: Why do you seek in the present to enjoy what is reserved for the elect in the future? For in this life—that is, before the light—you cannot possess the glory of the heavenly reward in true happiness. Rather, after you have been humbled here for a time, hope that there you will truly be exalted forever—you for whom everything that appears pleasant and sweet to lovers of the world is bitter.

Thus the sons of the Church rise and proclaim her most blessed when, exalted by heavenly blessings, they behold how great is the blessedness of that homeland of which they have been deemed worthy to become participants. In the divine vision they celebrate her together with fitting praise. Her husband praises her when he rewards the good things that he himself bestowed. In what words he praises her is next shown, when it says:

—“Many daughters have gathered riches,” etc. By “many daughters” he means the churches of heretics and the crowds of the wicked. The daughters of Catholics are called either Christ’s daughters or the Church’s, because they too were reborn through the Lord’s sacraments and received the adoption of sons, which they did not preserve. Hence John also says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John 2).

These daughters gathered riches—namely, practices of good works: fasts, almsgiving, affliction, bodily chastity, restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and other things of this kind. These are truly riches of the Spirit when they are performed with pure sincerity of mind; but when they are done without the faith that works through love, they benefit those who perform them nothing.

Those daughters also gathered riches in vain of whom the Lord says: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I never knew you’” (Matthew 7). But the Catholic Church surpasses all daughters of this kind; with chaste faith and perfect works, she follows the footsteps of her Redeemer.

—“Deceptive is grace, and vain is beauty,” etc. The grace of praise that she receives from human beings is deceptive; the beauty of chastity or good works that a soul displays to human beings while lacking the fear of God is vain. But that conscience is truly worthy of praise which preserves the fear of God in all things. For this fear is the beginning and guardian of all virtues, as Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110; Proverbs 1, 9; Sirach 1). And again: “Whoever fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Ecclesiastes 7).

Because of this, blessed Job both flourished incomparably in virtue during prosperity and remained an unconquerable opponent in adversity: he could truthfully say, “For I always feared the Lord, as though waves swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight” (Job 31). The grace of pretenders, therefore, is deceptive; the adornment of fools’ works is vain.

The Church, however, which conducts herself temporarily in fear during her earthly sojourn, will offer the burning lamps of her virtues to her Bridegroom when he comes to judgment. Rightly praised by him, she will enter with him through the gate of the heavenly kingdom. How he praises her is taught in the concluding verse:

—“Give her of the fruit of her hands,” etc. These are the words of that husband of whom it was said, “Her husband, and he praised her”—that is, of our Lord and Savior. At the end he will command the angels to bring the Church, after the contest of this life and after the threshing of earthly afflictions, into the joys of the heavenly kingdom and to join her to himself as a companion of immortal life, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Gather the wheat into my barn” (Matthew 13).

“Give her,” he says, “of the fruit of her hands,” because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, modesty, self-control, faith, and patience. For this, repay her the reward she deserves, “and let them praise her in the gates”—that is, in the judgment or at the entrance to the heavenly homeland.

May it not be the empty approval of human beings, but the works themselves that she performed, that he examines, approves, and rewards—the one by whose grace these things were given. May he himself, in his mercy, grant that we may deserve to be praised by him in the future, by praising him with worthy service in the present life. Amen.

[Col. 1039]

## A Little Book on the Strong Woman. (C, S)

### ALEPH

[Col. 1039D]

“Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far away, and from the remotest boundaries.”

The Catholic Church is called the strong woman. A woman, evidently, because she is accustomed to beget spiritual children for God from water and the Holy Spirit. Strong, because she despises all things of this world, adversities and prosperities alike, for faith in her Creator. For when he appeared in the flesh, he found her indeed weak, but by his finding her—that is, by his gracious visitation—he made her strong. Hence, after her redemption, as he was returning to heaven, he joyfully said to the citizens above: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the sheep that was lost” (Luke 15:6).

Solomon, therefore, seeing the human race entangled in innumerable errors, and recognizing that no patriarch, no prophet, indeed none of the elect, except the sole Mediator of God and human beings, was sufficient for its salvation, says: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far away, and from the remotest boundaries.” As though he were openly proclaiming, in wonder at the Lord’s future grace: “Who possesses such virtue, who such merit, that from so many unbelieving and wicked nations of the world he might gather for himself one Church of the elect, and by his grace make her strong and unconquerable against all adversaries?”

Certainly, one like us is not meant here, nor is he to come in our time; but at the end of the ages God, made human, will descend from heaven, who will redeem us from death by his passion. This is what he says: “Her price is far away, and from the remotest boundaries.” “Far away,” that is, in the temporal order, since the time from the days of Solomon until the Virgin’s childbirth would pass; “from the remotest boundaries,” because “his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Psalm 18:7). He offered nothing else as the price of our redemption than himself. Hence the Apostle says: “He loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance” (Ephesians 5:2).

The price of the holy Church may also rightly be understood as having been placed far away, since the incarnation of the Word of God, his life among human beings, his passion, and his resurrection were far removed from the condition of our nature. For he was born when he wished and from the mother he wished, and he lived in the world without sin; and when he wished, and by the death he wished, he departed from the world. He also held the time of his resurrection and ascension in his own power, along with other things of this kind, in which he was as far removed from us as heaven is from earth.

But since the Lord granted the Church whom he redeemed not only to receive the word of salvation, but also constantly to fight for it and to preach this very thing throughout the world, it is rightly added:

### BETH

“He husband’s heart trusts in her, and he will have no need of spoils.”

He calls the husband of the holy Church her Lord and Redeemer, who also deigned to become her price. Hence the Apostle says to believers: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

When he says, “Her husband’s heart trusts in her,” the expression is plainly drawn from human custom. Just as anyone who has a strong, faithful, and chaste wife trusts in her completely—because she cannot do anything against his will, cannot even be touched by an adulterous thought, willingly endures adversities for his love, and desires to convert to his friendship as many people as she can—so, surely, our Lord and Redeemer trusts in the Church.

He knows the Spirit of grace whom he has given; he knows the power of love which he has infused into her heart. Therefore he does not doubt that she can not only by no means be corrupted from the integrity of her faith, but will also persevere in gathering many into the unity of that same faith. This is what follows: “And he will have no need of spoils.”

For the Church despoils the devil when, through her preachers, she recalls to the way of truth those whom he had deceived. And it is rightly said, “He will have no need of spoils,” because the Church will never cease restoring to the faith of Christ souls liberated from diabolical deception, until, when the course of the world has been completed, the predetermined number of her members has likewise been fulfilled.

But since whatever good the holy Church, or any faithful soul, does, it receives from above, it is rightly added:

### GIMEL

“She will repay him with good and not with evil all the days of her life.”

A soul repays Christ with good when, having received from him the gifts of life, it responds by living rightly; and when it diligently strives to make known to others what it has been able, with his help, to know or do.

After saying, “She will repay him with good,” he immediately and rightly added, “and not with evil,” because there are certainly people who repay the good they have received from the Lord with evil: either by defiling the mysteries of faith they have received with heretical impurity; or by blaspheming through wicked deeds the faith they preserve in their profession; or by corrupting through evil conversations the good morals with which they serve in right faith.

Nor do those repay the Lord with good who, having received it, do not take care to persist until the end of their present life in the things they have begun well. Therefore, after saying, “She will repay him with good and not with evil,” to show that perseverance in good is necessary, he added: “All the days of her life.” A similar statement is found in the Gospel: “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” (Luke 1:74–75).

What works, and especially what fruits of righteousness or holiness, one who strives freely to repay the Lord with the good received from him should chiefly pursue is subsequently indicated when it says:

### DALETH

“She sought wool and flax, and worked by the counsel of her hands.”

The strong woman—that is, the holy Church—is accustomed both to understand and to observe the beginning of this verse literally, according to the prophetic saying: “When you see the naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah 58:7).

She works, however, not with useless and blind labor, but with this purpose: that she may deserve to hear from her husband himself, namely Christ the Lord, at the judgment: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matthew 25:43); and, “As long as you did it for one of these, my least brothers, you did it for me” (ibid. 45).

She works “by the counsel of her hands,” that is, through those persons by whom she gives alms to the poor. In their devout work she employs this salutary counsel: that when she scatters and gives to the poor, she herself should not be praised by human beings for a time, but that “her righteousness should remain forever and ever” (2 Corinthians 9:9), and “her horn should be exalted in glory” (Psalm 112:9).

Mystically, however, wool—which is the clothing of sheep—may be understood as all the works of piety and simplicity that we render to our neighbors. In flax, which grows green from the earth but loses its natural moisture through long and repeated labor and reaches the grace of a new whiteness, the chastisement of our flesh may be signified. As we burn out its inborn stains of vice through self-restraint, we make it worthy to clothe us with Christ, according to the Apostle’s saying: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

The strong woman, therefore, seeks wool and flax and works by the counsel of her hands when the holy Church diligently seeks by what fruits of piety she may exercise herself and how she may cleanse herself from carnal allurements. She does both with the most prudent counsel—that is, solely with a view to heavenly recompense. The following verse also speaks more openly of this recompense, when it adds:

### HE

“She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from far away.”

He calls a merchant a trader, who is so named by the ancients because he diligently devotes himself to acquiring and multiplying merchandise.

The strong woman therefore became like a merchant’s ship. Just as a merchant’s ship, loaded with goods that are more plentiful in its homeland, crosses the sea to foreign lands so that, after selling what it has brought there, it may carry home more valuable goods, so the holy Church, and every perfect soul, rejoices to be laden with the riches of virtues by which it may purchase greater gifts of divine grace.

It is indeed an excellent exchange when, by doing the good things we are able to do, we first receive this reward from the Lord: that we may advance ever further toward doing greater things; and then that we may receive eternal life.

The soul, therefore, became like a merchant’s ship. Having crossed, through desire, the waves of the present world, it meditates only on the eternal joys which it hopes to receive in heaven. To obtain these more abundantly, it strives eagerly to do whatever it can and bravely to overcome whatever adversity confronts it.

Of this soul it is rightly said that “it brings its bread from far away,” because in all the temporal good it does, it awaits only eternal recompense; it desires only the fullness of the living bread—namely, the bread of him who promises his hearers with piety and power: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:5).

By contrast, the person who receives his bread nearby and does not carry it from far away across the seas is the one who, while appearing to live justly, seeks only the rewards of human favor and does not strive, with any thought of enduring life, to rise above and trample upon the things that pass away below. Concerning such people he thunders terribly: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:5).

### VAV

“She rose during the night and gave prey to her household, and food to her maidservants.”

Just as the entire course of the passing world varies through the perpetual alternation of day and night—and day was naturally created for working, night for resting—so the whole time of the present Church is distinguished by a twofold condition of rest and work.

She rests, as it were, at night when some of her faithful, interrupting their external concerns for a time, begin to devote themselves to themselves and to care spiritually for themselves, exercising themselves more privately either in sacred readings, or in prayers and tears, or in other studies of this kind.

She rises during the night when, in those same faithful, she eagerly girds herself also to care for her neighbors. She is accustomed to exercise this work of fraternal service in two ways: she calls those who were wandering outside to the grace of faith; and she does not cease to rouse those who have already been imbued with the mysteries of faith to devote themselves more fully to good works.

Hence it is rightly said: “She gave prey to her household, and food to her maidservants.”

She gives prey to her household when she places those whom she has been able to snatch from the ancient enemy by teaching among the society of those who have advanced in faith. She gives food to her maidservants when, with the remembrance of heavenly reward, she refreshes the humble who obey her commands with due love, so that they do not grow weary under their devout love.

### ZAIN

[Col. 1044B]

“She considered a field and bought it; from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.”

He calls a field the possession of the heavenly inheritance. Concerning it the patriarch, blessing his son, says: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27).

The scent of the saints is like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed, because with the whole intention of their minds they contemplate the fullness of blessing in the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

The Church therefore considered a field and bought it, because she diligently learned what the joys of eternal life are and strove to labor for their possession with all that she could.

She also planted a vineyard from the fruit of her hands, because from the fruitful deeds or words of her faithful she composed sacred Scripture, through which she might intoxicate the minds of hearers with faith and love for their Redeemer.

Nor is it unreasonable to understand the vineyard as a figure of the Church herself, who is represented by the strong woman, and to understand as the shoots of the vineyard those who are the woman’s children.

The woman planted the vineyard when the primitive Church, sending preachers throughout the world, scattered the seeds of faith more widely. She considered the field when she perceived that the whole world, bristling with the thorns of vices, needed spiritual cultivation. She bought it when, sending teachers everywhere, she entrusted the talent of the word to hearers, so that by believing she might subject them to the most blessed service of Christ.

She planted a vineyard in that same field when she established the Church among new peoples of believers, firmly grounding them in instruction filled with evangelical truth.

She planted this vineyard from the fruit of her hands because the apostles and their successors instructed the peoples whom they taught not only by word, but also joined to the words of their teaching the testimony of good works and signs of miracles.

Even to this day—indeed, until the end of the world—the strong woman considers the field, buys it, and plants a vineyard from the fruit of her hands. For the holy Church is always diligently seeking whom she may convert to the faith; and whoever she finds teachable, she buys for Christ’s service with the money of the word. In them she strives to plant Christ’s vineyard—or rather, to make them Christ’s vineyard.

And because whoever desires to teach another must first abstain from evil himself and exercise himself in good deeds, it is rightly added:

### CHETH

“She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm.”

The Church girded her loins with strength when, intent upon the desires of things above, she disdained to succumb to carnal allurements. She strengthened her arm when she prepared herself to perform works of virtue.

It is rightly said first that she girds her loins with strength and afterward strengthens her arm, because the action of a good work cannot be acceptable to God if a person does not first restrain from both flesh and mind the looseness of lust.

Hence the prophet says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah 1:16). And the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). The loins are girded so that you may not be subjected to lust; the lamps burn so that you may shine with good works.

### TETH

“She tasted and saw that her trade was good; her lamp will not be extinguished at night.”

When he says, “her trade,” he refers to that field of which he said above: “She considered a field and bought it.”

The holy Church tasted; every perfect soul tasted—that is, it recognized through the innermost desire of the mind that the trade of unfading life is good, by which, after abandoning temporal allurements, we purchase eternity in heaven.

She tasted—that is, she learned openly that it is good, through the persistence of preaching, to lead to the way of truth as many people as she can. Therefore the lamp of her devotion cannot be extinguished by any darkness of tribulations, or even by death itself.

The lamp of those people is extinguished at night, although it may appear to burn during the day, who, as the Lord says, “believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away.”

The lamp of those whose vessels of inward being are shown to lack the oil of love is also extinguished in the middle of the night when the judge comes. Having lost the reputation of false virtues, they suffer the true torments of their dark deeds.

But if we wish to understand “night” here according to what was said above—“She rose during the night,” that is, she prepared herself for work after rest—it is plainly said that the lamp of the holy Church is not extinguished at night. For when she rests from the business of action, she gives herself more freely to the light of heavenly contemplation; and when she ceases from public works, she takes greater care to devote herself either to hearing sacred readings or to divine praises.

This follows the example of a diligent woman, who is accustomed not only to attend during the day to necessary labors, but also frequently at night, after lighting a lamp, to care equally for the affairs of her household.

### IOD

“She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle.”

By “strong things” he means perfect works in the love of Christ, to which the Church joyfully submits herself in certain expectation of heavenly recompense.

For example: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, ‘Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you,’ etc.” (Matthew 5:43–44); and concerning the preservation of virginity: “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew 19:12); and concerning the despising of riches: “If you wish to be perfect,” he says, “go, sell what you have and give to the poor, etc.” (ibid. 21).

For the people of the synagogue, to whom it was said, “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19), were so much weaker in the work of righteousness because they were less lifted up by the hope of perpetual reward.

But the Church, which heard from the Lord, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4:17), rightly endures all hard things patiently for the sake of obtaining it. Hence again he says of her strength: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

“And her fingers,” he says, “grasped the spindle.”

Women usually hold the spindle in the right hand and the distaff in the left. On the distaff the wool is wrapped; it is drawn out, spun, and transferred onto the spindle.

In Scripture, the right hand often signifies perpetual life, while the left signifies God’s present gifts: the abundance of possessions, peace in the times, bodily health, knowledge of the Scriptures, and understanding of heavenly mysteries.

When, by the Lord’s generosity, we receive these and similar goods, we carry them as though wool wrapped around a distaff in the left hand. But when, for love of heavenly things, we begin profitably to exercise ourselves in them, we transfer the wool of the immaculate Lamb from the distaff to the spindle, from the left hand to the right. For from the goods of our Redeemer and from the examples of his works we make for ourselves a robe of heavenly glory and a garment of bridal love.

To grasp the spindle with the fingers signifies the very intention of discernment by which a person works. This is indicated because none of the limbs of our body is divided into more joints and flexures than the fingers.

Whoever can truly say with the Apostle, “Our way of life is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20), “from which place we also await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,” has surely grasped the spindle with the fingers of his right hand, because he has learned through diligent discernment to labor for eternal goods.

It is rightly said, “They grasped,” so that it may be commended more vividly with what zeal and what haste we ought to pursue the uncertainties of this life in exchange for certain rewards with the Lord.

What the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—or every perfect soul, works with the intellectual spindle is explained next:

### CAPH

“She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor.”

This may be understood of works of almsgiving generally performed for the poor, but it is better understood of the word of God, which grants the garment of salvation to souls. Of this blessed Job boasts, saying: “I clothed myself with righteousness, and I clothed myself with judgment as with a garment and a diadem” (Job 29:14).

The Church opened her hand to the needy when she revealed the mysteries of faith to those ignorant of them through the workers of truth. She extended her palms to the poor when she dispersed preachers far and wide to instruct nations lacking eternal salvation.

### LAMED

[Col. 1047A]

“She will not fear for her household because of the cold of snow; all her household are clothed in double garments.”

The cold of snow is the hearts of the reprobate, stiffened by the torpor of their infidelity. Of them the Lord says: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 25:12).

Those hearts are crushed by that most evil snow which, having fallen from heaven into the depths of darkness because of the merit of its original pride, nevertheless still presumptuously presents itself to fools as an angel of light and displays, to those ignorant of its deceits, an appearance like the whiteness of snow as though it were the brightness of its merits.

It is proper to the Lord and his angels to signify the radiance of their virtue in a snowy garment.

The Church will not fear the cold of the snow mentioned for her household, because she believes the Lord’s promise that “the gates of hell will not prevail against her” (Matthew 16:18).

“All her household are clothed in double garments”: with wisdom, namely, to refute the doctrines of heretical false brothers, and with patience, to endure the battles of open enemies.

Or certainly they are clothed in double garments because they have the promise of the life that is now and of the life that is to come. Now, during their temporal pilgrimage, they are aided by divine help so that they do not fail; then, in the eternal dwelling of their homeland, they are uplifted by the grace of the divine vision so that they may live happily forever.

Again, her household are clothed in a double garment: one of works, the other of the mind’s faith. They possess the coverings of deeds, and are imbued with the mysteries of their Redeemer and formed by his examples. Thus the Apostle’s saying is fulfilled: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”

The cold of snow may also be understood as eternal torments, which we read are mingled with fire and cold when it is said: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12). Fire and smoke ordinarily produce weeping in the eyes, while cold produces gnashing in the teeth. Hence blessed Job, speaking of the eternal punishments of the reprobate, says: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat” (Job 24:19).

But the Church will not fear these things for her household, because whoever perishes did not belong to the household, nor were they clothed in its spiritual garment, even though for a time they appeared to be instructed in its mysteries.

Finally, we read in the Gospels that a man was expelled from the house of that banquet who had presumed to enter it in filthy garments of works, and was cast into the outer darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12). He was rightly bound in the cold of punishment because he had neglected to possess the garment of piety.

### MEM

“She made herself a quilted garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing.”

A quilted garment, which through its varied weave is customarily made extremely strong, signifies the strong works of the Church and the diverse ornaments of her virtues.

Concerning these the Prophet sang in praise of the supreme King, namely that man: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 45:10).

“Fine linen and purple are her clothing.” Fine linen signifies the purity of chaste conduct; purple, the outpouring of precious blood.

Fine linen is white in color; purple dye is made from the blood of the living creature called the purple-fish, and itself has the appearance of blood. Hence the Fathers beautifully said that the holy Church, blooming with the flowers of the elect, possesses lilies in peace and roses in war.

Again, because fine linen grows green from the earth but through long and varied exercises, after losing its natural moisture and greenness, is brought to the beauty of a white garment, while purple is royal clothing: the Church is clothed in fine linen when the elect chastise their bodies and subject them to servitude; she is clothed in purple when they practice that same self-restraint not for popular approval, but to obtain the blessedness of the everlasting kingdom.

Thus the garment of virtues appears contemptible in the present to those who do not understand it, but in the future what it has been will clearly appear.

Hence John beautifully reports in the Apocalypse that he heard the voice of the saints saying: “Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give glory to him, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it has been granted to her to clothe herself in shining fine linen” (Revelation 19:7). The fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

### NUN

“Noble at the gates is her husband when he sits with the senators of the land.”

The husband of the holy Church, and of every soul, is the Lord. He appeared ignoble when he stood before the governor’s tribunal to be judged, when he endured insults, spitting, scourges, and even death on the cross. But he will appear noble when he comes to judge the world in righteousness, and all his angels with him.

“Then,” he says, “he will sit on the seat of his majesty, and all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, etc.” (Matthew 25:31–32).

“Noble,” he says, “at the gates is her husband,” because in former times people customarily sat at the gates to judge, so that those coming to the city from elsewhere might immediately receive the judge’s prepared answer; so that unfamiliar city buildings would not astonish peasants or shepherds; and so that the peace of the city within would not be marred by the continual disputes of litigants.

The Lord, therefore, will be noble at the gates of the city, because he who is now thought contemptible by many will appear exalted to all when the end of the world arrives and he opens the entrance to the heavenly homeland for the elect.

“But he will sit with the senators of the land.” “Truly I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

### SAMECH

“She made a linen garment and sold it, and she handed over a belt to the Canaanite.”

The fine weaving of the linen garment signifies holy preaching, in which one rests gently, because through it the mind of the faithful is refreshed by heavenly hope.

Hence animals are shown to Peter in a linen sheet, because the souls of sinners, gathered together mercifully, are held within the gentle repose of faith.

The Church therefore made and sold this linen garment, because she gave by speaking the faith which she had woven by believing, and received from unbelievers a life of upright conduct.

She also handed a belt to the Canaanite, because through the strength of demonstrated righteousness she extinguished the loose works of paganism, so that what is commanded may be maintained in life: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

The name Canaan is fitting. Canaan both produced the people of the Gentiles and is interpreted as “changed”; thus it signifies the Gentiles converted to the faith. Through a most blessed change they migrated from vices to virtues and from the devil to Christ.

Hence Psalm 45 was written in his praise, whose title is: “For the end, concerning those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah; a song for the beloved.”

The sons of Korah are interpreted as the sons of Calvary; they are the children of the Lord’s cross, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

How they are changed is taught by what follows in the same Psalm, where the beloved himself—that is, the Lord—says to the Church: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and the house of your father” (Psalm 45:11).

He desires her to be changed so that he may have her as a daughter, and commands her to forget the house of her former father, namely the ancient enemy.

### AIN

“Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day.”

Strength is for enduring the wickedness of the perverse; beauty is for exercising the glory of virtues. Beauty, because she practices righteousness; strength, because she suffers persecution for righteousness. Therefore she will laugh on the last day—that is, she will rejoice at the recompense of the heavenly kingdom, for which she grieved amid the conflict of the present life.

It is the custom of Scripture to use laughter for joy, as the Lord says: “Blessed are you who now weep, because you will laugh” (Luke 6:21); and blessed Job says: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter” (Job 8:21).

The Prophet set down a similar statement concerning the Lord and Savior of this strongest woman, saying: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength” (Psalm 93:1).

When he preached the Gospel of the kingdom, it pleased some; some spoke well, while others disparaged, tore at, bit, reviled, and insulted. To those whom it pleased, therefore, he clothed himself in beauty; against those whom it displeased, he clothed himself in strength.

Imitate your Lord, then, so that you may be his garment. Be adorned with beauty toward those who delight in your good works; be strong against detractors.

### PHE

“She opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue.”

She opened her mouth to speak only for the purpose of teaching wisdom, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Ephesians 4:29), “but only what is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear.”

Or certainly she opened the mouth of her heart to learn inwardly from wisdom itself the truth which she was to teach others outwardly.

The following statement clearly agrees with both senses, because the Church does both: “And the law of kindness is on her tongue.” That is, she did not immediately punish sinners according to the manner of the Mosaic law, but mercifully called them to the remedies of repentance.

She plainly learned this example of kindness from God himself and our Savior when a sinful woman was brought to him and he said: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7). Thus, on the condition that she sin no more, he mercifully absolved her from the crime she had committed.

### ZADIC

“She considered the paths of her household, and she did not eat her bread idly.”

She considers the paths of her household because she subtly investigates all the thoughts of her knowledge. She does not eat her bread idly because she demonstrates through works before the eyes of the eternal Judge what she has received by understanding from sacred discourse.

Again, the woman’s household is the dwelling of the heavenly homeland; the paths of that household are the commandments of righteousness by which one reaches the dwelling of eternal life.

The soul carefully considers these paths and diligently examines by what deeds it must reach the things above; and it does not cease eagerly to practice what it has learned must be done.

Nor does it eat bread idly when, receiving the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, it strives to imitate in action what it celebrates in mystery. It is very careful not to eat the Lord’s bread and drink the cup unworthily, thereby eating and drinking judgment upon itself (1 Corinthians 11:29), but rather, by suffering for Christ, shedding tears, and devoting itself to good works, to follow as far as it can the examples of his sufferings.

The strong woman may also simply be understood as not eating her bread idly, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). He also says of himself: “These hands have ministered to my needs and to those who were with me” (Acts 20:34).

Hence, rightly rebuking luxurious widows, he adds: “At the same time they also learn to go around from house to house—not only idle, but also talkative and curious” (1 Timothy 5:13).

### COPH

“Her sons rose up and called her most blessed; her husband praised her.”

What he knew for certain would happen, he reports in prophetic fashion as though it had already happened.

The sons of the Church will rise: all the elect at the end, endowed with the immortality of the flesh. Then they will proclaim as most blessed their mother, who begot them for God from water and the Holy Spirit, and who is now despised by unbelievers as though she were wretched.

Indeed, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Corinthians 15:19).

But because we are engaged in the present life for the sake of the life to come, rightly, when what we shall be has appeared, we will proclaim as most blessed our mother, who, gathered from all the righteous, is called the one dove, bride, and friend of Christ.

Her husband will also rise and praise her, saying at the judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, etc.” (Matthew 25:34–35).

He himself indeed, “the first fruits of those who sleep,” rose from the dead; but on the day of judgment he will show more clearly to all whom he judges worthy of his praise how great is the glory of that same resurrection of his.

What is said—“Her sons rose up and called her most blessed”—may also suitably be understood of the present time, when any of the faithful, having passed beyond the troubles of the world, are led to the heavenly kingdoms.

To sit sometimes belongs to humiliation; to rise belongs to glory. Hence it is said: “They would have repented long ago, sitting in ashes” (Luke 10:13), that is, having been humbled. And the prophet says: “I sat alone because of the presence of your hand, for you filled me with threats” (Jeremiah 15:17).

The Psalmist likewise says: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm 127:2).

This plainly means: “Why do you seek joy in the present, when it is reserved for the elect in the future? You cannot possess in this life—that is, before the light of heavenly recompense—the glory of true happiness. Rather, after you have been humbled here for a time, hope to be truly exalted there forever—you for whom everything that seems pleasant and sweet to lovers of the world is bitter.”

The sons of the Church therefore rise and call her most blessed when, exalted by heavenly goods, they see how great is the blessedness of that homeland whose participants they have been deemed worthy to become, and in the divine vision they celebrate her with due praise.

Her husband praises her when he rewards the good things he himself granted.

By what words he praises her is shown next, when it says:

### RESC.

Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all.

By “many daughters” he means the churches of heretics and the crowds of wicked Catholics. They are called daughters either of Christ or of the Church, because they too have been reborn through the Lord’s sacraments and have received the adoption of sons, though they did not preserve it. Hence John also says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

They have gathered riches—namely, good works: prayers, fasts, almsgiving, affliction, and chastity of the flesh; restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and other such things. These are truly riches of the spirit when they are practiced with pure sincerity of mind; but when they are performed without the faith that works through love, they benefit those who perform them nothing.

Those daughters also have gathered riches in vain, of whom the Lord says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I shall declare to them, ‘I never knew you’” (Matthew 7:22–23). But the Catholic Church surpasses all daughters of this kind; with pure faith and perfected in works, she follows the footsteps of her Redeemer.

## SCHIN

[Col. 1052A]

“Deceitful is grace, and beauty is vain; the woman who fears God shall herself be praised.”

The grace of praise that she receives from human beings is deceitful; the beauty of charity or of a good work that the soul lacking divine fear displays to human beings is vain. But that conscience is truly worthy of praise which preserves the fear of God in all things. For fear is the beginning and guardian of every virtue, as Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Sirach 2:16); and again: “He who fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Ecclesiastes 7:19).

This is why blessed Job flourished incomparably in virtue even in prosperity, and remained unconquerable by his adversary in adversity: for he could truly say: “I always feared God as though waves were swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight” (Job 31:23).

Thus the grace of hypocrites is deceitful, and the adornment of fools’ works is vain. But the Church, which conducts herself in fear during the time of her earthly sojourn, will offer lamps burning with virtues to her Bridegroom when he comes for judgment; rightly praised by him, she will enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom. How he praises her is taught in the concluding verse.

## TAU

“Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.”

These are the words of that husband of whom it was said, “Her husband praised her”—that is, of our Lord and Savior, who at the end will command the angels to bring the Church, after the contest of this life and after the threshing and affliction of earthly things, into the joys of the heavenly kingdom and to join her to himself as a companion of immortal life, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Gather the wheat into my barn” (Matthew 13:30).

“Give,” he says, “to her from the fruit of her hands,” because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, moderation, self-control, faith, and patience. Repay her the reward owed her for this, “and let her works praise her in the gates”—that is, in the judgment or at the entrance into the heavenly homeland. It is not the empty favor of human beings, but the works themselves, examined, approved, and rewarded by him whose grace, by giving it, enabled her to perfect these things. May he mercifully grant that, so that we may deserve to be praised by him in the future, we may praise him with worthy services in the present life. Amen.

[Col. 1051]

# FRAGMENTS OF ALLEGORICAL INTERPRETATION ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON, FOUND IN AN ANCIENT CODEX (C,S)\*

## ON CHAPTER 7 OF THE PROVERBS

[Col. 1051D]

“And behold, a woman met him, dressed in a prostitute’s attire, prepared to ensnare souls, talkative and wandering, unable to remain quietly at home, nor able to keep her feet still in her house; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait beside the corners.”

Every heretic, lacking manly understanding, is rightly called a woman. Since he strives to produce polished speeches, it is clear that he adorns himself outwardly with a prostitute’s dress, because he attempts, through the brilliance of his speech, to accomplish what he cannot supply through the grace bestowed by the Holy Spirit.

If he should at some point find someone resisting his paths, he suddenly attempts to overcome him, more from his habitual talkativeness than from any clear strength of manly reasoning. He is recognized as wandering because one whom the spirit of error drags along knows nothing of the stability of a sound mind.

Or “wandering” may properly be understood in another sense: everyone who desires to turn aside from the line of truth plainly seeks out byways, avoiding them by different routes. He is wandering because he weaves the snares of different sects by which he may entangle the souls of the simple.

This woman is remembered as impatient of quiet because she transgresses the boundaries of the Fathers. Without restraint, she rushes headlong in impatience, not knowing what true rest is or how it is to be sought. She does not recognize ignorance concerning certain matters that surpass the clarity of the human mind. She cannot remain, as it were, at home with herself, but, driven forward by various passions, walks as though on feet through the winding paths of error.

There is also another house from which she goes forth to wicked acts, namely, the Church, although she may appear to dwell in it bodily. Therefore she lays ambush for those who conduct the affairs of worldly business; likewise, she stretches her discipline toward others whom the breadth of carnal life attracts; and then she persists in deceiving the rest who frequent the corners of a dark life.

Or, through the threefold location of the places, the threefold meaning of sacred Scripture may appropriately be understood. The heretic lies in wait outside when he attempts to deceive the hearts of the simple, whom the history of the letter nourishes, by perverting it. And when he traverses the breadth of allegory, he often extracts from it certain things that the multitude of the faithful declares to be contrary to the faith. When one comes to the forms of mortality, since they are joined together by different routes according to the diversity of mortals, he similarly makes a practice of striving to corrupt something there.

## ON CHAPTER 30 OF THE PROVERBS

“There are three things too difficult for me, and a fourth I utterly do not know: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, and the way of a man in his youth.”

By the term “eagle” any spiritual man is signified who, after the manner of that bird, strives to fix the sharpness of his eyes upon the heavenly sun. No one can discern his progress, because there is nothing bodily there from which anyone might have the possibility of following the eagle’s track with some aid. For the spiritual person judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one.

The sweetness of contemplation can indeed be felt, but it has no form that can be imitated. In the same way, the serpent’s path is known only to itself, which it customarily makes upon a rock. By the rock the firmness of the heart is signified; by the serpent’s movement, the suggestion of the evil spirit. At times the ancient serpent, by suggesting shameful things to the hearts of the elect, attempts to impress its own track upon them. Yet those who are founded upon the firm rock cannot be violated, nor do they know how to receive the venom of a destructive journey.

This matter is accessible to no one’s understanding, because no one can recognize how great is the strength of this rock unless he himself also becomes a rock. Or certainly he professes not to know the serpent’s path upon the rock because he utterly does not know whether a struggle has arisen for the purpose of testing or destroying the one whom the serpent encircles. And if that person should yield even briefly to the tempter, what mortal, I ask, could know it?

Likewise, no one can in any way read with human eyes the course of a ship dividing the waves of the sea after it has passed. What, then, is this ship except some preacher, by whose conveyance we are transferred to the harbor of eternal rest while storms rage all around upon the swelling sea? He traverses the paths of the raging sea while cutting through the waves of human hearts with the oar of preaching.

Who, then, could discern how far this sailor advances in the midst of the sea, so as to attempt afterward to carve out the traces of his preaching once it has run its course? You see him cutting through the swelling waves; you also sense him, with his sails suspended, making a prosperous journey as the favor of the Holy Spirit breathes upon him and follows him toward the minds of his hearers. Yet you cannot measure how effective he is in either respect.

Or the ship wandering over the waves marks out the mind of any human being, whose course—that is, the intention by which it is driven toward either side—you entirely do not know. You see it sailing with a favorable course; but whether it will suffer shipwreck amid the storms or be able to reach the harbor of calm, you remain ignorant. For just as successive tides of the sea cover over what had been cut through at the ship’s prow, so the line of human life’s steps is forbidden to erase the intention by which the soul is carried.

A fourth follows, which he says he utterly does not know. For who can contemplate a fixed goal for slippery youth, which, like gusts of wind, is turned aside elsewhere? Let us pass over the beginning of youth, whose fickleness is known to very many. But because its other phase is harmful and destructive, though this is divulged by few, Solomon strongly urges that it be guarded against, while he professes that he cannot know its perplexed path.

Every heretic, therefore, because of the fickleness of his mind, being carried about by every wind of doctrine, is not unjustly called a youth. He is also designated by the name “man,” because he has acquired a manly cleverness of intellect. His path is pressed on every side by so many and such great windings that, when you attempt to trace it, you can generally find no mark impressed upon it.

Examine the deeds of Mani, and especially the letter called *The Foundation*. There you will find a path scarcely traceable by anyone, worn by a monstrous foot with vigilant ingenuity. Solomon does not know this: whence such subtle expertise comes to one mortal, while dullness of mind clings to another, when both share in reason. No one is inferior to another with regard to the form of the divine nature, without whose light no one can see the hidden things of truth; and yet many secrets of the Scriptures are sometimes disclosed to heretics that are concealed from devout men.

There is also another interpretation, which can suitably be referred to the person of Christ.

Christ is called an eagle because of the manifold significance observed in that bird. As that bird protects its nest, so he protects his bride, namely, the Church. And just as it never approaches a foreign nest in order to produce offspring, so Christ does not beget offspring outside the bosom of the Church.

For this reason, immediately after birth it exposes its young to the rays of the blazing sun. If they do not look upon the brilliance of that star with unflinching light, they are immediately driven away from the nest as degenerate, separated from the others who resemble their father. This aptly corresponds to Christ, because all whom the light of true knowledge does not illumine, even if they have been begotten within the Church, are nevertheless expelled and separated from the fellowship of the elect.

That bird also carries serpents aloft into the air on the propulsion of its wings, devours them, and extinguishes all their venom by its natural heat. So Christ, returning to the Father after triumphing over the prince of death, destroyed the malice of the ancient serpent by the ineffable power of his divinity.

Solomon professed not to know its way, for who can speak of the goings forth and return of the only-begotten Son of God, who willed to become incarnate, to die, to be buried, to despoil the underworld, and afterward to ascend into heaven while his disciples looked on?

He himself is rightly called a rock, upon whose foundation our weakness is made firm. The crooked serpent attempted to impress its venomous tracks upon him; but he, like true adamant, did not receive even the mark of that slippery movement. Rather, completely blunting it, he declared: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

He had endured the step of the *chelydrus*—a venomous serpent—when it said to him: “If you are the Son of God, say that these stones should become loaves of bread” (ibid., 3). Who, I ask, could fully examine the serpent’s cunning and the strength of the most powerful rock?

He is called the ship; he is also called the helmsman, while the prow is commended to the Holy Spirit. In it the apostles sit like rowers, and in it we too, placed aboard, make our way toward the homeland. We sail securely by scorning the song of the Sirens; we are struck by the repeated blasts of temptations, but are roused only so that we may not grow sluggish through the torpor of idleness.

How we are carried across to the farther shore of this sea without the damage of shipwreck—while the barking of the Scyllaean dogs resounds and the danger of Charybdis threatens—who among human beings, I ask, would dare to investigate?

In fourth place he sets the way of a man, knowable to no one. Who is this man except the one of whom the Apostle says: “Until we all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13)?

For who can estimate how many good things he provided for the human race while he dwelt on earth—not only by helping bodies afflicted with manifold sickness, but, what is more useful, by healing their souls, as the singular physician? Who came to him suffering hunger of body or soul and returned unfed? Who went to him weighed down by the burden of crimes and departed lacking health?

What, then? His path is accessible to no one. These are the things Solomon could not penetrate. He saw these future things in the spirit; but the understanding of the figure is one thing, and knowledge of the foreknown reality another.

## ON THE SAME CHAPTER 30 OF THE PROVERBS

[Col. 1056A]

“By three things the earth is moved, and the fourth it cannot bear: by a servant when he reigns; by a fool when he is filled with food; by an odious woman when she is taken in marriage; and by a maidservant when she becomes heir to her mistress.”

At times the earth—that is, the heart enticed by earthly desires—is moved when it is bent toward consenting to sin. What causes this movement he indicates by saying: “By a servant when he reigns.”

A servant administers a royal scepter when some hired man usurps the pastoral chair. The earth that he himself moves, having lost the stability upon which it is founded—the fruitful earth that endures forever—follows him as one that is itself mobile. For what if one mobile thing imitates another mobile thing? The one fleeing follows the one leading the way.

He flees because he is a hired man, “and the sheep do not belong to him” (John 10:13). At the beginning, the movement moves those subject to it, either by the example of a wicked life, so that they cling to its movement.

Moreover, the earth is moved either toward an outpouring of the commission of crime or toward the weakening of faith, when a fool is acting as king; for he has been filled with food. What is the food of the faithful people except the living bread of sacred discourse? Hence David says: “You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me” (Psalm 22:5).

Now when a fool—namely, any heretic—frequents this table and gnaws at the loaves he sees placed there—for he lacks the strength of humility by which those loaves are broken for both little ones and great—he withdraws as though satisfied and attempts to forge other loaves.

Hence comes the saying: “Do not eat with an envious man, and do not desire his foods, for like a diviner and a soothsayer he estimates what he does not know. ‘Eat and drink,’ he says to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the foods you have eaten and lose your beautiful words” (Proverbs 23:6–7).

No one can doubt that these things entirely suit the behavior of heretics, unless he favors them. For what diviners or soothsayers do not know, they are accustomed, according to their practice, to give as oracles: attempting to assert either that the things being asked about are false, or that one ought to judge concerning them by conjecture rather than by the form of truth.

If you eat their foods, you must first vomit up the loaves of the Lord’s table, since, unless your mind rejects the bread of faith, it is clear that you cannot receive the loaves of error. These are the beautiful words, namely, the Lord’s loaves, which you will immediately lose once you swallow foods of this kind. For “what partnership has Christ with Belial?”

Who is this odious woman who is joined to a man by the law of marriage except a soul possessing withered acts, which is rightly represented under the name of the fragile sex? The man to whom she is married suitably signifies the governing faculty of the mind. Hence, speaking to the Samaritan woman, the Lord says: “You have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18).

Yet she is recognized as odious not to the one to whom she is joined, but to the wise, who detest carnal life. When, desiring a life of pleasure, she subjects reason and compels it to serve her seductions, she enters, as it were, into a marriage covenant with the man she most desires.

When she reigns, therefore, the earth is accustomed to be moved, because the mind’s perception, which is prepared like a field of the Lord to receive and bring to growth the seed of the divine word, if it is entrusted to be guarded by such a woman, immediately abandons its purpose and imitates the filthy embraces of that wicked woman.

The fourth follows, which the earth cannot bear: namely, a maidservant succeeding her mistress by hereditary right. What, then, is this maidservant except human flesh, which by the law of nature has become accustomed to obey the commands of the soul?

At times this maidservant becomes mistress, when the shameful heats of the pleasures cherished by the woman just mentioned are transferred into acts of the flesh. Now that mistress, living in delights, is dead, and the inheritance passes to the maidservant, which completes all the crimes that the former arranges.

If you entrust pastoral care to this maidservant, what mortal, I ask, could endure the extent of the calamity that would then befall the kingdom over which she is placed?

These are the monstrous plagues by whose rule the earth of the human heart is moved and unstable work is carried away. These are the people who do not know how to enter the city, and who block the way for the others who hasten there with panting breasts.

## ON THE SAME CHAPTER

“There are three things that proceed well, and a fourth that walks prosperously: a lion, strongest among beasts, which fears no one’s approach; a rooster with his loins girded; and a ram—and there is no king who can resist him.”

Here the lion is placed as the one of whom it is written: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). He is called the strongest among beasts because “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25). He fears no one’s approach, for he says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

The rooster with his loins girded signifies the holy preachers, who announce the true morning amid the darkness of this night. Their loins are girded because they restrain the flowing excesses of lust from their members. Lust is in the loins. Hence the Lord also says to them: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35).

“And a ram—and there is no king who can resist him.” Whom else can we understand here as the ram except the first order within the Church, the priests, of whom it is written: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28:1)? By their examples they draw the people who walk behind them, like a following flock of sheep.

No king at all is able to resist those who live spiritually and uprightly, because no persecutor, however he confronts them, can obstruct their purpose. For they know both to run anxiously toward the one they desire and to reach him by dying.

Thus the lion is placed first, the rooster second, and the ram third. Christ appeared first, then the holy preachers, the apostles, and finally the spiritual Fathers placed over the churches—leaders of the flocks, because they are guides of the peoples who follow.

But we confirm this still better if, by explaining the rest of the same passage, we add what follows. For because the Antichrist will appear after these things, he added this as the fourth, saying:

“There is one who appeared foolish after he was raised on high. If he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth.”

He will be raised on high when he falsely claims to be God. But, raised on high, he will appear foolish because in that very exaltation he will fail at the coming of the true Judge.

“If he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth”—that is, if he had foreseen his punishment when he began to grow proud, he would not, though once well created, have been raised up in such a display of arrogance.

What was said above—“the fourth that walks prosperously”—should not trouble us. He said that three proceed well, and the fourth prosperously. For not everything prosperous is good, nor in this life is everything good prosperous.

The lion, rooster, and ram proceed well, but not prosperously, because they suffer the battles of persecutions. The fourth proceeds prosperously but not well, because the Antichrist walks in his deceit; yet, for the brief period of the present life, that deceit prospers for him.

Thus it is said of him under the figure of Antiochus through Daniel: “Strength was given him against the continual sacrifice because of sins, and truth will be cast down to the ground; he will act and prosper” (Daniel 8:12). What Solomon calls “walking prosperously,” Daniel calls “prospering.”

## ON CHAPTER 31 OF THE PROVERBS

“Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest they drink and forget judgments and pervert the case of the children of the poor.”

“Lemuel,” in our language, means “in whom God is”; but his mother, who is said to have instructed him in this kind of vision, is divine wisdom. She therefore exhorts her son, in whom God dwelt through the sevenfold Spirit, not to offer wine to kings for drinking.

Who these kings are, from whom the drink of wine is entirely withheld, his father made clear to us when he said: “Now, therefore, understand, O kings; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10).

He would indeed be accused of giving wine to kings, by which the minds of those who drink are alienated, if he did not show how gravely the flattering concern of this world impedes the minds of those who have entangled themselves in earthly affairs.

Thus, if someone keeps silent about warnings of salvation and, as a result, a sick person who could have been healed incurs death, he is certainly considered to have struck the fatal blow.

“There is no secret,” he says, “where drunkenness reigns.” Although this may be understood of bodily wine—for no drunk person is master of himself, and therefore, like a clay vessel, he pours out everything—there is nevertheless another wine that is accompanied by no secret.

What, then, is represented in this passage by “secret” except some mystical wisdom, which plainly is not accessible to the lovers of this world? No secret of wisdom, therefore, is found where the reign of drunkenness is shown to exist. If you wish to investigate the hidden things of wisdom, make the insolent reign of drunkenness stand far away from you.

How great a calamity proceeds from this drink is proclaimed by the resulting forgetfulness of judgment and the perversion of the case concerning the children of the poor. The memory of the aforementioned kings is vigorous in discerning judgments to the extent that it is clearly removed from the heat of worldly anxieties. They are sober, therefore, insofar as they grow slack with regard to the allurements of the passing age.

Who is this poor one, whose children’s case those drunk on the Babylonian cup pervert, except the one who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9)? The case is perverted in judgment when an innocent person is punished by an unjust judge and a guilty person deserving punishment is granted impunity.

As for the fact that he uses the doubtful particle, saying, “lest they drink,” I think he wished to make known that the power of free choice is inclined toward either alternative, and he subtly indicates that it is especially liable to incline toward the worse if it is not held back by the bond of love or fear.
