Or by Lemuel, which, as we have already said, is interpreted as “in whom God is,” human reason, made in the image of God, is suitably designated. His mother, namely the grace of God, warns it not to give a harmful drink to the kings—that is, to the inner senses of the human being.

As long as these obey reason, they are rightly called kings, because the external actions of a person are ordered through them, accompanied by royal judgment. Whenever they draw into their interior the drink of fleeting happiness, they suddenly become deprived of the memory of discipline and, amid the darkness of a shameful affection that has arisen, cannot distinguish what must be avoided from what must be done.

Then they pervert the case of the poor man’s children when they change the works of the spirit—which ought to be poor in its consideration—from the recompense to come into a carnal affection. For the cause of our labor is the fervent, unfading love of rest.

Rejecting wine of this kind, Solomon compels his flesh to serve the spirit, so that with free movement he might turn his mind toward drinking in the instructional words of wisdom, so that grace might be added to his head and a necklace to his neck.

## ON CHAPTER 26 OF THE PROVERBS

[Col. 1059C]

“As one who throws a stone upon the heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool.”

Anyone educated in secular literature should know that, according to the error of the pagans, Mercury was the god of those who habitually devote themselves to exchanging merchandise. Since traders are almost all intensely occupied with gathering wealth, from which the fuel of avarice grows, it seems appropriate that, through the name of the chief deity, the name of the one who serves him should be signified.

Thus, by the name “Mercury,” any avaricious person is expressed. What, then, does it mean to throw a stone upon his heap? This must be considered.

It was the custom among the ancients that, if they found an avaricious person among their neighbors, they would immediately run to the public road, and each of them, carrying a stone, would gather a heap as a disgrace to the miser. Later, whenever a traveler saw the stone heap from a distance, he would, according to ancestral custom, take up a stone and throw it onto the heap.

Therefore, just as those people are considered foolish who devoted themselves more to collecting stones than to curing the miser’s disease, so without doubt those are called devoid of understanding who attempt to increase the number of fools—who are rightly called stones—by giving them honor.

Perhaps if assemblies of the people piled up a heap of divine testimonies against those who exalt fools, indeed men of stone, to the pastoral chair, and likewise against those who are unjustly promoted, they would grow numb for a while under the pressure of so great a plague.

For what? Do you suppose that one whom wisdom has not promoted can benefit others, when he has no knowledge at all of the rule of discipline and does not know the homeland to whose joys the people subject to him are invited?

“Certainly not,” you say.

## ON CHAPTER 18 OF THE BOOK OF WISDOM
When quiet silence held everything, and night had reached the midpoint of its course, your almighty Word, O Lord, leaping forth from heaven, from the royal seats, rushed down as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction: a sharp sword, bearing your undisguised command. Standing, he filled everything with death, and, while standing on earth, reached even to heaven.

Another translation has “midst of silence,” signifying the same thing as “quiet.” Even in the middle of the night, there is a quieter silence around the nation of God, where there is no hearer, although there may be someone who knows how to speak about God. Hence David says, “I was mute and humbled, and I was silent from good things, and my pain was renewed” (Psalm 38:3). The man of God is silent with the greatest sorrow; the wicked are silent in another way, despising the majesty of their Creator. The heart of the one is crushed by anguish, while the mind of the other is dissolved in foolish delight.

Another silence concerning God follows when there is a hearer but no preacher. Hence it is said through Jeremiah, “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4:4). We see this happening daily, since the wickedness of human life has prevailed to such an extent that no one doubts that this misery reigns both among those set over others and among their subjects.

Likewise, a “midst of silence” arises most deeply in the human heart when there are no people willing to apply their hearing or ears to preachers, and no teachers are present to open the word of God. Hence, through David, it is said, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 52:4). For when the only-begotten Son of God assumed our humanity, this error had not yet occupied the minds of mortals.

This silence, to be sure, did not hold everyone, but everything, because every creature except man praises its Maker by its own form. At that time, however, scarcely anyone knew how to contemplate the Creator’s praise in the beauty of the world’s structure. Consequently, not only man but also the other creatures observed the “midst of silence”: man because he disregarded the use of reason, and the inferior creation because no one knew how to refer its most fitting order to the Fashioner of all things. Thus night had reached the midpoint of its course.

What else is signified by the word “night” than ignorance of God? And what by “course” except perseverance in that same blindness? Night completes the midpoint of its course in its customary way when, never turning aside, it does not deviate from its purpose of wickedness. It was likewise the midpoint of the course because the aforesaid error was running commonly through all.

Then the Almighty leapt forth from heaven, from the royal seats, as a stern warrior. By “royal seats” are expressed the angelic powers in which the Lord sits. By saying that he leapt forth, he indicated his unexpected coming. He truly appeared as a stern warrior because he seized and bound the strong man who was guarding his courtyard in peace, plundered his spoils, deprived him of his ancient authority, despoiled hell, and returned victorious to the place from which he had come.

He came leaping into the midst of the land of destruction. What else was the human race than land transferred beyond the boundary of justice? To bring it back within the limit of mercy, the Father’s Word descended, so that he himself might cultivate it, sow its crops, and watch over it as it gave birth. Or, appropriately, he called the Jewish people the land of destruction—the people whom the boar from the forest destroyed.

A man from David’s seed according to the flesh came into their midst and appeared leaping forth. Or he approached the midst of the land of destruction when he proved that the human heart—called “the midst” for several reasons—was worthy of divine destruction. In this way the wicked sometimes return to the way of justice when it has first been demonstrated to them with manifest reason that destruction issuing in condemnation awaits them. For they cannot be restrained by the bond of heavenly love; rather, terrified by fear of Gehenna, they must be recalled to the worship of their Creator.

As soon as the Lord enters the land, the destruction of vices follows: darkness cannot endure light. A person sees where he lay and perceives the cords of sins by which he was dragged away and made an exile. May he himself also leap with powerful strength into our land, which lies beyond its boundary; may he drive away the hostile band that attempts, after its ancient fashion, to possess once more the dwelling place of our breast.

This Word is the sharp sword reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, the discerner of thoughts. What more is there to say? No creature is impenetrable before its edge. This is the sword by whose blow a son is separated from his father, a mother from her daughter, and—what is more difficult—a person from his own desires.

For the Son of God bears the Father’s undisguised command, since whatever the Father has, the Son also has. What is it to bear an undisguised command except to proclaim to human beings, with equal right, an order without pretense? He is the messenger of the Father’s will; he bears his command; he strikes, wounds, and heals; he raises up, crowns, and glorifies. “The Father judges no one,” for “he has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:22–23). Whoever detracts from one likewise detracts from the other. For Truth itself says, “Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

He bore the Father’s command when he remained obedient to him unto death (Philippians 2:8): “Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

Let us too bear his command, putting ourselves to death together with our vices and desires. Let us submit our stiff necks to his commands and take up his easy yoke, by which all burdens are shown to us to be exceedingly light. This is the sign that we are called his friends: that we obey his commands. For he himself says, “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

“And standing,” he says, “he filled everything with death.” When the Son of God put on our flesh, he appeared among human beings as if rising from the bed of the Law, in which he had long lain hidden. Finally, he filled everything with death by saying openly to all, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

He filled everything with death when, standing outside the contagion of every stain—being born a virgin from a virgin, pure from one who was pure—he asserted that the kingdom of heaven could be forfeited not only by deeds but also by thought. For he says, “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).

Who, then, is free from the dominion of death? Before he had stood, scarcely anyone knew this, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “I did not know sin except through the Law” (Romans 7:8). “I would not have known coveting unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

Or the Lord stood when, after triumphing over the prince of death, he rose from the dead. For as long as he endured the passions of human flesh, he lay, as it were, with us, as a participant in our corruption. But when he had risen, it was said of him, “Jesus stood on the shore,” although the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus (John 21:4).

Afterward, when the disciples had been sent to preach the Gospel to every creature, everything was filled with death: the soul was shown to be bound by original transgression, and the outer person was proved to be submerged in the enticements of the flesh. For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

“And reaching to heaven,” he says, “while standing on earth.” As a human being he was among us, while as God he ruled heaven. When he did what belongs to man, he stood on earth; but when he performed the works said to belong to divine power alone, he reached to the summit of heaven. Thus, governing all things, he both stood on earth and did not abandon heaven.

He likewise stood on earth when he turned earthly hearts toward the pursuit of his discipline. He stood in heaven when he asserted that those held entangled in earthly desires could ascend to fellowship with the citizens above. He clung to the heavens on high when he governed those whose manner of life was in heaven, lest they fall.

This is the Word full of truth, which contains solely the form of the Lord’s Incarnation.

This may also be interpreted morally. The first silence, I say, is the will to sin, while the opportunity to carry out the conceived evil does not at all present itself according to the desire of the wicked person. This indeed seems to flow from the overflowing mercy of the heavenly fountain, when the result of wickedness is withheld from the depraved mind, lest the person be punished more severely if he has not at some point repented of his criminal desire.

There is also another silence, which the mind of a wicked person preserves when, while the sanctions of both Laws are set before it, it deliberately decides to sin but is restrained solely by fear of punishment.

The “midst of silence,” however, is that which is more serious and more abominable than the others: when a person wishes to sin and is able to fulfill what he wickedly desires, yet neither through fear of divine regard nor through reverence for human beings does he cease from doing what he has impiously resolved to do.

## ON CHAPTER 38 OF ECCLESIASTICUS

When a certain wise man was praising craftsmen according to the quality of their works, he added the work of the potter, saying:

“Thus the potter sits at his work, turning the wheel with his feet. He is always occupied because of his work, and all his work is counted. With his arm he forms the clay, and before his feet he bends his strength. He will give his heart to complete the smoothing, and vigilance will cleanse the furnace.”

Afterward, taking up the craftsmen whose preeminence he had described, he says:

“Without all these a city is not built, nor will they inhabit it, nor walk about in it, nor leap into the assembly.”

Do you think it could be doubted that a city cannot be built without the potter’s work? “Who,” you ask, “unless insane, would think that?” It follows, then, that the significance of this craftsman, like that of the others whom he discusses in the same passage, must be understood in a mystical sense.

The potter sits at his work when any teacher of the Church attempts to shape minds occupied with earthly affairs, so that they may become vessels to be assigned not to dishonor but to honor. He turns the wheel with his feet when, through evident works, he joins the hearts of his subjects to his own will.

For what is the revolving nature of the human heart except a wheel set in motion? Nothing can turn it more suitably or swiftly according to one’s direction than the example of a religious life, so that the earthly mind, gradually shaped and thoroughly refined by the torches of heavenly love, may advance into a vessel of election.

The activity of the potter is unknown among the multitude of human beings, because no one can know how much fruit he has poured into the hearts of his hearers. He forms clay with his arm when, through the example of his labors, he invites an earthly heart to become what he himself is.

Furthermore, his strength bends before his feet when his teaching is said to correspond to his works. His strength likewise bends before his feet when the work is distributed according to the strength of his spirit; or because the state of the soul rests upon humility alone—for anyone is strong enough to be founded upon it. Alternatively, the craftsman places strength before his feet when intention does not turn aside from works, or when he places works before strength, as though submitting strength beneath his feet.

After this, he applies himself to completing the smoothing. For what else is smoothing than the completion of a vessel? Indeed, when a human being becomes heavenly, having cast off the contagion of the first parent, the form of the completed smoothing shines forth in him.

Finally, vigilant watchfulness is exceedingly necessary to him, so that he may be able to cleanse the furnace in which the vessel is fired. After the work of preaching has been completed, the preacher still has the labor of vigils, so that, if any dirt has clung to him, he may wipe it away with a diligent hand.

What, then, is the furnace kindled by a heavenly bellows except the pastor’s mind, which is burned over the destruction of its members? It must therefore be cleansed, since you will rarely find anyone carrying out the office of preaching whom either the favorable breeze of approval has not struck, or the harshness of judgment has not rebuked, or more lenient correction has not scourged. Hence one must necessarily keep watch in the administration of preaching.

Likewise, when the task has been completed, the work of careful examination must be applied, lest anything remain hidden and mixed in that might obscure the reward of strenuous labor.

## ON CHAPTER 8 OF WISDOM

“Wisdom reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly.”

What are these ends, and what is the middle between the two that this Wisdom encompasses? We know from the account of Scripture (Genesis 1) that, after the world’s structure had been distributed into its proper forms over the number six, supreme Wisdom rested on the seventh day from all the work it had performed.

This is the first end, namely, the completion of perishable things. The other follows when there will be a new heaven and a new earth. Thus Wisdom reaches from the end at which all things revolving beneath the sun are said to have been completed to the end at which they will pass away.

The Wisdom under discussion reaches mightily when each thing, just as it was created, does not transgress the boundary assigned to its nature, by which it subsists; when, master of its own right, it does not desire what belongs to another, preserving the beauty of the most beautiful order.

This same Wisdom orders everything sweetly because it has bestowed upon the individual forms of things the law of the sweetest tranquility. For, being itself sweet, it could create nothing harsh or unpleasant. This is the lofty depth that no one can behold or penetrate.

In the human soul, three powers of nature are recognized as active. There is the rational, the desirous, and the irascible power. In discerning what is good or evil, it uses the aid of reason. Since, however, by the command of nature it desires what is better than anything else, no one doubts that it possesses desire flowing from the source of reason. Hence the saying, “Desire, like newborn infants, the rational milk.”

First, because it is indignant against guilt, it is naturally said to possess a movement of salutary anger. Hence David says to sinners, “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). It is as though he were saying: “Because, in despising reason, you have rejected salutary desire and anger, which punishes excesses, be angry with yourselves. By becoming angry, drive from the cavern of your heart what you have introduced by taking wicked delight in it. Then beware lest you fall into the same ruin again, attending to what the Lord says in the Gospel to a certain person: ‘Go, and sin no more’” (John 8:11).

Finally, let us carefully investigate what the two things are that resist the three powers mentioned above. There is no doubt that carnal desire resists spiritual desire, while carnal anger, opposing justice, conversely resists the other anger, which is inseparably the companion of justice.

These are rightly said to inhabit one house, because such an internal quarrel takes place within the dwelling of the inner person. What the evangelist Luke divided according to the number five, the Apostle Paul here certainly comprehended under the number two, when he says, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17).

## ON CHAPTER 8 OF PROVERBS

“Not yet were the abysses, and I was already conceived; the springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood firm with their massive weight.”

By the name “abysses” are appropriately expressed the hidden mysteries brought forth by the prophetic mouth. The hearts of the saints, from which many-branched streams flow to water the flock entrusted to them, are suitably signified by “springs.”

But what are these mountains except the company of martyrs, whom the love of the Holy Spirit draws with greater weight toward God, so that neither threats, nor the allurements of the world, nor the carefully devised cruelty of tortures, nor even burning plates of iron raking through their innermost organs can overcome them? Hence David says, “In a weighty people I will praise you” (Psalm 34:18).

## A JUDGMENT ON SOLOMON

Solomon, a man of such great wisdom—can it be believed that he thought there was any usefulness in the worship of idols? No. But he was unable to resist the love of women that was drawing him toward this evil, doing what he knew ought not to be done so as not to grieve the women whose charms he passionately loved.

Although Solomon had sinned, he nevertheless performed penance, writing Proverbs, in which he says, “At last I did penance, and I considered where I should choose discipline.”

That remarkable Solomon, who deserved to be joined to the Wisdom of God as its attendant, fell into the embraces of foreign women. Ensnared in the bond of lust, he polluted himself by the error of sacrilege when he fashioned an idol of Chemosh, the god of the Moabites.

But since afterward he acknowledged his fault through a prophet, was he therefore deprived of heavenly medicine? Or perhaps I never read in the Canon that he repented or obtained forgiveness? Hear his penance, which is not recorded in public laws. Perhaps I shall say something acceptable precisely because he repented not before the face of the people but in the secrecy of his conscience, with God as witness.

He obtained forgiveness on this account: when he had been released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of kings who had pleased God. Yet we know that this had been denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained in the perversity they had adopted until death. Therefore, because he deserved to be buried among righteous kings, he was not excluded from forgiveness; but he could not have obtained that forgiveness without penance.

The books of the Hebrews say that Solomon was dragged five times through the streets of Jerusalem as an act of penance. They also say that he came into the temple he himself had built with five rods [and] four experts in the Law, so that he might be beaten by them. They, however, agreed in common counsel that they would not lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed; consequently, frustrated by them, he was deposed by himself from the kingdom.

“Since,” he says, “you see elephants subjected to you and lions made subject, know yourself, O man.” This saying is not, as they report, by the Pythian Apollo, but by the holy Solomon, who says, “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women.”

Nor shall we be surprised that, in the opposing category, the worst kings precede rulers as a type of transgressors, since we teach that the best kings—David, Solomon, and Josiah—and the patriarchs and prophets preceded as figures of the Lord Savior.

[Column 1065]

## ALLEGORICAL EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS (C, S)

### BOOK ONE

## ON THE GRACE OF GOD, AGAINST JULIAN

[Column 1065C] As I am about to write, with the help of heavenly grace, on the Song of Songs, I thought the reader should first be warned to read with the greatest caution the little works of Julian, the bishop Celanensis of Campania, which he composed on this same book, lest, through the abundance of his flattering eloquence, he fall into the pit of harmful doctrine.

But, as the saying goes, let him pick the grape in such a way that he also avoids the thorn—that is, let him search out and select sound meanings in Julian’s statements, so that he may no less avoid the unsound ones. Or rather, let him do what Maro says:

> You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground,  
> Flee from here, boys; a cold snake lies hidden in the grass.

That is, let him restrain himself entirely from reading Julian, since there are authors who have expounded the same book both with sound meanings and in simpler words.

For Julian is, as a most skilled rhetorician, so fierce an opponent of the grace of God after Pelagius that his writings show this even more openly—those writings in which, against the most vigorous champion of that same grace, Augustine, he raged irrationally. For the sake of this quarrel, he first composed a little book *On Love*, under the pretext that he wished to remove love from the most shameful pleasure, but in reality to confirm his own heresy.

In brief, to compress several points into one, he teaches that by the freedom of our will we can do the good things we wish, although we may accomplish them more easily with the help of God’s grace. He compares this to travelers who can indeed complete a journey on foot but, undoubtedly, with less effort when horses are available to carry them.

Thus he forgets the Apostle’s admonition: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (1 Corinthians 2).

And, what is more serious, he opposes the one who did not say, “Without me you can do a little,” but rather, “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15).

He teaches that only those whom both learning and piety have made clear-sighted and educated can behold the mysteries concealed in the Law. He has forgotten the grace of God, which has revealed the secrets of Scripture even to the uneducated and ordinary, as the Evangelist says: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

The same Evangelist testifies that these men were uneducated when he says: “When they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they were astonished” (Acts 4).

Julian says that a holy and noble love, implanted in us from the very beginning of life by nature’s inclination, persists with the mind’s own powers, without any loss of its original vigor, right into extreme old age. He is plainly incredulous toward the Lord’s statement, “Without me you can do nothing,” and also toward the Apostle’s words, “We all offend God in many things” (James 3).

It is remarkable where Julian learned that a holy and noble love was implanted in us from the beginning of life by nature’s inclination, when the blessed Apostle, born from the stock of the patriarchs, says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2).

How was this “by nature,” except that, when the first man sinned and abandoned holy love, vice grew in place of nature?

It is remarkable where Julian found—or thought that he could find—even a single human being in whom holy love, relying solely on the powers of the mind, persisted into old age without loss of its vigor. Yet he who, because of his preeminent love, was worthy to recline in the bosom of his Creator found no such person among those who enjoy God’s grace. Rather, he testified through a humble confession: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Julian says that our love, just as it derives from the body in being disturbed and impetuous, derives from the mind in being lofty and continuous. Both claims, however, are shown to be contrary to the truth.

If our love derived from the body rather than from the mind in being disturbed and impetuous, the Lord would not say: “For from within, from the heart of human beings, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, greed, wickedness, deceit, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness. All these evils proceed from within and defile a person” (Mark 7).

Again, if our love possessed its loftiness and continuity not from God’s daily grace but from nature or the powers of the mind, the Apostle would not say of his holy labors, to which he devoted himself with lofty and continuous love: “I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15).

And again: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; rather, our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3).

But even if he possessed his good works—not from the Lord but from himself—in which, without any contradiction, lofty and continuous love holds the citadel, he would have thanked the Lord in vain for things the Lord had not given him, saying: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 2).

Julian says that, so long as our love desires nothing from the will of the gentiles, it is moved as though solely by the mind’s choice and possesses delight in its actions: free from disturbance and rejoicing in liberty.

To say this openly is to claim that, except for what pertains to the goadings of the flesh, it lies within the choice of our mind how much it submits itself to love; and that love itself, directed solely by the movement of the mind—that is, without being acted upon by any grace of God—possesses the perfection of good works, freely and subject to no disturbance. Everyone who is wise plainly understands how far this is from the truth.

Why does so great a multitude of the faithful, seeking to love the Creator with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength, and each one seeking to love his neighbor as himself, not always obtain what it desires? It is because love is not moved solely by the mind’s choice, as Julian thought. Rather, as Paul knew, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5). Therefore it is not equal in everyone, because each of us has gifts of grace that have been given differently.

Why are we so often hindered by adversities arising not only from outside but also from the mind itself, and why are we unable to accomplish everything good that we desire? It is because the person is deceived who says that our love, by the sole choice of the mind, possesses in its actions delight free from disturbance and rejoicing in liberty.

The Psalmist sings the truth when he says: “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he greatly desires his way. When the righteous person falls, he will not be shaken, because the Lord supports his hand” (Psalm 36).

Here he plainly indicates that we cannot be free from the disturbance of vices even amid the frequent aids of the Lord’s protection, nor should we rejoice in all the steps of our actions because of nature’s liberty, but because of divine direction.

Julian vainly wishes genital pleasure to be excepted as the only thing that is not moved according to the choice of our mind—as though the fury of anger, pride, avarice (*philargyria*), gluttony (*gastrimargia*), vainglory (*cenodoxia*), and other such passions were not conquered with far greater labor than the incentives of lust.

These passions arrive to disturb our mind even before the time of puberty, and, although lust has often been subdued or has ceased through nature, they nevertheless do not stop attacking us.

Julian says that the assistance of the Holy Spirit is given—and continues to be given—in response to our prior efforts and merits, so that we may love the human race more deeply. It is useful to set down his words in order:

> “When, therefore,” he says, “the wise mind, which subjects pleasure to the dignity of love, both stirs and orders desire, it never oversteps the limits of duty, but through efforts and merits advances toward such greatness and beauty that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins to fan its noble fire. Then that love comes into being which attempts to embrace not only relatives or fellow citizens but the human race itself in its embrace.”

A Catholic reader can easily observe how many and how great the blasphemies contained in this one sentence are.

For it is clear what he attributes to the freedom of human choice and what to spiritual grace. He testifies that the human mind can become wise by itself, possess by itself the dignity of holy and noble love, subject the pleasure of the flesh to this love by itself, and by itself both stir itself toward the virtues and order desire.

He says that the mind itself advances through its efforts and merits toward such greatness and beauty that it becomes worthy of the Holy Spirit’s assistance. When that Spirit comes, he does not say that the mind is helped as a darkened house is helped by a flame or torch when it is kindled and illuminates the house. Rather, he says that it is helped as wind helps a burning or shining fire, so that it may shine more brightly.

The fire, indeed, could be kindled, burn, and consume a great forest even without the wind’s breath; yet, driven by the wind, it becomes more and more aflame. This is what he signifies by saying that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins to fan its noble fire.

Julian had placed such great goods of the mind before the Spirit’s arrival, and after all this he says that the grace of the Holy Spirit begins in it—as though grace were an assisting force arriving afterward, rather than an inspiring power that comes beforehand and is the author within us of good efforts and merits.

Observe, however, what he believes is accomplished in the noble fire of the wise mind by that fanning:

> “Then,” he says, “that love comes into being which attempts to embrace not only relatives or fellow citizens but the human race itself in its embrace.”

You see, therefore, since he attributes so much power to our mind, what he attributes to the Spirit of grace: he says that the Spirit comes late to assist the mind itself and then infuses into it not that love by which God is loved, but only that by which the human race is loved.

He has forgotten—or is unconcerned about—the apostolic faith, which says, “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

It would be a lengthy task to bring forward all the absurdities that Julian put into this book and refute them with testimonies of the truth. Let these few examples suffice; from them one may infer how detestable the others are.

After these and countless similar arguments, with which he completed his first book by disputing against the grace of God, he polluted the second book with the same plague of heresy.

Finally, in explaining the statement, “Your breasts are better than wine,” he philosophized most shamefully about the nature of milk and soon attempted, even more shamefully, to transfer the quality of that nature to confirmation of his error. Since setting the whole passage down would be both horrifying and excessively long, we have thought it sufficient to include a part.

Accordingly, assuming the role of those against whom he was fighting under the name of Manichaeans, he says, among other things:

> “For he asserted that our opinions were driven to such a point by the foaming waves of error that we turned our accusation against the author himself; and, to lessen the guilt with which the crimes of the will were evidently burning us, we subjected the very nature of the body to disgrace, swearing that we came into this world incapable of goodness and full of iniquity. Finally, that scarcely anyone could be led to justice—not, I say, by reason, but not even by the instruction of the sacred Law. This opinion was indeed disparaging to the nature of flesh and blood. But after the mediator of God and human beings took up the saving mystery, so that he might assume the nature of mortal man in order to give an example of consummate virtue, he showed that all crimes arose from conduct, not from seed. Finally, when the wills had been turned toward better things, he showed that not only the precepts of the Law but also those of the Gospel could be fulfilled.”

These words of his must be answered briefly. We do not at all turn an accusation against the author of our nature when we say that we were conceived in iniquities and born in transgressions. Rather, we confess that in the first parents of our nature we were made in his likeness, so that, immortal and without sin, we might live in the delights of paradise with the help of his grace.

If those first parents had taken care to preserve that most blessed purity of primitive life, and had not trusted the enemy more than the Creator, their holy and undefiled descendants would still inhabit the delights of paradise, knowing neither death nor sin.

But when, without any necessity imposed by nature and solely through the carelessness of a wandering mind, they consented to sin, and were immediately excluded by the just judgment of the Creator from the place of paradise’s delight and punished with death for the sin they had rashly contracted, they left its contagion to their stock and race.

Thus it happened that we too, though unwilling, were bound by the guilt of the sin they had voluntarily committed, so that not even infants—who can will nothing good or evil—can be free from it, unless by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Thus Julian is proved to be mistaken when he says, “Guilt was kindled in us solely by the crime of the will.” Later he explained his meaning more openly, saying, “All crimes arise from conduct, not from seed. For what we have received from Adam as original belongs to seed; but what belongs to conduct, or to will, weakness, and ignorance, is the sin that we ourselves add.”

He is proved to be mistaken when he criticizes those who bring disgrace upon the nature of our body—not the nature in which the first parent was created holy and immortal, but the nature that became corrupt after their transgression—by saying, “I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7).

And likewise what the same Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, but the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5).

These things so oppose one another that you do not do what you wish. He is shown to be mistaken when he censures those who assert that we come into this light incapable of goodness and full of iniquity. For we truly confess that all human beings come into this light full of iniquity, bearing the guilt of the first transgression; but that we are born incapable of goodness—far be it from us to swear this. The heretic, however, in order craftily to deceive the weak, joined the truth of Catholic confession to the falsehood of his impiety.

He is shown to be mistaken when he says that we swear no one can be led to righteousness not only by reason, but not even by the teaching of sacred law. On the contrary, we confess that by both reason and the teaching of holy law we are led to righteousness, with the Lord’s help; but without his grace we cannot be justified either by the resources of natural reason or by the prescriptions of divine law, as the Apostle testifies: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3)—that is, the letter, when it commands, kills if the Spirit is not present to grant that the commands of the letter be fulfilled. And the Spirit gives life by granting that what the letter commands may be accomplished.

But when he says of the Lord, “So that, in order to provide an example of consummate virtue, he might assume mortal human nature,” he more secretly vomited forth the poison of his heresy, because he says that “the Lord, coming in the flesh, bestowed upon us not gifts but examples of virtue.” Hence shortly afterward he says: “By assuming flesh, then, he condemned the sins of conduct—not, of course, by changing the nature of the flesh, but by changing its works, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us according to his example.”

Likewise, in his exposition of the verse “Your neck is like necklaces”: “When,” he says, “a beautiful neck is adorned by nature with the ornament of gems, skill undoubtedly increases its happiness; and, as though they were worthy of one another, the honor of the necklaces and the beauty of the neck come together.” Thus also in you, whose nobility instruction shapes, so that the virtues which nature begins, discipline may complete. He should have said instead: “Grace begins, grace completes, grace crowns.”

Likewise, after countless passages of this kind, which a devout reader will very easily detect in his own little works, in explaining the verse “I will take hold of you and bring you into the house of my mother; there you will teach me,” he more openly disclosed what he insanely thought against the faith, saying of the Lord:

“Already in infancy he showed many things that we ought to learn. First, that he himself is the maker of all those born from the union of male and female, since, without the agency of a man, he fashioned a body for himself from a virgin; next, that no sin is innate in human beings, since he, although clothed in the reality of flesh, existed free from every stain; finally, that our origin cannot, except impiously, be attributed to the works of the devil, since it would rejoice in the true God not only as its creator but also as its indweller.”

By saying these things he not only constructs his error, but also advances it through this very example. Scripture testifies that sin is innate in human beings, for it says: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial, into the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). Indeed, blessed Job testifies that this condition is coeval with human beings from conception itself, when, pleading with the Lord, he says: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?” (Job 14).

What consequence can there be, then, in saying that no sin is innate in those born from the union of male and female because the Son of God, without the agency of a man, fashioned a body for himself from a virgin, and, clothed in the reality of flesh, existed free from stain? What logical connection is there in a human being establishing the innocence of his birth by the example of the Mediator of God and human beings born in the flesh, when the archangel said of his birth to the virgin mother: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1)?

But to our mother after the guilt of transgression the just Judge said: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in pain you will bear children, and you will be under the power of your husband” (Gen. 3). Nor did he make this other claim—namely, that our origin cannot, except impiously, be attributed to the devil’s works, since it would rejoice in the true God not only as creator but also as indweller—either Catholic or logically consistent. For although the devil inflicted sin upon the first parents, he nevertheless did not take from them the natural course of the blessing they had heard: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1).

We are therefore not deceived by that impiety which Julian reproaches us with, as though we attributed our origin to the works of the devil; we know that our origin was created by God through the work of the primordial blessing. But far be it from us to say that, after the evil of transgression and before the remedy of the second regeneration, which takes place through water and the Holy Spirit by the gift of God’s grace through Jesus Christ our Lord, our origin rejoiced in God.

We have thought it necessary to note these few passages from the aforesaid work of Julian, selected from many others, as a warning to readers, so that, instructed by these examples, they may look more vigilantly through the remainder of his reading, in which he often inserts statements that are no less harmful among salutary teachings. For in other little works as well, despite the vigorous opposition of the most holy and learned bishop Augustine, he does not hesitate to affirm the same heresy of his.

Finally, in the book he wrote On the Good of Perseverance, he defends, as he himself maintains, the goodness of nature and the freedom of our will with great determination against the impiety of Mani. But, as truth demonstrates, he persists with great obstinacy against faith in heavenly grace.

“For this,” he says, “is perseverance, which chiefly asserts the power of free choice, its goodness, and the freedom of its nature and of the movements of the human mind, while it shows that every good of the mind is voluntary and never subject to any chance. But that I have free movements neither of the flesh nor even of the mind is taught me not merely by apostolic writing but also by my own thoughts. These thoughts, when I am willing and striving—as I say nothing of other matters—do not allow me, with fixed mind and tireless desire, to devote myself to the practice of prayer. If I had free movements of the mind, I would wish to keep my mind intent upon prayers throughout the entire time of prayer, just as I can most easily arrange the members of my body whenever I wish, in whatever posture or place of prayer.”

And shortly afterward:

“For it arms,” he says, “and kindles the excellent mind of each person, while it continually reminds him of his freedom and drives away from him every fear.”

How much better would he have defeated Mani if he had said: “The grace of God has made the mind of each of his elect excellent and has kindled it toward the pursuit of virtues, while continually reminding it of its weakness and of the fact that without grace it can do nothing; and while driving from it all confidence in its own virtue, it persuades it to sing to God: ‘I will guard my strength toward you’” (Ps. 58).

And again, after much in which he praises the freedom of our will, he says:

“For, as the most learned and orthodox have brilliantly argued, no one can ever truly be harmed except by himself; nor is there anything at all by which anyone can be made miserable against his will. What, then, will virtue fear except its own failure, by which a human being is harmed forever?”

This opinion cannot stand anywhere except among heretics, because it is plainly established that Adam’s sin harms all human beings—not by themselves, certainly, but by him who, through the guilt of the first crime, condemned the whole human race perpetually, except those whom Christ’s grace sets free.

The malice of heretics harms those whom it drags unknowingly and unwillingly to destruction, even though they desire to know and hold the Catholic faith. But Julian feared that, if in so large a volume he attributed everything by which we might live rightly to the freedom of our will, he would be detested and anathematized by everyone as an open enemy of God’s grace. Therefore he also mentioned grace at this point, but so covertly that he did not say that it gives all virtues, but only that it assists and strengthens perseverance in us.

“For it belongs to divine grace,” he says, “to love and strengthen perseverance, so that it may guard the other virtues and defend virtue against everything that resists it.”

Here too he used a very cautious word: he did not say that grace gives perseverance, as though we had not possessed it previously, but rather that it assists and strengthens it, as though perseverance had already arisen from us—just as the wind helps a flame of fire, which it did not itself kindle but which was kindled elsewhere, so that it may burn more brightly; and, lest it be extinguished, strengthens it by blowing. As we have shown, he made his meaning clearer at greater length in his book On Love.

Near the end of this little book Julian himself openly reveals the intention with which he labored throughout the little works he examined in making such assertions.

“Mani is scandalized,” he says, “because we confess what is fabricated”—that is, while denying our true Lord. “He is offended because we assert that nature is good and that the human being has free choice.”

But in the book he wrote for Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, On the Institution of a Virgin, he also discloses what he thinks about the power of free choice. Some of our people, reading this book attentively, rashly believe it to be by the holy and Catholic teacher Jerome, failing entirely to perceive that both the sweetness of its beguiling eloquence and the perversity of its seductive heresy plainly prove that this little work is not his. Rather, in the Dialogue of Atticus and Critobulus, which he published while Pelagius was still alive, when Julian was still being nourished by him as a little boy, like a royal serpent in its cave, Jerome himself had already attacked and crushed Pelagius’s faith—or rather, his impiety—with divine utterances.

In this book, therefore, and in other little works, Julian declares that he has confirmed the same heresy of his, writing:

“Whenever I have to speak about the formation of character and the conduct of a holy life, I usually first display the power and quality of human nature and show what it can accomplish.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, since I have followed this order of exhortation in other little works as well, I think it must be observed above all here, where the goodness of nature ought to be declared more fully, in proportion as the life to be formed is more perfect.”

Likewise, in the course of the same book:

“For how many philosophers,” he says, “have we both heard of and read about, and have ourselves seen, who were chaste, patient, modest, generous, abstinent, kind, rejecting at once the honors and pleasures of the world, and lovers of justice no less than of wisdom? From where, I ask, did people alienated from God obtain these things that please God? From where did they obtain these good qualities, unless from the goodness of nature? And since we see that they possess either all the qualities I have mentioned together, or one person possesses one and another another, and since all share one nature, they show by their example that everything can exist in everyone which is found individually in individuals. If people thus show, even without God, what they were made by God to be, consider what Christians can accomplish, whose nature has been restored for the better in Christ and who are helped by the aid of divine grace.”

And after much of this kind, speaking of blessed Job:

“O man,” he says, “evangelical before the Gospels, and a disciple before the apostles’ commands! By opening the hidden riches of nature and bringing forth from himself what we all could accomplish, he showed this to everyone.”

Again, shortly afterward:

“We do not defend the goodness of nature,” he says, “in such a way as to say that it cannot do evil; indeed, we also confess that it is capable of good and evil. But we vindicate it from this one injustice: that we should appear to be driven to evil by its fault, since we do neither good without the will nor evil, and since it is free always to do one, although we are always capable of both. For why are some to judge and others to be judged, unless it is because within the same nature there is unequal will, and because, although we are all capable of the same things, we do different things?”

And shortly afterward, recalling that Adam was expelled from paradise and Enoch carried away from the world, he added:

“For neither would the one have deserved punishment nor the other election from a just God, unless each had been capable of both. The same is to be understood of the brothers Cain and Abel, and also of the twins Esau and Jacob; and it must be recognized that will alone is the cause when, in the same nature, merits are different.”

And again, shortly afterward:

“Nor is any other cause responsible for the difficulty we too experience in living well than the long habit of vices. When it infects us from childhood and gradually corrupts us over many years, it afterward holds us bound and enslaved to it, so that it appears to possess a kind of force of nature.”

Likewise, after much in which he admirably instructs a virgin dedicated to God—and he truly would have completed a very useful and salutary work if he had taught her to implore divine grace for assistance in everything, rather than trust in the freedom and strength of her own mind—just as, in the book we mentioned that he wrote On the Good of Perseverance, he would have greatly benefited those devoted to virtue if he had not interspersed poisonous errors.

But if “a little leaven,” as the Apostle testifies, “corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5), how much more does the greatest quantity of poison?

“We attribute iniquity to the just and cruelty to the pious,” he says, “when we complain that he first commanded something impossible. Accordingly, we think that a human being is condemned by him for things he could not avoid.”

And shortly afterward:

“He who is just could not command anything impossible; nor will he who is pious condemn a human being for things he could not avoid.”

In each of these individual statements, which I have excerpted from one of his little books, the multitude of errors is readily apparent to every learned person. I have therefore gathered so many of them together in order that those who maintain that this book was written by the Catholic blessed Jerome’s pen might be convicted by the larger number of proofs of error, and might consequently become more cautious in reading one whom they have learned to be a heretic.

I have also thought it useful to respond briefly to all these statements together, since, as I have said, their wickedness may thereby become clearer to everyone. When he therefore says that “many philosophers possess patience, chastity, modesty, and other virtues from the goodness of nature,” it is established that whichever philosophers did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, could possess no true virtue and no true wisdom. Whatever taste of wisdom or image of virtue they possessed, they received wholly from above—not only as a gift of their first creation, but also through the daily grace of the one who does not abandon his creature, and who, without abandoning it, bestows his gifts upon human beings as he judges—great gifts upon the great and small gifts upon the small.

But when he says that “everything can exist in everyone which is found individually in individuals,” he contradicts Scripture, which says: “For not everything can exist in everyone, since the Son of Man is not immortal.” This plainly suggests that only when this mortal nature has put on immortality can all the good qualities of the virtues exist in everyone; and even then they will exist not through the goodness of nature, but through the grace of him of whom it is written: “That God may be all in all.”

Our daily proofs of weakness also demonstrate that everything cannot exist in everyone, since so many are found who, despite striving with the greatest effort, can never attain the virtues they see others possess.

When he says that human beings without God show what they were made by God to be, he is so far from the truth that not even people close to God can show, in this life at least, what they were made to be by the first parent. For who could be greater in wisdom or life than the one who, before paying the debt of the flesh, was caught up into paradise—or into the recesses of the third heaven—and contemplated the way of life of the heavenly citizens and heard their conversations? Yet he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner human being, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7). It is clear that the parents of the human race, as long as they preserved the goodness of nature undefiled, could not have said this.

When he says that the nature of Christians has been more fully restored through Christ and that they are helped by the aid of divine grace, if he wishes this to be understood only of what has been granted to us in the forgiveness of sins through baptism, it is heretical; but if it refers also to his daily grace, by which he never ceases to restore and assist us in mind and body, it is Catholic.

When he says that blessed Job opened the hidden riches of nature through his outstanding virtues and showed from himself what we all could accomplish, how much better would he have said that Job opened the ineffable riches of divine grace and showed in himself that it could grant these things to all whomsoever it wished?

When he says that we are not driven to evil by a fault of nature, since we do neither good without the will nor evil, he contradicts the Apostle, who says: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For the willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishment of good. For I do not do the good that I want; rather, I do the evil that I do not want” (ibid.).

When he says that it is free for us always to do one thing, although we are always capable of both, he contradicts the prophet, who speaks to God in supplication: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps” (Tobit). He also makes himself greater than the Apostle, who said: “I myself, with my mind, serve the law of God; but with my flesh, the law of sin” (Rom. 7).

When he says that the reason some judge and others are judged is only that within the same nature there is unequal will, and that, although we are all capable of the same things, we do different things, he contradicts the Catholic faith, which also confesses that infants are to be judged—those who, placed in the same nature, were taken away without baptism before they could do or will, or even know, anything good or evil.

When he says that Esau and Jacob and others of the same kind were distinguished solely by will, so that they had different merits in the same nature, he contradicts the Apostle, who, speaking of them, says: “For when they had not yet been born or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works, but from the one who calls—it was said to him: ‘The elder shall serve the younger’; as it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. 9).

When he says that no other cause makes it difficult for us to live well than the long habit of vices, he contradicts Scripture, which says: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb” (Ecclus. 40).

When he says that the Lord, because he is just, commanded nothing impossible, he speaks truly if he is referring to the help of the one to whom the Catholic voice pleads: “Lead me in the path of your commandments” (Ps. 118). But if he trusts in the powers of his own mind, he is refuted by the truthful statement of that same just Creator, who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 13).

When he says that the one who is pious will not condemn a human being for what he could not avoid, he contradicts the judgment of that same pious Redeemer and just Judge, who says even concerning infants: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). Nevertheless, as Saint Augustine says, “the punishment or condemnation of all who, besides the sin they inherited originally, added no further sin will certainly be exceedingly mild.” Yet such people cannot be wholly exempt from condemnation, since the Apostle plainly says that “death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin” (Rom. 5).

And as though someone might ask why it reigned over all who had not sinned, he immediately gives the reason, adding: “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (ibid.)—that is, not on account of their own sins, but because Adam, the transgressor, generated children like himself.

We must therefore say concerning this question what we have heard the same Apostle Paul say. Discussing the unequal lot of Esau and Jacob, the twins born from one intercourse, he says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’ Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 11). And after being greatly wearied by this question, he concluded: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (ibid.).

We have thought it useful to offer these preliminary remarks from Julian’s little works as a warning to readers. From this point let us turn our pen to an exposition of the Song of Songs, and in this exceedingly difficult book let us diligently follow the footsteps of the Fathers and, with the help of that grace of God which we defend, devote whatever salutary effort we can.

In this work I warn the reader not to judge me excessive because I have wished to explain at greater length the nature of the trees and aromatic herbs, of which this book contains very many, according to what I learned in the books of the ancients. I did this not out of a desire for arrogance, but to compensate for my own ignorance and that of my people, who were born and raised far beyond the inhabited world—that is, on an island in the Ocean Sea—and can learn of what takes place in the chief regions of the world, namely Arabia and India, Judea and Egypt, only through the writings of those who were present there.

## HEADINGS IN THE SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 1077C]

I. The Synagogue longs for the Lord to come in the flesh and, when he comes, meets him with devoted love.

II. The primitive Church complains that she has been darkened by the persecution of the unbelieving Jews, and therefore tremblingly invokes the help of her beloved Redeemer.

III. Rebuking the Church, the Lord admonishes her, fearful as she is, concerning the grace given to her against all the ambushes of her enemies.

IV. Strengthened by God’s words, the Church recalls his manner of life, his passion in the flesh, and his resurrection.

V. The Lord praises her after she has been strengthened; and, returning his praise, she desires to rejoice with him during the slight peace of the present life.

VI. Recalling the joy of the virgin mother, the Lord also embraces in his bride the virtue of chastity as worthy of praise.

VII. Brought into knowledge of heavenly mysteries, the Church desires to be refreshed and rest under the protection of her Redeemer.

VIII. He himself adjures believers not to disturb the Church’s peace.

IX. Appearing in the flesh, the Lord stirs the Church to preach, because the winter of long unbelief that had oppressed the world has passed; and at the beginning of her work he commands her to detect and refute the foul wiles of heretics.

X. Favoring the Lord’s commands, the Church repeatedly prays that he come to her aid through the hidden grace of inspiration.

XI. The Church of the nations explains in what order she came to the faith of Christ; and he, rejoicing with her desires, commands the faithful not to disturb her rest.

XII. The Synagogue marvels at the faith inspired in the Church, devoted through mortification of the flesh and the power of prayer.

XIII. She replies that she has come, delighted by the bed and the couch of the peaceful king—that is, by the rest of souls and inward refreshment—and especially by the beauty of the king himself; and, in order to behold his appearance, she stirs even those who were admiring her.

XIV. Delighted by the Church’s faith, the Lord praises and commends each of her members individually—that is, each of the faithful—in a fitting utterance of praise. He foretells that the fury of her persecutors will be bent toward reverence for her, for whose love he himself accepted the wounds of the cross.

XV. He describes the sweetness of the doctrine preached by her teachers, the fruits of their works, and the fervor of their most delightful reputation.

XVI. He entrusts her to the winds of tribulations to be tested, so that her steadfastness may be proved more fully.

XVII. Conscious of her devotion, she prays that he come to inspire her.

XVIII. The Lord testifies that he has already come to her and has been delighted by her pious works; he also commands the heavenly citizens to rejoice with her good works.

XIX. The Church, resting from the tumult of the world, is roused by the Lord’s voice to correct certain people in whom her hope and love had begun to grow cold. Excusing her ministry through her love of repose, she begins to be kindled to action by his hidden inner prompting; but the result does not immediately follow what she has begun. Therefore, seeing the virtues of great teachers, she casts away whatever remained clinging to her of the desires of the world.

XX. In some of her faithful, the same Church entreats the more perfect to commend her also to the Lord at the time of her compunction or prayer.

XXI. They, in return, ask that something be told them about her virtues, so that, kindled by their sweetness, they may burn more intensely in her love.

XXII. She fulfills their request and, singing appropriate praises of her virtues and power, asks again in whose minds her traces are accustomed to be found.

XXIII. She responds to the pious desires of the saints that he delights in fruitful works and gathers the perfect into eternal joys through the virtues of chastity.

XXIV. Hearing this, the Lord praises the Church’s devotion and praises her activity; yet he teaches that he is not greatly desired in this life.

XXV. He says that the perfection of the whole Church is preferable to the many churches throughout the world, the many gatherings of false brothers, and the many choirs of the innocent.

XXVI. Hearing the Lord praise the Church, the Synagogue too is stirred to admire her, especially because she is terrible to all her enemies through the unconquerable contest of virtues, which the Apostle teaches will occur at the end of the world.

XXVII. The Church replies and declares through her teachers what caused her military preparedness: namely, concern for all the churches of which the one Catholic Church consists.

XXVIII. The Synagogue says that, having confessed these things at the sudden astonishment caused by the preaching of the Gospel, she had necessarily been thrown into confusion. The Church, rejoicing in her salutary beginnings, asks her to return to recognition of her Redeemer.

XXIX. The Redeemer himself, assenting to her exhortations, testifies that nothing is more to be seen in her than diligence in virtue.

XXX. Again describing, as usual, praises of his beloved, he first indicates, in the joining of her thighs [junctura feminum; see note below], the union in himself of the peoples who believe in him and love him.

XXXI. Seizing the word from his praise, she heaps praise upon him and begs him to come, so that, with his cooperation, she may undertake the pious labors either of action or of preaching.

XXXII. Beginning from the Church’s new origin, she desires the Lord to become incarnate, so that, through the aid of his assumption of humanity, she may be relieved as if by support, and may deserve to ascend to contemplation of the divine glory, as though to the embraces of his right hand.

XXXIII. Rejoicing with his desires, she adjures believers from the Jews not to disturb the faith of the nations.

XXXIV. Obeying his commands, they marvel with suspicious minds at the suddenness of her way of life.

XXXV. He also admonishes the Church herself concerning the love by which he redeemed her through the tree of the cross, and commands her always to carry his memory in heart and deed.

XXXVI. He also addresses the Synagogue concerning what should be done with the primitive Church from the nations, since she does not yet have among her own people those capable of being appointed teachers.

XXXVII. He adds that if any among them is eminent in life and speech, he should be instructed in the divine writings so that he may be promoted to the rank of teacher; but if they are of simpler nature, the examples of the saints should be set before them, by which they may be strengthened more fully in the faith.

XXXVIII. She replies that she has been made eminent by his gift and that, in her more perfect men, she is qualified for the rank of teacher.

XXXIX. The Church adds that, called into the peace of her Creator, she possesses many peoples, signifying that the nations of the Gentiles belong to her.

XL. Favoring these things, the Lord declares that he cares for the whole Church and commands those who have been blessed also to undertake the ministry of preaching.

XLI. The Church, obedient to his commands, entreats him to make himself present more often in the hearts of the faithful, so as to help her spiritual endeavors.

## THE SONG OF SONGS HAS THE FOLLOWING LITERAL TEXT

### CHAPTER ONE

The voice of the Church:

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest perfumes. Your name is poured-out oil; therefore the young women have loved you. Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes.”

The king has brought me into his chambers; we shall exult and rejoice in you. We shall remember your breasts more than wine; the upright love you.

Again, the voice of the Church:

“I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like Solomon’s skins. Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me. The sons of my mother fought against me; they appointed me keeper of the vineyards, but I did not keep my own vineyard. Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents. I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry on Pharaoh’s chariots. Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove. Your neck is like necklaces. We shall make golden chains for you, worked with silver.”

“While the king was at his couch, my nard gave its fragrance. My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he shall remain between my breasts. My beloved is a cluster of henna in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

“Look, you are beautiful, my beloved; look, you are beautiful, your eyes are like those of doves. Look, you are handsome, my beloved, and comely. Our couch is flourishing. The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.”

### CHAPTER TWO

“I am a flower of the field and a lily of the valleys. As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters. As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat beneath his shadow, whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.

“The king brought me into the wine chamber; he ordered love toward me. Strengthen me with flowers, support me with apples, for I am sick with love. His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it.”

The voice of my beloved:

“Look, this one comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a doe and a fawn of the stags. Look, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, peering through the lattice.

“Look, my beloved speaks to me: ‘Arise, hurry, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter has already passed; the rain has gone away and withdrawn. Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; the fig tree has produced its green figs, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance. Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come.

“My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the shelter of the wall, show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face beautiful. Catch the little foxes for us, which are destroying the vineyards; for our vineyard has flowered.’

“My beloved is mine, and I am his, who pastures among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline. Return, my beloved; be like a doe or a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of Bethel.”

### CHAPTER THREE

“On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him. I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.

“The watchmen who guard the city found me. ‘Have you seen him whom my soul loves?’ A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves. I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of my parent.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it.”

“Who is this that rises through the wilderness like a column of smoke from perfumes of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer? Look, Solomon’s couch is surrounded by sixty mighty men, among the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most highly trained for war, each man’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.

“King Solomon made a litter for himself from the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold, its upholstery of purple. Its interior he lined with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.

“Come out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon wearing the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart.”

[Note: “[Col. 1079] Thus there and several times below in the Exposition of the Song of Songs. In the Vulgate, femorum. EDIT.”]

## CHAPTER IV

How beautiful you are, my beloved, how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within. Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet. Your cheeks are like a slice of pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within. Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline. I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come. You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck-hair. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses all spices. Your lips drip honeycomb, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense. An enclosed garden is my sister, my bride; an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of orchard trees; henna with nard. Nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon. Myrrh and aloe with all the finest perfumes. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow forcefully from Lebanon. Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.

## CHAPTER V

Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his orchard trees. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, my friends, and drink; drink deeply, beloved ones.

I sleep, but my heart is awake. The voice of my beloved knocking: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.”

“I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?”

My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch. I rose to open to my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh. I opened the bolt of my door for my beloved, but he had turned away and gone. My soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought him, but I did not find him. I called him, but he did not answer me. The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me. The guards of the walls took away my cloak.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am faint with love.

“What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?”

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands. His head is the finest gold. His locks are like raised palm clusters, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside overflowing channels. His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers. His lips are lilies, dripping first-rate myrrh. His hands are turned work in gold, filled with hyacinths. His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires. His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases. His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars. His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. Such is my beloved, and such is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.”

“Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned? We will seek him with you.”

## CHAPTER VI

My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies. I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me; he feeds among the lilies.

You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely like Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array. Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away. Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of sheep that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your eyes.

There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines saw her and praised her.

Who is this woman who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array?

I went down to the garden of nut trees, to see the fruits of the valley, to inspect whether the vine had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded. I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.

“Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you.”

## CHAPTER VII

“What will you see in the Shulammite, except the dances of the armies?”

How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince! The curves of your thighs are like necklaces made by the hand of an artisan. Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine.
