Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed by lilies. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twin offspring of a gazelle. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head is like royal purple bound in channels.

How beautiful you are, and how lovely, most beloved, in delights! Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters of grapes. I said, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” May your breasts become like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like apples. Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy of my beloved to drink, and of his lips and teeth to savor.

I belong to my beloved, and his desire is toward me. Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field and stay in the villages. Let us rise early and go to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers are producing fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed. There I will give you my breasts. The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates. All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you.

## CHAPTER VIII

Who will grant that you were my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother, so that I might find you outside and kiss you, and no one would despise me? I would take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house, into the chamber of her who bore me. There you would teach me, and I would give you a cup of spiced wine and the juice of my pomegranates.

His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it.

Who is this woman coming up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?

“Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated. Set me like a seal upon your heart, like a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is harsh as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers overwhelm it. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, he would utterly despise it.”

“Our little sister is small, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for?”

“If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her. If she is a door, let us enclose it with cedar boards.”

“I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers, from the time I came to be in his presence as one who has found peace.”

The Peaceable One had a vineyard in that which has a people. He entrusted it to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit. My vineyard is before me. Your thousand, O Peaceable One, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit.

You who dwell in the gardens, your friends are listening; let me hear your voice.

“Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.”

# BOOK TWO

The Song of Songs, in which that most wise king, Solomon, described the mysteries of Christ and the Church—that is, of the eternal King and his city—under the figure of bridegroom and bride. Whoever wishes to read it must first remember that the entire congregation of the elect is generally called the Church. Nevertheless, for the sake of distinction, that portion of the faithful which preceded the time of the Lord’s incarnation is specifically called the Synagogue, while that which followed it is called the Church.

For the Old Scripture commonly designates the faithful people of that time by both names. Both names are Greek: *Synagoga* means “assembly” in Latin, while *Ecclesia* means “convocation.” It was thought more fitting that the faithful of this time be called by the latter name because of their fuller knowledge of spiritual understanding. For to be called together is proper to those who know how to hear and discern; stones and any other senseless things can merely be gathered together.

Both these portions of the righteous are one and the same, sharing in the faith and love of Christ, although they possess sacraments differing according to the circumstances of their times. The apostle Peter bears witness to this when he says: “Why are you testing God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also are” (Acts XV).

For just as we hope and believe that we shall be saved after the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection has already been accomplished, so also the earlier portion of the Church, still awaiting that same incarnation, passion, and resurrection of the Lord and Redeemer as future events, believed that it would be saved through his grace, whose coming it ardently desired.

Therefore this portion’s voice first resounds in the song of love. When the holy prophets repeatedly both showed it the way of life and promised the coming of him who, proceeding like a bridegroom from his marriage chamber, would bestow upon the whole world the grace of a new blessing, it began, passing beyond the voices of the heralds, to desire more greatly the presence of its own King and Savior, saying:

## CHAPTER ONE

### I. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is plainly to say: “I beseech you, do not always appoint angels or prophets to instruct me. Let him who has so long been promised come at last, enlighten me with the light of his presence, and, as though offering me a kiss, let him strengthen me by speaking to me with his own mouth. Yet let him also patiently receive the touch of my mouth—that is, let him not disdain to hear and instruct me when I ask him about the way of salvation.”

It is clear that this desire was fulfilled when, as we read in the Gospel, “As Jesus sat on the mountain, his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew V). Again, when he recalled to his disciples the dignity of his presence—that is, of his coming in the flesh—he said: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X).

At that time, too, he opened his mouth to promise the joys of the heavenly kingdom, unheard of through the ages [perhaps, “in the age”], just as previously he had often opened the mouths of the prophets through whom he promised his coming to the world.

After the Synagogue, desiring the Lord’s coming and hearing the prophets proclaim him, said, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”—that is, “Let him himself impart to me the gifts of his teaching”—it suddenly turns its words toward the one whose coming it ardently desired and adds:

### “For your breasts are better than wine.”

It is as though it were plainly saying: “I desire you to come and to be refreshed by your own eyes because the sweetness of your presence surpasses incomparably all the gifts that you sent through the heralds of your coming.”

By “wine” he means the fervor of legal knowledge, while by “breasts” he means the beginnings of evangelical faith. Concerning these Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians III). And again: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians II).

The breasts of the bridegroom are therefore better than wine, because the beginnings of the New Testament immediately make all whom they regenerate through water and the Spirit fit to enter heavenly life. The long observance of the Law could in no way accomplish this—not even in those who, kindled by a taste of heavenly sweetness, could truly say to God with the Psalmist: “And how excellent is your inebriating cup!” (Psalm XXII). The Apostle confirms this when he says: “For the law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews VII).

If the breasts of Christ—that is, the beginnings of the Lord’s faith—are better than the wine of the Law, how much more does the wine of Christ—that is, the perfection of evangelical teaching—surpass all legal ceremonies! If the sacraments of his incarnation send people into life, how much does knowledge of his divinity glorify them, and how much does the vision of it glorify them?

The bridegroom himself also indicates that he possesses not only milk but wine when he says later: “I drank my wine with my milk.” How greatly his wine surpassed the wine of the Law he signifies mystically in the Gospel, where, when the old wine failed at the symbolic wedding of the Church, he himself made new wine from water, plainly worthy of greater praise.

And rightly he calls them “breasts,” which are a woman’s bodily members, so that at the very beginning of the song he may show that he is speaking figuratively. Likewise in the Apocalypse, which is itself also a figurative book, John says of him: “I saw one like the Son of Man in the midst of seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe” (Revelation I). He adds: “And girded around the breasts with a golden belt.”

Nor did the bridegroom himself—that is, our Lord—shrink from assuming the figure of the female sex when he says through Isaiah: “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord. If I grant generation to others, shall I be barren?” And again: “As a mother caresses someone, so I will console you” (Isaiah LII). And in the Gospel he says to the unbelieving city: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew XXIII).

### “Fragrant with the finest perfumes.”

The finest perfumes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which the breasts of Christ are fragrant, because the holy teachers—ministers, that is, of evangelical milk—advance through the anointing of the Spirit into the love of virtues.

The perfumes with which prophets and priests were visibly anointed under the Law were indeed good; but the finest are those with which the apostles and their successors have been invisibly anointed. Concerning these Paul says: “It is God who anointed us, who sealed us, and who gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Corinthians I). The apostle John likewise says: “Let the anointing that you received from him remain in you” (1 John II). “You do not need anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about everything,” and so forth (ibid.).

They are also fragrant with the finest perfumes when they spread the reputation of their good works or preaching far and wide, as they themselves say: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place” (2 Corinthians II).

He explains why his breasts are fragrant with the finest perfumes when he adds:

### “Your name is poured-out oil.”

There is no reason to wonder if his members give off the fragrance of perfumes, because he himself received his name from oil, so that through anointing he might be called “Christ,” that is, “Anointed One.” This is surely the anointing of which Peter says: “How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts X).

The Holy Spirit is commonly understood under the designation “oil,” as the prophet bears witness when, in praise of the same bridegroom, he says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm XLIV).

His name is therefore not oil that merely drips but oil poured out, because, as his forerunner says of him: “God does not give the Spirit by measure. For the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John III).

He is also rightly considered, in his elect, under the name of poured-out oil. When he appeared in the flesh, he flowed forth upon them most abundantly through the gift of his Spirit, so that what had previously been held hidden within one people, the Jews, he has now suffused with manifest grace to the ends of the whole world. The prophecy has been fulfilled that said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II). Explaining this, the apostle Peter says: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift, which you see and hear” (Acts II).

His name is therefore poured-out oil, because that which he is is rightly named: he is rightly called full of the Holy Spirit, since by that same gift of the Spirit he acts, anointing the hearts of the elect.

### “Therefore the maidens loved you.”

By “maidens” he means souls that, reborn in Christ, have cast off the filth of the old human being. They cling all the more closely to the love of their Creator as they recognize that solely by his grace they receive both the remission of sins and the gifts of the Spirit, through which they advance in virtue.

Hence they openly profess and say: “The love of God—that is, the root of all virtues—has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V).

Nor should it be doubted that the earlier saints also loved the Lord with perfect love, and that their devout throngs may figuratively be called maidens. Through faith in the truth they trampled upon the examples of the ancient sinner and pursued, with unwavering hope, the rewards of the new life.

Thus one of them, already certain of future blessings, speaks to his soul, saying: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm CII). But these words apply more appropriately to the heirs of the New Testament, because through the washing of grace they are specifically born to God as adopted children. They love him all the more as they receive greater gifts from him, so that, once freed from the flesh, if they have lived rightly, they may ascend to the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

### “Draw me; we will run after you.”

Up to this point the voice is that of the Synagogue—that people which preceded the Savior’s incarnation in devout faith. At the beginning of the song, while the prophets proclaimed him for a long time, it responded: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”—that is, “Let him appear himself and, speaking mouth to mouth, grant me examples of how to live and bestow gifts.”

Then, in the verses that follow, it indicated what his gifts were and how greatly they were to be loved by chaste souls. At this point the voice of the Church is added—that is, the voice of those who came to faith after the time of his incarnation.

The former first prayed that the Lord would come and bring it a kiss of peace. The latter, knowing that he has already come in the flesh and already returned to heaven, no longer asks him to descend to it in this manner; rather, it desires itself to follow him to heaven.

Since it sees that this cannot be accomplished by its own power, it rightly implores the guidance of the one to whom it longs to come. “Draw me,” it says; “we will run after you.” It is as though it were plainly saying: “We would gladly run in your ways, follow the traces of your works that you marked while living on earth, and reach you as you preside in heaven. But because without you we can do nothing, we ask that you deign to give us your hand and help us to run to you by your support. Thus alone can we either run rightly or complete our course: if we run with you as our guide and helper.”

Therefore the Apostle, who glories by saying, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy II), plainly teaches elsewhere whether he could direct his steps by himself or whether he ran because the Lord drew him, saying: “But I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians XV).

It is fitting that, although the singular is used—“Draw me”—the plural follows—“We will run,” because the Church of Christ throughout the world is one, yet it consists of many souls of the faithful. These are called maidens in this passage, specifically because of the life of their new manner of conduct.

### “The king brought me into his chambers.”

The chambers of the eternal King are the inward joys of the heavenly homeland. The holy Church has now been brought into them through faith, and in the future it will be brought in more fully through possession of the reality.

The bride, that is, the Church of Christ, speaks to the maidens, namely, to faithful souls who have recently been reborn in Christ and are his members. “For this reason I beseech the bridegroom to help us as we run after him, giving us his hand so that we do not fail; for I have already tasted beforehand the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom. I have already tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet. I have already learned, through his revelation, the good things prepared for me in heaven.”

Then, turning to the one who revealed these things to her, her King and Lord, she hastens to give thanks for his benefits, saying:

### “We will exult and rejoice in you,” and so forth.

This is plainly to say: “We do not exalt ourselves over the gifts we have received. Rather, in everything in which we live well, we exult—or indeed, we shall always exult and rejoice—in your mercy, remembering throughout how mercifully you have refreshed us and how you have deigned to temper the harshness of the Law with the grace of evangelical faith.”

### “The upright love you.”

For this reason we shall not exult and rejoice in ourselves but in you, remembering your gifts, because all who are upright in heart have learned that you must be loved before and above all else. Those who prefer anything to your love cannot be upright at all, since from you alone they have everything good that they possess.

It should also be observed that earlier he said, “The maidens loved you,” but now he says, “The upright love you.” We must conclude that by “maidenhood” he meant nothing other than uprightness of heart, since those who have put off the impurity of the old human being and put on the new human being have been created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth.

Again, “The upright love you,” because in reality no one except the upright can love the Lord. Whoever violates the uprightness of righteousness by deed, word, or even an evil thought, vainly claims to love the Creator whose commands he despises. For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments, as the evangelist John testifies (1 John V).

After the holy Church has been led into the chambers of Christ—through knowledge and hope of heavenly blessings—and after it has learned to love him with an upright heart and to rejoice and exult in his grace alone, it remains to show what contest it undergoes for that love and for acquiring the blessings it has tasted, and what affliction it endures.

### “I am black,” and so forth.

Black, certainly, under the adversity of afflictions, but beautiful through the splendor of virtues; indeed, all the more beautiful in the sight of the inward Judge the greater the afflictions of foolish people by which it is harassed and, as it were, disfigured.

By the daughters of Jerusalem to whom she speaks, she means souls imbued with heavenly sacraments and sighing for the dwelling of the heavenly homeland. Consoling it in its tribulations, the holy mother says to these: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.”

It is as though she were plainly saying: “I appear exceedingly contemptible in the eyes of my persecutors, but before the God of truth I shine gloriously through my confession of the truth.” Therefore you should not grieve in the exile of this labor, since you remember that you are citizens of the heavenly homeland and are hastening toward the vision of eternal peace through the adversities of the passing world.

### “Like the tents of Kedar,” and so forth.

Kedar was the son of Ishmael, concerning whom it was said: “His hand will be against all, and everyone’s hand against him” (Genesis XVII). The truth of this prophecy is demonstrated even today by the nation of the Saracens, hateful to everyone, who are descended from him. The Psalmist, beset by anguish, likewise affirms it when he says: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul was a long-time sojourner. I was peaceable with those who hated peace” (Psalm CXIX).

David is not in fact recorded as having suffered any hatred from the Ishmaelites; rather, wishing to exaggerate the evils he endured from Saul and his other adversaries, he lamented that he was harassed by the wickedness of a people that never cared to be at peace with anyone.

Solomon, by contrast, was peaceable both in name and in life. Indeed, as Scripture testifies, all the kings of the earth desired to see Solomon’s face in order to hear the wisdom that God had given in his heart.

Thus, when it says, “I am black, but beautiful, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon,” the words are to be distinguished so that she is black like the tents of Kedar but beautiful like the skins of Solomon.

The holy Church has often been darkened by the afflictions of unbelievers, as though it were the common enemy of the whole world, fulfilling the Lord’s word: “You will be hated by all because of my name” (Matthew X). Yet she is always beautiful in the sight of her Redeemer, as though she were truly worthy for the King of Peace himself to visit.

It should be noted that Kedar, by its very name, which signifies darkness, indicates either perverse people or unclean spirits. Solomon too, whose name means “peaceable,” indicates the same through the mystery of his name. Concerning him it is written: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom,” and so forth (Isaiah IX).

When the Church is said to be black like the tents of Kedar, this is presented not as truth but according to the estimation of foolish people, who even suppose that it provides a dwelling within itself for vices or malignant spirits.

But when she is called beautiful like the skins of Solomon, this is presented as an example of truth. For just as Solomon used to make tents for himself from the hides of dead animals, so the Lord gathers the Church for himself from those people who know how to renounce carnal desires.

Hence he said to everyone: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew XVI). And the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians III).

Some, reading this statement—“I am black, but beautiful”—in this way, say that the Church is black in her carnal members, or in her false brothers, like the tents of Kedar, but beautiful in her spiritual members, like the curtains of Solomon.

Yet if we consider what is written concerning the Lord—“We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isaiah LIII)—which was said not of his sin, for he had no sin at all, but of his passion, it is clearly established that the Church too declares herself black not because of sins or the vices of sinners, but because of her temptations and sufferings, by which she is continually exercised.

The same meaning is confirmed by the words that follow, when it says:

### II. “Do not look upon me because I am dark,” and so forth.

This is plainly to say: “Do not marvel, O daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls devoted to God—that I am despised by human beings, because the heat of the temptations that I continually endure for the sake of my inward beauty has made me outwardly dark, although heavenly grace has granted me inward beauty.”

This resembles the apostle Peter’s statement: “Beloved, do not be surprised by the fiery ordeal that comes upon you for your testing, as though something strange were happening to you, but rejoice as you share in Christ’s sufferings” (1 Peter IV).

At times the Lord himself is signified by the name “sun,” as when it is said of his ascension: “The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.” At other times his elect are signified by it, as he himself says: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matthew XIII).

But in this passage the heat of tribulations is more appropriately represented by the name “sun,” in accordance with what he himself says concerning the seeds cast upon the rock: “When the sun rose, they were scorched, and because they had no root, they withered” (ibid.). Explaining this afterward, he says: “When tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, they immediately fall away” (ibid.), thereby declaring that tribulation and persecution are represented by the name of the sun.

Therefore, just as those who remain quietly at home often have whiter limbs, while those who work in a vineyard, garden, or any other open-air occupation generally have their bodies darkened by much sun, so the more earnestly the holy Church girds herself for spiritual battle, the more fervent she sees the snares of the ancient enemy rising against her.

And just as the sinner is often praised in the desires of his soul and the one who acts wickedly is blessed, so sometimes the righteous person is reproached in the virtues of his soul and the one who acts rightly is cursed. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; we are blasphemed, and we entreat” (1 Corinthians IV).

He himself teaches the faithful to disregard, indeed to rejoice in, the stain of this blasphemy, for whose sake the Lord says: “Blessed are you when people curse you; and when they persecute you and say every evil thing against you,” and so forth (Matthew V).

Therefore, because the holy Church sees that she is adorned inwardly with faith and virtues but testifies that she is scorched outwardly by persecutions, it remains to show from whom she suffered the first fury of persecution. It follows:

### “The sons of my mother fought against me,” and so forth.

This is the voice of the primitive Church, which receives the battles of tribulation from the Synagogue itself, from which she derived her origin according to the flesh, as the Acts of the Apostles teach most fully.

In this statement it should first be noted that the bride of Christ rightly asserts that she has been discolored by the sun, since she used to work in his vineyard, like an open-air laborer, cultivating or guarding it.

There was one vineyard of Christ in Jerusalem, namely, the primitive Church, which was founded on Pentecost—that is, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection—through the coming of the Holy Spirit. At that time the apostles themselves were its guardians.

But after persecution arose in the time of the blessed martyr Stephen and everyone except the apostles was scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, it happened that there were several vineyards—that is, that churches of Christ existed in several places—because those who had been scattered here and there preached the word.

Through the working of divine providence, the very dispersion of the Jerusalem Church became the occasion for establishing a greater number of churches. Hence it is appropriate that our manuscripts read, “They were scattered”; in Greek it says *diesparisan*, that is, “they were disseminated throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.”

And shortly afterward: “Those who had been disseminated went about evangelizing the word of God.” For the Jewish persecutors, although they wished to drive the Church away, unwillingly spread the seed of the word more widely. By persecuting the one Church in Jerusalem, they unwittingly caused many churches to arise throughout the world.

When the primitive Church had said that she was darkened by afflictions because the sons of her mother—that is, the Synagogue—had attacked her with murderous hatred, she immediately added how much she had advanced through the assaults of those same afflictions, adding in the person of those entrusted with the task of preaching:

### “They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”

It is as though she were plainly saying: “The harshness of my persecutors brought me this advantage and benefit: I became the keeper of many vineyards, namely, the churches of Christ, after the multitude of persecutors had scattered the primitive vineyard—that is, the Church which I had first begun to plant and guard in Jerusalem.”

The statement that she did not keep her vineyard must be referred not to her mind but to her location. For at that time a considerable portion of the Church withdrew from Jerusalem because of the persecution, yet it retained the entire integrity of the faith firmly in its heart. Indeed, as we have said, it also undertook the ministry of preaching with devoted lips.

Some think that the statement “They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep” should be distinguished in this way: by “vineyard” the Church of Christ is signified, while by “vineyards” are understood the many decrees of the Law and the various traditions of the Pharisees.

“They made the Church,” they say, “a keeper among the vineyards,” because they compelled the faithful to be circumcised and to observe the ceremonies of the carnal Law. Among them was the one who said: “In all the synagogues I frequently punished those who believed, and I pursued them even to foreign cities” (Acts XXII).

Therefore he did not keep his vineyard, since through him many of the faithful were scattered from Jerusalem, like branches of the heavenly vineyard. Yet its root he was in no way able to uproot.

But because the greater the adversity by which the wicked test the faith of the elect, the more earnestly they must invoke the Redeemer’s help, the holy Church, after lamenting that the sons of her mother had risen against her and that her vineyard had been shaken by their assault, remembers the Lord’s promise: “In the world you will have tribulation; but be confident, I have overcome the world” (John XVI). Turning her anxious heart toward him, she prays, saying:

Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, etc. She rightly calls him whom she beseeches for protection “the beloved of her soul,” because the graver the danger from which she longs to be rescued, the more dearly she loves him through whom she knows she is to be rescued. Something similar is found in the Psalmist’s words: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII). This plainly means: “I do not cease to love you with my whole mind because I perceive that, without your grace, I can possess no virtue.”

She also indicates that he is a shepherd when she says: “Where you pasture, where you lie at midday.” This agrees with what he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me” (John X). [Col. 1092A] He pastures his sheep and lies among them at midday because, lest the hearts of his faithful wither inwardly in the heat of temptations, he refreshes them with the remembrance of heavenly sweetness and, in his mercy, is accustomed to dwell among them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The Lord pastures me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has settled me” (Ps. XXII). Hence John says: “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

Since, therefore, many false prophets go out into the world saying, “Look, here is the Christ,” or, “There” (Matt. XXIV), Christ’s Church must always discern, through careful investigation, who those people are in whose confession and conduct he himself may be found; and she must beseech him in devout words to deign to reveal himself: “Tell me,” she says, “whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie [Col. 1092B] at midday.”

Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions, etc. It is as though she said plainly: “Because the many-sided persecution of those who oppose me afflicts me like the heat of midday, I beg you, my Redeemer and Protector, to declare in what places I may find those who are refreshed by the grace of your presence, and which teachings among all the others accord with the harmony of your evangelical truth. For, if you delay your help any longer, I may perhaps encounter gatherings of the erring; without your guidance I can in no way enter the way of truth.”

Heretics may appropriately be called his companions, insofar as they bear either a profession of his name or his mysteries. Did Christ’s bride not do this when pseudo-apostles came to Antioch—namely, [Col. 1092C] his companions—proclaiming, “Unless you are circumcised according to Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts XXVII)? Already wearied by no small measure of agitation and controversy, she finally sent Paul and Barnabas to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem to establish more certainly what the truth of the Gospel was. When the conflict had ended, it was proved that the Lord Christ was the shepherd and indweller among those whom James, Cephas, John, and the other apostles instructed, and that his pure fold—his Church—was to be protected from the flocks of his companions, that is, from the peoples of the heretics.

Did Christ’s bride not do the same in the times that followed, whenever the sons of her mother fought against her—that is, whenever heresies arose from within her [Col. 1092D] against her? She immediately brought together councils of the Fathers and diligently sought to determine what the truth of the faith was. But because that same bride, namely Christ’s Church, having sought the help of his presence in her tribulations, adds the words “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions” from the perspective of those who are weak, he at once reproves her same fear with a kindly rebuke, as though saying the Gospel saying: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV). For what follows is:

III. If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go forth, etc. “Why,” he says, “do you speak as though you could in any way be abandoned by me in some temptation, and complain that, in guarding our vineyard from its enemies, you have been blackened by excessive heat like the midday sun? [Col. 1093A] I myself have already made you beautiful among women—that is, among the synagogues of other doctrines—through the bath of regeneration; but I have ordained that you should be made much more beautiful through the testing of tribulations.” If perhaps you do not know these things and do not [now?] remember that “no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. II), go forth from my company and follow the tracks of the flocks; that is, imitate the actions of the erring, although I have determined that you should rather be the guardian of my one flock, for which there would be one fold and one shepherd.

And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds. That is: nourish lost hearers by following the teachings of foolish teachers, having abandoned the words of the wise, which are given through the counsel of the one shepherd by means of teachers. [Col. 1093B] For I commanded you, if you love me, to pasture my lambs—that is, souls serving me simply and innocently—on the word of salvation. I wished you to devote such care to this office that you would prefer to suffer every adversity, even to undergo the torment of death itself, rather than cease feeding them.

But if you do not know that you have been betrothed to me under this condition, pasture your own kids instead: joined to wandering teachers, provide for the luxurious and proud. They are rightly called kids, and your kids, namely those who are to be placed on the left at the judgment. They are yours because they are not instructed according to the rule of my commandments but rather according to your own errors—that is, according to those errors by which you were held before you were joined to me.

The Lord does not speak these words as a command but rather as a threat, [Col. 1093C] indicating what befalls those who, unable to endure the adversities of temptations, separate themselves from the unity of ecclesiastical peace. Thus in the Gospel, when he says: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. XII), he does not command us to make it bad but teaches what reward awaits evildoers.

Since the Lord does not want holy Church to be ignorant of herself, but desires her diligently to learn what gifts she has received from him and what she ought to suffer or do for love of him, he consequently discloses to her what her condition is when he adds:

I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots. He calls his cavalry the army [Col. 1093D] of the children of Israel, whom, freeing from Egyptian slavery, he led through the Red Sea into the wilderness and brought into the land of their promised inheritance. In that same sea he drowned Pharaoh’s chariots, which had pursued them in an attempt to drag them back into servitude.

He calls it cavalry because, just as a charioteer is accustomed to preside over cavalry, so at that time the Lord himself ruled that people, guiding it along the way of salvation. To this cavalry he compared his Church, whom he made his beloved through the water of regeneration. For just as the people were greatly terrified when Pharaoh’s chariots came upon them, yet were saved by heavenly protection, so he taught the Church always to trust in his protection amid the threats of persecutors.

Moreover, the fact that the people of God were then [Col. 1094A] illumined by a pillar of fire, while the Egyptian troops were enveloped in the densest darkness, so that throughout the whole night they could not approach one another, continues always to be enacted in the night of this present age. For the heavenly dispensation, separating the righteous from the reprobate according to a fixed order, shines its grace upon the former and leaves the latter in merited blindness. [Col. 1093D]

Again, when they reached the Red Sea, the children of Israel were freed after the waters had been divided, while the Egyptians, when the waters returned upon them, were drowned with their horses and chariots. Is it not clear that the wave of death itself, which all mortals must encounter, carries the wicked away to destruction but opens a path to salvation for the devout?

The other events that we read were done for that same cavalry of God—that is, the Israelite people—during the time of the Egyptian persecution, [Col. 1094B] the more carefully they are explained, the more clearly they are found to have prefigured the holy universal Church, of which that people was a part.

And since this verse teaches how the Lord protects the Church amid adversities, it remains to show how greatly the Church herself preserves the love of that same Lord and Protector when adversities confront her. It follows:

Your cheeks are beautiful, etc. The nature of the turtledove is said to be such that, if it is deprived of the companionship of its mate, it is never thereafter joined to another. This is fittingly applied to the chastity of the Church. Although she has been widowed by the death of the Lord her bridegroom, she nevertheless retains such a great remembrance of him—knowing that he has risen from the dead and now reigns in heaven—that she can in no way admit the companionship of outsiders. Content with love for him alone, she hopes one day to come to him. [Col. 1094C]

Hence, instructed by the words of the outstanding teacher, she is accustomed to proclaim that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither powers nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom. VIII).

Since the seat of modesty is customarily in the cheeks, it is rightly said to holy Church, who fears that she might stray from the way of truth by following the examples of the wicked—this is what she means by “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions”—in the response of Truth itself: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove.” This means: “I have adorned you with so great a virtue of salutary modesty that you may recoil, uncorrupted, from the chastity of the faith promised to me, [Col. 1094D] moved neither by any desire for transitory things nor by hearing any wicked doctrines.” What is the principal reason for preserving this great sobriety he makes clear by adding:

Your neck is like necklaces, etc. Through the neck we convey food into the body to refresh it, and through it we utter words by which we disclose the secrets of our heart to our neighbors. Hence the person of teachers is rightly signified by the neck of the Church. Through the word of edification they instruct the unlearned, and through this same ministry of instruction they transmit the food of salvation to the members of the holy Church entrusted to them.

This neck is rightly compared to necklaces. Necklaces are ornaments customarily hung around the necks of maidens. Although the word “necklace” often designates all the ornaments of married women as well, [Col. 1095A] the steadfastness of spiritual teachers is fortified and adorned with the insignia of heavenly virtues, since they demonstrate through their deeds what they teach in words.

“Murenulae” are likewise ornaments of a maiden’s neck: chains woven of gold rods and sometimes varied by the addition of silver rods, as this interpretation shows; they derive their name from their resemblance to the serpent called the moray eel. These appropriately signify the woven fabric of the divine Scriptures, by which the beauty of the holy Church increases when each of the faithful, having examined the sayings and deeds of the Fathers, strives ever more earnestly to shine with virtues himself.

The gold of which he says the murenulae are to be made is the brightness of spiritual meaning; the silver with which he says they are to be patterned is understood as the splendor of heavenly eloquence. When he promises in the plural, “We will make for you,” he speaks of those through whom, with the Spirit of God acting and cooperating, sacred Scripture has been ministered to us—many of whom were still to come at the time when Solomon sang these words. [Col. 1095B]

He places golden murenulae patterned with silver around the bride’s neck because the Church has prepared the divine texts to be learned by those whom she would appoint over her faithful by the right of teaching. He places murenulae fashioned by the craftsman’s art around the neck when each faithful soul, in all that it says and does—indeed, in all that it lives and breathes—continually attends to the holy Scriptures and carefully directs its understanding and words according to their examples.

Thus this little verse is joined to the preceding one: the cheeks of the holy Church are beautiful like those of a turtledove—that is, her modesty remains inviolate [Col. 1095C]—because frequent meditation on the divine Scripture does not allow her to go astray.

The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “We will make for you likenesses of gold with silver inlays, until the king is at his resting place.” In this sentence, the word “gold” properly expresses the brightness of the heavenly homeland. In this life the likenesses of that brightness, not its incorruptible reality, are shown to us through the holy Scriptures, as the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” that is, through likenesses; “but then face to face” (1 Cor. XII).

Indeed, Moses himself, to whom, as we read in Exodus, God spoke “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exod. XXXII), knowing that he had not seen God’s glory itself, [Col. 1095D] prayed, saying: “If I have found favor in your sight, show me your way, that I may know you”; and again: “Show me,” he said, “your glory.” The Lord also showed this very thing when, in answer to him, he said: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII).

The vision of the divine face, then, has not been denied to us altogether, but has been denied to those still living in this mortal condition; it has been promised in the future to the pure in heart. In the present, a likeness of this face and of perpetual blessedness was shown not only to the Fathers, when the Lord appeared in angels, but is also shown clearly today to us who read the writings of the Fathers. We strive always to retain in our minds what they said about the glory of the heavenly homeland and continually to sigh for the vision of these things. [Col. 1096A]

These likenesses are made with inlays of silver because, through the brilliance of spiritual sayings, the heavenly mysteries are disclosed to us. And since we need the comfort and assistance of such likenesses only in this life, and not in the future one, it is fittingly added:

Until the king is at his resting place. That is, until Christ is in his hidden place and has not yet appeared to us in the glory of his Father, to repay each person according to his work. Then, as Isaiah says: “The eyes of the saints will see the king in his beauty” (Isa. XXXIII). Hence the Apostle says: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Coloss. VIII).

Christ the King was at his resting place—that is, in his hidden place—not only before [Col. 1096B] his incarnation and ascension into heaven, but also during the time when he appeared visibly in the flesh to the world. For even then he did not show his faithful, who dwelt with him in the flesh, either the glorification of his assumed humanity or the eternal glory of his divinity. Rather, he promised these things as the reward of faith to all the elect in the life to come.

Our edition, however, which has been translated from the Hebrew source, joins the final part of this verse—“Until the king is at his resting place”—to the following verse, which must now be discussed. After receiving such gifts and promises from her Creator, the Church immediately replied and, by adding the following words, declared with what devotion of works she had received them:

While the king was at his resting place, etc. [Col. 1096C] She calls the king’s resting place the time of his incarnation, through which he deigned to humble himself for us and to bend down so that we might be raised up. In that resting place he wished both to refresh his Church with living food and himself to be refreshed by her good works.

Hence he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever” (John VI). Again, speaking to his disciples about the peoples who believed in him, he says: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John IV).

“Nard” signifies the fragrance of good action. “While the king was at his resting place,” she says, “my nard gave forth its fragrance,” because when the Son of God appeared in the flesh, the Church grew fervent in heavenly virtues. This is not because she had no spiritual and devoted men before his incarnation, but because [Col. 1096D] without any doubt she then devoted herself to stricter pursuits of virtue, when she learned that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom would immediately lie open to all who lived rightly as soon as the bonds of the flesh were loosed.

It should be noted that the literal figure of this verse was also fulfilled in the works of Mary Magdalene, who represented the type of the Church, when, while the Lord reclined at table, she poured ointment of nard over his head and feet, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, as the holy Gospels testify.

In one of them the nature of this nard is also described, when it says: “A woman came with an alabaster jar of costly ointment of spikenard” (Mark XIV). Its tips, as it were, spread out into ears; for this reason perfumers celebrate both the spikes and the leaves of nard as possessing a twofold value. [Col. 1097A] Physiologists write that it is principal among perfumes, and therefore it was rightly prepared for the anointing of the Lord’s body.

It is a shrub, they say, with a root that is heavy and thick; the shrub is short, black, and brittle, though fleshy, fragrant like cypress, harsh in taste, and with a small, dense leaf. There are many kinds of it, all precious, but the Indian variety is more precious still.

IV. My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me, etc. We read that this was also fulfilled literally in our Savior when, after his passion had been completed and his body had been removed from the cross, Nicodemus came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They took his body and bound it in linen cloths with spices.

The beloved of the Church therefore became a bundle [Col. 1097B] of myrrh when the Lord, anointed with myrrh and aloe and wrapped in linen cloths, was enclosed. This bundle dwells between the bride’s breasts when the Church meditates without interruption, in the innermost part of her heart, on the death of her Redeemer. Who does not know that the heart has its place between the breasts?

A bundle of myrrh will dwell between the bride’s breasts when every soul consecrated to God strives, with an attentive mind and as far as it can, to imitate the death of him by whom it knows itself to have been redeemed, mindful of the Apostle’s saying: “All who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. V).

But because the glory of the resurrection immediately followed the death of our Mediator and Savior, the bride rightly adds:

[Col. 1097C] My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me, etc. On the surface of the literal text, the sense of this verse is as follows: Just as the island of Cyprus is accustomed to produce clusters larger than those of other lands, and just as in the Judean town called Engaddi more distinguished vines are born than elsewhere—since from them flows not wine but the liquid of balsam—so my beloved is joined to me by a love surpassing all others, so that no creature can tear me away from affection for him.

Typologically, however, just as myrrh signifies the sorrow of the Lord’s passion because of its bitterness—for although it is healthful for treating illnesses, it is bitter to the taste—and because he both received myrrh-mixed wine to drink from the soldiers and was anointed with myrrh by the disciples for burial, as we have said, so the cluster [Col. 1097D] suitably announces the joy of his resurrection. “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII). Thus the Lord became a cluster of Cyprus in the resurrection, having been a bundle of myrrh in the passion.

He rightly dwells between the bride’s breasts because he who was transformed into a cluster is the same one who is of the vine. For this reason the holy Church never removes the memory of the Lord’s death from her heart: the one who died for her sins also rose from the dead for her justification. To her, as she follows his footsteps, he offered the example of rising after the anguish of death.

He is also appropriately remembered as being in the vineyards of Engaddi. For, as we have said, balsam is produced in the vineyards of Engaddi; it is customarily mixed with olive oil in the preparation of chrism [Col. 1098A] and consecrated by pontifical blessing, so that all the faithful may be marked with this anointing through the laying on of the priest’s hands, by which the Holy Spirit is received. By it also the Lord’s altar, when it is dedicated, and other things that ought to be sacred, are anointed.

Thus the vineyards of Engaddi most fittingly signify the divine charisms. The bridegroom is in the vineyards of Engaddi because the Lord himself, appearing in the flesh, is full of the Holy Spirit, and he himself bestows the Spirit’s gifts upon believers.

He calls the balsam trees vineyards because they rise in the manner of vines, which cannot support themselves without props. They are more like vines than myrtles and are distinguished by perpetual foliage; their height remains within two cubits. Their seed is similar in taste to wine and red in color; [Col. 1098B] their branches are thicker than those of the myrtle. At a certain season of the year they exude balsam.

Farmers are accustomed to cut their shoots with sharp stone or bone knives, for contact with iron damages them. Through these incisions a sap of extraordinary fragrance flows out; it is caught in beautifully glistening drops on wool and then gathered in small horns. Since it flows through a fissure in the bark, it is more often called opobalsamum—for *opē* in Greek means “cave.” The more generous vein of each tree is tapped three times during the summer heat. The tear has the highest value, the seed the second, the bark the third, and the wood the least.

All these things, if carefully considered, most aptly fit our Redeemer. He appeared humble in the flesh yet full of grace and truth; he was wounded for iniquities [Col. 1098C] and poured forth from his wounds for us the sacraments of life and salvation. Hence he himself, who is the power and wisdom of God, says in Ecclesiasticus: “My fragrance is like unmixed balsam” (Ecclus. XXIV).

The order of the words is truly remarkable: first the bride says that, while the king reclined, her nard gave forth its fragrance; then she compares him to a bundle of myrrh; third, she calls the same one a cluster of Cyprus; finally, she recalls that he is in the vineyards of Engaddi. For first, while the Lord reclined at table, a devout woman anointed him with nard; then the disciples anointed the crucified one with myrrh for burial and wrapped him in linen cloths; after this, when the joy of the resurrection soon arrived, he distributed spiritual gifts to the faithful.

Nor should it be passed over that Engaddi is interpreted as “the spring of the kid.” [Col. 1098D] By this name the bath of holy baptism is plainly indicated. Into it we descend while still sinners and deserving of the left hand, but we ascend cleansed from the foulness of sins and destined to be counted among the lambs.

And when she was signifying the joy of the Lord’s resurrection by saying, “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me,” she rightly added immediately, “In the vineyards of Engaddi,” that is, “of the spring of the kid.” This plainly means: “In the spiritual gifts that are bestowed upon the faithful from the time of baptism.”

Thus far the Church has enumerated the gifts she received from her Redeemer and testified to the pledges of his love. He immediately replied to her in return for these gifts:

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, etc. [Col. 1099A] Behold, you are beautiful in pure works, by which you conduct yourself soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age. Behold, you are beautiful in simplicity of heart, because you persist in good works for the sake of the hope of eternity alone, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God.

Your eyes are like those of doves: the eyes of your heart are simple and pure, wholly free from every duplicity of deception and pretense. Therefore they are greatly blessed, because “such as these will see God.” Again, your eyes are like those of doves because your perceptions are endowed with spiritual understanding. Since the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, the terms “dove” and “doves” rightly signify spiritual understanding and gifts.

Christ’s beloved also has eyes like those of doves because every soul that truly loves him inwardly is not inflamed [Col. 1099B], like a hawk, by desire for external things, nor does it contemplate inflicting anything hostile on any living person. Such is said to be the gentleness of the dove, which considers everything it encounters with a simple, mild, and humble heart.

Hearing that the Lord had granted her a twofold beauty—of works, namely, and of intention grounded in the simplicity of a pure heart—she immediately replied in a devout voice:

Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and lovely. It is as though she plainly said: “Whatever beauty, simplicity, and spiritual grace I possess, I received from you, who have bestowed them. Through you I possess both the forgiveness of sins and the power to perform good works.

“But you are truly and incomparably beautiful and lovely, because you are God, [Col. 1099C] begotten eternally from the Father before the ages; and when the time of my redemption came, you were conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin mother. You were not merely free from every stain of iniquity but also full of grace and truth. You came into the world and lived in the world; indeed, you bestowed upon all who share in your grace the gift of becoming beautiful in virtues themselves.”

You are therefore beautiful and lovely—that is, wondrous both in the eternity of the divine nature and in the dignity of the humanity you assumed. Since the splendor of this beauty is accustomed to become known to hearts that are withdrawn from external activity, the more freely and clearly they rest, according to the Psalmist’s words, “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. LV), she rightly adds:

Our couch is flourishing. At times the holy [Col. 1099D] Church rests with the Lord, her bridegroom, as though on a couch; at other times she stands with him in battle against her enemies. She stands in battle when, in the face of the more violent assaults of temptations, she wages the contest of faith against the wicked even unto blood. She rests on the couch when, with times of peace smiling upon her, she renders him free service and directs the tranquil gaze of her mind toward contemplating the glory of his majesty.

Thus the same couch is rightly called flourishing, because all the saints make use of the tranquility of peaceful times and devote themselves especially to sacred reading, fasts, prayers, and the other fruits of the Spirit when they cease from the labors of tribulation. They raise themselves higher in contemplation of heavenly things [Col. 1100A] when they receive a time of calm free from outward disturbance.

The Church’s couch may also rightly be understood as consisting of flowers, not only because of the works of purity by which the elect attain the fruit of eternal life, but also because of the offspring of the faithful, whom the Church is accustomed to beget for God from water and the Spirit, fragrant with the flower of faith. She devoted herself to this activity with all the greater zeal, cooperating with the Lord and with the word confirmed by him, the more fully she received from him a quiet and peaceful time free from the persecution of the envious.

It should also be noted that throughout the whole text of this little book the bride always desires to remain with her beloved in the house, on the couch, or in some other interior place, which is more fitting to the female sex. The bridegroom, however, [Col. 1100B] in what is fitting to the male sex, calls his beloved outward to works—namely, to vineyards, gardens, and other such places. For the holy Church, if it were possible, would always desire to converse with the Lord amid the tranquility of worldly peace, and to propagate and nurture a heavenly offspring for him.

But he himself ordains that she be exercised by frequent tribulations in the present, so that she may reach eternal goods in a purer state and, if all temporal circumstances should perhaps proceed prosperously, may not become so enamored of dwelling in this present exile that she sighs less for the heavenly homeland.

Thus Christ’s bride, desiring to lead a peaceful life in him, next indicates what sort of houses she wishes to receive him in, saying:

The beams of our houses are cedar, etc. [Col. 1100C] She calls the various gatherings of the faithful throughout the world her houses, and from all of these the universal Church is constituted.

The beams and ceilings designate the various orders of the faithful in those same houses of the Church. Both are customarily placed high up, but beams are made for strengthening, whereas ceilings contribute more to the beauty of houses than to their fortification.

The beams therefore signify holy preachers, by whose word and example the structure of the Church is held together so that it can stand. Through the strength of their teaching they hold back the storms of heretical assault, lest they overthrow it.

The ceilings are compared to the simpler servants of Christ, who know how to adorn the Church more by their own virtues than to defend it with words of doctrine and fortify it against the attacks of perverse teachings.

The ceilings hang attached to the beams because it is necessary that all who desire to shine with lofty virtues in the holy Church cling with their whole mind to the words and examples of the highest Fathers, by which they are lifted away from earthly ambition. [Col. 1100D]

It is fittingly said that these beams are of cedar and the ceilings of cypress, because both trees are known to possess an incorruptible nature, exceptional height, and an outstanding fragrance. This suits those who can say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. II); “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III); and, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation?” and what follows (Rom. VIII).

The fact that the scent of cedar is also accustomed to drive away serpents, according to the poet’s words,

> Learn also to burn fragrant cedar in the stalls,  
> and to drive out the heavy serpents with the scent of galbanum,

is appropriately applied to the high ceilings—that is, to teachers—who by the power of the heavenly word are accustomed to repel the venomous teachings of heretics and drive them away from the seduction of the simple.

Who does not also see how well suited to these same holy preachers is the fact that their resin, called cedrine, is so useful in preserving books that those coated with it neither suffer from moths nor grow old with time? The holy Scripture has been composed through the spiritual understanding of these preachers, and it can be corrupted by no heretical cunning or consumed by the passing age of the world—so much so that “until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished” (Matt. V). [Col. 1101B]

When the Lord said this about the Law, how much more did he leave it to be understood of his Gospel?

The cypress, too, in that it is suitable for treating bodily ailments and does not surrender the beauty of its foliage to any force of the winds, expresses the steadfastness and activity of those who adorn the holy Church, like ceilings, with the loftier ornaments of virtues.

Thus the bride—that is, the holy Church, or every elect soul—marvels at the beauty of her beloved; she praises the softness and purity of the flowering couch; she proclaims the inward beauty of her houses, in which she may fittingly receive her beloved.

But because the labor of the present age is more appropriate than rest, and because in this life the elect, with Christ’s help, are exercised more in devout actions than they enjoy peaceful leisure, he summons the bride to exercises of labor [Col. 1101C] and to enduring the company of the wicked, adding:

## CHAPTER II.

### VI

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys,” and so forth.

You delight, my beloved, in flourishing through hidden virtues in quietness; but remember that I am the flower of virtues, from whom alone every spiritual fruit arises, and in whom alone you can possess a flourishing repose. I am the flower of the field because I desire the grace of my fragrance to become known throughout the breadth of the whole world. This can in no way be fulfilled unless you occasionally interrupt the quietness in which you delight and gird yourself for the duty of preaching, by which you are to be exercised.

I am also the lily of the valleys rather than of the mountains, because I habitually disclose and reveal either the brightness of my glorified humanity or the splendor of my eternal divinity among those who humbly submit themselves to the acceptance of my rule in faith and love, and who seek to follow my will rather than their own. Although they delight in the leisure of my inner contemplation, nevertheless, when I command them, they do not refuse to advance to the labor of preaching.

Indeed, I have granted you a share in my brightness so that you might be compared with a lily—namely, by the radiant perfection of your works and by the precious brilliance of a pure heart. But lest you should wish to have the security of quietness in this life, know that for the present you must live among the reprobate and endure daily the goads of the wicked; in the future, however, you are to hope for repose with the elect alone.

“For as a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” For you must suffer adversity not only from those who are in every way alien to you in mind and profession, but you are also often more sharply pierced by the wickedness of those souls whom you had rejoiced to receive among the number of your daughters through the fountain of regeneration and through faith and participation in the heavenly sacraments.

It may reasonably be understood that, in the words “I am the flower of the field,” the undefiled birth of the Virgin is signified. Likewise, in what follows—“and the lily of the valleys”—the humility of the parents of that same one may be understood. For he himself appeared as a flower in a garden—not of the countryside, but of the field—when from the flesh of the untouched Virgin mother he assumed flesh ignorant of sin and full of virtue. Of him Isaiah said: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11).

He himself sprouted as a lily in the valleys, since he chose humble and poor parents from whom God would be born as man. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The valleys will abound in grain” (Psalm 64). He himself is the grain, because he refreshes us with the bread of life; he himself is the lily, because, like the gleam of gold in whiteness, he has divinity in its name.

Beautifully, in the lily the outer whiteness first gradually opens, and only then does the grace of the golden color hidden within become visible: for when the Lord was born into the world, he was first recognized as an exalted man by those who truly believed in him; as time proceeded, it became known that he was true God. All the elect, moreover, through the sacraments of his assumed humanity, advance toward contemplation of the divine splendor.

When the Church, wearied by adversities, had said to the Lord, “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely; our bed is covered with flowers,” and the rest that follows—plainly desiring, in tranquil times, to devote herself to contemplating that beauty and comeliness and to produce for him flowers, whether of good works or of faithful souls—he replied: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” It is as though he openly said:

“Remember that I, who was able to be born from a Virgin, who am God before the ages, appeared humbly in the world as man at the end of the ages. I have always shown myself the companion of the humble and of the poor in spirit; by the steps of humility I reached death. You, however, must cease seeking the security of quietness in this world. Rather, like a lily among thorns, shine forth whiter and gentler; and even when afflicted by the barbs of those who are close to you, display the truth of your beauty more graciously.”

After the Lord had praised the Church because she had preserved the chastity of her faith uncorrupted among the spikes of the faithless and had shone forth more gloriously amid the horrors of the wicked, she immediately raises him up with greater praise in a reciprocal response and declares that he alone stands out as holy among the faithful works of the good.

“As an apple tree among the trees of the forest,” and so forth.

This is what the Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord? Or who is like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88). Therefore, just as an apple tree, pleasing in sight, smell, and taste, ordinarily surpasses the wild trees, so the God-man rightly surpasses all who are merely human and holy; and the merit of those who are sons of God by grace is transcended by the power of him who is Son by nature.

Hence John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1). Hence the apostle Paul says: “Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a son over his own house.”

Let the cedar shine; let the cypress raise itself on high; let the other trees of the forest display the marvels of their beauty, fragrance, and virtue. The apple tree surpasses them all, for beyond the sweetness of its fragrance and appearance it also contains within itself the power to nourish those who eat it.

Let the righteous shine, each in his own virtues; he surpasses them all who, born from the Virgin, supplies us with the means of everlasting life. Therefore it is aptly added:

### “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat,” and so forth.

It is as though it were openly said: “For this reason I decide that my beloved is to be preferred above all, because I see that only under the protection of his compassion—whose desire has always inflamed me—I have found refreshment from the heat of tribulations, and because I feel the exceedingly sweet fruit of his gifts, by which I trust that I shall continually be restored.”

The holy Church desired to breathe for a while under the shadow of her author when she lamented that she had been darkened by the excessive sun of persecutions, because the sons of her mother were fighting against her. She implored his present help and anxiously cried: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie at midday.” Weary not only from the burden of afflictions but also enticed by the memory of his beauty and comeliness, she said: “Our bed is covered with flowers.”

She showed that she had obtained what she desired when she said: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired, I sat, and his fruit is sweet to my throat.” It should be noted that above she had declared the beams of her houses to be cedars and their ceilings cypresses; yet she did not recall that their protection was sufficient for her, nor that she was content with their height and beauty as objects of contemplation. Instead, she diligently sought only the tree of life, in whose shadow she might rest and by whose fruit she might be refreshed.

For although all the saints can set before us the exalted examples of their virtues, demonstrate by preaching the path of heavenly life, and offer the support of their intercession before the Lord, nevertheless we must say to none of them, but only to our beloved Savior: “The children of men will hope under the protection of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35).

Hence it is rightly said: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” For the only Son is rightly preferred above all the sons of God: like a shady tree, he protects us from the heat of the persecuting world; like an unfading apple tree, he refreshes us with heavenly sweetness.

How great is the sweetness and power of his refreshment is shown in what follows:

### VII

“He brought me into the wine cellar,” and so forth.

“As soon,” she says, “as the sweetness of his grace touched the throat of my heart, I felt myself so restored in spirit and transferred from delight in earthly things to desire for heavenly things, as though I had been brought into a wine cellar and refreshed at once by the fragrance and the drink of new wine.”

Therefore he who gave such blessings rightly turned her toward loving him in return with an unquenchable love.

In a typological sense, since the grace of the Holy Spirit is commonly signified by the word “wine,” the Lord bears witness to this when he says that “new wine must be put into new wineskins” (Matthew 9; Mark 2; Luke 5)—that is, the fervor of spiritual gifts must be poured into pure hearts.

The wine cellar is to be understood as the Church, within whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is ordinarily given and received. The beloved therefore brought his beloved into the wine cellar because the Lord fashioned the Church, gathered from the whole world, into one house for himself and consecrated it with the gift of his Spirit.

Since this structure rests principally on the foundation of charity, with him as its builder, she rightly added, after saying that she had been brought into the wine cellar: “He ordered charity in me.”

“He ordered charity in me,” she said—that is, in his mercy he granted me to possess an ordered charity: so that each person might love the Lord his God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength; might love his neighbor as himself; and might endure even an enemy by loving him.

The one of whom the very arranger and giver of charity says, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me,” and so forth (Matthew 10), either does not know or neglects to preserve the order of this charity.

Yet the ordering of charity may also rightly be understood as referring to its strengthening, because what is placed carelessly is weak, whereas what is arranged in order remains firm. Thus the Lord may appropriately be said to have ordered charity in the Church, since he is recognized as making it solid in the hearts of his faithful through suitable stages of growth.

What is said—“He ordered charity in me”—may also be understood in this way, as though it were said: “He himself loved me with an ordered charity.” That is, he joined all my members, all the elect, to himself in devoted love; yet he embraces the more excellent among them with a greater affection, as is fitting, when it is said: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13).

He loved them all; yet a more indulgent love is indicated toward one when it is said: “That disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 21). In the Church, according to distinctions of merit, he loves some more than others.

Again, “He ordered charity in me”: “He himself loved me first, and by loving me gave me the ability to know how to love him in return.” Hence he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). The apostle John says likewise: “This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4).

Again, “The Lord ordered charity in the Church,” because the charity with which he chose her before the ages he revealed through certain stages of growth as time progressed. For, as the Apostle testifies: “God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5).

As the manifestation of that same charity advanced, John says: “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be the children of God” (John 3).

Again, concerning that same perfect love, than which none greater can exist and which itself can never diminish, the Lord says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him,” and what follows (John 14).

When he said in the present tense, “Whoever loves me”—which no one can do unless he has first been anticipated by his love and unless the grace of his Spirit has kindled him to love him—why did he immediately add in the future tense, “will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him”? Surely because the one who is meanwhile loved by God so that, by believing, he may be able to love, will then be loved by God so that, by seeing him, he may love him more fully. Once his face has been revealed, he will love him with all his strength more truly, insofar as he suffers nothing from lower things to impede that love.

The Lord therefore orders in the Church the charity by which he himself loves her and inflames her to hold rightly to love of him and of her neighbor. How greatly that charity raises up the mind, once it has perfectly absorbed it, away from love of fragile things, the following verse teaches when it says:

“Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples,” and so forth.

The soul that truly tastes the ordered charity of its author languishes from love, because when it is inflamed to seek the light of eternity, it grows weary of love of the temporal. It becomes colder toward devotion to the passing age in proportion as it rises more ardently to contemplate the joys of the everlasting kingdom.

But let us see, soul, what bed she who burns with such love seeks, on which she may rest when weary.

“Strengthen me,” she says, “with flowers; surround me with apples.” In the flowers, the tender beginnings of virtues are signified; in the apples, perfection.

The soul, therefore, languishing from love, beseeches the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, those souls who have preceded her in heavenly desire—to help her beginnings with good examples and to recall frequently for her what kind of beginning, progress, and end they had in traversing the way of virtue. Thus, by contemplating them, as though by the most pleasing fragrance of flowers and apples, she may recline more softly and sweetly in affection for her Creator.

This may equally be understood of the works of the saints that we have before our eyes and of the deeds or sayings of earlier fathers that we gather from the meadows and groves, as it were, of the Scriptures.

“His left hand is under my head,” and so forth.

In Christ’s left hand, his temporal gifts are signified; in his right hand, the blessedness of everlasting life. Hence elsewhere it is written concerning him who is the power and wisdom of God: “Length of days are in his right hand; in his left, riches and glory.”

The holy Church, and the soul wholly devoted to love of its Redeemer, therefore shows what kind of repose can exist in this life, which she had sought so earnestly, and how she desires to recline with her beloved on that bed flourishing with virtues during the pilgrimage of this exile.

“His left hand,” she says, “is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” She calls the principal faculty of the mind her head. Her beloved places his left hand beneath the bride’s head when the Lord strengthens the hearts of the faithful who still dwell in this life by the knowledge of him, raises them up through participation in his sacraments, grants them the pledge of his Spirit, and supplies them with the consolations of the holy Scriptures.

His right hand will embrace her when, after this life, he promises her the everlasting kingdom of heavenly life. It is rightly said that the left hand supports the head and the right hand embraces her, because we receive temporal gifts as assistance for this pilgrimage, whereas we shall see the heavenly rewards without end.

The bride, who above, languishing from love, sought to be strengthened with flowers and surrounded with apples, now rightly testifies that she has the beloved’s hand beneath her head.
