For although every lover of his Creator rejoices in the flowers of virtues; although he delights in the progress of his neighbors, with whom he himself may arrive at the sight of the Creator’s face; and although it is sweet for him to remember the examples of the ancient saints, by which he may be stirred more ardently to love either God or his neighbor—nevertheless, those who truly desire to rest have one and only one hope: to be sustained by the hand of their Author.

First comes the left hand, so that through it they may deserve to reach the embrace of the right. For his right hand will embrace no one whom his left hand has not first received for nurturing; that is, no one will behold his exalted splendor in the future who has not faithfully reclined in the present to receive the mysteries of his humility.

Did not Paul, who taught that he was the most faithful minister of this bride, saying, “I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11), seek to place the bridegroom’s left hand beneath her head so that he might lead her to the embrace of the right? For he says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2).

Again, he urges her to reach toward the embrace of his right hand when he says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3), and, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (ibid.).

“His left hand,” she says, “is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” It is as though she openly said: “May the temporal benefits of my Lord and Savior assist me, so that I may find some rest from the desires and disturbances of the world; but the promise of eternal things, by which I shall be rewarded forever, delights me far more.”

How pleasing to the Lord himself is such repose of his bride—that is, of the Church or of any elect soul—is indicated by his following response, when it says:

### VIII

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields,” and so forth.

By the daughters of Jerusalem he means souls aflame with desire for their heavenly homeland. The bridegroom adjures them not to awaken the bride resting in his love, nor presume to disturb her, happily lulled to sleep, amid the agitation of human affairs.

Whoever importunately obstructs the mind of any elect person while it is speaking with God in devout prayers, or meditating on divine commandments or promises in sacred readings, certainly awakens Christ’s bride from blessed sleep before she wishes it.

She wishes to awaken refreshed by this most joyful sleep, because she knows how to devote herself to divine service at the appropriate time and to return at the fitting time to attend to the necessities of human frailty.

Whoever, therefore, does not fear to obstruct the faithful while they are intent on heavenly pursuits surely harms the virtues by which he believed himself to be strong. Hence the bridegroom rightly adjures the daughters of Jerusalem by the does and stags of the fields not to do this.

By the does and stags—clean animals, hostile to poisons—the works of spiritual virtues are signified. In proportion as these excel in purity, so are they accustomed to despise, indeed to destroy and eliminate, the poisonous devices of the ancient enemy.

Beautifully, after saying “does and stags,” he added “of the fields,” so as to express the endurance and simplicity of pure minds, flourishing in sincere faith, in which virtues arise and are nourished.

Thus the bridegroom adjures the daughters of Jerusalem by the does and stags of the fields not to awaken or rouse his beloved until she herself wishes it. It is as though he plainly said:

“I call all the faithful to witness, and I adjure each one by the virtues that he desires to nourish with a pure heart, not to despise the devout efforts of his brothers, nor thoughtlessly obstruct them by violating what is sacred. Rather, let each person rejoice in the progress of his neighbor as in his own, and fear to inflict loss upon his brothers’ spiritual gain as he would fear to inflict it upon himself. For a person diminishes his own virtues when he refuses to spare, indeed refuses as far as he can to assist, the virtues of his neighbor.”

The bride gladly accepts this adjuration of the bridegroom and immediately replies:

“The voice of my beloved.”

The implied sense is: “This is the voice that I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken me while I rested in his embrace, before I myself wished it.”

The soul filled with God must greatly rejoice when, amid the adversities of the world, it happens to receive his consoling voice, either through the gift of hidden inspiration or through meditation upon or hearing of the sacred writings.

For although we are not yet permitted to gaze upon the face of our beloved, much has already been granted to us in that, meanwhile, we are refreshed by the sweetness of his words in the holy Scriptures.

Much more is granted to those who receive the higher gift: with the pure gaze of the mind lifted toward heavenly things, they taste in the present something of the sweetness of the life to come.

Hence, after the rejoicing bride had said, “The voice of my beloved,” she immediately desired also to see that beloved, though she was not yet able to do so, and added:

“Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains,” and so forth.

He calls mountains and hills those who transcend the general conduct of the holy Church—like the flourishing plain of the fields—by the singular purity of their minds. The more lightly they make themselves by rising above desire for earthly things, the more capable they become of contemplating heavenly things.

Concerning such people Isaiah, when describing the advent in the flesh of the Mediator between God and humanity, says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it will be raised above the hills” (Isaiah 2).

That mountain is rightly said to be on the top of the mountains and raised above the hills—that is, to be higher than exalted people—because in the last days he appeared as a man among human beings, but as God he existed with the Father before the ages.

When the beloved comes upon these mountains, he is said to leap and to cross over these hills because the Lord habitually illumines the hearts of the exalted through the frequent grace of his visitation.

He is beautifully said not to remain on these hills but to leap, or to cross over them, because the sweetness of inner contemplation is as elevated through knowledge of heavenly things as it is brief and rare, owing to the heaviness of minds still held down by the burden of the flesh.

“For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9).

Nor should what the beloved himself promises his bride in the Gospel be considered contrary to this: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

He remains always with all the saints through their faith and love and through the help of his grace; but he appears more excellently, for a time, to the few exalted ones to whom he wishes, and when he wishes.

For it belongs to the few—and to those who, because of the height of their hearts, are compared with mountains and hills—to say: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5).

To all the faithful, however, it is said: “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God” (1 John 4). It belongs to the whole Church faithfully to hear: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.”

It belongs only to the perfect to say: “We did not make known to you the power of our Lord Jesus Christ by following cleverly devised myths, but having become eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1).

An evident example of this vision follows when it says:

“My beloved is like a doe,” and so forth.

All who know how to investigate the natures of these animals carefully find many features in them that apply most suitably to the beloved of the Church, that is, to the Lord Savior. But in this passage we should attend especially to the fact that they delight in dwelling on the heights of the mountains and in making extremely swift leaps. For this reason they are seen by us more rarely than oxen, asses, or other such animals, which, once tamed, we use whenever we please.

This is very appropriately applied to the height of heavenly contemplation, which does not lie within the will of the human observer but in the grace of God, who appears when he wishes.

I believe that Isaiah—the preeminent mountain—saw him seated upon a high and exalted throne not when he himself chose, but when the Lord wished. He also saw the heavenly hosts singing to him the praises due to him.

Paul too, himself a mountain who greatly despised earthly things and touched the stars with his summit, was caught up into paradise and caught up into the third heaven not when he himself decided, but when it pleased God; and he heard secret words that a human being was not permitted to speak.

It accords with both the humility and the truth of the assumed humanity that the Lord is compared not with a stag but with a fawn and a young one of the stags—that is, with smaller animals—since among human beings he appeared not only as man but as a humble man.

He became a fawn of the stags because he assumed true bodily substance from the flesh of the preceding fathers; for he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1).

David himself says: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41). And again: “He made my feet like the feet of a deer” (Psalm 16).

But concerning the other stags, who are plainly companions of his life, he says: “The voice of the Lord prepares the stags” (Psalm 28). For he prepares stags when he supplies the faithful with the gifts of virtues.

That they may direct the course of their minds toward higher things; that they may thirst unceasingly for the fountain of life; that by their spiritual sense of smell they may draw out and trample down the heretical serpents of speech from their hidden places of deceit; that they may chew over the word of life; and that in the upright steps of their actions they may maintain the measure of saving discernment—these things arise not from their own power but from divine generosity.

The voice of the Lord therefore prepares the stags because his grace places the saints in the citadel of virtues.

From these stags, then, was born the fawn rightly beloved by the bride—that is, by the Church or by any faithful soul—for Christ is descended from the fathers according to the flesh, and is “God blessed above all forever.”

Since in these verses the loftiness of the contemplative life has been expressed, it remains to show the perfection of the active life, which is common to the whole Church. It follows:

“Behold, he himself stands behind our wall,” and so forth.

Now the beloved remains near the bride; now he appears leaping upon the exalted mountains, because our same Lord and Savior offers himself for a time to the more perfect, whenever he wishes, to be seen “through a mirror and in an enigma,” while he always grants all the elect the invisible grace of his presence.

Concerning this manifestation of his presence it is rightly said now: “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall,” because he remains with us—indeed, he remains in us—in such a way that he cannot be seen by us, as John testifies when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4). “If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us” (ibid.).

The wall that shuts us off from his sight is the condition of our mortality, which we merited by sinning. In our first parent we were created in such a way that, if we had never consented to sin, all the elect would always behold, without weariness and without any labor, the light of divine contemplation. Now only a very few of the more perfect attain to seeing it, with the greatest labor, by purifying their hearts through faith.

But in this wall divine mercy made windows and lattices from which he might look upon us, because he opened the grace of his knowledge to our minds, however weighed down they may be by the blindness of this age, and continually refreshes us with the light of his hidden inspiration.

Since through the outlook of this inspiration the merciful Creator chiefly works to summon us away from love of temporal things toward earning the joys of heavenly peace, it is rightly added:

“Behold, my beloved speaks to me: ‘Arise,’” and so forth.

“All things have their season, and everything under heaven passes through its appointed times” (Ecclesiastes 3). Christ’s bride, therefore—the Church, or any elect soul—has a time for resting; she also has a time for rising to labor.

Thus, just as above he adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken or rouse her until she herself wished it, now, with his voice changed, he himself commands her to rise and hasten to him. He no longer consents to enter her bed, however richly it may flourish with heavenly pursuits; rather, as the continuation of the song teaches, he commands her to go out with him to cultivate the vineyards and drive away the harmful beasts from them.

He adds, to call forth and kindle her zeal, that once the winter winds have passed, the springtime warmth now assists the diligence of the laborer; that the arrival and songs of the spring birds make rural places more pleasant than courtly ones; and that the growth of the flowers promises farmers hope of the future harvest.

But since we have touched only briefly on the surface of the literal text, let us now turn our pen to search out the meanings of the allegory.

Above, under the figure of the fawn and the young one of the stags, it was said how the Lord reveals the inner mystery of heavenly things to the contemplation of the exalted. Under the figure of him who stands behind our wall and looks through windows and lattices, it was said how, though he is still invisible, he repeatedly illumines the whole Church by the gaze of saving compunction.

It remains now to make known how he incites that same Church either to the duty of preaching or to the practice of good works.

“Arise,” he says, “hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.”

Rise from that bed which is exceedingly dear to you, in which you delight to care for yourself through psalms and prayers and the other disciplines of life. Hasten and come also to devote yourself to the salvation of your neighbors through the diligence of preaching.

For we hasten toward the Lord who calls us by as many steps as we perform works of virtue for his sake.

### IX

“For now the winter has passed,” and so forth.

This is what the Apostle says: “The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light” (Romans 13).

Just as the darkness of night is expressed by the austerity of winter and rain, so the storm of unbelief is represented by them—a storm that ruled the whole world until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

But when the Sun of justice shone upon the world, the ancient treachery of wintry unbelief immediately withdrew and was driven away, and flowers appeared upon the earth, because the beginnings of the nascent Church now shone forth in the faithful and devout dedication of the saints.

“The time of pruning has come.”

This refers to the one whom the Lord mentions in the Gospel. Having said that he himself was the true vine and that his Father was the farmer, he immediately added: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will remove; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15).

The work of pruning may also rightly be understood in accordance with what the Apostle says: “Having stripped off the old man with his actions, put on the new” (2 Corinthians 3). Explaining this elsewhere, he says: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4). And again: “Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his own hands at what is good” (ibid.).

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

The voice of the preacher has been heard in the land that has now begun to be ours, since it received the word of faith. Concerning this land it is also said in the psalm of the first day of the week—that is, of the Lord’s resurrection, which took place on the first day of the week—“The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Psalm 24).

The voice of the turtledove, which by its call usually signals the departure of winter and the arrival of spring, suits those who know how to say: “The darkness has passed, and the true light is already shining” (1 John 2).

The voice of the turtledove, which sounds humbly and expresses a groan in place of song, accords with those who, remembering their sojourn and the homeland promised to them, are accustomed to say: “And we ourselves, although we have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.” They also cry out to their hearers: “Be sorrowful and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into grief.”

The bird itself, which loves chastity and always dwells on mountain ridges and the tops of trees, imitates the life of those who testify for themselves and their companions: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7), and, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

Moreover, its customary avoidance of human roofs and human society, and its preference for dwelling in forests and solitudes, prefigures those who, although placed bodily in the world, are separated from the world in mind and desire rather to see heavenly things.

“The fig tree has brought forth its unripe figs.”

They call *grossi* the primitive, immature figs, unfit for eating; even if shaken, they fall at the slightest touch.

The fig tree brought forth its *grossi* when the turtledove sounded, when the Synagogue brought forth many people through the apostles preaching in Judea—people who had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. They preferred to maintain an imperfect and, as it were, immature observance of the legal letter rather than receive in it the sweetness of spiritual understanding.

Apponius explains this verse as meaning that the fig tree brought forth its *grossi* when the Synagogue produced the apostles, who, born from it, supplied believers with the sweetest nourishment of doctrine.

And because, when the Synagogue brought forth either the apostles who preached the Gospel or those who insisted on preferring the ceremonies of the Law to the Gospel, the faith and salvation of the whole world nevertheless followed, it is rightly added:

Vineyards in blossom gave forth fragrance. For by the blossoming of the vineyards is signified the beginning of the multiplying Churches, whose renown was spread far and wide from that Church which was first planted in Jerusalem. For what is more pleasing than the fragrance of a flowering vine? Indeed, juice pressed from their blossoms makes a kind of drink, suitable both for health and for pleasure. Who would not readily see what this signifies when compared with the good reputation of virtuous action? The likeness, therefore, of the vineyards from which wine is produced—which gladdens the human heart—applies both generally to the Churches of the faithful and particularly to each of the elect, who bring forth for themselves spiritual joy and gladness. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (1 Cor. III). And, as the Psalmist says, “All the glory of the daughter of kings is within” (Ps. XLIV).

Saint Jerome explains these verses as follows: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land: the turtledove, a most chaste bird, always dwelling in lofty places, is a type of the Savior.” And shortly afterward: “Immediately the turtledove says to the turtledove: The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs—that is, the precepts of the old law have fallen, and from the Gospel the flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.”

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1111]

“Arise, my friend, my bride, and come,” etc. If, according to the Apostle’s interpretation, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X), what are the clefts of the rock except the wounds which Christ accepted for our salvation? In these clefts the dove dwells and builds its nest, whether when each gentle soul, or when the whole Church, places the sole hope of its salvation in the Lord’s Passion, trusting that through the sacrament of his death it is protected from the snares of the ancient enemy, as from the seizure of a hawk, and striving in him to bring forth spiritual offspring, whether of children or of virtues.

Hence Jeremiah, addressing heretics under the figure of Moab and calling them to the unity of ecclesiastical faith, says: “Leave the cities and dwell in the rock, inhabitants of Moab. Be like the dove nesting at the summit of the cleft” (Jer. XLVIII).

The wall, moreover, which is customarily built of stones for the protection of vineyards—for in Isaiah’s song it is said, “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill, and he surrounded it with a wall” (Isa. V)—signifies the guardianship of the heavenly virtues with which the Lord surrounds the Church, his vineyard, lest it be devastated by the incursion of unclean spirits, like savage animals. Hence the Psalmist says: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. XXXIII). And the Apostle, speaking of angels: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. I).

In this wall, therefore, the bride and beloved of Christ finds refuge for herself, like a dove finding a cavern, while the holy Church learns that, through angelic assistance, she must defend herself against the devil’s deceits. Accordingly, the Lord exhorts this same Church—and every soul devoted to him—to the practice of pious and fruitful labor, saying: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come.” Then follows, through the words “Arise, my friend, my bride, and come; my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the cavern of the wall.”

It is as though he openly said: After the storm of pagan life has been removed by heavenly mercy; after the flowers of a life that brings salvation have already emerged on the earth; after, in the manner of pruning, the heavenly husbandmen have begun to separate the unjust from the just and vices from virtues with the discerning sickle of instruction; after the herald of salvation has already sounded throughout the world; after the world itself has been converted to the knowledge of the truth and the most delightful report of a new life has been spread among the nations—I beseech you, O great multitude of faithful souls, beloved by me, to whom I have bestowed the gifts of my friendship, whom I have deigned to join to myself as a bride, to whom through the infusion of my Spirit I have imparted the simplicity of a dove-like mind, for whose health and life I myself accepted wounds and death, to whom I have granted the assistance of heavenly protection against invisible enemies—I beseech you, since you have been made the recipient of such gifts, not to grow slack through idle leisure, but rather to hasten to gird yourselves for the diligence and zeal of the required struggle, for the sake of eternal rest.

“Show me your face,” etc. You who desire to hide in the secret place of secluded rest, like a dove in the clefts of the rock or in the cavern of the wall, I ask you to come forth into the public sphere of action, to show your faith through your works, and to declare outwardly, for the example of others, what beauty you possess within.

For I, who perceive the hidden things of the heart, consider that you show me your face when I see you display for the benefit of your neighbors an action without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind. For “whatever one does for one of these least ones, one does for me.”

Let your voice sound in my ears—that is, the voice of praise or preaching: words that either praise me in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, or, by preaching, rouse the mouths and minds of your neighbors to my praise. The bride therefore shows her face to the Lord in the things she does in his sight, and she shows the sound of her voice in the things she speaks beneficially before him.

It should also be considered more attentively that he says, “Show me your face.” “Yours,” he says, not another’s—that is, holy and undefiled: “For such I made it, cleansing it by the washing of water in the word; such I perfected by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, setting the light of my countenance upon you.”

“Let your voice sound in my ears,” not a stranger’s—that is, the voice which I taught you to have on the day of your betrothal, by which you promised to preserve your chastity for me.

Again, “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” means: show your face to me, not to others. Remember to give your voice to my ears, not to those of others; that is, take care to perform good works and speak holy words for the sake of love of me, not for any other reason. For whoever devotes his good deeds or words to human approval shows the beauty of his face or the sweetness of his voice to outsiders rather than to the Creator.

Even according to the literal sense, women who, for the deception of foolish men, strive to adorn the face of their bodies and soften their words beyond measure are transgressors of this commandment of the Lord. Therefore they remain unworthy of that outstanding praise with which the Lord glorifies his bride and adds:

“For your voice is sweet,” etc. The voice of that soul is sweet to the Lord which knows how to announce the Lord’s words sweetly to its neighbors or to sound forth praises to the Lord himself, saying with the prophet: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII)!

That face appears beautiful to the Lord which strives to make itself worthy of seeing his face, and which is accustomed to say to him from the depths of its heart: “I have sought your face, Lord; your face I will seek; do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. XXVI).

Yet concern for our own purity is not sufficient for us if we do not also correct those who err, insofar as we are able, and if we do not take care to defend the weaker against their snares. Hence it follows:

“Catch for us the little foxes,” etc. Foxes that destroy vineyards are heretics and schismatics. Would that we did not know how much they are accustomed to tear with the teeth of perverse doctrine the flowering vineyards of Christ—that is, the inexperienced minds of the faithful!

Christ therefore commanded his bride, laboring piously with her attendants, whom he customarily calls the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, with preachers exalted through holy humility—to catch the little foxes: that is, to strive immediately to detect and defeat the tricks of the deceitful. Otherwise, once they have grown larger with time, they will be driven away from the destruction of his spiritual vineyards only with greater difficulty, the longer they have been accustomed to graze upon them.

And beautifully, the one who had earlier spoken of vineyards in the plural again used the singular: “For our vineyard has blossomed.” Thus he calls many vineyards one vineyard, just as he wished the many Churches throughout the world to be called one Church. He said that the vineyards blossomed in order to show the peoples of the elect sprouting widely. And fittingly, when he warned that the foxes must be caught, he immediately designated the vineyard by a singular name, so that he might teach that heretics must be pursued and crushed above all for this reason: lest their attack divide the faith of the Church—which ought to be one—and tear it into parts.

The nature of foxes also aptly corresponds to the character and words of heretics, since they are exceedingly deceitful animals, hiding in ditches or caves, and, when they appear, never running along straight paths but always through winding turns. Anyone can readily understand how these traits correspond to the deceptions and frauds of heretics.

Nor should it be passed over that, when he was speaking to the children of the Church, he did not say, “Catch foxes for yourselves,” or “Your vineyard has blossomed,” but, “Catch for us the little foxes, for our vineyard has blossomed.” By this he more powerfully kindled all who were able to defeat or correct the wickedness of heretics or bad Catholics, showing that they served him in this work and demonstrating that the vineyard they were defending belonged to him, the rewarder of pious labors.

Accordingly, the bride and beloved, with the simplicity of a dove-like heart, rightly responds at once to such an expression of his affection:

## X. “My beloved is mine, and I am his,” etc.

The meaning of this response extends all the farther because it appears to be expressed so briefly. It may rightly be understood in this way: “My beloved is mine, and I am his”—let us be joined to one another by true and sincere love.

It may also be understood thus: “My beloved is mine.” He had promised me such words of divine exhortation, consolation, and promise, and I will always offer him the clear face of my way of life, the pure voice of my speech, and my gratitude.

It may also be taken, with great appropriateness, in this way: because pronouns often carry considerable force, the Church—that is, the whole multitude of the elect—says, “My beloved is mine,” and no one else’s; and again, “My beloved is mine,” not another’s, meaning that he grants me the perpetual favor of his love and returns its fruit. “And I am his,” not anyone else’s; I, and no other human multitude, meaning that I am always joined to him in complete devotion of humility and obedience.

All these meanings are aptly suited to what follows:

“He who feeds among the lilies.” That is, he who is accustomed to rejoice in the most pure and sweetest fragrance of my virtues, who delights in the most pleasant fruit of the Churches shining throughout the world.

Thus the holy universal Church is designated sometimes by the plural name “lilies,” and sometimes by the name of a single lily. For, as it says, “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters.” Likewise, through “vineyards” in the plural, where it says, “The vineyards are in blossom,” and again through “vineyard” in the singular, where it adds, “For our vineyard has blossomed,” the same Church—which is one alone—is represented.

It is called in the singular because “the heart and soul of the multitude of believers was one” (Acts IV). Yet it is most appropriately named in the plural because that unity of heart and soul among the faithful is no longer contained in only a few, but in a multitude of believers.

It should also be noted that lilies correspond to the acts of the saints in this respect as well: they are accustomed to heal limbs scorched by fire. When the saints discover that the hearts of their neighbors have been burned by the flame of vices, they immediately offer them the help of fraternal love by which they may be healed. And lest the heat of greed or lust, pride or anger, or the fervor of other crimes overwhelm them, they diligently supply them with the cooling refreshment of their consolation and exhortation.

Some interpret the Lord’s feeding among the lilies as his feeding among the most pure choirs of virgins—and rightly so, since they shine outwardly with chastity of flesh and inwardly stand out with the radiance of an undefiled heart.

Again, the Lord feeds among the lilies—that is, among the most pleasing virtues or multitudes of the saints—for the same reason that he is born among them: because he, the Mediator between God and human beings, willed to become of one nature with his Church. Hence the Church is customarily called his body, and he himself the head of the body, the Church.

He feeds among the lilies when the number of the faithful within the Church is increased through the fountain of regeneration. He feeds among the lilies when the faithful, who are certainly his members, advance in the love of heavenly things through the most radiant examples of earlier believers.

It should also be noted that above the beloved is remembered as feeding, while here he is said to be fed. The bride says: “Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you feed, where you rest at midday.” He is fed in us because we are his body and members from his member; he feeds us because he is our head, from whom we all rightly glory, each one saying: “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies”—meaning that afterward he will exalt us also and gather us to the head.

And because this feeding of the Lord, which takes place in the progress of his saints, continues to the end of this age—for once they have arrived at the vision of him, they will have no further progress to make—it rightly follows:

[Col. 1116B] “Until the day breathes,” etc. That is, until the eternal light of the age to come rises and the shadows of the present life—that is, ignorance and error, in which even we faithful, who use the lamp of God’s word, are meanwhile deeply clouded—bend and pass away.

For when that day, desired by all nations, begins to breathe forth, that is, to reveal itself, the Lord will no longer feed among the lilies—that is, among the gatherings of the saints—but will then rather refresh them with the eternal vision of his glory. “I shall be satisfied,” he says, “when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI); and, “Blessed are those who hunger now, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V).

Nor is it contrary to apostolic speech that he compares the present life with the shadows of night and the future life with day. Of the life we now lead the Apostle testifies: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XV). For, to put it briefly, this present life of the faithful, who cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, is day in comparison with unbelievers, who know or love nothing of the true light; but in comparison with the future blessedness, where the true light is seen without end, it is still a most profound night.

Yet because the holy Church knows two spiritual lives in this age—one active and the other contemplative—and because divine Scripture customarily speaks now of one, now of the other, and now of both, earlier, when mentioning the contemplative life, it says of the Lord: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer.”

Then, beginning to speak of the active life: “Behold,” it says, “he stands behind our wall,” and so forth, until it says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed.” When all these things are carefully considered, they encourage us to the duty of good action.

Then it spoke of both together: “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows bend.” For in both lives the beloved feeds among the lilies, because the Lord of his elect delights both in their pure outward activity and in their inward sweet contemplation of eternal things, and is himself refreshed in his members.

This continues until the day of true light breathes forth, because then we will neither be afflicted by the labor of any good work nor will even the more perfect contemplate heavenly things fleetingly and for a moment through a mirror and in an enigma. Rather, the whole Church will see the King of heaven himself in his beauty forever. Because every taste of this vision, however slight, delights the bride of Christ greatly, it fittingly adds:

“Return; be like a gazelle, my beloved,” etc. Since you have aroused and urged me to cultivate the vineyards—that is, to establish and multiply the peoples of the faithful—and since you commanded that the rotten cunning of those who attack these same vineyards be driven away like little foxes; since you wished me to show you my face, even though you have not yet promised to let me clearly behold your face, but speak to me by showing me only a partial knowledge of yourself, as through windows and lattices, I ask you to return frequently from general instruction to illuminate more sublimely the hearts of the perfect.

Just as the sight of a gazelle or a young deer on the mountains is rare but delightful to those who see it, so may you present in exalted minds whatever traces of your greatness you can. I ask you to reveal, even to some of my members along the way and from afar, a glimpse of the sweetness of immortal life which you promise to all your members as their reward.

The name “mountains” also aptly applies to the minds of those who have learned to open the eyes of their hearts to the contemplation of heavenly things, when it says, “Upon the mountains of Bether.” For Bether is interpreted as “rising house” or “house of watchfulness.” Those who rise in mind more diligently than others toward the desires of heavenly things, and who watch more earnestly to receive them, rightly see the heavenly mysteries more excellently than others.

If, however, it is read as some manuscripts have it, “Upon the mountains of Bethel,” that is, “the house of God,” there is no difficulty at all. For it is clear that the hearts of the righteous may rightly be called the mountains of the house of God, in distinction, of course, from the mountains of Samaria and of Esau and others of this kind—that is, from heretics and all the proud.

In another edition, in place of this name, we have seen written in Latin: “Upon the mountains of juices and spices.” This equally suits the minds of the saints, who are not dried up by empty thoughts but, like aromatic trees, are always refreshed by the health-giving juices of inward sweetness and love. These juices and spices have frequently been signified in this book under the names of frankincense, myrrh, aloe, and other such things.

But because lovers of the truth come not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, and from both peoples one Church of the faithful is gathered, it remains, after the calling of Judea and its sweetest conversation with its Redeemer, to relate specifically in what order the Gentiles attained to the knowledge of salvation and with what love they held fast to what they had found. Accordingly, the voice of the beloved Church from the Gentiles follows.

# CHAPTER III

## XI. “In my bed by night I sought,” etc.

Long ago, she says, with great zeal I sought the Lord whom now my soul loves completely. Even then I loved him, although I did not yet know him, insofar as I loved reason, wisdom, truth, and the worship of God.

But because I sought him in my bed—that is, while still subject to the allurements of my flesh—and because I sought him by night—that is, in the darkness of profound ignorance—for no angel, no prophet, and no certain teacher had shown me the light of divine knowledge—I was entirely unable to find the one whom I sought.

When I had truly discovered that I had by no means attained the truth I was seeking, I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, gird myself for the labor of the search that brings salvation, travel through lands and seas, attend publicly and privately upon the instruction of all whom I heard to be wiser, and diligently seek out whatever true wisdom or certainty I might find anywhere that could lead to eternal blessedness.

But although I traversed the world with immense labor and distinguished among the sayings of the wise, I could learn nothing certain or indisputable about the way of truth. That these were the aspirations of the Gentiles, who desired to know God but did not yet know him, is demonstrated by the studies of the philosophers, who traversed so many lands in their investigation of truth and wisdom and composed so many volumes.

Scripture also testifies to this when it says: “The Athenians and all the foreigners residing there devoted their time to nothing except either speaking or hearing something new.” The Apostle’s speech also testifies to it. Preaching in the council of those same Athenians, he said: “As I passed by and observed your objects of worship, I found an altar on which was written, ‘To an unknown god.’ What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you. The God who made the world and everything in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by human hands” (Acts XVII).

The devotion of Cornelius the centurion also testifies to it. He learned to seek knowledge of the divine worship from God through prayers and almsgiving.

Again, the action of the Ethiopian testifies to it. Coming from the ends of the earth to the Lord’s temple, he approached in order to worship the one whom he did not know. He burned with such love for the truth he did not know that, sitting in his chariot, he devoted himself to the writings which widespread report had declared to be divine.

But when the Lord saw his perseverance in the search for truth, he at last deigned to reveal himself to one who had long been seeking him. To the man whom he had inspired to seek, he granted the gift of finding. In accordance with what he had long before promised through the prophet:

“The needy and the poor seek waters, and there are none; their tongue has dried up from thirst. I, the Lord, will hear them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare mountains, and springs in the midst of the plains” (Isa. XLI).

These are the springs of which the thirsty Psalmist said: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI). These are the rivers which he himself promises to his faithful, saying: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII).

Hence it rightly follows:

“The watchmen who guard the city found me,” etc. The watchmen who guard the city are heralds of the truth. With pious solicitude they continually keep watch over the protection of the holy Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, and they labor through the word of preaching lest it be corrupted by the faithless.

These watchmen therefore found the Gentiles intent upon investigating the truth and showed them what they were seeking: Philip opened the light of the Gospel to the eunuch and instructed him in the knowledge of the prophetic words he was reading; Peter filled Cornelius and his companions with the heavenly grace they so greatly desired; Paul made known to the Athenians the God whom they worshiped without knowing him; and others showed to others the presence of their Creator, long sought and desired.

It was as though the Gentiles, who were to be transformed by the Lord’s gift into the bride of Christ, said to the watchmen of the city: “Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?” They said this when they most gladly lent their ears to the teachers who came to them and eagerly took care to discern whether the way of truth was truly the way they preached.

“Shortly after I had passed by them,” etc. Whoever wishes to enjoy the teaching of truth must not approach it hurriedly and carelessly. For one who desires the beloved to come must pass through his preachers most diligently and mingle familiarly with their assemblies, so that he may thereby deserve to attain more closely to the knowledge of the one whom they preach.

We also say that we have “passed through” a book when we have read it through to the end. Hence the angel says to Daniel concerning the mysteries he saw: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII).

“Shortly after I had passed by them,” she says, “I found the one whom my soul loves.” The seeker of truth must pass through the watchmen—that is, as has been said, mingle and unite himself with the assemblies of faithful teachers and review their sayings or writings through frequent meditation.

When he does this for a short time, he immediately finds the beloved whom he was seeking, because, in accordance with the words of Paul and Isaiah, “The Lord has made a brief word upon the earth” (Rom. IX)—namely, the word that says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark XVI).

And concerning this the Apostle says: “But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth.’ This is the word of faith which we preach: that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. X).

“I took hold of him and will not let him go,” etc. The more urgently I held on to the one I had found, she says, the more slowly I had found the one I was seeking. I declare that I will never let him go, but I strive always to persevere and advance in his love, so that I may also endeavor to bring back to faith in his name the Synagogue through which I received the hearing of the word and the ministry of regeneration.

For it is certain that at the end of the age Judea will receive the faith which it now attacks in unbelief. This cannot happen except through the teaching and ministry of those who will then be found faithful among the Gentiles. For the Apostle plainly says: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

What the Church says—“I took hold of him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me”—must not be understood as though she were going to release Christ after instructing the people of the Synagogue in faith in his name. Rather, it means that she loves him with such affection and seeks what belongs to him with such diligence that she strives also to bring her related people under his authority, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us” (Ps. XXIV).

For there is no reason why one who raises his eyes to God in order to ask for mercy should turn them downward after finally receiving mercy. The greatest sign of mercy received is that one always keeps one’s eyes fixed upon God and contemplates his glory without end.

It should also be noted that, even according to the literal sense, the sequence of this chapter was fulfilled in Mary Magdalene, who also bore the figure of the Church. When the Lord, whom she loved with her whole living mind, had been taken from her sight by death and burial, she sought him in her bed, held by such love for him that, even when his limbs had been laid down for rest, the memory of him did not slip from her heart.

She sought him by night—that is, during the two nights in which he rested in the tomb—but still did not find him, because the time for his resurrection had not yet arrived.

At dawn she rose with spices and, anxiously seeking him, came to the tomb. Yet even then she did not immediately find the one she was seeking. First the angels found her, the guardians, in fact, of the Church. When she questioned them about the Lord and heard that he had risen, she finally came to see him.

She took hold of him and did not afterward release him, having truly learned that he had conquered death. She also hastened to bring him into his mother’s house, because she preached his resurrection to the assembly of the disciples who had preceded her in Christ and who had been stirred to piety by their examples.

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles,” etc. If we consider the preceding verses, we will not find in them that the bride reached rest or sleep. Rather, we find that she sprang from her bed and, through the greatest labor of seeking, arrived at the discovery of her beloved.

How, then, does this same beloved adjure the daughters of Jerusalem not to rouse her or awaken her, unless perhaps the soul that knows how to rest in divine love is lulled as if by the most blessed sleep?

Just as a sleeping person closes the eyes of the body to external things and often opens the eyes of the heart in the vision of hidden things, so a mind devoted to heavenly love withdraws itself from concern for visible things in order to awaken more perfectly and freely to the contemplation of invisible things.

Nor is it surprising that love is compared with sleep, since by desire for visible things it turns the mind’s perception away and directs it toward the desire for invisible things. Indeed, it is also compared with death, as this same song says: “Love is strong as death.” For just as death destroys the body, so the brightness of the inner life destroys attachment to outward pleasures.

Therefore the daughters of Jerusalem are rightly adjured—that is, each of the souls of the faithful who anxiously sigh for fellowship with the heavenly citizens—not to rouse the beloved, meaning that they should not obstruct a mind devoted to God from its intent pursuit of heavenly desire through an untimely intrusion.

This can also rightly be understood of the Church’s condition as a whole, for to disturb its peace is to oppose Christ’s will. Since enough has already been said above about this, it is sufficient to speak more briefly now.

Let the reader remember only this: the verse is repeated here in the song of love so that the Lord may show that he takes no less care of the Church gathered from the Gentiles than of that gathered from the Jews, but exercises equal concern for the peace of both, since from both he gathers one most beloved house and family.

Indeed, Judea once believed that it alone was beloved by God and that the word of salvation was entrusted only to it, not also to the uncircumcised Gentiles. Luke bears witness to this when he says:

“The apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. When Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision disputed with him, saying: ‘Why did you enter the house of men who were uncircumcised and eat with them?’”

And in another place: “On the following Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted the things spoken by Paul” (Acts XI; XIII).

Thus what she who adjures the daughters of Jerusalem says—not to rouse the beloved—may also be understood as a command to those who had preceded the Gentiles in faith from among the Jews: that they should not disturb those who had come from the uncircumcision to faith or oppose their salvation.

The words “until she herself wishes” may also be understood to mean that the Church from the Gentiles would voluntarily submit herself to vigils and labors for the Lord.

For this reason there immediately follows the exclamation of the same daughters of Jerusalem, who marvel that the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out upon the nations.

## XII. “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?” etc.

“Who is this?” they say—how worthy of such praise, how worthy of such a miracle! She has not been cleansed by the mystery of circumcision, nor yet washed in the font of regeneration, and already she has been filled with the new grace of the Holy Spirit; already she speaks in tongues and magnifies God. We do not remember that this ever happened among our people from the time when either the covenant of circumcision was given to our fathers or the washing of baptism was given to us.

“She comes up through the wilderness”: she rises from the lowest pleasures to the heights of virtues, lifting her eyes toward the eternal mountains—or rather, lifting them and desiring to reach the one who dwells in heaven.

She comes up through the wilderness—that is, through the midst of those nations which bore no fruitful harvest of virtues, which no prophet of God from his people, no patriarch, and no angel who came to them had instructed in a more salutary way of life. Her faith is all the more miraculous because, having only recently recognized and embraced it, she preserves it invincibly, in accordance with what the Lord himself testifies in her praise: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; you hold fast to my name, and you have not denied my faith” (Rev. II).

This was also said as an example of the people of Israel, who, freed from the darkness of Egyptian slavery, went up through the wilderness on the way to the promised land.

Hence “wilderness” may also rightly be understood in a good sense: as designating a way of life separated from the allurements of the world and devoted solely to searching out God’s law and observing the heavenly commandments. Hungry and thirsty for righteousness, it feeds only on the manna of the heavenly word and drinks from the fountain of life that flows from the spiritual rock.

Hence the Psalmist sings eagerly and ardently: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh longs for you in a desert and trackless and waterless land” (Ps. LXII).

The Church therefore comes up through the wilderness in order to arrive at the promised kingdom. But how she comes up is shown when it follows:

“Like a slender column of smoke from spices.” Smoke usually arises from fire; born aloft, it seeks the heights and gradually withdraws from human sight.

The Church rises in its likeness. Kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit with love for its Creator, it strives toward heavenly things with every effort of the virtues. Nor does it desist from what it has begun until, withdrawn from human affairs, it is caught up into the invisible joys of heavenly life.

And just as smoke at one and the same time partly rises and partly disappears in the higher regions after it has arisen, so the Church, until the end of the age, is continually born anew in some of its members through the grace of the Holy Spirit, while in others, who were previously born to God, it is continually gathered up toward heavenly things.

It is rightly compared not simply with smoke, which can spread in any direction, but with a slender column of smoke, so that both the unity of its faith and its uncomplicated ascent toward higher things may be signified.

But concerning the enemies of God, who are lifted up not by any vision of heavenly desire but solely by the arrogance of pride, it is said that, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, they will fail like smoke. And because, just as worldly desire burns in the mind of the wicked, so, by contrast, virtue blazes and smokes in the heart of the good, rightly, when it had said, “Like a slender column of smoke,” it added:

From the spices of myrrh, etc. Myrrh, which is suitable for embalming bodies—as the sacred rite of the Lord’s burial also demonstrates—signifies abstinence from the flesh. Incense, which is customarily kindled before God in prayers, expresses the power of prayer, as the Psalmist also testifies in prayer: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Psalm 140). The entire powder of the perfumer signifies all works of virtue. These are compared not to whole spices but to spices reduced to powder, so that we may be admonished to discern carefully the good things we do [Col. 1122D] and to examine them, as though through a sieve of diligent discernment, lest anything unsuitable remain in them. The perfumer who prepares and sifts this powder is understood either as the person himself who devotes himself to the practice of virtue, or as the Lord, the giver of virtues.

It should be noted that, when mentioning the spices, he rightly names first myrrh, then incense, and finally the entire powder of the perfumer, in accordance with the order which the Lord also sets forth in the Gospel, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12). In other words: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33). Mortify the desires of the flesh, and offer to God the acceptable vows of the heart.

Therefore the beloved, the heavenly bride of the bridegroom, ascends through the desert [Col. 1123A] like a rod of smoke from spices of myrrh, incense, and the entire powder of the perfumer. For whether it is the holy Church or any perfect soul, it grows daily toward higher things through progress in virtue; moved by the flame of charity, it returns to its author the sweetest ardor of abstinence and prayer—or rather, of all the fruits of the Spirit.

The beloved may also rightly be understood to ascend like a rod of smoke from spices of myrrh, incense, and the entire powder of the perfumer because that one and the same Church is built from the many persons of the faithful. Since they flourish with different virtues, some, like myrrh, devote themselves more earnestly to mortifying the pleasures of the flesh, after the example of him who said, “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9) [Col. 1123B]; some, in the likeness of incense, devote themselves especially to frequent prayers; others labor to offer God the fruits of other good works. Yet all, kindled by the one fire of the Spirit, like a single rod of smoke, seek the heights of heavenly life with undivided zeal in every respect and with shared devotion.

Nor should it seem contrary to the attentive reader, but rather quite consistent, that this same beloved is described both as devoted to sleep and as ascending through the desert. She is shown sleeping when the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured not to awaken her. And the daughters of Jerusalem themselves testify that she is ascending when they immediately reply, “Who is this who ascends through the desert?” At one and the same time she both sleeps and ascends: she withdraws herself, as far as she can, from external cares and carnal desires [Col. 1123C], while through progress in good action or thought she draws near to the vision of her Creator. When she is said to ascend through the desert, the destination and cause of her ascent are also indicated, as is added in the voice of the Church herself—the one who is ascending:

### XIII. Behold, Solomon’s couch, etc.

Her ascent, then, is toward Solomon’s couch and litter—that is, toward the couch and litter of the peaceful king, namely, our Lord and Savior. The couch is that on which she may rest forever in peace; the litter is that from which she may be refreshed without end by the food of life.

The reason for her ascent is that the middle of the litter toward which she ascends is spread with charity. Although the ascent to it is purple—that is, bloodstained through excessive struggle—the sweetness [Col. 1123D] of the charity recognized to be present in it greatly invites the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, souls of religious mind, to climb up to it.

Solomon’s couch, therefore, is the glory of heavenly blessedness, in which the king of peace himself rests forever with his saints. The beloved of that king, namely the Church, advances toward this couch daily through the desert of this world and has already arrived there in part, insofar as she has sent her faithful ahead to future rewards. She will arrive there in her entirety when, at the consummation of the age, the Creator himself, the king of that heavenly city, gathers his elect from the four winds and, as he says elsewhere, “girds himself, makes them recline, and, passing by, ministers to them.”

In this life also, Solomon’s couch is the peaceful way of life of the saints, withdrawn from worldly disturbances [Col. 1124A]. Having suppressed or quieted the conflicts of vice, it imitates the happiness of everlasting peace. Hence the prophet says: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Psalm 71)—that is, in the lofty contemplation of future blessings. The apostle Peter likewise says: “If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you will be blessed, for the Spirit of the glory of God rests upon you” (1 Peter 4:14).

The statement that “sixty strong men, chosen from the strongest of Israel, surround Solomon’s couch” fittingly applies to both couches. For holy preachers protect the Church’s present quiet and peace against the attacks of heretics, while the more perfect continually contemplate, with fixed attention, the inward rest of the heavenly homeland. It is rightly said, therefore, of the couch of that king of peace [Col. 1124B] that strong men surround it. It is rightly added by repetition, “chosen from the strongest of Israel.”

Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” because those who desire either to protect the Church’s present peace by preaching or to behold him who is in heaven by contemplation must be vigilant, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened, and take care to render themselves worthy of the divine vision. “Chosen from the strongest of Israel,” he says, because all who strive toward the joys of the divine vision are rightly designated by the name Israel. But the strongest among them, he says, are those who are either raised up by the gift of heavenly contemplation or undertake the ministry of preaching in the proper manner.

They are also appropriately designated by the number sixty, because such people expect the denarius of eternal recompense for the perfection of good works. God completed the adornment of the world in six days [Col. 1124C] and rested from his works on the seventh; therefore the number six appropriately signifies the light of perfected action, for which eternal rest is hoped. That the rewards of good works are represented by the number ten is known to everyone who knows why those laboring in Christ’s vineyard received a denarius as their wage.

### All holding swords, etc.

Those holding swords are the ones of whom the Apostle says: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). They are thoroughly trained for those battles about which the same Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, etc.” (ibid.).

They are rightly called thoroughly trained, because those who, enclosed in flesh and placed on earth, fight against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places require great skill in warfare [Col. 1124D]. Indeed, they require great skill—or rather, great grace from God—when the frailty of the flesh fights against an archangel, stirred up to battle through so many thousands of years.

### Each one’s sword upon his thigh, etc.

The thigh commonly signifies carnal descent. Hence it is written: “All the souls of those who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy” (Exodus 1). The soldiers of Christ have a sword upon their thigh when they restrain the movement of carnal desires with the severity of the spiritual word.

They do this because of the terrors of the night—that is, lest the snares of the ancient tempter overthrow them if he finds them secure and unarmed, and, after conquering them, defile Solomon’s true couch, which they ought to have guarded [Col. 1125A]. This may equally be understood of both couches mentioned above: the present peace of the Church and the future peace of the eternal King.

Holy teachers fear lest the condition of the present Church be violated through the darkness of heretics. Those accustomed to open the eye of the mind to the contemplation of future joys fear lest the night of demonic disturbance obscure the light of divine revelation within them.

If the strongest of Israel, in whom there is no deceit, who are thoroughly trained for battle, have a sword upon their thigh because of the terrors of the night, what ought I and those like me to do? How greatly must we serve the Lord in fear, since we are less instructed for spiritual combat and less strong for accomplishing what we describe? Our one refuge is wholly to cling to him and place our hope in him, since he cannot be conquered; with the prophet, we must seek his protection, saying more and more often: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 36).

He is my light, namely, to train me for battle; and my salvation, to make me strong and unconquerable in battle. For if we persevere in preaching, perhaps we too may deserve to hear with that same prophet: “His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night” (Psalm 90).

Some interpret the strong men who surround Solomon’s couch as angels who fight for the peace of the holy Church against the aerial powers. Their interpretation appears to conflict with the statement, “Each one’s sword upon his thigh.” For how can those who have no flesh, from whose nature they derive their existence, bind or restrain the allurements of the flesh with the sword of abstinence? [Col. 1125C]

The Church coming from the nations therefore says: “Behold, seventy strong men, chosen from the strongest of Israel, surround Solomon’s couch,” and so forth—as though she were openly saying:

“Why are you amazed, daughters of Jerusalem”—that is, peoples believing from Judea—“that I ascend through the desert in the likeness of sweet-smelling spices of virtue? See that the king to whose fellowship I hasten is peaceful; behold, that couch of his inner rest is safe from the snares of the wicked and accessible only to the good, and I hasten to reach it. But, if you delight to hear more about his riches, I shall unfold them further.”

### King Solomon made himself a litter, etc.

The litter is so called because it either carries the bodies of those sitting or reclining at a banquet, or is customarily carried from place to place as circumstances require. The holy Church is rightly compared to it [Col. 1125D]: she raises believers to the banquet of eternal blessedness, and she herself is carried throughout the entire world through the ministry of her preachers.

The Lord made this litter for himself from the wood of Lebanon because he built the Church from souls strong in courage and steadfastness. The trees of Lebanon greatly excel in height, beauty, and their naturally incorruptible character.

### He made its columns of silver.

“James, Cephas, and John,” he says, “who were considered to be pillars.” He made these columns of silver because, to confirm the faith and support the condition of the Church, he established the holy teachers with the brilliance of heavenly speech.

### A golden backrest.

He made a backrest in the litter [Col. 1126A] when he promised the faithful the hope of everlasting rest. “Take my yoke upon you,” he says, “and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11). He made this backrest golden because he prepared for us the radiant glory of the eternal rest of the divine vision. Hence it is said: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14).

### A purple ascent.

True purple is dyed with the blood of shellfish. Solomon’s litter therefore has a purple ascent because our King and Lord “loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Revelation 1). The ascent to this litter is found to be purple alone because no one enters the Church unless imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion. Hence he himself says [Col. 1126B]: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6).

### He spread its middle with charity, etc.

He spread it with that very charity with which he suffered for us: “No one has greater charity than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). As the Apostle says: “God commends his own charity toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5).

Through this charity he prepared the middle of his Church like a floor spread out, where faithful souls might rest softly, because he filled its entire interior with love of the things above. This is what he added: “For the daughters of Jerusalem”—that is, for souls aflame with desire for heavenly things.

For the more greatly God commended his charity to us by suffering for us [Col. 1126C], the more people he kindled to love him in return and to suffer for his sake. The purple ascent may also be understood particularly of those who shed their blood for Christ. They are rightly said to have ascended to the golden backrest by a purple ascent, because they reached the charity of everlasting rest through labor and by the craft of tribulation.

The following appropriately applies to them: “He spread its middle with charity.” For this reason they are ready to pour out their blood for the heavenly King: he has inflamed the middle of his litter—that is, their hearts—with his charity.

Hence, when the Apostle was describing the purple ascent of the litter [Col. 1126D], saying, “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing,” he immediately took care to add a statement about the golden backrest, saying: “Testing produces hope, but hope does not disappoint.” Then he concluded with the charity with which its middle was spread: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts” (Romans 5).

While the daughters of Jerusalem were amazed and praising the Church from the nations, which ascends to heaven like a rod of smoke from spices, the Church herself gives the reasons for her ascent. She explains that the couch of the peaceful king, toward which she hastens, is protected from the attacks of the wicked; that his litter, where she hopes to be refreshed, although its ascent is arduous, nevertheless has a backrest radiant like gold [Col. 1127A]; and that its middle is spread with his charity, for which reason she hastens to ascend, knowing that “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

After these words, in a marvelous and fitting order, having recounted the gifts of her king, she begins also to praise his very appearance and adornment. She invites everyone to behold him; and after she herself has been summoned, she takes care, in assuming the office of evangelization, to summon others as well. Accordingly, the text continues:

### Come forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.

The daughters of Zion are the same as the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls sighing for the joys of the heavenly homeland. Zion is called “speculation” or “watchtower,” while Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” Both names suit the inhabitants of that same heavenly city [Col. 1127B], where they enjoy perpetual peace and always contemplate the face of their Creator.

“Come forth, therefore,” he says, “daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon.” Come forth from the turbulent way of life of the world, so that you may be able to see the king of peace. Come forth in mind and action from the midst of Babylon, you who desire to have a share in the heavenly Jerusalem, in accordance with the command of that true Solomon, who says: “Come out of her, my people, lest you become participants in her sins.”

For this reason he himself, wishing to separate us from fellowship with the world and summon us to heavenly joys, chose to suffer for us outside the walls of the city, as the Apostle beautifully and fully explains, saying: “Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Let us therefore go out to him [Col. 1127C] outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13).

And because our same Lord Jesus Christ must be confessed not only as the true Son of God but also as the true Son of man—the Son of God born eternally before the ages, but the Son of man made in time at the end of the ages—it is rightly added immediately after the words, “See, daughters of Zion, King Solomon”:

### In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.

This is plainly to say: “See the Lord in the humanity which he received from his Virgin Mother and placed at the right hand of the Father’s majesty.” His mother crowned him with a diadem when the blessed and undefiled Virgin, conceiving from the Holy Spirit, supplied him from her own flesh with the material of that most holy flesh [Col. 1127D]. Appearing in it to the world and dwelling among us, he destroyed the kingdom of death by dying and restored life to us by rising again; and by ascending into heaven he exalted that flesh with the glory of an everlasting kingdom.

When the daughters of Zion see King Solomon in the beauty of his natural being, they gaze in astonishment also upon the diadem with which his mother crowned him. For the elect, while believing and confessing the glory of the Son of God to be equal to that of the Father and the Holy Spirit, also recognize that the assumption of human nature—in which he conquered the dominion of death—has been glorified forever, not by the power of its own substance but through the operation of the Word who assumed it, that is, the only Son of God.

One of the daughters [Col. 1128A] of Zion, herself most noble and already gone forth from the boundaries of earthly desire, spoke in supreme amazement at the vision of this diadem: “But we see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2).

### On the day of his betrothal, etc.

This refers to the time of his incarnation, when he came forth from a virginal womb as a bridegroom from his chamber in order to join the Church to himself. That was the day of the gladness of his heart, because he rejoiced that, through the dispensation of that same incarnation, the world would be led to the recognition and vision of his eternal divinity.

Hence, when many had gathered to his faith, it is written [Col. 1128B]: “In that hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones’” (Luke 10).

Hence the Redeemer himself, after the human race had been led back to the heavenly realm through his blood, speaks to the citizens of heaven, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke 15).

Therefore, when the daughters of Jerusalem had earlier marveled at the bride’s arrival and said, “Who is this who ascends through the desert?” and so forth, she aptly responds by praising the bridegroom’s couch, praising his litter, and finally praising the bridegroom himself, toward whose embrace she hastens.

She recalls the humanity assumed for her sake into God, which the mystery of the incorruptible Mother brought forth when the time of his response arrived [Col. 1128C], so as to show that she rightly longs for the glory of his divine vision, for whose sake he had assumed the appearance of human nature.

Thus, deservedly, she who subjected herself so greatly to the praises of her Redeemer, and who, in order to praise him, invites her own companions—the daughters of Zion—with the zeal of maternal affection, herself also receives from that same bridegroom and Redeemer a worthy recompense of praise. His voice now follows:

## CHAPTER IV

### XIV. How beautiful you are, my beloved! etc.

He called the Church beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful because he saw her to be praiseworthy both in action and in preaching. In action, because she ascends toward him through the desert like a rod of smoke from spices; in preaching, because she strives to make even her neighbors ascend to fellowship with him, saying: “Come forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.”

It is rightly presented first in action and afterward in preaching, following the example of the one of whom it is written: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

### Your eyes are like those of doves, etc.

Your perceptions are excellent and venerable through contemplation of spiritual things. By them you have deserved to see and understand my gifts, which you recently expounded, and my diadem, which you praised. Since, as we mentioned above, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, spiritual grace is rightly signified by its name.

### Apart from what lies hidden within.

Apart from the invisible reward in the heavenly places, which cannot yet be seen by you while you are journeying on earth. For this is the greater beauty of glory, which cannot presently be assessed worthily.

And beautifully, when he praises the simplicity of her eyes—that is, her knowledge of hidden things—he first calls her “beloved,” in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

### Your hair is like flocks of goats, etc.

If the keenness of spiritual perceptions is rightly understood in the bride’s eyes, the purity of innumerable general thoughts may suitably be understood in her hair. In the saints, even when such thoughts are sometimes formed for the administration of temporal matters, they never cease to be formed with a view to heavenly things.

For it is written that Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that no delay might be caused for him in Asia. For he was hastening, if it were possible, to celebrate the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem (Acts 20). In this matter he was occupied with thoughts concerning an earthly journey, but he undertook that earthly journey with the intention of receiving a heavenly reward.

The same may be understood of the craft of tentmaking which he practiced with Aquila and Priscilla. The thoughts with which they carried it out were indeed temporal, but they were drawn to this work by their contemplation of eternal things, so that through this earthly labor they might assist the ministry of the Gospel, which was heavenly.

Hence the bride’s hair is aptly compared to flocks of goats that have ascended from Mount Gilead. These animals are clean and are accustomed to climb steep rocks or trees in search of food. In the same way, as we have said, the thoughts of the elect, although they deal with earthly matters, nevertheless aim at heavenly things; and even when they care for the support of the flesh, they direct the mind’s gaze rather toward the soul’s welfare and heavenly nourishment.

The preachers of the holy Church may also be understood in the bride’s eyes. Through them the heavenly mysteries, which the general multitude of believers neither sees [Note: [Col. 1129] This passage appears mutilated. Perhaps one should read: “Through whom the heavenly mysteries … the general multitude of believers sees,” with the words quae and neque deleted. EDIT.].

The faithful peoples may be understood in the hair. Although they are less learned in seeing and guiding the steps of the Church, they nevertheless provide her with the greatest adornment through the multitude of their service.
