The Lord himself, when he preached through disciples sent out to preach that “you will be hated by all because of my name,” immediately added by way of consolation: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21). This is plainly to say: “Although the hatred of persecutors rages, they cannot snatch away even the least of those who belong to me—that is, even a hair from your head.”

The hair is rightly compared to such flocks of goats. For goats commonly signify sinners. Since the whole Church truly confesses that it cannot be without sin, how much more must this be acknowledged by those whose life is spent among the common people, since “we all offend in many ways” (James 3)!

The faithful therefore have sin, but through daily progress in good works they nevertheless strive toward that life in which they will be free from every sin. For this reason it is aptly added concerning these same goats: “Those who have ascended from Mount Gilead.” For all who have been joined to the body of their Redeemer dwell upon the mystical mountain.

The does, however, have ascended from that same mountain when they seek its higher slopes for the sake of pasture. This occurs when the humble, conscious of their sins and frailty, are inflamed by fear of their own weakness and continually strive to raise themselves toward the heavenly pastures of life in Christ.

We read in the book of Numbers and in Chronicles that Mount Gilead had very good and abundant pastures. This suits that lofty and exceedingly fruitful mountain, of which the city built upon it—that is, the holy Church—customarily says: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a pasture of grass” (Psalm 22).

The name of the mountain itself is also fitting: it is called “heap of testimony.” The Lord is the heap of testimony, because in him the multitude of all the saints, namely the living stones who have been proved by the testimony of faith, is gathered and united, as the Apostle says.

The bride’s hair, therefore, is compared to flocks of goats which, grazing on this mountain, continually strive to ascend higher. Whether they are the temporal thoughts of the elect or the more fragile multitudes of the Church, the less they find themselves free from fault, the more earnestly they seek the help of the one whom they understand must free them.

### Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, etc.

Just as the Church’s more fragile people, still devoted to earthly activities, are signified in the hair, so the more perfect—those suited to govern the Church—are designated in the teeth. The former excel in number, the latter in firmness. The former refresh those within by the word; the latter, although they grasp less of the inner mysteries, adorn the Church outwardly with good works.

Would not he to whom it was said, “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10), rightly be called the God of the Church? “Kill,” that is, teach them to anathematize the evil in which they were and what they worshiped; then insert them, once made good through their profession of the true faith, into the unity of your body, which is the Church of Christ.

Indeed, the same teachers were earlier designated by the name of eyes. They are eyes because they perceive sharply the secrets of spiritual mysteries; they are teeth because they rebuke the wicked with the word of truth and, once reproved and cleansed, transfer them into the holy members of the Church.

They are the Church’s teeth because they prepare for her little ones the bread of the word of God, which those little ones are not yet able to chew themselves. Pious nurses commonly break pieces of bread with their teeth and, while nursing, place the small chewed portions in the mouths of infants, until they gradually wean them from milk and bring them to the use of bread.

Thus the holy mother Church has teachers who, like breasts, offer the milk of gentler instruction to beginners. She has these same teachers, who are not ignorant of how to offer the bread of stronger teaching to those making good progress. But, so that they may advance properly, it is necessary to invite them gradually and step by step to learn higher things; first, the clearer matters among the spiritual mysteries, examined with careful and diligent exposition, must be entrusted to them as though already chewed by the teeth, so that by practicing these things frequently they may gradually become capable of the inner mysteries.

These teeth are rightly compared to a flock of shorn sheep that have ascended from the washing, because they have been cleansed in the fountain of baptism and stripped of their possessions.

It belongs to everyone to be purified by the washing of Christ’s life, since “unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit,” and so forth (John 3). But it belongs to the perfect—especially to those entrusted with the care of feeding his sheep—to renounce everything they possess. The first and chief teeth of the Church, namely the apostles, and a very large multitude of that primitive Church, are indeed recorded to have done this.

### All bearing twins, etc.

Christ’s sheep bear twin offspring because all whom the holy teachers beget for God through preaching are instructed in the twofold love of God and neighbor. They bear twins because the disciples whom they teach are imbued with knowledge of faith and right action.

“And none among them is barren”: among the sheep of the supreme shepherd there is no one who does not produce the offspring of good works. Among them are also many who rejoice in the offspring of both works and teaching.

Nor will those be counted among the barren who, washed in the fountain of salvation, are immediately taken from this life. They had offspring of faith, which either they themselves professed on their own behalf or others professed on theirs; they also had the intention of good action, which, had they been allowed to remain, they would have practiced in fellowship among Christ’s sheep.

Of such people it is written: “Made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled a long age” (Wisdom 4). “His soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity” (ibid.).

### Your lips are like a scarlet thread, etc.

The bride’s lips are compared to scarlet because the Church never ceases to preach the price of the Lord’s blood, by which she was redeemed. Rather, she diligently sings: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

It should be noted that her lips are compared not simply to scarlet, but to a scarlet thread. A thread customarily binds the hair. If the faithful peoples are understood in the bride’s hair, what is the thread that binds them and fits them more suitably to the head except the doctrine of truth?

By this doctrine the unformed minds of believers must be strengthened and applied more diligently to the love and worship of their Creator, lest, left unbound, they run loose into empty acts and withdraw from the embrace or adornment of the true head, and lest by untimely laxity they impede the very eyes—that is, those who ought to have shown them beforehand the light of righteousness.

For just as the good deeds of disciples sometimes become an example of virtue to their teachers, so their negligence more often produces harm to their teachers’ good action.

“Like a scarlet thread,” he says, “are your lips, and your speech is sweet,” because the Church customarily strengthens and, as it were, dyes with the memory of the Lord’s Passion her doctrine—which restrains the minds of the weak from wantonness.

Nothing restrains the pleasure-loving more effectively from carnal desires than hearing or recalling that the Lord of glory deigned to become incarnate and suffer for them. Hence the Lord considers such speech sweet, because he receives it with great pleasure when he sees us recounting and meditating upon this among ourselves—the very purpose for which he came to us from heaven.

If we say that thoughts are figured in the hair and the spiritual perceptions of the faithful in the eyes, the conclusion of the exposition is the same. We restrain the unceasing wandering of superfluous thoughts by no other means more effectively than by frequently remembering and continually recounting the Lord’s blood.

We also often reject harmful thoughts when we turn them over in an unwary mind, then suddenly, recalled to God, imprint the sign of the holy cross upon our breast and cast away what we were wickedly contemplating. In this way we bind our hair with a scarlet thread, because we restrain the looseness of our thoughts with the triumph of the sacred blood.

If this salutary bond is absent [Col. 1132B], they defile the entire beauty of the head by their wavering. For they disturb the mind’s tranquility and cover the sharpness of the eyes, because through the wicked meditation of carnal things they obscure the grace of spiritual perception.

### Like a fragment of a pomegranate, etc.

We have already taught above that the cheeks signify modesty, since, when we blush, a sudden redness commonly suffuses them. Because the pomegranate is rose-colored, it suitably signifies the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, just as scarlet does.

It was fitting that the manner of our redemption should be made known through the frequent repetition of figures in the sacred song, as also in the other writings of prophecy. Since the holy Church is not ashamed of the cross of Christ, but rejoices in insults and sufferings for Christ and customarily bears the banner of his cross upon her face, she is rightly said to have cheeks like a pomegranate.

It is not without significance that she is compared not to a whole pomegranate but to a fragment of it. In a split pomegranate both the portion of redness that was exposed is visible and the portion of whiteness that had been hidden within is revealed.

The bride therefore has the redness of a pomegranate in her cheeks when the Church confesses the sacrament of the Lord’s cross in words. She also displays the whiteness of that split fruit when, pressed by hardships, she proves the purity of her heart both in action and when the cross of her Redeemer reveals what saving grace it contains within.

She likewise displays the pomegranate color in her cheeks when her first and most eminent members—the holy martyrs—shed their blood for Christ. She adds the white when those same martyrs shine with miracles either during their suffering or after their suffering has been completed.

Nor should it be passed over that a pomegranate encloses a great abundance of seeds beneath a single outer rind; hence it is also called a “seeded apple.” These seeds cannot be seen while the fruit remains whole, but when it is split, their countless number becomes clear.

So too the holy Church, the more she is compelled to be broken by adversity, the more clearly she shows how many grains of virtue she contains beneath the covering of one faith.

It is rightly added: “Apart from what lies hidden within.” Everyone can hear the Church’s confession of the life-giving cross, and everyone can see the Church’s hardships. Unbelievers, together with believers, can also observe and marvel at the brilliance of her charisms, which heals the weak, raises the dead, cleanses lepers, casts out demons, and performs other such works [Col. 1133A].

But the Church alone knows how greatly she is held by the love of invisible life, how intensely she burns with the vision of her Creator, and how ardently she loves the progress of her members.

As the tower of David is your neck, etc. We have already said concerning the neck that it signifies the holy teachers, who continually increase the Church by nourishing it with spiritual sustenance and strengthen it in faith through words of holy exhortation. But the fact that the neck is placed in the middle and joins the body to the head also aptly suits those through whose ministry the Church is joined to Christ, since they have handed on to it the nourishment of life received from the Lord himself. Concerning them the Apostle, commending the grace of the Gospel, says: “Although it first began to be spoken through the Lord, [Col. 1133B] it was confirmed to us by those who heard it” (Hebrews 2). Hence it is written of the same matter: “He gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds; and all ate and were satisfied” (Matthew 14). This was done bodily in such a way that it also signified the Lord’s spiritual deeds: namely, that he entrusted the heavenly bread of teaching to the first members of his Church, that is, the apostles; they then set it before the body of that same Church subject to them; and thus, through ministers of the word succeeding one another in due order, its salutary nourishment reached its fullness throughout the whole world.

This neck is rightly said to be like the tower of David. For if the city of David is the Church of Christ, the tower in that city is the unconquerable steadfastness of preachers, who, for defending the structures of the faith and repelling the weapons of its enemies, have been built [Col. 1133C] higher than the other faithful by the strong hand of the desirable King—for this is what the name David signifies. The battlements with which this tower has been built are understood as the defenses of the holy Scriptures or of divine spiritual gifts. [Col. 1134A] The Lord made the bride’s neck like a tower when, by giving the grace of the Holy Spirit, he made the first teachers of the Church invincible against their enemies. He added battlements to that tower when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24) and prove, through the words of the preceding fathers, that the words of his preaching were true. He added battlements to the tower when he also bestowed on them gifts for performing signs, so that by new works of virtue they might establish that what they preached as new was divine, and, by healing bodily diseases, more easily draw those whom they instructed toward the salvation of the soul.

A thousand shields hang from it, etc. The thousand shields hanging from the tower of David are the innumerable protections of divine defense. Through them the holy preachers themselves were assisted by the Lord, so that they could not be defeated by their enemies [Col. 1134B]; and they also teach their hearers to be aided against the attacks of enemies, whether visible or invisible. “The entire armor of the mighty” means every form of preparation, whether of action or of heavenly teaching, by which these same teachers not only escape the ranks of evil spirits but also overcome them, when by preaching they snatch many whom those spirits had held deceived from their power and transfer them from vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy.

And rightly, where spiritual warfare is mentioned, the tower of David, not the tower of Solomon, is set forth as the example. The name and person of each king very often customarily represent the eternal King; but since David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance,” this name is rightly applied where the Lord is teaching the Church to wage war against her enemies. Thus she proceeds fearlessly into battle because she remembers that she is aided by him [Col. 1134C] who cannot be defeated, and strives to conquer with greater urgency because she knows that his face is desirable—the face of the one to whom she will come after the enemy has been overcome.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1133]

[Col. 1133C] Two breasts of yours, etc. The same mysteries of Christ and the Church are repeated in many ways and through many kinds of figures, but each repetition always contributes something new, either supplying an argument for the same mysteries or, through its very novelty, delighting the minds of the hearers more fully. [Col. 1133D] The teachers who above were designated by the names of eyes, teeth, or neck are now expressed under the name of breasts. They can rightly be called eyes because they perceive the hidden mysteries of the sacraments; rightly teeth because, by correcting the wicked, they metaphorically chew them and transfer them, softened and humbled, into the body of the Church; rightly neck because, by preaching eternal joys to the entire body of the Church, they supply it with something like vital breath and prepare the nourishment of teachings by which it may be restored to salvation.

They are now also most appropriately called breasts because they pour the milk of the saving word into those who are still infants in Christ. It is not without reason that, with a numerical qualification, he says “two breasts,” since no woman customarily has more or fewer than two breasts. He says “two breasts” in order to indicate that the infants of two peoples—the Jewish people [Col. 1134C] and the Gentile people—are to be nourished for faith. Thus Paul says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we might go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision,” and so forth (Galatians 2).

But Peter, sent [Col. 1134D] to the circumcision, see what he says: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational, guileless milk, so that by it you may grow into salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious” (1 Peter 2). By saying this he also explains the mystery of the Church’s breasts, declaring that it is rational to desire and taste milk because the Lord is sweet. Again, let us see whether Paul, who was sent to the uncircumcision, also performs the office of the breasts. For he says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

These two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe, since they are the offspring of her to whom this song so often says: “Be like, my beloved, a doe or a fawn of the stags.” They are like the fawns of a doe because, with [Col. 1135A] the purest eyes of their hearts, they discern what must be done and what must be avoided; they perceive with keen minds the path of the virtues on which they must walk and the winding turns of words that must be shunned; and they rejoice to fly with the swift course of good works from the valley of tears to the place that God has appointed, so that, walking from virtue to virtue, they may deserve to see him in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of eternal dwelling.

For fawns are especially distinguished by the swiftness of their feet and the sharpness of their eyes; hence those who are commanded to point out the way of knowledge and virtue to the inexperienced are appropriately compared to their nature. “Like two twin fawns of a doe,” he says. They are rightly called twins because, formed in one and the same faith and renewed by the same sacraments, the teachers of both peoples gather into the one Church of Christ all [Col. 1135B] whom they raise. Hence Peter says concerning those who believed from the uncircumcision: “God, who knows hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us; and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15).

Who feed among the lilies, etc. The holy teachers feed upon the pure and shining flowers of the divine Scriptures. And, so that the milk of saving doctrine with which they nourish the little ones may not fail, they continually read in the writings of the fathers what they ought to do and how they ought to teach; they fill their breasts, as it were, with life-giving juices, and do so until the end of the age. For after that day has dawned which the Psalmist desired when he said, “One day in your courts is better than a thousand” (Psalm 83), there will no longer be time either for teaching or for learning.

[Col. 1135C] Then the prophecy will be fulfilled which says: “No longer shall each one teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all shall know me” (Jeremiah 31). When all the darkness of this world has been entirely bent down and consumed, the saints “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13), each receiving rewards according to what he has learned, done, and taught.

As far as natural reasoning is concerned, it is beautifully said that the withdrawal of night is the inclination of the shadows, because the darkness of night, as the philosophers say, is nothing other than the shadow of the earth. The sun, circling around the earth, carries light and day with it; on the other side, namely where it is absent, it leaves the shadow of the earth. This is that primordial division by which God divided light from darkness.

These shadows, when the sun sets, then begin gradually to rise; and as far as the setting sun has descended beneath the earth, so far do they grow and rise, until, with the sun positioned beneath the middle of the earth at midnight, they themselves, fully erect, occupy the middle of the earth [Col. 1135D]. Then, as the sun gradually advances, they too gradually decline toward the west, until, when dawn appears, they disappear completely, having wholly inclined themselves.

The shadows of the earth do not reach the stars because the sun, created larger than the earth, makes the shadow pointed; before it can reach the stars, the shadow fails, while the sun’s radiance, diffused on every side around the earth, freely beholds the stars that it illuminates.

Night, therefore, is the present life; the sun of righteousness is Christ. [Col. 1136A] The mass of earthly desires often hides his light from us, so that he is not seen. As he justly withdraws from us, so we become darkened; as he mercifully returns, so we are illuminated. But we shall truly enjoy his light when, after all the darkness of the present affliction and blindness has been inclined and dispersed, we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Yet, mindful in every way of our salvation, he did not leave the night of this life wholly dark. Rather, as though fixing stars in the heavens, he set before us the examples of the saints, by which we might walk with an unimpeded step along the path of our works.

I will go to the mountain of myrrh, etc. Myrrh expresses the mortification of the flesh or the endurance of sufferings for the sake of piety; frankincense expresses the devotion of lofty-reaching prayer. The mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense are the very elevation [Col. 1136B] of mind belonging to those who productively overcome the struggle with the flesh and ardently raise themselves toward the love of heavenly things.

The Lord goes to that mountain and hill because he deigns frequently to visit and inhabit the hearts of those who devote themselves to virtue. Hence he says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Corinthians 6). Thus, while praising the Church and enumerating the individual members of her virtues, the Lord suddenly adds: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” This is plainly to say: “I will frequent and glorify with a gracious and merciful illumination those whom I regard as exalted in the virtue of suffering or prayer. I will often come and make my dwelling with those whom I see cleansing themselves from bodily defilement and perfecting the sanctification of the Spirit in divine fear.”

[Col. 1136C] He does not propose to abandon the one whom he has been praising and go to others, but because he intends daily to add new peoples to that same Church of his and spread her throughout the whole world. These words may perhaps also appropriately be understood as referring to the calling of the synagogue, since the speech concerns the Church from the Gentiles and the calling of the synagogue that will take place at the end.

For he gives an answer to her desire, expressed earlier when, after finding him, she said: “I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house.” In the immediately preceding verse he taught that the Church of the Gentiles would never let him go, when he said: “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a doe, which feed among the lilies, until the day dawns and the shadows decline.” That is: there will be teachers in you who instruct the two peoples and, united in humble and chaste love [Col. 1136D], bring them into concord until the end of the age, when the day of eternal recompense appears. Then, because he is also going to call Judea, he indicates it more clearly by adding: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” This does not mean that, when he comes, he can find her already elevated in virtues, since, after receiving a bill of divorce, she had long ago departed from his faith; rather, by coming he will make her worthy of his fellowship. Therefore he immediately and appropriately adds what follows concerning the surpassing beauty of the one and the same Church, which is to be gathered either from Judea or from all the nations throughout the world:

You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, etc. You are beautiful not only in the more eminent members of the elect, whom I have specifically enumerated, but also in those who appear small [Col. 1137A] and fragile; you shine with the beauty of virtues and are free from the stain of vices. For he blessed all who fear the Lord, “the small together with the great” (Psalm 113).

Hence John says in his Apocalypse concerning the heavenly homeland of this same Church: “Nothing defiled shall enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, but only those who are written in the book of life of the Lamb” (Apocalypse 13).

These words do not mean that in this life any saint can be wholly free from every fault or perfect in all virtues, since it is truthfully written: “There is no one righteous on earth who does good and never sins” (Ecclesiastes 7). Rather, they mean that the holy Church, insofar as she is the Church of Christ, is pure in right faith and clean in works. If any impurity or wickedness touches her, it does not belong to her but must be expelled [Col. 1137B] from her as something foreign, with every effort and as quickly as possible.

The saying of blessed John is similar: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin” (1 John 3), because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin when he has been born of God. Insofar as the seed of God’s grace by which they have been reborn is present in them, they cannot sin; insofar as they do sin, the rebirthing grace has for a time withdrawn from them, so that they may recognize what they are in themselves—those who had been living righteously through that grace.

After this life, that grace will introduce them, cleansed from every evil and shining in complete beauty, into the city in which, as has been said, nothing polluted can enter. Then this saying will truly be fulfilled in the bride beloved by the Bridegroom, toward which she now strives with all the effort of virtue: that she be altogether beautiful [Col. 1137C] and have no stain in her.

Come from Lebanon, etc. If we follow the Hebrew etymology, Lebanon means “whiteness”; if the Greek, “frankincense.” Indeed, above, where we read “to the hill of frankincense,” some manuscripts have “to the hill of Lebanon.” It is readily apparent to everyone that both names signify diligence in virtue.

The bride of the Lord, that is, the Church or the holy soul, comes to the Lord not only when, summoned from the body, she receives the reward of everlasting recompense; even while dwelling in this age, she advances toward better things by however many increases in good works she makes, and by as many steps, so to speak, she approaches him who alone is good. She reaches him, however, when, released from bodily bonds, she deserves to see his face.

[Col. 1137D] The Lord sees the bride situated in Lebanon and urges her to come to him, because when he sees a faithful soul adorned with good works and offering him the incense of pure prayer, he is pleased with her pious efforts and exhorts her to persist in what she has begun. He does this either through the hidden prompting of his inspiration, through meditation on the divine Scriptures, through the exhortations of other believers, or even through the adversities or benefits experienced by those who labor. Through a kindly providence toward her, he acts so that, whether worn down by the troubles of her present exile, she may desire more ardently the homeland of everlasting rest, or, lifted up by present progress in goodness, she may more sweetly long for the unfailing joys of the heavenly city.

He commands the bride a third time to come from Lebanon because he requires in his elect the progress of good [Col. 1138A] action, saving speech, and pure thought. Or certainly, he says: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come: come by the excellent life that you practice while living in the body; come, released from the body, to receive the soul’s everlasting life; come a third time, having received your body again, to see the complete joys of the resurrection.”

And because many of the elect receive an everlasting reward not only for the purity of their own lives but also for the correction of those whom they instructed, the text appropriately continues:

You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, etc. Amana, Sanir, and Hermon are mountains of Cilicia or Judea, providing lairs for lions and leopards, as well as for other wild animals. They plainly signify the proud hearts of unbelievers, in which unclean spirits have their dwelling. [Col. 1138B] In contrast, the Lord says through the prophet concerning the elect: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 7).

Lions signify demons because of their pride; leopards, because of their cruelty or the variety of their wicked arts. When the holy Church, through her preachers, has rescued such souls from the power of darkness and turned them toward recognition of the true light, the preachers receive the crown of life not only for themselves but also for those whom they have won for the Lord, according to the saying of Proverbs: “The crown of the aged is their children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Proverbs 17).

The Apostle says concerning those whom he taught: “What is our glory, or hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?” (1 Thessalonians 2).

[Col. 1138C] It should be noted that he does not say, “You shall be crowned from Amana, Sanir, and Hermon,” but “from the summit of Amana” and “from the strength of Sanir and Hermon.” When the ignoble common people are converted by the Church to the Lord, she obtains a crown from the sides of the mountains in which the beasts had hidden, because she receives a reward from the salvation of a rebellious people. But when she brings the leaders of wickedness themselves, the notorious persecutors, onto the way of life, she is crowned from the summit and peak of the mountains, because the palm of recompense grows with the labor of the struggle.

A similar thought is expressed in what follows: “From the lairs of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” The lairs of lions among the mountains of leopards are those who, [Col. 1138D] driven by the fiercer rage of evil spirits, prevail by force and fraud in harming Christ’s flock. When the Church has chastised them and recalled them to the grace of humility and piety, she too will be crowned through them, because she will rejoice in their everlasting salvation.

Those who possess no opposing strength and pursue the good only through deceit are not called lairs of lions but, more appropriately, lairs of foxes. Hence the Lord says to the scribe who deceitfully promised him service but had no power against the Church: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8). By the name of foxes he signified that man’s frivolity and deceitfulness; by the designation of birds, the exaltation of his mind. But when the Church has saved these people as well, the Son of Man comes to rest there through the merit of humility and sincerity [Col. 1139A], where previously wicked spirits had arrogated dwellings for themselves of boastfulness and frivolity.

You have wounded my heart, my sister, etc. This passage can be understood simply, since he may have wished, by mentioning a wounded heart, to express the greatness of the love he has for the Church. He rightly calls her both his sister and his bride, because he has joined her to himself by the covenant of the heavenly bridal chamber and because he also deigned to become human and naturally to be her brother.

It may also be understood according to what Isaiah says: “He was wounded because of our iniquities; he was crushed because of our crimes” (Isaiah 53). He then explains what is especially the cause of his receiving this wound, saying:

With one of your eyes, etc. We said above [Col. 1139B] that by the eyes of the Church are understood either her spiritual senses or those who customarily see and demonstrate her spiritual realities, namely, her teachers. In the hair, moreover, is understood the multitude of the people. Although they cannot reach the height of that saying in which the Lord says, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matthew 19), they nevertheless tend toward heavenly things by that path of good actions which he mentioned beforehand, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid.).

There, however, when the eyes and hair are described in the plural, a multitude either of rulers or of hearers is indicated. Here, by “one [Col. 1139C] of your eyes,” the unity of the teachers or of the spiritual knowledge that they teach is commended, concerning which it is written: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4).

Likewise, in “one lock of your neck” the unity of those who customarily cling to their spiritual teachers with devout affection is praised, covering them with their reverent services as hair covers the neck. For above it was evident that the same teachers are indicated by the neck of the Church.

Luke designates the unity signified by the lock when he says: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4); nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them (ibid.). What the neck, to which that lock was attached, was doing, he indicates immediately afterward, saying: “With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” (Acts 6).

[Col. 1139D] He therefore says: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” As though he were plainly saying: “In the whole form of your body, by which you are spread far and wide throughout the world, O Catholic Church, you appear beautiful and spotless to me. But this is what wonderfully inflames me to love you above all else: that you are shown to possess the unity of the same faith and love both in your distinguished faithful and in those subject to them. This is what led me to receive the wound of death for your life. I desired you to pursue unity in all your members—in the greater and the lesser, in the stronger and the more ordinary—so that with one [Col. 1140A] and undivided understanding in all you might strive toward that life in which the unity and glory of true peace reign.”

How beautiful are your breasts! etc. Just as teachers are understood by the neck, eyes, and teeth, so they are also understood by the breasts. The difference is that they are to be understood under those names when they speak wisdom among the perfect or rebuke those who contradict; but when they become weak to the weak in order to win the weak, they are rightly said to perform the offices of breasts, because they impart the milk of simpler teaching to those who are little in understanding—namely, to those who are not yet able to grasp the bread of more exalted teaching.

They are teeth when they correct the restless; breasts when they console the fainthearted and support the weak. And rightly he praises and marvels [Col. 1140B] at the beauty of the breasts of his sister and bride, because it is a great work before God and a virtue worthy of wonder when one who is capable of revealing higher mysteries of truth to the perfect does not disdain to instruct the weak in the first rudiments of faith.

The Lord rightly declares such a soul to be his sister and bride, because he judges her worthy of his love and union when he sees her becoming an imitator of his work. For he himself, in order to make us strong from weakness, did not shrink from becoming weak for a time—or even from dying—so that we might live.

Although he was the bread of angels in his divinity, he wished to remain hidden through the assumption of flesh, so that he might nourish human weakness and make it capable of receiving that same heavenly bread. Since an infant is less able to eat bread, by eating [Col. 1140C] the bread itself the mother, so to speak, incarnates it and, through the humility of the breast and the nourishment of milk, feeds the infant from that very bread.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). This is the everlasting food with which the angels are restored, because they are satisfied by seeing his glory. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.), so that the wisdom of God, which consoles us like a mother, might also restore us from that same bread and, through the sacraments of the Incarnation, lead us to the recognition and vision of divine love.

The holy teachers likewise turn the bread on which they themselves are sublimely nourished into milk with which to feed the little ones. The more deeply they contemplate the eternal joys in God, the more humbly they sympathize with the weakness of their neighbors.

Your breasts are more beautiful than wine. [Col. 1140D] This verse was already expounded at the beginning of this song, where it was said: “For your breasts are better than wine.” It was understood there that these words also demonstrate the beginnings of evangelical faith, which surpass the whole power of the Mosaic Law, since the Law brought no one to perfection and, as it was unable to introduce even its eminent worshipers into the kingdom of heavenly life, whereas the grace of faith leads those reborn in the font of baptism—even infants and those who die at the very beginning of life—to heavenly joys.

Many proofs show that the ceremonies of the Law may be compared with wine, but the clearest is that at the mystical wedding of the Church the wine fails, so that, through the Lord’s wondrous action, much better wine is made from water. This mystically signified that [Col. 1141A] the literal observance of the Law would come to an end, and that what was veiled in the letter would be revealed by the grace of the Gospel. The water would intoxicate the wedding house of heaven with spiritual love—that is, the holy Church, whom Christ deigned to consecrate as his bride.

The breasts of the bride are therefore more beautiful than wine because the beginnings of evangelical faith surpass the legal decrees, even those shown to have breathed something of the taste and considerable sweetness of virtues.

But we should attend more carefully to these words. Above, the breasts of her beloved bridegroom were praised; here, by contrast, the beloved praises the breasts of his bride and sister and declares them preferable to wine. This reciprocal exchange should not be thought to have been inserted into the sacred song without purpose; rather, it serves to commend more deeply the unity of Christ and the Church. He is the head of the body, the Church, and she is the body of this head. Hence the Apostle says: “The two shall become one flesh. This mystery is great; I am speaking, however, of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

[Col. 1141B] For this reason, by a similar example, the breasts of the bridegroom and the bride are praised as though they were the very same breasts, because the teachers of the Church are the teachers of Christ: teachers of the Church because they teach her; teachers of Christ because they teach at his command, because they teach her his precepts, and because by teaching they urge her toward fellowship with him.

Thus the Apostle says: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ” (Romans 1). Again he says: “We are your servants through Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4). And elsewhere: “Everything is yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas” (1 Corinthians 3).

[Col. 1141C] And the fragrance of your ointments, etc. The fragrance of the Church’s spiritual ointments is the renown of her spiritual gifts, concerning which it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

When Mary Magdalene, as a figure of the holy Church, anointed the Lord with nard, it was written: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (Matthew 26). This mystically foreshadowed that the whole world would be filled with the devoted services that the Church performs toward her Redeemer.

If, as was proved above by evangelical authority, the observance of the Law is rightly expressed by the name of wine, what prevents the name of spices from indicating the most [Col. 1141D] fragrant renown of the saints of that time? “The fragrance of your ointments,” he says, “is above all spices,” because, without any doubt, the renown of the Christian faith, spread much more widely throughout the world, has grown beyond the fame of the righteous who belonged to the former people.

This faith introduced a public contest with the world by renouncing the worship of the gods, and endured public persecution from the world until it conquered. It is not fitting for Christ’s bride to be compared with low and worthless things—with wine, which the taste consumes, or with spices, which the breeze is accustomed to disperse—since even the praise due to the legal observance would be exceedingly slight if it were said to transcend cups of wine or spices suited merely to the senses of the flesh.

Your lips, my bride, are a dripping honeycomb. A honeycomb is honey in wax; honey in wax is the spiritual sense of divine [Col. 1142A] utterances contained in the letter. It is rightly called a dripping honeycomb. The honeycomb drips when it contains more honey than those waxen chambers can hold. Such indeed is the fruitfulness of the holy Scriptures that a verse customarily written in a short line may fill many pages if, when carefully searched out, it is shown to contain within it such a great sweetness of spiritual understanding.

Let us give one example. The Psalmist says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem” (Psalm 147). According to the literal sense, he exhorts the citizens of that city, in which the temple of God stood, to offer him praise. According to allegory, however, Jerusalem is the Church of Christ spread throughout the whole world. According to tropology—that is, the moral sense—every holy soul is rightly called Jerusalem. According to anagoge—that is, the understanding leading upward—Jerusalem is the dwelling of the heavenly homeland, which consists of holy angels and human beings.

[Col. 1142B] The saying that Jerusalem means “vision of peace,” and that it is commanded to praise the Lord, suitably applies to all these meanings, although they differ greatly. A single holy soul cannot offer God as much praise as the whole Church throughout the world; nor can the universal Church, while she journeys on earth away from the Lord, be as perfect as she is when she reigns blessed in heaven in the presence of her Lord. Nor can the peace of the saints, which meanwhile consists in the hope of seeing God and being freed from evil, be equated with that vision of peace possessed in reality by those who, freed from every evil, enjoy the supreme good.

[Col. 1142C] The bride’s lips are therefore not merely full of honey but also a dripping honeycomb when the teachers of the Church demonstrate that an abundant variety of inner sweetness is present either in the figures of the Law, the prophetic sayings, or the Lord’s own words and mystical deeds; and from these they prepare the sweetest nourishment of his members—that is, of the faithful who are good hearers—and the most wholesome feasts for their minds.

There is no contradiction in the fact that above the bride’s lips were compared with ribbons and now with a honeycomb. Here the honeycomb delights by satisfying the throat; there the ribbons bind and restrain the hair. The one restores inwardly; the other binds outwardly. The same teachers are ribbons in the saving commandments and a honeycomb in the heavenly promises: ribbons when they restrain us from the flow of carnal pleasures; a honeycomb when they promise us the gifts of heavenly joys. Likewise, they are ribbons in what they openly [Col. 1142D] teach must be done or avoided; a honeycomb in those things that, having been enacted or spoken figuratively, reveal what hidden saving mystery they contain within.

Honey and milk are under your tongue. Milk signifies the instruction of the little ones; honey signifies the teaching appropriate to the more perfect. The Apostle teaches about milk when, reproaching certain people who had fallen away from faith, he says: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food.” Wisdom teaches concerning honey when it says: “As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so one who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by power” (Proverbs 25).

He does not forbid eating honey but eating too much of it, because we are not altogether forbidden to search out the majesty of God, especially since it is sung in praise of the righteous: “They shall speak of the magnificence of your majesty and of your holiness” (Psalm 144). Rather, we are recalled from attempting to investigate things that exceed our measure. Hence elsewhere he says concerning lovers of heavenly wisdom: “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are satisfied, you vomit it up” (Proverbs 25).

[Col. 1143A] It is fitting that honey and milk are said to be under the tongue. The word of God is on the tongue when it brings it forth in speech; it is under the tongue when it diligently meditates in the heart what ought to be brought forth. It has honey and milk under the tongue when it rightly knows how to distinguish what should be said to beginners, what to those who are progressing, and what to those who are perfect in knowledge and love. When the proper time for ministry arrives, it distributes these things through the ministry of the tongue according to the capacity of its hearers.

And the fragrance of your garments, etc. The garments [Col. 1143B] of the Church are her works, as John testifies. Speaking of her future blessedness, he says: “The marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, and it was granted to her to clothe herself in shining, spotless linen” (Rev. XIX). For the linen is the righteousnesses of the saints. And blessed Job says: “I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself in judgment as with a garment and a diadem” (Job XXIX).

In the frankincense, as has often been said, the heavenly desires of the righteous and the fervor of their frequent prayers, reaching upward, are indicated. Hence the fragrance of the bride’s garments is rightly compared to the fragrance of frankincense, because everything that the holy Church does for the Lord returns the equivalent of prayers on her behalf. Nor can the apostolic command, “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V), otherwise be fulfilled, unless everything we devoutly do commends us to our Creator as though through intercession. For neither the Apostle himself nor any of the saints could devote themselves perpetually to prayer in such a way that they did not devote another part of their time to sleep, food, or the other necessities of this life. But because the righteous continually do what is right, through this the righteous pray without ceasing, and they never cease from prayer unless they incur sin. Therefore the fragrance of their garments smells like the fragrance of frankincense, because the reputation of the good works they perform rises in the divine judgment as prayers do.

This verse harmonizes with the one mentioned above: “And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” There, under the name of ointments, the infusion of the Holy Spirit is shown, by which the hearts of the faithful are enlightened [Col. 1143D] and prepared for spiritual combat; here, under the word “garments,” the deeds of the righteous that are outwardly visible are indicated. Hence, by a beautiful distinction, works performed by human beings are compared with the fragrance of frankincense, whereas gifts bestowed by divine generosity exceed the measure of comparison, since the fragrance of the Church’s ointments is said to surpass all spices.

Since frankincense is so often mentioned in this song, and its typological significance is established, I would like to instruct briefly those unfamiliar with the nature of the spice itself. It is a tree of Arabia, similar, they say, in bark and leaf to the laurel, emitting sap like an almond tree; this is collected twice a year, in autumn and spring. For the autumn harvest, the trees are prepared by cutting their bark during the fiercest heat of summer. A rich foam then bursts forth and thickens when congealed. When the nature of the place allows it, whatever has adhered to the tree is scraped away with iron, using a smooth palm-leaf vessel to receive it; for this reason it appears bark-covered. This is the purest and whitest frankincense.

The second harvest takes place in spring, after the bark has been cut during the winter. It comes out red and is considered not comparable with the first; it is said to be whiter when taken from a young tree, but more fragrant when taken from an old one. The drop that hangs from it in a rounded form we call “male” frankincense; the drop dislodged by shaking we call manna. The frankincense-bearing region is called Sarvia, a name which the Greeks say signifies “mystery.” It is inaccessible on every side because of cliffs, and on the right it rises in crags from a sea inaccessible to ships. Its length through the forests is one hundred miles by one route, or, as others report, eighty; its width is half that. High hills rise there, and trees that grow spontaneously descend and spread across the plains. The soil is generally clay, with few springs, and those nitrous.

These remarks concerning the nature and location of frankincense have been stated briefly, as we found them in the books of the ancients. Almost all of them, if one attends carefully, correspond figuratively to the virtues of the saints, especially because the region in which it grows is called “mystery.” The fact that the trees grow spontaneously aptly applies to those whose supreme virtue is not compelled by laws or decrees, but is admirable because of voluntary offering, as the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything that you have,” and so forth (Matt. XIX).

What does the fact that, when the trees are cut, the tear of frankincense flows forth indicate except the compunction of the humble in heart, from which pure prayer, sweetened by tears, is usually born? The fact that the region has rare but nitrous springs suits those from whose belly, as Scripture says, “rivers of living water”—that is, gifts of spiritual teaching—flow forth (John VII), also suitable for cleansing the minds of their neighbors. For nitre is especially useful both for treating illnesses and for washing away stains.

The fact that the region is surrounded on every side by the protection of cliffs and crags corresponds to the merits of those of whom the Lord speaks in the parable: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard and set a hedge around it” (Matt. XXI). For the Lord planted the Church by establishing her in the precepts of life, and he set a hedge around her by the guardianship of his protection, defending her on every side so that she could not be destroyed by wicked spirits or human beings.

Wisely, after the Lord had praised the individual members of the Church one by one, he finally commended with fitting praise the ointments with which she was entirely anointed. None of her members, whether small or great, lacks consecration through the spiritual infusion of this anointing; for whoever lacks it is not in the body of the Church. He also praised her garments, that is, her works of righteousness, because her entire body is adorned by them. No one in her merits eternal life unless clothed in righteous works—works performed either by that person himself or, if he was an infant, by others in him and on his behalf.

But because it seemed tedious to the excellent lover to praise the members of his bride individually, and because it seemed inadequate to match each of her parts with individual precious things, he praises her as a whole [Col. 1145A] and compares her at once with several of the greatest substances, adding:

## “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride,” etc.

The garden is the Church, which produces a variety of shoots of spiritual works; these are subsequently enumerated under the names of various spices. She is also a fountain overflowing with salutary teaching, by which she waters the minds of her faithful as though they were beds of spices that she had prepared and arranged. Hence it is written: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XX). The Apostle likewise says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III). “I planted,” as though in the Lord’s garden, the spices of virtues; “Apollos watered,” as though from a sealed fountain of heavenly teaching; but the Lord, like an employer of his laborers, helped them so that they would not labor in vain.

This garden is enclosed because the Church remains fortified by the protection of her Lord and Redeemer, so that she may never be violated by the wicked invasion either of unbelieving human beings or of unclean spirits, nor be trampled down and hindered from producing heavenly fruits. This fountain is sealed because the word of faith contained in the Gospel, guarded by its seals, can never be disturbed by any attack of those who go astray. “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. IV).

Whoever attempts to break the seal of the living fountain errs and cannot profane the fountain of life. Rather, when the wicked intrudes, he kills himself in this attempt, after the example of the Egyptian army, which was destroyed in the mystical baptism of the Red Sea. The people of God were saved there, while the Egyptians, presuming to enter the holy place not by believing but by pursuing, were destroyed.

And because the same holy Church, designated by the name of a garden irrigated by a sacred fountain, was first planted in the small soil of Judea but soon expanded throughout the entire world, it is rightly added:

## “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates,” etc.

Because the primitive Church, which was in Jerusalem, produced abundant peoples for God from water and the Spirit, it is rightly said that the sacred garden, assisted by the irrigation of the divine fountain, sent forth from itself a paradise—not a paradise of just any trees, but one of pomegranates with the fruits of other trees.

For the pomegranates, which are red with a bloodlike color, signify the triumphs in the Church of those who, after the general washing of the sealed fountain, were also baptized in their own blood. The fruits of the trees signify the general works of the virtues, or those who perform the works of the virtues. Yet the pomegranates, which this garden is said first to send forth from itself, may also rightly be understood as the whole company of the baptized, because the regenerating fountain was consecrated as a mystery of the Lord’s Passion. For “all who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of God, we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

After the many pomegranates, the fruits of trees and spices follow, fittingly worthy of such a beginning. For after the ascent from the fountain, sprinkled with precious blood through which we become children of God, there must follow the fragrant fruitfulness of virtues, by which the grace of our regeneration itself is adorned and continually grows.

## “With cyprus, with nard, nard and saffron.”

Cyprus is an aromatic tree in Egypt, with leaves like those of the jujube and a seed whiter than coriander. It is boiled in oil and afterward pressed; the substance called cyprus is produced, and a royal ointment is made from it. The finest is in Egypt, the second in Ascalon of Judea, and the third on the island of Cyprus. Some say that this is the tree called privet in Italy.

We read concerning manna that it was like white coriander seed; and since the seed of cyprus is said to be of the same quality, it fittingly signifies the same heavenly blessing as manna. This seed is put into oil and boiled when the gift of heavenly grace is received by hearts enlightened with the richness of love; and when the flames of temptations are brought upon them, its virtue—how great and of what kind it is—is made more clearly evident to all.

Nard, which bears the type of the Lord’s burial, is attested by the deed of Mary, who anointed him with this spice when the moment of his Passion was approaching. He himself explains it, saying: “In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial” (Matt. XXVI).

The Lord’s garden, or fountain, produces cyprus when the Church teaches her children above all to seek the grace of heavenly refreshment, to preserve the light and anointing of love in their hearts, not to be overcome by the fire of tribulations, but rather to show by that very occasion how great and what kind of seed of divine grace they have received.

Cyprus is joined with nard when the Church either more diligently instructs the same people in faith in the Lord’s Passion, or teaches them to imitate that Passion by suffering themselves. Saffron, as though possessing a flower of golden color, displays those who shine with a greater grace of love. Just as gold surpasses other metals, so love surpasses all virtues. “Now,” he says, “faith, hope, and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love” (I Cor. XIII).

In contrast, Jeremiah, lamenting the destruction of his fellow citizens, says: “Those who were raised among saffron flowers embraced dung” (Lam. IV). Those raised among saffron flowers embrace dung when those who once appeared to glow with the most pleasing flowers of love later begin to plunge themselves into the foul mire of vices.

The further fact that saffron is said to bring the comfort of cooling relief to the burning limbs of the sick also corresponds to acts of supreme virtue. Such virtue is accustomed to moderate the mind’s heat from carnal pleasures and to kindle it toward the joys desired in the heavenly homeland.

But nard is said to disperse and warm the chill of cold limbs. It is obvious that the memory of the Lord’s Passion drives the sluggish fear of death from the hearts of the faithful, inflaming them and making them eager to imitate his death—not only by putting their own vices to death, but also by laying down their lives for him.

## “Cassia (fistula) and cinnamon,” etc.

Fistula, which is also called cassia, is counted among the aromatic trees. It has a sturdy, purple-colored bark and is said to be highly useful for treating disorders of the internal organs. Because of its shortness, some count it among fragrant herbs. Precisely because of this shortness, it rightly signifies the humble in spirit, theirs being the kingdom of heaven. They are, as it were, clothed in purple, always mindful of the Lord’s Passion and always ready to suffer for the Lord, like the one who said: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII).

This virtue especially has the habit of chastising and removing among us the movements and wantonness of the soul, like pains of the internal organs, when, reflecting on what God suffered for us, we recognize that we suffer less than we deserve.

Cinnamon represents the same virtue. It too is a tree short in stature, but outstanding in strength and fragrance, and for medicinal uses it is twice as effective as fistula. Hence it may aptly be understood that Scripture intended to express the progress of humility by placing cinnamon after spikenard. For cinnamon is said to be darkish or ash-colored, and this suits the minds of the humble, who, conscious of their own frailty, know how to say to God in their daily prayers: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). And again: “I reproach myself, and I repent in dust and ashes” (Job XLII).

It is fitting that after fistula, purple in color, cinnamon, a tree of ash-colored appearance, is placed, because through remembrance of the Lord’s wound contempt for our own virtue arises in us. Its bark is valuable; because it is round and slender like a reed, it receives the name cinnamon. For *ammomum* in Greek means “unstained.”

“Fistula and cinnamon,” he says, “with all the trees of Lebanon.” Just as fistula and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the righteous, so the trees of Lebanon indicate their exalted actions. These possess not merely the fragrance and healing power of fistula and cinnamon, nor do they display only the glory of bark; they also rise to great height and immense strength. Hence they are suitable for greater buildings, as this very song testifies, in which it was said above: “The beams of our houses are cypress.” And again: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the trees of Lebanon.”

Fistula and cinnamon therefore grow in the Lord’s garden with all the trees of Lebanon, because those who are admirable in humility and patience in the holy Church await the palm of heavenly reward together with those who firmly fortify that Church by preaching or by performing virtues.

Myrrh and aloe express restraint of the flesh, because these spices naturally prevent the bodies of the dead, when anointed with them, from decaying, as the evidence of the Lord’s burial also testifies. For just as the corruption of dead flesh signifies the rottenness of lust, so its preservation, when typologically understood in a good sense, most aptly demonstrates the virtue of restraint and chastity, which restrain our members from vices.

The first ointments are those of which the Apostle says: “Strive for the greater gifts, and I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XII), and so forth—the passage in which that great master of speech wonderfully discusses the great virtues among which love holds the chief place.

The conjunction is indeed beautiful: myrrh and aloe arise in the Lord’s garden together with all the first ointments, because when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive the greater gifts of the Spirit. Scripture contradicts the opposite view, saying: “Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. I). “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (ibid.).

Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, up to five cubits in height, resembling a thornbush. The Greeks call it *acanthon*; its drop is green and bitter, and from this it received the name *myrrha*—“myrrh.” All these features aptly correspond to mortification of the flesh, which is felt as bitter for a time but is most gladly accepted in hope of the ever-flourishing homeland, namely that of which Peter says: “He regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven” (I Pet. I).

It is rightly compared with a thorn, because, in order to preserve the mind forever, it temporarily afflicts the body with the pricks of labor. Moreover, the fact that its naturally flowing drop is more precious, while that extracted by wounding the bark is judged inferior, shows to whom it is not evident that greater virtue before God belongs to the one who strives to chastise and subject to servitude a healthy and vigorous body, even while worldly abundance smiles outwardly, than to the one who, pressed by illness or other adversities of the world, restrains the flesh from wantonness unwillingly and constrains it to the remedy of abstinence?

Nevertheless, this too should rightly be counted among the great virtues: when someone patiently, humbly, and gratefully receives the scourges of paternal correction and, disciplined by them, arrives at the gifts of the promised inheritance.

Aloe also, if considered more attentively, is aptly likened to those who practice restraint. It is a tree of exceedingly sweet and powerful fragrance, so that the ancients burned its wood on altars in place of incense. Yet it gives off an exceedingly bitter sap, though one suitable for many medicines. So, too, restraint and the curbing of carnal pleasures are bitter in the act itself, but glorious by the merit of virtue and most pleasing to the inner judge.

## XV. “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters,” etc. [Col. 1148D]

The fountain of gardens arises within the enclosed garden of the Lord, because from the primitive Church there proceeded into the world a heavenly teaching that would produce for the Lord many churches—that is, spiritual gardens.

Of this fountain it is rightly added: “A well of living waters.” What is a well except a fountain? Yet a well is always deep, whereas a fountain is also sunk into the depths, but may likewise be found at the highest point of the earth. Thus one and the same teaching of the Church is the fountain of gardens, because it produces spiritual fruits in those whom it instructs; and it is a well of living waters: a well, indeed, because it is not open to everyone. It is not situated in plain sight, but is stored in the hearts of the saints through the revelation of the Holy Spirit.

Hence none of the rulers of this age knew it. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But,” he says, “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (I Cor. II).

It is called “of living waters” because the divine and heavenly utterances, which continually and unfailingly emerge from the invisible treasures of divine grace and lead into life all whom they wash and irrigate, are living waters. For those waters are customarily called living which flow eternally from a spring, in contrast with those which are collected in cisterns by an abundance of rain, or in pools, or which rush for a time with great force through torrents when the snows melt, but disappear when fair weather returns.

To these may rightly be compared the brief and swollen boastfulness of worldly teaching. It often seems to pour forth innumerable and profound rivers of eloquence and learning in many forms; but all these things soon dry up, as though they had never existed, when the Sun of righteousness and the summer of evangelical brightness dawn.

The Lord himself complains of them through the prophet, saying: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. II). Isaiah likewise says: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt”; and shortly afterward: “The water from the sea shall dry up, and the river shall be desolate and dry” (Isa. XIX).

“A well,” he says, “of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon.” By Lebanon he speaks of the Church herself, who is both white and exalted through her life. For Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness,” and she pours forth streams of salutary wisdom to her hearers, as though to fields lying beneath her.

The Lord likewise says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist, explaining this, adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John VII). Living waters flow from the belly of the believer when holy preaching flows from the hearts of the faithful.

“These waters flow,” he says, “with force from Lebanon.” He rightly added “with force,” so that he might signify not only the descent of the living waters to us but also demonstrate that the power of their coming is unconquerable. Just as no one can hold back rivers rushing down from a high mountain, so the outflow of apostolic speech, because it proceeded from a heavenly spring and was divinely impelled to run, could not be overcome by any contest with opposing powers or diverted from its course. Rather, souls surrendered before they ceased to be irrigated by the life-giving teaching.

Such is the saying in the Psalm: “The force of the river makes the city of God glad” (Ps. XLV). It rightly makes the Church glad, for she has not only received from the Lord a river of living waters, but that same river comes with such an impetus of heavenly grace that no obstacle of an opposing power can impede it.

The well of living waters may also suitably be understood as signifying those who habitually strive to draw out whatever earthly thought they find in their hearts, bring it forth by devout confession, and cast it away. Thus, by chastity and humility, they prepare within the hidden place of their breast a dwelling worthy of God, and by diligent cleansing of themselves they open within themselves an entrance for living waters—that is, for heavenly gifts—through the channels of hidden inspiration.

They do this after the example of the blessed patriarch Isaac, who, when the Philistines obstructed him, used to dig wells useful to himself and his household. When the Philistines, out of envy, attempted to fill them in, he would cleanse them again by chaste labor and continue digging deeply until living water answered him.

Such is our contest with the evil spirits. They strive, by thrusting the rubble of vices into our senses, either to disturb the water of wisdom within us or, if they can, to exclude it from us altogether. But we should counter them with vigilant diligence, driving out through frequent prayers and watchfulness the temptations we discover that they have introduced into us, so that we may become capable of invisible gifts.

But because the Lord had said that his garden was enclosed, irrigated by a living fountain, and planted with fragrant spices and trees; because he had declared that it possessed waters of wisdom by which it was irrigated, and little wells on account of the hidden mysteries, and living waters on account of the eternity of the blessings to which they lead those who drink; and because he had asserted that these waters flowed forth with persistent and utterly unconquerable force—it remained, once everything had been firmly and orderly arranged, that access for adversaries to test it should by no means be denied, but rather that it should be shown that it could not be harmed by many torrents flowing from various directions. Indeed, the more it was tested by the blasts of adversity, the more fully the inner sweetness of its fruits would be revealed.

Hence, in the Lord’s own voice, the following is now added:

## XVI. “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind,” etc.

By the north wind and the south he indicates the frequent storms of temptations by which the Church was to be assaulted, so that it might become known how much spiritual grace and how much inner virtue she possessed.

If we think there is some difference between the names “north wind” and “south wind”—one being cold and the other clearly warm—it is not unreasonable to understand by the north wind the harshness of the frightening world, and by the south wind the allurements of the deceiver. For the Lord himself proves that the garden is tested by this twofold assault when, explaining the parable of the good seed, he says:

“The one sown on rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is temporary. When tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he immediately falls away. The one sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless” (Luke VIII).

The Lord may seem to say in the imperative: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden.” But he does not command the wicked to do evil; rather, he permits them to use their free will as they wish. He can himself make from their evil deeds the good things he wills, while by an unalterable judgment he repays them with the torments they have deserved for their evil.

Thus the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he might afflict his people (Exod. X); but shortly afterward, when those who were afflicted had been liberated, he punished forever the one who had afflicted them. And when he says concerning blessed Job, “Behold, he is in your hand” (Job I), speaking to the head of all the wicked, and that one went out and struck him with the greatest plague, does it not seem that the Lord said to the most turbulent and harsh of the winds: “Blow through my garden, and its spices will flow”?

The spices did flow from the garden shaken by the winds when the holy man, struck by adversities, scattered far and wide such steadfastness in virtue, of wondrous fragrance, that even us, placed at the final limit of the world and of the age, he has filled with the indescribable sweetness of his fragrance.

When the Church hears that she is to be tested by the blasts of temptations, she does not contradict the provision and ordering of her beloved. Rather, so that she may neither be overcome by adversity nor corrupted by prosperity, she seeks his help in everything—he who brings forth the winds from his treasuries and, as blessed Job says, “made a weight for the winds” (Job XXVIII). In other words: “He does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to endure” (I Cor. X).

# CHAPTER V

## XVII. “Let my beloved come into his garden,” etc.

May the Lord come into his Church, so that he himself may preserve her undefiled and always fruitful in the harvest of faith. May he who promised to remain with me until the consummation of the age graciously reveal the presence of his coming to me especially when he sees me being assaulted by greater temptations from my enemies, and may he kindly grant that he himself be more beloved by me than all else.

For I am confident that, so long as I can truthfully say, “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII), and, “He will rescue me from my strongest enemies and establish me upon the heights of the heavenly kingdom” (ibid.),

“and may he eat the fruit of his trees,” and may he willingly look upon and gratefully receive the works of his saints, in accordance with what he himself said to his disciples concerning the Samaritans who would believe in him: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John IV). He makes clear that he was speaking of the calling of the nations when he adds: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John VI). “Lift up your eyes and look at the regions, for they are already white for the harvest. And the one who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life” (John IV).

In contrast, when he was hungry, he sought fruit on the Jewish fig tree; and because he found none, he condemned it to perpetual barrenness. He did this figuratively, signifying that he indeed hungered for the salvation of the Synagogue, but that the Synagogue, because it had utterly rejected the fruit of salvation, was to be punished with the retribution of eternal unbelief.

The saying may also be understood more specifically as spoken by the voice of the perfected members of the Church, namely those who remember that they serve God with sincere and steadfast intention: “Let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees.” It is as though they were saying openly: “Would that the Lord might come quickly, so that in his kindness he might restore to us the reward of our devout dedication! Just as we have always endeavored to love him and return to him the fruit of righteousness that he himself gave, so may he reveal to us the most blessed recompense of his love by receiving us to himself.”

Although it is fitting for the saints to say this at all times, how much more so when they see the condition of the present Church shaken by storms of temptations! The Lord himself, immediately responding to their desire with a welcome voice, testifies that he has already done what they requested.

## XVIII. “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”

“I have come,” he says, “very often into my Church; indeed, during the time of her pilgrimage, do not cease doing this in any way. I come to correct those who have gone astray, to help the weak, and to strengthen those who doubt in the faith; to be nourished, as by the sweetest foods, on the perfected fruits of those who act well; to defend those who are struggling from the ambushes of their enemies; and to reward the victors over their enemies with the crown of my perpetual vision.”

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

By myrrh are signified those who have either ended their lives through martyrdom or have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. By spices, in general, all those distinguished by the reputation of good works are signified.

He gathers his myrrh with his spices when he cuts off his martyrs, together with the other elect, from this life by a kind of sickle of death, once each has reached the maturity of the perfection granted to him, and leads them to the inward joys of heavenly blessedness.

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey,” etc.

Those who know how to investigate the sweetness of spiritual meanings in the sacred writings and to clarify them through preaching for the salvation of their hearers are compared with a honeycomb. Those who desire willingly to taste the meals of the word set before them and to feed on them without satiety are likened to honey.

Likewise, the strong and exalted preachers of heavenly things are represented by wine, while the hearers who are still weak are represented by milk. [Col. 1152C] When the inner judge approves the life of all these people—different indeed in the modes of their pursuits, but united in one hope of heavenly reward—he eats, as it were, the honeycomb with the honey, and drinks the wine with the milk.
