But he is not only delighted by the devout deeds of the elect; he also urges his faithful to such a banquet of the mind—that is, to rejoice together in the holy desires of the good—when he adds:

“Eat, my friends, and drink,” etc. That is: you also, who are my friends because you do what I have commanded, and who are most dear because you embrace me with complete love—fill your hearts, I beg you, with the deeds of the saints as with choice foods. Nor should you merely take care to recall these things; turn their memory itself to the fruit of imitation. This is what [Col. 1152D] it means, after eating the honeycomb and honey, and after drinking wine and milk, to become intoxicated: not merely to rejoice in the admirable virtues of the good, but also to follow them, and through recalling them to shake off the torpor of our mind and kindle it more vigorously toward the love of eternal things.

Conversely, the prophet says to certain people: “You have eaten, but you have not been satisfied; you have drunk, but you have not become intoxicated” (Haggai I). The mind has eaten the food of the life-giving table but is not satisfied; it has drunk the cup of salvation but is not intoxicated—if it has learned the words of Scripture and become acquainted with the examples of the righteous, yet has not changed its own life or corrected its conduct. It has drunk but is not intoxicated if it joyfully hears the precepts of life, but remains sluggish and lazy in fulfilling them.

[Col. 1153A] But if, in the statement above by the Lord—“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, and drunk my wine with my milk”—we wish to understand that he transferred his saints from this world to the heavenly realms and introduced them into the fellowship of the heavenly citizens, who are indeed his body, it will follow that this exhortation of his, of which we are now speaking, was addressed to those same citizens of heaven. For when he had said that he had eaten his honeycomb with his honey and drunk his wine with his milk—that is, that he had gathered the saints to increase his heavenly body—he immediately turned his face and words to the inhabitants of heaven, saying: “Eat, my friends, and drink, and become intoxicated, my dearest ones.” In other words, he was saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke XV).

[Col. 1153B] And by a most fitting comparison, those whom the Lord, rising from the dead, took with himself from the underworld and carried up to the heavenly kingdoms are likened to that honeycomb and honey—those who had pleased him from the foundation of the world. The sweetness of the holy souls whom he lifted to eternal joys in heaven is thereby compared to honey. In the honeycomb, however, there is no lesser happiness for those who, in both body and immortal soul, deserved through him to ascend to the courts of the heavenly city. Of them the Evangelist plainly testifies: when the Lord was dying on the cross, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; after his resurrection they came into the holy city and appeared to many (Matthew XXVII). Those who rose from the dead when the Lord rose must also be believed [Col. 1153C] to have ascended with him when he ascended into heaven. Nor should faith be given in any way to the rashness of those who suppose that, after later returning to ashes, they were shut up again in the tombs that had previously been opened—by those to whom they had appeared alive shortly before—in the manner of the dead.

Thus the Bridegroom ate his honeycomb with his honey when the Lord brought to eternal life all who had faithfully served him from the beginning of this life: some rejoicing in the immortality of the flesh, others still awaiting the rewards of resurrection. He raised them all together to the blessedness of ineffable glory among the fellowship of the angels.

[Col. 1153D] Up to this point the Lord had praised the beauty and virtues of the holy Church at great length, beginning with the words: “How beautiful you are, my beloved! How beautiful you are! Your eyes are like those of doves.” This praise was carried so far that she was even set before adversaries as one to be approved. When this began to take place, she invoked the unique help of the same Redeemer; and he, delaying her requests not at all, gathered under the names of myrrh and spices those who had been tested by afflictions or adorned with other virtues and brought them to the heavenly homeland. He also declared that the whole life of the holy Church—which is distinguished in its teachers and in its hearers—was pleasing to him under the names of honeycomb, honey, and milk. When these matters have been completed, there follows the voice of the Church, desiring to cling to the Lord in the secrecy and silence of contemplation rather than, through the labor of preaching, to provoke against herself the weapons and fury of the wicked.

### XIX. “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

It is as though she were saying: “When the storms of persecutions have for a time ceased, [Col. 1154A] I have begun to enjoy a little rest in the Lord even in the present life. I use that leisure most willingly, yet I do not cease, with the whole desire of my heart, to keep watch for the rest that knows no end.”

“I sleep,” because, by his grace, I enjoy a measure of tranquility in this life while worshiping him. I have not been given over to as much labor of preaching as the primitive Church endured, nor have I been struck by as many conflicts with the faithless as the countless throngs of the nascent Church suffered in its early days.

“And my heart is awake,” because the more freely I am at leisure from external assaults, the more deeply I see within that he himself is the Lord.

The holy Church says this in those who, amid the calm of temporal life, [Col. 1154B] desire to serve the Lord through psalms, fasts, and the other prayers and almsgiving of a quieter life. But because this life is one of labor, not of rest, she immediately hears the voice of the Lord awakening her and urging her to the sweat of preaching, so that during the time of this exile she may remember that the taste of the rest she desires has not been entirely denied her, nor its eternal enjoyment withheld. For it follows:

“The voice of my beloved, knocking: ‘Open to me, my sister,’” etc. The beloved knocks at our door when the Lord arouses us to advance in virtue and reminds us of the joys of the promised kingdom, just as we knock at his door when we seek from him advancement in virtue and entrance into the kingdom, remembering his promise: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke XI).

He also declares that he himself knocks at our door [Col. 1154C] when he says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation III).

We open to the Lord who knocks in two ways: either we open the inner chamber of our heart to receive the fervent love for him that we have already possessed for a while; or, by preaching, we unlock the hearts of our neighbors to receive his fear or love, which they have not yet possessed.

There is also a third knocking of the Lord at our door: when he warns us, through preceding illnesses, that we are to be taken from this life. Concerning this he says in the Gospel: “You also must be like people waiting for their master, when he will return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him” (Luke XII). We open immediately to the Lord knocking in this way if we receive death gladly and do not fear being brought before his judgment, remembering that we have pleased him by good works and have always honored him, according to the Psalmist: “The honor of the king loves judgment” (Psalm XCV).

[Col. 1154D] Yet in this passage, if it is considered carefully, the Lord seems to seek rather that opening of the faithful soul which takes place in the instruction of its neighbors. For it is clear that she had already opened her own heart to him, since, freed from the bonds of the flesh, she desired to depart to him and could say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” It is clear that the beloved had already entered into her, since she honored him with so many and such great titles, saying: “My sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled.”

“My sister,” because you have become a co-heir of my kingdom; [Col. 1155A] “my beloved,” because, having escaped the yoke of servitude, you have become acquainted with my secrets; “my dove,” because you have been enlightened by the gift of my Spirit; “my undefiled,” because, withdrawn from busy activities, you have been raised to divine contemplation.

But when he says, “Open to me,” he undoubtedly requests that the minds of those who were not yet worthy of all these things be opened to him through preaching, as the words that follow also make clear:

“For my head is full of dew,” etc. Christ’s head is God, as the Apostle says (I Corinthians II). His locks are the thoughts gathered in the minds of his faithful, which do not stream down in scattered disarray but remain bound together through discipline.

The dew and the drops of night, [Col. 1155B] which fall from above amid darkness and cold, represent the minds of the wicked: obscure and blind, always desiring the things that are on earth. Of such people it is said: “Because lawlessness will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV).

The Lord commanded us to love him and to love our neighbor. But when we honor him with less love than we ought, and when many—even worse—are held by no feeling of charity toward him at all, what is this but Christ’s head being full of dew? And when all the wicked pour out hatred rather than love upon the servants of Christ, who gather themselves into the custody of their minds and cling more closely to the love of their Creator, do not his locks become wet with drops of night, and do they not endure heavily the pressing cold of blind persecution?

When such a time therefore descends, the Lord rightly awakens the Church [Col. 1155C] from the sleep of the gentle pursuits in which she delights. He commands her to devote herself to the word of preaching and, through frequent exhortation, to warm and enlighten the hearts of the wicked and open to himself those that had been closed against him. By entering, he can dwell there through faith. He prefers that she attain the salvation of many through labor rather than possess quiet among the few who had been saved, even though that quiet was made commendable by frequent meditation on heavenly goods.

When summoned to the labor of preaching, the Church replies to the Lord:

“I have taken off my tunic,” etc. As though she were plainly saying: “I have abandoned the affairs of frail things; why should I put it on again?” For whoever girds himself for the office of preaching and undertakes responsibility for governing souls must also attend to providing the support of temporal necessities for those to whom he preaches eternal things.

[Col. 1155D] Therefore the Church, in those who prefer to care for themselves in secrecy rather than be occupied with the burdens of laborious action, recalls that she has taken off her tunic and cannot put it on again. Since the tunic figuratively signifies the occupations of this age, the Lord himself bears witness to this when, speaking of the coming of his final judgment, he says: “And whoever is in the field, let him not turn back to take up his tunic” (Matthew XXIV). He mystically warns that one who has occupied hand and mind with the advancement and fruits of spiritual things must not return to seek the world’s pleasures, which he had cast aside.

[Col. 1156A] “I have washed my feet,” etc. I have already washed my thoughts—which once used to touch the earth—with frequent tears of secret compunction, and, as far as conduct made possible, rendered them worthy of heavenly entrance. Thus I can say: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Psalm CXXI). That is, although I have not yet deserved to enter the walls of the heavenly city itself, I have nevertheless already striven to purify my thoughts so thoroughly that, by repeatedly fixing the gaze of my heart upon it, I remember having tasted in advance certain beginnings—by no means insignificant—of its joys. How then could I leave the summit of contemplation and again be polluted by the filth of the world?

[Col. 1156B] Apart from the concern for temporal support that we have mentioned, it is very difficult for even an outstanding teacher not sometimes to be disturbed by some fault of vainglory or by anger—anger, if he is not humbly heard while speaking of divine and heavenly things; vainglory, if, while humbly obeying him, he acquires many crowds of believers for the Lord. Anger is troubled when he is criticized; vainglory swells when his speech is praised.

Hence James says: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you will receive a greater judgment; for in many things we all stumble” (James III). Hence the Lord himself washed the feet of the disciples returning from preaching, signifying that even the greatest preachers cannot be entirely free from sins, at least in all the thoughts by which they touch the earth. Yet he graciously washes these thoughts, whatever they may be.

The holy Church therefore takes delight in the gentle and salutary pursuits [Col. 1156C] of a quiet life, in those who have deserved to experience such things; and she excuses herself from the office of preaching, saying in a certain manner with Moses: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you are going to send” (Exodus IV).

But because the Lord wishes our love for him to be recognized chiefly in our love for our neighbors, when Peter three times professed that he loved him, he replied three times: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). Thus it is fittingly added:

“My beloved put his hand through the opening,” etc. The beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord kindles us invisibly, through a hidden compunction, to the work of virtue.

He puts his hand toward us when we desire to rest, when he recalls to us his work that he has accomplished in us—not merely that we should be human beings, but also that we should belong to him.

[Col. 1156D] He puts his hand toward us when he reminds us of the work he accomplished in himself for our sake: when, coming forth from the Father’s bosom into our public life, he deigned not only to become incarnate and live among us on earth in order to make us spiritual and heavenly, but also to die so that we might live forever.

Therefore our inward being rightly trembles at such a touch of his, because, recalling the work of his mercy, our conscience is afraid, according to the prophetic saying: “I considered your works and was terrified.” It hastens to rise up for the salvation of its neighbors, for whose sake God became incarnate and died.

The name “belly” commonly designates the heart, because just as food is digested [Col. 1157A] in the belly, so thoughts mature in the heart through diligent reconsideration. Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jeremiah IV). What benefit would it have been to his hearers if the teacher had complained that his belly was in pain? Rather, he strove to benefit them greatly by testifying that his own conscience was disturbed by their wicked deeds and filled with inward sorrow.

The “belly” may also be understood as the very weakness and frailty of those who hesitate to undertake the office of teaching, either because they consider themselves less capable or because they delight in the leisure of their quiet and shrink from the task.

The bride’s belly trembled at the beloved’s touch when, at the prompting [Col. 1157B] of divine compunction, the weaker members of the Church shake off the torpor of idleness, kindle themselves for the practice of good works, and rise to counsel their neighbors through preaching. This is what follows:

“I arose to open to my beloved.” To open to the Lord here means to preach the word of the Lord. We open to the Lord not only when we receive his coming into our heart through love, but also when, by instruction, we turn those who were accustomed to close their hearts against the truth toward receiving it.

The bride rightly recalls that she rose to open to her beloved, because whoever intends to preach the truth must first rise to perform what he teaches, lest, while preaching to others, he himself become reprobate. The following words appropriately accompany this:

“My hands dripped with myrrh,” etc. By “hands” are understood works, which are performed by the hands; by “fingers,” discernment, [Col. 1157C] by which works are directed. For no members of our body are divided into so many joints or more capable of bending than the fingers.

Thus, when the Lord was about to give his judgment concerning the adulterous woman, he first wrote with his finger on the ground and then pronounced the judgment that was requested. Mystically he admonished us that whenever we intend to chastise or judge others, we should first humble ourselves and carefully engrave an examination of our own conscience through diligent discernment, carefully considering whether we too may be tempted.

It has often been said that myrrh signifies continence of the flesh and martyrdom. Hence the meaning is clear: the bride’s hands drip with myrrh when a holy soul devotes itself to works of continence; and her fingers are full of thoroughly tested myrrh when, examining itself with vigilant discernment, it finds that it lives continently solely with a view to the heavenly reward.

[Col. 1157D] Those who strive for human praise and, as the Judge himself testifies, have received their reward appear indeed to let myrrh drip from their hands; but they do not have their fingers filled with thoroughly tested myrrh. For even if they give not only their possessions to the poor but also their limbs to the flames, if they do not have charity, it profits them nothing.

Since, therefore, one who wishes to teach another must himself abstain from carnal allurements and be prepared to suffer for confessing the faith, the bride rightly said, “I arose to open to my beloved,” and immediately added, “My hands dripped with myrrh.” And because this continence or suffering must be practiced solely with the intention of receiving an eternal reward, she rightly added: “My fingers are full of myrrh.”

[Col. 1158A] Likewise, the bride’s hands drip with myrrh when his workers—that is, holy teachers—subject their bodies to salutary mortification. Her fingers are full of thoroughly tested myrrh when they advance so far amid tribulations that their endurance is shown to be invincible, according to the Apostle’s words: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Romans V).

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.” The bride opens the bolt of her door to her beloved when each chosen soul makes the temple of its heart worthy of divine visitation and habitation.

She opens the bolt of her door to the beloved who knocks when, set aflame by a sudden inspiration with desires for heavenly things, she strives to open more widely the breast of her mind to receive a taste of that same heavenly sweetness.

Earlier she had said that the beloved had put his hand through the opening, [Col. 1158B] touched her, and shaken her with trembling. Inflamed intensely by this touch, she now desires not to be touched by his hand through the narrowness of the opening, but, with the door of her heart thrown open, to enjoy his most blessed embrace—that is, to be filled more fully with the sweetness of divine illumination, which she had already felt briefly and in very small measure.

But because the perfect vision of eternal joys is granted to none of the elect in this life, and is reserved as the reward of all the righteous in the life to come, it is rightly added:

“But he had turned away,” etc. [Col. 1158C] This is what the Psalmist says: “A man will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Psalm LXIII). For the higher the human heart, purified by faith and prayer, raises itself to contemplate the glory of the divine vision, the higher it discovers that which it seeks and to which it will ascend in order to attain it at the time of the promised reward.

Ecclesiastes expresses something similar: “I said, ‘I will become wise’; but it withdrew farther from me, and much more than it had been” (Ecclesiastes VII).

[Col. 1158D] Nor should it be overlooked that she does not simply say, “I opened my door,” but rather, “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.” She had closed the inner chamber of her heart with a bolt lowered from above, so that no profane or treacherous person might enter, according to Solomon’s saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs IV). She opened it to her beloved so that, after all the crowds of the unclean had been driven away, she might provide her Creator with free access within her.

Nor should it be thought contradictory that earlier we said that the bride opens to her beloved through the drops of night and chilling dew, when the Church or a faithful soul kindles the hearts of neighbors to praise the Creator whom they did not know or did not care about, whereas now we interpret her as opening the bolt of her door to that same beloved when, through advancing compunction, she opens her mind more widely to his entrance.

Both things take place at one and the same moment. For the inward inspiration that kindles anyone to gather souls for God commonly kindles that person at the same time to a more ardent love of the same Creator. Indeed, no other cause rightly urges anyone to teach than the love of God.

And when someone delights, through teaching, to open the soul of a neighbor [Col. 1159A] to seize the gifts of divine mercy, he must necessarily renew his own mind by doing this and enlarge it more generously for the entrance of heavenly grace.

Finally, the words that follow plainly reveal how greatly the bride was advancing while she labored to open to the Lord the hearts of her neighbors, which she had seen to be obscure, grievously bearing that the one for whom she herself was meanwhile burning should be weighed down by the unbelieving torpor of others, as though by the dew and drops of night. For it follows:

“My soul melted,” etc. “The more sweetly,” she says, “I received the voice and nearness of my beloved through the opening of secret compunction, the more sublimely everything cold within me grew warm, and everything rigid melted—so much so that I found sweetness in being dissolved into nothing but tears. And the one whom, when he touched me through his grace, I had been unable to hold even for a moment, I now delight to seek in his absence with weeping and groaning.”

[Col. 1159B] This too greatly increased my melting away from my former hardness and my pouring out of my soul within me: I see the love of many growing cold, while he himself complains that he is covered by the dark disturbances of the wicked, like drops of night. And because the wicked have destroyed his law, I have therefore taken greater and greater care to love his commandments more than gold and topaz.

“I sought him, and did not find him,” etc. This is the voice within the holy Church of those who, having passed beyond concern for fleeting things, are accustomed to walk only in the highest goods and always to love entrance into the heavenly homeland.

There is no doubt that they cannot always, as they wish, be affected [Col. 1159C] by a desire for heavenly things with one and the same force of sweetness. This virtue does not lie in the free choice of a mind raised to heavenly things, but solely in the gift of God, who raises and enlightens it.

Whenever a chaste soul either wishes to depart to the Lord or, while still placed in the flesh, to be lifted up by a taste of future blessedness, yet does not immediately obtain what it asks, then it must necessarily say with a groan: “I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.”

He is always found by those who seek him rightly, so that he may have mercy; he always answers those who call him rightly, so that he may provide for their perpetual salvation. But he does not always answer for the purpose of immediately granting himself to be found, lest he give those still journeying along the road of this exile in the present life what he promises to those who arrive in the homeland.

[Col. 1159D] Therefore, let us say many times each day, bending the knee, to the Father: “Your kingdom come.” We do not doubt that we are heard, nor do we immediately receive what we ask; rather, we patiently and joyfully await the fulfillment of our prayer until we attain it at the end.

“The watchmen who go about the city found me,” etc. The watchmen who go about the city are the holy teachers entrusted with the care of the Church, so that by word or example they may guard it from the incursions of wicked doctrines and kindle it more and more toward fear and love of its Creator.

These watchmen go about the city because, throughout all the places [Col. 1160A] of the holy Church, which is spread in every direction across the whole world, their bodily presence and living voice, or their teaching and work inserted in writings, are found.

When they find the bride wearied by seeking her beloved, they strike and wound her, because they further inflame with the word of their teaching the soul they find anxious with heavenly love. When they extinguish whatever earthly thing they discover to remain in her and render her, as it were, insensible to all lowly concerns, they wound her as though by striking her.

For when the Apostle describes the armor of God and says, “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI), what wonder is there if someone is said to be struck and wounded when touched by this sword? By the blow of this sword one receives the wound of which it is said elsewhere: “I am wounded with love.”

“The watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.” [Col. 1160B] The watchmen of the walls are the same supreme teachers when they also strive to instruct those who are capable of governing and fortifying the Church.

I believe that Timothy, Titus, and other such workers of truth were the walls of the city of God; and when Paul gives them exhortatory commands, what should he be understood to be except a watchman of the walls?

He shows himself to be a watchman of the city, which he diligently went about, when, listing his labors, he says: “Apart from those things that are external, there is my daily pressure, my concern for all the churches” (II Corinthians XI).

He likewise shows that he is a watchman of the walls when he says to Timothy: “But you, be watchful; labor in all things; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry” (II Timothy IV), and other words of this kind.

And to Titus he says: “For this reason I left you in Crete, [Col. 1160C] so that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in each city, just as I instructed you” (Titus I).

[Col. 1160D] The watchmen of the walls take away the bride’s cloak when she has been struck and wounded, when the apostles or apostolic men remove from some soul touched by divine love the restraints of passing things, so that, freed from lowly concerns, it may seek the face of its Creator with a freer course.

The cloak is the same as the tunic mentioned above when she says: “I have taken off my tunic,” signifying the entanglements of earthly things.

### XX. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find him,” etc.

The bride rightly languishes with love when, struck and wounded by the sword of the Spirit, she casts off the garment of carnal desire. For in proportion as a holy soul grows strong in God, it becomes weak and feeble with respect to affection for this world.

Nor is it surprising that a perfect soul is said to languish with regard to the things of the world, since the Apostle does not hesitate to call those who have perfectly abandoned the world dead: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Galatians VI); and of himself: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (ibid.).

The daughters of Jerusalem are the citizens of the heavenly homeland, some of whom are still journeying on earth, while others already reign there.

But in this passage, when it says, “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am languishing with love,” she seems to address that portion of them which remains on earth and has not yet deserved to see the Lord perfectly, although it often finds him when it receives him through love into its own breast.

The bride therefore adjures these daughters of Jerusalem that, if they find her beloved, [Col. 1161A] they should tell him that she is languishing. For we are this bride, and the friend of this same God and our Lord, insofar as, clinging to him, we become one spirit with him. Set aflame by desire for eternal things and sighing for the face of our Creator, whom we do not yet see, we come to his servants, whom we believe to lead an angelic life on earth. We earnestly ask them, during the time of their devoted prayer, to commend us also to the Lord and intercede for us, so that we may deserve to see his face.

This is precisely what we do: we adjure the daughters of Jerusalem to report to God the greatness of our love and to ask for heavenly assistance for us, just as for themselves, so that we may behold his glory.

Accordingly, a response of this kind is given in every respect [Col. 1161B] by those same daughters of Jerusalem, one that plainly accords with the devout fellowship of the faithful. For it follows:

### XXI. “What is your beloved beyond a beloved?” etc.

This is plainly what one faithful brother says to another faithful brother: “I beg you, because I perceive that you burn with the love of the Redeemer, speak to me also about him; strengthen me with salutary exhortation, so that this same love may increase in my heart through his benefits and gifts.

“For some time now, conscious of my sins, I have begun to possess his fear. But now, as my mind grows stronger, I have become more secure concerning the forgiveness of my sins, and I delight to hear something about his love.

“Tell me, then, please: what is your beloved beyond a beloved?” That is, what is he like insofar as he ought rather to be loved than feared?

You have a word of this kind in the song of Isaiah: [Col. 1161C] “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a hill, in a fertile place,” and so forth, until he says: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved sapling” (Isaiah V).

“Beloved beyond a beloved” may also be understood as the Son from the Father, rightly believed and confessed as “light from light, God from God.” For just as the Father and Son have one charity and one divinity, so they also have one love, as John testifies when he says: “Everyone who loves him who begot loves him also who was born from him” (I John III).

There follows the bride’s fitting response to those who ask.

### XXII. “My beloved is white and ruddy,” etc.

He is white because, appearing in the flesh, he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (I Peter II). He is ruddy because he washed us from our sins in his blood (Revelation I).

He is rightly white first and then ruddy, because he first came holy [Col. 1161D] into the world and afterward departed from the world bloodied by his passion.

“Chosen out of thousands,” because, from the entire human race, the one Mediator between God and human beings—through whom the world was reconciled—was chosen. He alone among mortals was deemed worthy to hear from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III)—that is, in whom I found no fault that could offend me, and every weight of virtue in which I could rejoice.

[Col. 1162A] Thus Ecclesiastes aptly says of him: “I found one man among a thousand; but among all these I found not one woman” (Ecclesiastes VI), implicitly meaning one radiant with perfect righteousness. That this is what these words should be understood to mean is shown by the sentence that follows: “This alone I found: that God made human beings upright, but they themselves have entangled themselves in innumerable questions.”

“His head is finest gold.” The Apostle says that “the head of a woman is man, the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (I Corinthians II). This head is finest gold because, just as nothing is considered more precious among metals than gold, so the singular and eternal goodness of God rightly surpasses all the good things that he himself has made.

### His locks are lifted like palm branches, etc.

The locks of the Beloved’s head are the hosts of the saints who cling to God in faithful service; and rightly are they likened to lifted palm branches, because they await the sweetness of everlasting reward. Hence the Psalmist says: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm” (Ps. 91). They are rightly called black, like a raven, because they recognize that they cannot possess this sweetness from themselves but hope to receive it from him who says: “As a branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me” (John 15). Indeed, they discover that of themselves they were nothing but darkness, as the Apostle reminds us: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Nor is it surprising that before the washing of regeneration we are compared with the blackness of ravens, since the Truth who teaches even the apostles already following him says to them: “If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Matt. 7). But let us also see whether the Lawgiver detected anything raven-like among the lifted palm branches in the locks of the Bridegroom. For when he had perceived the light of divine glory, he immediately recognized and rebuked the darkness of human depravity, saying: “Lord and Ruler, merciful and gracious God, patient and of great compassion and true, who keeps mercy for thousands, who takes away iniquity, crimes, and sins—and no one is innocent before you by his own merits” (Matt. 7).

The locks of the Bridegroom, therefore—that is, the companies of the righteous—are like lifted palm branches and black like a raven, because through the mercy of the Ruler they strive toward the joys of victory, but recognize that this is not through themselves. This verse may also be understood of the spirits who eternally cling to their Creator in the heavenly homeland: the more deeply they behold the glory of unchanging and everlasting majesty, the more truly they discern how weak and insignificant everything created is.

Apponius interprets the Bridegroom’s locks as the powers of the angels and adds:

> “By saying ‘lifted palm branches,’ he taught that these ministries never bend away from their power and office, but always remain exalted; just as the locks of palm trees, always retaining the strength of their greenness, are lifted upward.”

Julianus speaks of them as follows:

> “The locks are also represented by another comparison, in which the form of curls seems nevertheless to imitate the gleam of gold. ‘His locks are like lifted palm branches,’ so that they may evidently appear curled and ruddy.”

A little later he says:

> “It is as though he said: The companies of saints, both human and angelic, serve his divinity and continually celebrate the king’s honor with praise. They are so conspicuous in the dignity of their ministry that they excel like palm branches and shine like gold. Yet they understand so deeply the one whom they serve that they not only assume no pride, but seem, because of their exceeding humility, dusky and black.”

Moreover, another translation, instead of “lifted palm branches,” used a single expression: “his locks are fir trees.” We know, indeed, that *abies* is called *elatēs* in Greek and is never altered by the weakness of decay. Hence *elatēs* here appears to be a Greek word, not a Latin one—that is, the proper name of a tree. Pliny the Elder also seems to support this when, writing about perfumes, he says:

> “There is also a tree belonging to these same perfumes, which some call *elatē*, which we call fir; others call it palm, and others spatha.”

From these words it may be inferred that *elatae* are trees bearing some resemblance to a palm or a fir and suitable for making perfumes. For this reason our translator said “lifted palm branches,” that is, “firs of the palms,” so that we should understand not the ordinary kind of fir suitable for buildings and ships, but the special kind suited to perfumes. This also fits the figures appropriately: the Bridegroom’s locks are compared with trees used for perfumes because the hosts of the saints, who cling familiarly to their Creator like locks to a head, are filled with the grace of virtues. As they diligently serve the divine Majesty, they adorn the Bridegroom’s head like locks resembling perfume-bearing trees.

Finally, when Mary Magdalene poured nard upon the Lord’s head, she made his hair resemble lifted palm branches—that is, aromatic trees—as a mystery of great devotion.

### His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.

John reveals what must typologically be understood in the Bridegroom’s eyes. When he recalls seeing the Lamb with seven horns, he immediately added an explanation: “Which are the seven spirits sent forth into all the earth” (Rev. 4). By “seven spirits” he means the seven gifts of the one and same Spirit, which Isaiah distinguishes according to the well-known order of divine activity, since “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

He delights in dwelling in those minds that make themselves clear like living waters; they permit nothing filthy, nothing dark, nothing that ought not to be approved by all lovers of truth—or rather, by Truth itself, which searches hearts and kidneys—to remain within them. And rightly does he say not “above pools of water,” but “above streams of water.” For if you ask where these waters flow and toward what they hasten, the fountain of life from which they arise reveals itself: namely, our Lord, from whom the hearts of the elect receive whatever is pure and luminous.

“It will become in him,” he says, “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). Those who appear to possess purity of speech or conduct, but either conceal or do not know that through this same purity they must strive toward the heavenly kingdom, are surely likened not to streams but to pools of water. Those who, by openly retaining their uncleanness, provide a dwelling for evil spirits are likened not to clean waters but rather to muddy wallows, in which swine delight.

Swine therefore delight in marshes, while doves delight in streams of water, because unclean spirits seize upon unclean breasts as a fitting dwelling. But “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5), and they are filled with the light of divine gifts. Since these gifts are given freely to the faithful, solely from heavenly benevolence, it is appropriately added:

### Which have been washed in milk, etc.

The gifts of heavenly generosity and compassion are rightly signified by the name of milk, because mothers who nourish their little offspring provide them with milk as nourishment freely and from the natural cause of affection. The doves, therefore, to which the Bridegroom’s eyes are likened, have been washed in milk, because “by grace we have been saved through faith, and this is not from ourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

These doves—that is, the gifts of the Spirit—are said to have been washed in milk even though they have never possessed any impurity, just as the Psalmist says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings; silver tested by fire, approved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12:7), although it is clear that they have never contained any earthly pollution requiring purification by fire. So too the Son, coeternal with the Father, is rightly believed to have been born from the Father, and rightly, truly, confessed and believed never to have been unborn. Scripture contains countless other examples of this kind.

These doves also dwell beside streams that are completely full, because grace of the Spirit most willingly inhabits any hearts overflowing with love of the virtues, so that it may illumine them with the more exalted regard of its presence—those hearts that vigorously strive toward heavenly things with the purity of sincere intention.

If we wish to understand the preachers of his word by the Bridegroom’s eyes, we shall find that they are like doves above streams of water: like doves because they are simple, and above streams of water because they have been enriched with spiritual grace. Streams of water often signify the holy Scriptures, which themselves are frequently represented under the name of waters. The preachers attentively devote themselves to these Scriptures, so that, instructed by them, they may more easily recognize and avoid the devil’s snares.

Doves commonly settle beside streams of water not only for drinking, washing, or the pleasantness and cleanliness of the place, but also so that they may foresee in the clarity of the water the shadow of a hawk approaching and thus escape the danger threatening from the enemy. The significance of this natural image is plain: we need continual meditation on the divine utterances, so that, as we read the deeds and sayings of the saints, we may carefully examine by what kind of open attack, and by what engines of deceit, the ancient enemy attempts to fight against and overthrow us.

As soon as we perceive his future snares, let us enter our one refuge—the clefts of our rock, that is, the defenses of faith in the Lord—and strive to protect ourselves by the sign of his Passion. Let us also swiftly seek the cave in the wall, that is, seek the frequent intercessions of the saints, whether angels or human beings, on our behalf before the mercy of our loving Creator. This is necessary for all the faithful, but especially for those upon whom has been imposed not merely care for themselves, but also the burden of governing and instructing others.

These are the firmest and safest defenses of the holy Church. For this reason the Lord earlier said to her: “Rise, my beloved, my bride, and come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock, into the cave in the wall.”

It is rightly said of these same doves—that is, the spiritual ministers of the word—“which have been washed in milk and dwell beside streams that are completely full,” to indicate that first of all they have been refreshed by the washing of baptism. This is appropriately expressed under the name of milk, since among the sacraments numbered under this term are those through which the infancy of the holy Church is accustomed either to be born or to be nourished.

If we believe that there is some distinction between streams of water and completely full channels, the instruction of the Old Testament may be understood by “streams of water.” Its worshipers truly know how to say to God: “The children of men shall hope in the protection of your wings” (Ps. 62), lest they be snatched away by the snares of aerial powers as by the talons of hawks. “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10).

In “completely full channels” the perfection of evangelical teaching may suitably be understood, for its fullness is such that nothing greater can exist, at least for those dwelling in this life. The Evangelist distinguished the two when he said: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Since knowledge of both Testaments has been granted to teachers of the truth, the Lord’s eyes are rightly said to be like doves above streams of water, washed in milk and dwelling beside completely full channels.

## BOOK FIVE

### His cheeks are like beds of spices, etc.

Just as the lips of the Lord express the words he spoke, so his cheeks express the modest piety and severity of his countenance. If it could rightly be said of an ordinary human being, “The wisdom of a man shines upon his face,” how much more did the fullness of virtue and wisdom shine for those who considered the face of that man who is the power and wisdom of God?

“His cheeks,” he says, “are like beds of spices planted by perfumers.” Just as beds of spices, properly and orderly arranged, offer those who look upon them great delight both in fragrance and in appearance, so the Mediator between God and human beings, appearing as a man, illuminated those present by the sweetness of his virtues or teaching and drew the absent to himself through his reputation.

By the perfumers who planted these beds understand the prophets and apostles. They committed not only his words but also his conduct to the sacred pages, with entirely harmonious testimony: the former narrating the mysteries of his future incarnation, the latter recounting its events.

I believe that the following should be referred to the appearance of his cheeks: that he rejoiced in spirit, congratulating the faith of the little ones; that he grieved over the hardness of the hearts of unbelievers; that, about to raise Lazarus, he rejoiced for the sake of the disciples, so that they might believe; that, seeing his weeping sisters or friends, he himself wept and was troubled in spirit; that, as his Passion approached, he began to be sorrowful and troubled; that he allowed no time for laughter or empty words; that he did not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears; and that, “like a sheep led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

### His lips are lilies dripping the choicest myrrh.

They are lilies because they promise the splendor of the heavenly kingdom; they drip the choicest myrrh because they proclaim that one must reach it by despising present pleasures. “From that time,” he says, “Jesus began to preach and to say, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near’” (Matt. 4).

Again, his lips are lilies because by their whiteness he commands us to shine with holiness; they drip the choicest myrrh because he orders us to endure courageously whatever adversity may arise in order to preserve this holiness.

His lips displayed lilies when he taught his hearers to be poor in spirit, meek, mourners, hungry and thirsty for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and peacemakers. He promised each of these the reward of everlasting blessedness. He added myrrh to the lilies when he immediately continued: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Again, his lips shone like lilies when, in one and the same person, he taught that he was truly God and truly human. The golden color within suitably corresponds to the truth of the divinity that was in Christ, especially since it is threefold and thus represents the one undivided glory of the Holy Trinity. The whiteness outside appropriately signifies the purity and holiness of the humanity he assumed.

Those same lips also dripped the choicest myrrh when he foretold that, although impassible in his divinity, he would suffer in the human being he had assumed bonds, scourging, spittle, insults, and death. His lips imitate both the appearance and the fragrance of lilies when he says: “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his work” (Rom. 2:6; Matt. 16:27; Rev. 22:12). They drip first-rate myrrh when he says: “But first he must suffer and be rejected by this generation” (Luke 17:25).

### XXIII. His hands are turned work of gold, etc.

After the lips, the Church praises the hands—that is, the works—of her Redeemer after his words, because he showed by his deeds that what he taught in words was to be believed through his works. Thus, when he taught on the mountain, the crowds marveled at his teaching. But so that faith might follow their wonder, when he descended from the mountain he cleansed a leper who asked it by the mere touch of his hand.

For the same reason, when his fellow citizens marveled at his deeds, they said: “Where did this man get such wisdom and mighty works?” (Matt. 13). Wisdom refers to the lips, while mighty works refer to the hands.

He rightly declares that his hands are turned work, signifying that he possesses both an effortless power and an indescribable skill in action. For it is evident that turning work is more readily and more indescribably accomplished than other crafts. Someone who works with an axe, chisel, hatchet, or hammer works with far greater labor and requires frequent application of a rule and careful observation by the eyes lest he make an error. But one who turns on a lathe does not need an external rule; by means of the tool he uses, he can preserve the direction of his work within the tool itself.

The Lord’s hands, therefore, are turned work, because he has at hand the power to do whatever he wills, for “he spoke, and they were made.” Finally, he said: “Take up your pallet and walk.” Immediately the man who had lain paralyzed for thirty-eight years rose, took up his pallet, and walked (John 5:8–9).

His hands are turned work because he himself holds the entire rule of righteousness. Unlike our poverty, he does not need to learn in the sacred writings lest his work deviate from the truth. Hence it was said of him: “How does this man know letters, since he has not been taught?” (John 7:15). He knew because he himself was older than the writings and the law—indeed, he was the judge of the very Lawgiver.

“His hands,” he says, “are turned work of gold, full of hyacinths.” In gold, which surpasses all metals, the excellence of divinity has repeatedly been shown to be signified. His hands are therefore of gold, because no believer is unaware that the mighty works he performed as a human being were accomplished divinely.

They are rightly also said to be full of hyacinths, because they awaken us to hope for and love of heavenly things. Hyacinth is a gem of the color of the sky. The Lord has hyacinths in his turned hands so that he may adorn the vessels of election that he prepares for glory with gems of this kind—that is, so that he may gladden the hearts of his elect with desire and expectation of heavenly glory.

If we understand by hyacinths the pigments bearing this name, this too does not depart from a fitting signification of truth, for hyacinth is a pigment of purple color and pleasant fragrance. Hence the poet, gathering together precious things as examples of love, adds:

> “Gifts are laurel and sweetly ruddy hyacinth.”

The Lord’s hands were also full of purple flowers, because, as he was to die for our life, he suffused them with the redness of his own blood when they were pierced by nails.

Yet another translation teaches that the name *hyacinths* here should be understood as gems rather than flowers; it reads: “His turned hands of gold are full of *tharsis*.” For among the Hebrews *tharsis* is the name of a stone that we call chalcedony.

### His belly is ivory, etc.

The belly occupies the most vulnerable place among our limbs, since it lacks the bones that would protect it and encloses the flanks, every wound to which is exceedingly dangerous. Ivory, moreover, is the bone of an elephant, an animal said to possess extraordinary chastity and cold blood. Hence its death is often sought by the dragon’s ambushes, since the dragon desires to cool its burning entrails by drinking the elephant’s blood.

The sacred history testifies to the color of sapphire when it says: “They saw the God of Israel, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24:10).

The belly of the Beloved therefore signifies the fragility of his humanity, by which he was made like us. Ivory indicates the beauty of chastity, by which he remained in the flesh free from the corruption of sin. Sapphires express the sublimity of the heavenly virtues with which he shone in the flesh.

“His belly,” he says, “is ivory, distinguished by sapphires.” It is as though he plainly said: The fragility of mortal substance will truly exist in him, but this fragility, wholly free from the wantonness of mortality, will shine instead with the splendor of divine works.

He beautifully said that his belly was wholly ivory, but not wholly clothed in sapphires; rather, it was distinguished by sapphires, so that partly ivory and partly sapphires would appear. His belly was ivory because the fragility he had assumed was entirely free from sin, so that no more corrupt heat could be found in it than in the bone of a dead elephant. It was distinguished by sapphires because amid the sufferings of his assumed humanity he displayed frequent signs of perpetual divinity.

To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he was born a little child for us; to the power of divinity, that he was born of a Virgin, and that this same birth was proclaimed by angelic voices and celebrated in mysteries. To the power of divinity belongs the fact that, indicated by a star, he was shown worthy of worship by the Magi; to the fragility of humanity, that he was driven from his homeland by the plots of a treacherous king.

To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he could be led and tempted by the devil; to the power of divinity, that after defeating and repelling the devil he was honored by angelic ministries. To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he asked a Samaritan woman for water; to the power of divinity, that he testified that he could give her the fountain of living water.

To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he grew weary from traveling; to the power of divinity, that he promised eternal rest to those who followed him. To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he slept in a boat; to the power of divinity, that when awakened he commanded the winds and the sea.

To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he was crucified and died; to the power of divinity, that at his death the elements trembled, both earthly and heavenly. To the fragility of humanity belongs the fact that he was prepared with spices and buried; to the power of divinity, that he rose and ascended into heaven.

To the fragility of humanity belongs what Isaiah says: “He had no appearance or beauty, and we saw him despised” (Isa. 53:3). A little later: “His face was as though hidden, and he was despised, and we did not esteem him” (ibid.). To the power of divinity belongs what John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1).

Christ’s ivory belly was therefore distinguished by sapphires, because his immaculate and undefiled incarnation shone forth through the frequent miracles of divine exaltation.

It should be noted that Scripture says of the color of sapphire that its appearance is like the sky when it is clear. By the name “clear sky,” the sublimity of divine majesty is not inappropriately represented. The Psalmist attests to this when, describing the incarnation of the same Redeemer, he says: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its summit” (Ps. 18).

This is what he himself says of himself to his disciples: “And you have believed that I came forth from God; I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28).

The Bride also saw the appearance of sapphire in the ivory belly of her Beloved when, through the voice of her first shepherd, she said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). For in the holy, innocent, undefiled Son of Man, set apart from sinners, she recognized the pure fullness of divinity.

### His legs are columns of marble, etc.

By the name of the Lord’s legs are signified the courses of his incarnation, by which he deigned to come for our salvation. They are rightly compared with columns of marble, because they are strong and straight. What is stronger than marble? What is straighter than a column? Did not the Psalmist behold the firmness of marble in his legs when he said: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run his course,” and the rest (Ps. 88)? Did he not also see the straightness of the columns when he again said: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways” (Ps. 144:17)?

For this reason, when he was placed on the cross, his legs were by no means broken, although the governor permitted it, just as his garments could not be torn. The tunic remained uninjured, to signify that the unity of the Church—which is his chosen garment, without spot or wrinkle—must never be violated. His legs remained untouched, to signify that the mystery of his coming in the flesh, sacred and inviolable, endures against every hammer of perverse doctrine. For Pilate is interpreted as “the mouth of a hammerer.” But although the hammer, with an impious heretical mouth, prepares to strike, the marble columns stand, firmly repelling the blow of the striker. Though mad doctrine says some mad thing about the Lord, evangelical truth stands victorious.

It is fittingly added of these columns: “Which are founded upon bases of gold.” The golden bases are the counsels of divine providence, in which, from eternity before the ages, all that was to be created in time in the world was ordained; in them both the incarnation of our Savior and our salvation in him were predestined. The Apostle testifies: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and immaculate in his sight in love” (Eph. 1). And the apostle Peter says that we were redeemed by the precious blood of Jesus Christ, as of an immaculate and undefiled Lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested in the last times (1 Pet. 2).

Therefore the marble columns, to which the Lord’s legs are compared, are founded upon his golden bases, because all the footsteps of our Savior—by which he willed to come from heaven to earth, to live on earth, after earth to descend to hell, and after hell to rise from the tomb and return to heaven—are firm as marble, straight as heaven’s power, ordered as columns by the rule of the divine command, as founded upon golden bases. Of these bases he himself says: “For I have not spoken of myself, but the Father who sent me has himself given me commandment what I should say and what I should speak” (John 12:49). And if you wish to know why the bases are golden, hear what follows: “And I know that his commandment is eternal life” (ibid.).

### His appearance is like Lebanon, etc.

“Why,” he says, “should I labor further to describe each of his members? I shall comprehend the whole in brief.” Just as Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia, is renowned and distinguished for its height and extent, so our Lord rightly surpasses all who have sprung from the earth by the grace of his greater exaltation. As that mountain is productive of noble trees, so he raises up all the saints by his protection lest they sink down to the depths, and preserves those rooted in himself lest they be shaken by the winds of temptations. As all the glory of the forests yields to the beauty, strength, height, and fragrance of cedars, so “my beloved is fairer in form than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon his lips; therefore God has blessed him for ever” (Ps. 44:3), together with the rest that the following psalm describes of him—things greatly surpassing his measure and fellowship.

It should be noted that the same Beloved is compared both with Lebanon, which produces notable timber, and with the cedar, which Lebanon itself produces among other trees: as though one and the same person produces and bears trees, is produced among the trees, and is borne by himself. For our Lord Jesus Christ, while by the grace of his divinity he gives birth, nourishes, and sustains all the elect from the beginning of the world to its end unto life, also made himself a human being among human beings when he willed; and he filled that human being with the grace of his Spirit, though far more highly than all others. For it is said of them: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4); but of him: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure. For the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3).

The Lord, therefore, is chosen like the appearance of a cedar, because he surpasses, by a unique and singular dignity, the entire grove of the holy Church in which he was born. His appearance is like Lebanon, which brings forth among excellent trees even the cedar, because among his elect he also created himself, the human being he willed to be, like the tree of life in the midst of paradise. It is as if a painter painted himself too among others, in his proper place, with the suitable colors; or as if a historian, relating many things about many people—for example, the lawgiver Moses or the evangelist John—also described of himself, in his own place, matters worthy of remembrance.

Thus the mountain of whiteness—for this is what the name Lebanon means—that is, our Redeemer, among innumerable fruitful trees which it brought forth to praise the Lord’s name, also brought forth a cedar, a tree more excellent than the rest: namely, himself, who would not only praise the Lord’s name but would himself come blessed in the name of the Lord.

### His throat is most sweet, etc.

If in the Lord’s lips, above where it was said, “His lips are most shining lilies,” we understand the words of his mouth, what should we understand in his most sweet throat but at times the savor of those same words? Many who read or hear can repeat the Lord’s words and can most easily investigate the mysteries of faith; but very few are found who truly feel in the palate of their heart how sweetly these things taste. Hence it is said in the outstanding praise of the saints: “They shall utter the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and shall exult in your righteousness” (Ps. 144:7). Those exult in God’s righteousness who have learned to taste inwardly, with love, the abundance of his sweetness and to utter its memory by preaching it also to their neighbors. But one who has not yet learned to taste his sweetness must necessarily fear rather than exult in the righteousness of his judgments.

Thus Peter, uttering to us the memory of the Lord’s exceedingly abundant sweetness, which he had well tasted, says: “Desire the reasonable milk without guile, that by it you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2). Again, because the vital breath is conveyed through the throat to the lips so that one may speak, just as in the Lord’s lips we may understand the words he spoke, so in his throat we may most fittingly understand the inward and hidden disposition of his piety and kindness, through which it came about that he spoke outwardly to us.

For Paul says: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:13). When he gave us hope of the appearing of the glory of the great God, his lips will be lilies; when he taught us, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, to live soberly, justly, and piously, those same lips will drip the choicest myrrh. But that eternal grace, which appeared to us, when it willed, in this promise and teaching, is itself his throat, rightly most sweet to us, since apart from it we can possess no sweetness at all.

Finally, the Beloved himself showed what the sweetness of his throat can accomplish not only in spoken voice but also in breath itself, when, appearing to his disciples after the resurrection—to the first members, that is, of his Bride—he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

“And he is wholly desirable.” The whole Christ is God and human being—that is, Word, soul, and flesh—and he is wholly desirable, because what the apostle Peter says, “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12), must be understood not only of the unchangeable majesty of his everlasting divinity but also of the glorified substance of his assumed humanity. I shall say something more: he was wholly desirable even before the glorification of his humanity; he was wholly desirable from the very beginning of his conception to the triumph of his Passion: desirable to his mother, when she said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38); desirable to the blessed womb that bore him; desirable to the breasts that nursed him; desirable to the angels, who immediately at his birth sang the hymn; desirable to the shepherds, who, having seen him, glorified and praised God; desirable to the Magi, who came from the East to seek him and, when they were granted to find him, worshiped him with gifts offered; desirable to the aged Simeon, who awaited to his last age the vision of his birth promised to him and, when he received him in his arms, blessed God and joyfully beheld death; desirable to Anna the prophetess, who, seeing his birth, likewise rendered to the Lord the due praises of her confession; desirable to all who saw him at twelve years of age in the temple, marvelous among the elders and teachers in heavenly wisdom; desirable to the disciples, who, when he called, most promptly left everything they had and followed him; desirable to those same disciples when they said, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 8:68); desirable to all the people and the tax collectors, who, hearing his word, justified God; desirable to Peter on the mountain, when he says, “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4); desirable to the thief on the cross, when he prayed, “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Nor is he desirable only to those who loved him when they saw him in the flesh, but also to those of whom he himself says to his disciples: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17). He is desirable also to us, who were born into the world after his ascension into heaven and possess, together with the earlier saints, his common promise: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and will receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John 14:3).

### Such is my beloved, etc.

The more devoutly the Church, or each holy soul, loves God, the more familiarly it has God as a friend. For one who, because of weakness of mind or consciousness of sin, still keeps the divine commandments with servile fear must call him rather Lord than father or friend, because he has not yet been able to attain that apostolic perfection by which he deserves to hear: “But I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). Abraham too, because of his outstanding faith and love, was called God’s friend; and the Lord speaks to Moses as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend (Exod. 33:11). Having heard the character of the Beloved, about whom the daughters of Jerusalem had inquired, they add another question, saying:

## “Where Has Your Beloved Gone?” etc.

For the sake of poetic elegance, the persons speaking are varied. In reality, the daughters of Jerusalem designate the same Church of Christ that is expressed under the name of bride. She is called by the name of the daughters of Jerusalem, or of Zion, because she consists of many souls who derive their origin from that heavenly city which is the mother of us all. She is called bride, sister, friend, or by some similar name in order to signify that she is one and not divided, although she is spread far and wide throughout the world.

The varied conversation of the speakers among themselves concerning the bridegroom is, as we said above, that pleasant exchange among the faithful of Christ by which they incite one another to love him. The bride had adjured the daughters of Jerusalem that, if they found her beloved, they should tell him that she was languishing with love for him. For it is the common joy of the whole Catholic Church that all the elect should pray to the Lord for her welfare.

The daughters of Jerusalem had asked the bride what her beloved was like, because faith in Christ can be learned and taught only within Catholic unity. After hearing the description of him, which they had earnestly requested, they also ask where he has gone, because this too must be learned within the unity of the holy Church: namely, in whose heart, above all, and in what kind of way of life the Lord is accustomed to be found.

When, therefore, we come together and speak about the Lord with pure intention, we are all daughters of Jerusalem—all of us who aspire perfectly to things above and truly profess that we are pilgrims on earth and have our homeland in heaven. Yet each of us is rightly said to speak with the bride of Christ and to seek an answer from her, when he carefully ensures that he neither wishes to say nor to hear from a brother anything other than what the rule of Catholic peace prescribes.

The Church is called the most beautiful among women because, although there is great beauty among the churches of Christ throughout the world, like women spiritually fertile with blossoms, still greater is the beauty of that one Catholic Church, which is completed from all those churches as from her members. Far be it from us to understand “women” in this passage as the synagogues of heretics, schismatics, pagans, or erring Jews. The bride of Christ cannot be called the most beautiful among those women who are shown to possess no true beauty.

Rather, they are the beautiful churches of Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea, and countless others of this kind, wholly consecrated to God throughout the world. The one Church that consists of them all is rightly called the most beautiful.

## “Where Has Your Beloved Gone?” etc.

The beloved is said to go away and withdraw, not because the Lord ever abandons those whom he has already acquired and proceeds to acquire others, but because the power of the divine nature can be present everywhere. Thus, when he wishes to join others to himself, he goes or withdraws toward them, while nevertheless preserving in the grace he began those whom he had already gathered to himself.

This accords with what he says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers, and lead them to the entrance of the tent of meeting; and I will take of your spirit and give it to them” (Num. XI, 16). He did not diminish the grace once given to Moses; rather, he made them participants in the grace that Moses possessed. It is like a flame of fire: when you light a candle from it, you kindle the candle with its light, while the flame from which you light it remains undiminished.

It may also rightly be understood that the beloved goes away and withdraws from the bride for a time when, although we desire to be inflamed by love of him even to the shedding of tears, and with fixed, unwavering intention to persevere in prayer, and to transfer the whole mind from carnal desires to eternal things, he does not always grant what is desired according to our wishes.

Rightly, therefore, we ask those whom we believe to know, and whom we judge worthy of such an inquiry, where the Lord has gone or where he has withdrawn. We desire that they point out to us the presence of those who, by greater signs of virtue and purity of mind, show that divine grace is in them, so that, instructed by their examples and conversation, we too may deserve to advance more and more in love of our beloved.

And they rightly say, “We will seek him with you,” because any soul that attempts to seek Christ without the fellowship of the holy Church will no longer rightly be counted among the daughters of Jerusalem, but among those of whom the mother of holy Samuel, representing the Church, says to the priest of the despised Synagogue: “Do not regard your handmaid as one of the daughters of Belial” (I Sam. I, 16).

## CHAPTER VI

### “My beloved has gone down into his garden,” etc.

It is already known what the beloved’s garden is. He himself said: “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride.” His garden is the Church; his garden is every elect soul.

And well, after saying, “My beloved has gone down into the garden,” he added “his”—that is, the garden which he himself made, cultivated, planted with the spices of virtue, watered with the fountain of his grace so that it would not fail, and enclosed with the wall of his protection so that it would not be profaned by outsiders.

This is the garden of which he himself says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and planted in his garden; it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of the air rested in its branches” (Luke XIII). The mustard seed is the word of the Gospel, humble in appearance but ardent in power. God himself, both God and man, received it from the Father and sowed it in his Church, giving it such growth that, like an outstanding tree, it extended the branches of faith and virtue far and wide throughout the world. In these branches the angelic spirits also rejoiced in the salvation of humanity, and the citizens of heaven believed that their rest had been increased when earthly people were recalled to heavenly things.

Nor was it without reason that the same beloved was seized in a garden, suffered crucifixion in a garden, was buried in a garden, and rose victorious from the dead in a garden. He wished to be believed to be a gardener by Mary, who first deserved to see the glory of his resurrection, because in his own garden—that is, in the Church—among the other plantings of divine charisms, he had taken care to plant the virtue of patience in this life through contempt of death, the hope of ending this life in blessed repose after the dissolution of the body, and the desire for blessed immortality in the restoration of the body.

He is appropriately said to have gone down into his garden, rather than to have entered it. The beloved’s dwelling is on high, because he dwells in the heights and looks upon the lowly (Ps. CXII). The garden’s place is low, in the valley of tears. Yet the one who descends into it from above has himself established in its heart the ascent by which they may reach the place of heavenly happiness.

Hence it is rightly said above of this same garden, that is, the Church: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness like a column of smoke from spices?” It is therefore a wondrous dispensation of heavenly mercy that the Lord is said to descend into the Church, while the Church is said to ascend to the Lord. Divine grace descends to us from above, enabling us, once assisted, to ascend upward.

This was mystically signified in Exodus, when the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai and Moses ascended. The latter ascended in order to receive an increase of virtue; the former descended in order to bestow it.

After saying, “My beloved has gone down into his garden,” he also explains how that garden has been established and with what produce it is fertile, immediately adding: “To the bed of spices.” The bed of spices is the mind of the faithful. Taught the discipline of right faith, it is arranged as though with equal sides on either hand; repeatedly turned with diligent cultivation by the spade; and cleansed of useless weeds. For it examines itself with careful scrutiny and strives through attentive thought to ensure that the heavenly Farmer finds nothing profane, nothing unclean, nothing opposed to the things that are truly conducive to salvation.

It strives to make itself worthy for the beloved himself, the sower of righteousness, mercifully to plant in it the spices of virtue by his grace and to water them with his frequent assistance, so that they may never dry up.

The soul beautifully expresses its heavenly desire at the beginning of the forty-first Psalm, according to the Hebrew truth alone, saying: “As a bed is prepared for streams of water, so my soul is prepared for you, O God” (Ps. XLI).

When the Lord descends into his garden, or to the bed of spices, what he does there is shown when it is immediately added:

### “That he may feed in the gardens,” etc.

He feeds in the gardens because he delights in the pious labors of the saints. He feeds in the gardens because those who are his members produce fruits of righteousness. And we should understand the saying about almsgiving not only in a bodily but also in a spiritual sense: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these my brothers, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

He gathers lilies when he leads the righteous, who have attained the perfect whiteness of merits, out of this life and brings them to the heavenly kingdoms.

The following two verses expand this further through the stimulus of immense love, adding:

### “I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine,” etc.

I prepare for my beloved a pleasing pasture in beds of spices—that is, in the pure hearts of the faithful—and my beloved, who feeds among the holy desires of chaste minds, repays me for this return of grace by fulfilling the desires of those faithful whom he has nurtured.

He fulfilled them by plucking them from this paradise of sacred delight and gathering them into the secret chambers of the heavenly dwellings. There, before the sight of his glory, they will shine with eternal immortality of flesh and spirit, like the double appearance of lilies—that is, both golden and white—and, like a most fragrant odor proceeding from them, they will spread the imperishable reputation of their virtues among all the inhabitants of the everlasting homeland.

Up to this point, it is the voice of the holy Church, seeking and praising her Lord and desiring to see his face. But since he can never be absent from those who love him—for “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst”—even if one of his own is shut in among lions, held in the depths of the sea, or enclosed in the belly of a sea creature and thus separated from other mortals, he is there with him.

His voice therefore follows, declaring that he has always been present to those who seek him, speaking about him, and that he has heard what they were saying. He repays their devotion toward him with worthy praise, saying:

### XXIV. “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely,” etc.

Jerusalem is said to mean “vision of peace.” By this name the dwelling of the heavenly homeland, which possesses perfect peace, is very frequently signified.
