“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely like Jerusalem.” The Church, or every holy soul—which is a portion of the Church—is sweet and lovely like Jerusalem when, through the integrity of pure conduct, the sweetness of divine praise, and the delight of mutual love, it immediately imitates the heavenly city, in accordance with what Isaiah says: “As the new heavens and the new earth that I am making shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring stand” (Isa. LXVI).

The Church is also terrifying, like an army drawn up in battle array, when with steadfast intention in pure prayer she repels every attack of the demonic army; when, through frequent preaching of the heavenly word, she shatters all the weapons of wandering doctrine; and when, by the continual examples of good works, she rebukes even the perverse conduct and life of false believers and brings them back to the path of truth.

The Church is terrifying like an army drawn up in battle array when every faithful person remains in the vocation to which he was called; when those who govern give their subjects the form of salutary teaching and perfect action; when those who practice continence cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord; and when married people so use this world that, through diligent generosity in almsgiving, they do not neglect to acquire for themselves the rewards of the age to come.

The prophet teaches that the Church consists in this threefold distinction among faithful persons when he asserts that only three men—namely Noah, Daniel, and Job—would be delivered at the time of heavenly vengeance.

When each of these preserves his own rank undefiled, they display an army properly arranged, and thereby make the bride of Christ invincible to all her enemies. Likewise, every perfect soul, when it devotes itself to virtue in such a way that it leaves no place for vices among them, remains truly terrifying to its enemies like an army drawn up in battle array.

For example, if it pursues continence in such a way that it does not retain the virtue of humility; or if it practices works of almsgiving without restraining its tongue from the fault of excessive speech; or if it persists in frequent prayers while neglecting to show affection and love to its neighbors—such a soul is less terrifying to its enemies, because it has arranged the camp of its virtues less perfectly: it has firmly ordered faith in one part, but has left another part inactive.

Yet because the one and same Church of Christ partly already rejoices with her King in heaven and partly still wages war for him in the world, the words, “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely like Jerusalem,” may be understood of that part of her which, having completed her struggle and finished her course, has already received the crown of righteousness.

But what follows—“Terrifying like an army drawn up in battle array”—may appropriately be understood of those who, still held in the body, resist with strong faith the enemy lying in ambush around them like a roaring lion.

Again, the Church is beautiful, sweet, and lovely like Jerusalem in what she inwardly accomplishes spiritually and worthily before God. She is terrifying like an army drawn up in battle array because she strives to extend her spiritual rule throughout the whole world, even against the resisting powers of the age.

Indeed, the former dominion of the Romans, Greeks, and other peoples was like an army arranged in battle array, because it oppressed the world with great power. But it was not sweet and lovely like Jerusalem, because it neither knew how to hope for nor to imitate the joys of the life of peace.

The Church, however, is beautiful, sweet, and lovely like Jerusalem because she is accustomed to live a heavenly life on earth. And she is terrifying like an army drawn up in battle array because she strives to draw even the minds and conduct of barbarians from different nations into her way of life.

Yet because she has not yet deserved to see the face of her beloved, whom she seeks with the greatest longing, she next hears:

### “Turn your eyes away from me,” etc.

It is as though he were saying plainly: “I gave you dove-like eyes, by which you might understand the secrets of the Scriptures, distinguish virtues from vices, and recognize the paths of righteousness by which you must still come.

“But beware of attempting to direct those same eyes toward me in order to see me. ‘No one shall see my face and live’ (Exod. XXXIII). There will be a time when, freed from the bonds of the flesh, you will come to me. Then what I promised will be fulfilled: ‘Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him’ (John XIV).

“But now, while you remain in the body and are a pilgrim away from everlasting goods, turn the eyes of your mind away from contemplating the divine majesty and essence. For they have made me fly away—that is, those spiritual senses of yours by which you desired to know me perfectly. Although they rise very high, they are not sufficient in this life to comprehend me perfectly. They can reach only the point of recognizing that the glory of the divine nature is of such sublimity that it can be seen only by those who have been wholly removed from visible life and introduced into the invisible.”

We are therefore commanded in the present life to turn the eyes of our inquiry away from knowing God’s substance, because those eyes make him fly away from us—not because he whom we seek withdraws farther away, since he promises, “Seek, and you will find” (Luke XI), but because, through his revelation, we learn that the more deeply he is sought with a pure heart, the more certainly his incomprehensibility is comprehended.

Something similar is found in the Psalmist: “A man draws near to the deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). It is as though he were saying in other words: “Human frailty raises the attentive eyes of its heart to see God, and those eyes make him fly away, because the senses, exercised and enlightened by that very inquiry, recognize that the eminence of divinity is more excellent than they had hitherto been able to conceive.” Thus they understand most truly what is said in another Psalm: “There is no end to his greatness” (Ps. CXLIV).

By this response the Lord wished to satisfy the desire of the holy Church, with which she openly sought him carefully and not in an obscure saying, longing to see the one whom she loved, as the earlier verses of this poem abundantly declare.

He therefore urges her, with a proper discrimination of times, not to seek on the journey the reward reserved for her in her homeland, but to remember that meanwhile she must walk by faith in order to arrive at sight. The evangelist John beautifully distinguishes these times, saying: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

But lest the Church perhaps take it hard that she cannot yet enjoy the full contemplation of her Creator, he enumerates the manifold pledges of the Spirit that he has granted her, so that she may bear more patiently the delay of that one supreme and singular good which she has not yet received but will receive in the time of eternal recompense.

The text continues:

### “Your hair is like a flock of goats,” etc.

These verses, together with those that follow and those set out above, have already been explained as fully as our capacity permits. Yet it should not weary us to repeat in explaining what the author of the sacred poem did not weary of repeating in writing, whether to recall what was said earlier or, with the help of divine grace, to accomplish something new and useful.

The repetition of these or countless other things already stated in Scripture is an indication of firmness: it shows that the word is God’s and that it is truly fulfilled, as the patriarch Joseph testifies when interpreting the king’s dream.

In the bride’s hair, therefore, the manifold sublimity of her thoughts is signified; in her teeth, the firmest stability of her words. The teeth cooperate with the lips and tongue in speaking, while the hairs arise imperceptibly from the head and do not hurt when cut. What wise person would grieve when the superfluous frivolity of his thoughts is removed, rather than rejoice?

Thus, in a great mystery, the teeth of the lawgiver are read as unmoved when he was full of days; and no razor ascended upon Samuel’s head because he was a perpetual Nazirite— that is, holy—to the Lord. This signified that “not one iota or one stroke would pass from the law until all things had taken place” (Matt. V), and that the prophetic mind found in itself nothing of loose thought that the strictness of penitence ought to cut away.

The bride’s hair is rightly compared to a flock of goats. For the law commanded that any soul that sinned through ignorance, once it recognized its guilt, should offer God an unblemished female goat as a sacrifice.

Our hair is compared with a flock of goats when, in penitence for the errors of our thoughts, we offer the Lord tears of compunction and prayers of supplication.

The flock of goats may also appropriately be understood as so designated because goats customarily seek their food among steep rocks or thickets. The thoughts of the elect, always striving toward heavenly things, rejoice to feed in high places, not in the low pleasures of earthly things.

Of these goats it is rightly added: “Which appeared from Gilead.” Gilead means “heap of testimony.” By this name the mind of the righteous is rightly called when it proves through clear signs of virtue that it has renounced earthly desires.

Mount Gilead received this name because Jacob and Laban made a heap there as a testimony of friendship or agreement that they would not harm one another, when Laban had sought his idols among Jacob’s possessions and had not found them.

Laban therefore signifies the world; Jacob signifies the mind that supplants vices. Laban seeks his idols among Jacob’s possessions and does not find them when lovers of the world examine the hearts of the elect and discover nothing of their own in them.

Jacob also makes a heap as a testimony that he does not touch Laban’s substance and boundaries. When the abundance of virtues has been gathered within him like living stones, the mind devoted to God says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed goal, the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. III).

Laban also brings stones for the construction of the same heap when the world itself, through its temptations, provides the faithful with an occasion for virtue.

An agreement is made between Laban and Jacob that they will not harm one another when the righteous person declares: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

From this heap, therefore, a flock of goats appears, to which the bride’s hair is compared, when a multitude of lofty and frequent thoughts is generated from a faithful mind. And from this flock we offer God an unblemished goat for the sins we have committed in ignorance when, having recognized our sins, we punish them with humble contrition of heart.

Gilead is the name not only of a mountain but also of a city founded upon it. Hence it can rightly bear the figure of our Lord and Savior, as well as of the Church or any holy soul situated in him.

Earlier, where the added phrase occurs, “Your hair is like a flock of goats that have ascended from Mount Gilead,” we understood it to have been spoken of that incomparably exalted mountain which says of itself: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

Here, however, where the name of the mountain is omitted and the text simply says “which appeared from Gilead,” nothing prevents us from understanding it as spoken of the city built upon that mountain—that is, the Church or the righteous soul.

A holy soul may rightly be called a heap of testimony, built upward through the gathering of various virtues. The whole Church is also rightly designated by this name, to whose peoples the apostle Peter says: “As you come to him, a living stone rejected by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves, like living stones, are being built upon him” (I Pet. II).

This also suits the Lord, as we said above, to whom the assembly of all the elect is joined—those who bear testimony to a pure conscience through pious confession and upright deeds.

### “Your teeth are like a flock of sheep that have come up from the washing.”

We have said that the words of the holy Church may be understood in the bride’s teeth. They are therefore rightly said to be like a flock of sheep, because nothing but the brightness of virtue and innocence is seen in them, as they seek the grace of their Creator in everything—whether by teaching, praying, or speaking his praises.

The sheep are rightly said to have come up from the washing, because nothing filthy, nothing unclean, nothing that has not been purified in the fountain of knowledge proceeds from the mouth of the righteous, in accordance with the apostle’s exhortation: “Let no evil speech come out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV).

By contrast, anyone who brings forth shameful, insulting, harmful, or even idle words from an obscene heart has teeth resembling not sheep coming up from the washing but rather pigs emerging from the mire.

The text rightly adds:

### “All bearing twin offspring,” etc.

All the sheep to which the bride’s teeth are compared bear twin offspring in abundance, because every word of the elect is fertile with the fruit of the twofold love—namely, love by which God and neighbor are loved.

Every word speaks of the perpetual health of mind and body. Every word is accustomed to arm its hearers with the weapons of righteousness that must be held on the right and on the left. Every word desires to discuss the promise of life, both the present and the future. Nothing proceeds from the mouth of the righteous that is not beneficial to the fruit of eternal salvation.

The sheep to which he compares the bride’s teeth are appropriately said to bear twin offspring, because by what we say we are able to benefit our neighbors and instruct them in the way of virtue; but by what we think soundly, we benefit ourselves.

Before the inward judge, on the altar of the heart, we ourselves offer a living sacrifice. For the benefit of our neighbors, however, we disclose by words only what we carry on within.

Thus, someone who sought to please the Creator with such a sacrifice said: “In me are your vows, O God, which I will repay with praises to you” (Ps. LIII).

If, as was said above, we understand the preachers to be represented by the teeth and the hearers by the hair, this fits extremely well—not only because the former provide the body with speech and nourishment, while the latter provide the head with pleasing adornments, since they offer the instruments of salvation, but also because the former are placed first on the face like forerunners, while the latter, like successors, cover the back part of the head.

It is therefore evident that those who are still inexperienced and more fragile ought to listen to the words of their elders and obey them. The teachers themselves, however, must not only fulfill the divine commandments but also increase the flock of the supreme Shepherd by preaching.

### “Like the rind of a pomegranate,” etc.

It was said above that the cheeks of the Church signify the mark of her modesty, while the pomegranate represents the ministry of the Lord’s blood.

The bride has cheeks like a pomegranate because the faithful soul is not ashamed either to confess the passion of its Redeemer in words or to imitate it in deeds. Setting aside every shame and confusion that brings death, it delights to proclaim openly: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

And appropriately: because he had compared the cheeks of the Church to the rind of a pomegranate, he therefore added, “Apart from what is hidden within you.” The rind of a pomegranate displays only redness on the outside, but conceals within itself the many seeds with which it abounds.

So the soul devoted to God and healthfully modest strives in every way to protect itself by the power of the life-giving cross. Yet beneath the sign of that same cross it contains many kinds of virtues that are scarcely visible outwardly but refresh the mind inwardly.

### “There are sixty queens,” etc.

Queens and concubines alike approach the king’s bed and bear sons to the king, but both do not ennoble the king’s head with royal diadems.

Both therefore signify souls devoted to preaching the truth, generating spiritual offspring for the eternal King through the word of faith and the fountain of saving baptism. Yet there is a considerable—indeed, no slight—difference in their minds.

The queens are those minds that serve doctrine with the kingdom of heaven in view. The concubines are those who proclaim Christ insincerely, motivated only by the advantage of carnal and temporal pleasures.

The apostle speaks of such people: “Whether Christ is proclaimed through pretense or through truth, in either case I rejoice, and I shall continue to rejoice” (Phil. I).

The Lord himself distinguishes them from one another, saying: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

Both approach the king’s bed, but both do not reign with him, because those who destroy their teaching by their deeds deprive themselves of the consolations of the everlasting kingdom.

Therefore the former are rightly included under the number sixty, while the latter are included under eighty. The number ten signifies knowledge of the divine law because of the Decalogue; the number six, in which God completed the world, signifies the perfection of good works.

Since five multiplied by twelve makes sixty, the number sixty of the queens may also be interpreted in this way: those who regulate all the senses of their body—sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell—according to the rule of apostolic teaching are rightly represented by the number sixty.

They are called queens because those who now follow the commandments of the apostles, whose number is twelve, through all the functions of their members will then be joined with those same apostles in everlasting joy with the King.

The number eighty, when understood in a bad sense, not unreasonably signifies the cares and entanglements of earthly and temporal matters. The course of this age revolves through the four seasons of the year, and the world itself is divided into four regions: east, west, north, and south.

There are therefore sixty queens because all souls that follow the knowledge they have received through the perfection of sacred law with good action now wage war in the kingdom of faith, and in the future will enter the heavenly wedding with the true King.

And there are eighty concubines because those who expend the knowledge of truth and the mystery of the word, which they appear to practice, upon the pleasures of weak and passing things will, when their lamps have been extinguished at the bridegroom’s coming, be excluded from the gate of the heavenly kingdom through their pleasure in temporal things.

### “And there is no number of young women.”

Understand the young women as souls recently reborn in Christ that are not yet capable of the ministry of preaching. Therefore, as though not yet noble and not yet suited to the royal bed, they attend the queen in the faithful watchfulness of service, because they rejoice humbly to obey the commands of the holy Church.

Of such persons we read above: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you.” That is, they are souls that do not remain old through guilt but have already been renewed by grace.

Their number is without limit because the total number of the citizens of the heavenly homeland surpasses the bounds of our estimation.

This cannot be understood of our peaceful King, the true Solomon, as though he did not know the number of his faithful. For if he “counts the number of the stars and calls them all by name” (Ps. CXLVI), how much more would he know the number of his elect, whose names he wrote in heaven and whom he foreknew before the ages?

### XXV. “My dove is one, my perfect one.”

There are indeed sixty queens because faithful souls abound throughout the world who devote the knowledge of the word they have received to multiplying the offspring of the Church, with a view to attaining the kingdom of heaven.

There are also eighty concubines because there are souls who devote themselves to doctrine with earthly things in view. Although they themselves succumb here to carnal allurements, they nevertheless generate spiritual offspring for God by preaching.

There are also young women whose number is without limit, because innumerable groups of the Christian people are found who, although they are not yet able to be promoted to the office of governance and teaching, nevertheless obediently and faithfully offer the devotion of their faith and conduct in service to the holy Church, the bride of Christ.

Yet above all these—the true and the pretended members of the Church alike—the universal Church herself rightly excels. In these faithful members, from the beginning to the consummation of the age, from the rising of the sun to its setting, and from the north and the sea, she praises the name of the Lord.

In her praise it is beautifully said: “My dove is one, my perfect one.”

She is one because she admits no division of schism. She is one because there is not one Church before the law, another under the law, another under grace, one gathered from circumcision and another from uncircumcision. Rather, just as there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God the Father of all, so there is one Catholic multitude of all the elect, subject in every place and age of the world to the one God and Father.

Luke teaches why she is called Catholic, saying: “The churches throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace; they were being built up and walking in the fear of the Lord, and they were filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit” (Acts IX).

For what is expressed here in Latin is, in Greek, *catholos*. Hence it is plainly evident that the Church is called Catholic because she is built up throughout all parts of the world in one peace and in one fear of the Lord, and is filled with one and the same consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Because she shares in the unity of the Spirit, she is also rightly called a dove. For the Spirit descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove, in order by this form to display both his own simplicity and that of the Lord upon whom he descended.

Because the Lord made his Church a participant in this simplicity, he rightly calls her his dove; and he rightly calls her perfect—not only because she is completed as one Church from all the peoples of the righteous, but also because she is perfected by receiving all the gifts of virtue and all the divine charisms.

One is her mother’s chosen one, her who gave her birth. The mother and parent of the present Church is the one of whom the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4). She is rightly both called and is the mother of us all, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). Hence it is also said in the Apocalypse of John: “And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God” (Rev. 21). The holy city Jerusalem comes down from heaven from God because everything good that the present Church knows and does, hopes for, and receives, she has received from above—either through the King of heaven himself or through the ministries of the heavenly citizens [Col. 1183B].

She is therefore one, chosen by her mother, the one who gave her birth, either because that heavenly city approves only those from human society whom it sees serving God in the unity of its faith and love. As for the Donatists, or any others who separate themselves from catholic unity, whether by open schism or by profane conduct: because they refuse to possess the perfection of dove-like simplicity, that city separates them from the lot of the elect at the judgment and places them on the left.

The word “mother” and “parent” may most appropriately be understood as designating the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church herself has been reborn to God and consecrated, since in Hebrew “spirit” is called *ruga*, a feminine noun. The Lord himself teaches that this is rightly called the mother and parent of the Church, saying: “Unless someone is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). Immediately distinguishing our spiritual generation from our carnal one, he added: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3).

For this mother and parent, one dove of Christ, perfect and chosen, has been appointed, because, after all the crowds of schismatics have been abandoned, spiritual grace will raise to the joys of the heavenly homeland the Church that she now nourishes and protects in the unity of catholic peace.

## “The daughters saw her and called her most blessed,” etc.

Here he seems to mean the same daughters whom above he called young women, since there he brought forward queens, concubines, and young women together, while here he introduced daughters, queens, and concubines [Col. 1183D]. Great, therefore, is the praise of catholic unity: the motherly grace that gave birth to her chose her forever, and the daughters whom she herself through the Spirit begot for God and nourished do not cease, as soon as they see her—that is, as soon as they learn the chastity of her life and hear of the gifts of the inheritance promised to her—to pronounce her blessed.

Queens and concubines also raise her up with just praises: that is, whether they are truly participants in her kingdom, or those souls who cling to her in name only but remain earthly in hope and disposition, they all acknowledge that she is worthy of everlasting praise. For all understand with certainty that nothing true and steadfastly good can be found apart from her fellowship.

But because, before the end of the world, Judea too is to be gathered into the grace of her Redeemer and herself is to praise the same perfection of the holy Church together with the others, the following is appropriately added in the voice of the Synagogue as she marvels:

## XXVI. “Who is this who comes forth,” etc.?

This Synagogue, converted to faith in Christ, speaks here, astonished that the Church has been raised by divine grace to such a height that, although she is most humble, she cannot be overcome by any power of worldly empire.

“Who comes forth,” she says, because she has not been content to remain in one place or to appear for a short time. Rather, throughout the whole world she continues to extend her faith and renown and, throughout all the ages of the passing world, to contend for the crown of everlasting life.

She comes forth “like the rising dawn,” because in her the rising of the true light is now shown to the world after the darkness of ignorance has receded. Her heralds admonish us, saying: “The night is far gone; the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light,” and so forth (Rom. 13) [Col. 1184B].

### “Fair as the moon, chosen as the sun,” etc.

She is “fair as the moon” because, illumined by the Sun of righteousness, she advances in majesty and fills the night of this age with the light of heavenly knowledge and evangelical conduct. She is “chosen as the sun” because she receives within herself the image of that same Creator and Illuminator by walking in all righteousness, holiness, and truth, and by giving him true thanks, since “the light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4).

Again, she is “fair as the moon” in the night of the present life, where, as the condition of the times changes, she is now bright to the world, now despised and oppressed; now full of the radiance of virtues, now disgraced by the vices of the wicked. In many ways she follows the course of the waxing and waning moon.

She is “chosen as the sun” in the future day of blessedness, where, with the state of eternity remaining unchanged, she will shine in the true vision of unchanging light, when the promise is fulfilled: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Cant. 6) [Col. 1184C].

She is “terrible as an army set in ordered ranks,” because no clouds of adversity have ever been able to restrain her from displaying in herself both the beauty of the moon and that of the sun: the moon’s beauty in the laborious light of good action during the present time, and the sun’s in the hope of everlasting blessed reward.

She is rightly “terrible as an army set in ordered ranks,” because the more perfectly she arranges the order of virtues within herself, the more terrifying both the whole Church and every faithful soul become to the aerial powers. For anyone who does not know how to maintain the necessary order in certain good practices—for example, vigils, fasts, manual labor, meditation on Scripture, the word of preaching, or the restraint of silence—goes astray. Such practices, though often usefully maintained, are sometimes also salutarily interrupted according to circumstances.

There are, however, higher gifts of virtue without which one cannot attain life: faith, hope, and love. For this reason they must never be absent from the hearts of the faithful, regardless of time or place or the consideration of those who give instruction. Therefore, whatever soul continually fortifies itself with the more eminent virtues and, when the place and hour are appropriate, diligently girds itself for the practice of lesser ones as well—that soul is terrifying to all adversaries and advances like an army intelligently and firmly arranged in battle order [Col. 1185A].

While a small crowd of believers from the Jews continued these words and reverently admired the Church’s struggles, she assented to the one praising her and immediately explains the reason for her military equipment, answering in the voice of the teachers—that is, the leaders of her spiritual warfare:

## XXVII. “I went down to the garden of nut trees,” etc.

The garden of nut trees is the present Church, where we are scarcely able to look into one another’s consciences. Nuts are all fruits covered with a harder skin, whereas all soft fruits are generally called apples (*mala*). Thus the life of the righteous is rightly compared with nuts: they preserve the sweetness of spiritual fruit in the innermost heart, yet cannot make known outwardly to their neighbors how great that sweetness is [Col. 1185B].

Therefore the mother Church must always maintain a carefully ordered battle line in her teachers, since she must fight on behalf of and defend from the enemy those whose thoughts and hearts she often does not know.

The passage may also be understood in this way: just as a nut or almond has an exceedingly bitter outer covering and is enclosed by a very hard shell, yet, once the harsher and harder parts have been removed, the sweetest fruit is found within, so every correction and labor of self-restraint by which the holy Church is exercised seems bitter for the present but produces in the future the sweetest fruit, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s saying: “All discipline at the time seems not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Heb. 12).

By the “fruits of the valley” he means the fruits of humility, as in the Psalm: “And the valleys will abound in grain” (Ps. 65), because the humble overflow with nourishment from heavenly grace.

The fruits of the valley also signify the good works of the faithful of the holy Church, performed in the depths of the earth but, through merits advancing toward the heavenly kingdom, leading their workers there. Concerning these the Psalmist likewise says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, to the place he appointed for them” (Ps. 83).

“And the bride went down to my garden,” to see the fruits of the valley, when the teachers of the Church come down from the height of their secret repose and divine contemplation—of which they are often granted a share—and turn their mind to consider the condition of that same Church. Thus they diligently investigate how far each of the faithful has already advanced in good works and how much he still needs the assistance of teachers, and they supply those who need cultivation with the fruits of life [Col. 1185D].

### “To see whether the vine had flowered,” etc.

He inspects whether the vine has flowered when he carefully examines whether, anywhere, the hearts of those whom he teaches are proposing to undertake new zeal for virtues—virtues by which we are spiritually intoxicated—according to the Psalmist’s saying: “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83).

He inspects whether the pomegranates have blossomed when he diligently observes whether any can be found who desire to be poured out in their own blood in imitation of the Lord’s Passion, following the admonition of the Apostle Peter: “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought” [Col. 1186A].

Thus the Church proclaims her evangelical labors to the Synagogue, which marvels at them. But the Synagogue, pierced by a salutary fullness, confesses that because of the cause of her profane blindness and ignorance she had remained for a long time deprived of so great a salvation, answering in this manner:

## XXVIII. “I did not know; my soul troubled me,” etc.

“I did not know” the gifts of spiritual grace by which you have been illumined by the Lord to bring forth the fruits of faith among all nations.

An inward anxiety of mind troubled me because the New Testament was suddenly introduced in place of the old. The preaching of the Gospel suddenly filled the whole world, replacing the books of the prophets and the Law, which I knew to be divine and written by the Holy Spirit.

Like a swift chariot, it traversed in a short time not only Judea and Samaria but also the boundaries of all nations, while I looked on in wonder and astonishment. It is rightly compared not simply with chariots but with a quadriga, because it has been entrusted to memory by the authority of four writers, while the one Spirit of God, through Jesus Christ, directed both the minds and the hands of those writers in composing it—just as one might see a four-horse chariot prepared to run with the harmonious speed of four horses, yet guided by the control of a single charioteer so that it travels along a straight course [Col. 1186B].

I had indeed heard long ago that four authors wrote about Jesus with equal agreement. But who moved them by his Spirit, what usefulness and truth their writing contained, and how much glory and salvation it held—alas, how late I was permitted to perceive and know!

When he calls the heralds of the New Testament the “chariots of Aminadab,” the name “Aminadab” signifies the Lord the Savior. As though presiding over a chariot, he filled the hearts of the preachers with the grace of his Spirit, so that through them he might reach the peoples who were to believe in him, with the word of saving doctrine going before [Col. 1186C].

Aminadab, who was the great-grandson of the patriarch Judah, indicates the Lord the Savior both by his person and by his name. By his person, because through him the genealogy of the Lord’s incarnation descends from Abraham to King David and through David to Joseph and Mary. This is understood in the same way that the name of Judah himself, and those of David, Solomon, and the other fathers from whom Christ descended according to the flesh, are sometimes taken by the prophets as figures of Christ. Thus we read: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. You have lain down; like a lion and like a lioness, who will rouse him?” (Gen. 49). And again: “I will cleanse them, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, and my servant David shall be over them” (Ezek. 37). Also in this very book: “Go out and see, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon” (Cant. 3) [Col. 1186D].

By his name, however, Aminadab—interpreted as “my people’s voluntary one,” or “the one of my people who offers himself willingly”—aptly designates the Mediator between God and human beings. Although he was God before the ages, he was united to flesh and appeared, when and how he willed, among the people of the Church as their merciful Redeemer. Through voluntary goodness he became a portion of his people, whose Creator and ruler he was by natural power.

When the Synagogue confesses the long slowness of her mind, by which she was hindered from understanding the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, the Church immediately answers with consolation and exhortation:

### “Return, return, O Shulammite,” etc.

Return to recognition of your Redeemer, from whom you had wandered so miserably while turned away for so long; so that, instructed in his mysteries, you may become worthy to enter the heavenly life.

Return to the peace of our kinship, which for so long, because of religious disagreement, you thought should be rejected.

“Return, return,” so that we may look upon you. Return in purity of faith; return in perfection of works; return together to the Lord’s love, so that with rejoicing eyes and hearts we may contemplate the appearance of your chastity, which we have long desired. When the love of Christ joins us to one another, may both of us be built in him, as in the cornerstone, into one house of faith [Col. 1187B].

I do not remember having read the name “Shulammite” (*Sunamitis*) anywhere else. It seems to be the name of some noble woman, either a proper name or derived from a place, who at that time was distinguished by great renown for wisdom, beauty, or virtue.

But if “Shulammite,” as some report, is interpreted as “despised” or “captive,” the name suits the Synagogue when, on account of the guilt of unbelief, she withdrew from the grace of her author. Insofar as she was captive under the yoke of sin, she remained unworthy in view of divine mercy. Yet the Shulammite is asked to return, so that through the obedience of returning to the Lord she may deserve to be released from the bond of guilty captivity and restored worthy to the sight of her Redeemer and Savior.

While the Church urges the Synagogue to return to the grace of her Redeemer, the Redeemer himself assents to her devout exhortations, suddenly inserting his own speech and declaring that the consolations of her exhortation are already about to reach their fulfillment. For he says:

# CHAPTER VII

## XXIX. “What will you see in the Shulammite?” etc.

It is as though he were openly saying: “You grieve that the Synagogue has remained turned away for so long, and you entreat her to return to me; you rejoice to behold her face adorned for me. But know that the time is near when you will see in her nothing of her former unbelief and estrangement, but only works of virtue and spiritual struggles.

“What, then, will you see in the Shulammite,” he says, “except the choirs of camps”—that is, the army of peace?

In choirs, the voices of singers harmonize; in camps, the hands of lovers fight. What, then, will you see in her except the choirs of the elect, who with one heart and one soul proclaim the praises of their Creator? These are also the choirs of camps, because by serving the Creator they drive back and disrupt every force of the enemy [Col. 1187D].

He said this and, to praise the Church herself—the Church whose concern for the salvation of the Synagogue he rejoiced to see—turned with his customary sweetness to add:

### “How beautiful are your steps,” etc.!

He appropriately began her praise with her steps and concluded with the grace of her mouth. For this is how he ended: “And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples; your throat is like the finest wine.” Above, beginning with the eyes, he seemed to have finished by praising only the upper members. This change both supplies beauty to the poem and provides a suitable place for the mysteries being sung.

Because he saw that she did not remain idle in secure repose but was accustomed to advance toward the contest of preaching, he rightly first marvels at the beauty of her steps—that is, at the steadfastness of her works, through which she wished to set examples of virtue before those whom she instructed.

Concerning these steps the Psalmist prays to the Lord: “Make my steps firm in your paths” (Ps. 16), that is, direct my actions along the narrow road by which one reaches life.

These steps are in sandals when our actions are strengthened by the examples of the righteous who went before us to God. We are shod with the skins of dead animals when, imitating the earlier saints whom we read to have been clothed in works of righteousness, we enter the way of virtue with greater confidence and purity.

Concerning these sandals the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6). Whoever proclaims the peace of truth to others must first adorn and strengthen the steps of his works with the examples of those who came before, lest he show his followers any way of living or teaching other than the way trodden by the fathers—indeed, by the Lord himself—remembering the apostolic command: “Be imitators of me, brothers, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 14).

By teaching in this manner he ascends to that height and beauty of virtues of which prophet and apostle speak: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Rom. 10) [Col. 1188C].

He calls her “the daughter of the prince,” namely of the one about whom it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). Among other promises of heavenly gifts, he himself speaks to her through the prophet: “You will call me Father, and you will not cease to follow after me” (Jer. 3).

It should be noted that blessed Jerome, who was knowledgeable in Hebrew truth, writing against Jovinianus about the daughter of the prince, placed “daughter of Aminadab” in this passage and declared that this verse could also be understood of a virgin dedicated to God. He says: “Beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of Aminadab,” which is interpreted as “the people who offer themselves willingly.” Virginity is voluntary; and therefore the steps of the Church are praised in the beauty of chastity.

From this it is clear that those greatly err who interpret the chariots of Aminadab above as the army pursuing the Church, whether of unclean spirits or of wicked human beings, since it is plainly more appropriate to understand them of the prince of princes himself and of his chosen people [Col. 1188D].

## XXX. “The joining of your thighs is like necklaces,” etc.

Scripture commonly signifies the succession of offspring by the thighs. Thus it says: “All the souls who entered Egypt with Jacob and who came out from his thigh, apart from the wives of his sons, were sixty-six” (Gen. 46).

Accordingly, the offspring of the Church—her spiritual generation, brought to completion through the mystery of the word and the washing of regeneration—is rightly understood in her thighs.

The joining of her thighs is the concord of two peoples: Jews and Gentiles. United in one faith, they complete the universal Church, which is made fruitful and grows by spiritual offspring until the end of the age [Col. 1189A].

This joining is compared with necklaces because catholic faith is demonstrated by the testimony of good works. These necklaces are fashioned by the hand of an artisan, because the works of virtue through which the Church is built as one from two peoples are established by the ineffable generosity of our Creator.

He is the artisan of whom the Apostle says: “He came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2). The Psalmist speaks of his marvelous workmanship: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 117).

The Apostle also recalls this artisan in praise of the patriarch Abraham: “For he was awaiting the city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Heb. 2).

After the bride’s feet have been shod, the joining of her thighs is rightly praised, because through the ministry of preachers the unanimous union of believing peoples is brought to completion. The joining of the thighs is appropriately recalled in these passages because, at the end, Judea, gathered into the faith, has been promised as a participant in both peoples and is to be united in Christ. The text continues:

### “Your navel is a turned bowl,” etc.

The navel, which is the most fragile member of our body, appropriately signifies the weakness of our mortality.

Our navel becomes a turned bowl “never lacking drink” when, reminded of our mortality and weakness, we strive to offer the cup of saving speech to our neighbors, so that, by showing them mercy, we may receive in return the blessedness of heavenly mercy.

There is no objection to understanding this also of the general almsgiving represented by a cup, concerning which the Judge himself will say: “I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25).

A bowl (*crater*) is a larger vessel with two handles. Concerning it the poet says:

> When the first rest follows the feast and the tables are removed,  
> they set out the great bowls and crown the wine.

This bowl is rightly said to be turned on a lathe. A vessel worked on a lathe is completed more quickly than by other crafts, so that the speed of extending mercy may be indicated—whether to those who need an earthly drink, or to those who need a heavenly drink, or to those who need both—according to Solomon’s saying: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you can give immediately” (Prov. 3) [Col. 1189D].

It should also be said, as we mentioned above, that turning is less explicable than other arts, because it produces from itself the rule by which it completes its work with disciplined circularity. Thus it rightly suggests the simplicity of a truly devout mind that gives alms with pure intention.

Someone who gives a drink to the thirsty in order that an equitable rewarder may grant him an abundance of earthly drink, or who offers the cup of the word to the erring so that the Lord may provide him with a greater store of knowledge by which he may appear admirable to human beings, is not compared with a lathed bowl but with one made by other tools. Although commanded to perform the work of mercy, he seeks from the Lord not the upright and indescribable reward of sustaining his weakness but a temporal one [Col. 1190A].

The bride’s navel may also be understood as a turned bowl never lacking drink because the Church—or every holy soul—the more fragile she remembers herself to be and the farther she knows herself still to stand from the immortality and incorruption she hopes for in the future, the more diligently she ensures that she is continually refreshed by cups of God’s word and warmed by his love, saying with the Psalmist: “And your cup that intoxicates—how excellent it is!”

### “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed with lilies.”

The belly signifies the same condition of our mortality as the navel. It is itself a most certain and powerful judge of our weakness: by daily nourishment it restores our body so that it does not fail, until what we hold as promised comes to pass: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6) [Col. 1190B].

Our belly, then, is like a heap of wheat when, mindful of our fragility, we prepare in the present life the fruits of good works by which we may be perpetually refreshed.

He says “a heap of wheat,” rather than simply an abundance of wheat, to signify virtues growing upward into height. And because a heap normally rises broader at the bottom and becomes narrower at the top, this figure rightly corresponds to our good actions: the higher they are in merit, the fewer workers they find.

You will see more people giving alms to the needy from their possessions than leaving all they possess; more good married people than celibates; more abstaining from bodily enticements than laying down their lives for the truth [Col. 1190C].

He rightly asserts that this same heap of wheat is enclosed with lilies, so that we may understand that everything good we do is done for the sake of seeing eternal love, and that no hostile snare finds entry into the threshing floor of our heart, when we surround all our works on every side with the regard for heavenly reward.

The heap of wheat may also be understood as the works of almsgiving that we perform for Christ’s poor, concerning which he himself says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25).

After the bowl abounding in drink, it is fitting that the bride’s members should be compared with a heap of wheat, so that she may be shown to give the poor both drink and bread. This can be understood both of spiritual and bodily refreshment—that is, of the things with which we instruct the mind of our wandering neighbor.

Spiritual instruction itself is recognized to contain a cup in some passages and the bread of life in others. It has the likeness of a cup in clear statements, but of bread in mysteries.

It offers a cup in those matters that can easily be understood as soon as they are heard and require no other exposition, such as: “You shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness” (Deut. 5), and: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22).

It gives bread when it entrusts to its hearers words that are more difficult to understand and that, like food reaching our entrails by chewing, reach the inner regions of our understanding through exposition. Such is the whole sequence of this poem, and such is the saying of the Law: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20). Mystically, this admonishes us to sanctify the light of spiritual grace, in which alone we possess true rest: that is, to keep it ever undefiled in a holy and chaste heart, as we receive it on the day of redemption.

These and similar words, whose meaning we reach only through the labor of exposition, are rightly compared with a heap of wheat, which is brought to the use of our nourishment only through considerable labor—grinding, sowing, baking, and chewing.

Clearer passages are appropriately compared with a bowl never lacking drink, because the clear commands and promises of God abound in Scripture. Just as drink can be swallowed without delay or labor, so these passages can be understood as soon as they are heard and, once understood, stored for the increase of our salvation, as though in the belly of memory [Col. 1191B].

The bride may also most aptly figure the undefiled womb of the divine font, from which we are reborn as a new creation. It is like a heap of wheat enclosed with lilies because, by regenerating and consecrating all whom she brings forth in Christ, she teaches them to persist in good works, with the sole regard of heavenly glory.

She is like a heap of wheat because she cleanses those whom she washes from all the chaff of sins and, through a second generation, conforms them to the one who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

She is enclosed with lilies because those whom she releases from the entanglements of sins in which they had been carnally born, she also adorns and strengthens with the light of heavenly gifts [Col. 1191C].

### “The two breasts,” etc.

We have discussed this verse at length above. Now, however, it should be recalled briefly that she rightly praises the bride’s breasts after her belly, because the holy Church gives the little ones whom she generates in Christ from the most holy womb of the saving water the milk of gentler instruction for the nourishment of beginners, until she gradually trains them to receive the bread of higher wisdom.

The breasts of the Church are therefore those who instruct her little ones—that is, those newly reborn in the faith. They are appropriately said, with the addition, to be two, because from the two peoples—namely, the Jews and the nations—the saving font gathers those whom it washes and brings forth through the heavenly mystery [Col. 1191D].

They are rightly compared with two fawns of a gazelle because true teachers take from the words of both Testaments what they preach.

These same fawns are rightly said to be twins because the Testaments were issued by one and the same author, namely the one of whom Ecclesiastes says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply; they were given through the counsel of masters by one shepherd” (Eccl. 12).

The bride’s two breasts are therefore like two twin fawns of a gazelle because the teachers of beginners do not preach their own ideas to them or adulterate the word of God. Rather, “as from God, in the presence of God, in Christ” they speak. He is the one shepherd who makes one fold from two flocks of sheep.

Burning with desire for him, the bride cries above: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday.”

He is the one master of masters, for he commanded his disciples—and our teachers—saying: “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28).

The name of gazelle (*caprea*) is also rightly attributed to him, since it is a clean animal, distinguished in sight and in running, cleaving the hoof and chewing the cud, and, like all clean quadrupeds, armed with horns.

If the saints are fittingly compared with such an animal’s nature because they have a divided hoof in their discernment of good and evil; because they customarily speak and, as it were, ruminate on the good things they distinguish from evil; because they have learned to direct the eye of their heart far ahead, that is, toward contemplating heavenly goods from the earth; because they desire to penetrate the path of virtue more eagerly by their own running; because they rejoice that they have received purity of mind and body through the grace of their Creator; and because, raised up by the confidence of faith against the power of this world, they customarily say to God, “Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. 43)—how much more does the nature of this animal suit the one whom it signifies, who possesses all these gifts of virtue in himself and grants them to others according to the measure of his giving!

### “Your neck is like an ivory tower.”

Since both voice and speech proceed through the neck, and since food by which all the body’s members are nourished ordinarily enters through it, the neck rightly signifies, as we have indicated above, the form of teachers, who strengthen the whole body of the Church both by the voice of exhortation and by the nourishment of their life [Col. 1192C].

This neck is like an ivory tower because teachers provide the holy city of God—that is, the Church—with both adornment and strength, and with the beauty of their life. Because they are proved already dead to this world, they appear like ivory to all who see them; and like a lofty, impregnable tower they defend the city of God against the attacks of every enemy.

When they say, “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications, destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10), they show themselves to have been set like a tower as a defense of the holy city.

And when Paul, describing his own life and that of his fellow workers, says, “Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God; I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2), he signifies that in the cross he possesses the quality of ivory—a dead bone, indeed, but marked by outstanding beauty [Col. 1192D].

Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, etc. The same holy preachers who, because of the nourishment of the word, were compared to the bride’s neck are also signified by the eyes: this indicates their inspection of hidden things, which they themselves learn in secret so that they may proclaim them openly and, through what they have received by secret meditation, supply the holy Church with manifest nourishment by their teaching.

These eyes are rightly compared with the pools constructed at the gate of the city of Heshbon. He calls that city also “the daughter of the multitude” because of the abundance of its inhabitants: just as those pools, with citizens continually flowing toward them, used to provide an uninterrupted supply of water, so preachers never cease to offer streams of doctrine to their hearers. They themselves are continually filled within by these streams, just as pools abound in water through living springs.

This corresponds also to that once-famous *probatica piscina* (“sheep-pool”) at Jerusalem, into which, when an angel descended at the appointed time, the water was stirred; and whoever among the sick descended first was healed. For there is one God, one faith, and one baptism. When the Holy Spirit descends into the fountain of life, he washes one people of the faithful with the grace of the second regeneration. This pool is rightly called *probatica*, that is, “sheep-related,” literally indicating that sacrificial victims used to be washed there by the priest; but figuratively expressing that those who are to be brought to the holy altar and offered to God as a sacrifice ought to be washed in the waters of regeneration.

Heshbon is suitably placed as a figure of the Church, either because of its name, since it is interpreted as “a girdle of mourning,” or because it was once the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and, after he was killed, it was attacked by the children of Israel. For it is clear that the Church was once enslaved under the power of the devil, the king, that is, of all the wicked; but after he was expelled and renounced, it became the city of its Redeemer.

And now the Church, which had previously been called “the nations,” received this name when, in place of the wanton and fleeting joy of this world, it girded itself with a most salutary girdle of mourning: a girdle, indeed, so that it might restrain the loins of its mind from every impurity; a girdle of mourning, so that, made wholly external and alien to temporal joys, it might hope to receive joys fixed confidently in heaven.

This city, that is, the Church—which is also called “the daughter of the multitude” because of the abundance of peoples flocking to the faith—has pools at its gate. The bride’s eyes are compared with these pools because no one can enter her who has not first been sprinkled with the water of saving doctrine, cleansed by the bath of the water of regeneration, and consecrated by a drink from the life-giving fountain.

This was most clearly and beautifully prefigured in the tabernacle or Solomon’s Temple. At their entrance stood a basin or bronze sea, where the priests who were about to enter washed their hands and feet. This was certainly done for the sake of a mystery: the Lord was to provide for us the washing of heavenly doctrine and the fountain of regeneration, so that, initiated by it, we might enter either the fellowship of his present Church or the dwelling of his eternal house, which is in heaven.

[Col. 1194A] Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, etc. Since odors and foul smells are usually distinguished by the nose, the ministers of the word of God—who, for certain reasons already mentioned, had been signified by the neck and eyes of the Church in the figure of women—are now also signified by the nose, on account of the most salutary discernment that the Fathers have shown to be the mother of virtues.

For, as though through the function of smelling, they are able to recognize better than others in which actions or words the good fragrance of Christ is flourishing, and which exhale the deadly stench of wickedness. Every teacher, and indeed every believer, greatly needs careful discernment, lest vices conceal themselves under the appearance of virtues: lest they carry something wolf-like beneath a sheep’s clothing; lest cunning be mistaken for prudence, greed for frugality, the desire for vengeance for justice, hardness for fortitude, or obstinacy for assumed steadfastness.

Thus teachers, and rightly all the elect who have received this grace from the Lord, are said to be like the tower of Lebanon, because they are able to distinguish the fragrances of virtues from the foulness of vices. The tower “which looks toward Damascus” signifies that they hold the most exalted position in the holy Church and always watch with the most vigilant eye of the mind against the snares of the ancient enemy.

It has often been said that Mount Lebanon signifies the Lord the Savior and his Church. By contrast, it is abundantly clear that Damascus figuratively indicates the city of the devil, that is, the reprobate multitude either of angels or of human beings. For Damascus was the metropolis of all Syria and had kings who were exceedingly impious and powerful. Since they rightly bore the type of the devil, they repeatedly brought wars and captivities upon God’s people; these plainly prefigured the temptations and snares of the devil, by which he continually attacks the Church.

Moreover, the fact that Damascus is called “a drinking of blood” or “an eye of blood” corresponds to the signification of those who delight in the allurements of flesh and blood—including the shedding of blood inflicted upon the innocent. It also corresponds to the most perverse intention of demons, who strive spiritually to slaughter us and to take away from us the eternal life that we possess in Christ.

Against both these kinds of enemies the Psalmist prays to the Lord, saying: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Psalm 50). Whoever, then, is firmly established in Christ and diligently surrounds himself and his own with vigilant care, lest they be overcome by such wars—whether openly inflicted through human beings or secretly through the devil—may rightly be called the nose of Christ’s bride and be like the tower constructed on Mount Lebanon facing Damascus. For, skilled in discernment and exalted in life, he provides continual watchfulness so that the Church may never be disturbed by sudden assaults of evil.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1193]

[Col. 1193D] Your head is like Carmel, etc. In the head of the bride, the mind of the faithful soul is rightly understood, because just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are directed by the mind. Hence the thoughts themselves, which issue from the human mind in countless numbers at every hour and moment, are aptly figured by the hair.

The prudent reader should remember that what is said of one elect soul is to be understood of the whole Church. For although the multitude of believers differs in merit, it nevertheless has one heart and one soul, insofar as all, through one and the same faith, hope, and love, aspire toward the courts above.

Scripture relates that Elijah prayed on Mount Carmel with bent knees and obtained rain from the Lord after a long drought. Therefore the bride’s head is like Carmel, because the hearts of the elect are exalted through their manner of life and offer the Lord an ascent into themselves through daily progress in virtue.

For Elijah is called “the Lord God,” who prays to the Father in these people and, as though over parched fields, calls down rain from heaven, because he invisibly kindles these people to pray to God and, through their prayers and merits, frequently bestows his gifts upon the world in peril.

The name Carmel, moreover, which is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” suits the bride’s head—that is, the Church’s mind—which knows well that it ought to glory not in bodily but in spiritual circumcision. Concerning this the Apostle discusses many things in his letter to the Galatians, and the prophet teaches, saying: “Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4).

The Jews refused to possess this knowledge when they took pride only in the circumcision that is outward. For this reason they did not know how to have a head like Carmel: they had placed their minds in lowly things and in the glory of the flesh. Thus they are deservedly reproved by the voice of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, who says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7).

“And the hair,” he says, “of your head is like royal purple joined in channels.” As we have said, the hair of the bride’s head signifies the thoughts of the faithful soul. Royal purple signifies imitation of the Lord’s passion, and the hair of the bride’s head is rightly compared with it, because every thought of the elect is fortified by faith in the holy cross, and the whole inclination of their heart is ready to suffer for the Lord, so that they may deserve to be raised with him.

The statement that this purple is “bound in channels” may be understood either as referring to dyed wool, which, before being spun, is kept divided in channels, or to wool that is to be dyed after the blood of the murex has been placed in channels, being divided there into portions and dyed separately while bound.

For when murexes—that is, sea snails, also called shellfish—are cut with iron, they emit tears of purple color. When these are collected, purple dye is prepared. Both explanations produce mystically one and the same meaning.

The channels [*canales*], then, which receive the royal purple, are the innermost hearts of Christ’s faithful. The wool, which is placed in the channels bound there in order to receive the purple color and afterward to be taken up as the king’s ornament, is the humility—most gentle and mild—of the faithful conscience. Through sufferings and works of righteousness it advances toward the raiment of the eternal King. “For all who were baptized into Christ,” he says, “have put on Christ” (Galatians 3).

This wool, bound in channels, is dyed purple because the virtue of humility, fixed and as though tied within the hearts of the elect, is continually stirred by the remembrance of the Lord’s blood to endure temporal tribulations. Through this endurance it may reach participation in the Lord’s kingdom.

What we have said about purple bound in channels—that dyed wool already made suitable by the murex is kept in separate compartments before being drawn out into threads—belongs to the figure of a higher virtue. For it expresses the humility of those who have already been so exercised by frequent tribulations for the Lord that it is evident they cannot be overcome by any pressure of adversity.

They say that a perfect purple dye never grows pale under any sun or sprinkling of water, but that the color once received customarily endures. Therefore the hair of the bride’s head is like royal purple bound in channels when the thoughts prepared in hearts devoted to God are also ready to die for Christ, so that they may deserve to reign with him.

This purple, brought out of the channels, becomes an ornament for the supreme King when, given the opportunity to suffer, they show what they have carried in their hearts, bravely for the glory of their Redeemer, and are ready to endure every adversity of the world—and, if it should happen, death itself.

This was aptly prefigured in the Acts of the Apostles by Lydia, that seller of purple. Since she feared God, she was the first in Macedonia to believe and be baptized with her household when Paul was preaching. She received him into her hospitality, both when he first preached the word of faith to her and afterward when he suffered at the hands of unbelievers beatings, imprisonment, and chains.

By her craft, faith, and service she signified the Church from the nations, which, instructed in the confession of the Lord’s passion, would itself pour out its blood for it and would receive into its innermost heart the teaching of the apostles, expelled by unbelievers.

How beautiful you are, etc.! Earlier, in praise of the bride, it is said: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army drawn up in battle order.” There she is called, together with beauty and loveliness, “terrible as an army drawn up in battle order”; here she is said to be beautiful and lovely in delights.

As far as ordinary human experience is concerned, it is difficult for one and the same person both to live in delights and to be terrible like an army arranged for battle. Delights soften the mind and prevent it from applying itself to military matters. But where the delights are spiritual—that is, where the desire for eternal sweetness fills the throat of the soul—there the soul becomes terrible to spiritual enemies, and it shatters all their weapons like an army drawn up in battle order.

Indeed, the more firmly it perceives the taste of inward satisfaction, the more terrible it becomes to those who, through the bitterness of proud tyranny, have utterly lost the glory of the sweetness above, for which they were created.

It is fitting that, after the lover of the holy soul had said, “How beautiful you are, how lovely!”—that is, “How perfect you are in faith and work”—he immediately added, “Most beloved in delights.” For it is fitting that the soul whom the Lord sees devoted to heavenly delights should be most beloved by him. The more abundantly the pure mind tastes the food of life, the more greatly it burns with love for that one; and the more ardently it loves what is above, the more perfectly it is loved by the author and giver of heavenly goods.

The holy soul, therefore, is most beloved by the Lord in delights, because while it ardently hungers for the joys of inward refreshment, the love of its Creator increases in it. And because such a soul already tastes, even amid the struggle of the present life, no small portion of the joys of future reward, it is rightly added:

Your stature is like a palm tree, etc. The stature of the Church is the uprightness of its good works, because it refuses to bend toward earthly desire and raises its whole self toward the attainment of heavenly things. Concerning this the Apostle admonishes: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act courageously” (1 Corinthians 16). Concerning this also the Lord himself says: “I am the Lord, who rescued you from the slavery with which the Egyptians oppressed you, so that you might walk upright” (1 Kings 10).

The palm is the adornment of a victorious hand. Among the ancients, moreover, whoever won in a contest was crowned with a palm. Thus the bride’s stature is compared with a palm tree when every inclination of the faithful, raised upright in love of heavenly things, meditates, while standing in the battle line, upon the prize with which it will be rewarded as victor when the contest is ended.

Again, because the palm tree appears rough near the ground but displays beauty and the sweetness of its fruit at the top, the stature of the Church—or of any faithful soul—is rightly compared with it. Such a soul bears harsh labors for the Lord on earth but hopes to receive from the Lord a most welcome reward in heaven.

The palm is rough near the earth because the elect suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. It is beautiful and sweet at the top because they rejoice amid afflictions and exult, knowing that their reward is abundant in heaven.

Again, since the palm is clothed with enduring leaves and preserves its foliage without succession, who does not see that it represents the stature of faith? As the condition of the passing world changes, faith retains the same words of right confession, like leaves that never return once they have fallen, and preserves among its elect, undefiled to the end of the age, the same perfection of works that began at the beginning—like the beauty of the palm.

“And your breasts,” he says, “are like clusters of grapes.” As has often been said, the breasts of the Church are its teachers when they provide Christ’s little ones with the milk of their first instruction.

But these same breasts are compared with clusters of grapes when the teachers reveal the mysteries of the divinity, by which Christ is equal to the Father, to those to whom they had entrusted the first sacraments of his incarnation. The same teachers who had earlier said, “We judge that we know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2), later say to those capable of receiving stronger food: “Their fathers are the ones from whom Christ is descended according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (1 Corinthians 11).

Or certainly the breasts of the Church are compared with clusters of grapes when teachers, at one and the same time, open the great mysteries or precepts of Scripture to mature hearers and entrust to the simple-minded, according to what they can receive, the nourishment of life.

To the simple-minded they say: “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments: You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother; and, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” To the mature hearers: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess, and give to the poor” (Matthew 19), and other sayings of this kind.

These breasts are also compared with clusters of grapes because the Apostle says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are self-controlled, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5). They perform the office of breasts when they temper their words for the weak according to what they are able to hear. They are compared with clusters of grapes when, beside themselves in spirit, they are intoxicated with sublime things by the abundance of the house of God—the house of God that is not made with hands but is eternal in heaven.

But because all holy people have received whatever good they possess through the gift of heavenly grace, it is rightly added:

I said, “I will climb the palm tree,” etc. The only reason that the breasts of the Church are compared with clusters of grapes is that the Lord has deigned to ascend into her and enrich her with his grace.

For the fact that teachers preach both humble things to the little ones and sublime things to the perfect, that they condescend to the inexperienced and are temperate with them, while they themselves are sublimely intoxicated in contemplation of heavenly things, is not their own merit but a heavenly gift.

Earlier it was said concerning the Lord: “My beloved went down into his garden” (Psalm 86); now he himself says: “I will climb the palm tree.” The same Church, or the perfect soul, is the Lord’s garden and is also the palm tree.

But there is a difference between the Lord’s descending into it and ascending into it. He descends into it when he sends heavenly grace from above, by which it can itself become heavenly and be transferred to things above. He ascends into it when he reveals the knowledge of his majesty more and more to the faithful; when he inspires in those who are making progress a love of the heavenly homeland, as though by certain steps they were reaching toward the heights; when, to those to whom he had previously said, “When you have done all that is commanded you, say, ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke 17), he gives greater gifts and adds: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends” (John 15). And again: “Go and tell my brothers” (John 15).

The Lord therefore descends into his garden when he bestows heavenly gifts upon the faithful; he ascends into the palm tree when he graciously grants increases of virtue to those same elect as they advance, until he brings them to perfection. Concerning these virtues it is appropriately added:

I will grasp its fruits. He grasps the virtues of the faithful soul so that, by the most salutary touch of his compunction, he may continually make them more fruitful through greater blessing.

The fruits of the palm may also be understood as each of the elect, whom the Church—his palm tree—produces for the Lord. He grasps these fruits when he strengthens his own people in faith and love and protects them by his protection so that they may never fail, until they reach the full maturity of life, according to the Psalmist: “You gave me the protection of your salvation, and your right hand received me” (Psalm 17).

In what follows—“And your breasts shall be like a cluster of Cyprus”—this too may be understood: those who willingly and simply proclaim to their neighbors the little that they know are sometimes intoxicated with a greater gift of wisdom.

This happens when the Lord ascends into the palm tree and grasps its fruits, because unless his grace grants us progress, and unless his grace strengthens our hearts, we are able to possess neither great things nor even small goods.

The name of the palm tree may aptly signify also the most victorious tree of the cross. The bride’s stature is rightly compared with it, because the holy Church is raised through the passion of its Redeemer so that it may stand upright, stable, and immovable.

It is rightly compared with this tree because the saints who preceded the time of the Lord’s incarnation signified the mysteries of his passion either by prophesying or by suffering, while the saints of our own time glorify the same triumph of his most holy passion: all by believing and confessing, and many also by dying.

When the bridegroom says, “I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will grasp its fruits,’” this corresponds to the age in which Solomon sang these words, when the Lord repeatedly promised through the voices of the prophets that he would come in the flesh for the redemption of the human race; when he proclaimed that he would climb the tree and, dying for his bride, return victorious to life after destroying the dominion of death.

The fruits of the palm that he said he would grasp are the later glories that followed his ascent of the cross: the glory of his resurrection and ascension into heaven, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and the salvation of the believing world.

To this meaning the following also aptly corresponds:
