And your breasts shall be, etc. The first teachers of the Church, namely the apostles, received, after his passion and resurrection had been completed, a much greater knowledge of saving doctrine than they had possessed before.

This occurred when, appearing after his resurrection, he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures; when, sending the Spirit from above, he granted them knowledge of all languages; when the mockers falsely said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2).

But they truly were affected like clusters of grapes, because they were refreshed by the grace of spiritual gifts. Thus the saying was truly fulfilled that new wine is to be put into new wineskins, and both are preserved (Matthew 9).

To either interpretation the following aptly corresponds:

And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples, etc. In the fragrance of the mouth is the good reputation of speech; in the throat, the very function of the voice devoted to God. Both are worthy of praise in the Catholic Church and in every elect soul, because the voice itself, which instructs those present, and the reputation of its speech, which reaches those absent either through letters or through those who have heard, are shown to be full of virtue and grace.

The fact that he compares the fragrance of the bride’s mouth and throat with apples and the finest wine may be distinguished in this way: apples retain all their force in their freshness, while wine derives its value from age. Therefore the voice of the speaking Church and its reputation are rightly compared with both, since both their beginning and their perfection are worthy of wonder.

Again, since the virtue and fragrance of the finest wine are greater than those of apples, it is rightly said: “And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples. Your throat is like the finest wine, surpassing the grace of apples.” The present address of the holy Church surpasses the reputation that the speech of its hearers can spread about it.

Thus far the bride has been praised. When the praise reached the point of saying that her throat was like the finest wine, she seized the word from the bridegroom’s mouth and, moved by great love, eagerly sought to bring this saying to fulfillment herself.

She understood that the word “finest wine” signified the Gospel, in which alone there is eternal salvation for believers, and she said:

## XXXI. Worthy of my beloved to drink, etc.

The finest wine, she says, with which he compared my throat, is worthy for my beloved to drink, because the word of the Gospel, which he has deigned to place in my mouth, is so sublime that it ought to be preached to the world by no one other than my beloved himself, my bridegroom and Redeemer.

He himself, appearing first in the flesh, opened the heavenly path to the human race through the mystery of regeneration. He himself first preached the sacrament of his passion, resurrection, and ascension, through which the world would be saved, and afterward left it to be preached by his faithful. He himself drank the cup of salvation and thus offered it to the Church to drink.

Nor should it seem absurd that it is said to be “chewed by his lips and teeth,” when wine is being discussed. It is clear that chewing belongs more properly to food than to drink. Speaking figuratively, he calls the beloved’s lips and teeth the holy teachers, as has been demonstrated above, because they chew the finest wine that he himself drank when they delight in examining repeatedly the word of grace that they teach and in discussing it with one another.

Some understand this response of the Church to have been subtly introduced into the Lord’s speech in this way: when he praised her by saying, “Your throat”—that is, “the sweetness of your confession”—is like the finest wine, she immediately assented to his words and added: “Worthy of my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew.”

It is as though she were saying openly: “I now greatly desire my beloved to judge, by careful examination, the affection and sincerity of mind that I have toward him. For I trust that, even if he examines it as thoroughly as he usually examines a drink or a food when he carefully endeavors to taste or chew it, he will already prove it worthy of his praises.”

For this reason the first shepherd of the Church answered the Lord when he questioned him: “You know that I love you”; and again: “You know all things; you know that I love you” (John 15).

To this beloved, then, she adds, still moved by the great ardor of the same love:

I am my beloved’s, etc. I am my beloved’s, and not another’s. To him I devote the whole service and offering of my obedience.

“And his turning is toward me,” so that, while I remain in mortal life, he may always help me by his present regard, lest I grow weary through laboring, lest I carry lamps without oil—that is, good works without love—and at the end may bring me with him into the immortal joys of the heavenly bridal chamber.

The statement, “His turning is toward me,” may also be understood as spoken especially in the figure of the Synagogue, that is, of the people who preceded the time of his incarnation.

When it had heard him promise above, “I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will grasp its fruits’”—that is, “I will climb the wood of the cross, on which I will die, and, taking the fruits of the resurrection, I will offer them to believers to nourish them unto eternal life”—it rightly proclaims with joy: “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me.”

This means that he who was accustomed always to be present to me by an invisible presence may deign to appear to me also in my own nature and form.

The following words aptly suit lovers of both periods:

Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field, etc. The earlier saints greatly desired the Lord’s coming for the salvation of the human race. Hence, praying, they say: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Psalm 79).

They desired him to go out into the field—that is, for him who was invisible with the Father to appear visibly to the world—according to Habakkuk, who, in prophetic fashion, sang future things as though they had already occurred: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Habakkuk 3).

They themselves also wished to go out with him into the field, so that they might announce as present to the ages the grace of the Gospel which, seeing from afar and greeting it, they had proclaimed as future.

They longed to dwell with him in the villages—that is, to entrust the word of faith even to the pagans. For who does not know that pagans derive their name from villages in Greek, because they are far removed from the habitation, or even the knowledge, of the city above?

What do you think Isaiah, Jeremiah, Joel, and the other prophets would have done—those who, prophesying before the dispensation of Christ’s future appearance in the flesh, endured so many adversities for proclaiming him—if it had happened that they lived with him in the flesh?

The following words also, in no small measure, fit very suitably with the prayers of the faithful among the ancient saints.

But the Church of our own time, burning with an equal devotion, rightly cries out: “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field.” You raised the man whom you assumed for my salvation and placed him in heaven at the Father’s right hand. I ask, through the presence of your divine grace, that you deign to come to me more frequently.

You command me to cultivate my field, in which you sowed good seed—that is, you command me to preach throughout the whole world the Gospel that you gave. But because I can do nothing without you, I beg you to go out with me into the field: wherever you wish me to preach the word, be my fellow worker and helper.

We read that he himself said that, when the day of judgment comes, of two people working in a field, one will be taken and the other left (Luke 17). The one who cultivated the field of his own heart or that of his brother with the Lord’s cooperation will be taken. But whoever trusted that the fruits of doctrine or good actions came from himself will rightly be left by the one whose help he had neglected to seek.

“Let us dwell in the villages”: let us approach the hearts of foreigners also, teaching them. Let us not visit these places merely in passing, but let us remain among them until we make what is pagan civilized, what is foreign and alien familiar to us—or rather, our own.

Let us rise early to the vineyards, etc. Let us dwell in the villages in such a way that we also rise to cultivate the vineyards. Let us make our dwelling among those who have already been converted to the faith in such a way that we also strive, by evangelizing, to acquire others among whom we may dwell.

And rightly, when she says, “Let us rise to the vineyards,” she first adds, “Early.” For “early” signifies the rising of the true light, through which the world was rescued from the power of darkness.

“Early, then,” she says, “let us rise to the vineyards.” It is as though she were saying openly: “Because the night of ancient unbelief has departed, because the light of the shining Gospel has already begun to appear, let us rise, I beg you, to the vineyards—that is, let us devote ourselves to instructing Churches for God throughout the world.”

Let us see whether the vine has blossomed, etc. The vine blossoms when the Church receives the first beginnings of faith and confession. The flowers produce fruit when the faith and confession of the saints become ready also to perform works of righteousness, lest their faith be found idle or dead without works.

Pomegranate trees blossom when those who have advanced in faith and right action receive the desire to suffer for righteousness. Since pomegranates appear to be blood-colored, they aptly express figuratively the passion either of the Lord and Savior or of his faithful.

In each of these matters the bride rightly seeks the presence of her beloved, saying: “Let us go out into the field, let us dwell in the villages, let us rise to the vineyards, let us see whether the vine has blossomed,” and so forth.

For the Church is in no way sufficient—without the grace of him who, about to ascend into heaven, promised, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28)—either to go out into good works, to remain steadfast in the practice of good action, to rise toward salvation and the purpose of doing good, or to discern how far the souls of its hearers have progressed.

If we wish to understand these words as spoken by the person of the ancient righteous, we may appropriately understand “early,” when it says, “Let us rise early to the vineyards,” to signify the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

Many prophets and righteous people desired to see the times that the apostles saw. They longed, if it could be, to remain in the flesh until the new light of his coming, so that they might hear the words of the one teaching in the flesh, cling to his promises, and, with him present in the flesh, speak afterward of him to those who would believe.

The remaining words may be understood in the same sense as above:

There I will give you my breasts—that is, there, where we have come to see whether the vineyards and pomegranates have blossomed or are bringing forth fruit.

It is clear that the breasts of the Church are its teachers, the teachers of its little ones. The Church gives these breasts to the Lord when, in his service, it presents the deeds and words of its preachers, so that, just as nurses carefully suckle infants, those preachers may strive to conduct themselves in such a way that, through both sight and hearing, those who are still inexperienced may progress in Christ, reach the strength of spiritual maturity, and become worthy to hear the words of blessed John:

“I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the evil one” (1 John 2). “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2).

The Church rightly, after entreating the Lord, saying, “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field,” and the other words that follow, concludes in this way: “There I will give you my breasts.”

It is as though she were saying openly: “For this reason I entreat you so earnestly: that you may undertake spiritual labor with me, through which I may continually acquire new peoples for you and may learn to discern the condition of those who have already been acquired and how far they have advanced in faith.

“For I am striving most diligently to devote the tutors of my little ones to you, so that I may set before them nothing to follow, either by example or by word, except what you yourself have commanded.”

He knew that he belonged to these breasts who said: “We became little ones among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2), so greatly did we desire you.

The bride gave such breasts to her beloved, and not to anyone else, when, hearing him say, “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13), she immediately took care to obey his commands.

The mandrakes have given forth their fragrance at our gates. The gates of Christ and of the Church are the very same teachers, who were also signified by the term “breasts.” They are breasts because, as has often been said, they suckle His little ones and infants, laboring with continual diligence so that perfect praise may also proceed from their mouths to the Lord. They are gates because, through the ministry of the word and of regeneration, they introduce those whom they instruct into the dwelling of the holy city. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI).

Accordingly, John says in the Apocalypse concerning that same city [Col. 1203C]: “And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates” (Apoc. XII), because, plainly, the first teachers of the Church—that is, the twelve apostles—were chosen. At such gates, then, the mandrakes gave forth their fragrance when the apostles and their successors spread the renown of spiritual virtues far and wide. The Church therefore rightly beseeches the Lord to come there to bring heavenly aid to her preaching, where she knows the preachers themselves to be fragrant with outstanding virtues.

But whoever carefully investigates the other properties of the mandrake, and the medicines to which it is suited, will certainly discover that it is appropriately adapted to signify the virtues of the faithful. It is an aromatic herb whose root resembles the form of a human body [Col. 1203D]; its fruit is sweet-smelling and about the size of a Matian apple. Hence the Latins also call it *malum terrae*, “earth-apple.” It has the property that it frequently induces sleep when the sick are afflicted by the distress of wakefulness.

A person is tormented by the worst wakefulness when he seeks to strip his mind of the cares and desires of this world but, delayed by the practice of evil habit, is still unable to obtain the rest he seeks. Yet whoever earnestly strives to heal his weakness through the diligent practice of spiritual pursuits will, as the battles of his vices gradually recede, arrive at that quiet of mind of which the bride speaks earlier in this poem: “I sleep, but my heart is awake”; that is, “I rest from the cares of temporal things, and my heart remains awake in the contemplation of everlasting goods.”

[Col. 1204A] Likewise, when the bodies of certain people must be cut because of disease, the bark of this plant is infused into wine and given to them to drink, so that, once rendered drowsy, they may not feel the pain. The meaning of this property in relation to spiritual medicines is readily apparent. The soul grows grievously weak when it has been subdued by the heavy burden of vices; and it is offered to physicians for healing when holy teachers exhort it to resist carnal pleasures. But because what was once held with great love cannot be abandoned without severe pain, it seems to be cut away by the one who withdraws the soul from its long-established habit of enticements.

Yet, lest such cutting should perhaps appear intolerable to the weakened soul, a salutary potion must be given, so that, beneficially lulled to sleep by it, the soul may not feel the pain of the incision. [Col. 1204B] The punishment of the eternal fire of Gehenna, which will torment souls neglectful of their salvation forever, must be recalled to mind; and the glory of the heavenly homeland, where the souls of the righteous who have been received there will reign with Christ without end, must be brought back to memory. This is the potion of salutary teaching, which renders the soul, long languishing away from God, or asleep to this world—or rather dead to it, so that it very easily endures—and even rejoices—that all the pleasures to which it was previously attached should be taken away.

Likewise, that mandrake is said to heal those who suffer from nausea, so that they are unable either to retain food or to take pleasure in eating it. The food of the soul is the word of truth. Those who are unable either to receive it by hearing or to retain what they have received by hearing in the stomach of memory are held by a wholly evil and dangerous sickness [Col. 1204C], since the life of those who disdain either to preserve the bread of life once received or at least to partake of it must plainly be despaired of.

Frequent examples of the saints and the present pattern of virtues usually provide a remedy for this sickness: when some person who is fastidious and negligent, having seen or heard of the works of the good and recalling the glory of the heavenly reward, also seeks to imitate their good actions and labors in this present life, so that he may deserve to be regarded as a co-heir of their everlasting happiness. Whoever is such a person has, as it were, been led through the fruit of the mandrake to the hope of salvation and life.

Those teachers who possess such abundant grace of the Spirit and such zeal for piety that whoever sees or hears them is immediately changed in mind and begins to follow their way of life rightly bear the form of the mandrake, because they fix the nourishment of life in the hearts of those who are nauseated.

[Col. 1204D] The bride beautifully promises her beloved not only the fruits of vineyards and apples, rich in delights that give life, to look upon, but also the fragrances and health-giving juices of mandrakes. She boasts that she possesses not only those things that can be eaten and drunk, but also those that can make food or drink pleasing and sweet to those who find them distasteful. For the Church brings before the sight of her author the gifts of the heavenly word—namely, the foods and drinks of life—and brings forth suitable ministers who, by preaching, carry these things to the hungry and thirsty. Moreover, by first tasting them herself—that is, by practicing them beforehand—she makes them sweet even to those who find them distasteful.

[Col. 1205A] She brings forth, as it were, vineyards: innumerable companies of the elect. She brings forth pomegranates, troops of martyrs made precious by the splendor of unconquered confession. She brings forth spiritual gifts, by which she kindles the hearts of the sluggish to behold and imitate the examples of the good.

## All new and old fruits, etc.

The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises of the New and Old Testament. The Church has preserved them all for her beloved because she knows that he alone gave the commandments of both and repaid those who kept them with fitting rewards. She knows that he alone either proclaimed commandments or promised rewards: lesser ones through angels to his ancient servants, and greater ones through himself to us.

In this statement the Church powerfully refutes the sects of the Photinians, who deny that the Lord and Savior existed before Mary; and she also refutes the madness of the Manichaeans, who dogmatically assert that the God of the Law is one and the God of the Gospel another.

[Col. 1205B] Likewise, the new and old fruits are the righteous of the New and Old Testament. None of them, however distinguished by exceptional holiness, could enter the innermost sanctuary (*adyta*) of the heavenly kingdom before the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord and Savior had been accomplished.

The Church of that time, which is now called the Synagogue for the sake of distinction, said: “All new and old fruits I have kept for you, my beloved.” As though she plainly said: “I know with complete certainty that no one can be saved except through your grace, and that no mortal can already become perfectly blessed before you, having become mortal, open the way of true blessedness to the heavenly realms. For all the righteous whom I have seen I have preserved in sure faith for your most holy coming, through which I have learned that they will reach perfect happiness.”

[Col. 1205C] The Church of the New Testament also expresses a similar statement through the voice of her first shepherd, thus testifying against those who thought otherwise: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they also were” (Acts XV).

The following statement proves that this is the true interpretation of the present passage, for it continues:

## CHAPTER VIII

### XXXII. Who will grant me my brother, etc.?

For both in many passages, and in all of them, and especially in this one, the poem testifies that nothing carnal or literal is being expressed, but that the whole is intended to be understood spiritually and typologically [Col. 1205D]. What woman could suddenly desire that her beloved—her chosen one—should no longer be a young man as he had been, but should be born again as an infant brother to her, and be nourished as a little child at the breasts of her mother, when she was accustomed to find him already grown?

This, therefore, is the voice of the ancient righteous, who believed that the Lord and Savior was consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit in divinity and worshiped him with due service, but desired also to see him in human form and consubstantial with human beings, so that they might see fulfilled in him—the one of whom these things had been foretold—the things they had known through prophecy.

[Col. 1206A] They longed to hear that most fitting declaration of their Creator, which he uttered with his hands extended toward the disciples: “Behold my mother and my brothers” (Mark III). They desired to receive that delightful announcement which the same disciples received after the triumph of the resurrection: “Go and announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matt. XXVIII). The beloved himself bears witness to them, saying elsewhere to the same disciples: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see the things that you see, and did not see them, and to hear the things that you hear, and did not hear them” (Matt. XIII).

What he says, “Sucking the breasts of my mother,” cannot be understood specifically of that glorious Mother of God, of whom it was truly said, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke X), and of whom he himself says in the Psalm: “From my mother’s womb, you are my God” (Ps. XXI). This is plainly to say: “You who were my Father before the ages, from the time I began to be human you are also my God.”

[Col. 1206B] For Solomon—or any righteous person of that age—could not call blessed Mary his mother, since she was destined to be born in the world so much later. Rather, he calls his mother the Synagogue, namely, the substance of human nature, from which she herself had been born and from which she desired the Redeemer of all to be born and nourished.

Burning still with immense love for his birth, she added:

### And I shall find you outside, etc.

The beloved was within, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). But so that he might also be found outside, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

The patriarchs saw the Lord, and the prophets saw him, but inwardly—that is, in spiritual contemplation of the mind—not through the gaze of bodily eyes. They saw him in an image, in the form of an angelic substance; but they could not see his very nature, which he revealed through angels in whatever manner he wished.

[Col. 1206C] Indeed, the lawgiver himself, who was worthy to hear, “I will show you every good thing” (Exod. XXXIII), heard again: “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII).

Blessed are those who were worthy to say to one another: “We have found the Messiah, which is called Christ” (John I), and again: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph of Nazareth, of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote.”

To such people also aptly applies what he says: “So that I may find you outside and kiss you” (Song VIII). The Synagogue kissed the beloved whom she had found in those who, in the assumed reality of the flesh, were now worthy to see him face to face in truth and to speak with him mouth to mouth.

[Col. 1206D] This is the kiss: that most loving gift of his mouth and that mutual exchange of conversation which the Synagogue sought above all in this poem, beginning: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

She fittingly adds her wish: “And now let no one despise me.” The Church was despised by outsiders as small and worthless so long as she was confined within the narrow boundaries of Judea. But when, with the Lord’s coming in the flesh, she began to spread among all nations, she became terrifying to the world, as though she would fill the whole earth and overthrow the worship of all gods.

[Col. 1207A] That she was not an object of contempt but rather of terror, like an army drawn up for battle, was demonstrated especially by the fact that war was publicly declared against her throughout the whole world. Yet in that war, whether by living or by dying, she prevailed and became still more terrifying to the entire world.

The Church was also despised by unclean spirits, who boasted that they had deceived the human race, dragged it from the heavenly homeland into this exile and manifold misery, and that no human being could exist entirely free from their domination. But after the Mediator between God and humanity, the human being Christ Jesus, came into the world, was tempted, and conquered the very enemy by whose temptation the first-formed man had once been conquered; after he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil; and finally, by dying, destroyed him who held the power of death; after he led out with himself from the underworld the entire multitude of the preceding righteous and brought them to the joys of that kingdom which the first-formed man had lost, and placed the sign of his victory on the foreheads of the faithful—then the good life of human beings was no longer despised by them.

[Col. 1207B] They see that they have been conquered by a human being, and they grieve that the human race has been transferred to the kingdom which they themselves lost through pride.

It is also permissible to believe that the holy angels despised human life less after they saw God and their Lord love the human race to such an extent that he himself chose to become human, live among human beings, and die.

[Col. 1207C] Hence, before his incarnation, they patiently allowed themselves to be worshiped by human beings. But when John began to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, the angel forbade him, saying: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God” (Apoc. XII, 17).

Therefore that ancient multitude of the elect rightly sighed for the coming of the same Lord Jesus and said: “Who will grant you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you, and now no one may despise me?” To this it fittingly adds:

### I will take hold of you, etc.

The Synagogue speaks in this way, just as Paul says: “We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep” (I Thess. IV). Although he knew with certainty that he could not remain in the flesh until the day of judgment, nevertheless, because of their participation in one and the same brotherhood, he joins himself to the number of those who will be found alive in the flesh at the Judge’s coming.

[Col. 1207D] Here, therefore, the ancient people of God speaks in the person of that part of itself which would see him appearing in the flesh: “I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother.” I will receive you as you come with ready and faithful devotion; I will embrace your teachings with eager desires and await your promises. I will also lead you, returning to heaven after the dispensation of the flesh has been completed, with joyful eyes, and I will proclaim you joyfully to all with a joyful voice.

This is the house of his mother: namely, the blessedness of the heavenly homeland, for whose dwelling human nature was created. If no one had sinned, the entire human race would have passed from the delights of paradise, in which the first human being was placed, into that homeland to possess it forever, without passing through bodily death.

The Church therefore promises to lead the Lord into this house—not being able to accomplish this by her own power [Col. 1208A], but desiring through her prayers that it be accomplished, and proclaiming through her praises what must be accomplished or has been accomplished. In this way the Psalmist could exalt him to the heavens, although he said: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me” (Ps. XXIX).

This is plainly to say: “Because you have deigned to assume the nature of my weakness, I rightly confess the praises of your power, which has glorified that nature, with unwearied delight of mind.”

### There you will teach me, etc.

“There you will teach me”—in that very substance of the flesh in which I shall find you outside and kiss you—there you will give me the commandments of your Gospel, which the prophets, the Law, and the Psalms promised. There you will teach me to hope for gifts greater than those I read of in the Law and the prophets.

[Col. 1208B] Or this must be understood more profoundly: “There you will teach me in the house of my mother, into which I rejoice to lead you with a joyful procession of the eyes and desire to lead you also with the praise of words.” For there he taught and teaches the Church through that part of her which he has received to himself there. There he will teach the whole Church when, after the universal judgment has been completed, none of his saints will be anywhere except in heaven with him.

What he will teach there he himself indicates in the Gospel. In that sweetest and most generous discourse which he held with her immediately before his passion, he says among other things: “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly”—that is, “I will show the Father openly to you.”

### And I will give you a cup of spiced wine, etc.

The Church gives the Lord a cup of wine when, having received his benefits, [Col. 1208C], she returns to him a great fervor of love. She gives wine not pure but seasoned, as it were, with the mixture of noble spices, when that same love is proved also by the testimony of good works.

If we wish to offer him a cup of devotion worthy and acceptable to him, we must possess not only works that demonstrate love for the Creator, but no less those that prove the fraternal love within us. He himself clearly distinguishes these when, warning his disciples not to perform their righteousness before people in order to be seen by them, he immediately adds three kinds of good action in completing the statement: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting. He plainly indicates that our righteousness ought to consist in these three.

All that we mercifully do to relieve the needs of our neighbor [Col. 1208D] belongs to almsgiving. Everything we perform with devout piety in order to appease our Creator belongs to prayer. The whole chastening of the mind, by which we strive to abstain from vices and the contagions of the world, belongs to fasting.

And because the holy Church offers her beloved not only purity of life but also, in many of her members, receives the precious cup of death for love of him, she rightly says, “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine,” and adds, “And the juice of my pomegranates.”

The pomegranates are the same as the *mala punica*, “Carthaginian apples.” They are called *granata*, “seed-filled,” because of the multitude of their seeds, and *punica*, “Punic,” because they abound especially in Africa and around Carthage. Since they signify the blessed martyrs, their very rosy color is an indication of this.

[Col. 1209A] She rightly calls it the juice of the fruits, not a drink, unmixed wine, or *sicera*, so as to indicate the fervor of unquenchable love in the heart of the triumphant army. New wine—that is, wine taken immediately from the winepress—is usually more fervent; and therefore it appropriately corresponds to the most ardent virtue of those who do not hesitate to pass through iron and flames in order to reach the vision of the Creator.

For who does not see that just as this drink is said not only to heal the heat of the stomach and a diseased belly but also to benefit the other internal organs, so the fervor of charity, the more abundantly it overflows, the more it covers—or even extinguishes—the multitude of sins?

[Col. 1209B] Let the ancient congregation of the righteous, desiring to see the coming of its author in the flesh, say: “There you will teach me, and I will give you a cup of spiced wine, and the juice of my pomegranates.”

As though she openly declared: “There—that is, at the very time or place in which I find you outside and am found worthy to speak with you—you will present to me the commandments and gifts that are fitting for the Son of God appearing to human beings in human form; and I will offer you the service of an undivided heart, the service that is truly owed to God.”

For his coming grants to the Church, laboring amid the adversities of the world, heavenly rest—meanwhile in hope, and in the future in reality. She rightly adds:

### His left hand is under my head, etc.

By his left hand she signifies the sacraments of his incarnation and the gifts of his present presence; by his right hand she signifies the rewards that the elect will receive in the future. Among these is not only the vision of divine majesty but also the glory of his glorified humanity, of that same one Mediator between God and humanity.

[Col. 1209C] The bride therefore rightly desires that his left hand be placed beneath her head and that his right hand embrace her, so that now she may rest from the disturbance of the world through his temporal supports, and then enjoy his manifest vision forever.

Indeed, no disturbance ever interrupts the eternal rest of the saints. Hence it is rightly said, “His right hand will embrace me,” because the presence of the divine majesty will surround his own on every side in the heavenly kingdom, so that no memory of misery may violate a happiness worthy of God, nor any fear of its end constrain it.

[Col. 1209D] Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any longer, because the former things have passed away.” And again: “And night shall be no more. They shall have no need of the light of a lamp or of the light of the sun, because the Lord God will illumine them, and they will reign forever and ever” (Apoc. XXII).

But the rest granted to the faithful in the present life can by no means be perfect, because the ancient enemy, death, has not yet been destroyed. Hence it happens that the fortunate rest of the good, and a kind of most welcome sleep that renders their minds, intent upon divine things, as though insensible to this world, is often disturbed by the attacks of the wicked—namely, those who, ignorant of the blessedness of such sleep, have instead grown accustomed to remain awake through love of the passing world.

[Col. 1210A] Would that only those who openly belong to the world and attack the peace of the Church held such hostility, and that the Church herself did not also contain within her those who impede her spiritual pursuits by their carnal conduct. Yet because she herself gives birth to many such people, the Lord warns them not to presume to disturb the minds of the faithful who are devoted to the Church’s prayer, reading, or other acts of piety. When he heard the desire of her heart, he immediately added:

### XXXIII. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not stir up, etc.

Such souls are rightly called daughters of Jerusalem, because through the bath of regeneration they have been joined to the body of the holy Church, and because they are striving toward the heavenly kingdom, although upon the foundation of right faith they build not gold, silver, and precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw.

[Col. 1210B] “Do not stir up,” he says, “my beloved with the tumult of carnal disturbances, and do not make her rise from the quiet of her peaceful devotion, in which she delights to stand before the sight of her Creator. Until she herself wills”—that is, until, after properly completing the duties of divine service, she consents, warned by the necessities of human weakness, to return to the common care of human frailty.

And because, after Judea had gathered to the faith of the Lord’s incarnation, a multitude of the nations also followed and hastened to share in the same grace, Judea, astonished at this unexpected conversion, suddenly exclaims:

### XXXIV. Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, etc.?

The Church of the nations comes up from the wilderness because, after having been abandoned by her Creator for a very long time, she reached his grace as the steps of faith and good works advanced [Col. 1210C], fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah, who says: “The wilderness and the dry land shall rejoice; the desert shall exult and blossom like a lily” (Isa. XXXV).

“Overflowing with delights”—namely, those of which the bridegroom says above: “How beautiful and how lovely you are, most beloved, in delights!” That is, in desires for the heavenly life.

“Leaning upon my beloved”: rightly leaning upon him, without whose help she could not only fail to ascend to heavenly things but could not even rise again. For both progress in virtue and the very beginnings of faith can be ours only if the Lord grants them.

[Col. 1210D] Judea was all the more astonished at this grace of the new conversion of the nations because she believed that she alone, together with those who were admitted into her rite through the mystery of circumcision, belonged to it, as the Book of the Acts of the Apostles most openly testifies.

When she had said in astonishment, “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights?” she concluded in still greater amazement: “Leaning upon my beloved.” “My beloved,” she says—that is, the one whom I thought loved me alone and was unknown to the other nations.

In response, he who is our peace, who made both one and, coming, preached peace to us who were far away and peace to those who were near (Eph. II), urges her to remember the grace through which she herself was rescued from the gravest evils and converted to the way of truth, and to rejoice together with the salvation of others, since the author of salvation and life is rich toward all who call upon him.

### XXXV. Under the apple tree I awakened you, etc.

[Col. 1211A] The apple tree most aptly expresses the wood of the holy cross, on which he himself deigned to hang for the salvation of all. In praise of it the Church said above: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.”

Under the apple tree, therefore, the Lord awakened the Synagogue, whom he recalled from eternal death through faith in his passion. Under that same tree her mother and parent was corrupted and violated—namely, the greater and older portion of the same people.

This was the portion which, seduced by the persuasion of its rulers, chose Barabbas instead of the Lord, foolishly crying out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). It too was beneath the tree of the cross—not humbly entrusting itself to the faith of this tree, but obstinately invoking vengeance from it upon itself.

[Col. 1211B] Separating from her society the people who consented to believe, the Lord exhorts them to retain in a steadfast heart the memory of the grace bestowed upon them and also to join to it works worthy of the faith they have received. For it follows:

### Set me as a seal upon your heart, etc.

“Set me upon your heart” through thought, and “upon your arm” through action, so that inwardly there may be “love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I), and so that the same devotion of the heart, which the inward judge sees, may also be proved outwardly to those who observe it by the display of good works, to the glory of the Father who is in heaven.

He rightly says, “Set me as a seal.” We often carry some sign tied to a finger or arm, so that we may be reminded of the thing whose frequent remembrance we desire. In this same manner the Lord wishes us, always reminded by the present seal, to retain his commandments, according to what he himself commands when speaking of the Law: “It shall be as a sign in your hand and as something suspended before your eyes, for remembrance” (Exod. XIII).

[Col. 1211C] If we continually carry his memory in our breast, then he who bestowed this grace upon us will also remember us forever and preserve us, as though in place of a seal, happy through his presence in the heavenly kingdom. Thus he promises to the distinguished leader of his people: “I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, and I will set you as a seal, because I have chosen you, says the Lord” (Haggai II).

[Col. 1211D] Against this, condemning and rejecting him who turned to apostasy after faith, he says: “Though Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring upon my right hand, I would tear him away from there” (Jer. XXII).

Or this must be understood more profoundly: a seal, wherever it is placed, is usually an indication of secret things, precious objects, and things that must not be violated. Thus it is written of the Lord: “He shuts up the stars, as under a seal” (Job IX)—so that they may be opened only with the permission and command of the one who sealed them.

This is why Abraham received the sign of circumcision, “a seal of the righteousness of faith that he had while uncircumcised.” Through the circumcision he received in the flesh, it was signified that the faith he had already received before circumcision was effective for the cleansing both of the heart and of the body. We too now possess that faith without circumcision of the flesh, and in it we are justified, according to the saying of the prophet and apostle: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. I).

[Col. 1212A] Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ must be set as a seal upon our heart and as a seal upon our arm, so that we may understand everything he did or said in the flesh to be secret and heavenly.

Because he himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God, we set him as a seal upon our heart when we learn the things he said as though they were truly the words of divine wisdom. We set him as a seal upon our arm when we strive to hear and follow, according to our measure, the things he did as though they were true examples of virtue.

[Col. 1212B] Likewise, we set the Lord as a seal upon our heart and arm when we keep his commandments in the present life in anticipation of receiving the reward which we are not yet able to see.

“Because love is strong as death,” etc. This love, or zeal, can rightly be understood both in our Lord and Redeemer and in his elect. For the love with which he loved us was strong as death, since it was so great that through it he went to death itself for our sake. Hence he says: “Greater love than this no one has, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). The zeal with which he was jealous for us was hard as hell, because no temptations of hostile enemies could turn him back from concern for our salvation, just as hell itself cannot be softened by any torments of the wretched or changed from the severity of its sentence. This comparison certainly appears austere; but the more austere the comparison, the more closely it commends the affection of the Lord who is zealous for us. Concerning this, after expelling the faithless from the temple, he says to the Father: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68). And the greater his zeal is shown to be, the more grievous the condemnation that follows us if we despise it.

The love of his faithful, too, is strong as death, because not even through the bitterness of death itself can they be torn away from it. Hence they confidently say: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8). Their pure and God-devoted zeal is likened to hell, because just as hell never releases those whom it has once seized, so the stubbornness of their ardent zeal never grows cold at any time.

This is the zeal by which Phinehas, inflamed, struck down the fornicators in the wilderness; this is the zeal with which Elijah burned when, after the waters of heaven had been suspended and then recalled after three years, after the prophets of Baal had been killed and the people’s heart had been turned back to the Lord, he said: “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord of hosts, because the sons of Israel have forsaken the covenant of the Lord: they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword” (3 Kings 19); this is the zeal Peter employed when he brought the neophytes who had lied to God to their death; this is the zeal of which Paul writes to the Corinthians: “I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God. For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 11).

The greatness of perfect love, or zeal, has appropriately been introduced at this point, where, while Judaea marvelled, the Lord was directing her attention to the new conduct of the Gentile Church and urging her to recall to mind the gifts of piety granted to her. For after the corruption of her parent and mother, she herself had been raised through the tree of the cross in the first resurrection [to] grace. [Col. 1212C]

Thus this statement can fittingly be applied to what precedes: “Remember, O Church gathered from the Jews, that through the wood of my passion you have come to life; and never forget that the greatness of my love and zeal for you brought me even to death. Nor should you be surprised that I have received into my faith the crowd of the Gentiles whom you see inflamed with such love and such zeal for accomplishing my will that it seems easier either to persuade death to stop carrying souls away from the world, or hell not to receive those carried away, than to persuade them ever to depart from my faith. Do not think that you can please me merely by an outward profession of words. Rather, if you wish to come to life, set me as the memorial of your will like a seal upon your heart; set me upon your arm. Imbue your mind with so much love, whether divine or fraternal, and be so zealous that the fullness of the heavenly citizens may not be completed without the gathering of your people, so that your love itself and your zeal itself may not be changed or diminished by any condition of adversity or prosperity.” [Col. 1213A]

Some understand the statement “Zeal is hard as hell” as referring to the envious zeal that the Synagogue often held against the Church of the Gentiles. Concerning this we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “But on the following Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of the Lord. When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with zeal and contradicted the things spoken by Paul” (Acts 13). This zeal is hard as hell because it consumes with the plague of impiety the soul that it has seized. Hence it is written: “Zeal has seized an unlearned people, and now fire consumes the adversaries.” [Col. 1213C]

If this is understood in that way, the Lord rightly admonishes the Synagogue not to remain bound by such zeal against the Church when she sees the Church rising from the wilderness of vices and overflowing with heavenly delights, cleaving to her beloved with an irrevocable mind, lest, by envying the good things that she herself could have possessed, she lose them.

After this statement, he adds further observations by accumulating remarks on the power of love, saying: [Col. 1213D]

“They are lamps of fire and flame.” Fire, that is, in the same love by which they burn inwardly; but flame in the practice of righteousness, by which they also shine brightly and widely before others. Were they not lamps of fire who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24). Did the Lord not will us to be lamps of flame, to whom he says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works” (Matthew 5)?

These are the lamps which, when the bridegroom comes, the virgins who possess them will enter with him into the bridal chamber of the everlasting kingdom. They have placed his love and fear upon their heart and arm—that is, they have subjected all their thoughts and actions to his commands. But then the lamps of the foolish are extinguished, because the works by which they seemed to shine before human beings will grow dark when the inner judge arrives and reveals the intentions of hearts: they performed their good works under the pretext of transitory praise. [Col. 1214A]

“Many waters could not extinguish love,” etc. By “many waters” and “rivers” he means the assaults of temptations, which do not cease to attack the souls of the faithful, whether visibly or invisibly. Through open adversaries of the faith, through false brothers, and through the hidden snares of the ancient enemy, they attempt to overcome them. Yet temptations can in no way seize hearts that are accustomed to be rooted and founded in love. The promise of truth stands firm, in which it is said: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43); and in the Gospel, concerning the house built upon a rock: “When the flood occurred, the river struck against that house, but it could not shake it, because it had been founded upon the rock” (Matthew 7). And because, in whatever mind love of eternal goods abounds, the worth of fleeting things immediately becomes contemptible, it is rightly added: [Col. 1214B]

“If a man were to give all the substance of his house,” etc. This statement requires no explanation of its words. The apostles themselves above all, and afterward an innumerable crowd of believers, demonstrated by their own examples how true it is: for the love of truth they left behind everything they seemed to possess in this world, and considered that they had lost nothing, provided that they received true goods in heaven. [Col. 1214C]

The Lord clearly signified this in two consecutive parables in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and in his joy he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13). Again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes away and sells everything he has and buys it” (Matthew 13).

Hence the outstanding preacher said most excellently: “For the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as refuse, that I may gain Christ and be found in him” (Philippians 3).

But if the reading found in certain codices is followed—“He will despise him”—a very different sense results, namely the one commended by the Apostle when he says: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13). Therefore, if a man gives all the substance of his house to the poor for love—that is, in order that he might love—the judge himself, seeing that his heart is empty of love, will despise him as though he had given nothing. [Col. 1214D]

Although this appears contrary to the preceding sense, it nevertheless declares no less clearly how lofty and how necessary the virtue of love is. Both interpretations lead to the same conclusion: that we should always carry love in our work as a seal.

### XXXVI. “Our sister is little,” etc.

The Lord speaks these words to the Synagogue, which marvels at the faith or reception of the Church of the Gentiles. With great providence he now calls her their sister in charity—that is, both his own sister and the Synagogue’s—so that the Synagogue might recall that the presence of her Creator had been made known through grace, and might rejoice more and more over the fraternal fellowship granted to her by grace. [Col. 1215A]

The Lord Savior’s sister is both his entire Church, gathered from the two peoples, and every holy soul—not only because he assumed the same nature in which he himself became human, but also because of the gift of grace by which he gave those who believe in him the power to become children of God. Thus he who was the only Son of God by nature became, by grace, the firstborn among many brothers.

Hence there is that most sweet statement of his to Mary: “Go instead to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20). [Col. 1215B]

When he therefore says, “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts,” he indicates the early period of the Gentile Church’s birth, when the number of believing peoples was still small and she remained less capable of preaching the word of God. Read the first book of the Acts of the Apostles, which extends from the eighteenth year of the emperor Tiberius to the fourth year of Nero, and you will find that many crowds of Gentiles believed through the preaching of the apostles; yet nowhere in that entire period of approximately thirty years will you find that they preached. [Col. 1215C]

The Church of the Gentiles was still little and was not yet sufficient to generate or nourish children for Christ through instruction. Therefore the Lord admonishes the Synagogue, using fraternal charity, to rejoice in her salutary beginnings and to apply to her depravity [smallness] the aids by which she might grow. As though offering fraternal counsel concerning her interests, he adds:

### XXXVII. “What shall we do for our sister,” etc.?

He addresses the Church; the Lord addresses every chosen soul when he admonishes it concerning eternal salvation, either through the hidden illumination of his Spirit or through the open voice of preachers. In this address the heavenly goodness takes account of the measure of our strength and bestows its gifts according to the capacity of human beings.

He therefore says: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?” As though he were saying plainly: “The Church of the Gentiles is indeed small in number and is not yet sufficient to undertake the ministry of the word. What, then, does it seem to you, O Synagogue, should be done for the care of this sister of ours at the time when I begin to address her through my apostles and the successors of my apostles? Shall we, as though she were still a little one, entrust to her the small secrets of heavenly mysteries? Or shall we make her greater through increase, so that, progressing well, she may be capable of more perfect virtues?” [Col. 1215D]

While she remained silent, listening rather to what he himself wished, he immediately revealed what ought to be done, adding:

“If she is a wall, let us build upon her battlements of silver,” etc. The Lord himself is often signified in sacred Scripture by the name “wall” or “door.” He is rightly called a wall because he fortifies his Church on every side, so that she may not be plundered by enemies; and rightly a door because it is only through him, or through the fellowship of this Church, that we enter either the Church’s enclosure or the walls of the everlasting kingdom. [Col. 1216A]

For he says of himself: “I am the door of the sheep; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). And again: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). The prophet, foretelling the future gifts of the Church, says of him: “A wall and a rampart will be placed in her” (Isaiah 26). The wall is the Lord himself appearing in the flesh; the rampart is the revelation of prophecy. By proclaiming from the beginning of the world that he would become incarnate, prophecy greatly assisted the structure of the Church.

Yet he who, by appearing in the flesh, deigned to make the Church his sister also gave her a share in his name, so that she too might be called both wall and door. [Col. 1216B] She is a wall in those who, endowed with greater learning and the virtue of the Spirit, are able to fortify and defend the minds of the faithful against the incursions of the erring by bravely resisting the weapons of wickedness. She is a door in those who, although less equipped to repel the sophistries of heretics or pagans, are nevertheless healthfully imbued with the simplicity of the Catholic faith and, by preaching, open the entrance of the kingdom to those who desire it, leading them through the mystery of the second regeneration into the courts of heavenly life.

Similarly, he does not refuse to bestow upon the more perfect members of the same bride other names of virtues that are unquestionably appropriate to them. For example: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 10); and again: “Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves” (Luke 10), although he himself is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1), the spotless and undefiled Lamb who took away the sin of the world. [Col. 1216C]

“If she is a wall,” he says, “let us build upon her battlements of silver.” It is as though he were saying plainly: “If the Church of the Gentiles is capable, in some of her members, of opposing the teachings of the perverse, possessing men suited to teaching—whether naturally gifted with intelligence or trained through philosophical instruction—let us by no means take away from them the ministry of teaching the truth. Rather, let us assist them by giving them the pages of the Holy Scriptures, so that they may more strongly and easily guard the weak from the snares either of deceitful doctrine or of corrupting example.”

The silver battlements are the divine heights of eloquence, concerning which it was said above: “Your neck is like the tower of David, which was built with battlements”; and concerning which the Psalm says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested in fire, tried upon the earth” (Psalm 12). [Col. 1216D]

“If she is a door, let us fit her together with cedar boards.” If there are in her people who know how to instruct the little ones in the word of simple teaching and lead them into the inner chambers of holy conduct, let us set before them the imperishable examples of the righteous of former times. Through these examples they may more effectively fulfill the office just mentioned. It has often been said that cedars signify the virtues of the elect.

The figure of boards expresses the breadth of their hearts, in which they may receive the memory of heavenly words. Concerning this the prophet says: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 119). [Col. 1217A] The Apostle wished his hearers to be adorned with such boards when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own inward parts. In return—I speak as to children—be enlarged yourselves” (2 Corinthians 6).

Hence Solomon also admonishes the lover of wisdom, saying: “Write it upon the tablets of your heart” (Proverbs 7).

Hearing these counsels or promises of her Redeemer concerning herself, the Church no longer awaited the assent or response of the Synagogue to whom he was speaking. Instead, she immediately sprang forward and answered him with a devoted voice:

### XXXVIII. “I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers,” etc.

I am rightly called a wall because I am constructed from living stones, because I am united by the bond of charity, because I have been placed upon an immovable foundation, and because no blow of the heretical battering ram can overthrow me. For “the firm foundation of God stands,” bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his.” [Col. 1217B]

There are also in me some who, endowed with greater grace, surpass the general life of the faithful by the special height of their virtues as far as a tower surpasses a wall. They nourish those who are still little and weak in faith with the simpler milk of exhortation, as though with breasts, and repel all the darts of the perverse through exceptional power of speech, like a secure tower.

Yet I was able to possess all these things not by the choice of my own freedom, but, from the time when I was made before him as one finding peace, I received them through his gift—that is, from the time when he deigned to grant me the gift of his peace through the word of reconciliation. [Col. 1217C]

For by my own diligence I could neither come before him, from whom I had withdrawn so far, nor recover the peace I had lost. Rather, I gratefully received what he freely offered. From the time when he himself bestowed this gift upon me, I immediately progressed through the growth of virtues and profess that I may rightly be compared to a wall and possess breasts like a tower. For I constantly drive hostile forces away from harming that city, and I strive always to raise up new peoples for it.

Because I could do this only through the gift of the peace granted by him, I wish to say more about the virtue of that peace:

### XXXIX. “There was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one,” etc.

The Church speaks this either to the Synagogue, which she saw envying her—or, to put it more mildly, greatly marvelling at her conversion to the Lord—or certainly to her attendants, whom this poem customarily calls the daughters of Jerusalem. [Col. 1217D]

The “peaceful one” whom she names is her bridegroom and beloved, the “Father of the future age, the Prince of peace” (Isaiah 9), whose figure Solomon foreshadowed both through the peaceful condition of his reign and through his very name.

The vineyard belonged to the peaceful one because through his grace the Catholic Church was established throughout the world. It is mentioned in many places in Scripture, but most explicitly in the evangelical parable, where it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard,” etc. (Matthew 20). [Col. 1218A] There, by the laborers of the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, it is plainly expressed that the one and same Church of Christ, throughout the entire period of this age—which is comprehended under the symbol of a single day—is cultivated by the unceasing labor of spiritual teachers.

Again, the vineyard belonged to the peaceful one in that peace of which he had said that it had been made before him as though finding peace. For whoever neglects to possess peace does not belong to the Church of Christ, even though he may appear to confess Christ and obey his commands.

“For his place was made in peace.” And the Apostle says: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12). [Col. 1218B]

The very appearance and form of the most beautiful vine also sets before us the fellowship of this peace for imitation. To quote the words of blessed Ambrose: “For imitation of our life, it first fixes a living root; then, because it is of a flexible and perishable nature, it grips whatever it has seized with tendrils, as though with arms, and by these it rises and lifts itself up.”

The people of the Church resemble this vine. They are planted by a kind of root of faith, restrained by the shoot of humility, and, lest they be bent or driven away by the storms of the world, they embrace their neighbors with those tendrils and rings, as though with the embraces of charity, and rest in their union with them.

This vine is dug around when we are relieved of the burden of earthly cares. Nothing weighs down the mind more than such anxiety and desire, whether for money or power. Once dug around, the vine is tied so that it may rise, when our affection is lifted by the example of the saints and does not lie low and despised; rather, each person’s mind raises itself toward higher things, so that it may dare to say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). [Col. 1218C]

This vineyard has peoples because the holy Church has been gathered not from the single nation of the Jews but from the peoples of every nation. The Church of the Gentiles added this especially in order to show that she too could belong to this vineyard, and that Judaea ought not to glory in the uniqueness of the divine knowledge granted to her, since the Psalmist says: “Praise the Lord, all nations” (Psalm 117). Moses himself foretold: “Rejoice, nations, together with his people” (Romans 15).

Because the Lord takes great care that this vineyard remain undefiled, and because it is greatly necessary for human beings to become participants in it, it is rightly added: [Col. 1218D]

### “He entrusted it to keepers,” etc.

The keepers of the Church are the prophets; the keepers are the apostles; the keepers are the successors of the prophets and apostles, who, at different periods of the world, were appointed to its governance by heavenly command. The keepers are the armies of the heavenly host, who throughout the age of this fleeting world care for the Church’s well-being, so that it may not be disturbed by the invasion of evil human beings or spirits.

A man brings a thousand silver pieces for the fruit of this vineyard because every person who makes progress for the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom abandons all worldly things. The fruit of labors performed temporally for the Lord is the reception, with the Lord, of everlasting rest and kingdom. Concerning this he said: “I appointed you to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain” (John 15)—that is, “to work, receive your reward, and for that reward itself never to come to an end.” [Col. 1219A]

Scripture customarily calls a man one of perfect virtue. Indeed, *vir* (“man”) takes its name from *virtus* (“virtue”). Such a man—that is, a mind exalted by the grace of virtue—brings a thousand silver pieces for the fruit of this vineyard when he leaves behind all temporal possessions in order to deserve to receive eternal goods.

By the term “silver pieces” he signifies every kind of money that ought to be abandoned. By the number one thousand, which is perfect and complete, the totality is customarily signified. Therefore, by the thousand silver pieces that the man is said to bring for the fruit of this vineyard, the totality of what every perfect person leaves behind for the Lord is indicated. Although these things may sometimes be small in monetary value, they are judged great and abundant by the estimation of him who weighs not the sum of the money given but the conscience of the person giving it. [Col. 1219B]

This is the same meaning as the statement given above in other words: “If he gives all the substance of his house for love, he will treat it as though it were nothing.” The thousand silver pieces here stand for all the substance of the house that is abandoned. Love, however, which, when the other charismatic gifts cease, embraces us perpetually in our heavenly homeland, is itself the fruit of the vineyard. The blessed, who now labor in that vineyard while hungering and thirsting for righteousness, will then be satisfied by it.

The voice of the peaceful one himself follows, for he teaches how great is his care for his vineyard—that is, the Church—what he preserves eternally for those who leave behind their possessions, and what singular reward he intends to give to the keepers of that vineyard, namely its teachers. [Col. 1219C]

### XL. “My vineyard is before me,” etc.

“You have been tested,” he says, “and I have entrusted my vineyard to keepers who would cultivate it both by their words and by their examples. But know that I committed its care to keepers in such a way that I nevertheless continually observe what is done in it. I see with what disposition and diligence each person labors there; finally, I behold how many snares it endures from adversaries and how many open conflicts it withstands. And why say more? Behold, I am with it all the days, even to the consummation of the age.

“But when this has appeared, I will then repay with fitting rewards all who labor in my vineyard, or for my vineyard, or against my vineyard. Those who have distributed all the goods they possessed or could acquire in the world for the fruit of the vineyard—that is, for the hope of the heavenly inheritance—and have given them to the poor will certainly obtain the fulfillment of their hope. Indeed, they will receive in heaven gifts greater than they knew how to hope for, since ‘eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.’” [Col. 1219D]

Those who served as keepers of the vineyard by preaching or by shining through more exalted deeds will be rewarded with a double recompense above the other righteous. Hence it is said to Daniel through the angel: “Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12). [Col. 1220A]

This is also what is meant here concerning those who despise transitory goods for the sake of receiving eternal things and who, because of the steadfastness of their unanimous hope, are designated by the term “one man.” “A thousand of yours,” he says. Immediately he explains what greater reward is reserved for those who guard the state of the Church with greater diligence, adding:

“And two hundred for those who guard its fruit.”

The number one thousand and the number one hundred, since each is a perfect number, are rightly understood as signifying perfection and the fullness of eternal recompense. The number two hundred, that is, a doubled hundred, signifies the greater rewards of perfect teachers. Concerning these rewards, even as they begin in this life, the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching” (1 Timothy 5). [Col. 1220B]

“‘A thousand are yours, O Peaceful One,’ he says: ‘the thousand silver pieces that you brought for the fruit of my vineyard remain with me, the Peaceful One, preserved in their complete number. You need not fear in any way that you will lose through the forgetfulness or ignorance of the just judge anything of the good works you have done. For I come to gather the works and thoughts of human beings together with all nations and languages, and to repay each according to what they have done in the body.’

Again, because peacemakers are so called because they are accustomed to make peace, just as those who keep the laws of peace are called peaceable, the silver pieces which the saints distribute in truth are peacemakers for them: they open for them the way to the vision of everlasting peace, customarily expressed by the name of the heavenly city and mother of us all, the new Jerusalem. They scatter among the poor of Christ the patrimonies that they preferred to give away rather than possess themselves.

“And two hundred for those who guard its fruit.” “Silver pieces of the Peaceful One” is understood, so that the complete sentence is: “A thousand silver pieces are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred silver pieces of the Peaceful One are for those who guard its fruit.” [Col. 1220C]

For those who undertake a double labor in the present—living soberly, justly, and devoutly, while also protecting through their preaching that the fruit of the Church does not fail or fall prey to enemies—will receive a double gift in the future.

Therefore the same distributor of gifts immediately encourages his Church, or every soul devoted to good works, to persist as far as it can also in preaching the word of truth:

“You who dwell in the gardens, listen; make me hear your voice.”

[Note: In the Vulgate Edition, with a substantially different meaning, that verse reads: “You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen; make me hear,” etc. Bede himself appears to have read the verse in this way, since below, in his exposition of this passage, he has: “But our friends also listen, namely the angels,” etc. EDIT.] [Col. 1219D; Col. 1220D]

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Because our conversation, which has continued at length, must now be brought to a close, hear what I chiefly ask and demand of you. Nothing is sweeter to me in every respect than for you to dwell in gardens—that is, to establish your dwelling in the cultivation of spiritual fruits. Do not build yourself a hut there by hasty labor, as though you were about to leave shortly; rather, with a steadfast and unwavering mind, await my coming there.

“For you know that I often descend to my garden, to the bed of spices, in order to feed in the gardens and gather lilies—that is, to see, assist, and reward the good efforts of your labors. Next I ask this gift from you: make me hear your voice by preaching, as far as you are able, both my commandments of the Law and the promises of reward. Whenever you do these things, remember that you do them with me always listening to you, for I am always accustomed to be present at your prayers.

“But our friends also listen—namely, the angels, whom I have given you as helpers against the daily struggles with evil spirits, and the spirits of righteous human beings whom, taking them from your assembly, I have gathered to the vision of my glory, to which you too will one day wholly belong. Both are your friends; both observe your deeds and words. They greatly rejoice when they see you acting courageously for the attainment of the blessedness in which they themselves rejoice. They exult whenever any of your faithful happen to enter there, and they hasten to receive them in their arms.” [Col. 1221A]

When he had said these things, the Church immediately assented and replied: [Col. 1221B]

### XLI. “Flee, my beloved,” etc.

This passage can rightly be understood both of the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension and of what takes place daily in the Church. The beloved flees after addressing his bride and sister, because, having completed the dispensation of our Redemption, he returned to the heavenly realms. He is compared to a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices, because he frequently appears through the grace of compunction in the hearts of his faithful. These hearts are mountains of spices because, rejecting base desires, they are held by the love of heavenly things; and, purged of the stench of vices, they are filled with the fragrance of particular virtues. Thus they say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III), and, “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Corinthians II).

It was fitting that, at the conclusion of the sacred song, mention should be made of his Ascension and of the grace that followed it. A little earlier, the desired joys of his Incarnation had been expressed when the bride said, “Who will give you to me as my brother, who suckled the breasts of my mother?” The fruit of his Passion had also been brought forward, when he himself said, “Under the apple tree I awakened you.” And again: “For love is strong as death.”

“Flee, therefore, my beloved,” she says, “and be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices”—as though she were plainly saying:

“Since you appeared in the flesh and deigned to bestow upon me the commands and gifts of heavenly life that I had always desired, now that the task of your loving dispensation has been completed, return to the heights, to the Father’s bosom. Yet, I beg you, do not entirely withdraw from me the light of your frequent visitation. Rather, as a gazelle or young stag—although these are untamed animals, unaccustomed to human approaches, they are nevertheless often seen in the mountains—so, I ask, remember to deal with me: although you remain bodily in the heavenly realms and do not again visit human dwellings, still grant me the frequent protection of the divine presence. For only in this way shall I be able to fulfill that greatest command, which you gave me as a final farewell: that I should always inhabit the gardens of virtue and always make you hear the voice of my confession and preaching.”

This sentence may also, as we said, appropriately be understood of the daily condition of the holy Church. The beloved flees from the bride who dwells in the gardens and whom he was addressing when, from a mind intent upon good works, he temporarily withdraws either the grace of virtue that he was accustomed to provide or even subjects her to the storms of temptations in order to test her, so that she is compelled rightly to say, “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face from me?” and so forth, to the end of the psalm (Psalm XII).

He is compared to a gazelle and a young stag appearing upon the mountains of spices when, as he himself judges appropriate, he either removes the dangers of the temptations besieging her by restoring to her the light of his protection, or restores the accustomed gifts of virtue that he seemed to have withdrawn.
