To say nothing of the great charisms of the great—such as the healing of the sick, the raising of the dead, the expulsion of demons, certain knowledge of hidden things, the clear contemplation of heavenly joys, and other gifts of this kind, which cannot always be present even in the outstanding members of the Church—it is evident from our own weakness that we are by no means always able in the same and unvarying manner to persist in the sweetness of prayer, shed tears either from consciousness of our guilt or from desire for the heavenly homeland, suffer with a grieving neighbor, or confront approaching temptations. Thus, at times, although we strive greatly to employ these goods, we cannot; and again, at other times, although we apply ourselves to them less, we enjoy an abundance of them.

How does this happen, unless because the beloved now flees and now revisits our mind, in a loving providence that accomplishes both purposes: through the grace bestowed, we grow in progress toward virtue, and through the grace withdrawn, we learn to preserve the virtue of humility? He temporarily withdraws the desired effect of virtue so that, when it is later restored, it may be held more firmly; he restores what was withdrawn so that the spirit, exercised by frequent renewal, may strive more ardently toward heavenly things.

Therefore, when she says, “Flee, my beloved,” she is not speaking as one who wishes this. For who would want to drive from their own presence the one whom they love? Rather, she speaks with fervor for his will, remembering his custom: often, in the midst of conversation, he has left her and gone away, so that he could be found only through diligent and prolonged searching. She also remembers her own condition, since during the time and place of this pilgrimage she cannot see him continually.

What does she add? “Be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” She pursues him with intense desire and supplication, knowing that in the present life this is her greatest happiness: since she cannot possess continual vision of him, at least to be consoled by his frequent visitation. This happiness is granted only to those who, through contempt for earthly things and desire for heavenly joys, deserve to be called spiritual mountains of spices.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1223]

[Col. 1223A] In the exposition of the Song of Songs, which we explained in five books—for we composed the first volume of this work specifically against Julian, in defense of the grace of God which he attacked, and through the withdrawal of which he perished—we followed the traces of the Fathers in such a way that, meanwhile, we left untouched the works of our beloved father, the pope, blessed Gregory, beloved by God and human beings. We judged that it would be more pleasing to readers if, since he discussed the matters explained in this volume throughout his various works, scattered here and there, and since these discussions are numerous and copious, we were to place them all together as though collected into a single volume. This we are now about to do, with the Lord’s help.

Let this, then, be considered the seventh book on the Song of Songs, collected indeed through our labor, but composed from the words and understanding of blessed Gregory. If someone should perhaps think that our little works are rightly to be despised, let him have readily available for reading the sayings of one whom it is certain must in no way be despised. If, however, someone reads these works of ours as well, captivated by affection for them, let such a great architect place a golden summit upon the marble buildings of our smallness.

I have heard that Paterius, a disciple of that same blessed Pope Gregory, collected and arranged in a single volume, in order, whatever Gregory had explained in parts throughout his works on the whole of sacred Scripture. If I had that work at hand, I would fulfill the intention of my undertaking much more easily and perfectly. But since I have not yet deserved to see it, I myself have taken care, as best I could and with the Lord’s help, to imitate it.

### From Book XXVII of the *Book of Job*

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Col. 1223C]. The mouth of God may designate the only-begotten Son, just as he is called God’s arm, because through him the Father accomplishes all things. Of him the prophet says, “And the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (John XII); and John says of him, “All things were made through him” (John I).

Thus he may also be called the mouth, as though by the name “mouth” the Word were plainly indicated, just as we too customarily say “tongue” for words. When we speak of the Greek or Latin tongue, we mean to indicate Greek or Latin words. We therefore rightly understand the mouth of the Lord as the one through whom he speaks everything to us. Hence the prophet says, “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken this” (Isaiah LVIII).

Therefore the bride says to him in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” as though she were plainly saying, “Let the sweetness of the presence of the only-begotten Son, my Redeemer, touch me” [Col. 1223D].

### Again, above, in the same book

And when Matthew saw the Lord giving commandments on the mountain, he said, “Opening his mouth, he said” (Matthew V). It is as though he plainly said: “He then opened his mouth who had previously opened the mouths of the prophets.” Hence also the bride, desiring his presence, says of him, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I). For as many commandments as the holy Church has learned from his preaching, so many kisses of his mouth has she received.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXX

“For your breasts are better than wine.” These are the breasts—that is, the teachers—which, fixed in the chest’s hidden chamber, give us milk to drink. For, clinging to the secrets of supreme contemplation, they nourish us through subtle preaching.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIV

“Therefore the young women loved you.” Sacred Scripture often uses youth to signify newness of life. Hence, when the bride comes, it says, “The young women loved you” (Song of Songs I): that is, the souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism, who do not fail through continuing in the conduct of the former life but are adorned by the manner of life of the new human being.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII

“I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” True preachers do not grow proud of the light of righteousness. Rather, through the grace of humility, they confess in themselves the blackness of sins. Hence the Church of the elect also says, “I am black but beautiful.” And John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (I John I).

### In the seventeenth Homily of the Gospel Exposition

“They made me keeper of the vineyards,” and so forth. The holy Church says this concerning its weaker members. For our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the practice of daily labor. But, although placed as keepers in the vineyards, we do not guard our own vineyard, because, while we are entangled in external activities, we neglect the ministry of our own action.

### Again, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXX

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves,” and so forth. The Lord feeds when he takes delight in our actions. He lies down at noon when, amid the carnal desires of the hearts of the reprobate burning with passion, he finds refreshment in good thought among the hearts of his elect.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, in the same place

“Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women, go forth,” and so forth. Each elect soul recognizes itself as beautiful among women when, even though placed among sinners, it remembers that it was created according to the image and likeness of its Author, so that it may walk in accordance with the order of the likeness it has received.

If it does not know itself, it goes forth, expelled from the secret place of its heart, and is scattered among external desires. Once gone forth, it departs after the tracks of the flocks, because, abandoning its inner life, it is led onto the broad way and follows the examples of the peoples. It no longer feeds lambs but young goats, because it aims not to nourish innocent thoughts of the mind but wicked movements of the flesh.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXV

“While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” The virtues of those who are progressing, when known to other people, spread fragrance like a sweet scent. Hence Paul says, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Corinthians II).

Hence also the holy Church, exuding a certain fragrant sweetness in its elect, speaks in the Song of Songs, saying:

“While the king is at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” [Col. 1225A];

as though it were saying more plainly: “As long as the king remains hidden from my sight in the repose of heavenly secrecy, the life of the elect is exercised in wondrous fragrances of virtue, so that, while it does not yet see the one it desires, it may exude fragrance all the more ardently through desire.”

When the king has been placed at his couch, the nard gives forth its fragrance: while the Lord rests in his blessedness, the virtue of the saints in the Church supplies us with the grace of great sweetness.

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily III, Part II

“Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I am sick with love.” For one who loves her bridegroom ardently, there is ordinarily one consolation amid the delay of the present life: that, because her own vision of him is postponed, the souls of others may advance through his word and may burn with the torches of love for the heavenly bridegroom.

Hence the bride says in the Song, “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I am sick with love.” For what are the flowers except souls already beginning a good work and breathing forth the fragrance of heavenly desire? And what are the apples among the flowers except minds already perfected in good things, which reach the fruit of good work from the beginning of holy reconciliation?

She who is therefore sick with love seeks to be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if she is not yet permitted to see the one she desires, it is a great consolation for her to rejoice in the progress of others. Let the soul, then, sick with holy love, be supported with flowers and apples, so that she who is not yet able to contemplate the face of God may rest in the good work of her neighbor.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book VI, according to the interpreters of the Septuagint

“I am wounded with love.” The unhealthy soul, struck down in the blind love of this exile, neither saw the Lord nor sought to see him. But when struck by the darts of his love, it is wounded in its depths by an affect of piety and burns with the desire for contemplation. In a wondrous manner, the soul that had previously lain dead is brought to life by the wound, unto salvation.

It burns, it pants, and even desires to see the one from whom it had fled. Thus, by the blow it is brought back to salvation, being recalled from the turmoil of its own love to the security of inward rest.

### In the section entitled “The Rule of the Pastor”

“His left hand is under my head,” and so forth. The Church has placed God’s left hand—namely, the prosperity of the present life—beneath its head, pressing it down through the intention of supreme love. God’s right hand, however, embraces the Church, because it is held with complete devotion beneath his eternal blessedness.

Hence it is written again, “Your right hand, O Lord, shattered the enemies” (Exodus XV). The enemies of God are advanced by his left hand and shattered by his right, because the present life often exalts the wicked, while the advent of eternal blessedness condemns them.

### In the twenty-eighth Homily of the Gospel Exposition

“Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills.” In coming for our redemption, the Lord made, so to speak, certain leaps. Do you wish, beloved brothers, to know his very leaps? From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross he came to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven [Col. 1226A].

Behold: in order to make us run after him, he made certain leaps of the truth manifested through the flesh. He also “rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Psalm XVIII), so that we might say to him from the heart, “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily I, Part II

“Behold, he stands behind our wall.” The holy Church, now plainly desiring to see the Lord in the voice of the bride, says: “Behold, he stands behind our wall.”

For he who displayed to human eyes that which he assumed from mortality, while remaining invisible in himself, stood, as it were, behind a wall to those who sought to see him openly. He did not present himself to be seen manifestly in majesty. He stood, as it were, behind a wall: he displayed the nature of humanity which he had assumed and concealed the nature of divinity from human eyes.

Hence it is added there, “Looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice.” Whoever looks through windows or latticework is neither seen wholly nor wholly unseen. Thus the Redeemer appeared before the eyes of those who doubted. If, while performing miracles, he had endured nothing as a human being, he would plainly have appeared to them as God; and again, if, while suffering human things, he had done nothing as God, he would have been thought merely human.

But because he both performed divine works and endured human sufferings, he looked upon human beings as through windows or latticework: he appeared as God through his miracles, while remaining hidden in his sufferings, and he was seen as human through his sufferings, yet was recognized as more than human through his miracles.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVII

“Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come.” Since the holy preachings, that is, the rains together with winter, will cease with the present life, the voice of the bridegroom rightly says to the soul that is departing and hastening toward eternal summer, “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; for winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed.”

When winter passes, the rain withdraws, because when the present life is brought to an end—the life in which the cloud of ignorance and the sluggishness of corruptible flesh had bound us—all the ministry of preaching ceases. Then we shall see more clearly through ourselves what we have now heard more obscurely through the voices of the saints.

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily IV, Part II

“Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove,” and so forth. Whether it is the holy Church or each individual elect soul, it is a friend to the heavenly bridegroom through love, a dove through the Spirit, and beautiful through the beauty of its conduct. When it is led out from the corruption of the flesh, winter has certainly passed for it, because the sluggishness of the present life has departed.

The rain also has gone away and withdrawn, because when it is led out to contemplate the almighty Lord in his own substance, drops of words will no longer be necessary, as though the rain of preaching had to be poured down. What it was able to hear only faintly, it will then see more fully.

Then flowers appear upon the earth, because when the soul begins to taste in advance something of the sweetness of eternal blessedness, it smells, as it departs, what it will possess more abundantly in the fruit after it has gone forth.

Hence it is added there, “The time of pruning has come” [Col. 1227A]. In pruning, sterile branches are cut away so that those which are fruitful may bear fruit more abundantly. The time of our pruning therefore comes when we abandon the fruitless and harmful corruption of the flesh, so that we may attain the fruit of the soul. That fruit will be most abundant for us: the vision of God.

### In the twenty-fifth Homily of the Gospel Exposition

“On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves,” and so forth. We seek the beloved on the bed when, amid the slight rest of the present life, we sigh with longing for our Redeemer. We seek him by night because, although the mind is already awake in him, the eye is still dim.

But whoever does not find the beloved must rise and go around the city—that is, traverse in mind and inquiry the holy Church of the elect. Let him seek him through the lanes and streets: that is, let him observe those who walk through narrow and broad ways, to see whether he can discover any traces among them and search them out. For there are some even among those who live in the world who possess something in their conduct worthy of imitation.

As we seek, the watchmen who guard the city find us, because the holy Fathers who guard the Church’s constitution meet our good efforts and teach us by word or writing. When we have passed them a little way, we find the one whom we love, because our Redeemer, although human in his humanity among human beings, was nevertheless above human beings in his divinity.

When, therefore, the watchmen have been passed, the beloved is found, because when we see that the prophets and apostles are beneath him, we understand that the one who is God by nature is above human beings. He is first sought as though he could not be found, so that, once found, he may be held more firmly.

### Again, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII

When the Church was seeking its Redeemer, it did not wish to place its hope in those ancient preachers. It says, “When I had passed them a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” For it could not find him if it had not wished to pass beyond them.

### Again, in the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily VI, Part II

Thus the bride, anxious with holy desires, speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, and I did not find him.”

She seeks the beloved on her bed when, in the leisure and repose she desires, she already longs to see the Lord; when she already desires to go forth to him and pants to be free from the darkness of the present life. But she seeks him and does not find him because, although she desires him with great love, she is not yet granted to see the one she loves.

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily X, Part II

“Who is this who ascends through the desert,” and so forth? The holy Church of the elect, when it rises from this world in holy prayers with ardent love, ascends through the desert it is leaving behind.

It explains how it ascends: “Like a column of smoke from spices.” Smoke arises from incense, and the Psalmist says, “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL). Smoke customarily draws out tears. Thus smoke from spices is the compunction of prayer conceived from the virtues of love [Col. 1228A].

Yet this prayer is called a column of smoke because it asks God for heavenly things alone. It advances uprightly, so that it does not turn back to desire earthly and temporal things through worldly ambition. It should be noted that it is called not a “rod” but a “little rod” (*virgula*), because at times, in the heat of compunction, the power of love burns with such subtlety that even the mind itself that has deserved to possess it through illumination cannot comprehend it.

It is rightly said, “Of myrrh and frankincense.” According to the law, frankincense is burned to the Lord in sacrifice. By myrrh, dead bodies are embalmed so that they may not be corrupted by worms. Those who mortify the flesh so that the vices of corruption may not rule them offer, therefore, a sacrifice of myrrh and frankincense; and they burn before the Lord an offering of their love, fragrant in his sight.

They offer myrrh because they afflict themselves and, by afflicting themselves, preserve themselves from vices; frankincense because they love the vision of God, for which they burn inwardly with the deepest longing to arrive, and because they present themselves to him in holy virtues.

Hence it is added there, “And all the powders of the perfumer.” The perfumer’s powder is the virtue of one who acts well. It should be noted that the virtues of those who act well are called powders, not perfumes. Whenever we do any good, we reconsider it and, lest anything improper be present in it, examine it through the judgment of reconsideration. Thus we make powder from perfumes, so that through discernment and love we may kindle our action more subtly for the Lord.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book VII

“Behold, Solomon’s litter, sixty mighty men,” and so forth. The strength of the righteous is to conquer the flesh, resist their own pleasures, extinguish the delight of the present life, love the hardships of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, despise the allurements of prosperity, and overcome in their hearts the fear of adversity.

Sixty mighty men, from the strongest of Israel, surround Solomon’s litter, because all the saints without doubt contemplate the inner rest that they desire.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX

“All holding swords and most skilled in warfare.” Paul explained what is signified by the sword in divine Scripture when he said, “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

Solomon does not say, “All having,” but “holding,” because it is not merely remarkable to know the word of God but to do it. He has the sword but does not hold it who knows divine speech but neglects to live according to it. Nor can one who does not exercise the spiritual sword he possesses be skilled in warfare, for he is wholly unable to resist temptations.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XX

“Each man’s sword upon his thigh,” and so forth. The terrors of night are the hidden ambushes of temptations; the sword upon the thigh is vigilant discipline pressing down the allurements of the flesh.

Therefore, lest the terror of night—that is, a hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is necessary that the sword placed upon our thigh press down through discipline. Holy men are so certain of hope that they nevertheless remain always suspicious of temptation. To them it is said, “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling,” so that rejoicing may arise from hope and trembling from suspicion.

### On the same subject, in the section entitled “The Rule of the Pastor,” Book VI

The sword is placed upon the thigh when an evil suggestion of the flesh is subdued by the sharpness of holy preaching. Night expresses the blindness of our weakness, because whatever adversity threatens in the night is not seen.

Each one’s sword is therefore upon his thigh because of the terrors of night: holy men, while fearing what they do not see, stand always prepared for the struggle.

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily III, Part II

“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon,” and so forth. It should not be thought that Solomon, a king of such greatness, who abounded in such immense riches that the weight of his gold could not be estimated and silver had no value in those days, made himself a wooden litter.

Rather, Solomon is our peace-bringing king, who made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. The woods of Lebanon are exceedingly imperishable cedar trees. The litter of our King, therefore, is the holy Church, which is constructed from strong Fathers, as from imperishable cedar trees.

It is rightly called a litter because it carries souls every day to the eternal banquet of its Creator. Its silver columns were made because holy preachers shine with the light of sacred utterance. There is also a golden reclining place with the silver columns, because through what the holy preachers say with clarity, the minds of their hearers find the radiance of inward love upon which they may recline. Through hearing what is expressed luminously and openly, they rest in that which shines in the heart.

The silver columns and the golden reclining place were made because through the light of speech the brightness of rest is found within the soul. The inward radiance already illumines the mind, so that through intention it rests there where the grace of preaching is no longer required.

But to show what kind of ascent leads to that which is revealed within as bright, he immediately adds concerning the same litter: “Its ascent,” he says, “was purple.” True purple, because it is dyed with blood, is rightly understood in the color of blood. And because, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, a very great multitude of the faithful reached the kingdom through the blood of martyrdom, our King made a purple ascent in the litter: one reaches what is seen brightly within through the tribulation of blood [Col. 1229D].

What, then, are we to do? What hope will there be if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues? Yet our consolation is also present. Let us love God as much as we can; let us love our neighbor; and then we too shall belong to God’s litter, because, as it is written there, “He paved its middle with love.”

Have love, and without doubt you arrive where both the silver column is raised and the purple ascent is held. For that this is said on account of our weakness is plainly shown when it immediately adds, “Because of the daughters of Jerusalem.” The word of God, which speaks not of sons but of daughters, signifies by the female sex nothing other than the weakness of minds.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book IX

“How beautiful you are, my beloved,” and so forth [Col. 1230A]. He calls her beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful because one beauty belongs to her moral character, in which she is now seen, and another belongs to her rewards, by the appearance of her Creator into which she will then be raised.

All the elect are her members, because they walk straightforwardly in all things. Her eyes are called the eyes of doves because they shine with great light and sparkle with the miracles of great signs. But how great is the miracle that can be seen? The inward miracle, which cannot be seen, is more wondrous. Of this he plainly adds, “Apart from what lies hidden within.” The glory of an open work is great, but it is far incomparable to the hidden reward.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book III

“Your lips, O bride, are like a scarlet ribbon,” and so forth. A ribbon binds the hair of the head. The bride’s lips are therefore like a ribbon because, through the exhortation of the holy Church, all the thoughts spread through the minds of hearers are bound, lest they flow loosely away, lest they scatter themselves through unlawful things, and lest, once scattered, they weigh down the eyes of the heart. Rather, they gather themselves toward a single intention, while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them [Col. 1230B].

He rightly asserts that it is scarlet because the preaching of the saints blazes with the fire of love alone.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXIII

“Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep,” and so forth. We understand the teeth of the holy Church as those who, through their preaching, crush the hardness of sinners. They are rightly compared to sheep that have been shorn and washed because, taking up an innocent life, they laid aside in the washing of baptism the old fleece of their former conduct.

### In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily IV, Part II

“Your neck is like the tower of David,” and so forth. In the neck is the throat, and in the throat is the voice. What, then, is signified by the neck of the holy Church except its sacred utterances? Since a thousand shields are said to hang upon it, the whole number is indicated through this perfect number, because all our defense is contained in sacred speech.

There are God’s commandments there; there are the examples of the righteous. Therefore, upon the neck of the Church—that is, in the preaching of sacred speech, which because of its defense and height is said to resemble the tower of David—a thousand shields hang. For as many commandments as are found there, so many are the protections of our breast.

Behold: as we hasten to become strong against fierce powers, we find in this tower the armor of our mind. From it we take the commandments of the Creator; from it we take the examples of those who went before us, through which we are armed invincibly against our adversaries.

It should also be noted that the tower is said to have been built with its battlements. Battlements perform the same function as shields, because both protect the combatant. Yet there is a difference between them: we move a shield wherever we wish for our protection, whereas we can be defended by battlements but cannot move them. The shield is in the hand; the battlement is not held.

What, then, is the difference between battlements and shields except that in sacred speech we read partly of the miracles of those who went before us and hear of the virtues of their good works? Their miracles testify how truly they spoke about God, because they would not have performed such things through him unless they had spoken truthfully about him. Their works testify how devout, humble, and kind they were.

What, then, are their miracles except our battlements? We can be fortified by them, yet we do not hold them in the hand of our free choice, for we are unable to perform such things. A shield, however, is in the hand and gives defense, because the virtue of patience and the virtue of mercy, with grace preceding us, are both within the power of free choice and protect us from the danger of adversity.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIV

“Your two breasts,” and so forth. What are the two breasts except the two peoples coming from Judaism and the Gentiles, who, within the body of the holy Church, are fixed in the hidden place of the heart through the intention of wisdom?

Those among these peoples who are elect are compared to gazelles and young stags because, through humility, they understand themselves to be wicked and sinful; but when they run through love, if any obstacles arising from temporality confront them, they pass beyond them and, by making leaps of contemplation, ascend to the heights.

To accomplish this, they contemplate the examples of the saints who went before them. Hence they are also said to feed among the lilies. What is signified by the lilies except the life of those who truly say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Corinthians II)?

Therefore the elect, so that they may be able to attain the highest things, having seen the fragrant and radiant life of the righteous, now thirst eagerly to see the Lord; they burn with the heat of love to be satisfied by contemplation of him. But because, while placed in this life, they are not yet able to do so, they are meanwhile nourished by the examples of the Fathers who went before them.

Hence the time of this feeding among the lilies is appropriately defined when it says, “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” For we need to be refreshed by the examples of the righteous until, when the eternal day breathes upon us, we pass beyond the shadows of our present mortality. When the shadow of this temporal existence has passed and mortality has inclined, because we see the inward light of that day itself, we no longer desire to be inflamed with love for it through the examples of others.

But now, because we are not yet able to look upon him, it is supremely necessary that we be stirred by seeing the deeds of those who followed him perfectly.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVII

“You will be crowned from the head of Amana,” and so forth. What is signified by the name of lions except demons, which rage against us with the fiercest cruelty? And because sinners have been called to the faith, whose hearts were once dens of lions, the Lord is believed to be crowned from the dens of lions when, through their confession, he is acknowledged to have conquered death. For the reward of victory is a crown. The faithful therefore offer him a crown as often as they confess that he conquered death through the resurrection.

### In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XV

“Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Many of the righteous, when they see certain people acting perversely—people who must be struck by harsh rebukes—assume harshness of tongue, but conceal kindness beneath the tongue of their mind.

Hence, in the voice of the bridegroom, it is said to the holy Church, “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Those who do not wish to reveal the sweetness of their mind to the weak, but strike them with a certain harshness when they speak, and nevertheless, amid harsh words, secretly insert something of sweetness—these have sweetness not upon the tongue but beneath the tongue. For among the harsh things they utter, they release certain gentle and sweet words by which the mind may be refreshed through kindness.

### In the section entitled “The Rule of the Pastor,” Title XV

“Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates.” What is signified by the pomegranates except the unity of the faithful? For just as many seeds are protected within a single outer rind in a pomegranate, so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, whom an inner diversity of merits contains.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVII.—“Rise, north wind, and come, south wind” [Song 4:16; Col. 1232B]. By the south wind, which is naturally warm, the Holy Spirit is suitably signified; whoever is touched by it is freed from the torpor of his iniquity. Hence it is rightly said in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow.” The north wind is commanded to rise so that the hostile spirit, which constricts the hearts of mortals, may flee. The south wind comes and blows upon the garden so that its spices may flow forth, because through the coming of the Holy Spirit, when the human mind is filled by him, the reputation of its virtues is immediately scattered abroad; and thus the tongue of the saints rightly says, like a garden blown upon by the south wind: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2).

In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily II, Part II.—“I sleep, but my heart is awake” [Col. 1232C]. Contemplative life possesses a very pleasing sweetness: it snatches the soul above itself, opens heavenly realities, shows that earthly things ought to be despised, reveals spiritual things to the eyes of the mind, and conceals bodily things. Hence the Church rightly says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” One sleeps with a watchful heart when, by advancing inwardly through contemplation, one rests from restless outward activity.

Likewise in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII, on the passage cited above.—“I sleep, but my heart is awake.” As though she were saying: “While I lull my outward senses to sleep from the cares of this life, with an unoccupied mind I perceive inward things more vividly. Outwardly I sleep, but inwardly I keep watch, because, while I seem not to sense outward things, I grasp inward realities attentively.”

[Col. 1232D] In the Gospel Homilies, Homily XXV.—“My soul melted,” and so forth. The human mind that does not seek the vision of its Creator is badly hardened, because it remains cold within itself. But if it begins to burn with desire to follow the one whom it loves, it runs, melted by the fire of love. It becomes anxious with desire; everything that formerly pleased it in the world grows worthless; nothing outside the Creator delights it; and what previously gave pleasure to the soul afterward becomes exceedingly burdensome. Nothing consoles its sorrow so long as it does not yet behold what it desires. The mind grieves; even light is wearisome to it. By such a fire the rust of sin is boiled away in the mind, and the kindled soul, like gold—for through use it had lost its appearance—becomes bright again through the fire.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVII.—“The watchmen who patrol the city found me,” and so forth [Col. 1233A]. The watchmen find the bride while she is seeking, and they wound her, because when diligent teachers find a soul already seeking the appearance of its Redeemer, they wound it with the darts of heavenly love through the word of preaching. If any covering from its former way of life still remains upon it, they remove it, so that, once it has been stripped of such a burden, the one whom it seeks may be found by it more quickly.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXIV.—“His head is the finest gold.” Since God is Christ’s head, and nothing among metals is more brilliant than shining gold, the bridegroom’s head is called gold because his humanity exercises dominion over us through the radiance of his divinity.

In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily VIII.—“You are beautiful, my beloved,” and so forth [Col. 1233B]. Since Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” and by that name the heavenly homeland is expressed, the holy Church is called sweet and beautiful like Jerusalem, because the desire of her life is already compared with the vision of inner peace. In loving her author and longing to see his appearance—of whom it is written, “Into which things angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1)—she is said already, through the very desires of her love, to resemble the angels. The more she is made pleasing to God, the more she acts so as to become terrifying to wicked spirits.

How she is terrifying is shown by the comparison that follows: “like an army set in array.” Why is the holy Church to be feared by her enemies like an army set in array? This comparison is not without profound significance and must therefore be examined carefully. We know and it is evident that an army’s line appears terrifying to its enemies when it has been so compacted and massed that it seems broken at no point. For if it is arranged so that an empty space is left through which the enemy can enter, it is plainly no longer terrifying to its enemies.

Therefore, when we draw up the line of battle against wicked spirits, it is supremely necessary that we always be united and bound together by charity, so that we may never be found broken by discord. For however many good works there may be among the good, if charity is absent, discord opens a breach in the line, through which the enemy can enter and strike us.

In Homily IV on Ezekiel, Part II.—“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden things” [Col. 1233D]. The cheeks are the spiritual parts of the holy Church, which now shine within her through miracles and appear venerable, as it were, upon her face. When we see many people perform wonders, prophesy future events, abandon the world perfectly, and burn with heavenly desires, the cheeks of the holy Church grow red like the rind of a pomegranate.

But what is everything that we admire when compared with that of which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2)? Therefore, when he admired the cheeks of the Church, he rightly added, “apart from your hidden things.” It is as though he were saying openly: “The things in you that are not hidden are great; but the things that are hidden are altogether ineffable.”

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIX.—“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” [Col. 1234A]. The holy Church, desiring the rewards of heavenly life, is called dawn because, while she abandons the darkness of sins, she shines with the light of righteousness.

Yet there is something subtler that we should consider by reflecting on the nature of twilight or dawn. Dawn and twilight announce that night has passed, but they do not yet display the full brightness of day. While they drive away the night, they receive the day and hold a light mingled with darkness. What, then, are all of us who follow the truth in this life, if not dawn or twilight? We already perform certain things that are beginning to shine, yet in some respects we are still not free from the remnants of darkness.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXX.—“Your nose is like the tower of David,” and so forth [Col. 1234A]. Through the nose we distinguish pleasant odors from foul ones. What, then, is signified by the nose if not the prudent discernment of the saints? A tower is placed high for observation, so that an approaching enemy may be seen from afar. Therefore the nose of the Church is rightly said to resemble a tower in Lebanon, because the prudent discernment of the saints, looking carefully all around and set on high, detects fault before it arrives and, the more watchfully it anticipates it, the more firmly turns away from it.

In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily XI, cited above.—To preserve the truth of preaching, it is necessary to maintain the height of upright living. Hence it is also rightly said in the Song of Songs, in the voice of the bridegroom of the holy Church: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.” What praise is it, my brothers, for the nose of a bride to be compared with a tower? But since through the nose we always distinguish pleasant odors from foul ones, what is signified by the nose if not the discernment of watchmen?

That nose is called like the tower of Lebanon because the discernment of those set over others must always be fortified by vigilance and must consist in the height of life—that is, it must not lie in the valley of weak conduct. For just as a tower is placed on a mountain for observation so that approaching enemies may be seen from farther away, so the preacher’s life must always remain fixed on high, so that, like the nostrils, it may distinguish the foul odors of vices from the fragrances of virtues, foresee the attacks of evil spirits from afar, and, through his prudence, make the souls entrusted to him cautious.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XII.—“Let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the blossoms are bringing forth fruit” [Col. 1234C]. The vines flower when the minds of the faithful propose good works; but they do not bring forth fruit if, overcome by certain fears, they grow weak and fall away from what they had proposed. Therefore one must not look merely to see whether the vines are flowering, but whether the blossoms grow strong enough to produce fruit. For it is not remarkable if someone begins a good work; it is very remarkable if someone perseveres in a good work with right intention.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVI.—“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights?” [Col. 1234D]. Clearly, unless the holy Church overflows with the delights of God’s words, she cannot ascend from the wilderness of the present life to higher things. She therefore overflows with delights and ascends because, while she is nourished by mystical understandings, she is raised each day to contemplate heavenly realities.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII, according to the Seventy Interpreters.—“Who is this who comes up, made white?” [Col. 1235A]. The holy Church does not naturally possess heavenly life; but when the Spirit comes upon her, she is adorned with the beauty of gifts. Therefore she is remembered not as white, but as made white.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXX.—“Set me as a seal upon your heart.” A seal is placed upon things so that they may not be violated by the presumption of plunderers. The bridegroom is therefore placed upon the heart as a seal when the mystery of faith in him is impressed upon the custody of our thoughts, so that that unfaithful servant—namely, our adversary—when he observes the signs of faith, may not presume to break in by temptation.

In the Gospel Homilies, Homily VII.—“For love is strong as death.” As death destroys the body, so the charity of eternal life destroys love of bodily things; for whoever it has completely absorbed, it renders, outwardly toward earthly desires, like one without sensation [Col. 1235B].

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX.—“Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.” The age of the holy Church is described just as the age of every individual person is described. She was little when, newly born, she was not yet able to preach the word of life. Hence it is said of her: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts,” because the holy Church, before she advanced through the growth of virtue, could not offer the breasts of preaching to the lowliest hearers.

The mature Church, however, when joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, conceives through the ministry of preaching and carries children in her womb; she brings them forth by exhorting them and gives them birth by converting them [Col. 1235C]. Of this stage of her life it is said to the Lord: “Young women have loved you” [Col. 1236A]. All the churches that together constitute the one Catholic Church are called young women—not aged through guilt, but renewed through grace; not barren through old age, but, in the age of their mind, suited to spiritual fruitfulness.

In the exposition of Ezekiel, Homily II, Part II.—“You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear your voice” [Col. 1236A]. The holy Church dwells in gardens; every soul that has already been filled with the greenness of hope and good works dwells in gardens. The hope of this world is dry, because everything loved here quickly withers. The apostle Peter urges us to hasten, saying, “Into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.” Therefore she who already dwells in gardens ought to make her bridegroom hear her voice [Col. 1236B], that is, to utter the song of good preaching in which the one she desires may take delight. “Friends are listening,” namely, all the elect, who desire the words of life so that they may live again for the heavenly homeland.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVII.—“Flee, my beloved.” “He has fled from us,” we say whenever what we wish to remember does not come to our mind. “He has fled from us,” we say when we do not retain in memory what we want. Therefore, after describing the Lord’s death, resurrection, and ascension, the holy Church, filled with the prophetic Spirit, cries to him: “Flee, my beloved; flee.” As though she were saying: “You who became perceptible through the flesh, surpass the understanding of our senses through your divinity, and remain incomprehensible to us in yourself.”

# [EXPOSITION ON THE SONG OF HABAKKUK]

[Col. 1235]

## ADMONITION

[Col. 1235C] It is established from the Epitome of the History of the English People by Bede the Venerable that the exposition on the Song of Habakkuk was written by Bede himself. In that work he carefully compiled a catalogue of all his writings, among which is listed “One book on the Song of Habakkuk.”

This book has been transmitted to us by two very ancient manuscripts: one from Fleury, whose script approaches an age of approximately nine hundred years; the other from Corbie, from about the same period and written at least eight hundred years ago. A third manuscript, somewhat more recent, only about five hundred years old and belonging to the monastery of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris, has also transmitted it. All three consistently retain Bede’s name, so that no doubt remains that this exposition is genuinely his work, especially since its style agrees entirely with his other works and it is not found attributed anywhere to anyone else.

The blessed man undertook it in response to the urgent requests of his sister, who had devoted her virginity to God in some monastery, as may be gathered not only from the beginning of this work but also from its conclusion, where he says: “May it happen, dearest sister and virgin of Christ, that we too, loving him, may be made worthy of such a name.”

This is confirmed especially by the Corbie manuscript, at whose end these words are added: “Here ends the exposition on the Song of the prophet Habakkuk, addressed to his sister, a virgin of Christ.” No surviving record, so far as I know, has yet disclosed either her name or the monastery in which she consecrated herself to God.

Bede’s sole purpose in this work was to explain the prophet’s words according to the version of the Seventy Interpreters and briefly to represent the Incarnation of the divine Word, Christ’s passion, the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the nations. Learned readers will easily perceive how successfully he accomplished this.

MARTENE

[Col. 1235]

## ALLEGORICAL EXPOSITION ON THE SONG OF THE PROPHET HABAKKUK (C)*

[Col. 1235D] The song of the prophet Habakkuk, which you have asked to have explained for you, dearest sister in Christ, chiefly proclaims the mysteries of the Lord’s passion [Col. 1236D]. Hence, according to the custom of the holy, universal, and apostolic Church, it is solemnly repeated every week in the morning praises on the sixth day of the week, the day on which that same passion was completed.

It also mystically describes the event of the Incarnation itself, the resurrection and ascension into heaven, the faith of the nations, and the faithlessness of the Jews. For the prophet, contemplating the condition of the present age, had seen the peace of sinners and the afflictions of the righteous; he had seen the wicked abound in riches while the innocent were subjected daily to scourges; he had seen impiety in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice; he had seen the tears of the innocent with no one to console them, and their inability to resist the violence of their calumniators, deprived of everyone’s assistance [Col. 1237A; Note: alternatively, “of their worshipers”].

Knowing also that these and countless similar things could by no means occur without divine providence, he was [Note: alternatively, “is”] greatly troubled in mind and, sighing heavily from the depths of his heart, cried out to the Lord: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? I shall cry aloud to you, suffering violence, and you will not save?” (Hab. 1:2).

And again: “Your eyes are pure; you cannot look upon evil [Note: alternatively, “upon what is evil”], and you cannot behold iniquity. Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself, and you will make human beings like the fish of the sea and like a creeping thing that has no ruler?” (ibid. 1:13–14).

Yet amid these things he immediately recalled [Note: alternatively, “he led [it] into the lands as an example” (in terras eduxit sub exemplo; uncertain)] the dispensation of the Lord’s Incarnation and passion, which he had understood through the prophetic Spirit. He realized that he had complained far too harshly [Note: alternatively, “as was fitting”] about the afflictions of the saints in this life, for whom eternal rest had been promised in the future, since not even the Son of God himself [Note: alternatively, ipsa, a feminine form], appearing in the flesh, would leave the world without the suffering of the cross [Col. 1237B]. He was to be born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mother, live in the world without any sin, and pray to the Lord for his own ignorances. Thus he begins:

“Lord, I heard your report [Note: alternatively, “your hearing,” or “what was heard of you”], and I was afraid.” The Lord Savior’s “report” is what he heard from the Father: that he should come in the flesh, be born into the world, live among the weak as the Almighty, among sinners as the Just One, among human beings as God; perform heavenly works; teach heavenly commandments; promise heavenly gifts; be tempted, scourged, mocked, and killed; destroy our death by his own death; rise from the dead and ascend into heaven; and, having sent the Spirit from above, illuminate the world with the grace of truth.

He himself frequently mentions this report in the Gospel, saying: “But the one who sent me is true, and what I have heard from him, this I speak in the world” (John 8:26). And again: “But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). John the Baptist also says concerning him: “The one who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” (John 3:31–32).

The prophet therefore heard this report of the Lord in the Spirit and was afraid, because he had complained about the sufferings of the righteous in the world, although even the Lord himself, who makes the way of salvation and life prosperous for us, was to have a deathly departure from the world. He was afraid because he had complained about the tribulations of the saints, who are not only to be rescued by the Lord from tribulations but also to be crowned eternally with the Lord.

“I considered your works, and I was terrified.” These are plainly the works by which he redeemed the world, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross, so that, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb. 2:14). The more intently anyone considers these works, the more deeply he trembles at the works of his own frailty.

“In the midst of two living creatures you will be known” [Col. 1238A]. “In the midst of two living creatures” may be understood as “in the midst of Moses and Elijah” [Note: in one witness, “in the midst” is absent]. For there he was made known to the three disciples on the holy mountain: he told them that he was to die and said that he would suffer in Jerusalem. There he was made known as one who would rise and become immortal, when his face was glorified like the sun and his garments shone like snow. There it was made known that he was the Son of God, when a paternal voice from heaven said to him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5).

It may also appropriately be understood as “in the midst of two robbers.” Crucified between them, he was made known by dying to be a human being. But when the sun was darkened, the earth shaken, and the other miracles occurred around the cross that the Gospel recounts, he was made known to be God [Note: alternatively, obscuro, “with the sun darkened”]. By appealing to the Father on behalf of his executioners, he made known how compassionate he was. Through this example, the prophet, who foresaw these things in the Spirit, was admonished not only to endure patiently the afflictions of the wicked but also to extend the grace of his kindness to them while they persecuted him.

“When the years draw near, you will be known; when the time arrives, you will be revealed.” He indicates the years and the time of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

The prophet saw these times and years as still far off and greeted them from afar when he said that, as the years drew near and the time arrived, the Lord would be revealed and known. For earlier also he had heard the Lord say to him: “Because the vision is still for a distant time, and it will appear at the end and will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because coming it will come and will not delay” (Hab. 2:3).

Hearing this report [Note: alternatively, “command”], and considering the works of the passion, he was afraid and terrified, because he had been troubled [Note: alternatively, “was troubled”] by the transitory happiness of the wicked and the temporal affliction of the good. Nevertheless, so that he might make fitting repentance for his ignorance, he soon became confident that he could obtain pardon for his error. Thus he adds:

“While my soul is troubled within me, you will remember mercy in your wrath” [Col. 1239A]. “While my soul is troubled,” he says, shaken by the fitting sorrow of satisfaction and repentance because of fear of your wrath and judgment, which I fear I have carelessly incurred, “I believe that I shall quickly obtain the mercy of the pardon I have sought from you.” Here we must consider the marvelous speed of divine compassion. He says that his mind was troubled only because of God’s wrath, and immediately he adds that God had turned from wrath to mercy.

A similar statement is found in the Psalmist: “I said, ‘I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. 31:5). Yet such indulgence may apply to the smallest faults. Our offenses, however, are much more serious and therefore require greater and more prolonged repentance, together with tears and almsgiving [Col. 1239B].

Thus far the prophet has briefly explained the fear by which his mind was struck when he heard and carefully considered the event of the Lord’s Incarnation and passion. He then immediately describes more fully what that report was and what those works of the Lord were, by contemplating which he was so deeply shaken [Note: alternatively, “by example”; alternatively, “at once”]. He continues:

“God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shadowy and densely wooded mountain.” Lebanon is the highest mountain of Phoenicia, distinguished by tall, incorruptible, and aromatic trees. Scripture testifies that the Lord’s Temple in Jerusalem was made from them; therefore in Scripture the Temple itself is sometimes designated by the name Lebanon. Hence comes the saying of Zechariah concerning the Chaldean army that was to come against it: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1).

God therefore comes from Lebanon because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, scattered the first seeds of the Gospel in the Temple itself and from there filled the entire world with the growth of his faith and truth. Hence Isaiah says that “the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3).

He scattered the first seeds of faith there not only through the apostles, who, after his passion and resurrection, were filled with the Holy Spirit and by preaching there laid the first foundations of the Church—afterward their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. 18:5)—but also through himself. First, in that same Temple, he bore witness to the faith that was to be held in him, when he sat among the teachers at the age of twelve, questioning them like a human being of tender age but answering the teachers like God of eternal majesty. When his parents sought and found him, he himself indicated that he was God and the Son of God, saying: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke 2:49).

It should be noted, however, that this verse reads as follows in the Hebrew truth: “God will come from Thaeman,” that is, “from the South.” In the literal sense this has an easy meaning, because Bethlehem, where the Lord was born, lies south of Jerusalem. When, on the fortieth day of his birth, he was brought by his parents to Jerusalem so that a sacrifice might be offered for him according to the law, God indeed came from the South [Col. 1240A; Note: in one witness, “of his birth” is absent].

“And the Holy One,” he says, “from the shadowy and densely wooded mountain.” The Holy One is the same Mediator between God and human beings who above is plainly called God. Concerning him, Gabriel, announcing the Gospel to the Virgin Mother, said: “Therefore the holy one who will be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

The mountain from which this Holy One is sung as coming may be understood as the kingdom of the Jews, from which he derived the origin of his flesh. Concerning this mountain Daniel saw a stone cut without hands—that is, Christ, begotten without human agency—who, crushing the kingdoms of the world, would fill the whole earth with the glory of his name (Dan. 2:45).

That mountain is rightly called shadowy and densely wooded. It has many fruitful trees, that is, many holy men laden with the fruits of virtues. They nourish our hunger with the sweetest taste of their teaching and, by the protection of their intercession, overshadow our frailty, lest it wither from the inner greenness of love beneath the heat of tribulations [Col. 1240B; Note: alternatively, “lest they relieve the hunger of our mind”].

To this image the Apostle Peter aptly corresponds: a remarkable tree of this mountain, he not only refreshes those who hunger and thirst for righteousness with the fruit of his teaching but also saves the weak by the shade of his body (Acts 5:15).

These holy and exalted men can also be designated by the name “South,” from which God is said to come, because of the love by which they are accustomed to burn in the Lord and the teaching by which they shine before human beings. God comes from this South because he deigned to become incarnate from such people. God comes from this South every day when, as we read or hear their words or examples, love or knowledge of the truth is generated more perfectly in our hearts.

He continues:

“His majesty covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.” Having described the dispensation of the Lord’s Incarnation, he immediately added the mystery of the ascension, by which that same humanity was to be glorified, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his course reaches to its end” (Ps. 18:7).

“His majesty covered the heavens,” because the one who through the Incarnation was made a little lower than the angels was crowned with glory and honor through the resurrection, placed through his ascension above the works of the Father’s hands, and had all things subjected beneath his feet (Ps. 8:6). When the apostles preached, the whole earth was filled with his praise [Col. 1240D].

This is briefly yet most clearly contained at both the beginning and the end of that same psalm, where it says: “O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth! For your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens” (Ps. 8:2).

Even before his passion and resurrection, when the Word made flesh dwelt among us, his majesty covered the heavens, because the assumed humanity, though still mortal, already surpassed the heavenly powers. “And the earth was full of his praise,” since the powers of heaven truly knew that he was the creator of the earth, as he was of all creation through his divinity, while at that time he dwelt [Note: one witness adds “and was seen”] on earth through his humanity. Hence, at his birth, they sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

“His splendor will be like the light.” The splendor of the virtues and teaching of the Lord Savior will illuminate believers; hence he is called the Sun of Justice in Scripture. But since that splendor could not shine perfectly upon the world unless he himself [Note: alternatively, ipsa, a feminine form] first tasted death for a time, overthrew the kingdom of death [Note: alternatively, “cast it down”], and, rising from the dead, granted the world hope and faith in resurrection, it is rightly added:

“There are horns in his hands. There his strength of glory was established.” By “horns” he means the crossbeam of the wood of the cross, which he held fastened to his hands, so that, conquering every death by this kind of death, he might establish the strength of his glory in the hearts of the elect, lest they be held back from his love by any terrors or enticements [Col. 1241B]. He also promised them the future glory of incorruption, through which “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 15:26).

Finally, on the holy mountain, in the presence of Peter, James, and John, his splendor shone like light. They delighted in the sight of this splendor, but how fragile and weak they still were was demonstrated at the time of his passion. After he had received the horns of the cross in his hands, however, the strength of his glory was established there, so that neither terrors, nor blows, nor death itself could drive him from the hearts of the faithful.

In the manner of the prophets, “horns” may also signify the kingdoms of this world [Note: the material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Fleury manuscript]: “The elevation of the human mind, whether good or reprobate, may be designated by the term ‘horns.’”

“There are horns in Christ’s hands,” because he is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15). There are horns in his hands so that, humbling one and exalting another, he may break all the horns of sinners, by which they are vainly lifted up, and exalt the horn of the righteous—that is, their desires devoted to God, by which they strive to overcome all the battles of the wicked and of vices.

“And he established firm love as the strength of himself” [Col. 1241C]. Through inward love, the saints loved Christ’s strength even before the passion; but this love was not firm until, after completing his passion and resurrection, he gave them the grace of the Holy Spirit more fully. Then it became so firm that not even the horns of kings—that is, the power of the arrogant [Note: alternatively, “the horns”]—could break it [Col. 1241D].

“Before his face the word will go, and it went forth in the fields.” Before the Lord came in the flesh, the words of the prophets went before him, bearing witness to his coming. These same words went forth in the fields when, through the preaching of the apostles, they were spread throughout the entire world.

The word of preaching preceded the Lord not only in the prophetic writings but also in the apostles, when they proclaimed to the world the advent of Christ already completed in the flesh. The word went before his face because, naturally, the teaching of truth first reaches the ears of those who are to be instructed [Note: alternatively, “formed”]; afterward faith and understanding of the Word illumine their hearts and make them worthy to have God dwelling within them [Note: alternatively, “worthy”].

This is symbolically indicated in the Gospel when the Lord himself sent his disciples to preach in every city and place where he himself was going to come. We see the same order taking place even today: the Lord follows his preachers, because first the teacher’s word must be heard, and then the light of truth must be fixed in the hearer’s heart [Note: alternatively, “by light”]. Hence it is appropriately added:

“His feet stood, and the earth was shaken.” When, through the preaching of a teacher, the traces of truth are fixed in the minds of the hearers [Note: alternatively, “of the listener”], the mind itself is immediately shaken and disturbed as it considers itself [Col. 1242B].

The Lord’s feet may also appropriately be understood as the teachers themselves, through whom the word is ministered, since he who is present everywhere through himself is carried throughout the whole world through them, as through his feet. These feet stand, and the earth is moved, because the more firmly holy teachers persist in proclaiming and guarding the truth, the more quickly earthly hearts are shaken into doing penance for their errors.

And because this act of repentance must in no way be attributed to the human preacher but to the one who gives illumination, it is rightly added:

“He looked, and the nations melted away.” This is plainly to say: “The Lord had mercy, and the nations repented.” With such a look he also looked upon Peter when he denied him; and Peter, pierced by the memory of his sin, immediately melted into tears [Col. 1242C].

“The mountains were crushed violently” [Note: in one witness, “mountains” is absent]. By mountains he means the proud—those who exalt themselves through the kingdom, wisdom, or riches of this age. When the Lord looked upon them [Note: alternatively, “when he inspired them”], they were not merely crushed but violently crushed, when, through his mercy, some such people not only abandoned their empty and arrogant elevation but also attacked it in their lives as well as in their preaching [Col. 1242D; in the Fleury manuscript, “as well as in their preaching” is absent].

Saul and Matthew, for example, were mountains: the former was exalted by the wisdom of worldly learning, the latter by the mammon of iniquity. But when each was converted to the teaching of humility, he became a disciple of Christ. They were indeed mountains violently crushed.

“The everlasting hills melted away.” As with mountains, the name “hills” expresses proud people, though perhaps inflated with less arrogance and yet not free from the guilt of swelling pride. They must therefore be healthfully brought low so that they may deserve to be raised up by the Lord [Note: alternatively, “so that they might deserve”].

They are rightly called “everlasting hills” because, while they are humbled temporarily and melt away from the swelling of pride, they are raised up and glorified forever by the one who says: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Another translation has “hills of the age” more plainly in place of “everlasting hills.” This distinguishes them from the hills of the Lord, that is, holy men who, because of the sublimity of their minds, despise all temporal and lowly things and are worthy of such a name. Concerning them the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71:3).

The paths of his eternity I saw before his labors. The paths are the paths of the Lord’s temporality, by which he came into the world so that for a time he might appear to human beings; but the paths of his eternity are those by which, having bodily departed from the world, he returned to the Father, with whom he remained eternally even while he dwelt temporally in the world. These paths he himself desired when, as his passion drew near, he said to the Father: “I have glorified you upon [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another reading: the whole earth.] the earth; I have completed the work that you gave me to do” [Col. 1243B] (John XVII, 4). Immediately afterward he added, concerning the paths of eternity: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (ibid., 5).

The prophet saw these paths of eternity before the labors—namely, before the labors of the incarnation and passion—concerning which it was said above: “God will come from Lebanon,” or “from the South,” and: “Horns are in his hands,” along with other such expressions, many of which are found in this same song. Of these labors the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II, 8). Then, concerning the paths of eternity and what the Mediator between God and human beings would merit through these labors, he added: “Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II, 9–10). And because through those same labors of his, and through those same paths of his eternity, when he had completed the labors of his passion and returned to the Father, not only the people of the Jews but also the peoples of the nations were destined to reach everlasting rest, it is aptly added:

“The tents of the Ethiopians shall tremble, and the tents of the land of Midian.” Who does not know that the Ethiopians and Midianites are peoples of the nations? By these names all the nations of the Gentiles are indicated. Upon hearing the saving preaching of the Gospel, they were to be shaken with salutary fear, so that, just as the prophet heard and feared the still-future report of the Lord, contemplated the works of his future incarnation, and trembled, so the nations, when the same report was announced to them by the apostles and his works had already been accomplished, would begin to serve the Lord in fear and to exult before him with trembling.

He fittingly placed the Ethiopians first, since they are at the ends of the world, mystically indicating that the sound of the preachers would go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the inhabited world. Within this same mystery, the official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, received the first fruits of the Gentiles—faith and the sacraments of Christ—when Philip preached to him [Col. 1244A]. The nation of the Midianites, however, took its origin from one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah, who was called Midian; it is in the desert of the Saracens, toward the east of the Red Sea, in Arabia.

Let the Ethiopians, then, tremble at the name of Christ, so that it may be signified that his faith will reach the ends of the world. Let the Midianites also tremble, so that the peoples of the Mediterranean regions may likewise be shown to be destined for salvation. But when he does not say, “The Ethiopians and Midianites shall tremble,” but rather, “The tents of the Ethiopians shall tremble, and the tents of the land of Midian,” he uses the figure of speech found in the Gospel: “The whole city went out to meet Jesus”; and in the Psalm: “And your cup, intoxicating” (Psalm XXI, 5). The city itself did not go out, but those who were in the city [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another reading: went out]; nor was it the cup itself that intoxicated, but what was in the cup. This figure of speech is called in Greek metonymia, that is, “transnomination,” when what is contained is indicated through its container.

“Are you angry, Lord, at the rivers, or is your fury against the rivers, or your wrath against the sea?” By the names of rivers and sea the hearts of unbelievers are expressed. They are rightly called rivers because, with the whole force of their intention, they flow downward toward lower things; and sea because inwardly they are darkened by troubled and bitter thoughts and raise themselves above others with the swollen whirlpools of boastfulness.

“Have these,” he says, “sinned so grievously—those who plunge their minds from heavenly desires into the pursuit of low things, and who, unstable through the arrogance of their spirit [Note: [Col. 1243D] Another reading: “unstable.”], raise themselves against their neighbors—that the anger they deserve should remain against them forever? Or will you bestow the grace of your mercy upon all who sin throughout the world, whether more lightly or more seriously?” For I indeed perceive that you will send apostles to preach your glory to the nations; but who will believe is a matter of your knowledge, not of human knowledge. For this is what follows:

“For when you ascend, you will ascend upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.” That is, [Note: [Col. 1244D] Another reading: “when ascending”; another: “you ascend.”] you will ascend into the hearts of your elect through the illumination of grace [Note: [Col. 1244D] Another reading: “through whom”], so that under your guidance they may walk the path of the virtues; and, carrying you throughout the whole world by evangelizing, they may proclaim to the world the life of everlasting salvation.

The figure of this riding was also manifested literally in the Lord, when, making his way toward Jerusalem, he sat upon a donkey, while the crowds going before him, following him, and coming to meet him sang: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John XII, 13). In that riding salvation resounded, for it signified their spiritual journey by which, with the Lord leading through the apostles, they are led to behold the realms of the Jerusalem above, “which is the mother of us all” (Galatians IV, 26).

“Bending your bow, you will stretch it over the scepters, says the Lord.” By the bow he means the unforeseen arrival of the divine judgment, by which he foresaw that even the scepters—that is, the kingdoms of the world—would be judged. Thus the prophet indicates what the Lord does in his horses, that is, in the apostles and their successors, whom he fills and governs with his grace: “Bending,” he says, “you will stretch your bow over the scepters”; that is, by threatening through teachers, you will threaten that your judgment will come suddenly, so that whoever is terrified by the threat of anger as by a drawn bow, and takes care to implore your mercy, will not experience the discharge of the arrows—that is, the threatened punishment of everlasting penalties.

By prefacing, “Bending, you will stretch your bow over the scepters,” and adding, “says the Lord,” he signifies God the Father, concerning whom the Son himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

“The earth shall be split by rivers.” Here he does not mean the rivers that he feared above on account of the Lord’s anger and fury, but rather those of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” And the Evangelist explains: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John VII, 38).

The earth is split by these rivers when the hearts of carnal people, watered by the word of saving doctrine, crush the hardness of their unbelief by humbling themselves and open the inner recess of their thoughts, which had been wrongly closed, to receive the words of saving reproof or exhortation. This is explained more fully in what follows:

“The waters shall see you, and the peoples shall grieve.” The hearts of sinners, split open for the recognition and confession of the truth by the repeated address of teachers, like an inundation of frequent torrents, meanwhile see God through faith and grieve that they have so long withdrawn from him through guilt. But when the grief of repentance has ended, they will see him more fully in the future by direct vision and rejoice forever in the blessed sight of him.

What is said—“The earth shall be split by rivers”—can also be understood in this way: the earth is to be split so that rivers might newly arise from it. Ancient histories often report this happening, namely, that when an earthquake occurs, rivers that had not existed appear. Anyone who wisely understands that the earth is as full of countless veins of water as the human body is full of veins of blood does not doubt that this can happen. In this sense the earth is split by rivers when a carnal conscience, split open for repentance, advances through the gift of divine grace so greatly over time that it can itself bring forth streams of doctrine for others [Note: [Col. 1245D] Another reading: “rivers”], and water their parched hearts, either by its example or by its speech, so that they may produce the fruits of the virtues.
