“Sprinkling waters along the paths, the abyss gave its voice from the height of its vision.” The same teachers are represented by the name “abyss” who above were represented by “rivers”; but they are called rivers because of the force of their stronger assault, by which they cut through the hardness of an earthly mind so that it may do penance for its errors [Col. 1246A]. They are rightly called “abyss” because of the depth of knowledge with which they are inwardly filled, as Solomon testifies: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man” (Proverbs XVIII, 4).

Thus the abyss gives its voice while sprinkling waters along the paths when holy preachers, filled inwardly in their hearts with the deep knowledge of truth, present the ministry of the word outwardly to their hearers, gradually and in portions, according to the capacity of the weak, bringing forth what they themselves inwardly comprehend all at once in great abundance. By “paths” he means works, either those of the teachers themselves or those of their hearers. They sprinkle waters along their own paths when, wherever they walk, they continually display examples of right living to those who observe them. They sprinkle waters along the paths of those who observe them when, by teaching and living alike, they show them beforehand the paths of action by which they ought to walk [Note: [Col. 1245D] Another reading: “may walk.”]

But if the reading is, as some manuscripts have it, “You will scatter waters along the paths” [Note: [Col. 1245D] Thus in the Floriacensis and Corbeiensis, very ancient manuscripts; the Michaelinus has “many manuscripts.”], it is clear that this is said of God, who himself scattered the waters of life from the fountains of Israel far and wide among the nations of the whole world, saying to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

After saying that “the abyss would give its voice,” he aptly added, “from the height of its vision,” because what the holy preachers proclaim outwardly as something wondrous to us proceeds from that fountain of wisdom by which they themselves, contemplating the heavenly joys, are inwardly illumined even more wondrously. Did not the great abyss give its voice from the height of its vision when the Apostle Paul said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. I speak as to children: be enlarged yourselves also” (II Corinthians VI, 11)? [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another reading omits “Did not.”]

How and in what order it came about that the world was sprinkled with saving waters, and that the abyss of heavenly wisdom thundered over the earth, is shown next, when it says:

“The sun was raised up, and the moon stood in its order.” The sun was raised up—that is, the Sun of Righteousness, the Lord, after his passion and resurrection, was raised into heaven. Having sent the Spirit from the Father, he illumined the Church and extended it throughout the whole world, so that it, in its order—that is, after the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation had been fulfilled—might rise from its long sickness of unbelief and stand firm in faith, act manfully, and be strengthened in his love.

And because he had compared Christ to the sun and the Church to the moon, he aptly turned again to the same sun and immediately added:

“In the light your arrows shall go forth, in the brilliance of the flash of your weapons.” The arrows of Christ are his words, by which human hearts are pierced, so that, after receiving a saving wound, the faithful soul may say: “I am wounded by love.” These arrows go forth in the light because, through the ministry of teachers, the words of truth have been made openly known to the world [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another reading: “brought forth”], in accordance with what Truth himself commands them [Note: [Col. 1246D] Another reading: “commands”] ասում: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” [Col. 1247A] (Matthew X, 27).

And because the clarity of miracles also followed the words of light, he added [Note: [Col. 1247D] Michaelinus, omitting “he added,” repeats the text: “In the light your arrows go forth.”]: “In the brilliance of the flash of your weapons.” With arrows combatants strike their adversaries; with weapons they protect themselves from wounds. Thus the sayings of preachers, by which they overcome the perversity of unbelievers, are appropriately signified by arrows, while the miracles by which they confirm the truth of their preaching are signified by weapons.

The arrows of Christ therefore go forth in the light, and they go forth in the brilliance of the flash of his weapons, because what he did in greatness, what mysteries he revealed, what commandments he set forth, and what rewards he promised have now become known throughout the whole world, brighter than the sun, through the writings of the Gospel. Holy teachers, too, because they are children of light, shine with light and brilliance in whatever they do or say by his gift.

“In your threat you will diminish the earth, and in your fury you will cast down the nations.” By threatening the severity of the judgment by which the wicked are condemned [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “are damned”], you will salutarily humble those who used to place earthly things above heavenly things, so that, as their earthly desires are gradually diminished, they may begin to set their minds on and seek the things above. By bringing down fury, you will condemn forever those who, through their insolent exaltation [Note: [Col. 1247D] Michaelinus reads “insolent”; Floriacensis and Corbeiensis read “eternal” (*aeterna*)], refused to be humbled for a time. The Psalmist prays that this may not happen to him, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chastise me in your fury” (Psalm VI, 2).

“You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones.” The Mediator between God and human beings went forth from the Father and came into the world, not to judge the world [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “to judge”], but so that the world might be saved through him [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “might be saved”].

By “your anointed ones” he means all the elect, who are most rightly called by this name from the anointing of spiritual grace. Hence the Psalmist says of those who wished to harm the saints and were restrained by divine prohibition: “He reproved kings for their sake: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’” (Psalm CIV, 14).

He saved his anointed ones—not those whom he found already anointed [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “that”], but those whom, by going forth from the Father and appearing in the flesh, he made his anointed ones, that is, his christs, through the Spirit of adoption. Concerning this anointing the Apostle John admonishes his hearers: “Let the anointing that you received from him remain in you” (I John II, 27).

In some editions this verse is found as follows: “You went forth to save your people through Jesus Christ your own.” This is understood as having been said to the Father, because he went forth to save his people through Jesus Christ, his Son [Col. 1247D]. For “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” And because that same going forth—that is, his coming into the world—was destined to bring not only the resurrection of the faithful but also the ruin of unbelievers, it is aptly added:

“You sent death upon the heads of the enemies; you raised the bonds up to the neck” [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “to the crown of the head.”] He who brought [Note: [Col. 1247D] Another reading: “offered”] the joy of salvation to his elect, whom the prophet had called his anointed ones [Col. 1248A], himself sent eternal death upon those who neglected to be anointed by his grace. This is also known to have been fulfilled bodily in the very nation of the Jews, which persecuted the Lord, appearing in the flesh, even unto death. After it had crucified him, not many years later, when the Roman army descended upon it, it was condemned to enormous destruction, except only those who had withdrawn into faith in the grace of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “had believed”]; moreover, it was deprived of its kingdom and homeland.

This is what he says: “You raised the bonds up to the neck”—namely, to the neck of the kingdom against which they had previously raised themselves in opposition to the Lord. Concerning this, the most blessed first martyr Stephen said to them even as they raged against him: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII, 51).

The Lord raised the bonds up to the neck when he sent a hostile army for the overthrow of the proud nation—not only of the Jews, but also of all who refused to accept the humility of the Christian faith. The Lord casts down pride [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “has laid low”], in accordance with what the Psalmist sings concerning the saints: “And two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance upon the nations, rebukes among the peoples, to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron bonds” [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “manacles”] (Psalm CXLIX, 6)—iron, that is, because they are eternal, and once caught in them they can never be released [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “ensnared.”]

If someone says that it should be read in the plural, “You raised the bonds up to the necks,” the meaning is the same. For the just Lord will cut off the necks of sinners.

“You cut off the heads of the mighty in alienation; the nations shall be moved by it” [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “are moved.”] In place of “alienation,” the Greek has ἔκστασις (*ekstasis*), which some have interpreted as “astonishment,” others as “mental transport.” Whether it is called astonishment, alienation, or ecstasy of mind, the meaning is the same: someone is so disturbed and stupefied by a sudden miracle that he is removed from the ordinary sense of his mind.

This happened to the Jews, as the frequent testimony of the Gospel reveals, saying that they were astonished and amazed at the teaching and powers of Jesus: “From where does this man have all these things? Do we not know his father and mother?” (John VI, 42). And in the Acts of the Apostles, after the lame man had been healed by Peter and John at the temple gate: “They were filled,” he says, “with astonishment and ecstasy” (Acts III, 10). In this ecstasy—that is, in amazement or mental bewilderment—many from the people were moved to believe in the Lord.

But the heads of the mighty—that is, the chief priests and elders—were cut off from the lot of the faithful through their unbelief. [Note: [Col. 1248D] Another reading: “mounted” (*montatae*).] The nations were also moved by it when, after hearing or seeing the powers of the Lord and his apostles, they were so astonished and amazed that, having anathematized and rejected the gods whom they had worshiped, they received the new faith of Christ with devoted minds. Concerning them it is aptly added:

“They shall open their mouths like a poor man eating in secret.” For just as a poor man, remaining hungry for some time, if he should happen to find food somewhere, immediately strives to refresh himself with it in secret and does not wish to bring it out into public, lest someone else seize it and he himself perish from hunger, so indeed the peoples of the nations, when the bread of the word was offered to them through the apostles—bread from which they had long remained hungry—immediately opened the mouths of their hearts and began to taste it with complete avidity.

They devoted themselves all the more to hearing or reading the Scriptures because they remembered that for so long they had subjected their ears and minds, in the most wretched kind of poverty, to doctrines that were useless and even harmful. The order by which the poverty of the nations reached the banquets of the word is indicated when it immediately continues:

“You sent your horses into the sea, disturbing many waters.” By the sea he means the world; by the horses of God, the holy preachers; and by the many waters, the peoples of the nations. When God’s horses were sent into the sea, the many waters were disturbed, because, once heralds of the word had been scattered throughout the world, the hearts of the nations were thrown into turmoil—some toward believing and receiving the sacrament of faith, others toward contradicting or even persecuting the heralds of that same faith [Note: [Col. 1249D] Another reading: “to pursue [the heralds].”]

Hence the Psalmist fittingly says: “All who saw them were troubled, and every human being feared; and they proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds” (Psalm LXIII, 9). For when all were troubled, not all feared and proclaimed the works of God. Rather, only those who remained human beings feared and proclaimed God’s works; those, however, who had been alienated from human reason were compared to senseless animals and made like them. Although such people were troubled and stirred by the powers of the saints, they nevertheless refused either to fear God or to proclaim or understand his deeds.

It is fittingly said above concerning these horses, namely, the holy preachers: “When you ascend, you will ascend upon your horses”; and now it is added concerning the same: “You sent your horses into the sea,” so that from both statements it may be gathered that the Lord sent preachers into the world in such a way that, while they preach, he himself is never absent from them. Rather, just as a charioteer guides horses, so he is always present in governing their minds.

“I kept watch, and my belly trembled at the voice of the prayer of my lips.” Following the customary manner of the prophets, he calls his mind his “belly” [Note: [Col. 1249D] Another reading: “his.”] For just as food is received into the belly, by which the body’s strength and life are refreshed, so pious thoughts are received into a holy mind, by which the life of the inner person is sustained and preserved, lest it fail [Note: [Col. 1249D] Another reading: “be destroyed.”]

“I kept watch,” therefore, says the Prophet, carefully contemplating the future passions and later glories of Christ, the rejection of his people, the faith of the Gentiles, the disturbance of those same nations at the new preaching, and the persecution that unbelievers would stir up against believers. “And my heart trembled” at those things that I foresaw and spoke as destined to come.

Or certainly, contemplating the differing condition of the human race: “I kept watch over myself,” he says, more diligently, with a trembling spirit [Note: [Col. 1249D] Another reading: “with an agitated spirit”], lest I should sin in deed, in word, or in heart; and lest, while preaching to others, I myself should become rejected. It should be noted that he says he trembled at the voice of the prayer of his lips, although throughout this entire song he appears to have prayed nothing at all, but only, fearing and trembling, described the future mysteries of Christ and the Church.

Yet the person who calls his song a prayer is not mistaken, for he placed this title over it: “The Prayer of Habakkuk the Prophet for ignorances.” Whatever a holy man says is entirely prayer to God; everything he does, when his sincere intention is to please the Lord, pleads before God on his behalf and commends him to the Lord.

“And trembling entered my bones.” Just as Scripture sometimes signifies our carnal actions by the word “flesh,” so by the word “bones” it usually designates strong and spiritual deeds [Note: [Col. 1250D] Another reading in Flor.: “of the bones”; in Corb.: “of the bone.”]

“Therefore,” he says, “my heart trembled at what I foresaw was destined to come into the world, and whatever spiritual strength I thought was present in me trembled as though wholly fragile, when I looked upon the greater virtues and sufferings of blessed Christ and his apostles.” This is explained more clearly in the following words:

“And beneath me my strength was troubled.” He fittingly says that his strength was troubled not in himself but beneath himself, because, carried away into contemplation of heavenly mysteries, the prophet saw himself somehow raised above himself [Col. 1250C]. The higher he is made by the light of contemplation, the more imperfect he sees himself to be in the merit of his actions. Raised up to behold the things above, he is rightly disturbed by what he had done among the things below.

The prophet’s strength was troubled, his bones trembled, and his belly quaked not only because he recognized that he was less than perfect in action, but also because he saw that all who wish to live piously in Christ would suffer persecutions. He also saw that Christ himself, who would enter the world without sin, would not leave the world without the punishment of sin, in accordance with what he had indicated at the beginning of his song [Note: [Col. 1250D] Another reading: “had signified.”]

Yet this fear and trembling did not remain without consolation. Hope in the future rewards diminished and lightened the present adversities [Note: [Col. 1250D] Another reading omits “rewards.”]. For this is what follows:

“I shall rest on the day of my tribulation, so that I may ascend to the people of my migration.” He rests on the day not only of recompense but also of tribulation who does not doubt that through temporal afflictions he will obtain [Note: [Col. 1250D] Another reading: “will accomplish”] eternal joys, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “For by hope we have been saved” (Romans VIII, 24). And again: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans XII, 12).

This is the rest of the elect in the present life: having abandoned the desire for lowly things, they strive with the full intention of their minds and by the daily steps of good works [Col. 1251A] to ascend and migrate into the fellowship of those who have gone before them in Christ. When the contests of their sufferings have ended, they receive the crown of life, following the example of those who were once carried away to Babylon and were afterward led back from Judea to their homeland under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Scripture calls them “the children of the migration,” and reports that with great devotion they restored the holy places that the enemy had destroyed. This is a most evident figure of our condition.

For in our first parent we were carried away from our heavenly homeland and brought into the Babylon of this age, that is, into confusion. But by the gift of the Lord Jesus Christ, the great King and High Priest—whose type Zerubbabel and Jeshua prefigured—we have rightly been called back again to our homeland and to the vision of supreme peace, which is what the name Jerusalem signifies [Col. 1251B]. This is so only in such a way that, meanwhile, in the Jerusalem of the present Church, exercising ourselves in pious labors, we are prepared in due course to enter the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all.

If it is read without distinction, as it is found in certain manuscripts—“I shall rest on the day of tribulation,” without adding “my”—it can be understood according to what is sung in the Psalm concerning the righteous: “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Psalm XL, 2). That is, on the day of judgment, when everlasting tribulation will seize the reprobate, everlasting rest will receive the righteous.

Even before that final and universal judgment, however, the saints rest on the day of tribulation, ascending to the people of their migration when, transferred from the world through good works, they are joined in heaven to the joys of the righteous who went before them, while their persecutors, likewise removed from this life, undergo the torments of Gehenna, where they will be tormented forever.

The day of tribulation can also be understood as occurring in this life, when, as the scarcity of temporal goods grows heavier, those who had loved such things excessively grieve as though surrounded by miseries. But every elect person, although bodily enduring the same hardships, possesses rest in the Lord through the fixed hope of the mind, knowing that the more heavily he is pressed down among things below, the more exaltedly he will ascend after his afflictions into the eternal fellowship of the citizens above. To this interpretation what follows aptly corresponds:

“For the fig tree shall not bear fruit [Note: [Col. 1251D] Another reading: “does not bear”], and there shall be no produce on the vines. The work of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no food. The sheep shall have no food, and there shall be no cattle in the stalls. But I shall glory in the Lord and rejoice in God my Jesus.”

For when the abundance of worldly things fails, and carnal people and all lovers of this life are thrown into turmoil [Col. 1251D] [Note: [Col. 1251D] Another reading: “each carnal person”], the righteous are not saddened by the loss of temporal [Note: [Col. 1251D] Another reading: “good”] advantages; rather, they rejoice in possession of the heavenly kingdom promised to the poor of Christ, remembering his promised consolation, who said [Note: [Col. 1251D] Another reading: “his promise and consolation, in which he said”]: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.”

And what marvelous faith, hope, and love the prophet displays! The Son of God had not yet appeared as a human being or received the name Jesus from his parents, yet the prophet, foreseeing that same name in the Spirit, testifies that he rejoices amid adversities in the one who, born in the flesh long afterward, would open for the faithful the gate of the heavenly homeland [Col. 1252A].

If anyone seeks a figurative interpretation of these verses as well, the fig tree, vine, and olive tree represented the synagogue of the Jews: it offered God the sweetness of good works, the fragrance of fervent love, and the richness of a merciful spirit. The sheep and oxen were also present typologically within that same people [Note: [Col. 1252D] Another reading: “types”]: sheep, namely, those who humbly heard the voice of the supreme Shepherd; oxen, those who diligently bore the yoke of the Law and, by assiduously teaching and correcting the hearts of their hearers, prepared them to produce the fruits of good works, as though plowing the Lord’s earth.

For those who lived spiritually, the fields of the divine Scriptures, spread out most widely, produced spiritual food. The one who had become like an animal before the Lord delighted in this pasture, always clinging to him and saying: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me” (Psalm XXII, 1).

But this fig tree, when the Lord came to it for the third time—that is, in the giving of the Law through Moses, in diligent reproof and exhortation through the prophets, and in the offering of grace through himself [Note: [Col. 1252D] Another reading: “in the obligation of grace through himself”]—neglected to bear the fruit of virtue. Therefore, condemned to eternal barrenness, it was given over to a curse.

The produce failed in the vines once belonging to the Lord—that is, the fruit of love among the crowds of the Jews. For this reason, when he was thirsty, they offered him vinegar instead of wine: when he sought in them the sweetness of the virtues, they offered the bitterness of vices; when he desired their virtues, they brought forth their vices.

“The work of the olive” failed when that same people fattened the heads of the wretched with the oil of flattery and falsely voiced the prophet’s words with deceitful mouths, saying: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of God” (Psalm LI, 10). Therefore, at the time of the final recompense, it will bring lamps that have gone out and, together with its darkness, will be excluded from entry into the heavenly homeland.

The fields yield no food when that same people, with the pages of the divine writings opened, is unable to find the pasture of truth through right understanding. The sheep fail for lack of food because, where the refreshment of inward sweetness is absent, there is no source from which the innocence of a simple life may arise.

Thus it is said: “The sheep have failed for lack of food,” that is, because food was lacking, just as the Prophet says in the Psalm: “And my flesh was changed because of the oil” (Psalm CVIII, 24)—that is, because the oil by which I might be refreshed or made fat [Col. 1252D] was absent.

Finally, certain manuscripts have it as follows: “The sheep failed because they did not eat; the oxen are not in the stalls.” For indeed, among the Jews the stalls of the heavenly writings abound; but because those who might carry the gentle yoke of the Gospel do not savor the nourishment of heavenly understanding in them, they are absent.

Considering all these things as destined to come upon the unbelieving part of his nation, the prophet immediately shows what he himself would do with the faithful of that same nation—or rather, with the fellowship of the whole Church, which was to be gathered throughout the world [Note: [Col. 1252D] Another reading: “was to be collected”], or was already elect in Christ [Col. 1253A]:

“But I,” he says, “will glory not in my own righteousness but in faith in divine protection. I will rejoice in God Jesus, that is, in my Savior, because I understand that salvation is found not in me but in him.”

And as though we were to ask him why he gloried in the Lord and in God Jesus, whom he called his own through the grace of great love, and why he rejoiced, he immediately indicated, as though giving the most just reason for that same joy, and thus ended his song:

[Note: [Col. 1253C] Al., “Lord.”] The Lord God is my strength, and he will establish my feet for completion, and he will set me upon the heights, so that I may conquer in his splendor.

As though he were saying openly: “My strength is indeed disturbed beneath me”—that is, while I contemplate the condition of human frailty, which is below; but as I raise the eyes of my mind toward the grace of divine assistance [Col. 1253B], I trust that in him I can exercise strength. He himself is able to lead the steps of my works to a firm conclusion; he himself can set me upon the heights, so that we may despise as worthless, through contemplation of eternal blessings, every exaltation of worldly power [Note: [Col. 1253C] Al., “as nothing”]. I shall conquer all the temptations that come upon me, whether from adversity or from the allurements of the world, in his love in which I shall be—that is, while in everything I do I seek not my own glory but his, remembering that I received from him whatever good I accomplish.

For rightly are those helped by the Lord so that, having overcome temptations and been proved, they may reach the palm of the heavenly calling, who refer the whole cause of their victory to his praise. Some manuscripts read: “And I shall conquer in his song,” which refers to one and the same meaning [Col. 1253C]. For whoever knows how to give thanks to the Lord from the heart in all the tribulations he endures conquers in the Lord’s song, knowing that “all things work together for good for those who love God,” and, with blessed Job, habitually sings: “Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job XV, 21).

Finally, the apostles Paul and Silas, amid blows, darkness, and [Col. 1254A] the bonds of prison, were singing a hymn to God; and therefore, divinely aided, they suddenly emerged victorious. For although their feet seemed to be fastened in the stocks, the steps of their works were nevertheless brought to completion in virtues.

Beautifully, the end of this prophetic song answers to its beginning. Whoever, after hearing and considering the works of the Lord appearing in the flesh, fears and trembles faithfully, comes to this: having despised the things that in this life are borne along in varied conditions like the waves of a tossing sea, he glories and rejoices in him alone, whose joys he is able to enjoy perpetually. He is helped by him so that he is neither broken by the adversities nor weakened by the allurements of the present world. He sings the praises of his grace in the present, so that he may deserve to conquer, and in the future, because he has conquered, he never ceases to sing them.

It also comes about that such a soul [Col. 1254B] conquers the world in the Lord’s splendor—namely, in that same splendor of his, recalled to mind more often during the time of struggles and perpetually beheld in the time of rewards, according to what he himself promised: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

It should also be noted, after the prayer—or song—of Habakkuk has been expounded, that his name too, which is interpreted as “embracing,” accords with the meaning of that same prayer. For it is evident that he embraced the Lord with the inward love of his heart and clung to him, since he testifies that he glories and rejoices in him alone. Would that it might come to pass [Note: [Col. 1254C] Al., omits “come to pass”], dearest sister and virgin of Christ, that we too, loving him, might be made worthy of such a name. For if we strive to embrace him with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, he too will deem us worthy to embrace us in the arms of his love [Col. 1254C], remembering his promise in which he says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). Thus we shall deserve to be numbered among the members of that bride who joyfully sings to her creator, namely her heavenly bridegroom:

> “His left hand is under my head,  
> and his right hand will embrace me.”  
> Amen (Song of Songs 2:6).

Here ends the exposition of the Song of the Prophet Habakkuk, addressed to the virgin, sister in Christ.

### Allegorical exposition on Samuel

Book One. 499

Prologue. Ibid.

Chapter One.—Elkanah, a man of Ramathaim, has two wives: Peninnah, rich in sons, and Hannah, mourning the reproach of barrenness. Ibid.

Chapter Two.—Amid prayers and tears, Hannah vows to the Lord that, if she receives a son, she will make him a Nazirite; and when the priest Eli blesses her, she returns home with her household. 505

Chapter Three.—Hannah names the son born to her Samuel; and, after weaning him, she dedicates him forever to the Lord with gifts and sacrifices. 507

Chapter Four.—Hannah, worshiping with her husband in the tabernacle, speaks a hymn of thanksgiving to the Lord. 509

Chapter Five.—While Eli’s sons profane the priestly office, the boy Samuel ministers before the Lord, girded with a linen ephod; and, when Eli blesses her, Hannah is made fruitful with sons. 512

Chapter Six.—Eli’s sons increase their sin, even disregarding their father’s warnings; but Samuel, advancing in age, pleases both God and human beings. 515

Chapter Seven.—A prophet comes to Eli and declares what will befall his household because of the guilt of contempt. 516

Chapter Eight.—When Eli’s eyes grow dim, Samuel sleeps in the temple of the Lord; responding to the Lord’s fourth call, he learns what will befall Eli and reveals it to him in the morning. 519

Chapter Nine.—Israel is defeated and put to flight by the Philistines, Eli’s sons are also killed, and the ark of God is captured. Hearing this, Eli immediately falls backward and dies; his daughter-in-law also dies after first giving birth to a son, Ichabod, which is interpreted as “inglorious.” 524

Chapter Ten.—When the Philistines carry the ark of God into the temple of Dagon, Dagon himself is struck first, and then the people and the land are also punished with a fitting plague; the ark remains among them for seven months. 529

Chapter Eleven.—Instructed by their priests and diviners, the Philistines send back the ark of God with due veneration. The men of Beth-shemesh, receiving it first, offer sacrifices to God. 532

Chapter Twelve.—After some of the Beth-shemites are struck because they presumed, as they deserved, to look upon the ark, the men of Kiriath-jearim receive it and guard it for twenty years. Then, at Samuel’s admonition, Israel abandons its idols and serves the Lord, while Samuel offers a burnt offering. When the Lord thunders, the Philistines are terrified and flee. Samuel judges Israel and builds an altar to the Lord at Ramah. 538

### Exposition on Samuel

Book Two. 545

Prologue. Ibid.

Chapter One.—When Samuel grows old, he appoints his sons judges over Israel. But when they turn aside from the right path, the people demand that a king be appointed for them. At the Lord’s command, Samuel explains the right of a king, but even so he cannot turn them back from their most evil purpose. 548

Chapter Two.—While seeking his father’s donkeys, Saul comes to Samuel. Samuel receives him graciously and tells him that the donkeys have been found; in the morning he anoints him king with holy oil and foretells what will happen to him. 554

Chapter Three.—Samuel summons the people to Mizpah and seeks and finds a king by lot: Saul. At last, when he returns, the chosen portion of the people follows him. 564

Chapter Four.—Jabesh-gilead, besieged by the Ammonites at Gibeah, is reported to Saul; and when Saul arrives with an army, it is delivered early in the morning. 567

Chapter Five.—After the king has been appointed, Samuel proves himself innocent and just; and, to strike terror into the stubborn people, he calls down rain from heaven during the season of harvest. 571

Chapter Six.—Saul and Jonathan choose soldiers for themselves from among the people; and after Jonathan strikes the Philistine garrison, the same men terrify the Israelites with larger forces. 573

Chapter Seven.—When the people have dispersed from him, Saul offers a burnt offering; Samuel reproves him for acting foolishly and informs him that another is to be anointed king in his place. 577

Chapter Eight.—Because Israel has no weapons on account of the scarcity of smiths, the Philistines devastate its land in three divisions while Saul looks on; and Jonathan, crawling among the crags with his armor-bearer, becomes the origin both of the battle and of the victory. 581

Chapter Nine.—Saul adjures the people not to eat before the enemy has been destroyed, and not to eat with the blood after the enemy has been destroyed. He forbids the building of an altar; and, although he seeks an oracle from the Lord, he does not merit one because of Jonathan’s guilt. Nevertheless, the people rescue Jonathan so that he does not die. 588

Chapter Ten.—Saul conquers Israel’s enemies throughout the surrounding region, distinguished by the glory both of his sons and of his soldiers. 592

Chapter Eleven.—Saul, ordered to destroy Amalek, commands the relatives of Moses to withdraw so that they may not perish with the others. Because he violated the command in part, he hears, when Samuel’s cloak is torn, that the glory of the kingdom will be torn away from him. Moreover, after Samuel himself kills the king of Amalek, he refuses to see Saul any longer. 594

### Exposition on Samuel

Prologue. Ibid.

Chapter One.—At the Lord’s command, Samuel anoints David the Bethlehemite as king after bringing him from the pastures. Soon David shines with the perpetual grace of the Spirit, so that he even relieves Saul, who is seized by an evil spirit, by playing the lyre. 603

Chapter Two.—Goliath terrifies the Israelite camp for forty days by challenging them to single combat, but at last he is defeated by David with a sling and a stone. 609

When the women meet the returning army, they create in Saul the fuel of perpetual hatred and envy because they prefer David to Saul in their praise. Finally, when Saul is seized by an evil spirit, he tries to strike David; but because he cannot, he removes him from himself and appoints him tribune over a thousand men. 624

Chapter Six.—Saul tries to strike David but cannot, and orders the house into which David has fled to be guarded. David places an image in his stead and, leaping through the window, goes to Samuel. Chapter Seven.—Jonathan and David renew their covenant; and when Saul plans to kill David, Jonathan signals him to flee by means of an arrow shot. 639

Chapter Eight.—Ahimelech the priest gives David and his companions the consecrated bread and Goliath’s sword, while Doeg the Edomite watches from hiding and plots. 648

Chapter Twenty-One.—When the people are stirred into an uproar because of hunger and scarcity, Nehemiah adjures the nobles and officials not to exact interest from their brothers but rather to give money for them. 899

Chapter Twenty-Two.—Nehemiah explains how much mercy he personally showed to the people. 900

Chapter Twenty-Three.—Sanballat and his associates try to draw Nehemiah away from building the wall, even hiring domestic agents to plot against him; but when he detects these plots, the wall of the city is completed in its entirety. Ibid.

Chapter Twenty-Four.—When the city of Jerusalem has been built, the gentiles are terrified; Nehemiah lists the singers and assigns guards to the gates. 902

Chapter Twenty-Five.—To find inhabitants worthy of the city, Nehemiah rereads the census book of those who first went up from Babylon to Judaea. 903

Chapter Twenty-Six.—In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem, and when Ezra reads the law of Moses, they listen attentively. Ibid.

Chapter Twenty-Seven.—They celebrate the Feast of Booths, while Ezra reads the law of God to them day by day. 905

Chapter Twenty-Eight.—After the Feast of Booths has been completed, they assemble again to confess, read, and pray to the Lord. 908

Chapter Twenty-Nine.—Ezra’s prayer, or confession, in which he asks the Lord to remember the covenant he made with their fathers. Ibid.

Chapter Thirty.—The leaders, together with the people, make a covenant and write that they will keep all the Lord’s commandments and support the rites of his house. 909

Chapter Thirty-One.—The leaders from the sons of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi dwell in Jerusalem, together with a tenth part of the remaining people. Ibid.

Chapter Thirty-Two.—The line of Jeshua, the high priest, and those who were leaders of the priests and Levites in those times is set forth. 911

Chapter Thirty-Three.—The city of Jerusalem is dedicated with solemn rejoicing, and the guardians of the storehouses containing the treasury for the offerings of the holy things are listed. 913

Chapter Thirty-Four.—All foreigners are separated from Israel [Col. 1259], and the Levites’ portions and the priests’ firstfruits are stored in the storehouse of the House of the Lord. 920

Chapter Thirty-Five.—After returning from Babylon to Jerusalem, Nehemiah once again cleanses the storehouses of vessels belonging to the gentiles and restores there the things appropriate to the House of the Lord. Ibid.

Chapter Thirty-Six.—Nehemiah diligently insists that the Sabbath’s rest not be violated by trade with the gentiles. 921

Chapter Thirty-Seven.—Nehemiah purifies the Jews from foreign wives and establishes the orders of the priests and Levites, each in his own ministry; finally, he commends himself to God’s memory for good. 923
